# Table of Contents

1º/ Van Helmont - *The Origin of Medicine* <note>original: "Ortus medicinae" — This is Van Helmont’s most famous work, published posthumously, which laid the groundwork for modern chemistry and physiology.</note>... Amsterdam, 1648, 800 pages.

2º/ Van Helmont - *Unheard-of Minor Medical Works* <note>original: "Opuscula medica inaudita" — A collection of shorter treatises on specific medical conditions, including his famous work on "the stone" (kidney stones).</note>, Amsterdam, 1648, 110 pages.

3º/ Van Helmont - *Unheard-of Doctrine of Fevers* <note>original: "Febrium doctrina inaudita" — Here, Van Helmont challenges the ancient "humoral" theory of medicine, arguing instead for chemical causes of illness.</note>. Amsterdam, 1648, 115 pages.

4º/ Van Helmont - *The Tomb of the Plague* <note>original: "Tumulus pestis" — A treatise on the plague, suggesting it was caused by an "archeus" or vital spirit being disturbed rather than by bad air or astrological alignment.</note> — Amsterdam, 1648, 88 pages.

<term>Van Helmont</term> <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont (1580–1644) was a Flemish physician and chemist who is considered the father of pneumatic chemistry (the study of gases).</note>
<term>Amsterdam</term> <note>The Latin variations "Amsterodami" and "Amstelodami" both refer to Amsterdam, which was the premier center for intellectual and scientific publishing in Europe during the 17th century.</note>
<term>1648</term> <note>This year is significant as it marks the first time Van Helmont's son, Francisco Mercurius van Helmont, published his father's collected manuscripts together.</note>

# TO THE UNSPEAKABLE WORD,

## The Author offers this humble burnt offering.
<note>original: *Holocaustum vernaculum*. In this context, "holocaustum" refers to a biblical "whole burnt offering" or a total sacrifice, while "vernaculum" suggests something domestic, personal, or in the author's own simple style.</note>

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'O' decorated with elaborate foliate and floral scrolls within a square border.</image-desc>

Almighty, Eternal, and Incomprehensible Being! Origin of all Good. You have entrusted to me a Talent <note>A reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents, where a servant is expected to invest what his master gives him.</note>, which I bring forth into the market to earn interest: But I acknowledge and confess my trifle <note>original: *nauci*, meaning something of no value</note> of a power, my vile and misusing uselessness. Thus submerged in the abyss of my own Nothingness, I pray to You, All-providing Good, that You might mercifully look upon this book, You who are the Eternal Beginning and End of all Wisdom. Let Your saving Will be done, Lord, in the grace of Your Love, through this dry wood, food for worms, fuel for the fire—your useless servant, the son of your handmaid. Unless You complete me anew and guard all Your gifts, they will perish in me forever. This I frankly confess from the knowledge of my innermost core <note>original: *meditullii*</note>, before You, Lord, to whom all things are thoroughly known in truth: and before the World, to which most excellent truths remain hidden. I am astounded by the Abundance and Magnitude of Your benefits toward my worthlessness <note>original: *floccitatem*, literally "flimsiness" or "a tuft of wool"</note>. Thus prostrate, I celebrate Your most glorious Name, and I call upon it from above, O most Faithful Lover of mankind; JEHOVAH! O Holy and Incomprehensible Name! at all times, it alone is to be sanctified, and it alone freely sanctifies its Saints. Mercifully look down from the throne of Your Omnipotence upon the miseries of the living; help the children of men, since it is Your delight to be present with them. Remember the word of Your promise, no longer as the God of our Fathers, as in former times, but now declared as God our Father: No longer the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; but as the God JESUS, the God of MARY our mother, and He who was made our Brother in the love of Your Grace. Of all [my] desires...
<meta>catchword: meorum (my)</meta>

<summary>This page contains a formal Latin dedication to God (Jehovah/Jesus), where the author humbly offers his work as a spiritual sacrifice. He emphasizes his own unworthiness and the transition from the Old Testament conception of God to a New Testament relationship through Christ.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, Tetragrammaton, humility, Parable of the Talents, divine wisdom, Christology, spiritual sacrifice</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s introductory prayer and dedication. Having established his own "nothingness" on the previous page, he now explores how human language and thought attempt to grasp the divine, leading into a discussion on the nature of spiritual worship.</meta>

the end and aim of my efforts tends toward this: that Your incomprehensible Name may be sanctified, not only because You are called Thrice-Greatest and Best <note>original: *Ter-Optimus-Maximus*. This title, "Thrice-Best-Greatest," was a common Renaissance adaptation of the Roman title for Jupiter, used here to signify God's supreme perfection.</note>; but also because You alone are the All, to whom the vow of all sanctifying Love properly belongs, since You do not need us, nor can we devote anything else to You. The Prophet cried out, *Ah, Ah, Ah, Lord, I cannot speak; behold, I am a child* <note>A reference to the biblical book of Jeremiah 1:6, where the prophet expresses his inadequacy and lack of eloquence before God.</note>: but to this I reply *O, O, O, Lord*, my thoughts fail, and they melt away into a bare vow of Love for the Sanctification of Your Name; for behold, Lord, I am nothing but Nothingness, nor am I anything else, except insofar as it has pleased You that I should belong to You. 

O All, of All, and my All-encompassing vow, I rightly seem to offer to You in my native tongue, and even to vow to You, the Fief of my Essence <note>original: *Feudum meæ Essentiæ*. Using legal terminology of the day, the author describes his very existence as a "fief"—something he does not own outright, but holds in trust from God, his feudal Lord.</note> and of my Self, which, having been invested by You, I use and enjoy with the help of my neighbor. For although the first conception of the soul exists beyond words, and thus without its own language: yet I feel it to be still raw and not yet set apart, until it is refined and, joined to the mind, passes into thoughts, words, and writing. This rawness, I perceive, makes the object of the first conception weak and unstable, and quickly obscures it again. For that reason, Your Eternal Wisdom has permitted it to be carried further, even unto the mind.

It is true indeed, that You wish to be adored in Spirit by men, but not in such a way that it remains in the indistinctness of the first object. On the contrary, even the Angels, pure and simple Spirits, though they may adore You purely in thought as Spirits; yet they busy themselves with a certain melody unknown to us to sanctify Your Sanctifying Name without ceasing. Therefore, You command that You be loved not only from the whole soul and the whole Spirit; but also from the whole heart and all one's strength: so that prayer established spiritually, and bare adoration, at the very least exclude oral prayer that is void of the soul's attention.

Grant, most beloved Lord, that I may suggest this to my neighbors, Your servants, through a comparison: An Organist, hearing a new melody, at first plays it not without difficulty; his soul perceives the sound in part, but his fingers (as the builders of sounds, just as other limbs are the fashioners of words) do not follow so harmoniously,

<summary>The author discusses the transition from "raw" wordless prayer to structured thought and language, arguing that God deserves the devotion of the mind and senses as well as the spirit. He introduces a musical analogy of an organist to explain the difficulty of expressing divine inspiration through physical means.</summary>

<keywords>sanctification, Jeremiah, Fief of Essence, philosophy of language, angelic worship, organist analogy, spiritual prayer</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's analogy between the physical act of making music and the spiritual act of expressing thought. He uses the technical world of musical notation (tablature) to explain how the "raw sound" of a spiritual impulse is translated by the mind into a specific, usually native, language.</meta>

...nor is it granted to them to achieve the absolute perfection of a song so quickly, fast, and distinctly. When such a person sees organ tablature <term>tabulatura</term> <note>Tablature is a form of musical notation that tells the player where to place their fingers on the instrument, rather than indicating the pitch and duration of notes as in standard staff notation.</note>, he plays immediately; for his grasp is accustomed to sending the music to his fingers at the first sight of the tablature. But when a song is constructed according to the laws of Music <note>That is, standard musical notation on a staff.</note>, rather than being converted into tablature, he plays with greater difficulty, as he is less used to it; for the tablature familiar to his Spirit must first be composed from the Music before he can play. It is a matter of even greater difficulty and rarity for lute <term>testudo</term> <note>original: *testudinis*. Literally "tortoise shell," a common Renaissance term for the lute due to its curved back.</note> tablature to be performed spontaneously on the organ, or organ tablature on the lute <term>chelys</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for a lyre or lute.</note>.

The logic seems no different to me regarding the first conception of the soul—like a sound that is still raw—when the mind desires to be reduced into words or writings. Lacking this clarity, not a few people get stuck on a good object of thought, which vanishes without fruit because the mind remains indistinct. Furthermore, I feel that the first idea of the soul follows the mind's accustomed instinct, so that it may be perceived there, refined into words or writings. But truly, since a human being is imbued from the start with the character of their native tongue <term>vernacula</term>, holding it as something incorporated or inspired; and since, moreover, they are accustomed to communicating their thoughts (as they turn into meditations, languages, or writings) to the mind in that native tongue, it seems inconvenient and strange to the soul to take the object of the first conception—already depicted in words in the mind via the native tongue—and bestow upon it a foreign idiom against its innate habit. In this, the intellect labors, and through the act of translating, it overshadows, weakens, and fatigues itself; it even alienates the pure and plainly spiritual concept of the original object.

Indeed, I have found it to be true that every object of the first thought that passes into words is always first held in the native tongue. I discovered this in a man who used nothing but the Spanish idiom and was known as a Spaniard; having been lethally wounded and out of his mind, he spoke much, but only in Italian, and he barely understood when addressed in Spanish. I likewise saw a sick German man, who sat or lay just as they placed him, like a statue; he was never able to respond to questions, nor did he understand what his wife or any of his children said in any language other than his own German, even though within his own home he had constantly used the Italian and French languages. In fact, a little later, when he was freed from this waking coma <term>coma vigili</term> <note>original: *Comate vigili*. A medical state where a patient appears awake but is unresponsive or shows primitive reflexes; the author uses these cases to show how the "essential" language remains when the conscious mind is damaged.</note>, he could hardly be persuaded to believe that this had happened.

<summary>The author argues that human thought is fundamentally tied to one's native language, using the metaphor of musical tablature to describe how the soul's "raw" ideas are processed. He supports this with early neurological observations of patients who, during brain trauma, reverted to their primary languages despite being multilingual.</summary>
<keywords>linguistics, native tongue, musical notation, tablature, neurology, soul, thought expression, translation, Spanish language, German language, Italian language, waking coma, cognitive processing</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the author's philosophical discussion on how thoughts are translated into "tablature" (language) to a formal, prayerful dedication of the work. *And so, O Lord, I have laid down the humble dedication* <term>dedicatiuncula</term> <note>original: *dedicatiunculam*. A diminutive form, emphasizing the author's humility in offering this "little dedication" to God.</note> *of my book in the native tongue before Your most high Throne; specifically, the melody of my purpose, that suffering of my neighbor which You did not disdain to cast down upon me. To You be all honor! I proceed now to make known to my neighbor the wretched ignorance of the Pagans* <term>Ethnicorum inscitia</term>, *by which those who are Your sick have hitherto been led astray by the Academies* <note>The author refers to traditional universities, which he believes teach medical theories derived from ancient Greek (pagan) sources like Galen, rather than through divine inspiration or the study of nature.</note>, *and thus miserably destroyed, notwithstanding the Prophetic commandment issued in Your name:*

> *Thus says the Lord: Do not teach in the manner of the nations.* <note>original Latin: *Hoc dicit Dominus; Nolite docere, ad instar gentium.* This is a variation of Jeremiah 10:2, which traditionally warns against learning the ways of the heathens.</note>

*Therefore, O Lord! grant that my soul may retain the gifts granted to it for Your honor, so that I may impress Your Goodness—the portion of my debt—upon my neighbor in this Way of Death. Be to me, O Lord, my every Pole-star, You who alone are the Way, the Truth, and the Life. This is the only thing we ought to love. You, my Angel, Guardian, and Intercessor, who behold the Almighty Good, obtain in my name that which I lack; follow in the footsteps of Raphael,* <term>(the Divine Physician)</term> <note>original: *Medici Divini*. In the biblical tradition, the Archangel Raphael is the angel of healing.</note> *who carried to God the works of burial for the dead performed by night* <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit, where the Archangel Raphael recounts how he brought the record of Tobit’s pious acts—including burying the dead at night—before the Holy One.</note>; *carry to God this work now performed in the night of my darkness, taking diligent care that man hereafter might not be so destroyed, nor undergo death so quickly. Offer this my work before the Most Holy Trinity* <term>Sacro-sancta Trinitas</term>; *to whom I dedicate it! Do so, for the Glory of God* <term>DEI Gloria</term>!

<meta>catchword: AMI-</meta>

<summary>In this devotional dedication, the author presents his medical work as a spiritual offering to God and the Archangel Raphael, positioning his "native" approach to healing as a divine alternative to the "pagan" teachings of contemporary universities.</summary>

# TO THE FRIENDLY READER

->Sends Greetings<-

## FRANCIS MERCURY VAN HELMONT,
### Philosopher through the One in whom all things consist,
### A wandering hermit.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap "C" containing an ornate floral pattern and a central heart shape.</image-desc>

I had once decided, amidst many wandering thoughts, that it would be difficult to persuade myself to write anything for the use of my neighbor to be published in this present age; since I hate the feigned, variegated, vain, and deceitful words for which those of the world thirst. But now, compelled by the reasoning and letters of many just and wise men from various kingdoms and states—who, by a pledge of salvation, urged me that I was bound to commit to the press all the writings of my piously departed father; and to attach to them when and how he met his final day, and in what state he left the aforementioned writings; and furthermore, to supply those things which were lacking, so that the human race might be reclaimed for life from many errors, torments, and destruction. This is what extorted from me the decision to leave all other things behind and to survey the said writings. Having done this, I condemned myself to their approval and suspended my previous purpose, offering the following short narrative in plain and simplest words, in the mother tongue <note>While the text here is Latin, the author likely refers to a "mother tongue" style of plain, unadorned speech, or perhaps a Dutch version he drafted first.</note>, following the tenor of my father's previous dedication, imitating him by chiming in with that same intention of his.

My father's death occurred on the thirtieth day of December, in the year one thousand six hundred and forty-four, at six in the evening, while he was still in full possession of his reason, and after he had first requested and received all his sacred solemnities and funeral rites <note>Referring to the Last Sacraments of the Catholic Church.</note>. His illness was his life itself <note>original: "Morbus sibi fuit ejus ipsa vita." A poetic expression suggesting his intense life of study and physical constitution eventually wore him down.</note>, which remained with him for seven weeks, beginning in this manner: At one time, because of a cold and foul-smelling mist, he suddenly returned home on foot at noon; which was the cause for him that when he attempted to write a short letter of about fifteen lines, or indulged in a too lengthy discourse, his breath would fail him to such an extent that he was forced to stand up and draw breath through the nearest window. By this, on two different occasions, pleurisy <term>Pleurisy: A painful inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs, often causing difficulty in breathing.</term> was brought upon him, from which he nevertheless recovered entirely. Indeed, on the day before his passing...

<summary>Francis Mercury van Helmont introduces his father’s posthumous medical and philosophical works, explaining his initial reluctance to publish and detailing the onset of his father’s final respiratory illness in late 1644.</summary>

# PREFACE

...I was standing upright, he was still writing to a certain friend in Paris <note>original: "Parisios"</note>, and among other things wrote these following words; *Praise and glory to God forever, to whom it has pleased to call me from this world; and as I conjecture, no more than twenty-four hours of life remain;* for today I endure the first attack of Fever <note>original: "Febris"</note> because of the weakness of my life and its failing, by which I must reach my end. This followed exactly as he said, after he had bestowed a special blessing upon me, which I consider a huge legacy. I do not expand here at length upon the specific nature of his disease because of the shortage of time; especially since I must mention it in my *Compendium on All Things to One* <note>original: "Compendio meo de Omnibus ad Unum"</note>, which, God willing, I am striving to publish shortly.

A few days before his death, he said to me: *“Take all my writings, as well those raw and uncorrected as those thoroughly purged, and join them together; I now commit them to your care; perform everything according to your judgment. It has so pleased the Almighty Lord, who attacks all things strongly and directs all things kindly.”* Therefore, attentive Reader <note>original: "Lector"</note>, I ask that you do not judge me unfairly at first glance because I have seen to the printing of the rawer writings mixed with the more mature ones, without restoring or correcting them. Know that a great and laborious desire to advance this work was the cause: Nevertheless, you will finally find that the eager reader will be satisfied in every way in this and the aforementioned things, and then you will judge that I have performed all things rightly and faithfully, seeking nothing for my own profit, which will shine more fully from this preface of mine. I call God to witness, to whom my vow to tend to the help of my neighbor is known. Therefore read and reread this writing, and you will not regret it forever: for in the highest truth I tell you, I have brought these things forth out of mercy alone, noticing that men, because of their own self-importance, have so little at heart the salvation <note>original: "salvationem"</note> of eternal and temporal life.

Halt your old inner-outer steps, enter the eternal royal way; discard those innumerable bypasses which I myself have worn down with great labor and difficulty while seeking where I might arrive at the knowledge of truth, meanwhile striving to find the ordering of all created things and their harmony <note>original: "harmoniam"</note>, and that by all internal and external means which I could imagine. I then directed all my senses so that I might become known to those called Wise Men <note>original: "Sapientibus"</note>, hoping at last to find some untaught Wise Man <note>original: "Sapientem"</note>, in whatever places I might stay, whatever nations I might call upon, and of whatever profession or condition they might be. I spoke according to their appetite, so that I might bind them to me in conversation, and I shared the whole cause to the best of my ability. By this and other ways, I attained several clear fundamental insights and arts, all of which I deliberately pass over here: And when I understood them individually and universally, I discovered only the highly esteemed handiwork <note>original: "opificium"</note> of man, which the more foreign, vain, and futile it was, the more...

->TO THE READER.<-

...to be carried away and worshipped; recognizing this as a form of servitude, I voluntarily turned away from it, as one who pursued plain simplicity.

Descending, I was ascending toward essential and hidden properties, and it seemed that the understanding of certain Latin books was lacking for my assistance; to this end, I frequently read through the New Testament <note>original: "Testamentum Novum"</note> in both the Latin and German languages simultaneously. By this means, within a few days, I might not only understand the Latin style, but also discover in the aforementioned Testament the perfect, long-desired, simple, and eternal truth, and the Unique life—that One (namely, GOD) <note>original: "Unum (scil. DEUS)"</note> who demands only Unity and is opposed to all Duality or Plurality. Likewise, whatever God created, He created everything in that One and through that One; otherwise, He would not have maintained order. 

And so that I might better recognize and enjoy this lovable, free, and unique One in all things, I applied myself to quiet study; outwardly I dressed in simple clothing, while inwardly drawing my spirit closer and practicing healing. I did many things known only to God. Thus, for the sake of preserving health and increasing strength, I lived soberly for many years; I abstained from meat as well as fish, wine, and beer, to such an extent that I incurred the contempt and disgust of my relatives, who reproached me (with good zeal, I suppose), saying: "What unusual thing is he attempting now? He makes himself unfit for every status and function, whether Church-related or secular. He will finally be driven to madness when he finds nothing new for his delight, or he will devote himself to magic arts, or plot a new heresy <note>original: "hærefin"</note>." It is the same with him as with the other children of the Sages—they persist in their stubbornness. 

Others added: "His parent is to blame, for indeed he raised all his children wrongly; from their youth he applied them to <term>Pyrotechnia</term> <note>literally "fire-art," a term used at the time to describe chemistry and alchemy</note>. Now having become moody, he has lost his chance for happiness; when the Infanta of Spain, Isabella Clara Eugenia <note>The sovereign of the Spanish Netherlands from 1598–1633</note>, would have received him and intended him for noble service under her nephew, the Prince-Cardinal <note>Infante Ferdinand of Austria, a military leader and governor</note>, he resisted. It would have been better if he had died in place of his brothers, from whom some good might have been expected; this one is of no use. If he craves studies, let him submit himself to the Doctors, as is the custom for others; or he should be forced to take a wife, who might shake these strange ideas out of him." 

In response, others replied that it was too late, saying mockingly: "He plays the philosopher; he is too stubborn; he is seen nowhere except with all sorts of foreigners and eccentric people <note>original: "personis heteroclitis"</note> of every profession and business. He will yet run into misfortune; for he cannot pretend, he spares no one—neither the great nor the small—when he discovers injustice. Now we are cast down from all hope; he must be reduced to the point of bankruptcy <note>original: "ad incitas"</note>. For his entire inheritance, both what he possessed and what was yet to come, has passed to his sister; and moreover, he departed joyfully on a journey from here, saying that never..."

# ->PREFACE<-

...that he would return: Who ever remembers such things! Something else must take his place, about which we are not entirely certain; yet he should not be considered so foolish as to cast off his old skin <note>original: "veteres ut abjiciat exuvias"; a metaphor for his old life or social status.</note> unless better and more certain things were at hand. Our conjectures fail us, since he embarked on this without consulting us; let him look out for his own end; since he once needed us, he is now considered a stranger.

After I overcame these and many other misfortunes with a calm and joyful spirit, I immediately wove together the following series to unburden my conscience. This was related to me at my request by a man unknown to the world, a God-fearing man; I will summarize his main points through Questions and Answers <note>original: "Interrogata & Responsa"</note>, in which the subsequent questions will sometimes point to more than was clearly declared in the preceding answers. This was done intentionally, so that the reader might likewise exert some effort in the meantime, and it would be clear that the aforementioned answers are abundant.

At one time, this friend of mine came to visit me. Among other things, I asked him if he still remembered the promises he had made to me—to provide certain materials to be joined to my father’s Work <note>Van Helmont is referring to the writings of his father, the famous alchemist and physician Jean Baptiste van Helmont.</note> for the further instruction of the kind reader. He replied to me:

"Listen, Brother: last night, as I was continually weighing and ruminating on your words and on the new and unheard-of commentary on the *Poimander* of Hermes Trismegistus <note>The *Poimander* is a foundational text of Hermeticism, a mystical philosophical tradition. Hermes Trismegistus was its legendary founder.</note>, my lamp was extinguished. I had withdrawn from natural food for the body for a time so that I might devote myself entirely to the interior. Then, after I had suffered a heavy trance <note>original: "deliquium"</note>, I saw—with the use of my eyes suspended—certain transparent, heavy, dark, and compact things created in their beginning, middle, and end by a certain Light which also penetrated my very self. At that moment of vision, I found myself placed upon a transparent, living, spherical, double platform <note>original: "suggestu"</note> without a base, held fast in its own beginning, irradiated by the stars, and inscribed everywhere with a circular letter, which some call the Zenith and others the Nadir. This vision spoke to me by its very appearance: 

'Hear, see, understand, and speak to *the One in All, and All in One* <note>original: "Vnum in Omnibus, & Omnia in Vno"</note>; the time has appeared for all the blind to see, and for those who see to remain blind. *Follow me, and I will lay open to you my illuminated lights. My heart, most stable, created both old and new, is hung as a prize* <term>brabium|A Latinized Greek word for a prize or reward in a contest, often used in a spiritual sense to mean the 'prize' of eternal life.</term> *for every man, its quality expressed as an unknown thing. Step forward, strive! You are able to reach the bottom of my necessary body, with all its durable, resting, and active members. These are whole parts, praising their Creator individually and universally through their effects—the Creator who made me perfect, so that I might help you and those like you in a moment of necessity; for I am subject to you, and besides me, there is nothing.*' Hearing these things, it was clear they were true; and by that very sign, I saw the prize hanging, over which, as if in a frenzy, I uttered these words:"

# ->TO THE READER.<-

"You are young, as are your children who shall be born from you: for your brothers are like you, equal to you in age; your body was created most bright, most heavy, highly compact and visible; your only two colors are blue and red, which contain all the colors of the Universe; and she who shall transform you into black darkness is a white and red virgin; at each turn you will bear ten children to her, while your virginity remains unharmed; since you and your children are established as Light, whose parts are whole, and neither heat nor cold nor any sharpest sword shall loosen your bond; for Salt is your father, and the Moon your mother <note>The speaker uses alchemical allegories: Salt represents the "fixed" or physical principle, while the Moon represents the "volatile" or reflective principle.</note>: therefore hear all things without seeing, and see without hearing, and speak inwardly in silence: All in One; then you will know the twofold, united One in All; and you will be able to loosen the eternal bond, and to bind it, without loss of time."

With these things said, a profound shuddering awe <note>original: "horror"</note> pervaded me, and soon turning toward my own kind, I saw countless men there of all nations—learned and unlearned, Sages, noble and ignoble, young men with the old—who were all divided against each other in a struggle for the sake of knowledge and the science of truth. I, seeing the depth of this division, attempted by a vow to prepare myself for the grafting of mutual **Harmony** <note>original: "Concordiæ"</note>. I first noticed that a certain small book—part of another yet to follow—titled *Unheard-of Medical Works* <note>original: "*Opuscula Medica inaudita*"; this refers to a collection of treatises published by the author's father, Jan Baptiste van Helmont, in 1644.</note>, had partly stirred up this disagreement. This book had called back pious young students and other cultivators of truth from the long and murky night into the dawn, so they might believe that a more perfect light, hitherto unknown, remained, from which this dawn might shine for them. And the more deeply they inspected the aforementioned little book, the more they rejoiced that they found in it the promised arrival of the desired **Perfection of Light**. 

This so increased their spirit that one of them did not fear to propose this parable in a loud voice in public to certain **University Professors**—men otherwise famous and Christian, yet ungrateful—prefacing it with Questions and Warnings: "It is no wonder that these words of ours seem harder to the Flesh, since they are spiritual, concerning which the flesh cannot pass judgment; just as he spoke who had never looked upon the light because of a disease of his sight: and when he saw even the smallest bit of Light, he detested it, claiming among other things that it was the worst poison, because it brought him intolerable pain. For that reason he remained incurable—he who in his stubbornness could suffer no mention of a cure, since he loved darkness rather than light, and so was made a son of that same darkness." 

Some of the Professors realized this simile was aimed at them; unable to restrain themselves and seized by fury, they shouted: "You novices and seditious sowers of **heresies**, it would be fitting to burn you alive with your followers!" Having said this, the raging men rushed toward the house of the Senior Professor, and there they called an assembly by night, so they might foresee what was beginning...

# PREFACE

...so that this new Doctrine might be subverted. The Patron <note>original: "Patronus"; here referring to a protective head or leader of a guild or academic body</note> of this family was a most greedy old man, and as he was the eldest in age, he began the speech first, after he had received everyone with a formal greeting, saying:

"Brethren and sons sworn to our Profession, it is well known to you that our Doctrine is firmly established; concerning which nothing is to be doubted, since it is so ancient, nor has it ever endured any adversity from the nations that could brand it with a stain. In our days, it is by no means to be allowed that it should perish through this schismatic <note>In this context, "schismatic" refers to a philosophy that breaks away from established tradition, likely the chemical medicine of the Helmontians</note> Doctrine, or that the glory, esteem, and the excellence we have committed to the printed press should perish entirely. Let us strive with all our strength to preserve them: by doing this, we shall make ourselves immortal to our descendants, and we shall carry off a solemn reward for our distinguished deeds. Let us be in harmony, and then we shall achieve much.

First, I will express my own opinion: If anyone among us opposes our purpose, let a fine <note>original: "mulcta"</note> be imposed on him by a majority of votes, suited to each person's means. I, as the first, will bind myself to this written agreement <note>original: "apographo"</note>; and as soon as anyone becomes liable for a fine, the money resulting from it shall be set aside for the purpose of suppressing our enemies. Furthermore, lest discord grow among us, and so that we may conveniently reach a suitable conclusion, it is necessary that everything carried out here be recorded in writing."

To all of this they immediately obeyed, and put it into effect; moreover, they urged him to proceed as he had begun, saying: "These two propositions are just and fair; since through this doctrine of ours we have all acquired wealth, it is also fitting and just that the things gained from it should serve our Doctrine and defend it, so that we may reach even greater riches."

The aforementioned Elder, hearing these things, added with a grateful and pleasant face and gesture: "I consider it most necessary also to win over the other University Faculties <note>original: "Scholarum Facultates"</note>, so that they may join us and enter into a mutual alliance, since it affects their interests as well. Once this is obtained, we will soon implore the Magistrate to condemn that seditious little book to the fire, under a further interdict <note>A formal prohibition or ban, often issued by religious or legal authorities</note>, so that those who use it should suffer punishment of their property and body.

Secondly, we should take pains to immediately trick the only son of the author of the said little book, who possesses the rest of the writings by hereditary right. We should promise him a certain sum of money through a third party, as compensation <note>original: "redhostimentum"</note> for his father's books, which we would claim were to be sent to the press. We will pretend to stand on his father's side, so that by this pact we might at least find out where he keeps them hidden, so we might get hold of them to be burned in the fire. For when these see the light of day, we shall suffer even greater losses. Nor would any other remedy be available than to arrange for a book to be published under the author's name containing perverse doctrine or hellish arts <note>original: "stygias artes"; likely referring to magic or heresy to discredit the author</note>, and to scatter it throughout the whole world; also...

->### TO THE READER<-

...so that this might better succeed, the aforementioned heir had to be removed from our midst, lest he obstruct our undertaking. All of this may be freely perpetrated without sin, since we can demonstrate and confirm these actions by the accepted use and doctrine of many celebrated writers of a certain predominant Order <note>This likely refers to a powerful religious or academic society that provided moral justification for the guild's actions.</note>. Having finished these remarks, he asked the primary Doctor following him to likewise strive with all his might to subvert the opposing doctrine and preserve the profitable one; to which he, the second in rank, complied.

He was, in other respects, an upright and sincere man, who had secretly recalled many miserable souls from the underworld <note>original: "orco"; a poetic reference to death or the grave</note> by his integrity. With this integrity, he corrected—whenever the opportunity was granted—the formulas of remedies, reducing the quantity and violence of the treatments prescribed by his aforementioned colleagues. This man was also highly skilled, and he awaited the coming arrival of **Elias the Artist** <note>original: "Eliæ Artiſtæ"; in alchemical tradition, a messianic figure expected to appear and reveal the secrets of the "Great Work" and the true nature of medicine.</note>, whom he longed for desperately. He had learned of him many years ago from one of the brothers devoted to his Profession; otherwise, he was powerful in reason and firm in health—a man who, when dying, seemed to know something beyond the common lot of men.

Once, before his death, he went to minister to the poor for free out of charity, performing many works of mercy in Hospitals <note>original: "Noſocomiis"</note> and Prisons, until he contracted the common disease. This soon brought his fellow Professors to him, who exulted to test upon him the fruits of their professed theory: these men, having held the usual Consultation, drew his blood in large amounts, administered *Purgatives* <note>original: "Cathartica"; harsh medicines used to induce vomiting or bowel movements, then believed to "cleanse" the body.</note>, and thus completely destroyed his strength. 

But it happened conveniently that his remaining vigor and his youth overcame the disease: it appeared he had regained his lost strength, by which it was confirmed to him that the Professors and Licentiates were true Physicians. He considered, based on their reports, that he had deserved death and owed his life to their torments <note>The narrator uses "torments" ironically to describe the painful medical treatments of the 17th century.</note>; hence they carried off a double reward, though not according to their merits. The young man, returning to his former pious path, was oppressed a second time by the same evil, and by their work he hoped to escape the same butchery <note>original: "carnicinam"</note> again. But, alas, his spirit failed him, and with sound reason and knowledge of the truth, he cried out to this brother of his: 

*“It is finished with me, as with every individual; and it will last as long as these so-called Physicians truly feel and see this present state for eternity. But now they forget the past, believing they possess the present; they deny the future when they cannot see it, and thus they take no care for a longer life. For they were never deprived of it, like some other fleeting good that can be repaired; but possessing only a single life and losing it, all will be over. It is a vain thing to apply oneself to studies when no necessity presses. The servant is conquered, who ought to serve us, perpetually calling out with all his qualities; he who names this man his Master will unknowingly be his slave <note>original: "mancipium"</note>, although all...”*

-># PREFACE<-

...men, with few exceptions, are bound by this slavery, which even now and in the future robs the greatest part of humanity of their lives. I despair for this temporal life; for those who are said to bring aid lack any true knowledge of it, and they are forced to spend their time in the disputes and disagreements that arise among them—in the hatred and envy with which the aforementioned Doctors <note>This refers to the elite medical establishment mentioned on the previous page.</note> never ceased to struggle. Being few in number, they scurry about day and night, excelling in wealth as they scrape together a massive sum of money from the healthy, the sick, and the dead alike. Thus they have been able to frequent their circles in harmony, which will persist until the end times appear. You shall recognize those times when you see the number of younger Doctors of Medicine and **Licentiates** <term>Licentiatorum; a degree rank below a full Doctor, granting the right to practice</term> increase so much that they have scarcely enough work to sustain them.

The Elders will be hostile toward the Younger and the newcomers because their daily income will be diminished, and because they will find that these newly arrived juniors—forced to learn more certain methods to earn a living—cure some of those sick patients who would have met their deaths under the care of the elders. At this, the Elders will be envious, wishing in their hearts that all the sick people who might summon the younger doctors would instead perish. Finally, they will revile them publicly before all the People, saying:

> "These wicked young men heal with incantations; it is necessary that their practice be forbidden."

With these and similar words, they will labor to subvert them. They will offend God, so that He might give courage to the Younger and to other pious and industrious men to achieve that which they shall propose to the Elders in these words:

> "When we invited you to permit us to publicly heal certain sick people from the **hospital** <term>nosocomio; from the Greek word for an infirmary</term>, establishing a **prize** <term>brabium; a reward or trophy, often used in the context of a competition or race</term> for the benefit of the poor, and challenging you to do the same—so that whoever failed to produce results would pay a penalty—you refused. You do not seek the needy, but you create them; in this, you act like beggars who loathe those like themselves and do not want their number to increase. For you have secured for yourselves the houses and places of certain rich men, where a more generous handout resulted from your deceitful words and rituals, so that you might leave these arts and houses to your children as a dowry."

This is the very thing you cherish in your hearts, but it shall turn out badly. Because of this public discord, which shall spring from avarice, that long-standing fraud will become known to the World. People will look only to the true Doctors, who shall be judged by their good fruits, and who will follow in the footsteps of the **Samaritan** <note>A reference to the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), the biblical model of a true healer who helps without regard for status.</note>.

When he had finished these words, he felt his life failing him. Therefore, with his eyes turned upward, he added sorrowfully:

> "Merciful Lord, shorten the term of human health <note>original: "Salutis humanæ"; this refers to both physical health and spiritual salvation.</note>, and change the Doctors' fading doctrine of the flesh into the genuine love of the Spirit, so that the innocent may complete their lives to your glory. I pray you, O my Savior, do not hereafter count my death as a sin against the Doctors; for they know not what they do. But deign to open their sight, so that they may support the truth, and so that the People may proclaim of them what was once said of **Saint Paul** <note>original: "Divo Paulo"; likely referring to Paul’s transformation from a persecutor of the truth to its greatest advocate.</note>."

When this was finished, he committed himself entirely to the Divine will...

-># TO THE READER<-

...granted to truth, and he breathed out his last breath in the arms of this his brother, who continually meditated on these aforementioned words.

This man, in his turn, brought forth the following: "We are all bound, brothers in Christ, to champion the truth; which is accomplished no better than by attacking and defending. Hence let us pursue two things: one, that the strengths of our enemies become known to us; the other, that we add greater strength to our own, and thus be more confirmed in our purpose." After they had heard all this, they forced him to undertake this duty under threat of a fine, to such an extent that he had to take up this task as if it were a voluntary gift. And he replied: "I, second of the Elders, desiring to be taught by anyone in this difficult matter—I, a servant of truth—do to some degree grant the first two propositions. But to the third I can in no way agree: namely, to suppress the aforementioned books with prohibitions and the marks of censure <note>In this period, the medical and ecclesiastical authorities often worked together to "censure" or ban books that challenged traditional Aristotelian or Galenic medicine.</note>. For if we strove for that, we would act altogether preposterously; we would imagine we were extinguishing them in one place, only to revive them in a thousand others. Men are no longer so ignorant and incautious as they once were, when they surrendered all copies of a book for the sake of offering up their obedience—a fact that is especially clear to the **Printers** and **Booksellers**, who make a profit from them here and there, and they cannot be forbidden or hindered. 

Does not the matter itself speak of this everywhere? One need not look far. This very author published a dissertation entitled *On the Magnetic Cure of Wounds* <note>original: "De Magneticâ vulnerum Curatione". This refers to Jan Baptista van Helmont’s controversial work on sympathetic magic and weapon salve.</note>, which was stolen from him, and about fifty editions were printed by his enemies. Against this work, they published in great numbers three different books by theologians and doctors of medicine from all over Europe—who cultivate their own atheism—consisting of blasphemous censures. They easily obtained these censures because they live in every region under every kind of religious habit and mask, wherever money or merchandise abounds. They scattered these censorious notes everywhere in temples and other public places, by which the little book became known; it was hunted for by everyone. I knew many who sought it at a high price, yet were not able to obtain it. For none of the **Engravers** <term>Chalcographorum; literally "copper-writers," referring to printers who used copperplate engraving or general publishers</term> had found out anything about it, since they [the enemies] kept it for themselves. It was copied at least fifty times for the sake of gathering the opinions of censors, so that they might ruin its author, causing him a loss of more than fifty thousand **Imperials** <term>Imperialium; high-value silver coins used in the Holy Roman Empire</term>.

Furthermore, because the aforementioned little book, or Disputation, was approved by all wise, learned, and fair-minded men, a great injustice was done to the author. God looked out for him elsewhere and blessed him, so that it might not be suppressed according to their desire. And behold, during the detention <note>Van Helmont was famously placed under house arrest by the Inquisition for his "Magnetic Cure" treatise.</note> he suffered because of this, he published another little book as a precursor, to be followed by this other principal one, so that it might be clearly evident that writings of this kind have little fear of the censor’s rod.

Fourthly, it is impossible for the original manuscript <note>original: "autographum"</note> of the book or the writings to be seized from the heir by craftiness or by a price, only to be destroyed by fire before they can be printed. For I have learned that certain arrogant men offered the aforementioned heir a thousand crowns <note>A significant sum of gold currency</note> in hand, using a certain **Bookseller** as their front. They even bid a further thousand in collateral on this condition: that he surrender all the writings of his father which he possessed, without keeping a single copy for himself. But the heir, being free from the lust for money, smelled a fraud; he listened to the man, asked many questions, looked into every detail, and so utterly confounded him that the man finally broke out into insults in his imprudence, retracing his steps homeward with his journey wasted. These and many similar experiences which the heir has endured have bred a mistrust in him, so that he demands only such security from anyone who aspires to those works that he cannot be deceived. I have understood, moreover,—if I remember correctly—that in the meantime he has seen to it that they are printed by an honest and faithful man who will busy himself with selling them throughout all the lands of the earth.

Fifthly, if one were to suborn forged books to the Author, containing foreign and false Doctrine, it would be made plain to all. For the method of the Discovery <note>Likely referring to the "Chemical Invention" or the alchemical process described in the books</note> is now open everywhere; furthermore, by doing so, we would only rouse the heirs, and he would cry out so loudly (in accordance with the meaning of his name) that he would be heard by everyone. He does not lack the means, though he lacks an inheritance; for it is asserted—and it is the truth itself—that he has found **Elias the Artist** <note>A legendary figure in alchemical lore, predicted by Paracelsus, who would appear at the end of time to reveal all the secrets of nature and medicine.</note>, and has made him an intimate friend. With his help, he will propagate the **Philosophy of Pythagoras** <note>original: "Pythagoræ Philoſophiam"; in this context, it refers to a mystical understanding of the harmony of nature and the elements</note>, whose final tablets he has dug out with unwearied labor through the <term>metallic rod</term> <note>Likely a dowsing rod or a specific alchemical tool used for "mining" philosophical or literal truths</note> at the direction of his Father.

Since things stand thus, let us not provoke him; let us spare our efforts and save our expenses. For if this Doctrine holds any evil purpose, it will collapse of its own accord all the sooner; but if it descends from the divine, and we fight against it, we would not be equal to the task, and we would spend our labor and costs in vain, bringing destruction upon ourselves now and in the future. 

When all the remaining Doctors had heard these solid reasons, they gave him great thanks and honored this <term>Confutation</term> <note>A formal logical argument intended to disprove or check an opposing view</note> as a settled matter. Upon hearing these things, he was seized by <term>Apoplexy</term> <note>A sudden stroke or loss of consciousness, often attributed to intense emotion or "humoral" imbalance</note> out of grief and fear, so much so that he met a very sudden death. His sons broke out in wailing, the neighbors were awakened and flocked to the spot; ignorant of what had happened, they found this entire family in the greatest consternation. Similarly, a student who had observed this crowd approached and immediately looked out for his own advantage. For when he saw all their writings lying scattered here and there and abandoned, he took them up, hid them under his cloak, and soon withdrew. As soon as the day had dawned, he gave anyone of his friends and patrons the opportunity to read them; they spread the word and made it known everywhere. ...it was reported that he had obtained **Pythagoras’s Testament**, and to the Supreme Lord of hidden treasures it was told; he immediately committed you to custody, because you had not brought the found Testament of Pythagoras into the open, which ought to be acquired not by theft but by gift. > Be of good courage; you must undergo this Sentence which our Lord has passed upon you, which begins in this manner: By the mandate of your supreme Lord, to whom it is certainly established that you, **Mercurius van Helmont**, have found by digging up the treasure which he had commanded his subjects to seek out; accused by them, and convicted by certain and full proofs, you are condemned to death, unless you publish that very **Testament of Pythagoras** complete and intact <note>original: "sartum tectumque," a legal phrase meaning "in good repair" or "entirely preserved"</note>, and likewise reveal most fully by what path and knowledge you found it. Once these things are performed, liberty shall be awarded to you throughout all his Empire.

Listening to these things with a sad heart, and then being raised up again with eagerness, you knew for certain that you would not escape death by denial; wherefore you replied to the Delegates in the following way:

> I pray you, Lords Sages as well as Prudent ones, if I have any influence with you, witness my grateful mind before our Lord for so merciful a sentence with which he has deigned to honor me. Demonstrate to him that I retained that Testament imprudently, not knowing it was required to be handed over. I now prepare to provide it, with all the experience and **Science** by which I obtained it, and indeed to whomever it pleases the Lord, provided his Goodness grants me the space of an entire **Week**, within which I shall satisfy the Lord, so that I may recover my liberty according to the tenor of the Sentence. I hope this will not be refused; for in truth, and according to legitimate computation, I need two days—namely that of **Saturn** <note>Saturday</note> with that of the **Sun** <note>Sunday</note>—so that I may begin and perfect the whole web <note>original: "telam," often used metaphorically for a complex work or alchemical process</note> within myself, or arrange each thing in order, which I shall distinctly signify on the coming day of the **Moon** <note>Monday</note>, and so thereafter through the whole following week.

Since you have bound yourself by a specific and ample term of days, we shall remain with you continuously to inquire into your concepts, which you will form during these two preceding days.

You rejoiced in that company: for whoever looked upon them gathered from their dress and gestures that they were pious men; since their countenances bore a divine joy, and...

...and you said to them: "Since the day is drawing to a close—a time I must use to prove my obedience—know, my Sages, that I have set no fixed time for gathering my memories, nor do I need such a thing, as I have no use for it. However, considering that today is the first day of the week, and tomorrow is the Lord's Day—the seventh day, on which He completed all things and rested—it seemed fitting to me to distribute and organize my **Knowledge** <term>Scientia; here referring to the deep, alchemical understanding of nature's secrets</term> according to the days of the week. Thus for us, as fleeting beings, the first day is considered the last; if I were to count backward starting from Saturday <note>The day of Saturn</note> to complete the whole week, I would need forty-two days, which would surely cause boredom in many because of the great length of time. Therefore, I will instead recount everything briefly.

I, **Mercurius**, was raised from my earliest years in a secluded **Hermetic School** <note>A school dedicated to the mystical and alchemical arts of Hermes Trismegistus</note> by my Father. Though I was steeped in those teachings, my restless spirit was not satisfied. I longed to understand the entire **Sacred Art**, or the **Tree of Life**, and to experience it fully. I refused to set my hands to the work until I understood it thoroughly, from head to heel <note>original: "à capite ad calcem", a Latin idiom for "completely"</note>. Furthermore, I had determined in my mind that through the verification of truth, one could reach the ultimate end without the help of external instruction. I began to categorize all creatures: first the external and corporeal ones, and then the internal, spiritual, and **body-forming** <note>original: "corporificantes," referring to the vital forces that organize matter into living forms</note> ones. I then brought these parts back together into a single Whole. I found I could not subdivide or truly know the corporeal things without joining them to their spiritual, body-forming counterparts. I looked upon them with a fresh perspective, placing them all in their proper order as I saw fit. In this, I was free from the biased, false, and stubborn opinions of the Heathens, for I never attended the Universities <note>original: "Academias"</note>, as is quite evident from my unrefined style. Nevertheless, take careful note: I utter no useless word; every word signifies something and belongs to the whole.

My spirit could find no joy or interest in temporary and fleeting things. I constantly thirsted and gasped for things that are perfect and eternal. From the necessary but momentary created things, I looked up toward myself, and from there toward **God**, who created **Heaven** and **Earth** together—a concept that profane philosophers cannot grasp. Those who desire to reach this state must worship God through firm **Faith**, with humble **Hope**, and in true **Love**. Only then will they attain a perfect knowledge of themselves and of all other creatures—knowledge of them before their beginning, in their **Being** or essence, and after their **Transmutation**, which I shall speak of more broadly and clearly.

You speak of the Light of the vessel and the Soul; are these two distinct Lights, or do they together form a single one?

**Mercurius**; There is but a single eternal Light, present in all parts wholly and eternally, externally and internally, as it is eternal life and the entire eternal portion inspired into man by Almighty God; as Moses testifies in the second chapter of the Book of Genesis:
> *Man was made into a living Soul* <note>original Latin: "Factus est homo in Animam viventem"</note>: *which Soul constitutes the seventh day, as is demonstrated in that very chapter: Thus the Heavens and the Earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God ended His work which He had made: and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had done. And He blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it He had rested from all His work which God created and made.* (Namely, making man into a living soul.)

**The Sages**; If this Light is the seventh day, what do you think of the preceding six days, and of that which appears in the eighteenth chapter of **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note>:

**Mercurius**; In the beginning God created all things, the Heaven and the Earth, and whatever was created: which Moses, at the opening of Genesis, encompasses within the first day, where he indicates the formation of the remaining five days, saying:
> *In the beginning God created the Heaven and the Earth; and the earth was without form and void; and darkness was upon the face of the Deep: and the Spirit of God moved upon the waters. And God said: Let there be Light. And there was Light. And God saw the Light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.*

To the extent that Man constitutes the sixth day. These days are distinct from one another so that Man may know himself—what he is, what he must do, and what power he has, or can have, through his Spirit, insofar as he is man (not likewise insofar as he is Soul) over the things created in the preceding days; as it is written in the aforementioned chapter of Genesis:
> *And God said: Let us make Man in our image and likeness: and let him have dominion over the fish of the Sea, and over the birds of the Heaven, and over the beasts of the whole earth, and over every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.*

**The Sages**; You satisfy us, and furthermore, you indicate that Man is the sixth day; and that He separated the Light and the darkness on the first day, which Light or Spirit He called day, and whose Blood, Flesh, or darkness He called Night—which evening and morning constituted the sixth day, and so on for the remaining five, although according to the particular nature of each. But you make no mention of the Seventh day?

**Mercurius**; The Seventh morning, Light, or life, is the Spirit of God Himself, as has been said; and therefore, in Moses' description of the seventh day, it is not expressed that the seventh day was made of evening and morning, as was the case with the preceding six

This being so, at least one Deified Man would have existed; brought to this state by his necessary struggle, he would enjoy in his life the same Grace as Christ our Savior after his resurrection. So that more men of this kind might now be procreated, and so that all might also enjoy that same Grace for which Adam was created, and acquire it through that very struggle, it pleased the Lord God to send the aforementioned sleep, lest Adam, while sleeping deeply, should have contributed anything to the construction of Eve; instead, she was now established by God through this sleep.

The curious might further ask: Why was Eve formed from Adam's rib, and not from his flesh? I return this answer: Adam was the first man, Eve the second, built to be his helpmate and for joined procreation. Now, propagation in man consists partly—as in other living creatures—in Union or Nourishment, as has been said; and it must further be observed in every growth of created things in this world, before they are able to grow up (because they consist of two things: one must first perish, namely the Body and Form, which consist of water and earth, and arise from the light of the Moon and the stars, as the lights of the Night, each according to their different natures, without exception). So that this too might be perfected in Adam, the Lord God removed a rib from Adam, which is bone, according to the "Becoming" <note>original: "Fieri"; the process of creation or the state of being made.</note> in Adam, the offspring of the veins (which to the Belgians <note>The author refers to the Dutch/Flemish language here; the words for "veins" (*aderen*) and "vipers" (*adders*) are phonetically similar.</note> also sounds like vipers), which is ruled by the Moon; as will be found, when the Moon waxes, the marrow of the bones likewise increases, like the waters, and decreases with it. It will further be found that when flesh is burned by fire, it loses its form, but the bone does not; indeed, it is so stable that the examiners of the purity of coinage make their crucibles <term>crucibles: heat-resistant vessels; here specifically referring to cupels made of bone ash used to refine gold and silver</term> from it, in which they melt and test Gold and Silver. So that the Bone, or Rib, is nothing but Human earth and retains nothing else, insofar as it is the second production in Man, like Earth from the Waters, insofar as from the pri-

...let it be debated between you and Adam, since he himself had to struggle against his own darkness, so that he might subdue it just as you do.

**Mercury:** There is no other reason, except that darkness increased in man through the touching and eating of the fruits of the Forbidden Tree <note>The "Arbor prohibita" refers to the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil in the Garden of Eden.</note>, to such an extent that Darkness now holds the primary place over the light and possesses it, just as, in Adam [before the Fall], the Light possessed his darkness and illuminated it before his fall.

**Sages:** How was this done?

**Mercury:** This was done by a fermenting, contagious, dark, and deadly eating.

**Sages:** What do you mean to suggest by that? Explain yourself through analogies.

**Mercury:** Just as there was darkness upon the face of the Deep <note>original: *Abyssi*; referring to the primordial chaos in Genesis 1:2</note> before the Spirit of God moved over the waters, in a similar way you will find that any vessel or enclosed and moldy place will make anything introduced into it—even for a very short time—equally rancid and further infect it, without any of the original and primary ferment and mold decreasing. Furthermore, to demonstrate that this moldy place is also dark, we learn from coopers <note>original: *doliariis*; craftsmen who make wooden barrels and casks</note> who, wishing to know and experience whether a barrel is moldy or not, open its orifice and lower a lit candle through the bunghole <note>original: *umbilicum*; literally "the navel," here referring to the central opening of the barrel</note>. When the vessel is clean and infected by no mold, the lamp lowered into it will remain burning until it stifles itself with its own generated vapor; but if the barrel is moldy, the flame or lamp cannot even penetrate through the barrel's opening to the thickness of the wood <note>The author suggests the foul air or "darkness" of the mold is so thick it physically repels the light or prevents combustion.</note>. It clearly appears, therefore, that darkness also exerts itself and makes other things dark, just as Light works; and this happens when darkness overcomes Light, or Light overcomes darkness. These and similar darknesses must exist before all Light; and the more stable they are, the more stable is the body arising from them. It must now be further noticed that, just as temporal Light illuminates outside of itself—one more than another according to their stability, size, or union—in a similar proportion and way, darkness pours out rays outside of itself, as was related. Just as burning and consuming fire can, through its light, ignite, burn, and excite many seeds into growth <note>original: *Crescentiam*; in an alchemical context, this refers to the "increase" or "vegetation" of a substance</note> according to the measure of their more stable nature; which you will clearly perceive by this well-known experiment: it is seen and felt that the closer a fire is lit, the more it shines and heats. This Heat and Brightness are one and the same thing as long as they are in the Fire, as can be proven by the collection of those hot rays with the aid of a certain burning-mirror <note>original: *speculi ustorii*; a concave mirror used to focus sunlight into a single point to create intense heat or fire</note>, by which the hot rays are gathered together again and become like those existing in the fire: namely, hot and burning. ...the light <note>original: *ducum*, likely an OCR error for *lucem* (light), continuing from the previous page's mention of a candle</note> we permit to burn freely, we will perceive, by the light which shines forth through the fire, that at various distances from here other created things are scorched; specifically, in the nearest vicinity they are more stable and combustible, and as far as the rays are spread, to that extent the Heat is also diminished, and it will ignite less stable created things. The reason is that what is made quickly must also necessarily perish quickly; for this reason, cold and damp Regions produce greater fruits than hot and arid domains, yet they are less durable than other smaller, hotter ones, because the Light that is within them is more divided. This is true in both beasts and men; the men of damp regions are coarse and large, nor can they endure as much Heat as Men living in high, arid, and scorching regions, as the facts themselves bear witness. Indeed, you will find it even in the corpses of those slain by violent death, as Histories relate and we can still experience daily: when a slaughter has been made, the men who had come from cold and watery tracts to wage war against those of hotter provinces—when both sides have been killed—could be distinguished long afterward. This is because those from the colder regions rotted quickly, while those from the hotter ones dried out and remained preserved. In the heat, these latter remained whole because their <term>balsam</term> <note>In alchemy, "balsam" refers to the "radical moisture" or internal preservative fluid that keeps a body from decaying.</note> is more durable than that of others, according to whether they contain more or less moist matter, or participate more or less in the Nocturnal Light. Those who are more deprived of it enjoy more of the diurnal Light.

Just as now the Sun is the perfect and greater diurnal <term>luminary</term> <note>original: *Luminare*; a source of light, specifically a celestial body</note>, so the Moon, the Planet nearest to us, is the perfect Nocturnal Luminary. These are perennial in their Essence, and they likewise render those bodies perennial and durable which are born and reborn by their help. Furthermore, as there is but one Sun and one Moon, the things created from them can be prepared in no other way than similar to them, being also unique and perfect—such as Gold, which the Philosophers called the Sun, and Silver, which they called the Moon, and the other five metals likewise according to their nature, following the other Planets. In this, the philosophers acted rightly and maintained the truth, because these are the only perfect bodies; Fire cannot harm them, and they remain stable within it. Gold lives in Fire, and therefore the Philosophers distinguished it by the name of the <term>Salamander</term> <note>A mythical lizard said to live in fire; here used as an alchemical code for gold's ability to resist melting away or oxidizing in extreme heat.</note>, which is now falsely considered to be a mere Animal. 

Temporary and fleeting fire possesses its own fire only in part, as was said; but the Sun is the Fire and perennial life, and it can only live in what is similar to itself, which must also be a stable body. And just as the Body is temporary in all things—except for these two aforesaid [Gold and Silver] which are similar to the luminaries and participate in them entirely—by the same reasoning that Bodies return to their first Essence, so too the Light must return to its Origin. For the fleeting cannot reach the perennial. these darknesses are perpetual, yet perpetual Light can also dwell within them, first according to the Spirit, then according to the Soul; and since this spirit is eternal, it illuminates the eternal darkness. The darkness then coalesces into Light, and becomes **Silver**, which is twofold <note>In alchemy, silver is often considered "dual" because it is a "perfect" metal but lacks the fixed "sulfur" or heat of gold.</note>, constituting the Body in the Flesh and Bones of **Gold**, which is threefold <note>Gold was often described as "threefold" because it was seen as a perfect balance of Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt.</note>. Just as the Sun is now the great light of the day, so it overcomes the Moon, and the Silver is entirely converted into Gold. Through this, the other five terrestrial planets <note>The "five terrestrial planets" refer to the other metals known to alchemy: Mercury, Venus (Copper), Mars (Iron), Jupiter (Tin), and Saturn (Lead).</note> can be transmuted and brought to a similar perfection, since they too are nocturnal Lights. Furthermore, it should be known that there are countless Minerals, differing from one another like the stars, all of which await their perfection. Some of these can reach their final perfection more easily and quickly than others. Gold and Silver, no matter how minutely they are divided, can be reunited without loss because all their smallest parts are whole and enduring. Nevertheless, they can be rendered "failing" <note>original: *caducæ*; referring to a state where the metal loses its purity or stability</note> because they have not yet joined into one; however, this destruction cannot begin from within the metals themselves—neither in the case of Gold nor Silver—because they are stable.

Now certain Lovers <note>A common term for "Lovers of Wisdom" or alchemists.</note> might ask, in what way would this happen? I reply: in the same way it happens in all created things, and as occurred in Eve, by the increase of darkness, which takes its origin from the beginning of their bodies, as has been related. Indeed, darkness can increase so much that it could turn the entire spirit into darkness. But if the Moon—or the spirit of the Sun—calls the Soul or heat to its aid before it is subjugated and conquered, the Spirit will be strengthened. It will not be as it was before its corruption, but through this struggle and victory it will be so strong, and its Spirit will be so greatly multiplied, that it will be able to make ten of its imperfect brothers <note>The "imperfect brothers" are the base metals (like Lead or Iron) which the alchemist seeks to "heal" or transmute into gold.</note> stable. However, it does not acquire freedom or complete and eternal Union through this one battle; rather, it must repeat this conflict many times, which will grow ever greater according to the increase of the Spirit and the gloom, until it reaches the end. Then it shall suffer no more, and the watery body or darkness will be entirely consumed. Then it is a pure, everlasting, united, and twofold Light, which will illuminate all things without detriment or diminution, and it will be able to perfect all its brothers into things like itself, while retaining its own power. And when this happens in the Sun, the light of the Moon is changed and absorbed into the Sun, so that the Sun likewise becomes eternal, united, and threefold—which is the ultimate state in eternity (outside of man). And from this it can be demonstrated that the Evangelist John, in the third chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, uses the same comparison, saying:

...dedicating himself to serving each and every one of you with all his strength. Having seen them, he advised publishing them, adding: "If anyone desires more, provided they are fit for the knowledge, I will never fail to serve anyone more fully as the occasion arises <term>pro re natâ|A Latin idiom meaning 'as the matter arises' or 'according to the circumstances'.</term>. # PROPHECY
## CONCERNING THE AUTHOR,
### EXPRESSED IN A POEM.

1. Medicine before Hippocrates appeared naked and wandering. 2. A saying of Hippocrates, inviting her to the cities. 3. In admiration, she responds to Hippocrates. 4. The praise due to Hippocrates. 5. Hippocrates was the first of healers; how he cultivated Medicine. 6. Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD) was a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> gave her the ornament of language, but did not nourish her, nor did she grow because of him. 7. The Arabs <note>Refers to the medieval Islamic physicians, such as Avicenna and Rhazes, who preserved and expanded upon Greek medical knowledge.</note> did the same. 8. The followers of both these sects have done the same until now. 9. Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> sought the title of 
<column-break/>
Monarch of secrets and Prince of healing, but unsuccessfully. 10. Medicine scorns pagan worship. 11. She wishes for a mirror, so that she might come forth clearer by reflected light. 12. The Author’s book will serve as a mirror for posterity. 13. Medicine explains her own and the author’s destinies through the prophet. 14. Medicine praises the Author’s studies. 15. The prophet explains the desired fruits of his labors. 16. The judgment of Medicine concerning the Author’s book.

---

<margin>Medicine. 1.</margin>
By chance, the most sorrowful daughter of Latona’s lineage, <note>original: *Latogigenæ*. A reference to the goddess Latona, mother of Apollo. In this allegory, Medicine is personified as the daughter of Apollo, the god of healing.</note>
    Was wandering through wild places to dwell among fierce beasts.
And hostile to her own prayers, then pondering her fate,
    She blamed the unmerciful gods and the cruel deities.
She argued: and with her senses disturbed by excessive anger
    She strayed, and the cause of her error was her grief.
<margin>Aesculapius.</margin>
Thus a double disaster: for she knows her wretched brother <note>Aesculapius, the god of medicine, who was killed by Zeus/Jupiter for bringing the dead back to life.</note>
    Perished by the flame of wrathful Jove.
While he broke the iron laws of the three sisters, <note>The Fates (Parcae), who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note>
    He is said to have perished by the celestial fires.
From this comes an uncertain wandering with wavering steps,
    From this many a tear comes to her sorrowful cheeks.
<margin>Hippocrates. 2.</margin>
The <term>Man of Cos</term> <note>original: *Cous*. Referring to Hippocrates, who was born on the Greek island of Cos.</note> saw her wandering, and having seen her, he loved her.
    Indeed, her beauty, rivaling snowy roses, pleased him.
He spoke: "I think the Dryads <note>Tree nymphs in Greek mythology.</note> are here, my Nymph,
    And the wanton crowd of the Horned God. <note>original: *Cornigeri Dii*. Referring to Pan, the god of the wild and shepherds.</note>
For your presence hallows these fields; it hallows them
    With a proud beauty that befits a Greek goddess.
Why does it please you to visit the mountain valleys?
    Why the peaks that resemble rocky heights?
Do not city palaces with high roofs please you?
    Does not the civic crowd of famous men please you?
Does not a dwelling more suited to a delicate life please you?
    And to enjoy a more excellent condition?"

<summary>This page features a poetic allegory describing the "birth" and wandering of Medicine as a goddess, mourning her brother Aesculapius before being discovered by Hippocrates. It serves as a historical and mythological justification for the author's new medical system.</summary>
<keywords>Medicine, Hippocrates, Aesculapius, Galen, Paracelsus, mythology, allegory, history of medicine, prophecy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the allegorical poem introduced on the previous page.
