# PROPHECY CONCERNING THE AUTHOR,

Let the humble peasants and the unlearned youth grow cheap in value; let the rustic roofs of the small cottages grow vile. <note>These lines conclude the speech of Hippocrates from the previous page, where he argues that medicine should move from common folk-remedies to a majestic, organized art.</note>

<margin>3.</margin>
The graceful Nymph <note>Medicine, personified here as a divine maiden.</note> was awestruck by the face and the majesty of the speaker, and by the bearing of the great man. Soon, every tear vanished from her purple-tinted face, and no complaint sounded with a mournful tone. She cast her starlike eyes down toward the green earth and gave signs of certain joy to those who were weary. Having meditated on the words spoken to her for a brief moment, she replied to the old man of Cos <note>original: *Coo... seni*. Referring to Hippocrates, who was born on the Greek island of Cos.</note> with these words: "These words of yours are pleasing; you are the one among mortals whom I desire. What you have offered will be like a gift to me. I shall dwell with you; through you, I will drive away both plagues and pestilences. Indeed, when Disease sees you, she herself will feel sick."

<margin>4.</margin>
Bright Cynthius <note>original: *Cinthius*. An epithet for Apollo, the god of both the sun and healing.</note> rises from the Eastern waves and sinks his horses in the Western abyss. Your glory shall climb higher than any kingdom; indeed, your praises shall lick the highest stars. Posterity shall cry out that you are the one and only master, and there will be no spark by which your praise could further increase. Living fame shall celebrate you throughout the wide world, until the Fates <note>The three goddesses of destiny in Greek mythology who spin and cut the thread of life.</note> finally snap your destiny.

<margin>5.</margin>
The man of Cos, offering deserved thanks for such a great gift, bestows these presents upon the naked Goddess. He wraps the snowy Nymph in a pure linen cloth <note>original: *sindone*. A fine muslin or linen garment.</note> which surpasses the lilies scattered in the white snow. Golden-haired Apollo never saw anything like it, whether he is rising or washing his glowing chariot in the Western sea. For a long time, Medicine remained adorned with such beauty; thus did the ancient Fathers <note>The earliest physicians of antiquity.</note> cultivate her.

<margin>6.</margin>
Until Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD), whose complex systems dominated medicine for centuries.</note> arose five centuries later; he was entirely devoted to ornament, but he did not provide food for her mouth. To be sure, he gave her garments soaked in Tyrian purple <note>original: *Tyrio... murice*. An expensive dye symbolizing luxury and status, but here implying that Galen’s medicine was more about "dressing up" the art with words than providing substance.</note>, which a twisted fringe adorned with many knots.

<summary>Medicine accepts Hippocrates as her master, leading to a golden age of healing until Galen arrives centuries later, who is criticized for favoring ornate language and status over the practical substance of the art.</summary>

### EXPRESSED IN A POEM.

<sig>A 2</sig>

Bright studs distinguish her shining belts:
Beautiful linens enrich the maidenly head.
<margin>7.</margin>
Avicenna <note>original: *Avicennas*. The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> comes, the glory of the Arabian race:
It is said he grew old in the robes of a scholar to be entreated.
<margin>8.</margin>
In a number greater than can be counted, many of his followers came,
Who did nothing except polish the robes they were given. <note>A critique of the "Scholastics" who merely commented on old texts rather than performing new research.</note>
<margin>9.</margin>
At last, the great Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss-German physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> from Swiss shores,
Showing off, declared himself to be of the lineage of a Goddess.
<margin>10.</margin>
However, she <note>Medicine, personified as the Nymph.</note> despises the bright gems and precious necklaces:
"That does not help goddesses at all," she says.
Ornaments that breathe nothing of ancient dignity
Are more of a disgrace the more they are a product of artificial art.
What purpose have a thousand robes? A thousand displays of luxury?
This vain labor does not suit our divine nature.
To have sought mere ornaments for countless years,
Alas! One should be ashamed to have stayed awake for such guilty trifles.
<margin>11.</margin>
And oh, that it were allowed for me to see how beautiful I am!
Might I not be even more beautiful in my own judgment?
Might our beauty be gazed upon by the judging Goddesses?
And might all men approve of our divinity?
But perhaps, Nymph, they fear that if you see your own face,
You will despise everyone, and wish to live for your beauty alone.
If you had not seen your own reflection, Narcissus,
The water you gazed upon would not have been the crime of your death.
He was a mortal; I am the daughter of a God, a Goddess,
I do what I desire, I go where the Goddesses have willed.
Who will give me a mirror? I seek a mirror; through it I shall be rendered
more bright, and every blemish will be gone from my whole body.
<margin>12.</margin>
Who will give me a mirror? Goddess, cease your justified grief.
For behold, he prepares that glass which will reflect your face.
Jan Baptist <note>original: *Ioannes Baptiſta*. Referring to Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), the author of this work.</note> shall give it, whose name is from Helmont,
Whom pleasant Brussels nurtures in her bosom.
Whether the spirit, departing from a vessel, enters into a vessel, <note>A reference to Van Helmont's pioneering work with "gas" (a word he coined) and the chemical transformation of substances in sealed containers.</note>
I swear by this genius of yours, greatest Old Man of Cos! <note>original: *maxime Coe*. Hippocrates, the legendary father of medicine from the island of Cos.</note>

<meta>This page continues the allegorical poem where Medicine, personified as a Nymph, addresses the state of her art. Having previously critiqued the followers of Avicenna and the boastfulness of Paracelsus, she now speaks a prophecy regarding the "Author" (Jan Baptist van Helmont), framing his work as a divine remedy for the "labyrinth" of traditional medicine.</meta>

### A PROPHECY CONCERNING THE AUTHOR,

<sig>D3.</sig>
<sig>D4.</sig>

*In this mirror, you will marvel at the reflected form,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which holds sway over disease, over death, and over ill-favored Fate.* <note>original: *Parca*. One of the three Fates in Roman mythology who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note>
*Destructive old age shall not snatch away its accustomed beauty,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Nor shall there be a wrinkle of age upon its ancient brow.*
*Thereafter you shall not be hindered by a labyrinthine turn,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*For the straight path lies open from every trail,*
*Said the Nymph to the Prophet.* <note>original: *Vati*. The "Vates" or Seer/Prophet to whom the personification of Medicine is speaking.</note> *The Ruler of Olympus* <note>A classical reference to God.</note> *decreed*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*That the world should be scourged by unusual evils throughout its sphere,*
*So that the wretched mass of human kind might come to know*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*How great is the ignorance of the common medical crowd.* <note>original: *Medica... plebis*. A sharp critique of the established medical practitioners of the 17th century.</note>
*Indeed, He willed that the chosen ones should shine forth against*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The number of diseases and a new barbarism.*
*And on the other hand, He willed that the ignorant rabble—*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The fierce murderer of many men—should fall apart of its own accord.*
*Each one, clinging to the worn-out words of his master,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Thinks that the touch of the pulse* <note>original: *tactus*. Refers to the traditional diagnostic method of feeling the pulse, which Helmont felt was over-relied upon by Galenic doctors.</note> *is the peak of the medical art.*
*While they wander through circuits, and restore the opinions*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Of their ancestors into new works and new centuries.*
*Hence they have not dared to advance their step beyond the man of Cos,* <note>original: *à Coo*. Referring to Hippocrates, the famous physician from the Greek island of Cos.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Nor do they think they can seek the art any further.*
*But what shall the mortal race do, now accustomed*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*To this law of healing? To suffer everything in their own skin?*
*Always treading the fixed footprints of the ancient fathers,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Alas, the credulous crowd perishes by its own deception.*

# THE AUTHOR’S PROMISES

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial D featuring an intricate design of scrolling vines, leaves, and floral motifs.</image-desc>

I shall speak of the errors of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university medical faculties of the 17th century, which primarily taught the ancient Greek doctrines of Galen and Aristotle.</note> regarding those things which they have rashly judged to be the foundations of nature; then, in the failings of Nature, I will show defects, or diseases, unknown to those who came before. Specifically, I will show that these do not arise from the mixing, battle, opposition, or disproportion of the elements, nor likewise from those qualities which they falsely claim are the primary and genuine properties of the elements. For this reason, their meditations on "complexions" <note>The "complexion" was the specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) thought to determine a person's health.</note>—whether in a balanced or unbalanced state—are vain. I will also teach that the four humors <note>The traditional medical theory that health was governed by four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> are mere trifles, and that everything attributed to them thus far was devised by the heathens <note>Helmont frequently attacked "heathen" (pagan) authors like Galen and Aristotle for leading Christian medicine astray.</note> and their evil demon, to the destruction of the human race. Indeed, the composition, connection, qualities, and effects of the humors—and the diseases dreamed up from them—are mere fictions; likewise false are the teachings on laxatives, and the choices, withdrawals, and reductions of humors that they suppose. To be sure, these vain hopes, uncertain healings, and dangerous experiments conducted in such a state of ignorant laziness have constituted not a medical art, but uncertain conjectures that seek out excuses and cover their errors with the earth. Finally, I will show that they have sold vain and harmful hopes as if they were truths; that bloodletting <note>original: *Phlebotomia*</note> never helps except by accident—specifically due to a lack of better art and gentler medicine—but that the cutting of veins always takes away from a long life. Cauteries <note>The practice of burning the skin to create a "derivative" sore.</note> too were introduced without foundation, after they had already explored the uncertain and faint help of their own remedies in vain.

Furthermore, I will reveal that "Tartars" <note>original: *Tartaros*. A term used by Paracelsus to describe stony or sandy deposits in the body, like kidney stones or gouty crystals.</note> are not the perpetrators of illnesses. Similarly, diseases do not arise from the "three principles" <note>The Paracelsian chemical principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, nor from the "essentials" of which Chemistry <note>original: *Chemeia*</note> boasts. I will also uncover the vanities or fictions of the "catarrh" <note>A term for "downward flow"; traditional medicine attributed many illnesses to mucus "dropping" from the brain.</note>, showing that there is no disease born of such a parent. Finally, I will establish that the errors regarding "vapors" <note>original: *ventos*, literally "winds" or gases within the body.</note> must be corrected. Lastly, I will prove that the Heavens are immune and harmless from "seminal" diseases <note>He argues that diseases come from internal "seeds" or spiritual blueprints, not from astrological influences or the stars.</note>. I shall expose the inventory of medicines and the abuses of physicians alike, for the sake of charity on both sides. Meanwhile, I will conduct an "anatomy" of diseases <note>Helmont uses "anatomy" here to mean a deep structural analysis of the cause of a disease, rather than just cutting open a corpse.</note> through their true roots, and I will explain several of them by separating them from common error as the occasion of the argument arises. Indeed, I have represented the tragedies of Apoplexy, Leprosy, Asthma, Dropsy <note>original: *Asciten*</note>, Gout <note>original: *Podagram*</note>, the formation of stones <note>original: *Lapidescentiam*</note>, uterine disorders, and finally of Poisons and the Plague. I will show that healings and cures should be established not through "contraries" nor through "similars," but only through "endowed" and "appropriated" remedies <note>He rejects the Galenic rule of "contraries cure contraries" and the Paracelsian "like cures like" in favor of specific medicines that match the specific "essence" of the disease.</note>. Toward this end, it was truly necessary to destroy the entire Physiology of the ancients and to renew the physical teachings of the Schools. Lastly, I will treat the root of life (which no one else has done). I ask the Lord God that

### INDEX OF THE FIRST COLUMN

1. **The Author’s Intent.** 2. *The origin of Medicine, and the continuous corruption following from it.* 3. *The origin of Schools and Sects.* 4. *The credulous laziness of the Europeans who followed.* 5. *Medicine, which was introduced by Galen, was thereafter driven in a circle, like a millstone.* 6. *The ruinous blindness of the Schools.* 7. *The construction of a shameful Catalog of "Incurables."* 8. *Arguments against Bloodletting, based on its indications.* 9. *The errors regarding purgatives.* 10. *The entrance of scoundrels into medicine.* 11. *Several of Galen’s deceptions.* 12. *The ease with which Galen acquired his dominance in the art of healing.* 13. *That sharpness of mind was of no value, nor were the pagan schools.* 14. *How much one can actually progress in pagan schools.* 15. *Why medicine is the highest and most obscure of sciences.* 16. *The goal of Medicine has stood neglected.* 17. *The errors regarding medical goals are demonstrated.*

### COLUMN I

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap Q featuring floral and fruit ornaments</image-desc> Although self-love <note>original: "Philautia"</note> frequently shuts out the knowledge of truth—even though nothing more precious has been given to man—I nevertheless deemed it a work full of Christian piety to teach how much the disciplines handed down to me have progressed. I have therefore deliberated upon a clearly unusual matter: namely, to overturn the cups of giddiness and sluggishness with which the Schools have hitherto been intoxicated, <margin>2.</margin> luring the world and deceiving it for twenty-one centuries. First, Hippocrates—a man of a most rare gift and a participant among the Adepts <note>The "Adepts" refers to a semi-mythical group of masters who possessed secret knowledge of nature and alchemy.</note>—published several of his wearying experiences without any varnish <note>original: "sine fuco," meaning without artificial coloring or deceit.</note>. Since very few of his genuine works survive, and even those were subsequently forced to serve the opinions and commentaries of others: although most of his <margin>3.</margin> works are now considered adulterated trash. Others could not endure his industry; for such is the decay of the days, that virtue and truth soon have envious rivals accompanying them from their very birth. Hence, everything human has always been liable to ruin. Indeed, things that were once embraced out of charity in ruder but more sincere ages,

<column-break/>

soon found themselves turned toward profit, convenience, luxury, and glory. Thus, a display of piety succeeded charity, and vanity born of profit destroyed compassion. In this way, the purity of healing migrated into tongues, boastings, controversies, quarrels, and conjectures; and having abandoned the faithful trust of prior observations, they erected "theorems" softly suited to sluggishness and giddiness. Then Galen, five hundred years later, built up hypotheses of "complexions," humors, and "degrees" <note>Galen categorized medicines and bodies by four degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>. He promised a mathematical demonstration, by an easy method, of those things which Nature alone can measure—matters she has reserved for herself in secret, and which she finally revealed only to the Spagyrists <note>original: "Spagyris." These were alchemical physicians who believed in separating and recombining substances to find their "essence."</note>. Meanwhile, Galen dispersed his theorems into a vast mass, which the talkativeness of the Greeks later increased immensely, and which the Schools, even to this day, superstitiously worship because they have made trophies for themselves from the labors of others. From this point, study passed into a "profession" and into Universities. Since the Romans (whom the Greeks call Barbarians), the successors of Galen, were not ashamed to propose him as their author. For they jumped from the act of *healing* to being *Healers* <note>original: "Medicos"</note>, and they erected "Medicine." And so they erred at the very threshold, and even to this day, they have written an omen for themselves in their very name. For they do not cherish Medicine or act as Doctors because of the *work* of healing, but only because of *speaking* <note>Helmont is making a wordplay between "Medicus" (doctor) and "dicere" (to speak), suggesting they are merely "speakers."</note>; they are "Doctors of Speaking," and their profession is "Medicine," and their whole curative art, by their own confession, is destined to be merely "discursive" <note>original: "sermocinalis," meaning related to speech or rhetoric rather than action.</note>. By this prophetic etymology, they denoted that they could not hope for honor from the art, since they acquired their name only from speaking. Later, the Moors <note>original: "Mauritani," referring to the Islamic scholars like Avicenna who preserved and expanded Greek medicine.</note> promised the prize of victory, just as Greek influence had almost withered away in these studies. But the Europeans, despairing, as if the whole power of their minds were exhausted, <margin>4.</margin> chose to stand by barbaric inventions and to cultivate foreign ideas.

<meta>This page continues the author’s sharp critique of the academic medical establishment, specifically targeting the legacy of Galen. # THE AUTHOR'S PROMISES

<columns>

...to have cultivated their inventions, they thought was enough for themselves. However, they did not think it ungenerous to reduce those same fictions into new categories every day; indeed, they considered it an honor to be wise only by way of a commentary. From this, the cup of laziness imbued the Schools with a lethargy, where everyone preferred to agree rather than to investigate. 
<margin>5.</margin> Because of this, medicine has made no progress since the time of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>; instead, through **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> it has actually moved backward, and thereafter it has been driven around in a circle. From this, the Schools conceived a sort of dizziness; and Galen’s deceptions, imitating the song of the cuckoo, rotated forever in that same circle. For while studies are directed toward profit, medicine is rotated around a millstone. 
<margin>6.</margin> Indeed, since the Schools even today recognize hardly any remedies besides bloodletting <note>original: "venae sectionem"</note> and a collection of laxatives, all their effort is such that they presume to remove all bodily ailments through blood, dung, baths, searing irons, and sweat. This results in nothing but the diminishment of the body and its strength, as well as the putrefaction of the blood—which they call "purging"—and a miserable butchery. 
<margin>7.</margin> Hence it has happened that they themselves, marveling at their own vanishing effects, have built up a massive troop of "incurables." As if driven by desperation, they make only shameful mention of those diseases and have introduced "palliative care" <note>Treating symptoms without curing the cause.</note>—a practice full of calamity and despair. 
<margin>8.</margin> Only a **Plethora** <term>Plethora: An old medical term for an "over-fullness" or excess of blood, used to justify bloodletting.</term>, I say, is called the indicator for bloodletting; yet in other respects, this practice is harmful. The lack of appetite and the aversion to food at the start of an acute illness easily deplete any "Plethora" within the first few days as the disease ravages the body. Nor has the empty fiction of "revulsion" and "derivation" <note>Theories that humors could be drawn away from or toward certain parts of the body.</note> been of much use, as I have demonstrated in my own discourse on fevers. 
<margin>9.</margin> As for laxatives, since they only drain the fresh blood from the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "Mezaraicis venis," the veins supplying the intestines.</note> and transform it by making it putrefy in different ways according to the nature of their own poisons, they have truly, until now, given only a faint hope of healing—one full of confusion, anxiety, and uncertainty in the outcome. Therefore, we are blind, unless with great courage...

<column-break/>

...we go to meet such a slaughter of mortals, moved by the sighs of the sick, the orphans, and the widows, and finally by a pity for the dead. For besides the fact that the aids the Schools offer the sick are so uncertain and untrustworthy, I ask you to pity with me the human lot, which has subjected life and fortunes to an art filled with conjectures and uncertainty. It has even admitted every kind of scoundrel and harlot to rage with impunity against our kin. 
<margin>10.</margin> When I consider such laziness and blindness of the Schools and the ages, I praise God, three times glorious, that He has revealed much truth in Himself to the "little ones," which He has hidden from the great men and the academic chairs. Therefore, marveling at the abyss of God's judgments, I holily adore Him. 
<margin>11.</margin> Furthermore, Galen—seizing the glory of his predecessors for himself—expanded his art, which was content with a few rules, into immense volumes. It pleased him, of course, that all bodies be formed from the four **Elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and take their entire essence from them. And so, according to this standard, he confirmed four qualities, as many simple "complexions," then four pairs of complex qualities, and from there also the four **humors** <note>Blood, Phlegm, Yellow Bile, and Black Bile.</note> as our constituent parts—things that others had dreamed of before him. Then, from the struggle and discord of these humors (both the simple ones and his own invented ones), he established almost all diseases and the goals of healing, just as he decided health was derived from their balance. He also claimed every disease was a mere **disposition** <term>diathesis: a physical state or constitutional predisposition.</term> in quality. For this reason, he argued that remedies are only "contraries for contraries" <note>The principle of *contraria contrariis curantur*, e.g., using "cold" medicine for a "hot" fever.</note>. Compelled at last by this necessity, he copied out the powers of simple medicines word-for-word from **Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist.</note>, distinguishing elementary degrees but everywhere neglecting their "seminal" and "specific" power, because he did not know it. 
<margin>12.</margin> By this very "ease" of the art, he gained and held the leadership of healing; and the next generations were lured by such a shortcut. Thus, a lethargic sleep crept into the Schools through the gates of laziness. To wake them, I pray God may give His honor...

</columns>

...matter, and may mortals reap the fruit I desire from my labors! Many will grumble, I know well, grieving that their own and their students' wearying lectures will be diminished if I resign the solid truth of Medical science to the gift of the glorious God alone, and hope very little in the sharpness of human wit.
<margin>13.</margin> But let them snarl as they will: man is a blank and empty slate (*tabula rasa*), and must acquire his doctrine from elsewhere, from the one and only Teacher. Of whom it is said that the disciple never surpassed that Teacher, because there is only one Father, and one Teacher, who dwells in heaven. From whom comes every good thing, all light, and the clarity of Understanding. As Christians, indeed, we profess the Lord Jesus as the unique wisdom of the Father, the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "α & ω"</note> of all essence, truth, and knowledge. And so, since every good gift—not only of virtues but also of knowledge—descends from the Father of lights; who could learn the token of Medical science from the pagan Schools? For the Lord created the Physician, not the Schools. 
<margin>14.</margin> The pagan schools can indeed possess historical knowledge, observing things that are contingent, regular, and necessary. This is the science of remembering facts. And they can attain Mathematics, which is the science of applying things to measure. And finally, they can promise a rational science, which is deduced from either of these through the adaptation of discourse. And if only they had provided, through those means, something solid and sincere to the extent they were able! They can, I say, know historically the ebb and flow of the stars and the sea, that water tends toward a level and downward, deriving various consequences from this and establishing them as axioms. They may know, I say, the art of bread-making and adapt the necessities of causes, somewhat connected, to reasoning. But to understand and know these things from the very source, or *a priori* <note>reasoning from cause to effect, rather than just observing the result</note>, is granted to no one without the special favor of Christ the Lord. 
<margin>15.</margin> Therefore, the science of healing is the last of all and the most hidden, so much so that it is no wonder that even today...

<column-break/>

...its first principles are still missing from the printing presses. The more clever among the heathens argued that the world consists of its own law, and that things have their roots in the whole and in species, by which they promised they would be preserved forever by their own power, and thus that independence, or a deity, resides within things. Alas! Hence, like drunkards, they have stumbled in the darkness around dismal deities and blindness, away from true Philosophy and the truth of Medicine. And therefore, they necessarily remained ignorant of created things, and of their seeds, roots, and knowledge. Thus, the knowledge of Nature was indeed attempted by the heathens through childish conjectures, but it was never attained in the slightest. Therefore, I have grieved with compassion that, until now, the principles of physics <note>meaning *Physica* or natural philosophy, the study of the natural world</note> have not been drawn from elsewhere. Just as I have resolved to uncover these in this work, I humbly pray that God grant my talent may not result in a punishment of retribution, even if in this labor I have not been able to achieve as much as I wished. For the entire faculty of Physics has been brought down to man; 
<margin>16.</margin> therefore, it ought to concern his life immediately, and all its defects. All Physics, therefore, culminates in the use of life, the discovery of causes, of disease, and of remedies. Regarding this last pivot, little sweat has been spent so far, nothing is known, much indeed is promised, and most things are neglected; I find that it has been long expected, and everywhere it is in error. For the knowledge of diseases contains the science of causes, of dependency, and of their appropriation to the guardian powers of our body. 
<margin>17.</margin> In these matters, they have hitherto "erred by the whole width of heaven" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to be completely and utterly mistaken</note>. But the discovery of a remedy presupposes the aforementioned knowledge, and furthermore of the powers and strengths—I mean the manner and means of acting—and the application, preparation, and deduction of those remedies, according to the specific needs of the parts and the objectives. It also necessarily contains the knowledge of <term>simples</term> <note>individual medicinal ingredients, usually herbs or minerals, not yet mixed into a compound</note>, their powers, actions, changes, defects, alterations, differences, and connections or dependencies, both among themselves and with respect to the vital powers. Each of these truly desires...

### COLUMN II

<margin>1.</margin> I have had to approach Philosophy from the very beginning <note>original: "Ab ovo," literally "from the egg."</note>. A matter, I say, never investigated theoretically, and even less attempted or known through practice. That is, I have decided to make public an unheard-of truth. For unless we deal with diseases in the same way as other arts deal with their objects; and unless we are able to promise and foresee the certain outcome of diseases—responding to the patient's wish in the manner of
<margin>2.</margin> other craftsmen—it is a sign that the means and the end are left to a conjectural and uncertain Art. In such a state, ignorance is the leader, and the path is the track of uncertainty; eventually, darkness seizes both the traveler and the guide as they move through unknown paths. I know that many will be 
<margin>3.</margin> angry with me. Primarily those who will attribute my plainness <term>ruditatem: a lack of polished academic rhetoric</term> and severity in criticizing to intolerable boasting. Then, there are those who are displeased by everything not produced by their own judgment, who mock and dread everything new; as well as those who, claiming to know everything, refuse to learn. However, I could not bury my talent because of those who hate me, nor fail to reveal my zeal to my neighbor. Therefore, I will unfold the gifts of knowledge granted to me, without envy, deceit, hope of profit, or the vain glory of ambition, for my neighbor’s sake; and I will gladly show how far they have satisfied my 

<column-break/>

experience. I hope that once the truth is shown, those endowed with richer talent will easily become more useful to the State than I. For it is fitting that disciplines should become wealthier day by day by proceeding through additions. Those who come after will therefore be 
<margin>4.</margin> obligated to those who came before. Indeed, it is believed to be a great help to have leafed through the books of many before me, because it is easy to add one's own ideas to the discoveries of others. But in the task I have undertaken, every kind of help from the Academics was weak, and the advice and support of my ancestors was therefore of no use to me. Insofar as I differ from them, it is very easy to discern that the pen of every writer has been ignorant and "diseased" <note>The author suggests that the medical texts themselves are as corrupted as the diseases they fail to cure.</note>, and that the judgment of no one has profited me at all—indeed, it has significantly hindered me. Therefore, I sincerely and candidly protest and profess that the writings of my ancestors have fought against me for some years regarding the glory of truth. But when I bring forth all things 
<margin>5.</margin> new and unheard of, I will not interpret the discoveries of others, nor will I contend with authorities; and I have appeared to myself as a new author of a Medicine that was, until now, known in name only. Therefore, the gifts for which God the Creditor has inscribed me—a poor little debtor—in His book, I have put out at interest <note>A biblical metaphor for using one's God-given talents rather than hiding them.</note>. All these things are paradoxes. I admit it. For if they existed elsewhere, I would consider myself a useless brawler, a waster of my days, a redundant repeater, and presumptuous. Therefore, if it pleased the Father of Lights <note>A title for God from the Epistle of James.</note> to increase the number and wickedness of diseases in the days of our ancestors, I believe it is equally not unfitting to hope that His Goodness has opened His treasures so that at last—quickly, safely, and gloriously—He might anoint the scars and wounds which the Father of Mercies has inflicted. Specifically, 
<margin>6.</margin> He who from the beginning established the Physician as a Mediator between God and man. Indeed, He has taken delight in willing to be "conquered" by the Physician; He testifies that He created the Physician for this very purpose with a peculiar praise and chose him. It is truly so. For God does not sooner punish a man, make him weak, or threaten to kill him...

# THE AUTHOR'S PROMISES

...wishes for Himself an opposing Physician, so that He might overcome Himself—even while sending down deserved punishments—through the gifts of His own mercy. This is the Charity of the Most High, more precious than any fleeting thing, which He has bestowed from ages past upon the Physicians He has chosen. He, the incomprehensible one, who disposes all things sweetly.
<margin>7.</margin> Such Physicians are prepared in their mother’s womb (for this phrase, *the Most High created him* <note>original: "creavit ipsum Altissimus." A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1, "Honor the physician... for the Most High created him."</note>, implies this), performing their duty with no regard for profit. They reflect purely upon the pleasure (indeed, the command) of Him who alone is truly merciful, and who orders us, under the threat of hellish punishment, to be
<margin>8.</margin> like our Father. *Obey those in authority* <note>original: "Obedite præpositis."</note> is a precept indeed; but *honor your parents, honor the Physician*, is a more binding command than "obey," since we are sometimes forced to obey even those beneath us. For the Physician is a Mediator between the Prince of Life and Death. I stop here, soon enough, considering the benefits granted to me, though I am unworthy. Furthermore, I neither seek a kind reader nor fear a critic <note>original: "Momum," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and harsh criticism.</note>. Let it be permitted to displease both, for those who are allowed to do so will find fault with every
<margin>9.</margin> labor and science. For God has so decreed that new things continually find harsh and, for the most part, ungrateful censors. I have renounced with great effort the desire to please Courts and Nobles, or to hang upon the whims of others; I have always judged this to be a form of slavery. On the contrary, I consider it true freedom not to be subject to anyone but God. For although it was difficult at first, I chose this kind of austerity, which was my habit; I then made it natural through practice, and finally found it sweet. And I wish that this habit had grown in me not out of arrogance, but from the possession of a more careful science! For I am mindful of the word: *God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they are put to shame, because the Lord has despised them* <note>original: "Deus dispersit ossa eorum, qui hominibus placent..." quoting Psalm 53:5.</note>. I know for certain that if it pleases the Giver, he will pour dew upon my fate and grant growth, and thus my concepts will be profitable to the human Commonwealth, if my days are fulfilled. If not, He at least knows

<column-break/>

my inner heart, and I shall expect the rewards of His Mercy. Let God, therefore, stand between me and the world, for He shall judge both. May His name be thrice gloriously sanctified, and may His sanctifying will alone be done in all things. Amen.

### ->COLUMN III<-

<margin>1.</margin> Charity prays, desire seeks; and necessities, out of compassion, knock at the soul. This is how understanding is given. Truly, I was ashamed, even from my youth, that a worker called to a task would promise to do it and stand by his promises,
<margin>2.</margin> while I, called to a sick person at the beginning of a disease—when their strength was still intact—would allow that person to perish. Full of dread, I believed it would not be enough to say: *It is not always in the Physician's power that the sick man be relieved* <note>original: "Non est in Medico semper relevetur ut æger," a famous line from the Roman poet Ovid.</note>. From this arose a license to proceed recklessly and continue in medical work by saying: "I shall be excused because I did as much as I could, according to the theorems of the art." This is a hollow excuse if my knowledge is everywhere defective, and the very hypotheses of the art are rotten at their root. It is surely
<margin>3.</margin> the ignorance of healers, persisting in bad treatment, that is almost a capital crime; indeed, it cannot be expiated before God, where "a man will give skin for skin" <note>original: "pellem pro pelle dabit homo," quoting Job 2:4.</note>. For it is a sign that such a Physician did not enter through the door, but through the window, and has claimed a false name for himself. For my part, even from my tenderest years, I held science above riches. 
<margin>4.</margin> Healers used to ask me, of course, why I cured less according to the way of Galen <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over 1,500 years.</note>, and why I refused to follow them like a flock of sheep following those who went before. They even promised me many gold coins annually...

# THE AUTHOR'S PROMISES

<columns>

...turning toward profit, as many of his peers did; but after their theorems became suspect to me, I anxiously sought a safer path. For I longed to know more than to be enriched. And would that this desire in me were purely for God’s sake! At least sufficient riches came along with some degree of knowledge. Soon I learned to doubt even more the constancy of Galen’s theorems <term>Galen’s theorems: The traditional medical teachings of Galen (129–216 AD), which relied on the balance of four "humors" and dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</term>, after I had seen that the very axioms of the Schools were ulcerous; then gradually, through discourse and experience, I confirmed this concept more and more: namely, that the seeds of ignorance, by the same contagion, had penetrated into the root of healing and the minds of
<margin>5.</margin> those healing. Therefore, I immediately abandoned all the books of everyone, the meticulous hair-splitting <note>original: "acribologias," referring to overly precise or pedantic arguments.</note>, and the empty promises of the Schools, firmly believing that *every good gift comes from above from the Father of Lights* <note>original: "omne donum bonum, de sursum venire à patre luminum." A quote from the Epistle of James 1:17.</note>, and even more so, the knowledge of
<margin>6.</margin> Adept Medicine <term>Adept Medicine: A term used by alchemists to describe medicine reached through divine insight and chemical laboratory work rather than ancient textbooks.</term>. I traveled through several foreign nations and found nearly the same laziness and ignorance among them all. I did find some who were more curious to know, more tenacious in their purpose, and more cautious in their presumption; but they were equally, if not more, ignorant than the rest. Meanwhile, I was honestly weary of my past labor and the anxiety suffered in learning. In the multitude of books, there was nowhere solace or knowledge, but only vain promises, abuses, and
<margin>7.</margin> many errors. Thus I long ago considered the art of healing to be a mere imposture introduced by the Greeks, until finally the Sacred Scriptures instructed me better. I considered the Plague the most calamitous of diseases, in which everyone would desert the sick, and faithless helpers, distrusting their own art, would flee faster than the unlearned commoners and the simple plague-healers. I proposed, therefore, to dedicate one period of time to the wretched people infected by the contagion. Although no medicine had then become known to me except common ones, God nevertheless preserved my innocence from such a fierce enemy. For I visited them of my own accord, not called upon, not so much to help—

<column-break/>

—as eager to learn: yet all seemed to be refreshed with hope and joy when they saw me. I myself, relying on the hope that I would eventually possess the knowledge of an Adept through God’s sheer grace, persuaded myself of this. After a decade of wandering and study, and after receiving my degree in the medical art at Leuven <note>original: "Lovanii."</note>, finally in the year 1609, now married, I withdrew to Vilvoorde <note>original: "Vilvordiam," a town in the Duchy of Brabant.</note>, so that, less distracted, I might proceed through the kingdoms of plants, animals, and minerals. By curious analysis, opening bodies and separating all things, I intended to investigate for a full seven years. I investigated the books of Paracelsus <term>Paracelsus: A 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who famously burned the books of Galen and promoted the use of chemicals in medicine.</term>, which were covered in derided obscurity, and I admired that man and treated him with great honor—until finally an understanding of his works and
<margin>8.</margin> errors was granted to me. For no friend (that thief of days), no wine, or banquets detained me (as I could not yet bear wine then); but continuous labor, through sleepless nights in succession, accompanied my desires. And finally having been taught that bodily powers are bound to their principles, and that they cannot be worthily known without unlocking the barriers, I sang a hymn to my Lord, because I did not yet regret my age, labors, expenses, and neglected profit, being compensated by the sweetness of Adept knowledge. Meanwhile, Reader,
<margin>9.</margin> I am indignant with myself that I am scarcely allowed to open my concepts in truth without damaging the reputation of previous authors. But the license of previous ages has encouraged me; it made Galen unpunished—indeed, praised—even though he frequently found Erostratus, Asclepiades, Protagoras, Erasistratus, Herophilus (I do not mention Moses here), and many earlier ones guilty of error. Indeed, he even frequently criticized Quintus, his own teacher, whom he nevertheless testifies to have followed in most things (though he was an empiric). But what harm will it be to those who tread the worn path, yet are ignorant of a safe way of
<margin>10.</margin> healing? For who has understanding that he did not receive for free? I confess indeed that the errors of the Schools, the imprudences...

## T H E A U T H O R’ S C O N F E S S I O N .

1. *The Author’s Murmur.* 2. *Doctors in Ireland are preferred to those of Italy.* 3. *The Romans lived better without Doctors.* 4. *A dream shows the Author his own soul.* 5. *The manner of the mind in understanding.* 6. *The nature of the mind’s deputyship <term>vicariatus: the role of the mind acting as a representative or substitute for a higher power.</term>.* 7. *The nature of the soul’s appearance.* 8. *The Mind asked the Author his intention in writing this book.* 9. *The subterfuge of "I-ness" <term>Egoitas: a philosophical term for self-consciousness or the essence of the "I".</term> in the Author.* 10. *The mind’s response.* 11. *Confession of incidental vanity.* 12. *What the Author saw after repentance.* 13. *Another intellectual vision.* 14. *The Author’s repentance.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring scrolling foliage and a central face/mask.</image-desc>

<margin>1.</margin>
When I had read through this work of mine, and had grasped the content of the book as if in a single point in my abstract Intellect, I said with a sigh: O the cares of men! O how much emptiness is in things! <note>original: "O curas hominum! O quantum est in rebus inane!" This is a quote from the Roman satirist Persius.</note> To what purpose is it to pursue the errors of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities of the time that taught ancient Greek and Roman medicine without questioning it.</note>? What utility will the Christian world feel? Whether we know that diseases proceed from conceived entities <term>entities: "entia," formative principles or spiritual origins of disease in Van Helmont’s theory.</term>; or finally, whether they spring from heats or fictitious humors <term>humors: the traditional medical belief that health is governed by the balance of four fluids: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</term>? For, miserable man, have you not labored in vain? For what purpose is such a brilliance of Theory? Do not all these things contain the fuel for presumption?

<margin>2.</margin>
For I remember that the nobles of Ireland give a field to a domestic healer, not indeed one who returned trained by the Academies, but one who would heal the sick. He has, namely, a book left to him by his ancestors, filled with remedies. And so the heir of the book is always the heir of that field. That book depicts the signs of diseases and local remedies. And the sick Irish are healed more happily, and are far stronger than the Italians, who have in every village their own petty quacks <term>Medicastros: a derogatory term for unskillful or fraudulent doctors.</term>, living off the blood <note>original: "cruore," implying they drain the resources or life of the poor.</note> of the miserable. I said therefore to myself: What vain error has led you

<column-break/>

astray? What great thing did you recently meditate upon, if the Academies mock your little disputations and trample them underfoot? And although you may not have written for the sake of your own little glory, yet all things in the hands of men are vain. You thought indeed that if you did otherwise, you would have buried the talent granted to you.

<margin>3.</margin>
Indeed, did not the Romans live for five hundred years without doctors, and with far happier health than they did afterward when the Greeks were conquered? From whom did they secretly receive Doctors? Would it not be a happy age if the thorns of theory, together with the thistles and briers of the earth, were burned, and leaving the weeds behind, we ate only the wheat? Certainly, I know not whether from the fatigue of reading, or truly from sleep creeping in, these insults to truth—unworthy of a response—terrified my soul.

<margin>4.</margin>
At least a great quiet soon invaded me, and I fell into an intellectual dream, quite memorable. For I saw my soul, small enough, in human form, yet free from the distinction of sex. Immediately I stood stuck in wonder at the spectacle, not knowing what "I-ness" <term>Egoitas: the quality of being a self; the subjective "I" that observes its own existence.</term> was in me, which could discern a soul distinct from itself, and understand the intellect outside of itself? And then a certain light entered into the soul, in comparison with which the visible light of this world seemed to contain foul darkness. For that light was not different from the soul itself. Therefore it had nothing like itself among sublunary things <term>sublunary: the realm below the moon, i.e., the physical earth, which was thought to be imperfect and changeable compared to the heavens.</term>.

<margin>5.</margin>
Then I immediately understood that we who are now joined with the flesh are, through the same flesh, abstracted from the true and luminous intellect: and that the soul understands in peace and quiet, not in ambiguity...

He recounts a mystical dream in which he observes his own soul as a genderless being made of divine light, realizing that the human body obscures true understanding.</summary>

# THE AUTHOR’S CONFESSION.

...by which, and led by a strained reasoning, it induces for itself blind images of the truth, intricate fallacies, and persuasions of truth—mostly ill-fated—neither rejoicing in a foray into similarities, nor purifying likenesses and their proportions through relationships to make them equal, nor lowering itself downward to the underlying faculties, which are prone to analysis and synthesis; nor weighing all things when agitated by the various breaths of certainty, passions, and the confusions of infirmities. 

<margin>6.</margin>
But I noted that, since the mind's prior majesty was now void, another generation had arisen. In this, the sensitive soul <note>original: "anima sensitiva," the part of the soul responsible for sensory perception and basic life functions in the Aristotelian tradition.</note> would act as the mind’s deputy. This soul, which stood in need of the arousal of confused knowledge, determinations, and disciplines, now fills the place of true understanding and arrogates all "I-ness" <term>Egoitas: a term Van Helmont uses for self-consciousness or the ego-driven identity of the individual.</term> to itself. From this I learned that it happens that we do not perceive that we understand anything, as long as the principal agent of this wretched and fleeting intellection has not translated its power as far as the limits of the senses. For this reason, we do not even remember that we understand, unless such an action is propagated in us through the economy of the senses. Nor do we notice that we know, except when a certain mutual transfer of faculties occurs, and, as if the angles of actions were folded together around a center by opposing stage-actors. In this duality of intelligence where I was placed, the threat of the Lord—who is to judge our justices—concerning the soul turned over in my mind. 

<margin>1. Eccl. 13.</margin>
For I had proposed to investigate all things that are under the sun; and that God, thrice glorious, had given to the sons of men their own occupation 

<margin>7.</margin>
to exercise themselves. The soul, therefore, decided to examine itself in the proposed image of itself. According to that saying: *For who knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?* <note>original: "Quis enim scit, quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est?" (1 Corinthians 2:11).</note> Afterward, the soul opened the eyelid of the right eye. Indeed, it was not shaped like a human eye—distinct with membranes, a pupil, and various fluids—but rather, the eye was a single, luminous little globe, like the star Venus appears 

<column-break/>

from afar. This eye, although it was by far the most beautiful in its brilliance, nonetheless struck me by its unfamiliarity. It shone as much inward, toward the depths of the soul, as outward through the whole soul. It cast a ray into the splendor of that understanding, previously hidden, which had fabricated for itself a distinct "I-ness." 

<margin>8.</margin>
It demanded an account from the "thymosis" <note>original: "thymosi," from the Greek *thymos*, referring here to the spirited or passionate part of the sensitive soul.</note> or spiritedness of the sensitive soul. Namely, whether in the composition of this book, with a always resigned will, he had offered everything nakedly to the most placid goodness and will of God? Or whether, indeed, he had ever presumed anything of himself, like those preoccupied people who spend their whole life thinking about the inscription on their tomb? Or what posterity would think of him? 

<margin>9.</margin>
But the "I-ness," refusing to tolerate the light of the discussing Intellect, tried to submerge itself within the body, fleeing the examination of contemplative truth. But in such visions, in which the Intellect apprehends the "I-ness," the latter stands as if outside the body. Therefore, unable to hide itself from the ray of the soul that shone through it, it sought a diversion in a completely unusual way: as if out of shame for the matter and the novelty of the place, it asked for a delay until the day after tomorrow, hoping that by tomorrow the Intellect would perhaps be unmindful of 

<margin>10.</margin>
what it had begun. But the soul said: *Each day has its own burden* <note>original: "Quaeque dies suum onus habet," echoing Matthew 6:34.</note>, and requires its own account. There is no need for delay for a confession of truth; tomorrow will provide no help. Thus, the withdrawal 

<margin>11.</margin>
and delay were removed. Then the "I-ness" confessed: "I admit, and willingly detest, that the general fragility of men has repeatedly contaminated me, composed as it is for custom, believing that honor, by merit and worthiness, should nourish all arts, according to the dictates of the Gentiles <note>Referring to the secular or pagan philosophers who believe that the pursuit of honor is the proper motivation for science and art.</note>." Having said this, the "I-ness" itself felt its own foulness. And from that point on, the Intellect, worn out by grief, sighed as it were: recognizing my poverty of understanding—and how painfully needy it is—within the body, which nonetheless still desired the applause of men and vain [glory]...

<summary>Van Helmont describes a spiritual vision in which his soul examines his "I-ness" (Egoitas), revealing his secret desire for human honor and fame. He confesses that his intellectual pursuits were tainted by a worldly desire for recognition rather than being purely dedicated to God's truth.</summary>

<keywords>Egoitas, sensitive soul, spiritual vision, self-examination, intellectual pride, confession, divine judgment, thymosis</keywords>

--- Page 56 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Author's Confession" from page 14. Van Helmont is deep in a spiritual reflection, moving from the philosophical analysis of the soul to a personal account of his struggle with intellectual pride and a transformative mystical vision. The catchword from the previous page was "Non" (not).</meta>

...having obtained a doubtful **little glory**. Indeed, by a special privilege, all honor and glory belongs to God alone. I realized then that I had declared war against God and had introduced a separation into the universe by my vain efforts. For the universal order of things is such that everything, primarily and as an ultimate end, and totally, exists for the honor of God. Therefore, so that my labor would not be entirely rejected (since it was still far from goodness), it was necessary for this mark of "self" to be seriously purged. To this end, repentance was looked for and expected from above, with earnest pleading. 

<margin>12.</margin> When this repentance arrived, the other of my eyes finally opened. For I saw then that the investigation of all things under the sun was a good gift, descending from the Father of lights into the sons of men, as a pursuit and a festive correction of past ignorance; otherwise, the danger of empty self-satisfaction would constantly attack from the side. 

Wherefore, I humbly asked the Lord, out of the pleasure of His piety and with total displeasure for my own vanity, that He would spare me and deign to mortify the **I-ness** <term>Egoitas: a term Van Helmont uses for the self-centered ego or the human tendency to claim divine gifts as one's own achievement.</term> that was always reflected back upon myself. 

<margin>13.</margin> Meanwhile, with a resolved mind, I decided to bury this book in the fire; and I would have done this very thing and was ready to carry it out, had not another **intellectual vision** <term>intellectualis visio: in mystical theology, this is a vision perceived directly by the understanding or the mind, rather than through physical sight or mental images.</term> presented itself to me. For I saw before me a tree by far the most beautiful, spread out as if across the whole horizon; its magnitude and breadth left me remarkably stunned. It was sprinkled with countless fragrant flowers of a most calm and luminous color; each of them had a bud behind it, a pledge of future fruit. I plucked one for myself out of so many myriads, and behold: the scent, the color, and the whole grace of the flower immediately perished. At that same instant, the understanding of the vision was given to me. Namely, that each of God's gifts are like flowers, even more glorious than Solomon on his throne—representing great expectations if they remain on the tree. But if a man appropriates a gift for himself, or dares to pluck it from its origin, although the flower vanishes from him, the plucker remains a debtor for the promised fruit.

<column-break/>

Therefore, I decided from then on to leave God’s gift on its tree and not to claim anything for myself by plucking it. I willingly confess my past ingratitude toward the tree. 

<margin>14.</margin> Because whatever I have of it was freely bestowed and granted to me conditionally for a time. Furthermore, from the bottom of my soul, I detest my vain and foolish ignorance, because I originally thought I could reflect back into myself this gift that falls upon me like a foreign ray of light. For just as stinking smoke comes from dung, so does the **pride of erasure** <note>original: "fastus lituræ." This likely refers to the vanity an author feels regarding their own writing, editing, and intellectual "polishing."</note> rise from letters. I used to delight in a **being of reason** <note>original: "ente rationis," a philosophical term for something that exists only as a mental concept rather than a physical reality.</note> rather than in solid truth, thinking it would be honorable after death—something that no one will rightly value. Namely, that honor would be the applause of the many, according to the judgment of those who err. 

I shudder at it, therefore; I repudiate from this moment on and renounce any praise that anyone might ever give me. Now at last I perceive what stains the love of **vain little glory** <note>original: "gloriolæ," a diminutive form emphasizing the insignificance of human fame.</note> possesses, and I have openly declared war against it. Knowing, indeed feeling from my past vision, that although it is easy not to receive praise while it is not being given, it is nevertheless difficult not to be delighted by it when it is offered. For I have experienced how dreadful it is, in the world to come, to have attributed to oneself for some frivolous reason even a part of the glory that is owed entirely to God. 

I desired, therefore, that this book should come forth for the common good with my name suppressed, to bear witness that I henceforth despise the common breeze of popularity. But the decree of the **Powers** <term>Potestates: the governing authorities, likely referring to the religious or civil censors who required authors to identify themselves.</term> stands in the way: *Every soul is subject to the higher powers.* <note>original: "Omnis anima subjecta est potestatibus," a reference to the Epistle to the Romans 13:1.</note> May God, the fountain of all good light, help me to continue seriously mocking myself, since formerly vain presumption crept in sometimes from behind and occasionally from the side; may it no longer plague me in any way hereafter. He will dew upon these fates—if perhaps it pleases Him—the things that will grow which I have sown for the use of my neighbor. Meanwhile, I wish, O faithful of Christ, to be judged unworthy, evil, ignorant, and rash, provided that my neighbor does not thereby suffer harm in the art of healing.

He renounces personal fame and explains that he only publishes his name under his book due to the requirements of established authorities.</summary>

For he did not consider me useless or ignorant in vain. ### THE STUDIES OF THE AUTHOR.

*1. The birth and life of the Author. 2. The Author laughed at the masked efforts of the Professors. 3. The nakedness of the Author. 4. He pursued more solid sciences in his leisure. 5. Astrology became worthless. 6. He spurned a Canonry. 7. What progress was made in studies at Louvain, among the Jesuits. 8. Stoicism was displeasing. 9. Stoicism to be rejected by command. 10. The Author was drawn into Medicine as if by chance. 11. The defects of the herbalists. 12. Medicine flows only from above, and therefore cannot be handed down by rules. 13. <margin>1.</margin> In the year 1580, the most calamitous year for all of Belgium <note>Refers to the upheaval of the Dutch Revolt/Eighty Years' War.</note>, my father died: I was the last and most worthless of my brothers and sisters. For I was being educated in studies. By the year 1594, I had finished the course of Philosophy, which was my seventeenth year. And so, since I had only my mother, I seemed at Louvain to have been made entirely my own master and judge. Wherefore, I saw that no one was admitted to exams unless they were masked in a long gown and a hood <note>original: "tunica talari, & cuculla larvatum"; Van Helmont viewed academic regalia as a deceptive 'mask' of wisdom.</note>, as if the garment itself promised learning;

<margin>2.</margin> I began to realize that the Professors, for a long time, had exposed the young men who were to be presented in the arts to ridicule. I marveled at a certain kind of delirium in the professors, and indeed in the whole world, as well as the simplicity of the youths' credulity. I withdrew into a calculation, so that at least by my own judgment I might know how great a Philosopher I was; I examined myself to see whether I had attained truth or knowledge.

<margin>3.</margin> I discovered that I was puffed up by the letter <note>Refers to "the letter that kills," or superficial, bookish learning.</note> and, like one who had eaten the forbidden apple, plainly naked, except that I had learned to argue with craftiness. 

<column-break/>

I had learned how to dispute with others. Then for the first time it became clear to me that I knew nothing, and that what I did know was of no value. For the "Sphere" <note>The *De Sphaera Mundi*, a standard medieval astronomical textbook.</note> in Physics seemed to promise some knowledge, to which I had therefore added the Astrolabe, the use of the ring <note>An astronomical ring or portable sundial.</note>, and the theories of the Planets; at the same time, I cultivated Logic and Algebra for the sake of amusement, whenever the reading of others brought on boredom: to which I connected the elements of Euclid.

<margin>4.</margin> And I had made this teaching a companion to my nature, because it contained truth. But by chance, the *Cyclognomica* <note>A work by Cornelius Gemma attempting to link all knowledge into a universal system.</note> of Cornelius Gemma, like a second Metaphysics, came into my hands. Since it uniquely commended Nicolaus Copernicus, I did not stop until I had made him familiar to me. From this I learned vain eccentricities and a different circuit of the heavens; thus, I realized that whatever I presumed to have acquired about the heavens with great labor was not worth much time.

<margin>5.</margin> Therefore, the study of Astronomy began to become worthless to me, because it promised little certainty and truth, but many empty things. Having finished the course, since I knew nothing solid or true, I refused the title of "Master of Arts"; I was unwilling that the professors should play the fool with me by declaring me a Master of the seven arts when I was not yet even a disciple.

<margin>6.</margin> Seeking truth and knowledge, rather than appearance, I withdrew from the schools. A rich Canonry <note>A church office with a guaranteed income (prebend).</note> was promised to me, provided I would devote myself to Theology; but Saint Bernard deterred me, saying that I would be "eating the sins of the people" <note>A common medieval trope warning that clergy living on tithes or endowments were sustained by the sins of their flock.</note>. I asked the Lord Jesus to deign to call me where I would please Him most. For it was the year in which the Jesuits had begun to teach in Louvain

He describes his decision to refuse his Master's degree and a lucrative church position to seek genuine knowledge, eventually turning toward the Jesuits.</summary>

...to teach philosophy <note>original: "docere philosophiam"</note>, even though the King, the Nobles, and the University were against it. And because this had been forbidden to them by Pope Clement VIII, their students—who were aspiring to academic degrees—flocked to the preparatory schools. Others, particularly the wealthier ones, were enticed by the attractive study of Geography. Another of the Professors, Martin del Rio <note>Martin Antoine del Rio (1551–1608) was a Jesuit polymath famous for his work on magic and demonology.</note>, who had previously served as a judge of the Spanish Court and later sat in the Council of Brabant before being drawn to the Society of Jesus, was lecturing on *Magical Investigations* <note>original: "Disquisitiones magicas"; Del Rio’s most famous book, a massive treatise on witchcraft and the supernatural.</note>. I took up both lectures eagerly. Yet, in the end, instead of a harvest, I gathered only empty stalks and a most wretched collection of scraps, devoid of any real judgment.

<margin>7.</margin> Meanwhile, so that not an hour should pass without fruit, I read Lucius Annaeus Seneca, who pleased me immensely, and especially Epictetus. Thus, in moral Philosophy, I seemed to have found the very juice of truth. Immediately afterward, I thought that this must be the discipline for which Pythagoras required so many years of strict silence, excellent judgment, and therefore remarkable obedience. Finally, with only a few things changed, I saw a Capuchin friar as a "Christian Stoic." This study for the sake of eternity certainly appealed to me, but my rather frail health stood in the way of such great austerity. I prayed to the Prince of Life several times to give me the strength to contemplate the naked truth and to love it directly; this desire was increased in me by Thomas à Kempis, and later by Johannes Tauler <note>Thomas à Kempis and Tauler were famous Christian mystics who emphasized internal devotion over outward ritual.</note>. And since I presumed that through Stoicism I was making progress in Christian perfection, and trusted in it with certainty, finally, after some delay and exhaustion in that exercise, I 

<margin>8.</margin> fell into a dream. I seemed to have become an empty bubble <note>The "bulla" or bubble is a recurring motif in Van Helmont’s thought, representing the fragility and vanity of human existence.</note>, whose diameter reached from the earth all the way to heaven. Above me leaned a coffin, while below, in place of the earth, was an abyss of darkness. I was immensely terrified, and at the same time, I fell outside of all knowledge of things and of myself. Returning to myself, I understood in a single concept: That in Christ Jesus we live, move, and have our being. That no one can even say the name of Jesus for salvation without the special grace of God. That one must pray continually: and lead us not into

<column-break/>

temptation, etc. Indeed, an understanding was given to me that without special grace, nothing but sin awaits us in any of our actions. Having seen and tasted this knowledge, I marveled at my former ignorance; and I recognized that Stoicism held me like an empty and swollen bubble between the abyss of hell and the necessity of imminent death. I recognized, I say, that through this study, under the appearance of moderation <note>original: "specie mediocritatis"</note>, I was becoming most arrogant—as if, relying on the freedom of my will, I were renouncing divine grace, and as if we could achieve whatever we wished through our own selves. "Far be such a sin from me," I said. Therefore, I judged that this blasphemy might be forgiven in Paganism, but was unbecoming of a Christian; and so, on this account, I considered Stoic philosophy to be hateful.

<margin>9.</margin> Meanwhile, as I grew weary and tired of reading too many other things, I leafed through Mattioli and Dioscorides <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli and Dioscorides were the primary authorities on botany and herbal medicine in the 16th century.</note> for recreation. I concluded that nothing is so necessary for mortals as to minister to their own needs by admiring the grace of God in vegetables and gathering their fruits.

<margin>10.</margin> Soon after, I discovered that the herbal art <term>herbal art<gloss>Botany and the study of medicinal plants.</gloss></term> had not grown at all since the days of Dioscorides. On the contrary, today people only argue about the illustrations, names, and appearances of plants handed down by him. Nothing of their virtues, properties, or uses has been added to the original discovery and histories—except that later writers have made up "degrees of elementary qualities" <note>The Galenic system categorized medicines by four qualities (Hot, Cold, Moist, Dry) and four degrees of intensity.</note> to which the entire temperament of the herb is supposed to be attributed. But when I discovered that perhaps two hundred herbs of a single quality and degree had diverse properties, and that several herbs of different qualities and degrees worked in harmony (for instance, in wound-healing potions) to produce the same effect, I began to hold in low esteem not the herbs themselves—which are the talismans of divine love <note>original: "pentacula divini amoris"</note>—but the Herbalists themselves. And as I wondered at the cause of such instability in their effects, and such great obscurity in applying and 

<margin>11.</margin> healing, I searched to see if there was any book that handed down the axioms and Rules

<margin>12.</margin>
Medicine? For I used to think that medicine <note>original: "medecinam"</note> could be taught and handed down through formal instruction, much like the arts and sciences, and thus it was a matter of tradition—not merely a gift. Since medicine is a science, and "every good gift comes down from the Father of Lights," <note>A reference to James 1:17.</note> I imagined it must have its own theorems and its own leading authors. I thought these authors were equipped with infused knowledge, much like Bezalel and Oholiab <note>Biblical craftsmen from Exodus 31 whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom and knowledge.</note>, whom the Spirit of the Lord had inspired with the causes and understanding of all diseases, along with the knowledge of the properties of things. I therefore considered these enlightened men to be the foremost professors of the healing art. I asked myself: was there not another who had described the gifts, properties, applications, and harmonies of vegetables, from the hyssop even unto the Cedar of Lebanon? <margin>13.</margin> A certain professor of medicine answered me that nothing of these things was lacking in the works of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the dominant authority on medicine in Europe for over a millennium.</note> or Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note>. But as I was not prone to blind belief, and could not find the certainty I sought among the writers, I began to suspect the truth: that the Giver of Medicine remains its continuous dispenser. <margin>14.</margin> Thus, anxious and uncertain as to which profession I should commit myself, I looked at the customs of the people, the laws, and the decrees of Princes. I saw that Law <note>original: "jus"</note> consisted of human traditions—uncertain, unstable, and devoid of truth. Indeed, because there was no stability in human affairs and no core of real science, I felt I would be leading a useless life if I spent it on the mere opinions of men. Finally, I realized that governing myself would be difficult enough; to judge the property and lives of others was obscure and beset by a thousand thorns. Therefore, I utterly rejected the study of law and the governance of others. On the other hand, the hardship of human life and the will of God—by which everyone must protect themselves as long as possible—pressed upon me. I was leaning with a singular greed toward the most peaceful knowledge of natural things; and since the soul arrives as a servant to its own inclinations, I slipped imperceptibly into the science of nature.

<column-break/>

I read, therefore, the *Institutes* of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany.</note> and Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), who introduced the term "physiology."</note>, through which I realized I had looked upon the whole science of healing as if through an epitome, and I smiled to myself. Is this how the science of healing is handed down? Without a theorem, and without a teacher who has drawn the gift of healing from an Adept? Is the entire history of natural properties really confined to the elementary qualities? <note>Referring to the traditional system of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry qualities.</note> <margin>15.</margin> So, I read the works of Galen twice, Hippocrates once (whose *Aphorisms* I learned almost by heart), and all of Avicenna. I seriously and attentively read through perhaps six hundred authors—Greeks and Arabs as well as moderns—noting down in commonplaces whatever seemed unique or worthy of the pen. <margin>16.</margin> Finally, rereading my collected materials, I recognized my own poverty. I was ashamed of the labor and the years I had spent. I noticed that all the books sang the same old song as the *Institutes*; there was nothing solid, nothing that promised the science of truth or the truth of science. Meanwhile, from the very beginning, I had purchased every kind of "simple" <term>simples: individual medicinal herbs or minerals used as remedies, as opposed to "compounds" or mixtures.</term> from a merchant so that I might keep a small amount of each in my possession. Then, from a pharmacy assistant—a collector of simples—I obtained all the common plants of our country. In this way, I learned to recognize many of them by their appearance. At the same time, I reflected that while I knew the faces and names of these simples, I knew nothing of their true properties. <margin>17.</margin> I then wished to accompany a practicing physician; but soon, I was repeatedly disappointed by the insufficiency, uncertainty, and guesswork of the healing art. I knew how to dispute any disease as a matter of logic, yet I did not know how to fundamentally cure a toothache or the itch. Finally, I saw that fevers and common diseases were cured neither certainly, nor scientifically, nor safely. As for more serious ailments that do not cease on their own, they were mostly relegated to the catalog of incurables. It then occurred to me that the art of medicine was an invention full of imposture, despite which the Romans had lived happily for five hundred...

<meta>This page continues the author’s spiritual and intellectual crisis regarding the state of medicine.
