<header>STUDIES OF THE AUTHOR.</header>

...years had passed. I considered the healing art of the Greeks <note>Refers to the Hippocratic and Galenic traditions that dominated European medicine.</note> to be false: indeed, I saw that the remedies themselves, used as mere experiments, helped no less without a method than those same remedies, when used with a method, failed most people. In both cases, I detected the fallacy and uncertainty of the canons of healing, which were based on the "diversity of temperaments" <note>The "complexions" or four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) used by ancient physicians to explain health.</note>. I said, with a grieving heart: 
<margin>18.</margin> "Good God! How long will you be angry with mortals? You, who until now have disclosed not even one single truth of healing to your Schools? How long will you deny the truth to a people who confess your name—a truth more necessary in these days than in those past? Or does a sacrifice to Moloch <note>An ancient Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice; the author is suggesting that current medical ignorance is a form of human sacrifice.</note> please you? Do you wish the lives of the poor, the widows, and the orphans to be consecrated to you under the most wretched torture and despair of incurable diseases? Why, then, do you not cease to destroy so many families through the uncertainty and ignorance of those who heal?" I fell on my face and said: "Lord, forgive me if my love for my neighbor has swept me beyond my limits. Pardon, pardon, Lord, my indiscreet charity; for you are the radical good of goodness itself. You know my sighs, and that I confess I am nothing, I know nothing, I am worth nothing, I can do nothing, and I have nothing. I am needy, naked, empty, and void. Give, Lord, give knowledge to your creature, so that he may intimately know your creation—himself first, then the other things besides himself, on account of your mandate of Charity—and at last, 

<margin>19.</margin> in you, find all things, and above all things."

<column-break/>

When I had prayed intensely out of great weariness and exhaustion of soul, I was by chance led into a dream, and I saw the whole universe in the presence of truth as if it were some formless chaos, which was almost mere nothingness. And from there I drew the concept of a single word, which signified to me the following: *Behold, you and what you see are nothing. Whatever you strive for is less than nothing itself in the sight of the Most High. He knows all the ends of things to be done; you, at least, should attend to your own salvation.* Indeed, within that concept was an internal command that I should become a Physician, and that one day "Raphael" <note>The Archangel Raphael, whose name in Hebrew means "God heals."</note> himself would be given to me. Immediately thereafter, and for thirty full years following, I labored through the nights in order, at my own expense and to the detriment of my life, so that I might acquire a knowledge of the natures and properties of vegetables and minerals. Meanwhile, I lived not without prayer, reading, the scrutiny of things, the weighing of my errors, and the recording of my daily experiences. At last, I recognized with Solomon <note>A reference to the Book of Ecclesiastes, attributed to King Solomon, which stresses the vanity of human knowledge.</note> that I had mostly twisted my spirit in vain until then, and that the knowledge of all things under the sun is empty, as are the vain investigations of curiosity. And he whom the Lord Jesus has called to wisdom—he, and no other—is the one who shall come to it. Indeed, he who reaches the summit will still be able to do very little unless the kind favor of the Lord shines upon him. Behold, thus I grew up, became a man, and now also an old man—useless, and ungrateful to God, to whom belongs all honor.

## THE HUNT FOR THE SCIENCES,
### BEGINS FROM "KNOW THYSELF."

<margin>1.</margin> Reason <note>original: "Ratio"</note> is thought to be the life of the soul, or the very life of our life. However, I believe that the Almighty alone is the way, the truth, the life, and the light of the living and of all things; but Reason is not this. And therefore, our mind ought to be *Intellectual* <note>The author distinguishes between "Reason" (logical, step-by-step thinking) and "Intellect" (direct, intuitive spiritual perception).</note>, not *rational*, if it is to reflect the closest likeness of God. This paradox must be elucidated for the investigation of all things knowable, and especially for those who have achieved mastery <note>original: "Adeptorum"</note>. In my view, all Philosophy begins and proceeds from the knowledge of oneself—whether it be natural philosophy or moral philosophy. Therefore, I shall set forth the Intellect and the hidden knowledge of ourselves, so far as I can reach with my meager ability. For the undisputed opinion of the Schools <note>The academic establishment of the time.</note> holds that God has bestowed nothing more precious upon man than Reason, <margin>2.</margin> by which alone we are distinguished from the beasts,

<column-break/>

while we share a common nature with the Angels. I, too, was persuaded and believed this from my tender years. But after my judgment had matured and I had once gazed into my own soul, I felt entirely otherwise. Meanwhile, I confess that I prefer to be wise in secret rather than to wish to seem wise; I have always been more eager to learn than striving to teach. Nevertheless, I was obliged to teach certain things, lest I be found to have buried the talent I received. <margin>3.</margin> For this reason, Reason once showed herself to my soul in a certain vision, in the form of a thick and dark mist. She proposed that she was the nurse, the guide, and the protector of the mind, so ordained by God for the attainment of every good, even solid good. Indeed, she protested that she was the helm of the life-course, the prow and the stern of the mind, and thus the inventor of all sciences. At first glance, the soul welcomed Reason with gratitude and desired her to rest within itself, with pleasure, in joy and jubilation. For the mind had once so persuaded itself, having been so taught. <margin>4.</margin> Yet soon, lest it sin through the lightness of its belief, the soul began to challenge Reason with its own weapons, saying: "If, therefore, you, Reason, are destined for my service, it is not I who should follow you, but you who should follow me. After all, you affirm or demonstrate nothing through discourse that I have not first instilled in you. In what way, then, do you—now a disciple—claim guardianship over your mistress, a daughter over her parent?" This first argument, born of my own arrogance, taught me that nothing is closer to the soul than pride; yet the soul covered this haughtiness, arising from disobedience, with the cloak of virtue, so that it might not be led away by credulity. Reason, however, replied—not indeed directly, but only so as to generate fear in the mind, and thus by way of scruples, draw the mind into its own wishes. It said, naturally, that no salvation of the soul is acquired without reason; <margin>5.</margin> that mortals would surely perish under the allurements of the senses unless vices were restrained by the reins of Reason. To which the mind, filled with indignation, said: "Begone! None of these things come from you or through you; the knowledge and execution of these things come from faith..."

...reason, <note>original: "rationem," completing the word from the previous page</note> out of mercy, I suspect. On the contrary, **Faith** commands that for its own sake, we desert you. For your flexible imposture has birthed a hundred divisions and cracks in faith, even among the most refined men. Moreover, every such division has its own "rational" introduction of sophistry. For **Reason** produces nothing on either side but **opinion** <note>original: "putationem," referring to mere human supposition as opposed to certain knowledge</note>, in place of faith. Faith, however, comes from grace; it is not from you, you deceitful thing. You delude all the most sagacious men who trust in you, and miserably lead them away to a pit of miseries. Finally, my mind considered, through faith, that there was only one unique form and essence of truth, and that every **intellect** was always and only concerned with what is **true**. <margin>6.</margin> Wherefore, in this choice, my mind is determined to prize the **Intellect** above **Reason**. Therefore it began to fear lest Reason—which craftily deceives so many myriads of men under the appearance of piety, truth, and Religion, through a multiplicity of errors—might seduce the mind itself like a gentle flatterer and a clever seductress. <margin>7.</margin> The mind therefore suspected that Reason would not only fashion persuasions for the sake of fallacy and its own advancement whenever the mind chose it as a Judge or Assistant, but also that Reason would plainly give itself over to the service and flattery of desires, even those of the most religious men; and that it would bring with it more opinion, rashness, and stupidity than science and truth. Indeed, Reason is easily swayed by tongues, wavering now to one extreme and now to the other; it would find, fashion, and spread out "reasons" everywhere according to the whims of desires. Nay, not rarely does it proceed by reasoning until it falls outside the bounds of what is reasonable, remaining indefinitely indistinct and uncertain in the very ignorance it promised to unravel. Frequently, too, Reason has driven souls mad when, <margin>8.</margin> trusting too much in its persuasions, they surrendered themselves to it. To others, finally, it has cut the thread of life through tasteless, troublesome, indiscreet, and fruitless anxieties. The mind therefore conceived a weariness toward the Empire of Reason, and even more so

<column-break/>

because it knew Reason was a domestic servant of its own household <note>A reference to the faculties of the soul acting as "servants" to the higher mind.</note>, yet this handmaid presumed to take over the entire dominion of the soul. <margin>8.</margin> And the mind, remembering the divine word, *that a man’s enemies are those of his own household* <note>A citation of Matthew 10:36, here applied metaphorically to the internal faculties of the man.</note>, conceived a loathing for Reason. And although this aversion on both sides was not yet sufficiently established, it nevertheless *gathered strength as it went*. From then on, the soul began to contemplate Reason no longer as a part or power of itself, but as a foreign guest, plainly severed from the being of the mind and neutral to it. This occurred after the soul knew, through faith, that once it was separated from the body, it would no longer have need of reason; <margin>9.</margin> that reason was therefore frail and mortal; and indeed, that it had come to us along with death, in the <margin>10.</margin> **corruption of nature** <note>This refers to the "Fall of Man" in Genesis, suggesting that discursive reasoning is a result of original sin.</note>. For the mind knows that after death, it will possess all its knowledge simultaneously: full, naked, not successive <term>successive|Step-by-step or logical progression from one thought to the next</term>, not extorted by the force of premises, not conquered, not deceptive, debatable, or doubtful. Nor will the mind, after death, make "demonstrations" so as to conclude, drag, force, deduce, or reflect one thing from another, whether that be for the purpose of conceiving or notifying. Therefore, the mind seized <margin>11.</margin> this frail Reason—which is a fugitive from the soul—by its cloak, and stripped it of every garment even unto nakedness. And then it was confirmed to the mind that Reason had been left to us as a **stigma** from the torturer, to serve as a memory of our calamities and our fall. And that the **knowledge of good and evil**, acquired by the eating of the apple, was this very Reason itself, so greatly adored by mortals. From then on, the mind strove to withdraw, not indeed against, but away from the <margin>12.</margin> **use of Reason**: namely, by abstaining from all discourse <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to the process of logical reasoning (discursive thought) rather than speech.</note> in the contemplation of a thing as it is—good, true, and existing in act. However, I could not obtain this immediately, because Reason continually followed the unwilling soul like a shadow follows a body; it arrived unbidden in the council of the mind by right of old possession and because the gates of our council were not sufficiently guarded. And under this title, the presence of Reason was thereafter even more burdensome, sadder, more wearisome, and cloudier to me.

<margin>22.</margin> Because of this, I soon observed that the discourse of **Reason** thins out, overshadows, hampers, and suffocates that noble act of understanding by which the sciences of the premises, implanted within us, are known. It exists, I say, more to weary the soul that follows it and to cover the skull with gray hairs, than to produce within us a true knowledge of the truth. 

<margin>23.</margin> For I found that the soul, wishing to know through the "hunt" of **Reason**, for the most part embraces half-lies and false satisfactions in place of truth as the reward for its labor. For thus the deceived mind gazes upon lies, disguises, fraud, and in short, mere supposition, in the place of truth, so long as it does not yet doubt the impostures of **Reason**. For thus far it has happened that there are so many impostures and false doctrines, both in Religion and in the art of medicine, that I cannot survey any corner of the Schools where truth has not been overturned by the brooms of **Reason**. 

<margin>24.</margin> Thus I saw **Reason** naked,

<column-break/>

and I learned that in every instance **Reason** brings forth nothing but a "supposition of truth," by which means it buries the intellectual intellect. This is because the mind cannot simultaneously embrace and follow two lights that are so different. By such suppositions, however, the wretched world is everywhere led away and deluded. And first of all, [the world is deluded] because everyone thinks **Reason** is the **Image of God** <note>original: "Iconem Dei"</note> and our greatest treasure, etc. Please! Let **Reason** be sought on a doubtful question by ten wise men, separately; and notice how much they differ from one another, how each is deluded by his own **Reason**, and how each fights strenuously for his own supposition. Truly, when my mind stripped **Reason** of its clothing, I observed that the world is deceived primarily by its own supposition: that it calls the investigation of the knowledge of things through their causes the "inquiry" or "discovery" of **Reason**. 

<margin>25.</margin> In this, I first detected the disguise and the most miserable condition and impoverished nakedness of **Reason**; indeed, it is ashamed to appear except under the cover of a false <term>etymology</term> <note>original: "Etymi," referring to the naming or definition of a concept</note> and a borrowed cloak. For **Reason** is in no way the cause, part, or essence of the thing caused; much less does the Rational faculty in man actually "touch" things. For a thing is that which it is in itself, without any reflection upon it by human **Reasoning** or discovery. Let the outer garment of **Reason**, therefore, be a mask. A cause, to be sure, is the beginning and origin of the thing caused. **Reason**, however, is nothing of the sort. Finally, I noticed that the Schools give **Reason** a place in the middle of the essence of the mind, and from this they name the soul "rational" as if it were an essential property—as if **Reason** were given to the soul as a lamp in its innermost essence. Whereas, in truth, in the mind (which is the closest image of God), there is no place for reason. This is because the soul, when separated from the body, does not use the discourse of **Reason**. Indeed, even when the soul, still an inhabitant of the body, understands anything intellectually, it plainly refuses all use of **Reason**. For when it uses **Reason**, it clearly tastes of its corporeal foundation.

<margin>27.</margin> Soon after, as **Reason** was stripped bare, a similarly trivial shroud immediately presented itself, born from the mere opinion of reason. This opinion holds that whatever is related to the truth, **Reason** judges to be "Reasonable" and consistent with **Reason**. Yet, **Reason** and truth are distinct at their very roots. For truth is a <term>real being</term> <note>original: "ens reale," meaning something that exists in reality</note>, a true thing; but **Reason** is a <term>mental being</term> <note>original: "ens mentale," an object that exists only in the mind</note>, problematic and merely apparent. Hence, the "being of **Reason**" is actually a "Non-being," born from opinion as its mother. For the rational faculty, and the **Reason** derived from it, often embraces falsehoods as truths, and laughs at truths

<margin>28.</margin> as if they were false. From this, I finally observed in earnest that **Reason** does not align with the conformity of the thing proposed through <term>discourse</term> <note>the step-by-step process of logical argument</note>, nor with the knowledge of the conclusion we find. Indeed, **Reason** is not properly a judgment of the external man or of his imagination, by which he rubs his perceived truth against the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species scientiarum," the mental forms or categories of knowledge</note> of the sciences which people believe are innate to man. Thus, a straying imagination first constructs a knowledge

<margin>29.</margin> that is agreeable to itself. But **Reason**—that steward in the mind held in such high regard—is nothing other than the relationship of that aforementioned conformity (found through discourse) with the innate forms or ideas in the <term>phantasia</term> <note>the faculty of imagination or mental representation</note>. This conformity, because it is inherently confused, obscure, and shifting, must necessarily be unstable due to the nature of the subject it inhabits. In this way, even the most refined **Reason** can be deceptive within itself; nor is it necessary that it compel, contain, or

<margin>30.</margin> conclude any certainty within itself—except for **Mathematics** <note>original: "Mathesi"</note>. This is because **Mathematics** consists plainly in the measures of things that can be measured. This is why more heretics are converted by the example of a Christian life than by the reasoning of debates. Finally, the fitness of that relationship to the innate forms in the imagination may be called rationality or reasonableness.

<margin>31.</margin> Reasoning, however, or <term>logic</term> <note>original: "logismus," from which "syllogism" is derived</note>, is the act by which the conformity of such a 

<column-break/>

relationship is brought close to the forms born in the imagination, or (as my opinion holds) finally awakened. By "taking off the shoes of reason" <note>An allusion to Moses at the burning bush; a metaphor for setting aside worldly logic to perceive the divine or natural truth directly</note>, I found many things in nature which the intellect judges to be necessary, but which **Reason** rejects as impossible.

<margin>32.</margin> From then on, I knew that **Reason** does not dwell within the true intellect, but outside of it. This is because truth is formed immediately in the intellect; for truth understood is nothing other than the <term>adequation</term> <note>original: "adaequatio," the perfect correspondence or "leveling" of the mind to the object it perceives</note> of the intellect to the things themselves. The intellect knows things as they are; therefore, in turn, the intellect is verified by the things themselves, through the things themselves. Since the being of things is, in itself, always true, and their essence is truth itself, the intellect that is carried above them is always directly true.

<margin>33.</margin> But since the imagination, or its **Reason**, is a certain oblique way of understanding—proceeding through arguments and discourse rather than through the transformation of "adequation"—this rational mode is therefore a deceptive and abusive form of intellect. However, the good, the right, the one, and the true always hold themselves in one and the same way in the intellect, because in the intellect they stand at the point of "adequation." But the evil, the crooked, the oblique, the false, and the manifold are created in many ways through **Reason** in the imaginative part of the soul.

<margin>34.</margin> I have thus come to know for certain that **Reason** should not be held in such high esteem as it has been until now. Furthermore, **Reason** and discourse flourish quite clearly even in brute animals. For it happens that an old fox is more cunning than a younger one through a rational discourse confirmed by the memory of experience. Indeed, bees count. If there are thirty hives arranged in order, a little bee flying out in the morning counts from which hive she departed; then she does not return or enter until she first recounts the order. ...they return to the numbered hive: whose citizens, although they are strangers, kill that arriving little bee. In this way, thieves destroy all the hives in a single night. For the serpent was more cunning than the rest of the living creatures. With a single example, which stands for a thousand, I will demonstrate the nature of rational discourse in beasts. 

A neighboring farmer kept a hunting dog, which was put in charge of the nightly guarding of the estate. It happened that during a full moon, a wolf was prowling around the farmhouse; the dog immediately barked at it and pursued the fleeing wolf. The wolf, however, driven by hunger, turned back toward the dog and began to chase it. But the dog, fleeing and leaping over a <term>dark thicket</term> <note>original: "furvum." This likely refers to a dark patch of brush or a specific farm structure used for concealment</note>, retreated to safety. From there, it barked continuously, waking its master and alerting him to the wolf's presence. 

The following day the wolf returned, and the dog attacked it by barking, just as it had the day before. This time, the wolf feigned flight until it knew by calculation that its companion, a wolf it had brought along, had hidden itself beneath the dark thicket. When the first wolf turned back toward the dog, the dog fled from the pursuing wolf, thinking it could retreat to the thicket as if to a most secure fortress. But the other hidden wolf leaped out, caught the dog in its jaws, and prevented its leap over the thicket. Thus, I have noted remarkable cleverness in all brutes, even in many insects. 

<margin>35.</margin> Therefore, I consider it a contemptible definition by which man is depicted as a <term>rational animal</term> <note>original: "animal rationale," the standard definition of man in Aristotelian philosophy</note>, as if this were a description of his essence. If the "end" or purpose is the first of all causes, according to Aristotle, then man should have been defined by his ultimate purpose and the specific properties intended for him in creation. Therefore, the definition of man should not have been begged from the fountain of paganism, which was entirely ignorant of creation and its purposes. Indeed, just as my philosophy is unknown to the heathens, so in turn theirs is worth nothing to me. For I write for Christians, for whom it is shameful to follow pagans against the truth of the Gospel. Nor do I wish to be considered a brawler over names, as often happens when discussing the purposes, prerogatives, choice, and dignity of the **Divine Image**. Above all, I reject the follies

<column-break/>

of paganism perpetrated in definitions, especially that of man. Indeed, by the testimony of St. Anthony, as described by the Blessed Jerome, Paul the First Hermit was recorded among the number of the saints. In that same account, we read of a <term>Faun</term> <note>a mythological creature, usually half-man and half-goat</note> as a speaking, rational animal: indeed, one recognizing the God of nature and of the Christians, worshipping Him, and entreating Anthony to pray to God for him and his kind. 

It is clear, first of all, that this Faun was not a human, based on Anthony’s assertion and its monstrous shape. Finally, it is gathered that it was not an <term>evil demon</term> <note>original: "Cacodæmonem"</note>; for a demon is so proud that it would not even know it could be saved by prayer, nor would it wish to ask anyone to pray for it, nor prostrate itself to seek pardon. For the Blessed Jerome calls the Faun neither a man nor an evil demon. The Faun is therefore neither of these, by the same witness through whom that famous Paul obtained the first place among the Hermits and was recorded among the Saints. Therefore, a Faun is an animal using reason, speaking a native language, but it is not a human. 

The same was true of a <term>Satyr</term> <note>another half-human, half-animal spirit of the woods</note> long ago, which was seen alive and then preserved in salt and shown for money, carried through Egypt, Phrygia, and Greece. Finally, in Scotland, Zeeland, and elsewhere, monsters have been fished up with semi-human figures, using reason, and even practicing mechanical arts. 

Doubtless, man alone was made in the **image of God**, to the exclusion of all others. These "rational brutes" in their own elements are also different from one another: they are, however, mere <term>simulacra</term> <note>shadowy likenesses or imitations</note> of us, and not images of God. 

<margin>36.</margin> Man, therefore, is a living creature in a body, through an immortal soul, for the honor of God, sealed according to the light and in the image of the **Word** <note>original: "verbi," referring to the Logos or Christ</note>, the first model of all causes. For the day and its light once existed without the Sun, and the Sun will one day be without light. But the soul of man cannot be considered without the divine image, while the Kingdom of God, with all its spiritual gifts, is more intimate to the soul than the soul is to itself. Therefore, I am rightly indignant that the Schools follow the philosophy of the heathens...

...pagan teachings, they badly imbue the youth, and they even now delight in acorns <note>A metaphor for crude, primitive knowledge versus refined "bread"</note>, though the feasts of primary truth have already been found. *Lord, the light of your countenance is impressed upon us* <note>original: "Domine lumen vultus tui, impressum est super nos." A reference to Psalm 4:6</note>. For no one perfectly knows an image, nor whether it responds well to its archetype, if he has not first recognized that archetype. Therefore, as many as define man poorly do not recognize God, nor do they recognize themselves in their essential <margin>37.</margin> qualities. Thus, the Philosophical Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic tradition of universities based on Aristotelian logic</note> have rested more on the teachings of the Pagans than on the teachings of Paul. Hence I observe that those Schools have meditated on man only according to his corpse; they have not considered him according to the intention of the Creator, or the "efficient cause," nor according to man's final destinations. Otherwise, the Almighty would have fallen short of His target, if the "end" is the first of all causes in the act of creating, and if there is anything to be considered as "first" in the adorable Author of all things. Therefore, a creature ought to be defined by the intention of the efficient Creator. For He does not err in His ends, He who fashions the very properties that flow from the goals of those destinations. Wherefore man, although from his body he possesses certain animal and corporeal conditions, nevertheless, by divine intention, he was created as a living image of God in an immortal substance. He was made so that he might know, love, and adore God, according to the light of the archetype impressed upon him. But after man lived in the flesh as an animal, God said: *My Spirit shall not remain with man, because he is flesh* <note>original: "Spiritus meus non permanebit cum homine, quia caro est." Reference to Genesis 6:3</note>. <margin>38.</margin> For that very "genus" <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category, like "animal"</note> belonging to the thing being defined in the definition of man—which the Schools call "animal"—is the very thing God calls a degeneration, a turning away of ways, a corruption of nature, and the destruction of His intention in creating. Moreover, it is beyond doubt that the "constitutive difference" <note>The specific trait that distinguishes a species from others in its genus</note> of man, or "rationality," also belongs to the beasts. At the same time, there is a poverty of logic in any definition entirely destitute of a true constitutive difference. Furthermore, Reason having now been stripped even unto its nakedness, I acquired a complete distaste for it, because it seemed to me a hollow skeleton once the masks and <margin>39.</margin> robes were removed. Finally, I beheld its narrow poverty and

<column-break/>

restless foulness, while I was especially mindful of the confusions and uncertainties with which it had habitually entangled me. I began therefore hereafter to observe that my intellect profited more through figures, images, and dreamlike visions of the <margin>40.</margin> imagination than through the discourses of Reason. Nay rather, frequent discourses ordinarily render a man morose, wrathful, mindless, stormy in his judgment, and unstable or weak, and thus also of delicate health. But at last I looked more deeply into the progress of figures and ideas: and I found then that they were still girded with miseries and anxieties. This was because the images were alienated (on account of their "otherness" from the truth of the thing itself, and because of the inexcusable deformity of every likeness that is removed from actual identity). And then I judged thus, because the distinction between images of the Imagination and intellectual images had not yet become known to me—those images which, after abstractions, remain in the very center of the soul. <margin>41.</margin> For I used to be weary most of the day concerning some knowable thing; and even if its basis and manner were unknown to me, I resolved that it was to be extracted by me through images. At last, when I felt myself hindered from proceeding further because I was benumbed, I fashioned within me some image of the thing not yet perfectly known, adorned with a possible proximity to its <term>quiddity</term> <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note>. Under which image, after looking at it in my imagination for a long time <margin>42.</margin> and as if speaking to it, I finally fell asleep, being remarkably exhausted by study. I did this so that I might excite at least a dream-vision of the thing, through which I might extract that desirable knowledge. According to the saying: *Night unto night shows knowledge* <note>original: "Nox nocti indicat scientiam." Reference to Psalm 19:2</note>. And it is truly a wonder how much light such visions opened to me, especially when the body had not been recently fed. For I do not deny that I have many times acquired the <term>quiddities</term> of the sought-after thing by this means of "knocking"—though they were usually covered under the cloak of a riddle, or confused, and for the most part still subject to pluralities and othernesses—provided that a period of seeking had come before.

He claims that true intellectual progress comes not from logical reasoning, which he finds exhausting and hollow, but through imaginative "dream-visions" and intellectual images centered in the soul.</summary>

...with aids and attached supports of prayer and others. And a holy man said to me (to whom I had opened every corner of my conscience, and the weariness of my labors and years through sleepless nights), *“Ah! Would that I had labored as much, and spent as much in loving God, as you, wretched man, have in the investigation of things to be known—of which the last day will not demand an account or reckoning from you!”* Indeed, I praised the Lord then, because He had freely granted me some closer means of knowing and learning than Reason would be—for Reason never penetrates to the prior <note>The "prior" refers to the first cause or origin of a thing</note>, and only rarely to the posterior <note>The "posterior" refers to the secondary effects or results</note>, and even then with much uncertainty. For I believed then that the original misery of our corrupt nature could not progress any further toward the light, once it had been tasted, than through the aforementioned images of the Phantasy <note>In the psychology of this era, the "Phantasy" or imagination was the faculty that created mental images from sensory data</note>.

<margin>43.</margin> Therefore, by the persuasion of that man, I ceased to desire, seek, or investigate anything more narrowly; I stripped myself of all curiosity and appetite for knowing. I withdrew myself to rest, or “poverty of spirit,” resigning myself to the most lovable will of God, into a state of almost not being, not acting, into a mere state of desiring nothing and understanding nothing. This was especially because I knew the manifold imperfections in my cognitions, feeling a deep indignation toward myself for having spent so many and such great labors for the sake of fleeting science. Thus, I was wonderfully displeased with myself; I asked the Lord that He would sweep entirely out of my mind every knowable thing and its profane desires. Under this title, I often offered my whole mind to His good pleasure. Meanwhile, after two months in this renunciation of the sciences and naked poverty, it once happened to me again,

<margin>44.</margin> that I understood with the intellect. I was sitting beside my Athanor <term>Athanor: A self-feeding furnace used by alchemists and chemists, designed to maintain a steady heat over long periods for chemical transformations</term>. However, I soon returned to myself, and I did not know how long that light had lasted. I knew only this: that the novelty of the unusual thing, the wonder, and the joy then snatched away that light, and caused me to fall back into my former confusions of darkness, because Reason had not yet been mortified <note>In mystical writing, "mortified" means to subdue the ego or the rational mind so it no longer interferes with divine experience</note>.

<column-break/>

Aristotle, although entirely devoid of this light, nevertheless seemed to have described from elsewhere another man's sensation concerning the labor of Sophia <note>Wisdom</note>, or the Adepts <note>Those who have attained the "Great Work" or ultimate knowledge, usually in an alchemical context</note>. *“It is better to be ignorant than to know by a mere inscription”* <note>original Greek: "Βέλτιον ἀγνοεῖν ἢ ἐν ἐπιγραφῇ εἰδώς."</note>. By the silent suggestion of another, no doubt, he calls those better disposed than if they were “knowers”—that is, by means of logical demonstration, by which means alone he otherwise always boasts that all science in man arises. At least I recognized that I must bid farewell to Reason and Imagination, as though they were animal faculties (and this because of the misery of our Fall), if we are to be drawn by hope into the depths toward the solid knowledge of truth.

<margin>45.</margin> I knew likewise that what was required was a smooth transition of the intellect, and a peaceful transmutation of itself into the form of the thing to be understood; at which point, namely, the intellect for a moment becomes as if it were the understood thing itself. Since, however, the intellect is perfected by understanding, and nothing is perfected except by that which shares a common bond <note>original: "symbolum"</note> with it in its nature, I therefore concluded that the intellect and the things understood, as such, must be—or become—of the same nature. This must happen without labor or restlessness, but with leisure, in its own proper light, with abstraction, prayer, and the absence of any other created help. But if some outside help intervenes, it will then be with the labor of an aroused desire, outside the intellect. Furthermore, the Poets, who are sometimes subservient to this truth, signify this transmigration and transfiguration of the intellect (which is otherwise natural to it) by the name of Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology, here used as a metaphor for the mind's ability to take the shape of the things it understands</note>, though in the form of a fable. I, however, now knew even more clearly that this transmutation of the intellect must occur because the intellect in itself is entirely pure, simple, unique, and undivided.

<margin>46.</margin> For this reason, it would also possess a single, simple, uniform, and unambiguous act, which is plainly undivided from the intellect itself. Otherwise, the intellect would lose the homogeneous simplicity of its unity through the duality of “otherness.” Nevertheless, I have found sufficiently that it is not within the full and free power of our will...

...[by the] power [of this light], to thus enjoy one's own intellect now. And as for this, more is required than merely thinking, striving, hoping, or wishing. This is not only because of the lack of habit—since from childhood we have continually become accustomed to obeying the imagination through animal acts—but much more because the will itself, along with the Memory, must be entirely absorbed during that moment of movement, and as it were annihilated within the intellect. This is indeed a mystery of immense weight.

<margin>47.</margin> For otherwise, as soon as someone thinks about his own soul, or about any thing, as if it were a "third" thing—with a sense of "otherness" <note>The author uses "alteritas" (otherness) to describe the feeling that the thinker and the object of thought are separate. He argues true understanding requires this gap to be closed.</note> or separation outside the intellect—by that very fact, it is not yet the thought <margin>48.</margin> or operation of the pure and solitary intellect. 

But when the soul thinks of itself, or of anything else, as if it were itself—without the "otherness" of the thinker and the thing thought, and without attachment, outward-turning, or relation to duration, place, and circumstances—then, indeed, such a thought is truly intellectual. Yet even then, it is not necessarily "illuminated," although this intellection is a far nobler form of thought than that which rushes in through chance occurrences. This is true whether those thoughts arrive through images without any logical sequence (as if they were poured in), or whether they are drawn from experiences and observations, flowing in as if by their own accord. 

Since the soul, in that state of light, apprehends the inner and prior essence of the thing understood, the intellect itself, by a kind of migration, transforms itself into the very thing it understands. From this, it evidently follows: If intellectual knowledge consists of the "likeness" of the thing understood being within the intellect itself, then the Kingdom of God <note>original: "Regnum Dei"</note> comes to us and is reborn whenever we adore God’s Goodness, Power, Infinity, Glory, and Truth in spirit—doing so intellectually and through a sense of His "presence" in faith. In this way, it is a delight for God to be with the children of men. 

Certainly it is so. Our intellect is drenched, as if with a new dew of perfection, whenever it intellectually contemplates something super-heavenly: because for a moment, it migrates into that thing and tastes it. <margin>49.</margin> Then, truly, there flashes within 

<column-break/>

the image of God <note>original: "imago Dei"</note>, and it becomes glorious. (Good God, how far you lead mortals!) 

But truly, let not such intellectual thought be confused with the use of specific words or languages; nor with the constraints of the senses or of Reason; nor with some swift concept of a whole logical argument <term>logismus</term><note>A technical term for a logical syllogism or a calculated chain of reasoning.</note> gathered up all at once; nor with a dependence on a sequence of things previously thought; nor hedged about by circumstances of "here," "now," "white," "big," "bitter," "similar," "peaceful," and so on. In the pure intellect, one thing does not exist without the other; nor does it exist with the other under a sense of "otherness." It cannot even be conceived through Reason or imagination, nor thought of through mental images or "ideas." 

Rather, in that state—right here and right now—the senses, Reason, imagination, memory, and will are all melted together into the pure intellect. They stand in a kind of darkness, obscured by the superior light of the intellect. Then—then, I say—a certain light falls upon the Soul. And that is (in my judgment) everything that could ever be expressed by word, thought, speech, or writing. 

Whether that light is altogether supernatural, or whether the intellect is ignited this way by its own nature, I would rather experience than try to define. This one thing at least I know: it does not happen without grace. Therefore, whether the intellect is transformed, or whether it transforms itself into the likeness of the thing understood, it surely has need of divine help—<margin>50.</margin> and indeed, singular help. For then the Soul gazes upon its own intellect under the form it has seized within that light. In that "mirror" of itself, it beholds itself intellectually, without the reflection of "otherness." Thus it conceives the knowable thing, together with all its being and properties. Because this light of knowledge does not flow out away from the intellect; instead, it remains reflected within, upon the intellect, perfecting it in all truth and perfect certainty. 

Indeed, some <margin>51.</margin> Rabbis <note>The author likely refers to Jewish mystical traditions (Kabbalah) which he frequently studied and cited, sometimes with caution.</note> fear this state of the soul as dangerous. The mystical School <note>Likely referring to the tradition of "Rhineland Mystics" like Tauler or Ruusbroec, who wrote about the soul's union with God.</note> also dreads the danger of arrogance and "spiritual adultery." Both, however, [avoid it] as harmful...

[The Adepts] avoid [this state]. They think that if it were to strike too often, or persist too long, it would bring certain death, along with a sickness that the Rabbis call *Binsica* <note>original: "Binsica Rabbini vocant" — Likely referring to the Hebrew *Neshiqah*, the "Kiss of Death," an ecstatic death where the soul leaves the body to unite with God.</note>. This is properly an atrophy of the imagination <note>original: "Phantasiæ Atrophia"</note>. However, I pray they pardon me if I feel differently. First, because the organs of the imagination do not labor in this; they sleep motionless, as if they did not exist. Therefore, they suffer nothing in return. Furthermore, this act is not in our power: for I believe that primary act belongs to Mercy <note>original: "Clementia" — often used here to mean Divine Grace or the kindness of God.</note>. Mercy never gives, performs, causes, or admits anything disordered. Thus, even if Mercy were to flow more frequently or longer, it would not contain or imply any disorder. I pray, therefore, that the Father of Lights <note>original: "Pater luminum" — a title for God from the Epistle of James 1:17.</note> may deign to go before and follow me with His clarity, to lead me to a calling in His grace that is pleasing to Him. And so this light, falling from above upon the soul (at a time when the soul is less bound and restricted by the organs of the body, and is in itself impassible and immortal), cannot harm life. Indeed, after receiving such a small amount of light, I find that a man can endure a three-day fast with hardly any suffering. Because of this, it occurs to me that the friends who accompanied Job could have remained by him without food or drink for a full nine days. Furthermore, in my opinion, this light—without the help, effort, or labor of the understanding—so disposes the intellect that it enters into its own freedom; otherwise, through the servitude of the body, the intellect is entirely unstable, dark, and confused. In other respects, the intellect does not use physical organs beyond or outside itself. Therefore, it is neither fatigued like the imagination <note>original: "Phantasia"</note>, nor is it subject to diseases, changes, disturbances, alterations, alienations, or mixtures from 
<margin>52.</margin>
within itself. For no error, imposture, lie, or deceit falls into the intellect while it stands in that light. Neither do lethargy, sleep, or defect dwell within it; nor does it look for help from any created thing, such as the body, Reason, or any power of the imagination; but it carries its 

<column-break/>

native light above the entire scope of Reason. Indeed, what is more, the intellect is not provoked then by any power lower than itself, nor by things themselves as they are known—which are liable to fraud, imposture, and lies. For things stand in the nakedness of their own being before the intellect, as if to be shaped by it and given life through transmigration. Thus, all things are in their own intellect in such a way that all things are the soul's own intellect. Yet, even so, although the intellect—through the intellectual act—transforms itself into the form <note>original: "speciem" — the "species" or mental image of a thing.</note> of the thing understood, it nevertheless preserves its own unmixed property and essence, to which it returns as soon as it ceases from that act. The soul possesses this prerogative by Mercy, that it may be the Image of God <note>original: "imago Dei"</note>: and therefore, it is a simple created light, unknown. Thus, whenever 
<margin>53.</margin>
it conceives something foreign within itself, it must necessarily cease from being the simplest light, the divine image, or transform itself into the shape of the thing conceived. This happens so that the essence of the thing conceived is a naked essence, yet essentially within the intellect—just as the apple tree is within the seed of the apple. It follows from this that intellectual knowledge is free from all error. This is because Reason, which causes us to stumble everywhere, is absent. In the intellectual concept, essences stand naked and stripped: the soul, in that moment, beholds them as such in the mirror of its own intellect, just as the eye beholds itself in a mirror through the reflected ray of itself. Therefore, nothing is considered true except 
<margin>54.</margin>
insofar as it is conceived as such in the intellect. For this reason, Aristotle was forced to admit that the principles of essence and the principles of the Intellect are exactly the same. That is to say: the truth of essence and the truth of intellectual knowledge are one and the same. And therefore, just as being (or existence), the true, the good, and the one are interchangeable; so in turn, essence, goodness, and truth must melt together in the unity of the intellect into the form of the mind. ...of the intellect and the thing understood: because before the act of understanding, every reciprocal relationship, repercussion, <margin>55.</margin> and reflection upon one another is first annihilated. For the intelligibility of a thing itself is nothing other than the arrival and approximation of the unity of the intellect and the understood—or rather, the destruction of "otherness" in the relationship. To make this clearer with an example: the understanding **intellect** is not different from the thing understood, any more than a direct ray of light is different from its own reflection. Thus, the essence of the thing understood, in the light of the intellect, becomes a spiritual and essential splendor. Indeed, through a migration toward unity, it becomes, in a way, the intellectual light itself. This is something that cannot happen to the souls of brute animals. <margin>56.</margin> Therefore, our soul, in understanding itself, in a way understands all other things as universals; they exist in an intellectual way in the soul, as in the image of God. For this reason, surely, the understanding of ourselves is by far the most difficult, the last, the best, and the most useful. For one who knows the divinity of the soul cannot help but prefer it to all fleeting, foul, and worthless pleasures. <margin>57.</margin> The difficulty of this aforementioned understanding consists primarily in the fact that the soul is the image of God; and this image, both in itself and regarding the archetype <note>original: "typi" — the original pattern or model (God) that the soul reflects.</note> it represents, is nearly impossible to grasp through understanding. Furthermore, since the soul does not possess within itself any image of itself that is distinct from itself, it is utterly unable to understand itself through "ideas." Since it is simple and uniform, it does not understand itself through an image; nor would it be harmonious or fitting that, because of the soul's supreme or uniform simplicity, it should use different modes and means of understanding when looking at itself versus the modes and means it uses for other understood things. Hence, out of necessity, to preserve its uniform simplicity—as is proper for the image of God—the soul must understand all other things without a <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie" — in scholastic philosophy, this refers to the mental form or representation of an object.</note> distinct from the things themselves. But since the soul lacks its own specific image of the divine likeness, so that it might

<column-break/>

transform itself intellectually into itself, it therefore cannot properly understand itself in an intellectual way, except in the light and faithful testimony of Him whose image it is. For the knowledge we have of God belongs to tradition, faith, and therefore to merit. Yet this knowledge is clearly "negative," in so far as God is not "this" or "that" which can be conceived by the senses or the mind. And consequently, the knowledge of the soul, as a divine image, carries with it a "negative abstraction" of other things, which it calls "non-being." Now, no concept, no figure, and no understanding corresponds to non-being. That is to say, since privation is the companion of negative abstraction, and since negative and privative things lack a corresponding idea or species, the light of knowledge that the soul has of itself is a gift of Mercy <note>original: "clementiæ" — Divine Grace.</note>; it is unearned, and never fully complete in this life. But if the fortunate soul should at some point conceive God within itself through the beatific vision <note>The direct perception of God enjoyed by the saved in heaven.</note>, then by that same ray of light, it will look upon and know God, itself, and all other things within. For this reason, the more the soul understands itself intellectually, the more it progresses in the most useful knowledge that can be had of created things in this life. Because in the light of its own light, it gazes, in a way, upon the properties, essences, effects, differences, distinctions, and defects of all things. Wherever this knowledge has once arrived, there all the cloudier speculation and assistance of **Reason** <note>The author distinguishes between *Intellectus* (direct spiritual intuition) and *Ratio* (discursive, logical reasoning).</note> withers away; just as, conversely, true intellect is suppressed within us under the decrees of Reason. <margin>58.</margin> Therefore, since the proper object of the intellect is the very essence of things, for that reason, "accidents" <note>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size.</note>—as if abstracted and severed from the things in which they exist—must be conceived by the imagination, and that through species and images; but by no means by the intellect. In the intellect, I find all accidents connected together at a single point, under the essence of the understood things. Indeed, accidents are not properly "beings" themselves, but belong to the beings upon which they depend. Therefore, accidents do not have an essence which moves toward the unity of the intellect...

<page-num>31</page-num>

<margin>59.</margin> ...the mind migrates, or into which the intellect transforms itself. Furthermore, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic philosophers, primarily those following the traditions of Aristotle in medieval universities.</note> divide the intellect into the **Active** and the **Passive**. For they want the **Active Intellect** <term>intellectus Agens: In Scholastic thought, the part of the mind that "acts" upon sensory data to create abstract concepts.</term> to be occupied with finding the means and premises of a demonstration; specifically, so that it may press the distinct marks of terms into the **Passive Intellect** <term>intellectus Patiens: The part of the mind that "suffers" or receives the impressions made by the active mind, like wax receiving a seal.</term>, as if into a layer of wax placed beneath it. They therefore call the Active "masculine," noble, and formal. But they liken the Passive to the "feminine" and to ignoble matter. They persuade their students of these dreams by arguing that nature everywhere works toward its own perfection, and that "acting" is always nobler than "suffering" <note>original: "passione" — here meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>. But I, for my part, pity such dryness everywhere. First, because a demonstration is not an effect or an offspring of the intellect, nor does it provide the means to the sciences in any way, as I have already sufficiently proven. Second, I once saw an Ethiopian quickly rotate a reed in a hole in a board with a piece of cloth placed between them; and not long after, the reed and the cloth caught fire. Then, I hid a reed in a glowing furnace, and the reed shone, ignited more quickly, more brightly, and more perfectly. Yet in this latter case, the reed did nothing; it merely "suffered" the ignition. To this extent, although the acting principle <margin>60.</margin> can sometimes be nobler than the passive one while the effect moves toward perfection—or while the passive subject must be perfected by the agent—nevertheless, while a union is "rotting" under a dungheap <note>A common alchemical and biological metaphor for transformation and generation through decay.</note>, I will not easily believe the agent is more perfect than the passive subject. I have shown enough elsewhere that in all of nature, Aristotle’s doctrine is empty and mere nonsense. How much less, then, would it hold up in the field of the intellect, whose being and operations depend solely upon the soul? For we Christians are compelled to believe that our intellect is an immortal spirit, a light, and the image of the Almighty. Just as its origin surpasses nature, so it cannot be fitted to nature's rules. Since it possesses the simplest kind of being, it is by no means divisible into the struggles of "active" and "passive," or into different parts. Since it also depends immediately, total-

<column-break/>

ly, and continually upon its original archetype <note>The "original type" refers to God, in whose image the soul is made.</note>, it follows that without a particular gift of Grace, it cannot understand anything at all. This is because the object of the intellect is Truth itself. Therefore, it does not understand with a perfect understanding except by receiving. But that which only receives is "passive"; it does not "act" within that process. For that which comes to the intellect through Grace is not the intellect’s own property. The Will, too, when it is passive—for instance, when it is ruled by the will of superiors—is nobler than when it acts of its own accord. Indeed, the **Imagination** <term>imaginativa: The faculty of the soul that forms mental images of physical things.</term> knows by acting, and for that reason, it grows weary. Aristotle knew this faculty, but he certainly did not know the intellect. For the intellect "suffers" or receives only by understanding through illumination. Indeed, it is more troublesome, more servile, and more obscure to work while understanding than to be passive. This is because by being passive, the intellect receives a nobler light, granted freely. Finally, since in the act of understanding it always migrates into the form of the thing understood, the intellect—participating in that infinite light—is perfected without the weariness, trouble, and labor of "thinking." The understood light shines within the very light of the intellect while understanding. Thus, things themselves seem to speak to us without words, and the intellect penetrates them even when they are closed, just as <margin>61.</margin> if they had been cut open and laid bare. Therefore, the intellect is always perfected by being passive and by receiving. But the **Imagination** (or the "animal intellect" known to Aristotle) only looks at things from the outside and forms images of them for itself according to its own opinion. With all the weariness of labor, it runs around them in circles. It sees, of <margin>62.</margin> course, the "bark" and the "husks," but it never reaches the "kernel." This is because the **Phantasy** <term>Phantasia: Another term for the imaginative faculty that processes sensory appearances.</term> does not enter the thing; nor, in turn, do things enter and satisfy the imagination. ...began supernaturally, and today they remain constantly the same as they were from the beginning. I understand, therefore, that the causes of natural things presuppose a cycle of change. And although the bodies of the Elements <note>The traditional four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> have come under the domain of nature, the study of them is irregular and foreign to true Philosophy. <margin>3.</margin> For those who before me believed that the four elements flowed together through mixing to create every single body, viewed the elements in a pagan manner; they attempted through their own fictions to make the elements "marry" and obey. Therefore, every natural body requires nothing other than corporeal beginnings, which are mostly subject to the change and succession of days. Nature, however, does not consist of an indefinite and impossible **hyle** <term>hyle: A Greek term used by Aristotle to describe "prime matter" that has no qualities of its own until "form" is added.</term>, nor does it have need of such a principle, nor of "privation" <note>Aristotle argued things change because they lack (privation) a certain form.</note>. Instead, order and life are present in the **efficient cause** <note>The agent or force that brings something into being.</note> by necessity. Every thing is empty, void, dead, and idle, unless it is established by a vital or seminal principle, or is eventually so established. Indeed, these laws of nature would collapse unless a specific order existed within things and intervened to bend private interests toward the sustenance of the common good or necessity. Aristotle dictated four causes that constitute things, but these made even their own Author ignorant of nature. For first, he confuses the "beginning" with the **material cause** <note>The "stuff" something is made of.</note>. Specifically, he calls the first cause "indefinite matter," or a sub-lying corporeal mass that stands in need of formal determination. Then he confuses the second cause—the internal essence or **form** of a thing—with the other of his principles. Finally, he calls the third (external) cause the "efficient," and names the fourth the **end** <note>Also known as the "final cause" or purpose for which a thing exists.</note>, toward which every thing is directed. <margin>4.</margin> He claimed this "end" was the first of the three prior causes in the mind of the efficient agent. Thus, he suggests natural things are not only begun by a "being of reason" <note>An abstract concept rather than a physical reality.</note>, but also that they lurk, as if lifeless, within the mind of the efficient cause through this "end." But if he investigates natural causes poorly, he does

<column-break/>

far worse when he substitutes a supernatural "end" in the mind of the **First Mover** <note>Aristotle’s term for God or the primary source of all motion.</note> for a natural cause, or requires a mental concept of a purpose in non-living things. <margin>5.</margin> Truly, I am not accustomed to serving the ears of others through the laziness of agreeing without weighing the facts; I have found the three latter causes in the knowledge of nature to be faulty—indeed, extremely harmful. As for the first of the four, I shall shortly show it to be a myth. For first, since every cause, according to nature and the succession of days, is prior to its effect, surely the "form" of a completed thing cannot be the *cause* of its production. Rather, it is the final **Entelechia** <term>Entelechia: A Greek term for the full realization or "completion" of a potential.</term> of generation, the very essence and perfection of the thing generated. All other things are directed toward its attainment. Therefore, I consider "form" to be an effect rather than a cause of a thing. <margin>6.</margin> Furthermore, since form is the goal of generation, it is not merely the act of generating, but the act of the thing already generated. It is a potential made possible during generation. However, matter (the subject of generation) exists in "actuality" just as its internal act is an internal agent, the efficient force, or the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: In this philosophy, the "Archeus" is the internal master-builder or vital spirit that directs the growth and life of a living thing from within.</term>. It is therefore false to say that the more "form" a thing has, the more it possesses of actuality, being, virtue, and operation. <margin>7.</margin> Because form is not acquired or possessed in parts or degrees, beings are not capable of having "more" or "less" of a form. Indeed, even if they were so capable, the activity of the agent does not belong to the form itself, but to the **Archeus**, of which I will speak soon. <margin>8.</margin> Form is therefore indivisible. For whatever Aristotle attributes to "form" or to the final perfection on the stage of things, actually belongs properly, directively, and executively to that agent, the seminal Archeus. <margin>9.</margin> Finally, since Aristotle’s efficient cause is "external" (just as he says a blacksmith is to the iron), I easily recognized that he traded his fictions for true foundations. His entire speculation wanders around artificial things and the external parts of nature. In truth, the entire efficient cause in nature is internal and essential. <margin>10.</margin> And although a father who generates a child is "effective," in the order...

The preceding plant of that seed is a remote cause, a natural occasion for the seed, which by itself and immediately builds and produces the plant with the help of a stimulus. Otherwise, if the parent herb were the efficient cause of the produced herb, the parent cause could not be burned without the produced herb perishing at the same time. Therefore, the seed is the internal, immediate efficient cause of the produced herb. For this reason, after a diligent investigation of all things, I have not found any dependence of a natural body, except strictly upon two internal causes: <margin>11.</margin> **matter** and the **efficient cause** (to which some external stimulating factor is usually joined). # CAUSES AND BEGINNINGS
## 36

Water, of course, is the beginning "from which" things are made; and **ferment** <term>Ferment: In this context, not just yeast, but a vital, creative principle or "spiritual enzyme" that gives form to matter.</term> is the seminal beginning "through which" they are made. That is, it is the disposing force from which **seed** <note>The Latin text frequently uses "femina" and "femine," which in this context and typography are archaic forms or printer variants for "semina" (seeds). I have translated them as "seed" for clarity.</note> is soon produced within matter. Once this **seed** is acquired, it becomes life itself—the "middle matter" of that being—running its course until the thing reaches its final period or ultimate state of matter. Now, **ferment** is a "formal" created being <note>A "formal" being is one that provides the "form" or essential nature to a thing, according to Aristotelian philosophy.</note>, which is neither a substance nor an accident. Instead, it is a neutral thing, much like light, fire, the *magnale* <term>Magnale: A term used by the physician-philosopher Paracelsus to describe a great, invisible power or atmospheric spirit.</term>, or "forms." It was established from the beginning of the world in the various regions of its dominion so that it might prepare, excite, and precede seeds. This is what we call **ferment in general**. Each of the things I am assuming here I will eventually demonstrate in its proper place. I will not deal with fables or non-existent things, but with principles and causes in relation to their goals, actions, and generations. I consider **ferments that truly and actually exist, and which are individually distinct by species.**
<margin>25.</margin> These **ferments** are therefore gifts and "roots" established by the Lord Creator until the end of time. They are durable and sufficient for continuous propagation, and they excite and create their own proper **seeds** from water. Surely, just as He gave the earth the power of germinating from itself, He gave as many **ferments** as there are types of fruits to be expected. Thus, even without the **seed** of a preceding plant, they can proliferate their own juices and fruits from water. Therefore, **ferments** bring forth their own **seeds**, and never those of another. That is, each acts according to its own nature and properties. As the Poet says: "Indeed, nature lies within the soil" <note>original: "solo natura subest"</note> and "Nor does every land bear all things" <note>original: "Nec omnis fert omnia tellus" — a quote from Virgil’s Georgics.</note>.
<margin>26.</margin> Indeed, there is a certain order placed in locations by divine will—a certain reason and immutable root—for producing certain established effects or fruits. This applies not only to vegetables, but also to minerals and insects. For the depths and properties of lands differ, and this is due to some cause that is innate and coeval <note>Existing from the same time of origin.</note> with that land. I attribute this to the **formal ferment** created within it. Consequently, different fruits sprout and burst forth spontaneously in different places; and if their **seeds** are transferred elsewhere,

<column-break/>

we see that they usually grow more weakly, like **supposititious offspring** <note>Children substituted or placed where they do not belong; used here to mean plants grown outside their natural habitat.</note>.
<margin>27.</margin> What I have said about the **ferment** placed in the earth, you will find equally in the air and the water. For these also do not lack the Roots, Gifts, and **fermental** Reasons which, being stable, bring forth fruits dedicated to specific places and provinces. This is proven not only by the persistence of those fruits, but also by the spontaneous and abundant outpouring of un-sown seeds.
<margin>28.</margin> **Ferment**, therefore, holds the nature of a true "beginning," and it differs from the "efficient cause" in this way: the efficient cause is considered as the **immediate active principle in the thing**, which is the **seed**, and acts as the **motivating principle toward generation**, or the **constitutive beginning of the thing**. But **ferment** is often prior to the **seed**, and generates the seed from itself.
<margin>29.</margin> And so **ferment** is the **original beginning of things**, a **power implanted in the earth or in locations**, rather than in the established seminal things themselves. However, the **ferment** that grows within established things along with the properties of the **seeds** behaves as an **efficient cause toward the seed of things**. But this "seminal ferment" is not the same as one of the two original principles; rather, it is a product of that principle and an effect of the **individual seed**, and is therefore fleeting and perishable. Elsewhere, the **originating ferment** <note>original: "fermentum principians"</note>
<margin>30.</margin> established in the boundaries of the elements remains immutable and constant, subject neither to change nor to death. It is therefore a power grafted into locations, placed there by the Lord Creator for its own ends in the succession of days. Meanwhile, the **seed** in things and its **fermental power** is a thing that, once the scene of its "tragedy" <note>A metaphor for the life cycle or the drama of existence.</note> is worn out, ends in an **individual epilogue** <note>Death.</note>. For although a thing may successively proliferate from itself, this happens only by the power of the **ferment** it once drew in; consequently, the ferment never ceases to produce spontaneous fruits in its own locations—fruits which are often more successful than those grown from the **seed** of previous parents. These things are easily recognized in minerals that are born spontaneously; but in plants and animals, which generate through the **successive fertility of the seed**, this is not so obvious, nor is it in other living creatures.

<summary>This page defines "ferment" as a divinely-ordained, formal principle residing in specific locations (earth, air, water) that precedes and generates seeds. It distinguishes between the permanent "originating ferment" of a place and the temporary "seminal ferment" of an individual living thing.</summary>

...while they might appear to have a promiscuous sex arising from putrefaction <note>The author refers to "spontaneous generation," the old belief that small creatures like insects or worms were born directly from rotting matter without parents.</note>, they soon propagate through mutual intercourse. Indeed, the nature of the **ferment** is the same everywhere. Thus, the ferment is the same beginning in both cases. For in the **seed**, it is either instilled by the parent and takes on an identity with it, or it is imprinted upon matter from elsewhere by external causes; at the very least, in both cases, it holds the place of the true internal efficient power.

<margin>31.</margin> 
Indeed, the Creator of all things designated specific and stable places for certain ferments within the storehouse of the elements, as if in a pantry of seeds, as prototypes for those efficient powers. Other things He dispersed through individuals and species, as if they themselves were "places." In some areas, He willed these beginnings to be stable, according to the nature of the bodies in which they reside; in others, He willed them to be transient, passing from hand to hand to continue the chain of existence. He willed them to differ in this: that the stable ferments of places should be the primary, universal, simple, and starting beginnings of seeds (the efficient powers of natural causes), which would impregnate the element of **water** within itself, in the air, or in the earth. Conversely, the "falling" or transient ferments, drawn from parents, would concern only prepared matter and would sit immediately in the "bosom" of the seeds. Therefore, they would also contain the internal necessity of death.

Another universal beginning of bodies, which is **water**, is the unique material cause of things. Water possesses the nature of a "beginning" within itself—in its manner, purity, simplicity, and its progress of starting things—just as it does at the end of dissolution, to which all bodies return through the reduction 

<margin>32.</margin> 
to their ultimate matter. I will soon demonstrate this in its proper place through examples. Thus, a "beginning" differs from a "cause" only theoretically; the "beginning" is an actual being that initiates (and thus causes), while the "cause" is the term of a relationship to the thing caused (the effect), perhaps closer to a theoretical concept. Or distinguish them as you please. I, at least, understand that causes initiate and beginnings cause under the same name, whether in the bosom of the elements or in the family of material seeds themselves.

<column-break/>

Therefore, in the history of natural things, I consider matter to be mostly impregnated by seed, running its course from its first life to the ultimate end of that concrete thing. I do not, however, consider the **Aristotelian "prime matter"** <term>Prime Matter (Materia Prima): In Aristotle's philosophy, a pure potentiality without any qualities. The author rejects this as a logical impossibility.</term>, or that "non-being" which is 

<margin>33.</margin> 
impossible. Instead, I consider the real beginnings of the conceived efficient cause: the first gifts, roots, treasures, and impregnating ferments of all beings. Or, if the reader prefers to conflate the "efficient cause" with the "ferment" of things, and the "matter" of bodies with the "element of water," I am happy to stop being so distinct, provided it is understood how these things behave in the "light of nature." At the very least, I have discussed the beginnings and causes of bodies as I feel and have experienced them. I also promise great light to those who once make this theory their own.

<margin>34.</margin> 
In the first place, they will find Aristotle's axiom to be false: *That a generator cannot be part of the thing generated.* <note>original: "Quod videlicet generans, nequeat esse pars generati."</note> In truth, the effective principle of generation is always an internal agent, an internal worker, and a generator. This is clear enough in those living things that emerge from putrefaction with only a "mother." In those cases, there is no external generator of the same kind; rather, the seminal mass itself, or the generative seed, guards within itself everything it needs for the economy of generation.

It is not enough simply to have warned of this pair of causes; rather, it would be helpful to more clearly explain the "efficient power," or the primary **Cosmocrat** <term>Cosmocrat: From the Greek 'kosmos' (world) and 'kratos' (power). A ruling force or "world-governor" that directs natural processes.</term>.

<margin>35.</margin> 
Wherefore, I assume here what I will demonstrate elsewhere: namely, that in the entire series of natural things, nothing new arises that does not take its origin from a seed, and nothing happens that does not happen by the necessity of the seed. The "tragedy" that ends at the finish line is nothing but the period or epilogue of exhausted seeds—unless, perhaps, they are forced to depart violently. 

<margin>36.</margin> 
For this reason, I exclude **fire**. Fire was given not for generation, but for destruction. Most importantly, it has a peculiar origin that is not seminal. It is a thing unique and unequal among all created things (as I shall discuss in its proper place). Finally, I exclude...
