# CAUSES AND BEGINNINGS

The influence of the heavens, which due to their most general purpose, possess no **seminal power** <note>original: "potestatem seminalem." The internal blueprint or vital energy that allows a seed to grow into a specific organism.</note> within themselves. This is because they are perhaps too far removed from the lot of things that can be generated. Therefore, these influences are read by the Creator as "Signs, seasons, days, and years" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14.</note> and are intended for no other purpose; they are not intended for the seminal causes of things.

<margin>37.</margin>
Furthermore, among the efficient and seminal causes in nature, some are "efficiently efficient," while others are "effectively" so. In the first class are the **seeds** themselves and the **spirits** that dispense them; these causes belong to the lineage of essences and, through their high level of activity, are rightly distinguished from the material cause. Those that are "effectively efficient," however, are the host-vessels themselves and the immediate organs of the seeds—such as external **ferments** <note>In this context, a "ferment" is a transformative agent that acts like yeast, turning raw matter into a specific substance.</note> and the dispositive materials that lead toward the "otherness" of transformation. This also includes the dispositive powers of circumstances, which foster, excite, and promote growth.

<margin>38.</margin>
For even when a seed is given, not just anything will grow from it indiscriminately. Furthermore, our student will learn of the character of **Aristotle**, who was prone to founding axioms; whenever he found something that fit his own concepts, he immediately turned it into a Rule, binding roots taken from weak authority into a universal law. Subsequent ages, prone to laziness, admired these axioms of his and thus easily came to worship both the man and his rules. Consequently, he also introduced mathematics into nature with a violent interpretation, wishing for natural causes to obey numbers, lines, and the letters of the alphabet—an utterly ridiculous audacity. For example: noticing that fire would burn dry wood faster than wet wood, he immediately meditated upon a universal axiom.

<margin>39.</margin>
"The action of active agents exists only in matter that is prepared" <note>original: "Quod actus activorum, tantum essent in materiam dispositam." A famous Aristotelian principle suggesting that a cause can only work if the material is already "ready" for it.</note>. Yet this is hedged about by much ignorance. For first, because he saw fire, an external agent, run toward combustible matter, he then judged that every other agent in nature must act in the manner of fire—not knowing that fire does not act

<column-break/>

in the manner of a seminal agent, but is a unique type of creature. He therefore judged, with equal ignorance, that every efficient cause must necessarily be external, just like fire. He was also deceived in this: that he established that every natural agent requires "prepared matter." On the contrary, an agent in nature prepares its own underlying matter for itself. For every design of a natural agent acts for no other end than to prepare the matter placed beneath it for goals known to itself—or at least destined for generation. Indeed, from the single juice of the earth and a single garden, four hundred different plants grow and bear fruit. If the Agent finds a friendly "disposition" in the matter, well and good; if not, it prepares the same for itself with easy effort. What if I later demonstrate that all tangible bodies proceed immediately from the single element of **water**? By what necessity, I ask, will an agent require a pre-existing preparation of matter? Or if it does pre-exist, who was that "preparer" or precursor to the Agent? Is the Agent not sufficient by itself to prepare whatever matter it inhabits? But if you say it is a **ferment**, you must at least recognize that both causes do not differ in nature from the product, except in maturity; nor is the Agent distinguished from the ferment. If the Schools were imbued with a discipline of better substance, they would surely know and recognize that their Aristotle fails his own Rules—those which he first erected as true premises for scientific demonstrations. He himself would have been driven mad by the "monstrous generations" of stones within us <note>A reference to "calculi" or kidney and bladder stones, which the author views as a natural process of matter being "prepared" and hardened internally.</note>. And though mathematics was cruder before the birth of **Euclid’s Elements**,

<margin>40.</margin>
Aristotle, being far more skilled in math than in nature, nevertheless strove to subject nature to the Rules of that science. For he knew that the circle is the most "capacious" of shapes on a plane. Suddenly, therefore, he forced this into a universal axiom: even round ulcers and wounds are more difficult to heal than any others of equal size. But surely a wound penetrating from a broad dagger is more difficult to heal than a round one in the flesh. In ulcers...

# NATURAL MATTERS.

Indeed, an anal fistula or a tear duct fistula are more laborious to heal than any leg ulcer extended in its circumference. He <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or a contemporary follower of his logic.</note> was surely deceived by a preference for "Rules," thinking that the healing of a wound proceeds only from an external agent—a plaster—and that this "exteriority" is not just a matter of the body's surface, but a geometric concern regarding the distance of the wound's edges from its center. I will recount a history. A military wagoner infects his wife with the **Venereal plague** <note>original: "lue Veneris," a common historical term for syphilis.</note>. For lack of a remedy, this spread into an "eating" ulcer. I saw at least one instance where it devastated the fleshy membrane from the ear into the neck, shoulder, and elbow, back through the shoulder blades, and along the entire side of the ribs and chest. As this membrane is thicker in women, it contained a deeper cavity. She said she had many other smaller ones through her abdomen and down her legs; she exhibited a human body almost without skin. By my authority, the woman was brought to the hospital at Vilvoorde <note>A town in the Duchy of Brabant, near modern-day Belgium.</note>, though the nuns refused her. But "Mars" <note>A reference to military authority or forceful intervention.</note> prevailed, for sometimes even nuns must obey for a time. The garrison surgeon dipped **aqua fortis** <note>original: "Chrysulcam." Literally "gold-dissolver," referring to nitric acid, used here as a harsh cauterizing agent.</note> into the raw muscles using soaked lint, causing incredible pain; her pitiful wailing shook the house. Passing by, I asked why he had done this. He said it was an ulcerated, total **cancer** <note>original: "Carcinoma." In this period, the term was often used for any spreading, malignant-looking sore.</note>, and the sooner she died, the luckier she would be. A complaining nun, hearing this, said she was not bound by the rules of her house to host Cancer, leprosy, or the plague, etc. Therefore, immediately before dusk, they carried the woman to the suburbs and dumped her on a dunghill. A poor peasant, pitying the unknown woman, built a small hut of branches to protect her from the rain and applied cabbage leaves to draw away the flowing pus and ward off the harsh weather. He told me the story. I provided **Paracelsus's Coral** <note>original: "Corallatum Paracelsi." A chemical medicine made from red mercuric oxide, believed to have powerful healing properties.</note> prepared with egg white, and in 26 days she was entirely recovered. Indeed, the massive ulcers were covered with skin in a sudden rush, though a few tiny cracks remained at the start,

<column-break/>

maintaining a longer duration. Soon, a dying relative left a house and field to this poorest of women. Her husband died behind some bushes; she married again, now wealthy with a herd, a flock, and fields. For in the husband and the surgeon, I saw robbers; in the nuns, fickleness; in the peasant, a Samaritan; and in the woman, I marveled at Job <note>A biblical reference to the patient sufferer who is eventually restored.</note>. I knew then that the God of Job is the same eternal and almighty Ruler of the universe. From Him, although man has stolen the titles of majesty—Highness, Excellence, Clemency, and Lordship—He has reserved at least one for Himself alone: **Eternity**. In respect to which, man is a mushroom of a single night, rotten by tomorrow. Let the Schools know, therefore, that the rules of
<margin>41.</margin>
**mathematics** <note>original: "Matheseos."</note> poorly fit nature. For man does not measure nature; nature measures herself. Nor will a pagan, ignorant of the paths, show the way any better than a blind man can show colors he has never seen. Therefore, besides the ignorance of nature in its root and essence, the Schools have failed to know the causes of things: their number, their requirements, and finally the flows of maturation, slowness, and speed. Likewise, they ignored the compositions and resolutions of bodies, made both by nature and by art; they also ignored the necessity of **seeds** and **ferments** <note>The active agents of transformation in Helmont’s chemistry.</note>, as well as their ends, dispositions, defects, restorations, deaths, successions, contiguities, and dependencies—precisely because they taught that a "natural agent" was something foreign and strange to the things themselves.
<margin>42.</margin>
Consequently, they also ignored the births of "forms" and the properties proceeding from them. In their place, they set forth fortune, chance, time, vacuum, and the infinite, even though these are alien to nature and contain ridiculous disciplines. Indeed, they followed an Author <note>Aristotle.</note> who believed the world was unfolded from eternity to eternity by its own powers, yet he contradicts himself by denying the infinite. Since the Prime Mover, who will endure eternally and do all things in eternal power, necessarily includes the infinite.

# THE ARCHITECT-ARTISAN.
<note>original: "Archeus Faber." The Archeus is a central concept in the work of Jan Baptista van Helmont. It refers to a semi-spiritual, internal vital force that acts as a "master smith" or "architect," directing the growth, functions, and healing of a living organism.</note>

1. *The Archeus is the efficient cause.* 2. *Its nature in seeds.* 3. *Its properties and differences.* 4. *The composition of the generative aura.* 5. *The birth of seminal ideas.* 6. *The seminal clothing of the Archeus.* 7. *The dwellings assigned to the seed with their caretakers.* 8. *The union of stars imitated in seeds.* 9. *The First Mover <note>original: "Primum mobile," referring to the outermost sphere of the heavens that provides motion to all others.</note> has no substitute in man.*

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'T' featuring floral and foliate scrolling patterns.</image-desc> I have touched upon the origin and causes of natural things, and—lest I seem to have proposed an internal "efficient cause" <note>The "efficient cause" is an Aristotelian term for the primary agent that brings a thing into being.</note> for no reason—I will more conveniently explain this "artisan," the Vulcan <note>The Roman god of the forge and fire; here used metaphorically for the internal "smith" of life.</note> of generations. Therefore, whatever comes into the world through nature must have within itself the beginning of its movements, an awakener, and an internal director of its generation.

<margin>2.</margin> Every single thing, however hard and opaque it may be, nevertheless encloses within itself—before it reaches that solidity—an aura <note>A subtle vapor or breath of life.</note>. Before generation occurs, this aura foreshadows the future generation within the seed (which is fertile up to this point), and it accompanies the generated being until the end of its "stage" or life cycle.

<margin>3.</margin> This aura, although it may be more brilliant in some things, is nevertheless compressed into the form of sap in vegetables, and in metals, it is thickened into a very dense, uniform substance. Yet to each thing has fallen this gift which is called the <term>Archeus</term>, containing the fertility of generations and seeds as an internal efficient cause. That artisan, I say, possesses the image of the thing to be generated; at the beginning of that thing, he composes the plans for the tasks to be carried out.

<margin>4.</margin> Indeed, the Archeus consists of a connection of the vital aura (acting as the matter) with a "seminal image," which is the inner spiritual nucleus containing the seed's fertility. The visible seed, however, is merely the husk <note>original: "siliqua."</note> of this. This image of the Archeus—flowing down from the "idea" of its predecessor, or seizing that same idea from the storehouse of external things—is not some dead likeness. Rather, it is marked with full knowledge and adorned with the necessary powers for the things to be done in its destiny; thus, it is the primary organ of life and sensation.

<column-break/>

For example: a pregnant woman, through her own desire, shapes a cherry in her fetus on that part of the body where she moves her hand in longing. <margin>5.</margin> That cherry, I say, becomes real within the flesh—green, pale, yellow, and ripening to red—following the same stages by which trees bring forth their own cherries. Indeed, that same cherry on a fetus turns red sooner in Spain than it does in Belgium <note>referring to the warmer climate accelerating the "ripening" of the birthmark.</note>. Thus, a cherry is made through imagination. In the same way, through the imagination of desire, the vital image of living creatures is transferred into the spirit of the seed, destined to unfold itself through the course of generation. <margin>6.</margin> But since every bodily act must end in a body, it happens that the Archeus—the Artisan and Rector of generation—immediately clothes himself in a bodily garment. In living creatures, he travels through all the hiding places and recesses of his seed and begins to transform the matter according to his own <term>entelechy</term> <note>A term from Aristotle meaning the realization of potential or the "vital principle" that guides an object toward its finished state.</note>. For here he places the heart, there he designates the brain, and everywhere he establishes an immovable inhabitant as a presiding officer, determined by his own universal sovereignty, according to the requirements of the parts and the goals of their destinations. <margin>7.</margin> Finally, that presiding officer remains as the internal curator and rector of those goals until death. Another part, however, remains fluctuating and assigned to no specific member; it maintains a watch over the individual "pilots" of the limbs—bright, yet never ceasing its work. <margin>8.</margin> Furthermore, just as things below the moon express an analogy of the higher heavens within themselves, so each thing is more perfect in its imitation of the stars the more vital it is. This goes so far that sick people seem to carry "sensible almanacs" <note>original: "Ephemerides sensibiles." An ephemeris is a table of celestial positions; here, he means the sick can feel the "weather" or "stars" in their bodies.</note> within themselves, aware of future storms. Truly, the planetary spirits shine forth most clearly in the viscera, just as the changes and powers of the firmament appear in the universal Archeus that flows into us. <margin>9.</margin> The "First Mover," however, never had a specific organ in men; rather, it occurs only under the Archeus of the womb through an analogous meditation, as if in the final completion of created things. For perhaps woman, for that reason...

## USELESS LOGIC.
<note>original: "LOGICA INUTILIS." The author here begins a systematic deconstruction of Aristotelian logic, arguing it is a hindrance to true scientific discovery.</note>

<margin>I.</margin> **I** shall be called a presumptuous brawler, one who is displeased that any of his predecessors should know anything—like a wild boar completely uprooting a vineyard. But I know that it would go badly for me if my soul stood subject to human judgments. For from a man

What if I shall show the ignorance, laziness, impieties, and cruelties of physicians regarding things that ought to be held at the highest price—the loss of which is irreparable and, finally, most dangerous to souls—and if I am answered with contempt, mockery, and sarcasm? <margin>3.</margin> Truly, I congratulate myself even now, and live content in the hope of that reward. # LOGIC IS USELESS.

<margin>4.</margin> As Jerome says in his prologue to Isaiah <note>original: "in prologo Isaiæ"</note>, let them read first and despise later, lest they seem to condemn things they do not know out of a prejudice of hatred rather than a reasoned judgment. But I do not care whether I am read and criticized, or not. It is enough for me that I have satisfied my duty. For I had no swelling of ambition <term>thymosis; an ancient term for an emotional "boiling" or swelling of pride</term> to make myself known; I willingly confess that I possess nothing good worthy of imitation. Indeed, this book would have been submitted to the press without a name, if it could have been done without causing offense. From my youth, I began to grow accustomed to the "itch" of study, so that while the Physicians, Surgeons, and Apothecaries <note>original: "Seplasiis"; literally "sellers of ointments"</note> spoke against me, the rest of the common folk spurned me as a Spagyrist <term>Spagyrum; a follower of Paracelsus who uses alchemy to separate and recombine substances for medicine</term> and a Philosopher. Only a few favored me, and I have withdrawn myself from their favor as much as I could. Certainly, I have spent much of my life and labor, and taken away much of my own useful leisure, to satisfy the requirements of this study. Praise be to the First Truth, to whom alone belongs the reward for good deeds. In whose mirror I saw—and have held as a fixed rule—that the judgments of men are mostly diametrically opposed to divine ones. I saw that the common breeze is foolish, full of errors, shameful, and always harmful; but the universal Judge is a stranger to error.

<margin>5.</margin> I shall begin, therefore, with the verbal arts. Logic consists of three members: Definition, Division, and Argumentation. First, they teach that a definition consists of the "genus" of the thing defined and its "constitutive difference." <margin>6.</margin> But since hardly any other constitutive difference of a species is known besides "rational" and "irrational"—which are supposed to be specific and closest to individuals—and since one of these two is actually a negative term <note>The author means "irrational" is just the absence of reason, not a positive trait</note>, and I shall prove the former to be sometimes frivolous; therefore, with one foot removed from the tripod, the Logician must necessarily fall, having relied on such a seat. <margin>7.</margin> Especially because Division is such a wretched limb of Logic that it may rightly be doubted whether it remained almost neglected by the Schools themselves due to its ridiculous sterility. For the knowledge of the whole and the complete comes before that of its parts. And it is of the essence of the "universal" to be "one in many," and therefore it is more knowable. For he who knows the "one and useful" knows the many

<column-break/>

and the particulars; but not the other way around. This is because the "one and useful" exists in the intellect, whereas plurality, or division, exists in the senses. For the more something is divided into parts, the closer it approaches the infinite, and it is therefore less knowable, sliding toward irregularity, and more subject to change and opposition. But since logic deals with universals, and it is said in the *First book of Posterior Analytics* <note>original: "1. Posterior."; referring to Aristotle’s work on logic and demonstration</note> that we err less in universals than in particulars: certainly logic, leading us through Division to singular things, is so far from leading us to science (according to their own Aristotelian principles) that it rather thrusts us into <margin>8.</margin> errors. Indeed, if we look more closely at the limb of Division, it can complete no part of Philosophy; it is a mere naked method of dividing, so raw and crude that hardly a single hypothesis, axiom, property, mode, or process is dictated even to young students.

Therefore Logic, being sterile and deprived of two feet of its tripod, has long since collapsed in my view. Indeed, Philosophy is impoverished and worthy of pity when it boasts that it produces sciences with such narrow equipment and such small and defective tools. <margin>9.</margin> But the third limb of logic [Argumentation], raised on high, is held in great weight among the practitioners of the verbal arts—though it is equally unsuitable for the true uses of nature. For nature hates brawls and does not willingly bear discords. The world has indeed allowed itself to be deceived by Aristotle, because he boasts that logic is the mother of the sciences, and that we know nothing except through demonstration. And lest common people <note>original: "Idiotæ"; refers to the unlearned or laypeople</note>—many of whom are shrewder and more skilled than Logicians—should laugh at this loud, Stentorian <note>original: "Stentoris"; referring to the Greek herald Stentor, known for his incredibly loud voice</note> arrogance, he makes Logic natural and innate to us. Beautifully, then, he extols the method of disputation he invented with much praise, and removes all knowledge from man as if from a blank slate <note>original: "rasa tabula"</note> unless he has surrendered himself to be taught by Logic. I truly continue to wonder at this vanity, as well as the credulity of the world. Especially since reasoning, or natural...

### LOGIC IS USELESS.

...natural logic <note>the OCR begins with "lem," likely the end of "naturalem" (natural) from the preceding page</note>, he was compelled to grant it to humans as a natural gift. Thus, he might value his Philosophy—that supposed discoverer of all sciences—no longer as some hidden, profound knowledge, but as a certain natural brawling of quarreling and a method composed for that very purpose. Therefore, at this point, we must inquire how much truth, power, 
<margin>10.</margin> and utility it actually possesses. As for me, I know that every dispute eventually gives birth to a conclusion; however, every conclusion merely introduces an opinion. Indeed, I hold that even the strongest form of reasoning (which they call a **Syllogism** <term>Syllogism; a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises, e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal</term>) has never actually provided any true science, nor is it fit to do so. Therefore, one should expect even less knowledge from any other formula of argument. 
<margin>11.</margin> Among the nineteen formulas of syllogisms, twelve conclude negatively. But no negation ever gave birth to science, since it contains something privative <note>meaning it defines what something is NOT rather than what it IS</note> and teaches that nothing exists by denying that something is. 
<margin>12.</margin> True science, however, must be positive, since it concerns only what is positive. Finally, since the basis of every syllogism rests on the idea that if two things agree with each other, they must agree in some third thing (and the conformity of this agreement must appear in the conclusion itself), it follows that the knowledge of that conformity must necessarily pre-exist in us before the conclusion. Thus, I must have already known in a general sense everything that is demonstrated through the conclusion. For that knowledge lies hidden within us, like fire beneath the ash; it brings itself out into the open through the natural power of discourse whenever the need arises, no less than through the rules of Logic—a fact which even Aristotle himself did not dare to deny. Otherwise, anyone seeking knowledge through Logic would, in some way and to some extent, already have to know what they are seeking. For if they did not already know and recognize it, how would they recognize it once they found it? Unless, of course, the Logicians prefer to believe that knowledge sought through demonstrations is 
<margin>13.</margin> found by mere chance. At best, the knowledge we draw out through demonstration was already within us previously, and only becomes 

<column-break/>

a little more distinct through the Syllogism. However, it remains, as before, tied to doubt. This is because every conclusion necessarily follows the "weaker part" of the premises <note>a rule in formal logic stating that if one premise is negative or particular, the conclusion must also be</note>. Hence, it is written with the doubt of its opposite. Indeed, the conclusion of a Syllogism usually denies specifically what its premise was as a universal negative, and it does not dare to infer anything affirmatively where there is anything negative in the premises. This is a sign that it teaches nothing through assertion, but most willingly denies. Furthermore, since science lies hidden under the ash in the intellect, the intellect can shake off the ash whenever it seems necessary to itself; it has no need for syllogistic modes and forms for this. Indeed, since according to Aristotle one should not dispute except with those who admit the principles (which he thinks are primarily true), it happens that from dissimilar principles, an unrelated conclusion often follows. 
<margin>14.</margin> For instance, from false premises: "Nothing adorable is the Creator" and "Every idol should be adored," there follows this true conclusion: "Therefore, no idol is the Creator." It cannot be judged, therefore, that the conclusion of Syllogisms compels by necessity. For from a lie, a falsehood otherwise follows necessarily in the true intellect and true science. From the impossible follows the impossible, and from the absurd comes nothing other than another absurdity. This is proven by the whole of **Mathematics** <term>Mathesis; the Greek-derived term for the mathematical sciences, often viewed in this period as the peak of certain, logical demonstration</term>. Therefore, just as truth and the knowledge of it are not contained or hidden in a lie, it follows that the knowledge of a conclusion is not necessarily enclosed in the premises. For either it is false that "no tree of lies produces the good fruit of truth," or it is false that a true conclusion can be born from false premises as if they were principles. Indeed, since it is evident from this that there is no necessary dependence of the conclusion upon the premises, it is also easily understood why the soul has made such meager progress up to now through demonstration. 
<margin>15.</margin> Wherefore the Blessed Augustine says: *“Just as in false sciences there can be true conclusions, so in true sciences there can be false conclusions.”* 
<margin>16.</margin> Indeed, when I scrutinized the nature of demonstrations more deeply, I found demonstration to be...

# USELESS LOGIC.

...and that knowledge exists in the teacher, but not in the learner: and thus, it serves not so much to discover knowledge as to display what has already been discovered. In the learner, however, the Syllogism blows the ash away from the fire <note>original: *cinerem difflat ab igne*; a metaphor for revealing what is already there but obscured</note>. Since whoever syllogizes already knows distinctly beforehand that which he strives to have granted to him through the conclusion. Namely, he knows the terms, the middle, and the mode <term>Mode; in logic, the classification of a syllogism according to the quantity and quality of its premises</term>. For no one syllogizes with unknown terms. Therefore, demonstration has appeared to me to serve schoolmasters who rouse beginners to attend to those things which they themselves already know. These people have certainly, up to now, discovered few and useful sciences, however much they boast that they hunt for "middle terms" <term>Middle term; the term that appears in both premises of a syllogism but not the conclusion, acting as the bridge between them</term> through demonstrations and acquire sciences. For every syllogism first conceives an opinion of a thing and persuades itself that it is certain: then, in order to establish it for itself or for learners, it seeks terms, a middle, and a mode, so that it may force its demonstration into form. Therefore, the Syllogism is not for discovering sciences, but rather to demonstrate discovered opinions to others. And since the Syllogism produces in the learner a certain recollection <note>original: *reminiscentiam*</note> of what he knows, and nothing else—and true sciences are not acquired through recollection, as if all knowledge of all things had pre-existed within us—

<margin>17.</margin> Hence, the Syllogism cannot give birth to or discover sciences; it only makes clearer those insights that have already been discovered and known.

<margin>18.</margin> But I know and admit that the knowledge of my intellect dwells immediately in the intellect, and (according to Aristotle) since those immediate sciences (that is, intellectual ones) are indemonstrable <note>In Aristotelian logic, the first principles of a science cannot be proven by that science; they must be self-evident or known by intuition</note>: it also follows that any true or intellectual science is indemonstrable. That is, true sciences cannot proceed from demonstration. Indeed, every demonstration consists of discourse and reason. It is, of course, a simple and perfect reasoning:

<margin>19.</margin> But (according to Aristotle) the knowledge of principles is not in Reason: but entirely above it. Therefore, to know through a Syllogism cannot be intellectual or essential, nor can it be

<column-break/>

originating or *a priori* <term>A priori; knowledge that proceeds from causes to effects, or from theoretical deduction rather than observation</term>: but it is only a supposed opinion deduced from established hypotheses, categories, or rules of the one syllogizing. (I have written more and sufficient things on this matter elsewhere.) Not without merit, therefore, did the blessed Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> <margin>In Psalms 140 & 143.</margin> compare the art of syllogizing to the plagues of Egypt: and he calls the demonstrations of Logic the "gnats" <note>original: *Cyniphes*; referring to the third plague of Egypt, often interpreted as biting gnats or lice</note> of Dialectics. However, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> wished for those things to be avoided altogether.

> *Doing nothing through contention... and to contend with words is useful for nothing else but the subversion of the listeners: since these things extinguish faith and the merits of faith.*

<margin>20.</margin> But they say: Logic is the discoverer of "middles." That is, it is for the discovery of middle terms and form for the sake of demonstration. Do you perhaps think the Apostle did not know what, and how much, Logic could do? That he spoke outside, beyond, and against the spirit of truth when he ordered that Logic be avoided? Or should more be granted to such a flabby argument than to the Apostle’s command? But truly, logic does not find the means for producing, having, doing, or knowing: but only for showing some supposition more concisely: and even for attacking the truth, it discovers composed brawls. For that reason, the Apostle calls Logic by the sufficiently despised title: *contentions*. Which he certainly would not have done if she were the mother of sciences, the discoverer of useful means, or if she were profitable to Christians. Therefore, the Schools, by teaching otherwise, by doing otherwise, by assuming logic to be necessary and using it daily, <margin>21.</margin> oppose the Apostle's precept. Discovery in Logic, therefore, is not properly discovery, just as demonstrable science is not true and intellectual science. Because we do not properly "discover" what we already know in some way, just as we do not "discover" what we already have in our hand or in a chest; but things not known before are properly discovered, just as things not held or possessed are acquired through discovery or gift. For when someone shows me calamine stone <term>Calamine; a mineral (zinc carbonate) used in historical metallurgy</term>, the preparation of Cadmia <note>an ancient term for zinc ores or the deposits found in smelting furnaces</note>, its content of copper, the mixture, and the uses of brass <note>original: *Aurichalci*; a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc</note>, which

...what I did not know before, he teaches, demonstrates, and gives knowledge of that which was previously unknown. But Logic never taught such things. Thus, logical discovery is merely a repetition of what was already known. And because Logic does not know the unknown, it cannot teach it. Indeed, our spirit was already in possession of that which they solemnly promise can be found through logic. Since it is impossible to know whether the premises are true, apparent, or false unless a knowledge of the terms was already within us, along with every awareness of their equivalence and confirmation. 

Therefore, the entire ministry, duty, and utility of logic consists in only two things. <margin>23.</margin> Namely: so that the teacher may impress his own thought distinctly upon the listener; and so that the listener may stir up a reminiscence or recollection through the connection, adaptation, equivalence, and conformity of the terms. This is certainly not the inventive function of the sciences, but rather a subsequent following of discourse toward that which had already been discovered. Finally, nothing that happens in this way belongs to the sciences at all, but only to words <note>original: *dictiones*; referring to verbal expressions rather than empirical reality</note>. 

<margin>24.</margin> Wisdom alone—the son of the eternal Father of Lights—gives the sciences. The means of acquiring the sciences are only to pray, to seek, and to knock <note>A reference to Matthew 7:7, suggesting that true knowledge is a divine gift rather than a result of human logic</note>. Meanwhile, I marvel at such great blindness in the Schools on both sides, by extolling and magnifying Logic so much. I would certainly wish that the Schools would say: what science has Logic ever brought to light? Perhaps Geometry? Music? Glass-making? Printing? Agriculture? Medicine? Hydraulics? Mineralogy? Warfare? Arithmetic? Carpentry? Or any use-

<column-break/>

-ful thing at all? Not at all. Therefore, the logical Schools must finally admit with a blush that the same thing has happened to Logic as has happened to Galenic doctrine <term>Galenic doctrine; the medical system of Galen (2nd century AD), which the author views as outdated and deceptive</term> until now. Namely, that through boasting, impostures, and ignorance, it has deceived a credulous world. The Gentiles, by prostituting demonstrations and selling sciences, had no other light than that which flowed from corrupt nature—seduced by obscure thoughts—into disorder and confusion, slavishly obeying the changes of circumstances and the thoughts born from them. 

I have occasionally shared these things with learned men, who finally admitted that Logic is served up to youths at that age because they cannot bear any more solid food, and thus it serves them to sharpen their wit. (If only Logic were not used for various abuses, and once swallowed in youth, did not produce an age fertile with ruinous wits and logical deceptions!) To them I say: <margin>25.</margin> It is not free from imposture if they meanwhile recommend Logic as true Philosophy and as the discoverer of the Sciences. 

They say, "at least Dialectics <term>Dialectics; the art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions</term> is highly necessary for Theologians so they may refute the subtleties of heresy." I judged that this was a desire to be "wiser than the Apostle" <note>original: *sapere supra Apostolum*; likely referring to St. Paul’s warnings against worldly wisdom</note>, and thus to recommend the abuses of the Schools over sacred things. For Evangelical truth does not seek Logic or contentions; instead, it demands piety of life in faith, an example of living, incorrupt conversation, and abstinence from lusts and the pride of life, so that the word of the Lord may become fruitful. Many testify with me that enough has been debated by illuminated Doctors since the beginning of the Church.

<margin>1.</margin>
The Schools have sworn such loyalty and finality to their Aristotle that even today they call him, by antonomasia <note>original: *Antonomasiam*; a rhetorical device where a title or epithet replaces a proper name</note>, "The Philosopher." Yet, I find him to be utterly ignorant of nature. I am not reluctant to describe several reasons that have driven me to this conclusion—and I do so with no other purpose than to ensure that, henceforth, neither Professors nor students are led astray by habit and the custom of giving assent, nor allow themselves to be led by the blind into a pit. Otherwise, I act as no man’s advocate; I am no more an enemy to Aristotle than I am to a non-entity.

<margin>2.</margin>
In the first place, Aristotle defines nature as follows: *The principle of motion and of rest in those bodies in which it exists primarily and not by accident.* In this, I find more errors and ignorance on the part of the definer than there are words. First, the word "exists" <note>original: *inest*</note> shows that he is speaking of a body that really exists, and not of his impossible prime matter <note>original: *hyle*; the formless "stuff" Aristotle imagined as the basis of all things</note>. 2. He implies that such bodies do not belong to the category or substance of nature. For it is not the property of bodies to exist within other bodies "primarily and not by accident." 3. He removes all "accidents" <note>Non-essential properties, like color or size</note> from the catalog of nature, as if they were outside, beyond, or above nature, because accidents exist "by accident." 4. He likewise excludes from nature those bodies that have motion or rest "by accident." 5. The being of things is within nature—nature itself—before the day of their motion or rest. For it is necessary that something exist before it can move, be moved, or rest. Thus, the principle of *being* precedes the beginning of moving or resting; yet nature cannot exist before its own 

<column-break/>

existence. For if the beginning of motion or rest were posterior to "being," then nature would be posterior to natural being. 6. What if God, after Creation, had commanded neither motion nor rest (since "rest" for Aristotle presupposes the end of a motion)? Then there would have been a creature, but no "nature" as defined here. For in the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth. There was already a nature that Aristotle did not understand; it was surely once a Creature, and existed in actuality before, or without, the nature defined here. 7. Bodies in which the beginning of motion is external and accidental—for example, when the Sun’s heat moves a seed to grow, or when a pregnant woman, by accident of her imagination, transforms the embryo—would not fall under "nature," nor would that accidental beginning. 8. To "rest" is not merely "not to move," but to cease from motion; therefore, "not moving" is a more general state than "rest." Thus, nature taken absolutely would only exist after nature’s existence had already begun. 9. If the principle of motion in a thing is "nature," and the efficient cause is properly called the "beginning of motion" (which he says is non-elemental heat), then it follows that either the efficient cause must be internal (which contradicts Aristotle), or that nature, as the beginning of motion, does not exist intimately and primarily within bodies. 10. Every external efficient cause would be a beginning of motion in a thing "by accident." But every efficient cause, according to Aristotle, is external. Therefore, no external efficient cause is "natural," which contradicts his own second book of the *Physics*. 11. Anything moved by mathematical principles, or a mill moved by wind or a stream, would not be moved by nature.

<margin>3.</margin>
I, however, believe that Nature is the command of God, by which a thing is what it is, and does what it is commanded to do. This is the Christian definition, sought from the Holy Scriptures. 12. Then, for the "constitutive difference," he takes matter, or the body, in which said beginning of motion exists. Christians, however, are bound to...

# AND THE IGNORANCE OF GALEN

to believe that nature is every creature, including the body and its accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color or weight, as opposed to its "essence."</note> no less than the very beginning of motion itself. 13. Furthermore, although death is, in itself, the beginning of rest in a corpse, Christians believe it is not a "creature"—that is, not something created by the Lord—and therefore it is not "nature." Although it occurs according to natural processes, this happens not because of the essence of death, but because of its natural causes.

4. Aristotle, however, elsewhere touching upon nature just as falteringly, says:
> *Every power of the soul seems to participate in a certain other body (for he does not dare to affirm it positively and simply) than those which are called elements.*

For just as souls differ, so too does the nature of that body differ: the seed contains the cause of fertility, namely heat—which is not of fire, but a spirit in the foamy body of the seed; and the nature which is in that spirit corresponds in proportion to the element of the stars <note>Aristotle's theory of "vital heat" suggested it was a celestial substance, different from ordinary fire.</note>.

This discourse, so praised by the Schools, contains almost as many errors as it does syllables. At last, the Writer of the *Natural Philosophy* <note>original: *Naturalis auscultationis*; a reference to Aristotle's *Physics*</note>, appearing deeply anxious, does not know what he calls, or ought to call, nature. For first, he says the power of the soul is corporeal; thus, he excludes the intellect from the powers of the soul. 2. He says that the power of the soul—which he later calls mere heat—participates in another body than those called elements. It is as if it participates only in a body above the elements, a celestial one. 3. It is absolutely false and ignorant to say that any power of the soul "participates" in the body, even if it is bound to the body. For every power is an accident; and no accident or quality can be a "participant" in a body. On the contrary, it is the Body that is a participant in its accidents. 4. He claims souls do not differ except in respect to that body (which he finally calls mere heat). Yet, if all souls and their powers participate in a celestial body, then souls do not differ by reason of that body, in which he said they all agree. Or, if there is any distinction between souls, let it be by reason of the body of matter, or an unnamed, 

<column-break/>

neglected client <note>The author uses "client" metaphorically to refer to matter as a subservient or dependent entity</note> that was plainly unknown to Aristotle. Thus, with such an apparatus of words, he has said nothing but trifles. 5. If souls only differ by grace of that body, then the "act" would be determined by the "potency," and the species by the matter, and not by the form <note>In Aristotelian logic, "form" gives a thing its identity; the author argues Aristotle's logic here accidentally suggests matter defines the soul</note>. 6. To say "the seed contains the cause of fertility" is childish and redundant. Indeed, a seed is defined as being a seed only if it possesses the cause of fertility. 7. He claims every power of the soul participates in a body other than the elements. Yet he insists that the bodies of all living things are necessarily mixed only from actual elements. 8. He claims the seed is not fertile except through heat. As if fish were not more fertile than quadrupeds, and as if fish were not actually cold! 9. He does not recognize that common moderate heat from coals can foster eggs into chicks. He is ignorant that all heat belongs to a single, most specific kind of quality, distinguished only by degree. 10. He is ignorant that heat only warms by its own nature (*per se*), and it would only fertilize by accident (*per accidens*). Therefore, although that heat might be the principle of motion and the power of the soul (that is, "nature") in itself; yet, insofar as it fertilizes seeds by accident, it would be a beginning of motion by accident. Therefore, in respect to the same nature, it would be a beginning both *per se* and *per accidens*—or, it would be nature and not nature at the same time. 11. He confuses the quality of heat with the spirit and aura of the foamy seed; yet these are as distant as the categories themselves. 12. He says heat is the spirit of the foamy body, and the nature in that spirit is heat. Therefore, spirit would be within spirit. 13. He says nature is in that spirit; yet that spirit is not the "nature" defined by Aristotle as the subject of Physics (even though this spirit is the principle of motion in the seed and of life in living things). He denies even more strictly that the foamy body of the seed belongs to the census of nature—as if the true seed of things were the foam, and not the interior invisible nucleus <note>original: *nucleolus invisibilis*; likely referring to the vital spark or formal principle within matter</note> within the corporeal seed—but claims that only the power of souls (which to him is nothing but heat) is nature. 14. # ARISTOTLE'S PHYSICS

...every power of the soul were circumscribed by heat, he would exclude from the ranks of nature all other bodies and any accidents <note>In this philosophical context, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or weight.</note> whatsoever. 15. That power of souls, by which they differ from one another, he claims is heat alone—not indeed a fiery heat, but one corresponding in proportion to the "element of the stars" <note>Aristotle's *quinta essentia* or aether, which he believed provided the vital warmth for life.</note>. What kind of correspondence could exist between such varied categories? 16. He denies that this power of souls comes from the "ancestry of the elements." By using the plural, he does not reject just one element, but with the strength of a total negative, he rejects them all. 17. Every power of the soul, he says, is mere heat—not even responding to the heat of the stellar element, but to the element itself. 18. He does not recognize any heat other than fire, nor any element of fire other than the "culinary" kind <note>The "culinary" fire refers to common, earthly fire used for cooking or warmth, as opposed to "elemental" or "celestial" fire.</note> (because he distinguishes elemental heat from the stellar element); yet by his own authority, he fenced off fire between heaven and air, and it was not the culinary kind. 19. Finally, whenever he had to state positively what "nature" was, he evasively says it is now the power of the soul, now the fertility of the seed, and finally a non-fiery heat—a heat he never felt nor truly knew. He makes a fifth element out of the firmament of stars after having cast away the other four by denial. And so, he runs in circles with his evasive denials; lest he be caught, he denies that nature is from the lineage of the elements. As if it were enough to have said: "it is a chimera, not made of the elements, but of the fifth stellar element." It is not a body, not an accident, but a heat responding to the element of the heavens, rather than to the heat of those heavens. 20. And he would not even say these things *are* so, but only that they *seem* so to him. Yet, according to his own logic, many things "seem" to be that in fact are not. 21. And if you do not believe it, go and see for yourself, or wait forever. 22. As if the entire action of nature were written in heat alone! 23. Metals also, which he elsewhere writes are condensed by cold alone 

<column-break/>

because they flow when heated, would now be considered outside the realm of nature. 24. And as if the seeds of plants—because they are not "foamy"—were not endowed with fertility, or did not contain nature within themselves! 25. He denies, therefore, that in animals which are actually warm, the heat is "elemental" (a claim I shall prove true in its proper place), while forgetting his own axiom: *That the cause must be of the same species as its effect.* I say that he does not realize that our heat warms other things by simple, elemental heat. And conversely, not only does elemental heat (which he places in the sublunary fire, distinct from the culinary) warm us, but even culinary fire warms us to a degree suited to our nature. They must, therefore, be of one and the same species. 26. Finally, he rashly asserts that nature—or the power of the soul, or the "seminal truths"—is nothing other than that celestial heat. 27. Thus, he recognizes heat (which is actually cold in a fish) as the cause of fertility, since he distributes it to every power of the soul. This is truly selling trifles as Philosophy. And whenever he fears his nonsense will not find a buyer, he summons us to the "element of the stars." After he has (it seems) summoned us through one trifle and many denials to this "proportion of the stellar element." It is truly shameful for Christians to still follow this man as a patron in Physics, when we believe by faith that before the stars were even created, plants germinated by their own seminal power. 

<margin>5.</margin> For in nature there is always found an agent, matter, and a product (or effect), as well as an instrument and a disposition. Every agent measures its instrument and adapts the dispositions toward the end of the product. <margin>6.</margin> Heat, however—whether you want it to be elemental or celestial—can indeed be a "disposition" produced by the seed, and likewise its "instrument"; but it can in no way be the "seminal agent" that measures and adapts its own dispositive instruments. For the operation of heat is nothing other than to heat, whether that is said to be "elementally" or "firmamentally." Therefore, the operation of heat in generation is not ordered toward the end of the disposi-

For if that heat were this seminal agent, or the nature of seeds—aside from the fact that it would need as many specific differences as there are species of generated things in nature—it would necessarily possess outside of itself a measured and clearly determined instrument (since existence is not granted without essential properties) for the introduction of any specific essence. Indeed, since the knowledge of natural truth necessarily depends <margin>7.</margin> upon its nature and essence, Aristotle, who was ignorant of the essence <note>Original: "quidditatem."</note> of nature, also did not know its truth; thus, he offered nothing but his own dreams to be taught in the Schools. Therefore, whoever looks to heat as the sole instrument of nature, and takes this instrument itself to be the seminal and vital nature, is like someone who thinks a bodyguard is the King, or that a file is the blacksmith. Rather, heat, as heat, is not even a proper instrument of nature; it is merely a common byproduct in warm things, a companion and an accidental product. The knowledge of nature and essence is not gathered from improper, adjacent, and accidental effects, but from the knowledge of principles, which (as is evident) the Peripatetic School <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway in the Lyceum where Aristotle taught while walking.</note> has ignored until now. The principles of Bodies, however, are water and seed (or Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire/craftsmanship; here used metaphorically for the active, transformative principle), corresponding to the two sexes. They suppose Matter—or rather, an impossible corporeity combined with mathematical abstraction—to be the principle, the support, and the nursery of nature. Just as such a thing will never exist, so too will it never have the energy to initiate or cause anything. Likewise, "Privation" is offered as another principle, which the Schools themselves rashly admit is a mere non-entity. And finally, they teach that "Form"—the end of generation, the peak and ultimate goal of intention, and the product itself—is the *beginning* of nature; a truly preposterous delirium! They suppose the effect to be the beginning. 

In another book, he sells the "causes of nature" as principles—namely matter and form, omitting privation—as if to discuss causes for once. As if the principles of nature began by means of causality! Furthermore, "Fortune" and "Chance" are treated in a specific book as if they were proper passions of nature. Events of chance do not deserve a place in the contemplation and doctrine of nature. Finally, "Vacuum" and "the Infinite"—things irrelevant to the knowledge of nature, and almost entirely privative or plainly negative—have obtained their own treatises. Time and Place are estimated by the Schools as internal documents of nature no less ignorantly than impertinently. And lastly, they introduce "Local Motion" into nature just as futilely and with the same blurred lack of distinction, insofar as it serves Mathematics. 

I certainly wish that in the brief span of a young man’s life, <margin>9.</margin> they would no longer be imbued with such trifles and lying sophistry. During that useless three-year period, or even the whole seven years, they should instead learn Arithmetic, Algebra, the elements of Euclid, and then Geography—including the details of seas, rivers, springs, mountains, provinces, and minerals. Likewise, they should learn the properties and customs of nations, the nature of waters, plants, animals, and minerals.

It is far from the case that by the perishing of their life, they were corrupted by that very fact.
<margin>17.</margin>
Therefore, death in living things is not properly the corruption of life, nor of the living being, but the extinction of life. And although in some cases the corruption of the body follows, this is certainly incidental to life and the body. This is evident, since corpses are preserved from corruption by art. 
<margin>18.</margin>
Thus Aristotle already confuses privation <note>the absence of a quality</note> with corruption, and does not distinguish his principle of "non-being" from being through <margin>19.</margin> corruption. Finally, the forms of things are not subject to corruption, and therefore they do not rot; rather, they are annihilated. Therefore, the removal or extinction of a form cannot involve any corruption on the part of the form. I hate, moreover, metaphors in natural history and the family of essentials. For these have introduced the errors of the Schools <note>the traditional university system based on medieval logic</note>, the quarrels of disputation, and the worship shown to Aristotle. However, if Aristotle is ignorant of nature and unaware of all physics, truly Galen has everywhere manifested an even greater ignorance.

<column-break/>

<margin>20.</margin>
For first, I will make it clear that there is no "fourness" of elements, nor is their meeting responsible for bodies believed to be mixtures; much less is there a struggle or battle of qualities or <term>complexions</term> <note>the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note>, or causes of diseases. And so the treatise on elements does not properly belong to Medicine. I indeed find Galen to be a diligent and boastful describer of opinions without judgment or discretion. Nor did he perceive nature, diseases, causes, and defects better than he did the decrees of Hippocrates and <margin>21.</margin> Plato. Twice, indeed, I have read through those volumes of Galen with attention, but I found Galen’s poverty and indistinct ignorance struggling with his rashness. For those books touch on nothing less than the doctrine of Hippocrates or Plato. Nor does anything of Hippocrates have anything in common with Plato. And so I have not found anyone who would judge them worthy of commentary, nor as having been written about the preservation <margin>22.</margin> of health. This one thing is constant in Galen: that having suppressed the names of the authors, he willingly snatched the inventions of others for himself; he is entirely poor in judgment whenever he expresses the feelings of his own will. These things concerning the two vanguards of physics I ought to declare so that the Schools may abstain from worshipping these masters.

# THE ELEMENTS.

<margin>2.</margin>
I will now and again approach the <term>Anatomy of the Elements</term> <note>original: "elementorum Anatomiam"; a metaphorical term for dissecting or analyzing the fundamental components of matter</note>, so that it may be clear how much has been erred until now regarding the causes of diseases. I shall report Paradoxes everywhere, and things unusual to the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic institutions dominated by Aristotelian and Galenic thought</note>; and it will be hard for those who believe that all truth flowed from Galen to fall away from the doctrine they have soaked in. Galen—in many volumes and with the tedious boasting of the Greeks—handed down that every body (earth, water, air, and fire excepted) consists of the marriage of these four joined together, and thus from this, a body is called a "mixture." Furthermore, he claimed that the entire similarity and diversity of bodies arises from the unequal confluence and continuous battle of these four elements. The later Schools, however, still dispute undecidedly whether the elements persist with their own forms within the mixture, or whether, in each mixing, they are deprived of their own essential forms, which they might then reassume by a "peculiar indulgence" upon being separated from the general form of the mixture. Finally, they command that all infirmities and the primary fuel of our mortality descend from this inequality and the "duel" of the elements. It is truly a wonder how much has been brawled and written over these things: and it is piteous how much these loose dreams of trifles have until now deceived the world, prostituting empty and pernicious nonsense in the marketplaces of the Schools as medical science; and thus so harmful a delusion has deceived the obedience of the sick in the act of healing. 

<margin>3.</margin>
Therefore, setting aside the impostures of the Pagans <note>The author classifies Galen and Aristotle as "Pagans" whose authority should be secondary to Christian revelation</note>, I direct my experiences and the light granted to me according to the authority of the Sacred [Scriptures], in the sight of which light the "night-birds" <note>A metaphor for those who prefer the darkness of old, unexamined doctrines</note> flee. It is therefore most deeply to be grieved that darkness is still taught in the Schools of Christians, while the light of truth is available. In the beginning, therefore, the Almighty created Heaven and Earth before the first day had dawned. Then, on the first day, He created light and divided it from the darkness. On the second, He created the firmament, which would separate the waters above from the waters that were below it, and He named it Heaven. It is conspicuous from this, therefore, that before the first day, the

<margin>4.</margin>
over which the Spirit (whose name is Eternal) was carried, so that He might fill the fresh creature of water with His blessing. It is clear, therefore, that the creation of Heaven, water, and earth occurred before the [first] day, and is not numbered among the six days of creation described thereafter. It pleased the Eternal also to rest on the seventh day, which, in respect to the aforementioned creation, would have been the eighth, if it had been a day. And therefore, it was not referred to in the count of days, because the creation of elemental matter occurred before light was born. Finally, by this text, the <term>firmament</term> <note>original: "firmamentum"; the sky or expanse of the heavens</note> is not only the eighth star-bearing heaven, but at the same time also that which we, by our own authority, distinguish into seven "wandering" spheres <note>The seven planets of traditional astronomy: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. Although that <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest, fiery heaven, believed to be the dwelling place of God</note> joined with two companions is taken as one, another perhaps remains as the third: the "abyssal retreat" of the fountain of light, the inscrutable couch of the Divine Majesty. ->## THE ELEMENTS.<-

<margin>6.</margin> I consider the **waters** to be nobler than the **earth**: indeed, I hold that water is purer, simpler, more invisible, more constant, closer to the first principle, and a greater participant in celestial power than earth is. Therefore, the Eternal One willed that Heaven should contain the waters above itself, and something further still (on account of which it is called Heaven), which we call the air, the ether, or the **vital breeze**. Therefore,

<margin>7.</margin> no mention is made of the creation of water and air, because the etymology of "Heaven" <note>original: "Cœli etymon"; the author refers to the Hebrew *Shamayim*, which some early modern thinkers interpreted as a compound of "fire" and "water" or "there" and "water"</note> included both. And for this reason, I call these two elements

<margin>8.</margin> **primigenial** <note>meaning "first-born" or original</note> in respect to the earth. But nowhere do we read anything concerning the creation of **fire**: therefore, I do not recognize it among the elements, and I reject its name as part of paganism. Nor,

<margin>9.</margin> likewise, do I agree with **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> that fire should be recognized as a "supralunary" element under the name of the luminaries and stars, as if it were not created from the beginning; yet this would be necessary if it were to claim the lot of an element. I deny, therefore, that God created four elements, because he did not create fire as a fourth. And for that reason, it is a vain idea that fire flows materially into

<margin>10.</margin> the **mixture of bodies**. Consequently, the four-fold foundation of elements, qualities, temperaments (or complexions), and

<margin>11.</margin> diseases falls apart. For our **mechanics** <note>the author's term for experimental chemistry or laboratory work</note> has revealed to me that every body—such as a rock, a stone, a gem, flint, sand, marcasite, clay, earth, fired bricks, glass, lime, sulfur, etc.—can be transmuted into an **actual salt**, equal in weight to the body from which it was made. And this salt, when distilled several times with the "circulated salt" of Paracelsus, entirely loses its fixity and is finally transmuted into a liquor, which also eventually passes into **tasteless water**. This water is equal in weight to the salt from which it flowed. Indeed, I have learned how to reduce plants, flesh, bones, fish, and anything similar into their "mere three" <note>the *tria prima*: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>, from which I afterwards produced tasteless water. Metal, however, because of the "anatic" <note>original: "anaticam"; likely referring to a proportional or equalized union</note> joining of its seed, and sand (<term>quellem</term> <note>a specific term used by the author to describe the primordial, gritty earth</note>) are reduced into salt with the greatest difficulty.

<margin>12.</margin> I have learned therefore through fire that God,

<column-break/>

before the first day, created water and air, and out of water created the elemental earth, which is the sand called <term>quellem</term>. Because this was to be the future basis for man, the leader of all creatures, it had to be created at the very beginning, even though by its own nature it was not truly primigenial. For this reason, I find only **two primitive elements**, even though neither is explicitly mentioned in the Holy Scriptures, because they are encompassed by the title of Heaven. Truly, along with those two, He created the earth at the same time. On account of which He created two great luminaries: the Moon, as the lesser, to govern the water by its light; and the greater, the Sun, to shine upon the earth.

<margin>13.</margin> I shall soon show that these primigenial elements are never transmuted into one another. Truly, in the earth, the decaying water acquires a "local" or "insown" seed. Thus it passes either into a liquor (<term>Leffas</term> <note>a Helmontian term for the vital juice or "sap" that nourishes plants</note>) for every plant, or into a mineral juice (<term>Bur</term> <note>a Helmontian term for the metallic "liquid" or first matter of minerals</note>), according to the species chosen by the direction of the seeds. These seeds, from the ferment of the earth (first "empty and void," then soon after filled by the blessing of the Spirit moving over the waters), are brought to fulfillment.

<margin>14.</margin> My experience with fire has taught me that the "three firsts"—namely, the **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** of water—always remain undivided, whether the water is meanwhile raised as a vapor in the form of a cloud, or rarefied into invisible things, or finally even fluctuates in the original form of water.

<margin>15.</margin> For as to Paracelsus’s claim that water is utterly annihilated by evaporating: let that be his own ignorance, which should not be overlooked even by a novice distiller. Indeed, I have found that water raised into the atoms of clouds always remains the same in number and species as the water which the "atoms of the mercury of water" show to us in the image of a cloud. Moreover, a separation of the three firsts never occurs in water, much less any essential transmutation. For-

<margin>16.</margin> -asmuch as it is a simple outward turning of the internal parts by fire, which return back inside as often as the vapor is condensed into drops. *1. Fire is neither an element, nor materially mixed into bodies, nor is it matter, nor does it contain matter in itself. 2. Earth is not part of a mixture. 3. <margin>1.</margin> Therefore, Fire is not an element, nor is it materially mixed into bodies; for I shall show that fire is neither matter, nor does it have matter within itself.

<margin>2.</margin> Indeed, earth is never encountered—except as itself—mixed into any natural body from which it might be recovered by any labor. I have therefore grieved, and felt indignant within myself, that the very basis of the art of healing is stuffed with such trifles, and that the sick are forced to obey such mockeries.

<margin>3.</margin> However, I give the name of **original earth** or the **virgin element** to the constant body of sand itself: the rest of the earth, of every kind, I call the "fruit of the earth," born of mineral offspring. This is proved more than sufficiently through **Pyrotechnia** <note>the "art of fire," or chemistry</note>. For that sand is the original earth is proved first by its difficult reduction into water; for sand is more quickly reduced into water from flint or even Diamond than it is from common sand (the *quel-lem*).

<margin>4.</margin> Furthermore, the mattock <note>original: "ligo," a digging tool</note> also proves this; because by digging, various layers are encountered near the light, variegated in color and thickness. Even if, according to the rustic

<column-break/>

etymology of the Schools <note>referring to the traditional university scholars who followed Aristotle</note>, these are believed to be black, white, yellow, or red earths, etc., they are nonetheless fruits of the earth and consist of seeds. Beneath these layers lies the sand, which is also many-fold in its varieties of depths in different places; finally, beneath all of those, sits the grit, which our people call the *Keybergh* <note>Flemish for "Quay-mountain" or "Stone-mountain"</note> or the siliceous mountain, from which the origin of rocks and mountains and the primary riches of mines flow. At the very last of all, the white or "boiling" sand (*quel-lem*) reveals itself in the living and vital bottom, which the mattock never penetrates. For however much sand and water you take from there, just as much succeeds in place of what was taken, filling the same space. This unmixed sand, I say, is a kind of "sieve" or strainer, and the foundation of nature, through which all waters are filtered, so that they all maintain a mutual communion from the beginning of creation to the end, and from the surface of the earth all the way to the center.

<margin>5.</margin> Moreover, the water held in this foundation of sand is perhaps, in actual fact, a thousand times greater than the entire mass of seas and rivers flowing on the surface of the earth. This is easily verified by assuming the entire surface of the earth were still covered by waters to a depth of 600 paces. It follows, therefore, when the relationship to the earth’s diameter is considered, that there is easily a thousand times more water below the earth than above it. For dry sand absorbs at least nearly four times its volume of water in the same space. I do not mean, however, that even if the *quel-lem* is the final depth for a digger, that all the layers are found spread out in that exact order everywhere. For the aforementioned sand, which sometimes sinks perhaps a thousand paces below the horizon, at other times boils up in the open air, or even, not rarely, on the very peaks of mountains.

<margin>6.</margin> Regarding this matter, the Schools are ignorant, along with their Aristotle...

# E A R T H.

<meta>catchword: tritio-</meta>

The followers of Aristotle stubbornly maintain <note>original: "Aristot. mordicus tenent"; referring to the "Peripatetics" or Scholastic philosophers who followed Aristotle's teachings as absolute truth</note> that all true springs owe the cause of their permanence to air that has been condensed into water. However, they are unable to defend this position; for on the peaks of the highest mountains, springs frequently gush forth where there is no other mountain of equal height nearby, nor any pipe extending from both sides for this purpose. Therefore, with a haughty brow, they remain silent and keep still regarding this unusual miracle <margin>7.</margin> of nature. Truly, as long as waters wander within the living and vital depths of the earth, and are held within the "boiling sand" <term>quellem</term> <note>a Flemish term used by the author to describe a spring-source or quicksand where water defies gravity</note>, they are not, I say, compelled to obey the hydraulic laws of position. It is no different than blood: while life is nourished within the veins, it likewise knows no "above" or "below," and is present in the forehead just as it is in the feet. But the moment it falls from the veins, or the waters gush out from the boiling sand, they do not cease to flow downward in obedience to the laws of position. Therefore, the sea, in its own depths, swallows the waters received into the sieve of "virgin sand," exactly according to the Wise Man <margin>8.</margin> <note>A reference to King Solomon in Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full."</note>; though all waters flow into the sea, it never overflows. This is because there is a continuous duct, like a single thread, established from the virgin sand into the springs, brooks, rivers, and the sea, to moisten the earth and enrich it with minerals. From there, the driven waters are partly absorbed back into the depths by the boiling sand and partly carried away by the air. Thus, the whole world distributes its waters and yields them into various fruits. I have meditated with admiration on how the Almighty has set the necessities of ungrateful mortals <margin>9.</margin> as the very goals of all things. I return to the earth. I have found it certain that the "original earth" nowhere concurs spontaneously in the mixtures of fruits, nor does it fall in by chance, nor is it taken up by nature—nor, once taken up, is it ever found through the work of nature or art. Therefore, the logic of "mixtures" <margin>10.</margin> <note>Aristotelian "mixture" (mistio) suggested that elements combine to form a new substance</note> fails; the count of elements, qualities, and temperaments <note>The "four humors" or balances of hot/cold/wet/dry that dominated medieval medicine</note> ceases; and thus, those deceptive futilities, stubbornly or ignorantly cultivated by the Schools until now, are false. For even if dust or ash is left behind from a man or from wood by fire, "earth" is nonetheless never extracted from it.

<column-break/>

Otherwise, our cemeteries would soon <margin>11.</margin> swell up with the accumulation of material. Earth, therefore, is at most a permanent **matrix** <note>a mold or container</note>, but not the **mother** <note>the actual material source</note>. If earth ever flowed into fruits or mixed bodies, it would either persist in them (and thus be found through the analysis of art or nature, and return from there—which is false), or it would be entirely absorbed into the mixture and cease to be earth, having been transmuted into something else. In that case, the amount of earth elsewhere would decrease (which I will soon show is equally false). Or, through death and the dissolution of the thing, it would return again into earth, and there would be a daily and repeated return from "privation" to "habit" of one and the same element. Or if it did not return into this earth, it would remain transmuted into fruits, and thus long ago the entire earth would have been converted into fruit, and nature would have lost its stability and mocked the Creator's original goals; or the earth would have returned into another element from the dissolved mixture. The absurdity of this is clear. Indeed, <margin>12.</margin> it is not in the nature of water or air to convert a foreign element into its own substance. Hence I will soon demonstrate that not a single drop of water has ever been turned into air, nor conversely has air been changed into water. Yet these changes appear less laborious than the change of earth into water or air. Therefore, if nature has not yet attempted the easier transmutations, how can one presume it does the more difficult ones? Otherwise, the earth would have been absorbed and annihilated by the waters and air, which are so much more vast, contiguous, and active. But the Father of the Universe, being a lover of harmony, hates discord and strife, especially among the elements; He created them not to be at war, so that they might be the stable pillars of nature. He directed the elements toward their destined ends and laws of duration. Namely, that the earth should bring forth and nourish its fruits for His honor and for the use of man. However, neither the honor of God nor human necessity required anywhere, or in any way, the battles of elements, their voracities, or their struggles for destruction—nor the commutation of one into another.

<margin>13.</margin> Thus, Earth is never taken up, nor does it materially rush in of its own accord, into the constitution of bodies outside of itself. No mixture in nature is formed correctly—coalescing firmly under the unity of a natural composite form—except between juices and spirits. Conversely, no powdery mixture tends toward generation; instead, it is merely an "apposition" <note>a mechanical placing of things side by side without true chemical bonding</note>, which soon and spontaneously falls apart again. Accordingly, all earth, mud, and every tangible body is truly and materially the offspring of water alone, and is reduced to water again through nature and art <note>the term "art" in this context refers to alchemy or early chemistry</note>.

<margin>14.</margin> Nor does it stand in the way that bricks are baked from mud and sand, or glass from sand and ash. For whatever mud there is, it eventually resolves spontaneously into salt, while the same sand remains which the mud had drawn into itself. Likewise glass, which passed into an artificial composite by art and without a seed: so by art again, once the bond is loosened, it returns to its pristine beginnings, such that the same number and weight of sand is entirely drawn out from it—the very same sand which, through the flow of the furnace, had coalesced with alkali into a transparent stone, or glass. For from this it is clear that sand, or the element of earth, never flows together for natural and seminal <note>referring to the "seeds" or blueprints of life</note> generations. And as often as it serves the craftsman's arts, the sand always persists unchanged within the glass, hidden by the glowing flow of salt and taken up into the transparent glass. For silver does not cease to be silver when it is dissolved by *Chrysulca* <term>Chrysulca</term> <note>literally "gold-puller," an early chemical term for acid, usually nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</note>, even if
