the eye has lost sight of it and it has acquired transparency. Therefore, since original sand or earth <margin>15.</margin> resists both art and nature, and cannot by any aids (except for the single fire of an artificial Gehenna <term>Gehenna</term> <note>an alchemical term for an intense, destructive fire or a specialized furnace capable of total reduction</note>) depart from its primeval constancy through nature or art—under which artificial fire the sand flows, and finally becomes water, because it has the power to act upon any sublunary thing without reaction—it follows also that original earth is never taken up in any way for the seminal generations of nature. Nor does it <margin>16.</margin> prove anything that some unskilled person might wish glass to be the ultimate subject of art, and that it therefore cannot be destroyed by art or fire. For he will be instructed if he melts glass dust with more alkali and exposes it to a damp place; he will soon find all the glass resolved into water. If *Chrysulca* is poured into this, adding enough to saturate the alkali, he will immediately find sand settling at the bottom, of the same weight as was previously suited for making the glass. Therefore, earth persists unchanged, although it seems to have been mobile and moved throughout the whole world. Indeed, a mole, by <margin>17.</margin> digging through a mound, causes the flooding of a large tract; thus a lowly animal can move the earth from its center and the world from its place, if we believe the center of gravity holds its place, and we see the seas recently resting upon the back of the earth. <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring floral and scrolling vine motifs.</image-desc>At the very least, after the Eternal One separated the waters from the waters by the firmament, He gathered the sublunary <note>referring to the region below the moon, i.e., the Earthly realm</note> waters and called their collection the "Sea." Directly opposite this, the Dry Land stood out, which He named "Earth"; and both constituted a single globe. This globe was somewhat more prominent in the middle of the earth for this reason: in the center of the earth, it gaped with an immense abyss, from which a spring burst forth, destined to moisten the land. For if the earth had not been much higher in its center—beyond the usual roundness of a globe where all lines are equidistant from the center—then the spring could not have flowed down from there to the lower sea; instead, it would have stagnated immediately at its source. From this, I conceive that in the beginning, the Earth was continuous and undivided, since the whole of it had to be irrigated by a single spring. Finally, it had no islands; rather, the entire globe showed the sea on one side and the land on the other. This was indeed the face of the world before the flood. Afterward, during the flood, the earth gaped into various sections, and from the abyss of these rifts, waves erupted in abundance. The floodgates of both the lower abyss and the heavens were opened so that they might utterly submerge the entire globe of the earth.

<margin>2.</margin>
Great God! You intended to prune Your vine of its useless branch and to punish the world as it deserved, yet You could not yet refrain, mindful of Your paternal affection, from separating the land in the midst of Your most just anger. You tore it apart for the greater utility, necessity, and convenience of mankind. The sea, which previously stood as a single mass on only one side of the globe, You sent across various shores of the earth, and You did not cease from a new blessing upon the ungrateful work of Your hands. For upon the earth, guilty in Your sight, You abundantly poured out vital vortices of super-celestial waters, which far surpass dew in fertility. The earth, truly intoxicated by these, shone forth again and returned unceasingly to its accustomed labors. Finally, that single spring and source of waters, which You had placed in the heart and summit of the earth, was thereafter diffused into a thousand veins which pierce the globe of the earth almost everywhere for far better uses. Indeed, You even washed the sea into almost every bosom of the land, so that there might be a greater society of mortals. Blessed and fortunate, therefore, be Your punishment; what then shall the gifts of Your blessings be? Lord, keep us, according to the immensity of Your goodness, among the number of those who will praise Your magnificence forever, in the sanctification of Your name.

# WATER #

In turn, the Schools <note>The academic authorities of the time, typically Aristotelian philosophers</note> easily promise that these things are interchanged; but before I descend to that point, I shall elucidate another paradox. <margin>13.</margin> Namely, that the globe composed of earth and water is indeed round from the East, through the West, and back to the East; yet it is not so from the North <note>original: "Aquilone"</note> to the South <note>original: "Austrum"</note>, but is instead oblong, or of an oval shape. This fact has especially deceived many sailors. It is because the waters glide with a swifter course from the North to the South than they do otherwise from East to West. For a great many waters always descend from the North through rivers, and these never flow back toward the North. Thus the Danube glides into the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea</note> along with many others; the waters descend through the Hellespont, and nothing returns from the Mediterranean. Whatever once falls into the Mediterranean is never scattered back into the Ocean. For the Nile, always descending in a straight line from the Mountains of the Moon <note>A legendary mountain range in East Africa, long thought to be the source of the Nile</note>, merges into the Sebennytic mouth <note>original: "Zebenuticum," one of the ancient mouths of the Nile delta</note>, entire with all its branches; meanwhile, the Mediterranean neither grows larger nor becomes saltier. This, however, would be entirely necessary if the waters poured in were to exhale from the sea only as bare vapor. But Eternal Wisdom made the Mediterranean deeper than the Ocean in most places, so that the virginal sand, like a sieve, might drink up the waters together with their salts. For human necessities (which seem to have dictated a law to God out of His goodness) required springs and rivers falling from the highest peaks. Finally, the waters poured out from the source-matter <term>quellem<gloss>a primal, flowing substance or spring-source</gloss></term> through springs, draw the following waters after them by continuity, and thus they also drink up the waters of the seas by sucking them from the bottom. Therefore, properties were added to places by Divine Providence because of these necessities. The flow of the Northern sea, below Kent in England <note>original: "sub Angliæ Kentonia"</note>, anticipates the flow of the Western sea by almost half an hour. From this, I conjecture that the land and the sea rise toward the Northern region. For Scandinavia <note>original: "Scandia"</note> is so named from "ascending" <note>original: "à scandendo," a popular but false etymology suggesting the land "climbs" upward</note>, being the entire Northern land. And the Northern sea would not freeze if it were salty. If it is fresh, it denotes that the salt of the Ocean cannot be mixed with it while ascending, but rather that the Northern waters rush incessantly down a slope.

<column-break/>

For it is likely that, both in the first mixing of the abyss and in the flood of the Cataclysm, all the waters were mixed once and again, and the mixing of these was therefore called the "sea." Those waters, therefore, which were once salty at the beginning and soon thereafter became fresh: it is certain that they have continually flowed downward, because they are fresh today; and thus Scandinavia is situated far higher than Egypt. But let us merely imagine that the earth established a rim for the sea of ten feet on the shores on both sides, and let us maintain a uniform roundness: at the very least, the Nile—which is carried headlong in a straight line from the South into the Mediterranean Sea for a thousand leagues—if it followed only the roundness of the sphere (which is not sloped anywhere, but rather behaves like a plane in relation to the center), it would have at most a drop of ten feet from its source all the way to the sea. This would be to call the Nile a quiet pond, not a running river. Indeed, when a trench was being planned from Ghent <note>original: "Gaudavo"</note> to Bruges <note>original: "Brugas"</note>, a drop of 18 feet in height was discovered, the measurement having been taken at night by the flame of a candle <note>A 17th-century surveying technique to establish a level line over long distances</note>, and this was after subtracting the roundness of the sphere. If, therefore, in a slow-moving channel, there are 18 feet of descent over eight leagues, the Nile, flowing just as slowly, would need a height of at least 2,230 feet at its beginning. But if it flows in the manner of the Nile <note>i.e., swiftly</note>, it will necessarily need four times that at minimum: or nine thousand feet. Now, if the Nile measures this height of the earth over 15 degrees, from the Southern Tropic to the Mediterranean Sea, where the figure of the globe is still spherical, what may we not then conjecture from the Mountains of the Moon all the way to the South? This tireless fall of waters from the North promises a remarkable elevation of the earth. <margin>14.</margin> So it is. But from this, one cannot conclude that all the waters will immediately desert the North, given that elevation; <margin>15.</margin> for the laws of position are silent where water falls toward the center of the world from all sides. And so it was a necessity of the universe and a rule of its properties. For I imagine a sublunary place without a tangible body, but a smooth flint stone from the Heavens... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page</note>

It would express for us the figure of the world. Let us imagine a round stone outside the highest Heaven. Therefore the shortest night is at most only 7 hours. In the winter solstice, however, the sun rises 15 minu- <margin>21.</margin> tes before eight, and sets 27 minutes before four. Therefore the shortest day is at least 7 hours and 42 minutes. It detracts from the roundness of the sphere to have more light than darkness. Finally, modern voyages have seen the Sun in the north for a month before the perfect roundness of the heavens would have permitted it.

<header>AIR</header>

## A Mathematical Demonstration that Air and Water are Primal Elements, and are Never Mutually Interchangeable by Cold or Heat.

The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic academics who followed traditional Aristotelian philosophy.</note> still hold with their Aristotle that air is moist to the eighth degree—that is, supremely moist—but warm only to the fourth degree, or moderately so. To water, however, they grant the highest degree of coldness, with a diminished or moderate moisture. Thus, they command that air be twice as moist as water, based on the idea that air, through its own compression and gathering together, generates water. But I ask you: what is this other than selling dreams for the truth? For if air were condensed, its moisture would also become denser, greater, and more palpable in the water than it was previously in the air. Since condensation by no means creates a new essential form, nor is it the principle of generation <note>term: generation (the process by which a new substance comes into being)</note>, what is this but irrelevant nonsense? At the very least, water would be nothing but air condensed tenfold (or rather a hundredfold) in its moisture, and thus more active; therefore, it would moisten a hundred times more, and more strongly, than air. <margin>18.</margin> It is so far from the truth, then, that water would be less moist than air. But if mere condensation were to dispose air toward a new form, since that same disposition of the internal efficient cause is a necessary cause of the thing generated, it must remain the same in the product. Therefore, if condensed air were water, there would now be only two elements: namely, water and earth. Meanwhile, water would be just as moist as the air was previously, in which only condensation intervened. This is merely a joining together of parts, not a formal transformation of one thing into another. Indeed, in every way, the form resulting from the moisture of air condensed a hundredfold would be at least a hundred times moister, and would moisten more, than the original air. But surely water does not moisten

on account of its density (otherwise, earth would moisten even more), because moisture alone moistens, and not density. Otherwise, quicksilver <note>mercury</note> would moisten wool or the hand more than water does. For whatever moistens more is itself moister; and vice versa, whatever is moister in the nature of the elements also moistens more. Nature laughs at those who demand faith in place of known senses based on a dream, and who still teach the shameful fictions of Aristotle as truth. But the Schools say: "Thus it must be taught because of the axiom: *That because of which a thing is such, is itself more such.*" <note>original: "Propter quod unumquodque est tale, illud ipsum est magis tale." A logical principle suggesting that if air makes water moist, air must be even moister.</note> (As if one should lie to God for the sake of an axiom's honor!) They claim water is not moist except because of air; therefore, air must be moister than water. But they will sweat more than enough before they prove this foundation. In truth, air in itself is neither moist nor warm; whatever moisture is in it is a foreign content, never reaching the nature of the air itself, even though vapors are contained within the pores of the air. For what does it concern the nature of glass if it has enclosed water within itself? I shall soon show that it is impossible for air and water to be changed into one another. Thus, through absurdities, the Schools 3. suppose entirely impossible theorems. It is also absurd and impossible that condensed air becomes water and serves as the perpetual source of springs. For I have seen air in an iron tube of one ell <note>a historical unit of length</note> compressed to the space of nearly fifteen inches, which then, by its own explosion—like a gun driven by gunpowder—sent small balls through a board. This certainly 4. would not happen if air, when compressed, could be forced into water. Especially since that experiment would succeed no less in the most intense cold of winter than in the heat of summer. If therefore air, compressed by force while the tube and the weather are cold, is not changed into water, by what authority do the Schools establish their fictions about the condensation of air as the source and continuation of springs? For cold in nature does not have

Indeed, no trace of moisture is found in the aforementioned tube <note>original: "canna"; likely referring to a pneumatic pump or syringe used in experiments</note>; on the contrary, a piece of leather moistened at the end of the thrusting piston dries out immediately. It is also ridiculous to prove that air is 5. humid by the origin of springs, and then to turn around and prove the origin of springs by the assumed humidity of the air. Both arguments of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval system of philosophy and theology based on Aristotle</note> arise from a lack of truth and are a childish begging of the question <note>original: "petitio puerilis principii"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</note>. And so that they may adorn the four elements with qualities, they assign to each one "excellent" quality and one "diminished" quality; thus the Schools command Nature to obey their own fictions. They say, therefore, that air is 6. "diminishedly" hot. This is because they want it to be near the fictional element of fire: that is, either because it borrows that diminished quality from its neighbor, changing its own native character at the whim of its neighbor—which is irrelevant when the conversation concerns native properties—or because it possesses that quality by its own nature, and although it is diminished, it nevertheless has it, and thus it had such a neighbor. This is equally irrelevant and 7. unfortunate. And so that they may prove the moderate heat of the air, they introduce "Antiperistasis" <note>A philosophical concept where one quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being "trapped" by cold</note>, an equally futile invention. Namely, they imagine that the air is hot in its uppermost part due to the proximity of fire (and thus they feign a heat that is not essential, but borrowed by accident and improper) and that it is likewise hot near the earth from the reflection of the sun's rays. This heat is a stranger, occurring by accident within such a small space; therefore, it is a fictional property of the air. Yet they claim the middle region of the air is miraculously cold because of Antiperistasis. Specifically, because it is surrounded on both sides by warm parts of the air. They say something similar happens in deep wells, which are cold in summer and 8. lukewarm all through the winter. But I marvel at the profound stupidities of the Schools and the "down-dragging" <note>original: "Catochum"; likely from the Greek 'katochos', implying a state of being possessed or held down by old dogmas</note> of the ancients. 1. Because from this entire structure of theirs, it appears that air is generally cold, not moderately warm. 2. Since fire is not an element in nature, much less beneath the hollow of the moon, it cannot heat the upper air except in dreams. 3. For if air were hot of itself and by elemental property, then it would be hot always and everywhere, even in deep wells. 4. If indeed it is heated by something else congenial to it, then besides the fact that it would have something mixed with it whereby the simplicity of its elemental body would cease, it would also always and everywhere be hot in that way; or finally, it would be hot because of some adjacent agent, by accident. This is irrelevant whenever an assumption regarding essentials must be proven. Therefore, if air is not hot of itself, it is necessary that it be cold of itself, since those two qualities successively exclude each other in nature. 5. If fire is never cold or humid, and water is never dry, then air can never be less than intensely humid and "diminishedly" hot, if the Schools speak the truth. 6. They claim a middle region of the air which is scarcely half a mile distant from us, unmindful of their own doctrine. They say the diameter of the air exceeds the diameter of water tenfold, and this in turn is ten times greater than the diameter of the earth. If this fiction were granted, the semi-diameter of the air would be more than 570,000 miles deep. Therefore, a half-mile would be as nothing in respect to the middle of the air. Schools, I pray you, wake up! For if air were warm spontaneously and by its own nature, for what reason would it be cold in its middle? Is it because its neighbor on both sides is warm? But then the air would not feel indignation, but rather joy, from the conformity of a neighboring nature. For why would air strip off its native property simply because it touches air creeping on both sides that is conformable to itself? For how will lukewarm water poured into lukewarm water grow cold because it finds lukewarmness on both sides? Or if a cold thing is placed between two cold things, will it therefore become warm in its middle? I cannot sufficiently marvel at the unpolished rudeness of the Schools, who hand down the doctrine of Antiperistasis, which desires such great credulity rather than judgment. For even if that fiction were pleasing while the air near the earth is warm, it certainly could not hold in the frosts of winter.

It is so clear from this that, either out of a stubborn zeal, the followers of the Peripatetic school <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> teach known falsehoods so as not to break their oath to the word of **Aristotle**, or else they believe no judgment remains for them to honestly perform their duty; they think they have done enough if they simply follow the herds of those who went before them. **Antiperistasis** <note>term: Antiperistasis. In this, we see by mechanical demonstration that the air in deep wells and cellars remains stable at the same point of heat, whether one chooses to measure it in winter or in the greatest heat of summer. 10. For we see mechanically that a limb almost frozen grows warm again under snow and is preserved from "blasting" <note>frostbite or gangrene</note>; whereas otherwise the air would soon proceed to freeze it totally, or if it were suddenly brought to a fire, it dies because of the hasty action of the other extreme. Therefore, it is better to go through the middle: if one goes from the cold air, through the snow, the water, and then into a relaxed warmth. Therefore, snow is less cold than the air. 12. But why do they invoke its density for the moisture of water to dampen it (which is ridiculous)? At least they might have said something plausible if they claimed the same density of water did not flow because of the cold. Pay attention, therefore, whoever you are who strives to work for the health of the soul by **healing**, to what kind of patron the Schools still defend. With what plan have they made the elements, complexions, and degrees of qualities the basis of healing—they who, led only by a sluggish credulity, gave names to the number, essence, use, properties, fruits, and passions of the elements according to their pagan blindness? See how slavishly the Schools have borrowed the **elemental qualities**, and wished them to obey the pleasures of their dreams; they have combined, increased, blunted, and diverted them like sallow fabrications, and passed them down as the causes of natural things, the knowledge of diseases, healings, and the devastation of the **temples of the Holy Spirit** <note>The human body</note>. Air, therefore, water, and earth are cold by creation, because they are without light, heat, and participation in life. Heat, therefore, is a stranger to them, external to the elemental root. But air and earth are, of themselves, dry; only water is moist. These are the qualities of those bodies, which no one may vary at his whim. Air, however, has vacuities (as mentioned elsewhere in its place) in which it drinks up and holds vapors. This is the state, order, and complexion of the elements. And this touches the medical profession only indirectly. Thus, in the Schools, that which is of least use is investigated most as if it were of the greatest moment, and I shall show that what is of the greatest moment has been neglected until now. This is because the entire labor of healers has yielded to mockeries and useless brawls. Therefore, if the elements do not enter into a mixture, the doctrine of the Schools is vain regarding the number, composition, temperaments, unequal concurrence, contrariety, proportion, struggle, and **degree of the elements**; for degrees are bound to the seeds of simple things, not to the element. These are vain trifles—whether the forms of the elements remain in the mixture—since they are not present: as the element...

## I. *That Air and Water are bodies that cannot be changed into one another.*

Although I have demonstrated in the presence of many that Heer <note>Henri de Heer (1570–1636), a rival physician at Spa</note>, in his *Apologue* against my booklet on the waters of Spa, impertinently used my own instrument; nevertheless, he does not fail to involve me in his stupidities. For he says: I wished to produce perpetual motion. He did not even recognize that in this he contradicts himself. For in the instrument, motion ceases after the water has ascended or descended according to the temperature of the surroundings. Nor can this motion be called "perpetual" any more than a weathercock <note>original: "velum templi," literally a temple sail or cloth</note> destined for the changing of the winds. Heer thus reveals that he does not know what perpetual motion is. For I had made my instrument public so that, according to my doctrine on the springs of Spa, I might prove that air undergoes the common rarefaction and compression without any change to its element. For Heer says: the spirit of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid</note> penetrated the substance of the glass; which no one will concede who knows that far more subtle liquids are preserved even in fire. Nor did it help that I had affirmed to him
<image-desc>A drawing of a glass instrument, possibly a thermometer or a chemical apparatus, with a bulb at the bottom and a long, thin stem.</image-desc>
that Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a famous Jesuit mathematician and astronomer</note> in the College of the Roman Society <note>The Jesuit Roman College</note> sixty years ago had enclosed water in glass of this shape, of which not even the smallest drop had perished. This was shown by a line marked there with a diamond. Heer, however, boasted among the unlearned <note>original: "Idiotas," meaning those lacking formal education</note> that he had once been a Professor of Mathematics at Padua. Therefore, I wished to demonstrate on paper his total ignorance of mathematics. But he became mute in my presence. Regarding the demonstration, it proceeded thus: A figure of the glass was drawn, in which A and D are two spheres filled with air. A, the upper one, is closed on all sides from the outside. D, however, is the lower globe, open at the end of the Channel F. Moreover, A and D are connected from a single piece of glass through the channel B C E, in which there is a liquor of vitriol (so that it would not spoil), which I told the inquiring Heer had been made red by the soaking of roses so that it would be more visible. Let that red liquor, therefore, be B C. Upon this figure, I constructed this problem:

<margin>13.</margin> **Given.** That vessel D is as tightly closed as vessel A is, according to his hypothesis. **Required.** To be demonstrated: That the water B C cannot move. Likewise, that it cannot show the temperature of the air. Likewise, that it could not have dried up or exhaled. Pushing against the water B C, it will destroy the **equilibrium** through excessive action. Thus, in D, the air will be compressed and condensed through restriction, so that it yields to the expansion made in A.

**Demonstration.** Therefore, according to the **hypothesis of Heer** (that compressed air is converted into water), the liquid would never have been missing from the vessel. However, his own observation maintains that, although the glass was exquisitely closed on all sides, the water nevertheless dried up and became air. He cannot admit this drying in an exquisitely closed glass without his hypothesis being destroyed (namely, that compressed air changes into water); nor can that hypothesis stand unless he admits the continuation of the liquid. Yet this contradicts his own observation. Likewise, he cannot admit the movement of the liquid B C unless he admits the glass is open at F; and consequently, he must confess that he erred in his observation. And although he was forced to confess by the force of demonstrations before he vomited out his **Apology** <note>a formal written defense</note> full of every kind of slander against me, he nevertheless persisted in it, revealing his own ignorance.

<margin>1.</margin> **P** <note>Large ornamental initial P</note> It is already well enough established that water, by the force of heat, is raised in the form of vapor; this vapor is nonetheless nothing but thinned water, and remains as it was before, and therefore, when struck back by an Alembic <note>A distilling apparatus</note>, it returns to its original weight of water. One might suspect, however, whether water, consumed by the cold of the air, might be changed into the nature and properties of air. For after the Deluge <note>The Biblical Great Flood</note>, the Almighty sent winds to dry the face of the earth. And even today, under the freezing North Wind, water is absorbed more quickly than by summer heats. Also, a fountain under the most chilling cold, falling into a basin in a continuous stream, is prevented from freezing by the motion of the falling spring: yet a certain vapor is seen to ascend, which soon becomes invisible and is snatched away into the air. The presumption is that the entire nature of air is consumed at least by cold, if <margin>2.</margin> not by heat. First, I respond: granted that absurdity, the Schools <note>The traditional academic authorities/Scholasticism</note> have nothing to gain for themselves from it; for air would then be moist of itself—far from it, that air (as they maintain) would be much more moist than water. Rather, it is at least dried water. For a transmuted thing always loses the properties it had in its starting point and borrows the qualities of the transmuting agent. For either all air would have once been water, or only that air would be moist which was born from water: while the other, original air would have been dry from creation. And thus there would be two airs, essentially different. However, that air in its purity is dry by internal property is clear from the objection, especially regarding cold. For if air, from its root, were moist, winds would not have been sent to dry the earth. But if indeed the waters of the flood were truly changed into air by the winds, there would be much more air after the flood than before. Consequently, either some part of the world would have been a vacuum, or certainly, we would now be suffocated by the compression and density caused by such a new mass of air (which will later be revealed through the mechanics of a candle), or an equal part of air would have had to be successively annihilated during the generation of so much new air. Since the Text <note>The Bible</note> maintains that such deep waters, and the entire surface of the earth, were dried at once by the winds. Or, if before the flood, the waters had been air in the floodgates of heaven, then at least during the whole flood, there would have been a vacuum in those floodgates of heaven: if indeed water is (at minimum) a hundred times thicker and more compressed than air. Therefore, I propose as a thesis: <margin>3.</margin> Water never perishes, not even through cold, nor can it be changed into air by any efforts of nature or art; and conversely, air, in no age or by any disposition, can be reduced into water (not even for a single droplet). For water does not tolerate a vacuum, nor its own compression by any moving force. It is only compressed by a seminal thickening, through its formal transmutation. On the opposite side, air cannot exist without a <margin>4.</margin> vacuum (which I shall prove in its own chapter), and therefore it tolerates its own compression and dilation. They are therefore two stable elements, differing from each other in nature and properties, such that it is impossible for them to be changed into one another. I confess indeed that an aqueous breath ascends from the basin of a fountain, like a mist, made of the smallest atoms of water; which breath, although it becomes altogether invisible a short distance away, does not therefore invalidate the given doctrine. 5. Than at first. Because it is an element and a body, it is impossible for it to be reduced into a greater simplicity than its own destination allows. Since thinning through the division of parts is nothing other than a kind of simple grinding <note>original: "trituratio"</note>. For example:

6. Beat gold into sheets, then into the thinnest gold leaf, then into painters' gold, and soon grind it smooth again upon marble. Then, with cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note> and salt, fashion it into an impalpable powder <note>original: "alcool"; here meaning a fine powder rather than liquid alcohol</note>, separate the cinnabar by fire, and wash away the salt with water; repeat this as often as you like. Finally, with sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, antimony, and sublimated mercury, drive it through a retort. Repeat this seven times, until all the gold is reduced into the form of a volatile, pomegranate-colored oil. For it is a body most highly smoothed—indeed, it remains a hard, solid, malleable, and most fixed body—which now only *appears* to have turned into the nature of an oil. But truly, that deceptive liquor is easily reduced back into the original weight and body of gold. If, therefore, gold does not change its original nature through so many "slaughters" <note>original: "lanienas"; a vivid term for violent chemical processes</note>, nor lose its seed in any way, much less will water change, being a simple element destined by the Lord of things for the constancy of the universe.

7. Even if water possessed the three common principles and truly consisted of salt, sulfur, and mercury mixed together <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsian alchemy</note>, it nevertheless does not allow any separation of these, because of the exquisite simplicity of its nature and the most stable perpetuity of its constancy. For when bodies are thinned to the highest degree, so that they can be thinned no further, if the thinning were continued, they would finally pass into another substance while retaining their seminal properties. And thus far the *Alkahest* of Paracelsus <note>The hypothetical "universal solvent" capable of reducing any body to its prime matter</note>, by penetrating all bodies of nature, transforms them by thinning. This does not happen in the elements of water and air because, on account of their supreme simplicity and the priority of their destination, they refuse to migrate or be transformed into anything prior or simpler. Therefore, while breaths <note>vapors</note> impregnated with the odors and seeds of composite things are carried from the lower regions to the middle region of the air: there, because of the most subtle division of vapors by the cold, they are indeed reduced as much as is possible for nature into the simplest and primitive purity of elemental water. But in that ultimate fineness of itself and the subdivision of atoms, all seeds, odors, and ferments which they brought up with them die away, and return into the first element of water (from which they were materially formed). Hence clouds, as long as they are clouds, smell foul in the mountains; but not after they have been thinned there by the highest colds into the final division of fineness. And this was a necessity in nature, that not far from us, a region of the air should be most frigid. For this reason, water always remains entirely as it is, or without any division of the three [principles], it is transformed into fruits, and goes where the seeds call and lead it. Indeed, skillful investigation has shown me that, in a certain way and in an analogous sense, the three first principles are in water, yet they are not divisible from one another by any art or passage of days. For an element would cease to be a simple body if it were separable into something prior or simpler. But in corporeal things, nothing is given that is prior or simpler than an element. Water, therefore, is most similar to the internal Mercury of metals, which, when it is already stripped of every stain of metallic sulfur, coheres to itself with such an indissoluble bond that it radically rejects every division possible by art or nature. Hence the occasion was given to Geber <note>An 8th-century alchemist, often associated with the "Summa Perfectionis"</note> to say that in the series of things, no moisture is similar to Mercury, because of its homogeneous simplicity, remaining forever constant to itself even in the torment of fire.

From this point, however, since I have surveyed it for thirty solid years with great labor and expense, and have found Mercury to be equal to water, I shall therefore endeavor to explain its nature, as far as the present discourse requires and the thinness of my judgment allows.

9. The <term>Spagyrists</term> <note>Alchemists who practiced the art of separating and recombining natural substances</note> first confess that the substance of Mercury is utterly intolerant of any intrinsic division, and they give the reason: that its parts of water are joined to earthy parts in a homogeneous and unified proportion by the temperament of water (while the airy and fiery parts are suppressed in silence, because these would fly away if they were present, nor do they contain the cause of constancy required here); and to that extent, these two cannot desert each other because of their just temperament, embracing one another even against the will of fire.

10. They were deceived, primarily, by the error of the ancients concerning the necessary flowing together of the four elements into the composition of mixed bodies. But certainly, that error was not to be indulged by the Spagyrists, who did not dare to bring forth the air and fire of Mercury when its constancy was being discussed. Then, in whatever way it might have been "married" to the earth—whether by art or by natural proportion—it could never acquire constancy in fire, nor truly ever be radically joined to the earth. This is because water, in whatever way it is mixed with earth, does not cease to be water.

11. For neither the mode nor the proportion will ever cause water to degenerate from its essence; nor could any connection with earth obtain that result. But water, remaining water, is born to always fly away from the fire. It is truly ridiculous to suggest that water would love a proportionate weight of earth more than an unequal one, and for the sake of that "love," would more unwillingly desert that temperament of earth. Indeed, while there is talk of the mixing of the four elements, it is understood to be about pure and entirely unmixed elements; and thus unstained by any blemish of mixing, or otherwise prevented by any disposition. For water does not carry a scale with it, nor does it have regard for weighing the earth to be mixed with itself so that it might be more tenaciously connected to the same.

I marvel greatly that the lurid error of the mixing of elements, received into all the Schools, has given birth to such stupid absurdities, and that by that single absurdity, they block the door to the discovery of sciences and causes. Mercury does not admit or contain even the least bit of earth in itself, as it is always the son of water alone. Indeed, earth and water can never be forced into any natural body, or be driven into an identity of form, by whatever artifice that is attempted. For bricks, if they are baked into a tile-like stone from moist earth, do not contain water except for the sake of the ductility of the mud; otherwise, the earth has the seed in its own salt, from which the mud may turn to stone through the cooking of <term>vitrification</term> <note>The process of turning a substance into glass or a glass-like state through heat</note>.

12. Therefore, there is only an outpouring and an apposition of parts of water and earth; but not a celestial admission. For whatever must go into a composite, and be converted from diverse things into this "something," it is necessary that this be done by the work of **acting spirits**, embracing each other to the extent that they promote the matter by transforming it into a new generation. But the elements are bodies, not spirits, and much less do they act upon one another. Therefore, the earth would first have to lose its own being and be reduced into a juice before it could marry the water, so that by embracing the water impregnated with seed, it might lead it into the fruit destined for the conceived seed. But what agent would there be that would change the earth? Since simple earth would only be transformed into a neighboring simple thing? Surely another equal element would not cause it: since nothing of that sort has been seen to belong to water or air. Nor finally, would the earth intend its own corruption by itself.

Therefore, although a part of the earth may be homogeneously reduced into water through art <note>meaning alchemy or human skill</note>: I deny that this happens in nature alone; since in nature the agent is lacking, by means of which alone the "virgin of the earth," or the true <margin>13</margin> [substance], is summoned. This serves as a lesson for Chemists: that the Earth, although created in the first constitution, is nevertheless properly—at least—the fruit of water. Therefore, generations or mixtures never occur in nature except through the impregnation of water. Therefore, the only constancy of bodies in fire is found in the family of minerals, and indeed, it is most pure and perfect in metals. <margin>14</margin> For this reason, the Eternal did not create a moisture that, in its own constancy, is to be compared to metallic mercury. There is, therefore, in Mercury itself—just as in the elements—a proximate reason for indestructibility. Indeed, a certain external sulfur is detected in Mercury, containing the original blemish of the metal. Because this blemish is original, it is therefore difficult to remove from it. When this is finally nonetheless separated by art, the experts say that the Mercury has been cleansed of its superfluous sulfur and superfluous moisture. Indeed, thereafter it can be precipitated into the form of earth by no fire, on account of its greatest simplicity, by which it is compared to the element of water. For it has lost the earth (that is, the sulfur), which earth in its central essence is no less from the element of water than its remaining, purified Mercury—even though it previously held that earth most deeply committed to itself from its origin. If, therefore, in its pristine state, Mercury possessed an equal temperament of earth and water: then at least after the removal of that sulfurous earth, it would have lost its pristine indivisibility; instead, by a contrary relationship of proportion, it has thereafter confirmed for itself a far firmer [indivisibility] forever. For Mercury is found, after it has been despoiled of that sulfur, to be changeable by no fire. *Because it is Mercury of Mercury.* <note>original: "Quia est Mercurius de Mercurio" — a phrase implying a doubly-refined or essential state of the substance.</note>

by a change of salt <note>original: "falis mutatione," likely a typo for "salis mutatione"</note>. This certainly would not happen if the dissolving agent were joined to the substance being dissolved at the smallest level, and if it were not stopped by the Mercury of that solid body. Therefore, the inner Nucleus of Mercury is not reached by dissolving agents, <margin>18.</margin> much less is it pierced through. But those ignorant of the truth, struck by the novelty of this paradox, will rave: if water cannot be compressed, and its parts do not collapse into one another, and yet gold is made from water alone, where then does gold or lead get its weight? Especially since water has no pores <note>void spaces</note> ten times larger than the water itself. First of all, while this doubt does not remove all uncertainties, it proves nothing against the matter of gold being taken from water alone. For if gold were made of the four elements in proportion—and air and fire are light—I would similarly ask: where does gold get its weight? But if it were from earth and water alone, where does gold get its tenfold weight? Therefore, an argument that does not push away its own difficulties carries no weight against its opponents. 

But since an interpreter of nature ought to be ready to investigate and provide the causes of nature, I shall speak from what has been established: the Seed of gold has the power of transmuting water into "this specific thing," which is far different from water. Wherefore, it is consistent with nature and reason that in transmutation, water undergoes such compression, collapsing, and uniting in its body as much as stones or metals outweigh water, and as much as the necessity of the seeds requires. Inasmuch as nothing comes from nothing, weight must come from another body of equal weight. In this process, just as there is a change of matter, so there is a transmutation of the entire essence. And so water, while it submits to the laws of the seed, is also bound by the rules of its own weight, condensation, collapsing, and dimensions. For if water in the form of vapor, a hundred times lighter than itself, flies off spontaneously and escapes the eyes, and yet remains water; why should it not, when it becomes "this specific thing" and is no longer formally water, also take on densities ten times greater than usual? In both cases, surely, the matter follows the properties of the seeds. 

The freedom of nature, therefore, is perpetual: to spontaneously perform and undergo compressions of the watery body, and to refuse to undergo them by any human artifice—indeed, mountains would sooner be overturned by gunpowder <note>original: "pulvere pyrio"</note>. Therefore, sixteen parts of water are compressed into the space of one when gold is fashioned from water. Wherefore, it is far from true that the penetration of dimensions is impossible, <margin>19.</margin> if nothing is more natural to nature than <margin>20.</margin> to condense the body of water. Indeed, although it appears in water that the first three dimensions <note>length, breadth, and depth</note> are pulled apart into one another, there is no hope [of separation], because in the absolute simplicity of water there is hidden a certain "watery sulfur" <note>a technical alchemical term for the active, combustible principle</note> which cannot be separated from the others without everything coming along at once. The "first three" [elements or dimensions] are not true things, but are only abstracted through the imagination. 

Therefore, since water varies as an offspring in both cases according to the diversity of its seeds: so many different kinds of earths, minerals, salts, liquids, stones, plants, animals, and meteors arise through their species by the "breath" of the seeds. For water rots in the earth, becomes the juice of the earth, gum, oil, resin, wood, berries, etc.; and that which recently was nothing but water materially, now burns and emits smoke. Not indeed that this smoke <margin>21.</margin> is air: but it is either a breath or a dry exhalation, a new fruit of the water, not yet totally deprived of the conversion of its seed. This is proven: for the body of air cannot cast a shadow in air; but whatever exhales from coal casts a shadow in the sun. For since air has a determined consistency and thickness conforming to its own simplicity, it follows that whatever is denser than air is not air. Furthermore, that which exhales, having been thinned out by the heat of fire, is still denser than air, and for that reason it casts a shadow. That substance will certainly become much thicker in the cold, and will become visible in the clouds. Therefore, whatever exhalations <margin>22.</margin> climb upward from the earth are joined to the clouds; to this extent the clouds even stink, not unlike water under the equator <note>original: "aequinoctiali"</note>; and there, having consumed the ferment and seed of their solid form, they turn back into pure water...

For while something exhales—whether it be of the nature of water, oil, or soot, or in the form of an exhalation—even if it does not take the seeds of the concrete matter with it, it at least carries upward the ferments. In order for these to be fully abolished from there, and so that the residual matter may return into water, it is necessary that in the "kitchen" of the coldest air, they are first raised into a subtle **Gas** <note>The author, Van Helmont, is credited with coining the term 'Gas' from the Greek 'Chaos'</note> and pass into another higher region, assuming a condition in the form of the smallest **atoms**. And so that the ferments may die there, as much by the cold of the place as by the subtlety of the atoms, as if by suffocation and extinction. For cold is, therefore, a principle—not indeed a vital one, but one of extinction. Inasmuch as it further subdivides the parts of the atoms by making them more subtle, as I taught above. And so under cold, wood is consumed even more quickly by fire, as if it were agitated by a blast. By which necessity, that place has always been cold from the beginning. Indeed, the Author of Nature <note>God</note> would not seem to have failed the necessities of His creatures. Cold, therefore, is native and vernacular to this place; it does not arise from the later chimera of **Antiperistasis** <note>A philosophical theory that one quality intensifies its opposite, e.g., cold making fire hotter</note>. Clearly, it was necessary that the matter of fruits, brought there, should return into its first being, and the infections of the ferments must therefore first be removed through the **mortifications** <note>chemical "killing" or neutralizing</note>, subdivisions, subtleties, penetrations, suffocations, and extinctions of the cold.
<margin>25.</margin> Air, therefore, is the place where all things brought to it are consumed, and proceed back into the pristine element of water. For in earth and water, although bodies risen from seeds gradually rot and turn into juice, they are not yet so close to the progeny of simple water that they are reduced into Gas. For soon in the earth, exhausted bodies drink in another foulness, ferment, and seed. From there they fly to "second marriages" and are propagated anew into succeeding fruits. But fire, the death of things, lacks seeds; subject to the will of the Craftsman, it consumes all seminal things, and translates their combustible materials into Gas. Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541)</note> asserts that the three beginnings are so
<margin>27.</margin> united in individual principles that by no help of art can one be entirely freed from the other. With all due respect to the man's authority, our mechanics <note>experimental chemistry</note> has proved the contrary of his assertion by means of the spirit of wine being converted into tasteless water, embracing its secret **Samech** <note>An alchemical term, often referring to a salt of Tartar or a universal solvent</note>. And so that man cannot even plead ignorance. For the spirit of wine, totally flammable, de-phlegmed, and oily, always passes—as much as half of it—into simple, tasteless, and elemental water by the touch of the salt of **tartar**. Again, the same happens by repetition for the remaining part. That man was indeed ignorant of the "quiddity" <note>the essence or 'what-ness'</note> of Gas (namely, with me, into wind) and finally the properties of cold in the air; indeed, he thought that the vapor of water was plainly annihilated. Which stupidity of idiocy is least of all to be overlooked in so great a **Distiller**. Especially since he wishes elements to be separable from fictitious elements, rather than the three firsts from the three firsts. Therefore, from the delivered anatomy of water, it is now sufficiently clear that simple water is not "raw"; and that fire does not remove from it a rawness which it does not have. That the whole action of fire is not upon the water, but upon that which is joined to it by accident. Galen <note>Ancient Greek physician</note>,
<margin>28.</margin> copying Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek botanist</note> word-for-word according to his custom, and wishing to measure the elemental grades of simples, did not approach this through the discretion of the tongue: and so he guessed that more fire had flowed into the mixture where there was more acrimony or bitterness.

He was unmindful of the doctrine he so often repeated: namely, that any single body consists only of three principles, but not of elements. This is because elements were not bodies, **but locations and empty matrices of bodies**, or of principles, devoid of all body. For even if they are not commonly believed to be so, among us the "unpolluted elements" are those which Paracelsus teaches can be sequestered from polluted ones by art. However, his description allows for air in one glass, common water in another, earth (whether from a garden or a field) in a third, and finally the flame of fire in a fourth. He then closes the vessels with the "Seal of Hermes" <note>An airtight alchemical seal made by melting the glass neck of a flask.</note> by melting the neck. And he claims the water boils continuously for a month in its vessel. As if that were possible and the glass would not shatter sooner! Especially since he commands the water to be closed up without any air at the very lip of the vessel (the glass being melted with the water inside), and finally, that a flame be captured in the glass; but the moment it ceases, it is no longer fire: **but is aerial soot**. Fire is not a substance. Finally, fire cannot be detained within the closure of a vessel. Elsewhere, he denies the element of fire exists except in the heavens; but now he calls the *Gas* of a burnt thing "fire." He exalts these trifles of his as causes of great moment, which, however, he did not dare to name. Because he anxiously thrust his dreams upon the world, in the hope of earning the name of "Monarch of Secrets" <note>original: "Monarchæ Arcanorum"</note> thereby.

As and Blas <note>Blas: a term coined by Van Helmont to describe the "astral" or "motive" force in stars and living things</note> are indeed new names, introduced by me because the knowledge of them was unknown to the ancients. Nevertheless, among physical principles <note>original: "interinitia physica"</note>, Gas and Blas hold a necessary place. Therefore, this paradox must be further expanded upon. 1. And first, in what way Gas is made from water, and how different that mode is from the one by which heat raises water into vapor. Likewise, how these things happen must be understood from the 2. anatomy of water. I shall repeat, therefore: that the thrice-glorious God, in the beginning, created the heaven and the earth, and the abyss of the waters. Moreover, the abyss began from the hollow of Heaven and ended upon the small globe of the earth. Nothing is read there concerning the creation of air, which is nevertheless a body, and created as an element; not indeed after the six days of creation so that it might fill the place where air now is. Therefore, 3. "Heaven" designates the air, and it is the matter of the Heavens, otherwise unknown until now. Then the Eternal created the firmament, so that it might separate the waters which were to remain under it from those which were to remain above it. 4. Now, the firmament was not like a floodgate <note>original: "catarafta"</note> or like an idle gap between the waters: but rather the operative principle of that separation. Just as the Sun is not a gap between day and night, although it was made to separate day from night; rather, the Sun is the maker of the day itself. Heaven, therefore, or air, is constituted as the separator of the waters, destined to last as long as the world itself. Wherefore it obtained two 5. distinguished powers: namely, extreme cold and a dryness proportioned to it. It does indeed have within it great lights <note>the stars and planets</note> which revolve in it, and which mitigate the innate cold in some way; yet the air does not fail in its duty as a Separator. And in that part where such separation ought to happen (which is near to us), there are no lights at all; indeed, not even many at a distance. However, the closer that air 6. reaches the chambers of the Blessed, the more it abounds with lights. Such is the disposition of the air. Now truly I shall approach the history of the "breath" <note>original: "halitus"</note>. Which contains vapor and Gas together, and thus the contents of the air must be examined. For Gas is not a dry and oily body, which the ancients called an 7. exhalation: but a companion of the exit, and moreover something aqueous, besides vapors, from which the body, mode, and progress of meteors <note>original: "meteorón corpus"; referring to all atmospheric phenomena like rain or lightning</note> will be known. I consider the body of 8. Water to contain elements within itself: a congenial mercury, liquid and most simple; and finally an insipid and equally simple salt. Both of these embrace within themselves a uniform, homogeneous, simple, and inseparable sulfur. I suppose these things, just as Astronomers suppose their eccentrics <note>mathematical models used to explain planetary orbits</note>, so that the weakness of our understanding may be assisted. Therefore, as the salt of water is moved and grows warm by the 9. smallest amount of time, being impatient of heat, it immediately climbs upward, as if to a place of rest and cooling, with a proportioned part of its Mercury. And so far also the sulfur, inseparable from both, must accompany them. These three thus connected are vapor, which, being led into the lukewarm air, hastens to ascend for the same reasons, until it reaches the places of cooling prepared by the Creator. Having been led there, the vapor, immediately laying aside the heat attached to it, as if repenting of its flight, would wish to receive resolution again in its Mercury and return to the former state of water. On this occasion, the Mercury of the water <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid or volatile principle of a substance.</note> is so congealed that it becomes incapable of dissolving its own Salt. For this reason, that vapor is immediately changed into Gas, and suspended in the form of Gas, it wanders about. Indeed, unless the cold were to dry out the Sulfur of the water <note>Sulfur represents the combustible or oily principle.</note> in its outer shell and divide it to this extent, all vapor (as seen in our glass vessels) and clouds, being heavier than the air, would immediately rush downward. Hence we see that when vapors occasionally fall outside their boundary (as happens soon after great frosts when a sudden south wind blows), the Mercury of the water having thawed, the Salt is easily dissolved again within its Mercury. Truly, the pressures of cold and heat command the beginnings of water to be turned either inward or outward. Thus, small rains and dew fall in the smallest atoms, as if they were descending and dissolved vapors. Therefore, it is not a new and substantial generation when vapor is raised from water, since it is only a thinning out due to the turning outward of the parts. Nor is it a new generation when the Mercury of the water dissolves the Salt, which it encloses within itself again and is changed into rain. This is nothing but the dissolution of the previous atoms of water and their gathering together into larger drops. For no change of essence intervenes where there is only a local 
<margin>¶ 1. division and a turning outward of parts. For example: yellow and malleable Gold does not change its essence while dissolved by *aqua regia* <note>A mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids used to dissolve gold.</note>, when it has the color of iron rust, nor when it turns black in *Chrysulca* <note>Another term for acid that dissolves gold.</note> and is crushed into the smallest powder.</margin>
<margin>¶ 2. Furthermore, so that you may understand Gas: First, consider that the air is made of separated things, and finally simple in its root, and thus simply cold and dry. Since, therefore, heat and cold are more active than moisture and dryness: Therefore the moisture of Mercury first suffers from the coldness of the air. And since the Mercury and Salt of water are colder than their Sulfur, they are more quickly affected by the coldness of the air—and first indeed the Mercury, because it is the coldest of the two companions. But since everything desires to remain in rest and without the change of vicissitudes,</margin>
and it is necessary for the elements to remain without destruction; therefore the Mercury and Salt of water hasten to protect themselves from the cold of the air. And so they condense, armor themselves, and freeze by the cold, which otherwise, having been changed into Gas, are lifted up (for it is always characteristic of the air to separate waters from waters) or otherwise they delay that change and flight. But if indeed the water, being agitated, does not freeze: then the cold and dryness of the air seize the three primes <note>Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt.</note> of the water, so that the Mercury of the water becomes incapable of dissolving the Salt in its moisture. And so the Salt, under the cold, in a certain way becomes clotted within the Mercury and Sulfur. Thus the Sulfur, being drier than the other two, suffers even more easily from the coldness than its companions, and more from the dryness of the air than from its coldness. Wherefore the Sulfur is dilated into the smallest parts, of which the individual clotted Mercuries and Salts expose their Sulfur outwardly, so that it may endure the dryness of the air. Wherefore, since the Sulfur is equal to either of the two, it is necessary for the remaining two to be divided and dilated to the measure of the Sulfur. Whence, by a very easy process, through the cold of the air, the Mercury with the Salt of the water are frozen within the Sulfur. Therefore, since the Salt and Mercury are unfit for moistening the Sulfur, they are necessarily changed into Gas likewise, and being more and more refined, they are subdivided even to the extreme and possible subtlety of the element. Gas, therefore, is not a substance or essence: but varies only as far as alteration. For in vapor, the Salt, impatient of heat, rises with the Mercury, and they have the Sulfur enclosed within them. And Gas turns the Sulfur of the water outward, dries it, and subdivides it. For vapor, while it reaches a place of cooling, mostly wanders about in the form of a cloud, semi-frozen, and does not ascend: but when the cold of winter arrives, when that region of the air already becomes cold beyond measure, soon the air becomes clear, the clouds disappear, and are changed into Gas. In the mountains of Switzerland and Savoy, the clouds fluctuate beneath one's feet; through their openings, we look down upon the world

# GAS AND WATER

<margin>14</margin> We know this because of the immense cold of the place: for whatever is above the clouds is without cloud, because all that vapor is gradually thinned out into Gas and ceases to be seen. The Sun indeed shines serenely in that part (unless it is snowing): but its heat is not perceptible, although I have seen a companion, on the side where the Sun's rays had struck him directly for a full half-day, have his face and neck scorched, exactly as if <term>blistering beetles</term><note>original: "cantharides"; used historically in medicine to cause skin blistering.</note> had been applied. And this happened without any sensation of heat or pain. For this does not happen because of the excessive subtlety of the air and heat. Indeed, it is the degree of heat, not its subtlety or purity, that burns. On the contrary, a denser body, like iron, burns more fiercely than a thinner coal. Much less does it happen because of the reflection of rays: for it burned on the side where the sun struck, but not on the opposite side where the reflection from the mountain struck. For the cold of the place causes the Sun's heat to be less felt. 

<margin>15</margin> From this it is certainly clear that cold is not a mere absence of heat, or a privation, or a non-entity. For here both stand together, they work simultaneously and distinctly, and indeed at an intense degree. And by their mutual tempering, they make the air almost the sweetest in the whole world. Yet the snow on the mountain is not melted by that burning of the Sun. This is because the cold of the snow and of the place together are equal to the heat of the Sun. However, insofar as a human is warmer than snow, the burning of the Sun naturally overcomes and powerfully burns, because human warmth excludes almost all the cold of the place, and the burning of the Sun acts almost alone.

<margin>16</margin> While vapors and clouds become Gas, they are refined, and the more refined they are, the higher they climb by subdividing, and the more they escape our sight. Otherwise, the Sun, because of the multitude and density of clouds, would never shine on us, and much less would it warm the earth. Therefore the stars twinkle, and the whole sky, though devoid of color, is splendid. 

<margin>17</margin> Yet it reflects a sky-blue. For although Gas is most subtle and invisible in its own body: because it still differs from the absolute transparency of the air, therefore in such great depth, it mimics a blue color. 

<margin>18</margin> For Gas, which I said gives a shadow in its first division, does not appear in a thousand of its subdivisions, except that in great depth it reflects the aforementioned color. 

<margin>19</margin> It is also frivolous to say that the air is carried away by the motion of the <term>prime mover</term><note>The "primum mobile," the outermost sphere in the old geocentric model of the universe.</note>. Because clouds follow the lead of the winds. But the motions of the winds are irregular, because they are the <term>Blas</term><note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a "pulsing" or "motive power" of the stars and nature.</note> of the stars; they are not the motion of the celestial spheres. 

Furthermore, far above the snows, the air is almost motionless. 

<margin>20</margin> Indeed, a Belgian merchant ascended a mountain in the Canaries <note>Likely Mount Teide on Tenerife.</note>, which today is considered the highest in the whole world. There was one guide, two masters, as many servants, and 5 Camels, one of which was designated for provisions and fodder. They ascended in the month of June, very early in the morning. They had scarcely traveled for an hour when they encountered cold, and all day they complained that toward nightfall it was so unusual that they had to add more clothes. On the third morning, about three hours after sunrise, they reached the summit of the mountain. There, the sand and the tracks of the camels, impressed a year before, were as fresh as if they were new, and the names of certain people were inscribed on the ground as if by a finger yesterday. For besides the air being by far the sweetest, they found no vegetation due to the lack of rain. Therefore they hurried to descend, the Camels not resting for the entire five days, except for the little time they took to eat fodder. For the whole three days, they were perhaps fifteen Italian miles distant from the horizon. But although this region of tranquil air did not feel the storms of the winds in that way, nevertheless it is necessary for it to have a flowing sweet breeze and an alterative <term>Blas</term>, not only because it suffers day and night, cold and heat: but it also transmits the <term>Blas</term> of the stars, admits the Gas from below, and suffers other consequences thereof. And just as that region transmits the alterations of the stars, so it also conceives and participates in them. For the Sun (let the judgment be the same for other stars) cannot help but be hot, which on the coldest mountains burns blisters.

He uses an account of a mountain climb in the Canary Islands to prove that the upper atmosphere is tranquil and preserves tracks for years due to the lack of wind and rain.</summary>

It is necessary, therefore, for those alternations to be hosted in that same place. In the same way, the rays of the stars, with full strength, transform the vast monarchy of the air, and they sow their own alterations. That is: In the immense space of the tranquil air itself, there is the **Gas of water**, which, through the most exquisite refinement of subdivision, has been forged many times over and subdivided by the cold through which it passed. This Gas, at least, would never spontaneously return to its original water, nor would it descend to the coldest places through which it escaped by climbing upward, unless the *Blas* <note>term: *Blas* — a word coined by Van Helmont to describe a "motive power" or vital force that governs the movement of stars and weather</note> of the stars 
<margin>21.</margin> above forced its descent. And so, there is no region of the tranquil air devoid of alternations, except that rain moistens only there, and the whirlwind of the winds does not serve to stir the waves. For since the Gas, which it guards within itself, has already been reduced to such a great subtlety of its own, and its individual atoms—as if breathed upon by fervors on the outer surface of the sulfur—cannot truly return into rain unless, by a gentle wind, they descend to the middle region, where they resume the beginnings of coagulation under the warm breath of the breeze. Namely, a certain opposite alteration to that from which the Gas departed must reduce the Gas back into water. For a gentle warmth in the tranquil air causes the atoms of Gas to fall, covered by their own sulfur; these, like a ruptured skin or like glass, are suddenly brought from warmth into cold and are broken. And thus the Mercury of the water <note>note: original: *Mercurius aquae* — referring to the "mercurial" or fluid principle of water in alchemical theory</note> dissolves its own salt, at which resolution the melted sulfur itself returns into the original water.
<margin>22.</margin> And such an inversion of the body of water, and that torture through the examination of cold, is necessary so that every force of ferment <note>term: *Ferment* — a catalytic power believed to cause all physical and chemical changes</note> is entirely removed from the heights. For otherwise, much corruption and much stench of mists would soon destroy mortals. Just as in molten silver, tiny atoms of gold sink to the bottom: so the atoms of Gas settle, and by sinking they grow large, which otherwise, due to the cold of the air, would be weakly lifted up again, unless a propitious warmth occasionally stood in the way in the coldest place. Thus, indeed, rains, showers, storms, thus hail, snow, mist, and frost arise from the alteration, by accident, from the *Blas*—both motive and alterative—in the coldest places. And so, Gas and *Blas* are the diverse colonies of the whole 
<margin>23.</margin> time of a meteor. At least from the cited examples I have learned that the Sun glows not by Accident, but by itself and immediately. And that heat is as 
<margin>24.</margin> intimate and proper to it as its own light is to it. Therefore, the air has its own depths no less than the earth, which the Adepts <note>note: "Adepts" refers to masters of alchemy and the secret sciences</note> call *Peroledos*. Thus, the invisible Gas 
<margin>25.</margin> is hosted in various layers of the air; if the waters have their own abysses and whirlpools, they have their own pits, so to speak, in the *Peroledos*, which the skilled have called the Floodgates of Heaven and the valves. For the Gas, falling from the depth of Heaven into the place of the clouds, is not carried without a director, *Blas*. Indeed, it does not fall except through layered and ordered valves. Namely, to the planets, 
<margin>26.</margin> all valves do not lie open indiscriminately: but each one, through its own *Blas*, is the key-bearer of its own *Peroledo*. I propose this to be examined by the Astrologers who are the indicators of meteors, and I promise they will find a rich storehouse of material. For in this way the winds sometimes hasten perpendicularly downward and strike the earth, while at other times they exit the valves laterally, destroying houses and trees, and even bringing pitiable slaughter to ships. A warmer breeze, however, announces the *Blas* of Heaven: that a wind is about to come from the depth of the air and lead the Gas downward with it. Whence the Gas is soon resolved again into vapor, and then into rain. Clouds, of course, then appear—not long before seen in no corner of the world—because the invisible Gas glides downward from the depth of the upper air, which into vapors and...

This is indeed the purpose of the air: to continually separate the waters from the waters <note>A reference to Genesis 1:6, where the firmament divides the waters above from the waters below</note>. But since one part of water is extended to at least a hundred times its own dimension when it becomes a breath <note>original: *halitus*</note>, and is thus subdivided, such is the order and law of the universe that individual things are moved for human necessity and the preservation of the world. 

<margin>27.</margin> Thus far, heavy things are indeed carried upward. However, I am not so anxious about the occasional causes of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning</note>; it is enough for me to have known that the breath rising from below—namely vapor and **Gas**—is the material cause of every meteor. 

<margin>28.</margin> Regarding the efficient cause, it is sufficient to know the *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a "pulsing" or "motive force" of the stars and planets</note> by the authority of the Holy Scriptures: *They shall be to you for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years.* <note>Genesis 1:14</note> This, therefore, is the restless destiny of water: that by continually proceeding upward and downward, not unlike the winds, in an unordered and irregular motion, they respond to the *Blas* of the stars. 

<margin>29.</margin> And so, the same and undiminished water which existed from the beginning of the universe, exists now, and shall exist until its end. Furthermore, I consider the *Peroledos* <note>Van Helmont's term for the specific regions or "flasks" of the atmosphere</note> of the air to be like the vessels of the stars, through which they unfold their *Blas* across determined places, as required for the uses and changes of the seasons. Especially since the upper and almost tranquil *Peroledos* contains the reason why there are winds, 

<margin>30.</margin> fruits, dews, and especially local weather. For since wind is flowing air, and thus possesses instability within itself, it is necessary to find the local cause of stability in the calmer *Peroledos*. Therefore, there are valves in the *Peroledos*, either closed or open, according to the *Blas* of the stars which they obey. Nor is it a wonder that there are invisible limits or boundaries in the air, restraining such great power and mass; for the visible world contains scarcely the smallest power of the "republic of things." For who would deny that under the rock of Scotland <note>Likely a reference to a specific landmark or "echoing rock" known to the author</note>, which 

<margin>31.</margin> is barely 12 feet wide and 30 feet high, there is some division of the *Peroledos* (to say nothing for now of the Equinoctial line and its wondrous properties)? When a war engine <note>A cannon or mortar</note> is fired on one side, not a single sound or tremor is heard on the other side of the rock (which for that reason is called "Fear"). So also, one must consider the lateral valves or doors of the *Peroledos* in the air, because winds mostly exit with a lateral motion, and are likewise carried by the *Blas* of the stars across their boundaries. 

From the aforementioned doctrine of **Gas**, I finally 

<margin>32.</margin> object to myself: If water is frozen by cold into snow, hail, and ice, then water will not be dissolved by cold into **Gas**—if the action and effect of a uniform agent and patient must be the same. Here it must be seriously noted: That water freezes itself; it is not efficiently frozen by another. For although cold has been thought to congeal until now, 

<margin>33.</margin> that is only occasionally, not effectively. Water, therefore, by a sense of its own mode, perceives the cold of the air—not indeed as a mere absence or privation of heat (as I have already demonstrated by an example common in Switzerland), but as a positive cause in its natural quality. Since, first of all, it is certain and confirmed by sight that cold air gradually consumes water, snow, and ice: the latter two more slowly, the former more quickly. Finally, it is obvious that whatever the air thus steals away, it immediately transfers into invisible **Gas**. If, therefore, the cold of the air hardened water into ice, the further action of the air would also immediately cease once the ice was made; but the consequence is false, and therefore so is the antecedent. For the moisture of water is easily dried and divided by the cold; wherefore the <term>Mercury</term> <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, the "Mercury" represents the volatile, fluid principle of a substance</note> and the salt of the water, feeling the frost of the air which wishes to separate the waters from the waters, and knowing they must endure the extension and drying of their moisture—and thus the entirely violent impression of the <term>Separator</term> <note>The "Separator" refers to the divine or natural force that divides substances into their constituent parts</note>—they desire...
