Indeed, it is not strong enough to accomplish this perfectly, since even in the ice, the sulfurous part of the water has already suffered a thinning of itself; and thus, even now, the ice floats upon the water. <margin>34</margin> However, although the sulfur of the water is thinned in the ice, it has not yet laid aside the nature of water. This is proven through mechanics. <margin>65</margin> Fill a large glass flask with pieces of ice, and let the neck be closed with the Seal of Hermes <note>An airtight seal made by melting the glass neck of the vessel shut.</note>, that is, by the melting of the glass in that spot. Let this flask then be placed on a scale, with a weight added to the opposite side, and you will see that after the ice has melted, the water will be heavier than the ice itself by almost an eighth part of its weight. Since this can be done a thousand times with the same water, always retaining the same weight, it cannot be said that any part of it has been turned into air. <margin>36</margin> For such is the eternity and constancy of the elements that, although water may depart into vapor, into Gas, into ice, or even into solid bodies; materially, however, it always remains the original water. In some cases, it is masked by arriving ferments and seeds; in others, it is varied only by the disturbances of the primary qualities in the *Resolleo* of Paracelsus <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe a state of matter resolved into its primary form without the influence of a "seed" or specific blueprint.</note>, that is, without a seed. From the aforesaid, however, several notable things arise:

1. That water has a certain kind of sense and choice, and thus all beings in some way participate in life. <margin>37</margin> *Come, let us adore the King, for whom all things live.* <note>original: "Regem cui omnia vivunt, venite adoremus." A liturgical phrase applied here to the vitalism of nature.</note>
2. Since water does not encrust itself in the structure of vapor, vapor is therefore more pleasing to the water, both in its cause and its manner, than Gas is. And this, in water, argues for something similar to choice. <margin>38</margin>
3. And that therefore vapor returns more readily into water than Gas does. <margin>39</margin>
4. That the change of water into vapor is, in respect to the Separator, oblique and as if by accident. But Gas consists of the proper destination of the air, by which the air separates the waters from the waters. <margin>40</margin>
5. That air is far colder in itself than water.
6. That it is dry by itself.
7. That unity, or the connection of integral parts, is as pleasing to nature as the division of the same is hateful.
8. That the structure of Gas brings forth another inward principle of water <margin>41</margin> (since it does not have a composite beginning) or a cause of some slight heterogeneity, other than that which is reached by heat in the birth of vapor.
9. That created things, the simpler they are, the more homogeneous they are: yet a total, simplest homogeneity is not found in bodies.
10. That the sulfur of the water, thinned in the ice, is the cause of the lightness in frozen things, and not the inclusion of foreign air. <margin>42</margin> For always and everywhere, water excludes a marriage with air.
11. That the cold and dryness of the air can do nothing else to the water than thin its sulfur. But the freezing itself, or hardening, is the water's own action, by which it places an obstacle against the Separator.
12. That the air acts upon the water without the water's reaction or the air's suffering. Since it is the Separator of the waters, established by divine law.
13. That even in natural, unfeeling things, reaction differs from resistance. For there is no reaction of water against the air, and yet water exists with resistance.
14. That the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Aristotelian academic establishment, which the author frequently critiques.</note> have erred because they dictated that every action of nature happens with a reaction of the sufferer and a suffering of the agent. <margin>43</margin>
15. That the transmutation of Gas into air is impossible. <margin>44</margin>
    1. For otherwise, the air would always increase immensely, and consequently, all water would have long ago ceased to exist.
    2. Because, besides what I have demonstrated elsewhere—that air can in no way return again into water—the same is now sufficiently clear from the aforesaid.
    3. Since it is proper to water to suffer from the air, and not conversely to react against the air. Therefore, air, once made from water, would always remain air: since there is no reciprocal agent that might transmute air back into water.
    4. Indeed, for air to return into water by itself fights against the general axiom: That everything, as much as is in itself, desires to remain in its being.
    5. Especially because air lacks in itself the principle of its own dissolution from decay and the alteration of parts, the causes...

## THE BLAS OF METEORS.
<note>The author, Jan Baptist van Helmont, uses the term "Blas" to describe a specific vital or motive force, distinct from heat or light.</note>

<margin>1. What Blas is. 2. The stars operate more majestically through local motion than through light. 3. What the motive Blas of the stars is. 4. What wind is, and from where it is moved. 5. Stars were made for us. 6. Diverse activities in Blas. 7. The activities of the stars are carried out through Blas, the executive motion. 8. The error of Paracelsus. 9. The two great lights <note>The Sun and Moon</note> exercise their own properties. 10. How the influence of the stars is referred back to the two lights. 11. The births of rains and meteors. 12. "Præcedines" <note>A term for early atmospheric precursors</note> arise soon from the falling waters, whence the ferments and seeds of things. 13. A history of Cyprus. 14. Resolution of the question concerning the stillness of summer air and the continuous breathing of winter air.</margin>

1. <note>Ornate initial 'S'</note> The Stars are for us as signs, seasons, days, and years. Therefore, they bring about the changes of the seasons, the storms, and the successions of time. For this work, they possess a double motion: namely, local <note>movement through space</note> and alterative <note>changing the quality of things</note>. Both of these, however, I designate by the new name **Blas**. And they excite this Blas more by their motion through 2. space than by their light. For indeed, on a dark night, the North wind often blows, followed by the South wind, and vice versa. Therefore, the Blas that breathes a warm wind does so not by the heat or light of the heaven itself, but requires position, direction, and connection. Whithersoever the light of the stars reaches, the valves open or close themselves. Let the motion of the stars, therefore, be the 3. key-bearer of the valves. This motion simultaneously moves the *Perolcdos* <note>original: "Perolcdos"; a term used by Van Helmont to describe the layers or "beds" of the atmosphere</note>, or the strata of the air. Therefore, not all heat comes from pre-existing fire or light, nor is cold merely the naked absence of heat. Rather, the motive Blas of the stars is a pulsive power, by reason of their journey through places and according to their aspects <note>astrological positions</note>. These circumstances in the stars cause the primary qualities in these lower regions, just as 4. in men, shame, anger, fear, etc., stir up cold and heat. And the stars have this by the gift of creation. To Hippocrates, wind is a flowing wave of air; but I, defining it by its causes, say that wind is flowing air, moved by the Blas of the stars. And that by a natural result; though at other times it is not rarely granted to an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmoni"</note> to cite winds even without Blas, or to increase a tempestuous Blas. Therefore, unless the air has Blas, it remains quiet, nor does it have the principle of motion from itself: but it comes to it from elsewhere. The motive Blas, therefore, stirs up winds, storms, and floods, through the diverse *Perolcdos* of the air, now upwards, now downwards, crosswise, lengthwise, and laterally, running through all the borders of the earth. Although the elements have no need of motion for themselves, human necessity demands it. 5. And since nothing could move itself (except for the *Archeus* <note>the internal vital principle</note> given to seeds), the Eternal was pleased to place in the stars an *enormontic* <note>original: "enormonticam"; a term derived from Hippocrates meaning "impulsive" or "stimulating"</note> motive force, not much unlike the command of our own mouth. Thus, Blas is a testimony to us that God, in His surpassing Goodness, made the elements and the stars for us, measuring their ends according to our conveniences. Thus, Blas moves not so much by light, rays, and motion as it is the general beginning of motion for the stars: no less...

# THE BLAS OF METEORS

6. It seems to look less toward the earth than toward the air and water. For the Moon rules the night according to the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "juxta Sacra"</note>, just as the Sun rules the day: although the moon, for half its course, does not run beneath the night. Indeed, it divides the globe of the earth into quarters, into two ebbs and flows of the Ocean every day. In this, it consumes nearly 23 hours. It is less by as much as the Sun and Moon have meanwhile moved away from or approached each other. Therefore, the *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont meaning the "motive power" or "astral pulse" that drives natural motions</note> also excites the tide in the waters, even when the wind is silent. Moreover, the alterative *Blas* consists in the production of heat and cold; and that especially with the changes of the winds. But the stars do not have or give humidity or dryness from themselves.

7. For humidity is not consider-able in nature apart from matter, as a naked quality, and therefore it is not brought to us from the stars. For all humidity is from water, which existed before the stars were born.

8. Therefore, Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> errs when he says that rains, snow, etc., are the fruits of the stars, such that they are cooked to maturity in the stars as if in leather bottles. Dryness also, in the air that separates the waters, existed before the stars: nor is it consider-able outside of a body, in the manner of a quality.

9. Heat and cold, however, are qualities more abstracted from the body. There are, therefore, only two great luminaries, and consequently at least two of their qualities are scattered into the air, from which all meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning</note> are moved. Namely, the heat of life is a property of the Sun; but cold belongs to the other star [the Moon]. The remaining stars also gave their names to these two luminaries.

10. Whenever, therefore, stars of the nature of the moon are carried through solar places, a lukewarmness occurs in the air; but if solar stars run beneath those same places, heat occurs, according to those qualities of the air. The *Gas* <note>Van Helmont's term for the "spirit" or "essence" of a substance, from which the modern word "gas" originates</note> of the air is also altered in different ways.

11. From this, the *Blas* heats uniformly through the depths of the air. Therefore, the *Gas* is either detained in its layers or brought down to us. Thus the atoms of *Gas*, invisible because of their extreme smallness, losing their constriction and the excess of cold, fall back into tiny droplets and hasten downward. But if indeed warmth affects the lower *Perolaedos* <note>A term used by Van Helmont to describe specific regions or layers of the atmosphere</note>, when the *Gas* arises downward, provoked by the *Blas*: summer showers occur. To be sure, the *Gas* congealed by frost, as soon as warmth arises, is liquefied and rushes headlong downward. <margin>12.</margin> For the Mercury of the water dissolves its own Salt, and Sulfur envelops these two. And so they fall into rain. But if this happens in the upper *Perolaedo*: the falling drops are frozen in the middle silver-white layers: and thus they are precipitated into snow and hail. But if warmth dominates through several continuous *Perolaedos* of the air: long-lasting rains follow. From this it also appears that an unequal *Blas*, in different depths of the air, produces different effects. For often the lowest *Perolaedos* are warm, and the day is plainly cloudy, with many clouds. At other times, the second and third *Perolaedos* are warm, while the lower one is cold. Whence snow. And thus the rest of the cohort of meteors is caused for us.

I trust that the causes and manner are now more clearly established through *Gas* materially, and through *Blas* operatively and motively, than heretofore. Whence Astrologers and Physicians will be able to presage things upon a more solid foundation. Meanwhile, I leave untouched the matters of prophecies, which God hides as portents through ministering spirits. I shall only relate what Brother Stephen de Lusignan, the last of the family of the Kings of Cyprus, of the Order of St. Dominic, recites in his *Description of Cyprus*, printed at Paris in the year 1580, folio 212, in French to this effect: <margin>13.</margin> *Toward the end, I underwent an earthquake at Famagusta, which lasted eight days. Afterward, however, there arose whirlwinds of winds, passing over the Island and entering the marketplace of Famagusta: for they soon took away the great palace there, destroying many houses, along with some men.* It would have been all over for Famagusta, had not some people perhaps arrived by chance. *Let the reader know, therefore, that it is customary for Eastern sailors, when they notice winds of that kind, to take a knife, with which they make the sign of the Cross in the air, and utter these words: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.* <note>original: "In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum" (John 1:1)</note>

Nor do I find any superstition in it, except that it is necessary for the knife to have a black handle. And thus I am unable to determine anything for certain. So he says. At least it is a marvel. That this diabolical storm should cease, and the devil spare the whole city, perhaps on account of the sin of a <margin>14.</margin> single sinner. Furthermore, concerning the *Blas* <note>Van Helmont's term for a motive power or vital force governing motion and change</note>, there is still something considerable. If in a great heat you hold a burning candle near the opening of a window, usually no trace of moving air is felt; but throughout the entire winter, however small the opening may be, it continually and annoyingly breathes a wind. But since the constriction of the air (let us now take "air" to mean its *Magnale* <note>The "Magnale" refers to a sheath or medium through which the Blas acts; a sort of spatial extension of a substance</note>) is no greater due to cold than its rarefaction is due to heat, the reason for the former seems no stronger than the latter for stirring up a wind. Therefore, there is a twofold local motive of the *Blas* in the air: One, indeed, which excites the winds, and thus includes violence and speed, from a native power or motion.

The other, truly, which follows upon the alterative *Blas*, on account of condensation or rarefaction in the air. This, however, since it is almost universal because of summer and winter, also produces a certain slow flow of air. And although the cold of the *Magnale* condenses equally, and thus far the air is unmoved by reason of the alterative *Blas* and the violent wind-force; nevertheless, since in the opposite sphere of the region <note>original: "sphæra plaga"</note>, the *Magnale* in the air is so greatly rarefied generally because of summer; it is necessary for the air in the northern region partly to recede and be compressed, and thus occupy a smaller place, and partly to be gently propelled by the rarefying and rarefied *Magnale* of the air contiguous to it from the other half of the globe. And this is the cause of the question proposed: namely, of the slow and unceasing flow in the winter air which we experience through a crack, however small, even when the wind has ceased. But it is not so under heat. For once the *Magnale* has been rarefied through the summer, the air stands unmoved among us.

...now awakened. Hippocrates calls wind "breath" or "flatulence" <note>original: *ventum, flatum*</note>; he recounts that all diseases arise from breaths, and places his *pneuma* <note>Greek: *τὸ πνεῦμα*, meaning spirit or breath</note> among the primary causes of illness. Truly, that was an age of simplicity and candor, for those more blessed ancestors did not yet possess such a great knowledge of diseases, nor were they so cruel or frequent. For not everything was granted to Hippocrates.

2. For the Almighty was pleased to create His own physicians even after Hippocrates. He was indeed able to show Hippocrates that there is a spirit within us, which he called *Blas* <note>A term coined by van Helmont to describe a localized vital motion or "astral" force</note>, inciting all things; this he then compared, by microcosmic analogy, to the breaths of the world, and restricted it to a series of breaths, whether they were participants in life or indeed in death, and contained the causes within. Whether these were finally excited from the heavens, reflecting the analogies of the celestial orb, or at last stirred by sublunary law, he left undecided. For the lineage of vital spirits had not yet been fully made known.

3. For no one before this had learned by experiment that the matter of **Gas** is actually water <note>Van Helmont believed gas was a transformed state of water</note>, and thus it was not yet known that the winds of the world differ entirely from the vital spirit. From the knowledge of winds, offered by me in the preceding pages, I now finally proceed to the examination of the air.

4. For I have said that it is proved through mechanics that water is not formed from the compression of air, however cold it may be; and thus, there has been an error until now regarding the mixture of elements, the origin of springs, etc. Moreover, that mechanics is true: because air in an iron tube of one ell <note>A traditional unit of length, roughly 2-4 feet</note> can be compressed to about fifteen fingers' width; from the expansion of this compressed air, the projection of a marksman's bolt through a board would occur, no less than if it were propelled from a **Gun** <note>original: *Sclopeto*</note>.

5. Which certainly would not happen if, under such great compression, air were changeable into water under the cold of an iron winter. From this I first learned the matter and conditions of air; that it sustains the compression and dilation of itself most easily, as far as sight indicates. Whence I considered it a necessary consequence that in dilated air, according to its twofold extension, there must be some free space and a **vacuum**. For instance, if from a space of 28 fingers, without any loss of air, the air is shut up within five fingers of the tube, it follows that nearly [twenty-three] fingers, and almost half the air, is devoid of body. One of two things is necessary under this mechanical proof: either that a vacuum is absolutely and ordinarily given in the nature of air; or the penetration of bodies <note>The impossible idea of two physical objects occupying the same space</note> occurs in compressed air (as was said).

6. Surely many will admit a vacuum with me as more tolerable than the existence of different bodies in the same place. Since a vacuum is not far removed from nothingness, and the action of nothingness is weaker than the action of a doubled being. And since Nature began from nothing, she is closer to nothing than to a double. Thus, Nature struggles more against the double. Indeed, gunpowder <note>original: *pulvis pyrius*</note> overturns mountains, mines, and cities. However, nowhere is an equivalent paradigm offered for a vacuum. Furthermore, I prove an ordinary vacuum in the nature of air again as follows:

7. In the middle of the bottom of a dish, let a piece of **candle** be placed, fixed to the bottom with its own wax. Let it burn, and let water be poured around it to 2 or 3 fingers' depth; then let a deep **glass gourd** <note>original: *cucurbita vitrea*, a chemical flask</note> be inverted over the flame, with the flame standing 3 fingers above the water, so that the mouth of the inverted glass stands upon the bottom of the dish. You will soon see that in the place of the air in the aforementioned glass, the water is drawn upward by a certain suction and ascends into the glass in the place of the diminished air; and finally, the flame is suffocated. In which several truths occur.

**First—Truths.** 1. And especially, it is beyond doubt that flame is ignited smoke. 2. That smoke is a body of **Gas**. 3. That soot ascends from the tip of the burnt smoke. 4. That one part of tallow or wax is easily extended into ten thousand times its own size. From this I conclude that the space of the air ought not to be diminished by the flame, but necessarily increased, unless some part of the space in the air was a vacuum, which is diminished. Nor otherwise from the absurdity...

It is not absurd <note>original: "absurdo caret"</note> that an element might be annihilated or consumed. Indeed, a cannon <note>original: "bombarda"</note> or fire-mines <note>explosive tunnels used in siege warfare</note> would not operate with that power known to our age, nor would the shattering of rocks and the greatest disruptions in mines occur, unless a tiny bit of powder, ignited in a single moment, produced ten times a thousandfold of flame. This flame cannot be contained in the previous space occupied by the powder; instead, it shatters everything, rather than smoke penetrating smoke or flame penetrating flame. To this is added the expansion of air through the heat of the flame, and not its compression, as otherwise commonly appears to be the case. Finally, let a sulfurous wick <note>original: "lychnium sulfuratum"</note> be lit and suspended by a thread in a glass flask <note>original: "lagena vitrea"</note>; let there be a little water in the flask, and let the flask be very well sealed with a cork stopper so that it cannot breathe. You will see the flame and the smoke of the sulfur fill the entire area of the flask where the air is, and finally, the fire is extinguished. However, no reduction <note>original: "imminutionem"</note> of the air occurs, nor a suction <margin>9.</margin> of the water upward, because water would have to be substituted in the place of the air; thus, suction would not gain anything here, nor compensate for the defect in the air. It is true, indeed, that when the lid is opened, suction is detected. But the flame does not cling so tenaciously to the candle that it is capable of lifting such a great weight of water; that flame is destroyed from its wick by the slightest breath. And so, the flame does not immediately raise the water: but the suction, caused by some part of the air being consumed, lifts the water, and it remains for many days, the water having been raised even after the extinction <margin>10.</margin> of the flame. For this reason, I have considered that air has pores <note>the author suggests air is not a solid block but has internal spaces</note> which would allow for a violent constriction of the air in a tube, and some natural annihilation in a dish. But that the air in the glass should be condensed <margin>11.</margin> because of the heat of the flame and the soot—that is contrary to Mathematics <note>original: "Mathesi repugnat"; here meaning the certain laws of physics</note>. The instrument which measures the degrees of the surroundings <note>an early form of thermometer</note> shows that heat expands air, but does not contract it. Therefore, the aforementioned objection attacks the assumed thesis, by which it is granted that an addition of matter occurs in the air through the new matter of the flame and soot. But if it is said that there is something flammable in the air which is consumed by the flame of the candle, then a new absurdity arises. Namely, that some body is either plainly annihilated, or burned by the flame and, by burning, is not dilated. Finally, assuming that something is consumed, it is at least necessary that this flammable thing be converted either into nothing or into something. Yet it is characteristic of fire that, by burning, it extends everything flammable, but does not compress it. As I showed before regarding gunpowder <note>original: "pulverem pytium"</note>. But if we say that the air in the glass is diminished by the flame, then I have my point: namely, that there is something in the air, less than a body, which fills the vacancies of the air and is utterly annihilated by the fire. Nor is this as if it were the nourishment of the fire itself. For although that may be impertinent to this question and place, nevertheless, that which is truly not a body can nourish nothing. Furthermore, since it is neither a body nor a fat <note>original: "pingue"; referring to the "oily" principle thought to fuel fire</note>, it cannot be inflamed, ignited, or frightened by fire, or consumed. Then I shall also demonstrate in the chapter on forms that fire is not a substance. That which is not a substance does not require to be nourished. Finally, since air is an element and simple, it cannot, in its nature, admit a composition or connection of diverse things. Nor are there, in the essential substance of air, diversities of parts, some of which might be consumed by fire, while others are not at all. For that reason, if fire had found a flammable part in the air, the entire air, ignited by even a single candle, would have perished long ago. Nor would the fire have ceased if, having need of nourishment, it had found it nearby in the air. Indeed, if air were burned by fire, the air would pass into something simpler and more primary, and would cease to be an element. The flame of the candle would be prior to and simpler than the element of air. It is observed that in the cavities of the air, far from the air extending itself, there is a contraction; and this is the sole cause of the diminished space in the air, whereby a flame <margin>12.</margin> is also immediately suffocated. For heat, external to a glass vessel, appears to dilate the air within; but a fire inside, on account of its own soot <note>original: *fuligines*; the particulate byproduct of combustion</note>, actually provokes the suffocation and compression of the air. Therefore, heat by itself dilates the air, as is evident through the machine that measures the degrees of the surroundings <note>likely a primitive thermoscope or thermometer</note>; but fire, because of its <margin>13.</margin> soot, compresses it. And so it follows that the soot acts more strongly through compression than the heat does in dilating. Furthermore, the soot is more troublesome to the air than its own natural vacuum—indeed, more so than the dilation of its vacuum. Since the dilation of the space of the air, caused by heat, is pleasurable to it compared to the compression caused by soot. From this, I conjecture that the individual members of the universe possess a certain sympathetic sense. <margin>14.</margin> And so, since air essentially possesses porosities, it feels pain if those are filled and overburdened by a foreign <term>Gas</term> <note>The author, Van Helmont, famously coined the word "Gas" from the Greek "Chaos."</note>. However, unless the air possessed empty porosities (at which point the doctrine of Physics founded on the "negative vacuum" <note>The Aristotelian idea that "Nature abhors a vacuum."</note> falls), bodies would by no means admit their own dilation or a foreign Gas. Indeed, through their commutation into Gas, they would require a thousand times greater capacity, and thus space <margin>15.</margin> would fail for the breathing out of effluvia. Air, therefore, was created to be a receptacle for what is exhaled; wherefore it is also necessary that it possess a vacuum in its pores. Yet it receives those exhalations by a fixed rate and a just proportion of itself: and when it has its vacancies filled to the just measure, the air flees, and by its flight, it forces every flame into a pyramid. But if the air, hindered from flight, is burdened with excessive soot, it fills itself up <margin>16.</margin> and becomes cramped by the soot. These things have not yet been weighed by the Schools <note>The traditional academic authorities following Aristotle.</note>, and therefore they thought that fire lives and is nourished by air; nor do they have proof for this, except from a contrary sense: because fire, shut off from air, is soon suffocated. The extreme ignorance of the Schools is quite plain here. Since fire is not a body, insofar as it is fire, nor is it a creature of the primary constitution: for it neither lives nor is nourished, being more like death itself. This will be made manifest in the discussion on the "origin of forms." Air, however, is a simple element. For the suffocation of fire does not presuppose a necessary life, nor nutrition; nor is there an increase of fire accordingly, even if it be built up with plenty of open air. Neither does fire consume even the smallest bit of air, or convert it into its own substance (of which it has none) as if it were its nourishment. These are fables. For fire deprived of air perishes, not indeed because of denied nourishment or a shared life, but from a lack of space, being unable to contain the soot; by the compression of which, the suffocated fire is extinguished. Indeed, by too much and rapidly blown air, a flame perishes immediately in another way; since a flame less tenaciously fixed to the wick is carried away by the blast, and once removed from the wick, it has no further subsistence in the air, just as it has no substance in itself. Therefore, the pores of the air, filled with soot, fly away and yield their place to other incoming air, so that they may also receive their own amber-like portion of Gas. This flight of air stirs up the wind, as it requires. In the Salt-works of Burgundy, a flat dish filled with water, placed next to the grate of a furnace, freezes much more quickly than any other exposed to the open air and frost, on account of the continuous influx and passage of air—which the Schools wrongly thought flowed in for the life or nourishment of the flame. Therefore, the vacancies of the air are filled moderately; but if they are overburdened, it soon closes the place, the empty porosities being consumed, so that by suffocating the exhaling fire, it may turn it away from its undertaking. This is innate to all created things through <term>philautia</term> <note>Self-love or the instinct for self-preservation.</note>. For in no other way does water encrust itself with ice, than lest it be snatched away into Gas by the cold of the air. There are, therefore, necessary vacancies in the air, so that, according to their capacity, they might host evaporable <margin>17.</margin> outpourings; for the sake of which, the air must sustain compression and dilation...

...he made use of. For otherwise, if the vacuum of the air were removed, the slightest motion would move almost the entire universe in its continuity; mortals nearby would be suffocated and collapse, soon overcome by rising exhalations, just as often happens in the shafts of mines. In those places, miners are suffocated, not from a total lack of air—for it is most abundant—nor always because of a suffocating poison, but chiefly because the air in the shafts, being filled with the **Gas** <note>original: *Gas mineralium*; Van Helmont's term for "spirit" or "gas" derived from the Dutch *geest*</note> of minerals, is not renewed. Thus it also happens that lamps and torches are soon extinguished of their own accord, along with the diggers.

18. For this reason, they bore through the shafts and, using various machines, exhaust the air filled with exhalation and pour in and breathe in new air. Truly, air rejects excessive exhalation no differently than water rejects air, or anything else violently coupled with it in the same lodging. Imagine a brass flagon: let there be water at the bottom, **A**; air, **B**; a stopcock <note>original: *robineta*</note>, **C**; and the opening of the flagon, **D**, through which air is forcefully blown in with a siphon or a syringe <note>original: *clysteris*</note>. Then the stopcock is turned so that it violently holds the air beneath it. I say, therefore, that when the stopcock is quickly turned to give the air an exit, it will not only blow out the compressed air **B**, but along with it, the water **A** will fly upward in its entirety with great force. The air, therefore, sustains the sudden compression of its vacuum; for that reason, it also carries the water **A** out with it. This surely shows a vacuum to be more plausible than a "compression of air," which approaches the forced penetration of a body. Now, therefore, regarding the "impossible vacuum" of Aristotle, it has become an ordinary requirement of nature.

19. Nevertheless, those porosities of the air, however much they are actually void of all matter, nonetheless contain within themselves a created being—that is, something real, not a figment, nor merely empty space.

20. But it is something between matter and spirit, incorporeal, clearly a medium and a neutral thing; from the number, I say, of those things which, in the chapter on Forms, I denied were either Substance or Accident. It is a **Magnale** <note>A term used by Van Helmont to describe a "great thing" or a neutral, non-material medium that transmits celestial influences</note>; because it has no likeness among created things, it refuses to be manifested by anything similar to itself.

21. This **Magnale** is not light, but a certain form assisting the air, acting as its companion and joined to it as if in a certain marriage. Assisting, I say, not joined to its essence; therefore, it resides in the pores. Through this, clearly, the **Blas** <note>Van Helmont's term for the "impulse" or "motive power" of the stars and nature</note> of the stars is extended everywhere and with instantaneous motion, immediately and without hindrance. It is not through thousands upon thousands of generations of "species" <note>A reference to the Scholastic theory that light and influence travel by creating successive "images" or "species" through a medium</note> that celestial influences strike the lower world. These are the fables of the Schools, invented so they are not forced to concede that a single "Accident" can migrate from subject to subject; they prefer to believe that thousands of generations of species of light are made in an instant while the Sun, so far away, vibrates its rays toward us. Because the Schools establish this as an **Impossibility** <note>original: *Adynaton* (Greek)</note>, I will teach that the course of Nature is ordinary within the limits of the **Great Thing** <note>original: *Magno*</note>.

22. Now, therefore, the **Gas** and **Blas** of Nature are sufficiently established, as is the path by which the **Blas** descends to us. Regarding the wind, the doctrines of the Schools must be added.

23. First, the Schools of Aristotle teach that wind is a dry exhalation (but not air) raised from the earth by the power of heat; when it is prevented from climbing upward by a cloud, it runs about laterally as if furious, and produces the strength of such great mass. As if it had lost its original lightness through the first repulse of the clouds, and therefore raged laterally! As if the texture of the clouds were continuous, and no entrance or passage through the clouds were granted to an exhalation once repulsed by a tiny cloud! As if a flagon filled with air were to run about under water! And as if it had lost its prior upward urge, so that forgetting to climb, even if it did not find a continuous cloud, it would thereafter prefer to be carried laterally. For they did not consider that the lateral motion of the winds must...

For Aristotle writes that the salt of the sea (which he nevertheless thought was co-eternal with the world) has its origin from exhalation. (He did not recognize exhalation in the slightest: since it is volatile, and sea salt is fixed: for the water of the sea, otherwise fresh, cannot fix the volatility of exhalation, any more than sal ammoniac <note>original: "salem armeniacum"</note> itself). He also dedicated all meteors, and especially winds, even earthquakes and comets (of which the one in the year 1618 was a thousand times larger than the earth), as well as stones, cliffs, and rocks, to exhalations. His dreams lacked an adequate storehouse from which such great exhalations might come. And nevertheless, the Schools subscribe to these trifles, and do not wake up from their trance <note>original: "Catocho," a Greek-derived term for a cataleptic state or rigid trance.</note> unless Aristotle expressly strikes against their faith.

Galen, however, thinks that wind, or "flatus," is vapors raised from water and lakes by the force of heat; but that it is subsequently air, resolved from a mixed body. He says both are cold, assimilated to a decrepit age, lacking innate heat, and to cold affections. Stumbling, of course, in each and every point, he expanded childish dreams into an immense scale in place of the truth. For in Galen's time, the art of distilling had not yet become known; he never saw rose water, nor <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>. Indeed, he had read Dioscorides poorly, writing along with Pliny that quicksilver, because of its immense weight, could not be held in leather or wooden cases, but only preserved in metallic boxes. As if a single ounce of it weighed more than an ounce of lead! For this reason, Galen was bound to be deeply and inwardly ignorant of the highest principles of Philosophy and the innermost principles of Nature—the seminal resolutions and exaltations of any properties whatsoever.

Finally, to show the presence of vacuum in the air, it is fitting to investigate more deeply the nature of its rarefaction and condensation. First of all, whatever I have said so far about the rarefaction of air, I confess was done for the sake of the common understanding:

->otherwise, properly speaking, although air<-

<margin>27.</margin> seems to be compressed and expanded in a space of place; yet the rarefaction itself is not of the air itself—that is, that the body of the air itself becomes thinner by itself, in the way that breath <note>original: "halitus"</note> is made from water. For I have already shown several times that breath is a cloud of atoms of water, separated from each other by the intervening parts of the air, and that therefore water, in breath, always remains water, and suffers nothing else except its own extension and division into atoms, performed by its "Separator." For if the body of air were to be rarefied, this would be either insofar as it changed into another body, thinner, rarer, and simpler than itself—which is to invent a new and unheard-of element, actually cold, thinner than others, and simpler than air. Or, the air would be rarefied through the separation of atoms and the intervention of another unknown body; and then the intervening body would admit degrees of rarity; and therefore the rarefaction itself should be referred not so much to the air as to the intervening unknown body.

Yet there is rarefaction, not of the air, but *in* the air; and that is not only due to admitted soot (as in the mechanics of a dish) but due to the naked quality of heat (as is evident through the instrument measuring the qualities of the surroundings <note>A reference to an early thermometer or thermoscope.</note>). Therefore, whenever rarefaction appears in the air, it is absolutely necessary that it happens through the increase of the <term>Magnal</term> <note>A term used by Helmont to describe a neutral, non-elemental fluid or "gas" that occupies space and carries light/heat.</note>. This signifies that the vacuum in the air is increased, and the pores of the air are dilated and extended. So much so, that it is far from the case that because of heat, the air sustains rarefaction by itself and in its own body, and the body of the element is changed: rather, it is coagulated, or at least compressed, and the porosities of the vacuum extend themselves, or the Magnal itself is multiplied in the air. Wherefore <margin>28.</margin> it is also an improper way of speaking when we indicate that air is rarefied by itself, when it is rather thickened or compressed by itself: while the Magnal...

## ANOMALOUS METEORS.

Indeed, it is innate to itself, and therefore it is extended. From the aforementioned, however, it is deduced that the body of the air is led to its proper extension under the influence of cold. And again, it follows from this that cold is natural to the air. But the *magnale* <note>The author uses "magnale" to refer to a subtle, quasi-spiritual substance or "great work" within the air that mediates physical effects.</note> is contracted under cold. Whenever the *magnale* is constricted, the influence of the stars is scarcely constricted toward us. And from this, it is obvious why the Land of Promise <note>The Holy Land/Palestine.</note> is very warm—that is, why in a warmer zone, the Heavens are more fortunate in their kinship with the earth, the fruits more abundant, and more flavorful. The *magnale*, therefore, like light, is created and annihilated easily. For what is the vacuum of the air in itself is almost nothing in respect to bodies. For it produces from nothing, and into nothing it can also be reduced. But not without the air's resistance, because it has need of this vacuum for itself. Alas! how nearly nothing is the whole of nature, which began from nothing. In the aforementioned instrument <note>Likely a primitive thermoscope or weather glass.</note> measuring the surrounding environment by the heat or cold of the Sun, a larger or smaller place for the air is discerned; however, toward the rarefaction of what is contained, we feel the air being expelled. If its spirit—its position—is closed off, it is felt to be choked by the lack of air. Therefore, by looking deeply, the vacuum of the air—hence the *magnale*—is increased and diminished; however, the air itself does not rarefy. So also condensation, or the compression of air, is not in respect to its body, but only to the *magnale*.

# ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA

21. ...to accuse [nature] due to our ignorance of its causes. I shall relate at least one story that is worth a thousand. In the year 1554, in the territory of Liège <note>original: "Leodiensi"</note>, the tower of Kuringen <note>original: "Curingiæ"</note> was carried away by thunder and appeared nowhere. Finally, after a fortnight, while a grave was being opened in the small grassy area of the cemetery to bury a cobbler, behold—under the undisturbed green sod—first a brass rooster appeared with an iron cross, then the pinnacle of the tower, and finally the entire tower was excavated. I myself saw, by a single clap of thunder in my presence, several tens of thousands of oaks and hazelnuts burned in their first buds and leaves—namely an entire forest in a place called "The Grove" near Vilvoorde <note>original: "Vilyordiam"</note>—where meanwhile the numerous Birch, Beech, and Alder trees, though densely mixed in confusion with the others, remained unharmed by the thunder. At other times, however, with a single strike, it hits many things far apart simultaneously. For who can sufficiently explain the thousand various tricks and mockeries of the Craftsman <note>The "Craftsman" here refers to the Devil or a deceptive spiritual agent.</note>? It is enough that many spiritual actions concur, which are foreign to the ordinary course of nature, being equally powerful at a distance as they are nearby.

22. Therefore, that terrible voice of Thunder strikes the earth, kills silkworms, shakes beer and forces it to turn sour, makes the hung meat of a slaughtered ox flaccid, and curdles milk with a sudden ferment of acidity, etc. However, salt placed on the outside, at the rim of the jar or vessel, averts effects of this kind. Surely a weak resistance against such a great agent, if in nature the one resisting must prevail over the agent.

23. But what of it? The Evil Demon <note>original: "Cacodaemon"</note> hates salt, and therefore in his "Sabbaths of Sows" <note>A derogatory reference to witches' sabbaths.</note>, salt is said to be perpetually lacking; he is well aware that salt is exorcised for holy water, and sometimes a baptizer uses salt. Even unblessed salt ruins his commands. If, therefore, the tree is known by its fruits, so the author must be known by his works—all the more so because such weak remedies resist such great strength. Nor does it truly suggest the contrary that God, appearing to Moses on the mountain in perpetual lightning and thunder, surrounded the mountain in the presence of Israel. On the contrary, it is confirmed from this that the crash, thunder, and lightning belong to the ministering spirits—evil and executing spirits—since under the threat of death, Israel was barred from ascending the mountain. For I do not see that the thunders were at the peak of the mountain, but below, around the mountain. Nor did the Almighty appear to Elijah in a whirlwind or a strong wind, but in a gentle breeze.

As a corollary, I shall cite here the decree of the Church, which prescribes certain formulas in the blessing of a bell, confirming the same presidency over Thunder that I have prescribed in this chapter. For in the words of its exorcism, they have: *Let all the snares of the enemy, the crash of hail, the gale of whirlwinds, the onset of tempests be driven far away; let the hostile thunders and the blasts of the winds be tempered, etc. Let the right hand of your power lay low the powers of the air, and hearing this bell, let them tremble and flee. Before its sound, let the fiery darts of the enemy be driven further away, along with the flash of lightnings, the onslaught of stones, the damage of tempests, etc.*

Doubtless, all these exorcisms conspire against tempests. For hail, wind, rain, clouds, etc., are natural meteors; but the tempestuous hurling—surpassing the natural fall of a body of grain or the flow of wind—is understood to be done by malignant powers. These things are indeed confirmed regarding tempests of the air, hail, and sea; but in Thunder, it is not only the hurling of lightning or stones, but furthermore the crash of the thunder itself that depends on the powers of the air and our enemies. This is because no mere crashes could naturally produce these effects unless portentous and hostile powers mingled and played their part.

-> **The name is improper.** <- 2. Nicolaus Copernicus, through many phenomena, contended that the earth moves in a circle with the orb of the moon; and since no motion is proper to a globe except a spherical one, and that does not suit the earth according to the decree of the Church, I have therefore removed the name "motion" from the earth and changed it, so that it is instead said to "tremble" in fear. For the earth, being passively struck or threatened by some immense force, is shaken as if by fear and horror; it does not leap for joy. Indeed, it seems to endure something mournful and horrific, outside the usual course of nature. Therefore, having first established the name "tremor," the appearance of the event follows.

3. Truly, it was night, between the third and fourth day of April in the year 1640, a quarter past the third hour after midnight. The moon was two days away from being full, and it was the Wednesday before Easter, when Mechelen <note>original: "Mechlinia"</note> (where I then was for certain reasons) trembled significantly and leaped with three repeated attacks. In each invasion, the tremor lasted a little less than the time it takes to recite the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "symboli Apostolorum"</note>. Each attack was immediately preceded by a certain bellowing in the air, as if the movement of wheels, such as those by which great war engines are carried through the streets, were shaking the ground. The night, I say, was serene, clear, and devoid of wind. Indeed, because of a legal case then being reviewed, I was returning home a little before midnight. I was staying near the Dijle river in the Teutonic Commandery, commonly called Pitzenborch, according to the custom and humanity of the Illustrious man Lord Wernher Spies von Bullensheim, of the Teutonic Order, Provincial Commander of Koblenz <note>original: "Bulliniæ confluentiae"</note> and Commander of Pitzenburg, Lord <note>term: "Toparcha" - a local governor or lord of a district</note> in Elson, Herren-nolheum, etc. I was received there, removed from the streets by about 70 paces. I later learned from friends that at almost the same moments, and in the same three repeated turns separated by an equal interval, a similar thing occurred...

## I.
**D**iscussing the tremor of the earth, its causes, and its purposes, I shall begin above all with the name. It is usually called "motion" <note>original: "Motus"</note>, but that name seems to me too general and very improper. For while the earth or any other heavy body hastens downward, it is said to move itself, just as flowing water actively moves a wheel. But in a tremor of the earth, the motion seems to be passive, and thus by accident...

# EARTH TREMOR.

->EARTH TREMOR.<-

With a thousand accompanying bellows, the earth was heard to tremble at Brussels, Antwerp, Lier, Ghent, Mons in Hainaut, Namur, and Cambrai. Subsequently, we heard that the same had occurred in Holland, Zeeland, Friesland, Luxembourg, and Guelders; indeed, even as far as Frankfurt am Main, the shaking was no less severe. At Metz, buildings were several times demolished, and new structures collapsed near Thionville <note>original: "Theonpolin"</note>. Westphalia also trembled, as did Amiens <note>original: "Ambiavum"</note> and the neighboring coasts of France. All these regions surely trembled at the same moment, even if, due to the globe of the sphere, the clocks announcing the hours of the days necessarily differed. The tract of land extends at least three hundred and sixty leagues; in every smallest location of that circle, the ground quivered with equal dread. For the watchman in the vast tower of the cathedral of Mechelen was shaken no differently than any man lying in a humble hut. No differently, I say, did the dweller by the Scheldt <note>original: "Scaldis"</note>, the inhabitant of the islands, or the citizen of the fields feel it, than those who dwelt upon the higher hills. The fortune of all and each was then equal. Finally, I learned that ships in the harbors of Holland and Zeeland were buffeted in their masts and yardarms, even without any wind.

Regarding the immediate causes of such a great effect, there is <margin>4. Much agreement.</margin> much agreement among writers. Moderns, I say, swallowing the dictates of Aristotle, have not yet retreated a finger's breadth from them. Although they have added their own inventions to the precepts of the ancients. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval university system based on Aristotelian logic.</note> therefore teach that the earth trembles because of air, wind, or an exhalation <term>exhalation: a vaporous or smoky gas thought to be trapped underground</term> gathered beneath and in the caverns and pores of the earth, which, seeking an exit and eventually making one for itself, causes the earth to leap up. For from this, not infrequently, bursting forth through gaps and fissures, it gives rise to fatal diseases. This is the tradition of the Schools, received throughout the whole world for twenty-one centuries. If this had seemed to me consistent with the designs of the Divine Will, I would have refrained from writing. But it seemed to me to be sown with weighty anxieties and inevitable absurdity, containing no small amount of "old wives' tales." Indeed, the human race so willingly sinks into a stupor that, as if hope of learning were cut off, they command that all the treasures of the sciences be exhausted in Aristotle alone, and that further investigation should cease. I, therefore, shall first show the impossibility of that doctrine, and then I shall set forth my own opinion, established not by pagan dreams, but confirmed by the doctrine of a higher authority.

For first of all, the earth is actually divided into certain layers, soles, or bottoms. Indeed, the external bottom of the earth is visibly sandy, clayey, muddy in other places, dungy, gray, white, yellow, black, red, etc., playing with various diversities. Beneath this, there is generally gravel, and this itself is distinguished everywhere by great variety. Beneath this bottom, however, there is finally the flinty mountain (which they call *Renberch* <note>A Germanic mining term for "pure rock" or bedrock</note>), the layer of rocks, and the origin and first root of minerals. And finally, everywhere beneath this bottom, there is living sand, boiling gravel, *Dref*, or *quellem* <note>original: "quellem" - likely referring to "Quellgrund" or quicksand/spring-fed soil</note>, which, carried by waters in its continuity, extends even to the center of the world. And although all the aforementioned bottoms do not everywhere succeed each other in order, nevertheless the *quellem* is everywhere the final layer of the world, although it is not infrequently immediately exposed to the air and visible. (As concerning the origin of springs, in the book on the springs of Spa). This being once supposed, I say that the place where the exhalation would be—which is believed to be the cause of the earth tremor—would have to be situated in some place between one of the said layers, since in the earth there is no place outside the aforementioned strata. To the subversion of that doctrine, however, a demonstration is required which, from a sufficient enumeration of the layers, shows it is impossible for an exhalation of this kind to be contained or raised in any of the said bottoms, or if it were raised there, that it could not have the power to form a tremor of the earth. As to the first of the three members (namely, that no exhalation can be contained beneath the earth...

### E A R T H

I shall prove [the nature of the earth that actively causes its trembling]. It is not primarily located beneath the outermost, muddy, or first layer of the earth, which is near the air and designated as the habitation of mortals. For if that were so, the tower of St. Rumbold <note>The cathedral tower in Mechelen, Belgium</note> would not have trembled, nor would the buildings constructed immediately upon the *source-rock* <note>original: "quellem"; likely referring to the solid bedrock or spring-bearing strata</note>. Nor would ships, far removed from the sandy bottom in deep waters, be affected by a whirlwind of winds. For granted that the floor of the Sea might tremble just as other inhabited land does: nevertheless, without wind and storm, the surface of the water would not maintain the same steady shaking as that trembling sand. Yet this is found to be false, for even flying birds, having felt the trembling of the earth, would not fall as if struck—a sign that the air itself also trembles. Indeed, the elements shall one day melt in the sight of the Judge. Therefore, if the water trembles no less than the quiet earth itself, it is indicated that its cause is within the globe; or rather, that earth and water, by the same blow of percussion, together with the air, feel the dread or bear witness to the hand of the Striker <note>A reference to God as the "Percutientis" or Smiter</note>. Furthermore, an exhalation <term>exhalation: in early modern science, a dry vapor trapped underground thought to cause earthquakes</term> cannot dwell in any sandy depths as the cause of the tremor: because then the marshes, meadows, and places where the *source-rock* is spread immediately beneath the mud would not have trembled. This, like the preceding point, is far from the truth of the facts. Thirdly and finally, such an exhalation cannot be hidden beneath the *Keybereh* <note>A local geological term, likely referring to a specific hard clay or gravel stratum</note>. For in the entire circle where the earth then trembled, with few places excepted, the foundation of *Keybereh* does not exist at the same moment. Finally, an exhalation sufficient to shake such a mass with equal fury could neither arise nor be detained within the *source-rock*. Inasmuch as the *source-rock* (not infrequently near the air) is connected even to the center of the universe by its continuous unity and the mixing of waters, it would easily blow out such an exhalation before it could lift such a great mass all at once. Indeed, this assertion is inexcusable, because such an exhalation would break out at the weaker, less heavy, and less resistant part: that is, in the place of least weight. And so, under the thesis of a given exhalation, the tremor could not be equal in all places. This contradicts the facts. For before an exhalation could lift such enormous weights through such vast and varied spaces of soil and water simultaneously and in a single moment, it would have sought and found the yielding and weaker places through which it would have made a way for itself to burst out. Otherwise, the exhalation would fight against the rules of nature, proportion, and motion, which would elevate all of Belgium and great parts of Germany equally and at the same time. Especially 7. where the capacity of each place to house the exhalation is not equal, nor is the burden of the overlying load or the resistance of the weight equal; just as an equal arousal of that exhalation is impossible, so that it might act equally through so many tracts at once, in almost a single moment. Which is to say, it is impossible—if an exhalation is posited as the motor of the earthquake—to have equality in the simultaneity and power of motion through such a vast space, through such great differences of soil and sky, resistance, and irregularity of weight: since such an acting exhalation, measuring its own efficacy by the variety of places, the difference of the moving force, magnitude, activity, and speed, would necessarily be unequal and would have to obey the inequalities of the locations. Therefore, the quantity, origin, 8. power, lodging, and speed of exhalations are ridiculous, if they were to shake so many cities, mountains, valleys, hills, watery places, meadows, rivers, seas, islands, and such a vast mass, scattered far and wide, at one and the same moment, uniformly and repeatedly, and would find or make an exit for itself more quickly than it sought one. Now, however, to the 9. point: namely, that in the aforementioned strata of the earth, the arousal of an exhalation which might be the cause of an earthquake is impossible: let any natural "outflow" <note>original: "Aporrhea"; a Greek-derived term for a discharge or emanation</note> be examined through its causes. The exhalation that can be supposed as the mover of the earth is not, first of all, a vapor or watery breath, because that most swiftly returns again into water through compression, as happens daily in our...

in our distilling vessels <note>original: "alembicis"</note>: but an exhalation, according to Aristotle—which is especially necessary in these terms—is a hot and dry effluvium from bodies (and usually also oily) from dry parts, raised by sharp heat into the form of air, or a rising smoke. But I would wish the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university professors who taught traditional Aristotelian philosophy.</note> to answer: what, then, will that actual, equal, and connected heat be, beneath the sea, rivers, ponds, meadows, and beneath everything? For it is necessary that the heat and dryness be actual and strong, which are sufficient for such a remarkable effect in that place; and not merely potential qualities—bare, remote, possible, or imaginary. What is that heat, by whom and from where is it stirred up, in the deepest cold? What is that heat so brief, so strong, and so interrupted, which ceases after a few rigors of trembling, and does not seek the earth anew by trembling? For if the cause of such great motion is in heat, there will not be, at least after the motion, a cause of such sudden rest within that heat. Finally, what is this dryness, connected to fire, which immediately beneath the earth and waters, uniformly throughout all Belgium, should kindle a fire—the patron of such great exhalations—once the waters have been dried out? <margin>11.</margin> But come now, let us imagine in jest, and let us grant, that there is actual heat beneath the water and earth which is capable of igniting: at least, would that great and stubborn heat, and its unusual action, stir up exhalations before the dryness of the matter? This would certainly be an anomalous effect, hitherto never seen among fire-workers <note>original: "pyrotechnicos," referring to chemists or engineers who work with fire.</note>. Again, let us imagine other absurdities: that an actual, violent fire in water, or beneath watery places, could be born there without tinder, and be sustained without fuel, and proceed and persist for a long time. But at the very least, it could not excite vapors—and much less enclosed exhalations—breaking forth more tightly, which would not immediately suffocate that fire and render the sufficiency, strength, and successive generation of those exhalations void. Indeed, in the shafts of mines <note>original: "cuniculis mineralium"</note>, if they are not refreshed from time to time from above by a new breath of air, the lamps are immediately extinguished, and at the same time the miners are deprived of their standing and their lives. But if they are to subsist as fire and as exhalation until there is enough, let respiration be granted. Now, by that very fact, its offspring—the motive exhalation—will first breathe out through there; or if there is no place for sufficient respiration, the fire will necessarily be suffocated, nor will there be a place for such a great successive exhalation, or for the repeated onset of an earthquake. Let us imagine again, not indeed fire or actual heat, being hosted beneath the waters in the aforementioned soles of the earth: but that all of Belgium had in all places something similar to gunpowder <note>original: "pulveri tormentario"</note>, which finally, beneath the waters, by its own maturity or by a secret conspiracy of the stars, is ignited at once and everywhere, and to that extent supplies an instantaneous exhalation, equal in every place. But not even under such trifles <margin>12.</margin> would all of Belgium then leap up more than once, and it would have gaped open in the softer, less deep, and less heavy places, and some fragments of it would have leaped into the heights, and a chimney for that exhaling flame would have followed in that same place. But Belgium and part of Germany would not have trembled in such a way. For as soon as the earth had risen to a peak somewhere and gaped open, it would not have trembled more often, like a feverish rigor. For the supposed action of ignition would occur only so that the penetration of bodies might be hindered. Therefore, as to the third point: <margin>13.</margin> That even granted a sufficient exhalation beneath the earth, a tremor of the earth is nonetheless impossible. I have indeed already begun to prove this through certain granted fictions. Otherwise, in whatever way the exhalation is taken, and wherever it is supposed to be among the strata, the earth would not tremble from it: but elsewhere, where there were the least resistances, it would rise into a heap or a hump until it gaped, and the exhalation, by breathing out through a huge abyss <note>original: "voraginem"</note>, had made a way for itself. Since these things are not found to have happened, the tradition of the Schools also collapses. <margin>14.</margin> For first of all, so that it may be more clearly established, there is another action, and another mode of action,

<header>OF THE EARTH</header>
...when, due to the fear of the penetration of bodies <note>A reference to the Aristotelian principle that two bodies cannot occupy the same space at the same time</note>, the matter bursts apart; and that nature works differently because of the supposed lightness of exhalations striving to break out. Observe the mechanics of this. Take a large glass flask, thick and strong; pour into it four ounces of *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid</note>, prepared from saltpeter, alum, and vitriol, each dried separately. Into that water, throw one ounce of powder of sal ammoniac; and immediately let the neck of the glass be closed by melting it shut. This is what is called the **Seal of Hermes** <note>An airtight, or "hermetic," seal</note>. As soon as the spontaneous action begins, the vessel is filled with a copious (though invisible) exhalation, and even if it were imagined to be stronger than iron, it soon dangerously bursts into fragments because of the "fear of penetration," and not by reason of the lightness of the many exhalations. For even if it bursts because of the multitude and compression of the lightest and invisible exhalations, their lightness nevertheless has no importance in this. For if it did, the glass vessel itself, before its disruption, would be lifted spontaneously into the air and fly upward. Because it is a task of less effort to lift a weight of 3 or 4 pounds than to shatter a very strong vessel. Therefore, the exhalations which break the glass would much more powerfully elevate the glass, if the aid of "lightness" were not a vain concept. The Schools <note>The Scholastic philosophers following Aristotle</note> would beg for help from exhalations to explain the trembling of the earth. If, therefore, exhalations are not able by their own lightness to lift the vessel in which they are enclosed, much less could they lift such a vast and massive bulk of earth.

<margin>15.</margin> Finally, since every exhalation belongs to some body, and every body, if it be separable, is divided into **salt, sulfur, and mercury** <note>The *Tria Prima* or three primary elements of Paracelsian alchemy</note>: the mercurial part becomes the watery part of the body. Therefore, it is necessary that every exhalation be of a salty and oily matter. And that this part be raised up before the watery part. This has not yet happened in our glasses under the steady action of heat. If, therefore, the exhalation is salty, it is easily soaked into the earth; which can be seen in absolutely all waters and exhalations of any salts whatsoever: which, by acting upon the earth, are coagulated within it and lose all activity. Therefore, if they were stirred up within the earth, they would fail before they even existed, or would have ceased in the very making. But if it is an oily exhalation, that surely, when deposited in the earth, reassumes its former appearance of oil and thus grows together. Since this happens easily, it cannot be imagined how an exhalation, by its own lightness, could make such a mass of earth and immense weight stagger sooner than it would decide to coagulate. And in any event, there would be no place for anything but a single elevation of the earth, and a single subsidence of the same after some gap was found; but not for the exciting of a trembling trepidation. But let these be the dreams of those in watery places, meadows, muddy spots, ponds, the sea, rivers, etc.

<margin>16.</margin> Therefore, the absurdities which I previously conceded in jest, I will now attack in earnest. First, I ask, what is this heat so unusual, which from the year 1580 until the year 1640 was not seen in Mechelen <note>A city in the Low Countries, modern-day Belgium</note>? Just as no earthquake was seen? Why not every year? Why in April, during a very cold night, when it had snowed much the day before? Under a continuous North Wind? And not under the Dog Days <note>The hottest days of summer</note>? Is it because the interior of the earth is hot then? Why then not every year in January? But this argument of the Ancients fails after the discovery of the instrument that measures the degrees of the surrounding air <note>An early thermometer</note>. For

<margin>17.</margin> wells and caves are found to be of equal heat and cold throughout the whole year. Again: why does such great heat, the stirrer of exhalations, cease so suddenly? Especially where it stirs up a motor for an exhalation of such great mass? By what kindling is it lit under the water? On what food does it live and subsist? How is it not suffocated in that place? By what privilege does it look down upon the respect of bodies, places, and weights? By what prerogative, finally, does it stir up an exhalation of such vastness, without moist vapors, out of wet bodies? Or if it draws out vapors at the same time in the ordinary manner, why do these not mitigate the heat? Or extinguish it?

<header>TREMORS.</header>

## TREMORS.

Do they suffocate at the same time, along with their sisters <note>likely referring to related seismic phenomena or "vapors"</note> and the subsequent exhalations? Or what is this exhalation that shakes the vast tower of Mechelen <note>original: "Mæchliæ"; referring to St. Rumbold's Tower in Belgium</note> with no more regard than it does a humble hut? And why does it ignore the resistance of such immense weight? Does it act equally upon what is near and what is distant? Or does it find the collected power of its center everywhere and equally across the entire surface, so that it acts everywhere at once in a single moment, uniformly and with equal strength? Why, by the necessity of natural causes, is the thread not broken at its weakest part? Instead, all things undergo and even endure the same law of violence simultaneously. Certainly, if these things are considered rightly, there is found in the tremors of the earth a certain operative force of infinite power, which raises mountains and towers without regard for lightness or weight, as if nothing were able to resist this motive virtue.

<margin>18.</margin> Furthermore, I have proved that if there is any exhalation that is the efficient motive cause of the earth's tremor, it is neither from the lineage of salts, nor of sulfurs, nor of mercuries (since this is not an exhalation, but a vapor of watery parts). It remains, therefore, that it is not an exhalation: but the **Gas** <note>The author, Van Helmont, famously coined the word "Gas" to describe spiritual or volatile substances distinct from air</note> itself; not a stirred-up effluvium of bodies caused by heat, but rather the effective residue left after fire. Namely, the **Gas** of the flame of fire alone, or of the soot born from it. But neither of these exhalations can be the effective cause of the earth's tremor. Therefore, if none of these exhalations is the mover of the earth, there will be none at all (since no other is found), and consequently, it is an empty fiction of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Scholastic/Aristotelian university teaching</note> which they wish to be believed regarding the tremor of the earth. But if, seeking a loophole, they say they do not mean an exhalation excited by heat, nor one produced by necessity, but an "anonymous outflow" <note>original: "anonymam aporrheam"</note> established by its own causes—just as Aristotle writes that all rocks, stones, minerals, and even the salt of the sea, comets (though a hundred times larger than the globe of the earth), and all winds come forth from certain anomalous and unexplained exhalations, distinguishing winds therein from the air—this, I say, is to choose to rave with Aristotle and to remain, like him, ignorant of physics. Finally, it is impertinent to have cited Aristotle and to wish to defend one's errors through his authority. Nevertheless, I shall deal with the Schools by reason: so that since they proclaim themselves so rational, they may hand over their weapons to reason.

<margin>19.</margin> I say, therefore: No exhalation can be lighter, simpler, or more subtle than air, because air is a simple body of an element, while an exhalation is a composite body; and so, whatever it may be, it has within itself a heavy body which air lacks. Yet air is not lighter than a body that is without weight. That is, air is not lighter than itself, nor can it lift anything besides itself except through the motion of a blast or flow—that is, through **Blas** <note>A term coined by the author to describe a "motive power" or "astral influence" governing motion</note>. When this ceases, even the body it lifted sinks. From which I conclude that air or wind, whether enclosed or free, cannot lift the earth by reason of its lightness alone. Unless perhaps it is struck by an external and violent mover; but in this case, the force of the exhalation ceases, since it is merely the medium or organ of motion, not the principal motive force. Much less is this suitable for an exhalation, which is thicker and heavier than air insofar as it contains water.

<margin>20.</margin> I prove this through Mechanics. A bladder distended with air emerges from the water, not primarily because air is lighter than water, but because water is a heavy and fluid body; therefore, it does not allow itself to be pushed out of its place by a lighter body. The primary urge of water is to join itself to the water from which it was separated; the secondary urge, and as if by accident, is to squeeze out whatever is lighter than itself by its own settling. Gravity, therefore, not lightness, operates in this work, for a reason soon to be stated. Suppose a bladder capable of holding 3 ounces <note>original: "℥ iij."</note> of water is placed in a small pit and covered with earth. Truly, it will not shake off even half an ounce of the dust poured over it. Indeed, the bladder would not even seek to place itself outside the dry sand, being heavier—
