to stand out more prominently. It is therefore ridiculous to suggest that a bladder, weighing half an ounce, would ever fly up into the air of its own accord due to any lightness of the air. If, therefore, a great amount of air does not lift a bladder, much less certainly will air rise up when it is pressed down under the immense weight of the Low Countries <note>original: "Belgii"; referring to the Netherlands/Belgium region</note>. Elements, to be sure, look primarily and only to themselves; but they act as a whole for their own sake. Therefore, a glass bottle, filled with air and buried, attempts in vain to emerge from the earth; this is because air is everywhere in its own natural place, as long as there is a space not filled by another body, nor does it seek an exit. Therefore, if there are caves beneath the earth, the air in them naturally rests from all local motion. But in places where sand collapses like a fluid body, there, because the dust fills the vacuum and falls by its own weight, it accidentally squeezes out the air. But that movement of earth or water does not happen effectively because of the lightness of the air: or because the air, by the proper motion of its own lightness, moves itself upward and <margin>21.</margin> climbs. But (**Note**) in this, gravity itself is the efficient, active, primary, and total cause: since gravity has real weight and is an active quality. Conversely, the lightness of air is effective of nothing, since it has no weight and necessarily signifies "nothingness"; nor can it have any energy for acting. From which it follows: 1. That the lightness of air performs nothing: nor could a bladder, even if it were huge and weighed only six grains, be lifted spontaneously by the enclosed air, however great it might be; otherwise (which is false) air would be lighter than that which has no weight. 2. That air does not stand out above water because of its own lightness as an acting quality, or as the driving force of floating: but rather gravity is the real quality which expels the air. 3. And therefore, the theme of the Schools is absurd, in which air, or an exhalation, is established as the efficient cause of an earthquake because of its lightness, as if by lifting the earth it would shake it. Wherefore, <margin>22.</margin> since it has now been sufficiently proven: 1. That there is no place in the strata or soles of the earth where any airy body might be hosted, whether it be wind or an airy exhalation: but the deeper such a place is sought, the greater the difficulties that arise, both because of the greater abundance of water and the heavier burden of the earth from above, so that it would require almost infinite power to cause a tremor of the earth. 2. Next, that there can be no fire, heat, dryness, or alum <note>a mineral salt often associated with subterranean heat in early chemistry</note> as an exciter of an exhalation of such power: or its correlative. No possibility of such an exhalation subsists there in nature. And finally, thirdly: That no exhalation, by reason of lightness, performs anything or lifts a heavy body, much less so vast a region of the earth. I conclude, therefore, that whatever has been taught hitherto concerning the tremor of the earth is a hollow fiction of the Schools. Which again must be more strongly confirmed from abundance. Wherefore I will teach that the manner of the tremor of the <margin>23.</margin> earth taught by the Schools is utterly impossible. Let us imagine absurdities again, so that as if by a "rule of falsehood" <note>a logical method of proving a point by showing the absurdity of the opposite</note>, the error of the Schools may be detected. Let us grant, for instance, a bladder made of ductile material, a thousand times stronger than any iron, spread underneath (at some unknown depth) through the whole of the Low Countries and Germany, beneath the base of mountains, cities, seas, and rivers. And a thousand huge bellows, most firmly and perfectly attached all around. In order, therefore, for them to be able to lift the whole of the Low Countries at once, it is necessary that those bellows, and their posts and axles, be as strong as would be sufficient for the weight to be lifted. Next, a hand or agent would be required of such strength that it could lift the whole of the Low Countries in its palm, or otherwise it could not compress those bellows full of wind. But such an agent does not exist in the sublunary nature of things: even if the other granted absurdities were present. Therefore, the lightness of air or of a vain exhalation, and its innate desire to break out, is frivolous. Therefore, I do not hesitate at all to deny that wind is the cause, lest the honor due to my God be clouded over. The Schools, because they have hitherto been ignorant <margin>24.</margin> that lightness is not an active quality, and so—

<header>T R E M O R.</header>

which would be much less capable of overturning mountains. They had observed, however, that at times a mine, previously covered, soon after a trembling of the earth, vomited forth a foul poison and created a gap for itself: 
<margin>25.</margin> they are therefore, through thoughtlessness, inclined to refer the cause of the earth's trembling to this.
To make these things appear more clearly, let us imagine again the aforementioned "bladder" beneath Belgium, <note>The author frequently uses Belgium/the Low Countries as a hypothetical location for his geological models.</note> expanding with an airy body either of its own accord or by the influence of the stars (for when reason fails, the ignorant always recur to the stars and distant causes, and to witnesses that cannot be summoned). Suppose there are no bellows, nor openings anywhere around it. Then at least the body of the whole of Belgium, lying upon it, would press upon the aforementioned bladder with its own weight in such a way that, if it did not burst, it would at least vomit out its contents in a weaker and less heavy part. Once this happens, the cause for the compression of the bladder and the fall of Belgium is indeed present, along with the opening of some gap. But the cause for the *lifting* of that bladder is not yet findable, and much less the cause for the repeated succession of throbbing and trembling. Finally, such a bladder and its substance are not even possible; without which, even if there were a space in the earth, it is nonetheless not fit for receiving that exhalation. Indeed, behind the boundaries of the aforementioned bladder: at least the air or exhalation does nothing to lift the earth by its own lightness. Rather, if the earth should fall, it still finds no cause in the lightness of the trapped air: since it encloses the total cause in the fist of its own gravity: and the expression of the air must be measured according to the scale of the overlying weight. Therefore, assuming the bladder again, if some air or wind blew from the outside into the aforementioned bladder—compressed, lying on the ground, and empty of any body—no matter how strongly it blew, it would nonetheless never inflate the bladder, since the overlying Belgium would compress it. But if, instead of wind or air, a fiery exhalation is sought; I have already demonstrated the impossibility of fire and the fabled nature of an exhalation of such great effect throughout all of Belgium. Finally, that continuous bladder fails, which would need to be so strong and durable as to sustain on its back Belgium, the seas, the rivers, and much more besides. For even if I were to grant its existence: it is not that I think it exists, but that even if it were assumed, such great absurdities follow that they are eventually dashed against the "impossible" <term>adynaton: a rhetorical or logical impossibility</term> of the Schools.

The origins of this dream were given to the rustics <margin>26.</margin> (from whom the Schools received them) by mountainous places, sulfurous areas, and the dwellings of minerals. Ah! Is not the sluggishness in investigating the causes of effects to be pitied everywhere? Mount Soma, or Vesuvius, near Naples, has now burned for several centuries with sulfur and marcasites <note>marcasite: a brittle mineral (iron sulfide) often confused with pyrite in early modern geology</note>. It had, however, a gap in its summit through which the smoke and flame might breathe out, which was quite ample—perhaps the width of three arpents <note>arpent: an old French unit of area, roughly an acre</note>. However, the chamber nearest the flame, being already quite scorched and full of cracks, finally around December 16, in the year 1631, suddenly fell in one collapse into the abyss of the flame. Now, it is a property of certain metals as well as glowing marcasites during melting that if any water falls upon them, the whole mass leaps apart: therefore, the molten sulfur with the marcasites in the bowels of Vesuvius did not endure the falling scorched fragment of rock without a huge cataclysm; indeed, the flame vomited out everything that had fallen in from above, and more. Nor was this enough. In addition, several springs were released from above into the furnace of the fire. But what do molten sulfur or whirlwinds of soot have in common with the trembling of the earth? Does sulfur burn throughout the whole of Belgium? For a trembling of the earth had preceded that of Naples and accompanied that <margin>27.</margin> "Sodom-like" danger. And although they coincided, they do not therefore share a single root, as they obey different causes. That trembling of the earth, announcing a marvel, enclosed within itself a portent, and always encloses something of the sort. But the vomiting forth of metallic veins occurs by its own natural causes. It is truly a wretched sophism to argue from a non-cause as if it were a cause.

<meta>The author continues his investigation into the nature of the Earth, specifically challenging the Aristotelian theory that earthquakes are caused by trapped underground vapors (exhalations).</meta>

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>EARTH</header>

For the chimney <note>The author likely refers to a volcanic vent or crater</note>, having long since had an open path for exhalations, does not allow it to be believed that trapped vapors are the cause of that trembling of the earth. Would that the Schools <note>The Scholastic universities following Aristotle</note> had paid attention to their Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note>: that often, when an earthquake is imminent, birds fall from the sky as if struck by fear while the wind is silent; and in a calm harbor, triremes <note>Ancient galley ships</note> suddenly bounce. But what connection exists between the air and the sea and an exhalation trapped beneath the earth? Does the air tremble when the earth does? Or is a tiny tremor of the air enough to kill birds, which fly in any wind? Or because the sand of the sea (and indeed without any opening) might jump up half a foot, must the surface of the deep sea, devoid of wind, tremble along with the ships?

<margin>28.</margin> An original manuscript by the Curate of St. Mary’s across the Dijle <note>original: "Dilcam"</note> in Mechelen <note>original: "Mechliniæ"</note> was shown, in which he had written that in the year 1540, for three days, once every day, the earth trembled before a lightning bolt ignited its Sand Gate <note>original: "portam Arenariam"</note> and the gunpowder <note>term: "pulverem pyrium" (fire-dust)</note> contained within it. From this, the city, struck by an ill-omened disaster, fell, almost utterly shattered. Finally, in the year 1580 at the second hour of the afternoon, while the fury of the winds ceased, the city shook, two days before the English invaded Mechelen and seized it as plunder. But what do these events, happening out of fatal necessity in the chain of causes, have in common with a dreamed-up subterranean exhalation? For what could a supposed exhalation portend beyond or outside of itself? Why would it contain the significance of a future military invasion? Or a coming lightning bolt that would ignite the vessels of gunpowder kept there, shaking the sand tower and destroying the whole city?

For before Mount Vesuvius tortured its own bowels and covered many small towns with mineral clods <note>volcanic ash and debris</note>, denying hope to the farmer for the future, thick darkness preceded beneath the Sun; the air trembled mournfully for its own reason, as a prognosis of the threatened future disaster. The disaster itself followed its own natural causes. But the preceding signs have nothing at all in common with the occurrence of the future fire.

Since it is now established that there is no place among the strata of the earth, nor any exhalation lying beneath; and even if it were beneath, it would be impossible for it to cause a tremor of the earth: let it be certain, however, that the earth truly and actually trembles, whether by a discontinuity of the strata or the opening of some gap. I have considered that tremor in the earth to be no different than in the air when a clapper <note>term: "batillum" (the tongue of a bell)</note> strikes a bell. For as long as the bell trembles without a crack, it gives a tone. The Earth also, while it is shaken by its own supernatural clapper, emits a dull tone, because its body is composed of contiguous sand and water even unto its center; yet it is not a continuous whole in the sense of a single unit. It can tremble without a break in its contact, and all the more freely if metal is bent without the tearing of the whole. The Earth also, in its trembling, has its own internal clapper, more majestic than the voice of thunder. But because the blow is muffled by sand and water, it is shaken with a certain tone while it trembles; however, the bellowing that is heard from time to time is not of the earth, but foreign: it is not proper to the trembling of the earth, but the accidental wailing of spirits, which is called *Baleno* <note>A flash or shriek</note> by the Italians.

Finally, weighing the cause of the earth's tremor, I know that there is a motive force primarily in the air, by which the air carries out the impulse <note>term: "calcar" (spur/stimulus)</note> conceived from the stars. *Indeed, let the stars be for you as signs, seasons, days, and years.* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14</note> I know, moreover, that in the sea and deep lakes there is a motive force of their own, by which they experience tides without winds—by which, I say, our ocean rolls for six hours, and elsewhere for six constant months, in a single flow. I know, finally, that the earth is at rest and has no active motive force proper to itself. I believe, therefore, that the earth trembles and fears whenever the Angel of the Lord strikes it.

<margin>30.</margin> > Behold, there was a great earthquake: for the Angel of the Lord descended from Heaven. (Matthew 28:2) <note>The original text cites "Matth. 1. 8." but the quote is from Matthew 28:2</note>

# ANOMALY.

For the word among the Hebrews <note>original: *Ebræos*</note> contains the cause, as if one were to say: this is surely the sole cause of the earthquake, by which all things, without resistance, tremble equally like a light reed. In the Book of Revelation <note>original: *Apoc.*</note>, a third part of mortals, trees, or fish perishes by the very fact that the Angel poured out his vial <note>original: *lagenam effudit*</note>. For abstract spirits <note>purely spiritual beings like angels or demons</note> act by divine power, and nothing can resist them. Even the Evil Demons <note>original: *Cacodemones*</note>, whenever they are permitted to act with free power, act without the resistance of bodies or the reaction of defiance. For matter is the subject of another monarchy <note>the physical realm</note>; it cannot react against a spirit, which it touches in no way and affects by no physical object. Just as the Angel uses the liquid poured from the vial for the aforementioned slaughter, so for the shaking of the earth, he mostly employs a sound <note>original: *tonum*</note>. Indeed, a wandering sound was heard in the air, not unlike the creaking of driven wheels. There followed from this a tempestuous murmur like wind (yet without wind), and by that very act, the entire stretch of such great Provinces trembled together with immense horror. This same sound accompanied the trepidation of the earth on three individual occasions.

Almost the same thing happens with lightning. Lightning indeed burns and melts, but truly it does not "strike" in the sense of physical impact. According to the saying: *The voice of thunder* <note>original: *Vox tonitrui*</note> shall beat the earth, because it strikes. For instance, silkworms <note>original: *bombices*</note> die, milk curdles, beer turns sour, and a slaughtered ox hanging up retains flaccid meat unfit for salting—and this happens by the sound of thunder alone, while the lightning there is harmless. Therefore, let the voice of thunder and the *voice of the earthquake* be the sounds of the ministering spirits.

The stars, however, do not excite the motive and alterative force of the air or water through sound; rather, they act by their "aspect" alone, which they call "influences." This has action and direction in an instant, just like light or sight. Otherwise, many years would be needed before the audible forms <note>original: *species audibiles*</note> could travel from Saturn to the regions of the Atmosphere <note>original: *Meteori*</note>. Furthermore, a sound, even if great, gradually fails along the way.

As for the fact that the earth trembles along with a storm of winds, or sometimes successively through villages, cities, and as if street by street, running through them in a rolling motion: all of that is by accident, and according to the will of Him who shakes the earth as a portent. Likewise, the fact that it trembles more often elsewhere, but very rarely in living Belgium: this does not change the driving cause. It stands, of course, at the will of Him who encloses the universe in His fist, who can shake the earth at His nod and alone perform wonders. At His look, the earth shall sometimes smoke, and the melted mountains shall fall.

However, the fact that at other times chasms have appeared after an earthquake, and foul poison and arsenical fumes have exhaled: all of that is linked to its natural causes. These are not the *effects* of the earthquake except by accident, and they are certainly not the *causes*. This "blindness of causes" regarding the earthquake was invented with the Devil as the author, so that mortals might set aside all fear of the Divine <note>original: *Numinis*</note>, and thus bypass—if not totally neglect—the ends which God set for Himself (namely, to seriously venerate the power of His Majesty, so that being mindful of the crimes of their past lives, they might repent).

> Alas! What powerful hand with force unknown <note>original: *Deb! qual possente man con forza e ignote*</note>
> Causes the ground to collapse and sink?
> It is not trapped vapor as others believe,
> Nor does a dreamed-of screeching strike the soil:
>
> Certainly, the earth resents and shakes,
> Because the foot of the sinner grows heavy upon it:
> And it impatiently demands our bodies,
> To fill up its empty caverns.
>
> The language of heaven, which reproves man,
> Is the whirlwind, the thunder, the lightning, the flash;
> Now the earth also speaks in horrendous notes,
> Because man, who wishes to be entirely earthly,
> Understands not the foreign speech of heaven:
> Let him at least understand the speech of the earth.

Notwithstanding these things, there was no lack of one who said <margin>31.</margin> that he, from the deepest well of the castle of Leuven, had foretold by a certain omen that an earthquake would soon occur, because the water of the same well, three days before, stank with the odor of sulfur, and its infection, a yellowness...

I see, since they claimed the turbulence of the water betrayed it. But let that good man know that the well in question is 115 feet deep, because it is cut down to the castle by 93 steps from the adjacent street. And so, on one side, that well is no deeper than the neighboring wells, although on the other side, where it is adjacent to the castle hill, it is deep, as I have said. But since there is no vein of sulfur underlying the hill, the water could not have breathed out sulfur, because there was none. If, however, he suggests that sulfur was brought back: a sign might have preceded it as a warning from God; but it had no sulfur, which is neither present there nor was it ignited; therefore, it could not have caused the earthquake in all of Belgium <note>The author is likely referring to the significant earthquake of 1580 or 1640 which affected the Low Countries.</note>. Thus, there is no natural reason why the water in that well should be more disturbed by sulfur than in the neighboring ones, where no such thing was seen. Finally, it should be known: that an earthquake does not happen by a long preparation of causes starting three days prior. Because then the earth could not be elevated uniformly at once. Indeed, if some breath of sulfur had already made a premature exit for itself three days before, by that very act, it would have already found its way out and would have expired sooner through that well, before it could have lifted such a great mass all around. Indeed, having found an exit, it would have made the water sound with its blast and bubbling, and it would have erupted much more easily in the streets so much lower down, and the exhalation would have broken through in the neighboring areas, disrupting the hill itself more easily by rising into a mound; but the earth would not have trembled. Therefore, I reject the example of this event, as long as the arguments of impossibility I have opposed to it are not overcome.

<margin>32.</margin> Therefore, the earth trembles, not because it feels in the manner of an animal, or because it is afraid: but it announces something similar to us, and speaks to us as it were, accusing that Angel, or rather the hand of an angry God.

<margin>33.</margin> Moreover, the earth is struck and trembles at the command of God, denoting that sin has ascended from the earth into Heaven, crying out for vengeance before His throne. To be sure, the striking presupposes indignation, and indignation presupposes an accumulated measure of sin. The end <term>Finis; the purpose or goal</term> of the earthquake, truly, is that the sinner may amend his ways, and the righteous man may guard himself both against sinning and against the threatened punishment of sin. Therefore, an earthquake always threatens punishments. <margin>34.</margin> Furthermore, individual transgressions have punishments conforming to them. Namely, lust and impurity have expiations and penalties in the form of plagues and diseases. Adulteries, truly, pay their penalties through diseases, imprisonment, infamy, poverty, also sterility of offspring, premature death, or similar things. According to that saying: > *He who sows in the flesh, shall reap in corruption.* <note>A reference to Galatians 6:8.</note> Moreover, the pride of life is punished through poverty, sterility, wars, devastations, sudden death, the calamitous loss of friends, etc. Avarice finally pays its penalties through frauds, thefts, deceptions, the loss of some limb, etc. But if two or three sins flourish together among a people, then the punishments are also mixed. Namely, inclemencies, tyrannies, the breaking of vows or oaths, deceptions, extortions, plagues, sterilities, wars, etc. But if sins are connected in the powers, whether the princes, both of the Church and the secular world, and the Judges: the prophecies are full of the fact that because of their injustice, > *kingdoms are transferred from nation to nation.* <note>A common medieval and early modern political-theological trope based on Ecclesiasticus 10:8.</note> If these things happen with the rise of heresiarchs <term>leaders of heretical sects</term>, scandals, and other subversions, and especially where the poor suffer together: it is a sign that these evils proceed from filth, inclemencies, ambition, avarice, the breaking of vows, and drunkenness. For indeed, the prophecies abound with threats that > *Jerusalem shall be plowed like a field: the city shall become like a heap of stones: the plague and the enemy shall carry off all the prey, and shall lead the princes of the Church bound: the holy place shall be contaminated, so that they are a derision to the nations.* If the wars do not touch upon religion, only the sins of the Princes and Judges are noted. <margin>35.</margin> But the earth is struck and trembles chiefly because of the sins of blood <note>original: "peccata sanguinum"; likely referring to murder or violent oppression</note>, which cry out to a vindictive heaven. Therefore, after an earthquake, those punishments are to be expected which are due to enormity, cruelty, and injustice, according to what is deserved.

## A N O M A L Y.

worthy. Therefore, a *foul* trembling <note>original: "Tetræ"</note> denotes nothing if not the judgments of a God who avenges. Indeed, good comes from an evil cause, insofar as it contains a punishment for the unrepentant. Thus, from the Sunday of the Lord's Resurrection, the earth trembled, signifying the desolation of the city and of the Jewish Monarchy, which the Gospel predicted with the Lord's tears, and which Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Romano-Jewish historian</note> described as its destruction. As was foreseen by Daniel, Isaiah, and Psalm 10. Moreover, while the earth's trembling runs through the streets, as it were, it signifies the tumult of city against city, and that the villages shall be deserted. For a friend saw this chapter while it was still in draft form; he immediately perceived that a natural cause was lacking and agreed:
<margin>35.</margin> It was a most rare crime of men to have slaughtered the innocent Son of God in return for His benefits: wherefore a most rare kind of expiation <note>original: "piaculi"</note> ought to rain down upon that nation, raised with such great favor, lasting until the slaughter of the people and the destruction of the Republic.
<margin>37.</margin> But he was indignant that I had depicted the manner—that the earth had been struck not indeed with a staff, but by a sound—and he laughed at the conjecture. "Why," he said, "did God not act through gunpowder, through wind, exhalation, and vapor? Why did He not simply speak, and the earth was moved? Since God has a thousand ways, and it is not certain which means He used." Especially if I gave the reason why a trembling earth does not necessarily gape open—using the example of a bell trembling after a strike—certainly he ought not to have been angry with me. For I did not intend that He who surpasses every measure should bind Himself to a specific manner and means. As for that friend interjecting natural means: such as wind, vapor, exhalation, or gunpowder laid beneath Belgium. These things had already been sufficiently refuted in writing as being possible in nature; therefore, they are brought forward again impertinently, as if God had need of those means.
Inasmuch as when God acts miraculously, He often even uses natural things, but then He does not use things that are thought to be co-causes: for those means are and contain mysteries rather than the force of some causality. God therefore uses those means out of mere good pleasure, to designate some mystery. And so I took up the conjecture of a striking sound <note>original: "toni percuffientis"</note> (not because I am conscious of the divine counsel, or a curious investigator) from the Word: *The voice of thunder shall beat the earth.* Moses struck the waters of *Egypt*, and they were turned into blood, and frogs covered the land of *Egypt*: he struck the sea with a rod, and the waters stood still. He struck the rock, and it brought forth a spring. Elisha urged the *King* to strike the earth, and was indignant with him because he had not struck it more often, because the number of arbitrary strikes contained the number of victories and the turns of the enemy yet to yield. Therefore, with my friend's peace preserved, I have explained myself.
I gladly confess, I say, that I do not wish to scrutinize divine mysteries. However, I desired to pursue the manner and means which God uses in the trembling of the earth only by conjecture, not so that I might become known for such a discourse. Nor finally did I publish these things as a brawler: but so that the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of Wisdom, might arise from the trembling of the earth. Master Streithagen, Canon of Heinsberg, described a chronogram <note>A poem where certain letters, usually Roman numerals, add up to a date</note> of this earthquake in his *German Florus*, on account of its strangeness and the breadth of the locations:

> **V**ar**I**o**V**s **L**an**D** **I**n **A**pr**IL** **VV**as a**LL** **S**tr**V**ck **I**n t**V**-**MV**t:
> fro**M** **I**nso**L**vte **C**rash **C**o**V**ere**D** bo**D**Ies **L**ean.

### THE FICTION OF ELEMENTAL COMPLEXIONS AND MIXTURES.

1. That earth is seen not to be a primary element. 2. That fire is neither an element nor a substance. 3. That all visible things are materially composed of water alone. 4. Why the place of the air, which is called the middle region, is cold. 5. What the three first principles of the chemists are. 6. Certain bodies are not reduced into the three first principles. 7. The inconstancy of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a seminal figure in toxicology and occult medicine.</note>. 8. The error of the chemists. 9. The reduction of the three first principles into the water of a cloud is demonstrated. 10. The volatile salt of simples is fixed by melting together. 11. The three first principles did not exist before: but they come to be in the separation, and are indeed a new creation. 12. The oil of things is nothing but water, once the seed of the concrete matter is removed. 13. The same is proved in charcoal. 14. What the *Gas sylvestre* <note>original: "Gas sylvestre"; a term coined by Van Helmont to describe carbon dioxide or "wild gas" released during fermentation or combustion.</note> of things is. 15. How Gas is born in grapes. 16. The Gas of wines. 17. Why many grapes may be harmful. 18. That the Gas of must is not the spirit of wine. 19. The erroneous opinion of Paracelsus. 20. Double sulfur in tin: whence its lightness. 21. Gunpowder proves Gas. 22. Certain things transmute each other into Gas. 23. The incompatibility of certain melted substances. 24. That Gas is materially neither earth nor air. 25. The same by the supposition of falsehood, and seven absurdities. 26. A mixture is not converted into an element by the force of a conquering element. 27. The mechanics of the *Alkahest* liquor <note>original: "liquoris Alkabest"; the hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists.</note>. 28. All Gas is from the element of water. 29. Proved by the mechanics of charcoal. 30. By mechanics, that every vegetable is totally and materially from water alone. 31. Thus every stone is from water. 32. Dregs, and all fatness, are from water alone. 33. All soot is from water alone. 34. All sulfurs are reduced into soot and Gas; these, however, are reduced into water. 35. Why fire cannot make air out of water. 36. Ash and glass are from water alone. 37. The Gas of salts is nothing but tasteless water. 38. The Gas of fruits is nothing but water. 39. The fictions of the Schools concerning exhalations. 40. Physics is in darkness without Pyrotechny <note>The art of managing fire, here referring to chemical laboratory practice.</note>. 41. The spirit of life is materially the Gas of water. 42. Sweat before death is not sweat, but a melting of the liquor. 43. It is easily seized by an endemic Gas.

1. I have called two elements primitive, <margin>2.</margin> air and water, because they do not recede into each other: but earth, as if born from water, because it is reduced into water. But if water is changed into an earthy body, that happens by the power of a seed, and thus it then puts off the simplicity of an element. For example, from water comes flint, which is broken into sand. But indeed that sand resists less in the reduction to water than the sand of marble, which is virgin earth. Therefore the sand of marble, a gem, or a flint, betrays the presence of a seed. But if virgin earth is finally led into water with much labor, and was created in the beginning as an element: yet it seems to have become something other than its simple self; and therefore I have called those two primary. I have denied that fire is an element or a substance: but rather death in the hand of the craftsman, given for great uses. I mean an artificial death for the sake of the Arts, which the Almighty created, but not a natural one. <margin>3.</margin> Now I undertake to demonstrate that the bodies which are believed to be mixed are materially the fruit of water alone, and have no need for the marriage of another element: namely bodies, whether opaque or transparent, solid or flowing, homogeneous or dissimilar. Consider stones, sulfurs, metals, honey, wax, oils, bone, brain, cartilage, wood, bark, leaves—finally all and each are totally reduced into entirely tasteless water, and thus consist of and are contained by simple water alone. Indeed, most of them are destroyed by fire, and soon spontaneously give up a part of water. Although this may in some way reflect the nature of the concrete thing, at last, once the contagion of that concrete seed is removed, that water—or the mercury of things—returns into the simple and tasteless water of rain. Thus finally oils and fats, separated by fire, with a little alkali salt added, assume the nature of soap and pass away into elemental water. Indeed, whatever things are burned in an open fire are spontaneously reduced into water in the very hostelry of the clouds. <margin>4.</margin> That was surely the necessity of the cold of that place (as I have already taught above), so that whatever things might rise there from the lower parts would, by the mortal cold and their own division into a Gas of almost infinite atoms, forget their seeds. They are namely...

Namely salt, sulfur, and mercury—or salt, fluid, and fat—exist in very specific species:
<margin>5</margin> not indeed as certain universal bodies that are common to all species, but as "similar parts" <note>Latin: *partes simulares*, a term from Aristotelian biology referring to tissues that are uniform throughout, like bone or flesh</note> in concrete bodies, distinguished by a triple variety according to the requirements of their seeds. Therefore, if the seminal properties remain more tenaciously in those three when they have been separated, then through what has been admitted, the impressions of the properties are removed and alienated. Whereupon they subsequently migrate into the 
<margin>6</margin> element of water. Certain bodies, however, refuse to be divided into three; into salt, with the addition of the fluid *Alkahest* of Paracelsus <note>The *Alkahest* was a mythical universal solvent sought by alchemists</note>, they finally break down, and the salt, by migrating into tasteless water, is destroyed. This fact has caused the *Pyrotechnia* <note>The art of chemistry/fire-working</note> to be ignored and despised in the Schools. But I have a war not only with those ignorant of nature and the despisers of investigative Philosophy, but also with Paracelsus, the Leader of the Chemists:
<margin>7</margin> for whom, since it was difficult to turn aside from the accustomed path, he wished those Three to consist of a commission of elements; and sometimes he thought the elements of the world themselves were not bodies, but empty places or "matrices" of things. Elsewhere, truly, he denies that whatever is corporeal is elemental, but is only a mass of the three primaries. And again elsewhere, he taught how to reduce the elements themselves (even the flame of fire) into the four elements by a method. And thus the elements cease to be "naked" in the place of the three principles. But the flame itself (which is nothing but ignited soot), when enclosed in glass, soon perishes into nothing in that very instant. So much so that glass made in a glass furnace, with glowing fire and closed up, could never contain anything 
<margin>8</margin> except air. Inconsistent with himself, he made himself ridiculous, and those individual points are to be refuted by me in the appropriate places. For the Chemists have believed until now that the elements lie hidden in the three primaries. They had seen, for instance, air and fire fly out together from burning wax, and they thought that the water therein claimed the air and fire for itself. They reckoned that the earth truly flew away with the soot. They reasoned similarly regarding those things which leave behind charcoal and ash:

substituting ash for earth. They believed the fruits of the earth and minerals were like the innate pledges of water, but stirred up by the marriage of the three other elements. But I come to the matter at hand. Let there be a perfectly rectified *aqua vitae* <note>Literally "water of life," referring to concentrated alcohol or spirits</note>
<margin>9</margin> which burns entirely oily in its homogeneity: for that, through the salt of tartar <note>Potassium carbonate</note>, which is related to it, is immediately changed for a 1/16th part into salt, and all the rest becomes simple elemental water. And a single part becomes salt, although it was homogeneous with the other, and thus the water is reducible into water, because in the actions of bodies and spirits, while being dissolved, various coagulations of the solvent occur. Similarly also in the operation 
<margin>10</margin> of fire, salts which were previously volatile are partly melted into a fixed alkali, not otherwise than saltpeter and arsenic—both volatile—are fixed by melting. Therefore, the three primaries are not only separated, but are sharpened, changed, and vary the nature of the concrete thing; thus through fire they become a "new creature": not indeed created anew, but produced through fire. Thus a roof tile is no longer the potter's earth, but is now stone. Thus ash and smoke are no longer wood, nor is alkali or sand glass. Because the power of fire does not produce seeds, but by consuming them, it transmutes and alters individual bodies by separating them.
<margin>11</margin> Furthermore, no one would dare to say that the Salt of Tartar, in the case proposed, produces an element from a non-element, as if the salt were the father of the element of water: but the sulfur of the wine, once the seed is taken away, leaves the matter of the *aqua vitae* as it is. But the part which is fixed in the salt of tartar assumed the condition of salt, though it was previously fat. Before, it was entirely combustible, volatile, and of the same condition as its companions. Immediately, therefore, once the seed of the vinous sulfur is destroyed, it is nothing but elemental 
<margin>12</margin> water. Thus every oil, materially, is simple water, which a little bit of seed transfers into a combustible mass and the mask of sulfur. If one were to change substances into their families, it would not be difficult to see that they also return into water. Indeed, fire, by burning away the fat <note>original: "pinguedinem"; referring to the flammable principle or "sulfur" of a substance</note>, causes it to fly off into the air toward the clouds, and there, by the coldness of the place, it sometimes congeals into water. For fish, born by the power of a seed, transmute simple water into their own fat, bones, and flesh; it is no wonder, therefore, that fish are materially nothing but transmuted water, and return into water through the alchemical art. I shall demonstrate through mechanical means that all vegetables, too, and meats, consist of water alone. Indeed, all things, if not immediately, then at least with assistance, assume the nature of water again. Every stone, rock, and mud also migrates—either spontaneously or through additives—into an alkaline salt (for it is alkali, which was not salt before, yet once combustion is completed, the salt remains). Thus, ash becomes pure salt by its own alkali. Moreover, every alkali, when fat is added, is reduced into an aqueous liquor, which finally becomes pure and simple water (as can be seen in soap, the blue of lapis lazuli, etc.), whenever the "seed of fatness" is laid down through fixed additives. Otherwise, it is not the property of fire to create water (but rather flame), but merely to separate heterogeneous parts. Therefore, if water is made from sulfurs, and not through the fire's own transmutation, it is necessary that sulfurs be begotten from pure water. Since water is not separated from oils, but truly becomes from them: because water was not present in them formally <note>as a finished product</note>, but only materially; namely, once the mask of the seeds has been pulled away.

<margin>13.</margin> Furthermore, every piece of charcoal (which is made from the melting together of sulfur and salt, acting upon each other during burning), even if it were toasted in a glowing furnace until the final day, provided the vessel is closed, it indeed becomes ignited—and there is true fire in the vessel, just as in charcoal that is not enclosed—yet none of it is consumed, being unable to be consumed because its outflow is hindered. Therefore, charcoal, and universally all bodies which do not immediately turn into water, nor are yet fixed, necessarily belch forth a **wild spirit** <note>original: "spiritus silvester"</note>. For example, from 62 pounds of oak charcoal, one pound of ash is produced. Therefore, the remaining 61 pounds are that wild spirit, which, even when ignited, cannot escape from a closed vessel. This spirit, <margin>14.</margin> hitherto unknown, I call by the new name of **Gas** <term>Gas: a term coined by van Helmont, derived from the Greek "chaos," to describe invisible vapors that cannot be contained or solidified</term>, which can neither be constrained in vessels nor reduced into a visible body, unless the "seed" is first extinguished. Indeed, bodies contain this spirit, and sometimes they depart entirely into a spirit of this kind, not because it exists in them actually (since it could not be held back, indeed the whole compound would fly off at once), but it is a "congealed spirit," coagulated in the manner of a body, and it is excited when a ferment is acquired, as in wine, unripened grape juice <note>original: "omphacio"</note>, bread, mead <note>original: "hydromelite"</note>, etc. Or it is excited by a foreign additive, as I shall say regarding sal ammoniac, or finally through some alterative disposition. Such is the "breathing upon" in respect to an apple. For a grape is preserved and dried unharmed: but once its skin is ruptured and wounded, it soon conceives the ferment of boiling <note>fermentation</note>, and hence the beginning of transmutation. Therefore, the wines of grapes, apples, berries, and honey, as well as crushed flowers and leaves, once the ferment is seized, begin to bubble and boil, whence comes **Gas**: but from crushed raisins and common things, **Gas** is not immediately given due to a lack of ferment. The **Gas** of wines, if much of it is coerced within casks, renders the wines furious, <margin>16.</margin> "mute," and harmful. For this reason, eating grapes in abundance has often produced a morbid **Gas**. <margin>17.</margin> Since the spirit of the ferment is in an uproar, and since it is disobedient to our digestion, it associates itself by force with the vital spirit; indeed, if anything is ready to be secreted as sweat, that thing becomes lumpy through the stubborn acidity of the ferment, and produces significant troubles: griping pains <note>original: "tormina"</note>, diarrhea, and dysentery. Sometimes in my early studies <note>original: "Tyrociniis"</note>, <margin>18.</margin> deceived by the authority of ignorant writers, I believed the **Gas** of grapes to be the spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note> in abundance. But useless experiments taught me that the **Gas** of grapes is merely something on the way to becoming wine, but is not the spirit of wine itself. For the juice of grapes differs from wine no differently than a mash made of water and flour differs from beer <note>original: "cerevisia"</note>. For that which comes between the two...

The other <margin>21.</margin> part, however, is a sulfur that becomes oily. For gunpowder expresses the history of *Gas* most closely. For it consists of saltpeter (which the ancients wrongly thought was nitre, which even today is brought in abundance, dried from the flooding of the Nile), sulfur, and charcoal; because when joined, if they are ignited, there is no vessel in nature which, if closed, would not burst apart because of the *Gas*. For if charcoal is ignited in a closed vessel, none of it perishes. But if sulfur is sublimated in a closed glass, it ascends entirely from the bottom without a change of its species. Saltpeter also, when melted in a closed vessel, gives an acid liquor that is partly watery, while for the other part it is changed into a fixed <term>alkali</term> <note>A basic salt that remains after combustion.</note>. Therefore, fire [would produce] air, <margin>22.</margin> or rather *Gas*, from each individual part, which it would otherwise produce from the three connected parts if air were involved. Therefore, those substances placed together convert each other into *Gas* through destruction. Moreover, that intolerance between sulfur and saltpeter is not indeed from a "marriage of potentials" between cold and hot (as is believed), but because of the incompatible flow of boiling oil and wine, no less than water; or of molten copper and tin with wine. For in such great heat, when they touch each other in their smallest parts, they are either turned into *Gas* or they fly apart. For in this way lead, <margin>23.</margin> roasted with mercury and sulfur, goes off into a sudden flame, leaving behind a dross of almost no weight, yet dilated to the size of the lead. Wherefore, <margin>24.</margin> if *Gas* were air, all gunpowder would be air, and the lead itself would be entirely air. But it is not possible for fire to produce now air, now water, as an ultimate reduction from the same elemental fruit, unless fire were to lose its uniformity of acting at the same time—a property instilled in it by the Creator. Finally, it has already been sufficiently demonstrated above that air and water can never be transformed into one another. Therefore, if by fire, or any other medium, gunpowder and saltpeter are notably reduced into elemental water, their transformation into air is not possible. Moreover, several thousand pounds of gunpowder, when ignited at once, have given nothing except an inflamed *Gas*. This, in the clouds, finally returning into water, has coalesced. Furthermore, charcoal is reduced into stone by certain springs. I also know ways by which the whole of saltpeter is converted into earth, and all sulfur, once dissolved, may be fixed into an earthy powder. What if, therefore, these three earths contained three or four elements? At least the greatest part would be occupied by earth, and not reducible into the original *Gas*; nor is it consistent with reason that a body, which flies away entirely into an aerial *Gas*, should be converted into air or into earth at the whim of man. Finally, since the three aforementioned powders, under the hand of the Craftsman <note>The chemist or alchemist.</note>, finally become water, which thereafter can no longer return into earth or air through human skill, it follows also that the conversions of sulfur, charcoal, and saltpeter into *Gas* or into earth are not ultimate states, just as they are not true elements of air and earth. Finally, let us measure these things with common sense: <margin>25.</margin> as if the aforementioned simple substances were turned now into air, and now indeed into earth, because there was a mutual transformation of the elements into one another.

Let it stand here as a thesis, against which enough was demonstrated in the chapter on the origin of forms: namely, that fire is neither an element nor even a substance. These things being granted, it follows that the aforementioned three simples in <term>gunpowder</term><note>Latin: *pulvere pyrio*.</note> are not reduced into air by air while they fly off into <term>Gas</term><note>The author, Van Helmont, famously coined the word "Gas" from the Greek "Chaos."</note>, nor are they reduced into earth by earth while the saltpeter verges into earth through a certain sulfur; indeed, coal and sulfur are changed through waters into stone and into earth. This distilled juice, with alkalis added, is entirely reduced into tasteless elemental water. Nor indeed is this a wonder. For I shall show in its proper place that absolutely all vegetable things arise materially from the element of water alone. If <margin>28.</margin> therefore every mixed body returns at last into mere rainwater: it is necessary that every Gas proceeding from mixed bodies be materially from the element of water. <header>THE PIGMENT OF THE ELEMENTS.</header>

## THE PIGMENT OF THE ELEMENTS.

I have learned by a mechanical experiment <note>original: "mechanica"; here referring to a physical or practical demonstration</note>. For I took an earthen vessel, in which I placed 200 pounds <note>original: "tt", the symbol for libra/pounds</note> of earth dried in an oven, which I moistened with rain water, and into it I planted a trunk of a willow tree, weighing 5 pounds. And finally, after five years had passed, the tree that had grown from it weighed 169 pounds and about three ounces. However, the earthen vessel, with the earth planted in it, was covered by an iron plate coated with tin and pierced with many holes, so that the dust flying about should not be mixed with the earth. I did not calculate the weight of the leaves that fell in the four autumns. Finally, I also dried the earth in the vessel, and the same 200 pounds were found, minus about two ounces. Therefore, 164 pounds of wood, bark, and roots had arisen from <margin>31</margin> water alone. Therefore charcoal, since it is entirely made of water, if it be reduced into a stone in some spring; it could not be changed into stone by means of water, unless it were also entirely water.
<margin>32</margin> That stone becomes, materially, mere water. For just as fish produce much fat <note>original: "axungiam", specifically animal fat or grease</note> from the waters: so in turn all fat, with alkaline salt, becomes soap, which then being distilled, returns almost entirely into water; which, when it is stripped of the "seed" of the soap through additives, <margin>33</margin> becomes tasteless water. Indeed, all soot is partly the volatile salt of the concrete <note>original: "concreti", referring to a solid or composite body</note>, preserved from inflammation because of the admixture of escaping water; and partly it is oil, which escapes combustion by the speed of its flying off. For in this way the acid liquor of sulfur drawn out through a bell-jar shows that a great part of the sulfur, untouched by the flame, has ascended upward, which is again safely separated from that liquor <margin>34</margin> through rectification. For sulfurs, or fats, even if they are distilled many times at any degree of fire: nevertheless they always remain fatty, and retain their own nature as long as they possess the "seed" of that concrete body. When flame, or "artificial death," touches these, they soon fly away into Gas, but not into water. This is because every Gas still retains some condition of its concrete body. For the soots of a flame differ by genera and species: which surely would not be the case if they passed immediately into the first element. Fire indeed simply destroys, but generates nothing: since it lacks the power of a seed; and those things which it cannot destroy, it either separates or leaves untouched: and these are hitherto called "fixed."
<margin>35</margin> However, fire is not able to change that which is materially water in itself into air. <margin>36</margin> For otherwise it would have the seed of air. It is already sufficiently clear that by no help of art or nature can water become air, or vice versa. Therefore wood, since it is entirely from water, its ash, and likewise glass, will be from water. <margin>37</margin> Moreover, the following mechanical experiment proves that the Gas of salts is nothing but water. Take equal parts of saltpeter, vitriol, and alum: dry each one, and having combined them, distill the water. This is nothing other than pure volatile salt. Take four ounces of this, and join one ounce of Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Salis armeniaci"</note> in a strong glass vessel, an alembic, secured by a cement (made of colophony wax and glass powder) poured on very hot; soon, even in the cold, a Gas is excited, and the vessel, however strong, bursts apart with a crash. But if you leave a crack in the joint of the receiving vessel, and after the spontaneous boilings you distill the residue, you will find a sub-acid water, which is converted into rain water by repeated distillation and the addition of chalk. Therefore, one part of the salts passed into water, but the other into Gas. But the salts that flew away as Gas are of a homogeneous nature with those reduced into water: Therefore, materially, the Gas <margin>38</margin> of salts is nothing but water. Similarly, I have already shown that the Gas of fruits is nothing but water, as originating immediately from water. Thus, when a dried grape is distilled into elemental water, it remains water; but if a fresh one is once wounded, must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> and much Gas are drawn out. If therefore the whole grape, before fermentation, is turned into simple water: but when a ferment is applied, Gas is excited, it must be that this Gas will also be water. Since the disposition of the ferment cannot [create] from that which...

However, the **Exhalations** <note>original: "Exhalationes"; in Aristotelian physics, these were vapors rising from the earth to form weather</note> which the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university academics following Aristotle</note> claim are the daily material for winds, mists, comets, minerals, rocks, the saltiness of the sea, earthquakes, and all **Meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain and snow</note>—given that there is a storehouse in nature for these things and of such great mass—are but wondrous dreams, and are ignorant proportions of their own effects. What material, then, will be sufficient even for the daily winds? Indeed, it is utterly impossible for the Schools to have known nature, or the differences, causes, and properties of bodies, as many as have approached **Philosophy** without **Pyrotechny** <note>original: "Pyrotechnia"; the art of chemistry or "fire-working"</note> and have been deluded by pagan institutions until now. 

I have written elsewhere concerning long life, that the spirit of our life, the arterial spirit, is of the nature of **Gas**. 41. This is seen in palpitations, fainting, and **Swooning** <note>original: "hypothyimia"</note>. For how much of the vivid color, the vital light, and the full habit of the flesh is lost—and how the face itself immediately collapses into wrinkles—shortly after the aforementioned passions? For the spirit, which before unified everything with a calm redness, soon flies away and, overcome by a foreign air, is changed. Since the **Archeus** <note>The internal "vital workman" or governing spirit of the body in Helmontian medicine</note> is in itself a **Gas**, of the nature of a balsamic salt, if it encounters the "air" of another salt (just as **Sal Ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride</note> reacts when it meets the **Spirit of Saltpeter** <note>Nitric acid</note>), it easily and immediately dissolves through the pores, forgetting its duties and its household. Nor is it condensed into drops, because it is prepared from the arterial blood. 42. If any sweat exhales during fainting or death, that is the melting of the gore, not the arterial blood. Therefore, the vital **Gas**, because it is light and a balsam preserving from corruption, began to be likened to solar light from the first sketching of its birth. 

After the aforementioned faints, the innate spirits of the other members, like smoking embers, are again ignited by the solar light of the heart; just as the smoke of an extinguished candle, touching the flame of another, carries the flame back to the extinguished wick through the medium of the smoke. 43. Since the spirit of our life is a **Gas**, it is most powerfully and swiftly affected by any other **Gas**, namely because of their immediate contact. For nothing, therefore, operates more swiftly upon us than a **Gas**. This is evident in the **Grotto of the Dog** <note>original: "Crypta canis Siculorum"; a famous cave near Naples where CO2 pooled on the floor, suffocating dogs but not tall humans</note> near the Sicilians, in the **Plague**, in those suffocated by **Charcoal** fumes, and by fumigations. For men are often killed instantly in mineral tunnels. Indeed, in cellars where strong beer releases its raw **Gas**, a sudden death and suffocation easily break out. 

Wherefore I have grieved immensely, and pitying the human lot, I saw that by the thick negligence of the Schools, the higher remedies of fumigations are almost suppressed—by which not only are those in faints refreshed, but also the healings of many diseases are achieved. Anyone will more easily judge this with me when I explain odors in medical matters. Almost all medicines that restore strength have been neglected, and labor has been spent only on the diminutions of bodies: through the taking of blood, and loosening potions made of **Scammony** <note>A harsh purgative resin</note>, and through **Cauteries**, **Baths**, **Enemas**, **Sweats**, and **Spanish Fly** <note>original: "cantharides"; used to cause blistering</note>. For **Gas** is inserted deeply, and odors maintain a more immediate contact with the vital spirits than liquids do, if not by a poisonous stain, at least by their secondary qualities...

# THE MASS BY SEED.

The disposition of matter acquires and awakens through external warmth <note>original: "fomentis," referring to heat or applications that encourage growth</note>. From this, something similar to the **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is a central concept in Van Helmont's chemistry; it is the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that directs the formation of a living thing</note> is produced, which transforms, adapts, and increases its own sensory dwelling-place; it then proceeds to act upon the rest in proportion to the perfection and requirement of that vital breeze <note>original: "aurae"</note>. This seed, indeed, flourishes first with a certain generic fullness. For although it rejoices to have directed the mass laid beneath it toward the goal of the conceived ferment, it nonetheless frequently receives sparks of a more hidden light from elsewhere, and having taken a bold risk, it even aspires to become a **living soul**.

<margin>9.</margin> For this reason, not only do lice, bedbugs, fleas, and earthworms become guests and neighbors of our misery—born, as it were, from our innermost parts and excrements—but also, if a dirty shirt is pressed into the mouth of a vessel containing wheat: within a few days (say, 21), the ferment drawn from the shirt, altered by the odor of the grains, transforms the wheat itself, encrusted in its own skin, into **mice**. This is all the more admirable because such insects, distinguished by the signatures of their sexes, procreate with those that were born from the seed of parents. Thus, from this, the equality of both seeds and the vital strength of the ferments becomes conspicuous. What is even more miraculous is that from the grain and the shirt, the mice emerge not as infants, nor sucklings, nor tiny or premature, but entirely formed. In us, **phthiriasis** <note>A disease characterized by an infestation of lice</note> occasionally arises, and the louse emerges through the opened human epidermis; at other times it is generated in the pores, not indeed enclosed in the shell of a nit's egg, but tiny and barely visible. The flea, however, is always generated only externally, once the ferment is taken up. Nor was it enough for the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Aristotelian academic authorities, whom the author often critiques</note> to have said that such insects come forth from putrid things.

<margin>10.</margin> For even the eggs of birds rot significantly and stink immensely before the constitution of the chick. Therefore, life is present in those putrid things no less than in eggs. Nor is it enough to have doubted how such insects take a uniform and specific vital spirit from us, since natural generation presupposes an impressed seal of likeness. Indeed, in **anomalous generation**, the Archeus suffices—not the human one, but that which, in excrements, by a fermental power and for the sake of identity, always generates insects of a similar form. And so, although it may be a monstrous and anomalous generation in respect to us, it is nevertheless natural and ordinary in relation to the causes—namely, those giving us only the ferment and the warmth. Therefore, the ferment of the shirt, sprinkled through the wheat, resolves the matter through a backward movement, and thus a young mouse is formed, but not a newborn one. This is because it has regard for another mode of becoming.

<margin>11.</margin> In the former and vital seeds, the generator inspires the Archeus with a likeness of itself and a vital breeze, together with the mass of the seed. In the latter, however, only the odor of the ferment is breathed in from the containing vessels or the contagion of the surroundings. When these have been properly fitted together, they are soon formed into a plant or an insect; specifically, the breeze is awakened by the odor and the ferment of decay <note>original: "fracedinis"</note>, which is then exalted into the **governing Archeus**. As concerning "forms" elsewhere.

<margin>12.</margin> Seeds are thus made from the conception of the generator, making an image of itself, which disposes the matter toward the **idea** of a possible thing. For just as matter draws the disposition for transformation from an odor, so thereafter the disposition of matter occurs from the image, which procures and promotes a specific ferment. In this, however, there is an odor, or the quality of some decay, disposing the mass toward "otherness" and corruption. But the seed becomes a substance in which the Archeus is already present, which is a **spiritual Gas**, containing within itself the ferment, the image of the thing, and moreover, the disposing knowledge of things to be done.

# THE IMAGE OF THE FERMENT IMPREGNATES

Many animals, for the sake of restraining acidity, are compelled to eat chalk, lime, bricks, or clay. Therefore, the more subtle and volatile atoms of food are easily changed by the **ferment of the stomach** into a **windy Gas** <note>original: *Gas ventosum*; the author, Van Helmont, famously coined the word "Gas"</note> where the remaining part, at last, is content to be resolved into juice. For **Chemistry** is anxious in searching for a body in which a symphony of such great purity might play along with us, so that they could not be dissipated by a corrupting force. And at last, **religion** <note>likely used here in the sense of "scrupulous observation" or "natural law"</note> was amazed when a liquid was found which, being reduced to the smallest atoms possible for nature, being "unmarried," would spurn the unions of every ferment. Therefore, its transmutation is despaired of, as it finds no body more worthy than itself to which it might be wedded. But the labor of **Wisdom** <note>original: *Sophia*; referring to alchemical or divine wisdom</note> has created an anomaly in nature, which arose without a mixable ferment different from itself. That **Serpent bit itself**, revived from its own poison, and henceforth knows not how to die.

Indeed, because the **Schools** <note>The established academic authorities of the time</note> were ignorant of ferments, they also had to be ignorant of the fact that solid bodies are constituted from water and ferment alone. For I have taught that **vegetables** and grains, and whatever bodies are nourished by them, proceed from water alone: for a fisherman never finds any food in the stomach of a **Salmon**. If, therefore, the Salmon is made of water alone (even from rivers) and is nourished by it. Likewise, the **Sturgeon** lacks a mouth, appearing only with a tiny hole in the throat below, through which, besides water, the whole fish draws in nothing. Therefore, every fish is nourished and made from water equally: if not immediately, then at least if the water is pregnant with seeds and ferments. From the salty sea, almost every fish drawn out is fresh <note>sweet/non-salty</note>. Therefore, it converts salt into non-salt, or at least converts water into itself, not into salt water. Finally, **shellfish**, in place of bones, fashion stony shells for themselves out of water, as does the whole genus of snails. Therefore, the **salt of the sea**, which hardly yields to glowing fire, becomes sweet by the ferment in fishes; their flesh becomes volatile, and under nutrition, it is even entirely dissipated without residue or dregs. Thus also salt passes into the primeval element of water. And so the sea, although it receives salty rivers, does not become saltier day by day.

For the **purest water**, although free from all defilement, nevertheless under the **equinoctial line** <note>the Equator</note> becomes moldy and stinks; soon it turns yellow, then green, and finally turns red with a remarkable horror. *Which then spontaneously returns to its original state.* These things happen, of course, once the ferment of the place is conceived, and they cease when that ferment is consumed. Thus the purest water of a spring, by the stale ferment of a vessel, grows moldy, conceives worms, gives birth to gnats, and is even covered with a skin. **Marshes** grow stale from the bottom: hence frogs, shells, snails, leeches, herbs, etc. Even floating herbs cover the water, content only with the "drink" of the stale water. And just as stones come from springs in which a stony seed and ferment exists: so the **earth**, pregnant with metallic ferments, produces from water a metallic or mineral **Bur** <note>a technical term for a metallic embryo or raw ore</note>. But water elsewhere, enclosed in the earth, if it is near the air and agitated by a moment of heat, grows stale, and is no longer water: but is the juice **Lessas** <note>Van Helmont’s term for the vital sap or "juice of the earth"</note>, by the vigor of which—a stale ferment—the power of germinating herbs is conferred upon the earth. For that stale juice of the earth, by the stimulus of a little heat, ascends into vapor, becomes spongy, and is surrounded by a skin, according to the requirement of the ferments lurking therein. That staleness possesses the turns of the ferment and the powers of the seed, hastening gradually into the **Archeus** <note>The internal "vital director" or life-force of an organism</note> through seminal virtues, into whatever life it can. Therefore, the juice of the stale earth is **Lessas**. From this rises every kind of plant that lacks a visible seed, and sown seeds are promoted toward their destinations. There are as many rancid odors of staleness as there are messengers—and even promiscuous parents—of things. The vapor of the *lessas*, already condensed, turns pale at first, then yellowish, then a whitish-green. And finally, it becomes a saturated green. And once the power of the species is unfolded, it assumes various colors and markings. In this flow, it imitates the conduct of water under the equator. In this, however, it differs: that the water borrowed a ferment—too spiritual—from the **South Wind** <note>original: *Afro*</note> and the location, without corporal staleness...

32. Thus rain, conceiving a mellowing ferment <note>original: "fermentum fracidum"</note> in the earth, having become *leffas*, is drawn into the stomach-like roots by a certain suction. Observe the mellowing of a stained experiment. Soon from there it is carried to the bark, or the "liver" of the plant, where it is enriched by the new ferment of that organ, and becomes a herbal or woody juice, and finally, having reached maturity, it turns into wood, becomes a herb, or passes into fruit. Indeed, if the trunk under the earth should mellow <note>original: "fracefcat"</note> more quickly than the bark dries, it gapes open by its own ferment and emits a smoke through the bark, which at its beginning is a fungus, and finally hardens into a true root; and thus planted branches grow into trees by a shortcut of art. It is now evident, therefore, that there is no
33. mixture of elements: all bodies are made primarily and materially from water alone. Once the seed is acquired through the ferment, and once the seeds are exhausted, bodies finally recede back into the ancient hospitality of water. Indeed, ferments sometimes operate more powerfully than fire. For stones are turned into lime and wood into ashes, and there the fire stops; yet these same things, once a ferment is taken up in the earth, spontaneously return into the juice of *leffas*, and so finally into simple water. For otherwise stones and bricks spontaneously fail into saltpeter <note>original: "salem petra"</note>. Finally glass, unconquered by fire and uncorrupted by sharp air, may mellow and rot under the earth in a few years, and submit to the laws of water.

For those things which are liquefied in water soon return into water; but others are made volatile through ferments, and those which were compact and unmixable are brought into the necessity of transmutation through the ferments of mellowing, are opened up, and take up the counsel of separating. Truly the clearest springs, although they climb through rocks and sand from the tasteless bottom of nature (or the *quellem* <note>German: "Quelle" or source/spring</note>), purified far from the contagion of mud, ferment, and stain, may fall away in their progress: but they are destined for great uses: yet since they contract at least the hidden odors of the stone, imperceptible to us, they hasten toward other ends. Therefore brooks, springs, rivers, marshes, ponds, seas, and whatever waters are contained in a channel, soon conceive their own seeds, at least from the birth of the springs, and by frolicking, mature through their course. Clouds also, struck down by the mellowing of thunder, are fertile; but rains are heavy with dew or a conceived exhalation. Indeed, I have been taught by fire that dew is rich in sweet sugar. They say that boreal worms are born in the snow; therefore mountains covered with long-lasting snow produce grass which, though sparse, is yet most fit for fattening cattle; so much so that unless they are driven from the pastures in time, they will be suffocated by fatness. Moreover, waters which contain a "liquamen" <note>A dissolved substance or essence</note> 34. are called "corporeal" by Paracelsus <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note>, who ignorantly denies that they contain the element within themselves. Therefore, ferments play the entire scene in the world, through seeds, under the single element of water.

I take up the text: *The Heavens declare the glory of God: and the firmament shows his handiwork.* <note>Psalm 19:1</note> For this means: That the Heavens were primarily created to declare the immense Majesty, Power, Goodness, and Wisdom of God—the four columns upon which the entire globe of the universe stands and rests. Thus far, the Church admits meteorological predictions, the sterility or fertility of years, the seasons for sowing, the dangers of sailors, the deaths of Princes, Plagues, floods, and indeed whatever does not depend on the direction of our free will. To the extent, of course, that all these things are believed to be connected to the primary qualities of the elements by a contingent consequence. So much so, that although the Church allows the deaths of great men, the tumults of wars, and fires to be forecasted in almanacs <note>original: "ephemeridibus"</note>, she wishes them to be viewed not as free or arbitrary contingencies, and much less as necessary things, but simply as the effects of primary qualities and temperaments <note>original: "complexionum"</note>. In this, I have already demonstrated in the preceding pages how much error exists. Furthermore, I shall show here how far this has receded from Holy Scripture. If celestial influences hold the status of a "cause," then surely their effects will be connected to their causes by necessity, and thus far at least necessary, in the manner of other secondary causes whose effects follow necessarily once the causes are set—unless they are supernaturally hindered or changed. This is equally characteristic of all causes and involves no special status for the Heavens. But if celestial influences are only in the manner of a sign and a forewarning, they certainly carry no less necessity; indeed, a far tighter one, if we believe in the certain foreknowledge of divine providence and believe the works of the Lord's hands are pre-signified through the stars. <margin>12.</margin> But you will say: to what purpose are the announcements of Heaven, which no mortal knows, and which it is a crime for an Evil Spirit to know? Moreover, whether plagues arise and rage, or tyrannies, wars, devastations, tumults, or the beginnings of heresiarchs <note>Leaders of heretical movements</note>, by the Lord's permission, these will at least be as connected to their necessary and secondary causes—though they be arbitrary and occasional—as meteors are to theirs. For the work of announcing the works of the Lord's hands is not to be restricted solely to changes in the air: but absolutely, to all the works of the Lord's hands. Since if the Stars can be heralds of the threatened effects of God's wrath, which were committed to a striking Angel without secondary causes; why should they not likewise announce the works of the Lord assigned to secondary and free causes? For whatever God foreknows, He can also announce through His instruments if He wills: and the firmament and its lights are such proper instruments of God, according to the testimony of Scripture. Indeed, although I have dared <margin>13.</margin> to attribute more authority to Heaven than what has traditionally been granted to it by Sacred things. And although the stars foretell effects depending on free and contingent causes; yet I would not have it understood that the office of introducing the causality of the future is granted to the stars. For it suffices that they perform the duty of a herald in this, as a medium depending on divine prescience. For just as divine foreknowledge does not take away from man the freedom of judgment, and its knot with prescience does not take away the infallibility of events: it nevertheless contains no inevitability: much less <margin>20.</margin> does the foretelling of the firmament induce any necessity of contingency on the part of the will: although it falls entirely on the part of events joined to their free causes. Indeed, I have often wondered at those who reject the proclamation of the stars in free causes, as if they thereby made them necessary and took away the freedom of judgment: while meanwhile divine prescience causes nothing against free will: there is a far greater reason for necessity in the prescience of human glorification in God's hands than in the foretelling of the stars, which by its nature is bound to change because of the repentance of sinners and a fallible nature. For it happens that sometimes the stars foretell only threats, so that wandering mortals, through terror of punishment, may return to the path, like the Ninevites <note>The people of Nineveh in the Bible who repented after Jonah's prophecy of destruction.</note>.
