There are also some today, like lovers or the drunken, who predict the future, not knowing what, to whom, how, or why they portend. For thus in the writings of Josephus, a certain Jesus predicted the destruction of the Holy City with a continuous cry, and for that reason he was beaten. But the Apostles spoke from the Holy Spirit <note>original: *Paracleto*</note> in the tongues of all nations that were then under the sun; yet by the Hebrews and the pagans, they were held to be drunk on new wine <note>original: *musto*</note>. Although at that time in Palestine, no new wine was to be found. For those prophesying were glorifying the Lord Jesus. Nor is it read that they were then preaching, nor that any were yet converted.

They were therefore reckoned to be drunk on new wine, but not on aged wine, because among the gentiles, drunkenness from new wine would stir up Bacchic revelers <note>original: *Bacchantes*</note> or proclamations. It seems, therefore, <margin>25</margin> that prophecy from new wine—or otherwise prediction—is familiar to certain men who are almost simpletons, as if they were drunk; a constitution which the Holy Spirit calls the "gift of inebriation," which was known to the Jews, and <margin>26</margin> therefore falsely attributed to the Apostles. Furthermore, to demonstrate that the events of men are described in the Heavens <note>original: *Afris*, likely a typo for *Astris* (stars)</note>, out of a thousand I will relate at least three examples of diabolical predictions. These were extracted by evil spirits from no other source than the symbolic type depicted in the stars. <margin>27</margin> First: During the reign of Roderic IV, the last king of the Goths, the castle of Toledo, which had stood closed since the days of King Wamba, was opened due to the curiosity of Roderic; in it, however, nothing was found except a single <margin>28</margin> chest. In the chest was a linen cloth made of cotton, wrapped up, representing the clothing and persons of Africans. It was written therein: "When this castle and chest are unlocked, a People of this likeness and dress shall break into Spain and shall gain victory over the Spaniards." The Moors were depicted in the dress that they would wear 200 years later. There are two other modern examples. The Duke of Biron, having been seized by his King for the crime of treason <note>original: *laesae Maiestatis*</note>, soon asked from what region the Parisian executioner originated; when he understood he was a Burgundian, he groaned in fear and said: "Alas, I am undone!" For he had once learned from an augur that he must only beware of a mortal blow which a Burgundian would give him in the days to come. The Count of Loniguii, killed in a duel near Brussels, was itching for single combat <note>original: *monomachias*</note> and was quite bold because he had learned from fortune-tellers that he would be mortally wounded by a wolf <note>original: *lupo*</note>. However, the young man who was the partner in the duel for the Count of Saint-Amour had the surname "Loup" [Wolf]. He, having been lethally pierced, ran Loniguii through. Let the devil be the author of these predictions.

<header>CONCERNING LIFE, THE BODY, OR BORN FORTUNE.</header>

The Author. At the very least, it is a matter of faith that every victory of the brave is in the hand of the Lord. Let us grant that the devil incited Roderic <note>King Roderic, the last Visigothic King of Spain (d. 711)</note> to lose the Ark, and at the same time that he incited many Kings of the Moors to feign an alliance so they might invade Spain. Nevertheless, the devil could not have known that he would achieve this, given the free will of so many persons—much less that the Arabs would achieve victory (which the Lord alone gives to whom He wills)—unless he had first read the consent of the Lord depicted in the stars. For even an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmon"</note> could not have known this from the motion and light of the stars for two centuries into the future. In two other histories, the devil had already predicted not only the hour and place, but even the people killed and their names. Yet at the very least, a name is not bestowed by the Planets. 

<margin>28</margin> Furthermore, the commonly quoted Rule: *The stars incline, but do not necessitate,* seems to me contradictory to the Sacred text: *The stars shall be for you as signs, times, days, and years.* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14</note> Inasmuch as it is permitted to no mortal to extend the boundaries, effects, or purposes of the stars above, outside, or beyond the intention of the Creator. Therefore, whether they are merely premonitory signs, or finally the causes of seasons, days, and years: since for either purpose they are the means which God uses as secondary causes, they must have a relationship of necessity because of the power, certainty, and independence of Him whose means they are. 

<margin>29</margin> As for the "inclination" which the Schools <note>The "Scholastic" academic tradition of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> grant to the stars: it nowhere appears in the Sacred Scriptures that the stars are the causes of our inclinations. Rather, as often as the stars are the cause of causes, they are also the necessitating causes of the effects, in the manner of other secondary causes. For the Sun brings the day and the summer with no less necessity than a blazing wind <note>original: "flamen"</note> sets fire to the dry brush beneath the scythe. But where the stars obtain the nature of a sign, a herald, or a messenger: then they also do not exceed the aforementioned conditions, nor do they in any way assume the role of a cause. At the very least, they then foretell from infallible divine prescience, and thus they imply necessity—as far as it depends on themselves and on the free will of man—as premonitory signs of the works of the Lord's hand. 

<margin>30</margin> Even if they do not necessitate as future causes, they nevertheless necessitate insofar as they signify the will of the Lord. For free contingencies depend on their own causes; the primary cause of these does not intend those unfortunate effects which proceed from there by divine permission. Nor, meanwhile, are those things which are done immediately by free causes understood to be inclined by the stars (even if they are only foretelling them) toward producing their effects. Indeed, a strong, native, continuous, soliciting, and repeated inclination in some way implies a necessity over free will—which I do not allow to be inclined by the stars even in the smallest point. 

<margin>31</margin> Just as a friend is not the inclining or inciting cause of a war if he secretly announces to a Prince by letter that the enemy is preparing arms and plotting an invasion of a castle. However, the Schools defend themselves by that saying: *The wise man will rule the stars.* <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur Astris," a famous medieval astrological maxim</note> As if the stars prostrated anyone into slaughter, theft, homicide, adultery, sedition, drunkenness, etc., yet the wise man, by the liberty of his free will, were able to make such inclinations void; this they call "ruling the stars." But surely a poorly understood authority of the Sacred writings produces perverse consequences. 

<margin>32</margin> For in the first place, it is not the mark of a wise man to resist evil inclinations, but it is the mark of grace. Thus, a "wise man" is not understood in this context as one who is fortified with sufficient grace. For if he "shall rule the stars," he has nothing to fear from vicious inclinations, as the word "rule" <note>original: "dominari"</note> implies. Yet this is false throughout one's whole life. Finally, they also presuppose a falsehood: because it is in no way part of the stars' purpose to cause inclinations in us, but only that they be for signs, times, days, and years—and nothing more. 

<margin>33</margin> Finally, Heaven was created without stain. It is therefore absurd that it should stand in the place of the devil as a tempter for us, and what is more, as an "incliner"—which would pour into us a continuous spark toward vice and a headlong inclination.

->**THE STARS DO NOT NECESSITATE, INCLINE, OR SIGNIFY**<-

Far be it from the divine goodness that we should believe such things. Every wicked inclination does not come to us from the outside or from elsewhere: *but has grown within us from sin. From the heart come murders, adulteries, and evil thoughts* <note>A reference to Matthew 15:19</note>—certainly not from the stars. Therefore, under the humble protestation of my own insignificance, I renounce the opinion which teaches that the stars have the power to instill an inclination. For I was initially held back by various effects: that something almost beast-like flowed spontaneously into the living soul, moving about quite clearly. And although in the conceived embryo, some power first shines forth as if it were a certain <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>The basic level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition in Aristotelian philosophy</note>, that same power is eventually perfected and rises to the level of the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The level of soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared with animals</note>. And since the human seed is no less perfect than that of a beast, I thought that it also flowed at an equal pace and was finally perfected into a sensitive soul. Yet it is not so that this sensitive soul likewise passes into the nature of the human mind. For since no one can serve two masters at once who are not subordinate to each other without hating one of them—because they are incompatibly opposed—so in nature, a single body cannot serve two distinct souls. Let the sensitive soul be neither a substance nor an accident (as I shall teach regarding forms), but let the human mind be a spirit, even a living one, a substance in the abstract, and immortal. From this, it follows that if the sensitive soul is persistent, nature also willingly receives the human soul as its perfectly ultimate act, and both peacefully coexist within.

Having premised these things, I began to consider that a dog is a voracious, biting, envious, watchful, barking, and hunting animal, and for the sake of a single morsel, it is ungrateful and forgetful of all benefits, fawning, etc. All of these exist in the canine seed either as seminal or specific properties, and are not impressed by the stars. I recognized many of these as proper to the species, but some as peculiar traits inherited from the parents. Thus, the lineage of dogs differs in value. I realized, therefore, that similar conditions in a dog come from the lineage of the seed and are not astral. Consequently, when I observed similar inclinations in a man, I immediately judged that these too lay hidden in the human seed from some "canine" property. Finally, I noted that some animals are monogamous, while others are born from promiscuous and incestuous mating. Thus I noted the tame, the wild, the clever, those incapable of learning, the thievish, the cruel, the fugitive, the fearful, the wonderful, etc. These conditions—insofar as they are common to the whole species or dispersed through families—I learned come not from the Stars or from the <term>Almuten</term> <note>The "Almuten" is the planet with the most dignity or influence over a specific point in a birth chart</note> of one's birth, but arise entirely and solely from the seed. Therefore, I likewise judged that such inclinations in men grow into the newborn from some brutal property of the seeds. I also found among men entire families that were not infrequently furious, stupid, clever, insolent, petulant, etc. Whence some are called a *vipers' brood* <note>original: "natio viperina"</note>. Likewise: *Go tell that fox* (referring to Herod). <note>Luke 13:32</note>

Wherefore I began to remove talent, judgment, memory, morals, inclinations, and even the dispositions of death and fortune entirely from the stars. Finally, it is in the hand of the progenitor to generate a male or a female; yet the conditions, inclinations, talents, and properties of males are far distinct from those of females. For the Church prays for the *devout female sex* <note>original: "devoto femineo sexu"</note>; therefore, inclination or moral devotion is owed to the sex, not the stars. For horses are judged by the color of their hair; yet colors are varied by artifice at the time of conception. Furthermore, conditions and inclinations change through the ages of life. Children are certainly delighted by different things than men. For a sober youth sometimes becomes a drinking old man, or vice versa. A liberal adolescent often <margin>36.</margin> becomes a miser. Greed also often accompanies the female (who needs less and ought to desire less). These things certainly do not depend on the direction of the Stars, if the same *Almuten* governs the entire life. Indeed, I have distinguished inclinations so that one is that by which a person naturally leans toward professions, religions, or arts...

arts, sciences, trade, or the carrying out of business. This I call the **inclination of calling** <note>original: *vocationis*</note>. The second inclination concerns morals, virtues, and vices; which I call **moral** or **ethical**. The third regards health, diseases, and a long or short life. <margin>38.</margin> The moral inclination, however, is merely animalistic <note>original: *belluina*</note>; so I have already demonstrated before that it depends on the "being of the seed" <note>The *ens feminis*, referring to biological inheritance or the generative power of the parents.</note>. Indeed, the stars would be simply evil if they inclined a man toward vices. And the Creator would have erred in judgment, He who saw that everything He had made was good. Therefore, the inclination toward evil emanates from nature corrupted in its root and seed. From the heart flow evil thoughts, according to the light of the Gospel, and from the soul comes consent, just as a strong inclination comes from the habit of sinning. But good comes from grace, will, and practice. It is certainly by no means a stranger coming to us from the stars. Namely, the first constituents of our being were equally stained by transgression <note>The Fall of Man</note>; but they are unequally distributed and shared, based on the goodness of the seed, the mother's conception, education, etc., or the opposite.
<margin>39.</margin> And therefore all seminal inclinations grow, increase, or decrease according to the properties of the flows of the seed, toward their peak and decline.
<margin>40.</margin> That the third inclination arises from the weakness or strength of the seeds, and is entirely subject to the directing *Archeus* <note>A term used in Paracelsian medicine to describe the internal "vital force" or "alchemist" that governs the body's functions.</note> in nature, no one disputes except the Astrologer, who, poorly equipped, refers everything—even unto idolatry—to the movements of the stars, and attributes to himself the right of explaining them. He fails primarily to distinguish the power of announcing <note>predicting</note> from the effective power <note>causing</note>; nor does he know the seven elements. The fixed stars, however, contain particular tragedies. Therefore, when there are signs in the sun and moon beyond the usual course of nature, they signify portents of the future ruin of the universe. But that stupidity has become so common among the public that it is thought everyone should be believed in their own art. This is right, indeed, in that the Astronomer has learned to measure the motions and distances of the stars. But he is not therefore to be believed as if he were a prophet of the stars, unless he brings forth highly authentic credentials by which he may be believed, like Oholiab and Bezalel <note>Biblical craftsmen endowed by God with special skill (Exodus 31).</note>. I, therefore, for the vital inclination, praise the proverb: *the brave are created by the brave* <note>original: *fortes creantur fortibus*</note> and the good. Furthermore, as much as concerns the inclination
<margin>41.</margin> of fortunes. That, by its very etymology, falls outside the catalog of inclinations. I think, therefore, that all fortunes of all people, both prosperous and adverse, concern divine disposition, but not an "inclination," and much less do they depend on the stars, although they are pre-signified in the firmament. Since even this pre-signification demonstrates

I believe, therefore, that all the lots of all people are good in themselves, and are fully in the hand of the Lord. I believe, moreover, that the further anyone is from this opinion, the closer they are to paganism <note>original: *genilitati*</note>. The ethnic <note>pagan</note> schools saw, indeed, that living creatures have similar inclinations according to their species; yet, stunned by the plurality of moral inclinations in the human species alone—which expresses all the inclinations of all the beasts—and not knowing to what cause they should attribute such a number of inclinations, at the persuasion of the Evil Spirit <note>original: *Cacodaemone*</note>, through the augurs of the sky, they confusedly fled to the uncertain and momentary conjunction and elongation of the stars.

The human species is capable of all [kinds of] inclinations. For they have neglected to consider that brutes possess specific inclinations from the *seed-entity* <note>original: "ente feminis"; the vital principle within the seed that determines the nature of the offspring</note>, and that a horoscope is not owed to brutes. Yet man likewise possesses his own inclinations similar to those of the brutes. Therefore, at the very least regarding the moral inclinations of men, birth-charts are not to be investigated. For they do not come to man naturally from any other source than from the part of his body, which—whatever it may be—it owes to the seed-entity, no differently than the bodies of brutes. Indeed, the immortal soul is entirely simple and uniform; and since it is immortal, it cannot have its inclination from the falling and fleeting motion of the stars: but it only listens to nature, corrupted by sin in Adam and his posterity. Wherefore, in a distant grandson, there often resurface the manners, gestures, and inclinations of a grandfather never before seen. The Schools <note>The "Scholastic" academic philosophers of the medieval and early modern period</note> are content that these are given by the seed-entity, not by the stars. But, lulled by the habit of agreeing and by the importunities of the astrologers, they have neglected to weigh that the aforementioned inclinations of the grandfather are of no different dignity, nor separated from the assembly of other inclinations: and therefore they are held by the same law, the seed-entity. I do not know, therefore, by what merit they still teach today that man is so subject to the stars that he is continually tempted by them. [They claim] that moral inclinations—namely of vices and virtues—are taken from the hour of birth: But surely, *God established man in the hand of his own free will* <note>A reference to Sirach 15:14</note>. For the sensitive soul, the deputy of the mind, surely enjoys greater liberty than the souls of brutes, because of the seals suggested to it by the mind.
<margin>44.</margin> Indeed, brutal souls live content within a narrow latitude of the inclinations of their species: but the human sensitive soul ranges out toward all of them. For just as the human fetus, as soon as it begins to be nourished by its own portion, [is] not a plant of any one species, nor a brute of any one species, while the sensitive flows in together with the rational. Thus the human sensitive soul, not bound to a brutal species, wanders through the entire latitude of brutal

inclinations, and easily listens to foreign inclinations of the immortal mind introduced to it by its own pleasure. For the mind, slipping from its uncorrupted nature, easily falls by the motions and allurements of this [sensitive soul], and being always shaken from its place by unbridled appetite, it serves as a handmaid to the disturbance that drove it from its place.
<margin>45.</margin> Hence comes a foreign inclination. By frequent use or desire of this, a strong habit is formed, which finally imprisons the mind. It is clear, at least, that moral inclination is among the innermost properties of the sensitive soul, falling dispositively from the seed-entity. And that the stars have been allotted no power of causing anything in us, except through the *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont referring to a localized "motive power" or vital force governing motion and change</note> of the meteors. Furthermore, although an inclination of vocation, or a moral one, may change the vital [state]. As when a pruner becomes gouty; a brawler is wounded or killed: so the gilder miserably trembles; the digger of minerals, and likewise the Chemist, perishes by a blast. Yet those things happen only occasionally. Nor do they defer any right to the Astrologer. Away then, with the belief that the stars were created—or subsequently gained the right—to tempt, incline, destroy, make happy, or infuse sciences. For thus the force of merit and punishment is taken away, and the way is opened to Atheism and the fatalities of destiny.
<margin>46.</margin> Therefore *the wise man shall rule the stars.* <note>A common Latin proverb: "Sapiens dominabitur astris"</note> Not indeed that he is able to hinder, change, suspend, or invert the courses or lights of the stars: nor the successions of seasons, days, and years resulting therefrom. It follows, therefore, that the Wise man shall not rule over the effects which are coupled to the revolutions of the stars as causes; nor shall he rule the stars as signs, namely that he might change them at his pleasure: but only by foreseeing *that the seven wanderers* <note>The seven classical planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Sun, and Moon</note>, about to stir up a motive or alterative *Blas*, from which sterilities, colds, heats, high prices of grain or the like necessarily follow, he will be able to provide himself with necessities, and thus [avoid] the inconveniences born from the flux of the stars.

by meeting these advantages and, in a certain way, ruling from a later position. By this name, the **Astrologer**, not exceeding the limits of natural phenomena <note>original: "meteori"</note>, is numbered among the Wise in Holy Scripture. But if astrological predictions exceed this token by a rash daring, they are not only vain and conjectural, but are exposed by both pages of the Sacred Scriptures under the name of *Augurs of the heavens*. Thus Saint Ambrose rightly compares them to spider webs, which indeed serve to catch flies and gnats that entangle themselves, but are most easily broken through by a stronger animal. In this way, surely, these predictions only capture the credulous and those less <margin>47.</margin> firm in their faith.

However, I shall prove that they are in themselves vain and formed by conjectural rules. For they lean upon a double foundation: namely, the Null and the False. Regarding the nullity: it is because they wish to attribute to the seven Planets the form, inclinations, strength, character, fortunes, and <margin>48.</margin> death of the native, whereas God destined the stars only for signs, seasons, days, and years <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14</note>, and not as causes for the aforementioned things. And so, if predictions of this kind contradict the divine destination, they are by that very fact null and false.

Secondly: Because until now there is no agreement among Astrologers concerning the Scheme, *or the order of the heavens*. Namely, whether Mercury and Venus are carried in individual orbits below the Sun, according to **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century astronomer who placed Earth at the center</note> and all the ancient judicial astrologers; or whether they are rotated in smaller circles around the Sun. This is what the optical tube <note>The telescope</note> has recently explored. Therefore, the Aphorisms of predictions collapse, since they lean on that foundation *that those two planets are always lower than the Sun*.

Furthermore, if two of the planets (Venus being the greatest star besides the Sun) are carried around the Sun, and they possess such great power in Judgments and are so near to us, then surely those spots or stars in the Sun, or those very close to it, will be of far greater authority to refute all the aphorisms of the ancients. And the stars which have recently been found to revolve around Jupiter <note>The Galilean moons</note> prove by conjecture that the rules of the **Almagest** <note>Ptolemy's influential astronomical manual</note> were written on a false foundation.

Meanwhile, I shall remain silent regarding the **Copernican** opinion <note>The heliocentric theory</note>, which today does not lack its followers and is of no small authority, although they press their consent under silence. Yet once this opinion breaks forth, without doubt, all phenomena and predictions will fall.

Fourthly, the point of birth is uncertain. And since the stars vary at every single point, every prediction is necessarily uncertain. I myself, deceived in my younger years, attributed much to the significations of the stars; but when I could not satisfy myself by finding the point of birth through the notable accidents <note>significant life events</note> of the native—which is plainly necessary if those accidents proceed from the stars in any way—I finally described the accidents of a certain Great Hero. Namely, that in the 11th year of his age a wife of six years was married to him; that he obtained the rank of knighthood; that he traveled abroad until his 19th year; that he received a wound in a duel; and that his right thigh was broken by a fall in a carriage; with the precise hours added, along with observations of many other things.

Having added the fatherland where he was born on the 9th of June, between the 7th and 10th hour before noon in the year 1604, I myself approached the most skillful judicial astrologers, sending the question even into other regions, with a promise of 600 gold coins to whoever could divine the point of birth (known to us) from the aforementioned accidents. In the end, no one hit upon the true point; even he who came closest was still off by seven points, over half an hour away. Meanwhile, there were leaders among them who denied that between the 7th and 10th hour there was any such point through which accidents of that kind were signified; but rather that such a point was found just before five in the morning. In the truth of the matter, however, he was born in London in my presence, seven points after the ninth solar hour (not the clock hour). Consequently, with notable repentance, I mourned my credulity.

Furthermore, concerning the falsehood of the foundation of predictions, it is even more clearly established. Since they <margin>49.</margin> themselves admit their **eccentrics** <note>technical term for non-centered planetary orbits</note>, etc., are mere...

mere fictions; and almost impossible, invented only to save their theories. This implies that the spheres of the heavens and the movements of the stars are actually unknown. And so, once these absurd fictions are admitted, it is no wonder that many more related errors follow. I know a remedy—whereby a fetus that might otherwise remain in labor for a day and hours—once this drink is taken, the woman gives birth within a quarter of an hour. <margin>50.</margin> Saturn is cold and dry, a melancholic influence, and therefore envious, inciting one to theft and betrayals—plainly evil because it shares the nature of Earth. They claim Jupiter and Venus share the nature of Air and are cheerful, sanguine, and good; while the Moon and Mercury are cold and moist, sharing the nature of Water and phlegm, and are therefore mediocre. To the very hot Sun, they attribute a "mediocrity" <note>a balanced or neutral state</note>, yet neither moisture nor an element. Therefore, either the Sun will languish under this insult, or these fictitious elemental powers are wrongly attributed as the causes of the properties of the stars. For it is the property of stars not to change themselves, but to give an alterative *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont meaning a "vital motion" or "formative pulse"</note> to these lower things. In this, many falsehoods occur: 1. They plunge "evil" into the heavens as a causative force. 2. They claim the qualities of the Earth are wicked. 3. They place Fire among the elemental bodies. 4. They imply that the stars—or at least two of the elements God made—were not "good." 5. They falsely compare the stars in their causative property to elemental qualities. 6. They therefore falsely attribute to the stars a causal power over fortune, character, etc., based on a relation to the primary qualities. Therefore, since in judicial astrology <note>The art of forecasting future events or fate based on the stars</note> there are such exposures, falsehoods, and vanities—and in short, nothing but conjectures supported by merely lying rules—it is no wonder that the "Thousand-fold Craftsman" <note>A reference to the Devil</note> meddles in them, so that he may again have his four hundred prophets opposed to a single Micaiah <note>A biblical reference to 1 Kings 22, where 400 false prophets opposed the true prophet Micaiah</note>. Whoever you are, Reader, follow my example: do not seek to know things too high. No one doubts the heaven is "high," both in its location and in the profound ignorance of our blindness. For this reason, I certainly did not wish to inquire into celestial secrets, I who do not know even the smallest of earthly things. But if God reveals them of His own accord, sing thanks to Him with a grateful heart. Be certain He will reveal nothing except what looks to His glory and the benefit of mankind. I have written more on Epidemics in my treatise on the Plague.

...all things necessary for generation.
Therefore, the Almighty will no more grant His honor to any creature in this regard than in any other. Rather, He always remains the total cause, the perpetual Parent of things, the founder and Ruler of nature, persevering in creation. I profess, therefore, that just as in the beginning nothing was made without Him <note>original: "sine ipso factum est nihil," a reference to John 1:3</note>, so also today, the creation of any form whatsoever is a thing made from nothing, by that very same Being. This I say not only for matter, which was created once long ago, but also concerning any forms whatsoever. For just as the form is a kind of light of a thing, and the very peak of that light, so no one may father the forms of things except the Father of Lights <note>original: "Pater luminum," referencing James 1:17</note>, who gives all things to all, and is not far from every created thing. Nor shall I believe that the heavens establish the natural forms of things from nothing, or provide the seeds or the living animal, which they in no way possess. Because faith and religion alike teach me that even today, God is the immediate principle of things, everywhere present, working every perfection of all things. And therefore, whatever exists essentially anywhere—all that it is, can do, knows, and possesses—it owes entirely to God.

3. For indeed, creation regards and expresses a relationship to a thing existing in perfection; moreover, the perfection of a thing is its own internal, essential form. Therefore, its immediate origin can come from nowhere else than from creation. And thus, it comes immediately from the one ineffable Creator of things.

4. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholastic philosophers, typically followers of Aristotle in medieval universities</note>, therefore, holding the opposite view, were deceived when they perceived that light, by itself, produced true fire through glass. Light, I say, they thought to be an accident <note term="accident">In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality (like color or heat) that exists only within a substance, but is not essential to what the thing is</note>; but Fire they thought to be a substance, and in both thoughts they stumbled.

5. And so, being blinded toward the natural light of the Sun, they flee to it as if to the creator of the substance of fire; drawing back in doubt as to whether the heaven might still establish the form of fire, or whether any other artificial light might be equivalent in this work. For indeed, that laziness of the Schools always endures: having found one example (erroneous and imaginary), they immediately fall into a generalization, lest they be fatigued by investigating through specific types and find something that would force them to retreat from their possession of supposed knowledge. They could not understand the light of the Sun, I say, without simultaneously believing it to be the creator of all essential forms. But they stumble in the wrestling-ring, they fall, and they flee inconstancy.

6. For when they thought one essential form of fire was generated immediately by heat, rot, or friction—and now it is taken from another light without regard for or cooperation of the heavens—they sang a retraction. They attacked the heavens and their own prior opinion, and now they wish the creation of forms to be sought from these [mechanical causes], which they nevertheless freely and credulously yield to them, uncertain as to which Author the birth of forms should be attributed. Wherefore, when they saw fire taken from fire, and that there was fire potentially within a combustible object, they immediately, by the same logic, claimed that all seeds contain a potential form.

7. And to that extent, they claim that the actual form is eventually led out and procreated from a "potential disposition," which they call the potentiality of matter (a truly ridiculous notion). For in the beginning, they judged that the same thing happens in the generations of all seeds as they had experienced in light and fire. They began thereafter to stubbornly assert that every substantial form (I, however, grant an *essential* form to all things, but a *substantial* form to none except man, on account of the immortal mind) or "act" is drawn out without a medium from the power of matter. That is, it would be created by the Sun from the dispositions of matter—which is to say, from accidents. And as this "science" of theirs was birthed from the brain, like Minerva the daughter of Jupiter <note>A mythological reference to Athena/Minerva springing fully formed from the head of Zeus/Jupiter</note>, it was also anxious regarding the subject of inherence, inconstant, without sense, and soon split into various sects.

8. And first indeed, St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> teaches: *Accidents, in truth, do generate substance: but only in respect to the substantial form, of which they are the instruments.* In this, St. Thomas first fails his Aristotle, and wishes the efficient cause...

He speaks of these entanglements: *One substantial form does not make another out of itself: but its accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color, heat, or size, as opposed to the "substance" or essence.</note> actually do this. For nature is ignorant of such distinctions and has happily done without them until now. In nature's domain, every thing acts as it acts without a warrant of authorization. An accident, namely, acts according to how much and what kind it is in itself: not insofar as it has a commission from that of which it is an organ. For nature is ignorant of substitutions and all the deceits of Law. A thing works as much as it can without a diploma. For what pertains to the effect of producing forms, do accidents act insofar as they are organs of the substantial form, or in some other respect, if in the meantime the essential forms are truly and actually constituted by those very accidents? But surely an instrument, even if it generates something in Mathematics, is in no true sense a "generator" in nature, because it is external to the thing generated and specifically to its form; nor does it contain the essential Idea of the form, much less its Archeus <note>term: Archeus; the vital internal principle or "spirit-governor" that directs natural processes in Paracelsian chemistry.</note>. # OF FORMS

-> ON THE NATURE OF FORMS <-

And yet, since all natural things produce their like in species, it follows that they would want the essential form <note>The "soul" or defining essence of a thing</note> to be of the same species as its accidental forms <note>Non-essential qualities like size or temperature</note>. Indeed, it would mean that accidents had snatched away that prerogative from substances—namely, that accidents would produce accidents, and moreover, produce the essential forms of substances. The substantial forms, however, as if sluggish with idleness, would be on strike, having handed over the entire weight of the business to their deputies, the accidents. This would falsify their own axiom, and that of Aristotle: *That every agent is naturally born to produce its like.* <note>original: "Quod omne agens, naturaliter natum est producere sui simile"</note> For if that were true, accidents would be producing not only accidental forms, but even substantial forms—which they also teach are <margin>12.</margin> substances. Therefore, the axiom of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university scholars following Aristotle</note> seemed to me to be false and to contain a hint of Atheism: "That every agent which disposes toward a form, also gives the form itself." Since a substance differs in its category from accidents, their principles ought to differ no less. Truly, the active, moving, disposing, and essential principle of generations is the efficient cause itself, and the **Archeus** the smith <note><term>Archeus</term>: A term used in Paracelsian alchemy and medicine to describe the internal "master workman" or vital force that directs the growth and functions of a living body.</note>. Thus, it is God the glorious who ultimately creates the forms of substances. *Therefore, those whose principles are diverse in genus and category, their effects are equally distant: just as the same similar causes are similar to similar causes.* It follows from what has been said that heat produces heat, not fire; and much less does it produce the form of a chick. In short, it produces nothing other than heat. Because since the efficient cause is internal and belongs to the essence of the thing caused (which I will later demonstrate against Aristotle), therefore one and the same thing cannot be constituted by proximate causes that differ in species—much less by those that differ in their entire category. For "being" is not given without essential properties, just as an agent does not act without an organ or a medium. By what medium, then, or by what property outside itself, will heat be an agent in the production of a form or any substance? And by what contact will heat touch a form, so as to

produce this in another general object by the participation of its own being? Since <margin>13.</margin> among the Schools, who are imbued with pagan error, every form of a substance is a substance. From this, Christians must stand firm: that neither the heavens, nor the accidents that dispose toward a form, can create any substance out of nothing. For the creation of substance is proper to the Creator alone. Blessed Augustine therefore felt rightly: *If God <margin>14.</margin> contains all species within every substance (and indeed their individuals), how could He not have created all things? Or would He be unwilling to be the Architect of some things, for the making of which His ineffably praiseworthy mind possessed the art and knowledge?* Therefore, although the seed contains the image of the parent and its own **Archeus**, with all things required for generation: nevertheless, unless the essential being of the form depended originally, totally, exemplarily, perfectly, emanatively, and immediately upon God, nature would never work at all to acquire a form, because it would plainly lack active power if it were orphaned of that relative respect. Thus, in the first place, the heavens or the stars—moved by no mode of intellect—do not efficiently and immediately produce the essential forms of things through light, influence, concurrence, cooperation, or coupling. These are merely signs for us, for times, days, and years, whose duties no one is permitted to compel into new servitudes. Jeremiah says: *Learn not the ways of the nations, and be not dismayed at the signs of the heavens* <note>Jeremiah 10:2</note>, which the nations fear. If they are not signs, much less are they stars, because they do not have the character of causes, except that they exist for times, days, and years. Nor can a Christian, without sin, give them other duties. Indeed, according to Gregory: *The power of germinating from itself was bestowed upon the earth, just as the power of growing and multiplying was given to animals; to attribute this to the heaven, I judge to be a sacrilege.* But the Schools <margin>15.</margin> easily retreat from the Heaven to the disposing accidents. I, however, on the contrary, set down as my thesis: That accidents, neither by themselves nor as they are the organs of forms, produce <margin>16.</margin> substances...

the perfection of things, to derive from a universal and super-essential essence of perfection. Indeed, today they rather deride Plato, with his principle of the gods, and Avicenna with his *Cholecodea Pantomorphe* <note>original: "Cholecodea Pantomorphe" — likely a reference to the "Giver of Forms" or the "Universal Form-Giver" in Avicennian thought</note>. Yet these men saluted the truth from much closer than the Christians: who assert that the very lives of things, their substantial forms, and their "quiddities" <note>term: quiddity — the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note> are produced by the breathing of the heavens, the work of accidents, and the favor of material dispositions. I propose the blindness of these most rare men, committed even in the presence of light.

22. For they think that fire is a substance, and light is merely an accident <note>term: accident — in Aristotelian philosophy, a quality that does not exist by itself but only within a substance (like "redness" in an apple)</note>. In the good faith of their credulity, they have consented to the errors of the heathens, and have been seduced into many absurdities. 1. They are forced to absolutely deny that the forms of things are lights. 2. That lives, or forms, and lights, are placed among substances: since they do not acknowledge a middle being between accident and substance. 3. That although matter is a substance, standing-under and perennial; forms are instead privative substances, yet annihilable just like accidents. 4. That matter borrows its substantial being from a form that does not stand-under, but is annihilable. 5. That forms yield to matter in standing-under and 

23. subsisting. Which absurdities they would have noted by looking back, were they not so credulous. 1. For they would have known that the mind alone among forms is a substance. 2. But that all other forms are of the class of life, outside of accident and substance. 3. That it is impossible for matter ever to become an accident. 4. Because matter is not annihilable. 5. That it is impossible for an accident to be changed into a substance. 6. That an accident assumes degrees, but a substance does not. 7. And that therefore an accident, graduated on both sides, cannot lay aside its graduality to become a substance. 8. That even if light is reputed an accident, it will never of itself make fire, unless fire ceases to be a substance. 9. That the question is frivolous as to how an accident makes a substance, since it presupposes an impossibility. Therefore an accident shall not produce 

a substance out of itself, since this is impossible: Nor shall an accident make a substance out of a substance. For the question does not press how a substance is made from a substance, but how an accident produces a substance. For even if a dispositive and accidental operation intervenes in the production of a substantial thing: nevertheless, the production of the substance itself in no way regards the accident as its productive principle. Furthermore, since the two chief leaders of the Schools <note>note: likely referring to Aristotle and Galen, or Thomas Aquinas and Scotus</note>, groping blindly in the very sight of light and fire, have been led astray from the truth, I, a novice in Pyrotechny <note>term: Pyrotechny — the art of fire, here meaning chemistry or alchemy</note>, have deemed it worth the effort to demonstrate that fire is neither a substance nor an accident, <margin>24.</margin> but a peculiar creature, separate from both, which has no likeness to itself anywhere. Moreover, that culinary fire is not a Substance. Since there is no "elemental" fire at all—indeed, if there were, it would be of no use (as I shall show in its place). For the four elements cannot come together for the composition of bodies which are believed to be mixed. Because the substance of elemental fire does not descend from so many thousands of leagues to join its fellow elements in the constitution of those mixtures, and that rapidly and instantly at the pleasure of the seeds. Nor is it the property of fire to descend, just as it is not the property of water to call fire to itself for a mixture to be made in the future. For those commissions of the elements are the dreams of heathens and ridiculous mockeries, by which the Schools, without controversy, have hitherto allowed themselves to be circumvented. For if there were elemental fire near the moon; if it were true fire, it ought to have plainly the same properties as culinary fire: or at least this would not be fire, and the properties of this would not be essentially common to elemental fire. For celestial or elemental fire ought to actually consume and have nourishment—not indeed outside around itself, but within itself, thoroughly mixed: since one part of fire ought to be nourished as much as the other. In these things nothing of the sort happens, fire [would use] air as nourishment...

nourishment, being nearby, it would have devoured and consumed that nourishment of its own, and meanwhile, the Fire close to Heaven, being without nourishment, would have perished before then. I have also shown in its proper place how ridiculous it is to claim that air would be the nourishment of that fire, and even if that were granted, all air would have long ago been lacking; fire cannot make excrement out of air, nor anything purer, simpler, prior, or more subtle. On the contrary, if it made fire out of air, and there were no longer an element near the fire from which it could finally produce something else: then necessarily there would long ago have been no more air, but whatever was of an aerial form would be only fire. Or, if elemental fire ought not to be nourished, even though it possesses qualities that are greatly devouring, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval system of philosophy and theology based on Aristotle.</note> should at least have shown why fire is less nourished, or converts a neighboring guest into itself less, than the other elements are supposed to do. Likewise, why the fire of the kitchen should have this necessity of nourishment attached to it for its own sustenance—or else it fails—since it is true fire, and the primary element of fire itself is deprived of that same necessity. For they have not considered that true fire stands at the pleasure of the Craftsman <note>The "Artifex" or chemist/alchemist.</note>, and is led, reduced, and intensified for his uses. For he rouses fire at his will from things in which it is virtually present; nor even from all things indiscriminately. Otherwise, man would be the creator of fire, whereas he is merely its awakener. Furthermore, I call "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing, like the color of a shirt.</note> all the properties, powers, and qualities of things. But the Beings which have such qualities in themselves, beyond their own being, are not accidents: but rather the origin or the lodging-place of these qualities. Thus the heat of fire is its property and accident: neither is fire heat, nor is dryness heat. And since there is a distinct duality of these things, those two cannot be simultaneously in fire as if they were its immediate essence. But fire differs from both in such a way that it can rightly be denied that fire is heat, or that fire is dryness. Fire, therefore, has its own many properties and primary qualities.

Namely, heat and dryness. Likewise others, such as the power of separating, destroying, burning, making glass out of what is not glass, promoting, ripening, etc. Thirdly, light is in fire, as a property more intimate and formal to it. But the first and second of the aforementioned qualities in fire are mere accidents, in themselves separately distinct from the fire, of which the subject of inherence is the fire itself. Light, however, differs little from fire in essence, although in penetration and formal meeting, light receives a degree required for the entity of fire. Therefore, I shall show that fire is not a substance or matter; yet it is the subject of inherence for those accidents, or its aforementioned properties. Fire is, accordingly, a certain true and subsisting being, which nevertheless, as it is not a substance, so neither is it an accident: but a **neutral creature** <note>original: "creatura neutra" — a central concept for the author, describing things that exist but don't fit the traditional categories of 'matter' or 'quality'.</note> destined by the Lord for the uses of men, and given under the will of the same. I marvel, at least, that the Schools have hitherto not recognized, not inspected, and not investigated a matter so obvious: but believed it to be an element, and by the mere sight of fire, they fashioned a fourth element, and bolstered its existence with so many absurdities. Nor did they even once consider that if the highest heat were fire: that heat would have the other accidents of fire folded into it, and therefore the heat of fire would cease to be simple. Therefore, ignorance of fire, and the fact that St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> and Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note> subscribed to the playful inventions of the pagans <note>Referring to Aristotle and other Greek philosophers.</note>, gave cause for the errors described at the beginning of the chapter. <margin>25.</margin> My proposition, therefore, is that all forms of substances (the human soul excepted), likewise fire, light, place, the *magnale* <note>A term used by the author to describe a vast, subtle "greatness" or atmospheric medium.</note>, life, etc., are **neutral creatures**, between substance and accident. For I have partly treated the *magnale* in the section on the vacuum. I prove my proposition thus: Because they are actually something and a being; likewise they act, and have organs and properties: yet they are not substance, just as they are not accidents. Therefore...

For this reason, glass <note>likely a burning lens or magnifying glass</note>, which transmits all the gathered rays of solar light and collects them into a conical point in the air, teaches us that this united light is a true and actual fire; yet it is in no way different from the light itself, except by its concentration. But light is not a **substance**, according to the Schools <note>the "Schools" refers to Scholastic philosophers who followed Aristotle</note>; therefore, neither is that fire. Furthermore, that fire in the air is not different from the fire which is in a flame. For the fact that it has combustible material in a flame, but not in the air, is accidental to the fire: just as it is a matter of being nourished or not nourished. The major premise—that it is true fire—is proven because it performs all actions in the manner of fire: by heating, drying, igniting, burning, melting, etc. It possesses the same means and properties that true fire has. Now, no **accident** <note>term: Accident. In philosophy, a quality that cannot exist by itself (like "redness") but must exist in a substance (like an "apple").</note> acts through other means or properties outside of itself; yet connected light is an agent acting through properties and means outside of itself. Indeed, it is the property of light only to illuminate. Therefore, light is not an **Accident**. Nor does it matter if the light collected in the cone lives without nourishment: for it is enough that the light of the Sun or of a flame sustains that light in the cone without any other physical food. And so, it lives and subsists in the cone by the same privilege of the Sun or the flame. Truly, being nourished or not is accidental and secondary to its being; thus the question of nourishment is impertinent to the question of whether it exists. Therefore, in the point of the cone, there is true fire with all its properties, but a little above or below the cone, it is merely light, and no longer a burning fire. Yet since the same thing cannot be a **substance** in one place and an **accident** in another—and fire has now been found to be nothing other than mere connected light—it follows that a creature has now been found which is neither substance nor accident. For the essences of one and the same thing cannot belong to entirely different categories. And speaking absolutely and without any relation, this is true. Therefore, a mere actual fire has been found, which is nothing other than mere actual connected light. Therefore, absolutely all fire is essentially nothing but light. Nor is there room for the opinion that light, in its connection, becomes a composite different from itself when not connected: for we would only be driven to that by the difference of a fire that needs nourishment versus one that rejects it. Wherefore, looking more deeply into it: certainly culinary fire <note>ordinary kitchen or hearth fire</note> is in no way nourished. For nourishment, in and for itself, converts combustible material so that it may convert what it takes in for its own subsistence or growth. That does not happen to fire, which acts only for the necessary ends of its destiny. These are to separate separable heterogeneous things, and to change through flame those things which it otherwise only separates if they are not ignited. If, however, fire has need of air lest it be suffocated, this certainly does not happen primarily so that it may be fed by air, or sustained by it, or to convert the air into itself in any way, but only so that it may expel its soot into the air, which it produced by igniting the combustible material. Nowhere is a fire found that has ever appropriated anything from a burnable body to itself, or been nourished or increased by it—though the Schools have hitherto thought this without any controversy. They thought fire must necessarily feed not only on wood and coals, but also on air, and thus always necessarily be fed by a double food. Because, as will appear below, the rays in the connected cone still preserve their property and essence unmixed. And therefore it must be noted here that light is immediately in a place, but not in the air or the medium. These are: heat, drying, the stirring up of vapors and exhalations, combustion, melting, ignition, or the production of another fire from itself, and the generation <margin>28</margin> of its own likeness, along with illumination. A flame is indeed a fatty exhalation, a smoke ignited and illuminated, let it be so: but insofar as a flame is such and is true fire, it is not a different matter—ignited and not yet ignited; nor does it differ from itself, except that a light united in the center has come upon the fatty exhalation. There is surely there the production of a new fire—namely, of a flame, or a connected light. Yet it is not the procreation of any new matter or substance. <margin>30</margin> For fire is an artificial death, positive and not privative <note>Meaning fire is an active force of destruction rather than just the absence of something.</note>, more than an accident and less than a substance. Since the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic academics who followed Aristotelian philosophy, whom the author frequently critiques.</note> are still ignorant of this, it must be further declared—both because it is a paradox and pertains to the knowledge of forms, and because from ignorance of it, very grave errors have crept into the medical art. Therefore, to teach the irregular nature of fire, I shall propose several theses: <margin>31</margin> 1. That fire in a <term>flammable body</term> <note>original: "corpore phlegisto." From the Greek 'phlogistos,' meaning burnt or flammable.</note> is so united to the inflammable matter that it acts as its destroyer. 2. That inflamed matter is converted into a sooty Gas, which is not yet water; for although the fire has consumed the <term>seminal powers</term> <note>The "seminal powers" or "archei" were thought to be the internal blueprints that give a thing its specific form.</note> of the thing, some first fermental marks of the concrete substance remain. When these are finally consumed and killed in the air, that Gas returns into the element of water. 3. That every essential form exists for the being of the thing in which it inherently resides. And that fire also destroys fatty smoke, or coal, which it inflames, and converts it into <term>Gas silvestre</term> <note>original: "Gas silvestre." This is Van Helmont's term for carbon dioxide, literally "gas of the woods" or "wild gas."</note> (concerning which in its own place). 4. That every essential form is so united to its matter that once separated from it, by extinction or removal, it does not return again to the same habit or formal act. This does not happen in the case of fire. 5. That every arriving form is impatient of another total form. But a metal, or another fixed body, when ignited, returns always to its former state once the presence of the glowing fire is removed. 6. That every form of a substance has a specific matter in which it exists: but fire has wood, wax, oil, and as many subjects as there are signifiable species. 7. That every substantial form finally emerges in matter prepared by a preceding seed. Fire, however, lacks a seed; indeed, if there be any, it consumes them. 8. That the forms of substances do not have degrees: but fire admits of degrees by means of bellows. <margin>32</margin> From which I conclude that fire is not a substance, nor an essential form of substances: but the positive death and destruction of things, a singular creature, second to no <margin>33</margin> other. Whence I proceed to demonstrate it thus. It is beyond doubt that charcoal is far more porous than iron and has less solidity, yet ignited iron burns more than charcoal. Therefore, necessarily, the iron contains more fire in matter and form; but the consequence is false. Therefore, fire is not a substantial composite consisting of the matter and form of fire: because otherwise, if any substance were proper to fire, it would penetrate the dimensions of the body of iron. The Schools, in response <margin>34</margin> to this, answer against themselves: namely, that the compaction in iron is more matter than it is in charcoal; and to that extent it burns more powerfully, insofar as iron is capable of more fire. <header>THE RISING.</header>

The rays of the Sun do not, therefore, change these <note>the objects they strike</note> into cold things. Indeed, heat, cold, roughness, brittleness, sweetness, or bitterness do not act upon light; rather, only visible and opaque objects do. The Moon, therefore, possesses a luminous power of its own, which, as such, acts upon the warm light <note>of the Sun</note> and changes it into the opposite property. What if the Astrologer predicts the future colors of eclipses? Do not those colors promise some light proper to the Moon itself? For they are not conjectured from the medium or from vapors, because color cannot be predicted from the quantity of vapors in the calculation of a future Eclipse. Therefore, the colors of the failing Moon are <margin>47.</margin> indications of its own light. And in this, the rays of both luminaries differ: that the Sun strikes its light directly through its rays, but the Moon never looks directly at the center of the world, or the Earth, but always at its own eccentric center. For it does not look toward the center of the world except by accident—that is, when it is concentric with the world. Therefore, whenever it is concentric at the full moon and the new moon, there is an Eclipse. Let the head and tail of the dragon <term>Head and tail of the dragon: The ascending and descending lunar nodes where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic.</term> therefore be the nocturnal points in which the Moon is only directly opposed to the Sun in the eccentric diameter. Thus, the lunar rays do not strike the Earth directly, but are diffused into the eccentric space; and so, by way of influence, or through the action of governance (of which we shall speak in its proper place), it expands its powers into the night, or the nadir; whether it accompanies the Sun, or is truly distant from it by a whole diameter. Such indeed is the destination of the Moon, which the surges of the sea confirm, being no less accustomed to occur under the hidden Moon than during its fullness. There is, therefore, one purpose of the luminaries to rule the day and the night, another to separate the light from the darkness, and finally another to separate the day from the night. This repetition should not be attributed to a solecism <note>a grammatical error or absurdity</note>; for while the Sun shines, or the Moon returns the received light of the Sun, light is indeed sufficiently separated from the darkness. But the light of the Sun never rules the night, just as it does not shine in the night; therefore, so that the Moon may likewise fulfill its destination, it can never rule the night by means of <margin>48.</margin> light borrowed from the Sun. This is apparent enough, at least while it runs with the Sun by day as well as by night. Therefore, if even then the Moon must satisfy the divine intention, it is necessary that it possess another light entirely, by which it may shine every night and rule the night—and a far different manner of pouring out its light than that by which it reflects the light of the Sun. The Moon, to be sure, sends out its own expanded light beyond, no less than on this side of, the hemisphere of air, water, and earth. This is supported by the supposition of the center of the universe according to the opinion of Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer who proposed a geo-heliocentric system.</note>. Yet it is so that the action of its governance of light and influence operates more powerfully in the night, from which the Sun is absent. He who would separate day from night must separate the lunar properties from his own, even when the Moon is joined to him. This is proven by lunar diseases, which are aggravated toward night, even during a new moon. It acts so thoroughly through the bones and marrow of those who are shut up in a bedroom. This is not so native to the Sun. Therefore, the Moon occasionally influences the opposite part of the sphere more strongly than the one placed beneath it. This light, unknown to the ancients, is called "influence." But I would prefer to preserve the sense of the Sacred Scriptures: that it is said the Moon was created to give light at night, just as the Sun shines by day (that is, indifferently every night). It is therefore a property of lunar light, which they have called influence; and that is to have named the thing not from its effect, but from its causes. The bat, the dormouse, the mouse, <margin>49.</margin> the owl, and whatever things in the night, under the thickest darkness, distinguish their objects from afar and note the swiftest motions of objects—which our eyes could scarcely observe at midday; although some of these creatures display a glassy brightness <note>original: "glaucom nitorem," referring to the reflective layer in animal eyes</note>, they cannot, however, illuminate the medium with that brightness so as to see perfectly through it at a distance.

Therefore, it is necessary that in the thickest night and within a closed cave, there is some continuous light, by means of which such animals see perfectly. If this light is imperceptible to us, and yet truly exists, it is no wonder if the moon's own light has deceived our eyes. <margin>50.</margin> However, to make it known that **nocturnal animals** <note>original: "noctivaga animalia"</note> send out no light from their eyes—which would be for the purpose of illuminating the medium to distinctly recognize an object placed at a distance—and that they see only by means of **lunar light** <note>original: "lunaris luminis"</note>, let a **mirror** <note>original: "speculum"</note> be placed between the eye of the animal and its object, and this in thick **darkness** <note>original: "tenebris"</note>. Indeed, you will find not even the slightest bit of light reflected in the mirror.

Nevertheless, if you place a **thin candle** <note>original: "candelam tenuem"</note> at the end of a large hall, and at the other end of the hall there is a hole through which that weak light may pass into another dark hall, at the end of which is a mirror; certainly that weak light, vibrated directly by the ray of that **candle flame** <note>original: "flammae candelae"</note>, is received by the mirror and will appear. Yet it is not sufficient for a human to discern any object. Therefore, much less would the brightness of eyes—whose ray does not fall or appear in a nearby mirror—be fit for illuminating the medium so that all things might be perfectly discerned.

<margin>51.</margin> For there is beneath the earth, even at midnight, a light by which many eyes see, as witnessed in the Holy Scriptures and betrayed by beasts of this kind, which owes its origin to nothing if not the moon. For otherwise, there would be "tangible darkness" <note>A reference to the Plague of Darkness in Exodus 10:21</note>, which would far surpass our own darkness, however thick, because it would be deprived of all help from the moon. Nor is it a wonder that darkness has its own degrees. Since Hell has the "outer" or "extreme" darkness (because the Hebrew language lacks a superlative form) without the favor of the moon. For perhaps abstracted spirits have something that corresponds to our eyes for seeing, so that the whole does not see through the whole, whatever it is of itself; and some of these spirits are **night-blind** <note>original: "nyctalopes"; here used to mean those who see only at night</note>, while others are mute, **like bats** <note>original: "vespertilioni similes"</note>, as if they grow dim under the sun; therefore they appear more willingly to their own in the shadows and the middle of the night.

I will subjoin a history of this matter. In my **literary classes** <note>original: "classibus literariis"; likely referring to his time at university or a gymnasium</note>, I had a roommate born of honorable citizens. This man, with **closed eyes** <note>original: "clausis oculis"</note>, <margin>53.</margin> usually rose at night and wandered about; he would carry a **key** <note>original: "clavem"</note> with him, and having closed the lock behind him, he would open it again upon returning. And so, one evening I rose and secretly hid the key under the **pillow** <note>original: "pulvinar"</note>. But he, rising in his sleep, took the hidden key (as if it were visible to him) and departed. I followed him, having grabbed my tunic. He was climbing an ancient wall, the boundary of the College, covered in moss and hay. For there was an arch by which the wall supported the wall of a neighboring garden across the river. It was a **Full Moon** <note>original: "Plenilunium"</note> and a **frosty** <note>original: "pruinosa"</note> night. I shuddered at the sight and returned because of the cold. But my companion, returning soon after, placed the key into the hole of the lock so unhesitatingly that scarcely anyone with sight, even at midday, could do it with equal lack of hesitation. But in the morning, he was unmindful of everything. **For these walkers with closed eyelids** <note>original: "Palpebris enim clausis ambulones isti"</note> see clearly under thick darkness; without vertigo, they climb securely because they enjoy the lunar light.

<margin>54.</margin> Often a small wound becomes difficult to cure because it is inflicted on a luxuriant limb. Under the **equinoctial line** <note>the Equator</note>, all things rot quickly, not indeed because of an excess of heat (which is sometimes greater and more constant elsewhere, since under the line it rains several times daily), but truly because of the continuous proximity of the moon and the smooth shape of its globe (as I shall prove in its proper place). If a human or a beast, having died, remains overnight under the moon for even one night (for there the nearby moon strikes with a full ray), the following morning the corpse melts away in putrefaction.

On which occasion, it has been recorded among experiments: <margin>55.</margin> If anyone has **warts** <note>original: "Verrucas"</note>, **honey-combed tumors** <note>original: "Melicerides"</note>, **fatty swellings** <note>original: "Nattas"</note>, or similar **growths** <note>original: "excrescentias"</note>, and focuses the light of the moon into a cone through a **glass** <note>original: "vitrum"</note> <note>a lens</note> over them until they feel the cold within, they will thereafter easily vanish of their own accord. Nor is that a wonder, since defects of this kind obey the waxing **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"</note>. Hence they will also perish more easily during its waning. I know indeed that if the moon shines upon a wound, the lips of the wound soon turn livid...

Therefore, it is necessary that this warm light be of such great power that it preserves those many pounds—which would otherwise rush into coldness—from the cold by its continuous nourishment. <margin>87.</margin> and birds is Solar, just as the light of fish argues for a Lunar splendor.

# THE ORIGIN OF FORMS

For the example of the cold light of fish <note>original: "pifcium"</note> is not rare at night in tamarisks <note>original: "myricis"; a type of flowering shrub</note>, in the earth, and in combustible things. For it is a light, and once kindled, it is a glowing exhalation without fire or heat. For repeatedly, under the thickest darkness of night, I was able to distinguish the lines of my hand by the aforementioned light. Imagine in the same way that vegetables also obtain a twofold light, from the nature of light itself, and not from an element, because all things consist of a single element. Since the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional medieval system of philosophy and theology taught in universities.</note> have therefore been ignorant of the properties of lights, it is no wonder they have stumbled in the degrees of simples <note><term>Simples: individual medicinal herbs or minerals used in their natural state.</term></note>.

88. And so, hereafter, a different judgment must be given concerning the degrees of simples, according to the greater or lesser participation of light from their own ruling luminary. This is what Pyrotechny <note><term>Pyrotechny: the art of using fire, here referring specifically to Alchemical laboratory practice.</term></note> declares by the extraction of the light-being from the rest of the concrete matter. This is quite meager for many, but for the Adepts <note><term>Adepts: those who have mastered the secrets of Alchemy.</term></note>, it is very easy.

89. Indeed, through the fire of Gehenna, which is the *Alkaheft* liquor of Paracelsus <note><term>Alkaheft: a hypothetical universal solvent in alchemy, famously sought by Paracelsus and Van Helmont.</term></note>, it can be known how much of either luminary a vegetable possesses (even if unknown, bruised, or covered in decay), no less than by what shape it was adorned. 

90. And this is not by the persuasion of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist who advocated for Paracelsian medicine.</note>, who, when he had seen a weak lye <note>original: "lixivium"</note> congeal, thought the essence of a nettle <note>original: "urticæ"</note> remained in the salt of the ashes after incineration, because the beginning ice contracts its icicles <note>original: "ftirias"</note> into points.

91. Paracelsus is also mistaken when he writes that all vegetables cannot exceed the heat of the first degree. For the great luminaries have played wonderfully in the simples; and the seeds ascend to the fullness of degrees for the beauty of the Universe, and therefore all forms have the light of an essence-making quiddity <note><term>Quiddity: the inherent nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</term></note>, reduced to the union <note>original: "syzygiam"; a conjunction or pairing, often used in astronomy.</note> of either luminary. 

92. Nevertheless, the lights of the luminaries are not the constitutive forms of simples: because the light of the Sun, even in its simplicity, is combustible. It is shameful, therefore, to say that "man and the Sun generate man," <note>A common Aristotelian maxim: *Sol et homo generant hominem*.</note> because it is filled with the ignorance of paganism. 

Finally, the seeds of birds and quadrupeds are at first mucous, because they are perfected by the small help of the Solar light. <margin>93.</margin> They are, however, driven and thickened gradually, so that they suffice for the stability of their kind. Meanwhile, the eggs of fish are at first harder, and soon, with the light of the moon assisting, they soften into a mucus. <margin>94.</margin> There are, therefore, two great luminaries, and they suffice, just as there are as many primitive elements. The Sun presides over the air, as the moon over the maternal waters. Wherefore the fetus, by the light of the Sun, needs a continuous flow of air, just as fish are compelled to draw waters without ceasing for their sustenance and the refreshing of their light.

<margin>95.</margin> I have known, indeed, how to receive the light of the Sun into a flint stone (namely, by the preparation of the flint alone) so that outside the presence of the Sun, in the thickest darkness, that acquired light remains for a while; and the light is drawn in again by a new exposure of the flint to the daytime Sun, even if it is cloudy. <margin>96.</margin> This, therefore, was for us a necessity of inspiration not to be despised; namely, that the restoration of the luminaries contained in seeds by a certain kinship might happen: and not by the desired tempering of cold alone. Witness the fish. 

It suffices, therefore, that no form of natural things is produced by the Heaven, by the Sun, from a dreamed-of appetite of matter, or from any disposition of the feminine; since all these things are enclosed in a syndrome of accidents, nor do they know the way to creation out of nothing. For nature is never able of itself to ascend to the procreation of vital light. But Christ, the Lord of the Universe, is alone the life and parent of all things: nor will He give this honor to any creature. God alone, therefore, is the Father of lights. But He is not called so because He made the stars. For as He is not called the Father of stones, or of non-living things, so neither is He the Father of the stars. Indeed, He is not even called the Father of vegetables on that account, even though they have some vital light in them. He alone, therefore, is the Father of all lights, to whom alone the name of Father belongs. And He alone is to be called Father, who is in heaven. For

For even if a fleshly father gives of his own, from which the name of fatherhood is attributed to him; yet because he is not the giver of the vital lights, or the Creator of forms, the name of "vital fatherhood" is forbidden to be given to a creature. Therefore, God is the Father of lights, or of vital forms. And there are as many diverse lights of this kind as there are vital forms. For because souls are not known by a *prior* <note>original: "à priori" — reasoning from causes to effects</note> notion, they are called "lights" by a universal etymology, with a filial property, the correlative of which is Father. Yet, this fatherhood is understood by analogy. For although He truly creates all living souls: nevertheless, beasts do not assume the sonship of a proper name, because they do not bear the likeness of that Father of theirs. For their souls perish along with their life, in the manner of a candle's flame. Therefore, the mind of humans alone is an immortal substance, reflecting the image of the Father of lights: and for that reason, the power was given to it to become a son of God. Since we believe these things by faith, I am indignant that even today Christians teach that the forms of things and the souls of brutes are true and spiritual substances: and consequently that they are not vital lights, nor created by the Father of all lights: but are given and made by the Sun, and likewise raised up from a seminal power. As if a spiritual substance could be created from the power of matter! I judge that this is retained in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional medieval university system based on Aristotelian logic.</note> among the dregs of Paganism: and not without injury to the divine majesty, to whom all filial love is owed.
