Once I had explained my doctrine, I gradually fell into the history of vital principles, and consequently, I felt myself drawn into the necessities of disease and death; specifically, so that I might apply physical beginnings to the end of human destiny. And so I have arrived at the great *Oportet* <note>Latin: "It must be" or "The Necessity." The author refers to the inescapable laws of nature.</note>. I have come, namely, to the ebb and flow of life, and thus to the internal calamity of death. For this reason, all our physical consideration shall hereafter become Medical.

Indeed, Paracelsus, not being sufficiently consistent with himself in the discovery of the cause of disease, stumbled in the middle regarding the way and manner in which every thing inclines toward its decline. For the elucidation of this, I have already taught previously that fruits—which antiquity believed to be a heap of elements—are the offspring of water alone, impregnated by a seed, which disposes the water in certain places (acting as wombs) for the purpose of generation. For wherever water acquires an odor, it soon also conceives a ferment within itself, and then a seed, within the matter disposed by that ferment, once the disposition has begun. Indeed, many things come into being through odor alone. Often the root, the stalk, the pith, the leaves, and the history of the entire plant are born because of the flower of the odor, or the odor of the flower; and odor is the ultimate end of many species, as much in spices as in pharmaceuticals.

<margin>2.</margin> For instance, from sand, or simple earth and water, nothing grows unless they first contract a site, a mustiness, or odors. For far beneath the earth nothing grows musty, nor does a plant grow in pure sand. But when the time is near, the odor is musty, and brings forth its *Lessas* <note>A Paracelsian term referring to the vital power or "herbal juice" that causes plants to grow from the earth.</note> plants. Consider if one part of dung rots in the earth: it can impregnate water with five times its own weight and produce fruit. Indeed, all water is devoid of odor unless, in its own sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the combustible or soul-like principle of a substance.</note>, it has conceived a ferment of odor; certainly, in its simplicity, it remains without fruit, like rainwater. Therefore, in the deep layers of the earth, where there is a retreat far from site, rot, and corruption—even if there be no *lessas*—nevertheless the waters are impregnated by the hidden odor of the place. First, by an imperceptible contagion of a certain salt, they hasten toward richer colonies of fruits and burst forth.

Truly, a foreign fermenting odor dwells everywhere, which impregnates the sulfur of the water, and lying dormant there, finally thickens—as in minerals. Or, having thickened and been bathed at least in a denser vapor, it flourishes—as in plants and egg-laying animals. Or, right from the beginning, it burns in the form of a vapor—as in those giving birth to living offspring. The *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "chemist" or vital force that governs the functions of an organism.</note> therefore, once conceived, remains everywhere the guardian of life and the promoter of transmutations; and its change is immediately followed by the change of its life, namely from the first life and its matter, even unto the last. In this, indeed, the *Archeus* of things harmonize, insofar as vital things possess a certain splendor; yet they vary, insofar as they are precursors and managers of dissimilar forms.

However, they do not receive one another, lest their governance be disturbed; rather, for the sake of order (which they poorly explain under the title of *philautia* <note>Greek: "Self-love" or "Self-preservation."</note>), let the master remain who is the more powerful. They certainly expend the impressions of their ferment liberally, so that they may quell the foreign disturbances of a partner *Archeus* and subdue it. For just as under the immortal mind the subordinate forms of bone, membrane, etc., do not perish, so it happens in the transmutations of things. Thus, even if food, through every kind of transmutation, acquires the form of blood, <margin>4.</margin> it nevertheless preserves here the not-obscure accidents of the previous food, which therefore travel from one matter into another.

This is surely a harsh and paradoxical discourse in the Schools. Which I shall immediately prove by the example of a fact. Near the Mountains at Zoma, a pig, when the sea recedes, feeds on prawns, shellfish, etc. Its flesh tastes like fish fat, yet it is pork, forbidden to the Hebrews. <margin>5.</margin> It is therefore false to say that the species of things are like the species of numbers, to which if even a unity is added or subtracted, the species itself is immediately changed. For the single flesh of an animal takes on foreign flavors according to the variety of its foods. The Oak of Ireland likewise retains the properties of an antidote...

Nor does urine smell of turpentine, mace, or asparagus simply because some excrementitious part of the food remains in the flesh along with the blood. For Paracelsus occasionally mentioned "life" and "middle life" <note>original: *vita media*; a state of matter between its original form and its final assimilation.</note>: but he did not make it his own, even in his greatest necessity, when he dreamed of "tartars" <note>Paracelsus used "tartar" to describe stony deposits or toxins in the body, likening them to the crust in wine barrels.</note>. 7. Wherefore it is necessary that the same numerical accident migrates from the subject—that is, I say, it exists in the formally transformed thing just as it was previously in the transformable thing, even though the form of the subject it inhabited has fully perished. 

8. Because, even if the matter does not remain, the *middle life* sometimes persists, about which nothing has been heard in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Scholastic/Aristotelian universities.</note> until now. To be sure, the middle life remains in the transformed Archeus, not unlike the form of a bone after a man has died. 

9. For although there is a fermenting power in the stomach which dissolves what is ingested, and then these same things are perfectly transformed in other workshops <note>The "workshops" of the body refer to organs like the liver or heart.</note> of the body: nevertheless, nothing can be so perfectly transformed in us by the immediate flow of digestions through assimilation, but that the duller qualities of the prior concrete *middle life* remain. 

10. Which indeed, by necessity, having been afflicted by the nourishment of different climates, imprints very foreign contagions of properties into the solid parts. From this, so many dissimilarities of deformities of the one human nature occur: which certainly, I could never attribute to the vain "complexions" of qualities <note>A critique of the Galenic theory of the four humors/complexions.</note>. For pork is pork, even if the foul taste of fish fat remains in its middle life. This matter, never considered before, has made the entire contemplation of nature sterile. Indeed, this hinge of nature is neglected in the Schools. For it must be—it is altogether necessary—that the qualities of the middle life remain in transformed things. For unless this is granted, there will be no power in medicines, nor any occasion for diseases. For nothing works more happily for healing than that which, through its own transformation, has entered most deeply and is most closely united to that which must be healed. Thus a grain dies in the earth so that, through its middle life, it may stir up new offspring into a harvest. In foods also, although the former forms of the foods have utterly perished, the operative properties of the prior middle life nevertheless remain: and that through the second and third transformation of what is generated. To be sure, the native property of the middle life gradually fades away under the dominion of the ascending Archeus, by whose ferment the matter is subdued. This indeed is the great "It Must Be" <note>original: *Oportet*</note> in this valley of vicissitudes: it is not the whorish appetite of "impossible matter" <note>original: *hyles*; referring to the Greek *hyle* or prime matter.</note>. 

11. For Aristotle feigned a matter deprived of every accident, as well as of essential form, and he established this chimera for himself as the beginning of nature. And so he established as a material principle not a physical being, existing in act or possible in power: but a mathematical corporeality; not truly a "this something" or a beginning principle. Indeed, he thought nature would listen to shapes and measures at his imaginary pleasure. Meanwhile, so that this matter might be a principle, he feigned that a certain motive principle belonged to it—namely, a universal appetite for any forms unknown to it. These dreams, although ridiculous, conforming to no end, use, or necessity, and giving birth to many absurdities from themselves, are

Since there can be no appetite <note>original: *appetitus*; a philosophical term for a natural tendency or "desire" in inanimate objects to reach a certain state.</note> in that corporeity <note>The physical state of being a body.</note> that breathes toward any perfection which it did not previously possess within itself. <margin>12.</margin> For otherwise, in the consideration of nature—and indeed in its beginning state—the appetite of every being is carried toward a perfection, and not just any perfection: but that of the seed <note>original: *seminis*</note>, within the disposition of pre-existing, and thus already active, ferments. He was ignorant, primarily, that change arises not from the appetite of matter, but from the instruction of the seeds. Nor did the Schools once look back to see that the desire for remaining as one is—which is older, stronger, and more natural—is greater than the appetite for change; thus the Schools themselves contradict Aristotle, who claimed that every being, by its own natural effort, desires to remain as it is. For a thing must necessarily exist before it can think about or desire change. Therefore, matter ought to have obtained a perfected existence before it could grow weary of its old state and desire change. For to *be* comes before being *pleased*: and being pleased comes before being *displeased*: and nothing can be displeased, or desire change, except insofar as—once pleasure is attained and known—something more perfect and better is indicated as possible. For in cruder seeds, which have conceived their first ferments from odors; the odor precedes the complacency, and this in turn generates a desire for itself and for permanence. But in possible things, desire creates that same appetite for remaining, not for perishing through the mutation of its own being. But if, because of the internal obstacles of death, permanence is not granted: dissolution occurs in bodies, and from that comes weariness; from weariness one proceeds to aversion, as the governing power gradually fails, whence finally comes a destruction that was not intended, but follows through necessity. It was for the Schools to know that *being* always precedes the weariness toward *non-being*. That this weariness is not the intention of nature; but rather an imaginary metaphor for the subsequent defects of things. At the very least, this weariness ought to precede the appetite for non-existence. And much more so, the appetite for a new and unknown existence. Since a new existence is not given before the death of the present existence. Briefly, that the weariness of displeasure and appetite only suit a "non-entity" in dreams. And finally, that from such absurd, dream-like principles, nothing is to be expected except errors full of confusion. 
<margin>13.</margin> Change in nature, therefore, is not from the appetite of matter: but from the power of the efficient Vulcan <note term="Vulcan">A metaphorical name for fire or the chemical transformer/alchemist.</note>. In which the odor and flavor of the "middle life" generate the seminal image, which is the origin of transmutation. Nor are the Schools yet consistent with themselves regarding that appetite of matter; indeed, the Schools do not seem to have taught theoretical principles of nature for the sake of truth. 
<margin>14.</margin> For when they descend to the things themselves, they no longer accuse that appetite of matter for the corruption of a thing: but instead blame the air as the effective cause of all corruptions. 
<margin>15.</margin> But I know many things that are dried out under the air, which otherwise would rot immediately under the earth or water. Indeed, glass—the least of putrefiable things—remains in the air as if eternal. But when buried, after years, it admits decay, becomes wrapped in a crust, its dissolved salt fails, and its constituent sand remains. The air is a box, in whose porosities some things dispose themselves into alterations, some under the waters, and many also under the earth, according to the dispositions of the seeds. they scatter, they admit the same [odor] by a flowing and snatching wind, or they retain the same inside in a closed vessel. For if the former occurs: the empty pores of the bodies thereafter receive air, which, being shut up in the same place, becomes foul <note>original: "fracescit," referring to the spoilage of oil or organic matter</note> along with the odorous substance; from this, the residue of the odor receives a ferment, draws filth from the said foulness, and turns rancid or moldy. But if the latter should happen: then the air detained there becomes foul and leads the composite body to corruption, unless the odorous substance possesses the properties of a balsam: because the new ferment meditates a change of state. Volatile things, or those capable of exhaling and fleeing, easily waste away (because for the most part they have heterogeneities, in the absence of which distilled things are scarcely corrupted); one of these ferments the other, but they are as if suffocated and made foul by the element, or they conceive air, as before. Therefore, a ferment changes a thing insofar as it alienates its odor, according to the essence of the impressing thing, the vessel, the place, or the adjunct. Which things I prove by this mechanical [experiment]. Indeed, the juices of meats, of fruits, as well as any decoctions—otherwise quickly perishable—I preserve from rot for years, provided I pour a balsamic ferment into the air <margin>17.</margin> and keep it continually restrained. With me, therefore, corruption behaves as I have said. Forms are never corrupted: they do indeed perish. The human mind alone departs safe, but all other forms perish. Matter, however, neither departs nor perishes: but it is corrupted. And thus corruption belongs to matter alone. Corruption is, therefore, a certain disposition of matter, abandoned by the failing rector <term>Vulcan</term> <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, "Vulcan" refers to the internal fire or transformative power that governs a substance.</term>. <margin>18.</margin> For as long as the body sails with a healthy rector, it is happy and does not listen to foreign <margin>19.</margin> ferments. Nor is corruption, therefore, to be numbered among privations, if it consists of positive causes. Wherefore Aristotle’s other "beginning" in nature falls. For the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The vital force or "master workman" within a living being.</note> is not removed, dissipated, changed, or alienated of its own accord, unless it is infested by something new, under another ferment. Therefore, foreign ferments preside over all corruptions, and through the alterations of ferments, all corruption begins, ascends by degrees to a peak, and finally, having reached its period, is terminated. For there are some things in which the proper lust of the seeds is a cloak, and calls them away from the tenor of constancy to undergo the transmutations of change—not indeed because of an appetite for another form, but because the balsam implanted in their nature is easily scattered and perishes, such as meats and fish. Others, however, do not change their whole state and put on the anxious commands of new seeds unless rot is first excited. Such are wood, stones, and glass, which is most constant in fire. Between these, in a middle degree, are those things which, by the touch of the place, cover their surface with foulness or mold. Whence dispersed odors dissociate the marriages of the old seeds and meditate a new generation through dissolution. It is a natural symbol for air to incessantly separate waters from waters: and there are many things which do not tolerate such an alteration without stain; hence they immediately slide into a sudden disorder <note>original: "ataxiam"</note>. Corruption, therefore, just as it includes the extinction of the natural balsam, so the constancy of a thing desires its continuation. And indeed, for those things in which the balsam spontaneously flows away or expires, it remains associated with fixed things, is restrained by the barriers of dryness, or at least is cherished by a predominant ferment not foreign to the nature of the balsam. For in this way sweets, smoke, salt, pepper, "water of life" <note>aqua vitae / alcohol</note>, vinegar, and distilled oils preserve meats. But at least at the death of life, there is a great confusion of the thing on both sides and an opulent loss of powers. So much so, that the seeds serving the lower structure not rarely perish together, whence the "Vulcans" assisting the things, as if terrified by fear and like mercenaries, are the first to flee. Corruption, therefore, although it induces <margin>20.</margin> a transmutation with the perishing of another, is not a privation, nor does it necessarily follow generation, nor vice versa. Just as those things which, by their alternating presence, exclude each other, as light and dark-

Furthermore, since the "middle life" is so called in respect to two extremes: the <margin>27.</margin> **first life** will be that of the received and working seed, situated in the Archeus, which is endowed with the power of things to be done. For it is fitting to measure life itself from the Archeus, as if from a mediator and the organ of life. In the seeds, therefore, the first life thrives; but in the embryo, the middle life. The **last life**, truly, is when the total perfection of the constituted thing is present. This is indeed the last life of the thing, yet it is the middle life of the Archeus, if the first life of a new thing begins with the last life of the seeds. For in herbs, although the seeds seem to begin life while they swell and gape open, they nevertheless then rather die in their own last life, so that <margin>28.</margin> they may germinate in the first life of the thing to be constituted. Therefore, the first life of the fruit is the last life of the seeds. In the middle life, the herbs, roots, and stalks grow. But the flowers and fruits threaten the period of life. This must surely die in things if utility is to be hoped for from food and medicine. I except <term>amulets</term><note>original: "periaptæ"; objects worn or hung on the body for protection or healing.</note>, things hung upon the body, and those which act by the power of "governance" (of which I shall speak at another time). Surely the last lives of things must retreat, so that the thing may unfold its virtues in the juice to which the Archeus was married from the beginning, by laying aside the name and property of the last life, so that it may rise again to the middle. This death is not extinction and the true death of the thing, but rather a transformation. This will soon be evident in the apple. For a grain is eaten. Indeed, at that moment, the last life of the grain dies within; it is reduced into its own life, which our supervening Archeus overshadows, and it leads the middle life into its own first life through consumption, with the properties of the former grain remaining but dulled. In the death of the grain, or the last life of the seeds, the first life of a new creature arises. Briefly: as often as the Archeus of a thing is transplanted under a foreign leader, so often a change of life occurs, from the last to the first. This first is consumed into the new life of the thing and the middle life of the victorious Archeus, with only a clouded property of the middle life remaining, through which the retreat was made. Suppose an apple is cut through, whose internal pulp is rubbed upon <term>warts</term><note>original: "verrucæ"</note> until it grows warm, and the halves are tied back together with a thread until the apple rots: then you will see that the touched warts have disappeared. For as soon as the last life of the apple perishes, to which the impression of the warts was joined, the last life of the warts perishes, retreating through the middle life. Neither words, faith, nor confidence are required here. For if that apple is eaten by a pig or a mouse, the warts do not perish. This is because the stomach preserves the last life of the apple, as it were, in the retreat of the middle life, which the Archeus assumes for itself. But in death and the extinction of the last life of the apple through rot, there is no preservation, nor a retreat into the middle life. And so, with the death and extinction of the last life of the apple, the absent warts perish together with it, through a sympathetic action of governance. This, however, has deceived many, as the analogous flow of seeds was not rightly considered. For minerals, no less than the rest, are bound to their constitutive causes: and so they proceed out of necessity and the flow of their seeds. Therefore, they cannot lack the threefold distinction of seminal life. For whatever proceeds toward being "this something" without a parent (as minerals do) finds its seed in the lodging-place of locations. Wherefore some things are immediately in a place, but others are in a body situated in a place. The wind 
<margin>33.</margin> indeed flows incessantly in a place: yet every place has its own stable property; there are certain winds for Provinces, and fixed seasons. These I attribute to the place, not to the air or the unstable waters. God, therefore, not only endowed bodies with virtues: but also filled places immediately with the incomprehensible riches of seeds. Namely, He heaped up places with riches, which are to come forth into the light at a fixed maturity of days and put on the garment of water. For the earth 
<margin>34.</margin> was at first empty and void: namely, empty in a twofold way, because it was despoiled of its endowed powers, both in its own body and in the places of its recesses. Which you shall see thus. <margin>35.</margin> truly a being outside of light. And this happens as often as the aforementioned illumination is repeated. And so from this it is clear that light is a being, subsisting in a place immediately, and having no other being of inherence besides its own situatedness, separable from the created...

And so, if it were to migrate from the air into a stone, it could also migrate from the air into the neighboring air, if its existence is immediately from the air and not in a specific place. Indeed, it is all the same for light to migrate from a place (as its immediate subject) into the air, or into a flint-stone: the only difference is this: that the being of light does not subsist in the air except through a continuous feeding of light, just as a flame does not exist outside of combustible smoke. But if it should have a flint-stone as a suitable "tether" for itself (as happens when fire possesses iron), it persists in it for some time. For it happens from this that the sight perceives its object in a single instant, because both light and color are immediately in a place; but they are in the body of the medium <note>the air or water through which light travels</note> as if by accident and secondarily. For since "place" is its subject, it finds no resistance in the transparent bodies located there, so that in a single moment, light may vibrate from the eighth Heaven <note>the sphere of the fixed stars in traditional cosmology</note> all the way to the earth. Sound, however, or the object of hearing, is immediately in the "case" of the medium, and travels without a flow of air, from subject to subject. Even if the "Deaf Schools" <note>a derogatory reference to academic Scholastic philosophers who do not "hear" the truth of nature</note> become deaf to this. Odor, however, is not dispersed without the "odorable" substance, which is the *Gas* of the thing. This is dispersed through the voids, or the *magnale* <note>a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the vast, invisible spatial medium</note> of the air. And the *magnale* is the 37. case in which all *Gas* is reduced back into the first matter of water. Therefore, there inhabit 38. in places—not only lights and colors as immediate guests—but ferments and "Reasons" <note>original: "Rationes"; here meaning the formal, guiding principles or blueprints of things</note>. And these were located there by the Word of the Creator, so that they might be the roots of successive seeds until the end of the world. Minerals, therefore, are not scattered everywhere indiscriminately: but in certain years and places. For Swabia <note>a region in Southwestern Germany</note> can be as rich in copper as Cyprus once was. Therefore, cold is innocent, just as heat is useless, regarding the constitution 33. of those seeds. Indeed, both cold and minerals usually accompany each other in the mountains. For places which formerly lacked mines will one day, when the seed has matured, return their interest <note>repay the earth with riches</note>, not unequal to the wealthier ones. Because the roots, or the ferments of minerals, sit immediately in a place, and in the fullness of days, they breathe without weariness. When the seed has completed this, then the *Gas*, occupying the water in that same place, receives the seed from the place, which the sulfur of the water then impregnates, condenses the water, and gradually transplants it into mineral water. For it happens not rarely that a miner in the mines breaks the rocks, and a wall gapes open and gives a crack, from which a tiny bit of whitish-greenish water flows, which soon thickens like liquid soap (called *Burvoco* <note>a miners' term for a type of crude mineral marrow or "unripe" metal</note>), and then, its greenish paleness having changed, it turns yellow, or white, or a deeper green. For it has been seen thus, which otherwise happens inside without the wounding of the rock. Because that juice is perfected by an internal efficient cause. Therefore, the first life of the metallic seed is in the storehouse or pantry of the place, plainly unknown to man. But when the seed comes forth into the light, clothed in liquid and *Gas*, and begins to stain the sulfur of the water, that is the middle life of the seed. The last, truly, is when it now hardens. Moreover, the last life of the metallic seed is the first life of the metals, or at least closely joined to it. While that mass breathes sulfur and shuts its Mercury within: then, I say, is the middle life of the metals. The last, truly, is when it has acquired its own fixity and the stability of the vein. 40. Wherefore there is a more manifest progress and distinction of life and seed in metallic things than in the two allied Kingdoms <note>the Plant and Animal kingdoms</note>. Because metals do not require a specific shape, for while an image in living things flows from its parent; certainly the typical images of minerals are to be sought from the storehouses of Divine bounty. Hence also the 41. seeds of minerals are not defiled by the filth and lewdness of parents, nor do they offer themselves as monsters for that reason. But because they are untouched, they are therefore of narrow power in healing. Therefore, minerals, no more than other things, are to be despoiled of the possession of their "final life," if we expect obedience from them in healing. Otherwise, they will bring a languid help, and will cry out as if they have come in vain, because they have reached the ends of their destinations: but let them be directed toward the prevention of debaucheries and luxuries.

I shall repeat what I said above. In Eden, our <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital workman" or spiritual force that directs the body's functions, particularly digestion.</note>, being fully the master of all other Archei—whether of poisons or of nutrients—was able to subdue them for its own growth without any weariness to itself or any resistance from them. It was surely able, without difficulty, to remove and overcome every impression of the <term>middle life</term> <note>The "vitality" that remains in food or matter after its original form is destroyed but before it is fully assimilated into a new body.</note>. For the Archeus was then governed immediately by the immortal soul, and was therefore impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or being harmed.</note>. For God did not make death in Paradise; indeed, no "medicine of destruction" <margin>42.</margin> (that is, poison) was created on earth for man. But soon, once man was cast out onto the earth, it brought forth thistles and thorns. That is to say: although our Archeus acts as a victor and subdues the vital spirits of foods, nevertheless, the remains of foreign properties survive. The "final life" of the food indeed departs, but the "middle life" remains. For this reason, a weaker stomach feels a greater burden near the end of digestion than it does immediately after eating—as if the Archeus remembers its <margin>43.</margin> lost former dignity. These surviving qualities of the middle life, therefore, I call "ambulatory" <note>Moving or wandering properties that pass from one creature to another.</note>. <margin>44.</margin> Thus, what the <term>Schools</term> <note>The academic "Scholastic" establishment of the 17th century, which followed Aristotle and Galen.</note> shout is impossible is actually a common and necessary path in nature. It is as if it were necessary for the matter of generation to be stripped of every single accident of its prior being, and as if no previous dispositions could survive—as if every generation were preceded by total corruption or deprivation. They claim it is necessary that primary matter, or <term>summary hyle</term> <note>original: "hylen summariam"; the basic, formless stuff of the universe in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>, must actually be laid down and immediately precede generation, which they nonetheless claim happens in an instant. For unless the previous dispositions and the "ferments" of those things to be generated pre-existed in the process, anything could be generated <margin>45.</margin> indifferently from anything else. The poorly understood authority of principles has driven the Schools onto this rock; they think all accidents <note>Qualities or properties of a thing that are not essential to its nature.</note> depend immediately and originally on the "total form" of the thing. It is as if the form, arriving at the <margin>46.</margin> moment of generation, held all the characters of its seed within itself, and had infused them before

<column-break/>

it even existed. But if the properties that dispose the Archeus were sent in by the form of the parent, they differ at least in the individual being and would not belong to the form of the offspring. The Schools have neglected the <term>entelechy</term> <note>The actualization or "inner drive" of a thing toward its purpose.</note> of the seeds and the Archeus, as well as the actualities of subordinate forms. They did not know that from the beginning of generation to the end of the offspring’s spontaneous development, there is nothing but the flow of a single seed, which does not reach the "forms" of the generated things at all. Therefore, in the "middle life" of the Archeus, the powers of the seeds are hidden, rising toward vitality and acting as a foundation for the life or form of the living thing. Thus, when the Archeus of foods is transformed, the properties of the "middle life" migrate and are transplanted <margin>47.</margin> into the domain of the human Archeus, though they are much duller than they were originally. For this reason, it is a frivolous claim that no "accident" exists in the offspring that was not first in the seed (which they wrongly call "corrupted"). It is equally false that every lineage of accidents arises from the form of the thing. If that were so, the many properties and inclinations of men would be wrongly sought from the singular, simple, and homogeneous immortal mind. And if you should add the stars to the mind, these will quickly fail you. Help sought from so far away withers on the journey and fails before it arrives. It would also go poorly with seeds if every property and efficacy had to be borrowed from the "vital form" of a thing, which only arrives later. Thus, the clumsy <margin>48.</margin> dogma of the Schools holds that generation presupposes corruption, and vice versa. Otherwise, if the "middle power" consisted only in the total form and the final life of a thing, surely physicians would be deceiving the sick; for when the vital form is taken away from plants and animals, physicians still use them for the comfort of the weak. Indeed, they often see in the urine of a nursing infant the odors of things that the nurse consumed—for example, anise oil, mace, etc. What the nurse took smells in the urine of the suckling child, and for that very purpose they are given to the nurse; yet the Schools forbid that same accident from remaining as a guest in

The **Schools** <note>The Scholastic philosophers of the medieval universities.</note> indeed prefer to believe that light from the firmament to the earth, at every instant of location and motion, actually produces infinite **species of light** <note>original: "species luminis"; the visual forms or representations of light.</note>, propagating one another in a continuous thread at every mathematical point of the medium, rather than permitting light to be carried immediately through space by the vibration of a ray. <margin>49.</margin> Now, these are the reasons why the objects of sight move the imagination of pregnant women more strongly than the objects of the other, more corporeal senses. The first is: because the visible object is in its place immediately, and thus affects more, touches more closely, and penetrates the soul, because of a similar mode of existence. For they touch each other through an intimate contact. Second: the other senses serve sight. For example, a pregnant woman, having seen a **salmon** <note>original: "Sulmone"; likely referring to a salmon or a similar prized fish.</note>, is carried away by a desire to eat. Then, whatever she takes actually provides her with the taste of the salmon, and the sense of taste serves sight like a master; but the accident [entering] into the stomach, not having the salmon realistically in the visible object, perceives the fraud which the appetite commits against itself; therefore the woman becomes nauseated and weakened, with a palpitating heart. For the appetite feigns the taste of the salmon, but the uterus resents the falsehood; yet it cannot transform the food into salmon. Indeed, even if she eats another fish, and the transition is easy for those who share a **symbol** <note>A shared natural affinity or quality between two different things.</note>, she cannot from there form the desired salmon: because it is an object

<column-break/>

of taste, and not of sight. Whereas elsewhere, through a visual object, she easily transforms the fetus into a salmon or a duck, into a monster of that kind. Truly, the objects of taste, sitting immediately in some body, cannot, because of their corporeal thickness, form a transformative image.

<margin>50.</margin> Therefore, those who study the **adepts** <note>Masters of alchemy and the Hermetic arts who have "attained" the Great Work.</note> strive to promote the work of Wisdom through objects of sight, and specifically through the light of the moon. This is so that the soul may be touched by **formal light** <note>Light as a spiritual or essential force rather than just a physical one.</note> and "night unto night may show knowledge" <note>A reference to Psalm 19:2.</note>. As for the fetus, I certainly consider it like a foreign branch grafted onto the trunk of a tree, which, although nourished by the maternal fluid, soon lives within its own square. For it is not present as an integral part, but like a lodged soldier, it seizes everything at its whim, and expands the vessel itself by its own command. I consider the uterus, however, as an empty house, possessed and enlarged by a foreigner, into which pictures fall more easily than into a house that is exquisitely shut. Third: the object of sight is more spiritual, and therefore its image is more naked, more spiritual, and more active. Fourth: The **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical title for God.</note>, in this through a likeness, manifests by the mere thought of light that He created all things from nothing. The **species** <note>The visual forms or essences.</note> of things, I say, which He embraced in Himself from eternity, He produced into created being by thought alone. So too the imagination of the souls' lust, through the object of sight, pours out its own image in the woman, so that they might thus be fruitful by the command of God.

<margin>51.</margin> It could be asked here how the apparitions of spirits occur immediately in a place, in color, figure, and light, but not in a body; and consequently why they are seen by one person and not by another who is closer. By what way do lights and colors intersect each other in a place, the existence of each nonetheless remaining unchanged? In what way they penetrate each other and elude the rules of optics? That is, how **fascination** <note>original: "effascinatio"; the power of the eye to bewitch or influence matter through the imagination.</note> occurs. <header>THOSE THINGS UNKNOWN.</header>

<column-break/>

[Poisons] spread throughout the whole, and soon bring death; others, however, exert a topical <note>localized or specific to one area</note> poison, because their property, even if it penetrates by the nature of poison, dilates itself only according to the prescription of its own venom. This is surely the immediate action of forms upon forms, through the penetration of a **fermental union**, <margin>57.</margin> with a transmutation of our own substance. Therefore, a new poison is not properly stirred up in the **Archeus** <note>The "internal master-workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note>, as if it were forming a poison for itself. Just as elsewhere (such as in a fever) an occasional matter provokes the Archeus into a fury, not indeed for the sake of manufacturing other occasional febrile matters, but rather to produce naked **Ideas of fury**, dedicated to expulsion, which it depicts within its own substance. But the **formal lights** <note>The spiritual or essential essence of a substance.</note> of poisons penetrate the vital light, changing it efficiently and powerfully, because of the occasional poison inserted into them, which is present and radically penetrates our middle life, and disposes it toward the end of life, through the primary life of the poison. For there are **formal little fires** <note>original: "igniculi"; the sparks of vital energy in the body.</note>, whether animated or not, it matters not. For they act with formal license and liberty, by which they penetrate and insinuate themselves in a single point and in an instant. And they do what they are commanded to do by the Lord. One must then consider in what way they so easily destroy our life. <margin>58.</margin> 1. Whether, namely, they transmute ours into their own. 2. Or whether they drive the Archeus into a fury, so that, being out of its mind, it destroys itself and diffuses itself throughout the whole. 3. Or whether they mortify by a privation of light, namely, by blowing out the light of our little fire within the Archeus. 4. Or finally, whether they compress the Archeus under themselves, through their own virulent exaltation? It is certain first of all that this does not happen through **contrariety** <note>The old medical theory that "opposites cure opposites" (e.g., cold treats heat). Van Helmont rejected this.</note>, which, as is demonstrated elsewhere, never entered into nature. 2. It is certain that it happens through gifts bestowed upon the poison by God, which are called properties. 3. And it is certain that poisons act upon us in diverse ways, and that I have established a fourfold mode for the 

<column-break/>

differences of poisons. 4. And it is certain, finally: That God did not create death, just as He did not create poisons for the extermination of men, whom He had gifted with immortality; yet, once man's integrity was corrupted, those things turned out to be lethal to him which were not poisons to him before. There are, meanwhile, certain **fermental poisons**, which do not destroy us so much by the force of a luminous little fire and formal property, as by a certain almost smellable ferment. Thus, a single life fears many enemies from every side. For ferments of this kind approach closer to the nature of bodies. <margin>59.</margin> You see this in a **sulfur wick**, which, when lit and suspended in a glass vessel, will indeed burn and fill the vessel with the sublimated soot of sulfur: which, even if you make it exhale and then put the burning wick back in, is extinguished at the very moment it enters. Not indeed by the sulfurous smoke (which, since it is itself still sulfur, ought rather to be ignited), but by the **Gas sylvestre** <note>original: "Gas sylvestri"; a term coined by Van Helmont for the "wild spirit" or gas—like carbon dioxide—released during combustion or fermentation.</note>, whose odor alone extinguishes the new flame: not indeed by a material blast, but by its own odor. Indeed, it not only extinguishes a sulfur wick, but even the flame of a candle. And this is proven: for if you put a flame into a spacious vat, as long as the vessel smells of fermentation, or otherwise contains a little bit of fermented dregs, it blows out the flame of the wick or candle. The same thing happens proportionally, therefore, in the **vital little fires**, which you should understand as formal. In this way, surely, men are easily killed in caves and mines by the odor and the **Gas** of the place. Thus also pestilential poison often kills the vital light without delay. Because poisons of that kind are positive and "blowing-out" <note>original: "exsufflativa"; acting like a breath that blows out a candle.</note>, and mortal, but not privative. For they can be given no other name than that, by their virulent **Gas**, they efficiently blow out the formal light, the sensitive soul, or the substantial form of our life. And therefore they have a place among real beings, and indeed the most powerful ones.

Having sufficiently contemplated the integrity of Nature, I then gradually descended into its defects and alterations as I touched upon medical matters. I have shown, indeed, that there are not four elements in nature—and especially that Fire has neither the essence of an accident nor even of a substance, and much less the nature of an element. Therefore, the group of four elements and temperaments <term>complexionum</term> <note>The "complexions" were the four balances of humors: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic.</note> is broken and useless; and so is the forced adaptation of the four humors. Thus, although it is clear enough from this that the causes and essence of diseases have been left untouched in the Schools, I nevertheless wished to demonstrate this from their own theses in a special chapter elsewhere. In this place, however, I will demonstrate that nature does not know, and likewise does not admit by its own will, contraries.

In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth, and whatever is contained in the universe. But He placed the Man in *Paradise* after he had been created. For he did not have with him the lion, the sheep, or the Tiger as a contrary, or the wolf as a companion; nor, finally, any other animal that might lie in wait for him or the fruits of *Eden*. Indeed, the Almighty did not wish that man should see the sexual coupling <note>original: "brutalem copulam"; literally "brutal" or "animal-like" union.</note> of beasts, whom He desired to live in the innocence of purity (as I have said elsewhere concerning long life). He recognized that this authority had been given to him freely by divine grace, so that he might constantly adore such a massive responsibility in spirit, in return for so many benefits. For from the moment he gave names to all the brute animals, according to the specific nature of each, his own self-knowledge was also included. This is the pinnacle of Wisdom. For he knew himself inwardly (and certainly not as a brute animal) as a graceful and immortal image of divinity. Therefore, the animals were brought to him from everywhere primarily for the honor of God, and secondarily for his own utility, so that through the "negation" of the animals <note>By seeing what he was *not*—an animal—Adam learned what he *was*—a divine image.</note> which he had not seen before, he might draw out knowledge of himself, and thus not yield to the mockeries of the Tempter. <margin>3.</margin>
the fruit of the trees. At that time, every tree there was green with perpetual leaves, bore a succession of flowers, and finally produced perpetual fruit—neither worm-eaten nor falling before ripeness—just as it did not produce barren flowers. This was indeed the daily propagation, pleasure, luxury, and happy abundance of the plants in Paradise. For just as herbs fit for food are to us grains, legumes, vegetables, and spices, so too the trees there produced one of these—if not all four at once, or several connected together. Indeed, a manifold acorn there represented diverse grains. Olives and nuts likewise served as legumes. Just as apples served as vegetables. Trees were also the mothers of spices, offering herbs fit for seasonings. And finally, many things stood connected under a single species, just as even now an apple sometimes contains an oily kernel. All things surely flattered the human senses. But after the Majesty of man was made void due to his transgression, and

He pledged that in the fullness of time, he would die for man, so that his justice might be kissed by love. Whence came peace. Man was to be cast out of Paradise onto the earth, where he encountered more sterile trees, insufficient for the continuous necessity of food. But before he was driven away, since he was now ashamed of his nakedness, God clothed them both in tunics of skin. One indeed as a burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum," a sacrifice completely consumed by fire.</note> for his future passion. The other, without the breaking of its bones, was partly to be sacrificed and partly to be eaten as a peace offering <note>original: "hostiam pacis."</note>. He gave this to both humans, so that from the founding of the world, the Lamb might be at once a perpetual Sacrifice, a victim, and a meal—one and the same. The parents were clothed in the skins of these lambs. This first manner of sacrificing was thereafter imitated by the Gentiles. Although at least two

Just as he enriched the sea with a multitude of individuals, so he enriched the earth with a plurality of brute individuals. # THE NATURE OF CONTRARIES

...those offering sacrifice. Today only the Mohammedans <note>The author refers to Muslims.</note> and Calvinists fall short, being as it were destitute of Sacrifice. Therefore, let those who write that mortals before the flood were unaccustomed to eating meat yield their position; for it was written that "hereafter meat shall be like green herbs." <note>A reference to Genesis 9:3, where God allows Noah to eat meat after the flood.</note> Otherwise, it would have been in vain for Abel to have led flocks and herds, nor would the other <note>Likely referring to Cain’s descendants or the line of hunters.</note> have fallen in the hunting of wild beasts, and the name of Nimrod would be a hollow title. I believe, therefore, that mortals made use of animals, both domestic and wild; however, they hardly used fish before the flood. This was because at that time a single spring irrigated the whole earth, and the sea stood on the other side of the globe, while the other half was called the "dry land." Thus, fish belonged to the sea alone, while the whole world was an undivided continent; in the very center <note>original: "meditullio"</note> of which, a single spring irrigated the whole earth, divided into four rivers. For this reason, boats or skiffs were not yet known, and so fishing in the sea was unaccustomed. Nor did the habitation of men dwell upon the shores. For the single, vast continent provided enough pleasures for the Farmers, so that they detested the barren sea, bristling with a thousand storms. In Genesis, chapter 1, verse 28, we read that dominion over the sea was first given to man, then over the birds of the air, and thirdly over all living things that move upon the earth. Yet where food is discussed in chapter 1, verse 29, every herb and tree is given for food. And in chapter 1, verse 30, all the animals of the earth and birds of the air, and whatever moves upon the earth having a living soul, are given to men so they would have something to eat. Nowhere, however, are fish read to be granted, just as the fish of the sea were not brought to Adam to receive their names. From these things it is immediately obvious that there were no herbs, trees, or any reptiles contrary to man, or intended as a medicine for extermination. Likewise, the restriction to birds and things that move upon the earth excludes fish. Therefore, as the fountains and floodgates poured themselves out from the lowest depths at the flood (the breaking apart of the single continent), the fish, enticed by the 

<column-break/>

sweetness of the descending waters, remained in some of the rivers and marshes. Meanwhile, others ascended from the sea by the new permission and license granted by the flood. Therefore, let fish be considered meat: even if they were previously unused by man. I say meat, which from the flood onward would be like green herbs. Otherwise, the meat of birds compensated for the lack of grains, just as quadrupeds had long since from the beginning supplied the place of legumes. The First-Formed Man <note>original: "Protoplastus," referring to Adam.</note> therefore, outlawed to a land full of hardships, weariness, and repentance, through the leisure of his very long life, perceived his own nature—now defiled by corruption—and sought the means of its preservation. Finally, as necessity is the mother of talents and inventions, he began to meditate on how he might counter the internal calamities of life, and especially the injuries of the weather. In this labor, the elder of his sons <note>Cain</note> began to weigh the births of crops, and their successful or unfortunate yields. From this, the first Philosophy was **Agriculture**. 
<margin>7.</margin>
The other son <note>Abel</note> also noted the properties and fellowships of animals, from whose flock a tranquil life is led with certain hope. This was, of course, **Animal-Wisdom** <note>original: "zoösophia"</note>. But later, as their descendants made more 
<margin>8.</margin>
abundant progress, they wove the decrees of the stars together with the observations of their ancestors, and noted the announced 
<margin>9.</margin>

...having stolen them, he boasted that he had established the **theorems of the elements**, the **primary qualities**, the **complexions**, and the **humors**. <note>The author refers to the foundational Greek medical theories: the four elements (earth, water, air, fire), the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry), and the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note> To these, he dedicated all the works and fortunes of nature, both healthy and sick. Later, the Greek nation richly expanded upon these. Striving for the prize, the Moors <note>Referring to the Islamic Golden Age physicians like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes, whose commentaries on Galen dominated medieval universities.</note> built loose experiments upon these hypotheses. This, then, was the origin and fate of nascent Medicine, and these were its inventors. Within these limits it remained; no further progress was made thereafter.

**Galen**, cautioned by those who came before him, noticed that fire is extinguished by water and that water heated by fire vanishes. Thinking he "held a hare by the ears," <note>original: "lepore se auribus tenere" — a variation of the proverb "to hold a wolf by the ears," meaning to have a tenuous grip on a difficult problem or to be in a precarious position.</note> he boldly established almost all diseases and their remedies within those primary bodies and their qualities. For he said that fire was hostile to water and vice versa. Thus, by a universal decree, he sanctioned the idea that a meeting of four elements exists within us, continuously fighting one another in a state of war, and that a constant and inexcusable struggle of contraries occurs in us. Therefore, even if nothing attacked from the outside, an "intemperance"—that is, disease and ruin—would eventually arrive of its own accord. Death, I say, would erupt from the necessity of this elemental composition.

This might be overlooked in **Galen** <note>Galen was a pagan physician in the 2nd century AD.</note>. But it cannot be overlooked in Christians, unless they teach that there was the same necessity of composition in **Adam** before the Fall as there was after **sin**. If, for instance, **Adam’s** composition remained bound by four battling elements, he would have been naturally mortal from the start. Thus, all the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Scholastic universities that relied on Galen and Aristotle.</note> establish that only contraries are remedies for contraries. By these, every "excess" (labeled with the name of a disease) would be reduced back to symmetry. This plausible but foolish doctrine easily pleased everyone prone to the laziness of agreement. Indeed, because it could be easily grasped by common sense <note>original: "sensu rustico" — literally "rustic sense" or unrefined understanding.</note> and with great brevity, it was most greedily absorbed. Meanwhile, **Galen**—no matter how much he understood that amputation or restoration is privatively 

<column-break/>

opposed to a living being—nevertheless did not hesitate to reduce the removal of parts or humors to the series of contraries. He neglected the "family of privation" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should be present in a subject.</note> as if it were born of an adulterous union. From this, he assumed everything that differed in number, position, size, proportion, inflow, or outflow from the proper order as if they were contraries, simply to establish the stability of his own foolish Rule. It was as if **Medicine** did not operate physically, but stood by Mathematics alone. 

From this, finally, in a most general absurdity, he dictated that the natural indications of diseases are made through the opposition of contraries alone. For he wanted natural necessities to serve his own axioms; he did not build axioms that conformed to necessities. Therefore, as many theories as are offered to satisfy such ignorance are doomed to fall. Thus, there remains to this day a maxim adored by the **Schools** and the common folk alike, a kind of universal peak, which follows the well-worn path of healing through contrarieties—that is, through quarrels, lawsuits, wars, fighting, and "crises." For so it has been believed, so it has been done, and so it has been feigned until now, and that so far beyond controversy: for nothing is considered equally plausible and easy to agree with, and by its very ease of understanding, it deceives anyone who is unwary by delighting and carrying them away. 

But the knowledge of causes and the roots of healing grow from a much more hidden trunk than the common folk might pick flowers from. Nor did **Galen** consider that one of a pair of contraries must be spoken of just as often (according to **Aristotle**) as the other, because both stand under the same category and enjoy equal privilege. Therefore, he never investigated what that category might be under which positive coldness—or cold—stands as the contrary to a "putrid heat" so varied that he invented as many species of it as there are **fevers**. Indeed, where would he find a coldness that is contrary to a malignant, putrid, and "hectic" heat? And one that resists that heat with an equal number of degrees? What is this...

# THE NATURE OF CONTRARIES

...there would be a unique and individual action of cold, of so many different degrees and species, by which just as many heats, having been subdued, were forced into a balance. Indeed, as long as this was neglected by the **Galenists** <note>Followers of the 2nd-century physician Galen, whose system of "humors" dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, the proper remedy for every fever remained unknown, and remedies were applied based on guesswork and chance.

<margin>14.</margin> In these Galenic constraints, lies lie beneath both sides, conspiring toward the death of mortals. **Paracelsus** <note>The 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who famously challenged traditional medical authorities.</note> mocked Galen with a "Swiss sarcasm," <note>original: "helvetico sarcasmo"</note> although he himself repeatedly falls back into the same method, forgetful of his own constant reproof. For instance, he claimed that "coagulated" things are often the contraries of "resolved" things and their "resolvers"; indeed, he many times returns, unforced, to those exploded elemental imbalances. Finally, in a fever of contradiction, he established the cure for everything in the *similarity* of both nature and the causes of disease with the remedy itself. He is, in short, full of confusion everywhere.

<margin>15.</margin> I, however, under **Philosophical liberty**, being bound to no master, feel that if the connection of all afflictions is cut away by the removal of their causes, then every healing of diseases ought to be defined by that same law of causes. Thus, the correction, removal, and extinction of the **immediate efficient cause** (which fully includes within itself the removal of the resulting effect) would be the most important part of healing the flesh. It is not about "similarities," nor is it about the "contrarieties" of remedies. First, the products of diseases (for example, a <term>calculus</term> <note>A stone formed in the body, such as a kidney stone or gallstone.</note>), just as they retain their own active principle within themselves as a coagulated mass, so too are they very often cured by the removal of the effect alone. This is because the connection of the internal cause, or the immediate efficient, with its own matter is sometimes taken away at the same time. Add to this that the mere breaking of the connection between the efficient cause and the matter—and thus the shifting or loosening of their adaptation, and the extinction and calming of the privative disturbance in the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital director" or life force that the author believes governs the body's health and reactions.</note> (which sometimes includes mere deprivation within itself)—not infrequently completes the entire history of healing,

<column-break/>

without any "contrariety" or "similarity" of the remedy to the occasional causes. Paracelsus ought to have remembered this himself, if he had once looked back at his own <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcana" — powerful, secret alchemical remedies.</note>. For he would have quickly noticed that any one of those remedies defeats almost all diseases equally, without any relation to similarity or contrariety, but solely by the sprinkling of a **vital tincture**, a gift, a secret—that is, by an overflowing of goodness. Indeed, whatever happens or is born in nature, happens out of the necessity of **efficient seeds**.

<margin>16.</margin> Moreover, these **seeds** themselves do not operate at all for the purpose of similarity or contrariety (as is otherwise commonly thought), but only because they have been commanded to operate in this way by the Lord of things, who alone gave knowledge and goals to the seeds, known only to Himself from the beginning.

<margin>17.</margin> Otherwise, seeds go on, and they do not know where; they direct themselves, to be sure, as if they were powerful in knowledge, but they stretch through the means granted to them toward ends unknown to them. For we improperly call these the "intentions" of medicines or the "aims" of nature: not because they have fixed a goal for themselves from the start, as if they were powerful in mind and foreknowledge, but because, from a created gift, they are born to flow down spontaneously and naturally by their own direction toward those kinds of ends known to God. This is what **Christian Philosophy** dictates, but the **pagan school** <note>original: "Schola ethnica" — referring to the secular/Aristotelian universities.</note> is ignorant of it.

<margin>18.</margin> Therefore, even in the light of reason, I marvel at the audacity of the Schools, which did not recognize the "seminal entities" of nature in diseases. They chose instead to substitute the "qualities" of entities subsisting by themselves and of diseased states, wanting them to be judged by the judgment of the senses and of passion, as if they possessed antipathies and contrarieties by their own impulse. Indeed, I have become accustomed to philosophizing in such a way that I desire to measure things themselves from their radical foundation, according to the whetstone of **sacred truth**, as closely as human wit allows.

<margin>19.</margin> Therefore, to show that the theories of contrariety contain mere errors against nature, it must first be noted that **Aristotle's** invention regarding matter was futile...

# UNKNOWN THINGS
<note>original: "NESCIA"</note>

...to place before the subject of generation, both in a state of nature whole and in a state of nature corrupted (namely, by the sickness of disease), being deprived of every accident. (It is happily thus that it begins from a total deprivation of both accidents and forms, as if at the primordial beginning of things.) Every accident, therefore, both innate and supervening, consequently also depends on and flows
<margin>20.</margin> from the womb of the forms. In such a way that from the form and its prelude, in the **Archeus** <note>The internal vital force or "master chemist" that Helmont believed directed all biological processes.</note>, all activity, both of matter and of accidents, necessarily depends; meanwhile the **Schools** <note>Refers to the Scholastic tradition of the universities, which relied heavily on Aristotelian logic.</note> taught by this **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose theories on physics and biology dominated European thought for centuries.</note> (they still maintain even today) that nothing can be contrary to substances, whether material or formal. I do not see, therefore, from where accidents will beg for their own contrariety, especially those that are naked, immediate, and mere organs of their forms? For from where would they have drawn their contrariety, those whose matter and form (certainly the total principles of accidents) repel all contrariety far from themselves? Especially since accidents, considered in themselves, are not so much beings as they are *of* beings; and thus of themselves they are nothing,
<margin>21.</margin> and they can do or effect nothing. It is necessary, therefore, that if there is any intention of contrariety in nature, it must be primarily in the active principle, that is, in the heart of the forms. So much so that either the forms themselves (which they have without controversy placed in the number of substances) would be actually and potentially contrary to each other by primitive right. Consequently, the axiom of the Schools—"That there is nothing contrary to substances"—would be false. Or, accidents must have that same contrariety independent of the forms: and from their own nature, outside and against the possibility of the forms. That is, not to be the immediate media, products, and organs of the forms: but to arise, stand, persevere, and act from themselves, even against the will of the forms, outside and beyond the forms. To be, I say, independent beings, and no longer properties of beings. Or thirdly, at

<column-break/>

last it must be admitted with me that there is no contrariety in nature, except between free and elective agents. I add: if the equality of contraries stands, according to the aforementioned axiom: it is necessary that the relation of founding a relationship between contraries depends on a substantial root, or on a radical respect of contrarieties, and an intimate adequacy of proportion most deeply present. Which is to say: the essence of founding the relation of contrarieties (which would otherwise be prior to the very existence of the forms) is located entirely in the innermost substantial principle of the forms, which is completely incapable of contrariety. And this is true whether you look at God himself or another created substance. And so it is necessary that contrariety in nature includes a contradiction, both in its own beginnings and in those of Philosophy. But if you consider these things supernaturally, and in God, they are not contrary for that reason either. And so they will not flow from God into nature as contraries. And this is what I say. I urge even further: if one of the contraries is said in as many ways as the other: and nothing is contrary to substantial forms. Therefore there is also no friendship, symbolizing, or likeness between forms. Which is false. For from here the indelible character of things is established, because all things were created by God, the lover of peace. For after I submitted myself to be taught by better beginnings, I seriously recognized, whether I looked at substances or finally at accidents, that there is no contrariety in nature, except among **irascible** <note>Capable of anger, passion, or reactive force.</note> and living, moving beings. It is far from the case that the action of any agent upon a patient proceeds only from the relationship of contrary to contrary. I have therefore found contrariety only in the irascible power of sensing beings, and nowhere else. From where perhaps by
<margin>22.</margin> metaphor, or improper hyperbole, contrariety was twisted to apply to all the individual things of the world. ...led, likewise only through **Wrath** <note>Helmont uses "Ira" (Wrath) to describe the reactive force in living things, which he believes is the only place true "conflict" occurs.</note>—namely the action of the greater upon the lesser, the victor over the vanquished, and the stronger over the weaker—being stirred up due to the relations of contrariety. Therefore, the meaning of the negative axiom, which states that *nothing is contrary to Substances*, is equivalent to the thesis proposed in the title of this chapter: namely, that **Nature knows no contraries**. If there were any force of contrariety in nature, except in the irascible part of sentient beings (for I do not speak of terms and reasons established in Logic), it would surely be in the manifest and primary qualities of the elements: but in these there is no 
<margin>23.</margin>
contrariety. Therefore, it is nowhere else. This assumption is proven by the fact that the **Schools** <note>The Scholastic universities that followed Aristotle.</note> derive the primary contrarieties in mixed bodies from the contrarieties of the component elements themselves. But I have proven the secondary premise elsewhere, which must be repeated here: A young man descending in the morning from the Alps, which were covered with continuous snow, yet on the side facing the sun, his entire neck was burned into blisters or vesicles. And there the air is highly delightful, and as if infused with a new ether
> (learn meanwhile from this first, that cold is not a privative absence of heat; but a true entity.) <note>Helmont disagrees with the standard view that cold is just the "lack of heat." He believes cold is a physical substance or force in its own right.</note>
Therefore, in that same place, cold and heat—both intense at the same time in the same place, time, and subject of the air—endure one another. Which the Schools will not admit to be 
<margin>24.</margin>
possible in contraries; since they define contraries as things that wish to mutually defeat, break, expel, and kill each other, and lead to a middle, neutral state. It should be noted here in passing: there, intense cold is hosted immediately in the air; but intense and blistering heat is there on the part of the light, and thus immediately in the very place of the air, but in the air itself only mediately. But since that place penetrates the air through its entire substance, and the illuminated place simultaneously heats the air itself (which the light therefore penetrates at the same time), for that reason, in the same point of air, there is intense heat along with intense cold. The connection of both of which produces a pleasant and sense-friendly warmth,

<column-break/>

yet it is illusory. Because the effect of each connected quality brings forth great intensity beneath that warmth. And therefore warmth is not caused insofar as both qualities, being equally intense, break each other through a battle of contrariety and reduce themselves to a middle and plausible symmetry. Rather, the senses and the Schools (which allow themselves to slip everywhere according to sensory perceptions without internal investigation) are too improper and rustic judges of natural things. Likewise, boiling water poured into cold water in equal proportion, although they immediately stir up warmth in the mixture: nevertheless, each quality exists in an intense degree at that time, no differently than in the aforementioned Alpine air, even if the senses do not distinguish them. For it is not otherwise possible for that heat of the water, acquired through moments of degrees, to perish in an instant. Indeed, it is not a battle of contraries that immediately generated that warmth, nor the victory of the cold over the excelling heat while the prior heat is reduced: but the heat in the water is a passing <term>Relollæum</term> <note>A technical term used by van Helmont to denote a quality that is not essential or internal to a substance's "seed," but is an external, temporary influence.</note> because it was introduced by force. For that reason, when the fire from which it was produced ceases, the heat diminishes of its own accord immediately and stops when no longer fostered. That is, the heat in boiling water, divided through the smallest atoms of its subject, perishes of its own accord; it is not, however, conquered by contrariety in an expulsive manner. Because a <term>Relollæum</term> is an efficient quality,
<margin>25.</margin>
not proceeding from the **ferments** and **seeds** <note>In Helmont's chemistry, "ferments" and "seeds" (semina) are the internal blueprints that give a substance its identity and life.</note> of things. And it is twofold: namely, one in its own body, and the other in a foreign body. Among the internal *Relollæa* there are certain separable ones, such as cold in air and water. But others are inseparable, such as heat in the light of the Sun, a candle, and fire, which can never be cold. A foreign *Relollæum* is violent; if it is not fostered, it therefore perishes through its own moments and degrees. And therefore it is called "passing," such as is the heat in water. Therefore 
<margin>26.</margin>
air and water are not heated by fire through contrariety, but through the generation of a foreign *Relollæum*, insofar as it acts as it was ordered to act, in a manner divergent from the seeds of acting...

He argues that things like fire and water do not "fight" because they are opposites, but rather because of their physical properties and the way they occupy space.</meta>

### IGNORANCE
<note>original title: "NESCIA" — referring to things unknown or ignored by the established academic "Schools."</note>

<margin>27.</margin> manner of acting. Therefore, it neither acts toward, nor because of, a **form**. Likewise, while water extinguishes fire, or fire raises water into vapor, this by no means happens by the force of **contrariety** <note>The Aristotelian idea that elements "fight" because they are opposites.</note>. For the entire fire of the universe cannot destroy or diminish even the slightest moisture from a single drop of water. Therefore, the contrariety of fire would be ineffectual and foolish, or rather a vain and powerless battle. Furthermore, I have sufficiently demonstrated elsewhere—through <term>Mathematics</term> <note>original: "Mathesin"; Helmont often used mathematical/quantitative proofs to challenge qualitative physics.</note> and other means—that through no age, whether by art or nature, can air be converted into water, or water back into air. For fire is not extinguished by water because of the presence of a "contrary cold" within the water; for if that were so, boiling water would not extinguish fire. Indeed, fire burns more strongly under the blast and cold of the North Wind than the South; and only the coldest blast ignites fire more intensely. Therefore, water destroys fire, but fire does not destroy water. Fire does not yield because it is conquered by cold, but rather it perishes because it is suffocated. In the same way, boiling oil extinguishes a glowing coal. <margin>28.</margin> If, therefore, contraries ought to be under the same genus: fire cannot be the contrary of water. Since fire is not a **substance**, as I have sufficiently demonstrated elsewhere. Finally, if they were contraries: they would be primarily, substantially, and immediately contrary in themselves as simple things; and granted that, their action ought to be an equal and balanced fight. Which I have already shown to be false, just as I have shown that nothing is contrary to **substances**. It is in view of these two—namely fire and water—that the **Schools** <note>The university academics who followed Aristotle's teachings.</note> have imagined every mixture and every "contrariety of temperaments" in the universe. Is it any wonder, then, that the contrariety of nature dreamed up in the Schools is now held in suspicion, since their "privative contraries" exist without contrariety, equality, encounter, mixing, or the joining of forces?
<margin>29.</margin> Furthermore, **humidity** and **dryness** are qualities that are scarcely intelligible in the abstract (just as heat is considered in the hand, apart from or outside of fire—indeed, in a subject of its own, such as water); but humidity

<column-break/>

and dryness are rather the qualified bodies themselves. Nor are they acquired by parts and degrees (if the Schools will permit me) in the manner of "qualities." For humidity is not properly "produced": but when a moist body is added to a dry one, more moisture is applied, and thus humidity "grows" improperly. That is: humidity increases **quantitatively**, but not **qualitatively**. Water, however, never truly "dries out," though it may deceive the eyes by vanishing—as I have discussed elsewhere regarding <term>Gas</term> <note>Helmont coined the word "Gas" to describe the "spirit" or invisible state of matter that occupies space but isn't air.</note>. Finally, "dry" properly sounds like "juiceless," and contains only a negation of the moist. And although by the mixing of something dry, water may seem to be diminished in mud, the water nevertheless always preserves its own intrinsic humidity. Just as a dry body likewise preserves its dryness. For in their root, there is no "penetrating mixture," but only a placing of parts next to each other. Humidity and dryness are therefore so bound to the body that they can in no way be distinguished from it. And consequently, they <margin>30.</margin> are not **relatives** in the manner of heat and cold, which are introduced by degrees. All water indeed vanishes into vapor <note>original: "halitum"</note>; yet it never assumes even a minute amount of dryness. If, however, from flour and water, a mash or bread is made, and finally, through a conceived **fermental seed** of nature, they pass into stone—though these things are indeed coagulated, they merely cover and veil the original humidity of the water. But eventually, the original water is recovered from it. For it has not been "dried out," nor has it perished; though it be coagulated by the "seed of things." For I have elsewhere demonstrated mechanically and mathematically that all solid bodies are from **water alone**, and do not admit the encounter of other elements. Or rather: every tangible body is finally resolved into simple elemental water, such as falls in rain—indeed, it is equal in weight to its previously solid body. This single point destroys the entire framework of the "elements," the "temperaments," and the internal and unending war of qualities within us. Therefore, it is necessary that the Schools investigate other causes of diseases...
