### THE NATURE OF CONTRARIES
<note>original: "NATURA CONTRARIORUM"</note>

...to investigate. These things I have declared through the unheard-of principles of **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: "Physices"</note>. It is therefore a matter of wonderful stupidity to have dreamed that "moisture" arrives in degrees, or likewise that there is a "weakened" moisture and dryness within the elements. Indeed, it is a monstrous fiction to have introduced such stupid dreams into the families of diseases and healings, and to have confidently built the entire **foundation of Medicine** <note>original: "Medendi basin"</note> upon them. They have gone so far as to marry these categories of moisture and dryness together through entire classes, as much by mutual kinship as by the allurements of heat and cold. Clearly, they committed this single fault just to provide furniture for the vanities of their "temperaments."

<margin>31. Mourn for your neighbor.</margin> They are utterly ignorant that in nature, there is no penetration, radical union, or radical mixture of the moist with the dry—no "radical tempering" by which they might destroy each other 

<margin>32.</margin> in a formal embrace. I propose at least one question to all those who, until now, believe that "contrary elements" flow together to form the constitution of bodies (which they believe to be mixtures). I have resolved this elsewhere. Suppose they assume two heavy elements, namely **water** and **earth**, and two light ones. Also, suppose they assume that the penetration of physical bodies is impossible in nature. Thirdly, suppose they assume that **Gold** is, beyond controversy, a "mixed body" resulting from the real marriage of the aforementioned elements. If this is so, how is it possible for gold to outweigh water by at least sixteen times? For if there are parts of air and fire in gold, mixed in **equal proportion** <term>anatica</term> <note>From the Greek "ana," a medical term meaning equal parts of each ingredient.</note>: (for they assert this is absolutely necessary, since they attribute the eternal permanence of gold in the highest torture of fire to an equal mixture of the four elements). Therefore, the water and earth within the gold would have to outweigh their own matter by at least thirty-two times to create it. Does earth then "penetrate" itself at least thirty-two times while gold is being made from it? Thus, since weight infallibly reveals a heavy body, and weight does not consist of nothing, they must resolve this question for me before they 

<column-break/>

can pull me over to their opinion regarding the "mixtures" of elements. Meanwhile, I will have the opportunity to show **mechanically** <note>Meaning through physical experiment rather than abstract theory.</note> that solid and heavy bodies can yield an equal weight of water, entirely deprived of taste. There is no such "element" in nature, nor can elements—by any skill or effort of nature—ever be joined into a "formal unity." I have already discussed this more fully above.

<margin>33.</margin> It is therefore a "deaf" <note>Meaning nonsensical or absurd.</note> kind of doctrine to claim that the four elements are "contraries"; that they flow together for the composition of other things (which until now have been falsely thought of as "mixtures"); and that they even fight within such mixtures—where they are enclosed—just as they do in their simple state, because of their oppositions. And that, for this reason, they consume each other in an unceasing war, immediately rising again from "privation," devouring and then vomiting each other back out.

<margin>34.</margin> We must not tolerate this stupor of the **Academic Schools**, by which they subscribe to these trifles among themselves without a single scruple. They do not ask: what is that "appetite" in an element to expand itself? Or what "motion" would drive it beyond the boundary once established for it by the **Creator**? For in the first place, there is no hunger, thirst, poverty, or any similar defect to which they have been subject since creation. Nor do they suffer from defects, much less the *sensation* of defects. Since each element is in itself primary and simple, it does not admit "marriages," nor is it consumed by feeding, nor does it have or eject excrement through its own change, nor does it suffer from rust, nor does it degenerate by crumbling into some body purer, more primary, or simpler than itself. Therefore, there is no "necessity" for elements to hostilely consume each other. For "God saw all that He had made, and it was good."

<margin>35.</margin> If, therefore, two "good" things fought each other, that fight could not help but be a great and continuous evil, of which the Creator Himself would be the Author. It would follow that such a property of elements did not come from God, nor from sin: therefore, it would come from something greater than God. But if the elements are said to have been created by God in such a way that one continually changes the other into its own nature: it certainly would not be because of hostility...

...mutual; but for the necessity of nutrition. Although it presupposes something ridiculous, I have obtained what I wanted: namely, the removal of **contraries** <note>original: "contrariorum ablationem"</note>. Therefore, it is a vain evasion and a false invention. Indeed, this supposition cannot exist alongside the thesis itself. For if that excuse were assumed, a battle and resistance would necessarily follow. Otherwise, one element would immediately convert everything adjacent into itself. For there is no difficulty in overcoming where there is no necessity for battle or resistance. Because every single part of an element would have the same passion, motion, and desire to consume its neighbor, just as is supposed in the parts related to it. And thus, those activities would be so immensely intensified that it would, with easy effort and immediately, convert the element placed beneath it into its own nature without any reaction. And these things, once converted, would then incessantly convert others, one after another. At the very least, that highest air, which is furthest removed from water, pressed by a most tedious and long thirst, would have perished long ago, or at least would languish from weariness, deprived of its natural nourishment. Therefore, however these things are excused: at the very least, creatures would have been ordained by God with an appetite for disturbing the order and harmony of the universe and its first constitution; namely, to introduce dissolution and a primary disproportion by overcoming, destroying, and transforming its neighbor into itself. Truly, human frailties are the inventors of these fables, introduced <margin>36.</margin> by the **Pagan Schools** <note>The author refers to the followers of Aristotle and Galen, whose philosophies dominated medieval universities</note>. Because through ignorance of nature itself, the common crowd introduced laws, confusions, contrarieties, battles, hostilities, reductions, and repeated resurrections, so that men might excuse and adapt their own **irascible nature** <note>The human tendency toward anger and conflict</note> to things that lack it. The Schools, and the common people deceitfully taught by them, have undoubtedly estimated that in nature, it is greater, more glorious, and better to conquer than to be conquered: to subdue equals than to be subdued. But God taught us otherwise. Namely, at the peak of nature, it is more glorious to suffer than to inflict injury: it is more blessed to be overcome by a stronger force than

<column-break/>

to have cast down a weaker one. And since God cannot err in His estimations, it follows that the estimations of the Schools and the common crowd did not flow from the truth of nature, but surely from our own **spiritedness** <term>thymosi</term> <note>From the Greek 'thymos,' referring to the seat of anger and pride in the soul</note> and frailty. Therefore, they are erroneous and abusive, insofar as they are opposed to Divine judgments. Nor can those things which God has condemned in man be praised as glorious in the simplicity of law and the necessity of nature. But if there were any true contrariety in things lacking sensation, they would have rightly judged that it necessarily rises from, and presupposes, a concept of hatred and hostility, radically sealed in its first and formal beginnings. By reason of this, the **Agent** <note>The active force or element</note>, out of its own self-love, would stir up hatred for itself in the **Patient** <note>The passive element being acted upon</note>; or that hatred would have a dissimilarity and a drive toward "otherness" uniquely implanted in it by nature (because of repugnance). And in whatever way this is taken, it is to admit radical, seminal, and marrow-deep contrarieties in **substantial forms** <note>The essential nature or "soul" of a material thing</note>. Thus, the substances themselves would be immediately contrary to one another—unless they prefer to deny that forms are substances. But I am ready <margin>37.</margin> to teach that nature performs all things through its **middle properties** <note>original: "medias suas proprietates"</note>, with no goal of contrariety, hatred, or battle proposed for itself. Indeed, from faith we first believe it to be true that God is the Author and constant Ruler of nature, and that He expresses and testifies to His own goodness everywhere in His creation, as much as possible. Finally, that God is the fountain-source of love, concord, and peace; He also hates discords and contrarieties so much that if He could have founded the universe without strifes and contrarieties, it is beyond doubt that He did so. And yet He could do this most aptly, because He is Omnipotent, and He made all things as He willed; therefore, He also did so. The conclusion is evident: because nothing could resist Him, except that which He willed to make free; but He did not grant the seeds of things, or the agents of nature, the freedom of willing. Therefore, the agents of nature could not resist God. And consequently, He made the agents of nature according to the good pleasure of His love.

of goodness and peace. For instance, when I eat food, I never find a state of conflict within myself, nor within the food. Indeed, because of the necessary cycles of change in things, we do not like to call every harmful quality "hostility" or "enmity" between objects. Truly, one must speak precisely in Philosophy; elsewhere, words may change the meaning and alienate the very essence of things—especially here, where the entire medical <term>crasis|the healthy balance of the body's internal temperament</term> has been distorted to human ruin. For this idea of "contrariety" does not merely stain the face of nature with as many vices as there are active powers and properties; it even seems to accuse the Parent of nature Himself of being a maker and promoter of hatred and strife. Thus, the entire Universe would be nothing more than a hostel of hostility, a perpetual duel, and a true Fury <note>original: "erynnis"; a reference to the Furies of Greek myth who personified vengeance and discord</note>, nowhere expressing the image of its Creator. Therefore, contraries do not exist in nature from the Creator, who rejects them even in matters of choice—much less in those things which He Himself founded according to the pattern of the **Archetype** <note>The divine blueprint or original model of the world</note>. Finally, since a creature comes from nothing, it carries no properties from itself. If, therefore, contrarieties arose solely from error—from seeds distorted from their usual path—then they would at least not exist except in monstrous effects, and would thus be wrongly thrust into the systematic order of nature. Finally, it follows from this that the "contrarieties of seeds" would come from God alone; let a Christian judge the absurdity of such a claim. For until now, the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university professors and Scholastic philosophers of the 17th century</note> have never considered how much these two things differ: to have acted based on a *concept of contrariety*, versus something having operated through the *obedience of seeds* to the properties given by God. Therefore, to admit "contraries" is to establish that there are errors in the intention, the means, and the end of na-

ture. It must therefore be deeply understood that nature rejects contraries, if we hope to reach its innermost rhythm. As for what the Schools have invented regarding **radical heat** <term>radical heat|in medieval medicine, the innate warmth thought to be the source of life and vitality</term>: they have at least forgotten to marry a "radical cold" to it under the same vital principle, so that these contraries might enjoy equal rights. Instead, they have only opposed it with **Death**, which is outside of its category. For this reason, they have left that primary quality of heat a "bachelor," without a partner. They abandon their own false axiom, which states that contraries must belong to the same category and be spoken of in equal measure on both sides. For Death, being a privation and a "non-being," can in no way fill the role of a contrary, despite what the Schools say—as if it were the opposite of life or radical heat. For that which is not, and which is nothing, cannot stand in the same category as radical heat. I have dealt extensively with these fables and the fictions of "primeval moisture" in my treatise *On Long Life* <note>original: "De vita longa"</note>. Finally, the Schools, having crashed against the rocks, occasionally treat "potential" heat and cold; yet they do not treat them as contraries, since they claim heat and cold are connected and prevailing within every single drop or smallest atom of simple things. For instance, they explain the intense cold in opium, yet also the heat in its bitterness; and thus I have already exposed their science—derived from tastes and **Relollea** <note>A term used by the author to describe the specific elemental powers or properties acting within a substance</note>—as ridiculous through this single example. This is because the seminal and specific powers have been wrongly translated by the Schools into elemental qualities, or *Relollea*. For they divine a "cold" in opium, though it is not revealed by any judgment of the senses, simply because of its effects; they have, in a ridiculous dream, constricted the "seminal sleep-inducing power" to "cold." As if the Most High, when He sent sleep upon Adam, had stirred up cold within him! Or as if, after lunch, a noticeable cold would rise into our heads! Truly, the Schools on both sides demand that our intellect bow to an incomprehensible faith. What is missing in this passage I have explained more fully elsewhere regarding the actions and the knowledge of diseases.
<margin>38.</margin>
Thus far I have taught that qualities exist in the elements and operate without any regard for "contrariety." Now, indeed, I descend to the system of things. First, unity is not the contrary of duality, even though they differ by their distinctness. Likewise, neither "up" nor "down," nor "east" nor "west" are contraries; rather, they are oppositions of position that vary by perspective. Thus, what is "up" is "below" in relation to something else; nor is the right ear the contrary of the left, even though they are opposite. For I am not speaking of "contradictory terms," which only contradict in a relative sense, but do not possess hostile properties within the things themselves. Nor is my discourse about "privatives" <note>A "privative" is the mere absence of a quality, like blindness being the absence of sight rather than an opposing force</note>. Nay, I do not even deny contraries in the "irascible power" <note>The emotional capacity for anger or defensive spirit</note>; but I firmly affirm this one thing: that God did not make contraries in nature

<column-break/>

which would kill or attack each other through hostility. That is, I deny that there are contrary properties in natural things. I deny positive and real contraries in the sequence of natural actions. For virtue has its opposite in vice, which is of a "privative" nature <note>Meaning vice is the absence of virtue, not a separate "thing" created by God</note>. Nor is a flying creature the contrary of a crawling one; for the same silkworm <note>original: "bombyx"</note> is both. Nor is generation itself contrary to corruption; rather, it is a single flow of seeds from one point to another, through the exhaustion, removal, loss, or extinction of powers. Similarly, "large" is not the contrary of "small," nor "straight" of "curved." Since one and the same thing can be now small, now large, now straight, and now curved. The same holds true for sweet and bitter; hard and soft; rough and smooth; heavy and light; sharp and blunt; clotted and dissolved; or white and black. For any powers of things are absolute in themselves and do not concern themselves with others different from them. Because everything is exactly as it exists through itself; the fact that they are "opposed" by us, as if they were in disagreement, is unknown to the things themselves and is plainly accidental or foreign. Meanwhile, an axe does not cut wood, nor a knife slice bread because of "contrarieties" or "hostilities"; rather, each property acts, without reflecting on its opposite, because it was commanded to act. It is foolish to want things to be "contrary" when they have no claim to hatred, discord, victory, or superiority; therefore, there is no intention of contrariety in nature. Each thing acts, therefore, as it was commanded to act. For no war of contrariety is enclosed within the shell of an egg, even though the seed flows through various stages of disposition that are far different from one another. In both cases, the unity and concord of nature is preserved and remains; nature never contradicts itself—indeed, it shrinks from every "contrary" and whatever disturbs unity. Truly, in the seed there is a power to transform the water existing in the soil of a garden; and thus, that single water passes into a thousand different herbs: hot, sharp, bitter, acidic, and

Indeed, if any such power had been recognized at the threshold, the case should have been judged plainly from the start, where nature had the judge and witnesses on its side, and a just cause against the traitorous disease. # IGNORANT THINGS
->Z<-

<margin>43.</margin> Indeed, there are natural gifts that differ from "similars" <note>Similars: Remedies that share the same quality as the disease, as in "like cures like."</note>. Let those be the things in which our **Archeus** <term>Archeus: The "internal master workman" or vital spirit that governs the functions of an organ or the whole body.</term> finds its delights. For example: **Hunger** is like a very sharp disease, which kills in earnest with only a few days of patience. Yet it is not healed by a "contrary" food, nor even by a "similar" one. Nor does hunger prove a lack of consumed blood; otherwise, dysentery and bloodletting would necessarily make one hungry. Instead, in hunger there is a devastation of nourishment within the stomach itself, caused by the vigor of the **digestive ferment** <note>original: "fermenti digestivi"</note>—or "hungry" ferment—which preys upon the organ. This is why the sensation of hunger is ultimately like a "cough" of the stomach. Whenever the ferment of the stomach is well-disposed but has no object to act upon, it consumes the stomach's own nourishment. Therefore, food calms hunger not because it is the "contrary" of the ferment, nor because it is "similar" to it, but 
<margin>44.</margin> because it is the **appropriate remedy**. It is the same in the healing of any disease: what is required is the matching of the remedy to the indisposition of the Archeus and the removal of the occasional cause. This "appropriate suitability" of a remedy, or its "gift," presupposes a proportion in both degree and quantity, as well as an adaptation and application with a specific adequacy of conformity. Furthermore, this includes the indication and knowledge of the goal: the condition and requirement of our faculties, and their harmony with the remedy, which again assumes a proper dosage. For in this way, remedies do not merely respond to a parity of objects, but also to the specific directions of the **ferments** <note>Ferment: A vital power or "yeast" that triggers chemical and biological changes in the body.</note>.
<margin>45.</margin> **Paracelsus** <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541): A Swiss physician and alchemist who challenged traditional medicine and founded the field of iatrochemistry (chemical medicine).</note> once thought that no "simple" <note>Simple: A medicinal herb or single-ingredient remedy.</note> was fit for healing unless it first "died" <note>To "die" in alchemy means to be broken down or transformed through chemical processes like fermentation or heat.</note>. And again, elsewhere, he said it is not enough for a simple to die unless it is first reduced into the **Three Primes** (which he calls **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury**). This error of assertion stirred up frequent inconsistency in that author. In truth, there are not a few "simples" that explain their specific formal properties while the substance they inhabit remains intact. Examples that come to mind immediately are **Periapta** and many **Amulets**, 

<column-break/>

which he himself calls **zenexton** <term>Zenexton: A Paracelsian term for a powerful amulet or protective charm worn to ward off disease or plague.</term>. Indeed, we have noted with pleasure that **palpitations of the heart**, the infamous pain of **hemorrhoids**, flows of blood, **epilepsy**, "strangulation of the womb" <note>original: "uteri strangulatus"; a historical term for what was then called hysteria or uterine fits.</note>, and even **fevers** can be calmed by things hung on the body. On the other hand, many distilled remedies hardly know how to "die" or migrate into the "human family" <note>Human family: The internal environment or substance of the human body.</note>. Yet their effect on diseases is immense. Let Paracelsus also forgive me for saying that such an "Analysis" of simple remedies never occurs within our body. For I have sufficiently taught elsewhere that digestion never tends toward those three recent "Primes." Nor are we ever nourished by them, but by one and the same—or very similar—liquor of which we consist. Many things also lose their former powers through their first boiling. For **Asarabacca** <note>original: "Asarum"</note>, from being a vomit-inducer, thus becomes a diuretic. And for the most part, the specific property of a thing is destroyed by its division into those "Three Primes." For even if they retain some temperament of the whole, they are nevertheless a "new creature" fashioned by fire. Happy is he who knows how to remove diseases safely and promptly with **raw simples**. For this is the older method of healing noted in the Holy Scriptures: *That the Most High created medicine from the earth.* Indeed, a "specific being" cannot help but be altered by fire. Therefore, extracts and **magisteries** <note>Magistery: A concentrated medicinal preparation or extract in early chemistry.</note> are not infrequently weakened. For truly, while **Spagyria** <term>Spagyria: Alchemical medicine involving the separation and recombination of natural substances.</term> leads many things to a degree of greater energy—insofar as it rouses a "new being"—at other times it secretly weakens many things by stealing from them. Whoever thinks that Nature has polished nothing without fire accuses her of laziness and imperfection. Let the seeds of things be witnesses to this. For some sprout their own parts spontaneously; some indeed need reason and opportunity; very few truly require the art of preparation; and none, finally, admit fire or "analysis." For the powers that reside immediately in the lap of Nature act in the manner of an **influence**, and they do not willingly submit to fire. Those things, however, which are not indeed similar in their forms...

# THE NATURE OF CONTRARIES
->Z<-

<meta>catchword: appropriately</meta>

...ple; but they are immediately present in **heterogeneous** <term>heterogeneous: made of different kinds of parts, rather than being a uniform substance.</term> parts: very often they shine forth more in their abstract part. For in this way, mace, turpentine, and asparagus even paint their own symbol in the urine <note>original: "lotio"</note>. But the powers that rise from things through fire—although they owe something to their solid form, like tokens of that family—are certainly new and transplanted sprouts, usually vassals of another **Monarchy** <term>Monarchy: A term used by Paracelsus to describe a specific realm of nature or a particular chemical state.</term>. Just as I have written elsewhere regarding the faculties of medicines. For I have always highly valued the **Creator’s designation** in the endowment of **simples** <term>simples: Medicines made from a single natural ingredient, usually a plant.</term>. For indeed, according to His mind, most diseases yield to simples, driven out as if by the most ancient wedge. 

However, because I sing a panegyric for simples, I would not want this to be taken as a contempt for **Pyrotechnia** <term>Pyrotechnia: The "art of fire," referring here to chemical medicine or alchemy.</term>; rather, I speak only to those who admit nothing except those **three first principles** <note>The "Tria Prima" of alchemy: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, and who prefer the "sweats" of herbs drawn out by distilling far above their "bloody" juices. For let them first learn how to season the juices of herbs, and likewise the broths of meats, without salt, vinegar, honey, sugar, and fire, and how to preserve them from rot for years. Then at last they will easily despise distilled waters of herbs, no less than syrups. But when a disease has risen to a high degree and has married itself intimately to the failing nature of the patient, higher remedies are required than those which nature has produced spontaneously.

<margin>46.</margin> Finally, among many, I will perhaps be thought to have fought over **goat’s wool** <note>original: "de lana caprina" — a classical idiom for arguing about something trivial or non-existent.</note> and for a name alone. And they will say that I have striven to mask, by the etymology of the "opposite," that which is "contrary" to the **Schools** <term>the Schools: The traditional university authorities who followed the teachings of Galen and Aristotle.</term>. But this penalty awaits me only from the ungrateful. I address the healers and the Schools, who admit only those remedies for diseases which, being contrary by a hostile property, are thought to attack diseases by fighting them. And they teach that a healthy balance <note>original: "temperiem"</note> is acquired only through a contrary **imbalance** <note>original: "intemperiem," referring to an excess of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>. I rest my case in having demonstrated that no such things have existed in nature until now. Nor is it enough that they require superior strengths in a remedy relative to the disease; they even want this to happen with a war of contrariety, strife, and **crisis** <note>In ancient medicine, a "crisis" was the turning point of a disease, often viewed as a literal struggle.</note>;

<column-break/>

if victory is to be hoped for from it. Indeed, I have shown that powers of this sort are not found in nature. Likewise, that the **seeds of things** <note>original: "semina rerum" — the OCR reads "femina," but the context of natural philosophy confirms "semina," the internal blueprints of life.</note> do not act with the hope or effort of victory, nor by suffering their patient to be destroyed as if it were an enemy. Nor, indeed, by overcoming the activity of the patient. And thus, there is no contrariety, struggle, hatred, war, battle, or preference for arrogance or superiority in natural things. Instead, they act without intention or foreknowledge of the end. Insofar as they were so created by God, their Arbitrator, and so endowed: and thus they were ordered so to act.

It is clear, therefore, that contrariety—of the sort taught in the Schools as being inherent in all things—is exiled from all of nature, except for the **irascible faculty** <note>The part of the soul responsible for anger and competition, which Helmont believes exists only in sentient animals.</note> of living creatures. Thus, although **Self-love** <note>original: "Philautia"</note>, **sympathy**, **antipathy**, choice, and even some sense are attributed to non-living things, let it be understood as a certain analogy shining forth in effects and causes, rather than in the direction of the Creator or the destination of ends. This is because they are deprived of their own sense, choice, intention of acting, and foreknowledge of ends. 

But since any things of this sort clearly testify that they have a Director, who "powerfully moves their ends unto the very ends and disposes them sweetly" <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Wisdom 8:1.</note>, the explanations of those properties are testimonies that God, most glorious, holds the reins even of vile things, through powers given to them without their knowing. And thus they are totally upright, without knowledge of the end. That is, without the impulse, anger, struggle, and hatred belonging to those things. I am so far, therefore, from thinking that the actions of things and remedies happen through opposites (in place of contraries), that I have equally banished both opposites and contraries from nature. I have admitted opposites only by way of the relationship of terms, but not in the way in which they act upon each other. For ever since my manhood, I have realized: if things were contraries, or acted as such, then nature—totally, exemplarily, formally, and dependently—would not look toward its Creator. And concerning such a creature, it could not be said...

# IGNORANT THINGS
->Z<-

...it would be aptly said: *And God saw everything that He had made, and they were good* <note>original: "Et vidit Deus, quæcunque fecerat, erant bona" — a reference to Genesis 1:31.</note>: if nature could not unfold the properties implanted within it except through hostile hatred. Finally, how far those opposites (which I have categorized as "repugnant") differ from medical **contraries** <term>contraries: In Galenic medicine, these are opposing qualities like hot/cold or wet/dry used to balance the body's humors.</term>, is known to all who do not burn with the pleasure of reviling. Therefore, let the students take note whether he deals with me over a mere name—he who overturns the first principles of healing based on the Creator’s intention. For God willed individual things to operate according to the **gift of nature** <note>original: "dotem naturæ"</note> bestowed upon them, not through "contrariety" or a desire to destroy one another, but for ends known only to God beforehand. He is love and peace, not hatred, strife, or the fuel of opposition. Therefore, Created things must be weighed according to the intention of the Creator. A wolf has deceived the Schools, killing not just a single sheep, but the whole flock at once, if he could <note>The "wolf" here likely refers to Galen or the Aristotelian philosophers whose theories Van Helmont believed led physicians astray.</note>.

Contrariety exists in humans and beasts through the power of **thymosis** <term>thymosis: A Greek term for "spiritedness" or "anger"; here it refers to the emotional force or vital impulse that can change the nature of bodily fluids.</term>, which is absent from both the mineral and vegetable kingdoms. Finally, among mortals, Sins are opposed to virtues **privatively** <term>privatively: Opposing something by being the absence of it, like darkness is the absence of light, rather than a thing itself.</term>, since sin is considered a non-being. I think that habitual virtues are not the contrary of vices as long as they reside in the intellect; but only when their emanation from the intellect is in the "consent," wherein it is opposed to the *thymosis* of willing something else. This process first gives birth to anger, hatred, and rivalries—that is, contraries. For out of the heart proceed murders, adulteries, etc. However, a mere "non-being" does not proceed, nor does it fall under a concept, since it has no form of its own by which to represent itself. Therefore, sin is not merely a turning away from the Creator, but also a mental act of determined malice. A mental act always takes on a "matter" in which it paints the image of its own **Idea**, which it formed by conceiving or imagining; and so far, it flows out from the depths of the soul into the bodily faculties. Thus far I have discussed the created faculties according to the intention of the Creator. Namely, that the incentives of contraries or enmities are not given to things that exist without the animosity of the senses. 

<column-break/>

But it will be helpful at this point to show that, through this same *thymosis*, some things are indeed made that express animal hostility, such as the saliva of a rabid dog, the sting of serpents, bees, etc. Yet these things operate in the manner of poisons and virulent plants, which the Divine Goodness did not create for the sake of harming or killing, or for an evil end, but for other ends directed toward the glory of His majesty. 

But it will be very difficult for one accustomed to the old ways to stop attributing "hostile contraries" to inanimate things. It is hard for them to consider a thing (such as the saliva of a rabid creature or serpent), which was impressed with anger against man, without the "contrariety" we freely admit exists in the beast from which it flowed. But surely he will easily agree with me if he considers that poison—whether it be naturally created or prepared by a beast through the contagion of its anger—does not therefore cease to be poison and act according to the nature of poison. Its property is to act by a **natural force**; indeed, although it arises from the impression of anger, this quality is no longer "anger" in the poison itself, but a certain natural product. In it, there is indeed a "stigma" or mark of anger and opposition, but not the anger itself. 

And consequently, there is no similar product of "love" by which a man, being struck or anointed, might benefit as much as he is lethally harmed by the other product [poison]. From this it becomes manifest: that this poison, however much it was produced by anger and is lethal to man, does not act because of any "contrariety." This is because there is no opposite "contrary" that helps or promotes life in an equal way, just as this poison harms it. And so, if poisons of this kind were to act because of contrariety, then the old axiom would be false: that one of two contraries exists in as many ways as the other. Thus it has now been sufficiently shown that poisons may indeed be made from the anger of beasts; but it does not therefore follow that the poison of a plant acts [out of hatred], but rather because of its own natural...

the endowment implanted in it divinely; and it is not because of any contrariety <term>contrariety: the traditional belief that nature works through opposing forces like hot vs. cold</term>, as the venom of beasts is more capable of such opposition than other simple substances. Otherwise, the same must be judged concerning the poisons of sorcerers, witches, and the like; for even if these are composed and given to a drinker with the intent to harm, they nevertheless operate either naturally (and thus without any intention of contrariety or strife) or they operate by the power of a demon. This power is either solitary (and thus a truly hostile effect, because it comes from an enemy **Evil Spirit** <note>original: "Cacodæmone"</note>) or it is natural. And in that case, it works not by the force of opposition or combat, but solely through the unfolding of its own natural endowment. I have already shown above that this endowment is free from litigious 

<margin>49.</margin>

contrariety. Furthermore, on this occasion, the energy of poison prepared from **thymosis** <term>thymosis: from the Greek for "spiritedness" or "anger"; here referring to the vital force triggered by intense emotion</term> must be explained. It is commonly known that the **gore** <note>original: "cruor" — specifically the thick, vital blood</note> of a bull will strangle one who drinks it, but not the gore of an ox or a cow. I have elsewhere attributed this to the fury of the bull dying with a desire for vengeance, in the manner of serpents. A pig, however, though it dies with anger (perhaps why God forbade the blood of living creatures under penalty of indignation), dies with the fear of death. But the bull is stirred by such great fury that it suffers no apprehension of death. Therefore, its blood is poisonous, but its flesh is not, because its fury—arriving so close to death—does not have enough time to infect the meat. 

<column-break/>

A rabid animal, however, because it has been infected long before death, also taints its own flesh. Likewise, timid animals, such as the mouse, the toad, etc., sprinkle their flesh and bones with a certain fear from their very center, as I have demonstrated elsewhere in *The Tomb of the Plague*. Yet, here applies that axiom: *Dead beast, dead poison* <note>original: "Morta sa bestia morto il veleno" — an Italian proverb</note>. This certainly holds true in a venomous animal because it burns with the fury of vengeance at intervals. In short: if the powers and endowments of simple substances are adverse to us, it proceeds from divine ordination, not from an "Idea" of vengeance or hostile contrariety. For there is a great distance between being contrary to someone and having properties that are harmful by nature. The latter proves the order of God and the variety of powers established in nature, while the former suggests a hostility inimical to both God and nature. They differ, therefore, in their "end"—that is, in the institution and direction of God in nature. This is seen in the order, intention, and destination, and thus in the whole scope of the Divine mind. According to this, I consider contrarieties in beasts and humans, and not in other simple things, and least of all in the elements. And finally, this is not a question of terminology. I intend to overturn the "contrarieties" of the elements, the "combats" in falsely believed mixtures, and the "alternations of temperaments," just as I overturn whatever has been prattled on about life, disease, death, and remedies based on these false suppositions.

<image-desc>Decorative initial E featuring elaborate floral and scrolling vine motifs.</image-desc>Having now dispatched the elements, complexions, compositions, and natural causes for the sake of Physics—that is, having explained the ignorance concerning the beginnings of healing which surrounds mortals after the origin of "forms" was misunderstood—and having also taught the necessities of ferments and the "Great Oportet" <term>Magnum Oportet: "The Great Must," Van Helmont's term for the divine necessity or blueprint within nature</term>, <margin>1.</margin> I shall now examine the vital beginnings. The Schools have taught that in every local motion, it is necessary to establish an Immovable First Mover. I find this to be true neither by art nor by nature. In demonstration of this, a drunk man goes along with an unstable mind and foot on a swaying ship, yet he winds the weight of a clock. Therefore, in voluntary motions, an unstable first mover is not required. Likewise, the Sun, through glass, ignites gunpowder with its ray. This first mover possesses nothing within itself that is immobile. This is already evident in fire, as an anomalous being. Thirdly, in nature, every seed <note>original: "semen"</note>, once conceived in its proper place, does not thereafter cease to agitate the mass subject to it by its own motion. Therefore, the true and first mover of seeds in nature, and the craftsman of the entire universe, moves itself first, and by its own

<column-break/>

motion requires no further motion. And whatever excites any natural mover to move is its own proper and internal beginning of motion; and if it falls into improper places, it dies, and its motion ceases. <margin>2.</margin> The Aristotelians, therefore, who call nature the principle of motion, or the first mover, through an absurd forgetfulness, require the first mover to be immobile. And although seeds have need of external fostering or an exciter, nevertheless that excitation is not the internal motion, nor the mover of that same motion; it is merely an alteration, accidentally accelerating or maturing the power of its own motions, or the activity of the first mover, which would otherwise be too weak to move its own matter. Since this activity is a certain accidental "otherness" which in truth does not rest within itself (far from being immobile), it does not even remain in its original and single state. To be sure, it strengthens the Archeus <term>Archeus: the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the life functions of an organ or organism</term>, so that it may more powerfully unfold the strength of moving innate to it and direct it toward its ends. But if the Schools—however ineptly they treat Aristotle as a Physicist—wish in this place to refer to the one First and Supernatural Mover of all things, who is the independent beginning of all motion, I reject that as irrelevant outside of Physics. For that most glorious Mover gave to things powers by which, through themselves and by absolute force, they might move themselves or other things. It is, you see, impertinent to run back to God as the Mover to demonstrate the natural motion of bodies. <margin>3.</margin> Furthermore, the blasphemy of requiring God to be immobile of necessity so that He can move other things is not to be tolerated in a Christian. For God does not move through the contact of extremities, or through the attraction or expulsion of things; finally, the thing moved does not acquire strength from the immobility of the first Mover so as to require it beforehand. Rather, the divine will <note>original: "nutus," literally a nod or command</note> reaches from end to end mightily; it is not, however, constrained by the necessity of physical contact.

<summary>Van Helmont critiques the Aristotelian requirement of an "immobile first mover" in biology, arguing instead that life is governed by an internal, self-moving vital spirit called the Archeus. He asserts that biological motion is a gift from God but must be studied through its internal natural mechanisms rather than through abstract physics or theology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's investigation into the "Blas" (vital motion). Having listed 58 specific points of inquiry on the previous page, he now moves into a philosophical and physical critique of the Aristotelian "Immovable Mover," arguing instead for a more dynamic, God-given vital force within nature itself.</meta>

# HUMAN BLAS.

...oppressed by consequence, now led, or subjected to law: But [the Creator is] entirely free, moving all things as much by His own will and motion as by rest, indifferently and equally powerfully. Therefore, that His being is "immobile" does not imply the necessity required by the <term>Schools: the traditional university authorities who followed Aristotle and Galen</term>; rather, it is the mere good pleasure of His glory. For His command (*fiat*) passed into nature, which thereafter exists by moving itself. Thus, St. Gregory says a power was bestowed upon the earth by which it might thrust forth plants from itself. Therefore, it is a pagan doctrine, taken from <term>Mathesis: the mathematical study of mechanics and physics</term>, which necessitates the first mover to its own perpetual immobility so that it may move all things without end.

<margin>4.</margin>
This error might be pardoned in Aristotle, but not in the Christian Schools, who contaminate their young students with it. Otherwise, there would naturally be no motion unless it came from a motive principle which does not move other things unless it is itself moved through and in itself. Furthermore, in both artificial and natural things, if something is moved by an external mover, and the mover itself leans upon some immobile foundation during that motion—for instance, when a Sailor pushes a boat away from an immobile bank with a pole—the shore or bank does not move the boat, nor does it naturally contain a motive power in itself: rather, it is merely the medium through which the mover modifies his own motion. By stabilizing himself against this (as if against a bottom) through weight and the acting forces of mechanics, the mover fabricates his motion (which otherwise is entirely mobile and is moved actively). In this same way, a <note>original: "bombarda"</note> cannon explodes a ball more forcefully if it has an immobile, resisting body behind it. But surely, just as that body is not the source of motion, it is only through absurdity that it requires an "immobile mover," and it is ineptly compared to the First Mover [God]. Indeed, in natural terms, the first and total mover would be the ignited <note>original: "pulvis pyrius"</note> gunpowder, which requires no immobility to be moved, but needs a "modified organ" (the cannon) to move in a modified way. It is therefore impertinent to think that all motions are made by God, as the first mover, as if He moved the entire universe with a kind of stick.

<column-break/>

It is also impertinent, when investigating whether a mover as such must necessarily be immobile, to answer that the first mover will modify his motion and move more strongly if he is immobile or leans against an immobile foundation. Is this truly teaching Christian Philosophy? Truly, there is no doubt but that the stars, through their various aspects which they borrow from their motions, infuse a motive <term>Blas: Van Helmont’s term for a vital, pulsing motion or force inherent in nature</term> into the water and air, so that they might be for us for seasons, days, and years. Finally, the earth received an internal beginning for propagating plants before the stars were even born.

<margin>5.</margin>
Therefore, although brute animals are later than the stars, their seeds are not more ignoble than the seed of plants, nor are they bound to the stars by a link of greater subjection. Since the stars existed before the creation of sentient beings, it was appropriate that the human *Blas* should not indeed follow the lead of the stars, but at least imitate their motion—not as if they were its movers, but in the same way that we follow the tracks of a <note>original: "veredarii"</note> courier by our own free motion. In this way, perhaps, the internal organs chose the planets as their precursors. For each organ forms its own internal *Blas* according to the type of its own Star, which is therefore called "astral." This is because it imitates the tracks of heaven, both by the priority of the days of the precursor star and by the laws of their destinations in nature.

<margin>6.</margin>
Otherwise, in illnesses, as every effort of nature is symptomatic: so then the human *Blas* precedes and announces future storms; whereas in health, the human *Blas* ordinarily follows after significant changes in the weather.

<margin>7.</margin>
But brute animals, as they were created on a day before man, so their *Blas* always precedes and runs ahead of the *Blas* of the stars. Therefore, many prognostications of the weather are naturally drawn from beasts. To this, superstition was added, which contributed auguries and <term>haruspicia: the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</term> to the credulous and superstitious.

<margin>8.</margin>
However, the *Blas* which is directed toward local motion by the will of animals is in no way connected to the celestial movement above.

# HUMAN BLAS.

...above. For indeed, all carnal generation flows from the power of the seed: and the power of the seed flows from the will of the flesh: therefore, carnal generation has its own <term>Blas: Helmont's term for a fundamental vital power or inner motion</term>, serving the uses of its own ends, which flow from the beginnings of its own being. These are the will of the flesh and the lust of the masculine will. There is,
<margin>9.</margin> therefore, a twofold Blas in us. One, namely, which exists by natural motion; the other, however, is voluntary, which exists as a mover for itself through the internal will. From this, therefore, it is impossible for the predictions of the stars to conclude rightly within us. It has now been sufficiently demonstrated that there is something in the sublunary realm <note>The "sublunary realm" refers to the region below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay.</note> which moves itself locally and by alteration, without the Blas of the heavens or a natural immobile mover. Will, in the first place, is the primary mover of this kind, and the seminal being moves itself as well, both in the seeds and in those things constituted by them. Furthermore, just as God willed, so all things were made. From the
<margin>10.</margin> will, therefore, they were first moved. For hence, whatever insensitive things are moved, they are moved through a certain will of nature, as it were, or a pleasure; and they have their own natural necessities and ends. As is seen in the pulse of the heart, of the arteries, and in the expulsion
<margin>11.</margin> of many superfluities, etc. For Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> distributed the pulses quite skillfully; yet in this, he was deluded by Aristotle, who thought that the end and the efficient causes were external, and estimated that the purposes of the pulses were the total causes. For, passing over the proper Blas of the pulses, he only investigated the ends and necessities of nature, for the sake of which the pulses were not indeed created, but rather
<margin>12.</margin> modified. And so, consequently, he distributed the differences of pulses into a scheme only by their ends. Therefore, he did not touch upon the more important and efficient aspects. Thus, he constructed the causes of the pulses
<margin>13.</margin> under two heads of necessity. Namely, for the cooling of the heart—for which purpose the heart and the arteries would dilate themselves simultaneously—and for the exploding of sooty vapors <note>original: "fuligines". In Galenic medicine, these were the smoky waste products of "innate heat" that needed to be exhaled.</note> stirred up by heat. For which reason, surely, the Heart and the artery would compress and collapse themselves at the same time, for fear of suffocation. These two factors, by interweaving them variously according to strength, speed,

<column-break/>

weakness, hardness, and magnitude, along with their correlates, he compiled the differences of pulses with skillful investigation. And I wish that his other writings did not reveal that these things were described from elsewhere. The ancients, however, not content with two
<margin>14.</margin> ends—namely, cooling and the expulsion of sooty vapors—added a third, which was the nourishment of the <term>vital spirit: a refined, air-like substance believed to circulate in the arteries and sustain life</term> from the air. As if, indeed, air could ever become vital spirit! For if the spirit were increased or nourished by air joined to it (since a simple body is not digestible), then by mere mixing, the vital spirit would be made from air; and then the individual things of which they consist would no longer be nourished immediately. There was, therefore, an ignorance among the ancients, who did not know the constitution of the vital spirit, thinking that a little water mixed with much wine, or a little tin mixed with much molten gold, would become wine or gold. I will say here what I have perceived, after I have used discernment rather than the laziness of mere agreement. I began, therefore, first to consider that
<margin>15.</margin> heat does not reside in the heart primarily and of itself, but is a companion of life and the soul, a sign and a medium of operating in warm-blooded animals, derived from the nature of solar light. In fish, however, life is of the nature of "cold light," and therefore exists without actual heat—this is the truth. And therefore, that the pulse is not made in
<margin>16.</margin> nature for the sake of cooling the heart or blowing away sooty vapors, a dissected frog will teach. For in a living frog, you will see its heart and arteries move; the heart becomes red with each pulse, or through *diastole* <note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and the chambers fill with blood.</note>, and becomes paler through compression, even if it is not transparent. Nevertheless, although the ancients thought heat was the cause of the pulses, there is no one who has described that heat by its own internal heats—by what path, reason, and medium that heat is excited, kindled, and persists in us—because no one has meditated upon life and forms. And therefore, no one has understood the efficient cause of the pulses.
<margin>17.</margin> Indeed, no one until now doubts that heat flows from the heart, and no one disputes that the fetus is first cherished by maternal heat, until by the maturity of days, a heat of its own is kindled in it...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that human biological functions like the heartbeat are driven by an internal "Blas" and "Will" rather than external mechanical needs or stellar influence. He specifically refutes the ancient Galenic theory that the pulse exists solely to cool the heart or vent waste vapors, using the "cold light" of fish and frogs as counter-evidence.</summary>

# HUMAN BLAS.

<margin>18.</margin> ...the tinder is lit. But no one has investigated what that tinder is, or why, once ignited, it does not immediately perish but persists until the end; this is because everyone has overlooked the nature of life itself. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle whose medical theories dominated universities.</note> indeed imagine a fiery heat within us (contrary to Aristotle, who wished this heat to correspond in proportion to the element of the stars, and distinguished it from elemental and fiery heat). They claim it lives by feeding upon and consuming the "radical moisture" <note>radicale humidum: a medieval medical concept of a finite bodily fluid that acted as the "fuel" for life's lamp.</note>. From this, it would follow that the heart is the *wick* <note>original: "lychnium"</note> of a consuming fire. However, since the substance of the heart and the pericardium, as well as the blood, is not suited for fire, they were forced to admit that this fire is not fire, and the heat is not fiery, even though it "consumes." They told themselves it was enough to have described the tinder, the wick, or the beginning of heat metaphorically—as if nature admitted metaphors.

<margin>19.</margin> For I remember, in the first place, several young women <note>original: "virgines syncopizatas," referring to women who had suffered syncope or deep fainting spells.</note> who had fainted and were deprived of pulse and breath, as far as human judgment could discern. So much so that for several hours they were mourned among the dead; yet they revived, and having later married, they lived healthily and gave birth five or six times.

<margin>20.</margin> For they were icy cold as soon as the pulse had failed. Hence I began to doubt whether the pulse occurred for the sake of producing heat, rather than for the purpose of drawing in cold air <note>Van Helmont is questioning the Galenic idea that the heart beats primarily to "cool" the innate heat of the body with outside air.</note>. Thus, I began to regard the "final causes" of the pulse as nonsensical, and I suspected that the predictive part of medicine was thereby undermined. I prove it thus: for there is a septum, or partition, between each chamber <note>original: "sinum," literally "hollow" or "pocket," here meaning the ventricles.</note> of the heart, which is so porous in itself as long as one lives that, by the suction of the heart’s ears <note>auricles</note> (for it is considered "eared" on both sides by analogy, because it has parts like bellows), the venous blood from the vena cava (forming the right chamber of the heart through its passage) passes through and migrates into the left; it does not, however, go back from there to the right.

<margin>21.</margin> This is because the pores in the septum itself are triangular; the point of the triangle, ending in the left chamber, is more easily blocked, while the base of that triangle, in the right chamber, is never blocked except at death. But the blood of the left chamber

<column-break/>

is already arterial and blood in the true sense of the name, different in color and refinement from the crude blood <note>original: "cruore," referring to the darker, thicker venous blood.</note> still in the vena cava. Therefore, it was not without reason that I found it necessary to discover a new, or fourth digestion, in the "stomach" of the heart. For just as venous blood differs from the milky cream and chyle <note>chyle: the milky fluid produced from digested food in the intestines.</note> of the gut, so too does arterial blood differ from venous blood—although they are close in kinship, and a "clothing of the heavens" has, to some extent, reduced them into one family.

<margin>22.</margin> Yet in this lies the specific difference between the two: that the blood is "informed" <note>In Aristotelian terms, "informed" means given its essential nature and life-force.</note> by the immortal soul in the left chamber; the venous blood, however, is not at all so informed, but is merely illuminated by light, participating in the "sensitive form" rather than being shaped by it. For all other digestions require rest. But the fourth is perfected by an unceasing continuity of motion. This is not because the motion of the heart itself is the transformative formal cause, but rather that it concurs as a disposition. That is to say, in the left chamber of the heart, as if in a stomach, there dwells a singular ferment—intensely vital and luminous—which is the sufficient cause for the transmutation of venous blood into arterial blood, just as it presides over the transformation of blood into the vital spirit. Indeed, all venous blood naturally tends toward its end, which is nutrition; yet ultimately, it is dispersed and vanishes into a vapor, or into <term>Gas: Helmont's famous term for a spirituous substance or "wild spirit" that cannot be contained</term>, unless it is halted by the "clot of accretion." Arterial blood, however, has as its goal not to turn into soot or excrement. If that happens, it occurs through disease and by accident. Otherwise, the proper object of blood is to be translated into the vital spirit. If that spirit then also vanishes, let this be contrary to its intent—since every being naturally desires to persist. For the vital spirit is a light dwelling originally in the ferment of the left chamber, which illuminates new spirits produced from the arterial blood; it is because of this continuity of light, indeed, that the artery is raised <note>i.e., the artery pulses or expands.</note>. For the spirits thus become participants in life and its executors, just as they are executors of <term>Vulcan: a metaphor for the transformative power of heat or alchemy</term>, of continued heat. Human life, therefore...

# HUMAN BLAS.

...[is] a formal light, and in its own way the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>anima sensitiva: In Helmontian thought, the soul shared by humans and animals that governs the senses and movement.</note> is itself luminous; therefore, death follows immediately upon its being "blown out." This is because the immortal mind of man is enfolded within the sensitive soul, and the mind flies away at death while the other soul perishes. Far be it, however, that this vital light should be called "fiery," or said to be burning and devastating the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the innate bodily fluid that medieval doctors believed acted as the "fuel" for life's lamp.</note>, or that it should pollute the heart and arteries with a continuous production of soot. Rather, it is a **formal light** (as I have said before regarding forms), for no one could ever describe the inner essence of life otherwise, even if they had seen the formal lives of things in a state of ecstasy. This is because words and names are lacking by which these things might be named from their true origin. And although God might have shown the essence of life in its concrete form to someone, He will never grant the honor of teaching it to any creature. Since life in the abstract is God Himself, the Incomprehensible. Thus, by degrees, food and drink ascend into the <term>chyle</term> of the stomach, the <term>chyme</term> <note>original: "chymum"; the pulp of digested food further refined in the mesentery.</note> of the mesentery, venous blood, and finally through arterial blood, reaching the thinnest ether—the vital spirit, the very support of the soul. This transformation presupposes the movement of the heart. For it is not enough for the <term>ferment</term> <note>Van Helmont believed "ferments" were the chemical agents responsible for all bodily transformations, like modern enzymes.</note> to be efficiently productive so that blood may be animated and turned into spirit, and for that spirit to dwell in the left chamber of the heart; unless a pulsating motion also occurs, similar to the motion by which sour milk is changed into butter through a true transmutation. Indeed, through motion, there occurs a thinning of the blood—not into an acid, but into a salty nature—and it is not thereby turned into fat or butter, but into vital spirit, of the nature of salt, and thus of a <term>balsam</term> <note>A "balsam" in alchemy is a substance that preserves against decay.</note>. Thus, indeed, the blood, through motion, heat, and ferment, is changed into an ethereal offspring, the immediate home of the vital light. *Wherefore blood, water, and spirit are the same.* <note>original: "Quapropter sanguis, aqua & spiritus idem sunt."</note> For if that light is in the spirit, and the spirit is carried through the arteries into the whole body, that light must be continuous with itself throughout, since it is the nature of light to be extinguished if interrupted. Therefore, the arteries had to remain open, in such a way that they never remain <column-break/> compressed for long. Therefore, it was fitting for the pulse to dilate them, and not for them to be so compressed that the entire artery collapses into itself. For this reason, perhaps, the artery is not unfairly clothed in a double and harder tunic [wall]. For the discontinuity of that light is the reason why, in an instant, all the sovereign power of the brain perishes in those who are hanged. It is not because the spirit had vanished from the brain so quickly, but because the light was interrupted. Finally, if the pulsating motion did not occur, a lethal cold would soon arise, and we would be colder than a frog. To that extent, although many frogs live through the winter under the mud without breathing, they do not live without a pulse. Also, the ferment of the left chamber [of the heart] transforms its blood only with a slow sluggishness, and would transmit it everywhere too lazily; therefore, it would not satisfy the timely needs of the spirits. For let us imagine a leather bottle imbued with a scent, but filled only halfway with liquid. That liquid will hardly catch the scent of the bottle; but if it is shaken, that scent immediately forces itself through the smallest parts of the liquid. In this way, surely, the vital ferment of the left chamber is immediately given to the blood through the movement of the heart, and compels it to a swift obedience to its impression. For light is easily kindled by light: and therefore the blood, now animated, easily catches the light of that solar lamp and is adopted as "ethereal offspring." Thus, the **Blas** of the heart is the vital spirit, and consequently the fuel of its own heat; but the spirit thus animated is the mover of the heart, a fact almost neglected in the Schools. Consequently, also, that motion occurs because of the necessary heat established in our "solar" constitution and the construction of the spirit. I do not believe, therefore, that the pulse was instituted for the purpose of cooling the heart <note>This rejects the common Galenic view that the pulse was meant to "fan" and cool the heart's fire.</note>. For vital things do not fight under the lethal banners of cold, nor do they intend cold: they only intend vital things. Cold in us is, surely, a sign of death, because it is its companion. Therefore, whatever would produce cold in the fountain of life would intend the removal of life, and would lead to the destruction of the body's monarchy...

They think this even though such fire would have to be fetched from far away, from the ridiculous "fire in the hollow of the moon," which otherwise would not descend safely through so many 
<margin>25.</margin> regions of cold air to the ordinary constitution of simple things, unrestrained and according to the whim of lower things, contrary to its own nature. Thus, if the Schools had understood this fictitious fire under the circle of the moon to be **radical heat**, they would impertinently say that it subsists in us as if in a lamp of **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidi radicalis"; the innate fluid medieval doctors believed was the "oil" that fueled the "lamp" of life.</note>. Meanwhile, they dream that the fiery element (which they rashly imagine) lives with equal force without the need for nourishment or consumption. In this way, false authorities give birth to false themes, and through ignorance of causes, 
<margin>26.</margin> the principles of healing have perished. In my judgment, the Schools should at least have remembered that the very blowing of bellows does not cool a fire, but rather ignites it more. Nor do I see by what reason the motion of animals should be the cause of their own cooling. Finally, I know that fire can in no way be associated with other elements, even when cut into the smallest pieces, without being instantly extinguished. I also know it is impossible for a fire to exist which is not truly fire and supremely hot. And so, if Nature were to attempt cooling through the pulse, her effort would be foolish, vain, and impossible. From this, a horrendous conclusion follows: that God, in the ends He proposed for Himself, had actually 

<column-break/>

erred. Let the Schools, therefore, come to their senses. Furthermore, there must be a hasty transformation of **gore** <note>original: "cruoris"; the thicker, raw part of the blood.</note> into blood, and of this into **vital spirit**, lest after fainting spells and palpitations (under which the infections and dissipations of those spirits occur so quickly that the pits of **smallpox** <note>original: "variolarum."</note>, not previously visible, suddenly appear), death should rush in as a necessity. Thus, the help that is required immediately was not to be sought from afar or delayed. This is indeed the 
<margin>27.</margin> reason why the pulse becomes faster in a fever, and not for the expulsion of soot, nor a greediness for cooling. For if a 
<margin>28.</margin> thorn is fixed in the tip of a finger, immediately the pulse becomes hard, strong, and faster; and then, following the increase of the pulse, an increase of heat—not cold—is immediately present everywhere in proportion, and indeed both before and without the birth of any "soot." Then, at the beginning of intermittent fevers, for several hours and as long as the cold chill lingers, the pulse is small, rare, and depressed. Yet **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredo"; the Schools believed fevers were caused by rotting humors.</note> is present and kindled (if the Schools spoke the truth), and therefore the "soot" present in the Schools' theory is the cause of the **paroxysm** <note>A sudden attack or violent expression of a disease.</note>; they thirst greatly in the cold chill and vomit yellow bile. Therefore, the compression of the pulse ought to be very frequent, and the whole pulse by far the fastest. Especially since many who die in those fevers perish during the febrile onset in the cold, from a lack of spirits and as if suffocated. However, in troublesome heats, even in **erysipelas** <note>A bacterial skin infection causing redness and inflammation.</note>, **carbuncles**, or **Persian fire** <note>original: "ignis persicus"; an old term for various skin inflammations or shingles.</note>, etc., the vital spirit glows, provoked by the disease-causing agent, as if provoked to anger. This is evident in the aforementioned localized kindlings, even caustic ones. Where otherwise a tempered luminous kindling shines forth everywhere under vital harmony. Indeed, as seen toward death or a fainting spell, the corneal membrane of the eye is perceived to be deprived of light, not previously boiling with fire. Furthermore, the transformation of blood into spirit, which begins in the heart, is matured in the course of the arteries (or the **stomach of the heart** <note>original: "cordis stomacho"; Van Helmont viewed the heart's chambers as a place of "digestion" or maturation for the blood.</note>). [The stomach] and the primary motions of the heart, [those] of the mind and the sensitive soul, are truly **Saturnian** <note>original: "Saturnia"; referencing the astrological qualities of Saturn—slow, heavy, or sluggish—suggesting these motions are deep and foundational rather than rapid.</note> and sluggish. For the digestion of the heart is an integral transmutation of blood into spirit, without dregs or soot. Indeed, it contains no filth, nor does it admit heterogeneous things, nor does the spirit (the son of heat) degenerate because of heat. To be sure, it is an immediate operation of the sensitive soul, always uniform, similar to itself, and life [flowing] toward life breathed out through vital motions.

<margin>29.</margin> Therefore, the principal goals of the pulses are: 1. the conveyance of blood from the hollow of the **vena cava** <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart.</note> to the left chamber of the heart; 2. the increase of heat; 3. the manufacture of arterial blood; 4. and finally, the production of vital spirit. 5. I will repeat what I have said elsewhere: namely, that some forms shine, as in stones and minerals; some indeed shine with an added light, as in plants; others are even luminous, as in living beings.

<margin>30.</margin> Thus, a vital luminosity is given to the vital spirit through a kindled flame—not indeed of a fire-like nature, but one that is illuminating and specific (differing by species). Thus, fish live no less happily, and move more strongly, more vigorously, and longer

<margin>31.</margin> than warm beasts. The **Schools** <note>Van Helmont’s term for the academic medical establishment of his day, which followed ancient Greek theories.</note>, in place of what I have now demonstrated, assume that the blood in the liver takes on the nature of spirit, which they perhaps call "natural." This is the kind of aura present in all the juices of herbs; and from this, they claim the vital spirit is immediately born. But I derive the spirit from elsewhere, and from a far nobler lineage. Whether the Schools or I philosophize more correctly, let the reader judge, who has already drunk in both doctrines: remembering at least what I am about to say, namely that eventually the whole blood, and the nourishing liquid created from it—the immediate nourishment of the solid parts—is finally dispersed through the **diapheresis** <term>diapheresis</term> <note>original: "diapheresin"; the distribution of nutrients or sweat through the pores and tissues.</note> of the body

<column-break/>

without any dregs or **dead-head** <term>dead-head</term> <note>original: "capitis mortui"; an alchemical term for the worthless solid residue left after distillation or "death" of a substance.</note> residue. This is so the reader may suspect that blood is naturally inclined to become spirit at some point; which is not as easily presumed regarding the vapor of the blood. For they were ignorant that the whole blood of the arteries is not rarely turned into a spiritual **aporrhea** <term>aporrhea</term> <note>original: "aporrheam"; a Greek term meaning an outflow or emanation of particles.</note> or vital spirit. But if blood is changed into vapor in our glass vessels with a gentle warmth, it leaves behind a thick sediment and eventually charcoal at the bottom. Thus, the doctrine of the Schools is far removed from the knowledge of spirits; they think vital spirits are manufactured from a vapor or watery breath. For they neglected to see how in this vapor of blood—prepared from bread and water and the blood made from them—there is raised up not a watery breath (as they think), but a salty and illuminated spirit, and its heat is not merely heated, but heating. Indeed, no author until now has investigated this vital light by which the spirit is illuminated and, in a way, glows; so that life, light, form, and the sensitive soul become as one.

<margin>32.</margin> Finally, the rotten doctrine of the Schools confuses the purposes of the pulses and the breath. Namely, they think breath exists for the nourishment of the vital spirit—the "life of fire" (which they claim is fed by air), the cooling of the heart, and the expulsion of **soots** <term>soots</term> <note>original: "fuliginum"; the waste products or "smoke" that Galenic doctors believed the heart produced and needed to exhale.</note>. They intend to nourish and cool (or diminish) the vital heat. How these things can be combined at the same time, let others say. I am glad not to know. At the very least, in the greatest poverty of vital spirit, when its increase is most desired, the rising of the artery is then smallest and rarest. And vice versa, while spirit abounds, the rising of the artery is at its greatest. I confess indeed that breath is drawn by the reins of the will, or through the organs of voluntary motion; but the pulse is not. But since a healthy chest satisfies the goals of the pulse through its breathing, the pulse would not be necessary as long as one is cold and breathes enough.
