## Aa 2

->of pulses,<-

...of the pulses, and there must be another cause, or necessity, for respiration. Indeed, we perceive the necessity of panting; we also modify our breathing at will, and some can even suppress it entirely. But why do we not feel the necessities of the pulses, which are more vital and no less urgent? Especially since life—the origin of sensibility—is that which alone senses its every need, yet alone excludes us from every sensation [of the heart's movement]. Therefore, I conjecture from this that there are other necessities unknown to the ancients. <margin>33.</margin> I know indeed that no dregs, filth, or superfluities are expelled from the arterial blood or vital spirit (as I will show in its place); soot, however, is absent where there is no burning. Rather, the blood <note>original: "cruor"; refers to the vital, thicker part of the blood.</note> in its consumption, by the spontaneous guidance of heat, produces <term>Gas<gloss>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a chaotic, spiritualized substance or vapor that cannot be contained by vessels and lacks a fixed form.</gloss></term> just as water produces vapor. And that Gas (which the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle whose theories Van Helmont opposed.</note> call the spirit of the Liver, or the natural spirit of the blood) must necessarily be expelled subsequently; this stands beyond controversy. Otherwise, a man almost extinguished by cold would warm up faster if he held his breath for several hours (assuming breathing were only for the purpose of cooling); yet even in that state, he does not notably stop breathing, under penalty of death. The fish also lacks lungs and breath (for the bubbles they sometimes belch out are flatus, or the winds of digestion, not breath). Frogs indeed, and sea monsters that make sounds, have sacs performing the office of the lung, although fish are no colder than frogs. Indeed, frogs and swallows are hidden under mud all winter and live without breathing, yet not without a pulse. Therefore, there is one use for the pulses and another for breathing, and neither is for heat alone. For in the most acute and hot diseases, whenever breathing is greatest and drawn like a sigh, the pulse is small and swift, even while strength remains. Therefore, the use of breathing and the pulse do not correspond. Especially since we are better cooled by a large draft of cold

<column-break/>

water drunk all at once than if the same quantity were drunk in several sips. I say we are more refreshed by a single sigh than by many small and more frequent breaths. Just as a bellows does more with a large and continuous blast than with smaller, more careful ones, even if there are more of them. Whence to a man who weighs things well and is judicious, it can be sufficiently clear that there is another use of the pulses of greater moment: namely, that which regards the ferment <note>A vital catalytic principle Van Helmont believed directed all bodily processes, similar to how yeast transforms dough.</note> of digestions. <margin>34.</margin> To what end do I repeat this mechanism? Namely, that finally under the last digestion, all our blood perishes and exhales, leaving no dregs behind. However, whatever exhales through heat alone leaves dregs behind in both living and inanimate things (experts call this the **caput mortuum** <note>original: "dead head"; the useless chemical residue left in a retort after distillation or sublimation.</note>), which, when toasted, becomes charcoal. For the action of heat is everywhere simple, univocal, and homogeneous of itself, differing in effect only by reason of the matter it acts upon. Therefore, if the vital blood is to be so disposed in us that it is eventually blown away entirely without a "dead head," it was absolutely necessary for this to happen by another means than heat. Air, however, has always and from the beginning everywhere been the separator of waters from waters. <margin>35.</margin> This was unknown in the Schools. Namely, that for the whole blood to pass into **Gas**, it needs two wings for flying: air and ferment. Wherefore observe: as often as any blood in the outer body becomes unfit, or is not gradually disposed and undergoes stages so that the whole becomes volatile and able to fly across, in that moment **scirrhi** <term>scirrhi<gloss>Hard, painless tumors often associated with stagnant or improperly "digested" bodily fluids.</gloss></term>, nodes, and abscesses are conceived. But if it happens in the inner part: mostly fevers, apoplexies, epilepsies, asthma, pains likewise, and deaths follow. Let us see, therefore, what air or what ferment contributes to this. First, all the mucilage of the earth, which otherwise easily turns into worms—likewise starch, meat, fish, etc.—once frozen, lose their sliminess by that very fact and return to water. Insofar as air once

was best combined with ice (as I once said regarding the weight of ice) and so it is the first step by which air, a tenacious body, is resolved into water. Next, in the greatest cold and purest air, we are more voracious <note>meaning we have a stronger appetite</note>, yet we still sweat, and less is exhaled from us, with a slightly scantier and harder departure <note>referring to solid waste or excretion</note>. <margin>36.</margin> Accordingly, one sailing at sea eats twice, if not three times more (unless he is sick), and releases less excrement than when he is dwelling on land. Hence the proverb: *Water promotes digestion.* As if, indeed, the sailor were fluctuating in water and not in the air! However, this fluctuation <note>the tossing motion of the sea</note> refreshes the air for us, and thus digestion is made stronger. Therefore, if we eat more robustly and discharge less, it follows necessarily that more is exhaled or "vanished" from the body. This is to say that the purer air of the North <note>original: "Boreae"</note> and the sea contributes to the <term>diaphoresis<gloss>The process of sweating or insensible perspiration through the skin.</gloss></term> of the body, or prepares the blood <note>original: "cruorem"; referring to the thicker, vital part of the blood</note> for its own insensible perspiration. <margin>37.</margin> Clearly, for this reason respiration occurs: not indeed so that air might serve as food for the vital spirit, but that it might be connected to it, brought through the pulmonary artery and the pulmonary vein <note>Van Helmont uses the older terms "vena arterialem" and "arteriam venalem"</note> of the lungs; and the air thus brought into the heart receives a ferment, by which, together with the air, both prepare the blood for its total diaphoresis. Otherwise, many things become "fixed" and resist perspiration if they are urged by heat, though otherwise they were volatile in themselves. Wherefore <term>alkali<gloss>In Helmontian chemistry, a "fixed" salt that remains after combustion.</gloss></term> is not generated in ash by fire as an efficient cause, although it effectively proceeds from it. For the office of fire is indeed to ignite, consume, and separate, but not to produce anything. <margin>38.</margin> Since fire itself, the destroyer of seeds, is not rich in "seed"; yet from seeds all generation proceeds. Therefore, while alkali becomes fixed from a salt that was previously volatile, it is not the production of a new thing, but only an alteration of the thing. For alkali was materially present in the composite substance <note>original: "concreto"</note> before burning, and it flowed together with the mercury and sulfur <note>the three "Primes" of Paracelsian chemistry: salt, sulfur, and mercury</note>. However, while fire removes the mercury and sulfur, the salt—as a more subsisting principle—in the melting of the burning process,

<column-break/>

seizes for itself the neighboring part of the sulfur or "fatness." While it cannot sufficiently protect this part from the torture of the fire, the sulfur partly flies off under the mask of <term>Gas<gloss>Van Helmont’s term for a spiritualized, invisible substance produced by chemical reactions.</gloss></term> and acquires the smell of burnt matter <note>original: "empyreumatis"</note>, and partly, having seized the sulfur, it is incorporated by melting and becomes true charcoal. Therefore, the sulfur, now fixed by its "marriage" to the salt, does not quickly turn from charcoal into soot, but does so gradually, and only in an open vessel. And so, along with the previous sulfur (for from this the sulfur of a thing usually retains the sharp taste of volatile salt), and finally with the charcoal-sulfur, the proper weight of its volatile salt flies away. <margin>39.</margin> This indeed is nowhere more manifest than in the charcoal of honey. For if this is urged in a closed vessel, it remains unchanged by glowing fire; but in an open vessel, both depart so that thereafter no residue of ash ever remains. Materially, therefore, alkali salt pre-exists in the substance before conflagration. Since formally the whole salt in the substance was volatile, and not in the form of a more fixed alkali. This is now primarily clear in the blood <note>original: "cruore"</note>, which exhales entirely as a volatile substance through the pores insensibly, without any residue. But if it is burned, it leaves a great deal of fixed salt in its ash. Finally, pine wood, which gives little ash and even less salt in the preparation of "potash" <note>original: "cinerum clavellatorum"</note>, is turned entirely into alkali by calcination. For from Scandinavia there are brought to us wood-ashes <note>original: *Weedaschen*</note>, burned mostly from pine and some oak; when the moister air infects the barrels in which they are carried (namely, by the salt melting), the wood of the barrels, thus salted, melts like horn when burned and almost all degenerates into salt. Even the part that was ash becomes salt by reason of the salt it contains; this they then call pot-ashes <note>original: *Potaschen*</note>. Otherwise, the ashes of the same wood, when the salt is removed, remain ashes and do not become salt. From which it is certainly established that the salt from ash then makes something similar to itself through melting, and indeed a fixed thing. And therefore, in the substance, by reason of the salt and the melting, a fixity arises which otherwise did not exist.

Thus, while the **tartar of wine** <note>original: "vini tartarus"; the sediment or crust found in wine barrels, mostly potassium bitartrate</note> is burned, barely sixteen ounces of it give two and a half ounces of **alkali salt**; therefore, thirteen and a half volatile ounces perished during the **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its composition</note>. However, if these volatile parts are distilled and finally re-absorbed into their own remaining charcoal <note>original: "carbone residuo"</note>, they will still yield four and one-third ounces of salt through **cohobation** <note>the repeated distillation of a liquid over the solid residue from which it was just distilled</note>. Therefore, you may judge that what you see happen to the four and one-third ounces likewise applies to the two and a half ounces of the first alkali. To this point belongs what I have said elsewhere regarding **aqua vitæ** <note>literally "water of life," referring to concentrated alcohol or brandy</note>, fixed into the alkali of tartar; and the same happens to distilled vinegar. From this, it appears that the **volatile salt** of a thing is fixed within its own fixed alkali. Indeed, likewise, the entire ash was previously volatile and became fixed during the first melting of the combustion. However, the volatile salts, which were closer to the "essences," departed along with those essences in the first "torture" of the fire. Note, however, that although alkali may be made from the **spirit of wine** <note>alcohol</note> within the fixed salt of tartar, nonetheless, insofar as the salt of the *aqua vitæ* has been changed by its marriage to the essence, yet in the shared fixity of both, one is separable and distinguished from the other. For when **aqua fortis** <note>literally "strong water," meaning nitric acid</note> is poured on it, the alkali from the spirit of wine becomes reddish; the alkali of tartar, however, does not change color.
<margin>40.</margin> For this reason, there is a certain "republic" among alkalis, and those who counterfeit money labor greatly over the salt of tartar, while scorning the alkali of **saltpeter** <note>original: "salis petræ"; potassium nitrate</note>. Also, the alkali salt prepared here (as it is said) from the spirit of wine, through its association, changes the taste of the lixivium <note>lye or alkaline solution</note> of <margin>41.</margin> tartar: so that it turns into the **Balsam of Samech of Paracelsus**, which is astringent; whereas before it had the taste of lye, it lacked the balsam, and resembled a caustic substance. Finally, it fits here that decayed and rotten wood leaves behind almost no salt in its ashes. Indeed, the volatile salt departed with the sulfur through the **ferment of putrefaction**. And thus, there was as much volatile salt in the thing—or the **concrete** <note>the whole, solid substance before separation</note>—as is found to be missing in the ash. That is to say, all of it. From which it follows that the volatile salt, obtained from both sulfur and mercury, is materially the same as the 

<column-break/>

alkalized salt: and therefore the volatile is alkalized, <margin>42.</margin> and in turn, the alkali is volatilized, while the formal property of the **concrete** remains. It follows, finally, that the distilled sulfur of the concrete and the sulfur of the charcoal are of the same species, although the latter is imprisoned while the former is free. These things "mechanics" <note>here meaning chemical experimentation and observation</note> <margin>43.</margin> taught me, after I learned how to separate the three elements from ordinary concretes without **empyreuma** <note>the scorched, burnt smell or taste resulting from overheating organic matter</note>. I learned, namely, that every combustible body has within itself a volatile salt, which is fixed into an alkali by the seizing of its sulfur. Meanwhile, a part usually remains in abundance which escapes the embrace of the melting volatile sulfur. In this melting, the action upon the sulfur of the thing is vigorous. Understand this by the example of **distilled vinegar**. This, I say, since it is water <margin>44.</margin> impregnated with a volatile acid salt; if it touches anything by the "biting" action of its acidity, it is immediately coagulated, which is afterwards found as a fixed alkali through combustion. Indeed, if the acidic and volatile **spirit of vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid</note> corrodes mercury (which is equally volatile), the acid of the vitriol is fixed into true **alum**. Furthermore, applying these "mechanics" to the <margin>45.</margin> goal of total consumption in the **blood** <note>original: "cruore"; specifically the vital, thicker part of the blood</note>, I say: if air (let him who can, grasp the secret) primarily volatilizes the sulfur of the concrete with the total separation of its salt, this salt (which otherwise would be fixed into alkali in the charcoal by fire) becomes entirely volatile, and climbs upward, sometimes in a liquid form, and not rarely in the form of a **sublimate**; and it possesses the entire **crasis** <note>the specific temperament or healthy mixture of constituents</note> of the concrete. This salt has been demonstrated through mechanics; however, its demonstration is known to few, though we may make it known openly. At least from this, it appears that to the ancients, the true use of **air** in the pulse and breath was not known, because of their ignorance of the **Spagyric art** <note>alchemy/chemistry, specifically the art of separating and recombining substances</note>. At least from this, it is established by continuous necessity that air is drawn inward for a specific purpose: so that it may make the blood of the veins (which otherwise would not be dispersible by our heat, but rather condensable) plainly volatile, without any memory of a remaining **caput mortuum** <note>literally "dead head"; the useless solid residue left after distillation or chemical transformation</note>. In fish, however, the blood is not made volatile by heat, but by the vital ferments of the parts,

Because it is inseparable from heat, when the more watery part of the blood has exhaled, the remainder becomes clumpy and finally degenerates into a dry mass, unless by the unceasing drawing in of air and its union in the bed of the lungs and chest, the air itself is mixed into the sulfur of the blood, like a separator of waters, and carries out the sulfur—changed in its final state—together with the watery vapor, through **insensible Gas** <note>original: "Gas insensibile"; Van Helmont’s term for a vital, invisible vapor produced in chemical or biological reactions, distinct from ordinary air</note> transpired.

<margin>46.</margin>
This was not a mere function of cooling (as the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic medical tradition based on the ancient teachings of Galen and Aristotle</note> have thought, who are accustomed to measuring everything by heat and cold) but, with the addition of the **vital ferment** <note>original: "vitali fermento"; Helmont believed "ferments" were the chemical agents or catalysts responsible for all biological transformations</note> of the arteries (perhaps for this reason, and especially because the arteries accompany the veins throughout the whole body), it was a work of greater importance and necessity. And so, the pulse is no more for fanning away the **soot** <note>original: "fuligines"; in Galenic medicine, these were the smoky waste products of the heart's "innate heat"</note> of the blood than the blood is for the pulse, nor vice versa; but it serves most of all (besides the structure, illumination, and continuity of the vital spirit) to prepare the blood for exhalation without a **dead head** <note>original: "caput mortuum"; an alchemical term for the useless, inert residue left behind after a substance has been distilled or burned</note>, which is indeed entirely required by nature. Not indeed to chase away the soot produced by heat (though no soot properly exhales from moist things), but rather to prevent the ordinary actions of heat from generating vapors (which they indiscriminately call soot). Or to speak more accurately, to prevent the remaining part of the blood from thickening and causing total destruction once the vapors have departed from it.

<margin>47.</margin>
Consider how, when a finger is aching, hot, and wounded, an unusual pulse immediately shows itself in that place, because the entry of air to the blood hunted there and held in the edges is hindered. And there is a fear that the blood will congeal and

<margin>48.</margin>
harden into **pus**. But once the pus is formed, that fear is diminished, because it stops in its finished state. For before the wound, a hidden pulse, and soon a violent one, arises there, even before heat or the presupposed soot were present. Likewise also, as soon as some harm attacks the inter-

<column-break/>

nal membranes, the artery immediately, in a marvelous way, hardens throughout the whole person, and produces a hard, tense, vibrating, and even **saw-like** <note>original: "serratilem"; a historical medical term for a pulse that feels jagged or irregular, like the teeth of a saw</note> pulse.

<margin>49.</margin>
But by no means (as the Schools suppose) because the artery is dried out so that it might foretell what is in the heart, and reveal to the healer the quality and nature of the affected part. (Which is ridiculous!) For nature everywhere applies itself to maturing, promoting, or removing causes intentionally; it does not in any way concern itself with producing pathological, diagnostic, or prognostic signs. For these signs are noted and observed by the healer by accident and beyond the intent of nature. For if in the progress of nature something contingent is drawn into our knowledge, that is for nature an accident and entirely foreign; nature does nothing (except the stars) with the intention of foretelling. But whatever it does, it does from a command, which is its endowed property. Therefore, the artery does not produce a hard pulse because it has become more arid and drier; for there would be no hope, after the drying of the membrane, for an ever softer pulse, nor for the re-moistening of a part once dried out. Let old age itself be the witness, dry and juice-less. Finally, the channel or tube of the artery does not harden as a sign: but as a cause, end, and means of another intention. Surely, if the teaching of the Schools is true—that arteries pulse for the purpose of drawing in air to cool the heart—certainly if they were perpetually mindful of their own teaching as they should be, the arteries would at least draw in air more conveniently through that hardness of tension; since otherwise a soft artery collapses while drawing in, creeping like a worm, and falls in on itself in waves; and thus its mouth, which gapes open in hardness, is closed in looseness.

<margin>50.</margin>
Therefore, a hardened pulse indicates a contracted artery, but not a dried one. For if the pulse were produced for the purpose of revealing defects and the quality of parts, certainly in **apoplexy** <note>a sudden loss of consciousness or movement, similar to a modern stroke</note> the pulse would be very soft (because the brain, a completely medullary part, is determined to be the afflicted part), yet it is always hard there,

...and strong. Likewise, an **ossifragium** <note>original: "ossifragium"; literally "bone-breaker," likely referring here to a specific type of painful, hardening abscess or bone-related inflammation</note> would make the pulse the hardest of all. And once pus has already been formed, the pulse would be greater and more frequent than while it is being formed. This is because the preceding labor [of formation] brought about a lack of spirit, and the present pus or putridity needs quick ventilation. Similarly in a **phlegmon** <note>original: "phlegmone"; a term used in ancient and early modern medicine for a hot, red inflammation or localized swelling</note>, the **systole** <note>the contraction of the heart/arteries</note> would be more timely and much more manifest than the **diastole** <note>the expansion of the heart/arteries</note>.
<margin>51.</margin>
Since in the reality of the fact these things are not so, it is necessary that the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic medical tradition based on the ancient teachings of Galen and Aristotle</note> have erred regarding the purposes of the pulse. Furthermore, the coat of the artery, upon the arrival of sweat—however much harder it was before—softens again, even though there would then be a greater necessity for exploding away **soot** <note>original: "fuliginis"; according to Galenic theory, "sooty" vapors were the waste products of the heart's heat that needed to be exhaled</note> than for drawing in air. The artery, I say, ought then to be open and harder with frequent compression; it should not, with a large pulse, sink down more slowly like waves. Finally, in diseases of the lung, which is near the heart and filled on all sides with so many veins, arteries, and cartilages, the pulse is loose and wavy—and in an abscess of pus, with a certain intermission. The lung, I say, in its explosions of soot, most inconveniently timely, would need the hardest, most tense, and strongest pulse. Or perhaps is the double coat of the artery already soaked with the coming sweat? Does it soften thus far from an external moisture? Is it otherwise devoid of moisture? Will it resume its hardness after an hour of sweating? And will it compensate for its dryness with an alternating softness almost at will? For how full of weakness are the healing theorems of the Schools? Since in the aforementioned lung patients, a very loose artery and a wavy pulse reveal to us that breathing is given in obedience to the chest. For Nature is aware that there would be no need for a hurried pulse, nor for a stretched artery, where breathing takes up its duty first for the chest, and consequently or secondarily for the rest of the body; by this very thing it is shown to us that the use of breathing is for another end and another part than those over which the pulse is set. Therefore, as often as there is need for much air—instead of blood dispersed through the veins—so that it may volatilize that which threatens to become hardened, so often does the artery 

<column-break/>

tighten, stretch, and contract itself, but it is not dried out. That air, however, is drawn in not for the nourishment of the spirits, or the explosion of soot; but entirely as that which is in itself a **separator of waters from waters** <note>A reference to Genesis 1:6, here used in an alchemical sense to describe a substance that facilitates the separation of pure nutrients from waste fluid</note>, it may add a spur to the **ferment** <note>Van Helmont’s term for the chemical catalysts of life</note> of the final digestion, so that it may expel the whole nutritious liquor after its duties, without any of its own residue remaining.

Therefore, the inhaled air serves this ferment, not for cooling, not for the food of the spirit, nor as a bellows for soot. Otherwise, even the looseness of the artery is incapable of inhaling enough air. But the coming and prepared sweat, since it is already volatile in itself and flows out readily as far as the fluid, does not require much labor, nor the hardening of the artery. For as strengths fail, before the pulse becomes "creeping," it is wavy. Indeed, Nature having been weakened, she no longer contemplates a great labor. 

But the **apoplectic** <note>relating to a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note> pulse is the greatest and by far the hardest of pulses, especially near death. The Schools wish this to happen because they believe the pulse and breathing have the same inseparable necessity and end. Insofar as (they say) the heart wishes to compensate for the lack of breathing. But in the **uterine faints of virgins** <note>original: "syncopes virginum uterinae"; likely referring to what was then called "hysterical suffocation," a condition attributed to the movement of the womb</note>, in which breathing is extinguished and the strengths are strong (for they usually recover from it), the pulses are very small, in refutation of the preceding doctrine. So likewise the pulse of lung patients is wavy and languid, for whom Nature ought nevertheless to busy herself with the shortage of breathing. 

In apoplexy, however, why the pulse is hard and large must be investigated from the nature of the disease. Which I shall touch upon once in a formal book and in my treatise on the stone. Now, due to the proximity of the matter, I shall set forth two aphorisms. 
<margin>52.</margin>
The first of which is: *While pus is being made, there is greater labor and pain than when pus has been made.* Every **apostema** <note>original: "apostema"; an abscess or swelling</note> ending in pus necessarily contains an acidity which forces the blood into a clot. And therefore thereafter it is incapable of transpiration; wherefore Nature moves every stone <note>original: "omnem movet lapidem"; an idiom meaning she leaves no stone unturned</note>, and excites the arteries and breathing, so that through the air, the ferments may prevent an effect of this kind. And finally, accomplishing nothing, she ceases from that...

by nature. For not only is the **blood** <note>original: "cruor"; specifically the thicker, darker part of the blood</note> harmful to nature as it begins to clot, but also because it contains something foreign (for otherwise an **abscess** <note>original: "apostema"</note> would not form). Indeed, it is the property of an **acid** to coagulate all immediate nourishment; hence, pus is formed. Therefore, **Hippocrates** spoke more correctly than **Galen** when he said: *It is not hot or cold, etc., that are diseases: but the acid, the sharp, the bitter, and the harsh.* For as soon as a wound senses corruption, its edges swell and pus is created, unless a more violent force compels something worse, such as a watery discharge or foul matter, to flow out. Among the **unlearned** <note>original: "Idiotis"; meaning those without formal medical training</note>, pus is called "the good digestion of a wound," though it should more rightly be judged as the lesser of two evils. Truly, if a wound is fresh and protected from corruption by a balsam, no pus arrives. But when an **acidity** <note>original: "acor"</note>, which is the indicator of rot, contracts the bottom or the edges of the wound, pus is made. Often, indeed, worms are seen in wounds because of the decay. Even in kitchens, if meats begin to spoil, their juices turn sour. 
<margin>53.</margin>
For this reason, every wound-healing potion ought to contain a hidden **alkali**—and a volatile one at that—if it is to resist the accidents born from the acidity of corruption. This is because any alkali destroys every acidity it touches. In this way, **crab’s stones** <note>original: "lapis cancrorum"; also known as "crab's eyes," these are calcium carbonate concretions found in the stomachs of crayfish, used historically as an antacid</note> are diuretic and good for wounds, as is well known. For after being soaked in wine for a day, they taste like **lye** <note>original: "lixivium"; an alkaline solution</note>. 
<margin>54.</margin>
Another aphorism says: *The bellies are by nature warmer in winter than in summer.* However, the term **cavities** <note>original: "κοιλίαι" (koiliai); Helmont argues the Greek term refers to body cavities in general, not just the stomach</note> means "cavities," not "bellies." This aphorism is counterfeit; it does not match the neighboring passages, nor does it suit the genius of the Old Man <note>Hippocrates</note>. Finally, it is primarily false. For in winter, I eat hot things and drink liquids that are at least not cold; yet, after eating, I feel cold inside. I feel none of these things in summer. Indeed, in matters of touch, I take the sense of touch as the judge. The **Schools** <note>The Scholastic followers of Galen</note> make excuses, saying that external cold drives our internal heat inward, resulting in more successful digestion. First of all, I have sufficiently taught elsewhere that digestion does not come from heat. Secondly, after a meal, the internal cold is felt more in winter than in summer. 
<margin>55.</margin>
I do indeed admit that all heat comes from the **vital spirit** of the blood. If, therefore, through the cold, the spirit were driven inward along with the blood,

<column-break/>

there would be a danger of suffocation, and the pulse would give an indication of it, if the purpose of the pulse is to expel **sooty vapors** <note>original: "fuligines"; in Galenic theory, these were waste products of the heart's "fire" that needed to be exhaled</note>. Likewise, the pulse would be larger and faster in winter than in summer, if the hypothesis of the Schools were true. But the consequence is false: therefore, the hypothesis is also false. Or, if they want only the heat itself to flee inward, without the spirit, they must unwillingly admit that the same **accident** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like heat) that cannot exist without a "subject" (like matter)</note> can migrate between subjects. Finally, why would heat go inward toward its own source? And would this happen generally in everyone during winter? Could a healthy heart—which, due to an abundance of heat and fear of soot, would pulse with continuous necessity—not provide enough heat for itself because of the winter? Or why does it not stop pulsing rather than seeking back the heat it sent out, as if it were in ordinary poverty? The Schools skip over these matters with a light foot, as is their custom. 
<margin>56.</margin>
For they say that more food is consumed in winter than in summer because of the abundance of heat. And again, they predict a more abundant heat in winter because of the greater need for food. Namely, the same thing, in the same respect, would be the cause and the effect of itself—Father and Son, before and after itself. I, however, blame the air. Whenever the air is colder, it is also closer to its own natural quality and is a more powerful **separator of waters**; thus, it volatilizes the blood more into **Gas** <note>Van Helmont's coined term for a vital, spiritualized vapor, derived from the word "Chaos"</note> the colder the air is. This is no different from what has been said about sailors. Otherwise, the dreams of the Schools vanish regarding the heat of cavities and wells, as measured by an instrument that gauges the qualities of the surroundings. Regarding the human belly, it is the same if one stays in a lukewarm **heated room** <note>original: "hypocausto"</note>. The sensory organs, however, cannot exquisitely distinguish moments of heat when there is a six-month interval between them. This is because the organs themselves stand subject to the alterations of the seasons. Therefore, the application of sensible things to the organ of sense is deceptive due to the different seasons. Stomachs also seem warmer in winter because we require more food. And it is no wonder, because in summer we drink more freely instead.

<meta>catchword: tur.</meta>

<summary>Van Helmont challenges the Hippocratic aphorism that the body is warmer in winter, arguing instead that acidity causes inflammation (pus) and that digestion is not driven by heat. He critiques the Scholastic "Schools" for circular reasoning regarding internal heat and introduces his concept of "Gas" as a product of blood volatilization influenced by cold air.</summary>

only this last use of the pulse. Finally, I add this: there is no "animal spirit" <note>The traditional Galenic idea of a third spirit refined in the brain</note> in nature. Because the change that the vital spirit receives in the brain is not for a formal transformation; rather, it is a perfecting step toward its own destiny. <margin>§ 8.</margin> For the innate spirit intends to generate something like itself from the vital inflow, and it does this in each of the workshops of the senses, giving to that spirit the seal of its own organ. In this way, the optic spirit does not taste; yet the two do not differ in their fundamental nature, even if they differ in their duties. For in the vitality of the heart, it is animated once by the mind, and it becomes the mind's universal organ of life.

The Schools <note>Traditional academic medicine based on Galen and Aristotle</note> affirm that an endemic disease is drawn into the body from the surroundings through the arteries. I, however, was the first to doubt this, supported by many reasons and the great authority of truth. Consequently, I also believe that ointments applied to the pulse points for the purpose of being drawn inside are useless. First, these propositions contradict each other: "Air is drawn through the skin into the arteries," and "The contraction of the pulses is for the purpose of expelling soot <note>original: "fuligines"; waste vapors from the heart's "fire"</note> produced successively by the heart." <margin>3.</margin> For if soot is continuously produced by continuous heat, and the heart and arteries labor without ceasing to expel it, then certainly there will be no room or time for the movement of drawing air from the outside in. <margin>4.</margin> For if there is a successive, continuous, and unceasing expulsion of pulses from the center of the heart through the arteries, then the entire arterial channel must necessarily be filled with a continuous thread of soot from the heart all the way to the skin. Since the necessity of expelling this soot would be greater than the need to draw in air (for a fire is extinguished very quickly by smoke, but it is not consumed quite so quickly by a lack of cooling), there is no time allowed for the attraction of air. ...would increase the need for expulsion rather than satisfy the cooling of the heart. Therefore, as long as the hypothesis of soots <note>the traditional Galenic theory that the body produces "sooty" vapors as waste from "burning" blood, which must be expelled via the breath and pulse</note> stands, outside air is in no way drawn inward through the arteries. Thus, the Schools <note>referring to the established university medical authorities of the time</note> dictate their views without foresight, and yet they all subscribe to one another’s ideas. <margin>5.</margin> Indeed, from that same hypothesis, it follows that the artery would not rise by itself or as its primary action: but would only be raised primarily so that it might collapse, and finally by that effort lay down its burden and drive away the fear of suffocation. Since that would be the chief purpose of the pulses, the other—which is cooling—would become secondary compared to the first. Finally, if the arteries sucked in air, for what purpose, I ask, would that be done, when the struggle with the cruder local air <note>original: "endemici aeris," referring to air specific to a region which might be harmful</note> would do more harm than good? For it would not be for the sake of cooling the heart: since each individual pulse could hardly attract even a tiny bit of air through the smallest and outermost openings of the arteries. Would that air not be expelled immediately by the depression of the artery before it could be drawn further? Indeed, it would most quickly be united with the soot and heated by the arterial blood, so that the heart would feel no cooling within itself. This is especially true because that air would not reach the heart from the skin in a single draw, but with the many intervening depressions of the artery, it would grow so hot on the way that it would escape all hope of cooling. Therefore, if the arteries drew in air from the outside, the rising of the artery would necessarily always far exceed the depression in speed and size: which is a false conclusion. Furthermore, it is impossible that the air would keep its cooling quality untainted while being introduced gradually through so many winding paths of the arteries. Finally, the artery would not draw in air so that the vital spirit <note>the life-force believed to be carried in the blood</note> might take an increase from it. This is because, by the consensus of the Schools, the vital spirit is not made from air, but from the vapor of the blood, refined to the utmost in the heart and marked with the vital faculty. It is a dull assertion which supposes that the vital spirit is nourished by a simple element. For we are nourished by the same things from which we are generated. Therefore, since the air drawn in is an elemental body, it does not have

<column-break/>

the nature of the blood-spirit; and since air can never be made individual to a person by human determination, it cannot nourish a concrete body. As I have taught in its proper place. Rather, it always keeps the properties of a universal element and does not acquire the condition of the Archeus <note>Van Helmont’s term for the internal "master" or vital principle that governs the life of an organism</note>. For air is neither related to us, nor is it capable of vital light. Therefore, the artery will shrink from "exotic" air that has not first been refined in the proper workshops of the body to be adopted into its family. Nature attempts nothing in vain; she does not try to prepare air to become something for which it has no possible inclination. Otherwise, the vital spirit would be made in vain through so many expenditures and workshops of the digestive organs if it could be matured from the outside with such a light shortcut and without any cost. For the Schools have been deceived because it has been believed until now that fire must necessarily be nourished by air: and therefore, the vital spirit, as the author of all our heat, must need the element of air for its food. But I have already clarified above that fire is neither a substance, nor is it nourished by air, nor even by combustible matter—except that in hastening toward the end of its destination, it requires something flammable as an object, but not as nourishment. When the object is lacking, fire perishes in an instant once the goal of its destination is achieved. Indeed, since it is neither a substance nor an accident <note>a philosophical term for a non-essential property</note>, it also perishes from a lack of an object, because its object is also its subject. And so this is a most singular thing about it, and unknown until now. <margin>6.</margin> Therefore, the purpose for which external air would be drawn through the skin into the arteries ceases, the method ceases, and the possibility ceases, while the hypothesis of soots stands. Finally, if the artery were to suck in air through the pulse, it would suck it in indiscriminately, including regional [endemic] impurities, and thus such an attraction would be harmful. I have noted that this is false through frequent experience. <margin>7.</margin> Especially because whenever a foreign plague is contracted from the outside through breathing <note>original: "anhelitum"</note>, its adaptation <note>its initial take-over of the body</note> does not happen except near the stomach. This is made clear through the sensation of the place, anxieties, vomiting, sighs, headaches <note>original: "Cephalalgias"</note>, and delirium.

# ENDEMIC DISEASES.

Therefore, the part within us that perceives and forms the first movements of apprehension also feels the first attacks of the plague. I certainly grant that the plague is contracted by contact with a contaminated thing, and that pain is felt immediately, like the prick of a needle. But this does not prove that a flow of air occurs through the arteries, where the poison itself is suited to infect the skin and immediately burn it into a scab <note>original: "efcharam" or eschar; a piece of dead tissue that falls off from a wound</note>. It is, of course, one thing for the plague to be drawn inside through the arteries, or enticed by suction; and quite another for it to creep inward through contact, like the bite of a serpent, by the power of its own contagion. For plasters, baths, and oils alter the skin, and consequently they either proceed to alter further or they draw from the center to the skin—but it is not the case that material vapors sought from there are drawn inward.

<margin>8.</margin>
Next, the pulse does not function like respiration, which exhales whatever air is in the chest with a single breath; rather, the motion of the pulses is interrupted by its opposite, and is so frequent that it is exhaling no less than it is inhaling. Those alternating movements hasten so much that if they had drawn in any air, it would enter to no purpose, since it would be beaten out again in an instant. For whatever is closer to the openings would also be the first to be blown out. Thus, air would have no hope of ever being admitted more deeply, or of satisfying the cooling of the heart.

<margin>9.</margin>
Finally, the vital spirit lacks the generative power that would lead air through a formal transformation into spirit. Since that power belongs to the ferment and the "workshops" <note>the specialized organs or "offices" of the body where physiological changes occur</note>, without which blood is not made. For neither can blood generate blood; and even if the stomach's chyle <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note> were present in a vein or artery, blood would never be produced from it there. Therefore, air, even if it were a suitable body, could not become the nourishment of the vital spirit unless it had first been elaborated in the heart, made vivid, and individually illuminated according to the human species. Each of these requirements is at odds with the nature of the element [of air].

<margin>10.</margin>
Therefore, that failed invention is a trifling thing; the "cooling of the heart" by air drawn inward through the arteries is a fiction. And the "human Magnet" celebrated by Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a famous physician who used the metaphor of a "magnet" to describe how the body attracts substances from the environment</note> is likewise a fiction. Since the arteries suck nothing

<column-break/>

inward: air introduced in this way would be a greater burden to the arteries than the "soot" <note>original: "fuligo"; in old medicine, this referred to the "smoky" waste products believed to be produced by the heart’s heat</note> imagined by the Schools. If, therefore, the arteries do not draw in air, the flesh—which lacks cavities and is unfriendly to air—would certainly do so much less. Indeed, just as it is a mere invention that air is drawn from the outside to the heart through the arteries for its cooling, nourishment, and the increase of the spirit of the Archeus <note>the "Archeus" is Van Helmont's term for the vital governing principle or "internal master" of the body</note>: so it is an equally frivolous invention of the Schools that the sheer necessity of exploding the soot born in the heart would cause the arteries to depress <note>referring to the contraction or "systole" of the pulse</note>. <margin>114</margin> Indeed, in the preceding section I have already shown other purposes of the pulses at length. For whatever is made in the heart is either a pure being, entirely refined, and vital. For there is no "burnt-smelling" combustion <note>original: "empyreuma"</note> there, nor dryness, nor an efficient cause of soots. For it is foolish to have compared the factory of life to a destroying fire in such a way that one must imagine blood being burned there and giving off smoky soots. For if any foreign "outflows" <note>original: "aporrhoeæ"</note> occasionally reach the heart’s boundaries in an unnatural way, we immediately feel the "rhythm-less" <note>original: "arythmos"</note> failures of palpitations and intermittent storms. But if the production of soot were ordinary to the heart, how would it be separated from the vital spirit? And by what wall would they remain divided from one another? How would an "explosion" of soot be possible that did not simultaneously pour out the vital spirit intimately mixed with it? Are the Schools so devoid of pure doctrine that they cannot allow anything unpolluted, anything without excrement-like and dung-filled soot? Do they think the essential duties of life belong indifferently to both soot and the spirit of life? And that they have been mixed together until now? How could the depression of the artery tend toward a good end, destined by the Creator, if it blew out the vital spirit mixed together with the soot? Would that not bring death and destruction immediately? How could the Arbiter of things Himself, who is to be most highly honored, not have made death out of the contraction <note>original: "systolen"</note> of the pulse, even in the man He created? Finally...

...finally, if soot were the rhythm of the pulses (as they claim), who would be that separator who would force the soot out into the flesh rather than allowing it to go straight to the head through the aortas? What if the compression of the arteries were dedicated to the expulsion of soot? Since the arteries are pierced on the sides, so that they grant spirit and vital forces to the places they pass through, they would also expel soot there at the same time. This would surely be more harmful to all the internal organs than to the arteries themselves, because the arteries are thought to be refreshed by fresh air, but the organs are not. If they want soot to be expelled by the compression of the arteries, let them first show us that soot cannot be purged except through the final openings of the arteries, and that too while the spirit remains safe, though mixed with the soot. The Schools certainly maintain a doctrine polluted by soot <note>original: "fuligine"; Van Helmont is using a play on words here, suggesting their teaching is as "dirty" as the soot they describe</note>, and by the blind persuasion of laziness, they subscribe to their own guiding spirit, Galen.

<margin>¶ 12.</margin> Since they were ignorant of the matter, heat, sediment, content, and circulation of urine, and passed over the efficient cause of the pulses; and since they fled primarily to "heats" and "colds" and neglected the true goals, the entire <term>Tecmarsis</term> <note>From the Greek "tekmarsis," meaning the art of diagnostic signs or conjecture</note> of healing remained polluted. The Schools, therefore, have prophesied as if from a tripod <note>A reference to the Delphic Oracle's tripod; he implies they speak with unearned authority</note>, both in the knowledge of diseases and in their progress and end. Which I will later prove much more clearly.

<margin>¶ 13.</margin> Endemic diseases, therefore, wherever and however they in-

<column-break/>

-trant, affect everything: namely the head, the chest, and their subordinates. As much as they are powerful, so much do they work and achieve. For some imprint a stain on a part and then depart. Such as misty, foul-smelling, or rotten things. But some enter in the form of smoke and are inhaled as minerals, which are then coagulated inside in various ways. For some are spat out with phlegm, if they are not harmful. Others, however, cling tenaciously to the walls of the lung-pipes <note>original: "cannarum pulmonum"; refers to the bronchi</note> for life, and exercise their tyranny in their host. To this kind belongs whatever "smokes out" from the veins of minerals. Wherefore the smoke of minerals, because of its malice and arsenical poison, has become synonymous: for Arsenic and soot—or the smoke of metals—coincide. From this come hoarseness, heart tremors, fainting, asthma, pleurisy, pneumonia, coughs, bloody spit, consumption, abscesses, etc. Meanwhile, it is not clear that endemic diseases are drawn through the arteries, nor that they are immediately affected. But if Mercury produces tremors, at least that is irrelevant to the arteries. Nor do those whose bodies were treated with mercury ointments tremble for that reason; instead, they suffer from blisters in the mouth and throat, the uvula falls away, they develop ulcers, their teeth wobble and turn black, the head swells, and they salivate immense amounts of foul-smelling fluid. Likewise, the gilders, miners, and those who separate mercury, because they inhale a poison lethal to the head and the nerves, produce endemic diseases in us as much as they can.

<image-desc>Ornamental capital letter D decorated with floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
**I** have already discussed the **Archeus** <note>The internal "master craftsman" or vital force that governs growth and health</note> as the craftsman within the seed, and how he disposes all things both in generation and in the transmutations of food throughout the course of life. This duty properly belongs to the **innate spirit** <note>original: "spiritum insitum"</note>. Now, however, concerning how and from where the spirit fluctuating in the arteries is constituted—following the occasion of the **human Blas** <note>Van Helmont's term for the motive power or vital rhythm of an organ</note> already described—I have undertaken to explain their office and properties along this path.
<margin>1.</margin>
The **Schools** <note>The traditional academic medical establishment following Galen and Aristotle</note> teach that nourishment is first changed into **chyle** <note>milky fluid of digested food</note>, then into **chyme** <note>partially digested food</note> and **blood** <note>original: "cruorem"</note>, and so in the liver a certain **natural spirit** is formed, which, after a repeated digestion in the heart, is changed into the **vital spirit**, and finally in the brain becomes the **animal** or **sensory spirit**. Thus, the natural spirit is for nourishing the parts; the vital spirit is for preserving them; and the animal spirit is destined for the functions of the senses, motion, and the soul. But I believe one must philosophize far differently and progress further. For they knew of a certain spirit from **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek father of medicine</note> called the **source of motion** <note>original: "impetum faciens"</note>. Yet it was not enough to know that there was a certain spirit, or to have said by which organs it was made or what it did, unless they simultaneously explained its nature, substance, and properties, along with 
<margin>2.</margin>
its mode of formation. Elsewhere I have taught that from any plant or fruit, once the proper **ferment** <note>The agent of chemical transformation, similar to yeast</note> is applied, **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitae," referring here to distilled alcohol or spirits</note> is made. Since this is commonly known—while one manufactures water of life from grains, mead, and juices— 
<margin>3.</margin>
the proposition requires no further demonstration. Now, water of life is a volatile, oily liquor (insofar as it is entirely flammable) and entirely "salty" (insofar as it is sharp and biting; if held in the mouth for too long, it would burn the skin

<column-break/>

of the gums and lips). It is one and the same simple substance, thus containing only two, and not three, chemical principles <note>Van Helmont argues against the standard "Three Principles" (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) of Paracelsus here</note>. Indeed, it is such that, at the craftsman's will, the entire "water of life" may become salt or oil. This means those principles are not fixed starting points, but are changeable by human choice. 
<margin>4.</margin>
However, wine contains within its vinous part a spirit corresponding to the water of life; for this, without the ripening of other workshops <note>meaning other organs or digestive stages</note>, is snatched through the arteries of the stomach to the head. Thus, if more than what is right is present in 
<margin>5.</margin>
the stomach, drunkenness follows, because the spirit of wine flows more abundantly into the head than can be transformed in a convenient interval by the **human individuating determination** <note>The specific vital force that gives a human their unique identity</note>. For from this, the transformation is established, as well as 
<margin>6.</margin>
the operation of the ferment. Nevertheless, in wine, that spirit is milder than the "water of life" which is drawn out through distillation. This is seen similarly in olive oil. For the distilled version (which they call **oil of bricks** or the **oil of the philosophers**) differs far from the oiliness that is drawn from simple oil through mere digestion with the **circulated salt of Paracelsus** <note>A specific alchemical solvent supposedly capable of reducing substances to their first matter</note>. For the circulated salt is separated, identical in power and weight, after it has divided the olive oil into its different parts. For a sweet and double oil is separated from olive oil, just as a most pleasant spirit is separated from wine, set far apart from the sharpness of the water of life. From this, I consequently learned that whatever

Therefore, let it be understood that there are as many varieties of rotting, and as many different kinds of dung from one type of bread, as there are species of animals nourished by bread. Nay, furthermore, there are far more ferments of bread,
<margin>9.</margin> since bread rots in many more ways, as much spontaneously as by design. For what is said of bread, let as much be said of other foods. The **Schools** <note>The traditional academic authorities following Galen and Aristotle</note> indeed knew that nothing profits us which did not contain in its root a prelude to life (and therefore they admit air for the sake of increasing the spirit, deceived by the warnings of the poets who speak of "vital breezes"); they wanted, namely, in the **cruor** <note>raw, venous blood before it is fully vitalized</note>, a hepatic <note>liver-related</note> spirit to be natural,
<margin>10.</margin> existing in act, and flickering like a breeze. They thought, namely, that it was a vapor; unaware that vapor never becomes an uncoagulable <term>Gas</term> <note>Van Helmont's own term for a substance that cannot be condensed back into liquid</note>, a breeze, ether, or <term>wild exhalation</term> <note>original: "exhalatio sylvestris," Van Helmont's term for the gas produced by charcoal or fermenting wine</note>: but always remains water. They thought, therefore, that the vapor exhaling from blood drawn from the veins (just as from any warm liquid) was that spirit of the blood, from which the **vital spirit** would be materially manufactured. But truly the **cruor**, as long as it flows in the vessels of the Mesentery and the Portal vein, is devoid of spirit. Wherefore, even when summoned by laxatives, it is excreted rotten, without any notable sign of weakness: which does not happen so, if it has once reached the *vena cava*. Since then, homogeneously, the **cruor** is sealed with a prelude, so that it may become the blood of the artery and the spirit; and therefore, indifferently along with the blood, it is called in the Sacred Scriptures
<margin>11.</margin> the **red spirit**, in which the soul dwells. Although that is properly understood of the blood: inasmuch as the Scripture speaks in that same place of those whose throats are cut or who are killed, in whom the **cruor** is poured out together with the blood. At some time I will teach about digestions, that whatever is prepared in the stomach is made sour by the ferment there (even sugar itself), not indeed with the acidity of vinegar, unripe grapes, lemon, or vitriol; but by its own equal ferment,

<column-break/>

And that acid of foods is perfectly volatile. Nor does it stand in the way: that **chyle** in youths takes on the fixity of bone, as also in the fractures of bones. For the **chyle** of the stomach is the same after growth as it was for the youth. That whole [chyle] is finally blown away without any residue of itself: again it resumes the nature of bone in the Pore in the soldering of fractures. ...of growth, or by the separation of urine: but spirit is made by the thinning of what has been thickened. These two actions are so opposite that they cannot both belong to the liver alone. But if the **Schools** <note>The traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle</note> wish for the "natural spirit" to have pre-existed in food and to have received its perfection in the liver, [it would be lost]; for it easily evaporates by boiling, cooking, and roasting. And if any should happen to remain, it does not belong to the internal economy of our liver. I admit indeed that the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritum vini," meaning alcohol or ethanol</note> is the spirit of vegetables, and is easily snatched into the arteries as a simple "symbolizing" <note>an alchemical term meaning having shared properties or being compatible</note> substance, previously disposed to easily transcend into the **vital spirit**. But from this, the **Schools** prove nothing for their "hepatic" <note>liver-related</note> spirit. For the spirit of wine is snatched immediately from the stomach into the arteries without digestion, nor is it taken up through the stage of **cruor** <note>raw venous blood before it is vitalized</note> as a vital companion; from this, it is easily concluded that the vital spirit does not presuppose a natural one from the liver. And what I have said is clear: since those who suffer from fainting or tremors of the heart feel the spirit of wine admitted soon and immediately to the comfort of life; for even then they are not made drunk by a great abundance of wine.

<margin>13.</margin> Otherwise, while the wine still exists physically within the stomach, drunkenness proceeds from nowhere else than that the wine-spirit is snatched in abundance into the heart and head, and creates a confusion of the spirits already existing there, being himself a stranger not yet polished in the workshop of the heart. Let the **cruor** itself, therefore, be the "hepatic spirit," bodily, coagulated into matter, and the foundation for the vital economy. I allow this, as long as we understand it rhetorically: namely, that the cruor itself is the capable object and the matter from which spirit may then be made. But speaking philosophically, or properly, there is no spirit within the cruor made for it by the liver. This is because the labor of making blood, separating the watery fluid, urine, and sweat, falls upon the liver. Specifically, these things pass very quickly through the tiny sluice-gates of the small veins. For although the cruor may have undergone its "prelude" in the mesenteric vessels <note>veins connecting the intestines to the liver</note>, its true generation occurs—likewise the qualities of fibers and coa-

<column-break/>

gulation—during its very swift passage, along with its serum, through the tubes of hair-like thinness <note>Van Helmont is describing capillaries, though they were not yet fully understood by his contemporaries</note>. But if the generation of spirit were also to fall upon the liver: besides that generation being in vain, the liver would be overwhelmed by an excessive burden and a plurality of duties, like a donkey. It is enough for the cruor that, having become a citizen of the veins, it participates in life and is illuminated by the vital light. Therefore, just as by the ferment and labor of the heart, cruor becomes blood and volatile spirit: so, from the ferment taken from the arteries (the heart's deputy), they become so volatile that they leave behind no <term>amurca</term> <note>original: "amurcam," referring to the bitter dregs or sediment of oil</note> after their consumption, but depart by their total transpiration.

<margin>14.</margin> The heart, therefore, fashions blood from the **cruor**, which it fits and thins with the same effort; and it makes as much vital spirit in the blood as the thickness of the cruor and its resisting substance allows in that tiny space where it is agitated and shaken within the chambers of the heart. Indeed, it is not yet enough to know that cruor is spirit, and is likewise translated into arterial blood to give vital spirit, by whose favor it is informed by the mind and becomes animated. And from here at last, it is transferred into the chambers or "stomachs" of the brain, to receive there the various determinations of its character. Thus, it becomes the motive force in the spinal medulla, and the power of sight in the "optic workshops." If these spirits are led to the tongue by some error, they are plainly useless for taste. For this reason, it happens not rarely that fingers grow numb, or some movable part loses either sense or motion (leaving the other behind), because the parts are showered by a foreign or stray spirit.

<margin>15.</margin> For the authors of touch are unequal to motion, and vice versa. Furthermore, one must know the nature of the vital spirit. However, I have observed that they differ in an essential property: the spirit of the salt of **cruor** <note>raw venous blood</note> cures epilepsy, even in adults, whereas the spirit of the salt of urine does not. Therefore, it is clear that a salty and volatile spirit is contained within the cruor. But as to how the whole cruor, without any leftover waste, is transmuted by the **ferment of the heart** <note>the heart's unique catalytic power</note> into spirit—as much as can be said—I have explained in my treatise *On Long Life*. Because otherwise, the natures of things cannot be demonstrated from first principles, just as the operations of ferments cannot, because they are the essential causes in the transformations of <margin>17.</margin> things. The **vital spirit** is therefore saline, and thus **balsamic** <note>meaning it preserves against decay</note>, and a guardian against corruption; and this is not so much by reason of its salt, as by respect to the **light** conceived within its salt. Furthermore, air cannot become its addition or its nourishment. For although **aqua vitae** <note>literally "water of life," referring here to high-proof alcohol</note> is easily taken up into the vital spirit, this spirit is not oily or combustible; rather, the spirit of wine, by the mere touch of the ferment, easily ascends entirely into a volatile saline nature, so that it immediately loses its oily or <margin>18.</margin> flammable property. As I have shown through mechanical demonstration in the treatise *On Duelech* <note>Van Helmont's term for the formation of stones in the body</note>. Specifically, how in a single instant, aqua vitae is transmuted into a **white mass** <note>original: "offam albam," a reference to the "Offa Alba of Van Helmont," a chemical precipitate formed by mixing alcohol and ammonia</note> which is not flammable—which happens even more evidently to aqua vitae through the saline <margin>19.</margin> vital ferment. Therefore, the spirit of wine, without delay or further digestion, is immediately snatched into the heart through the arteries of the stomach, and restores the strengths, because it is perfected in the heart with very little labor. Yet it must not be thought that the vital spirit is acidic, just because the **spirit of saltpeter** <note>nitric acid</note> is mildly acidic and is eventually made from the spirit of urine. Because the spirit from which saltpeter is coagulated in the earth was not acidic while it was the spirit of urine. Thus, the vital spirit is salty, not acidic (for **acid** outside the stomach is hostile to the whole body), and it is closer to the spirit of urine than to saltpeter, and yet much more foreign to the spirit of saltpeter through

<column-break/>

burning, and the mixing of an added extract. Men easily perceive the saltiness of the vital spirit when they have had a numb limb, which, gradually regaining its sense of touch, suffers pricking and stinging—which are true signs of saltiness. The saltiness of the spirit can indeed be known; but its **light**, proceeding immediately and as from a fountain from the **Father of Lights** <note>a biblical reference to God as the source of all life and truth</note>, keeps away all further investigation by mortals. Furthermore, that the whole cruor is <margin>20.</margin> pure salt requires no stronger proof than that the whole cruor, in a uniform way, becomes **Ichor** <note>a thin, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer</note> through immediate degeneration in ulcers, **Ascites** <note>abdominal swelling caused by fluid accumulation</note>, etc. For the cruor is intensely red, but it becomes yellowish while it is being made into blood: because the redness turns yellow when it is dissolved, as it were, by the volatile salt. Whatever I have said so far is still a dead thing. The vital spirit performs the <margin>21.</margin> duties of life. However, the noble height of life does not belong to a liquor or an exhalation merely as they are salty. And so that it may live, it must necessarily have light from the Father of Lights, the life of all things. Therefore, it is necessary that the spirit, or **vital ether**, be illuminated by a light that is simply vital—and not even a universal light, but one that is specific and individualizing. Nor is it a fiery light, burning, inflaming, and visible in concentrated rays. Rather, it is a **formal light** <note>an animating essence or "form" in the Aristotelian sense</note>, belonging to the condition of the **sensitive soul**. At this word, the descriptions and further investigations of mortals must stop. To this end, imagine that **glow-worms** <note>original: "Nitedulas"</note> have light in their bellies toward nightfall (just as the bubbles of the sea have a nocturnal brightness, and many things which through rot proceed into the ultimate matter of salts). Yet this light is vital, and it is extinguished along with their life. Imagine a similar light in the spirit of life, which shines as long as it lives; and when it leaves the eyes of a dying man, they appear horny and defiled. And <margin>22.</margin> that light is sometimes extinguished while the matter of the vital spirit is still safe, as in the **Plague**, poison, **fainting** <note>original: "syncope"</note>, etc. Yet do not think that the essence of light is the same in us and in glow-worms, so that namely

# THE SPIRIT OF LIFE. #

...that lights differ only by a tone of degrees. <margin>3. 23.</margin> But in truth, there are as many species of vital lights as there are living creatures. This is an indication of the abundant divine generosity: that there are as many species and vital differences of lights (which we group under a single concept and word) as there are species of living things. Indeed, these lights are the very lives, souls, and forms of living beings. (I exclude the immortal mind, although it too is a certain incomprehensible light; I am dealing here with transitory lights.) Thus, through these lights themselves, all distinction of species exists. Therefore, the **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical title for God, here used to describe the source of all biological "vitality"</note> plays with an ineffable abundance of generic lights with much greater generosity than He does in the human face, where He shapes almost infinite varieties. There is, in fact, with Him a vast republic of lights and a legion of unremembered citizens, a likeness of which He expresses through the forms of living beings in the **sublunary world** <note>The earth, which in older cosmology was everything below the moon</note>. 

<margin>24.</margin> The **vital spirit** <note>original: "spiritus vitalis"</note>, therefore, is blood resolved by the **ferment of the heart** <note>a catalytic power Helmont believed resided in the heart</note> into a salty vapor and illuminated by life. This light in us is warm, of the nature of the Sun; yet it is cold in a fish, and never aspires to any power of heat. Therefore, our heat is not the consumer of the **original moisture** <note>original: "humidi primigenii," the internal fuel of life</note> (as I discussed in *On Long Life*), since fish have not escaped death thus far despite their coldness. <margin>25.</margin> Nor could the first men, who saw a thousand solar years before the flood, have had ten times more **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidi radicalis"</note> than we do, unless all their parts had been ten times larger. This is irrelevant. Since it is probable that Adam, fashioned by the hand of God, attained the most perfect stature—that of the Lord Jesus Christ—and did not exceed it. Finally, fish living under an icy sea would be naturally immortal if their radical moisture did not evaporate due to heat. There are some of our own religious men <note>likely referring to monks or friars in cold climes</note> who are so cold from their feet up to their bellies for almost the whole year that they do not feel they have feet. Therefore, they should at least 

<column-break/>

be longer-lived than us; indeed, their legs should remain youthful while the rest of their chest is shriveled with the wrinkles of age, if the consumption of the original moisture by heat was the inevitable cause of death. Likewise, both fish and such religious persons ought to refuse daily meals, because almost nothing would exhale through their pores. Or, if heat were of the essence of our life, certainly a body part languishing in continuous cold would either die or at least be transformed into a fish. <margin>26.</margin> From this it is evident that heat is merely an adjacent and accompanying sign of our life, but not its primary foundation. 

<margin>27.</margin> Let the **Schools** <note>the traditional academic establishment of the time</note> see, therefore, how ineptly they have restricted the entire **temperament of nature** <note>original: "naturae crasin," referring to the balance of bodily fluids</note> to heat until now. Far be it from us to philosophize so stolidly hereafter as to be ignorant that there is one kind of consumption of moisture by heat, which ends in thickening; and another quite different kind, which is promoted entirely toward transpiration by a thinning **ferment**. For the latter leaves no residue behind, while the former leaves behind a stone or charcoal. 

<margin>28.</margin> But if, at times, an increased heat rises within us so that it burns the limbs, causes gangrene, and like fire creates a scab, or sometimes eats away the flesh like a **gnawing dormouse** <note>original: "gliris," likely referring to phagedenic ulcers that "gnaw" like rodents</note>: these are indeed the works of corrosive, degenerate, and lawless salts, which have been proscribed from the vital Republic. Thus, through laxative poisons and diarrheas, the entire **cruor** <note>the thick part of the blood</note> is resolved into **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrilaginem"</note>; and through other poisons, the resolved blood flows out as **ichor** <note>watery discharge</note>, **synonia** <note>joint fluid or mucus</note>, venom, jaundiced excrement, and so on—often very sharp and burning with corrosive heat. For errors of this kind happen in life (they cease in a dead corpse) insofar as they take on a **thymosin** <note>a fermentative impulse or "vital anger"</note> from life itself, through the proper **Blas** <note>Helmont's term for the internal motive power or "pulse" of a living thing</note> of a corrupted nature. Thus life "heats the iron" with which it wounds itself in many ways, as I shall discuss regarding diseases. 

<margin>29.</margin> Finally, as to whether there is some "animal spirit" to be distinguished by species from the "vital spirit," or whether that dispute is merely a quarrel over names: I have said what the thing is in itself, to which a name can add or take away nothing. The vital spirit,

...through the Aorta arteries, it climbs into the head. In the middle of the brain, however, there is a single cavity <note>original: "sinus"</note>, which, when viewed from above, appears double; but when the "chamber" is lifted up, it reveals its unity. Furthermore, in this cavity, the arteries end in a certain wrinkled vessel <note>The choroid plexus, a network of blood vessels in the brain</note> of a completely different texture than the rest of the arterial structure. It is here, indeed, that the **vital spirit** flows out and exhales into the cavity of the brain to serve the primary faculties—namely, imagination, judgment, and memory. From here it also continues to be distributed into the openings of the nerves that begin in the brain. Thus, if it is to be called the **animal spirit** <note>In historical medicine, "animal" refers to the *anima* or soul/mind, distinguishing spirits of the brain from those of the heart (vital) or liver (natural)</note>, insofar as it receives its specific determination in the brain and acquires properties suited for its destined function, it does not, however, seem different from the vital spirit in its matter or its producing cause. Indeed, in the breadth of its own vital light, it is capable of all these properties without changing its native essence. For the same spirit that is pushed toward the tongue exercises the sense of taste, yet that same spirit does not taste in the fingers; rather, in both places, it takes on the particular character of the organs and puts on their property. If one's mind insists that it differs from the vital spirit, there would have to be as many essential divisions of spirits as there are duties, and as many ministries as there are pluralities of offices. Meanwhile, understand the matter and call it what you like: for I am not being contradictory out of some spirited passion against the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university authorities of the 17th century who followed ancient Greek and Roman medical theories</note>; I have simply been duty-bound, prompted by a higher authority, to reveal errors and teach what was unknown. If they detect my own errors with an equal mind, I shall truly rejoice, provided my neighbor attains the utility I hope for.

<margin>1.</margin> Because the entire foundation of nature is thought to turn on the hinge of heat, and the elements, mixtures, and temperaments have now been sent far away; therefore, to establish the lineage of the **Archeus** <note>The internal "vital architect" or biological spirit that Helmont believed directed the functions of the body</note> and the vital spirits, we must next speak of digestions. Because the Schools have enslaved these to heat, I will show that heat is not the proper organ of digestions. Indeed, the Schools were deceived by the metaphor of "digestion," introduced by a sort of poetic liberty borrowed from rustic common sense; they made **concoction** <note>original: "concoctionem," literally "cooking together"</note> a synonym for digestion. And since they knew that "boiling" was a form of concoction, they therefore transferred digestion to the category of boiling, and in both cases they judged heat to be the natural, total, and sole cause. For they saw that through boiling and roasting, many things become tender and are altered. Therefore, taking license from artificial things, they turned the kitchen into the wondrous transmutations of the viscers and food—not indeed in a similar way...
