# ->HEAT DOES NOT DIGEST AS AN EFFICIENT CAUSE,<-
# ->BUT ONLY STIMULATES.<-

...similarly: but they have handed it down entirely properly and closely, and through reputation this matter passed into belief, and then into a true dogma; they transferred all the duties and benefits of our nature into heats and temperaments, as if into total causes. This was mainly because they felt the bellies of humans and four-footed animals to be hot in actuality. Consequently, from then on, more effort was sweated out in increasing heat than in strengthening digestion. For they did not investigate further, even though the outcome often failed their hope. Thinking it sufficient that heat was found both in boiling <term>elixation; the process of boiling or stewing</term> and in the natural digestion of the belly, they fell asleep, expecting abundant help from it. Meanwhile they hesitated when they noticed that foods, through boiling, are not changed into juice by a complete metamorphosis. For they dissolved meats in a closed vessel into a finished broth—once the broth was pressed and strained—but they did notice the error, because the fleshy residues remained tenacious and hard, and would never liquefy into true **chyle** <term>The milky fluid of digested food produced in the stomach and intestines</term> through a true transmutation.
<margin>3.</margin> Yet through credulity and the antiquity of the error, they allowed their eyes to be veiled; seeking evasions and hiding places, they immediately thought themselves safe, provided they had implored different degrees of heat, if not even species and types (such as fiery, elemental, radical, corresponding to the element of the stars, etc.), and indeed the "moments" of heats, for help and excuse. So much so that for almost every moment of the degrees, there was its own constitution in di-
<margin>4.</margin> gesting. Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous physician and alchemist who often used chemical explanations for biology</note> also involved himself in this stupidity, wanting a single piece of bread, in so many species of animals, to take on a specific diversity of blood and dung, solely on account of the "moment" of the degree in heat. As if the breadth of heat could
<margin>5.</margin> establish a species, or vary it in substance. Furthermore, while the Schools presumed to have removed "every knot in the bulrush" <note>original: "scirpo nodum sustulisse"; a Latin idiom meaning to find a difficulty where there is none, or to solve a non-existent problem</note>, they then fell into spongy distinctions between natural digestive heat, and heat that is beside, or against nature.

<column-break/>

And finally, often against their will, they had to flee to the "sacred anchor" of hidden properties in digestions. This was so that, indeed, some heat would be the author of digestion, in disease as well as in health. Forgetting meanwhile that, just as they had
<margin>6.</margin> fashioned a single type of opposites, and each was spoken of in equal ways, so the condition of both should be single and uniform. Therefore they forgot to devise equal types and properties of cold. Namely, what sort of cold might be natural, digestive, and beside or against nature. Likewise, they ought to have taught some radical and original cold. Thus, if "radical heat" corresponds in proportion to the element of the stars and differs in its whole kind from any other warmth: then "radical cold" also ought to differ in just as many numbers and powers from any other cold, unless, for lack of truth, they are abandoning their wisdom as sterile. So indeed, although non-natural heat might proceed into natural heat, and vice versa, through an unheard-of license of women <note>likely a contemporary idiom meaning "fickle" or "unruly" reasoning</note>; nevertheless, they relegated native and febrile heat into distinct species (indeed even genera), so as to save the effects attributed to digestive heat. To the point that while they be-
<margin>7.</margin> lieved some birds consume things that otherwise defend themselves against the fury of fire, they acknowledged some "fire" more powerful than fire. For a dog consumes swallowed bones, which fire would never dare to convert into chyle. The diversities of these effects therefore forced the Schools to elevate heat into the "breadth of a predicament" <note>A term from Aristotelian logic meaning a broad category of being</note>, while neglecting the opposite colds in the meantime. Even though there is only a specific diversity of heat, which is unable to remove itself from the number of others.
<margin>8.</margin> For truly, whatever is taken into the stomach is finally transmuted once digestion is completed, and is far removed from boiling and other cookings prepared at any degree [of heat].
<margin>9.</margin> Because a single ignorance of **ferments** <note>Helmont’s key theory: that digestion is a chemical process of fermentation, not just heat</note> made digestions, and open...

# ->BUT ONLY AS A STIMULANT.<-

...remedies for <note>original: "ptiæ", likely referring to dyspepsia or indigestion</note> are unknown, and a fallacy of "non-cause as cause" is perpetrated. Therefore, this is no idle quarrel over mere names when fermental effects are ascribed to heat. Indeed, the resolution of this question changes the very intentions of healing. Consequently, I am accustomed to gladly inquire into the proper causes; for through the meditation upon these, utility follows, diseases tremble, and the vital strengths are invigorated. Therefore, the **ferments** <term>biological agents of transformation, similar to what we now call enzymes</term> are rightly indignant that they are believed to serve, against their will, under the principle of heat <note>original: "Helontio", a personification of heat or the sun-principle</note>. For it was never the nature of heat to lead a thing into a formal transformation. Since heat, by itself and primarily, does nothing but heat; yet by accident, it separates watery parts from the more stubborn ones. This uniform action of heat is by no means **digestion**, which is defined entirely by transformation. For even if digestion occurs in us with heat accompanying it, digestion itself is not heat, even if it is accidentally connected to heat.
<margin>10.</margin>
<margin>11.</margin>
For this reason, there is no actual heat in a fish, yet it does not digest less successfully than those warm-blooded animals; nor does it suffer ill from the things it has eaten, after the fashion of men.
<margin>12.</margin>
It is therefore frivolous to flee to the excuse of "potential heat" in the case of the fish. For in things perceived by the senses, the sense of touch alone is the Witness and Judge; one must not flee to dreams. For if digestion were to be attributed to heat—not to heat that is actually hot, but to a "virtual power"—then I have already gained my wish! Otherwise, what is that, I ask, but to quarrel ignorantly about heat as such, while meanwhile admitting there is something besides sensible heat that is the containing cause of digestion? For what can be said that is more foolish than that potential heat actually heats, and for the sake of this heating, digestion occurs? Shall a thing that exists only in "potential" now act "actually"? But at least in "canine hunger" <note>an insatiable, ravenous appetite</note> there is a very rapid digestion and an implacable hunger. Therefore, at such a time, a troublesome and hostile heat should be felt in us warm-blooded creatures, if digestion in us were performed by actual heat. For if a little heat causes a small digestion, and a moderate heat a moderate one: surely for a powerful

<column-break/>

and troublesome digestion, a great heat ought also to be present. Yet,
<margin>14.</margin>
although I have investigated this quite curiously several times, I have not found it to be true. Furthermore, this is notable: that the digestion of bread in a human, a dog, a horse, a fish, a duck, or a bird differs entirely in kind, no differently than the various types of blood and waste products born from them. For this reason, such varieties of digestion cannot arise from a single species of "digesting heat." Therefore, let the Schools establish and defend just as many types of heats and colds before they demand to be believed. I, therefore, take such a great difference in blood from the formal properties and specific ferments, and by no means from heat. Since
<margin>15.</margin>
I know perfectly well that whatever things have different essential efficient causes also have different effects and attributes. So it is that products different in kind necessarily require their own efficient causes that are different in kind. Otherwise, anything would produce anything else indifferently. Just as surely, one and the same thing arises from the same nearby causes. For how frivolous it is to have judged the vital and formal powers—the specific parents of transformations—to be the results of mere warmth?
<margin>16.</margin>
Truly, if digestion were the work of heat, a more successful and more abundant digestion would continuously follow a greater heat. For the more powerful any cause is in nature, the more powerfully it also perfects its own proper effect. Consequently, the stomach of a person with a burning fever <term>original: "causo", an acute, inflammatory fever</term> would digest more powerfully than that of a healthy person. But surely, in the stomach of a feverish person, nothing is rightly digested. For immediately,
<margin>17.</margin>
eggs, fish, meat, and broths turn into corpses <note>i.e., they rot or decompose</note> inside, and therefore they produce foul-smelling belches; if acidic belches follow these, **Hippocrates** <term>the famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</term> judged it to be a good thing, as much from the sign as from the cause. Yet there is heat in the feverish person; sometimes even that heat is temperate, specifically when it is not troublesome and does not excite thirst: nevertheless, digestion is hollow and useless.
<margin>18.</margin>
The more powerfully you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that heat is not the primary cause of digestion, citing the fact that cold-blooded fish digest well and that increased heat in feverish patients actually halts digestion. He concludes that specific "ferments" (enzymes) are the true agents of biological transformation, as evidenced by how different species produce different substances from the same food.</summary>

# ->HEAT DOES NOT DIGEST AS AN EFFICIENT CAUSE,<-

As is manifest in a person suffering from fever. In such a patient, one must immediately use the lightest food that is easy to digest. One must abstain from stronger foods, namely concentrated broths and juices: because in the absence of the **ferment** <term>the biological agent of digestion</term>, they easily putrefy, contract a foul stench <note>original: "nidorem", referring to the smell of burnt or rotting organic matter</note>, and are, as it were, turned into a corpse-like state. It is no different than if raw meat were tied to the breast, the soles of the feet, or the neck; far from being resolved into **chyle** <term>the milky fluid produced from digested food</term>, it soon putrefies and stinks after a few hours, even if it has been salted. The same occurs in an impure and feverish body, where heat is present but the digestive ferment is lacking. For if heat were the cause of digestion, then digestion would otherwise cease in a fever, yet heat is present; indeed, one would have to focus more on digestion than on cooling—especially if the heat is not excessively hostile.
<margin>19.</margin> Therefore, one should rather strive for the increase of heat than for cooling. Thus, the physician's aim would have to change: in a fever, one would have to think about increasing heat for the sake of digestion, nutrition, and the increase of strength. Nor would acidic things, "hungry" things <note>referring to sharp, corrosive substances</note>, or things of sulfur, vitriol, salt, nitre, citrus and the like be helpful; instead, heat would have to be excited and increased by sharp substances. He says something similar to madness who claims that snow cools insofar as it is white. So too is it ridiculous to assert that the specific ferment of the stomach digests because of the **vital heat** <note>the innate warmth believed by ancients to sustain life</note> existing within it. It is truly a cause for grief that the credulity and laziness of those to whom the care of life has been entrusted have turned cemeteries into mere dung-heaps, despairing of the investigation of physical properties—from which, nonetheless, they take their 
<margin>20.</margin> name <note>referring to "Physicians" or "Physicists"</note>. Paracelsus also, deluded by digestive heat and ignorant of the stomachic ferment, wondered that certain very hard things were changed into chyle in a few hours, and that bone was consumed in the warmth of a dog’s stomach. He, who aspired to a "Monarchy of Medicine," failed after he named this miraculous power; he was 
<margin>21.</margin> ignorant of it and did not know the ferments. For, being inconsistent with himself, he wrote elsewhere that this digestive property belongs no less to the closed mouth than to the

<column-break/>

stomach, and thus he claimed that Anchorites <note>religious recluses</note> happily spent their long lives without swallowing food. But surely that foolishness should be left to his own daring: while in the meantime, whatever perhaps remained within the cavities of the teeth is soon turned to a corpse-like state with a horrible stench, but is not digested.
<margin>22.</margin> For I remember that white and opaque glass, thrown out from my furnace, was swallowed by my chickens, who were deceived by the warmth of milk <note>original: "calorem lactis"; possibly a typo for "colorem" (color), meaning they thought the white glass was milk or curd</note>. Now, the fracture of glass is always sharp; yet it was discovered after a few days, when some chickens were killed, that the glass was diminished everywhere, bit by bit, had lost its sharp points, and had been made spherical. The rest of the surviving chickens and guests soon after a few days had ground down the remaining glass, even though they had also devoured the little glass spheres taken from those previously slaughtered. You will note, meanwhile, that glass resists waters that dissolve any metals <note>referring to strong chemical solvents or "aqua fortis"</note>. Indeed, in many birds the ferment is so powerful that unless they occasionally eat stones, chalk, or clay, they suffer ill from the abundance of acidity. On the contrary, the stomach of a feverish person, entirely foul-smelling, rejects foods eaten three days prior—not rarely still distinct to the sight—or sometimes turned into a yellow or rust-colored liquid, the aim of the ferment having gone astray. I learned the necessity of this stomachic 
<margin>23.</margin> ferment when, as a boy, I was feeding sparrows; I often stuck out my tongue, which the sparrow would grab with a bite and try to swallow for itself, and then I felt a great acidity in the throat of the sparrow. From then on, I knew why they were so voracious and digestive. Then I saw that the "stagma" <note>a distilled drop or oil</note> of sulfuric 
<margin>24.</margin> acid had soaked my glove <note>original: "chirothecam"</note> and immediately resolved the part it had moistened into juice. This confirmed to me as a beginner that foods are transmuted by acid, and thus there dwells in the stomach a ferment which immediately changes all ingested things, even if they are sweet, into acid. For this reason, all things provided for a sluggish appetite are also acidic: such as **verjuice** <term>the tart juice of unripe grapes</term>, vinegar, juice of lemon, of orange, mustard, and even 
<meta>The catchword "sal" indicates the next page likely begins with a discussion of "salts" or specific acidic salts.</meta>

# ->BUT ONLY STIMULATINGLY.<-

Salt and saltpeter, insofar as they contain within them a "hungry spirit" <note>original: "spiritum esurinum," referring to a sharp, acidic essence that seeks to consume or react with other substances</note> and a most gentle acid. Likewise barberries, currants, cherries, quinces, and the like. Thus far, they are pleasing to the dyspeptic sick <note>apepticis: those suffering from a failure of digestion</note>. Therefore, the contemplation of this **ferment** <term>the biological agent of digestion</term> is so necessary because it presides over the helm of life; and it is a matter of grief that the knowledge of it has been suppressed in the Schools until now.

<margin>25.</margin> And although the dryness of the whole body increases with old age, we do not grow old except by the scarcity, poverty, or extinction of certain ferments. Indeed, the stag, the raven, the eagle, the goose, etc., in the first years of their youth are far drier than we are, yet they endure for several centuries; indeed, in the eagle and the stag, youth is spontaneously renewed.

<margin>26.</margin> Moreover, this digestive ferment is not situated in just any kind of acidity. For neither vinegar nor lemon juice ferments flour; nor indeed is fermented flour necessarily a stomach ferment. But this is a "hungry" acid, a stomach acid, specific and human—so distinctly specific for each species of animal that it is uniquely appropriated to them. For mice, dormice, and swine would sooner perish of hunger than eat a kidney bean. In man, however, it generally aspires to the breadth of the whole genus.

<margin>27.</margin> Meanwhile, many shudder at cheese, or reject wine, milk, or other things because they cannot digest them. Therefore, whatever things struggle with our digestion are noted by the specific property of that ferment, and they strive to trample the ferment.

<margin>28.</margin> Therefore, the digestive ferment is an essential property, consisting in a certain vital acidity, powerful for transformations, and thus of a specific property. For a falcon will die before it will eat bread. I have already said elsewhere that if blood is distilled, by whatever degree of heat, it always thickens, dries, and leaves charcoal behind. Yet that very same blood exhales entirely through our ferments in the form of "insensible transpiration" <note>the process of moisture leaving the body through the skin without visible sweat</note>. Since heat always works in a single way <term>univocally: performing the same action regardless of the subject</term>, it cannot change food through digestion into

<column-break/>

chyle, then into blood, and then into the alimentary liquor, and finally cast it out through an insensible outflow without leaving any residue of its own. I say that a single heat cannot, in a youth, change blood into bone, nor in a bone-break, constrain blood into a callus <note>original: "porum," the hard substance that knits fractured bones</note>, while in adults and the healthy, it all flies away in exhalations. This is impossible unless, besides heat, there were other powers of cognition and sensation, which are the primary producers of these effects. For it is the property and nature of heat to consume moisture and retain the thicker part by drying.

<margin>29.</margin> For mice live on flour alone without drink, and they resolve it into their own juice or chyle. This is surely far removed from the aim of heat. Therefore, heat is not the author of digestion, but it is another vital faculty which truly and formally transmutes nourishment.

<margin>30.</margin> And I have designated it by the name of **ferments**. There are many ferments in us, as I will soon explain regarding the various stages of digestion. But since the ferment is occasionally lacking in the stomach, it is clear that its ferment is not its own, but flows to it and is inspired from elsewhere. Therefore, the **Spleen** <term>Lien: the Latin term for the spleen</term> lies upon the stomach in such a way—just as hens have the spleen very closely gathered around the stomach—that they digest more powerfully. Here I reveal the blindness of the Schools, which is highly to be wondered at and deplored with bloody tears.

<margin>31.</margin> For they have dedicated this noble organ, the Spleen, to be the sewer for the worst "atrabilious" excrement <note>referring to black bile, one of the four humors</note>—it, by whose aid alone we live and possess life and the "golden Saturnian realms" <note>a poetic reference to the Golden Age of health and abundance</note>. But as for the acidic and black excrement, which is occasionally rejected by the Spleen when imbued with too much ferment due to an indisposition of the organ, they have invented the name **black bile** <term>atram bilem: the humor of melancholy</term>. These things will become clearer later in our section on the *duumvirate* <note>the "duumvirate" refers to the author's theory of the governing pair of organs, the stomach and spleen</note> and on digestions.

<margin>32.</margin> Furthermore, before the conclusion of this question, it must be noted: among Physicians, there are only four degrees of heat, and as many of cold in simple substances, from the temperate even unto the caustic and the scarring—because regarding the virtual...

<meta>This page continues the critique of traditional Aristotelian and Galenic theories of heat. While the previous page focused on "ferments" as the true agents of digestion, this page systematizes the degrees of heat and argues that the qualities of "moist" and "dry" have been misunderstood by the academic "Schools."</meta>

# ->HEAT AS AN EFFICIENT CAUSE DOES NOT DIGEST, BUT ONLY STIMULATES<-
<note>original: "CAL. EFFICIENT. NON DIGER. SED TANT. EXCIT." — Heat acts as a catalyst or a necessary condition, but it is not the primary force that transforms food into body tissue.</note>

...act only by a quality that is merely actual and potential, which I shall touch upon elsewhere in its proper place. For this reason, the fourth degree of heat, among Physicians in the nature of things and to the 

<margin>33.</margin>
touch, is considered temperate <term>the balanced point between hot and cold</term>. But the Philosophers measure heat according to fire, and thus they imagine eight degrees leading up to fire: the fifth, sixth, and seventh of which they have not yet designated, because they are accustomed to believing in their own theoretical positions. They claim that only the eighth degree exists in the elements, and they believed the transition of the elements occurred here; for they thought they had proved something in fire—as if kitchen fire were an actual element—and nowhere else. I have already demonstrated that this entire dogma is worthless. It is especially ridiculous that they made a degree of heat in fire equal to the coldness of water, the moisture of air, and the dryness of earth. In this they were notably deluded, nor have they shown those same violent degrees anywhere else but in fire. They assert that in this eighth degree, the elements destroy, devour, and consume one another, no 

<margin>34.</margin>
differently than fire consumes wood. Next, the Chemists <note>Chymici: those practicing alchemy or chemical medicine</note>, after the fashion of the Physicians, made only four degrees within fire itself, caring little for the remaining elementary qualities because they had devoted themselves solely to **pyrotechny** <term>the art of managing fire for chemical transformation</term>. They distinguished these degrees such that the first starts from lukewarmness, within a wandering range, up to the fire for the "sublunation" <note>likely meaning the rising or distilling</note> of oily spirits. The second then goes from there up to the sublunation of dry spirits. The third continues up to a dark heat <note>obscuram ignitionem: the point where a substance begins to glow a dull red</note>. The last reaches the extreme power of a reverberating flame <term>a furnace where heat is reflected back onto the material</term>.

<margin>35.</margin>
For the sake of clearer teaching, I distinguish the degrees in chemical matters so that the first is where extreme cold is somewhat relaxed. For I, who imagine Chemistry as the handmaid and mimicking ape of nature—and subsequently its Mistress—subject all of nature to chemical speculation. Therefore, the second degree in nature is a heat such as that of water not yet frozen. The third is where it is mildly cold, such as well-water. Otherwise,

<column-break/>

absolute heat is deceptive to our touch (which is itself lukewarm), and whatever is less warm than itself is thought to be cold. And since the touch may be more or less warm, it provides an inconstant indication of heat. The fourth degree is a very slight lukewarmness. The fifth is truly lukewarm. The sixth is our own temperature <note>human body heat</note>. The seventh is already feverish. The eighth is the heat of the May Sun. The ninth is for distillation, and already exceeds what can be touched. 10. Distills with boiling. 11. Sublimates sulfur and dry spirits. 12. Liquefies and sublimates Pyrite. 13. Is in a brownish-red heat. 14. Is a glowing white heat.

<margin>36.</margin>
15. Finally, there is the ultimate vigor of the bellows and the reverberatory furnace. Lastly, although heat and cold are real qualities and admit of degrees, nonetheless humidity and dryness are not to be considered except in their concrete forms; therefore, they do not constitute qualitative degrees, but only quantitative ones. Because the "moist" in a single drop is just as deeply moist in dry clay as it is in its own element; this is because the moist and the dry do not mix at their root, nor do they enter or penetrate each other: therefore, they do not formally dispose or affect each other. For such appropriations belong to **seeds** <term>the internal "blueprints" or vital forces in Van Helmont’s system</term>, not to the elements. 

<margin>37.</margin>
Humidity, therefore, and dryness do not admit degrees, nor do they change or alter things for that reason. For they are not properly qualities in the abstract, but the very bodies themselves. Heat and cold, however, penetrate each other through their smallest parts, breaking and graduating one another. 

<margin>38.</margin>
Therefore, it is no wonder that the Schools <term>the traditional universities following Galen and Aristotle</term> have remained so silent regarding the degrees of humidity and dryness. For they assigned intense humidity to the eighth degree for Air, but for Water the same was relaxed or tempered to the fourth degree. Finally, they assigned intense dryness to the eighth degree for Earth, but for Fire, relaxed to the fourth degree. But these fables of "complexions" <note>neniae complexionum: "nonsense of the temperaments"</note>—both in the elements and in bodies, which they have falsely believed until now to be mixtures of elements—have fallen into ruins, shattered on all sides by the manifold necessity of their own collapse.

<summary>Van Helmont rejects the traditional Galenic system of four degrees of heat/moisture, proposing a more precise 15-degree chemical scale based on observable phenomena from freezing to white heat. He argues that moisture and dryness are physical quantities rather than shifting qualities like temperature.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from a critique of the nature of heat to a systematic dismantling of the traditional Galenic and Aristotelian model of digestion. The author, likely Jean Baptiste van Helmont, argues that the academic "Schools" have fundamentally misunderstood how the body processes food and disease.</meta>

# THE THREEFOLD DIGESTION
## OF THE SCHOOLS.

1. *The universal goal of this book.* 2. *The first digestion in the stomach.* 3. *The first region of the body.* 4. *Two wonders in this work.* 5. *The second digestion, and the second region.* 6. *The third digestion.* 7. *The final region of the body.* 8. *The forgetfulness of the Schools.* 9. *The state of growth.*

---

<margin>1.</margin>
It is not enough to have shown that there are not four elements in nature, nor their material mixtures and the resulting "complexions" <note>The four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic</note> and struggles; nor, finally, the meetings and combinations of humors <note>original: "humorum"</note> feigned from them, and their madness. Indeed, the "contrarieties" born from them and the *dyscrasia* <term>an imbalance of bodily fluids</term> are mere dreams of the pagans brought into Medicine and still worshipped by the Schools. Nor is it enough that I have shown elsewhere that the "three primes" <note>The Paracelsian principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> should be banished from the classification of diseases and healings; that I have refuted the causality of the Stars in healing; that I have hissed out the "winds" <note>gases or vapors</note>; and rejected the consumption of "radical moisture" <term>a vital fluid believed to be the fuel of life</term> as empty terrors. Finally, I have exploded the theories of Catarrhs and the hard, new invention of "Tartars" <note>original: "Tartarorum" — mineral deposits Van Helmont believed caused diseases like gout and stones</note>. Thus, I have shown that disease, both in general and in particular, has remained hidden from the Schools until now, and consequently, mortals languish under a conjectural art that is still fundamentally unknown—unless I myself reveal the proper causes of diseases. And since the causes of our internal enemies are mostly internal, I will first propose a history of bodily functions; after that, I will demonstrate some principles of nature, unheard of until now, which are necessary to know.

<margin>2.</margin>
The Schools claim that food and drink are transformed in the stomach, by the power of heat, into a liquid which, because of its resemblance to barley cream or ptisan, they called *chyle* <note>original: "chylum"</note>. They say this is then gradually drawn in and flows through the veins inserted into and accompanying the stomach and the whole duct of the intestines, and therefore connected by means of the *mesentery* <note>original: "mezenterio"</note> (which, in place of a third tunic, clothes, surrounds, and wraps the intestines).

<column-break/>

They say that the coarser residue is left in the intestines as useless dross, to be driven out through the anus.

<margin>3.</margin>
This cooking, of course, they called the first of the three digestions. And so, the first region of the body begins at the mouth and ends on one side at the anus, and on the other at the hollow of the liver.

<margin>4.</margin>
Two things are quite wonderful in this process. Namely, that in a few hours, hard food is resolved into juice, and that the veins end in the intestines with tiny openings—through these, I say, they drain off as much liquid as is ingested and produced daily. Yet they cannot drive away the "winds" <note>intestinal gases</note> which are subtler than that cream; however, no holes are found in the intestines, in life any more than in death.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nevertheless, the entire chyle passes through the veins of the mesentery into the liver <note>original: "jecur"</note>. In which, they say, the serum of the blood <note>original: "cruorem" — often referring to the thicker, clotted part of blood</note> is again separated for urine, which travels to the kidneys; but they claim the more substantial cream is changed into blood in the liver. In the first digestion, what is harder and opaque is excluded. In the second, however, the opaque is retained, and the transparent <note>original: "diaphano"</note> is excluded. Therefore, the second region and workshop of the body begins from the body of the liver itself and ends in the last branches of the *vena cava*.

<margin>6.</margin>
Thirdly, the blood <note>original: "Sanguis"</note> falling outside the veins and drawn into the nourishment of the solid parts is gradually perfected and transformed into a humor which they call "secondary." They divide this into four degrees of affinity before it is truly formed and admitted into the solidity of the solid parts. In this alimentary humor, therefore, the labor of the third and highest digestion is spent.

<margin>7.</margin>
And so they call this last workshop of the body the "habit of the body," and they forget the internal organs. Which, of course, also cook for themselves by the same right, and are nourished from it.

Therefore, I have first set forth the digestions as antiquity has known them until now, confirming them by mutual agreement; and now I shall subjoin those things which my own unique experience, under divine grace, has taught:

<margin>2.</margin> Beyond controversy, it is certain that food and drink are dissolved together, and equally, into a chyle <term>cremor: literally "cream," referring to the milky substance of digested food</term> that is entirely transparent within the hollow of the stomach. I add that this is done by the power of the first ferment, which is manifestly acidic and borrowed from the spleen <note>Van Helmont believed the spleen sent an acid "ferment" or vital spirit to the stomach to trigger digestion, a revolutionary idea that prefigured the discovery of gastric acid.</note>. That intestine is called the *duodenum*, from the measure of twelve fingers <note>The name "duodenum" comes from the Latin "duodeni," meaning twelve-at-a-time, because it was estimated to be twelve finger-breadths long.</note>,

<margin>3.</margin> and it is located immediately below the Pylorus. It is as if they are exotic thieves, putting their sickle into another's harvest. And this is certainly not by the vice of jealousy, as if they

<margin>7.</margin> Not much differently than how very sharp vinegar, through red lead <term>minium: lead tetroxide, used as a pigment</term>, immediately casts off its former acidity and straightway changes it into an aluminous sweetness <note>This chemical reaction creates lead acetate, also known as "sugar of lead," which has a sweet taste despite being toxic.</note>. ### THE SIXFOLD DIGESTION

...and the appropriate property of that ferment. Indeed, it is not enough to say—without proof—that an acidic ferment lives in the stomach for the first digestion and is the total cause of the liquefaction of harder foods, unless this is explained more clearly. 

<margin>11.</margin> First of all, the stomach does not possess this ferment within itself or from its own nature. For the appetite, digestion, and the general management of the stomach sometimes vanish and then return without the organ itself being destroyed; this is because these powers do not belong to the stomach alone. For this reason, I have said that the membrane of the stomach receives all the energy of its digestion and its functional service from the Spleen. Truly, the Spleen and the stomach together form a unique **Duumvirate** <note>original: *Duumviratum*; a Roman term for a "rule of two," here meaning the two organs work as equal partners.</note> within us. From this, the Poets established the golden and happy kingdoms of Saturn, and the free festivals of **Saturnalia** in the calendars. These ancients had sensed some history of an ancient truth <note>In traditional medical astrology, the planet Saturn was linked to the Spleen. Van Helmont suggests that ancient myths about Saturn’s "golden age" were actually coded observations about the Spleen’s vital role in health.</note>. Indeed, whatever is cast out by vomiting after food has been processed has an acidic taste and smell, even if the food had been heavily seasoned with sugar. Acidic belches occurring during diseases marked by sweating are considered by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> to be a good omen. 

<margin>12.</margin> For this reason, all sauces and seasonings for food used to sharpen the appetite are acidic. Such as the juice of lemons, oranges, and pomegranates; verjuice <term>omphacium: the juice of unripened grapes</term>, tartar, vinegar, barberry, vine leaves, mustard, and likewise sea salt, insofar as it contains an acidic spirit within it. In this respect, the "liquors" <note>Early chemical terms for concentrated acids.</note> of sulfur, vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note>, salt, and saltpeter are also recommended. However, I do not mean that the acid from any of these is consumed to increase the specific and appropriate ferment living in the Spleen. Far from it. For ferments have nothing else in nature, outside or beyond themselves, that can be worthily compared to them, since they are specific gifts of the vital nature. Therefore, a ferment, in its essence as a ferment, is a vital and free **arcanum** <term>arcanum: a "secret" or spiritual power that performs a transformation</term>, joined to no other physical quality. It is sufficient for seasonings that acids prepare the food for the easier entry of the splenic ferment.

<margin>13.</margin> Finally, although the ferment

<column-break/>

of the stomach has a specific sourness, that sourness is not the vital ferment itself; it is merely its organ or tool. For the stomach ferment has a singular acidity as its companion, divided by properties, genera, and species. But digestion in itself is the work of Life itself, of which sourness is the attendant instrument in this particular "workshop." In other "workshops of life" <note>The other organs involved in the subsequent five stages of digestion.</note> that follow, the life force associates itself with a different secondary quality as the servant of its purpose, adapted to the fermental and vital goal.

<margin>14.</margin> Because of this, it is not rare for a "sin" or error to occur in the stomach arising from the wrong degree of acidity. This is why **Orexis** <term>an abnormal or "adulterated" appetite, often referring to what we would call heartburn or acid reflux</term> and similar stomach troubles are caused by a corrupted sourness. This leads to stinging pains in the stomach, difficult digestions, and ultimately acidic belches and vomiting. If the ferment consisted purely of acid, then vinegar, oil of vitriol, and similar things would ferment a mass of bread and complete the transformation of our food perfectly. But they do nothing of the sort. Therefore, the ferment is a free and vital secret, and thus it adapts a "client" quality to its own ends as needed. Since ferments belong to the class of things that are "formal and seminal" <note>Higher-order spiritual blueprints that give form to matter.</note>, they separate themselves from the company of purely material qualities. If the ferment associates with a physical quality as a servant to better disperse its vital strength, consider that done as a help; thus, the ferment must contain a "duality" <note>A pairing of the spiritual power and the physical tool.</note>.

<margin>15.</margin> And for that reason also, that physical quality can err, either by being excessive or diminished in its degree. In this, I depart immensely from the **Schools** <note>The established medical universities of the 17th century.</note>. That it is nothing but a useless waste product, banished from the mass of the blood so that it does not infect it. 4. That it is therefore produced against the intention of nature. 5. That it is useful only for expelling feces and urine. 6. And that it is therefore a little pouch...

...of the gall <note>original: *fellis*; often referring to both the gall bladder and the bile itself</note>, that it is not part of the actual substance of the organ, but rather a sack, or a sewer for filth and superfluities. 7. Finally, they say that **blood-making** <term>sanguification</term> begins and is completed in the liver. To me, these truly seem like dreams. For in the first place, since bile is not required for the very makeup of the blood, it would not be necessary for that bitter thing—the gall or bile—to be procreated from every kind of food, unless it were propagated by its own specific agent in a unique workshop for a useful, vital, and necessary purpose.

<margin>16.</margin> For the gall seemed to me much less like a waste product than even the water found in the Pericardium <note>the fluid surrounding the heart</note>. At the very least, it is a wonder why fish living in water and cattle eating grass always nevertheless produce such a bitter liquid every day. Truly, that unchanging identity of the gall across so many different species seemed to argue to me for some necessity in the workshop of life. And so, the gall does not exist as a necessary byproduct of waste from whatever food is eaten, but rather as a necessary part of the organ's constitution.

<margin>17.</margin> I ceased to wonder at this when I considered what "tragedies of dominion" the womb might stir up—which is nothing but a sack and skin—and how it might take the place of a principal organ; considering, I say, what a great prerogative the membrane of the stomach claims for itself. It has even snatched the name and properties of the heart for itself above other organs <note>A reference to the "cardia," the upper opening of the stomach, which shares its name with the heart in Greek</note>. Thus I truly ceased to marvel that the name of "organ" was given to the gall bladder and to the gall itself—especially since many believe that the "irascible power" <note>the faculty of anger</note> is inborn within it.

<margin>18.</margin> I have indeed found, in the economy of human digestion, that the bodies and ferments of two organs—the gall and the liver—are connected for the sake of **blood-making** <term>sanguification</term>. The gall, without doubt, precedes the liver in the work of blood-making; thus it is closer to the stomach and intestines than the liver is. Indeed, the gall is nurtured in the bosom and lap of the liver, as if by a mother. It is the balsam of the liver and of the blood.

<margin>19.</margin> For truly, **blood-making** <term>sanguification</term> is not a transformation that can be introduced by a momentary arrangement. Furthermore, the liver is deprived of any large cavity inside which it could hold the juice to be turned into blood

<column-break/>

<margin>20.</margin> for a delay, or for the completion of digestion. That is to say, the liver in itself is a solid body having few and thin veins; therefore, the whole nutritive cream <note>original: *cremor*; the milky fluid resulting from the first digestion</note>, accompanied by such a large mass of "lotium" <note>liquid waste or urine-like fluid</note>, must pass through the liver in a swift transit. However, raw nutritive cream cannot be changed instantly into blood <note>original: *cruorem*; specifically the thick, red part of the blood</note> by such a swift passage alone. For this reason, perfect **blood-making** <term>sanguification</term> could in no way occur within the liver itself.

This is because the liver is not a kitchen; it is a steward <note>original: *oeconomus*; a household manager</note>, using its own blood-making ferment. Through this ferment, as if by a command, the liver executes the task assigned to it by the Creation, primarily through a series of successive arrangements. Therefore, the many veins of the **Mesentery** <term>Mesenterium</term> <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and contains numerous blood vessels</note> are the "stomach" of the liver itself, and the workshop where the blood is prepared. The liver breathes its perfection into the blood (which is still "naked" or raw) after it has been stored in the *vena cava*.

Indeed, since blood-making is a more exquisite kind of digestion and a more obvious transformation of matter than the melting of food into **chyle** <term>chylum</term>, it could not conveniently take place in one large vessel. Instead, it must happen in many narrower ones, which together equal a significant capacity. In these vessels, the fermenting **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>Van Helmont's term for the internal "vital director" or spiritual force that governs chemical processes in the body</note> may most strictly and closely touch and grasp every single part, communicating the ferment of its liver by changing it and breathing in vital power.

For the **Spleen** <term>Splen</term> breathes its ferment into the stomach—a wide vessel—even though the Spleen does not touch the food directly. In the same way, the liver, through its breath of life or ferment, breathes the act of blood-making into the veins placed beneath it. And just as food falls from the mouth into the stomach and there waits for the end of digestion, so from the intestines, the nutritive cream is immediately snatched into the "stomach" of the liver <note>the mesenteric veins</note>. 

<margin>21.</margin> But since that cream is plentiful, and a large part of it is waste (for it still contains urine within itself), it must first be unburdened of its waste so that it may be more conveniently turned into blood. For that cream is still entirely indistinct, and therefore does not yet recognize what is waste.

### THE SIXFOLD DIGESTION

What then will the liver do through a single action of **blood-making** <term>sanguificatio</term>? For shall the separation of waste, the transformation of the **chyle** <note>original: *cremoris*, literally "cream"; the milky fluid of digested food</note>, and the turning of that chyle into blood be performed and completed by one and the same operation? By no means. The chyle, to be sure, required a transmuting **ferment** <term>fermentum</term> <note>a vital agent that triggers chemical-like transformations in the body</note> distinct from the blood-making ferment. By this, the part of itself that is less fit is changed into pure waste; for the action of blood-making cannot make waste out of that which is not waste. Indeed, these two actions are too far apart from one another. For the action which prepares waste from the greater part of the chyle is not done by the coagulation of the blood and the separation of the more watery part.

<margin>22.</margin> Since the blood in the **meseraic veins** <note>the mesenteric veins that carry nutrients from the intestines</note> is not only not coagulated, but is not even yet capable of being coagulated as long as it remains in that "stomach." As is evident in dysentery, the separation of the watery waste from the blood occurs in the meseraic veins themselves, and indeed by a ferment and an organ acting far differently than that which is occupied with blood-making. There is, namely, a certain act which condemns a part of the chyle to become waste, but preserves the blood and leaves it untouched. Therefore, the production and separation of waste precedes blood-making.

<margin>23.</margin> And so, the "womb of the urine" begins before the meseraic veins. Yet the "womb of **Duelech**" <note>a term used by Van Helmont for the spirit that causes the formation of stones or calculi</note> is not yet there, because the ferment of the kidney changes the spirit of the urine in the liver and its surroundings. Therefore, by the ferment of the gall, whatever was acid in the chyle is changed into the salt of the urine.

<margin>24.</margin> Moreover, the "stomach" of the gall is the duodenum and the following passage of the neighboring intestine, and it ends at the beginnings of the mesenteric veins. But because this use of parts and ferments has been unheard of in the **Schools** <note>the established medical universities following Galenic tradition</note> until now, it must therefore be expanded upon with a longer discourse.

<margin>25.</margin> First, according to the standing doctrine of the Schools, blood is made in the liver, and together with the blood, bile is made at the same time. Therefore, the separation of the bile must also necessarily be, by motion and nature, later than the blood-making. For this reason, the gallbladder should be above the liver, and not below it next to the portal vein. Through

<column-break/>

supposition, I now grant the fictions of the **four humors** <note>the traditional theory that the body is governed by blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. At the very least, the blood would have been far more conveniently purged of superfluous bile than by the gallbladder (especially since the bile was still immediately mixed with the urine); and most of all, because they teach that the urine must be stained again by the bile—which would be in vain. For why should the bile be so precisely separated from the urine if it had to be added back to it again soon after? In any event, I reckon the liver is burdened with a useless and troublesome load by having the little sack of the gall hanging from it. A sack, I say, dedicated only to cast-off dung and to stirring up urine. And it is all the more an "unhappy" bladder because, since it is a membrane of a primary and "spermatic" <note>referring to the foundational tissues formed at conception</note> constitution, it must nevertheless be nourished by bile alone, since it lacks a vein propagated by running through the vesicle. For since we are nourished by the same things of which we consist, where will that little sack find its foundational nourishment from bile? Especially since there is nothing in bile but waste? If, however, it is said that the bile is collected in the sack beneath the liver for the purpose of wiping away the dregs of the bowels: at least the Creator would have more conveniently left the Agent—which creates the salt in the urine from non-salts to wash away and cleanse the intestines and stir up their waste—elsewhere, so that He might have freed the liver from the foul and tedious burden and companionship of the gall. Yet it is a matter of faith that our body was so skillfully fashioned by God that nothing in it is in vain, and nothing is diminished. Indeed, it is made far more ingenious and convenient than our intellect can grasp. Therefore, if the purposes of the gall given by the Schools were true, the kidneys would certainly have satisfied them far more conveniently than the Creator burdening the liver with such a useless weight. But the consequence proves its premise false: therefore the whole doctrine is false. If birds lack kidneys, a bladder, and urine so that they may fly more easily, but the gall only served to cleanse the blood, then at least the blood would more gladly have done without the purification of the gall than—

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the liver does not create blood and bile in a single step, but through distinct "ferments" that separate waste before blood-making begins. He mocks the traditional Galenic view of the gallbladder, asserting that the body's design is far more purposeful and complex than the "Schools" suggest.</summary>

### OF HUMAN NOURISHMENT

<margin>26.</margin>
...on the purification of urine <note>original: *lotii*</note>. That is to say: If nature is able to separate the drink in a bird without the need for urine, and consequently can do without kidneys and a bladder, would it not have been much easier for nature to have separated a tiny bit of bile along with the urine and the refuse of the bowels? Why instead would nature have burdened such a noble organ as the liver with a gallbladder <term>cystide</term>—a seemingly useless sack of excrement—thereby troubling the process of blood-making <term>sanguificationem</term>, even in birds? Certainly, nature is judged to have granted more importance to bile <note>original: *bili*</note> than to phlegm <note>original: *pituitæ*</note>, given that she created a specific little vessel for it. Indeed, it would be foolish if nature had placed bile in the lap of the liver merely as the dregs of the bowels and bladder, especially since nature could have easily allowed the bile to mix with the blood. Therefore, looking more deeply, I have observed that the gallbladder is like the kernel of the liver held within its cavity, carefully preserved from injury, while the liver is like the husk or bark of the gallbladder. Furthermore, the gallbladder is bound so closely to the **duodenum** <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> because its digestion and ferment must precede the digestion of the liver, or blood-making.

<margin>27.</margin>
For the watery, waste-like part had to be separated from the living **chyle** <note>original: *cremore*; the milky fluid of digested food</note>. This separation is not to be compared to whey and milk, which are only sequestered from each other when the milk spoils. Rather, in the chyle, the separation of the serum occurs alongside the refinement and preservation of the blood. That is: the ferment of the gallbladder perfects the chyle, preserves the blood, and breaks down the serum. These three things occur together at the exact point where the bile converts the **acid salt** of the stomach (which is harmful and corrosive anywhere except in the stomach) into a **salty salt** <note>Van Helmont is describing a chemical-like neutralization of stomach acid</note>. Furthermore, although I have said that blood-making happens after the separation of urine and the transformation of acid into salt:

<margin>28.</margin>
Nevertheless, both ferments—namely that of the gallbladder and that of the liver—begin at the same time, because neither is ever at rest. Because the work of the liver is of greater effort and perfection, it completes its task more slowly than the ferment of the gallbladder. For the aforementioned transformation of the chyle had to come first, so that the liver, relieved of a useless

<column-break/>

burden, might apply itself more conveniently to blood-making. Therefore, the second digestion (or that of the gallbladder) is distinct from the first and the third in its ferment, its organ, its vessel, its taste, its effect, and its purpose. All of this the **Schools** <note>the traditional Galenic medical establishment</note> have been ignorant of until now, because they err regarding the use of bile.

<margin>29.</margin>
In the **first digestion**, the stomach is the receptacle, but the spleen breathes an acid ferment from itself into the food, and from this comes an acid chyle. In the **second**, the thin intestines are the "stomach": the ferment is breathed in from the gallbladder to break down and separate the watery part, and the volatile acid is changed into a volatile salt. That this could happen by a swift contact, I will eventually show through several mechanical demonstrations—namely, how the oil of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note>, by the mere touch of Mercury, is converted into pure alum, vinegar, and salt, etc. Often, immediately after drinking, the urination is watery (though salty), and hardly has the mark of the first digestion been conceived before a notable part of the drink slips away through an error of the **pylorus** <note>the opening from the stomach to the intestine</note>. Consequently, the separation of urine from the blood was not done in the liver. Indeed, blood is not yet made in the liver if the chyle itself is still being prepared from the food in the stomach—consider how drinkers urinate very frequently during a meal. Thus, urine is also produced from a watery drink, even from a drink from which blood was not made; therefore, the generation of urine precedes blood-making there. Finally, in the **third digestion**, the **mesenteric veins** <term>venæ mesenterii</term> are themselves the "stomach," into which the liver breathes a bloody ferment, and its effect is red, salty blood. For wounds to the gallbladder are immediately fatal, but those of the liver are not.

<margin>30.</margin>
If, therefore, the gallbladder were at least only bile <note>meaning mere waste</note>, death would necessarily follow any leakage of the gallbladder. However, **jaundice** <term>icterus</term> is not fatal, even though the bile (as the same Schools teach) is diffused not just over the intestines, but equally throughout the whole body—far, wide, deep, and into the smallest parts. Therefore, either a wound to the gallbladder involves more than the leaking of bile, or jaundice is not actually leaked bile. Or both are true. Wounds of the bladder...

He challenges the Galenic view that bile is merely a waste product, using the non-fatal nature of jaundice to prove his point.</summary>

### SIXFOLD DIGESTION

<margin>31.</margin> Wounds to the bladder, even those inflicted above the pubic bone (according to Felix Wurtz, who in my judgment is the leader of modern surgeons), can be cured, even though urine—along with its "gall" (as they call it)—must necessarily be spilled out by that very act. Therefore, the gallbladder <note>original: *cyftis fellis*</note> is tied to the necessity of life and its integrity, because its injury results in sudden death. Nor is it merely the offense of the biliary waste that makes this death so swift. Furthermore, birds live happily without a bladder or kidneys, yet they are not without gall. For this reason, the necessity of the gall is more closely joined to life than that of the kidneys.

<margin>32.</margin> For life remains safe even with stony or decayed kidneys. Moreover, fish (according to the doctrine of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Galenic and Aristotelian medical authorities Helmont frequently challenged.</note>) abound in much phlegm and lack actual heat: they are nourished only by cold blood and a watery diet.

<margin>33.</margin> Finally, their excrements, which grow easily, did not require the "spur" of gall. Therefore, since the purpose, matter, and efficient cause of gall attributed by the Schools are lacking in fish, we would believe that the liver is tired out by the gall in vain—indeed, through an error of nature or even the Creator—unless we prefer to recognize the perpetual errors of the Schools and contemplate some greater importance for the gall as a necessary organ.

<margin>34.</margin> Hence, I establish that the gall is a vital organ <note>Helmont views the gallbladder not just as a sack, but as an active participant in the body's economy.</note>, and its very body is a bitter liquor prepared from the best blood: containing the balsam of the liver and blood. Whatever part of itself it happens to discharge into the **duodenum** <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> is its own excrement, a liquid already rejected by the gall.

<margin>35.</margin> I have shown at other times that these things are so, under the "deceptions of bile," using the example of a calf. Its mother’s milk, which is sweet, turns sour and curdles in the stomach, and thereafter provides the curd for cheese. The milk becomes a watery cream, but with little curdled milk. This cream contains urine and blood; the other curdled part, which begins to turn from pale to yellow, becomes feces <note>original: *ftercus*</note>. Soon, this mass falling into the **duodenum** proceeds to the **ileum** <note>the lower part of the small intestine</note> as a curd and turns more yellow the further it goes from the

<column-break/>

stomach, and finally turns green. Yet, there is no bitterness in the yellow, but a nitrous <note>salty/mineral</note> taste. In the green part, however, the smell of dung already becomes clear. The serous cream is soon greedily drawn and absorbed by the **mesaraic veins** <note>the mesenteric veins that carry nutrients to the liver</note> for the purpose of making blood <term>sanguification</term>. Similarly, milk is processed in infants, which is why modern physicians say they defecate entirely yellow—not from an abundance of bile, nor because of the dominance of the gallbladder, but because the fecal ferment <term>fermentum felleum</term> <note>Helmont’s theory that specific "ferments" or chemical catalysts drive every bodily process.</note> is weak. Therefore, the gall-ferment does not change the acid of the stomach into bitterness, but into saltiness, for reasons explained regarding the spirit of life. Pardon my readers' tender ears that I must discuss feces. I will show, therefore, that the taste of feces excludes gall, eludes the use of gall invented by the Schools, and proves that "bile" is a fiction.

<margin>36.</margin> A four-year-old boy had soiled the bed. Fearing the whip, he ate his own feces; yet he could not erase the signs from the linens. Questioned under threat, he finally told what happened. When asked about the taste, he said it was foul-smelling and somewhat sweet. Among other things, he had eaten a dish of peas; he complained that the undigested pea skins (the husks) were remarkably sour. For the vigilance of the gall-ferment over opaque and fecal undigested matter is not as great as it is over transparent things that must be prepared for the dignity of the blood. I happened to arrive on the same day and diligently asked him (even offering a reward) whether what he had eaten was bitter. He replied "no," repeating what he said before. Likewise, certain nuns were raising noble young girls as boarders; they preached constantly that those who ate luxuriously would share the fate of the "rich man" <note>A reference to the biblical parable of Dives and Lazarus.</note>, while only those who saved themselves through every kind of mortification <term>mortificatio</term> <note>The religious practice of self-denial or physical penance.</note> of the flesh would be saved. Therefore, a noble young girl, eager for her salvation and moved by this persuasion, ate her own feces and fell ill. She was called home by her parents and eventually told the story. She was asked...

...what its flavor might be, and he replied that it was foul and "watery-sweet." Thirdly, there was a Painter of Brussels <note>Likely a contemporary of Van Helmont; Brussels was a major artistic hub in the 17th century.</note>, who was prone to fits of madness. At the start of one such fit, he fled into a nearby grove, and there, far from the sight of men, he was found to have lived for 23 days on his own excrement. Soon after he was brought home, I visited him, and the Lord healed him. He had a perfect memory of everything that had happened during his madness. I asked him if he remembered the taste of the excrement. He said, "It tastes as it smells." Upon being examined by me regarding the primary tastes, he replied that it was not sour, nor bitter, nor sharp, nor salty, but "watery-sweet." Indeed, he said that the more often he ate it, the sweeter it always became. When asked why he preferred to eat excrement rather than return home, he said that throughout his madness he had been horrified by men, persuaded by his own delusion that men were searching for him to destroy him with a snare. It is clear, therefore, that there is not even a drop of gall <note>original: *fellis*</note> in excrement; for once a gallbladder is burst, no matter how well a fish is subsequently washed, the bitterness of the gall—conceived from even the slightest touch—is never removed.

<margin>37.</margin>
For if yellowness revealed the presence of gall, the excrement of infants would be the most "gallic" of all, yet it is licked by dogs because it still retains some of the flavor of milk. Furthermore, whatever is not fully processed in the stomach and has not taken on the "beauty of transparency," should not hope to be digested by the ferment of the gall in the intestines, even if it is tinted with a yellow color. This is because one does not proceed to the second or third stage of digestion unless the first is completed. Therefore, whatever is opaque and colored by heat in the Ileum <note>The final section of the small intestine.</note> is entirely proscribed as waste, and acquires a taste of putrefaction under a certain sweetness. This is no different from how sour fruits become sweet with a little heat. However, whatever was previously acid in the stomach becomes salty in the duodenum and is separated from the excrement; but if anything acidic persists that resists the ferment of the gall, cramps <term>tormina: severe, twisting abdominal pains or colic</term> immediately follow. Human excrement, however, putrefies—

<column-break/>

[column 2]

—because the "excrementitious ferment" presides over that place. That which is undigested and slips out of the stomach is not digested in the intestines either. It is ejected whole, yet it preserves—and subsequently increases—the portion of acidity it took on in the stomach. For this reason, bran in bread promotes its stay there because of the sourness; other things truly become more sour and stir up cramps. Therefore, shortly after the duodenum, the chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> begins to change its volatile acid salt into a corresponding saltiness, dissolved in the "cream" <note>original: *cremore*; Helmont uses this to describe the refined part of the chyle.</note>. The remaining and more "bodily" substance of the Cream, within the mesenteric veins, awaits "sanguification" <term>sanguificatio: the process of turning nutrients into blood</term> by the inspired ferment of the liver. Meanwhile, the salty fluid <note>original: *latice*; Helmont often uses 'latex' for bodily fluids.</note> is drawn through the liver by the kidneys and is committed to the kidneys and bladder for expulsion. Therefore, in the vessels of the Mesentery, the **Third Digestion** begins, which terminates in the liver. For as long as the blood <note>original: *cruor*</note> is in the mesentery, it is not yet digested, not yet fibrous, nor perfected. For this reason, the blood of the mesentery does not clot in cases of dysentery. At other times, however, if a vein in the stomach is ruptured, the blood immediately clots in the stomach.

<margin>38.</margin>
For the ferment of the liver is so inclined toward blood-making (as that is its unique and sole office) that even the veins, by "right of a fief" <note>original: *jure feudi*; a legal metaphor suggesting the veins hold their power and function as a grant from the liver.</note>, retain that power from the liver and from the innate *Archeus* <term>Archeus: the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the functions of an organ</term> that confirms it. Thus, in a corpse long after death, the blood in the veins does not thicken; yet if it is poured out elsewhere, it clots at once. For the "cream" running through the intestines thereafter becomes drier, its liquid being drawn upward into the veins. From there, the remainder putrefies more and more, so much so that when it has almost reached the ends of the Ileum, a good deal of more liquid excrement has already been generated. Before it has fully putrefied, it is snatched to the mesentery to be mixed as a "wash," useful for its own purposes. As I have discussed elsewhere regarding fevers, and likewise regarding the *Duelech* <term>Duelech: Van Helmont’s specific term for the stone-forming power or the stones themselves in the body, such as kidney stones</term>.

<margin>39.</margin>
The Schools <note>Traditional medical authorities following Galen and Aristotle.</note> believed that yellow excrement was bile and gall; they founded their entire demonstration for one of the "four humors" upon excrement. Thus, the door was opened for the miserable...

# THE SIXFOLD DIGESTION

...errors, and wicked throat-cuttings. For it mattered little until now that, with the substance of the urine's tint unknown, they constructed a false *Tecmarsis* <note>original: *Tecmarfin*; from the Greek *tekmar*, a sign or diagnostic token. Here, Van Helmont refers to the practice of diagnosing all diseases merely by looking at the color of urine.</note>. They claimed that bile and gall were the constitutive humors of our body and the perpetrators of all diseases—namely, yellow bile, and imagining a slightly more "digested" version as burnt or verdigris-colored, and from there, a dry and withered melancholy. They claimed the gallbladder itself was a sewer for excess bile, and that blood <term>Cruor</term> <note>Van Helmont uses the term *cruor* to refer to vital, circulating blood, distinguishing it from *sanguis*, which can refer to blood as a simple substance.</note> was nothing but an artificial body, a collection of several parts which, once separated, would be the same after death as they were during life. They did not see it as a body generated by Mother Nature through the true transformation of chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> into "univocal" blood. And finally, they based their healings on the removal of "perpetrated causes" that never were or are in nature. This truly surpasses the densest ignorance and makes the snoring of the academic Schools inexcusable. 

<margin>40.</margin>
But perhaps they will object to me: "You say," (they say), "that the veins avoid the chyle [cremorem] that has fallen from the stomach into the intestines. Therefore, the same task belongs to the veins of the stomach: to draw that acidic chyle into themselves without the intervention of the gall ferment—that is, without the change from acid to salt. And consequently, your 'gall ferment' is a dream and a fabrication. Indeed, a broth injected as an enema could penetrate to the liver without the gall's knowledge." (I resolved this question regarding the legality of the enema in the book on fevers).

<margin>41.</margin>
I respond: It is an old abuse of the Schools to attribute the same function equally to all veins. As if the veins severed in the arms were busy drawing chyle? First, I have already shown that the blood in the veins of the stomach is coagulable, whereas the blood of the mesentery <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note> is not. Next, it must be known that all acidic chyle is hostile to the veins, and they draw nothing hostile to themselves. From which it follows that the stomach veins draw nothing of the chyle beneath them; and all blood, before it is drawn in by the mesenteric veins, must have felt the "hand" of the gall ferment in the "stomach of the intestines" <note>Referring to the duodenum, where the gallbladder releases its ferment.</note>.

<column-break/>

Indeed, although the arteries dispersed through the stomach drive away the spirit of wine <note>Alcohol.</note>, they drink up no juice. For why would the arteries draw juice, since they never do any good with it? Since the making of blood is not the job of the heart, but of the liver; and since the juice drawn into the artery would necessarily be an obstruction and would have to spoil? If, therefore, the arteries have the gift of avoiding harmful things and at least drawing to themselves vital things destined for them by the Lord of things: Shall this discernment be denied to the veins in the stomach? 

For it would be poorly provided for horses by nature, who, content with a single drink in the morning, then feed all day on straw, hay, chaff, oats, or barley. For dry or juice-less things would soon contract mold in the stomach if the stomach veins drank up the drink. Horses would be thirsty all day. Therefore, the drink must necessarily remain in the stomach for a while, waiting there for the end of the future digestion, so that the acidic liquid—plainly hostile—is not drawn into the veins, nor the half-cooked chyle absorbed by the veins before its time. Therefore, the use of the stomach veins is different from that of the mesenteric <note>original: *mesaraicarum*</note> veins. And thus the objection falls. 

Because the mesenteric veins are the "stomach of the liver," and there is no other besides them; the stomach veins are not so. Let them at least be said to be for nourishing the stomach. Finally, wherever the Pylorus <note>The valve at the exit of the stomach.</note> is not tightly closed (as happens during long drinking sessions), the stomach almost continuously "urinates" from below through a thin thread, as it were, dripping into the intestine. In feverish people, however, whose pylorus suffers from excessive tightness, drink sometimes persists for three whole days, and finally more is rejected in a single vomit than was taken in two days. This certainly contradicts the idea that the stomach veins draw up the juice. It often happens to me, lying on my back in a carriage, that I hear through the jolting of the roads the chyle fluctuating in my stomach like a half-full bottle. And I have often gone to bed thereafter without dinner or drink; indeed, in the morning...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument regarding the physiological mechanics of digestion. He uses a personal observation of his own digestion to challenge the Galenic "Schools" on how the stomach, pylorus, and liver function, moving into his theory of the "Six Digestions" where each "region" of the body is defined by a specific digestive ferment rather than just anatomical location.</meta>

# HUMAN NOURISHMENT

...as the day before, I felt my stomach. Therefore, being somewhat curious, I provoked nausea in myself and vomited up a copious, transparent, acidic cream <note>original: *cremorem acidulum*; this refers to chyle, the milky fluid of digested food, which Van Helmont observed had become acidic in the stomach.</note>, so acidic that it set my teeth on edge. And although I did not feel a heavy burden before vomiting, I felt a lightness after it. From this I observed first: 

1. That even though 20 hours had passed, if the stomach veins had sucked up the chyle, I could not have thrown up so much from a moderate lunch the day before. 
2. That acidic cream is not attracted by the veins. 
3. That this acidic cream had not yet been dismissed from the stomach, not because of a failure of digestion, but because of an error of the pylorus <note>The valve at the bottom of the stomach.</note>. 
4. That digestion is distinct from the "expulsive faculty," since one can be completed while the other is absent or failing. 
5. That sometimes digestion bears the undeserved blame for the expulsive faculty, and vice versa. 
6. That just as I sinned by a too-tight closure of the pylorus, so drinkers sin by a too-negligent or loose pylorus. 
7. Indeed, at the start of illnesses, things consumed three days prior are not infrequently vomited up. 
8. That it is not the job of the stomach veins to draw in the chyle. 
9. That nevertheless, the doctrine persists which makes it a foolish thing to inject an enema through the anus to nourish a sick person <note>Van Helmont argues that since veins don't "suck" chyle greedily from the stomach, they certainly won't absorb nourishment from the lower intestines during an enema.</note>. 
10. That the upper orifice of the stomach errs in fevers by opening too much, causing thirst, while the Pylorus errs by its tight closure. 
11. That in fevers, both digestion and expulsion fail at the same time. 
12. That the "key" to the stomach's upper opening is in the spleen, and the key to the Pylorus is in the gall, because of the different seats of the two ferments. 
13. That the reason for the placement of the spleen and gall is based on their duties. For truly—

<margin>42.</margin>
The Schools <note>The academic medical establishment following traditional Greek/Roman authorities.</note> extend the "first region" of the body from one extreme, the mouth, all the way to the anus—and at the other extreme, to the hollow of the liver. But I, however, define the "regions" by their digestions, since without these, the "region" itself is merely a concept of the mind. For what does the exit of excrement have to do with digestion? What does it matter to the stomach that its dross is discharged through the anus? For the dung in the intestine is no more the "excrement of the stomach" than sweat is. Therefore, if the anus is part of the 

<column-break/>

first region because of the stomach's excrement, then the skin would also be part of the first region because of sweat, and the bladder because of urine. It is not the excrement, nor the exit of it, but the digestion alone that defines the limit of a region. And accordingly, there are 

<margin>43.</margin>
as many Regions as there are digestions. Finally, the "factory" of blood-making is not the liver itself in its own substance. For if it were, the liver of fish would also make their blood red; but since every thing generates something like itself, it would be necessary for either the liver of fish to be red, or their blood to be white <note>original: *cruorem esse album*; fish blood/fluid was often viewed as distinct from human red blood.</note>. Both of these are false. From this we learn that blood-making itself happens in its own "stomach of the liver," which is the complex vessel system of the mesentery <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>. Otherwise, the liver has too few and too thin vessels to properly refine the juice of such a great mass. Outside itself, specifically in the *vena cava*, the final 

<margin>44.</margin>
perfection of blood-making is inspired by the liver-ferment. And the Schools think that blood-making happens through the actual "brooding" or heat of the liver and the chyle, because they are 

<margin>45.</margin>
ignorant of any actions other than those that happen through long-lasting contact or physical grasping. Therefore, they believe every "agent" must necessarily "suffer" or be acted upon because of the resistance and reaction of the "patient" (the matter being acted upon).
