Whenever, of course, through heats and colds, figures and likenesses of mechanical devices (*which belong to the Schools of the organs and are their sacred anchors* <note>A metaphor for the last resort or fundamental principles of the Galenic medical establishment.</note>), they fail to grasp the matter: they immediately flee to miracles, or at least to the hidden mysteries of things. Terrified by the magnitude or the strangeness of the stunned matter, they rest in the laziness of investigation, in the admiration of occult properties. 

<margin>48.</margin> *Paracelsus* <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, for the making of medicinal vitriol from copper, orders that "decrepitated" <note>Salt that has been heated until it stops crackling.</note> salt be suspended in a pig's bladder in a kettle of boiling water, and thus all the salt will soon be dissolved. With this, he orders copper plates to be anointed, and promises that vitriol will be born in the air. I was indeed still in my *Apprenticeship* <note>original: *Tyrociniis*; his early years of study.</note>, yet I knew from *Philosophy* that salt could not be resolved into water by its own weight without a substantial transmutation of itself: and that this could not happen through the mere moistening of water. Yet, on the other hand, the authority of *Paracelsus* persuaded the opposite: namely, that without the addition of water (for otherwise the bladder would be in vain), the salt would liquefy into water. Therefore, as a *Beginner*, I decided to test this monstrous assertion of so great a man. But soon, with a slow heat, I found the water in the kettle to be not much less salty than that which was in the bladder, the neck of which was tied to the handle of the pot, protruding out of the water. From this I knew that the water penetrates inside and outside the bladder: namely, that the bladder is pervious to salt and hot water, but not to air. For 77 parts of rainwater resolve 23 parts of dried salt; but where even one of the 77 parts of water evaporates, a crust of salt floats upon the brine. In vain, therefore, does *Paracelsus* command the use of the bladder, since these things are done more conveniently without it. And this is besides the false supposition

<column-break/>

of it as well. I noticed, therefore, that at the degree of boiling heat, the bladder is porous; but not in the heat of our own internal economy <note>The natural heat of the living body.</note>. I concluded from this, therefore, that through the course of the veins, the intestines abound with more and tinier pores than elsewhere: to which pores others would correspond, being pervious through the course of the veins. Therefore, the "cream" <note>original: *cremor*; the chyle or digested food pulp.</note> passes through the intestines, partly by its own soaking in—just as the salt water soaked through the bladder—and partly by a specific sympathetic flow through the aforementioned pores, which are indeed open in life (just as they penetrate the bladder in heat) but closed in death. But wind, not being soaked up by moistening, is not absorbed by the intestines, nor is it sought by the veins; and therefore, it does not penetrate the intestines thus far. This is chiefly because it lacks the "path of congruity" and the *Blas* <note>Van Helmont's term for a motive or vital power, similar to a "star-force" within the body.</note> of movement by which wind might be drawn, and the "discerner of things to be drawn" <note>A vital faculty that selects what the body needs.</note> resists it. Therefore, the veins dispersed between the double tunic of the stomach lack the aforementioned pores—or are at least porous only where, being surrounded by the outer tunic, they may pour through the alimentary blood. Thus, the "kitchen" or digestion proper to the stomach is from the outside inward; but the "cooking" which happens in its cavity becomes universal, and is entirely recorded there as well. This is so that the digestion of both does not produce confusion. For there is a double cook in the stomach: one from the spleen <note>original: *liene*.</note>, and another proper to itself, which produce different digestions. Furthermore, the acidic ferment in the stomach dissolves foods into juice; but the ferment of the gall <note>The bile.</note>, by leaping upon the acidic chyle, separates the "chymus" <note>The refined matter for blood.</note> for the blood, and from there subtracts the "latex" <note>The clear fluid/serum.</note>, urine, sweat, dung, yellow liquid, and parts of the coarser dregs. Nor is digestion in the stomach, therefore, a formal transmutation of foods.

Dung differs essentially from chewed food: it should not be believed that what was not turned into any sort of cream by heat could be putrefied by heat alone in a few hours, but rather by the specific ferments of the internal "kitchens." For in this way, all wine is changed into vinegar, all quicksilver into gold, the whole egg into a chick, and all blood into final nourishment.

<margin>51.</margin> Whence I judge it false that there can be no nourishment without excrement. For the Schools <note>Referring to the traditional university-based medical authorities of the time, typically followers of Galen.</note> have meditated on dungs, but they have not considered that only homogeneous things concur for generation. Therefore, although separations of dross occur before the transformation of food, nevertheless, no more dross is made during the transformation itself—certainly after the state of homogeneity has been reached. Indeed, the separation of dross from a homogeneous substance is impossible, in which one part differs in no way from another. In foods, however, whether under the first ferment, there is heterogeneity because of the difference of the foods and their parts,

the inequality of chewing, and the unequal application of the received ferment. For food partly obeys the ferment more easily, and partly resists rebelliously, from which also a discordant capacity for the ferment arises.

<margin>52.</margin> That teaching of the Schools is also false: that the stomach cooks primarily for itself and only secondarily for the whole body, and thus it is truly nourished by the acidic chyle <note>original: *chylo acidulo*; the partially digested food in the stomach.</note>. And further, they claim that if it were not nourished by its own chyle, it would not want to begin or undertake the cooking. This is because, from "nature's self-love" <note>original: *Philautia naturæ*; the concept that every living thing acts out of self-interest.</note>, each thing acts intentionally for itself. 
1. This might have a place in a total agent, but certainly not in the direction of individual parts. 
2. Because no part in the body acts by its own whim of self-love; much less do the "workshops" <note>Referring to the digestive organs.</note> act this way, as they are dedicated to the service of the whole. Instead, nature obeys the assignments of the Creator in both cases, which were measured out by use and necessity by the Lord of things. 
3. We are nourished by the same things of which we consist: but we in no way consist of "cream." 
4. The stomach is nourished by no other material than the rest of the class of membranes, which lack this cream. 
5. Cream does not take on life except through the stages of blood; but the stomach cannot be nourished by food that is not yet vital. 
6. Cream is liquefied food, still possessing the *Archeus* and properties of food; however, the "spermatic" parts <note>The solid, foundational tissues of the body.</note> and those similar to the first constitution cannot be nourished by a liquor not yet determined to the human species. 
7. The veins are not dispersed into the stomach to flee the blood, but to diffuse nourishment. They do not contain "cream." Therefore, because the economy of the members is ignored, refutations sprout everywhere in the Schools; moving from a "non-cause" as if it were a "cause," they give birth to capital errors and deaf experiences, which must be paid for on the skin of others <note>A phrase meaning the patients suffer for the doctors' errors.</note>.

-> They gave me gall for my food; and in my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink. <-

...to be held as perfect vital blood;
<margin>63.</margin> For if the blood <note>original: *cruor*; referring to the thicker, venous blood or the clot</note> of the vena cava <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note> had begged for spirit from the liver, the right auricle of the heart would be in vain; yet that auricle works incessantly for no other purpose than that some spirit may be drawn from the left chamber through the septum of the heart, so that the blood in the vena cava, near the heart, may begin to be quickened by participating in that spirit. Since the auricle is on the left, and moreover there is the distinguished trunk of the artery, a stronger flow occurs from the left chamber. Consequently, only a small amount of vital spirit is communicated to the venous blood. Indeed, the blood of the liver is always soaked throughout by too much watery liquid, which it ought to be deprived of before it becomes a fertile and worthy support for the spirit. Nor, finally, does the liver have a suitable cavity within itself for fabricating the spirit. Therefore, just as I have seen intellectually through the whole scene of generation that there is only a single maker and ruler of the life of spirits in the seed, so too I admit only a single spirit in the vital economy.

<margin>64.</margin> For blood <note>original: *cruor*</note> indeed glides within the threads of the muscles and becomes flesh; but it does not easily pass over to nourish the internal organs and the fibers of the flesh. For a weak person, thinned by long illness, easily resumes his former state of flesh after convalescence, even after youth; but one who has been emaciated by a defect of some internal organ does not likewise rise again to his former state. And this is the difficulty in healing consumption and curing ulcers of the intestines. Meanwhile, external ulcers, which are far worse, are healed through medicines taken by mouth, even though they are further from the mouth than the internal ones. This is because the internal organs and membranes are nourished by "vital blood" <note>original: *sanguine*</note> more than by "venous blood" <note>original: *cruore*</note>. Furthermore, life has received its limit from God; therefore, whatever things are nourished by vital blood stop their growth at a fixed number of days. Meanwhile, the flesh of the muscles (which is nourished only by venous blood) and the fibers of the muscles (which are nourished by vital blood) grow without end whenever they fail, and in the destruction of certain parts, 

<column-break/>

they grow out immensely. Thus also fractured bones are solidified by a bony callus <note>original: *poro osseo*</note> at any age. But when the internal organs stop growing, all the spermatic fibers and those of the primary constitution also stop growing.
> *For which of you, by worrying, can add a single cubit to his stature?* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 6:27 or Luke 12:25.</note>
I have observed that pregnant women, long afflicted by notable sorrow, have given birth to smaller offspring. Primarily, therefore, I do not admit that a "hepatic spirit" <note>a spirit originating in the liver</note> exists within the blood. Secondly, I do not distinguish the "animal spirit" from the "vital spirit." Since in a single ship, only a single pilot stands at the helm, nor can several endure each other without confusion; neither do I admit a new digestion in the chambers of the brain for the sake of an animal spirit.

<margin>65.</margin> Just as the spirit does not differ in species from itself in the individual organs of the senses and the executors of movement—although the senses differ among themselves in species, as they also do from movement—so I consider it a confused argument that imagines several <term>Archei</term> <note>plural of Archeus, the "internal master-chemist" of an organ</note> in man. For <term>Gas</term> <note>Van Helmont's term for a volatile vital essence</note>, although it may have drawn a singular disposition from an organ, does not thereby prove a specific diversity.

<margin>66.</margin> Therefore, in the fourth and fifth digestions, there are no wastes <note>original: *excrementa*</note>, nor do they arise, nor are there dissimilar parts. Therefore, it is false that waste is produced in every nourishment. For blood and spirit harmonize in a univocal and vital unity. Truly, if any dregs from the prior digestions rush into the arteries or are born there, let that be a morbid, turbulent, and confused command. I am speaking now of ordinary digestions.

<margin>67.</margin> Finally, the sixth and last digestion is completed in the individual "kitchens" of the members. There are as many "stomachs" as there are nourishable members. In this digestion, surely, the spirit innate to each place cooks its own nourishment for itself. Under this digestion, as various dispositions occur, so also various errors of those dispositions happen. And so the diseases, which the <term>Schools</term> <note>the traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle</note> attribute to their four fictitious humors, should rather be attributed to "transmuted" things.

### HUMAN NOURISHMENT

...succeed consecutively until the true nourishment of the solid parts. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities following Galenic and Aristotelian medicine, whom Van Helmont frequently criticized for being too theoretical.</note> divide these transformations into four subordinate dispositions; and as if an error could never occur in these, they have forgotten the diseases which they ought to have attributed to this class. First, they say that because the blood <note>original: *cruor*; referring to the thicker, venous blood</note> within the extremities of the veins acquires the mucilaginous substance of **crude seed**. Next, in the manner of dew, it is diffused or falls into the empty spaces of the flesh; thirdly, while it is already being applied to the solid parts. And finally, when it is assimilated into that which is nourished. And from this it is truly informed: it assumes the nature of the solid part. 

These ideas are surely the dross of the Schools. For in the first place, the gore or blood does not turn white in the extremities of the veins, since the extremities do not possess any other power as a workshop than the entire preceding channel of the vein has. Thus the vein, although it is a vessel for nourishment prepared for the **kitchens** <note>original: *culinis*; Van Helmont’s metaphor for the internal sites of chemical transformation and digestion</note> of the solid parts, is nevertheless not itself the kitchen of the solids. For the individual solid parts foster their own proper kitchen within. Therefore, the gore and blood are not altered unless they are applied to the solids. This is because they are converted by the property of the solids into crude seed, and not by their own accord in the extremity of the veins. 

Secondly, the spermatic mucilage is not "dewed" from the veins into the solid. Indeed, mucilage is poorly suited to the nature of dew. Rather, a thin substance glides in, within the kitchens of each part, as fluid blood and gore, which are transformed only by the **ferment** <note>original: *fermento*; the vital agent Van Helmont believed was responsible for all biological change</note> of that location. Thirdly, there are no "empty spaces" in the flesh which they imagine are hungry for dew. Fourthly, nourishment is not applied to the solids in the manner of dew, which a little before was mucilage. Fifthly, nor finally is this dew united and assimilated to the solids: but whatever yields to being assimilated to them happens during the years of growth; thereafter, however, as gore and blood have crept into the solids by the continuous suction of nature, they are digested there, adapted, and finally expelled through **diaphæresis** <note>original: *diaphæreſin*; the dissipation of waste through the skin or pores</note>. Therefore, I consider these four dispositions, devised by the Schools and...

<column-break/>

...poorly arranged into a fourfold number (for perhaps a hundred dispositions intervene before a chick is formed from an egg—or, I say, before a solid part is formed from the blood), to be a result of the blindness <note>original: *Scotomiæ*; literally a darkening of vision, here used to mean intellectual ignorance</note> of the Schools. In this, they see nothing right or true, but look upon the very history of the matter as if it were stained; to them, that which has no nourishment of truth is true, being nothing but the excrement of fables. Therefore,
<margin>70</margin>
even the veins themselves, insofar as they are of the primary constitution, are nourished solely by arterial blood, and thus, perhaps for this reason, the artery accompanies the vein everywhere. For it happens from this that through more cruel bloodlettings, finally it is not gore, but a white matter <note>original: *albugo*; a clear or white fluid compared to egg white</note> that flows out, which is the immediate nourishment of the veins, due to the scarcity of gore. 

Furthermore, Paracelsus,
<margin>71</margin>
diverting nature on both sides to his own whims, says that in the digestion of the stomach, **putrid sulfur** is separated from two other beginnings. In the liver, however, **salt** is separated from **mercury**. He claims that gore is mercury, and the true nourishment of the whole integral body. It is not worth the effort to drag this man onto the stage any longer to mock him, while he himself invalidates this doctrine of his. For while investigating the origin of ulcers, he says that the whole gore is nothing but salt (he now makes no mention of mercury, unless he confuses mercury with salt in name and in fact), although the urine of those with ulcers contains not a crumb less salt than those who are not ulcerated. 

But surely it is shameful to regard the three "first principles" <note>The *Tria Prima* of Paracelsus: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which he believed composed all matter</note> of gore as if they were excrements, of which the blood is one of the three. He also everywhere compares milk to blood. He does not know that a transformed thing is no longer similar to that which is not transformed, just as a chick is not similar to the egg or the yolk. Specifically, he calls the buttery part of milk floating on the surface the **sulfur of milk** (meanwhile, the buttery part never floats on the blood, even analogically). The cheese, or the curds, he calls the **salt of milk**; therefore, the whey of the milk will also be the **mercury of milk**: and by consequence, the best part of it and the best nourishment of the milk...

<summary>Van Helmont rejects the Scholastic theory that nourishment occurs in four specific stages like falling dew, arguing instead that tissues have their own "internal kitchens" and ferments. He also critiques Paracelsus for inconsistently applying alchemical principles (Sulfur, Mercury, Salt) to the composition of blood and milk.</summary>

## 224 SEXTUPLEX DIGESTIO

...ment. And the whey of the milk will be the mercury, derived from the mercury of the blood. I will gladly, even laughingly, yield the whey to **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist; Van Helmont often agreed with him but here playfully disagrees on the priority of milk's components.</note>, and take the colostrum <note>The first milk produced after giving birth, which is thicker and richer in nutrients.</note> for myself. This is because butter retains the scent of the flowers upon which the cow feeds, 
<margin>72.</margin> but the whey does not. **Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel, a highly influential French physician of the 16th century.</note> truly thinks that butter is nothing more than the foam of agitated colostrum, being ignorant of the necessary presence of an **acid ferment** <term>fermentum acidum; the internal chemical agent Van Helmont believed was necessary for transformation</term> in the colostrum, so that it might truly be transmuted into butter through churning. Indeed, if a little ash, soap, sugar, or other substances that share the nature of lye <note>alkaline substances</note> are mixed into the colostrum, butter will never be produced, because the alkali destroys every acid ferment. This is why in winter, the churning of colostrum is more tedious before butter is born: because heat promotes acids and all forms of ripening. 
<margin>73.</margin> **Paracelsus**, however, elsewhere forgetful of his own doctrine, prefers colostrum to whey and cheese, both for health and healing as well as for the quality of the food. But the **Galenic Schools** <note>The traditional medical establishment following the ancient Greek physician Galen.</note> prefer thin and watery milk over the richer kind. Thus far, they rank sheep's milk as the lowest, then cow's milk, and thirdly goat's milk. Finally, they prefer donkey’s milk above the rest because of its thin substance and its great amount of whey. I, however, know this one thing: the milk of beasts grazed on dry pastures is the best, both for healing and for eating, as it is the least watery. For the goat (and the same judgment applies to its milk where the same logic holds), whose blood <note>original: *cruorem*; the thick, dark blood</note> the medical shops of the **Schools** prescribe—and sheep's blood is commonly sold in place of goat's—they command that the goat first be fed with diuretics. 
<margin>74.</margin> Therefore, the powers of milk must be measured by the health of the beast, its life, and its food, and not at all by its thickness or fatness. And physicians, when summoned to judge the milk in a wet nurse, come poorly prepared, behaving no differently than if they were judging blood drawn by bloodletting <note>original: *phlebotomiam*; the practice of bleeding a patient to balance their humors.</note>. That is, they are souls blinded by ignorance; though their eyes are open, they do not see. I have also observed that from the same cow, with an equal quantity of milk, there is a differing quantity of colostrum, even though she enjoys the same pastures. This is surely according to the cow's differing 

<column-break/>

<margin>75.</margin> state of health. Truly, for the sake of the blood, I hang the goat by its horns and bend its hind legs back to the horns; I remove the testes, and having received the blood from there, I release the bloodless animal to the butcher. This blood, when dried, is like glass and is very difficult to grind; it differs greatly from the goat's blood found in the medical shops. If taken in the weight of a drachm, it immediately puts one to sleep and cures pleurisy <note>original: *pleuritidem*; an inflammation of the lining of the lungs.</note>, etc., without any cutting of a vein; it will never fail you. 
<margin>76.</margin> For donkey's milk restores and recreates more, and indeed nourishes more, but not because it is more watery. For that would be judging the power of a kernel, never seen before, only by its shell. 
<margin>77.</margin> But the donkey, insofar as it is long-lived, has milk superior to other quadrupeds. For it is necessary that its milk also possesses an **Archeum** <term>The "Archeum" is Van Helmont's term for the vital internal director or life-force that governs the functions of an organ or organism.</term> endowed with a long life. And for this reason, surely, it only separates its colostrum much later, because it listens to corruption more slowly. For that separation tends toward duality and destruction. From this it is clear that since in childhood, nourishment is converted into our very constitution, donkey's milk confers a longer and healthier life to children compared to other foods. 
<margin>78.</margin> For this reason also, human milk, although it is most similar to us, most proximate, and nutritious, nevertheless yields to donkey's milk on account of longevity. Moreover, a donkey must be combed like a horse; indeed, from the taste of the milk, it can be discerned whether the donkey was combed that morning or not. 
<margin>79.</margin> Therefore, let the **Schools** learn to judge better concerning wet nurses, milk, and diet; likewise, let them judge the contents of urine, and not merely recognize bile or gall in the water or the stool. Let them know, I say, how to distinguish the urine of the blood from the urine of the drink. Furthermore, let them know that the drawing of fluid from the veins of the mesentery <note>The membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note> causes natural thirst, and not the exhaustion of the smaller veins 
<margin>80.</margin> due to the depletion of the blood. Otherwise, those with consumption <note>original: *phtisici*; patients suffering from wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note> would always be thirsty, and more so than those with dropsy <note>original: *hydropici*; patients with swelling from excess fluid.</note>; and repeated thirst would betray a repeated consumption of the blood, separated by only short intervals. 
<margin>81.</margin> It must also be known, toward the end...

He also critiques the medical establishment's methods for judging health through milk and urine, offering his own observations on thirst and the preparation of medicinal goat blood.</summary>

# HUMAN NOURISHMENT.

### Ff 2

...the end of the Ileum intestine, there is a small pouch which they called the **cecum** <note>Also known as the "blind intestine," the pouch at the beginning of the large intestine.</note>, in which sits a **fecal ferment** <term>fermentum stercoreum; an agent of transformation that Van Helmont believed turned waste into excrement</term>. Because this is a work of corruption and not of nutrition, its putrefaction is by no means to be counted among the digestions of food. For the fecal ferment does not proceed from any organ or vital faculty; and therefore, at this final stage of change, safer gripings occur when matter imbued with fecal ferment moves backward or contracts sudden stains of polluted rot. Furthermore, the cecum is a small but necessary receptacle for all waste. This is evident: for the **Wolf**, below the middle of its intestine, has two membranous bags or round pouches which serve as its cecum. For its food falls from the long passage of the intestine into one of the pouches, then soon into the other, and finally is led from there into the following intestine. <margin>82.</margin> However, **roundworms** <note>original: "Lumbrici"</note> are not generated in the duodenum, and much less in the stomach. Indeed, if they persisted there for long, they would be consumed like food. Where the **ferment of the gall** <note>bile</note> does not reach, that is the homeland of roundworms. For they are made from semi-digested nourishment which, when brought to its place like lukewarm milk, becomes encrusted with a skin, palpitates, and is gradually gifted with life. For roundworms scarcely creep upward out of their

<column-break/>

vital nest, except due to some foul obstacle or bad contagion that is horrid to them; thus, those that are cast up voluntarily through the mouth hardly portend anything good. Moreover, roundworms presuppose the ferment of the gall. Otherwise, in the **Celiac passion** <note>A historical term for chronic diarrhea or malabsorption, similar to what we call Celiac disease today</note>, continuous worms would be raised up. <margin>83.</margin> For the **chyle** <note>original: "cremor," the milky fluid of digested food</note> would rot immediately unless the gall seasoned the chyle with its salt. In the **rectum**, around the end of the colon, **threadworms** <note>original: "Ascarides"</note> arise, which are not roundworms generated from human substance or chyle, but from putrid scraps—just as worms arise in meat, cheese, fish, and ulcers. Therefore, threadworms are products of decay, unlike roundworms. Finally, roundworms exist in us without laying eggs <note>Van Helmont believed roundworms were spontaneously generated from food, rather than breeding</note>, whereas threadworms lay their own eggs. Common water boiled with **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, taken as a small and harmless drink, kills all worms, both in the intestines and elsewhere. The same applies in ulcers if that water is poured on them. Finally, I will add as a corollary: since the intestines in which roundworms are born cannot digest them, it follows that **enemas** sent in for nourishment are frustrated in their hope; the enema will sooner nourish the roundworms and threadworms than the human. Nature, therefore, has established with me **six vital digestions**. <margin>48.</margin> In the seventh number, she herself **Sabbatizes** <note>rests, like the Sabbath day</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the digestive system, shifting focus from the lower intestines and the formation of waste to the Pylorus—the lower "gate" of the stomach. Van Helmont argues that this organ is not merely a passive valve but a vital center of health with its own independent power.</meta>

# THE PYLORUS

...or drink it received, until the digestion of the stomach is completed and the **chyle** <note>original: "chylus"; the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>, or a creamy substance, is produced. For then, and not before, the Pylorus opens itself. However, the upper orifice of the stomach is closed, at least when fullness is imminent (if not enough is being swallowed), while the stomach begins to attend to its duty. These are the things I have found so far handed down by the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities who followed the ancient teachings of Galen and Aristotle.</note> regarding the pylorus. I, however, have discovered that a great hinge of health and illness turns upon the Pylorus.

<margin>2.</margin> For first of all, I have seen from time to time in fevers that undigested things are vomited today which were swallowed the day before yesterday. On the opposite side, in the **Coeliac passion** <note>A chronic digestive disorder where food passes through the body undigested; similar to chronic diarrhea</note>, the Pylorus is never closed. Indeed, some people, after they have been sumptuously satisfied with food, do not stop **playing the Greek** <note>original: "pergraecari"; a term meaning to carouse or drink heavily</note> the whole night through, and therefore urinate continuously. It is necessary, therefore, for their Pylorus to be remarkably open—not just drop by drop, but trickling in a continuous thread. Nor does it wait for any goal of cooking; for soon, or even from the beginning, it was not adequately closed, or at least it lies open with its folds somewhat drawn apart, after the stomach was not satisfied by the incoming drink. This occurs in healthy people when there is a failure in the closure of the Pylorus. There are others also for whom the Pylorus is a more stubborn guardian; they vomit drinks after they are half-finished. Inasmuch as the digestive power, not being equal to the whole of the drinks taken, ejects them when provoked. Indeed, it is an excessive obstinacy of the Pylorus 

<margin>3.</margin> when food from three days ago is ejected. These things certainly prove that the Pylorus is not only a **Gatekeeper** <note>original: "Janitorem"</note>, but also moderates the first and most evident digestion; and thus they prove the drowsy neglect of the Schools in this matter. For as a remedy to their insufficiencies, I say that the Pylorus is closed first of all, not indeed by a muscle, in the manner of the anus or the bladder, for it is not a servant of voluntary movement. Nor, finally, is it closed by contracted fibers, like a **cramp** or **colic** <note>original: "torminum"</note>.

<margin>4.</margin> For it performs its duty as gatekeeper without sensation or distress. But not otherwise than the **uterus** after conception, the Pylorus closes its lower mouth on every side by its own motive <term>Blas</term> <note>Van Helmont's term for a "vital motive force" or "impulse" that directs the movement of organs</note>. In this way, I consider both orifices

<column-break/>

of the stomach to be closed. It is such, however, that the upper orifice, once closed after a meal in a healthy person, easily opens itself anew at every persistent morsel or stubborn draft, since it can hardly bear for anything to hang over it from above in the throat. Although in the sick, and those suffering from hunger, its opening occurs with pain and great anxiety, because in those cases, that closure of the orifice depends on disorder. Therefore, the closure of the Pylorus is more stubborn and more accurate than that of the upper orifice. Finally, it is beyond doubt that the motive power of both parts does not obey the will, and so it is either natural or diseased. 

<margin>5.</margin> The Pylorus is said by the Schools to be subject to the **retentive faculty** <note>The supposed power of an organ to hold onto its contents</note>. But certainly, it shows absolute power when—even against the **expulsive faculty**, while the **digestive faculty** fails and the **attractive faculty** is nauseated, and thus others are ruined—the Pylorus often becomes stubborn, both in its closure (as I said happens above in fevers) and in its opening (as happens to those with the coeliac passion). 

<margin>6.</margin> For vomiting occurs while, with the Pylorus closed, the stomach contracts itself upward—not indeed through a shriveling of the stomach, but by a total movement of the stomach upward toward the throat. Thus, the Pylorus commands the vomit and does not listen to the retentive faculty. Since, therefore, the power of the Pylorus is not a follower of other faculties, nor subject to the fibers, but is **Monachal** <note>meaning "solitary" or "absolute," acting like a monk who follows his own rule</note>, and thus the fibers must obey its nod. It is necessary that this absolute power be vital and have its own motive <term>Blas</term>, like the uterus, independent of human choice. And it is all the more powerful because the <term>duumviratus</term> <note>The "duumvirate" or "rule of two," referring to the functional partnership between the stomach and the spleen in Van Helmont's physiology</note> of the stomach has now come to light. And although the Pylorus is often wearied by external and occasional causes (such as medicines, poisons, or filth), nevertheless its <term>Blas</term> is free to it, implanted in the part or its <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is the internal governing spirit or "master-workman" of an organ that directs its life-functions</note>. In this, however, I admire a certain superior force, similar to the influences of the stars. 

<margin>7.</margin> For the <term>Blas</term> of the Pylorus most closely expresses the <term>Blas</term> of the will; for even when an external stimulant rushes in toward closure or opening, it can nonetheless go against it at its pleasure, so that as long as the Pylorus is in good health, it moves for its own ends.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the Pylorus is an independent "gatekeeper" of the stomach governed by its own vital spirit (Archeus) and motive force (Blas), rather than being a passive muscle or a servant of the brain. He uses clinical observations of vomiting and chronic diarrhea to prove that the Pylorus can act against the body's other digestive faculties to preserve or eject food.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s revolutionary reassessment of the stomach's exit, the Pylorus. Having established in the previous page that the Pylorus is the "gatekeeper," he now explores its role as a "Rector" or "Governor" that possesses its own internal intelligence and motive force, which he calls "Blas."</meta>

# THE GOVERNOR

<margin>8.</margin> ...to its legitimate ends, or at least those that appear so to itself, by tightening or loosening the exit. Yet, when an inordinate man <note>A person living without moderation or discipline</note> transgresses against these ends, the Pylorus, as the sole moderator of digestion, often compels the man to pay the price through suffering. But since in this **Blas** <term>Van Helmont’s specific term for a "motive force" or "vital impulse" that governs the movement of organs</term> there can be defects, as if by an arbitrary judgment—not only from occasional causes, but even in its own motive principle when it becomes "mindless"—it may freely open or close itself out of season and in a state of fury, much like the womb. It is certainly a wonder that these things have remained neglected by the **Schools** <note>The traditional academic medical authorities of the time</note> along with the other principles of healing. Any power, and especially a motive one, easily wanders astray, excited as much by chance causes as by its own mindless whim; for these powers are free and, as it were, independent. In the error of this motive power, the Pylorus frequently and easily stumbles. Just as the womb, even when not shaken by external forces, throws itself about, ascends, or twists itself furiously to the sides, and alienates the throat, the gullet, and even the nerves that serve the will, acting against its duty—it tightens, opens, contracts, and repeatedly displays atrocious movements, hardly different from magic, insofar as an eccentric **Blas** <note>original: "Blas motivum"</note> is capable of stirring up various scenes of internal "storms." These matters must be carefully attended to by physicians, so that whenever the Pylorus wanders from its goals due to some irritating occasion, the doctor may immediately study how to remove the cause.

But if the Pylorus goes out of bounds by the error or "fury" of its own **Blas**, the physician must realize that he is dealing with eccentric powers and not with mere "matter" <note>The physical substance of food or waste</note>; he should by no means put his trust in evacuants <note>Medicines used to induce vomiting or purging</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> For let us consider a man in a balanced state, moderately fed: his Pylorus is adequately closed so that nothing drips through its cracks. Finally, when digestion is finished, the Pylorus opens itself. Certainly, this does not happen because of some stimulating "exotic quality" of the **chyle** <note>The milky fluid of digested food</note>; rather, it is because the Pylorus is "aware" of the things to be done in the stomach. Therefore, it is to be considered the moderator of digestion, in whose care the goals of the regime reside and where the keys are kept. For otherwise, if the Pylorus is closed

<column-break/>

longer than is right, that which was sufficiently digested does not cease to endure the further force of the digestive **ferment** <note>The chemical-like agent Van Helmont believed was responsible for digestion</note>, and is therefore "cooked" more than is right. It is not that the chyle is like glass in a furnace, which is cooked more excellently the longer it stays; rather, by too much delay, it is alienated and corrupted. This, in turn, must necessarily produce many difficulties, both in the stomach and in its neighboring parts. Nevertheless, if the Pylorus is not closed tightly enough, surely a fresh drink cannot help but be carried into the intestines along with its former raw qualities. Since stomach digestion is not the duty of the intestines, once they receive the **gall-ferment** <note>Bile</note>, the matter is changed into a foreign substance, eventually producing various infirmities in the veins. This is because the body proceeds to the "second digestion" while skipping the first.

<margin>10.</margin> In this way, tremors and twitching of the hands, palpitations of the heart, fainting spells, acute fevers, tumors, and unexpected bouts of arthritis leap forth. Likewise, the acidity of wine, not yet corrected by the maturity of the first digestion, is foreign to the veins; together with its innate **aqua vitae** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; literally "water of life," referring here to the spirit or potency of the wine</note>, it causes the veins' own nourishment to degenerate, and as an anonymous and unknown guest, it gives birth to unusual and unknown infirmities. It is almost the same if well-matured chyle slips into the **Duodenum**, and at that very instant new food is swallowed from above; be certain that a well-constituted Pylorus is immediately closed, even if the previous load has not been fully dismissed. Therefore, the portion of chyle that is detained becomes corrupted, grows more sour than is right, and contaminates the new food with a premature ferment. The whole mass becomes "exotic" <note>Foreign or harmful to the body's nature</note>, unless it is banished by the Pylorus before coction is complete—an act which excites various cravings, griping pains, and **Diarrheas**. Thus, an error of the Pylorus, whether its own or provoked by disorder, causes many difficulties. That the Pylorus closes immediately upon the arrival of new food is evident; otherwise, the new and raw food would slip out along with the chyle and appear in the excrement, as if produced by a **Celiac affection** <note>original: "affectu cœliaco"; a condition where food passes through the body undigested</note>. This is sometimes seen in "voracious" <note>Greedy or over-eating</note> children, whose Pylorus is not yet strong enough to...

He argues that most digestive illnesses arise when this gatekeeper opens too early or stays closed too long, leading to the corruption of food and systemic diseases like arthritis and tremors.</summary>

# THE PYLORUS

Therefore, those with weaker stomachs complain that great acidities arise within them, which they cast up in the morning along with yesterday's food, or at night along with the **chyle** <term>The milky fluid of digested food</term> from the previous noon and the dregs of the last-eaten meals. Furthermore, for a fuller understanding of these things, it must be repeated that it is not the function of the stomach's veins to suck up the chyle held within the stomach; likewise, vomiting occurs when the **Pylorus** <note>The lower opening of the stomach leading to the intestines</note> is closed, and the entire length of the stomach contracts from the bottom upwards toward the upper orifice. Finally, this movement is initiated by the Pylorus, which, if it were to open, would certainly relieve the stomach with much less distress. But since it does not open, it judges it unsuitable for health that those dregs be sent downward. Thus, it has appeared to me as the **Governor of Digestion**. This vomiting happens in two ways: namely, by the Pylorus’s own **Blas** <term>A vital, motive force or "impulse" specific to an organ</term>; in that case, it is painless. The other kind occurs from irritating substances; and that kind, even if it also happens by means of the Pylorus, is not by its own willing. Therefore, it is also troublesome and full of anxiety. <margin>12.</margin> At the very least, vomiting does not occur unless the Pylorus is closed; otherwise, that which is expelled by vomiting would instead fall down into the **Duodenum** <note>The first part of the small intestine</note>. For when vomiting occurs by the Pylorus’s own motion, everything it judges harmful to itself is removed in the first vomit. But if the Pylorus is provoked, then by repeated vomiting, other things are ejected than those which came out at first. Specifically, yellow yolk-like matter, then things that are more transparently yellow like rapeseed oil follow; these are believed to be bilious because of their bitterness. And finally, blue and green substances occasionally appear, which come right from the start after taking more violent drugs. <margin>13.</margin> Here, the Pylorus was open between the first and subsequent vomits, so much so that the Pylorus plucks upward to itself whatever lurks in the **jejunum** <note>The middle part of the small intestine</note> and its vicinity, so that it might wash away, as it were, the mark impressed upon it by the drug. Moreover, these things are usually bitter, both because they have endured the repeated and excessive, even angry, ferment of the bile, and also because they are snatched upward, contrary to custom, "into another's harvest" <note>original: "in alienam messem" — a metaphor for entering the stomach where they do not belong</note>, where they are corrupted into excrement, marked

<column-break/>

by the quality of the ferment that it immediately drank in. Therefore, the chyle in that place becomes bilious and bitter. Moreover, at this point, <margin>14.</margin> I look upon the **Schools** <note>The traditional medical authorities and universities</note> with wonder, for prescribing that foods of easier digestion should be eaten before those that are harder to cook, unmindful of their own doctrine. That doctrine claims that all the contents of the stomach are turned into a uniform chyle, and that the Pylorus is closed even from the beginning so that it lets nothing—not even a drop—slip away before digestion is completed. Finally, they claim that "cooking" <note>The process of digestion</note> is produced by the unceasing heat of the stomach, and thus digestion, once begun, continues from the start and never rests as long as its **Vulcan heat** <term>Internal digestive heat, named after the Roman god of fire</term> persists. They say each of the contents receives this digestive heat according to the capacity of the receiver. If this doctrine stands—since everything is reduced to a liquid chyle and mixed exquisitely in the "single pot" of the stomach—it follows that in a meal, those things which are harder to digest should be eaten first, so that they might be cooked for a much longer span of heat. <margin>15.</margin> Liquid foods (say the Schools) and those of prompter "cooking," if taken last, would putrefy if they had to wait for the final goal of the harder items taken. As if the digestive power were the parent of putrefaction! Or as if a mixing of the things eaten did not occur! Or a conversion into fluid chyle! But rather as if the things taken mouthful by mouthful would lie separated on the bottom. As if, I say, the Pylorus opened itself at fixed periods or turns, so that the order in which food was received might be preserved in sending out the chyle. If the Schools believed these things possible, at least the Pylorus would be endowed with greater discretion in observing the priorities of foods than the Schools so lazily neglect in their description of its duty. Furthermore, the closure of the Orifice <note>The upper opening of the stomach, the cardia</note> does not contribute to digestion, nor does it rule the appetite. The Pylorus, however, commands both. For sufficient satiety is usually present, yet we eat and drink further out of vice. Therefore, the closure of the Orifice is not from appetite, nor is it from fullness. # THE GOVERNOR

...ness, and an aversion to meat, soon begin from fevers and the onset of stomach diseases, and they have the [upper] orifice closed. Therefore, the orifice is neither closed because of fullness, nor because of the necessity of <margin>16.</margin> digestion, just as it is not continually opened because of appetite: if indeed it is closed without appetite, fullness, and digestion—and yet remains open after satiety during the process of digestion. For belches are emitted in the morning on an empty, void, and craving stomach; yet a belch signals the closure of the orifice. Finally, the orifice is closed in those who, pressed by long fasting, grow faint, and who have been weakened by a daily abstinence from food. For these people, the reopening of the orifice is very difficult, anxious, and painful. If, therefore, the orifice is not necessarily closed by hunger, appetite, fullness, and digestion, then the closure or opening of the orifice does not regard the needs of the vital powers serving digestion. Instead, the orifice primarily serves to prevent **chyle** <term>The milky fluid of semi-digested food</term> from regurgitating into the throat when a person is lying down. From this, it is first clear that the service of the **Pylorus** <note>The muscular valve at the bottom of the stomach</note> is more specialized than that of the [upper] <margin>17.</margin> orifice. Indeed, it is the governor of the entire stomachic economy, reaching even unto the last coil of the intestines. In this area, since the operation of the bile is completed, the bile itself ought to be built upon and lean upon the Pylorus. <margin>18.</margin> If there is not full agreement between these two, there arise diarrhea, griping pains, dysentery, hemorrhoids, and various disasters of the abdomen. It is also erroneous in **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years</note> and his modern Schools that we <margin>19.</margin> only hunger and thirst because of a scarcity of blood, and thus that as many ounces of blood must be refilled as are depleted. First, if that were always true, let the Schools choose: namely, either they make themselves into vain slaughterhouses through **phlebotomy** <term>Bloodletting, a common medical practice of the time</term>, or appetite is not actually excited by the "sucking" of the veins as they report a defect of blood. This is especially beyond doubt regarding health: for if hunger occurs because of a lack of blood, then bloodletting is poorly practiced during a scarcity of blood. But if this is considered in diseases—for instance, in a fe-

<column-break/>

-ver, where there is no appetite, there would likewise be no defect of blood. But if every day as many ounces of blood were supplied as were consumed—of which consumption hunger would be the indicator—then in a fever, either there is no consumption of blood, or hunger is not the sensation of consumed blood. But if blood is also consumed during a fever, bloodletting will be in vain. In any <margin>20.</margin> event, after two or three days of fever, just as much blood will have been consumed (since fever consumes and wastes the body more than healthy living does) as a "plethora" (the only indicator for bloodletting) would require to be removed. Consequently, if these theses about hunger are granted, bloodletting will be futile everywhere. For the Schools suppose that blood is dispensed from the **vena cava** <term>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</term> into smaller ones (as if the vein itself were the dispenser, and there were no difference between the vessel and the force that distributes things proportionally) and finally into tiny branches, through which it is dispersed into the body's tissues at last. And they believe that from the sensation of fasting alone, the last branches of the veins suck from the larger trunk, and this in turn sucks from the veins of the stomach and **mesentery** <term>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>. From this, they claim, hunger and thirst are finally felt. Given this, first: those whose veins are bulging would never feel hunger or thirst. Second: there would be no fluctuation of that sensation unless the larger veins were first emptied. Third: this thesis likewise contradicts the doctrine of the Schools, who teach that the stomach primarily digests for its own sake, and secondarily (or by accident) for the whole body—as if the stomach were subject to a common **philautia** <term>Self-love or self-preservation</term>. For if that were granted, the stomach would not digest, desire, or hunger for the body, but only for itself. Therefore, it would not feel hunger to supply the scarcity in the veins. Instead, the veins would primarily thirst and hunger, and the stomach would only do so by accident—not for itself, but because of the veins. Ignorance of the truth has made the Schools headstrong everywhere. They have not known, I say, that hunger is inspired into the stomach by the **Spleen** <note>Van Helmont believed the spleen was the seat of the "sensitive soul" and responsible for the impulse of hunger</note>; for the Spleen knows the goal of things to be done...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Pylorus as the "Governor" of the stomach's functions. Van Helmont is explaining how the Pylorus, rather than the upper opening of the stomach, controls appetite and responds to bodily trauma through its own "Blas" or vital internal motion.</meta>

-> ### THE PYLORUS <-

The stomach is the principal organ for governing the "decoctions" <note>The process of "cooking" or breaking down food in the body</note>; therefore, it is effectively placed in charge of the appetites, yet the *Pylorus* <note>The muscular valve at the base of the stomach</note> assists it as its *Governor and Executor*. For the *Pylorus* still possesses the decision, its own free *Blas* <term>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a vital, guiding internal motion or force</term>, of opening or closing itself. In a state of health, it moves according to its knowledge of the purposes for which the stomach creates digestion and appetite—appetites which are sent from the *Spleen*—as if the *Pylorus* were privy to the secret goals of the *Spleen*. However, in times of ill health, the *Pylorus* opens and closes itself perversely and in an inverted order, as if seized by a symptomatic madness. 

In fact, while I was once walking about to buy a villa, possessing a great appetite, I happened to twist my foot and fell. A chill immediately came over me, along with nausea, vomiting, and the total suppression of my previous desire to eat. But soon, I reset the twisted and semi-dislocated foot; and at that same instant, my original appetite returned to me, <margin>21.</margin> and the nausea ceased. Clearly, the upper orifice was open both during the appetite and during the nausea; but I had the *Pylorus* closed during the appetite, and shortly after, it was open during the nausea, and closed again during the vomiting. For as I have said, vomiting does not occur unless the *Pylorus* is closed and turned upward. In hiccups, however, there is an inversion of the stomach itself upward, which is therefore quite different from the aforementioned inversion of the *Pylorus* when one is about to vomit. That these things were so is evident: since the stomach, under the influence of great hunger, had nothing to vomit, and being greedy for food, the *Pylorus* by its own consent immediately closed itself. Then, as if driven mad by the twisting of the ligaments of the foot, it opened itself wide and summoned filth from the duodenum <note>The first part of the small intestine</note> to itself. Indeed, during the vomiting, in order to expel the collected "saburra" <note>Original Latin: *saburram*, referring to a gritty or foul accumulation of undigested matter</note>, the *Pylorus* closed itself; and it would have opened itself again for a new accumulation of filth, had the "madness" of the *Pylorus* not been quieted by the resetting of the minor dislocation. Since the appetite returned immediately upon the closure of the *Pylorus*, who does not see that the appetite supplied by the *Spleen* is governed by the *Pylorus*? I have said that the *Pylorus* snatches filth upward from the duodenum into the stomach; so that 

<column-break/>

the one who was previously thought to be a gatekeeper dedicated only to holding food in or pushing it out, might also be seen to attract harmful things. Although these things happen by a common force, by which all things once declared "outlawed" take on a hostile character and thereafter deteriorate; nevertheless, when the *Blas* of the *Pylorus* is "raging" toward the stomach, they are pulled in an inverted order. At least I have discovered in this that the *Pylorus* is not only the cause of appetite, nausea, and vomiting, but is also the sole perpetrator of *cholera, dysentery,* and *diarrhea*. I have learned by experience that the madness of the *Pylorus* is often calmed, and the aforementioned disasters corrected, by the application of a small remedy. It is truly a pity that "The Schools" <note>The traditional medical universities of the time, which followed Galenic and Aristotelian teachings</note> have considered nothing of these matters until now. All their assistance is placed in the *enema* <note>A liquid injection into the rectum</note>; they do not go to the "nest" of the evil. They turn themselves only to the passage of the byproduct, like a dog that bites the stone thrown at it. 

For I saw a young man, in excellent health and possessing a great appetite, who in the morning had eaten some fresh, ripe blackberries, well-washed, with buttered bread; and soon after he felt a pleasant sensation of cooling refreshment in his stomach. Then, perhaps half an hour later, his appetite being suddenly lost and accompanied by colicky pain, he fell into a diarrhea, having perhaps 70 bowel movements a day, milky in color. Immediately, the *Physicians* administered restrictive "cordials" <note>Medicines intended to invigorate the heart</note> both internally and externally. These included *quince juice* with *alkermes confections* <note>A famous red syrup made from kermes insects, pearls, and spices</note>, exhilarating *rose-based powders* <note>Original: *diarrhodonis de Spodio*</note>, *preparations of hyacinth* <note>Original: *diahiacinti*</note> and the like. Meanwhile, many enemas made from "chalybeate" whey <note>Whey treated with iron or steel</note> and similar rubbish were injected, and all was in vain. Finally, opiates were added to the other treatments; nature laughed at their learned ignorance and playful attempts, while the patient suffered from the useless <margin>22.</margin> remedies. At last, when he was placed in the ultimate danger of his life, the Lord healed him. I indeed administered two hard-boiled egg yolks, tempered with rose vinegar. That the diarrhea had arisen from a fault of the *Pylorus* is proven by the cast-down appetite, and the restoration of that appetite once the yolks were taken. For he felt the obvious help of the medicine while it was still within the stomach...

But if the hoof of a frisky beast becomes a luxury: it is said to bring certain destruction to those with dysentery. The *Pylorus*, therefore, is the **Governor** of the closing of digestion and appetite in the stomach: it even governs the long journey of the intestines, as much the contents as the wanderings of the neighboring veins. For they testify that the indigestions of food and excrement, corruptions, and rapid passages are the result of the indignation of the *Pylorus* alone, <margin>23.</margin> as confirmed by remedies. Thus, yesterday’s excess <note>original: "hesterna crapula," referring to a hangover</note> gives rise to vertigo, not so much at night as in the morning when the stomach is empty of food; and these dizzy spells usually cease as soon as breakfast is taken. This is because the *Pylorus* is then open and covered in filth: but then it closes itself at the arrival of breakfast, and, as it were, forgets the prior discomfort. <margin>24.</margin> Our rooster for two years ate bran and oats in the morning according to custom: but toward evening he refused to roost on the usual perches, lay on the ground, and the following morning turned away from food. Vertiginous, he ran sideways and often fell backward. Finally, he struck his comb and forehead quite hard against the earth and died before noon. Through dissection, however, several small flints were found, not indeed in the first sac or stomach <note>The gizzard or crop</note>, but in the inner and true stomach. A larger flint, however, had closed the *Pylorus*, and being smaller than a flint [that could pass], it had cut off the hope of passing through. Indeed, no other cause of such great vertigo and unusual death was found: except that the *Pylorus*, because it was closed by force and against its will at the site of "cooking" <note>digestion</note>, had produced a leek-green liquor <note>original: "porraceum liquorem"</note> above the larger flint. <margin>25.</margin> Which certainly could not have come from the gall-bladder, since the flint had blocked the passage from the gall-bladder through the duodenum to the stomach. Therefore, that green and leek-like liquor was born in the stomach by the fault of the <margin>26.</margin> closed *Pylorus*. Concerning thirst similarly, I have often observed 

<column-break/>

feverish people who were thirsty, who then vomited up the drink again along with four times its volume. Therefore, thirst is not necessarily due to a lack of moisture: nor even due to a penury of blood. It is not as if the same veins, for the same cause, are now the cause of hunger and now of thirst, and messengers of the lack of blood—indeed, sometimes both at once, hunger as much as thirst. Rather, the organ breathing a *ferment* <term>In Van Helmont’s theory, a "ferment" is a vital chemical agent that triggers biological processes like digestion</term> into the stomach excites hunger and thirst. For in fevers, an alkaline salt is the cause of the feverish state; hence thirst does not cease, even though the stomach flows with its own drink: for the drink does not reach that alkali. Thus, for instance, salty and peppery things prepare thirst, not otherwise than putrid alkalis; because they exclude the acid *ferment* from the stomach. Insofar as salt hinders the resolution and transmutation of food—that is, the entry of the digestive ferment breathed from the *Spleen*. Thus, a quantity of pure drink, peppery things, and hard and indigestible things cause thirst: not because they are "hot and dry" <note>A critique of the traditional Galenic system of four humors</note> in the midst of the waters held in the stomach, but because they resist the aforementioned ferment of the *Spleen* <note>original: "Lienis"</note>. Acids, on the opposite hand, insofar as they are similar to the ferment of the *Spleen*, soothe thirst. Thirst, therefore, in such cases, is not due to a lack of nutritive moisture: but due to the hindered ferment of the spleen, which, finally overcoming the aforementioned difficulties during longer sleep, causes sleep to take away thirst. Thirst also arises in fevers because of greasy, putrid, and coagulated things; not, however, because nutritive and cooling moisture is desired (as they think), but a "resolutive" of the harm. Thus, it does not so much indicate and demand nourishment as it does a remedy. And therefore thirst does not cease through drinking unless the drink brings a medium for the ferment to grasp. Since the *Pylorus* is the **Governor** of "cooking" <note>digestion</note>, and no less a moderator of thirst than of appetite, the sensations of both food and drink will also belong to the same Governor, who distinguishes the ends of digestions. Namely, at the beginnings of Tertian fevers <margin>27.</margin> <note>Fevers that recur every third day, like malaria</note>, a copious vomiting of yellow excrement, together with great thirst, infests the patient, and those two things concur with the closure of the raging *Pylorus*, and...

When his corpse was dissected, it showed no defect, except that a blackish broth was floating in the stomach with the Pylorus closed. 

2. A noble three-year-old girl, while an Italian doctor was boasting of a fever-reducing emetic, took a few grains of a certain powder. Perhaps it was because it was too late and life was already failing. The corpse of each was opened. And the same rotten broth held in the stomach was found to be the cause of the killing, with the Pylorus tightly closed. 

3. In the first stomach of those hens were found several of the aforementioned fragments, which were easily judged to have remained there for many days. They were diminished (since glass does not break except in points) both on the sides and at the corners; those fragments had become blunt on all sides.

2. That this closing of the Pylorus was "mad" <note>original: "furiosa"</note>; otherwise it would have opened itself and not caused such harm.

# THE HISTORY OF TARTAR.

*1. That the treatise on the four fictitious humors must be joined to this place for the sake of the work's completeness. 2. After discussing the rejected quality of elemental imbalance, we must then deal with Tartar and the three primary principles of the chemists. 3. The origin and life of Paracelsus. 4. He was the first to introduce Tartar as a cause of disease. 5. The battle of the Humorists <note>Doctors who followed the ancient theory of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> against Paracelsus ended poorly. 6. They thereafter used remedies borrowed from our fugitive servants. 7. The humors, which I have finally proven never existed in nature in a specific book, have long since fallen silent. 8. An epitome of what Paracelsus wrote in various places regarding Tartar.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D featuring floral motifs and scrollwork.</image-desc>It seemed fitting to me to place physical matters first in the order of medical practice; for I have always believed that the knowledge of all nature is only worth seeking for the sake of human health. Therefore, I have dealt only with the elements, so that I might drive away the fictions of the Schools <note>The established universities following Galen and Aristotle</note> regarding the composition of the four elements in every single body, which has been considered a "mixture" until now. I will show, I say, that there are no such mixtures of elements, nor any "struggles" between them, nor any imbalances or "complexions." Just as the catalog of diseases cannot stand in truth when based on these fictitious imbalances of elemental qualities. This means the Schools have, until now, been ignorant of the causes of diseases, almost all of which they have attributed to such qualities. Furthermore, the same labor now remains for me: I must write about the four false and fictitious <term>humors</term> <note>The traditional fluids believed to control health</note> and their stray corruptions, and show that such humors never existed in nature. Because of this, people have erred just as Perniciously in doctrine, knowledge, and the identifying of disease-causing agents, as they have in the resulting misguided remedies and

<column-break/>

all their directions and applications. And since I have already provided a specific book on this in the year 1644, printed at Cologne by Jodocus Calchoven and directed as a precursor to this work, and alongside it I published two others—one on <term>Lithiasis</term> <note>original: "Lithyasi"; the formation of stones in the body</note> and another on the "Tomb of the Plague"—in which I showed that the causes of those diseases have been ignored in the Schools until now. Therefore, it is enough for it to have been attested here. Nevertheless, those books should be transferred here for the sake of the work's completeness. Thus, the causes and essences of diseases have, until today, remained neglected by the Schools, and consequently, the sick have been left even more destitute of just remedies. Now at last, because Paracelsus recently
<margin>2.</margin>
dared to banish the general cause of almost all diseases to <term>Tartar</term> <note>Paracelsus used this term, originally referring to stony wine-cask deposits, to describe stony precipitates like kidney stones or gouty crystals in the body</note>; and although Paracelsus was the first to rashly satisfy this, he remained uncertain and inconsistent as to whether he should establish the Three Principles (which he rightly called the three principles of all bodily things)—namely Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—as the general cause of all diseases, rather than his introduced Tartar. And therefore, he left both of the aforementioned assertions still in dispute; yet the more illustrious physicians today have devoted themselves to Tartar. For this reason, since the truth of the causes and remedies of diseases is found in neither theory today, I have considered it a worthwhile task for the good of my neighbor to sweep away and avert both of Paracelsus's errors from the Schools. So that physicians, who are already leaning toward the doctrine of Tartar, may finally—after all errors are dismissed—take themselves to the true knowledge of diseases and remedies.

# THE TARTARS
<meta>catchword: cato</meta>

...and from there, may the person closest to me receive the benefit (which is the only thing I have desired). For the knowledge of things, according to the principles I have already handed down, is drawn from a definition; and a definition must truly be taken from a knowledge of causes. Therefore, in the midst of such great darkness and ignorance of medical matters on all sides, I will attempt to lead posterity—and indeed the **young students** <note>original: "Tyrones," meaning beginners or recruits</note> of today—into a true science of diseases and remedies. For I have long since lost hope that the elders will be willing to learn; they are too far gone, both through the laziness of agreeing with the inventions of the **pagans** <note>The author refers to ancient Greek and Roman physicians like Galen as "pagans"</note> (which they have already swallowed and converted into their own nourishment) and through the shame of learning from a poor little man like me, the least of the Philosophers.

<margin>3.</margin>
The father of **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who challenged traditional medicine</note> was the illegitimate son of a Master of the Teutonic Knights; he turned out to be a common physician, though rich with an excellent library. He entrusted his son, **Aureolus Philippus Theophrastus von Bombast**, to Trithemius of Sponheim. From there, wealthy with a storehouse of secrets, the son went to work on **Spagyric** <note>term: Spagyric—the alchemical process of separating and recombining the components of plants or minerals to create medicine</note> operations under Sigismund Fugger. For while there, he was not devoted to **Venus** <note>original: "Veneri deditus," a euphemism for lust or sexual pursuits</note>—for indeed, he had "castrated" his common path—nor did he waste his life in laziness or flattery, being hungry for knowledge. Around his twentieth year, while investigating various mines in Germany, he finally came to **Muscovy** <note>Russia</note>; in the neighboring regions, he was captured by the Tartars and led to the **Khan** <note>original: "Chamum," referring to the Mongol or Tartar ruler</note> by our "Sanuchus." From there, he was sent to Constantinople with the Khan's son. Finally, around the 28th year of his age, 
<margin>10.</margin>
he came into possession of the **chrysopoeic stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, believed to turn base metals into gold</note> which was given to him. Because of this, he turned toward Basel, where, since he was already famous for many healings of diseases, he obtained the chair of Medical Philosophy so that he might give himself entirely to **Spagyric** labors. Indeed, as the chrysopoeic stone had lifted his spirits and he saw the majestic equipment of physicians and their wandering errors, he had long since aspired to the leadership of the healing art. He taught at Basel for three full years and published a book on **Tartar** <note>Paracelsus used this term for stony sediments in the body, comparing them to the crust in wine barrels</note>, as well as on degrees and compositions. Both were 

<column-break/>

truly works of his own invention and burdened with many anxieties. Meanwhile, as each man is drawn by his own pleasure, and Paracelsus was indulging too much in his own concoctions, he began to despise the university chair and even the use of Latin; from which he almost fell away, thinking that the truth ought only to be spoken in German. Thus, although born with a rare talent, he was more successful by the gift of the **Azoth** <note>term: Azoth—a supposed universal solvent or spirit in alchemy, often associated with Paracelsus's secret remedies</note> than by the investigation of theory. It was he, I say, who first thrust **Tartar** upon us as the cause of almost all diseases and accused it, since he saw that he could not sufficiently trust the Schools of the Ancients, nor even his own "Three Principles." To him, as a patron, the modern Schools have subscribed. I too, as if having found a treasure, once congratulated myself and entirely agreed, until the Lord instructed me otherwise.
<margin>5*</margin>
First, the followers of Galen and Paracelsus disputed whether Tartar and **phlegm** <note>One of the four humors of traditional medicine</note> were not the same thing and merely synonyms. But finally, being stunned by the **coagulations** <note>Solid deposits like kidney stones or gouty crystals</note> and not daring to ascribe such a great crowd of diseases to phlegm alone, the more learned Galenists admitted the existence of Tartar; and they began to use remedies which they begged from **fugitive servants** <note>A derogatory reference to wandering alchemists or unlicensed practitioners</note>.
<margin>6.</margin>
And even if these remedies were all poisonous, filthy, and adulterated—and are even more so today—they nonetheless found their way into medical cabinets, so that they are brought out for use daily. At least when Tartar emerged as a theory, the **humors** <note>The four fluids (blood, phlegm, bile, black bile) supposed to govern health</note> almost failed in the minds of the more discerning.
<margin>7.</margin>
Therefore, the disgrace of healers arising from their failure to cure persuaded them to look back at chemical remedies. Neglecting the foundations of their own art, they began to use—without distinction—both those chemical remedies and wretched poisons as well as what their own **dispensatories** <note>official manuals of medicine</note> describe, doing so both to soothe fevers and to scrape away the phlegm of the stomach. Thus, having seen the laziness of Galen's remedies and theorems, the Galenists are gradually turning toward the theories of Tartar. Therefore, out of the many books which Paracelsus wrote concerning Tartars, I will draw together into a brief summary those things I have read.
<margin>8.</margin>
Nature, at first a beautiful virgin, from sin...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of disease, specifically focusing on "Tartar"—the stony deposits formed in the body. The author links the biblical curse of "thorns and thistles" to these medical obstructions and begins to critique Paracelsus's theories on the subject.</meta>

nature was polluted; not indeed by its own fault, nor was it for its own punishment, but since it had been created for the use of the ungrateful <note>The "ungrateful" refers to humanity after the Fall</note>, it was stained by the guilt of the inhabitants, so that at least through a defect of nature, it might to some extent atone for that guilt. The Creator repented, in a way, that he had ordered nature to obey the disobedient. Therefore, he decreed that the earth should henceforth produce thistles and thorns; under whose allegory the curse and origin of **Tartars** <note>In this medical context, "Tartar" refers to stony or sandy deposits in the body, like kidney stones or gouty crystals, named after the crust in wine barrels</note> are designated for us. This is surely the material of those things which prick us most sharply. Indeed, the words refer to the offspring of the earth, by the consumption of which they signify that diseases are eventually incorporated into us. For first, when these Tartar enemies enter treacherously through food and drink, they penetrate into the depths, mix themselves radically, and are closed up by an occult seal. Thus, some separate themselves immediately from the pure nourishment within: but others remain together with the nourishment, and when that is consumed, those that remain are coagulated in the form of slime, mud or a bolus, and finally sand or stone. These are then not only incapable of receiving the breath of life, but furthermore, boiling into a wild thorn, they become the intimate and immediate causes of all diseases, the daily nurses of mortal calamity. For as soon as the blood is converted into the substance of the nourished part and then consumed, this offspring of thorns often remains—a truly exotic coagulation, and often unfit due to its sharpness. For it hardens more every day, and stains its host with a thousand hostilities. In this

<column-break/>

matter, Tartar differs from the human excrement of food because the latter putrefies, while the former coagulates. Happy, therefore, is that stomach and liver alone which know how to banish the refuse of Tartar from the putrid excrement at the very threshold. Just as these thorns were procured for us by the ancient Tartarean enemy <note>A wordplay: "Tartarean" refers both to the medical deposits and to "Tartarus," the Greek underworld or Hell</note>, so the stone adhering to the sides of wine casks is called **Tartar**, because of its manifest pre-eminence, giving its name to the other classes of coagulable juices. For wine, in its vessel, is encrusted on all sides with a stony shell which is Tartar, distinct from the dregs. For these dregs fall to the bottom, incapable of coagulation, but the Tartar, stretched out everywhere, armors the vessel and preserves it eternally from putrefaction within. That guest, moreover, arriving through nourishment, is called **Foreign Tartar** <note>original: "Tartarus peregrinus"</note>, to distinguish it from that which grows within us by the **microcosmic law** <note>The "microcosmic law" refers to the idea that the human body—the "microcosm"—operates on the same principles as the universe or "macrocosm"</note>, a fatal spectacle. For whenever something violent rushes into us, by that very act the nutritional humors, deprived of life, become hostile, coagulate, and are called the **Tartar of the blood**. From this come abscesses, obstructions, and other calamities, according to the specific property and pleasure of each Tartar. And so Tartar, creeping from the mouth into the farthest reaches of the vessels, is also the principal cause of all diseases. These are the things concerning Tartar which I have been able to collect into one place from the scattered writings of Paracelsus.
