<meta>This page continues the investigation into "Tartar"—the stony residues found in both wine barrels and the human body. Having previously discussed the theological origins of these "thorns," the author now turns to a physical demonstration of how Tartar forms in wine, using this as a critique of Paracelsus’s theories on the causes of disease.</meta>

# TARTAR OF WINE

Before I reject the necessity that Paracelsus imagined for himself—namely, establishing that Tartar exists in every foodstuff in order to find the causes of disease—and so that the vanity of that fabrication may become manifest, it will be helpful above all to explain the manner in which Tartar is produced in wine. For it is from this (as people have begun to believe) that all causes of diseases establish their family and derive their name. The Cantabrians, whom they call Basques, before they were associated with our Dutchmen in the hunting of whales, often traveled near Greenland (which today is thought to have failed <note>The author likely refers to the "Lost Colony" or the cooling climate making Greenland inaccessible</note>). There, trapped by the cold beneath the reefs (which they call *Atalayas*), they had "cooked" wines, otherwise quite noble, which became frozen. <margin>1.</margin> Therefore, having removed the hoops from the cask, they exposed the naked ice of the wine, still in the shape of the original vessel, to the open air, so that in a single subsequent night, the remainder would be thoroughly frozen. <margin>2.</margin> Once this was done, they bored into the ice, and near the center of the ice they encountered a liquor the color of Amethyst: the pure **spirit of wine** <note>In early chemistry, the "spirit" refers to the alcohol content, which has a lower freezing point than water</note>, a fiery and vital liquor incapable of freezing. Thus, they drank the wine-ice melted by fire, having returned to themselves that tiny portion of vital liquor. This story is brought forward to the end that it may be established that the spirit in wine naturally flees from the cold and gradually withdraws itself from its own home toward the center of the wine. On the other hand, wines are set in the sun so they may turn sour; the spirit of wine flies away and leaves behind its sun-drenched corpse: vinegar. <margin>3.</margin> But since it is far more desirable for the spirit to retreat into the center of the wine than to vanish by flying away, necessity has caused cold and deep cellars to be found for the preservation of wines. Indeed, Austrian wines, working with a continuous heat like that of leaven, are viscous. For this reason, the cellars of Vienna are usually deepened by no fewer than a hundred steps. Spanish wines would endure the same, unless caution were applied by mixing in gypsum while they are pressed under the wine-press, which they call *Hiesso* <note>original: "Hiesso," a Spanish term for gypsum or plaster used to clarify and stabilize wine</note>. Therefore, in cold cellars, the spirit of the wine, on account of the cold, retreats to the

<column-break/>

innermost part of the wine and hides itself. <margin>4.</margin> Thus, the wine in the "bark" or outer layer all around, because the cold strikes the vessel, has less spirit than in its interior parts. From this it follows that, just as sun-drenched wines turn sour through a lack of spirit, so also proportionally, the outermost layer of wine in a cold larder is more acidic than in its central parts. <margin>5.</margin> Therefore, when the new wines (musts) are brought into the larder and when they have finished fermenting, their spirit soon flees inward, avoiding the cold; and thus the outer layer of the wine, having now also become slightly acidic, begins to act upon the dregs <term>fæx</term><note>The sediment or lees of the wine</note> still floating in the turbid wine. Indeed, it is impossible for there to be any acidity that does not immediately act upon a proportional object once it is found. This is surely the law and necessity of natural things. For example: vinegar, however weak, if it finds a **crab stone** <note>original: "lapidem Cancrorum," these are gastroliths—calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in historical medicine as an antacid</note>, cannot restrain itself from immediately acting toward its dissolution, changing it into a transparent liquor. <margin>6.</margin> Therefore the acid in the wine, now saturated with dregs and stripped of its own activity, inclines itself toward coagulation. However, it cannot be coagulated in the middle of the waves <note>i.e., the liquid wine</note>, but it has need of a fermenting wall, as it were, by which it may undergo a sort of putrefaction. Therefore, the coagulation occurs at the sides of the vessel, to which it attaches itself. This is according to a well-worn axiom of Chemistry: *Every dissolving spirit is coagulated by the same action by which it dissolves bodies.* <note>original: "Omnis spiritus dissolvens, eadem actione qua corpora dissolvit, coagulatur"</note> Therefore the more acidic wine, in its outer layer, dissolves the dregs; because soon the acid salt of the dissolving acidic spirit is coagulated together with the dissolved dregs, and it places itself against the neighboring side or curve of the vessel. This is done so that both (the dissolver and the dissolved) are not hindered from coagulating, but at least on one side are not surrounded by liquor. Thus, the **Tartar**, the new offspring of coagulation, is attached. <margin>7.</margin> Understand also that before it is coagulated, it is not yet "coagulum"; and therefore that acidic wine, with the dregs already dissolved by it, in the instant before it is coagulated, seizes the vessel and attaches and glues itself there by the "necks" of its own coagulum. Otherwise, it would settle to the bottom. This very thing...

This process serves as a scientific model to challenge Paracelsus's theories on how similar stony deposits form in the human body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Paracelsus’s "Tartar" theory. Having described how wine freezes and separates, the author now focuses on the specific formation of "Tartar" (wine stone) and why it is a poor metaphor for human kidney and bladder stones.</meta>

### HISTORY

<margin>8.</margin> ...the very essence of wine is Tartar, which is the subject of our discourse. Vinegar itself proves this to be the case; for wine that has been exposed to the sun and had its vessel heated by the sun's rays never contains tartar in the vessel, even though it remains vinegar. Yet the material is the same, differing only by cold or heat. In the former case, it exists with tartar; here, however, it is without it.

<margin>9.</margin> Most notably, it is clear from what has been said that the aforementioned Maxim of Chemistry <note>original: *Chymiæ*; referring to the alchemical principle that dissolution and coagulation happen as one process</note> errs in this: it claims that the dissolution of a body happens by the very same action as the coagulation of the spirit. Indeed, if there were not different moments of motion involved, the coagulated material would not cling tenaciously, glued to the cask as if it were poured there from a molten state. If it were coagulated during the very motion of dissolution, it would fall to the bottom in the form of a precipitate, rather than adhering to the sides. Conversely, no tartar is found in the region of the dregs <note>original: *fæcis*; the "lees" or sediment at the bottom of the barrel</note>.

<margin>10.</margin> Let there be another, more important point of note: it is entirely irrelevant to use wine tartar as an analogy for the coagulated stones within us. Therefore, the name, history, method, and purpose of wine tartar have been irrelevantly introduced into the causes of disease. These things will become manifest when I reveal the fiction of "tartar" in food and drink. At the very least, as far as wine Tartar is concerned: it is not a foreign visitor to the wine, produced from some exotic mother-matter against or beyond the nature of wines—nor was it added as a curse to atone for sins committed by wine. Furthermore, wine tartar is never coagulated by a coagulant unique to itself (although Paracelsus thought otherwise elsewhere), but tartar is coagulated only after the dissolving acidity of the wine is exhausted and saturated by the dregs.

<margin>11.</margin> That is to say: once the acidity is overcome by the dissolved content, it intends to produce a coagulation. However, it does not create a true stone, but a fictitious one, insofar as it is dissolved again in hot water, like an acidic salt in a liquid—which is commonly called **cream of tartar** <note>original: *cremor tartari*; a salt of tartaric acid still used in baking today</note>. All these things clearly do not match the coagulated stones in our bodies.

<column-break/>

Yet, through a supposed identity with tartar, these things have been pushed into every individual foodstuff by this wine-inspired fiction.

<margin>12.</margin> Finally, this point is also forced: that tartar is not an excrement of wine, except for one part, which is the dissolved dregs; a fact which certainly did not escape Paracelsus. He occasionally exalts wine tartar far above the wine itself, as the heir to greater virtues.

<margin>13.</margin> Therefore, he poorly aligns wine tartar—through an identity of being and formation—with "morbid tartars" (disease-causing stones). He calls these stones "excrement," or rather a "curse" rising from briars and thorns, or a "Cacedonic entity" <note>original: *ens Cacedonium*; a Paracelsian term derived from Greek for an "evil spirit" or malignant force</note> dwelling within the pure "Saphiric entity" <note>original: *Saphyrico ente*; referring to the "Saphiric" or pure, celestial essence of things</note> of nature. Therefore, even if there were some other wine tartar raised into the matter of diseases, they would still harmonize poorly, even according to Paracelsus's own mind regarding diseased tartars. And thus, he only irrelevantly attributed the cause of diseases to tartar.

<margin>14.</margin> For they do not agree in any way: not in matter, not in the efficient cause, not in the method or cause of coagulation, nor in the resulting product, the object, or the principles. For sand or a stone <note>original: *calculus*; a kidney or bladder stone</note> is not resolved by boiling, as wine tartar otherwise is.

<margin>15.</margin> The entire comparison is therefore metaphorical—a transference of name and property. It is a frivolous and bold rashness of assertion, defiling all created things with a "curse," so that everything, through and through, would be nothing but tartar. The audacity has progressed so far that they imagine tartar even in the marrow, though it is not coagulable; Paracelsus never even saw this, but asserted it by sheer daring. He now fabricates a "tartar" that is neither tartar nor coagulable. He does this so that not only everything that is coagulable and has solidity, but even any liquid—that is, the entire creation—would be nothing but tartar destined for the punishment of sin. When the young wine has finished fermenting, lost its sweetness, and assumed the qualities of wine, all the dregs fall to the bottom: then the transmutation of the more acidic part of the wine begins to act upon the dregs. Gradually, that which is more fruitful in the spirit of wine seeks the inner parts...

The author dismisses the idea that tartar is a "curse" or a universal component of all food and tissue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s chemical analysis of wine. He is arguing that "Tartar" (the crusty deposit in wine barrels) is a specific chemical product of fermentation and acidity, and therefore a misleading metaphor for human kidney stones, contrary to the theories of Paracelsus.</meta>

# THE DISCOVERY OF TARTAR

...it leaves the surface of the cask, and from there it begins to turn sour. Not finding a nearby object to act upon, except at the bottom, it gradually dissolves the material there; its acidity is formed and slowly becomes more established. Since every acid "boils up" as it corrodes, it happens that when the acid at the bottom acts on the sediment <note>original: *fæculam*; the fine dregs</note>, another substance rises from it and is substituted in its place. 

<margin>16.</margin> Therefore, the generation of tartar is a slow process. Tartar cannot attach itself to the bottom because of the restlessness of that constant bubbling. This is why "noble" wines, which are not easily abandoned by their fleeting spirit, do not turn sour quickly and produce little or no tartar. 

<margin>17.</margin> Old Rhine wines, however, lose their pleasant wine-like flavor as their acidity is absorbed by the dregs; yet they become <term>stomachic</term> <note>medicinally beneficial for digestion</note> because their spirits are not consumed in proportion to the dregs and acidity. Red French wines, unless they keep their dregs—which people therefore call the "mother" or "nurse"—dissolve their own tint and consume it with their acidity. Thus, by their second year, they lose their color unless they are very noble. Indeed, the tint of wines is a separable body. Noble red wines, because they turn sour more slowly, are preserved for many years. White wines that lack substance <note>original: *holigophora*; a Greek-derived term for "thin" or "weak" wines</note>, unless they are separated from the dregs, soon spoil. For once the dregs are removed, their mild acidity 

<column-break/>

does not find an object to dissolve, and the wine remains in its original state. 

<margin>18.</margin> Therefore, tartar is no longer wine nor dregs, but a "neutral" substance formed from both. That this is the case is clear from the fact that more tartar is dissolved in ten ounces of rainwater than in two hundred ounces of wine, no matter how much it is stirred by boiling. 

<margin>19.</margin> This is specifically due to the acidity of the wine, by which the tartar was coagulated in the first place. Finally, six ounces of <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate, obtained by burning raw tartar</note> dissolve seven ounces of crude tartar, because the lye of that salt consumes the acidity of the tartar. 

<margin>20.</margin> Printers prove that tartar consists of wine dregs and not just wine, for they prepare their ink from either wine dregs or tartar. Distilling both of these releases exactly the same odor and produces a similar oil. Tartar does not dissolve in cold water because the dregs of the wine surround the salt in the tartar so that cold water cannot penetrate deeply enough to dissolve it. 

<margin>21.</margin> Therefore, the "birth" of tartar occurs nowhere else except in wine-like juices that contain actual spirit of wine and are turning slightly sour because the spirit is escaping! Let the <term>School of Paracelsus</term> <note>followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, who popularized the idea that all metabolic diseases were caused by "tartar" or internal precipitates</note> realize from this how poorly their theory of tartar fits those very diseases for which it was invented. 

<margin>22.</margin> For our <term>calculus</term> <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> is in no way dissolved by boiling water. This is because Tartar should be numbered among salts, or juices coagulated by salt, rather than among actual stones.

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument against the "Tartar" theory of disease. Having previously explained that Tartar is a specific byproduct of wine, he now transitions into a critique of Galen’s ancient theories regarding how stones—such as kidney and bladder stones—form in the human body.</meta>

->### RASH THEORIES ON DISEASE.<-

<margin>1.</margin> Since Tartar <note>the crusty deposit found in wine barrels</note> first entered medical theory through the consideration of stones <note>original: *calculi*; mineral-like deposits in the body</note>, I have completed and sent to the press a treatise on **Lithiasis** <note>the disease of stone formation</note>, wherein I showed that Tartar is entirely foreign to the nature of these stones. Now, finally, I shall reveal that no disease whatsoever arises from Tartar, and that focusing on it in the study of illness is a fruitless endeavor.

<margin>2.</margin> Galen <note>a highly influential Greek physician of the 2nd century AD whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium</note> recognized that humans are burdened by stones and sand in the kidneys and bladder. However, he did not know to what cause he should attribute such hardness within us. Ultimately, he could find nothing that was able to be condensed into a solid, except for a single excrement which I call mucus, but which he labeled as **phlegm** or **pituita** <note>original: *pituitam*; one of the four traditional "humors" or bodily fluids</note>. Since he observed that a stone grows in the remote and outermost exits of the body, and thought that nothing had access there except for his humors, he boldly asserted that the same thing happens in the urine; therefore, a stone could be formed from nothing other than moist phlegm.

<margin>3.</margin> Because he marked this substance with the element of water and aqueous properties, he concluded it must harden within our "aqueducts" <note>the urinary tracts</note>. This discovery pleased him greatly, especially since the passage of a stone in the bladder is accompanied by a continuous excretion of mucus along with the urine.

<margin>4.</margin> He therefore thought that our internal fire—which he believed was one of the four elements that concur in our constitution—was necessary to harden the stony material and dry out the phlegm, even while it was in the midst of the waves <note>the urine</note>, for he knew of no other active agents in nature besides heat and cold.

<margin>5.</margin> For he did not know that all things once rose out of nothing; and now, through a necessary continuity in nature, each thing flows from a certain **genealogy of seeds** <note>Van Helmont’s theory that biological "seeds" or blueprints, rather than just physical elements, direct the growth of all matter</note>. It is not by a casual clashing of elements or by the power of supervening heat or cold that things can be so skillfully adorned with vital powers. Nor did he consider that such primary qualities, at their height or extreme, can generate nothing at all or contribute to a "new being," but at most

<column-break/>

can occasionally promote or delay the vital dispositions of the "seeds" in their simplicity—but not insofar as the elements are combined. I truly pity his labor, and the fact that all subsequent generations of the sick have paid the price for his gullibility, because he never properly measured the causes of **Lithiasis**, nor did he once seek them out within himself (as he ought to have done) before erecting a method of healing. Thus the soul becomes a handmaid to its own desires, and fashions plausible reasons for itself according to the whims of the disturbance that moved it to agreement with itself.

<margin>6.</margin> Therefore, a foreign judge must be summoned to weigh the reasons we have invented, lest we gullibly worship our own fictions and love them like a son, fighting for them against what is right, as parents do.

<margin>7.</margin> Let the fire, then, be that judge—the balance of all reasoning. But in Galen's time, **Pyrotechnia** <term>Pyrotechnia</term> <note>the "art of fire," referring here to early chemistry and distillation</note> was not yet known; among the initiates, it was hidden under an oath of silence like the secrets of Pythagoras. Indeed, Galen never even saw **rose-water** <note>original: *rhodostagma*; a distilled floral water</note>.

<margin>8.</margin> Therefore, he might be excusable in such a poverty of knowledge, and for his perhaps ambitious desire for the primacy of the healing art, if he had at least once cooked the mucus flowing from the nostrils or a stone-afflicted bladder in urine-like warmth, or dried it by itself without the urine. He would have undoubtedly found that this phlegm—which he thought hardened into the consistency of stone within us—never turns to stone by any degree of heat, ever or anywhere. No mucus (unless it is otherwise pregnant with the "seed" of stone) ever hardens; instead, it is either constricted into a light and crumbly crust <note>original: *tophum*; a porous volcanic stone or deposit</note> or resolved again into something like glue. This is how the "monarch of medicine" ought to have proceeded, rather than exposing himself to the ridicule of posterity and his more sharp-witted <note>original: *emunctæ naris*; literally 'of wiped nose,' meaning discerning or clever</note> contemporaries by filling massive volumes with such a dismal commentary on diseases, the miseries of the sick, life, and healing.

<margin>9.</margin> I do not, for my part, deny that some mucus occasionally turns to stone; but I steadfastly deny that this happens insofar as it is viscous or mucoid. It happens only if it is pregnant with a **stony seed**.

<summary>Van Helmont critiques Galen's ancient theory that kidney stones are formed by "dried-out phlegm," arguing instead that stones are created by specific chemical "seeds." He asserts that true medical knowledge requires chemical experimentation (Pyrotechnia) rather than just philosophical speculation on the four elements.</summary>

# THE DISCOVERY OF TARTAR

<columns>

For more brittle stones consist not of a pure and transparent liquid, but of a muddy and mucilaginous substance. Therefore, Galen’s doctrine—entirely moldy and full of phlegm—having been sown in stone, withered away. It remained sterile, without ear or fruit, in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established universities of the time which still taught ancient Greek medicine</note>, and there it fell ill beneath the Professor's Chair; now, soon to be shaken into dust, its brittle remains will vanish. Indeed, the ages that followed were more prone to believing than to investigating, following the herd of their predecessors, going not where one *ought* to go, but simply where others *had* gone. Under the leadership of sloth, the easy-going Schools have, until now, subscribed to such great ignorance out of respect for the unskillfulness of their ancestors.

<margin>10.</margin>
Wherefore Paracelsus, aspiring to a new "Monarchy" <note>Paracelsus often used political metaphors, claiming he would overthrow the "old regime" of Galen and become the "Monarch" of a new medical era</note> of the coming Elias the Artist <note>original: *Heliæ artiftæ*; a legendary figure in alchemy predicted to appear at the end of time to reveal all secret knowledge</note>, did not rest in the lukewarm and torpid dreams of those who snore. Seeking firmer principles for the nature of stones, he finally marveled at the tartar of wine during his inquiries. He conceived and nurtured a great hope in his mind, thinking that every stone—both in the great universe <note>The Macrocosm</note> and in the human body <note>The Microcosm</note>—was nothing but tartar.

<margin>11.</margin>
Then, progressing with the boldness of daring, he began to affirm that every solid body draws its hardness from the same "coagulum" <note>a thickening or clotting agent</note> as tartar. Thus, he was able to recant his earlier claim—that stones were a curse that came upon things later—and instead argue they were present from the very beginning by the destiny of their "seeds."

<margin>12.</margin>
Carrying forward this clever intent regarding Tartar, he concluded that just as tartar was a "stone" from wine—a metaphorical stone, I say, because it can be dissolved again in water—so too the kidney stone <note>original: *calculus*</note> was hardened by a similar thickening process from our food and drink. Thinking he had grasped the true origin of stones, he believed he "held the rabbit by the ears" <note>An ancient proverb meaning to have a firm grip on a difficult problem</note>. He was so pleased by his own daring, and so uplifted by the hope of his medical Monarchy, that he began to attribute almost all ailments to his "Tartar" in many volumes and lessons; he even believed the Plague originated from Tartar. This "happy and easy" command of his had such an impact that he promised himself total mastery over the art of healing.

<margin>13.</margin>
But when he saw clearly enough that the four elements, the "complexions" <note>temperaments or balances of qualities</note>, and the humors had failed to explain diseases,

<column-break/>

and that the true cause of illness was not yet known in the Schools—which he promised to have cracked open with his theory of tartar—he finally asserted, in order to establish the causes of disease, that all solid things are either pure tartar or contain it for the most part, to our destruction. As if the immense Goodness of God, in the act of creation, had been anxiously gaping for disease and the things that make us sick! Paracelsus’s labor and his rivalry in finding the cause of disease are intended for our benefit. Knowing the empty trifles and shameful idleness of the Schools, he strove entirely for the public good. I would have believed him—had he been less distracted by ambition—and thought that he might have reached the true foundations of healing through the most bounteous grace of God. But as ambition is swollen and always depends on the opinions of others, God allows ambition to always fluctuate in uncertainty.

<margin>14.</margin>
The inconstant Paracelsus, therefore, could never satisfy himself with his discovery of tartar. For this reason, he ran across now to "complexions," then to the Stars, then to the Three Primes <note>Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt—the core alchemical elements of Paracelsus</note>, and even invoked the four elements themselves to establish the causes of diseases. Indeed, he now accuses crystal (in the fourth degree of heat) of being a child of fire; but then, calling it a daughter of water, he says it is hardened by extreme cold. Then he affirms that a huge heap of glass, burnt by continuous fire and (frivolously diminished), turns into beryl. He forgets his own "tartar" theory and, addicted to the old ideas of "qualities" and "elemental degrees," he claims beryl is a child of Heaven and of a higher fire. He forgets that he himself had seen, in his own Swiss mountains <note>original: *Helvetiorum rupibus*</note>, ice lying frozen by immense cold for perhaps a thousand years, yet it was not crystal: it remained ice, just as it was from the beginning. Not yet finding full rest in his theory of tartars—though he dazzled the eyes and the trust of his followers and built a glorious name for himself—he fled to another anchor, the final hope of his hopes.

<margin>15.</margin>
He took the metaphor of the "microcosm" <note>The idea that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe</note> and treated it as literal truth, wishing us...

# RASH OPINIONS ON DISEASES

<columns>

...in every way and fully, to express the whole universe exactly according to the rule, and to contain it in reality through all the different varieties of lands, mountains, springs, stones, mines, plants, fish, birds, four-footed animals, reptiles, and stars as well, with all their properties, motions, storms, diseases, defects, and alterations. 
<margin>16.</margin> He asserts that unless we know and believe this thoroughly and fundamentally—knowingly, insightfully, distinctly, with total certainty and depth, and most specifically regarding every single thing created <note>original: "in unoquoque creatorum"</note>—we will be unfit for Philosophy, for the practice of medicine, or for disputing against his hypotheses. Indeed, he says that this indubitable "optic" science <note>By "optic," Paracelsus meant a science based on direct observation or "seeing" rather than just reading books</note> is ten times easier to learn than "unhealthy" Latin. By this boast, he is believed by his followers to have excelled in the knowledge of those who, by the recent testimony of the world, he alone conquered 
<margin>17.</margin> "incurable" diseases. So too Aristotle, aspiring to the title of "The Philosopher" <note>Aristotle was often called simply "The Philosopher" by medieval scholars</note>, despised those who spoke against his own (and indeed false) first principles. This is no different from how practitioners of the dark arts 
<margin>18.</margin> demand belief in themselves without demonstration. But let eternal praise and glory in every blessing be to my Lord, who formed us not in the image of the most impure world, but as a model of His own divine image. He adopted us through grace as children of election and co-heirs of His glory. Surely the condition of that "likeness" would be a thing to be grieved and pitied if it had subjected us beneath the law of all calamities—from the very creation and even before sin—to the point that we were merely the carvings of such a lowly thing. It would be as if the world were created for its own sake, and not for us as its ultimate end; or as if we were created for the sake of the world, of which we would be nothing more than icons! We would, for instance, be forced to develop stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> just so that we might represent the rocks and cliffs of the world. And so, all of us would be equally prone to stones, leprosy, and so on—otherwise, we would not all be equal "microcosms." Truly, since we are what we are by creation, and

<column-break/>

if a stone were formed simply to represent the cliffs, then death and disease would have been within us before we ever fell into sin. Away with such heresies! For we do not all suffer from the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, nor do those who suffer from it possess it so that we might represent thunder, or the trembling of the earth, or some unknown airy "Lorind" <note>A Paracelsian term for a type of atmospheric phenomenon or spirit</note> of its own inconstancy. Now, if even the smallest part of this theory were true, then according to justice, he who suffers the disadvantages of being a "Microcosm" ought also to receive the benefits—to the extent that, above all, we ought to be able to fly! For it is more reasonable that we should resemble birds than rocks or the storms of air and water. Away, therefore, with allegorical and moral interpretations of nature. Nature deals with beings as they actually and truly exist in their substantial entity, flowing from the root of the seed all the way to the final act of the tragedy. It admits no interpretation other than "becoming" and "being" arising from ordered causes. I also notice that Paracelsus, 
<margin>19.</margin> having invented "Tartar" and introduced it into diseases, still did not feel secure. Indeed, he mixes Tartar into the very first beginnings of our constitution, and thus does not even exempt the "seeds" of things from it. Rather, he wants Tartar to be mixed into the seeds radically, intimately, and most deeply, so that he might find a nursery for hereditary diseases. Forgetting this mixture 
<margin>20.</margin> once again, he says something ridiculous: He claims that a woman separates the tartar conceived from the male seed, snatches it into herself, hides it away, and, as if she had "anatomized" the seed, makes herself the "inheritance-seeker" <note>original: "heredipetam"</note> of that tartar. Conversely, he claims the spirit of wine can never be so purified through any possible circulations <note>distillations</note> that it does not still contain its own Tartar within itself—as if Tartar were the primary root of the universe or its immediate companion. But I know that if there is anything materially foreign in the seed, no generation follows. Finally, the seed of Adam, prepared materially in Paradise, would not have produced a more perfect offspring than that which was produced in him after the Fall. This is proved especially by

### THE INVENTION OF TARTAR

Cain and Abel. Finally, if **Tartar** <term>Tartar: A term popularized by Paracelsus to describe stony or hardening deposits in the body, like kidney stones or gouty crystals, comparing them to the crusty sediment found in wine barrels.</term> were so deeply ingrained in the seeds of life that it materially caused hereditary diseases many years after birth by separating itself from the whole, then surely that Tartar would not be so quickly separable by the "female magnet" <note>A reference to the womb's perceived attractive power</note>. For if anything were to be separated from the seed, it would be **Gas** <term>Gas: A term coined by Van Helmont (from the word "Chaos") to describe the invisible, spiritual essence of matter.</term>, which is diametrically opposed to Tartar.

Furthermore, if the womb were to separate something from the seed by drawing it out, it would follow the nature of things that "draw": they draw for themselves and to themselves, and then they stop. But if the womb extracts something specifically to separate it, then there would be no fear of hereditary illness, since the womb would have the power to sequester harmful things. Finally, even if diseases come into the arena of the body gradually, they were never materially mixed into the seed in the manner of Tartar. Neither Tartar nor "gouty chalk" <note>original: "creta podagrica"; refers to the stony deposits in the joints of those suffering from gout</note> pre-existed in the seed. Instead, diseases passed down from parents lie hidden

<margin>21.</margin>
"characteristically" <note>original: "characteraliter"; meaning as a formal blueprint or signature rather than a physical substance</note> within the "middle life" of the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: The "internal master" or vital spirit that Van Helmont believed directed all biological processes and growth according to a divine blueprint.</term>. The seal of this Archeus eventually bursts forth when its days have matured, and it builds a body suitable for itself; thus it becomes the Archeus of a disease, with all the required properties of its seeds. For disease is a natural constitution proceeding from a seed, 

<margin>22.</margin>
consisting of the Archeus as the efficient cause. Otherwise, it is a "rustic" <note>backward or unrefined</note> opinion held in the Schools <note>The traditional medical universities following Galen</note> that diseased bodies flow together materially to generate a hereditary defect. It also contains a level of idiocy to exclude disease from the number of natural agents and bodily entities, since the "morbific matter" <note>the physical substance of a disease</note> is often met right at the fingertip if one looks with their eyes. If, therefore, disease is counted among the entities of nature, why should it not be established by the necessity of its own seed? It is a crude Philosophy to suggest that Tartar was in the seed from the beginning, 

<margin>23.</margin>
and that thirty solid years later, it would begin its first principles of coagulation, planning its own growth and a sort of "particular Republic" for itself—all of this without any direction from the seed. God did not create death, nor did He therefore link Tartar,

<column-break/>

the matter of diseases, to the seeds of life. For if such stupid errors happened to the seminal Archeus, then the Governor of nature has abandoned the reins, and the human race will soon fall into ruin. Paracelsus’s statement is also absurd when he says that even the **spirit of wine** <note>distilled alcohol or ethanol</note> does not lack its own Tartar. For even if it were circulated for a century, it will truly never deposit any Tartar.

<margin>24.</margin>
For Paracelsus, who never saw or discovered that Tartar in the spirit of wine, wishes to be believed on his own "good faith," just as he does elsewhere when he thinks that whenever water ceases to be seen, it goes entirely into nothingness and is created anew at some point. It does not follow that because a salt is made from the spirit of wine, and that salt undergoes the coagulation of Tartar, that therefore the spirit of wine "contains" Tartar. For even if every coagulated thing were Tartar (which it is not), bodies do not contain the things that eventually become of them. For example: milk is made from grass, blood from milk, and from this, human seed is made. Yet grass does not contain a human within itself, nor does grass contain cow's milk. He therefore displays his total idiocy 

<margin>25.</margin>
by wanting every body, in whatever way it can be coagulated, to be "Tartar." This would mean all of nature is Tartar, simply to introduce a cause for disease even from the most purified liquids. He might as well have said that the "morbific matter" is the smoke of created bodies—but what would he have done then, except make himself a laughingstock? Is he not doing the same now, while he squeezes every body, whether already coagulated or capable of being so, under the name of "Tartar" just to find a cause for disease? For what new thing does he bring that was not known before, except the name "Tartar"? Did not **Galen** <note>The ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine until the early modern period</note> know that the material cause of diseases was coagulated or capable of being coagulated? By using the name "Tartar," therefore, he has at least dazzled the eyes. Yet coagulable bodies do not take on hardness from anywhere else except from the destination of their own seed—not in the way that wine and dregs constrain themselves through action. Primarily, these things are repugnant to the sacred texts and to his own

# RECKLESS THEORIES ON DISEASE

...theses which teach that diseases arrived in man through sin, and the thesis that **Tartar** <term>Tartar: For Paracelsus, a metaphorical and literal stony sediment in the body, like the crust in a wine barrel, blamed for causing obstructions and stones.</term> was sprinkled into virgin nature. Consequently, before the transgression, bodies would have contained their own internal coagulating agents, and not Tartar. For in the history of nature, he would have found—if he were not an **Idiot** <note>original: "Idiota"; here meaning an unlearned person or one lacking proper chemical insight</note>—that no liquid undergoes coagulation by the power of Tartar: but rather by the intention of the Creator, as it shines forth in the **seeds** <note>In Van Helmont’s biology, "seeds" are the formative, spiritual blueprints of all things</note>. Therefore, whatever is condensed is a "new generation," and not the maturation of some pre-existing Tartar. Otherwise, Tartar would not only have been in foods before the Fall: but all of nature would have been nothing but disease, and the punishment of death would have existed before the offense; thus death

<margin>26.</margin>
and the cause of death would have originated from the Creator. For Paracelsus, elsewhere weighing how flavors remain in things even after they are changed, wandered even further from the truth. He thought that essences do not die, nor are they destroyed, nor finally changed: but that they remain intact in the **dung** of animals. He convinced himself that even where no traces of flavor remain, or perhaps only faint ones, the original essences still survive intact. He was poorly taught by the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Aristotelian and Galenic academics whom Van Helmont frequently criticized</note> that the same "accident" <note>In philosophy, a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note> could not migrate from one subject to another. Thus, he would have had to deny the very transformation of things if he were pressed on the point. He claimed, for instance, that manured fields are fertile because the "undying" essences of vegetables in the dung enter the roots of the crops. He seemingly forgot his own doctrine elsewhere, which states that animal dung is stripped of every property of the solid matter and is only the "ultimate matter" of salts. Yet elsewhere he claims that dung contains the most potent matter of Tartar, and that the fields of **Bohemia**, which have not yet been manured, produce fruits that are less "tartarous" than those fattened with stony, earthy, or animal dung.

<column-break/>

When exposed to the open air for a long series of years, this earthy dung liquefies of its own accord. He claims this dung produces a more wild and stony Tartar in herbs than the dung that has been re-cooked and purified so many times into the matter of salts. In this respect, some types of dung wash out of linens like soap. Paracelsus reached such a level of absurdity with his "Tartar" that,

<margin>27.</margin>
whenever something might irritate the bladder or cause **strangury** <term>Strangury: A painful condition where urine is released drop by drop; often associated with stones or infection.</term>, he immediately calls it "frosty chalky Tartar" or something similar. As if "chalk" and "Tartar" were now synonyms! As if something could be **calcined** <term>Calcination: The process of reducing a substance to powder or ash by fire; Van Helmont is mocking the idea that this could happen inside a liquid environment like the bladder.</term> in the middle of urine without any heat! As if chalk did not presuppose a specific material from which it came—namely, stones! Since there is no ash that was not first charcoal. Finally, he acknowledges a "Tartar of the marrow" which cannot be coagulated. But how did he know of this, which he could never have seen? He wants to be believed in all things as one who perfectly knows the beings of the **Microcosm** and all their properties. But why does he now call Tartar a "non-coagulable being"? Is it not so that all diseases, whether they like it or not, must obey his fictional Tartar? As a Christian, I could not admit these "microcosmic dreams" as they were handed down by Paracelsus. That is to say, I cannot understand them literally rather than metaphorically—a sense that is always banished from the actual history of natural things. Nor do I tolerate his Tartars: instead, I will say along with that same Paracelsus, *“No one should be believed regarding what they cannot prove by fire.”* <note>original: "Nemini credendum, quod per ignem probare non potest." This is a foundational principle of the "iatrochemists" or chemical physicians: truth is found in the laboratory.</note> Therefore, I will not agree that chalk is burned inside us, nor that Tartar is born in us; I only recognize Tartar in winy liquids. I reject as a fable the idea that the "matter of Tartar" remains from generation to generation through the workshops of the digestive system.

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial E with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc> The more refined among the **Physicians** <term>Physicians: Referred to in Latin as "Medentes," those who practice the art of healing.</term> are gradually withdrawing from the schools of the **humorists** <note>Followers of Galen who believed health depended on the balance of four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note> in such a way that, along with Paracelsus, they now attribute almost all diseases to a single **Tartar** <term>Tartar: For Paracelsus, this was a stony, non-living sediment from food that supposedly caused all obstructions and stones in the body.</term>. Therefore, it was necessary for me to describe the beginnings of my own change of heart, and how far a youthful and reckless gullibility once led me astray. Meanwhile, since the counsel of judgment flows from the intellect through the grace of God, with the free choice of a willing consent, I would not wish to compel anyone. Let each, unforced, choose as much of the truth as the gifts received in their intellect shall reveal.

<margin>2.</margin> I, at least, being both greedy for natural truth and a dull-witted seeker of it, began to meditate on whether any Tartar exists in us with the property of persisting—having been neglected and passed through by every digestion within us—by a retained power of re-assuming its curdled form against our will. Such a thing would either be miraculous (that is, supernatural), or plainly natu-

<column-break/>

ral, or deceptive (that is, diabolical). This last, although it might not be above nature, is yet set apart into a peculiar class because of its unusual order in nature. However, whatever exists solely through **art** <note>original: "artem"; referring to human-made chemical processes as opposed to natural ones.</note>, since essential forms are excluded from the power of Craftsmen, the artificial being arising from it does not fall under medical consideration. Therefore, the aforementioned division of Tartar is commended by a sufficient listing of its parts. Finally, even if Tartar were diseased and thus far beyond the intent of human nature, it would not, in its own being, be beyond nature; for every material being is enclosed within the lap of nature. Therefore, whether Tartar is supernatural or merely natural, it would at least be a **creature** <note>original: "creatura"; meaning a created thing, part of God's original creation.</note>. Thus, Tartar would have been created from the beginning, since we read of no new thing being created after the Fall, nor of any matter being formally changed through the **curse** <note>The biblical curse on the earth following Adam's sin.</note>. Therefore, the Creator would have made the punishment before the fault, and death within the matter itself. <margin>30</margin> This is repugnant to the truth and to the Scripture. In whatever way Tartar is taken, therefore, it was not created by God; thus, it does not exist at all. The **seeds** <margin>40</margin> of thistles and thorns were indeed promised to the first Farmers, not because thereafter, through the curse, a new creature was transformed or mixed into every food as Tartar, which had not existed before the fall; for the curse would have preceded the sin, and the punishment would have been inflicted before the guilt. For Paracelsus ought to have known that in nature there are two "uterine sisters" among tangible things: namely, **Resolution** and **Coagulation** <margin>50</margin>, which alternately receive one another. For liquid becomes solid, and solids melt in turn. This is because this alternation is a law written in the **gas** <note>original: "aere"; Van Helmont often used the word for "air" to describe his concept of "Gas," the spiritual-material medium of physical change.</note> of bodies. Indeed, a solid body is never changed into another unless it is first reduced by resolution into its primary matter... <margin>60</margin>

He proposes instead that physical changes are governed by the natural cycles of dissolving (resolution) and solidifying (coagulation).</summary>

# THE HARMLESS NOURISHMENTS OF TARTAR

<margin>7.</margin> ...the matter of itself, which is a liquid—namely, that which it had before it was coagulated. Nor should it be believed that any body exists today whose matter was not created from the beginning; nor that after the first **six days of creation** <note>original: "sextiduum"</note> there was any vacuum in a body that was subsequently filled by a new creation of Tartar after the Fall. Much less should we believe that God created Tartar for us as thorns and thistles, which **Adam** <note>original: "Protoplastus," referring to the first-formed man.</note>, the chief transgressor, would not have felt much more principally, originally, and fundamentally—and consequently all the diseases alike which Paracelsus imagines to have originated from there. For God is no respecter of persons, but a just and severe avenger according to the merits of each individual.

<margin>8.</margin> Finally, many things prevent me from believing that some "Tartar" enters into us treacherously, and that although it is duly subdued and transformed by our digestion, it later, mindful of its own malice, separates itself from the company of good nourishment, retaining its ancient inclination for harm and its old hostilities of coagulation. For truly, even if Adam had not sinned, wine would not have been without its dregs, milk without its curd, rivers without stones, and food without excrement. To be sure, the channels for excrement <note>original: "emunctoria," referring to the body's waste-clearing organs.</note> existed before the Fall and were not merely destined to serve their uses after the transgression. Indeed, the very **Tartar of wine** <note>The potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine barrels.</note> first deluded this inventor of "Tartars," as he was unaware that this Tartar resulted from creation as a useful and good creature, having its own purposes according to the intention of God. How much more so, since this inventor of "morbid Tartar" confesses that Tartar is superior to wine; yet excrements are not superior to the bodies of which they are the waste. At the very least, it is not reasonable that an entity which emerged in nature from the curse of sin should possess great virtue. But if a body, insofar as it is coagulable, were "Tartar," then the entire universe would not be immune from this guilt—

<column-break/>

rather, it would be a son of the curse and not of creation. Finally, the Tartar of wine is dissolved by the boiling of water, and once the water has evaporated, it grows together again into a powder, which is now called **Cream of Tartar** <note>original: "cremor."</note>. But once it has been subdued by our digestion, it no longer coagulates into powder afterward. For just as it is the work of boiling water to dissolve, so it is the work of the **digestive faculty** to transform.

<margin>9.</margin> Therefore, a Physician would be of a wicked counsel who gave Tartar to be drunk if it could be coagulated again inside and treacherously cling to the vessels. For if, after digestion was completed, it retained any of its former power of coagulating, and to that extent gave birth to some hundreds of diseases, then the Tartar of wine itself would have every prerogative—under whose sign all the others have now given their names, according to Paracelsus. And yet, the Tartar of wine is not coagulated into its former state by digestion; on the contrary, it lays aside all hope of hardening, so much so that it cleanses away **mucus** <note>original: "muccagines."</note> from the stomach. Therefore, the "Tartars" of food will be even less able to do so.

<margin>10.</margin> Furthermore, if any "Tartar" from the earth entered into our food and resumed those earthly tendencies for hardening once swallowed within us, it surely would have first undergone those same laws of transformation in herbs and cattle, and thus in the foods themselves. Either it would have been banished and separated from them like wine-Tartar, or otherwise it would have lost its wild nature of coagulating within them. But since it did not exercise that treachery of hardening in the foods, nor retained or possessed the properties of Tartar: by what means, I ask, will it resume them in us rather than earlier, while it was an herb, or later, when it became the flesh of a beast? For how will it forget its treachery in its first transformation into an herb, and then in its second into a beast, and only recall it in us during its third transformation, along with the vegetable and the milk? But if it had been formally transformed, and had lost the being and property of Tartar while it put on the vital spirit and substance of **cabbage** <note>original: "brassica."</note>, grass, milk, and meat, and was truly made vital in these, having laid aside... <meta>catchword: deposita (laid aside)</meta>

# THE NOURISHMENTS OF TARTAR

...once the wildness of Tartar has been laid aside, how, I ask, and from where will the morbid Tartar that is to be coagulated find its old and unchanged principles within us? Or, if it has not laid aside its Tartaric properties while it was becoming grass, then chyle <term>chyle: the milky fluid formed in the stomach during digestion</term>, then cream, then blood, and finally milk—why does it not show itself as an open enemy? For Philosophy will not permit a thing to be both Tartar and cabbage at the same time, or to be living blood and Tartar simultaneously.

<margin>II</margin>
Therefore, if Tartar has lost its essence and passed into another form, it could not have retained its own nature. Much less could it have passed from a state of deprivation back to its original state <note>original: "a privatione ad habitum," a logical term for regaining a lost quality</note> within us more than it does in herbs or in beasts. Finally, if there were a "real Tartar" in things, it would surely persist through all the transmutations of the body, suffering nothing from the powers of this earthly world. It would undergo so many successive transformations and suffer nothing at all, unless it were consumed by us alone. But this is absurd—to grant a kind of eternity to excrement, which is not natural to its pure being. Indeed, either a field that has grown turnips for the fourth time and been fertilized would produce fruit entirely free of Tartar, or it is an absurdity that the Tartar, previously hidden, would only manifest itself at the third or fourth turn. Furthermore, if every growing thing had its own inseparable Tartar within it just as we do—but not in the milk and blood of beasts—then Tartar would exist by divine appointment <note>original: "destinatione"</note>. It would then be necessary that Tartar began from the very dawn of Creation and not from the rebuke of sin. But if Tartar were not a problem for other creatures, and only became Tartar for us, then its origin would be supernatural, and no disease would be natural. Every disease would then arise by a miracle, and our digestion would be more worthless and our life shorter than that of the lowliest little beast. For the digestion of those beasts leads to a true transformation, while in comparison to them, all the Tartars of our food would remain miraculously unchanged in their "first matter" <note>original: "prima materia," the fundamental substance of a thing before it takes form</note>. This, I say, is destroyed by Philosophy, which

<column-break/>

teaches that transformation never happens without the death and disappearance of the prior being, and the destruction of the starting point <note>original: "termini a quo"</note>, lest a single thing exist in two states at once. For the juice of a herb to become blood, the essence of the "herbal blood" must first perish, along with the properties of its **Archeus** <term>Archeus: the internal vital principle or "spiritual guardian" that Helmont believed governed the functions of each organ</term>, and thus all Tartar must also perish in the transformation of individual things. What if the stones in cherries, peaches, medlars, pears, and so on, were the "created Tartars" of those fruits? Surely they ought to be brought onto the stage of Tartars and into the causes of diseases even more than the Tartar of wine itself, which at least dissolves in boiling water. The Medical Schools would also be wicked and harmful, for they give the shells of such fruits, ground into powder, to their patients; for if whatever is liquefied by our digestions contained Tartar, it would necessarily increase our own stones <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>. Moreover, if Tartar were granted as the cause of diseases, then the cherry pit would necessarily have existed without its shell before the Fall <note>original: "ante peccatum," referring to the sin of Adam</note>. Thus, everything created would have been changed by sin, losing its prior nature and shape, growing now from a curse rather than the power of the blessing: *Increase and multiply.* In vain would the shells of such fruits be adorned with such beauty and marked by providence, keeping their specific identity everywhere, if they were merely the offspring and remains of excrement or Tartar, rather than the intended works of the seeds. Likewise, the liquid would pass through the stem of a cherry (a tiny thread indeed), becoming a Tartar of such hardness that it could not have hardened in the trunk or body of the cherry tree, but only around the pit. Indeed, Nature's purpose is stronger and comes first regarding the skin and shell of the cherry than regarding its wine-like juice. Thus, nature would intend the excrement before the thing itself. In us, however,

# THE INNOCENCE [OF FOOD]

...by the mere contact of the teeth, the tartar would soon harden. Tartar would also have to possess a remarkable knowledge, since it wanders about while not yet taken up by the plant, nor even while it is crushed and chewed by a beast; yet it would be formed into tartar only within man, while elsewhere it either refuses or does not know how to coagulate. Indeed, if tartar does not follow its own destiny in fruits, but only first in man, I would hardly believe that this mandate was divinely enjoined upon it while it enters into us as food. Rather, if any part of our food—contrary to its custom—degenerates within us, let that be our own fault, not the fault of things "pregnant" with tartar. But if tartar were truly hidden in things, the error would lie in the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that directs the functions of life and digestion</term>, arising from an ignorance of the laws of its own nature. 

<margin>12.</margin>
Let that be considered absurd: namely, to deny that through digestion, a substance can be digested and transmuted from its former appearance and the inclination of its own seed into the nature of the one who is digesting it. For indeed, from a single and uniform juice, four hundred types of herbs and just as many different trees are sumptuously nourished. It is certainly not the case that from that same juice, one part is separated for wood because it contains more resin and a stronger curdling agent, or that there are as many separations made from the juice of the earth as there are differences in the aforementioned plants. Far from it! Such a thing is unworthy of the *Archeus*, who fully knows the means of its own life and is strong enough to perfect the tasks it must perform upon the matter placed beneath it. For from seeds, nothing is ever "separated out" to become a root, a stalk, a leaf, flesh, bone, or brain. The diversity of the body’s members is not drawn from the reality of a single uniform liquid. For the *Archeus* does not stand in need of some tiny, imperceptible diversity pre-existing in the seeds—it is the *Archeus* itself upon whom all "otherness" depends, and of whose pre-existing disposition the *Archeus* is the principal and sole craftsman. From that same Vulcan <term>Vulcan: a metaphorical name for the internal heat or transformative power of the Archeus</term> flow the diversities of things, no less than the properties of those diversities. Otherwise, the *Archeus* would not be a transformer, but merely a ripener and a cook. 

<column-break/>

Was not wood merely juice in its beginning? And so, did not a mere herbaceous liquor harden by a power within the seed? It was not due to some pre-existing hardness in the matter. 

<margin>13.</margin>
That notion of *Paracelsus* is also absurd: that even if the material arrangements of different body parts do not actually exist as causes, there is at least a "spiritual human idea" present in bread, without which food would not be turned into nourishment. He calls this idea the "spoken anatomy" <note>original: "anatomiam effatam," a Paracelsian term suggesting that matter contains a blueprint or "word" that defines its purpose</note>, and boasts that it can be made visible through his art. I suppose that in this same bread there would likewise be the idea of a sparrow, a carp, a pig, an ox, a dog, a horse, an ape, and so on. These ideas would have to penetrate the "human idea" in the same mouthful of bread, to the point where *Paracelsus* could not always show a human idea, but would occasionally offer up a pig-like one—unless a spiritual separator were present to remove the other ideas from the human one whenever he wished, who reveals himself visibly in the human idea to whomever he chooses. Away with such "serious trifles" in the *Art of Healing* <note>original: "Medendo"</note>. Furthermore, when a bean is sown, a bean soon comes forth into the light; it has not lost the different parts that must be propagated into root, stem, sprout, and leaves. But even granted that a separation occurred in the seeds of things according to the variety of parts to be established, how much more carefully would the *Archeus* watch over the separation of Tartars from food? 

<margin>14.</margin>
Nevertheless, if some Tartar is granted to exist in food, it will surely never be let into the veins unless it has first been converted into true chyle <term>chyle: the milky fluid into which food is transformed in the small intestine during digestion</term>. That is to say, after it has ceased to be Tartar. Therefore, once the "clumping" quality is removed, it is no longer tartaric matter; otherwise, the entire universe would be nothing but Tartar. 

<margin>15.</margin>
For a certain young man who set sail with us from Calais traveled eighteen whole days to Bilbao, and daily he ate no less than he would have eaten in six days on land. Yet only once, on the ninth day, and again on the eighteenth, did he go aside to relieve his bowels; and the excrement barely exceeded the size of two eggs. From this I infer that such a great mass of food was changed and consumed into juice, and soon into nourishment capable of being dispersed through the body. If therefore...

# THE FOODS OF TARTAR

<columns>
if foods contained Tartar, and that young man had not excreted it, he would necessarily have fallen ill. This is because Tartar is certainly not digested or turned into good blood; instead, according to the laws of Tartar, once drawn into the veins, it ought to have coagulated. Yet, for more than four years afterward, he lived in good health. Thus, these Tartaric trifles <note>original: *tartareae nugae*; Helmont is mocking the complexity of Paracelsus's theories</note> fall apart.

Again: A man, quite emaciated from a long illness, recovered. He could not abstain from eating a great deal because he was extremely famished; yet he did not pass even a sixtyieth part of the food he consumed through his intestines. Thus, whatever he used to pass as excrement, he was now stuffing into himself to make flesh. In this way, a robust stomach easily digests even harder foods without harm or any "memory of Tartar." These same foods, when the stomach was previously more sluggish, the Archeus <term>Archeus: the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that directs the functions of life and digestion</term> would have separated and cast out as true excrement. Sometimes the Archeus plays the spendthrift within: while it is less pleasing to itself, it ruins superfluous things—which are otherwise harmless—and proscribes whatever it likes less, even if it is nutritious juice <term>enchymum: a term for the refined, nutritive part of digested food or chyle</term>. For whatever it does not wish to overcome, it does not attempt or attack; rather, it repels and condemns it. Whatever it does not dissolve into the appearance of a clear liquid, but leaves turbid or imbued with color, all of that it allows to run off as useless. But once a substance is fully dissolved, the Archeus selects what is suitable, retains it, adapts it through conformity, draws it inward, and hosts it within itself—having stripped it of every tendency to curdle. It only takes on a new form from the Archeus of the members that are to be nourished.

<column-break/>

Whatever the Archeus has once rejected is either waste in itself, or it soon becomes so because of that rejection. Indeed, whatever it has once repelled, it can never hope will be taken up later. It is clear, therefore, that if foods are not changed into good blood <note>original: *cruorem*; the thick, vital part of the blood</note>, this happens through a vice of digestion, and not because of some "Tartar." For a slower and more delicate digestion, which is nauseated by much manipulation <note>original: *mangonio*; Helmont refers to the artificial "dressing up" or processing of food</note>, reserves very little for itself from even a great deal of nutritious food. The rest, however, it treats with contempt through its abundance, as if terrified and indignant at its own sluggishness.

I remember a rooster that, when stuffed with wheat bran, excreted the bran entirely whole, without any of the flour's flower. But soon, pressed by hunger, it ate the excreted bran again; in that second dung, all the bran had turned into a liquid excrement. <margin>16.</margin> From this I learned that if anything appears among the excrement that is less broken down or changed, it is not the fault of Tartar, but an error of the digestive power. From this I also conjectured why the adult age is less prone to worms than old age or childhood. For in an adult, a single piece of bread is almost entirely converted into blood, whereas in the others, it turns into waste. Likewise, blood becomes bone, flesh, liver, <margin>17.</margin> cartilage, etc. It undergoes various hardenings, not because of Tartar, but because of the transformative power of the Archeus.

Finally, we are not forced to, nor can we, admit any "Tartar" in foods. Paracelsus was deceived because he saw a yellowish stone <note>dental plaque or tartar</note> grow on teeth. Although this stone has no equal elsewhere in the body or outside in the world, because it somewhat resembled a bladder stone in hardness, he rashly asserted that this dental stone was the "Tartar" of foods. Furthermore, he claimed it was harder the closer it was to the food and the mouth. Finally, thinking that no "food-tartar" reached the bladder, he said that kidney and bladder stones were only the "Tartars" of drinks, not of foods. He claimed it was a primary property of this substance to become harder the further it traveled from the mouth. <margin>18.</margin> This was truly a clever fiction <note>original: *commentum sane facetum*</note>, which imposed itself on him all the more harshly the longer he persevered in it. For he revealed that he knew the origin and material of neither Tartar, nor stones, nor even dental plaque. Therefore, he wrongly introduced Tartar as the father of all kinds of diseases. These things must certainly be explained more fully here. <margin>19.</margin> First, therefore, I will suppose a beer made from the best and most wholesome water (say, rain water, purified from all suspicion of Tartar) and...

Therefore, if Paracelsus was not merely dictating fables, that beer would never supply the material for a stone. On the contrary: the Tartar (which he imagines) in cereal grains would lose its "food property" of coagulating itself elsewhere, and would instead take on the property of the "tartar of drink" simply by the act of being cooked. 

And consequently, the same would happen to bread subjected to fire, as well as to all other foods; thus, Paracelsus’s aforementioned rule would apply only to raw foods. It would follow that someone who eats only cooked food would not be susceptible to dental stone <note>original: *lapide dentali*; what we now call dental plaque or tartar</note>. As if someone who drinks pure distilled water would not be subject to stones! Paracelsus himself denies this regarding the Emperor Frederick, who dreaded tartar; he claims that even those who drink pure, boiled water are subject to tartar, because once water has been boiled, it easily putrefies. 

Putrefaction, then—which usually causes Tartar to crumble—would now become the "mother" of tartar, even though putrefaction is otherwise the only thing that acts as an enemy to substances that have coagulated. As if indeed boiled meats or meat broths were not subject to putrefaction! Or were unhealthy simply because they were boiled! Or as if the Tartar in unboiled water acted in the place of a balsam <term>balsam: a restorative or preservative substance; here used ironically</term>. 

Why then does Paracelsus prescribe preventatives to be chewed with every meal, so that the drink does not turn into tartar, if the drink has already lost its tartar through boiling? Or, if water undergoes no change through boiling, why does he say it is unhealthy, quick to putrefy, and a cause of stinking breath? 

If urine <note>original: *lotium*; an archaic term for urine</note> is produced from drink that has been saturated with a mixture of foods, how can he claim that stones of the kidneys and bladder come only from the tartar of drinks, and not likewise from the general tartar of food? Does he perhaps intend to say that no one urinates solid foods? That would be a foolish thing to say seriously. If, however, he wants the drink to have the property of making Tartar harder the further it is carried through the body—well, then he distinguishes poorly between the tartar of food and the tartar of

<column-break/>

drinks. For the tartar from food would be mixed in just as thoroughly as the inherent Tartar of the drinks, if any existed. For what would the journey or the delay provide to the tartar of the drink? Or what would it acquire by flowing along to aid in its hardening? 

Indeed, a stone is not coagulated by heat, movement, or digestion (as will be shown in its proper place), but by a "seminal root" <note>original: *seminali radice*; Van Helmont's theory that stones grow from a specific vital 'seed' rather than just chemical settling</note> of its own internal coagulation. It would therefore be necessary for Tartar to cling less firmly to food than to drink. 

First, beer contradicts this: even though it is made of water and is not "Tartarous," it nonetheless produces stones and dental tartar no less than simple water does. Second, it is contradicted by those waters which, as they fall, immediately turn everything they touch into stone—and they do so less the further they have flowed from their source. 

Therefore, since the separation of waste occurs during digestion—a digestion which is absent in flowing water—the drink surely, under the first trial of digestion, would cast off all stone, even the hardest and purest kind. Furthermore, Tartar would have to be attached very loosely to foods if, by mere chewing, it immediately fixed itself to the teeth and separated itself from the foods in which it had previously hidden secretly through so many cycles of years and transformations of form (in plants, beasts, milk, etc.). 

<margin>20a</margin> But I ask you, what separating power resides in the teeth that, by the simple grinding of food by the molars, it would not only extract the Tartar from bread, but also simultaneously separate the coarse from the subtle, and the hard from the less solidly hardenable? If this does not happen through the sequestering and selection of tartaric parts, then the whole food would be of the same condition, and every bit of food would be equally tartaric. 

If that were the case, then God created death, and not everything He saw was good, if all foods were merely Tartar and excrement. Why then do cooking pots not have dental tartar attached to them to the thickness of several fingers? And why isn't it stinking and foul-smelling as it is on the teeth? For how could the Tartar of foods, by the mere [bite...]

# THE NOURISHMENT OF TARTAR
### 350

If bits were separated from food by the act of biting, could they really stick to the teeth if the teeth were simultaneously cleaning and wetting themselves through that very act of biting? On the contrary, this "Tartar" <term>Tartar: in early modern medicine, this referred to stony deposits (calculi) found in the body, which Paracelsus blamed for many diseases</term> would grow on everyone's teeth equally and without exception, because the conditions are the same for everyone: namely, teeth, food, and chewing. And yet, many people have teeth that remain immune to this stone. Indeed, beyond the Ethiopians <note>original: *æthiopes*; here likely referring generally to sub-Saharan Africans</note>, whose gums terminate in a sharp point above the tooth, these people in particular do not easily have stone attach to their teeth. Conversely, those whose gums are swollen and bloody, ending bluntly and fitting poorly against the teeth, frequently accumulate this kind of stone.

Prince Radziwill <note>Mikołaj Krzysztof "the Orphan" Radziwiłł (1549–1616), a Polish-Lithuanian noble who wrote a famous account of his pilgrimage to Egypt and the Holy Land.</note> recounts having observed thousands of jaws in Egypt from corpses already preserved with mummified balsam for two thousand years. He found not a single one where a tooth was missing, decayed, or even blackened. This is surely due to the excellence of the climate for the teeth and their brightness—which indeed pays a price elsewhere, since in that same place, barely one in three men is free from bleary eyes or a notable defect of the vision.

Finally, if it were a property of the teeth to separate this kind of Tartar from food, then the teeth of absolutely everyone would be smeared equally with foul tartar.

Likewise, if a connected series of teeth were held in the hand and passed through crushed food, or if food were pounded with that series of teeth like a pestle, and if that series were washed as much as a single draught of liquid (taken intentionally) washes our teeth, no stone would ever grow on those teeth. Much less would any stone grow that stinks like dental stone, which makes the breath smell like a corpse. Furthermore, a person with a fever, who for four days eats or chews nothing, still develops a mucilage <term>mucilage: a thick, sticky secretion; here meaning the film that precedes tartar</term> on their teeth that eventually turns to stone. Indeed, they have more of it than a healthy person. It is therefore clear that the stony mucilage, which first appears around the roots of the teeth where they emerge from the gum, is not the "Tartar of foods." Secondly, it shows that mere drink would also cause the same hardness nearby,

<column-break/>

which he falsely claims is unique to the "Tartar of foods."

Then there is the case of another person who eats nothing and drinks through a tube <note>original: *per cannam*; likely a reed or small pipe used for feeding</note> due to a defect of the mouth, palate, tongue, or throat, etc. Thus, he chews nothing and no nourishment touches his teeth; nevertheless, stone attaches to his teeth daily, no differently than in a person who eats.

Likewise, after every meal, even if the mouth and teeth are exquisitely washed, a new stony and foul-smelling mucilage still gathers around the teeth by morning. This could not have remained from food; and if it were the "Tartar of foods," it would be as diverse as the varieties of food are.

Yet the Carthusians <note>An order of monks known for their strict vegetarian diet, eating no meat.</note> have the same foul-smelling stone as meat-eaters. Likewise, those who live on simple bread and apples have no different stone than those who eat at least cheese and bread. Or consider those Irishmen who live on clover (which they call *Ciambroch* <note>original: *trifolio (quod Ciambroch vocant)*; an early reference to the Irish shamrock (*seamróg*), which was reportedly eaten in times of famine.</note>) and water instead of bread, or the Norwegians, content with raw and dried fish. They all agree in the same stone, with the exception of a few people of a more fortunate disposition.

<margin>21.</margin>
It was therefore a frivolous thing to base the discovery of "Tartar" as a cause for diseases on the "Tartar of foods" because of dental stone. For this stone certainly did not flow down from some dreamed-up "microcosmic" property <note>In the Paracelsian view, the human body is a "microcosm" reflecting the "macrocosm" of the universe.</note>, because the Macrocosm has nowhere fixed a stinking stone to its own teeth by chewing.

If, therefore, the stone does not come from the Tartar of foods, it certainly will not come from the Tartar of drinks either, since drink rarely touches the teeth, flows through quickly, and would wash away the same Tartar faster than it could deposit it. I will therefore explain from where the *Lithodontos* <note>original: *Lithodontos*; Greek for "tooth-stone."</note> derives its matter and its efficient cause. In this way, it will become even more established that the reasons for "Tartar" are vain.

<margin>22.</margin>
It is beyond doubt, then, that the tongue is clothed in a fringed tunic, like velvet <note>original: *Holoſerici*; literally "all-silk," but referring to the texture of velvet or plush fabric.</note>; and if any bit of food or drink becomes soaked in the mouth, it is caught within these fringes until they are filled with that same moisture. However, that is not any "Tartar" of food or drink, as if it were a "coagulable" part separated from a "non-coagulable" part; rather, it is the entire solid substance of the food, which perhaps by the saliva has become soaked—
