...it becomes wet and is trapped within that velvety surface <note>original: *holo-fericum*; likely a misspelling of *holosericum*, referring to the silk-like, textured surface of the tongue’s papillae</note>. Indeed, even if this filth is scraped off, it does not acquire the hardness of dental stone <note>original: *lapidis dentalis*; what we now call plaque or calculus</note> upon the tongue, no matter how much heat might dry it out. It certainly stinks, yet it does not possess the full, corpse-like stench of dental stone. For if the tongue is scraped with a blade <note>original: *scalpro*; a tongue scraper</note> or rubbed with a coarse cloth immediately after a meal, you will scrape away less mucilage the next morning, but it will be no less foul-smelling. You will find the same thing regarding the teeth. 

Understand, therefore, that this scum <term>scum: *saburra*, a term used in early medicine to describe the accumulation of waste or "dregs" in an organ</term> on the tongue is born not from food alone, but from saliva and the tongue’s own waste products. For if food is trapped in a cavity of a tooth—the same food whose waste is soaked into the coating of the tongue—and stays there overnight, it breathes out a far more foul breath than the aforementioned mucilage scraped from the tongue. 

So too, between the gums and the jaw, even if you wash your mouth after dinner, a certain white mucilage accumulates every morning; when wiped away with a cloth and dried, it smells with its own particular stench. In passing, I will note that this tongue-mucilage is the primary cause of the difficulties arising in the throat; consequently, those subject to these ailments have freed themselves by the frequent use of a scraper, specifically by scraping the tongue after every meal and every morning. Indeed, the tender neighboring parts, shrinking from this mucilage while it rots, become inflamed <note>original: *excandescunt*</note> through a harsh contagion. Thus, they ignite a slight inflammation <term>inflammation: *phlogosin*, a Greek-derived term for heat and swelling</term> due to the presence of this "foreign guest." 

However, that dental stone is not the child of saliva or of food, since neither one—nor even both together—can ever be coagulated into such hardness, and much less into such a stinking odor, which infects the entire air of the mouth and the foul breath ten thousand times every day. For a long time, I have marveled that a generation of such frequent, foul, and manifest growth remained unknown for so many centuries and to so many brilliant men. Trembling, I groaned: what, then, has been done in the Schools regarding more hidden matters! I shall say what Experience, the Mistress of things, has taught me: in the mouth, nothing circulates

<column-break/>

<margin>23.</margin>
except saliva, food, and drink. Yet dental stone is made of none of these; rather, in its first origin, it is like a white mucus, which then turns a pale yellow. From there, it finally grows into the hardness of a bladder stone <note>original: *lapidis vesicæ*; a kidney or gallstone</note> upon the teeth. It begins at the gums as a yellowish substance, and on the tooth it often manifests as black spots; indeed, it even makes the tooth decayed and black. Thus, the hardest and driest part of the entire body (that is, the tooth) rots most quickly. I have recognized, certainly, that the mucilage of food and saliva can thicken, but never into the consistency of stone.

<margin>24.</margin>
For that reason, it should be noted that the tooth is nourished not only at its base or root, but also laterally, from the gums themselves. The proof is in the gums themselves when they are bloody or less healthy and do not fit tightly to the teeth; they leave little pits or hollows against a poorly nourished tooth from the very start of their indisposition, and they stain the tooth with the blackness of their own extravasated blood. 

Finally, there is the fact that the tooth, beneath the gum, possesses an extremely sharp sensitivity, which it lacks outside the gum. In such a liveliness of sense, the tooth lives, and therefore it is nourished. Thus, the excrement of the gums was derived from the blood prepared for the nourishment of the tooth; likewise, it took on a certain determination or power of "dental hardness." Truly, when this waste product of the teeth drinks up the mucilage of food and drink, it soon hurries to harden into its destined stoniness. 

For what I said in my book *On Stone-disease* <note>original: *De Lithiasi*; Van Helmont's famous treatise on how stones form in the body</note> regarding the "stony seed" and "petrification" <note>original: *petrescentia*; the process of turning to stone</note> (or the manner in which stones are made) applies perfectly to the tooth and the construction of dental stone. For once it has received the seal of the coagulant and the "seed of stoniness" intended for the tooth, it retains that power even after it has become waste. This is not because it is the "Tartar of the Archeus" <term>Archeus: the internal "vital director" or spirit that Van Helmont believed governed the functions of each organ</term> in the way others claim, but because of the direction of the Archeus, by which it had already been destined for "tooth-making" <note>original: *dentificationem*</note>.

### ->THE NOURISHMENT OF TARTAR<-

A pointed gum-line is a sign of the best health in that area, and therefore it hardly ever creates dental stone <note>original: *dentalem lapidem*; known today as calculus or plaque</note>. Indeed, as long as the gum remains tightly attached to the tooth right up to its edge, it does not allow the tooth to produce waste, but rather preserves the tooth. Just as a tooth exposed by receding gums easily feels pain, rots, and allows stone to attach to it. For the eyes weep a fluid <note>original: *ichor*</note> which, in the morning on the eyelids, resembles amber <note>original: *succinum*</note>, and which has hitherto been called *Augstein* <term>Augstein: A German term meaning 'eye-stone,' historically used to describe amber or the hardened secretions found in the corners of the eyes</term> by the Germans because of the similarity. Indeed, the waste of the ears is like a yellow ointment, which is a great relief for the stinging of the nerves. It is not, therefore, unusual for the teeth to produce waste, and for this stinking matter—resolved from putrid blood—to be a "corpse" <note>Van Helmont often uses 'cadaver' to describe biological waste that has lost its vital spirit</note>. For the slime <note>original: *muccago*</note> from food that is pressed against the tongue dries out, yet it does not turn to stone unless it has been joined with the waste that bursts forth imperceptibly between the tooth and the gum. For since that is the waste of the tooth itself, it has possessed its own degree of hardness from the beginning. And so, in the form of a stony crust, it mimics the tooth to which it is attached. I have also observed that a tooth continues to grow through a true increase until the fortieth year. For a tooth that is opposite a pulled tooth exceeds its own row due to a lack of wear and enters the opposite space, until the aforementioned limit. Therefore, after the tooth stops growing, it hardly needs nourishment, or very little (since it is a substance that hardly dissipates); then, therefore, the gum becomes more fertile in waste and seizes a bit more nourishment; it becomes bloody and swollen, then soon shrinks and becomes as if decayed. From this comes frequent toothache <note>original: *Odontalgia*</note>, decay, cavities, and rot, especially for those whose growth stops prematurely in their youth. Therefore, just as teeth live by their own peculiar internal economy, so too they have their own ages, which <margin>25.</margin> I distinguish notably in this way: A tooth which, after a person's eighth year, reflects the brightness of opaque glass (which craftsmen call *Lattimo* <term>Lattimo: From the Italian *latte* (milk); a milky-white opaque glass developed in Venice to mimic porcelain</term> because of the color of milk) or the stone of a snail, is in its adolescence. This white color is brilliant and polished. Then it gradually turns pale; next, it turns a dull white, like ivory. This is the youth of the tooth. Then afterwards

<column-break/>

it turns a dark pale, as is seen in girls who have fainted or died. This is its manhood. And finally, it turns a pale yellow, like bone, and loses its original luster. Then the old age of the tooth begins. For as much as cartilage differs from a membrane, or a nail from a horn, by that much does a tooth differ from a bone. Moreover, toothache is frequent while the gum recedes and the tooth takes on the color of bone. Finally, however, the decayed, hollow, black, worm-eaten, and stinking tooth is the failing age of the tooth. Therefore, cold is an enemy to teeth. For it accelerates <margin>26.</margin> their old age. The grayness of hairs proves their old age, even beyond the old age of the person; and one hair turns gray long before another. So too, one tooth grows old before another. From this it is clear that each of the teeth lives on its own terms <note>original: *propria vivere quadra*; a Latin idiom suggesting each tooth has its own individual lifespan or "table"</note>. People of the South have brighter teeth than those of the North; they surely enjoy air that is kinder to teeth. The teeth of children before the seventh year easily feel decay, because they are pushed out of their socket by another growing tooth beneath them, are deprived of nourishment, and are burdened with dental waste. According to the injury of the gums, therefore, the injury of the teeth must be estimated; namely, from the plurality and ferocity of the waste. Not unlike the injured brain, which accumulates much mucus, or any other damaged part that piles up much filth; so the teeth and their nourishing parts, if they are injured, thrust forward no small amount of stony and putrid waste. Because this waste is not so much the remains of food as it is human waste: therefore, for all nations, dental stone is equally stinking. This fact deceived Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a physician who theorized that 'Tartar' was a metabolic disease caused by food toxins</note> and increased in us the suspicion of "Tartar." Hence it is manifest why, from <margin>27.</margin> the same urine, the same stone in the kidneys first grows together as something breakable, and then in the bladder becomes by far the hardest. It is not because there is "Tartar" in the urine, which becomes harder the further it falls down. That is a childish idea. Rather, truly, any petrifying juice has its own determined hardness, and not one borrowed from elsewhere...

This happens because once the surface of the kidney's functional tissue <note>original: *parenchymatis*</note> is worn away, the fibrous parts and the "spermatic threads" <note>Van Helmont uses "spermatic" to mean the formative, life-giving principles or "seeds" of an organ's structure</note> supply a similar white mucus from the formative nourishment. In this matter, people have erred until now, just as if you were to say that rye flour is stony by its own nature. In fact, the flour borrows from its additive what it did not possess on its own. Therefore, the mucilage in a stone is not "phlegm" <note>original: *pituita*; one of the four traditional humors</note>; rather, it is spermatic nourishment, secreted under the burden of disease, which is not petrifiable by itself, but only because of what is added to it. Indeed, it is by distinguishing causes *per se* from causes *per accidens*, sufficient causes from assisting ones, and primary causes from transplanted ones, that one arrives at <margin>29.</margin> true knowledge of the matter. # TARTARUS IS NOT...

<columns>2</columns>

...must be confirmed. First, I have shown that every stone is the immediate offspring of water, rather than of Tartar. Second, that the hardening <note>original: *concretio*</note> of any body results from a "seed" <note>the formative principle or internal blueprint of a substance</note>, and not from any "law of Tartar." Third, that this hardening is destined by the seed—by the integrity of nature, and thus from the gift of creation—and not from Tartar, which, according to Paracelsus <margin>2.</margin> is nothing but excrement. Now, a natural product arises from "mother matter," not from a "stepmother"; it proceeds from a seminal or efficient beginning, which contains from the moment of Creation all the patterns <note>original: *typi*</note>, Ideas, and the knowledge of the things to be done. Finally, I have shown that from the time of Creation, the patterns of Tartars were not placed within things for our ruin, just as no "medicine of destruction" was placed upon the earth.

What does it matter to the nature of Tartar (insofar as it is introduced into diseases) that a stone is the fruit of water, if that stone does not possess the condition of Tartar? Or what does it matter if Tartar is the fruit of wine, if nothing of the sort exists in other things? For how does it harm nature if a wandering imagination—deceiving itself with the name of stone or "calculus"—calls it Tartar? It is quite weak and without proof to assert that stones and every solid body agree in every property with the "tartar of wine." Indeed, such an assertion is made freely, without truth or probability. For the stone within us is generated by a different intermediary seed and process than the Tartar from wine or the stone from water.

<margin>3.</margin> There are, evidently, three "Monarchies" <note>or Kingdoms</note> of bodies in the universe: the Animal, the Vegetable, and the Mineral. Therefore, "stone" is threefold and distinct across each Monarchy. For a rock differs from the pit of a medlar fruit or a peach; and both of these differ again from the "stones" found in crabs, bezoars, snails, fish, the <margin>4.</margin> human stone <note>original: *calculo humano*</note>, and so on. These three types of stones are, in turn, far removed from the tartar of wine, which should not even be classified among stones, as it is a congealed liquor of salt. For a mineral is either a "rock" <note>original: *saxum*</note> that can be turned into lime, or a "stone" <note>original: *lapis*</note> that cannot be calcined, such as gems, marbles, and flints. Both, however, are now included under the single name of "rock" <note>original: *petræ*</note>.

<column-break/>

As for the vegetable stone, since it is combustible—like jet and other sulfurous mineral rocks—it is more like a knotty wood than a rock. The animal rock, however, is more like a stony bone (since it is partially combustible) than a true rock. To distinguish the human stone from the others, Paracelsus calls it <term>Duelech</term> <note>A specialized term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont for a stone formed in the human bladder or kidneys.</note>. This is because rocks, whether mineral or vegetable, are natural and necessary fruits, intended by the first design of Creation.

Only <term>Duelech</term> is a disease, and it is something like a monster. In other living creatures, however, the stone has obtained a beneficial purpose. From this it becomes clear that, although <margin>5.</margin> waters may beget rock, they do not therefore follow the essence, the seed, or the manner of generation belonging to the tartar of wine. For *Duelech* arose after the Fall <note>original: *post peccatum*; referring to the theological Fall of Man</note> as a morbid excrement; it does not arise from the intention of nature, nor from stony or tartaric matter. Instead, it is born by accident—by an error of the body’s governing faculty—as a diseased seed, bound by the necessity of the acting cause.

Therefore, I do not admit that Tartar exists in drink any more than in food. If it is potentially in wine, that happens by a connected necessity and by accident; it can have neither a place nor the power to act within us, such that "potential Tartar" could be made "actual" in our bodies. Thus, I do not admit a "tartaric generation" <margin>6.</margin> in drink, destined by God for our destruction. For what if bones are found in flesh, and the seeds of mineral rocks are established in waters? Does it follow that the seed and immediate matter of bones will be found in springs? Or that the seed and immediate matter of mineral rocks will be found in flesh or blood? If not <margin>7.</margin> in the blood, then surely not in drink or food. For death is not the work of God’s hands; and "God saw all that He had made, and it was good," both in the intention of His goodness and in the being of the creature. Therefore, there is no matter in water created to stir up the tragedy of Tartar or *Duelech* within us. If any evil now exists or comes to be during digestion, it certainly does not arise from the creation, destination, property, or efficiency of the matter...

# IN DRINK.

<columns>2</columns>

...by the efficient [cause] and final intention of the Creator: but it flows entirely from our own error and the corruption of nature. Specifically, through the intake of foreign seeds <note>formative principles or "blueprints" of disease</note>, the defective transformation of nutrients, or the insufficiently rigorous expulsion of harmful things, these conditions arise. If a pre-existing Tartar existed, dissolved in drink, it would surely putrefy within us immediately according to its own destination, occurring before the processes of digestion, putrefaction, and resolution; nor would it wait for the final exit of the urine to begin its plans for coagulation. Furthermore, it would turn into stone in everyone equally. However, since the stone <note>original: *calculus*</note> does not grow within the drink itself, but only in the waste products through the admission of the salt of urine and the help of other cooperating factors (as is explained abundantly in the book *On Lithiasis*), it is presumed that <term>Duelech</term> <note>a Paracelsian term for a stony deposit or "the stone" in the human body</note> does not consist of a tartar pre-existing in the drink. This is made clear through its mechanical resolution by fire. For when Duelech is distilled in closed glass vessels, it produces a foul-smelling oil, a spirit, and finally crystals of urine salt, exactly like those elicited by distilling human urine. For it is certain that the stomach, intestines, veins, liver, and kidneys do not generate Duelech by their own nature; much less do they sustain it, and even less so from <term>Tartar</term> <note>the crusty sediment found in wine barrels, which Paracelsus blamed for many diseases</note> already prepared and pre-existing in drinks. Otherwise, all people alike who generate human urine—in every person without exception, just as little stones grow in crabs without exception—would procreate Duelech. But Duelech turns to stone from a seed, produced finally in the urine through a transmutation of matter. That seed is so powerful that even if a sufferer of the stone drinks nothing but distilled water, they would not for that reason cease <margin>8.</margin> to generate Duelech. But people say: "Red wines generate a great deal of sand in those with the stone, therefore they contain sandy tartar." I would infer from this: If they contain sandy tartar, then they would produce sand not just in those with the stone, but in absolutely everyone. But since this only happens in those who are

<column-break/>

defective, it becomes clear from this that it is not a matter of the substance itself; rather, the sand is made from elsewhere. Indeed, the stomach of the defective would separate the sands before they ever reached the kidneys. <margin>9.</margin> The ignorance of the Schools <note>traditional academic medicine, particularly Galenic and Aristotelian</note> arises from this: they do not know, or do not weigh, that many things are made through transmutation which were in no way materially present. Indeed, only a ridiculous man would say that bones are present within grass. This dispute will cease once I have shown that Duelech is formed from things far removed from coagulation. For it does not follow that because certain wines contain more spirit of urine or volatile earth, they therefore contain the tartar stone; nor does it follow that the Tartar of wine materially generates human Duelech through its own separation. Ginger produces a great deal of sweat: therefore [according to them] ginger must materially contain a great deal of sweat. For the Schools pass judgment on the things of nature in a rustic fashion, being ignorant that many things are the work of an efficient transmutation—by the seed of a coagulant, I say, operating during the process of transmutation. These are by no means owed to the matter, nor to their "heats," nor to the fictional clashing of elements. <margin>10.</margin> Indeed, I saw two twins, raised by the same nurse and the same foods, of whom the elder had the stone, but the younger did not. For the milk did not contain more tartar for one than for the other. Likewise, the child of a certain President, born of two healthy parents, had four brothers and three sisters who were all healthy. Yet, having been nourished for only three months by a wet nurse who had the stone, he underwent a <term>lithotomy</term> <note>a surgical operation to remove stones from the bladder</note> once at age seven, again at age ten, and a third time two years later. On that last occasion, he expired under the razor. Certainly, these two histories did not occur because of the arrival of foreign tartar. <margin>11.</margin> Therefore, since there is no material existence in the things consumed—no truth, knowledge, necessity, or consequence—that can be made to fit Tartar: it was boasted far too loudly by <term>Paracelsus</term> that he had first discovered the cause of all diseases, calling himself the Monarch of secrets and...

# TARTARUS IS NOT THE ORIGIN OF DISEASE

<columns>
...the prince of medicine <note>likely referring to Hippocrates or Galen, whom Paracelsus frequently criticized</note>, and to have accused others of ignorance through his own invention. Nay, he even went further, claiming that from the "Tartars" of various regions, he could detect which diseases the inhabitants were prone to. For if Tartar was never part of the original creation, nor part of the curse [after the Fall], how then could it be the origin of diseases? It is truly a frivolous thing to claim one has investigated it through distillation and found that which never existed. To be sure, he had seen stones <note>original: *saxa*</note> generated at the bottom of waters. He also saw that in Styria, Savoy, and Valais <note>regions in the Alps famous for endemic goiter</note>, horrible goiters <note>original: *strumas*</note>—a pitiable sight—deformed the human appearance. Deceived by this, he concluded that from the "Tartar" of the waters come stones, goiters, and consequently everything that causes an obstruction. For he wrongly—and to the destruction of his followers—remained ignorant of the fact that all things arise from seminal agents <note>Van Helmont’s theory that "seeds" or formative blueprints direct the growth of all matter</note>, and it is granted to them to transform the matter laid beneath them according to the destinations and ends of those seeds.

<margin>12.</margin> For indeed, even if some drink is more harmful to those suffering from stones, that drink is nevertheless neither Tartar, nor does it contain it from that source, nor is anything of the form of Tartar condensed into **Duelech** <note>a Paracelsian term for a stony deposit in the human body</note> (as I have taught in its proper place); rather, it is the work of the [internal] operator upon the stone or mass, whatever is present in the waters by way of an actual seed. Moreover, if there is anything in wine, it will be by its own nature destined to become dregs <note>original: *fæcem*</note>, but it becomes Tartar only by accident; it does not, however, become Duelech. For you will interrogate the waters in vain by distilling them to see if they potentially become stone. Indeed, the rivers and springs teach us that without labor or expense. Furthermore, from wine there never comes stone, nor Tartar, and much less does Duelech arise. Nor will a plurality of dregs prove the presence of Tartar, just as they do not prove the stone. This is because Duelech belongs to a different family than Tartar. Hence, the richer wines are in Tartar, the healthier they ought to be against Duelech, if Tartar is otherwise drunk to wipe away filth.

<margin>13.</margin> I do indeed agree that stony waters are of a wild nature and a mineral condition, and they cause indigestion insofar as they contain foreign matter. But they do not for that reason materially contain Duelech in themselves, even

<column-break/>

though they occasionally destroy digestion and imprint a "stony middle life" <note>original: *petrofam vitam mediam*; the "middle life" refers to the state of a substance after it is eaten but before it is fully assimilated</note>, whereby the vegetative power of the human being, having been weakened, puts on that wild inclination. Yet this does nothing to support the Author of the theory of Tartars. For it is one thing to become "stony" occasionally, from the petrifying force of the "middle life" of things introduced into the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal vital spirit that governs the body’s functions</note> by way of impression and sealing; and it is quite another thing to become "stony" from liquid Tartar, dissolved in waters, which at last, in the period of a few days, resumes its former coagulation within the drinker. For I deny this latter process in nature, but I assert the former to be among the ordinary occurrences.

<margin>14.</margin> As far as goiters <note>original: *Strumas*</note>, or "Botia" <note>an old term for a swelling in the throat</note> are concerned, most people think they arise from drinking mineral waters, and Paracelsus also thinks they come from the use of "cachimial" waters <note>waters containing *cachimia*, an alchemical term for mineral dregs or immature metals</note>. But I would wish that, according to his own doctrine, he would show those *cachimias* in the waters by means of fire, which are specifically suited to coagulate only in our final digestion, and nowhere else but around the throat. I know, however, that he will never find such Tartar in the waters. Therefore, let him be condemned by his own law, which warns that no one is to be believed except insofar as he can demonstrate it by fire <note>referring to chemical analysis through heat</note>. I admit indeed that a "middle life" exists in water, whose property it is to excite the Archeus and infect it during the transformation of good nourishment—not by any foreign Tartar materially existing within it—into a stony hardness. For goiters, however, a matter is required which, by the property of its own Archeus, is born to block our throats and as it were to suffocate us, and this without the taste of astringency or earthy bitterness (for otherwise this taste, adhering in the heart of the matter and being ripened in the first digestion, would perish); and once transformed into nourishment, and retaining its former powers of "middle life," it performs its power around the throat more than elsewhere. This power, left to it by hereditary right in the nourishment and hence in the blood <note>original: *cruore*</note>, converts the nearby nourishment of the solid parts into a stony out-

...growth, which by the stifling power of the director <note>The "director" refers to the Archeus, the internal vital spirit Van Helmont believes governs the body’s functions.</note> moves toward the throat. And weighing this matter at Sion <note>original: *Seduni*, the capital of the Swiss canton of Valais, historically known for endemic goiter.</note>, I found that certain mushrooms are empowered with the aforementioned suffocating poison. I found them growing frequently from the roots of Larch, Fir, and Pine trees on the northward-sloping cliffs, where the black Agaric—an heir to the same "crime"—is also common on the trunks. I learned, therefore, that the entire soil of those places, being of a fungous nature, is contaminated by a property called *Leffas* <term>Leffas: a Paracelsian term for the "astral" or hidden mineral properties of the soil</term>. I thus came to believe that Goiters <note>original: *Strumas*</note> are born from the use of herbs and waters that have soaked up this *Leffas*. Furthermore, the fact that it is the power of the "middle life" of the Archeus that produces goiters in living things—and not some revived "Tartar" from mineral-rich water—is self-evident. 

<margin>15.</margin> Otherwise, a Goiter would appear no less frequently or slowly in the abdomen and liver than it does in the throat. For the minerals in the water do not specifically target the throat, nor would they promise such great hardness. Certainly, a Goiter would not be dissolved by an astringent and earthy remedy—a remedy by which I have many times seen massive Goiters vanish within a single month, and the suffocation caused by the poisonous mushroom suddenly cured. The remedy is as follows: 

**Recipe:** Take 3 ounces of sea sponge burnt to charcoal; 1 ounce each of burnt cuttlebone, long pepper, ginger, pellitory <note>original: *pirethri*, an herbal root used for its warming properties</note>, gall-nuts, rock salt, and charred eggshells. Mix these with the distilled water of the aforementioned sponges. Let it be dried out gradually. Take half a drachm of this powder with half an ounce of sugar during the waning moon, so that it may be swallowed while slowly dissolving in the mouth. Or make it into an electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note>. And the Goiter <note>original: *Bocium*</note> will disappear. 

Others, for lack of sponge, took the hairy growth that forms on wild rosebushes <note>known as a "robin's pincushion" or bedeguar gall</note>, which looks very much like the outer husk of a chestnut—shaggy and bristly—and they used the powder of this alone with great success. 

<margin>16.</margin> Likewise, I have used an ointment for goiters and hard tumors <note>original: *scirrhis*</note>: Take 8 ounces of laurel oil (not adulterated with hog's lard); 3 ounces each of frankincense, mastic, gum arabic, and fir resin. Distill this, then distill it again with potash <note>original: *cineribus clavellatis*</note>. 

If, therefore, a goiter or a hard tumor elsewhere were to 

<column-break/>

coalesce from a foreign "Tartar" <note>The Paracelsian idea that mineral crusts from food and drink cause disease.</note>, it would only grow harder when treated with warm remedies, and would not be so easily dissolved. Therefore, a goiter is a failure of the transmuting Archeus and not a coagulation of Tartar, just as I have clearly and abundantly demonstrated regarding *Duelech* <term>Duelech: Van Helmont’s specific term for the material that forms kidney and bladder stones.</term> For the Archeus transforms every mass placed beneath it, unless it yields, having been overcome by a more powerful "middle life." Thus, a Goiter is made from good blood, into which the stifling power of that "middle life" has been left behind. And the Goiter perishes once a remedy is taken, which does not work by dissolving stony matter—as would be necessary if it were made of Tartar transported there. Otherwise, it is altogether impossible for "Tartar" (if such a thing existed) to receive the breath of our life, to become living, to be fitted to our limbs, and to be admitted into the final digestion to receive the ferment of the blood—only to then be blown away through insensible perspiration, as happens to hard tumors born of vital blood when the aforementioned remedy is applied. 

<margin>17.</margin> Furthermore, this is no "quarrel over the shadow of an ass" <note>a Latin idiom for a trivial or useless dispute</note>. For it is not the same thing to deny that Tartar is materially present in food and drink (and that it remains through the "workshops" of digestion to eventually coagulate in the wretched), as it is to admit that things within us are transformed from good cream, chyle, or blood into something evil by the power of the "middle life," which transplants the directions of the Archeus. For just as the order of generation is one thing, so the order of prevention and healing is another in both cases. 

There is, therefore, no foundation of truth, appearance, or necessity for "Tartarization." For what purpose does it serve to invent "Tartar"—a stubborn principle of coagulation—which owes its very origin to a fiction? For the dispositions, coagulations, and resolutions of things depend upon their own seeds. *Duelech* is formed from the purest foods and drinks no less than from the less refined ones, if the "middle life" infects the Archeus poorly. Why, then, is it appropriate to render the foods and drinks which the Lord judged to be "good" infamous by the betrayal of "Tartar"? I truly believe this idea was found in "Tartarus" <note>A play on words: Tartarus was the Greek name for the underworld or Hell.</note> or from the devil, while...

# TARTAR IS NOT IN DRINK.

Satan would soon cast out the exile of the humors <note>The "four humors"—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Van Helmont believed were an outdated and demonic distraction from true chemical medicine.</note> from the medical Schools.

<margin>18.</margin> Indeed, since every thing is dissolved by the breaking of the bonds that bind it, it is helpful to have advised: coagulated things within us are not created through drying (with the exception of gouty chalk), nor through Tartar <note>original: *tartarum*; Paracelsus’s term for stony deposits in the body, named after the crust in wine barrels.</note> existing secretly within; much less so from any rocky or calcifying condition of the microcosm <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note>. For that chalk, after acquiring the opacity of *synonia* <term>synonia: Van Helmont’s term for the lubricating fluid of the joints, now called synovial fluid</term>, is thereafter gradually dried out. This is as I have written elsewhere regarding gout. Otherwise, in its beginning—just as with any *scirrhus* <term>scirrhus: a hard, non-cancerous swelling or tumor</term>, as well as with a **bolus, clay, mucilage**, sand, and **Duelech** <term>Duelech: a specific term used by Helmontians for a stony mass or bladder stone</term>—these are coagulated and resolved by seminal beginnings. They are dissolved and coagulated in a far different manner than if a persistent and immutable "Tartar" of any sort had, of its own accord, produced a foreign clot within us.

It is a fallacy <note>original: *sophismus*</note> to accuse a non-cause as a cause, or to neglect a cause as if it were a non-cause. If this fallacy usually brings great distress elsewhere, it certainly brings the greatest in healing, being full of dangers to life and damnation, as well as losses.

For one person digests well but separates with difficulty; another, however, excretes successfully but digests with trouble. Finally, a third digests efficiently and liquefies well, but transforms things vitiously within himself under the command of a foreign seed. It is one thing, therefore, to correct a foreign impression on the "middle life" 

<column-break/>

(which consists in the thickening of what is digested), and another thing to excrete what would otherwise cause harm if retained. And this is accomplished by dissolving and expelling. Finally, if there were any Tartar in the things consumed, ending at last in a persistent coagulation which it had treacherously brought inside with it, it would contain, at least in both cases, a despair of healing. And to that extent, a medicine of extermination would have been hidden in the earth by the Lord of things, established in nature from the beginning.

Lastly, there is no Tartar in foods, just as there is none in drinkable liquids. In water, there is indeed a "seed of stones"; but a stone is no more "Tartar" than a rock is bread. Therefore, the presence or power of Tartar can in no way be concluded from a petrifying <note>stone-forming</note> seed. Likewise, even if in growths or degenerated blood a power for **Duelech** or a **scirrhus** arises,

<margin>19.</margin> it does not lead to Tartar—much less does it mean that Tartar naturally resides in both the blood and the waste products. For whatever is born by accident from a foreign and alienated seed, and is compared by metaphor to the crusting found in wines because of its coagulation, is only referred back to "tartar" by a misused comparison. For nature hates metaphorical and poetic liberties. Therefore, Tartar is not the internal occasional matter of diseases.

# THE WANDERING GUARDIAN.

<margin>
45. The Guardian in the brain differs from other faculties.
46. That the diaphragm is porous.
</margin>

<margin>I.</margin>
The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the 17th century, which followed the ancient teachings of Galen and Aristotle.</note>, pointing their fingers at mucus from the brain and the spit of coughs, have said: "Behold, phlegm, one of the four constituent humors of our nature." And thereafter, one after another, they have always signed their names to this. This daring grew through playful arrogance, strengthened by the prescriptions of so many centuries and the signed authorities of the Schools. It is as if the brain had consumed the other three supposed or fictional humors for its own nourishment, excluding only phlegm—despite phlegm being most similar to the brain itself and, according to the mind of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose "humoral theory" dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, otherwise most fit to be totally transformed into blood. Sometimes, too, forgetting their own doctrine of the four humors, they have relegated this same mucus to be no longer "phlegm," or "pituita" <term>pituita: a Latin term for phlegm or rheum, often used interchangeably with mucus</term> properly speaking, but the "refuse of the brain," like a banished enemy or a superfluity resulting from digestion. They were rightly ashamed of that doctrine of theirs: because they recognized mucus as the excrement of the final digestion, and no longer a humor produced in the liver as one of the four parts of the blood. For indeed, excrement is repugnant to a vital humor. They therefore waver quite often, and stumble, and hesitate again, while they indiscriminately call a mucous man "phlegmatic" (on account of that waste and sickly affection), and thereafter measure and predict his strength, character, manners, and fortune from it. Meanwhile, unfortunate are the beginnings of the Schools, which define the essence, existence, and properties of phlegm—and of our own constituent elements and humors—from a waste product known to them. For the phlegm which, at the beginning of a cold <note>original: *Goryzzæ* (Coryza); the medical term for the common cold or nasal congestion</note>, flows from the nostrils as something watery (as they say) and thin, becomes thicker and yellow after some days, because it is thickened by the continuous cooking of heat. As if, perhaps, for a full forty days, it had waited within the empty skull without rotting, expecting thickening as its highest good!

<column-break/>

nor otherwise, being thinner, would it find enough cracks for an exit! These dreams do not deserve a rebuttal, except that they have transferred this method of healing into the destruction of mortals through serious credulity. I confess indeed that <margin>2.</margin> during my apprenticeship I believed that mucus, if it were not one of the four originating humors, was at least the waste of the brain's digestion. But later, withdrawing from the Schools with a freer investigation, I began to observe that I blow my nose rarely in summer, but very frequently in winter. Yet in both seasons, my brain and its functions are, by the grace of God, equally strong. For I considered, therefore, that winter blood is just as lively as that which I produce in summer (for life is placed in the blood by the Sacred Scriptures) and that the digestion of the brain, as well as of other parts, is equally healthy because it is complete. These things would not be so if the brain produced at least four ounces of excrement daily—and therefore drained sixteen ounces of blood for its nourishment alone—and produced such an abundance of phlegm (besides that, of course, which remained in the nourished part as a pledge of food) which it would otherwise leave in the blood during the summer. Or if they think this happens through a more exquisite digestion of the brain; or if they prefer to say the brain is ill-disposed due to the injury of winter air; however it is taken, it is necessary at least that the mucus be caused by some indisposition. Therefore, it is not caused by an abundance of phlegm, nor by a fault of the liver, just as it is not caused by a more exquisite separation of winter phlegm and a neglect of it in summer. Nor, finally, does that indisposition occur by a fault of the brain, any more than by a fault of the blood. Indeed, that is repugnant to the proposed thesis. Therefore, it flows from elsewhere. For if those wastes remained in the blood or the brain through the summer, which are otherwise excreted in winter, there would be no place to house the phlegm collected throughout the whole summer. Hence I propose this Thesis: Nasal mucus is more watery and copious, and <margin>3.</margin> therefore there is a continuous blowing of the same in winter, but not in summer. From which it follows...

If this occasionally harms the digestion of the brain: it will be either throughout the entire brain, or in its lower plane, where the cold strikes. It is not, however, an excrement consisting of the remnants of the final digestion, which they claim is dispersed like dew through the smallest solid parts. For this too would exhale as a vapor from the brain no less than from the whole body. If, therefore, mucus is naturally stirred up by occasional external causes and harmful weather, it must have its effective cause around the level of the brain where it encounters the air. But it is not caused by the cold itself. For that would imply the brain was conquered, overcome, and its powers extinguished. This conversion of that matter, since it is natural, is spread out like a breastplate <note>original: "lorica," a piece of Roman body armor</note> over the part 
<margin>5.</margin> struck by the cold. And since the matter becomes corrupted by the injury of the air, it certainly does not cling: but instead drips down like a continuous drop of water. This power, the maker of mucus, I call the **Guardian**. Let it suffice for now to have supposed this. Furthermore, the waste of the bowels and the bladder are the superfluities of the whole body and the parts in which they are made; they are indeed superfluous and useless from within. But sweat and insensible perspiration are "recrements" <note>refined waste products</note>, produced after the final digestion is complete and expelled after the very last function of all their parts. But mu-

<margin>6.</margin> -cus is of neither kind. This same change is entirely natural, ordained for a good end, so long as it arises from a well-constituted Guardian. Indeed, I greatly marvel at the sleepiness of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional medical academic establishment</note> through so many centuries. Because they saw mucus dripping through the nostrils, they immediately decided, as an unquestionable decree: that the same thing is nothing other than the waste of the brain. Indeed, whatever is thrust out through spitting and coughing (because the similarity of colors deceived their eyes), they dictated was nothing but falling waste from the brain. Nor did they once investigate in passing: If it is the waste of the brain, then it must be the residue of the final digestion. That is to say, when the blood, after it has been made into a nourishing humor and distributed like dew through the equal mass of the brain, would not be consumed there (even though it was already assimilated to the substance of the brain), but would instead depart through the pores by insensible transpiration without any residue. Instead, they claim that by a completely irregular defect, after it had taken on the lot of "spermatic mucilage" <note>The primary substance the body uses to build and repair itself</note> (for we are nourished by the same things from which we are built), it is as if the mucus is "recalled" from the distant, heterogeneous winding paths, and finally collected and expelled onto the shelf near the nostrils. For those who have stirred up such a biting laughter of self-satisfaction regarding the "uses of the parts" <note>A reference to Galen's famous work *De Usu Partium* (On the Use of the Parts)</note>, have not even once touched upon what the cause of such great abuse in this digestion might be. Since, if it were a waste product, it would be the superfluous part of digestion: Why would an old man consume more blood in his brain (because 
<margin>7.</margin> he wipes away more waste) than when he was a young man? Does the blood, already half-cooked and vital, then finally corrupt into a substance similar to seed? Such a confusion of corruption and alienation? In what way, in the middle of the blood's transformation into vital and seed-like mucilage, would the brain deviate with such a common wandering, and be corrupted by an error of abundant digestion?

Was it not clear from this that there was a need for another use, not yet known? One that does not come from hidden places everywhere—due to the identity of the brain's substance and the uniform digestion throughout—and from the smallest cells, with an ordered motion, corrupting its own proper nourishment, flowing back with the same force it entered, so that, now turning into waste, it might be gathered within the basin <note>original: "abacum," referring to the anatomical structure of the ethmoid bone or cribriform plate where mucus was thought to collect</note>? <margin>8.</margin> foolish labor for the brain. <margin>9.</margin> for now the nonsense of "Catarrhs," which they say rain down in such a large and continuous shower into the chest and the whole condition of the body. For how will the ruling powers <note>the vital mental faculties</note>, which they say dwell in the casing of the brain, remain safe while there is such noise, confusion, and such an abundant diversion of digestion? A tumult of returning mucilage and blood going expressly toward its own corruption?

But until now, it has not been thought of even once where such a great supply of mucus comes from: instead, the Schools <note>the traditional medical universities following Galen</note> have slept the "dream of Epimenides" <note>A legendary Greek poet said to have slept for 57 years; Helmont uses this to mean the medical establishment is oblivious to reality</note>, as if fed on lotus, provided they can hoard a little profit from the "Catarrh" they have made people believe in. For mucus is not 
<margin>10.</margin> ordinary waste from the blood. And the Schools could have easily noted this if they were not accustomed to subscribing to nonsense. Since after a great thirst, a large drink immediately produces a stagnant slime in the throat, in place of saliva. And so diseased conditions of the throat immediately thicken all saliva. 

Therefore, it is no wonder if the faculties—which I call **Guardians** because of their protective role—naturally attract a liquid other than blood from the entire lineage of our "reeds" <note>likely referring to the vessels or air passages</note> and adopt it for their own purposes. I call this liquid the *latex* <note>a clear, watery fluid distinct from blood</note> and will describe it in a specific section. This is 
<margin>11.</margin> no less successful, surely, than the way the kidneys separate urine <note>original: "lotium"</note> from the blood and draw it to themselves. I carry the same judgment regarding mucus.

<margin>12.</margin> a head cold <note>original: "Corizza"</note>, as long as the evil rages most and the north wind is fiercer, the mucus is also more watery, even while the brain's digestion and the health of the internal and external senses remain the same. Thus, thicker, stickier, scanter, and yellower mucus is praised toward the end of digestion (as they say). Finally, I consider that such a great amount of waste cannot be daily sequestered from our small brain because of the unsuitability of the nourishing blood.

<margin>14.</margin> Finally, I recall that the nutrition of solid parts occurs when the whole of the blood is transformed into food, without the separation of the pure from the impure—since such a separation would be too troublesome for the bones, nerves, organs, and so on. Therefore, solids do not provide any other waste in their feeding: except after the "hunger" of the parts has been satisfied by the nourishing fluid, the whole is consumed equally into a perspirable flow <note>original: "aporrhoeam," referring to invisible evaporation or perspiration</note>. That is to say, the waste of all solid parts does not happen while nutrition is in the process of being made, but only after it is completed. Truly, it then exhales entirely, according to the consensus of the Schools of medicine. Therefore, if the brain is held by the laws of solids and of all the internal organs—laws which the Archeus <term>Archeus: the internal vital spirit or "master-worker" that Van Helmont believed governed the functions of each organ</term> prescribes—there will be no mucus of the brain, nor will it give off anything in the place of waste, other than what it exhales entirely through the pores <note>original: "diaphæresin"</note> in the manner of other organs.
<margin>15.</margin> Finally, waste is relative to the digestion performed in the nourished part, because it presupposes that digestion. Nevertheless, mucus is not the waste of the aforementioned digestion, or the work of the vital Archeus would cease to be consistent in its digestion of similar parts.
<margin>16.</margin> Furthermore, if mucus were the waste of the brain, it would be collected from all sides, and would withdraw into a similar small cell; but it would not go to the basin <note>original: "pelvim," likely referring here to the infundibulum or the area above the ethmoid bone</note>. But the collection of mucus—that is, the common waste of the entire brain—from each imperceptible and tiny part of the brain would be difficult, and it would leave behind many blockages <note>original: "obstructiones"</note>, which, however, are never encountered. This is especially true because the brain is nourished through its body by few and thin veins, and no ducts or channels appear through which the mucus might be led away.
<margin>17.</margin> Similarly, the spinal cord would likewise have its own mucus, and while it struggled to evacuate it, this would have to happen either

<column-break/>

upward through the fourth sinus of the brain, or, falling downward (as a body otherwise fluid and deprived of life is born to always fall), it would block the common source of the motor nerves. This is especially so because mucus has the stickiness of mucilage; it would not be easily moved, but would always leave behind a gloomy fear of blockages. Finally, mucus, however it is taken and moved by warmth, never <margin>18.</margin> flies away entirely or disperses imperceptibly without leaving a residue of its dregs: instead, when its vapor is taken away, it is plainly hardened into a stone <note>original: "tophum," a hard calcium-like deposit</note>. Thus, it is a useless, indeed an impossible, waste for the solid brain, or for any of its similar parts. Truly, it is <margin>19.</margin> entirely contrary to the density of the brain, which, since it is not open with channels, would otherwise have to be continuously stuffed everywhere with clingy waste. Finally, looking toward the ends for which every thing was established by the Creator: no purpose <margin>20.</margin> would clearly appear as to why the brain should prepare mucus as the superfluous waste of its digestion, and thus far make itself an outlaw from the rest of the organs. For the entire nourishing liquid is eventually separated from the whole body through insensible transpiration, without any residue of itself. Since, therefore, there is such a conspicuous inequality of mucus in winter and summer, it could not come from the internal foundation of the mixture, but must come from elsewhere. Thus, mucus is not the dung of the blood, much less of the brain. For it happens <margin>21.</margin> to a healthy and sleeping person, for eight hours and more, that they eject no mucus at all; yet during that period, the brain completes its entire digestion. This is all the more true because the natural faculties of the brain, as of the entire body, are never on holiday. Therefore, mucus is not the waste of the thing, nor is it made by the intent of natural digestion. Nor is it a foreign waste, collected scatteredly through the brain and brought into the basin as its natural emunctory <note>an organ or part of the body that carries off waste</note>, nor is it manufactured by a defect of digestion. Since otherwise, it would be a continuous disease, especially in winter...

Then, as if it repented for its error, it produces first watery and then gluey waste, with which it intends to wash away the opposing filth. A cough <note>original: "Tussis"</note> arises from the sensation of something harmful attacking the larynx, from its beginning down into the depths of the lungs. Indeed, smoke, soot, sharp mineral exhalations, and also damp, foul vapors, etc., cause this distress. Finally, harsh cold overcomes the strength of the "host" <note>the body</note>, as if intending to extinguish the vital guest. A cough, therefore, is an effect of sensation: for as soon as the spirit dwelling in those parts is weighed down by a nuisance leaping in from the outside, the guardian immediately performs its duty. This "anonymous" faculty quickly calls for as much as it deems necessary from the mass of fluid and transforms it into mucus, which it pushes out toward the Larynx like dew. This is done so that the injury of the air does not affect the solid part itself directly and nakedly, but instead breaks itself against the aforementioned coat of mucus. But alas! when the

Not only does it take help from the fluid, but it even alters the substance of the nearby nourishment and turns it into a mucous glue. The closer the nourishment of the organ is to a glowing yellow or reddish heat <note>Van Helmont associates the colors of fluids with different stages of metabolic "digestion"</note>, the more the Guardian "slips" back into its former state when it falls, moving from red to the yellow of straw, and then closer to the appearance of egg white. Conversely, in those with "hectic" fever <note>consumptive diseases like tuberculosis</note>, the mucus becomes bloody and takes on the color of dark ashes. At that point, the substance of the nourishment itself departs in a transformed state, revealing the failing integrity of life in that place. Then, truly, the foul smell of a beginning corpse in the breath reveals the fainting of the *Archeus* of the lungs <note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont's term for the internal vital spirit or "master-sculptor" that governs an organ</note>. Thus, mucus serves as a barrier between the coming harm and the powers of the host. For this reason, it uses salty fluid as a stimulus for its own expulsion, to provoke the sensation of the larynx. There are also dry coughs when there is a 
<margin>35.</margin>
lack of salty mucus. Because old age is likened 
<margin>36.</margin>
to a deficiency, and the lung is the first organ to fail (as mentioned above), coughs are common in old age as if by its very nature...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that mucus and coughs are defensive reactions by a vital "Guardian" power rather than brain waste. He explains that the Guardian creates mucus to shield the lungs and throat from irritants, but when this power "stumbles" or "wanders," it leads to chronic illness and the breakdown of lung vitality.</summary>

-># THE WANDERING GUARDIAN.<-

<margin>37.</margin> because of their nature, these conditions are hardly silent, ceasing or being restrained only with difficulty; once nature is worn out, it does not easily admit restoration. This is the truth about the Cough <note>original: "Tussi"</note>. Regarding its remedy, nothing has been dreamed up that is actually useful. For first, they prescribed decoctions of herbs, such as Coltsfoot <note>original: "Tussilaginum"; literally 'cough-chasers,' a common herbal remedy</note>, but with such an unhappy outcome that almost every household mourns and detests it. When these decoctions were used with little success, it led the Physician <note>original: "Medentem"</note> to think of tablets made with sugar; eventually, they retreated to syrups and lozenges, hoping (I shall show the ridiculousness of this in its proper place) that by swallowing slowly, the saliva mixed with the thick syrup <note>original: "eclegmate"</note> would slip through the opening of the voice <note>original: "rima vocis," referring to the glottis</note> and into the larynx. They do not realize that the admission of such a "foreign guest" would cause even greater misery—constriction of breath, more coughing, choking, and spitting—than the cough itself, which is merely provoked by these unlucky fictions of "help." I have explained these things at length elsewhere as part of my system. 

Ah! And then came that wretched <margin>38.</margin> remedy made from a fox’s lung <note>In ancient "signature" medicine, it was believed that because foxes have great stamina for running, eating their lungs would cure breathing problems</note>. It was hoped that the power of the little animal's long-distance running, which it possessed while alive, would be imparted through sugar after its death. The Schools <note>Traditional medical universities</note> and their dispensaries are entirely ignorant of the fact that the lung is only a sieve for air, and it contributes nothing at all as an aid to the inspirations of long-distance movement. They are ignorant, I say, that it would give no more comfort to a limping or paralyzed man if he were to eat the feet of a hare or a <margin>39.</margin> deer every day. 

Finally, the Chemical crowd followed. When they saw that the ground becomes parched and sterile where "living sulfur" <note>original: "sulfur vivum," meaning native or pure sulfur</note> grows—and by "living" I mean naked sulfur, not that which is forced out of pyrites or elsewhere—they hoped that the mucus (the offspring of the Guardian) would likewise be dried up by sulfur. The Schools hoped to achieve this through "flowers of sulfur" <note>A powdered form of sulfur produced by sublimation</note>. Some therefore refined it with Aloe, saffron, myrrh, and roasted vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate</note>. Others then tried to dissolve it with lime and alkalis, which they named "Milk of Sulfur" (truly a foul-smelling thing). But it lost all credibility when that "milk"—or rather, that yellow liquid of sulfur prepared with lime—returned to its original sulfurous state as soon as vinegar was poured in. Indeed, they placed various masks upon the stomach to try to restore the failures of the <column-break/> Guardian situated at the threshold of the larynx, and to wipe away the harms it had perceived. In this way, both the hope and the purses of the sick have been deluded in various ways. I do not deny that properly prepared sulfur may help with Asthma. But <margin>40.</margin> that Asthma is not a guest of the lung, arising from its own internal "epilepsy" <note>Van Helmont often described sudden organ spasms as local forms of epilepsy</note>; for indeed, those sulfurs have no entry into the lungs themselves. Rather, the nest of that Asthma is around the stomach (as I will teach below), where the helpful sulfur does have an entrance. 

Furthermore, the "flowers of sulfur" sold in shops come from veins of copper. These veins are roasted with a slow fire to drive out the "thieving" sulfur; otherwise, the sulfur would snatch away a great deal of the copper's value. Therefore, anyone who knows why Arsenic <margin>41.</margin> took the name "smoke of metals" <note>original: "fumi metallorum"</note> should weigh the value of such a remedy. Certainly, the lung is hasty; it listens to its own destruction, and the restoration of a failing life is extremely difficult. The lung also gains hardly any help from foods, which have long since set aside the gifts of their native character through so many "offices" of digestion before they even enter the lung. It matters little even if they have reserved a tiny bit of their original scent from their solid form in the middle of their life. That is simply ineffective and unequal to the task of restoring weakness. This is all the more obvious in the "inn" of the lung itself: there, the power of the <term>Archeus</term> <gloss>the internal vital spirit that governs the life and health of an organ</gloss>—acting as a Guardian—willfully twists back, alienates, and corrupts its own nutrients that were meant to be assimilated. For this reason, I have rejected minerals for this purpose (except for the "Greater Secrets" <note>original: "majoribus arcanis"</note>), as they neither have entry nor have they contracted any familiarity with the Archeus implanted in the lungs. 

Otherwise, I have examined remedies by their individual classes. Those "wound-healing" medicines <note>original: "vulneraria"</note> have promised unique results; they pacify the Archeus, turn it away from corruption, and thus restrain the rages typical of a wound. I do not mean that I hope they can reach the lung or larynx in their original power (as I will reveal more conveniently elsewhere). But I at least considered that even if the failures of the cough were not continuous separations <note>of the tissues</note>, such that the phlegm was not actual pus, nevertheless, a wound-healing potion...

which would serve the whole human household as a kind of nourishment, which by its very nature would be responsible—both materially and efficiently—for restoring any deviation of the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The vital principle or "internal chemist" that Van Helmont believed directed all bodily functions</note> as well as that of the <term>Guardian</term> <note>The local vital spirit presiding over a specific organ or passage</note>. 
<margin>42.</margin> Therefore, the need for both Guardians was great, in order to wipe away the "inspired filth" <note>Inhaled dust and impurities</note> which, if brought inside, would otherwise gladly attach itself to the moist walls of the ribs, and the entire chest would soon be filled with mud. For this reason, both at the threshold of the larynx and before the organ of smell, mucus had to exude to catch those opposing impurities. Mucus, I say, was necessary and not water, because water would quickly hasten drop by drop to the bottom. Moreover, the internal parts had to remain moist so they would not crack from the continuous inhalation of air. Therefore, a certain distributive power—like that which dispenses saliva—had to be present to provide continuous moisture. I mean a moderate and slow moisture, which in healthy people ought to be borrowed from the mass of the <term>latex</term> <note>Van Helmont’s term for the clear, watery humor of the body</note>. But when the Guardians are unwell, they continually weep away a portion of their own nourishment, which they ought to have assimilated into themselves. This nourishment is altered in various ways into the form of water, or even transparent or opaque mucilage, according to the variety of the disturbances to which the 
<margin>43.</margin> Guardians have listened. Furthermore, the restoration of the Guardians from weakness is most difficult, and more dangerous in the larynx than in the nostrils, because it threatens <term>tabes</term> <note>Wasting disease or consumption, often associated with tuberculosis</note>; it always stands open and is disturbed by the abundance of air. Finally, it never satisfied me that the mucus of the nostrils—although not much different in color, taste, and appearance from the mucus of coughs—
<margin>44.</margin> should be the same as that which is coughed up from the internal pipes of the lungs. For I could not persuade myself that the same mucus would emerge from two such different organs. Indeed, if it were the same and identical, then that single mucus would not be the waste product of both. Thus, just as a Guardian in good health produces hardly any mucus, and then only as the opportunity arises, so when provoked, it produces mucus according to its own indignation and the property of the receiving organ. That is to say, once 

<column-break/>

seized by fury, it produces in its mucus something false, biting, sharp, and virulent, exceeding the proper limit in both quality and quantity! From this comes the erosion of the larynx, and from there, consumption, bloody spit, and so on. For even if a <term>vomica</term> <note>An internal abscess, usually in the lungs</note> produces various <term>apneumata</term> <note>Obstructions of the breath</note> and constrictions of the chest, it rarely produces a wasting cough. These coughs, therefore, I suspected to spring from an injury to the <term>aspera arteria</term> <note>The "rough artery," an old term for the trachea or windpipe</note>. 
<margin>45.</margin> That the Guardian does not reach the "quiddity" <note>The essential nature or "what-ness"</note> of the brain, I gather from a robust young man known to me, who every day, morning and evening, has been subject to miserable hawking and spitting for several years; meanwhile, he remains quite strong in his brain, nerves, and muscles. When one faculty is significantly injured while another is not at all, it is necessary that both are different in their properties and essences. Therefore, at the very least, the Guardian of the larynx and that of the head are far apart. 
<margin>46.</margin> After the air has been led through the lung into the chest, and pushes the transverse partition (which is called the diaphragm) downward into a circular shape, the diaphragm penetrates its own pores and strains the inhaled air. This is sufficiently shown by certain odors drawn in through the nostrils and finally returned through a belch. In this way, the smoke of charcoal prompts vomiting, and affects the stomach more quickly than the heart. Indeed, the smell of a corpse is felt around the stomach long afterward. So too, a pregnant woman carrying a dead fetus smells like a corpse in her breath. For that odor, passing through the uterus and the diaphragm, teaches us that the breath serves not only to cool the heart, but the whole body. Others have also shown that from the smoke of tobacco, the stomach is tinted with yellowness because of the soot. Likewise, the stomach dreads the odors of perceived laxatives, even if the drugs themselves are masked with sugar and spice, because by its own sense of smell, it perceives those same odors. Therefore, if the odor is air, it goes straight to the stomach. The plague itself, introduced through the inhaled breath, is mostly forged around the stomach; therefore, vomiting, headache, sleepiness, and so on, accuse and reveal an affected stomach.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that mucus is a specialized substance produced by local "Guardians" to protect the body from inhaled impurities. He concludes that the respiratory and digestive systems are more porous and interconnected than previously thought, as evidenced by how inhaled odors directly affect the stomach.</summary>

<margin>1.</margin> The beginning of Wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Now, the fear of the Lord begins from the meditation on death and eternal life. Indeed, many of the moderns, along with the Stoics, judge the end of Wisdom to be the knowledge of oneself. I, however, call the ultimate

<column-break/>

end of Wisdom and the prize <note>original: "bravium" — a term for the reward at the end of a race</note> of our entire life's course "charity" <note>Christian love/divine grace</note>, which accompanies us after other things have deserted us. Therefore, even self-knowledge, according to me, is merely a means toward the fear of the Lord. And the knowledge of life presupposes the knowledge of the soul. <margin>2.</margin> Since life and the soul are like synonyms. For it is a matter of faith that man was created in the image of God, from nothing into a living creature, and that his mind will never perish. But other souls, when they cease to live, return to nothingness <note>Van Helmont believed animal and plant "souls" were purely vital and temporary, unlike the immortal human mind</note>. The significance of this difference is discussed elsewhere in my work *On the Origin of Forms*. But so far it is not sufficiently clear in what that likeness with God, our Archetype, consists. I will say what I feel, under humble submission to the Church. There is no knowledge more burdensome than that by which the soul understands itself, though none is more useful. This is because the whole of faith establishes its base upon the indelible substance of the soul. Indeed, I have found many demonstrations concerning this truth published in books; but none of them provides a "reason why" with respect to Atheists, who deny a single and constant eternal deity. <margin>3.</margin> Plato indeed established three classes of Atheists. Namely, one which believes in no gods; then a second, which admits gods indeed, but claims they are unconcerned with us and despisers of small things, and therefore ignorant of them. Finally, a third class, which although it believes the gods are aware of even the smallest things, nevertheless supposes they are flexible and indulgent through a tiny little prayer. This kind of Atheist is most common among Christians today, especially those who profess themselves to be the most perfect. They certainly dare anything. They heavily impose burdens on the shoulders of others which they do not touch with a finger; they drain the purses of believers, and offer heaven for sale to the dying; they entangle themselves everywhere in secular affairs and unknown politics, to the extent that Religion...

<margin>4.</margin> People marry themselves to political affairs. Just as schoolmasters see themselves as fit to lead classes of boys, they ignorantly thrust themselves into steering the "helm" of the State. A supreme understanding is what should be wished for. If only it were permitted for Atheists to taste, for even a single moment, what it is to understand intellectually, so they might feel the immortality of the mind as if by touching it. I, for my part, am gladly ignorant of the rules or methods by which I could enlighten the intellect of another. However, I am rightly saddened that those who seek truth through study never arrive at its knowledge. Because they are puffed up by "the letter" <note>original: "litera inflati"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," implying they have book-learning without spiritual insight</note>, they lack charity; instead, greed and ambition hide their Atheism. I learned long ago that our mind understands nothing through the imagination, nor through figures or images, unless the miserable and wretched discourse of wavering reason is added. <margin>5.</margin> But when the soul comprehends itself intellectually, or within itself, reason fails it, as does the image of itself by which it represents itself to itself. That is, the soul cannot grasp itself through reason, nor through images. After I had known that the truth of essence and the truth of intellect have penetrated each other in unity and identity, I knew the intellect to be an immortal thing, separated far from fleeting matters. Indeed, the mind is not felt; yet we believe it to be within, not growing weary, nor agitated by diseases. <margin>6.</margin> Therefore, sleep, madness, and drunkenness are not symptoms of a damaged immortal mind; they are merely passions of the sensitive soul <term>sensitive soul: in Van Helmont’s view, the lower soul that governs the body and senses, distinct from the immortal Mind</term>, which is the companion of life. For even beasts endure such passions. I do not think it right for an immortal thing to suffer from fleeting things, nor to be subjected to or overcome by them. For indeed, the mind feels and endures the torments of hell, yet it is not overcome, nor is it extinguished. Thus, linked to a fleeting light <note>The "fleeting light" refers to the temporary biological life of the body</note>, it suffers from fleeting things. But as the mind is in us, and yet is not felt by us, so its continuous and unshaken operations are

<column-break/>

insensible. For that which is sensible in itself cannot be entirely spiritual and purely abstract. Indeed, even if it seems to us that we understand nothing through the total abstraction of discourse and separation from everything that can fall under the senses, the mind, or the intellect (and this at the beginning of contemplations), the mind still acts in these things in its own insensible way and with spiritual efficacy. This I perceived thus: <margin>7.</margin> for one who is confessing often does not feel the effects of contrition and grieves greatly over that insensibility. Yet, if asked if they wished to sin, they would perhaps answer that they would rather die. Therefore, in confession, there is an insensible operation of the mind, an effect of supernatural faith. Because intellectual actions are clients of a different Magistrate <note>Van Helmont uses "Magistratus" to suggest that the Mind operates under a different legal or spiritual jurisdiction than the physical body</note>. Hence, the mystics teach that in faith alone, without discourse or thought, the mind works more, and by working, also profits more than he who prays with many words and discourses, stirring up compunctions within himself. But happy is he who is permitted to perceive these insensible operations of the mind and reflect them into and upon the powers of the sensitive soul, just as operative faith begins. For these mostly leave their traces in life thereafter and excite the memory, which operates in faith along with grace. <margin>8.</margin> Atheists and libertines among Christians are the first to laugh at us, regarding the "Image of God" as a fiction, or that we were created in God’s image. <margin>9.</margin> But others, Atheists of the second class, believe not only that we were created in the image of God, but they imagine an identity within us with the immense and uncreated deity. They claim that man does not differ from God in substance in any other way than a part from the whole, and that he had a beginning with the One who has no beginning <note>original: "cum non principiato"; they believe the soul is co-eternal with God</note>. Not, however, in essence or internal property. This, indeed, besides being blasphemy, holds many stupidities. <margin>10.</margin> For whatever began is, by that very fact, a creature. Moreover, it involves an impossible imperfection in God,
