<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's philosophical inquiry into the "Mens" (the Mind or higher Soul). Having established its immortality, he now argues against the idea that the soul is a literal piece of the Divine substance, while simultaneously elevating the human mind's status above that of the angels due to the Incarnation.</meta>

-># THE IMAGE OF THE MIND.<-

<column-break/>

It is impossible even for God to create anything outside of himself that is equal to him in substance or essence. For it is established even through Philosophy that the individual parts of the infinite must necessarily be entirely infinite themselves. A creature, according to its substance, cannot be more infinite than it was according to its being, existence, and duration when compared to the Eternal Being. It is foolish, therefore, to believe that the soul is a part of the divine substance, or essentially similar to it, since the soul began from nothing in terms of its power, magnitude, duration, and glory. If, therefore, God could not make the human soul as a part of his own divinity—since the infinite has no parts or "lesser" portions—the soul was not made by God in that manner. Thus, it did not flow out spontaneously from nothing, nor did it make itself elsewhere before it existed. Therefore, those who believe that the "quiddity" <note>the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note> of the divine image located in the mind consists of an identity of substance and essence are immensely mistaken. These things stand apart from each other in every way by the boundary of infinity. The human mind would spontaneously slide back into the nothingness from which it began, and would be dissolved again, were it not preserved in being by the divine goodness. The mind possesses an eternal permanence from that point forward, not from its own being, but from the essence of eternity which is freely granted and preserved for it. It comes, therefore, from elsewhere, and from a source infinitely more powerful than itself. Let this suffice. The mind is a spiritual substance, a vital <margin>11.</margin> and luminous creature. And since there are many types and species of vital lights, this light of the mind differs from other vital things in this: it is a spiritual and immortal substance. Other vital lights, however, are not formal substances—even though they are "substantial forms" <note>A Scholastic term referring to the principle that gives a thing its specific identity; Van Helmont argues that while a plant's "form" makes it a plant, it is not an enduring "substance" like the human soul</note>—and therefore they recede into nothingness through death, not unlike <margin>12.</margin> the flame of a candle. Furthermore, the Mind differs from the Angels in that it is made after the image and likeness of the eternal GOD. For the mind possesses that light, and that luminous substance, as a gift of creation,

<column-break/>

since the mind itself is that vital light. But an Angel is not the light itself, nor does it possess an internal light natural to itself; rather, it is a mirror of the uncreated light. Thus, in this respect, the Angel falls short of the perfection of the true divine image. Otherwise, since an Angel is an incorporeal spirit, if it were luminous of itself, it would express the image of GOD more perfectly than a human. Furthermore, whatever GOD loves more is by that very fact more noble; but GOD loved man more than the Angel. To redeem the nature of Angels, he did not take on the form of an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmonis"</note>; whereas the thrice-glorious Lamb, the Savior of the World, assumed the nature of a servant to redeem man. Nor is this contradicted by the saying that "the least in the kingdom of Heaven is greater than John [the Baptist]." For the Son of Man is not less in dignity and essence than an Angel, even if he was "made a little lower than the angels" <note>A reference to Psalm 8:5 and Hebrews 2:7. Van Helmont argues that this "lowering" is a temporary condition of earthly life, not a status of the soul's essence</note>. For the Son of Man, by the lot of living, was made a little lower than the Angels while he was made man. So it was with John. Therefore, an Angel always remains a ministering spirit; but one never reads that an Angel is a "friend," or a "son of the Father," the "delight of the Son of Man," or the "temple of the Holy Spirit" in which the Thrice-glorious Trinity has made its dwelling. This, indeed, is the narrow prerogative of the divine image, which the eternal light imprints upon every man coming into this <margin>13.</margin> world. In the year 1610, after a long exhaustion from contemplation, in order that I might acquire some knowledge of my own mind—and because I then still thought that self-knowledge was a certain completion of Wisdom—I perhaps fell into a sleep. Carried away beyond the paths of reason, I seemed to be in a hall that was quite dark. At my left hand was a table on which sat a flask <note>original: "lagena"</note> containing a little liquid, and the voice of the liquid said to me: "Do you desire honors and riches?" I was struck dumb by the unusual voice. I walked about, weighing within myself what this might signify.

He uses this experience to explain why the soul must have a "figure" or shape, specifically a human one, which acts as a spiritual "seal" to form the physical body.</meta>

Meanwhile, on the right, a crack was seen in the wall, through which a certain light of unusual splendor struck my eyes; it made me forget the liquid, the voice, and my previous plan. For I saw that which surpasses any thought expressible in words. Immediately then, that crack disappeared. Returning then to the flask, but in sadness, I took it away with me. I tried, however, to taste the liquid, and with long labor, I opened the vial, and struck with horror, I fell out of my sleep <note>The author is describing a dream-vision that transitioned into a waking spiritual quest.</note>. But there remained a preceding and immense desire for knowing the soul: for which desire I panted for 23 solid years. Because finally in the year 1633, in the midst of anxious afflictions of my fortunes, yet with a "Sabbath" <note>original: *sabbatismo*; a state of spiritual rest or peace</note> of my life being offered to me from the security of an innocent life, I saw in a vision my mind in a human figure. It was a light, whose whole homogeneous nature was actively seeing—a spiritual substance, crystalline, shining with its own splendor. It was wrapped, however, on the other side by a cloudy part, like its own husk <note>original: *siliqua*</note>, and I could not discern whether that husk had any splendor of its own because of the superlative brightness of the crystalline spirit contained within. I easily noticed this, however: that the mark of sex was only in the husk. But the seal of the crystal was an ineffable light, so reflected that the crystal itself became incomprehensible. And this was not through any other negation, except that it not only cannot be expressed in words, but moreover, that you do not know the "quiddity" <term>the essential "what-ness" or nature</term> of the thing you see. And then I knew that this light was the same that I had seen 23 years before through the crack. I at least understood from this the <margin>14.</margin> vanity of my long desire. For however beautiful the vision was, the mind acquired no perfection for itself from it. For I knew that the mind, in a dream-like vision, had acted like a third person, and such a representation was not worthy of so great a desire. <margin>15.</margin> As for what pertains to the image of God, I could never conceive of anything, not even in the abstract meditation of the intellect, that did not, by that same effort, carry some

<column-break/>

figure before it, under which it stood in the mind of the one considering it. For whether I conceive a thing by imagining its idea, or whether the intellect transforms itself into the thing understood; the concept always stood under some figure. Nor could I consider the "quiddity" <note>essential nature</note> of the immortal mind, with its individual existence, as being stripped of all figure; nor could it fail at least to correspond to the human figure. For <margin>16.</margin> as often as a separated soul sees another soul, an Angel, or an evil spirit, this happens with the knowledge that these things are present to it, just as it distinguishes a soul from an Angel, or the soul of Peter from the soul of John. Indeed, a distinction of this kind occurs only through the vision proper to the soul, and this vision includes the external "otherness" and therefore the "figural" <note>shape-based</note> nature of the soul. For an Angel is in a place in such a way that he is not elsewhere at the same time. In this is necessarily included both a local and a figural limit. Furthermore, the human body, <margin>17.</margin> as such, cannot give itself a human figure: it therefore had need of a sculptor, who would be enclosed within the matter of the seed <note>original: *feminis*; referring here to the generative fluid or "thigh" in a biblical/anatomical sense</note>, and had descended into it from elsewhere. That sculptor, however, insofar as he might be a material force, has no more power of shaping from himself than the mass of the body itself. Therefore, something precedes in the mass which is plainly immaterial, yet real, and an effective beginning; it would be in anything that is to be shaped through a "sigillar" <note>seal-like</note> impression. Therefore, while the acting soul glides outward and surveys the body of the seed, in a certain aura, it sketches its own seal and figure, which is the cause of the seed's fertility. Otherwise, if the soul were not figured, but the figure of the body itself were born as if spontaneously: then a man missing a limb <note>original: *truncus*</note> would generate a child missing that same limb: because the body of that parent is not whole, and would at least be lacking in the spirit implanted in that limb. If, therefore, a figure is brought into the seed, it receives that image from a vital beginning outside itself and prior to it. But if the soul imprints its figure upon the seed, it will not represent a foreign or strange face, but will paint an icon of itself. For thus...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s discussion of the "Image of the Mind." Having previously described his vision of the mind as a crystalline, human-shaped light, he now transitions into a philosophical and theological defense of why the Mind must possess a "figure" or shape to function within the laws of nature and biology.</meta>

-># THE IMAGE OF THE MIND.<-

The souls of brute animals <note>original: *brutorum*; animals lacking human reason</note> preserve their own species through the act of generating. The Mind, however, although by virtue of its origin it stands above the laws of nature, nevertheless, once it has stepped across the threshold of nature and been incorporated and joined with another, it is thereafter constrained by nature's laws. This is because a uniform progression—ascent, descent, limitation, and end—must be maintained for all vital generations. Indeed, it would otherwise be full of absurdities if an operation of such magnitude (as is human generation and the continuation of the species) could happen without the cooperation of the Mind. It is necessary, therefore, for fertility to be granted to the seed through a participation in vital principles and a specific determination. This surely occurs in no other way than through the "sealing" of the soul within the spirit of the seed. From this, the matter obtains the required maturity and a "shadowed-out" figure, so that it may finally obtain from the Creator the formal light of life—that is, the soul of its species, whose likeness is expressed in that very figure. Furthermore, it is a matter of faith that our mind is a substance that will never perish. The fashioning of this substance anew out of nothing belongs to the Creator alone, <margin>18.</margin> who, if it pleases Him, adopts the mind alone into His own image. It also seems a logical consequence that the immense and ineffable God is of a human figure—and this by an argument *a posteriori* <note>An argument based on observing effects to determine the cause.</note>, if indeed <margin>19.</margin> arguments have any force regarding such an object. But because the physical body is often defective, many have thought that the glorious image of God the Archetype, represented in the Mind, consists only in the rational power. They are unaware that the rational force is merely a servant to the intellect; it is not of the Mind's essence, nor is it an inseparable companion. This I have already explained in my *Treatise on the Hunting of the Sciences*. Others, however, hold that the soul expresses the image of God most closely through the uniform simplicity of its substance and the triad of its powers: namely, Intellect, Will, and Memory. <margin>20.</margin> This comparison has always seemed like a feeble old-wives' tale to me—as if the Mind were the image of God only by some numerical value. For a true image involves a likeness of essence and figure, not merely 

<column-break/>

a parity of numbers. Indeed, if the soul, in its very substance, represents God Himself, then intellect, will, and memory will not be distinct powers, properties, or "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that can change without the thing itself changing.</note> of the soul. Thus, the likeness of the triad would cease to exist, and such an "image" would poorly fit the Original Type it is supposed to represent. Furthermore, it is absurd to compare the persons of the Trinity to memory or will, since no person of the Holy Trinity represents the "will" alone, nor is the "will" a separate person within God. Also, those three powers in the soul can in no way express the divine image or a close likeness any better than a bare triad of accidents heaped into the substance of the soul. In that sense, the soul would denote the image of God even less than any piece of wood does. For a piece of wood, through chemical analysis, expresses salt, sulfur, and liquor <note>original: *salem, sulfur, & liquorem*; the three chemical principles, or Tria Prima, of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>—and these are not merely three powers or a bare "three-ness" (like the mind in the aforementioned comparison to the divine persons). Any wood has three actual substances enclosed within the unity of the whole, separated in their individual existences, which in their connection make up the single substance of the wood. The mystic Tauler, however, <margin>21.</margin> divides the soul not into three powers, but into two distinct parts: namely, the lower or outer part, which he calls the "soul," and the other higher, inner part, which he calls the "ground of the soul" <note>original: *fundum animae*; Tauler’s *Seelengrund*</note> or the "spirit." He says that the image of God is specifically contained in this part alone. To this part, the Devil has no access, because the Kingdom of God is there. He assigns vastly different acts and properties to each part, by which he distinguishes them from one another. But at the very least, that holy man destroys the simple homogeneity <note>The state of being uniform or of one substance throughout.</note> of the soul, by which it ought most especially to express the likeness of God. Or at least, he denies that the image of God is propagated throughout the entire soul of man. Certainly, I do not easily believe in a duality of the immortal soul, or the "otherness" of a binary pair, if in its own essence

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the human Mind as the "Image of God." In the preceding text, he argued that the mind possesses a human-like "figure" or form. Here, he refines this by arguing that the Mind’s likeness to God is found in its simplicity and unity, rather than in complex faculties like memory or free will, which he views as temporary tools for earthly life.</meta>

-># THE IMAGE OF THE MIND.<-

...ought to exhibit unity. Rather, I believe that in the simplest unity—the indivisible homogeneity <note>original: *homogeneitate*; being of the same substance throughout</note> of the spirit—under the symbol of immortality, indissolubility, and identity, outside of all external connection, <margin>22.</margin> the mind is more closely assimilated to God. Therefore, the glorious image of God is not something separate from the soul, nor is it separable; rather, the mind itself is that glorious image, as intimate to the soul as the soul is to itself. For this reason, a likeness between the mind and God can neither be described nor even fully conceived, since God Himself is entirely incomprehensible; thus, a "character" or defining mark of identity and unity can never be thought of as the foundation for that likeness. It is enough that the mind is a spirit, beloved by God, homogeneous, simple, immortal, created in the Image of God—a unique being to which death adds nothing and takes nothing away from that which is natural to it in its essence of simplicity. <margin>23.</margin> And because by its very constitution and destination it is a partaker in blessedness, damnation is therefore something that happens to it "by accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing; here, it means damnation is not part of the mind's original design.</note>—that is, outside of its original purpose and because of a subsequent defect. Therefore, once the mind is separated from the body, it no longer uses memory, nor the process of "reminiscence" <note>recovering a memory through logic or triggers</note> by looking at place or duration; instead, a single "now" and "there" contains all things for it. <margin>24.</margin> Consequently, if any memory were to remain with it, it would be useless for eternity and a heavy burden. The same is true for reminiscence, since that is only brought into action through the discourse of reason, which is now dead. Thus, these no longer have a place in eternity, where the soul stands outside the necessity of remembering, in the gaze and enjoyment of naked truth, without setting, exhaustion, or defect. At the very least, the blessed soul would stand outside the aforementioned "trinity of powers" <note>Usually referring to the traditional division of the soul into Memory, Intellect, and Will.</note> and therefore would no longer represent the image of God—for whose sake alone it was created. Indeed, looking more deeply, I do not find in mortal man a singular memory or a separate power of the soul; but rather a bare mode of recollecting by which we, when forgetful, construct an "artificial memory" through the aid of the imagination (which is the

<column-break/>

intellect’s deputy <note>original: *vicaria*; one who acts in place of another</note>). This artificial memory is far stronger than their natural memory would otherwise be. <margin>25.</margin> Furthermore, when life departs, the will simultaneously recedes from the soul; it appears, therefore, to be added to the soul "accidentally." For God, after creating man, placed him "in the hand of his own counsel" <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 15:14: "He himself made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his counsel."</note>. This denotes not only a later addition but also that, in its own way, the will is not initially essential to the mind, but was added like a "talent" <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in the Bible, implying the will is a resource to be used.</note> granted by concession so that man might follow the path he prefers to choose. Otherwise, truly, in the whole scene of things, there is no power more ruinous to man than free will, since it alone gives birth to every discord between God and man. Therefore, such a faculty cannot have a place in the blessedness of eternity. Moreover, once the freedom of choosing is removed, the will itself either perishes or becomes a useless torment. For this reason, they say the will is "confirmed" in Heaven, or rather, it is taken away. That is, the inhabitants of heaven cannot "will," or "will to will," except what God wills. Those who are in charity and glory cannot help but will the things that belong to charity. Thus, the human will ceases when the freedom of willing is dissolved. Consequently, the will is a fleeting power of the soul because it cannot <margin>26.</margin> serve or benefit the blessed soul. Since it can no longer be put into action, it could only remain as a "wish"—which does not exist in Heaven, where there is full satisfaction and possession of all things desirable in every abundance. Therefore, the will would be a burdensome appendage to the blessed soul. Let it be enough to have stored up treasures in this life through the power <margin>27.</margin> of willing. Thus, the power of willing perishes with life, and the "substantial will" reveals itself—a will that is in no way distinct from the intellect and the essence of the mind, and therefore has a being distinct from the "accident" of free choice. For just as the power of fantasy is alienated through delusions and perishes with life, so also ceases the power of free <margin>28.</margin> choice. Plato’s *Parmenides* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato; Van Helmont cites it to support the idea that God’s nature is simple and lacks "accidents" or temporary qualities.</note> understood this to some extent: that in God there are no accidents...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the "Image of God" in the human mind consists of its essential unity and simplicity rather than temporary faculties like memory or free will. He contends that these powers are earthly tools that cease to exist or are transformed into a "substantial will" in the afterlife.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument regarding the "Image of God" in the human mind. On the previous page, he suggested that the mind, in its purest state, lacks the complexity of separate faculties and exists as a simple, unified spirit. Here, he explores how the mind’s intellectual light reflects the divine and distinguishes the "Intellectual Will" from the common, earthly will.</meta>

-># THE IMAGE OF THE MIND.<-

...nor should there be a duality <note>two-fold nature</note> distinct from its being. Therefore, I conclude that if the mind is to reflect His image, at the very least every property of the mind must melt together into an intellectual substance of simple light. Just as smoke, ignited by a flame, becomes one and the same with that flame in both its form and its matter. Thus the soul is a naked and pure intellect, and an image of uncreated light. <margin>29.</margin> Just as the eye sees nothing more truly or properly than the sun—and all other things only because of the sun—so the blessed soul understands nothing more truly than the light by which it is internally illuminated and which it enjoys; for it is upon this light that the soul totally and immediately depends. But just as the eye cannot endure a direct gaze at the sun, so the mind cannot understand God except according to the measure of Charity <note>original: *Charitatis*; divine or selfless love</note> it possesses, by which measure it also possesses God within itself in glory. For the mind’s free intellect, by the act of understanding, acquires a "usurpation" <note>here meaning a taking-up or mastery</note> of the thing understood, insofar as it transforms itself—through the desire to please and do well—into the unity of the light that penetrates it and, by penetrating it, makes it blessed. In this way, the mind primarily contemplates God through understanding; it is penetrated by light and thus the Image of God, which it reflects, transforms the mind and makes the mind like unto Himself.

<margin>30.</margin> However, those who have placed the image of God within Reason argue that the Law is the image of God, and that this Law is inscribed on our souls through Reason. Thus, they believe the soul is the likeness of God insofar as it is rational. But they fail to consider that while the soul might *contain* the image of God in this way, it does not follow that the mind itself is essentially the Law itself. This is no different than how the law and the soul differ in their "subjecthood" <note>original: *suppositionalitate*; a philosophical term for how a thing exists as a distinct subject or individual</note> of essence. For the Law did not yet exist when the soul of man was already created. I have shown in *The Hunt for Sciences* <note>original: *venatione scientiarum*; one of Van Helmont's treatises</note> that it is blasphemous to attribute the image of God to Reason. There is no similarity or comparison between the divine and a faculty as uncertain and falling as Reason.

<margin>31.</margin> I shall therefore speak my own views. The intellect has an Intellectual Will that is co-equal to it, substantially melted with it, and united to it. This is not a "power" or an "accident" <note>original: *accidens*; a temporary or non-essential property</note>, but the intellectual light itself—a spiritual substance and a simple, undivided essence. It is separated from the intellect only by the subjecthood of its being in an incomprehensible way, but not in its essence. Likewise, there is a third thing in the mind, which for lack of a better term <note>original: *defectu ethymi*; literally "lacking a root word"</note> I call Love, or perpetual desire. This is not a desire for having, acquiring, possessing, or enjoying, but for loving or pleasing. It is equal to the two previously mentioned parts and equally simple within the unity of the substance. These three are melted into unity under the single and indivisible substance of the soul. Furthermore, that Love is not some act of the will, but proceeds simultaneously from the substantial intellect and will as a distinct and glorious act. Finally, that Love is not a passion, but a dominant essence and a glorifying act. Therefore, the Will and Love discussed here have nothing in common with the "will of man" or the "will of the flesh." <margin>32.</margin> These are essential titles by which, for lack of better words, the mind represents the image of God in some way.

Because the intellect understands and intends God, it loves Him with the whole mind in a single, undivided act of love and pleasure—or desire—in its total simplicity. From the beginning of creation, these two (the intellectual Will and Love) were present with the intellect. One should not think they are only revived anew after death, since they belong to the essence of the mind and the Image of God. But as soon as the intellect yielded to the disturbances of the sensory imagination <note>original: *phantasiæ sensitivæ*; the part of the mind processing physical senses</note>, the intellectual Will and Love allowed for the entry of "will" and "memory" through the corruption of nature. These [earthly faculties] will pass away into nothingness along with the falling soul, while the integrity of the mind persists. Indeed, in ecstasy, the intellect, will, and memory often fall asleep, with only the fiery act of love remaining; this act is distinct from those three, yet it does not exist without the substantial intellect and will, to which it is otherwise equal. Therefore, while the others are, as it were, lulled to sleep, Love stands...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the true "Image of God" in humans is a unified trinity of Intellect, Intellectual Will, and Love, rejecting the idea that it resides in the fallible faculty of Reason. He describes these as essential, spiritual substances that persist beyond death, even as temporary faculties like memory and earthly will fade away.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the soul's nature. On the previous page, he described the mind as a pure, naked intellect and a reflection of divine light. He now moves to distinguish how this intellectual unity differs from the fragmented faculties we experience in our earthly, bodily existence.</meta>

-># THE IMAGE OF THE MIND.<-

...remains on the surface, as long as it has absorbed other things into itself. In this life, however, love comes before desire, because love is a passion of the **loving faculty** <note>original: *facultatis amativæ*</note>, which proceeds from that mental "suppositionality" (which is substantial love), and it reflects the image of the bodily faculty in this life. Therefore, individual things tend to rush toward disorder <note>original: *ataxiam*</note> and dissolution. But among the heavenly beings, that love establishes neither priority nor distinction from desire; it does not have the nature of a power, nor is it a habit or an act of willing, nor does it <margin>34.</margin> exist outside the intellect. Thus, the intellect is the **formal light**, and the very substance of the soul itself, which knows intuitively without the help of eyes—just as it discerns, wills, loves, and desires within its own unity, without eyes, whatever it comprehends within itself and indicates by its willing. For the mind then no longer remembers through the repetition of **images** <note>original: *specierum*; mental representations of things once perceived</note> of a thing once known; nor is it any longer led to knowledge through external circumstances. Instead, there is a single, simultaneous knowledge of all things understood, and an **intuitive gaze** within itself. It is such, however, that the mind may know one thing more "personally" than another, while the intellect reflects upon the things understood within a distinct unity of truth. This is not unlike how it works now in **artificial memory**, where that recollective memory is not an act distinct from the inductive judgment of the intellect. Therefore, this state is more natural to the mind once it has been freed from the turbulent fantasies of earthly understanding. <margin>35.</margin> For these things are not hindered by the fact that in living beings, memory may fail while judgment remains intact, or vice versa. These are, you see, heterogeneous faculties of the **sensitive soul** <note>the "sensitive soul" refers to the part of our nature responsible for senses and emotions, which we share with animals</note>, which are distinct in the body because they are conceived according to the "mode of the receiver" <margin>36.</margin> through the mortal soul. Indeed, I have noted that even in non-living things, a certain "deaf" knowledge of an object exists—as well as a sense and an affection for an object. These are what people have begun to call **sympathies**. This deaf perception of objects serves them in place of sight and intellect. For there is within them, besides (for indeed, whatever

<column-break/>

recedes further from the simplicity of the mind is, by 그 very fact, more prone to a multiplicity of functions) a certain vital power and gift of some goodness, value, and energy, directed toward the ends intended by the Creator. Just as there is also a third power, resulting from both of the preceding ones: which is a **joy** <note>original: *jubili*</note> at the meeting of things that help, or an aversion to things that harm. In these things, we observe a certain affection toward lowly things, as well as fear, flight, and so on. This triple grade is even more manifest in the "duller" insects and in men suffering from **insanity** <note>original: *vesanis*</note>, over whom no intellect presides, and in whom only the power of the visual light shines forth as a governor. Yet, in addition to this, there is in them the act of vital virtues and functions for which they exist. And thirdly, there is in them a far clearer act of joy or aversion. These things are explained far more powerfully in other "sensitive" creatures. To these creatures, a certain **sensitive imagination** belongs, along with a sort of discourse of reason; this shines forth in each of them more or less in place of an intellect. Thus, sagacity, will, and memory in them fall below the level of intellectual apprehension. However, their objects and functions are continually changing, according to matter, which is prone to divisions and individualities. This, of course, reveals the diversities of the "receivers." There is also in these creatures an emanative power of goodness and virtues, by which their souls lean more or less toward the exercise of their own virtues or ferocities. And finally, they have their own complacency, boredom, and **passion** <note>original: *thymosis*; a Greek-derived term for spirited anger or drive</note> in the consideration of objects. These are so united to the sensitive souls that it is hardly possible to look at two persons without soon becoming more attached to one than the other. Because of the "mode of the receiver," these things in the body will be more clearly manifested in man. Finally, I would not wish the <margin>37.</margin> **Image of God** in man to be considered as consisting of some **trinity of faculties** <note>referring to the traditional triad of Memory, Intellect, and Will</note>, which has so far been found to belong to other things in the system of the world. For the dignity of the Image of God is in no way shared by other created things. Since the Image of God is only...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's discussion on the nature of the mind and the soul. On the previous page, he was explaining how the mind functions through an "artificial memory" and how it relates to objects. Here, he distinguishes between the essential, "luminous" nature of the mind—which is a single, undivided act—and the fragmented "faculties" or "imagination" we experience while bound to a physical body and its organs.</meta>

...and it is intimate to the mind, and as proper to it as its own essence. The remaining **properties**, however, are not the essence of the mind itself, but are products of essences and come after them. For it is not worthy of the majesty of the **divine image** <note>original: "imaginis divinae"; the idea that the human mind reflects the nature of God</note> to be defined by mere qualities. Indeed, the properties of other things melt into the essence of the soul by the power of the divine image. But if they are judged as "attributes" or "products," it is only because of the wretched common way of understanding and habitual misuse of terms. <margin>38.</margin> For the mind is a single **act** <note>In philosophy, an "act" refers to something fully realized or in operation, rather than just a potential</note>: pure, simple, formal, uniform, undivided, and immortal. Within this act, the incomprehensible image of GOD incomprehensibly and essentially consists, and it gives form to the mind. So much so that in this image, even all the powers of the mind not only lay aside the nature of mere "attributes," but even gather their individual identities into an indistinct unity. This is because the soul is, in itself, a certain **substantial light**—or a substance so luminous that its individual existence is not distinct from the light itself. Its **intellect** is the light of the mind in such a way that the mind itself is purely a "lucid intellect." For in this light of itself, the mind, when separated from the body, <margin>39.</margin> sees and understands itself entirely through its whole being; for which purpose it has no need of either the brain or the heart. It is only in these organs, you see, that the substance of the mind seems to take on a "lineage" of distinct properties. Specifically, in the body, while the abstract intellect uses the bodily organs to which it is bound, it represents and takes on a **qualitative power** called **Imagination**. This happens because it is "sunk" through its seat in the **sensitive soul** <note>original: "animae sensitivae"; the lower part of the soul responsible for senses and movement, shared with animals</note> into the depths of that corrupt nature. This Imagination <margin>40.</margin> arises from a certain combination of the **phantastic power** <note>the faculty of forming mental images</note> of the sensitive soul itself and the splendor of the intellect, which has degenerated within the organs into the aforementioned qualitative power. Therefore, this faculty of imagination grows weary from its efforts; it fails, and not

<column-break/>

rarely, it even becomes insane, and the hair turns gray from the strain of imagining. But the mind, once separated from the body, never grows tired of understanding. Furthermore, in living beings, the imagination not only grows weary, but it also does not possess within itself any **intellectual species** <note>original: "species intellectivas"; the mental concepts or "forms" of things</note> that it has not drawn from sensible objects. Therefore, the intellectual power, which works together with the phantastic function of the sensitive soul, follows the nature of the physical organ and the will of the sensitive life—just as elsewhere in nature, an effect follows the "weaker part" of its causes. <margin>41.</margin> But the soul possesses everything it requires for knowing and willing—whether for once or for many times—entirely from itself, and not from anything external or foreign. For a **blessed soul** <note>original: "animae beatae"; a soul in the afterlife or a state of grace</note> does not derive its substantial "good will" from the thing it understands; rather, its goodness of love is its own, through which the blessed mind is "good" substantially and not just qualitatively. <margin>42.</margin> It possesses this prerogative because it is a "typical image" of divinity. Bodies, however, naturally and perpetually slide into the attributes of physical forms, variety, changes, and dissolution. <margin>43.</margin> Therefore, the **Love** or **desire** of the mind is not a function of some "appetitive power"; rather, it is the intellectual and willing mind itself. These are joined indivisibly under a single unity, in the greatest possible identity and simplicity. In mortal men, however, they are separated, as much because of the necessity of the organs and the differences in their functions as because of the mixture with the sensitive soul. <margin>44.</margin> For indeed, we now often desire things which the intellect judges should not be desired, and the will might wish for things that will not happen. It is necessary, however, that things whose operations are distinct must also be distinct at their root, in the same way that individual things are separated. In the mind, they are distinct only by a relative "suppositionality" <note>individual personhood or subsistence</note>; but in the sensitive soul, they are distinct according to their bodily and qualitative nature. <margin>45.</margin> Therefore, that loving desire of the mind is the very substance of the soul. And although in Heaven there is full satisfaction and perpetual enjoyment of all things desirable...

He distinguishes the tireless, unified understanding of the separated mind from the weary, organ-dependent imagination of the living.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the "Image of the Mind." On the previous page, he established the mind as a "substantial light" or a "lucid intellect." Here, he transitions into how the mind’s desire and will function both in our current earthly state and in the afterlife, specifically distinguishing between the mind’s divine essence and the "sensitive soul" that governs our bodily impulses.</meta>

# IMAGE OF THE MIND.

However, the desire of the mind—which is the pursuit of contentment—does not cease on that account, <margin>46.</margin> nor does this bring any "passion" <note>original: "passionem"; in a philosophical sense, this refers to being acted upon or suffering a disturbance, rather than just emotion</note> to the mind, any more than **Charity** <note>Love in its highest, divine form</note> itself does. Since, at their root, they are one and the same. Otherwise, if the aforementioned desire were to cease, either a sense of boredom or a numbing of enjoyment would soon arise in the heavenly realms. Therefore, this desire, or love, is the fuel of endless delight. It is clear, then, that in the mind, the **intellect**, **will**, and **love** are substantially born together as one.

In the **sensitive soul**, however, these operations are distinguished by the root of different faculties. This is why we can understand things we do not desire, and we also desire things we would rather not have, or things we do not fully know. Finally, we "will" (as when someone walks toward their own punishment) things we do not "desire," but would rather avoid. From this it happens that desire overcomes the will, and in turn, the will forces desire; thus, they are clashing commands. All these things occur in mortals as long as the sensitive soul draws its powers into a manifold disorder of division. Thus, impossible things are foolishly desired, as are things of the past, or we wish that present things had not happened. <margin>47.</margin> 

But the desire of which I speak is hidden within the mind; unless it were of the mind’s very essence, "he who looked at a woman to lust after her" <note>A reference to Matthew 5:28</note> would not sin before the consent of his will. Therefore, we now desire through the competing faculties of the mind within the sensitive soul, whose effects are rejected by the will and judgment. Even in its manner of operating, desire (or love) now acts one way, while the will acts another. Likewise, in the movement of time or duration, desire often precedes or follows the "willing," and one in turn overcomes the other so that it might restrain something distinct from itself. All of this occurs in transitory things because it arises from the **thymos** <note>original: "thymosi"; a Greek term for the "spirited" or emotional part of the soul associated with vital heat and impulse</note> of the sensitive soul. <margin>48.</margin> 

In the heavenly realms, however, that love rises again as the very substance of the mind; for there, nothing is desired that is not also willed. This, as much in its action as in its substance, is gathered into a single unity, although they may have different underlying roots. 

<column-break/>

This clearly surpasses the way of understanding available to mortals. Because in man, the **Kingdom of God** is indeed present now, but in an incomprehensible way; after death, however, that same Kingdom gathers all things into its own unity. Therefore, the primary **image of God** is in the mind, whose very essence is the very image of God. <margin>49.</margin> This image can neither be conceived by the heart nor expressed in words in this life, because it reflects the likeness of God; beyond this, there is no other image in us that can be presented to our understanding. Consequently, the mind itself is also totally unknown to itself. 

Next, in the **husk of the mind** <note>original: "siliqua mentis"; the outer layer or "shell" of the mind, often associated with the sensitive and vital soul</note>—that is, the sensitive and vital form—the same image shines back through its powers, but only as a receiver. This is because it has been overshadowed by animal generation, being transitory and defiled by impurity. Finally, the body has borrowed not so much the "image" of God (the essential light), but only the outward figure or shape. 

But the wretched mind, <margin>50.</margin> fallen into the "outer darkness" away from the uncreated light from which it separated itself, has lost the native light of the image because of "appropriation"—treating the light as if it were its own by right or merit. Because of this, it thereafter understands, wills, or loves nothing except itself, and for its own sake. Therefore, it will not represent the image of God (which is suffocated within it) when rising again, except in the bodily manner of Adam’s lineage—that is, only in its outward shape. 

Wherefore also it thereafter understands, wills, and loves everything with a blind perception, always addicted to itself. For it knows its own immortality just as it feels its damnation, and it complains of that damnation as an injustice done to it. This is because its self-love is only used to make excuses for its sins—as if they were committed in days of ignorance and innocence, caused by great fragility, the snares of enemies, and a lack of sufficient grace. It claims that eternal punishment is not deserved by merit for a momentary transgression. It rages, therefore, and hates God, especially because it knows the judgment of loss is unchangeable and the freedom to escape is shut off forever. Therefore, with hope cut off, into a final and persistent despair, from the very moment of its entrance, it passes to the place where there is no mercy...

<summary>Van Helmont discusses how the "Image of God" is unified in the mind but becomes fractured and conflicted within the "sensitive soul" during earthly life. He concludes by describing the tragic state of the fallen mind, which, by focusing entirely on itself, loses its divine light and falls into eternal despair.</summary>

...piety, compassion, consolation, or restoration. May the Almighty deign, in His goodness, to crush the snares stretched out in our path by infernal hatred, Amen. Let these things suffice regarding the soul, for the physical knowledge of oneself. Now, therefore, I enter into the study of nature, so that I may reveal the seat of the soul in the body.

I have written about the action of governance, and likewise about the **Duumvirate**, as befits a Physician, so that I might uncover the seat of the imagination and settle the dispute regarding the lodging place of the mental faculties. However, I remained in suspense for a long time, not knowing how a person with understanding could degenerate into a madman. I knew, indeed, that in foul things and poisons there resided certain inherent powers—not intelligent ones, certainly, but which corresponded to them by a kind of kinship—so that they might seduce our understanding into their service, even against our will. 
<margin>1.</margin> 
For example, the bite of a rabid animal, the sting of a tarantula, the eating of nightshade <note>original: "solani"</note>, etc. I also thought that within the thresholds of fevers there dwelt similar faculties. In this, a certain case immediately disturbed me: namely, that in the same fever, atrocious rages had succeeded ridiculous ones. This persuaded me that in the harmony of Madness, there were no discordant effects. For at first glance, I did not sufficiently notice that poisons can be softened or sharpened through maturation.
<margin>2.</margin> 
Then, I looked at the most "Lunatic" <note>One whose madness is tied to the moon</note> of cases, where it would attack and recede according to the alignment <note>original: "syzygia"</note> of its star, without any companionship of poison. Mania, too, would return and then fall silent, without any defect in the life occurring in between.
<margin>3.</margin> 
I remained entirely stuck, still unaware that beyond bodily poisons, there are also virulent images and impressions—the most absolute and effective masters of the vital spirits—to which those spirits obey as willingly as they do promptly.

# THE MAD IDEA.

...ly, our intellectual powers would obey, as long as we are shut in the prison of the body. <margin>4.</margin> Meanwhile, through faith, I knew the mind to be immortal, and by that right, its intellect remains unstained by the contagions of the body: for it was not fitting that what was immortal and infinite should be diminished or harmed by things that are fleeting. Therefore, on one hand, I willingly and humbly confessed my ignorance; but on the other, I contemplated the wretched and never-before investigated condition of the madman, and the remedies that are so meager in the face of the greatest and most pitiable evils. This is because the healers, imposing on the world with their hollow doctorates, persuaded themselves that they had surveyed all things, and that there was no cure for such a great evil: claiming that the brain had put on an "unequal imbalance" <note>original: "intemperiem inæqualem"; a technical term in Galenic medicine referring to a disruption of the four humors</note> as if it were a garment. Yet, when asked, they could not yet express this primary imbalance of qualities with a worthy definition. Therefore, scorning the sterile whispers of the Schools [the traditional universities], after I had noted that <margin>5.</margin> hypochondriac madnesses <note>At this time, "hypochondriac" referred to the *hypochondrium* (the upper abdomen), reflecting the belief that certain mental illnesses originated in the digestive organs rather than the brain.</note> were beyond controversy located in the *praecordia* <note>The area of the body around the heart and midriff.</note>, I first began to doubt whether that dreadful poison was carried to the brain through specific arteries? But at least this suspicion <margin>6.</margin> immediately displeased me, because then anyone would suffer from inexcusable insanity, unless perhaps in wise men those channels remained perpetually blocked, and were thus "diseased" in such a way that they did not become mad. At least I noted the difference between the delirium caused by fever and true mania; namely, that the latter often persists throughout a long life without the loss of general health, even into late descendants, without any disadvantage to the seed or to life itself. I often abandoned the matter as truly inscrutable, and often took it up again out of compassion. And finally, I saw clearly that I was <margin>7.</margin> leaning on false principles, led astray by credulity and the authorities of the pagans <note>Van Helmont often refers to the ancient Greek and Roman physicians, like Galen and Aristotle, as "pagans" whose errors misled Christian science.</note>, and that I was being deluded by the "unknown qualities" of diseases. I first conceived of it this way, and gradually becoming more confirmed in it, I stripped myself of the doctrine I had swallowed in the Schools regarding the soul and regarding diseases.

<column-break/>

Then, having moved my mind from the scrutiny of intellectual functions, I committed myself to the Lord in quiet and poverty: so that He might do with me whatever was pleasing to Him. Yet I was not so indifferent that I did not always desire to be of use to my neighbor. And so <margin>8.</margin> I asked the Lord that I might become known to myself—not merely by acknowledging my "abyssal nothingness" in a moral sense, but so that as a Physicist <note>term: Physicist (Physicus). In the 17th century, this meant a "natural philosopher" or someone who studies the physical laws of nature.</note>, I might behold the very powers of the mind. For I thought nothing so peaceful and useful, after the Wisdom of divine things, as once to behold my soul as the image of God. Therefore I revolved <margin>9.</margin> the question of the "seat" or "bed" <note>original: "thoro"; Van Helmont uses the term 'bed' or 'throne' to describe the specific physical location where the soul resides.</note> of the immortal soul, and I inquired within myself whether it was so "whole in the whole" <note>A common scholastic phrase suggesting the soul is entirely and equally present in every part of the body.</note> that it wandered as an exile without dependence on a "bed" or central throne, not bound to any certain home? Was it so "whole in the finger" that if the finger were cut off, the whole soul would depart from the whole body, or would it recede inward by a sudden movement of fear? And so I found the soul to be homogeneous, simple, and indivisible; otherwise it would not be immortal. Then I learned that it only shines upon the lower parts "radially," in the manner of sunlight, while in the meantime it hides as if in its throne, and from there shines through the whole, being entirely unknown to the sensitive soul <note>The "sensitive soul" or *anima sensitiva* was believed to manage basic biological functions and sensations, distinct from the immortal, rational "Mind" (*mens*).</note>; whose life, however, was the mind itself. Just as God, the essence of all things, is intimately present to each of us, yet is naturally unknown and unfelt by us. Then the debate <margin>10.</margin> entered my mind whether there were several centers, and those separated according to the vital necessities of the radical organs. But finally, I knew the mind was more bound to one organ than to another, both for the duties of seeing and of understanding. And finally, I was always brought back to the individual "bed" of a single organ. While I investigated the head and the heart, and weighed the ambiguities of authors, I realized immediately that I was falling back into the opinions of the pagans, to whom the knowledge of the true God was denied; and likewise the knowledge of the divine image, which me...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the soul's physical location. # THE MAD IDEA.

...nevertheless, it was the object of my investigation. I did not know where to begin such a heavy judgment, being destitute of authorities and companions.
<margin>11.</margin> Until at length, by the Lord's permission—though I was destitute of human help and labor—after many years of inquiry and the hope of knowing the "court of the soul," an unusual event happened to me, the story of which I shall tell. I was keeping watch over the poisons of plants, believing that such toxins were not harmful to Adam before his sin: since the Almighty created neither death nor the medicine of destruction <note>original: "medicamentum exterminii"; a reference to the Book of Wisdom 1:13, "God made not death: neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living."</note>, and so He sent out such terrible things, not indeed to kill man: but because man was forced to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow, and had been made liable to diseases: that even through those labors, medicines for those diseases might be produced.
<margin>12.</margin> Therefore, I promised myself that this toxin, acting like a guardian or a husk, covered some remarkable and "virgin" power created for great uses, and that through art and labor, these toxins would become mild and vanish. For this reason, I began to manipulate Monkshood <note>original: "Napellus"; also known as Aconite or Wolfsbane, a highly toxic flowering plant.</note> in various ways. And once, when I had prepared its root crudely, I tasted it on the tip of my tongue. For although I had swallowed nothing, and had spat out much saliva, I felt immediately afterward that my skull was being constricted from the outside, as if by a tight band. Then, several family matters suddenly came upon me; I paid a certain account, wandered through the house, and performed each task as required. At last, it happened to me (as never before) that I felt I could understand, conceive, taste, or imagine nothing in my head, as was my usual habit. Instead, I felt (with amazement) openly, clearly, discursively, and constantly, that this entire task of thinking was being performed in the *praecordia* <note>The "praecordia" refers to the area of the midriff, including the diaphragm and the region around the heart and upper stomach. Van Helmont believed this was the true "throne" of the sensitive soul.</note> and was expanding around the mouth of the stomach. I felt this so sensibly and clearly—indeed, I noted it so attentively—that although I still felt my senses and movement to be healthy and distributed from the head to the rest of the body, the entire faculty of reasoning was notoriously and sensibly in the *praecordia*, to the exclusion of the head, as if the mind were then meditating on its counsels in that very place.

<column-break/>

Full of wonder and amazement at that unusual sensation, I noted my own thoughts and conducted an examination of them, and of myself, in a more precise manner. And I clearly found, and weighed, that I understood and meditated much more clearly during that entire time. Indeed, that sensation by which I perceived myself to understand or imagine in the *praecordia*, and not in the head, cannot be expressed in any words. There was also a certain joy in that intellectual clarity. For it was not a thing of short duration, nor had it happened to me while sleeping, or dreaming, or otherwise ill; rather, it happened while I was fasting and in good health. Indeed, although I had experienced several ecstasies <note>spiritual or visionary states</note> before, I noted that they had nothing in common with this *praecordial* reasoning and sense of understanding, which excluded all cooperation of the brain. For with sensible reflection (as if I had been forewarned), I caught my head completely at rest in respect to the *phantasia* <note>the faculty of imagination or forming mental images</note>; for I marveled that the imagination was being celebrated outside the brain, in the *praecordia*, with a sensible, festive operation. Meanwhile, suspended in that joy, I sometimes feared lest this unusual event should lead to madness, because it had begun from a poison; but the preparation of the poison, and only the slight tasting of it, suggested otherwise. Meanwhile, although the clarity or joyful illumination of my intellect made that unexpected mode of understanding suspect, nevertheless, a most free resignation of myself to the divine will restored me to my former inner peace. Finally, after about two hours, a slight dizziness, repeated twice, came upon me. From the first, I perceived that the faculty of understanding had returned to my head; and with the second, I felt I was understanding in the usual way. Afterward, although I tasted that same Monkshood several times, nothing of the sort ever happened to me again. Indeed, I learned many things perfectly from that event.
<margin>13.</margin> And first, that just as certain preludes of the soul shine forth through ecstasies, so through this aforementioned experience, it appears that...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of his altered state of consciousness following his ingestion of monkshood. He has just described how his seat of reason shifted from his head to his upper abdomen (the midriff), leading him to challenge the traditional medical belief that the brain is the primary organ of thought.</meta>

# THE MAD IDEA.

In my judgment, I was so devoid of all fear that I contemplated my affairs as if they were not my own. For I looked back at them from a distance, as if they were cast into the mind of a man from another age.

16. I also learned that life, understanding, sleep, etc., are the works of a certain light, which does not require channels; since vital light penetrates vital light. Accordingly, the soul also withdraws, spreads, and pulls itself back by its own motion, and in entirely different ways in sleep, wakefulness, contemplation, ecstasy, fainting <note>original: "syncope"</note>, mania, delirium, rage, its own disturbances, spontaneous confusions, and even the violent impressions of certain simple substances. Because the mind encompasses an entire **Monarchy** <term>Monarchy: Van Helmont’s concept of a unified governing power within the body, directed by the vital spirit.</term> in spiritual matters, divided into many genera and species; no less than bodies differ among themselves, so too do the lights of the soul. 

<margin>18.</margin> 16. Finally, I learned that understanding, which arises through discovery and judgment—with reflection on places, circumstances, past events, things previously mentioned or sent—and thus directed toward absent things *as* absent, is performed as a final work in the **Brain** <note>original: "Cerebro"</note>, through the inflow of a ray from the **midriff** <note>original: "præcordiis"; the area of the upper abdomen/diaphragm.</note>, insofar as that kind of understanding presupposes memory. But that understanding which concerns the future, or abstract things, without regard for circumstances, as if they were present: all of this is forged in the **midriff**. And thus, the insane <note>original: "amentes"</note> view everything as if present, and babble as if about present things.

<margin>19.</margin> 17. Accordingly, poisons <note>original: "venena"</note> that have the power to dislocate the imagination do not primarily affect the **Brain**: but only the **midriff**. This is sufficiently proven by the story of the *Lawyer* <note>original: "Causidici"</note> who had drunk the seed of henbane <note>original: "hyoscyami"</note>, which I have related elsewhere. For whatever the stomach conceives is plainly transformed and migrates into another essence before even the smallest part reaches the **Brain**; and whatever does arrive there is already blood, which has cast off all qualities of its former state at the threshold of the primary workshops. Or finally, it slips out of the stomach and is pushed out as waste. 

<margin>20.</margin> And thus no simple substances, however they are taken, are materially applied to the **Brain**.

<column-break/>

Therefore, whatever the **Schools** <term>Schools: The traditional medical and philosophical authorities (Scholasticism) whom Van Helmont frequently criticized for following Galenic theory.</term> sell regarding **Head**-pills, lights, etc., is false. Indeed, neither do the pills draw anything out of the head, nor does the head give anything that it does not already have, except for mucus, which it sends to its own basin and nowhere else. But if any things strike, alter, or help the head, it happens entirely by way of the **midriff**, which has an unshakable action of **Governance** <note>original: "Regiminis"</note> over the head, as has already been sufficiently proven before. 

<margin>21.</margin> They have indeed correctly taught that dizziness and comas are stirred up due to the agreement of the lower parts [of the body]: but not without some chaff in the grain. For the **Schools** introduced thick, smoky, and sharp vapors. Then, and mostly in such cases, they want the **Brain** to be affected by the primary plague. It is therefore foolish to have applied remedies to the head—to the target, I say, and not to the archer. Because, clearly, they did not know the true internal efficient cause, its connections, nor the usual way diseases occur, and they completely neglected the action of **Governance** and the conspiracies of light. 

18. I understood also from this at last that the immortal soul <note>original: "anima immortalis"</note>, while it governed its body worthily before the Fall <note>original: "ante peccatum"</note>, understood everything intimately, visually, and without labor, weariness, or fatigue. 

<margin>22.</margin> Because within itself, in its own center and unity, without the aid of organs, it understood everything. But now, held in a foreign lodging and as if completely hindered, it has handed over the diversity of duties to the servant-like sensitive soul. 

<margin>23.</margin> In this place, I presume to give an account of the thoughts of others, since I cannot sufficiently answer for or grieve over my own. Namely, I have proposed to philosophize about the more hidden source of thoughts, and about the most abstract things—the vices and deviations of fluctuating and uncertain thoughts. Indeed, one must penetrate more deeply, where we must aim at the very powers of corrupted thoughts, and reach the fountain-like and occasional causes of such vices. The matter is truly arduous, obscure, and trackless, in which the theories <note>original: "theoremata"</note> of the **Schools** fail before even reaching the threshold.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the "midriff" (praecordia) is the true seat of immediate understanding and the source of mental illness, claiming that the brain only handles memory-based processing. He critiques traditional medicine for treating the head for ailments he believes originate in the stomach's governance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s investigation into the seat of the soul and the origins of mental illness. Following his experiment with monkshood, he is now developing a theory that madness is not a disease of the brain itself, but a disruption in the relationship between the immortal mind and the "sensitive soul" located in the upper abdomen.</meta>

### THE MAD IDEA.

...theorems and aids for the body—and even for diseases whose causes and effects fall under the senses or are proven through the dissection of corpses. In these matters, I say, the passive imagination reveals itself; 
<margin>24.</margin>
but the acting agent remains hidden. In other investigations, the flawed state is known from a concept of the whole; but in mental matters, the cause and manner of a violated understanding would be much more easily conceived than those of a healthy one. This is because the healthy faculty ascends more toward the **likeness of GOD**; whereas the defective faculty inclines more toward the meditations of a corrupted nature. Therefore, wholeness in mental matters is not demonstrated *a priori* <note>from cause to effect</note>; but deficiency becomes known, in a way, from the rupture of the connection of causes.

<margin>25.</margin>
Insanity, too, is always a subject of the most difficult teaching, because it encompasses within itself negation along with privation. For this reason, I decided that one must proceed by another path in the proposed case. I wondered if, by investigating the "mode of becoming" in any single type of insanity, I might find an exit for the others. I therefore proposed **Madness** <note>original: "Amentiam"</note> which arises from intense and persistent contemplation, fear, and passion. From there, I concluded that we must recognize the quality of the "poisonous" thing and the dispositions of the organs that concur when some simple substance—either taken in or generated within—has stirred up dementia. Once the knowledge of one kind of Madness is grasped, it will be easier to then measure their various differences, descending into the breadth of their modes, strengths, proximity, application, and the variety of their species. For this reason, I first decided to investigate the seat of the **sensitive soul**, whose wanderings, of course, 
<margin>26.</margin>
produce Mad states. Indeed, I considered that in whatever seat the "animal form" <note>the vital principle shared with animals</note> resided, the immortal mind—bound to it—would cohabit there as well, for the mind would reject a duality, discrepancy, or diversity of dwellings. Nor was it fitting that this mind be bound to the body without a medium, whereas the human seed (no less than that of a beast), by flowing down spontaneously, would be limited only to the "living soul" <note>the sensitive soul</note> exclusively. 

<column-break/>

And so it was fitting that the mind be bound to a social form and a formal light, with which it would best agree—as I discussed in the chapter on forms and the book on long life regarding the entry of death.

<margin>27.</margin>
Therefore, I first decided that the immortal soul had not chosen its home in the heart—a vessel so restless, surely, and distended by so many agitations and the various duties of the body. I also judged the head to be an unsuitable guesthouse for the immortal mind, because it is occupied with governing motion and sense. Most importantly, I saw that when the "conspiracy" from the lower parts is blocked, in a single instant the mental faculties perish as if cut off, and they do not perform the least meditation. Therefore, the head does not possess the proper operation of the sovereign mind. On the contrary, I have seen a poorly disposed **Duumvirate** <term>Duumvirate: A "rule of two," referring here to the governing relationship between the stomach and the spleen.</term> frequently disturb a head that was otherwise well-disposed, leading into Madnesses. Therefore, marvelling at the quietness of the **Spleen**, and likewise its abstraction from bodily governance, I intently considered this dilemma: If the mind, 
<margin>28.</margin>
the **Image of GOD**, is centrally in the head, it will be either in the borders or in the substance of the brain itself. It cannot be in the substance, since that lacks sensation and blood, and is destitute of the commerce through which the mind might be present to the whole body to which it is bound. That the head rules through sense and motion is disputed by no one. But that is a lesser, animal-like, and "beastly" governance. We are compelled to believe, however—taught by the disorders <note>original: "ataxias"</note> of diseases—that the head is ruled from elsewhere during mental suspensions and wanderings. I judged it indecent for the immortal soul to lodge in the cavity of the brain, or for the immortal soul to be wedded to a spirit that is wandering and fleeting from one moment to the next, rising daily from the blood. For this reason, it desired a more stable and quieter lodging than one that would be unstable by the hour. It rested rather in the center or middle of the body, in the parenchyma <note>the functional tissue</note> of an organ, from where it might speak equally with all members by reason of the unity and continuity of the implanted **Archeus** <term>Archeus: The internal vital workman or "spirit" that directs the functions of an organ.</term>. But since the organs of the body, with respect to the mind, are but dross and husks, the mind chose for itself the nucleus of the body: namely, the slight formal light of the small spark, or the sensitive soul, to which, it is clear, the mind is wedded...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the immortal mind does not reside in the brain or heart, but is "wedded" to the sensitive soul located in the spleen or upper abdomen, which acts as a stable center for the body's vital spirit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the "sensitive soul" (the mortal part of our spirit shared with animals) and its relationship with the immortal Mind. He is explaining that when these two become disconnected or when the sensitive soul is overwhelmed by bodily "dregs," madness and delirium occur.</meta>

### ON THE MAD IDEA.

...she wedded by the command of the Lord. And what God has joined, let no man separate without guilt. Meanwhile, the wretched state of mortals is to be pitied, because the Mind is indeed tied to the **sensitive soul** <note>The "anima sensitiva" in Helmontian theory is the mortal vital spirit that governs the body’s functions and feelings, acting as a bridge to the immortal Mind.</note>. To an entity that is certainly impure, devoted to lusts, allurements, and pleasures, the immortal Mind so easily assents, 
<margin>29.</margin>
as if by its own neglect it were now sleeping eternally. But it is not so. For the glory of divine mercy is so much greater, which by its grace alone freely resuscitates and sustains from the lethargy of death those whom it wishes to be saved. Otherwise, indeed, the sensitive soul—subject to diseases and **Madness** <note>original: "Amentiis"</note>—is always prone to any pleasures. 
<margin>30.</margin>
For the first degree of Madness shines forth in sleep; yet it is natural, while under the title of honest recreation and vacation, it plunges itself with the pleasure of rest into its own lodging. Furthermore, the eccentricities of natural sleep—its vices, defects, and manifest dementias—are all **sopors** <note>term: "sopores" refers to deep, unnatural slumbers or lethargic states like comas</note>. 
<margin>31.</margin>
Which, to be sure, no longer proceed from the sensitive soul’s own freedom and pleasure, but arise from excrementitious dregs, as if from fevers. For just as natural thirst is the sense of a lack of moisture, but a febrile thirst comes from the deceptive tricks of waste products, so these sopors are not caused by the natural faculty by which the soul stirs up sleep for itself; rather, the soul is seduced or overcome by the foreign deceptions of impurities. Therefore, these heavy slumbers, as well as **Apoplexy**, **Aphonia** <note>loss of speech</note>, etc., are not so much vices of an erring soul as they are its weaknesses, contracted through its "marriage" with corrupted organs. For the gatherings of impurities occasionally invade the "monarchic state" of the body as soon as the opportunity arises. It is not indeed necessary that such material impurities spread themselves into the "animate light" through a physical connection. For it is enough that they have a narcotic, poisonous power, fatal to the sensitive soul: because they alienate the **imagination** <note>original: "imaginativam"</note> just like the saliva of a rabid dog causes the fear of water. Thus also the Madness of neglect is introduced through those sleep-inducing things. That power is potentially and seminally present 

<column-break/>

in those dregs from the beginning, though once it has matured, it is very different from its origin. It is no different than an acorn compared to an oak. Therefore, these dregs impress an alien **fantasy** upon the unwilling sensitive soul, which is clearly seen in the effects of **opium**, **henbane** <note>original: "hyosciamo"</note>, and similar substances. 
<margin>32.</margin>
And every collection of impurities, besieging the sensitive soul in its original internal organ, puts to sleep the Mind's act of understanding, for the Mind is not able to shine freely into a sensitive soul that is so besieged. Wherefore the sensitive soul, deprived of its ruler <note>the Mind</note>, stirs up tumultuous storms and gradually raises its tempest into the "chest of the will," from which the irascible emotions are carried forth in a headlong and inverted order. Finally, the head brings forth its images of known things in a backward or jumbled connection. Whence it happens that mostly, once the deliriums are spent, no memory of the actions remains; because the sensitive soul, struck headlong by this "siege," moved everything in a backward manner. Whereas in other manias that are free from such dregs, the sufferers are mostly mindful of their actions. 
<margin>33.</margin>
For I have found many times that delirious people felt beforehand the intellectual images being sent down to the lower parts, then turbulent ones rising upward, and that the memory was the first thing to be weakened. Thus, I also concluded from this that the **intellectual power is located far from the head**. No differently than the parts remote from the heart feel the lack of "vital sprinkling" <note>blood/vital spirit</note> first of all. 
<margin>34.</margin>
In deliriums, therefore, I observed that the memory of things once conceived is the first to falter. Then, in its place, arises a troublesome and continuous recollection of a single thing, which behaves like a repeated dream, with a most annoying inversion and the "labor of sleep." Waking follows this labor soon after; namely, when the preceding dream-images have weakened the memory of the Brain, there arises from the **midriff** <note>term: "præcordiis," the upper abdomen/diaphragm area where Van Helmont located the sensitive soul</note> a certain waking dream with manifest delirium. Nor is it as it is in Apoplexy, heavy sleep, or fainting. 
<margin>35.</margin>
But it is a confused, unending propagation of **Ideas** formed in the midriff, vibrated upwards. And since in health no concept occurs without ideas, necessarily, even in delirium, there are their own mad Ideas.
