<meta>This page continues Jan Baptista van Helmont’s medical-philosophical treatise on the origins of madness. He is distinguishing between healthy thoughts and "Mad Ideas," arguing that insanity is not a failure of the immortal Mind itself, but a corruption of the "sensitive soul" and the vital organs.</meta>

### THE MAD IDEA.

But altogether under this distinction: that ideas in health are formed by the freedom of the soul, whereas insane ideas are like stamped marks, brought into the sensitive soul against our will, and therefore they violently lead it out of its proper orbit. It is far from the case that insane ideas are formed by the Mind, which is incapable of playing the fool. <margin>36.</margin> For it is clear that ideas follow the disturbances of the things from which they arise. This is most clear in the cases of the Rabid <note>Refers to a person or animal with rabies.</note> and the Tarantula: whose venom produces a specific, determined, and uniform madness, and ideas perpetually similar to itself. Thus also, a strong disturbance of our imagination forges an image and impresses it into some dregs, or at least into the nourishment itself, or even into a solid and constitutive part of us. From which, evidently, there is a continued propagation of new ideas, and their very diversity and breadth, in maniacs. Indeed, madness arises from fear, agony, envy, ambition, love, intense study, worry, shame, greed, and other similar disturbances. And those are all the more wretched which are stirred up without the disgrace of bodily wastes <note>Van Helmont argues that madness caused by "dregs" (bodily fluids) is easier to cure than madness rooted in the "spirit" itself.</note>, because they either persist continuously or return at fixed intervals of relapse. Otherwise, once the filth is consumed, the resulting stains cease of their own accord. But insanities, whether they rage with a continuous heat or repeat at intervals, have at least so defiled the spirit of the **Duumvirate** <note>term: "Duumvirate" (Duumviratus) refers to Helmont's theory that the stomach and spleen act as a secondary "government" of the body, controlling the vital spirits and emotions.</note> that they have radically impressed the storm of furious images received, <margin>37.</margin> in the same way as a birthmark is branded onto a fetus by the mother’s distress during pregnancy, lasting for a lifetime. Just as a cherry-shaped birthmark on a child turns green, yellow, and red every year along with the fruit of the trees, so also maniacal ideas, born from disturbances, have their own triggers for repetitions, periodic attacks, and intervals of worsening within the spirit of the **precordia** <note>The area around the heart and diaphragm, often considered the seat of the vital spirit.</note>, or even indefinite fuel for their continuation. This is clearly shown to us by **Lunaticism** <note>Madness associated with the phases of the moon.</note>, observing the alignment of that celestial body. Nor is it any wonder that these forms of madness behave like

<column-break/>

a stain in the Duumvirate; for the visual spirit is in the eye, and nowhere else in the whole body. Therefore, since the Duumvirate, by the radical appointment of the Lord, is continually occupied with phantasms, the occurrences brought upon it must so corrupt the management of the imagination that it accepts the replanting of the relapses of the conceived Idea. <margin>38.</margin> It should be noted meanwhile that a lunatic could not be healed unless the unclean spirit were cast out at the same time—whether this spirit was a companion of the nightly star [the moon] or the principal agent of the effect. I, at least, find in every mania a remarkable arrogance, by assuming some unmortified social passion, which both persists through life and shines forth when passed down to fierce descendants. Because the Mad Idea has penetrated the innate spirit, from which it finally violates the seed, having become natural to it. For I have curiously questioned many madmen, and healed not a few—both those who became insane through great disturbances, passions, and other diseases, and those who became mad by taking things upon themselves—and they told me that they fell gradually into **Mania**, usually with a prior sensation rising to them from the **hypochondrium** <note>The upper abdomen; in Helmont’s day, this was seen as the source of "melancholy" or "vapors."</note>, like a dark phantasm and a cloudy temptation of madness, by which they were at first pressed as if against their will, <margin>39.</margin> until the Idea finally acquired full dominion over them. When they returned to themselves, they were mindful of all their actions. For they confidently complained about everything: namely, that they were first stripped of all sequence of discourse, and that they remained in a precise immersion in a single concept; outside of which they thought of nothing else, with sorrow, distress, and persistence. For they thought just as if they were always looking at that concept in a mirror. Indeed, they did not even know they were then thinking that thing, or looking at it with their concept; although they thought so immovably that finally, under the entry and dominion of mania, if it happened that they were standing, they would have stood for several days without weariness, nor would they know they were standing. For it happened thus, because that Idea of foolishness, which...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s discussion on the nature of "Mad Ideas." He has previously argued that insanity is not a defect of the immortal Mind, but an "Idea" or spiritual image that becomes forcefully imprinted upon the "sensitive soul" or the vital spirits of the body, leading to a loss of reason.</meta>

### THE MAD IDEA.

...had driven away reasoning (through which they would have otherwise been relieved from immoderate and disordered weighing of thoughts) to the spirit, which is placed in charge of understanding, once it was impressed with a sort of dominion. Indeed, what these people did to themselves through long delay and continuous contemplation, others acquired through a sudden and violent disturbance in a brief moment. Meanwhile, some complained while weeping that they were oppressed by an unwilling and intrusive swarm of thoughts, like smoke rising from the depths. Even if they tried to suppress this through reasoning, the same troublesome and intrusive repetition of these same concepts would return. Others, however, who were no longer masters of themselves, or were otherwise beyond comfort, were repeatedly turned away from strong and fixed contemplation; whenever they slept or were at leisure, they returned with a sense of approval to forbidden speculations, which were nonetheless entirely distressing. Rejoicing in solitude, they withdrew from the conversation of others.

<margin>40.</margin> Because conceptual Ideas, still lacking a body, hold to the side of the intellectual light, they therefore penetrate our primary constituents—something not permitted to food or other physical bodies. They penetrate and clothe themselves in the airy body of the spirits, and by this means, they infect the vital forms of our parts.

<margin>41.</margin> Yet with this difference: that Ideas forged from the eccentricity of concepts enter and are admitted more powerfully, but are imprinted more slowly. In other cases, "dementing poisons" <note>Van Helmont often used the term "dementing poisons" to refer to substances or internal ferments that disrupt the mind.</note> gradually sow their ferment into their proper objects through disease; but eventually, they are stubbornly imprinted, as if sealed into nature itself.

<margin>42.</margin> It is a singular thing about maniacs that even if one lies naked on the ground, or spends the night on marble in the severest blast of the North Wind <note>original: "Boreae"</note>, he does not freeze, nor do his limbs die. To explain this, it is not enough to say: "The maniac does not feel the cold, nor does he know he is cold." For the deprivation or denial of knowledge or sensation provides nothing real; much less does it provide heat or strip the cold of its power so that it would cease to freeze the flesh. Indeed, even if a child in the cradle does not fear the plague, nor knows it is present, the Plague has not therefore lost its right over him. Therefore, there is some force that overcomes the cold and is not subject to the weather beneath the moon. And from this, it is most clearly seen that the Mind within us is immortal and incapable of suffering harm <note>The term "impassible" implies that the soul cannot be damaged or changed by physical forces.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>43.</margin> Truly, the Mind itself, noticing that the sensitive soul does not govern the man according to the requirements of our species, out of compassion for his innocent blindness, pours out an insensible ray by its own power (which is superior to the elements). This ray exempts the body of the Madman <note>original: "Amentis"</note> from the mortal nuisance of the cold.

<margin>44.</margin> Furthermore, since all Madness <note>original: "Amentia"</note> arises from an "efflorescing" conceptual Idea—a foreign one inserted into an alien field—this whole speculation is directed toward a useful end, and not merely toward curiosity or display.

<margin>45.</margin> I considered that a "mad Idea," once it has been imprinted into the radical principles of life (and thus propagated into families), cannot be removed along with the subject it has clothed. Therefore, a remedy had to be found that could kill, destroy, remove, or blot out that aforementioned image of Madness, or the stain already characterized.

<margin>46.</margin> This is not unlike a birthmark <note>original: "macula foetui impressa"</note> imprinted on a fetus: if the hand of a corpse (one long extinguished by wasting and stripped of all vital properties) is applied until the cold penetrates the marked part—which happens in the time it takes to say a *Miserere* <note>The "Miserere" is Psalm 51; its recitation was a common early modern measurement of time, lasting about a minute or two.</note>—the mark then vanishes of its own accord. In the same way, the Idea of mania must perish, while the immediate subject in which it dwells remains safe. This might happen by introducing the death of the Idea, or by generating an equivalent Idea, or one that drives out the foolish Idea. This explains why, until now, the remedy for Madness has been despaired of. No one until now has looked into the nature or properties of Madness beyond the imbalance of the "primary qualities" <note>The ancient Greek theory that health depended on a balance of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry.</note>. Indeed, Paracelsus himself, otherwise harmful regarding heats and colds, handed over all mania to heat and Bloodletting <note>original: "Phlebotomiae"</note>, making himself ridiculous in this...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that madness is an "Idea" imprinted on the body's vital spirit, which can even protect a madman from freezing. He suggests that curing madness requires "killing" this spiritual image, much like using a corpse's hand to remove a birthmark.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of how a "Mad Idea"—a corrupted mental image—takes hold of the human spirit. Having established that these ideas act like spiritual parasites, he now discusses the difficulty of removing them and begins recounting a dramatic case study involving a cure for rabies (hydrophobia) through near-drowning, which serves as a model for treating other forms of insanity.</meta>

### THE MAD IDEA

...offered light. The goal of healing seemed difficult (I confess), because a corrupted **Idea** of the phantasy, a seal-like mark or stain, had not only been introduced into the innermost point of the understanding, but impressed upon it. Furthermore, the restoration of the innate spirit was considered completely impossible. The longed-for help of the **Secret Remedies** <note>original: "Arcanorum"; these were high-level alchemical medicines believed to have specific spiritual powers.</note> was indeed implored, but their progress was slow because the stubborn enemy within resisted. But medicines were applied in which a "symbol" <note>An ancient medical concept where a remedy contains a spiritual likeness or "code" that matches the disease.</note> dwells: that is, a fermenting imagination of a sounder judgment. For just as there are poisons of the Mind that cause alienation for a time or for an entire life—which essentially introduce their own phantasy into us, such as those from a rabid dog or a Tarantula spider—so too do the fruits of the "knowledge of good and evil" exist within simple substances. These may appear poisonous at first glance, yet beneath them are guarded the richer treasures of mental restoration and reintegration. But since it is not safe to throw those remedies out to the common crowd of healers, due to the manifold abuse of the wits of this century; and finally, since "it is not every man’s lot to go to Corinth" <note>A Latin proverb (*Non cuivis homini contingit adire Corinthum*) meaning that not everyone can achieve difficult or expensive goals.</note>; I have therefore decided to proceed here by another way: the mortification <note>In a medical sense, "mortification" here means killing or neutralizing the diseased mental image.</note> of foolish images. Certain histories confirmed this consideration for me, which I will recount here as examples to be imitated. There is a castle situated by the sea, four leagues from Ghent, which they call the Sluice. I saw a ship sailing across, and in it an old man, naked, bound with ropes, with a weight on his feet. A belt was cinched under his armpits, by which he was tied to the yardarm <note>original: "antennam"; the crossbar on a ship's mast.</note>. I asked what this spectacle meant. One of the sailors said that the old man was now "hydrophobic" <note>Fearful of water; a classic symptom of rabies.</note> and had been bitten by a rabid dog long ago. I asked where they were carrying him at sea? Did they intend his death? "On the contrary," said the sailor, "he will soon return healthy." He claimed it was the "blessing of the sea" that it could instantly cure such madness. I offered a coin so that they would take me along as a companion and witness. We sailed for about an Italian mile,

<column-break/>

where the sailors opened a hole in the bottom of the boat, through which the entire ship was submerged almost to the rim. They were using that brine to refine Spanish salt. When that hole had been meticulously closed again, two men pulled down the end of the yardarm, raised the tip, and hoisted the old man high up, then cast him headlong into the sea. He remained under the water for the duration of a *Miserere* <note>Psalm 51; in the era before stopwatches, people used the time it took to recite specific prayers to measure duration.</note>. Afterward, they submerged him twice more for the duration of an "Angelic Salutation" <note>The "Ave Maria" or Hail Mary prayer.</note>. Then they placed him upon a rounded vessel, lying on his back, covered with a cloak. I suspected he had died, but the sailor laughed at my fear. For once the bonds were loosened, he began to vomit up all the brine he had breathed in, and soon he revived. He was a cooper from Ghent who, having been freed from the rabies, lived on in good health. From this—as our soul is a "handmaid" in finding reasons previously unknown—I immediately understood that the **Idea** of rabies, the mark of the impressed poison, had been "mortified" like a blemish in a fetus. For I knew that warts, likewise ulcers and other "exotic" growths that come later and are foreign to the original constitution, are separable from the body while the vital root of the individual remains. 

<margin>48.</margin> The sailor also related that the Dutch use raw salted herring, renewed every three days and applied to a rabid bite, to take away all fear of rabies. But where this was neglected, all were cured by this method of submersion. For since they dread water, it is no wonder they are cured through water. This remained afterward deeply stored in my mind: persuading me that this would not be useless in other forms of **Insanity** <note>original: "Amentiis".</note>. 

<margin>49.</margin> Thus it happened in Antwerp that a carpenter, persuading himself that he had seen horrific ghosts at night, became entirely insane from the terror. He was sent to the tomb of Saint Dymphna, the Virgin <note>St. Dymphna is the patron saint of the mentally ill; her shrine in Geel, Belgium, remains a famous site for psychiatric care.</note>, where those possessed by an evil demon are usually freed. This practice has been twisted into an abuse, so that all insane people are sent there indiscriminately, as if the fate of the possessed and the insane were the same. The carpenter, therefore, was kept there for a whole year, remaining insane despite the usual remedies being implored...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s discussion on the "Mad Idea"—a spiritual or mental disturbance—and shifts into practical, though startling, examples of how such ideas can be "suffocated" or cured through extreme physical shocks, specifically near-drowning. He then transitions into a discussion on rabies (hydrophobia) and the miraculous traditions of St. Hubert.</meta>

### THE MAD IDEA

...the middle; and when the money for the last six months was not sent from Antwerp, they sent the madman back, bound in a carriage. Having loosened his bonds, he leaped from the wagon into a deep, nearby pond. He was eventually pulled out as if he were a corpse and placed back in the carriage. Yet, from that moment on, he was free from his mania for <margin>18</margin> eighteen years. Encouraged by this example, I realized that not only is sudden rage curable, but even long-standing mania can be healed. I attempted this several times thereafter, and the outcome never failed me, except when, out of fear, I pulled the <term>Demented</term><note>In this context, "demented" refers specifically to those whose "Life Spirit" has been captured by a "Mad Idea."</note> out of the water too prematurely. At the very least, I learned from the example of the smith that it matters little whether the submersion happens in fresh or salt water, as the goal is the "suffocation" of the <term>Mad Idea</term>.

<margin>50.</margin> A certain woman known to me, highly commendable for her honesty, fell headlong from a bridge into a stream with a two-wheeled cart late one November evening. While the bystanders were busy tending to the horse, they neglected the old woman. She remained under the water until they had finished unloading several items of merchandise from the cart. Finally remembering the old woman, they carried her like a drowned corpse to a neighboring village. There, the host's wife placed the woman on a table in a prone position <note>Latin: *prono situ*; lying face down. Van Helmont is describing an early form of resuscitation technique intended to drain water from the lungs.</note> with her head hanging down. It so happened that in this way, she discharged the water she had swallowed into her lungs. This seemed like a mere fable to me, until a youth who had drowned while swimming was brought to a noble matron (my traveling companion) in Mons, Hainaut. She told the mother, who was wailing over the death of her son, to be of good cheer. She then stretched the youth out in a prone position across her knees. While he hung there limp and completely naked, he finally began to breathe again after vomiting up the water, and he revived before our very eyes. I remember another instance in the evening of the year 1606: returning from the Castle of Perla, two leagues from Antwerp, I came upon a crowd on the bank of the Rouen canal seeking a drowned youth, the only son of a wealthy widow. She was summoned and found the corpse lying on the ground in the straw; she took him into her lap and kissed him, weeping

<column-break/>

bitterly. I ordered her to turn the body over with the head and shoulders sloping downward, and the back facing upward. After a quarter of an hour, the youth began to breathe. Thus I learned that the drowned do not die easily, since both of the aforementioned youths had remained hidden under the water for perhaps half an hour. One should not cease praying as soon as someone who is believed to be dead stops breathing. Galen, for the treatment of rabies before the onset of the fear of water, prescribes calcined <note>Reduced to ash or powder by heat.</note> crayfish or crabs to be drunk for forty days.

<margin>51.</margin> However, if this ash does not sink immediately at the start, it is of no use, and thus its use has remained obsolete. Meanwhile, it is ridiculous that they add myrrh, etc., while burning the crabs. Or when they melt silver for the <term>Perfumer</term> <note>original: *Seplasia*; referring to the Seplasia market in ancient Capua, famous for ointments and medicines.</note> to prepare a cup, they add Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note>. The devouring flame consumes these antidotes before the animal is even toasted. Paracelsus, on the other hand, claims that hydrophobia is cured by sharp purgatives. But truly, the outcome did not match his promises. Therefore, the Catholics, despairing and not trusting in these kinds of remedies from the Academies, flee to St. Hubert in our lands, where they are healed through certain rituals.

<margin>52.</margin> This, however, is notable: if the rituals are not precisely observed, the rabies—which otherwise would have remained latent for a long time—attacks immediately, and the <term>Hydrophobes</term> <note>Those suffering from rabies/hydrophobia.</note> are brought low without hope. The Stole of St. Hubert is kept in a chest secured with six different keys, guarded by six different key-bearers. Every year, they cut off a part of that stole, yet the stole remains entirely whole, as it has for eight hundred years or more. There is no room for fraud, as it is not known today whether the stole is made of byssus <note>A rare, fine fabric often called "sea silk."</note>, wool, flax, or cotton; therefore, a new one could not be substituted every year. They cut a piece from the stole so that they may graft a thread from it into the skin of the forehead of each person bitten by a rabid animal. From this comes another miracle: he who has once recovered through the rituals by receiving a thread from the stole can delay the onset of the disease for another who has been bitten, lulling the approaching rabies for forty-day periods, and this for several years, until they are able to visit Saint Hubert at their own convenience.

Duumvirate nomenclature strikes the reader with the terror of novelty; therefore, I shall first give the reason for the name, and then explain its governance. <note>The "Duumvirate" is Van Helmont’s term for the joint rule of the stomach and spleen over the body.</note>

Before all else, the seat of the soul must be sought. For although the soul is everywhere its life is <margin>1.</margin>, yet just as the Sun is properly only in its own place in the heavens, even though its light is wherever it looks, exactly the same judgment applies to the central location of the soul. However, there is a dispute regarding the center of the soul, or its wrestling ground within the body. And the leaders, as if suspended in mid-air, fight over this matter, having no base on which to set their feet. For Plato fights for the heart, to which

<column-break/>

Bellinus and Dominic. They seek preservation and demand healing from the madness after the fact. But for <term>Amentia</term> <note>Dementia or insanity</note>, they do not, as far as I know, invoke any heavenly patron.

the Sacred Scriptures seem to give support, while they teach that murders, adulteries, etc., flow from the heart. Physicians, however, look to the head, as the residence of discourse and intellect. Especially because the heart, agitated by such tireless pulse-motion, could not help but produce a turbulent and restless soul. Those who baptize follow the opinion of the physicians. <margin>2.</margin> state that the immortal mind is so everywhere and equally in the body that they do not want it to dwell in any certain seat, no more than it can be constrained or bound by the body. This is a daily occurrence among those who have been dying for some time. 

<margin>3.</margin> A certain bride, wishing to celebrate her wedding in Opdorp, near the Scheldt <note>original: "Scaldim"</note>, because the local lord <note>original: "Toparcha"</note> was there, was greeted by her clients with the noise of muskets. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the true location of the soul within the human body. Van Helmont, having previously discussed the effects of rabies and the "spirit" of diseases, now moves to demonstrate his "Paradox": that the soul is not centered in the heart or brain, as commonly believed, but in the upper opening of the stomach, which he terms the "duumvirate" alongside the spleen.</meta>

->THE SEAT OF THE SOUL.<-

<margin>4.</margin> A certain woman was thought to have died: yet six hours later, a faint pulse was noted in both her arms by several people. A robust student struck another who was sitting at a table with his fist near the mouth of the stomach; the victim immediately collapsed with a foaming mouth and, before the Litany of Loreto could be read, his whole body was cold. A coachman, stabbed with a dagger near the mouth of the stomach, died immediately with a foaming mouth, deprived of all pulse and heat.

<margin>5.</margin> I shall therefore propose, under the humble censorship of the Church, a new Paradox: Although life is the indicator of the soul, and the soul is present wherever there is life; nevertheless, just as the soul (and the life of the whole body) does not fly away when a finger or a foot is cut off, nor can the soul or life be divided into parts—so that the soul in its integral whole is in no way divisible, even if death seems near when a more noble member is injured. Meanwhile, it is certain that life perishes immediately in a severed limb, even though a part of the soul is not thereby taken away from the whole. Therefore, it is clear that the soul does not reside centrally in every part where the operation and presence of life exists. It is necessary for the seat of the soul to be somewhere, like its own proper and central dwelling. From there, it sends out luminous and vital rays through the <term>Archeus</term><note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont’s term for the internal vital worker or governing semi-spiritual force that directs the body's functions.</note>, the organ of vital light. For the soul itself is a kind of light, a luminous substance in the mind; in other souls, however, it is indeed a light, but not a substance. As I have discussed elsewhere regarding the "origin of forms."

<margin>6.</margin> The Creator (to whom be all honor) maintained a certain progression of similarity, which instructs us regarding the throne of the soul, so that we may consider more abstract things by looking at denser ones. Indeed, one sees in a tree (an argument specifically drawn from the tree because of the prerogative of the Tree of Life) its own vital beginning. For in the root, as if in a kitchen, the foreign juice of the earth is cooked, altered, and distanced from the original simplicity of water, and it undergoes the arrangement of the vital ferment located there. Once "cooked," it is distributed from there so that it may be more and more refined and become similar to the tree, according to the necessity of each further "kitchen,"

<column-break/>

which has established laws for the inhabiting spirit. Thus, in the middle of the human trunk, there is the stomach, which is not merely a sack or a pouch, or a pot for food: but in the stomach, especially at its Orifice <note>The "mouth" or upper opening of the stomach where it meets the esophagus.</note>, as if at a central point and root, the principle of life, the digestion of food, and its preparation for life are most evidently established.

<margin>7.</margin> For whatever importance Physicians have ever placed on the Heart, they have, whether they like it or not, shared it with the stomach. Thus *Cardiogmus* <note>original: "Cardiogmus"; an archaic term for gnawing pain or oppression in the chest or stomach.</note> (the biting of the heart) and *Cardialgia* (heart-pain) are names that have misled people, having been borrowed from the heart when the pain actually originates in the stomach. Likewise, fainting, swooning, and epileptic seizures—which seem to hold the reins of life—take their origin from the mouth of the stomach. In bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"; the common medical practice of opening a vein.</note> this is a daily observation. Very often, as soon as a vein is opened, dizziness, as well as dimness and blurring of vision, are clearly felt to flow from the stomach; these symptoms cease as soon as a finger is placed on the open vein, and are felt again, rising from the stomach, as soon as the finger is removed. Finally, the authority of the Word confirms my paradox at the very threshold, when it asks:

<margin>8.</margin> *What thoughts have ascended into your heart?* <note>A reference to Luke 24:38. Van Helmont argues that if thoughts "ascend" to the heart, they must originate from a lower point: the stomach.</note> It does not say, "descend into your heart," nor "what thoughts are born or rise from your heart." For many times the stomach is called by the name of the heart, as when adulteries and sins are judged to arise from the "heart."

<margin>9.</margin> For every thought, in its first origin, must be born elsewhere than in the heart. The pulse and the violent, unceasing movement of the heart would prevent it. Indeed, thought ought to happen in stillness. Therefore, whenever thought is attributed to the heart, that way of speaking is according to the understanding of common people, taking the "heart" to mean the seat of the soul. And although the necessity of seeds in plants extends further to a multiplicity of functions and consequently moves into the diversity of different parts, the vegetative power does not therefore depart from its original vegetal bed, where it once fixed its seat for itself,

...nor does it migrate, or divide itself, because of the dispersal of the "kitchens" <note>original: *culinarum*; in Helmont’s physiology, these are the various sites of digestion or metabolic transformation throughout the body</note>. This happens in a much more formal and manifest way after the arrangement of the seeds <note>original: *feminis*, likely an OCR error for *seminis* (of the seed)</note> has decorated the animal figure and organized the variety of limbs. For then the sensitive and motive soul is granted, and it is housed nowhere else than in the root, from which it prepares all subsequent nourishment for itself.

<margin>10.</margin> To speak properly and to understand distinctly, there is not a specific "vegetative soul" in plants or beasts; rather, there is a certain vital power, acting as a precursor to the soul. The sensitive soul, however, takes up the reins of that **Archeal** power into itself, and that preceding vital power, which prepares the way, dissolves into the **Archeus** and thereafter submits itself to the sensitive soul. For the head is not yet occupied with animal reasoning, nor is the heart—though shaken by continuous pulses and working incessantly in the factory of the vital spirits and the transformation of gore into blood—yet an organ suited for the animal soul. Rather, when this soul finds its prepared guest-house in the root, it resides and remains there, and does not migrate elsewhere.

<margin>11.</margin> For in truth, the heart serves the stomach, while the whole of life is focused solely on the fabrication of the vital spirit. Indeed, the threshold of life for a newborn fetus begins with nursing and sleep, and continues this way for some time. Both of these take place in the stomach, where the vital forces are stabilized and preserved by the soul in that "root" through which the soul hopes to be primarily nourished, fostered, fueled, and increased in the future. For it was never the study or duty of the soul to wander or migrate from place to place to select a bed for itself, seeing as it is directed by an unerring intelligence and is established in its own certain seat from the beginning of life.

<margin>12.</margin> This center was designated for the origin of seeds from the beginning of Creation, with a command and a bond that the soul should not change its seat or seek out foreign places as if they were more convenient. For He who rules all things mightily and disposes them sweetly <note>A reference to Wisdom 8:1, a common theological citation regarding divine providence</note> knows the ends of every destination. There is indeed

<column-break/>

in the brain of a living creature a motive force and a sensory workshop. However, it does not follow that the soul, having been shaken from its original and primordial seat, has migrated from its radical guest-house—assigned to it by the Creator—to the head. For although the faculties and functions of the sensitive soul are indeed distributed among a plurality of parts, the soul itself remains unshaken in its original place where it was first bound and tied. Nor is it torn apart because of the diversity of its duties; for it accomplishes all things through the <term>Archeus</term><note>The internal "master-worker" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions</note> as its ministering organ, and is present everywhere by that vital ray, as if standing by.

<margin>13.</margin> Above all, it is easily felt that every impulse of the first concepts, and every initial and primitive agitation of disturbances, occurs near the entrance of the stomach. For if a gun should suddenly let out a crash, the shock of that same noise is perceived as a jolting near the "mouth" of the stomach. Similarly, if sad news is suddenly brought, that sudden and accelerated change is felt nowhere else than in that central guest-house of the soul.

<margin>14.</margin> So much so, that those who came before me, even if unwilling or unaware, placed the "concupiscible" <note>relating to the part of the soul responsible for basic desires and emotions</note> lodging of the soul in that same place. Because this is prior in duration to reasoning, motion, and the sensation of the external senses, it denotes—indeed, it proves—that the primordial guest-house of the soul is there. This seemed to me to be a piece of knowledge utterly necessary for the healing of diseases, as I shall demonstrate in the proper place regarding Illnesses.

<margin>15.</margin> For many have remained without hope of recovery because remedies were applied to the member assigned to the functions (such as the brain), and not to the root from which the error originated. Since the dwelling and the "court" where the edicts are formed were unknown, medicines were wrongly applied to the places where those edicts are executed. Because the location of the sensitive soul was unknown, it has been unrecognized until now that the soul receives the primitive stain, disturbance, and contagion of most diseases right there. And it is there that remedies must be appropriately applied, if the medicine for diseases is to be established from the root. In this matter, a very grave error has indeed been made...

# THE SEAT OF THE SOUL

<margin>16.</margin> ...hitherto. At the very least, the first movements or impulses, which are not within our power, have long been admitted to occur around the orifice of the stomach and to climb upward toward the head. It is certain, moreover, that every movement begins from a center, and therefore the center of the soul is wherever the beginning of concepts is felt. However, these are called "impulses not in our power" because they are the first concepts of the sensitive soul, still unordered and not yet purified by the command of the Mind.
<margin>17.</margin> Now, what I write concerning the seat of the sensitive soul, I also understand to be for the immortal Mind. Indeed, the Mind has no subject closer or more similar to itself in which to dwell than that vital light called the sensitive soul, in which the Mind is wrapped and, by divine command, bound by the bond of life. When the sensitive soul perishes through its own annihilation <note>Van Helmont believes the animal/sensitive soul is mortal and ceases to exist at death, unlike the immortal mind</note>, the Mind can no longer remain in the body; therefore, it hastens to the Being of beings <note>original: *Ens entium*; a philosophical term for God</note> so that it may pass to the places assigned to it.
<margin>18.</margin> Thus, the radical couch <note>original: *torus*; here meaning a foundation or primary seat</note> of the sensitive soul is in the vital <term>Archeus|The internal governing spirit or "master-workman" that Van Helmont believed directed all biological functions</term> of the stomach; it stands and remains there for the whole of life. This is not to say that the sensitive soul is housed in the stomach as if in a sack, skin, membrane, pot, prison, cell, or shell; nor is it contained in that seat in the manner of closed bodies within a purse. Instead, in an extraordinary way, it exists centrally in a point, as if in an atom in the very middle of a single membrane’s thickness.
<margin>19.</margin> It is in a place, yet not entirely "locally" <note>meaning it does not occupy space in the way a solid object does, but is present there spiritually</note>. Because every soul is a light given by the Father of Lights <note>A reference to the Epistle of James 1:17: "Every good gift... cometh down from the Father of lights"</note> and the Creator of things, and I have proved elsewhere that lights are immediately in a place and mediately in the air where they are located. Thus, the sensitive soul is in the place or seat of which I am presently writing. The Mind, however, being a luminous substance, penetrates the created light that is the sensitive soul, and in turn, this soul penetrates the Mind, dulling it with the contagion of the corruption of Adam <note>original: *contagione Adami*; referring to Original Sin affecting human intellect</note>. Regarding this, see the book on long life and the entry of death into man.
<margin>20.</margin> Therefore, the sensitive soul is fleeting,

<column-break/>

mortal, mere vital light, given by the Father of Lights, nor can it be explained in any other way or word. Since in the universe it has nothing similar to itself except the light of a candle—which, because it burns, can only be compared to that little fire by a distant analogy and a much unequal similarity, like looking through an outer husk <note>original: *siliquam*; literally a pod or shell</note>.
<margin>21.</margin> For that reason, clearly, although that sensitive soul is locally present in a place and dwells there, it is not contained by the place in any way other than how the flame of a candle is kindled in the air it breathes; and the light is in that flame just as life is in the aforementioned soul. There are, however, vital lights that do not burn at all, but are separated by as many differences as there are varieties of souls.
<margin>22.</margin> And for this reason, God is called by St. James the Father of Lights. Thus, the heat of living creatures does not come from the fountain-head of the soul’s light, but is the warming light of vital life; therefore, it is a product of life, not life itself. It is also a rival to solar light; just as in a fish, the vital light is actually cold, because it is of the nature of the moon. Because of this, God made only two—and sufficient—great lights for the life of sublunary things <note>referring to the Sun and Moon, which Helmont links to animal heat and fish vitality respectively</note>. However, the brightness of these lights, or the souls themselves, are subjects of inherent existence. And they are creatures situated entirely between substance and accident, for they belong to the realm of the intelligible world. Therefore, in the sensitive soul (and nowhere else in fleeting things), as if in a spiritual light made by the Father of Lights, the immortal Mind is joined. It is connected to the sensitive soul either by the hand of the Almighty (who is present everywhere) or through an Angel, by the bond of life—that is, the vital light.
<margin>23.</margin> This is an inseparable property of the aforementioned light. The immortal Mind itself is a bright, incorporeal substance, immediately reflecting the image of its God, because it received that image engraved upon itself during its creation, or at the very moment of <term>empsychosis|The moment the soul enters the body</term>. For both souls are created at once and joined by God, who will never grant His honor as Creator to any creature. Before the fall of Adam, however, there was no sensitive soul in man; how that soul descended into human nature along with death will be discussed in its proper place.

# THE SEAT OF THE SOUL

<margin>24.</margin> At the very least, through the arrival of the sensitive soul, death and the corruption of our entire nature entered, and the former majesty and integrity of our nature were blotted out. Indeed, while the mind was performing the duties of life directly, and was not yet "sensitive" <note>Van Helmont distinguishes between the "Mind" (unique to humans) and the "sensitive soul" (shared with animals), suggesting the latter only became dominant after the Fall</note>, immortality was also present, and the darkness of beasts had not yet occupied the intellect. <margin>25.</margin> Thus, man has indeed suffered a shipwreck in his nature, one that is beyond restoration; yet through rebirth, beneath the calamities of tribulations, man is exalted in a far more excellent way, as he is taken up by the image of God and adopted as His son. Furthermore, it is absolutely necessary that every impulse of the first movement, and the first concepts of the soul, should occur in the "bedchamber of the soul." Although this is felt most strongly around the orifice of the stomach, and God is wonderful in His works, it is because He was pleased to arrange such wonderful powers in the membranes of the stomach, the womb, and the meninges <note>The membranes surrounding the brain</note> <margin>26.</margin> that they present a kind of image of a Republic. Nevertheless, I have found that the Spleen serves as the ferment of the stomach—its Sun, its cook, and its director. Therefore, I have decided to call the conspiracy of these two organs the <term>Duumvirate|A term originally referring to a pair of Roman officials sharing joint authority; here, the joint governing power of the stomach and spleen over the body's health</term>. For although the digestive ferment and similar aids seem to represent a kind of servitude, in vital matters, servitude contains power and strength; thus, it also promises dignity and authority. So it is that just as the senses, the faintings of the whole body, and the privileges of digestion are most sensible, manifest, and open in the stomach, nonetheless, the vital breath—passing through so many arteries and so powerfully causing the stomach's digestions—has commanded that without duality, discord, or a preference of power, a single economy must be made of both organs. They conspire toward one goal with different duties, even though each attends to its own work individually, and is therefore separated by location. Truly, the effort of the Duumvirate is unique: a harmonious and resonant lyre of intention. Therefore, the Spleen, being nearby,

<column-break/>

leans upon the stomach from the outside, as if it were fostering it with the vital weave of the arteries. <margin>27.</margin> It is not that the arteries give all power to the Spleen, but rather the organs behave in the manner of the Stars. For although the Stars borrow light from the Sun, there is nonetheless in each a peculiar property and strength of acting, which is most evident in the Moon regarding the ebbs, flows, and floods of the sea. Suppose, then, that the arteries of the Spleen take the place of the Sun. Yet the Spleen itself has obtained a twin and innate dignity peculiar to itself, even though it enjoys the service of the heart in the preparation of the blood and the vital spirit. Therefore, the Spleen is the seat of the <term>Archeus|The internal governing spirit or 'master-workman' that directs the biological and chemical functions of an organ</term>, which, since it is the immediate organ of the sensitive soul, determines the vital actions of the soul residing in the stomach. For the sensitive soul hardly meditates on anything without the help of the Archeus, because it does not enjoy abstract thought like the Mind. The Mind, in its own retreat—sometimes through ecstasy, and without the aids of the Archeus or the bodily aura—contemplates many great things intellectually. Furthermore, in the wanderings of the Archeus, aversion, confusion, straying, and indignation are supplied. <margin>28.</margin> And the sensitive soul itself, like the <gloss>husk of the mind</gloss>, always uses the Archeus, whether it wishes to or not. From this source, certainly, all forms of madness (of which only a few have become well known) are called "precordial" <note>Literally "before the heart," referring to the upper abdominal area</note> and ascribed to the <gloss>hypochondrium</gloss> <note>The area of the abdomen under the ribs, housing the liver and spleen</note>. Yet these flow from the same seat, as well as from the same fountain of the soul, like the wounding of a single point. <margin>29.</margin> Remedies, too, hardly exit the enclosures of the stomach in a material way. Therefore, those things that are transferred to the Spleen are rare, which is quite obvious in the difficulties of treating a <gloss>quartan fever</gloss> <note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms every fourth day, which Van Helmont believed was rooted in the spleen</note>. For the immortal Mind, apart from its marriage to the sensitive soul, is read to have been inspired into Adam by Omnipotence. And that "breath of life" is called a substance; therefore, it is not found to be inspired into brutes <note>Animals</note>. <margin>30.</margin> The Mind, therefore, is originally bound to the Archeus as an organ is to its immediate mover; from this, the Mind could daily substitute a new Archeus at its pleasure from food, sufficiently and always, and keep it perpetually and equally strong.

<margin>31.</margin> ...and from here, to awaken an immortal life worthy of itself. For indeed, the immortal Mind, present everywhere, used to perform all the duties of life immediately through the <term>Archeus|The internal, semi-spiritual 'master workman' or vital force that Van Helmont believed governed all bodily functions</term> (which therefore borrows its vitality from the Mind). This Archeus consequently seemed somewhat superior to mortal things, a foster child of a more excellent monarchy than the <note>original: "sublunaris"</note> sublunary one. This was the state of things before Adam’s fall. But since on that same day of transgression they became guilty of death, a soul subject to death—the sensitive soul—arrived as the deputy and companion of the Mind. To this soul, the Mind soon transferred the arrangements for governing the body. 

For at first, there was an immediate marriage of the immortal Mind with the Archeus. Soon after the fall and the awakening of the sensitive soul, the Mind withdrew like a kernel into the center of the sensitive soul, to which it is bound by the bond of life. The Mind is not nourished by food, yet it could choose and prepare foods for its Archeus; the Archeus is now forced by tireless study to watch over its own sustenance and nourishment. And it prepares and applies this to itself gradually less and less aptly, due to the failing duration and power of the sensitive soul. 

So, I first had to speak of the Seat of the Mind, the material occasion of mortality, and the necessities of diseases and <term>ametry|A lack of proportion or 'unsoundness' in the body's rhythms</term>. For what is required here is demonstrated at length in the *Treatise on the Entry of Death into Human Nature*, along with an explanation of the Text: *Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land.* <note>Jeremiah 1:14. Van Helmont often used biblical passages to provide mystical foundations for his medical theories.</note> 

<column-break/>

As a corollary, therefore: <margin>32.</margin> the central place of the soul is the Orifice of the stomach, just as the root of vegetables is their vital place. The Mind sits in the sensitive soul, to which it has been bound ever since the fall. The brain, however, is the executive organ of the soul's concepts, insofar as it presides over nerves and muscles regarding motion; but regarding sense, it possesses in itself the faculties of memory, will, and imagination. 

Therefore, when the stomach fails, there arise paleness, tremors, dryness, <term>atrophy|The wasting away of body tissue</term>, griping pains, asthma, jaundice, paralysis, contractions, dizziness, apoplexy, etc. Indeed, the more famous of the physicians wonder that often extreme defects are overcome only through stomach remedies, and that a sickness of the stomach produces diseases far removed from itself. And the Moderns are amazed that wound-healing potions successfully heal wounds of the limbs, and that in Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist whom Van Helmont both admired and critiqued</note>, cancer, lupus, or an eating ulcer are healed by a drink. 

Therefore, the error of those who treat poorly affected external parts as if they were fundamental—and who transfer the entire remedy to the head when it is injured from below—has persisted until now because of ignorance of the Seat of the soul, life, and governance. <margin>33.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the "sensitive soul," the mortal part of the human spirit that governs physical life. Having previously argued that the immortal Mind retreated into the center of this sensitive soul after the Fall of Man, he now identifies its specific anatomical throne: not the heart or the brain, as traditional medicine claimed, but the mouth of the stomach.</meta>

### ON THE SEAT OF THE SOUL

<margin>1.</margin> Very often, the pit of the stomach <note>original: "Os stomachi," literally the 'mouth' of the stomach, referring to the epigastric region</note> cannot bear the touch of a hand, even if it is resting on the ribs on both sides. This is a clear sign that a most sharp and primary sensation lies beneath that spot—a sensitivity that one might otherwise expect to be found in the fingertips for the purpose of distinguishing touchable objects. Yet, the fact that it cannot endure a resting hand—even one offering a pleasant warmth and not weighing down with its own heaviness—reveals that life itself is the source of all sensation in that place. Because it is primarily affected in this way, it openly demonstrates that it is the sensitive soul, the first to encounter harmful things, and the vessel in which the immortal mind is wrapped.

<margin>2.</margin> But look, I look back at the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university medical authorities who followed Galen and Aristotle</note>, which freely admit that the tenderness of the stomach's orifice—or its excessively sharp, accurate, and primary sense—causes almost every instance of fainting <note>original: "syncope"</note>. They say these things, yet they do not reflect upon their own axioms regarding the heart, nor do they consider that this "sharp sense," as they call it, argues for nothing other than a vital readiness. It is not that one person happened to receive more or more open nerves than another. Meanwhile, they have never once considered that life, or the soul, resides in that seat. They are unwilling to look for the soul in a "sack" or a membrane; they have preferred to believe it is deposited in the bellows of the heart's chambers <note>original: "aurium cordis follibus," referring to the auricles</note> or in the lazy brain. For even though they would admit defeat when they notice powers disturbing or terrifying the whole body from the membrane of the womb, the Schools have not yet been granted the privilege of seeing and admitting that the same power is granted to the stomach.

<margin>3.</margin> Indeed, they were compelled by the complaints of many who were acting out of foolish lust <note>original: "stulta Venere lascivientium"</note>, who lamented that they were oppressed and anxious around the pit of the stomach with late-night wailing. But the Schools did not, therefore, call into doubt the traditions of the pagans, nor did they think it certain—even when briefly pricked by conscience—to wonder: whether perhaps the light of the vital beginning, or the entrance

<column-break/>

to life, was in that very place, which, being affected by primary irritating causes, would be the first to feel its own discomforts. For a command is not issued except from the court; likewise, the power of life is not delegated except by the presiding life, which is the soul. Indeed, from this it is first made manifest that unless a "character" <note>A 'character' in Helmontian chemistry/biology is a formative internal blueprint or vital signature</note> granted by the sensitive soul is imprinted upon the seed, the seed will remain sterile and monstrous. It is no different from the flower of a pumpkin <note>original: "Peponis"</note>, where no small pumpkin is seen attached to the back. Therefore, if the soul sits there as a guest, from which seeds originally borrow the character of their fertility, it is beyond doubt that the powers—both vital and reproductive—also lie hidden in that same place.

<margin>4.</margin> And furthermore, this seat of the sensitive soul does more than just moderate the digestive faculty of the stomach and rouse for this purpose the anonymous acidity of the stomach's ferment <note>Van Helmont was one of the first to identify the role of acid in digestion, though he called it a "ferment"</note>, allowing it to be regulated and limited according to the vigor of nature's laws. Truly, the life of the stomach itself presides over all the digestions of the entire body, however much they are dispersed into hidden or even remote corners. This is characteristic of the soul through a singular radiation and a participation, as it were, of its own life—as if by a simple and bare nod, and by the command of the <term>Duumvirate|The 'Duumvirate' refers to Van Helmont's theory that the stomach and spleen rule the body together as a pair of magistrates</term>, it compelled obedience toward itself from everywhere and from everyone. From this it likewise follows that the same vital vigor is spread in every direction; and by an erroneous path, its wanderings are also "transplanted" in a disease-causing way, even to the tips of the fingers.

<margin>5.</margin> In this way, that hostile acid—which, though it is pleasing and even equally required by the stomach—becomes an enemy when it enters "alien fields" <note>i.e., other parts of the body where it does not belong</note>. Nor must proof of that hostility be sought from afar. For instance, during the dog days of summer <note>original: "canicularibus," referring to the hot days of July and August</note>, when the light of the sun has entered in, they provide acidic broths tinged with an unusual color.

<margin>6.</margin> Therefore, when a "foreign guest" is carried from the stomach, through the vital beginning, to a foreign field, some "foreign defect" immediately follows, which usually betrays its presence instantly.

Disease is, of course, that which, if it is carried into the veins by an error of the ill-kindled Dual-Governance <term>Duumviratus: Van Helmont’s term for the coordinated chemical and vital rule of the stomach and the spleen over the body</term>, produces fevers. But if a hostile acidity is carried into the general state of the body or to the limbs, soon various abscesses and the errors of Gout <note>original: "Arthritidis"</note> are present. I speak of abscesses which, with very little physical matter—not unlike thorns or driven-in spikes—sting sharply; they finally hasten into pus, watery discharge, or foul gore.

<margin>7.</margin> This is surely the deceptive trap of "Catarrhs" <note>Catarrh was the traditional medical theory that diseases were caused by mucus or "humors" dripping from the brain into the rest of the body</note> which has entangled the Schools <note>The established medical universities</note> even to the modern day, through various "settlings" of non-existent humors, through flows, falls, and slips. And it was easy for Satan to cast down minds already prone to such things, seduced as they were by paganism. It is no different than how astronomers, having noticed the inexplicable position of the Moon and planets, invented "eccentrics" <note>complex mathematical circles used in old astronomy to explain planetary paths</note>—some relative and some simple—which they knew to be empty fictions, created out of the necessity of measuring the positions they found. But in the art of healing, it was easier for Satan to deceive his followers (that is, the pagans), because the physical senses were a busy and persistent persuader right at hand. Meanwhile, observation was neglected as the medical art began to be dragged toward profit. Indeed, from what has been set forth in my *Treatise on Catarrhs*, it is easily and necessarily concluded by anyone that there is no physical matter for these "Catarrhs," nor is there a "kitchen" in the head where they might be prepared, nor a channel through which they might flow down in such diverse ways, even to the most distant 

<margin>8.</margin> reaches of the body. Indeed, it would be far easier and more direct (though the only obstacle is the tradition once handed down to the Gentiles, which has blocked the path of inquiring after the truth through blind belief) to consider that from the very beginning of life, life is continued toward life; and finally, from a vital error, errors are scattered through the whole, and into the whole—into the containing parts as much as the contents. Finally, once this foundation has been ignored, every kind of remedy thereafter—recklessly and frivolously devised by descendants deceived by Satanic cunning—will be in vain. Would that those who come after me might 

<column-break/>

contemplate this enough with me! For then they would easily perceive, with tears, the great blindness of mortals, both among those who heal and everywhere among those being treated.

<margin>9.</margin> For the first sufferers of gout <note>original: "podagrici"</note> would step forward as witnesses and accuse the stomach; they would say they feel the first movements there, even febrile agitations like the precursors of an attack. Simply by the gaze and the irradiation of the vital light, an acidity is conceived and born there, which is erroneously transferred into the "fluid of the joints" <note>original: "feminale gluten"</note>, which they now call **Synonia** <term>Synonia: An early term for synovial fluid, the lubricating liquid in the joints</term>. This is the transparent, nourishing seed of the joints, deposited there more copiously because of the frequency of movement and the strong compression of the bones. For otherwise, the bones would grow hot and dry out from mutual friction. Although these things are much more fruitfully described in the chapter on **Gout**, it nevertheless 

<margin>10.</margin> helps me to expand upon them more clearly here. Truly, various diseases occur which take their origin centrally from the stomach, the beginnings and remedies of which have been ignored until now with ill omen. For in the hollow of the stomach, there are the acid, the bitter, the salty, the oily-smelling or putrid, the virulent, the tasteless, and so on. And especially the **acid**, which is the fermenting and digestive (or transformative) power; it is not native or natural to the stomach itself, but is prepared for it and breathed into it by the nearby "kitchen" of the **Spleen**. When this ferment is lacking, there is "indigestion" <note>original: "apepsia"</note> at home, "slow digestion" <note>original: "bradypepsia"</note>, a cast-down appetite, and a nausea for food—things which are immediately seen as local and crowded companions to fevers. For this reason, the Old Man <note>A common reference to Hippocrates</note> said: *Acid belches coming after oily ones are good.* Sometimes it also happens that too little ferment flows to the stomach; from this, "wasting" <note>original: "atrophiam"</note> is stirred up, and foods become difficult to cook <note>Van Helmont views digestion as a form of internal "cooking" or fermentation</note>. Indeed, the stomach, which seems to be deprived of ordinary feeling and perceives nothing except what is harmful, whenever it is unworthily affected by foreign things contained within it, immediately produces a watery liquid due to the scarcity of ferment, and struggles to push it out with nausea. ## II₂
<meta>catchword: Nor (Latin: Nec)</meta>

<page-num>296</page-num>

I say, therefore, that sometimes there is nothing but mere water, or a viscous slime—often even tasteless, and not rarely imbued with a strange sourness—which differs from the vital ferment as much as the dead differs from the living. Indeed, although they may share a similar taste, they are very far apart from one another, just as one can see in the bitterness of wormwood, and the squirting cucumber, or the bitter apple <note>original: "absynthii, & cucumeris asinini, vel colocynthidis"</note>. For when the drink and the food to be joined with it in the stomach suffer from a lack of living ferment, they immediately break down into a bitter yellow liquid. This is what the Schools <note>The established Galenic medical universities of the time</note> have until now falsely called "viscous bile," and even one of the four "constitutive parts of the blood." They remain ignorant, meanwhile, of what author or guide would cause pure bile to be separated in the liver from the blood it was born with and intimately mixed with—or how that solitary bile (which is certainly much changed from the bile floating in the blood) would be carried to the stomach. For there is no path from the liver to the stomach except through so many detours that they rightly accuse this invention of the Schools of stupidity. 

However, while the food approaches the stomach to be assimilated into it and nourish it, if it fails due to a lack of ferment, or because of some other storm arising in the stomach, it immediately rots and becomes infamous for its foul smell <note>original: "nidore infame," referring to the smell of burnt or rotting organic matter</note>. For when held in a warm place, that which has already entered the threshold of life and been counted among the soon-to-be-vital parts immediately rots and becomes stinking; indeed, if a delay occurs, it turns cadaverous. From this arise Cholera, lientery <note>A form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>, Celiac disease, and so on. Sometimes also the Archeus <term>Archeus: The internal vital spirit or "master-workman" that governs the functions of an organ</term> of the stomach, wishing to supply the lack of acid ferment, becomes indignant and produces a cruel, vinegar-like acid. From this come sharp hunger-pains <note>original: "Orexes"</note> and likewise griping pains <note>original: "tormina"</note>, as much in the stomach as in the intestines, which are usually cruel. But if a moderate acid flows, yet the abundance or harshness of the food is too great, then the whole meal turns bitter, and that yellow and thick excrement grows through such a degeneration. From this, a varied harvest of evils arises, kindled into diarrhea, unless the whole mass is immediately cast down at once. Sometimes even the Archeus of the stomach conceives a fury, and is kindled 

<column-break/>

by its own accord, so that the sourness does not strike the food, but infects the Archeus himself in a wandering way. It is then that Gout <note>original: "Arthritis"</note> is conceived. The Archeus, diffused through the whole body, most closely affects the joint-fluid <term>synonia: Van Helmont’s term for synovial fluid, which he believed nourished the bones</term> with its acidity, or rather the crude seed destined to be assimilated into the bones, and therefore deposited within the joints. It contaminates the joint-fluid of whichever part is weaker in its natural strength. For this reason, Gout is thought to choose, at its whim, whichever part it seizes. And because that sourness, received in the center of the stomach, is dispersed through the Archeus to remote places, it is therefore false that "defluxions" from the head are propagated through the nerves and veins <note>Van Helmont is rejecting the traditional view that joint pain is caused by fluid "dripping" from the brain</note>. 

In the same way, great griping pains in the belly provoke a harmful sourness in the stomach through the preservation of the parts; this sourness then, by a rare portent, causes the hands and feet to shake with contractions, and soon after dissolves them into paralysis. Thus, an improper sourness in the stomach, if it should seize the dewy and "spermatic" <note>In the sense of "generative" or "life-giving"</note> nourishment of the stomach—even slightly—provokes dizzy spells <note>original: "vertigines"</note>. These are more turbulent the more they regard the back part of the head. Apoplexy, however, arises when, by an entirely foreign motion and guest, a tasteless slime enters the veins of the stomach from its cavity near the orifice. It keeps the straightness of its own side and distinguishes a great condition from a minor one by the presence or absence of virulence. 

Furthermore, in chronic diseases of this kind, there is usually some "sealing character" <note>original: "character aliquis sigillaris," a signature or hereditary mark</note>. Thus, gout often flows from the beginning of the parents into the offspring, and there it patiently waits many years before its own fruit reaches maturity. Therefore, in the vital beginnings and radical organs of the stomach (which are the local or indwelling Archeus itself), that posthumous "gouty character," transferred by hereditary right, remains. Consequently, even that which is acquired through an irregular life sits in the Archeus of the stomach's orifice. When that Archeus, affected by weariness at the insolence of a foreign guest, sharpens itself for the expulsion of the same, the fruit of Apoplexy emerges.

# FROM THE SEAT OF THE SOUL TO DISEASES.

For that <term>gouty character</term> <note>original: "character podagricus"; Van Helmont views diseases as "characters" or "seeds" of information rather than just physical imbalances</note> is not silent, nor is it materially deposited within some nest, nor received in a secluded stable within the folds or wrinkles of the stomach, clinging like some foreign <term>tartar</term> <note>A term from Paracelsian medicine referring to stony or hard deposits in the body, like kidney stones or dental plaque</note>. Rather, it is a character entrusted to the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "master-workman" or internal vital spirit that governs the body's functions according to Van Helmont</note> of life itself. Let us imagine a unity of property and essence, by which that character—be it for gout, apoplexy, or epilepsy—lies buried, and is awakened at fixed stations of its own maturity, or is stirred up by certain consumed foods or odors. Then let us consider the natural acidity of the stomach which has now become degenerate, and likewise the tenderness of its orifice, which stirs up <term>syncopes</term> <note>fainting spells</note> and epilepsies (which testify to nothing except a sensitive perception, injury, passion, and disturbance of life, and thus a present enemy causing a riot through many things). Thus, if an unnatural acidity is excited and mixes with the Archeus—and since the Archeus presides over every digestion—this acidity is carried radially to foreign hearths to which it is entirely hostile: and from there, <term>Arthritis</term> <note>joint inflammation or gout</note> leaps forth. But if it is connected to food or drink, there are colicky pains, griping of the bowels, and other occasional disturbances of the parts. Yet if the acidity of the stomach should degenerate and associate itself with an opiate poison, penetrating toward the seat of the soul, epilepsy is immediately present. If, however, a foul mucus should arise, prone to bitterness, it stirs up vertigo, and rising more strongly, it excites <term>Apoplexy</term> <note>a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>. Indeed, it is not necessary to distinguish those things precisely from one another, as long as the matter or the occasioning cause is successfully exhausted.

<margin>12.</margin> At least certain external <term>periapta</term> <note>amulets or charms worn around the neck</note> protect against the fall and the epileptic seizure, which is a sign that either the "fruit" of the character is hindered, or the application of the occasioning cause to the Archeus is blocked: namely, in both ways the harmful thing is prevented, extinguished, or annihilated so that it does not mix with the Archeus. Furthermore, just as plants are usually accustomed to sleep in winter and be awakened, as it were, toward spring, so that they may put forth buds, leaves, flowers, or fruits; so the character of gout, epi-

<column-break/>

lepsy, etc., is also stirred into maturity at a fixed period, unless the importunity of provoking things anticipates it. At the very least, vertigo and apoplexy, etc., although they are counted among occasional causes, nevertheless sit closest within the very nest of life, in the Archeus, which is certainly implanted in the orifice of the stomach. For by what easy shortcut is the <term>Falling Sickness</term> <note>original: "Caducus"; a historical term for epilepsy</note> suspended and held back by things hung around the neck? It is because the entry of the harmful cause into the sensitive soul is hindered; it is the penetration of the harmful cause lurking in the Archeus toward the interior, which therefore utterly carries away the Mind: it certainly

<margin>13.</margin> leaves the pulse of the Heart behind, but it so ruins the sense, the imagination, and every principal power of the soul that for that interval they seem plainly abolished. Whence it should be noted with an iron pen <note>i.e., recorded as an unshakeable fact</note> that the soul so ruined does not dwell in the Heart, which does not falter at all. Gout, however,

<margin>14.</margin> just as it tends outward, so its character affects not so much the innermost shrine or seat of the soul, as the Archeus presiding over the digestions. These things happen because the hereditary gouty character was branded into the fetus from the beginning of generation, and long before <term>empsychosis</term> <note>the moment the soul enters the body</note>: and therefore it regards only the Archeus, not the soul, since the Archeus alone then bore the entire burden in itself. But that gouty character which is acquired through the excesses of life, even if it comes to an aged man, nevertheless preserves the nature of its own property. From this it becomes manifest that the character of any disease is indiscriminately admissible into the lap of the sensitive soul. So much so that, just as

<margin>15.</margin> a great terror has made many people epileptic for life, so a similar terror has thereafter rendered many people immune from gout. In the one case, terror generated an epileptic character in the <term>syndesmos</term> <note>Greek: "link" or "bond"</note> of life and the sensitive soul; that same terror, being one or two degrees milder and more external, killed the character of gout, and either rendered it frozen by fear or at least oppressed its root. # FROM THE SEAT OF THE SOUL TO DISEASES.

...Hippocrates (which, since it never existed anywhere, must be understood as the effect attributed to that bile) remaining in the <term>precordia</term> <note>The area around the heart and stomach; for Van Helmont, this is the primary center of life</note> (for he looked toward the seat of the soul, or the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>The "partnership" between the stomach and the spleen, which Van Helmont believed governed the body</note>, though it was not yet known). If this is scattered into the body, it provokes epilepsy; but if into the soul, it causes madness. Truly, that was the simplicity of the first age, which weighed things honestly but, for lack of <margin>16.</margin> supernal light, did not reach the depths of the matter. There are certain simple substances which, without causing sensory revulsion, produce true madness by being eaten; others produce sleep. Some bring the mad back to life, while others produce only delirium, or a kind of drunkenness. I would wish for the "characters" of diseases to be reckoned according to these similarities. For it is not only by taking in such hostile things that health, the mind, or life are alienated; rather, when harmful materials are conceived within, or even by "characters" alone, diverse properties are introduced into life or into the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal vital "workman" or spirit that governs the body’s functions</note>, the organ of life. And these are not only the good inclinations of fathers or grandfathers propagated into the seed, but also certain diseased "nurseries" <note>original: "seminaria"; seeds or points of origin for disease</note> which are born with us, just as they are threatened in simple substances. <margin>17.</margin> These things certainly deserve serious attention, especially whenever that hostile and morbid virus is coupled in various ways—now with the stomach's <term>ferment</term> <note>The transformative chemical power in the stomach</note>, now with the indwelling Archeus, and finally with the arterial spirit. Not infrequently, it also strikes radially at life itself, which is surely nothing but a central light, penetrable by any radial light. Thus, the vital light of the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The part of the soul responsible for feeling and reacting to the environment</note> is penetrated by a "foreign light" coupled to it, just as light passing through colored glass tints the simple light on a wall. Indeed, in the vital monarchy, which descends from the **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical reference to God (James 1:17)</note>, there are these living lights which shine elsewhere in the simple sun or in colored light, though assigned to a perishable state. And the combination of living lights is not only mutually tolerable,

<column-break/>

but also active upon one another. Thus it is evident from this that the **Father of Lights** holds the reins of life and of all nature. Therefore, in the splenic arteries, or in the very flesh of that organ, a property is already branded (which I call the **characteristic of the disease**) or even in the membrane of the stomach, the veins, nerves, or in their vital Archeus. These properties propagate themselves into the sensitive soul at intervals, or shine through by a continuous fuel, and they compel that soul to be their handmaid. So much so that the soul itself, or its life, or the vital Archeus, being provoked by turns, is driven into some movement of fury, madness, <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting</note>, vertigo, epilepsy, apoplexy, paralysis, contraction, and so on. The opposing side, <margin>18.</margin> being unwilling to learn, will accuse me ( *I know it well* ) of spreading a fog when I divert these sublunary things toward life, toward vital lights, or toward the invisible world where the Father of Lights presides. But I ask them to remember that this is the right path, which otherwise cannot be investigated from the source. Let them know that vital movements are only stirred by, and depend upon, life—whether we contemplate our own life, or the life and vital properties that appear to us as diseased, mortal, and hateful. Indeed, I look everywhere <margin>19.</margin> only for the common good of my neighbor, to open windows through which the **Light of Nature** <note>A Paracelsian term for the divine knowledge accessible through the study of the physical world</note>, which has been obscured until now, may reach the Schools and minds more gifted than my own. For this reason, I have cast aside the "complexions" of elementary qualities, as well as the humors, <term>tartars</term> <note>hard deposits or residues</note>, and such dreams of writers. I would wish in their place to introduce a true knowledge of nature and an investigation of ourselves. Finally, I have removed <term>Catarrhs</term> <note>The traditional medical theory that diseases are caused by "fluids" or "mucus" flowing down from the brain</note> from our midst as vain fictions and broken sticks upon which mortals have leaned until now. Thus, whatever deceived them through the fraud and trickery of "flowing humor" as a cause of disease, all of that must be referred back to the fruit and product of the vital cause: because—
