# FROM THE SEAT OF THE SOUL TO DISEASES.

<columns>
...and that which was thought in the Schools to flow materially from the head, is instead darted, shot, radiated, and propagated from the vital seat of the soul, by the common direction of the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal vital spirit or "workman" that governs the body's functions</note>, or instilled by a participation in life. Good God, how much I disagree with the traditions of the Ancients? Would that there were, or at least that You would create, those who might understand me, and foster the hope of the sick with a richer talent! But You, God, will act in these matters according to Your good pleasure, to whom I totally refer and offer each and every thing that I have, know, see, and <margin>20.</margin> am able to do. I return, therefore, to the path: I have shown elsewhere that, first and foremost, wound-healing herbs work by the power of a certain innate <term>alkali</term> <note>In 17th-century chemistry, an 'alkali' was a substance that neutralized 'acids'; Van Helmont saw this as a fundamental healing principle</note>. I have taught, for instance, that <term>Mercury</term> <note>The metal quicksilver</note>, whether precipitated or sublimated, is easily <term>revivified</term> <note>Restored to its liquid, metallic state from a chemical compound</note> when the clarified juice of a wound-herb is infused into it through boiling. From this it follows that the more excellent herbs in this degree are those whose boiled juice, when mixed with precipitated mercury and then washed away, revivifies the Mercury more easily and abundantly. For this reason, <term>crab stones</term> <note>original: "lapis cancrorum"; also called 'crayfish eyes,' these are calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish, used as an antacid</note> are more effective in healing if they are drunk with wine than with water; because those stones, in wine, very easily take on the power and flavor of a <term>lye</term> <note>original: "lixivium"; an alkaline solution</note>. And I pray that the Physician does not therefore dread the use of wine in a wound, a fever, etc. For by that very fact, as it tastes of alkali, it loses the powers and properties of wine. In this way, indeed, an alkali from the <term>linden tree</term> <note>original: "tilia"</note> is successfully administered, no differently than that powder of crab stones. For the goodness of God has invited us so that, because of the rarity with which that stone exists in a small space, mortals might be drawn into admiration of it, and from there also learn its powers and weigh its equally wonderful property, by which it benefits those who are wounded, bruised, or have fallen from a great height. <margin>21.</margin> And here a wonder immediately shines forth which has not yet been explained: namely, that a wound is healed in the foot, or even the leg, or in parts most remote from the mouth—places where no alkali has ever obtained physical access.

<column-break/>

Specifically, the alkali of this stone corrects the sourness which has been ignited, or is ready to be ignited, in the outer limbs or the habit of the body. For the power of the alkali does not pass from the stomach through the veins all the way into the toes. It is not admitted there, and even if it were admitted, it could not proceed free and unbroken through the previous stages and examinations of the digestions. For there is no one who does not know this, or who would not grant me what I have said. <margin>22.</margin> Therefore, it is entirely clear from this that although that alkali does not go materially all the way to the outer habit of the body, it is nevertheless sufficient that it disperses its property <term>radially</term> <note>Acting like rays of light from a center, rather than through physical travel</note> that far, provided it has forbidden acidity in the stomach, which is the source of the digestions and the Archive of Life. In this, the power of the stomach over all the "families" of digestions is manifested. Therefore, by a contrary sense, they once perceived that wine—because it easily turns sour inside us—ignites and perverts wounds, unless that acidic power of the wine is softened by the application of a wound-healing alkali. Indeed, the only detriment to a wound is the internal and <term>fermental</term> <note>A process Van Helmont believed was driven by specific 'ferments' or spiritual blueprints</note> sourness alone; when this is absent, the lips of the wound hasten to run together and close. For this reason, the Schools were deceived and universally forbade wine to the wounded. Today, the use of wound-healing remedies has disproved this, to the disgrace of the Schools. For the alkali does not materially go to distant parts to inhibit the sourness, since it cannot even penetrate to the <term>spleen</term> <note>original: "lien"</note>, the seat of the <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day</note>. It is sufficient, therefore, that it restrains sourness in the stomach, the Ruler of all digestions. Not indeed that it destroys the necessary acid ferment of the stomach, but insofar as it corrects and hinders the translation of that ferment to distant parts. This itself confirms the aforementioned paradox: namely, that the digestion of the stomach presides over the particular digestion of a thousand "kitchens" <note>Van Helmont's metaphor for the various local metabolic processes in the organs</note>; and further, that there is no material pilgrimage of the alkalis. <margin>23.</margin>

</columns>

<margin>24.</margin> Furthermore, it is better to drink the <term>alkali</term> <note>In 17th-century chemistry, a substance that neutralizes acids</note> of these stones <note>Referring to the "crab stones" or crayfish eyes mentioned on the previous page</note> than to drink calcined shells. This is because, even though they may help and the alkali in calcined shells is far more potent, they nevertheless harm the stomach's <term>ferment</term> <note>The vital chemical "yeast" or agent Helmont believed drove digestion</note> by their harsh power, or at least they tend to do so. In contrast, the crab stone is directed not so much against the ferment itself as against the *product* of that ferment. There is also an obvious reason why this stone, and herbs similar to it, can heal even great wounds located far away, yet provide no help at all for small ulcers in the throat, the larynx, or the bladder. For this confirms that every wound immediately turns sour (acidic), and if the acidity radiating from the stomach's vital digestion to the wound is blocked, it serves as a remedy. But an ulcer does not arise from the stomach's acidity; rather, it comes from a defect in the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital workman" or spiritual governor of a body part</note> of that specific part, or from a contraction of contagion. Consequently, an ulcer is not calmed by taking an alkali; instead, one needs "secrets" <note>Arcana; highly refined chemical medicines</note> that can penetrate anywhere. For food, drink, and medicines lose their specific power around the first digestion of the stomach; they do not go higher or travel further because they simply provide nourishment. Therefore, they strip away every mask that is unsuitable for nutrition and essentially spit it out, or otherwise change it into excrement. In this way, they also become useless for the intended healing.

<margin>25.</margin> But if the crab stone is a <term>diuretic</term> <note>A substance that promotes urination</note>, it is not because we should expect it to actually travel all the way into the bladder, or that its power remains untouched and unbroken until then. Far from it! Let it be enough if that stone strips the entire drink of its souring power. For it is that acidity alone—even if only a tiny amount of it is carried into the urine—that is capable of producing <term>strangury</term> <note>Painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>, <term>dysuria</term> <note>Difficulty urinating</note>, and the burning sensations familiar to <term>Lithiasis</term> <note>The formation of stones in the kidney or bladder</note>. For although acidity is normally overcome by healthy bile, even a tiny amount of it can be hostile in the urine and the parts that serve it, no less than to the rest of the household of digestions. Now, at last, I return to the "Right of the Duumvirate" <note>The "Duumvirate" is Helmont's term for the stomach and spleen acting together as the body's primary control center</note>, so that it may be clear how the soul, within its own body, exercises its commands in various ways. It acts by way of command, moderation, and governance, but also by way of ferocity, fury, and tyranny. For this, it does not need pipes, winds, vapors, soot, or—least of all—the help of heat, cold, or "flows" (catarrhs). The <term>Schools</term> <note>The traditional medical establishment following the ancient teachings of Galen</note>, seeing the effects of the Duumvirate and thinking they could link causes to each individual effect, attributed everything to "burnings" or "humors" and their settling in the body. They acted as if the things that happen naturally within us occurred only through the urgent necessity of weights, heats, and imaginary humors. And since they moved away from the soul and living powers toward artificial or dead mathematical examples, they finally found themselves working in vain. To their own surprise, and despite experience and the common observations of the people, they have placed most diseases on the list of "incurable," or into the category of things that heal on their own under the care of the kitchen. They have done this only after they have bled the veins and purged the bowels several times, even to the point of the patient's death or total exhaustion. And in the end, it is usually a "quack" or an old woman who cures those whom the "experiences" of the physicians had abandoned.

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' containing a small woodcut illustration of a landscape with trees and a building.</image-desc> It is a saying of **Hippocrates**: *In those whose vein in the upper abdomen pulses strongly, the mind soon grows sick.* For the artery of the spleen is very active; yet its pulse is not manifest as long as one is in good health and thinking clearly. But when things go wrongly, it soon announces madness with a strong pulse, reaching into the left ear, and often audible even to those sitting nearby. This is clear in the spine when pressed with a finger, whose pulse was previously unknown, but is then agitated with a troublesome and hard pulse before the finger even swells. Therefore, madness is shown to proceed from a disturbed spleen. Likewise—

<margin>2.</margin> The "Old Man" <note>Hippocrates</note> placed "black bile" in the <term>precordia</term> <note>original: "præcordiis"; literally 'before the heart,' but used by Van Helmont to mean the upper stomach and diaphragm area.</note> (for the name of the precordia implies that the stomach takes the place of the heart) and from there he predicted **Epilepsy**, if it entered the body, but **Madness**, if it entered the soul. Therefore, he derives both forms of mental impotence from the precordia. These states flourish most where their "occasional cause" is present.

<column-break/>

And so the Schools testify: where the workshop of madness lies hidden, there also in health is the seat of right judgment, according to their own axiom: *A function is corrupted in the same part where it is a complete function in the healthy; and vice versa.* <margin>3.</margin> For all forms of Madness (except for those related to deep sleep) take away wakefulness. This is a certain argument that sleep, stupor, wakefulness, and madness live in the same lodging. Just as sleep, wakefulness, imagination, and dreaming are powers revolving around the same subject, and occur in the same organ and lodging. I admit indeed that sleep comes after wakefulness, but that does not prove a variety of the "lodging subject." For it is indubitable that in an instant every operation of the Mind ceases through hanging, etc. Therefore, if the head were the <margin>4.</margin> proper place of the imagination, the operations of the Mind would persevere, yet they fall away as soon as light <note>The vital spirit or consciousness</note> is denied from the lower parts.

<margin>5.</margin> **Galen** proposes the ash of burnt crabs against the rabies caused by a dog. This rabies seethes in the "desiring" faculty, or in the fear of liquids—hence the name **Hydrophobia**. Therefore, rabies lies in the part belonging to the desiring power. For a lye <note>An alkaline solution</note> made from crabs is not suited to be carried to the Brain. Nothing goes there that has not first been transformed in the stomach; one does not reach the fifth or sixth stages of digestion except through the first and second. Thus, that rabies occurs by intervals—namely, when a cup is offered, it rages in the desiring faculty—yet no one has ever assigned the desiring of drinks to the brain. Therefore, when a rabid dog bit the finger of Doctor Baldus, that poison crept from the finger into the stomach, as if into the first organ of the sensitive soul. It reached even to the Spleen, which is curved toward it: whither the remedy of that lye is directed, so that it may be subjected to the <term>hypochondriac passion</term> <note>A 17th-century term for emotional or mental distress believed to originate in the organs of the upper abdomen (the hypochondria).</note>.

<margin>6.</margin> But lest the Schools detract from the dignity of the Brain, they concede that this madness indeed has a "point of origin" in the spleen, yet they insist the "point of arrival" is within the skull. In this, they say nothing that can be excused. For even if it ceases...

# THE RIGHT OF THE DUUMVIRATE.

Let the doubt cease for a time: it is enough that at the starting point, there is the first movement of a corrupted imagination. They will quickly respond: the humoral and occasional cause in the spleen is not to be accused; therefore, the construction of imaginations must occur outside the head. But soon, by the strength of more arguments, I will gradually reveal this.

<margin>7.</margin> *Petrus Bor Christiani* <note>Pieter Christiaenszoon Bor (1559–1635), a Dutch historian famous for his 'Annals of the Netherlands'.</note>, in his *Annals of Belgium*, relates that in the year 1564, in *Brussels*, a sow gave birth to six offspring. The first of these (for the last to be conceived is always the first born among animals) had a human head, face, arms, and legs, but from the neck down, the whole trunk of the body was that of a pig. For the mother was undoubtedly a sow. Therefore, the *Heart*, the *Spleen*, and the rest of the vegetative organs were similar to the mother's. Thus, although it had the head of a man, it possessed only a sensitive soul. It is surely a Sodomitic monster <note>A term used in early modern medicine to describe animal-human hybrids, often attributed to "unnatural" acts.</note> more like the mother than the father. So from a sheep mother and a goat father, a lamb comes forth which, besides the wool and the tail, has other sheep-like qualities. So a mule comes from a donkey father and a mare mother. And so a horse from a bull and a mare. In seven rabbits born from a dormouse father and a rabbit mother, nothing was like the father except the tail. If, therefore, that monster had a pig's soul, it follows that the condition of the soul depends not on the head, but on the lower members. And the very prerogative of the imaginative soul dwells in the *Duumvirate* <term>Duumvirate: Van Helmont's term for the stomach and spleen acting together as the body's governing center</term>, even though the head is the conducting part for concepts formed in the lower parts; it is indeed in the center <margin>8.</margin> and middle of the body. I have demonstrated elsewhere that the *Spleen* inspires the digestive ferment into the stomach: that is to say, the spleen is the beginning of vegetative life. But the vegetative power belongs to the sensitive soul, that is, to the *Duumvirate*. For there is not a separate "vegetative soul": but it is a vital power <margin>9.</margin>, a rival of the soul. The fetus, however, grows <note>original: "vegetatur"</note> before its animation <term>empsychosis: the moment the soul enters the body</term> solely by the influence of participation from the mother, so long as it is, as it were, an integral part of her. But soon after its own animation, it lives by its own "kitchen" <note>Van Helmont often uses the metaphor of a kitchen for the stomach's digestive heat.</note>. Therefore, there is only

<column-break/>

a sensitive soul in animals. Because this is also in man, and the Mind is bound to it, therefore the soul's concepts are first in the seat of the soul; perhaps, even if they are refined in the head, they nonetheless do not deny their source. Indeed, even if they were forged anew in the *Brain*, they would not for this reason require a journey, like a pilgrimage, for the succession of movements from the soul to the head. For the commands of the will are far coarser than concepts; yet, once the command of a motion is conceived, the finger of a lute-player executes it with the greatest speed.

<margin>10.</margin> Therefore, the actions of the *Governance* <term>Regimen: the vital governing principle of the body</term> radiate upon their objects with uninterrupted light. Thus, the discourse, matched to its own workshops, takes laws from both sides and, in turn, establishes others. Otherwise, the phantasms of the *Brain* are loose and confused if a harm from the *Spleen* intervenes. This is evident in hanging, febrile delirium, hypochondria, rabies, *Apopleptics*, *epileptics*, etc. From which it is clear enough that the *Brain* obeys the delirious *Duumvirate*.

<margin>11.</margin> For it is most agreeable to the truth that the wisdom of the flesh and blood (which belongs to the sensitive soul) has its seat in the most bloody organ of all. Therefore, we read in the *Sacred Scriptures* <note>Likely referring to Leviticus 17:11: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood."</note> that the soul and life are in the blood. For if you consider the organ of the spleen and its substance, you will judge its functional tissue <term>parenchyma: the essential functional parts of an organ</term> to be newly curdled blood, covered by a skin, and enriched with such a manifold weaving of veins and arteries that there is no other organ in the whole body that is so rich, having ten times as many arteries. But the *Brain*, in nearly its whole mass, has little vein or blood. The *Meninges* <note>original: "Menynges"</note>, or the coverings of the *Brain*, do have their small veins. And although in the cavity of the *Brain* there is an arterial vessel fit for breathing out spirits worked in the heart, the mass of the *Brain* is almost entirely bloodless <note>original: "exsanguis"</note>. It is no wonder then that the *Spleen*, under an exotic guest, forms foreign *Ideas* and strange concepts. While the spleen meditates on the expulsion of this guest, it excites a strong pulse, just as a thorn driven into a finger announces the present and hated guest.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the spleen and stomach (the Duumvirate) are the true seat of the soul and vital governance, using a 1564 account of a hybrid sow-human birth to prove that the soul's nature follows the torso's organs rather than the head. He further supports this by contrasting the blood-rich spleen with the bloodless brain, aligning with the biblical principle that life resides in the blood.</summary>

<margin>12.</margin> announces. For I have seriously observed the eyes and the grim face of the <term>hypochondriac</term> <note>In the 17th century, a "hypochondriac" was someone suffering from a physical disorder of the organs under the ribcage (the hypochondria), particularly the spleen, which was thought to cause melancholy and irrational thoughts.</note>, immediately as often as he would report to me his foolish and first conceptions: and as soon as I interrupted him in his beginning delirium, at that very moment his eyes and face would return to their original state of health. I marveled with compassion that such a swift and significant transformation of the whole face, so often repeated, could be propagated from the actions of the lower region into the "citadel" of the Brain. Furthermore, it is not only crude and uncomposed concepts that belong to the spleen; but even when the understanding of the Brain is lulled to sleep during dreams, a not-to-be-despised light of gifts reaches the Mind. <margin>Acts of the Apostles cap. 2. vers. 17.</margin> *And it shall come to pass in the last days: I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. And your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.* <note>original: "Et erit in novissimis diebus..." Van Helmont is quoting the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> These are, of course, significant dreams. *Night unto night shows knowledge* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:2</note>, if the watchful person first learns to withdraw his thoughts from things, place, and motion. <margin>13.</margin> I have also not asserted without reason that the first concepts of disturbances are felt in the <term>precordia</term> <note>The area of the chest and upper abdomen, surrounding the heart and stomach.</note>. For if sad news is brought to a hungry man, his appetite immediately vanishes. Therefore, the news and the appetite fall into the same "lodging." I have also taught elsewhere that the "stomach of the liver" is not some remarkable cavity lying open within the organ itself; but rather the veins of the mesentery are the casing for <term>sanguification</term> <note>The process of making blood.</note>, into which the liver radiates its first "breaths" of blood-making. But the "stomach of the spleen" is the stomach itself, which the spleen embraces and cherishes in such a way that it inspires it with the "Vulcan" <note>An alchemical metaphor for heat or transformative fire.</note> of digestion. Yet the spleen has another and proper "stomach" of its own, marvelous for the many-folded tortuosity of its arteries, by which the spleen "cooks" for itself alone. Under this digestion, if the smallest error should rush in, the spleen ceases its digesting and denies the necessary ferments to the external stomach. This is evident in fever, when in place of acidic digestion, <term>nidorous</term> <note>Smelling like burnt or decaying animal matter; refers here to foul-smelling belches.</note> belches occur, mimicking some kind of putrefaction. The Brain also, by its own insensibility, the spleen, as well as the <term>meninges</term> <note>The membranes covering the brain.</note> of the Brain, refer to the sto-

<column-break/>

-mach itself in this part. For the action of the stomach is authoritative, and it holds within itself a deputy-ship of the Heart, and it executes its duties, despite what the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic medical authorities of the time, typically those following Galen and Aristotle, whom Van Helmont frequently challenged.</note> might say. Nor does the spleen flourish with its concepts in vain, with such a fruitful, vital, and wealthy number of arteries: <margin>14.</margin> but as often as it lulls its own concepts to sleep with the delights of other nourishment, it gives a truce from work: that is, sleep. If these concepts are less than perfect, or disturbed by excessive anxiety of the stomach, it also produces confused dreams. <margin>15.</margin> No physician has doubted until now that the <term>ephialtes</term> <note>A traditional term for a nightmare, specifically the feeling of being pressed down by a heavy weight.</note>, or the incubus, is stirred up from the precordia: for it usually arrives after taking a larger meal of harder food. Or otherwise, when the stomach is laboring. Therefore, this happens not to one lying on the right side, but only to one sleeping on his back, or at least on the left side. This occurs when sleep is nearly sufficient. For they feel obscurely, they reason, they think they touch with their hands and see with their eyes: yet they are not able to move themselves. They feel themselves being heard, and they feel the oppressions. Otherwise, in sleeping, others (even the sick) move themselves freely. Indeed, the stomach is burdened and weighed down, and its concoction is not yet finished, and therefore it happens to those lying on their left side—the direction in which the mouth of the stomach is twisted. From this, it first becomes obvious: that the stomach commands movement, and especially in this, it moderates sleep, dreams, and movement all at once. For the dreams of the <term>incubus</term> <note>A nightmare.</note> are almost always the same, as is the inability to move, as long as the stomach, <margin>61.</margin> thus ill-affected, is distended by sleep. For the Schools assign the causes of the incubus to thick vapors invading the spinal medulla. And indeed, they attack these vapors because of the momentary resolution of that harm. For if the dreamers wake up immediately, the incubus also immediately ceases. And so, at the whim of the one waking up, those vapors ought to cease. Finally, I hear "thick vapors" accused in most causes of diseases: <margin>17.</margin> but I confess that in 50 solid years of distillations, I have never yet seen

He argues instead for the influence of the "Duumvirate"—the stomach-spleen axis—over the nervous system and the brain.</meta>

...to this place a thick vapor. There are indeed bodily exhalations in which a volatile thing is sublimated and climbs to the sides of a vessel. In this way, thick soots certainly ascend from sulfur, orpiment <note>Arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment.</note>, wood, arsenic, sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used in chemistry and metalworking.</note>, camphor, urine, and likewise from Mercury, lead, cadmia <note>A zinc-based oxide or ore found on the walls of smelting furnaces.</note>, copper, and so on; but I have not yet seen or known aqueous vapors, specifically thick ones, except among Academics who are ignorant of vapors. Indeed, however thick they might be, they would at least lose their thickness at the whim of the one awakening the person, and the heat that had stirred up such vapors would be stopped immediately. Both ideas are truly ridiculous. Finally, they suggest that the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>original: "medullam... spinali"</note> is affected because motion is denied in a dream. And thus, at the whim of the person waking, every affection of the spinal cord and every obstructing vapor would cease. This is equally full of frivolous thoughtlessness. But how can someone lying on their back send thick vapors from the stomach into the loins and the spinal cord, which is enclosed within the vertebrae and covered by membranes? Into a place where, as they say elsewhere, even the thinnest winds cannot penetrate? Especially since the position of such a person lying down would, by its nature, banish vapors from the stomach into the intestines, or carry them upward across the stomach into the navel, rather than downward to the enclosed spinal cord weighed down by the intestines? What does speech have in common with the spinal cord? Why would thick vapors from the stomach seek only the <term>recurrent nerves</term> <note>These are the branches of the vagus nerve that control the larynx; damage or blockage to them causes loss of voice.</note>? For the <term>Incubus</term> <note>Known today as sleep paralysis, often accompanied by the sensation of a weight on the chest and a terrifying "night-mare."</note> not only makes one hear internal whispers and allows them to wander—even to feel fear—but external things are also heard, both real and apparent. Yet one cannot move the tongue, no matter how much others might speak during the dream. Do the Schools perhaps think that the movements of the tongue are produced by the spinal cord? Those thick vapors would therefore be far different from dream-vapors, which do not impede the use and motion of the tongue, nor indeed of the whole body. For while they focus on the nerves to provide causes for immobility, the Schools themselves become mute and immobile. Since they never understand what they say, so

<column-break/>

too they do not understand how those thick (that is, impossible) vapors will penetrate the stomach, the abdomen, the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart.</note> extended through the back with its pulsating companion, the artery, and likewise the ligaments of the vertebrae. And how will these things become silent, be calmed, and cease in an instant if, by chance, the one suffering the Incubus is awakened? They would certainly have learned more correctly the action of the governance of the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>Van Helmont's term for the partnership between the stomach and the spleen as the seat of vital governance.</note>: namely, that an impediment offered to the stomach disturbs the Brain, the nerves, and corrupts the first conceptions by its vital governance alone, without vapors or tubes—insofar as it interrupts the comforts of the spleen. Thus, it happens that <term>apoplectics</term> <note>Those suffering from a stroke.</note> and paralytics can eat, hear, sleep, etc., yet cannot speak. For the Schools blame the blockage of the recurrent nerves. Why then does the Incubus not look to these nerves rather than the spinal cord? Why do remedies for the Duumvirate help apoplectics, those with vertigo, and those unable to walk or speak—with the drugs, I say, still present in the hollow of the stomach, while the effect on the recurrent nerves and the head has vanished? Does perhaps a <term>pica</term> <note>A disorder involving an appetite for non-nutritive substances.</note> have those nerves congested before speech?

<margin>18.</margin>
Will a cow, sticking out its mobile tongue into its nostrils, have its tongue tied? And does it lack recurrent nerves? Or otherwise, it will have them in vain if they are perpetually and naturally obstructed. A voluntary command is carried from the head to the nerves of the tongue. This is denied to a quadruped, but not to certain birds. Likewise, that command is not mastered at the first attempt, but gradually by customary practice. An apoplectic, however, does not release this command for execution because he is stunned, almost like a quadruped. Indeed, the concept of a donkey, by God's permission, once passed to its tongue <note>A reference to the biblical story of Balaam's donkey in Numbers 22, which was miraculously given the power of speech.</note>. Not indeed because the donkey was the organ of an Angel. For then it would have spoken the judgments of God, and not its own concepts, nor would it have complained about its beatings.

<margin>19.</margin>
On the occasion of the donkey, I will mention my own affairs. I was sitting on the last day of December in the year 1643, eager to write in a closed chamber; however, there was a great cold, and I ordered a brazier with lit coals to be brought, so that I might occasionally soothe the stiffness of my fingers...

# THE AUTHORITY OF THE DUUMVIRATE <note>The "Duumvirate" is Van Helmont’s term for the stomach and spleen acting as the primary governing center of the body's health and life force.</note>

...[she came] to that place. My little daughter arrived, and as soon as she smelled the harmful fumes <note>likely charcoal fumes</note>, she took away the brazier, and if she had not happened upon me, I would have died of suffocation. For I immediately felt a threatened fainting spell <note>original: "syncopen"</note> around the mouth of the stomach; I rose from my study <note>original: "museo"</note>, and while I was heading outside, I fell like a straight stick and was carried away as if dead. There was indeed a double condition: one from the bruised back of the head <note>original: "occipiti"</note>, which stole away my taste and smell and darkened my hearing; the other was the fainting, provoked from the stomach. For in those first days, my head spun with vertigo whenever I looked to the side, and much more so if I looked upward. I thought this was due to the concussion of the fall—the back of my bare head suddenly hitting the hard stone from my full height. But gradually I became more certain, and for many days I turned everything over in my mind. Thus I finally knew that the vertigo proceeded from the stomach, and was nourished there by the same root from which the fainting had arisen. For certain foods promoted that vertigo in me, especially around evening while they were not yet digested; and the "Nightmare" <note>original: "Incubo"</note> happens in almost the same way from nearly digested food. I also remembered how many times I had crossed the sea in the past: even if I was quite well and very hungry, nevertheless for many days afterward my head would spin and waver, until I had cleared the filth from my stomach with a light vomiting, in which that "spinning idea" was impressed. For I discovered that vertigo accompanied not only harmful foods, but additionally occurred at almost the hour when digestion was finished, and that by taking food and moderate wine, the vertigo was always immediately mitigated. Indeed, for a long time afterward, even though I had escaped completely free of it, I nevertheless suffered a relapse around evening from eating certain foods. Therefore, having experienced it, I believed (as the saying goes) "Robert who knows" <note>A play on the Latin proverb "experto crede Roberto"—trust the one who has experience.</note> that all vertigo climbs from below, without vapor or smoke; but rather, through the governance of action alone, the head listens to the stomach. And what is more, during the vertigo that threatened a fall, all reasoning began to spin, which was immediately restored once wine was taken.

<column-break/>

And so I understood that it was not indeed the food left in the stomach, but that the primary source <note>original: "fomitem"</note> of the fainting had received a harmful impression from the taint of an unworthy food. Hence, through the "Sulfur of Vitriol" <note>An alchemical preparation, often a sedative or tonic in Helmontian medicine.</note> I was also made free of it. Elsewhere I have explained the "Governor of the Pylorus" <note>The valve at the exit of the stomach.</note> with its twenty dignities, so that it might be established that the stomach is in every part and every corner the seat of the soul. Yet it is so that just as the mouth of the stomach presides over and dominates the head and the principal faculties, so also the Pylorus commands the lower parts. For I have observed a more atrocious colic turn into paralysis at one time, while at another it produced a contraction of the hands, feet, arms, and legs. I have also seen stomach pains so sharp that they took away all movement and caused a condition similar to Tetanus, which our local peasants call "the shot" <note>original: "injaculationem" / "Geschot"</note>, as if it were suspected and sent by witches; and a not uncommon sciatic pain accompanies these. To this end, I have seen bloodlettings, laxatives, enemas, plasters, ointments, cauteries, and similar things applied, and with a vanishing result. For the efforts of those who would ordain a remedy for the symptoms or the results, and bypass the springs gushing from the Pylorus, were crushed. I have observed that small, warm poultices <note>original: "fomenta"</note> for the most part calmed the storm, because they assist the internal and domestic *Archeus* <note>The vital, governing spirit that directs the functions of an organ.</note> of the intestines with a remedy and pacify him in his indignation. Wherefore I warn the reader to notice the stumblings of the Schools <note>The traditional Galenic medical universities.</note>, who attribute these things to their "catarrhs" and "flows of phlegm" as if to a sacred anchor of ignorance. But a certain history is worthy of note: A fifty-year-old man with a hernia, through neglect of his truss, suffered an intestinal hernia <note>original: "enterocelem"</note> which soon grew to the size of a head and hardened in a marvelous way. All night he renewed warm poultices of milk and cow dung and tried to push it back. But in vain. Indeed, it had turned into a single hard swelling, continuous like a pot, and it took away the hope that it could return,

...[be] possible, through an opening ten times smaller. Therefore, we offered a draught of wine that had been boiled once with crushed seeds (namely Anise, Caraway, Fennel, and Coriander, equal parts of each) and immediately the hardness was softened, and the hernia allowed itself to be pushed back. In this, the hardness along with such a great swelling must be carefully considered. For these surely did not owe their existence to wind or feces. Rather, the hardness lies beneath the Pylorus <note>The lower opening of the stomach leading into the small intestine.</note>. Therefore, it did not seem to be a body adjacent to the ducts of the ileum <note>The final section of the small intestine.</note>, but seemed to be a single continuous unit. Furthermore, the ileum did not subside when the patient lay down, nor did it rush forward spontaneously into such a mass; rather, it was thrust there by a more powerful force of the governing system. Finally, such a bump and such hardness does not protrude in women. For this reason, an injury to the Testis <note>In 17th-century anatomy, this could refer to the ovaries in women or the testes in men; here, Helmont links reproductive organs to stomach reactions.</note> excites the Pylorus into a rage. And therefore, the entire remedy consists in the mitigation of its rage. Moreover, I have seen several great nobles perish miserably, led away by hope placed in physicians who used topical treatments according to Galenic absurdities <note>References to Galen, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years and whom Van Helmont frequently criticized.</note>.

<margin>21.</margin> Furthermore, from here I return to the Duumvirate, in which the soul sits. For Plato established the Heart as the seat of the soul, in humans as well as in beasts. But the Galenic Schools attribute all intellect and madness to the head, and they think they are confirmed by the Church, which baptizes the head and not the Heart. Nor do the Schools look back to the fact that murders and adulteries come from the Heart. But the common people agree with me, who point their hand to the "mouth of the stomach" <note>The cardiac orifice or epigastric region.</note> as the vital beginning or seat of the soul, whenever they are pressed by distress—namely, as much by anxieties of the body and life as by mental afflictions. For I consider that in the fetus, the sensitive power is first hidden in the organ dedicated to nutrition, and that there is a notion of what is helpful and what is harmful. Finally, in the infant and the boy, senses form more distinct concepts, which movements obey. Therefore, the brain and its clients <note>The nerves and sensory organs.</note> are moved by sense so that they may obey the initiating concepts. But the soul has not therefore withdrawn from the organ that was first placed in charge of growth. For the entire spirituality belongs to the sensitive soul.

<column-break/>

For the head is baptized because the brutal sensitivity, through the organs placed there as a spectator, was where it first deceived Eve, and death entered. For on one hand, the Schools mock the terms *Cardialgia* <note>Stomach pain or "heartburn."</note> and *Cardiogmus* <note>A term for heart distress or stomach-related pressure.</note> as if they were rustic or barbaric; but then, on the other hand, they have observed that Fainting <note>original: "Syncopen"</note> flows so immediately from the mouth of the stomach as if it resided entirely there, and surely proceeded from there. And there, too, it is immediately restored by pouring in aromatic liquids. Moreover, in fainting, they have noticed that the intellect, sense, movement, and at the same time the pulse, all collapse together: and so, from the functions which are ascribed to the head and Heart together, they suddenly climb from the stomach. Yet without a deeper investigation, they attributed the whole mass of life, intellect, and soul to the head—unable to conceive that the principles of life belong to the Duumvirate, even though they are handed over into execution through subordinate organs. As if the principle of movement were in the muscles and bones because they move!

<margin>22.</margin> A certain lawyer had taken two drachms of crushed Henbane <note>original: "Hyoscyami"</note> seed instead of Dill <note>original: "Anethi"</note>, which had been prescribed to him for colic. Immediately he became so insane from it that he could not utter an intelligible word; and he was so mad that I have never seen anything more dull or foolish. He sat indeed upright next to the hearth, but he was entirely insane and a dull madman. However, through an emetic <note>A medicine that causes vomiting.</note>, he recovered within half an hour. Nasal powders <note>original: "errhinni"</note>, sneezing-powders, and medicated caps <note>original: "cucufe"</note> for the head would have been in vain, as would have been poultices for the Heart. Indeed, whatever of that seed he had drunk through the error of the apothecary's shop <note>original: "Seplasiae"</note> was still in his stomach, and the whole of it being wrapped in mucus, he soon threw it up through vomiting. Nor was any part of it able to evaporate from there as far as the head. Yet he was entirely innocent and insane, such that he understood nothing at all, though the motor functions of the head remained strong. From this, I gathered that the intellectual powers are struck in the Duumvirate. I even had him as a guest with me at dinner.

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument that the stomach and spleen (the Duumvirate) serve as the primary seat of the human soul and intellect, rather than the brain. He is currently providing clinical and sensory evidence for why the "midriff" or pit of the stomach is where thoughts and emotions originate.</meta>

# THE AUTHORITY OF THE DUUMVIRATE <note>The "Duumvirate" is Van Helmont’s term for the partnership between the stomach and the spleen, which he believed governed the body’s life force.</note>

...to feel oneself, faster than the movement of any vapors, a threatened fainting in the midriff <note>original: "praecordiis." In 17th-century anatomy, this refers to the area around the heart and diaphragm, specifically the pit of the stomach.</note>, and that all thought is suspended without sleep. From this, anyone who is not stubborn will clearly see that the primordial concepts of the soul are formed in the midriff, and if these are taken away, the light of understanding immediately fails as well. Likewise, a fearful person, in sudden terror, feels the sign of dread in the pit of the stomach <note>original: "ore stomachi," literally the 'mouth of the stomach.'</note>; if some great, unexpected crash (think of a nearby cannon shot) is suddenly stirred up, it precedes and cuts off all action of reasoning. 

<margin>24.</margin> Therefore, if the axiom of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities following Galen and Aristotle.</note> is true—that a damaged part is identified by the impairment of its actions—then the seat of both madness and fainting, and of every defect, should be found beneath the diaphragm. <margin>25.</margin> Indeed, those who are mad are for that reason very tolerant of hunger and thirst. For in the year 1615 at Alost, I saw a nine-year-old girl, quite a spirited little daughter of the hospital steward, who for three years had eaten nothing at all, except that perhaps every eight days or more she would drink about four spoonfuls of pure water. For she had ceased to eat after being significantly terrified by thunder. It is indeed beyond controversy that terror, sadness, and similar emotions primarily affect the midriff and immediately take away all hunger. <margin>26.</margin> They clearly reflect themselves into the stomach in a way that can be felt; therefore, they cannot be referred to the head, because no such disturbance is felt to seek the head, nor the heart—unless the pit of the stomach is mistaken for the heart. Nor is it even likely that if the head first grasped and felt sadness and sudden fears, it would immediately send them down into the stomach, rather than to the nerves over which it has more intimate control. Beyond being absurd, it would be cruel to torture a part not subject to it while leaving the subject part unharmed. Indeed, a greater authority of the stomach over the head is observed than that of the head over the stomach, which I have already demonstrated many times above. For indeed, drowsiness, sleep, wakefulness, deliria, and whatever symptoms are usually attributed to the head...

<column-break/>

...are mitigated and abolished by stomach remedies, not by head remedies. Hence the proverb: *A head worthy of hellebore.* <note>original: "O caput helleboro dignum." Black hellebore was the standard ancient treatment for madness and "melancholy."</note> For although there are many types of emetics <note>medicines that cause vomiting</note>, a peculiar power is attributed to hellebore for a brain that is mad. This is not because its toxic and harmful quality reaches the head; for while the hellebore is present in the stomach, and after it is rejected, contractions occur, such as those I noted above regarding griping pains. It relieves madness, therefore, because black hellebore, more than other commonly known emetics, unburdens old fevers of the midriff and the spleen <note>original: "lien."</note>. For it has already been demonstrated above at length and with many points that nothing strikes the head through the arteries or vapors. Therefore, the aforementioned diseases and their remedies concern the Duumvirate and do not affect the brain, except through its governance or through secondary affection <note>original: "deuteropathiam." A medical term for a condition where one organ suffers because another is diseased.</note>. <margin>27.</margin> For students who study excessively feel an internal fullness, composed of vertigo and anxiety with sighs, and they point to the pit of the stomach with their hand. Then they complain of headaches. But if they persist in their efforts, they perceive a certain fainting <note>original: "lipopsychin." From the Greek for a 'leaving of the soul' or a swoon.</note> around the pit of the stomach, and then their imagination is turned upside down. Therefore, unless they promptly desist from studying, they retain a madness that recurs at intervals for their whole life. Thus, where the harm is felt, there the ruin of the intellect resides, and the soul primarily dwells. <margin>28.</margin> The Schools, on the contrary, contend that the spleen is the sewer of black bile <note>original: "atra bilis." One of the four humors in traditional medicine, believed to cause melancholy.</note>, and that it discharges itself into the stomach with its dregs. And what I call the ferment of digestion inspired into the stomach, the Academies claim is an excrement of harmful humor, and thus they think the stomach's digestion is provoked by such dross. But after I knew for certain that black bile does not exist in nature, it was easy for me to depart from the tradition of Galen concerning both the humors and the use of the parts, and to desert the "Black-Bile Schools." Concluding by their own axiom: <margin>29.</margin> If the cause of madness is in the spleen, then the residence of the discerning intellect must be owed to that same place.

Morbid lethargy, as well as artificial sleep induced by opiates, are best overcome by alkaline washes <note>original: "lixivia," solutions of wood ash or lye.</note>, which are by no means recognized as remedies for the head. Furthermore, a person needing to urinate dreams that he is relaxing his bladder and urinating in a corner (for it happens to some that by this same consensus they wet their own blankets), yet the consensus given in sleep is inhibited. For even if the Brain sleeps fully through all the organs of the senses, the discerning power of the sensitive soul is not put to rest in the midriff <note>original: "hypochondrio," the upper abdomen below the ribs.</note>. For we often feel sleep in our eyes, but none around the stomach, and thereafter almost sleepless nights pass by. And therefore it is to be suspected that he described the same things word-for-word from elsewhere, having dissected an ape, as Vesalius proves; for the ape has the aforementioned plexus in its Brain. And so, although Galen was rashly deceived regarding that plexus, he nevertheless placed the seat of judgment in the Head because of that plexus—which does not exist. Why should the beginnings of imagination not rather be taken from the plexus of arteries in the Spleen, from the Saturn of the Spleen (from which the Saturnian kingdoms <note>A reference to the mythical Golden Age of peace and innocence.</note> of the innocence of first concepts are hoped to return)? So that the Spleen may communicate its decrees to the Brain through the influence of governance, without vapors or tubes and in an instant, just as I demonstrated above through the readiness of a lute player. <margin>33.</margin> For the First-Formed Man <note>original: "Protoplastus," referring to Adam.</note> must not be presumed to have been ignorant or stupid before the Fall, since he gave proper and essential names to all living creatures; but the state of innocence was guiltless regarding lust, which is covered by the word "nakedness." Indeed, the sensitive soul did not yet exist, and therefore the immortal Mind, intuitively understanding all things in its own Seat, looked upon itself in reflection, and intimately knew within itself the animals placed under its feet in the Image of God. But after man entered the way of corruption, just as fire comes from flint, so after sin did the sensitive soul come forth with the cooperation of the Creator, and hence the concepts of the Mind were obscured. <margin>34.</margin> Now, as for what modern concepts are: first, when I say that the first concepts or first impulses are formed in the midriff <note>original: "praecordia."</note>, I do not mean the impulses of the "irascible power," which the Schools falsely denied were in our power, as if they were entirely innocent of crime. Rather, I consider thereafter, through discourse, a truly weighty matter in the concepts of the soul, which are felt to be formed around the mouth of the stomach; and meanwhile, the Mind relegates these same concepts to the head, as if into a chest of memory for deposit. From this I perceive that although the soul resides in the midriff <note>original: "praecordia," the area of the diaphragm and stomach, which Helmont identifies as the seat of the sensitive soul.</note>, it has nonetheless placed the power of remembering in the head and the power of willing in the heart. Thus, both of these are perishable <note>original: "caducas," literally falling or transitory.</note> in this life and are the companions of the sensitive soul. <margin>36.</margin> animal-like powers of the soul, the soul itself has subjected them to bodily rules, after the manner of bodies. Otherwise, the Mind <note>original: "Mens," referring to the higher, immortal part of the human spirit.</note> is entirely undivided, and contains its own memory and will beneath the unity of the intellect. Yet, in a marvelous way, these are shrouded and lulled to sleep beneath the bond of the sensitive soul, to which the Mind is tied and connected. The Mind feels a law everywhere resisting its own law—that is, the law 
<margin>37.</margin> of the Mind. For the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Scholastic academic authorities who followed Galenic and Aristotelian medicine.</note> assign the "concupiscible" <note>The desiring or lustful faculty.</note> appetite to the liver and the "irascible" <note>The faculty of anger or spiritedness.</note> to the Heart. Indeed, if they had found more internal organs, they would have given separate lodging-houses to every single disturbance of the Mind, which are prone to disorder. Yet, otherwise, these things are felt remarkably in the Duumvirate, and seethe in those first movements. It is absurd to separate the desiring

<column-break/>

and angry faculties into different seats. For when someone resists a desired thing and becomes angry, it is at least one and the same power acting. Nor are the two aforementioned faculties sequestered into organs without doing an injury to the other powers. For fear, love, desire, hatred, sluggishness, and joy do not have their own diverse stalls. All such powers belong to a single soul; they are not the scattered servants of various disturbances. Indeed, when the soul is angry, or when it rejoices or loves—even if it is affected in different ways and paints various "masks" in its Ideas—this is not the duty or construction of the organs, but the passions of the one and only soul. Because these are the "works of the flesh" and variations of the concepts of the sensitive soul, they are manufactured by the soul in the seat of the Duumvirate. The Spleen, therefore, being intent upon its own reflections at intervals, and seeking delights and remedies for weariness, 
<margin>38.</margin> steals a third part of life from us through sleep. Just as it brings forth dreams while sleeping, so while awake, it propagates slightly more distinct and less somnolent cognitions and concepts. Truly, unless the Lord cherishes us by His grace, we dream throughout our entire life with confused concepts; indeed, we do not even perceive ourselves to understand, while, as the light of the Spleen is disturbed or ceases, the Brain hardly receives the first concepts of Ideas as they deserve. Sleep is therefore 
<margin>39.</margin> stirred up in the midriff, and notably manifests itself in the head; thus the head does not blush to obey the consensus of the midriff. Therefore, the "cold constipations of vapors" <note>Helmont is mocking the traditional theory that sleep was caused by cold vapors rising from the stomach to the brain.</note> are lying parents of sleep. For there is in the 
<margin>40.</margin> sulfur of the vitriol of Venus <note>original: "sulfure vitrioli Veneris," a chemical preparation of copper (Venus) vitriol that Helmont claimed had a narcotic but healing effect.</note> a narcotic power that is sleep-inducing, warm, and sweeter than honey, whereas in opium it is bitter. From this it becomes obvious that sleep is not a "privative force" that blocks and chills (especially after food and the drinking of wine), but a created faculty in the Spleen that is superior to wakefulness. So too, certain poisons alienate the Mind and use their own native "phantastic" power—by which they dispose ours (as in the "apple of Eve" <note>likely a reference to the poisonous thorn-apple or mandrake.</note>, the saliva of a rabid dog, the bite of a Tarantula, henbane, etc.)—according to their own pleasure. I at least believe that Venus is a function of the sensitive soul, and therefore must be located in that part where the first motions occur, even while we are sleeping. For nature was in no way more solicitous than in the distinction of the sexes. And so, from the beginning of the sketching of the fetus, it is immediately occupied in the organs of Venus. And perhaps this is even what the Ancients intended when they ascribed the spleen to Saturn—the first of the minor gods—and attributed to him the first paternity. Indeed, they depicted fauns and satyrs (a most lustful and scurrilous race) with the features of Saturn. Furthermore, nocturnal emissions <note>original: "pollutiones."</note> do not happen while one is awake: because sleep is an effect of the spleen, and is a delight to it. Otherwise, what commonality would the kidneys have with sleep? Does one not urinate more frequently while awake than while sleeping? Does sleep not (according to the Schools) suspend all excretions, except for sweat and useless seed? Certainly, a spontaneous emission would be more prone to happen to one who is awake than to one who is sleeping. However, such an excretion flows out during the sleep of lechery, so as to reveal that the organ for sleep, dreams, and emissions is the same, just as they are the handiwork of a single soul. For just as the making of blood <note>term: sanguificatio; the process of turning food into blood.</note> begins in the veins of the mesentery—acting as the stomach for the liver—so the "cooking" <note>term: coctio; the metabolic process of refining a substance.</note> of the sperm is performed in the testes by the spleen. For I remember men with stones in both kidneys who were nevertheless quite lustful. It would be absurd for a healthy and provocative power to persist under a disease of its own radical organ. For blood-making does not emerge correctly if the liver is badly affected, nor is vision fit if the eye is filled with sand. Nor will I ever believe that the kidneys, continually dripping with urine and occupied with the expulsion of excrement, never resting, are intended for luxury. It seemed, therefore, to be a "fecal dogma" <note>original: "dogma excrementosum."</note> to suggest that the motions for propagating the species, the summons of the vital faculties, and the character of the Mind, are forged in a stable of foreign filth. For the first motions of Venus

For if death entered through the first motions <note>A reference to the Fall of Man.</note>: it is consistent that this falling, degenerate life should also have had to take its beginning fundamentally from that same place. For in the trunk of the body, the 
<margin>44.</margin> orifice of the stomach holds the place of the center: from which the rays are most conveniently scattered both upward and downward. As for the fact that 
<margin>45.</margin> Abraham is written to have carried the Messiah in his loins: that has been foolishly led away from the spleen to the kidneys—from a most vital organ, I say, to a workshop and excremental sieve. It is a gift of God in this simple <note>term: simple; a medicinal remedy consisting of only one primary ingredient.</note>.

# ### ###

<header>The Right of the DUUMVIRATE.</header>

When the governance <note>Latin: *regimen*; the internal directing power of the body</note> is withdrawn, the strengths of the parts (no matter how primary they are) are immediately eclipsed. This is the cause of faints, apoplexy, epilepsy, palpitations, dizziness, and madness. And so it is that for those defects whose "occasional root" <note>The underlying cause or trigger of a disease</note> is consumed and vanishes of its own accord (as happens in milder fevers), their cycles and durations likewise fall silent of their own accord, so that they "forget to return"—regardless of how much the boasts of physicians
<margin>53.</margin> may vary on this matter. Indeed, those diseases whose roots cling more stubbornly are more deeply mixed into the constitution; otherwise, they entirely resist a spontaneous resolution. Consequently, they grow old along with the nourishments of the stomach and wait to bear their recurring fruits even at the very end of life. Therefore, an epitaph of "incurability" is now written everywhere for these diseases that do not cease on their own. This is because, until now, people have lacked the worthy "arcanum" <note>term: arcanum; a secret, powerful medicinal secret or "hidden" remedy used by alchemists</note> by which they might be uprooted. As long as the roots of these diseases only affect the "flowing spirit" <note>Latin: *spiritus influus*; the vital breath or energy that flows through the nerves</note>, they produce offspring specific to their own seed and host. Thus, epilepsy, because it besieges both types of spirit <note>The flowing spirit and the indwelling spirit</note>, crushes the faculties of both the body and the sensitive soul. In this way, he distinguished a "great" apoplexy from a "small" one: the minor affects the flowing spirit,
<margin>54.</margin> while the major besieges the "indwelling spirit" <note>Latin: *spiritus insitus*; the spirit fixed within a specific organ</note>. Likewise, there are "simples" <note>term: simple; a medicinal remedy consisting of only one primary ingredient, usually a plant</note> that cause drunkenness, sleep, lethargy, forgetfulness, stupidity, madness, rage, insanity, or delirium—precisely because they contain these qualities within themselves. For within the "Apple of the Knowledge of Good and Evil" <note>A reference to the forbidden fruit in Eden</note> there was such a power. There are other substances that provoke love, anger, or even feelings directed toward only certain persons. Thus, while the monarchy of the life and body remains stable, they disturb only the functions of the soul. There are, furthermore, those that observe certain stages. For instance, those who previously complained about being troubled by tedious or sad things against their will eventually succumb to actual madness. There are also things that instill cowardice or terrors regarding only specific objects. Others remember everything they did while in a state of rage, and only the 
<column-break/>
judgment of the mind is seen to be shattered. I say that all these strike at the head, but they do not *originate* from the head. This is proven by the "hypochondriac passion" alone <note>In the 17th century, "hypochondria" referred to a physical disease of the upper abdomen (the hypochondrium), often involving the spleen and stomach</note>. It foretells a storm and an approaching attack if a vein pulses with a strong and unusual turbulence. Yet, until now, the action of this governance has been neglected, and the animated faculty of the "Duumvirate" <note>The partnership of the stomach and spleen</note> has wandered as a stranger, while doctors have fruitlessly sweated over the false purgings of "black bile" <note>Latin: *atra bilis*; one of the four humors of traditional Galenic medicine, thought to cause melancholy</note>. That is, they have labored in vain by "melting away" the patient's strength. (Meanwhile, the "quartan fever" <note>A malaria-like fever that recurs every four days, notoriously difficult to cure</note> has always laughed at and cut down the hopes and boasts of the medical Schools.) Therefore, all power over madness and stubborn diseases has been wrongly attributed to "atrabiliary vapors" <note>Vapors supposed to rise from black bile</note>. Thus, it is clearer than
<margin>55.</margin> the noonday sun that in cases of madness, nothing is known; in apoplexy, nothing is put into practice; in "suffocations of the womb" <note>Historically called *strangulatio uteri*; a condition where the uterus was thought to migrate and cause choking</note>, nothing useful is achieved; and finally, in epileptic seizures, nothing is thought of except for empty tortures of the body, "liquefying" slaughters <note>Likely referring to excessive bloodletting</note>, and the vain loss of strength.
<margin>56.</margin> For often, doctors have tried in vain to help mania with massive doses of "soporifics" <note>Sleep-inducing drugs like opium</note>. Even at four times the usual dose, they barely bring sleep; therefore, the administration of these drugs is full of terror. But fury is not diminished by sleep or by chains. For narcotics produce sleep, but also "troubled dreams." Indeed, madness is nothing but a "waking dream." Therefore,
<margin>57.</margin> opiates bring a sleep that is harmful and full of labor. For whoever cannot resolve the "occasional cause" of a quartan fever from the Spleen should much less turn his hand toward curing madness. For madness, even without a "material error" <note>A physical lesion or structural damage</note> in the brain, usually sits in the hypochondrium, and for that reason, it is passed down to descendants. In this, indeed, does
<margin>58.</margin> "mania" differ from "delirium": the former lacks "filth" <note>Latin: *sordibus*; physical waste or humors</note>. Those who refuse to learn will laugh when I assert that one or a few "arcana" of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note> are effective against every disease. I will satisfy them on that point in due time. But for now, it is enough to repeat that there is one soul in man, located in the stomach as if in its own bed, from which all vital powers are drawn. And whatever disturbs this soul...

-># THE RIGHT OF THE DUUMVIRATE<-

# ### ###

<header>The Right of the DUUMVIRATE.</header>

[The disease root] disturbs or provokes: it is compelled to retreat through the unity of the remedy itself, if that remedy contains within itself the strength and essence of all the body’s members. 
<margin>59.</margin> To make this more manifest, I will share a case history. I once saw an obese body whose entire store of fat was dissolved into a fluid, which was then excreted through the urine. For I could not believe that the kidneys possessed the task of transforming fat—which was stretched beneath the skin—into water. Rather, I believed that this must be granted to the same faculty <note>The internal "intellect" or governing power of a specific organ</note> that originally formed the blood into fat. That is to say, it belongs to the same faculty, when it is altered, to convert fat back into fluid, just as its previous office was to produce fat from blood. 

It is not the "dignity of things" <note>The inherent quality of the food or matter itself</note> that makes us fat or thin. For quite often, many grow fat despite having wasted or stone-ridden kidneys. Instead, it is clearly evident from this that the stomach holds the "principality" <note>term: principality; the primary seat of governance and command in the body</note>. Just as a root governs the whole tree—directing this "comedy of digestions" <note>The complex, almost theatrical interplay of transformations within the body</note> in the leaves, fruits, and bark as much as in the wood, marrow, and branches—so too does the same occur within us, by the power of the Duumvirate. 

For one often encounters a Capuchin monk, burdened by long fasting and drinking very little (and that being only thin beer), yet who is endowed with a stout bodily habit. Conversely, one sees gluttons, raised on luxurious feasts, who are remarkably thin. Truly, as I ponder both these cases, I find that the foundational digestion of the stomach is the governess of all the others, which are subordinate to it. 
<margin>60.</margin> But it is at least a wonder how dissolved oily fat migrates back into its former watery fluid—indeed, back into the veins—and is finally drawn to the kidneys by a "summons" <note>Latin: *classica*; a trumpet call or military signal to assemble</note>. This entire process is truly shrouded in darkness unless we accept that a single life-force, from its own seat, has full power, authority, and faculty over the entire body. By this power, Hippocrates dictated that the whole body "breathes in and breathes out." <note>Greek: *ἄπνοιν καὶ ἔκπνοιν ὅλον* (apnoin kai ekpnoin holon). This refers to the ancient medical idea that the entire organism is a single, unified breathing entity.</note> In contemplation of this, I have said elsewhere that man is called an "animal" only by an injurious name. For he who gave proper names to all living creatures did not give 

<column-break/>

one to himself—because a true knowledge of himself was lacking, as it could not be found within the scope of mere "animals," nor did it exist there. He immediately saw that, even if no specific character presented itself to represent him to himself, there was something present in human nature that climbed above the lot of animated beings. And the Scholars could have sufficiently investigated this with Adam, if only they had considered for once why only man laughs. 
<margin>61.</margin> Indeed, laughter does not arise from the admiration of things present or past. For an infant often greets those speaking to it with a laugh. Therefore, laughter arises from the connection of the "double soul," <note>The Helmontian idea that humans possess both a sensitive soul, shared with animals, and an immortal mind given by God.</note> which beasts lack. 

To be sure, the sensitive soul—the fountain and origin of our first concepts—considering something pleasing to itself, conceives of it in joy just as the animals do. But while the Mind, in its penetrating light, feels itself to be a companion to the sensitive soul, it condescends (as if in wonder) to the pleasant concepts of the sensitive soul, marvelling that there is something worthy of joy: and from this comes laughter. For the Mind does the same thing in laughter as the sensitive soul does on its own in the body through the "tickling of an itch." <note>Latin: *titillationem odaxiſmi*; a reference to a tingling or prickly sensation that induces a reaction.</note> For anyone might jump if they even see a teaser threatening to tickle them. 

The soul, in its seat, understands and knows the matter; often it cannot find the full reason for this in the head, even though it may have distinctly known it at times, pronounced it, and furrowed it into the case of memory. It is clear, then, that the Duumvirate consists of its own intellect, belonging to the immortal mind, and additionally an intellect or "imaginative power" <note>Latin: *vis phantaſtica*</note> of the sensitive soul, using its various organs distributed in different ways. Yet the "college" <note>The unified assembly or governing council of these bodily powers</note> of these organs is celebrated within the seat of the soul.

I have now explained how the Duumvirate exercises its rights over the intestines, the heart, the head, and the nerves—even over dizziness and the principal faculties of the mind. It remains now to explain how much power it has over the lungs. Where, first of all, it is obvious...

-># THE RIGHT OF THE DUUMVIRATE.<-

# ### ###

<header>The Right of the DUUMVIRATE.</header>

<margin>62.</margin> Because those who, due to an overly sedentary life, find their breath easily cut off at the slightest movement, I have often freed them with a single emetic <note>original: "vomitorio"; a substance used to induce vomiting to clear the stomach</note>. From this, I remained confirmed in my belief that the entire difficulty was located in the areas bordering the stomach, and that the lung itself was to be held innocent. As for what concerns coughs, it is indeed clear that certain opiates work quite freely, and command not only that the patient sleep better, longer, or more quietly; but I remember that when the Laudanum of Paracelsus <note>A famous opium-based preparation created by the Swiss physician Paracelsus</note> was taken, even if it provided almost sleepless nights to the coughing patient, it nevertheless so pacified the cough and restrained the copious, yellow, and thick phlegm. Soon after, these were not only diminished in quantity but were also changed into pale mucous sputum, and then into white. Most importantly, when the opiate taken late was returned through vomiting in the morning, it testified that the suspended cough—and simultaneously the generation of throat-clearings, which had been so horrid in quantity and color—had ceased.

<margin>63.</margin> Especially regarding such sputa or throat-clearings, I believe I have abundantly demonstrated elsewhere that they do not flow down from the head into the larynx—which is the delusion of the "catarrh" theory <note>The ancient medical belief that mucus was a waste product "dripping" from the brain</note>. Therefore, it is sufficiently clear that they are manufactured without ceasing in the passage of the windpipe <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"; literally the 'rough artery,' the historical term for the trachea</note> itself. Consequently, a medicine still in the stomach, mixed with other foods from dinner, can restrain the ailment so that the nutritional fluid does not turn into a corrupt form in the larynx and withdraw into such copious mucus. In this, we see a conspicuous restorative or fortifying power, impressed upon the stomach, being carried to the "manager" of the lungs, and there extending its own authority. Just as I saw these things happen with joy and wonder in my early years, I thereafter studied how to increase that restorative power by retaining it, while suppressing the narcotic and harmful power of the opiate.

<margin>64.</margin> Immediately following this, I was made certain that the "dissolved flower of sulfur" <note>term: flower of sulfur; a fine powder produced by sublimating sulfur, used here as a respiratory medicine</note> achieves in this case what cannot be accomplished by the body of sulfur itself, even if similarly dissolved. And all of this is not because sulfur, as such, enters the lungs—nor would it be admitted under the privilege of being "flowers"—nor does it reach the respiratory organs in any unchanged way after passing the goal of digestion. Rather, it works only insofar as an "anodyne" <note>pain-relieving or soothing</note> power shines forth in the sulfur thus opened; this power, while still detained within the stomach, then hastens toward the spiritual governance of the lungs by the **Right of the Duumvirate** <note>The "Duumvirate" refers to Van Helmont's theory that the stomach and spleen act as a joint governing committee over the body's vitality</note>.

<column-break/>

Happy, therefore, is the sick person whose helping Physician knows how to separate the lethal elements from the poppy, while retaining the help that excites the power in the Duumvirate. Otherwise, the harmful is taken along with the beneficial, and one hinders the progress of the other. Thus, opiates should not merely induce sleep; they should at least restrain the withdrawal of the "spermatic" and nutritional fluid into a degenerate and exiled state—that is, into those frequent and horrid clearings and sputa which must be cast out. For it seems that the more copiously it is coughed up and cleared, the more abundantly it grows anew. Therefore, the restraint of this degenerate generation is clearly known to happen only through a restorative power awakened within the "pipes" of the Lung. To be sure, the harmful power of opium is blunted, so that without sleep (or at least not by the power of sleep itself), the freedom of breathing is introduced in peace, quiet, and without coughing, whistling, or snoring.

<margin>65.</margin> Now, the stomach is able to restrain the production of so much phlegm rejected by throat-clearing, insofar as its digestive power presides over all other digestions. Therefore, the aforementioned opiates heal the production of mucilage as long as that defect stems from a fault in the "digestive ferment" <note>Van Helmont believed digestion was governed by chemical "ferments" or transformative agents</note>. But they do not heal where it depends on the corruption of "innate strength" <note>The internal vital power of an organ</note>. For then, even against the will of the stomach, the body hastens toward wasting <note>original: "tabem"; a term for consumption or tuberculosis</note>; just as it is impossible for the stomach to restore a life already verging toward its setting sun.

# THE COMPLETION OF THE MIND. #

The majesty of the Mind is learned from the Wisdom of the Father. 18. Three desires are explained. 19. Their excellence. 20. Whatever the Lord’s Prayer concludes is new and unheard of. 21. The summit of loving desire. 22. The place of the sensible spark <note>original: "fomitis"; literally "tinder," used here to mean the source of passion or spiritual heat</note>. 23.
