Recent directors of the Mind, who entered through the windows, are exploded <note>original: "exploduntur"; rejected or driven out with disapproval</note>. 27. These shall fall in the maturity of time.*

<margin>1.</margin> I have already said some things regarding the origin and duties of the sensitive soul <note>The part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, which humans share with animals</note>: but not yet enough, and much less has been said regarding the immortal Mind: seeing as how by these two words almost everything we hold by faith regarding the human Mind is explained; and there is absolutely nothing that leads us into an open knowledge of it. For this reason, whatever we scrutinize concerning it is still wrapped in shadows and is plainly unknown. Indeed, we cannot comment on anything regarding the essence of the Mind, except for what we have learned by its working, and what we know has been given to us freely. For we are commanded to know and distinguish a man by his works.

<margin>2.</margin> Furthermore, that operation is not the most powerful operation of the Mind which human judgment forms and conceives for itself as a conclusion after drawing in a preliminary notion. Because not even the judgment of man itself belongs so properly to the Mind that it is its immediate offspring. Indeed, the Mind clings to the sensitive soul in us with such a tight bond that the distinct duties of each have hardly been separated from one another by the commerce of human

<column-break/>

custom. To be sure, all abstract speculation is believed to be the workmanship of the Mind alone until now, under which heading, of course, labors are felt in the head. This is especially believed because such things are thought to be foreign to beasts <note>original: "belluis"</note>. But I have already demonstrated elsewhere that bees observe numbers, and every morning distinguish their own hive from neighboring ones by numbers: and likewise, they count again upon returning, lest they deposit their burden of honey or wax in an unknown and ungrateful Republic. Yet nothing is so exotic to animals as the exercise of counting. So too we observe in beasts a certain imagination <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>, and no obscure marks of reasoning, and as it were a choice, selectively preferring one over another. And this is certainly even in unforeseen circumstances that they are not used to, nor have ever seen before, and much less been taught by a parent. For "the serpent was more crafty than the other living creatures." Therefore, if differences of sagacity are noted among animals, a place is left for suspecting that in man, those same operations are still far more skillful, powerful, eminent, and frequent than in animals, and that the sensitive soul of humans <margin>3.</margin> surpasses the animals in sagacity: unless the sensitive soul were a stranger to humans, and entirely exotic to its own nature. Indeed, man was chosen and raised up entirely in the image of God, and not so that he might degenerate into a specific and animal soul, and thus defile the image of God. Therefore, the sensitive soul remained an empty tablet in man: since it took its beginning from the Fall and the stain of corrupted nature, and thus it has hardly even obtained its own dignity of imagination that does not depend on every side upon the operations of the Mind; as will soon become more clearly apparent. And although <margin>4.</margin> sagacity is the daughter of judgment and reasoning, it is not for that reason a proper operation or fruit of the Mind. For the Mind, which since the first Fall has renounced all the duties of life to the sensitive soul, also by just merit...

These are not, however, the true and proper functions of the Mind. Indeed, as the Mind is now, since the Fall, shrouded by the light of the decaying soul, it therefore as if completely ceases from all governance of the body, and radiates its vital light into its "deputy," the Sensitive Soul. But its actions are not for that reason those of the Mind itself, which produces only abstract functions similar to itself.

I mean that Love which proceeds substantially from the other two. And from here, I feel that every proximate and entire function of the Mind begins in us. Furthermore, I have also demonstrated elsewhere that our life is now different and corrupt, after the sensitive soul—earthly, mortal, decaying, animal, and

It is, namely, a vital light created by the Father of Lights, and is a "neutral creature" between a substance and an accident. In beasts, this certainly subsists in itself, absolutely, and is determined into a brutish species. In man, however, because it comes later to an already corrupted nature,

# COMPLEMENTUM <note>The Completion or Supplement</note>

[The sensitive soul] is not of a determined animal species <note>original: "speciei brutalis"</note>: but is merely a vital light, and not life itself, as it is in brute beasts. This is because life is radially inspired into it by the Mind, which it envelops, and is, as it were, borrowed—just as the Moon receives its light from the Sun. And although this sensitive part of man far surpasses the souls of beasts in its shrewdness <note>original: "sagacitate"</note>, it nevertheless does nothing without the Mind. For from that Mind it draws its life; it cannot help but borrow its power of thinking from there too, to which it is so intimately bound that the Mind thoroughly penetrates the sensitive soul. To be sure, the human sensitive soul thinks by its own power, but it is illuminated by the Mind. And for that reason, every thought of our sensitive soul belongs to the whole man. For it happens exactly as it does with the Moon and the Sun: the Moon indeed has a light proper to itself, yet it shines more brightly with the reflected light of the Sun (as mentioned elsewhere regarding meteors), and its own light in the Moon is, as it were, eclipsed. Therefore, the sensitive soul in us thinks in various ways, and degrees of its breadth are felt through thinking. For, first <margin>9.</margin> of all, in mania, madness, folly, delirium, fury, drunkenness, and dreams, there are indeed various thoughts of the whole man; yet they occur with such a small light of the Mind that the Mind brings nothing but a faint glimmer, which it at least cannot refuse because of the close necessity of their bond. Therefore, the sensitive soul itself—because it is mortal and attacked by the injuries of fleeting things—succumbs to their persistence and thinks almost alone, aided by that tiny light of the Mind as a support for life. For this reason, those thoughts are free from sin <note>original: "peccati expertia"</note>, because the Mind does not think in them, but is instead clouded by the contagion contracted from the sensitive soul. Furthermore, as much as thoughts move away from that innocent contagion toward abstract discourses, so much more do they participate in the life of the Mind than in the sensitive soul’s own vitality. <margin>10.</margin> Truly, every sensitive thought is, of necessity, brought about by the service of the senses, and it does not exceed them, however much

<column-break/>

it may appear to abstract itself brilliantly from them. For whatever can be perceived by the senses does not yet reach the foundation <note>original: "fundum," often referring to the "ground of the soul" in mystical theology</note> of the Mind alone. This variety of thinking in the sensitive soul thus produces such a great breadth and variety in our judgments. Finally, just as the light of the Sun in the moon clearly loses its heat and takes on a coldness foreign to itself, so too in the vital sensitive soul, the ray of the Mind—though it is purely intellectual—transmigrates into the dominion of the sensitive soul. There, it even finds an earthly law, opposed to the law of the Mind. <margin>11.</margin> Wherefore, we must diligently ensure that, as much as possible, we withdraw ourselves from everything that can be conceived by the senses. For thus one goes to the mountain of the Lord <note>A biblical metaphor for spiritual ascent and mystical union</note>, which is the goal of our journey. Nor is it enough to have said this in passing, as if it sufficiently taught the naked operations of the Mind; nor is the path yet seen by which we may acquire any knowledge of the Mind. For such <margin>12.</margin> thoughts still belong to the whole man as long as there is any sense of "I-ness" <note>original: "egoitas"</note>, or as long as the Mind apprehends something outside itself with a sense of duality, and does not yet behold the thing as itself, transfigured. That is to say, the whole man looks upon the properties of himself or of other things in this way; it is not the naked intellectual light of the Mind that is working then, but rather a combination of both vital lights, penetrating each other. In this act—alas—the immortal Mind, as easily as it is prone to bad habit, willingly obeys its fleeting handmaid, the sensitive soul. So that we may eventually reach the desired purity of the Mind, thinking purely and nakedly in the abstract, we must first adopt the <margin>St. Dionysius to Timothy</margin> teaching of Saint Dionysius to Timothy <note>Referring to the "Mystical Theology" of Pseudo-Dionysius, which advocates for "unknowing" and stripping away sensory data to reach God</note>. For in order <margin>13.</margin> that divine things might be understood <margin>(for divine things are whatever the naked image of God beholds)</margin> and even in a subtle way, and to look upon divine mysteries, one must cast aside the senses, and the things of the senses, and whatever can be perceived by the senses. Furthermore, one must reject Reason, the actions of Reason, <margin>☛</margin> and whatever can be known and perceived by Reason.

# THE MIND

[it] can <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page.</note>: whether it be created or uncreated; so that you may go out from yourself, and from all knowledge of all those things, and come into the one unity of Him who is above all nature and knowledge. So says he <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic who taught that God is reached by "unknowing."</note>. For the mind is the closest **Image of Divinity**: Therefore, just as the eye looks at nothing more perfectly than the Sun itself (the clarity of whose light it nevertheless cannot endure), and sees all other things because of it; so the mind, properly, principally, and intimately, thinks and contemplates nothing besides that unity, and sees all other things because of that same unity. From this it becomes manifest that as long as anything is being thought that can be perceived by the senses or by Reason, it is not yet the pure and naked thought of the abstracted mind.

<margin>14.</margin>
The way of reaching that point, as described above, is indeed read about, but it is still far removed and almost impassable because of the total abstraction and banishment of all created things—and even of the uncreated <note>Meaning our human concepts or mental images of the Divine.</note>—from every consideration. That is to say, it is a denial proceeding through a setting-apart, until all activity of the mind is reached; this then excludes all thought and contemplation of the mind, and waits for the supernatural light of grace from above by doing nothing, but only by enduring after all <term>egoity</term> <note>original: "egoitatem"; the state of being focused on the self or "I".</note> has been exhausted. But since being completely liberated in this way does not reside entirely in our own power—and indeed suggests a grace of "rapture" <note>An ecstatic state of being "carried away" by God.</note> rather than the true, naked, and pure operations of the mind which I intend to examine in this chapter as a completion of the **Treatise on the Soul**—therefore, according to my own 

<margin>15.</margin>
poverty of judgment, one does not climb more closely to the super-eminent denudation of the mind alone and the abstract intellectual light through any action other than through the <term>Prayer of Silence</term> <note>original: "Orationem silentii"; a contemplative practice where the soul rests in God without words, images, or active thoughts.</note> in the spirit, in which it is the delight of God to be adored. In this way, He may illuminate that mind—as a naked image of Himself, reflected in the mirror of His divinity—in an emanative way. This is surely what the most glorious Goodness desires,

<column-break/>

<margin>16.</margin>
Moreover, so that the fruits or exercises may reveal the <term>quiddity</term> <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> of the Mind, I have thought that this cannot be had more powerfully from any other source than from spiritual exercises. By these, the mind itself extricates itself from the connected concepts of created things and those known through the service of the senses. For it is clear what the mind itself is while it has abstracted itself from the concepts that usually stain it, or could do so, or at least hinder it from reaching its own nakedness and purity, in which it is able to adore the aforementioned unity.

<margin>17.</margin>
The Lord Jesus, therefore, is the way, the truth, and the life. The way, I say, to Himself as truth, and to the life of the Father of lights. The way is therefore directed toward the attainment of abstract truth. His desire is that the hidden truth, which He painted in the mind as an image of Himself, should be known by us and adored in spirit. There He Himself is present as the **Kingdom of God**, with all His spiritual gifts. And therefore, the way and method of adoring in spirit cannot be more closely known or learned than from the Way and Truth Himself, and thus from the prayer which He dictated to us <note>The "Pater Noster" or Lord's Prayer.</note>, in which there are first three loving desires, or longings of love, and just as many petitions.

<margin>18.</margin>
For those desires are without any <term>egoity</term> <note>Self-centeredness.</note>, being naked regards toward God Himself, and therefore the purest of all things that can be desired or thought of out of love. And the first of these is that of which the Truth says: *Seek first the Kingdom of God and His Justice, and the rest shall be added unto you.* However, it is not the "Justice of God" that we should be made just (*for no living being shall be justified in the sight of God*). Rather, it is that His name should be sanctified, which is not only His due, and therefore just, but that loving desire justifies us. For it presupposes, first, Christian faith itself, and then His infinite goodness, by which He deigns to be **Our Father**. And indeed, in the word "our," selfhood is set aside for the goodness of God and our collective obligation, which otherwise is nowhere seen in the three desires. And thirdly, it displays His immense majesty, com-

### COMPLETION

to be measured from the habitation of the Heavens, which is the work of His hands. And so, with such things having been established, the longed-for **loving desire** is kindled within us. This desire does not merely wish for His name to be hallowed only through His only-begotten Son and our mediator—where **Deep calls to deep** <note>original: "Abyffus Abyffum invocat," a reference to Psalm 42:7, often used in mysticism to describe the deep part of the human soul calling out to the infinite depth of God</note>—nor does it wish only that the heavenly beings and the whole Church Militant adore His ineffable name. Nor is the meaning simply that His name should be hallowed on earth as it is in Heaven; rather, it is that it be hallowed **in us** and **through us**, once all <term>egoity</term> <note>original: "egoitate"; the state of being focused on the self or the "I"</note> and nothingness has been renounced. This is so there may be a naked and most pure reflection of the honor and delights of God, in that He is with us and is adored in the spirit of love. And therefore, the next following desire does not seek the "Kingdom of Heaven" for itself, but rather the **Kingdom of God**, which is within us, that it may come closer. This is not simply for our own sake, but because it is of His goodness to find delight in being with the children of men. For this reason, it is also desired that His will be done in us, over us, and through us, with a full <term>resignation</term> <note>The act of surrendering one's own will entirely to God's will</note> of our own wanting. These three desires proceed from the soul without "this-ness" or reflection upon ourselves, because they exceed all personality of the creature, so that God may be adored for His own sake.

<margin>19.</margin> Therefore, these excel every power of prayer, petition, praise, thanksgiving, and even glorification itself. For to give thanks acknowledges a benefit and involves the one who receives it. Glorification, praise, or even hallowing itself—insofar as it brings my "egoity" before the sight of God (even if it is meanwhile right and obligatory)—falls far short of the excellence of this most pure and loving desire, by which the hallowing of the Divine name is sought within us, in which **Deep calls to deep**. For who am I, that I should presume to hallow that Name in respect to the Infinite? I, who am surely nothing but a worm, a most miserable sinner? Therefore, the loving desire for hallowing so far excels the phrase "may your name be hallowed *through me*," as a miserable sinner is distant from the Son of God—

<column-break/>

<margin>20.</margin> —born of the Virgin <note>original: "Deiparæ virginis," literally the "God-bearer" or Mother of God</note>. For praises and prayers, both in the Mosaic law and today, were made through hymns, psalms, and petitions. But never, before the Truth was taught, did man attain the vigor, height, and depth of this loving desire to hallow the incomprehensible Divinity within us—in which there is more excellence than all creatures together can comprehend. For this hallowing is not desired because God is the "best," "greatest," or "generous," etc.; for those terms include the "egoity" of the one giving praise, which is incompatible with the Divine name.

<margin>21.</margin> Thus, the longing and desire of a loving soul, fervently desiring the hallowing of the Divine name in a naked and simple way, does not happen through any created thing below God, but through a **melting of the mind** <note>original: "liquationem mentis"; a mystical state where the soul's boundaries seem to dissolve in the presence of God</note> desiring in the love of God. For the minimum that this contains within itself is to offer oneself to God with the resignation of one’s whole self, and likewise to be willing to act and suffer anything, with a total loving offering of heart, soul, and strength, in obedience to the Divine will. In this loving offering, all thoughts except the naked desire of love are excluded as incompatible, because it transcends all self-reflection. Indeed, because it is "naked," it scorns every garment that Reason might provide for it.

<margin>22.</margin> For this love, so naked and excellent, arises in the seat of the mind and is felt in the very place where every first concept is formed, without image or fantasy. As long as it can be expressed in words, it is not yet the "abstracted naked thought" of the mind, which is described by **Blessed Dionysius** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian who taught that God is best known through "unknowing" and stripping away concepts</note> as being above everything that can be conceived by Reason, sense, or words. It is indeed felt, but without logical discourse or imagination.

<margin>23.</margin> Because in the naked concept of loving truth, Truth itself is struck, enjoyed, and approached by an inexpressible touch of the mind—indeed, it soon penetrates it. Otherwise, whenever ideas or concepts expressible in words are formed, they retain the mother-like frailty of the **Sensitive soul**, the weakness of inconstancy, uncertainty, and disturbances subject to the passions.

### COMPLETION OF THE MIND

24. Within the power of the Intellect—that is, the innate vigor of the Mind—and the longing of the loving soul, there is generated within us (much like a fetus in a longing pregnant woman) a certain **God-like being** <note>original: "ens Deiforme"; a state of being where the soul reflects the form and nature of God</note>. Or rather, the Mind itself is purified, and thus the Mind and the very image of God within it are set right. For this does not happen through sight or the sensual appetite, as occurs in a pregnant woman, nor is it conceived in the hidden places of the body, nor is it noted as a foreign fetus. Instead, it requires every faculty of the Mind, the soul, the Heart, and one's very strength. Therefore, that **Ideal being**, born of a loving desire, remains in the Mind itself, which it so disposes that the Mind transforms itself into a God-like image through grace flowing down from the divine.

25. But who am I, that I should write these things? Indeed, I fear I may be like a **church bell** calling the faithful to the Temple, while remaining myself high up in the tower, on the outside. But I have this much hope: if I advance in these aforementioned desires, I shall find my true self, for the more I neglect myself through humility, the more I shall truly exist.

26. Furthermore, there have recently arisen "directors of conscience" who take unto themselves all liberty of the Mind, especially when dealing with the **devoted sex** <note>This refers to women, particularly those in religious or lay-pious communities</note>. They have called this sex to themselves, saying that not only is Christ the "Anointed One" with them, but even Jesus the Savior is among them. Yet these men 

<column-break/>

err immediately, at the very threshold. For they call their "devoted ones" to perform contemplative exercises in groups—a thing which Truth itself <note>A reference to Christ, who is "the Way, the Truth, and the Life"</note> commands should be done in secret, after the door of the bedchamber has been shut. Next, they demand that honor, reverence, and wealth be owed to them under the guise of obedience and multiple vows. In this way, the **enemy** <note>The Devil</note> scatters his seeds as **tares** <note>original: "zizaniis"; weeds that look like wheat, from the Parable of the Sower</note>, suppressing what were otherwise good seeds.

<margin>27.</margin>
And for this reason, the Prophetess **Hildegard** <note>St. Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), a medieval mystic and polymath often cited by Van Helmont</note> predicted that eventually, secret lusts would be mingled with them, and they would fall just like Simon Magus, through the prayers of the Apostles—or rather, the Bishops and the faithful. Moreover, once someone has been led even a single time into the vigor of that holy desire, he will hasten to return there, spurred on by his own inner drive; having become familiar with the way, the path will be easier for him afterward. In the meantime, because not everyone reaches that height, God has made various "mansions" in His palace. So too has He ordained diverse means for this through **Charity**; I gladly omit these, as they are not the proper objects of our medical faculty. It is enough for me to have proposed the vastness of the Mind in its actions and the wandering power of forming "Ideas," both for the consideration of diseases and a healthy life, as well as for the exercise of virtues.

# THE SCABIES AND ULCERS OF THE SCHOOLS.

**Sf 2**

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap letter H at the beginning of the text, featuring intricate foliage and floral patterns within and around the letterform.</image-desc>**H**itherto I have shown that the causes of diseases handed down by Galen and his followers are erroneous and deceptive. It would now be proper to move on to the true doctrine of diseases—though it has remained unknown until now—were it not for certain matters that hold me back and divert me elsewhere, which rightly seem to require a preamble. For after I had treated the Plague, the Queen of diseases, in a published book, and at the same time spoke in a work currently under the press about **Lithiasis** <note>original: "Lithiasi"; the formation of stones or calculi in the body</note> as a monster generated both within us and outside us in the chamber-pots; and whereas in that same place I incidentally dealt with **Leprosy**, **Apoplexy**, **Paralysis**, **Stupor**, **Spasms**, and related diseases; yet I have said nothing at all regarding skin defects. Therefore, I deemed it worthwhile, before I complete this labor of mine by speaking professionally on the essence of diseases in general and in particular, to put forward certain specific points which I believe will throw open the doors to the understanding of diseases. And first, I shall touch upon diseases of the **skin** <note>original: "pellis"</note>, as they are more obvious to the senses. 
<margin>2.</margin>
For this reason, in my book on fevers, I recounted the beginnings of my "repentance"—the reasons why I was compelled to withdraw from the Method and doctrine of the Schools—to show the futility of the axioms by which the world is deceived. This deception occurs both through the drinking of purgatives and the estimation that diseases are created and cured by the ejection of fluids <note>The four "humors" of traditional medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, which the Schools persuade us are our constitutive parts, wandering about in improper quantity and quality. Therefore, I was not reluctant to bring back and repeat the same origins of my change of mind here. As a young man, about to say goodbye to a certain lady, I held her glove and her hand for a little while; she was suffering from a hidden and "dry" **Scabies** <note>original: "Scabie"; in this period, "scabies" referred to a broad range of itchy, scaling skin eruptions, not just the modern parasitic infection</note>. From this, I soon contracted not a dry, but a "sanious" <note>Oozing or discharging pus and serum</note> scabies, surely by the mere act of contact. And thereafter I observed many times that the towels of those with the itch produced the itch, and the hats of those with **tinea** <note>Ringworm or fungal scalp infections</note> produced tinea; just as the contagions of lepers and those with venereal disease are propagated through a shared **ferment** <note>original: "fermento"; Van Helmont’s term for a transformative agent or "seed" of disease</note>. And this is echoed by

<column-break/>

<margin>3.</margin>
the proverb applied to the incorrigible: Namely, that a single little bird may infect the whole flock with its own scabies. Indeed, such defects, transplanted by a virulent **tinder** <note>original: "fomite"; a substance or spark that carries infection</note>, are nevertheless judged by the Schools—without distinction—to be the fault of the **Liver** <note>original: "Jecinoris"</note>, excited by its untimely heat. As if the contagion on the skin of a single sheep could distemper the livers of all the other sheep! Truly, this single consideration was the first dawning of the light I attained. From this, the great "scabies" of the Schools was manifested to me, and they compelled me to look elsewhere, after I saw that the remedies of the Schools were vain and their greatest maxims were futile. Indeed, I summoned two of the more famous physicians of our city, almost rejoicing that I might now find out for myself whether their studies corresponded to practice. The healers, however, having seen the purulent scabies, immediately judged that there was an abundance of **burnt bile** <note>original: "bilem adustam"; also known as black bile or melancholy, thought to be caused by overheating</note> in me, along with **salty phlegm**, and thus that the blood-making process in my Liver was distempered. I was immediately glad that the things the Authors had sung to me were being confirmed by such experienced Masters. Inasmuch as I had learned in mathematics that all theorems are by far the truest things, I believed the same was common and inseparable from the rules of healing or axioms: thinking they were what they ought to be and what they promised. But immediately, out of my ancestral curiosity, I asked: what sort of "intemperance" of the Liver was this, which by one and the same act could kindle yellow bile more fiercely than is right, and simultaneously produce more **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitæ"</note> than is right? Since the act of the <margin>4.</margin> same root, or the same blood-making, could not be a "forked" generation at the same time and in the same organ—and so disparate—that it would abundantly produce fiery bile and, at the same time, cold, watery phlegm? These most experienced masters hesitated; standing stunned with arched eyebrows, they stared at each other for a long while. At last, the younger of them replied that the same intemperance of an ignited Liver did not therefore give a true...

# SCABIES AND ULCERS

...phlegm; but an abundant **salt phlegm**: for they claim the temperament of salt is hot and dry. To which I responded: "Then would the salt of the urine be created by a fault of the **liver** <note>original: "jecoris"; the liver was considered the seat of humor production</note> and an abundance of heat? And would meat broths made from unsalted meat take on no salt at all, even if they boiled with heat?" The elder physician replied: "These questions should be proposed to me in the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the formal academic settings where medical theory was debated according to ancient authorities like Galen</note>, not in practical matters, for which I have destined these hours for the profit of my family."

<margin>5.</margin>
He immediately asked which **Authors** I had consulted and what I had learned should be done. I said that for the cooling of the liver and the blood, a vein should be cut in the right arm below the **cephalic vein** <note>A common site for bloodletting in the 17th century</note>; then one should proceed with a cooling **decoction** <term>apozema: a medicinal tea or infusion made by boiling ingredients</term>, in respect to the scorched bile; however, moderate "cutting" and "thinning" agents should be mixed in because of the saltiness of the phlegm. I showed him a decoction from **Rondeletius** <note>Guillaume Rondelet (1507–1566), a famous French physician</note> which contained perhaps fifty ingredients, offering the richest hope for both goals. And since they did not know that I was a diligent and tireless taker of notes in the lectures, they wanted me to write everything down for myself. 

Thus, after a sufficiently generous bloodletting—performed in the spring of my youth and in a state of otherwise full health—I took the aforementioned decoction for three days. On the fourth and fifth mornings, I added enough **Rhubarb** and **Agaric** <note>Agaric is a fungus used as a potent purgative</note> so that nature would begin to obey the "calling" drug, and both offending humors would be made to follow. They praised everything, and most of all that I was eager to learn and obey. On the evening of the fifth day, I took **Fumitory pills** <term>Catapotia: an archaic term for pills or swallowable medicine</term>, because **Cordus** <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), a noted botanist and pharmacist</note> (whom I later called "Codrus") wrote that it was beneficial for both offending humors. (For I did not yet know then how to impose pills on the sick under a false name—pretending they moved the bowels because of the fumitory and not because of the ferocity of the poisonous laxatives). On the sixth day, therefore, I had at least fifteen bowel movements. Meanwhile, they praised my foresight, by which I had prepared the body to be so fluid.

<column-break/>

Soon, two days later, because the **Scabies** <note>A contagious skin infestation caused by mites, though then attributed to humors</note> had not diminished in its ferocity at all, I took the same drug again, with a significant aversion in my stomach; the purging succeeded poorly. They said my age of 18 years was "blooming" and prone to generating bile. And when they saw that the itching and pustules were not reduced at all, they decreed after two days that a third purgative must be taken. 

For then, toward evening, my veins were already exhausted, my cheeks had sunken, my voice was hoarse, and the whole condition of my body had wasted away and collapsed. Descending from my bedroom and even walking were difficult, because my knees could hardly support me. These things happened to me, a healthy man, merely from contact with a scabious hand. In the first instances, when I noticed such ample and foul filth being purged, I rejoiced.

<margin>6.</margin>
But too late did I consider that before the drugs I had been healthy in my internal organs; but now, with my appetite and digestion ruined, I had acquired great emaciation, while the Scabies remained healthy, along with a high and hoarse voice. Finally, so that I might see how much bile and phlegm I was ejecting, I urinated into a chamber pot; and I found that, through the laxative taken, I had ejected on three occasions nearly two buckets of foul and cadaverous bile, speckled with mucous shreds; which the Doctors asserted was that "salt phlegm." 

And while in the meantime I nourished large, purulent pustules over almost my entire body, especially on my legs, I asked whether the **pus** did not signify that the blood was at fault no less than the bile and phlegm. They said, since my strength was already flagging, they would remain silent about repeating the bloodletting, which would otherwise be appropriate given the persistence of the abundance of pus. I, however, considered it with regret, because I had been perfectly healthy before, except for the skin contagion caught from elsewhere; and because nothing is made from nothing, nor can any physical thing be located except in a place. Too late, therefore, I inquired: from where had such a great supply of bile flowed into me?

Therefore, with serious regret and at my own expense, I concluded from **Mathematics** <note>original: "Mathesi"; here meaning logical calculation or the science of weights and measures</note>: 1. That the name of "purgation" was a deception. 2. That the specific selection—meant to draw out this or that particular humor—was equally false. 3. That the very origin and existence of these "humors" was false. 4. That the cause of **Scabies** <note>A contagious skin disease caused by mites, historically attributed to internal "hot" or "salty" fluids</note> was a lie, falsely attributed to "burnt bile" and "salty phlegm." 5. That the **liver** <note>original: "jecur"</note> was innocent in skin contagions.
<margin>7.</margin>
6. That my scabies still persisted despite the purging, though not with the same intensity. 7. That its intensity had not diminished because some supposed humor (or several) had been led out, nor because their "abundance" had previously been at fault; for as soon as my blood was restored, the same scabies remained. Thus, the scabies had only been slightly lessened by the lack of blood volume <note>original: "plethora"</note>. At last, after perhaps three months, I recovered from the scabies by the simple application of a **sulfur ointment**. 8. That scabies is an affliction of the skin alone. 9. That the **Schools** <note>The medical establishment of the time</note> wrongly gave the names of "bile" and "phlegm" to ill-affected fluids, whether in the veins or outside them, whether harmful or harmless. 10. That any "purgatives" simply liquify, dissolve, and rot the blood and flesh indiscriminately, even while they remain in the stomach and intestines. 11. That it is false that blood returns into the "humors" from which it was supposedly born. 12. That in this case, an impossible regression would occur, from a state of deprivation back to a state of being. 13. That it is a deception to claim those three humors remain in the blood, flesh, and solid parts, only to be turned back by purgatives into what they were before the building of the flesh, etc.
<margin>8.</margin>

Thus, I could no longer doubt whether bile or phlegm were the cause of scabies. Gradually, by the grace of God, I understood this so certainly that I knew—through intellectual certainty and, as it were, through the science of sight—that there is no "bile" in nature, nor are there three humors united with the blood. Moreover, I have demonstrated in a specific book that the "masks" of phlegm and bile shown by the Schools are actually morbid wastes contrary to nature, the faulty products of bodily functions.

<margin>12.</margin> Likewise, ulcers are also formed, either from a poorly treated wound, from a bruise—such as **Cancer** in a woman—or from a breaking abscess. They may also arise from a poison generated within, which plants its malignancy in the external part and there fixes the properties of its virulent **ferment** <note>original: "fermenti"; in this context, a chemical-like agent that triggers a transformation in the body's tissues</note>. From this, whatever blood is distributed hourly to nourish that part is entirely turned into a virus <note>original: "virus"; meaning a poisonous or infectious fluid</note>, according to the lineage of its ferment. However, it is not the case that corrupted humors—supposedly sent there from the liver—rise again from death.

<margin>13.</margin> Therefore the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional medical universities of the time that followed ancient Greek teachings</note>, led astray by their blind belief in **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the Roman physician whose theories of "humors" dominated medicine for over a millennium</note>, have attributed these to their dreamed-up humors. They imagine these humors rising from blood and flesh because of the troublesome "unbalance" of some organ, which they blame on an "elemental battle" <note>Traditional medicine taught that health was a balance of the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>.

<margin>14.</margin> For Galen, in his work *On the Art of Healing* <note>original: "Therapeuticis"</note>, insists that an ulcer must naturally consist of two types of waste (it seemed enough for him to state this doctrine without proving it). One is a more liquid waste called **Ichor** <note>original: "Ichore"; a thin, watery discharge from a wound</note> or **sanies**, and the other is thicker—namely, **pus**. From this he concludes that every ulcer indicates, requires, and must be healed by a double medicine: one to dry out and soak up the watery discharge, and the other to wipe away the pus. (It is because of the failure of this method that many patients, finding no hope in the Schools, are relegated to the care of old women, to the shame of Galen).

<margin>15.</margin> How seriously did this man weave his fables? And how untouched are these trifles kept even today? For now, they no longer remember the fourfold humor and the fourfold waste that supposedly results from their corruption. Galen claims that pus is putrid blood, yet he forgets himself when he elsewhere teaches that blood, in its corruption, is entirely turned into bile. Finally, if purging medicines were to separate three humors from the blood individually at the Doctor's whim, he should remember that this would happen through the corruption of the blood as it breaks down into its preceding components (or

<column-break/>

else everything he invented about purges and humors is false). Therefore, in an ulcer, not just two, but four types of waste should emerge. Indeed, according to Galen, an ulcer without pus—such as a **Cancer**, a **malignant ulcer** <note>original: "Cacoëthes"</note>, or one that drains only a thin fluid—would be easier to cure than a purulent one. This is because it would only need drying agents, such as chalk or burnt bones.

<margin>16.</margin> For how stupid and insane is it to have taught that an ulcer must be cured by wiping away and separating the "fruits" or products of waste? Why not instead by cutting out the **root**, which they have never recognized as anything other than "unbalanced heat"? Every waste has a necessary relationship to digestion and the specific body part: true waste is the superfluous mass left over from digestion which the part cannot use and therefore separates.

<margin>17.</margin> Because the name "waste" <note>original: "excrementi"</note> implies the expulsion of the impure from the pure. Therefore, the watery discharge and pus are not the waste products of the ulcer or the body part, nor of natural digestion; rather, they are the products of the **seeds** or roots of the ulcer. Therefore, he who merely wipes an ulcer according to Galen's prescription labors in vain, especially in the more malignant cases. It is also a necessity that things which are not being nourished also lack waste. For nature never labors to "nourish" an ulcer.

<margin>18.</margin> Instead, a specific "corruptor" lives in the ulcer, which spoils the nourishing blood before it is even fit to be digested. To speak properly, dregs are not the "waste" of wine, but merely what settles out, because wine undergoes no nutrition or digestion. The ulcer, therefore, as such, is not nourished, nor does nature intend to nourish it. Thus, the discharge and pus are not the "waste" of the ulcer, but the products of the **Corruptor**; they are the indicators, signs, products, effects, or fruits of blood that has been depraved into harmful matter.

### OF THE SCHOOLS.

The destined blood is sent and distributed by **Distributive Justice** <note>original: "Justitia distributiva"; a philosophical concept applied here to the body's natural allocation of nutrients to its various parts</note>. This happens no differently for an ulcerated part than if it were still perfectly healthy. Once the blood arrives there, and because it cannot be changed into a true nourishing substance, it takes a risk governed by the **ulcerous ferment** <note>original: "ulcerosum fermentum"; in Helmontian medicine, a 'ferment' is a specific agent that directs a substance to transform into something else, like yeast in dough</note>. Therefore, the blood degenerates and is transformed at the root of the part where the corrupting agent is located and resides. This happens in the tissue itself, not in the cavity or channel of the ulcer. Otherwise, it would be necessary for pure and harmless blood to always fall into the ulcer's cavity and degenerate there by rotting—which both the eye and daily experience prove to be false.

<margin>20.</margin> Therefore, if the **Schools** <note>The established medical universities following ancient Greek traditions</note> wipe away an ulcer, whether with a cloth or a drug—though both do the same thing—they only remove the final product. They by no means reach the radical cause or the origin. If sometimes a bloody clot or mucus falls into the ulcer, it is because there is such a "storm of torture" in the surrounding parts (which are the true root of the ulcers) that a nearby eroded vein cannot hold its own blood. Even so, blood that happens to fall into the ulcer’s cavity is not seen to turn into **pus**.

From this it becomes manifest that blood degenerates not in the cavity of the ulcer, but in its margins. Thus, the vanity of **Galenic doctrine** <note>The teachings of Galen, which dominated medicine for 1,500 years</note> is exposed, as it places the healing of an ulcer merely in the removal of what is produced.

<margin>21.</margin> The root of every ulcer is in the bottom and the "lips" or margins—that is, it lives in the parts bordering the cavity. In these parts, there is a **kitchen** <note>original: "coquina"; a metaphor for the site where metabolic or chemical changes occur</note> where the blood is altered into corrosive **sanies** <note>a thin, greenish, or bloody discharge from a wound</note>, pus, and so on. Sanies is the product, or the positive effect, of ulcers. However, the cavity itself, which is commonly thought of by healers as "the ulcer," is a privative and deficient product. Just as a burned or destroyed village is not the "war" itself, but is an effect testifying to the loss, desertion, and destruction that occurred, so an ul-

<column-break/>

-cer is not merely the devastated cavity of the flesh; rather, this is a sign left behind by the ulcer. In the edges of the ulcer dwells the hostile corruptor and the guest, the virulent **ferment**, toward which we see the edges and bottom are variously altered.

<margin>23.</margin> Let the Schools take heed of what they teach when they claim the healing of an ulcer consists in removing the byproduct. Indeed, **pus** does not have the nature of an excrement, nor does it come from nature like waste; rather, it is the fruit of the ulcer, depraved by a "ferment" from an exotic Corruptor. Therefore, it degenerates, eats away, gnaws, and feeds upon the flesh.

Truly, larger ulcers lack pus; they only "weep" a continuous discharge, and sometimes ten times more than a fair distribution of blood would require. This blood flows out transmuted into sharp, consuming **ichor** <note>a watery, acrid discharge</note>. The Galenists never cure these with their drying agents, even if they add all their cleansing medicines, and no matter how loudly the followers of the books **On Local Remedies** and **On the Composition of Drugs** <note>original: "Catageni & Catatopus"; referring to Galen's pharmaceutical works *De Compositione Medicamentorum per Genera* and *De Compositione Medicamentorum Secundum Locos*</note> boast of their experiments.

<margin>24.</margin> For pus is only produced in closed or open flesh that is not yet entirely corrupted. Meanwhile, cartilages, bones, membranes, veins, nerves, and organs do not produce pus but merely "melt" and drip with ichor if they endure an ulcer. Thus, the corruption and "storm" of these parts is much milder than the tumults that occur in the flesh. Because the diversity of a remedy distinguishes the end for which it is intended, a drying medicine indicates a milder condition than one that must also be an **astringent**.

<margin>25.</margin> Therefore, because **Galen** and his followers have hitherto been ignorant of the causes of ulcers—the fuel, the womb, the subject, the efficient cause, the manner of formation, the seed, and the ferment—they have handed down nothing but ridiculous cures, remedies, axioms, and doctrine. Thus, it is no wonder that **malignant** <note>original: "cacoëthica"</note> and **spreading** <note>original: "phagederiaca"; from the Greek for "eating"</note> ulcers are not usually healed by the remedies of the Schools. For this reason, many distance themselves from the works of Surgery with great

# SCABIES AND ULCERS

They have removed the shame from Galen, his Greek contemporaries, and their Arab followers; just as I have touched upon in my treatise on the *Tomb of the Plague* <note>original: "Tumulo Pestis"; likely a reference to one of Van Helmont’s specific works or chapters regarding infectious diseases</note>. For indeed, milder ulcers, from which all malignancy has been removed—and which hasten toward the growth of new flesh and the restoration of the remaining cavity—drip only with **pus**. According to Galen’s rules, these are considered more difficult to treat than those flowing with **ichor** <note>original: "ichore"; a watery, thin discharge from a wound, often considered a sign of poor healing in ancient medicine</note>. However, ulcers that have already been mitigated are only irritated by "cleansing agents": they are far from being healed by them. Truly, if drying and cleansing agents were enough for all ulcers, the healing of any of them would be easy. Why then is the **Galenic School** <note>The medical establishment following the teachings of the ancient Greek physician Galen</note> so anxiously troubled about the choice of medicines, when dry cloths alone would satisfy both requirements abundantly? Surely a single cloth dries and cleanses at the same time? Let them be ashamed, then, and seriously ashamed, to pour out such nonsense from their chairs, their printing presses, and their mouths as medical axioms for the youth and for surgeons. And let them be ashamed to send these students out—prepared for the slaughter of mortals and the torture of those who trust them—under the flashy title of "healer" and "doctor." Therefore, it is not permitted merely to have wiped away and dried the pus and discharge; rather, the **hostile maker**, the corrupting agent sitting within the part, must be destroyed. This agent does not soften or diminish just by being dried or wiped.

<margin>26.</margin>
<margin>27.</margin>
<margin>28.</margin>

Namely, there is a "seminal destructive quality" and a poisonous impression that is exotic to the **Archeus** <note>original: "Archeo"; in Van Helmont’s system, the Archeus is the "internal chemist" or vital force of an organ that directs its functions</note> of that part. This perverts the good blood distributed to it: it naturally indicates that only its own removal will suffice. It is therefore a virus, a certain **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"; an active agent that causes a chemical-like transformation in the body</note> and contagion, rooted in the bottom, which corrupts the blood and the tissue. Let the Schools see, then, whether a **catarrh** <note>originally thought to be a "down-flowing" vapor from the head to other parts of the body</note>—raised as a vapor from the stomach to the level of the head—can give it a beginning or nourishment. And let them see whether **cauteries** <note>The practice of burning the skin with hot irons or chemicals to create an artificial sore</note>, applied at will, can sufficiently provide for that same habitual catarrh in place of drying and cleansing remedies—or even as a "revulsion" <note>A medical theory of drawing "bad humors" away from a diseased area to a different part of the body</note>—simply because of the continuity of the connection in their 

<column-break/>

root, their proportion, their application, their harmony, and even their dependent symphony. Indeed, whoever is ignorant of the activity and variety of ferments must necessarily try and explore everything by blind guesswork. There are, after all, just as many **ferments** of ulcers as there are different corruptions of ulcers and variations in the damaged parts. 

<margin>29.</margin>
<margin>30.</margin>

To this point, the testimony of **a single loaf of bread** <note>original: "unius panis"</note> will contribute much; for it can even be the guide for this entire dispute. This bread, when taken into a man, a dog, a cat, a horse, a cow, a hen, a goose, a duck, or a sheep, etc., undergoes as many determinations as there are differences in the ferments of their blood and waste that specifically (and even generically) emerge. Thus, blood that is of one single kind can sustain many kinds of ulcers and transformed corruptions of itself, according to the diversity of the "foreign ferments." And although a single **Archeus** is sufficient for generation, the means, lives, and modes of corruption are various: there are as many as there are families of corrupting agents. Therefore, the full and exact healing of ulcers is the removal of their specific ferment: not the "cooling of the liver," nor the wiping away of imagined bile or discharge. Finally, ulcers are not cured by the application of cleansing agents, even though, because of their malignancy, various degrees of corrosive cleansers might be used. It is not because **fixed realgar** <note>original: "realgar fixum"; a chemical compound of arsenic and sulfur</note>—treated with **saltpeter** <note>original: "salis petræ"</note> and turned into an astringent **sweetened sulfur** <note>original: "sulfur dulcoratum"; sulfur that has been chemically "softened" or neutralized</note>—extinguishes perhaps sixty varieties of ulcers because it gnaws and eats them away (for if that were so, it would not require "sweetening" with repeated **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritu vini"; highly distilled alcohol</note>). Rather, it works because it now possesses a mild poison that is capable of killing the "ulcer-maker" and the corrupter of the blood. 

<margin>31.</margin>

Once that agent is entirely dead, the flesh does not thereafter cease to grow back spontaneously from the bottom. Thus, the cavity of the ulcer indicates the growth of flesh and the scarring of the skin, so that once the **Corrupter** has been removed, restoration may take place. # OF THE SCHOOLS.

<margin>32.</margin> Those things which I attribute to a seminal and toxic **ferment** <term>fermentum: a vital, transformative principle that acts like a catalyst in both life and disease</term>, **Paracelsus**, in his usual manner, transferred into the mineral mines and salt-pits of the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: the concept that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe</term>. For because ulcers are mostly unpleasant due to their saltiness, he thought—according to his own **peculiar dialect** <note>original: "Idiotismum"; here referring to Paracelsus' unique and often obscure terminology</note>—to ascribe ulcers to the lineage of minerals and their distinct families. Now, I do not compose myself for quarrels, nor do I know myself to have been born for such a purpose. Therefore, I grieve for the man's vanity and his uncircumspect forgetfulness. For he boasts of man as a being taken from the **etymon** or **limbo** <note>original: "etymo, sive limbo"; in Paracelsian thought, the *limbus* is the primal matter or "great slime" from which the universe was fashioned</note>, an epitome of the entire universe; he imagines man as more glorious through the dignity of that "extract" than as the **Image of the Creator**. Yet elsewhere, he calls man a most calamitous monster, molded on all sides by minerals alone. Elsewhere, I say, unmindful of these things, he calls the whole human body **Cagastricum** <term>Cagastricum: a term used by Paracelsus for diseases or states originating from the "cagaster," an external or astral seed of corruption</term>: no longer consisting of various textures of salts, but proud only in the structure of a single **saltpeter** <note>original: "salispetræ"</note>. From this, he claims men were born as a "hard race," and therefore children of the earth. He essentially wanted all salts, stones, minerals, herbs, and so on, to lie hidden in man as if in their own nurseries. He believed they burst forth into action—not indeed as the offspring of confused seeds lying hidden in Chaos—but that by the mere separation of the **vital liquor** from its innate companions, they spontaneously regressed into their former mineral states. He failed to notice how absurd it is that, while the **macrocosm** <term>macrocosm: the universe at large</term> is composed no less of stars and plants than of minerals, the body would resolve itself into salts rather than into plants or four-legged animals. Thus, has **Paracelsus** not forgotten here not only seeds, vegetables, stars, and living creatures, but even himself? He fails to explain why his own seed—from which that mass of blood comes—once separated from the vital human beginnings, would regress into this or that mineral rather than something else.

<margin>33.</margin> For just as **Galen**, granting everything to "heats" and delirious with fevers, held the sovereignty of medicine for several centuries, so **Paracelsus**, reducing all things to a subterranean offspring and boasting of his "precious furniture," went mad for a time, and 

<column-break/>

aspired to that same sovereignty. But I ask you, who is that **Separator** who takes away and tears a part of himself from the **vital balsam** <term>balsamum: the natural life-force or preservative principle within the body that prevents decay</term>? And who, finally, is that **Corruptor** who would have changed a part torn from the vital lot into a mineral salt (which does not know how to rot within itself) or into a hidden metal, believable only by faith? Do you not call the dominion of the balsam "long life"? How then do you now call the separation of the balsam "death"? Or what seminal distributor within the human "limbo" is there who could twist one and the same liquor from the vital balsam now into **alum**, and now finally into **arsenic**? Truly, **Paracelsus**, after you constructed great fables with laborious and ridiculous investigation, because you did not know the **ferments** (to which one must come as active and seminal principles), you bypassed the beginnings of nature. Playing with the "limbo" of the microcosm according to your own whim, you exhibited yourself as ridiculous to posterity. For a full knowledge of ferments finds an easy path to knowing, removing, overcoming, and separating the poisons of any ulcers. For whatever happens in the course of nature, happens by the necessity and guidance of **seeds**, and moves toward its own ultimate period. It does not happen by the mere whim of a randomly decayed corpse or a falling part, which would supposedly hasten from privation back into its former being. Away with your trifles! For we do not have salt springs within us; we do not have reductions of blood into fictional and hidden metals. Nor are there minerals in us that, playing around, withdraw themselves from the vital beginnings and wait for the "author of withdrawals" so that they might return from a human existence into their former and destined mineral states, thus becoming the wombs and sources of ulcers. Nor indeed are there "microcosmic laws" in us any more than there are corresponding humors of the four elements in us, or their battles and grudges. For with **Nazianzenus** <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century theologian often cited for his views on the dignity of the human soul</note>, I cannot constrain man to the playful rules of the microcosm.

Here, he further distances himself from the literal interpretation of man as a "miniature universe" and discusses the treatment of wounds and ulcers through the calming of the "Archeus" or internal life-spirit.</meta>

# THE SCAB AND ULCERS OF THE SCHOOLS.

I prefer a thousand times over to be the **image of God**, rather than the image of a corruptible and torturous world. For although man vegetates and grows along with beasts and plants, the beasts are not, for that reason, the image of plants. Likewise, though man feels and moves, and even reasons alongside the animals, nothing but man **speaks**. An Angel, indeed, does not need to speak, just as he has no need for the organs of reproduction. If, however, a bird seems to speak, it merely imitates the tone of speech or its articulations. For there are no hailstones, snows, cliffs, rocks, metals, marbles, flints, or gems within us; nor is there a center of the world toward which all heavy things fall. Neither is there a **Stone** <note>original: "Calculus"; referring here to kidney or bladder stones</note> within us from the moment of creation, nor are there species of Porphyry, Jasper, and so on. A stone in a man differs from a true mineral stone no less than a Pear differs from a cow. Indeed, a pear is changed into the flesh of a cow much faster than a bodily stone could ever turn into a mineral rock. Therefore, the "microcosmic" name <note>The "Microcosm" is the theory that the human body contains all elements of the outer universe (the Macrocosm)</note> is merely **poetic, pagan, and metaphorical**, but not physical or true. It is equally fantastic, hypochondriac, and insane to have introduced all the properties and species of the universe into man and the art of healing. But human life and its remedy are far too serious for Proverbs and metaphors to play their stage-scenes with us.
<margin>34.</margin> Finally, **Paracelsus** is entirely ridiculous when he teaches that an ulcer or wound is nourished by herbs, balsams, or ointments. He seems to have written in earnest that these defects are "nourished" through remedies by true nutrition and the secretion of excrements, and that the lost flesh is truly, actually, and immediately restored from them. This I willingly indulge as part of his own **peculiar dialect** <note>original: "Idiotismo"; Van Helmont's term for Paracelsus’s unique and often nonsensical jargon</note>.
<margin>35.</margin> At last, for the cure of ulcers, there is the use of **Colcotar** <term>Colcotar: the red powder—iron oxide—remaining after the distillation of vitriol (sulfuric acid)</term>, applied in various ways according to the nature of the ulcer.

<column-break/>

For often a wash of macerated wine does the work; at other times, its powder is used after the careful separation of the salt. Sometimes it is boiled in linseed oil until it turns black, which is the basis of the **"Happy Ointment"** of **Felix Wurtz** <note>Felix Wurtz (1518–1574) was a famous Swiss surgeon who argued for gentler wound care over the aggressive methods of his time</note> for wounds. I say enough for the curious: namely, that Colcotar kills every corrupter of wounds.
<margin>36.</margin> Finally, regarding a wound, you should know that the very **separation of continuity** <note>The physical break or cut in the flesh</note> is indeed the immediate and sufficient cause and occasion, insofar as it opens and bruises the flesh, and so on. This requires consolidation, and by means of glue dissolved in wine (which is prepared, of course, from the skins of animals), it is soon glued together. This is especially true if the glue is made from the hide of a man who died a **violent death**—that is, one killed while his strengths were still whole.
But the alterations of the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body’s functions and healing</term> caused by the shedding of blood, and the conceived Ideas of revenge or indignation, which I call "wounds" in their own right (and not something foreign), or those inflicted from without, do not only need the gluing of the broken part. They require the **calming of the disturbed Archeus**. This is the purpose of oils, balsams, and plasters: they reconcile and bring peace to the injured, indwelling, and local Archeus. For this reason, the balsams of resins, flowers, and herbs were created; likewise those prepared from minium <gloss>red lead</gloss>, ceruse <gloss>white lead</gloss>, or Colcotar. To this also belongs the **Salt of Tartar** rectified by spirit of wine until it gains an astringent taste. This is the **"Balsam Samech"** of Paracelsus, just as his "Balsam of Soot" (made from Arsenic for ulcers, mentioned above) is so named because among experts, **Realgar** <term>Realgar: a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</term> is considered the "smoke of metals." It is called this not because it is not a simple substance existing by itself, but by similarity, because metallic smokes imitate the harmful nature of arsenic. Thus I close my teaching on external remedies.

<margin>1.</margin>
From the very principle by which the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities following Aristotle and Galen.</note> placed "contraries" in nature, they immediately and universally decreed that nothing is done in the sublunary world <note>The Earthly realm below the moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay.</note> without strife, war, fighting, and discord. To such an extent have quarrels, hatreds, and rivalries been estimated as the foundations or principles of nature, no less than self-love <note>original: "Philautia"</note>. Indeed, even into the

<column-break/>

<margin>2.</margin>
dances of the stars, they have introduced these same hatreds—credulous as they are—under the persuasion of the Astronomers. At the very least, they have established that in the whole earthly theater, nothing happens or is generated except through a relationship of superiority of the **Agent** over the **Patient**. They believe that the patient is forced by violence, tamed, altered, destroyed, and transferred entirely into the nature of the agent, solely through the relationship of the more powerful over the weaker. <margin>3.</margin> However, when the Schools saw that Agents gradually grew faint, either through age or through the exhaustion of acting, they likewise decided that this does not happen because the "seeds" or powers were drained, but rather because of the **reaction** of the patient alone. And so they established that every "patient" must necessarily react in turn, and to that extent every "agent" must likewise "suffer back," and cannot be weakened by any other cause. <margin>4.</margin> From this, consequently, I foresaw an omen: that eventually the seeds of natural things would undoubtedly be completely extinguished unless they were miraculously preserved. Yet, in both cases, I observe in the doctrines of the Schools a perpetual coarseness and a continued laziness in investigation. This alone has pushed away my former fear. For indeed, after I removed "contraries" from nature, I could not then, with sound judgment, find any reaction in the Patient; nor could I admit hostilities anywhere else in nature, except among living beings. For contrariety exists only in those things where there is an actual defense in the *will* of the Patient against injuries inflicted and sensed by the Agent. Therefore: there is nowhere a reaction of the patient upon the Agent, except where there is a "contrariety" conceived in the soul. That this is the ordinary and ordered state of things in nature, I shall demonstrate immediately. For in the first place, the Universe would remain as it currently subsists by the infinite power of the Word <note>The divine "Logos" or command of God</note>, if it had been so ordered. Infinite, I say, things would be in their successions and duration—though the creature itself is not "infinite" by the actual power of unity. And because this is a matter of faith, it requires no proof. There is therefore nothing among earthly things...

# THE UNKNOWN ACTION

<columns>

...[territo]ry, infinite in its own power. From this it follows that at length every particular agent gradually, even of its own accord, sometimes grows weary, and having fulfilled its duties, expires through the dissolution of its strengths, being circumscribed within the space of place, duration, and the power of its vigor: unless perhaps, by the anticipation of its end, or by impediments from the object, the appointed day of its own and limited expiration is evaded <note>Van Helmont argues that things stop moving or acting not because of "resistance" from an opponent, but because their own internal energy or "schedule" simply runs out.</note>. <margin>§.</margin> Furthermore, among natural agents, there are some having a motive power, which I have called the motive <term>Blas: A word coined by Van Helmont to describe a vital, internal motion or "impetus" within nature.</term>; the agents themselves, however, I call moving strengths. But the remaining moving things I call the alterative <term>Blas</term>, which clearly operate through the seminal power of a ferment <note>A "ferment" in 17th-century chemistry was a spiritual or material principle that initiated change and generation, like yeast in dough.</note>. And agents of this kind for the most part generate something like themselves. Finally, thirdly, there are certain anomalous or irregular agents. I shall speak of those three in order. Indeed, the moving strengths act upon their objects: 1. By a prevailing weight. 2. By a shape—round, angular, sharp, hollow, etc. 3. By the hardness or softness of the body, etc. 4. By an impressive <term>Blas</term> <note>original: "Blas impressivum"; a force "impressed" upon an object by an external actor.</note>, from a hand, a hammer, a needle, etc. 5. By speed. For unless a battering ram is struck with speed against a wall, or a hammer against a nail, even though the impressive force be robust, its <term>Blas</term> will nevertheless be sluggish. 6. By the impediment of a vacuum. And 7. finally, by the fear of the "penetration of dimensions" <note>This refers to the physical principle that two bodies cannot occupy the same space at the same time.</note>. However, it is clear that moving strengths do not in any way "suffer back" <note>original: "repatiantur"; the Scholastic term for an object reacting against an agent.</note> from their objects: for in the first place, in the nature of the aforementioned sixth and seventh points, the universe operates rather so that they do not exist, than that they might operate while they existed—much less that they should react. For an agent does not suffer back from an object that does not yet exist. Since that which does not yet exist cannot yet act, nor suffer back from an action. As for the first point, however—namely, that a greater weight cannot suffer back from a smaller one through any reaction of the smaller—this is clear. Because a smaller weight, placed on the opposite side, does not prove any reaction in the agent; rather, this happens because of a determination made either by the space

<column-break/>

of place (as in the distance from an axis), or because of the modified action of the greater weight. I prove in this way that this is not a true reaction: a smaller weight, simply and absolutely, suffers nothing from the larger one by which it is lifted; therefore, the smaller weight does not react at all, even though it is lifted and gives way. Indeed, the smaller weight only "determines" the action and gravity of the prevailing weight, insofar as every agent is of a finite and determinable action. That such a "determination" is not a reaction of the smaller weight is clear: for the same smaller <margin>6.</margin> weight, remaining as it is, becomes "greater" when it is moved further from the axis <note>This is a description of the law of the lever; a weight has more "power" the further it is from the fulcrum.</note>. Therefore, if there were any action or reaction in weights in the aforementioned case, it would have to be attributed to the space of place, and not to the gravity of the weight. Since one and the same weight, by the space of place alone, is varied and multiplied at the whim of the Artificer. But the space of place, or of distance, is something external to the essence of the weight, and plainly accidental. And so it can neither give a true and proper action nor reaction in weights. Therefore, the determination of actions in weights is not an essential and proper action or reaction of weight upon weight. Just as space, or the distance of place, does not have any internal power, or essential <term>Blas</term> of local motion, upon a ball shot from a cannon; but it only "determines" the finite force of the impressed motion, so that necessarily, through distance, the ball's acquired <term>Blas</term> gradually grows faint. For it is certain that the ball operates upon the medium at a distance; by which I mean that the ball has no activity in the gap of space itself, even though space "determines" the ball's <term>Blas</term> in such a way that it eventually perishes, because it is of a finite power. Likewise also in weights: a greater weight is indeed determined to a certain measure and power by a smaller weight; but that determination is not the true action of any agent, if local motion through place...

# OF GOVERNANCE

<columns>

...since it <note>The object or place where motion occurs.</note> (which is entirely external and accidental to the motion) is limited without any reaction: or if, through its duration, the motion should slacken of its own accord. But if the place and the duration do not suffer from the motion which occurs within them—that is, if the motion does not react upon the place or the duration—then there will be no true action of place or duration upon the motion either, even if a finite motion in a specific place and time should cease of its own accord. It matters nothing, therefore, to the concept of "reaction," even though a lesser weight limits a greater one to its own certain and defined boundary. Therefore, it is sufficiently clear from this that many things are thought to be agents and reagents upon one another because of the internal fragility of our own understanding. In reality, they neither act nor suffer upon each other, and likewise, they do not react or "re-suffer" reciprocally. Indeed, the action by which a greater weight lifts a lesser one, and the lesser yields to the greater—and likewise, by which the greater is determined and diminished by the opposing lesser weight (which otherwise increases the opposition to the greater)—this is not truly a natural action, or the force of <term>seminal properties: The internal "blueprints" or vital forces that Van Helmont believed directed the growth and behavior of all natural things.</term>. Rather, it is a relative respect of <term>Mathematics: In this context, "Mathesis," referring to the abstract science of measurement and proportion.</term> regarding place, duration, magnitude, and so on. These things are plainly external and accidental to natural agents. True actions and "re-sufferings" in nature are considered in the true and intimate joining of forces, which have no place in the things mentioned above. However, to show that these mathematical respects do not have an action flowing from the powers of things, but only a relationship of Mathematics (of which every "action," though it happens through bodies, does not belong to the body as such), it is enough to have shown through the aforementioned points that the determination of motions is far removed from the internal activity of motions. It is according to this internal activity that things were judged by the ancients to react and "re-suffer" in every action. For in this way, there are many impediments in nature which, even if they determine or even plainly take away the force of an agent, are still not to be considered as "reacting." And so, to speak most properly where a 

<column-break/>

natural philosopher must distinguish the essence of things—especially where the necessities of life are discussed—a lesser weight does not resist, and much less does it react against, a greater one. Instead, each thing hangs freely according to how much it weighs, without respect of one to another. But if a man opposes one weight against another—that is, a human intervention—the action of the weights does not regard each other reciprocally. From this, the things I demonstrated above against the "contrarieties of actives" <note>Van Helmont frequently attacked the Aristotelian idea that nature is governed by "contraries" (like hot vs. cold or heavy vs. light) fighting for dominance.</note> shine forth more clearly. For each agent, in the manner of a greater weight, acts freely and without a relationship of contrariety; it acts because it was commanded to act in nature, and as much as it is permitted to act. And so weight, or rather a heavy thing, hangs in itself according to how much it balances, absolutely and without respect to anything else greater, lesser, equal, or proportioned. For such "respects" belong to human industry, which, because of the handling of objects, invented measurements—both according to extension in length, breadth, and depth, and in the division of weights. Man, for example, established axles and lengths <note>Referring to the mechanics of a balance scale or lever.</note>, so that the entire consideration of a single body is artificial, and therefore changeable in its identity and unity. And consequently, weights as such by no means act or react upon one another naturally, or through a mixing of their properties, even though they may seem to do something "artificially." In the same way, light suffers nothing, even if the continuity of the light is hindered by a "suffering" wall. For otherwise, if a lesser weight truly reacted against a heavier one, the weight itself in the heavier object would be diminished forever, actually, and not only relative to the scale; thus, the pound would no longer weigh a pound, as before. And since nothing has been changed or taken away from the weights on either side, it is clear that these are only artificial relationships of moving strengths, and not a true reaction of the lighter weight. For as long as a pound weighs a pound, nothing is acquired or suffered in it by another weight placed opposite it.
