# UNKNOWN ACTION

...but on both sides, one is external to the other, foreign, accidental, and determinable by a relative foundation, so that it may serve human considerations. And whatever acts near us in this way, or seems to react: in truth, it acts not at all. As for the other moving strengths: If the impressed force of a strength should act by itself, but meanwhile is determined by the space of the location or its duration, or is weakened by obstacles, or finally if it acts in a modified way due to shape or hardness—at least in these cases, there is never any reaction from the receiver, or any <term>passion: In 17th-century philosophy, "passion" is the state of being acted upon—the opposite of "action."</term> <margin>7.</margin> created in the agent. For example: if someone strikes an anvil with a fist, and from there a wound or bruise results. There is not, in that blow, any reaction of the anvil, or any operation of hardness, or of an angle in the iron. For although the hardness resists, struggling against the striking fist, and the boundaries of resistance or struggle seem to necessarily include some force of reaction—nevertheless, this is an improper way of speaking, arising from a popular error of the ancients. For that is not a "reaction" of the anvil; rather, it is the very action of the fist itself, which I call **resilient** <note>original: "resilientem" — meaning "leaping back" or rebounding.</note>. For if the anvil truly reacted through its hardness, there would be no reason why the anvil would act only partially against the fist and wait for the blow in order to act. It ought, by its total hardness and weight together, to act even upon a resting hand and, in fact, plainly crush it. Nor would the action of the anvil be limited by the strength of the blow if it were truly a reaction of the anvil itself. Indeed, the same thing would happen to the fist whether it struck forcefully or modestly, or if the opposing fist were simply at rest: because in either act, the hardness of the anvil was the same. Therefore, that hardness of the iron does nothing, nor does it react, by any proper power of acting. For if the anvil had a power situated in reacting through its hardness, it would act in any strike equally and according to its full power—not according to the modification of the striking fist, which is entirely foreign to the anvil. Therefore, the fist truly and simply acts upon the anvil, and the anvil simply suffers the action, even if it

<column-break/>

takes no injury from it. But the fist suffers <note>In the sense of "receives the effect."</note> accidentally if it strikes more forcefully. However, the agent of this suffering is not the anvil, but the fist itself. Because there is only a single and unique action of striking and injury, which I therefore call **resilient**. And so the fist suffers and is injured by itself, through its own action; it happens "by accident" due to the strength of the blow, and "occasionally" due to the hardness or shape of the iron. These three things must be noted in a single strike. Since that which acts only externally, accidentally, and occasionally does not truly act by its own proper action. Therefore, there is no reaction in the anvil, just as there is no action. Instead, the striking and the hardness are the "occasional means" of the wound. One of these (namely, hardness) is a proper and internal occasion; the other (namely, the striking) is an accidental occasion. Finally, 8. there is another action of moving strength which has deceived many under the title of "reaction." For example, when a hand grasps a glowing iron: the hand, by grasping, acts truly and by itself, and the grasped iron itself <note>original: "patitur" — is the receiver of the action.</note> suffers in the grasping. But this iron, in turn, acts by a new and quite different action: by burning the hand. For that burning is not an action of the iron *insofar as it is grasped* (although that touch is the immediate occasion and the "cause without which it would not happen"), but it is a proper action of the iron *as something glowing*. Thus, the touch and the burning are entities entirely distinct and separable at their root. And so, both of those actions differ in their objects, even though they coincide during the act. Therefore, the burning is not a reaction of the iron as a thing grasped; or, it is not a reaction to the grasping. Even if the acting hand becomes a "patient" <note>A receiver of an action.</note> through an action of another class, it is because two entirely disparate actions concur: 9. namely, one of the grasping hand, and another of the burning iron. Finally, speed—when a <term>battering ram: A heavy wooden beam used to break down walls.</term> is dashed against a wall—is not the proper activity of the agent, but is a modification of the force moving by impression; and therefore it is external and accidental. Now, 10. as for agents acting through the <term>altering Blas: A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a vital, internal moving force or impulse that governs change in matter.</term>, they...

# OF GOVERNANCE #
### 333 ###

-> II. <-

...in no way do they endure reaction from their objects: because they generate through an absolute dispositive power <note>original: "potentiam dispositivam" — the power to arrange or prepare matter.</note> over those objects. This power, since it was divinely granted to nature, also acts without reaction. For example: If the entire globe of earth and water were made of flour, eventually that entire mass would be fermented by a single dose of bread leaven once introduced. This certainly would not happen if there were even the slightest reaction from the fermentable body. For a tiny bit of ferment would immediately be suffocated by the larger mass of the object. In the same way, the **seminal spirits** <note>In Van Helmont’s view, these are the "blueprints" or vital forces within seeds that direct growth and form.</note> arrange and alter the underlying mass according to the faculty granted and innate to them, with a remarkable prerogative, and without any reaction from the subject mass. Nor is it an objection that the stomach, in cooking harder foods, is felt as if to suffer back <note>original: "repati" — to undergo a reciprocal "passion" or reaction.</note> and endure a reaction from the things to be digested. For that is the talk of a crude peasant, or of [unskilled] physicians. Since unless the thing to be digested is cooked perfectly and within a fixed time, the digestion of it is hoped for in vain. For if it remains too long in the stomach, it is corrupted, and thus a new agent arises—it is no longer the original thing to be digested, once it has been corrupted. Nor does this new agent react in the manner of a glowing hot iron. This is because there are parts in that digestible material that are incapable of digestion with respect to that specific stomach. Neither does bread leaven ferment glass powder or flint sand; because it is a foreign and incapable object, untamable by it. Thus, the digesting ferment of the stomach ferments the flower of the meal, but not the bran. Meanwhile, the ferment of the meal suffers nothing from the glass powder: just as that powder does not react, resist, or truly struggle. Indeed, the altering ferments act in no way except upon those things having a **sympathy** <note>original: "symbolum" — a shared nature, correspondence, or "password" between substances.</note>: but they rest, cease, and sleep if they do not have their own proper object. Therefore, the impediments to agents, through the **altering Blas** <term>Blas: A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the inner motive power or "pulse" of a substance that drives its natural movements and changes.</term>, are incapacities, hardness, impurities, inequalities, and the requirements of moving space. Therefore, the action of these agents is limited to their proper object, and it arranges that object according to its decreed

<column-break/>

periods and methods. However, the intervening impediments are not "reactions" of the patient <note>In 17th-century physics, the "patient" is the object being acted upon by an "agent."</note>: but rather its own incapacities. For Silver does not "react" while it is being dissolved by **Chrysulca** <term>Chrysulca: Literally "gold-drawer," another name for Aqua Regia or a powerful acid used to dissolve metals.</term> with such great fervor; although the acid may meanwhile grow weary by acting and lose its strength. Rather, it is an innate property and gift of the spirits, who work by acting so that, by reaching their destined goal, they might perfect themselves and lead their objects to the ends naturally enjoined upon them. Distilled vinegar teaches this well enough while it dissolves "crab stones" <note>original: "lapidem cancrorum" — also known as crabs' eyes; these are calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine as an antacid.</note>, snail shells, corals, etc. For the acid spirit of the vinegar coagulates itself by acting, and what was otherwise entirely volatile and liquid becomes constricted—not only <gloss>that it might be</gloss> [solid] but also it changes its taste. For it compels and constricts itself into a tangible form, as if it rejoiced more to remain in the appearance of a solid body than as a liquor. However, it is clear that such coagulation and change of taste happen by the proper motion of the spirit of vinegar, and not by a reaction of the bodies standing in the solution. This is because there is no decrease in the weight of those bodies, not even by a single grain. Meanwhile, several measures of distilled vinegar undergo the aforementioned change. Thus, it does not seem consistent with reason that this happens solely because of the crushing of the stones, but rather because of the spirits’ own unfolding of their innate gift. Almost the same thing happens when **spirit of vitriol** <term>Spirit of vitriol: Sulfuric acid.</term> grows hot with Mercury. For the Mercury remains unchanged in its essence and matter, except that it assumes the appearance of snow: losing nothing of its substance in the meantime, yet the spirit of vitriol passes into true **Alum**. But if the spirit of **Aqua Fortis** <term>Aqua Fortis: Nitric acid.</term> (which, for its other half, is also spirit of vitriol) is combined with Mercury, that "snow" of Mercury is not made, nor does the liquid itself pass into alum. Therefore, it appears from this that the action is not proper to the Mercury, but to the spirit of vitriol, which arranges itself of its own accord in different ways according to its innate inclination...

Using examples like vinegar dissolving coral or acids reacting with mercury, he suggests that the changes observed in the solvent are self-directed fulfillments of its own nature.</summary>

# UNKNOWN ACTION #
### 334 ###

...toward various objects, changing itself differently. Therefore, the spirit of vitriol <note>original: "spiritus vitrioli"; an early term for sulfuric acid</note>, which is in aqua fortis <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid</note>, dissolves Mercury with a strong excitation of bubbles and a stormy boiling; and this happens far differently than when the spirit of vitriol is bare and simple. Indeed, this variety in acting reveals the various powers of the acting spirit, rather than those of the Mercury itself. For in one action, Mercury becomes invisible, while in another, it becomes white like snow. Furthermore, the spirit of sea salt <note>original: "spiritus salis marini"; hydrochloric acid</note>, although it is extremely sharp, is not changed at all by the company of Mercury, nor does it even act upon the Mercury. Thus, these appear to be effects of actions, and not of reactions.

So too, the gold-solvent <note>original: "Chrysulca"; another name for aqua regia, a mixture of acids</note> acts on all metals except gold; however, with sal ammoniac <note>original: "sale armeniaco"; ammonium chloride</note>, it acts only on gold, but no longer on silver. Therefore, these are unique properties of the spirits, and not reactions of the body undergoing the process—since that body, in its substance or weight, undergoes nothing except the mere and single division of itself. Therefore, spirits, stirred by acting through various "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing change</note>, undergo various metamorphoses; but if they remain drowsy and sleeping, and do not act on an object, they remain in their former qualities. At first, it seemed that this happened because of the touch of Mercury—since it is also a kind of spirit—but later, in the case of silver and gold, that whole theory fell silent.

Furthermore, I remember that a "lime" of silver <note>original: "calcem Argenti"; a metal reduced to powder by heat or acid</note> soaked up a liquor of sulfur which they call *stagma* <note>a term for a distilled drop or liquid essence</note>, which immediately laid aside all its harshness and sourness upon the silver, and by distilling it, changed this into a gall-like bitterness. Yet the silver remained the same as before in substance, weight, and powder. Therefore, that bitterness could not have been given by the silver. And for that reason, it was in no way caused by a reaction of the silver, but was made by its own accord from the property of the spirit of sulfur. For there is no less reason why the same spirit of vitriol, by acting in different ways, should also change itself into various forms, than that the same silver

<column-break/>

should grow fierce by "reacting" differently against different spirits under the boiling of those spirits. This is especially true while a metamorphosis occurs in the spirit through the act of doing, yet no alteration of substance or decrease in weight occurs in the silver while it is being acted upon.

These things can be demonstrated far more clearly by the Adepts <note>Alchemists who were believed to have attained the ultimate secrets of nature</note>. For them, one and the same liquor, the **Alkaheft** <note>Van Helmont's famous "universal solvent" which he claimed could dissolve any matter into its primary liquid form</note>, perfectly reduces all tangible bodies of the whole universe into their "first life" <note>their original, primordial state</note>, without any change to itself or any lessening of its powers. It is only brought under the yoke and changed by its own equal <note>i.e., only a substance of similar nature can affect the Alkaheft</note>. From this, it appears that a certain "sense" or perception exists in individual things, by means of which they move and unfold themselves differently around different objects. It does not follow, however, that the cycle of these movements and unfoldings, or the variety of the agents, should be attributed to a "reaction" from the things being acted upon.

It is just as when external warmth brings eggs to the stage of a chick: neither of the two suffers back from the other in a reciprocal way. For the vital spirit in the egg does not suffer anything back from the warmth, nor is that warmth in any way affected by the vital spirit of the egg. This supports what I proved before: namely, that things which "alter" do not act through contrariety <note>the Aristotelian idea that change happens through a struggle between opposites like hot and cold</note>. Therefore, the things being acted upon do not fight to defend themselves, nor do they react through opposition.

<margin>12</margin> That axiom is also false: "That every agent must necessarily act in an instant," and that its action is only delayed by the resistance and reaction of the one being acted upon. This is because a certain and fixed period of durations and dispositions is essentially included within every individual seed.

<margin>13</margin> For the falsehood of that axiom flowed from the fact that the Schools <note>The traditional university scholars of the time</note>, deceived by *Aristotle*, thought that fire should be compared to all other agents. When they saw that fire was almost instantaneous in some places, they believed the same should be applied to other agents. On this occasion, we must now speak of "anomalous" and "irregular" agents.

<margin>14</margin> First of all, it is manifest that *Fire* suffers nothing at all, nor does it endure anything through a reaction from the object being burned. For otherwise, a tiny fire would be enough to burn...

# OF GOVERNANCE #
### 335 ###

...burning the entire universe, if it were combustible. This would not happen if a combustible thing reacted even the slightest bit. Indeed, a river suffers nothing if a stick floats in it, and fire suffers even less if it burns the city of Saguntum <note>An ancient city in Spain, famously destroyed by fire during a siege by Hannibal</note> or if gunpowder is ignited. In nature, also, no formative principle <note>original: "feminale initium"; likely referring to the "seed" or generative spark</note> suffers from the matter upon which it acts. This is because it arranges the matter without any reaction, just as began to be clear in the case of "denied contraries" <note>A logical term referring to things that do not oppose one another directly</note>.

Furthermore, so that the falsehood of the aforementioned axiom <note>The Aristotelian axiom that "every action has a reaction"</note> may be more clearly seen, note that individual seeds <note>original: "femina"; likely a variant or typo for "semina," meaning seeds or formative germs</note> have their own periods and moments appointed by the Creator, by which they advance their course toward maturity. For rabbits, dogs, birds, humans, horses, and elephants cherish, perfect, and give birth to their offspring within fixed limits. It is certainly not because the seminal matter in a human is cruder, colder, or more rebellious than that of a cat. Rather, God has arranged the limits of each according to His good pleasure, and to inquire into His reason is not a matter for human judgment. For if the arrangement of seminal matter requires a longer labor, this does not happen because of its stubbornness or a reluctant strength, just as it does not come from the weakness or exhaustion of the acting agent, nor from holidays or the disturbance of passions.

Indeed, every agent in nature works without labor and without "passion" <note>In the sense of "undergoing" or "suffering" a counter-effect</note>; and therefore, it works without ceasing, rest, intermission, or trouble. For all things happen because of the communication of a "ferment" <note>A vitalizing chemical or spiritual principle that triggers transformation</note> and the determination of their "destination" <note>The internal purpose or blueprint of a thing</note>. For all things work purely through the reflection of their own destination toward the determining will of their Creator.

<margin>16.</margin> This is surely how Christians ought to philosophize. However, in local motion, in motive forces, and even in the practice of mathematics, the axioms of Aristotle do indeed serve a purpose—axioms which they have introduced into nature by the violent and persistent command of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian academic system of the time</note>.

<margin>17.</margin> For if damp wood is not burned as obediently as dry wood, this does not happen because of a reaction from the wood, or because the fire undergoes "passion." For even if the wood ceased from all combustion,

<column-break/>

the fire would not suffer more from the wood than it does from non-combustible gold. Indeed, if there were a certain active resistance—that is, a reaction—in damp wood as such, then surely water would also resist fire longer and more strongly than the resin of the wood or charcoal.

But the consequence is false. For water flies out of damp wood very quickly and before all else, even before the fire ignites the resin of the wood. Therefore, slowness in damp wood does not prove a reaction of the matter or the strength of the "patient" wood. Instead, the fire follows the laws of its destinations, by which it separates the more volatile things first, and then, in order, the less fleeting ones.

<margin>18.</margin> Thus, even if fire is placed under damp resin, which otherwise would have been immediately consumed by that same fire, nevertheless, because of the aforementioned laws, the fire patiently waits through the "torture" <note>A term often used in alchemy to describe the intense application of heat</note> and the departure of that water. Iron, too, placed between straw and fire, prevents the burning of the straw. But there is not, on that account, any reaction of the iron upon the fire, nor any "passion" of the fire from the iron. This was certainly not sufficiently investigated by the Schools. For although these axioms of theirs have a place in physical actions where an agent, out of necessity, cherishes and touches its object and thus inspires its power into it: nevertheless, this is entirely irrelevant in Agents that act upon subjects placed far away.

Indeed, besides the actions of the heavens (which are carried by influence, irradiation, and motion without the touch of the agent, but disperse their seeds solely by the *Blas* <note>A word coined by Van Helmont to describe the "stellar" or "vital" motive force in nature</note> of their powers), earthly things are not properly deprived of *Blas*.

<margin>19.</margin> For "fermental" odors produce highly active and seminal effects, and they transform an object in nature by their "suffumigation" <note>The process of being affected by smoke or vapors</note>, drawing it into their service. Similarly, "radial action" also concurs in nature: for the hoof of an Elk <note>original: "Ungula Alcis"; in folk medicine, elk hooves were worn as rings or amulets to cure epilepsy</note> is said to preserve the heart and head from "the fall" <note>falling sickness, or epilepsy</note> by its touch. Yet the seat of the evil is not in the finger, nor is there a journey from one end to the other, nor is the hoof's strength diminished by it.

...is [not] diminished by acting: rather it is strengthened, just as a magnet is strengthened by the address <note>original: "alloquio"; implying the proximity or interaction</note> of iron. Therefore charms or amulets possess a <term>Blas<gloss>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a formative, motive power or vital pulse, distinct from the soul</gloss></term>, by which they compel objects to obey them, like the heavens; they act only upon their own object, and not upon a foreign or neighboring one. And without any physical outflow, motion, suffering, or weakening, they bring forth their own merits. I know indeed that the Schools <note>The traditional academic authorities following Aristotle and Galen</note> cannot bear this; instead, they attribute these effects to vapors rising from the womb even to the smallest toe 

<margin>20.</margin> of the foot. This is because they submerge themselves in the mud of a "feculent Minerva" <note>An idiomatic way of saying their wisdom is "dirty" or "low-brow" compared to true natural philosophy</note>. But if a hysterical maiden <note>Referring to "hysteria," then believed to be a physical movement of the womb</note> sees everything perfectly, at least on one side, or only in one half, and sees only half of the needle she presses with her fingers, no matter how she rolls her eyes and head; if (I say) she sees many people gathered in a crowd, but only as far as the waist or only their half-profiles: will those vapors then be "halved," even though the pupil of the eye remains whole? Will these vapors (I say) allow many things to be seen and discerned at once, 

<margin>21.</margin> but each only by its other half? But the Schools have neglected the incorporeal **Blas** of governance, which acts without a physical outflow, just as the Moon makes the sea swell. For in uterine suffocation <note>A term for hysterical fainting or breathing difficulty</note>, as long as they are capable of speech, patients complain of a tension of the intercostals, and they believe a tight belt is cinched around their ribs, or a stick 

<margin>22.</margin> is extended from the lower parts to the throat, etc. Pay attention with me, I pray, oh Schools, to the double motive power within us, and turn away from this worn-out axiom of yours: namely, that the damaged action is of the same power as the healthy one. Since there is in us a **voluntary Blas**, and also a **Blas of the parts** themselves (as I have noted elsewhere regarding convulsions), note it at least in this place. If voluntary motion is natural, the will also suffers nothing from the muscles moved by it—indeed, it is not even moved by muscles that refuse to move. Nor, finally, is there a fatigue of the 

<column-break/>

faculty, but only of the body or the organs. Finally, because the muscles are moved by a troublesome **Blas** of the parts, there is no fatigue of the parts, even though the pain is intense and they do not feel a "tiring" of themselves; this is because convulsive movements, excited by the **Blas** of the parts, are made by a "dementing" faculty <note>A faculty acting outside of conscious control</note>, and thus they are hardly felt as fatigue.

<margin>23.</margin> Nor does it argue anything that moisture in wood, or the interposition of charcoal between the flame and the resin within the wood, retards the action of fire, lest the wood be consumed too quickly by its own voracity.

<margin>24.</margin> Since impediments do not act properly, nor do they react: but purely and simply suffer. They do indeed determine the action of the fire to some extent, or exclude it, as if they were incapable gaps, and nothing more. For it is proper and natural to fire to first consume water and lighter, dissipatable things into vapors before it ignites oily things by burning. Finally, after the oily things, it consumes the fat that remained more fixed in the charcoal. For water does not react against the fire, nor does the fire suffer. For whether water is in the wood or not, fire always acts in one way <note>original: "univoce"</note> and according to the purpose of its nature; it acts freely, and in a manner that convicts the aforementioned axiom of falsehood. Gold also, Talc, marble, etc., do not react against fire, even though they are not consumed by it. Their manifest incapacity stands in the way, because of which the fire does not act upon them through ordinary conflagration. For fire intends to illuminate those bodies that are opaque in themselves, so that they might become in some way translucent, which it finally achieves in their becoming white-hot. Indeed, fire strives by its own form to penetrate all things. Because flammable things cannot endure this without their own ruin, they are therefore ignited by burning, and once consumed, they withdraw. Nor does fire pretend to illuminate stones and metals in a single moment, according to the aforementioned axiom; but fire, in its nature of acting, accommodates itself according to the determination of each object. And so it is perpetually true that every natural agent...

He uses the examples of hysterical vision loss and the stages of combustion to prove that "fatigue" or "delay" comes from the physical organs or the nature of the matter, not from a reciprocal force acting against the agent.</summary>

Here, he applies this principle to the physics of fire and light, then transitions into a medical critique of how the "Schools" (the traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle) misunderstand the causes of disease.</meta>

### 337 ###

...acts naturally, and is received according to the capacity of the object receiving it. Therefore, the primary action of fire is to produce fire similar to itself in its object. In this process, some things burn away under the intensity of the fire; others, however, endure and wait for the fire's final intent. So much so that even if certain things cannot be cremated, the fire still acts upon them as much as it can to make them ignited <note>original: "ignita"; meaning glowing or heated to the state of fire without being consumed</note>. Similarly, light suffers nothing, even though it vibrates against the earth in a single instant from the Sun far away, or even if it is not transmitted through an obstructing opaque medium. Indeed, light suffers nothing from an opaque body, whether it passes through it or not. For it always achieves its intent, which is to illuminate, whether an impediment has intervened in the meantime or not. For the resistance or defiance of obstructing objects does not function by way of "reaction" (since agents suffer nothing in return), but is a matter of mere incapacity. Therefore, whether fixed objects are merely illuminated by fire and penetrated by light, or not, is entirely indifferent and accidental to those agents. For these things behave just like <term>leaven<gloss>ferment or yeast</gloss></term> in dough compared to glass powder. For the leaven suffers nothing, even though the inability of the glass to rise stands in the way of the leaven acting. For at the very least, there is no reaction where there is no action. This establishes the absence of reaction, struggle, hatred, or war between the agent and the patient <note>the "patient" is the object being acted upon</note>—the only kind of action, ironically, that the Schools have ever recognized.

<margin>25.</margin>
I will add other new points. I have said in my book on fevers that a poisonous waste in fevers is trapped in the <term>praecordia<gloss>the area of the midriff or chest, considered by Van Helmont to be the seat of the vital soul</gloss></term>, producing lethargy, delirium, etc. Therefore, the poison is "anodyne" <note>pain-numbing</note> and "insane." Likewise, in <term>epilepsy<gloss>original: "caducis," the falling sickness</gloss></term> there is an unfeeling and insane poison, causing affliction for a time, stable in the midriff. In hypochondriacal madness, there is a furious poison, or one that raves with a jest. In vertigo, it is a "spinning" poison.

<margin>26.</margin>
In Apoplexy, it is a poison that takes away sense and motion. Finally, in <term>syncope<gloss>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness</gloss></term>, it is a numbing poison that scatters the spirits. Hence it immediately removes sense and motion.

<column-break/>

But since the Schools do not look beyond their simple rules <note>original: "supra rus extendant," literally "extend themselves beyond the countryside"</note>, they thought that the "occasional matter" of these diseases was the very material from which the diseases arose, and that this was carried through the veins and arteries from below upward to the brain. However, I have refuted this elsewhere in my exposition of the <term>Aphorism<gloss>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</gloss></term>:

> *If in a continuous fever, after yellow urine, watery urine suddenly follows, it signifies future delirium; because the bile (as Galen believes) has been snatched up into the brain.*

Elsewhere, when the Schools noticed vertigos arising in the morning from yesterday’s overindulgence, they preferred to believe that the matter of diseases, in the form of vapors, is carried directly from the stomach into the brain through "anonymous tubes" and the gullet. And so they claim that <term>black bile<gloss>original: "atra bilis"</gloss></term>, following Hippocrates, is carried sometimes into the substance of the brain to produce Epilepsy, and at other times into the soul itself, and then it creates the passion of hypochondriacal madness. And they claim this happens through uncertain channels and guides, toward uncertain targets or objects.

<margin>27.</margin>
But since a single "melancholic humor" was insufficient to explain such great evils, the Schools then hesitated—not, indeed, concerning the four humors already established in antiquity, but concerning the malice of the humors, which remained unexplored and undifferentiated. Indeed, lest they be overwhelmed by the narrowness and sameness of the pathways (which could not account for such variety), they fled to the idea of "smokes and vapors." They claimed that various smokes from a single "black bile" penetrated the cavities of the brain and stirred up various atrocities. They safely wove these trifles as a pretext for gullible students, secure in the knowledge that they would never be forced to actually point out or look at these supposed smokes. Meanwhile, the Schools are worthy of pity for such laziness in investigating the truth until now, having been driven into such miserable straits. But surely the sick are more worthy of pity, for they have endured such "helpers"—hired at great cost—to the destruction of their own lives. For such patients must be lower and more miserable than such "agents."

<margin>28.</margin>
Thus the Schools neglected the actual substance of so many different poisons that lie in wait for the head and for life itself.

<meta>This page continues the critique of the "Schools" (the academic medical establishment of the 17th century). Having established on the previous page that spiritual forces act without physical "reaction" or loss of power, Van Helmont now applies this to the "human economy"—the way the body governs its own health and responds to disease.</meta>

### 338 ###

However, the Schools have carelessly applied that material <note>The physical matter of the body</note> to life—as if a disease-causing occasional cause merely triggered a disease-causing agent. Consequently, they have transferred the entire mention and consideration of this history into a physical context. Likewise, they have neglected the manner in which disease is formed and how the activity of a poison is carried to a living object. This is because they were utterly ignorant of the sink <note>original: "sentinam"; referring to a source of internal filth or toxins</note> from which those poisons are drawn, and they passed it over as if it were something entirely unheard of. They did this because they had neglected the **proper action of the human economy's governance**. Without this knowledge, however, nothing of what happens within us can be clearly understood. For only the "action of an agent upon a patient" was known in the Schools—which they insisted happens through a kind of encirclement, involving a struggle and "reaction" from the patient, along with the 
<margin>29.</margin> weakening and counter-suffering of the agent. But there is a certain action of a prior type, far different from the former, which those before me never mentioned, and which I call the **action of governance** <note>original: "actionem regiminis"; the internal vital power that manages the body's functions without physical contact</note>. This action occurs not only without any suspicion of "reaction," but even without physical contact; thus, it can act upon a distant or separate subject. This is called "magnetic" and "sympathetic" action—something derided by the modern Schools when it occurs between objects distant in space. But when it is confined within our own body, I call it the "action of mere governance" to distinguish it from magnetism. In this action, the Agent disposes of its own patient (the object within its sphere) as if it were a client by hereditary right, according to an innate order of laws subjected to it by a shared bond. Imagine the Agent here as a guardian and the patient as a minor. There is a similar action in the universe among the stars, both upon each other and upon things below the moon. While it is beyond controversy that this action is "influential" <note>acting through an "influence" or flow of power</note> in the heavens, it has been undeservedly suspected in things below the moon, and thus has been neglected and left barren until now. This is not the
<margin>30.</margin> action which the Schools recognized as the "consent of parts" or the "conspiracy of duties and necessities"; our present 

<column-break/>

action of governance is something else. For governance does not ask for "consent." Therefore, "consent" is primarily a deceptive name, containing either a mask or nothing but an imposture and a fable. For in reality, they want this "consent" to be stirred up, sought, and returned through vapors, channels, ducts, or fibers. Since these things do not exist in nature, nor are they required, they have nothing in common with the action of governance.
<margin>31.</margin> For the Schools nowhere admit the action of an agent unless it is applied to the patient by a medium, like a chain or a continuous channel. I say they deny the continuation of power stretched through the identity of a medium, unless it is carried to its proper patient through a kind of tube. And especially in the human body, they decree that nothing happens without the communication of pathways. This was the source of their continued and ridiculous necessity for "revulsions" and "derivations" <note>Standard Galenic medical practices of "pulling" or "draining" humors from one part of the body to another</note>.
<margin>32.</margin> Indeed, in the human body, Anatomy has been cultivated by this reasoning, as if it were the indubitable indicator and healer of all diseases. So much sweat has been poured into it that the Schools measure a "true physician" (forgetting their own Galen) by one who has poked around most in the filth of corpses, and who has discovered with his own scalpel those things that were published by his predecessors to the point of superstition. The error of such superfluous curiosity, and the pride of such insane doctrine—praised by the ignorance of the Schools—must be considered introduced by the Author of vertigo and darkness <note>Likely a reference to the Devil or a personification of spiritual blindness</note>. For it is
<margin>33.</margin> pleasing to him that we waste our time unprofitably under any title. For it was enough for Anatomy to know the site, the connection, and the uses of the parts—not to have spent a whole life in the **butchery of corpses** <note>original: "cadaverum lanienam"</note> to find the path of the smallest vein.

<margin>35.</margin> When one of the muscles must move while another remains at rest, the supreme Arbiter of things <note>God</note> established a variety of organs, so that the command of our will would be announced to the muscles solely through the assigned nerves, and then carried out through the muscles and bones. Because of this, the Schools <note>The academic medical establishment of the 17th century</note> have claimed that all our actions occur only through a linked chain of organs, across separate and distinct families of limbs. They did not notice that insects, with a single fluid stretched through their length, fulfill the various duties of veins, arteries, nerves, and viscera. Thus, I have seen a fly fly away even after its head was cut off, and the horned head of a hornet ( *which they call a "flying stag"* <note>original: "cervum volantem"; referring to a stag beetle</note> ) live and move six days after being severed. Therefore, the varieties of powers and organs do not depend on necessity; rather, the Creator chose to distinguish certain duties and ends through the blind and mutual dependency of organs only in the more "perfect" <note>more complex</note> animals. Meanwhile, this dependency and reciprocal exchange between limbs does not mean the action of governance ceases in man—an action I have 
<margin>36.</margin> already pointed out in insects. Indeed, in the human economy, many things are administered without any connection of "carrying canals" <note>vessels or tubes</note>. Because this remained a point of doubt, the Schools assigned the greatest glory of life and study to Anatomy. And whenever a connection <note>original: "syndesmon," from the Greek for "bond"</note> was unknown to them, they immediately fled to the "sacred anchor of ignorance" <note>An ancient idiom for a final, desperate resource</note>, attributing the cause to blind rising vapors or humors falling without order, with the astonishment one feels at an unusual thing. For after they had dissected at their whim those who were suffocated by the womb <note>hysteria</note>, or had fainted, or were extinguished by epileptic attacks or heart tremors—and had found no "highwayman" of life in the pathways who could be blamed for the murder—they retreated to the idea of blind vapors and foul breaths carried to the Heart and Head. So that even then,

<column-break/>

with no continuous commerce of pathways, they were forced to admit that those deadly vapors could be carried in every direction. <margin>37.</margin> I willingly admit those bodily actions where heat warms what is placed near it, and the way a belch rises from the stomach through the gullet into the throat and nostrils; likewise, that excrement grows in its own conduits, and to wander or stumble from these is a sorrowful thing. I admit too that the vital spirits are ordinarily dispersed into the body through the vessel-canals of their own viscera. I would be a madman if I did not confess these things. Finally, I admit the action by which the ferments of the viscera flow down into the "kitchens" of digestion along certain paths like rays, and are not carried by an oblique motion. <margin>38.</margin> But I do not overlook a third kind of action in the human body, which is called "influential" or the action of "governance." Although this does not ordinarily wander outside the body, it is nonetheless abstracted from any binding medium <note>it doesn't need a physical "bridge" to work</note>. Indeed, it acts not only by a direct and Solar ray, but also by another kind that penetrates the whole structure of parts imperceptibly—much like the moon, which affects whatever it looks upon even obliquely, as I have noted before in my new writings on "meteors" <note>Van Helmont often used meteorological metaphors to describe biological processes</note>. This, I say, is the action of governance or dependency, radiating and penetrating in every direction without the "allurement of connection," yet only toward its proper object. Note here what I have said elsewhere: that a beard is generated in a man by the testicles, which is what distinguishes him from a castrated man <note>The author argues that the testicles "govern" the growth of a beard through vital influence, not through a direct physical pipe or tube</note>. <margin>39.</margin> Besides this action of governance, I recognize two others that are natural but marvelous. There is therefore a third action proper to incorporeal Spirits. These do not require a direct ray to act, nor the sight of the object, nor its proximity, disposition, or connection. Instead, they act by a mere "authoritative nod" (for they lack extremities with which to touch the bodies they intend to move, or even the media by which they might move those bodies) through a far more effective influential power. That action is similar to the way the soul signifies its choice, or its "nod," to the organs to which it is bound. For you have diminished, O Lord,

Not rarely, the womb binds a single tendon in the foot or the throat, or completely compresses the entire gullet as if it were a localized disease; while in the meantime, no exhalation <note>original: "exhalatio," referring to the Galenic theory that "vapors" from the womb caused hysteria</note> is sent, directed, or received by that nerve or location. For by its mere "aspect" <note>an astrological and vitalistic term meaning influence or gaze</note> it contracts the lung so much that it entirely deprives the person of breath. The stories told here about harmful vapors are trifles. Indeed, such a vapor would convulse the intestines, stomach, and diaphragm—which are closer—long before it reached the lung alone. Elsewhere also, the throat rises to the height of the chin and then sinks again, and this is not the result of vapors. Rather, the dominion, the governance, the aspect, the influence, and the command of the womb are such. For it affects whichever part it wishes, and sometimes destroys the whole, because that whole is subject to it. For as long as it is not shaken by the perturbations of the soul, the womb stands on a "straight foot"—indeed, it slumbers. But once it is attacked by perturbations <note>emotional disturbances or passions</note>, it thereafter produces its own overflows throughout the entire body, which are sometimes lasting even unto death. 

<margin>44.</margin> Since the womb, by its own monarchy, distinguishes the whole woman from the man, and is the universal parent of that distinction, it is no wonder that by that same governance it can agitate all parts, even the most remote, no differently than the near ones, whenever it wishes. 

<margin>45.</margin> It is certain to one searching deeply that the operations of the sensitive soul <note>the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement</note> follow a similar order and progression in their work; thus, if the womb strikes down health through a spiritual governance, by an equal privilege, this power has been granted to the soul in acting upon the womb. For if a pregnant woman, moved by a desire (as I have repeated elsewhere), looks at a cherry and touches her own forehead, the fetus immediately receives the mark of the cherry. This is not merely a bare "spot" of a cherry, but a cherry that turns green, white, yellow, and ripens into a deep red color every year, in unison with the fruits on the trees. Indeed, what is far more wonderful: that which happens to the fetus in Brabant <note>a region in the Low Countries, modern-day Belgium/Netherlands</note> happens much earlier to a fetus in Spain—namely, where the cherries 

<column-break/>

ripen sooner. Therefore, thought seeks the fetus by a direct path; certainly not through the direction of fibers or straight rays, or a channel of physical leaning or proclivity, nor through a "consensus" <note>a medical term for organs feeling in sympathy with one another</note> of the brain and the womb, but by the sole reciprocal action of governance. 

Furthermore, even if no fetus is present, the "Ideas of the imagination" do not therefore cease to be painted upon the walls of the womb. Since these ideas are foreign to the womb, it easily goes mad, impatient with these exotic pictures. There is, therefore, an open path from the sensitive soul into the womb, and vice versa. This is what Hippocrates first noted: namely, that "the whole body is one that breathes out together and breathes in together" <note>original: "totum corpus exspirabile, & conspirabile esse," a famous Hippocratic maxim regarding the unity of the organism</note>. From this it happens that certain uterine symptoms can hardly be distinguished from enchantments. For in this way, the womb binds the lining of the lung so tightly that it transmits no air at all into the chest. There is no communication of vapor here, no path, no approach, no target, or method; much less is there an affinity with "catarrhs" <note>runny fluids or phlegm</note> in this area, since it begins and ends without any material inflow or outflow. 

<margin>46.</margin> It is, therefore, the sole action of governance by which the raging womb agitates all things. It is not, however, a binding, proximity, leaning, or "consensus"; rather, the superiority of monarchal power and the vital dependence of the parts are what must be considered. For the governing parts act with absolute power, not bound by the proximity of locations or physical positions; they act equally fiercely regardless of the body's posture. And what is far more narrow: the governing force reaches its end or target unsullied, without the contamination of any intermediaries. The womb often lives and riots even after the death of the woman which it brought about. To such an extent does it possess a singular monarchy, which a duality explains <note>likely referring to the dual nature of the soul and body, or the womb's semi-autonomous life</note>; nor does it obey the body, to which it then prescribes laws. For it is not violently shaken by anything other than the perturbations of the soul. Therefore, besides the singular sensations of smell, taste, and touch, it also excels with a certain "brutal intellect" <note>an instinctive or non-rational intelligence</note>, whence it rages and roars if all things do not respond to its will. It rages, I say, by twisting itself upward, downward, forward, backward, or to the sides, with unspeakable torment of pain.

As long as this frenzy is confined within its own dwelling <note>original: "hospitio," referring to the womb itself</note>, it excites only local pains. But when it seizes or "looks upon" distant parts, it grips and strangles them like a cramp, in no other way than by a fury incited against them. I remember that I once saw women who had been "strangled by the womb" <note>This refers to "hysterical suffocation," a condition where it was believed the womb moved upward or sent influences that constricted the throat</note>, whose corpses were bruised and blackened in those parts where they had suffered pain before death. Nor does the womb pour forth its flows unless an inordinate madness opens its veins to overturn the innocent treasure of life. Thus, it does not contract the nerves and muscles, make the limbs lame, dislocate tendons, relax muscles, or shrivel and wrinkle membranes, except by the sole action of its governance. Unless it were agitated by fury, it would otherwise maintain a duality in harmony with the woman's life; for as long as a thing preserves its unity, it desires to remain in its state of being. When, therefore, this frenzy acts outside the womb, it causes fainting fits, apoplexy, strangulations, tremors of the heart, and sudden death, almost at its own whim. But the frenzy of the womb alone is the lesser evil. However, when it flies over into the **sensitive soul** <note>In Van Helmont's philosophy, the soul that governs the senses and vital functions, distinct from the rational, immortal soul</note> (with which I have shown it shares a common bond), it pours a true mania of its own fury out from the **hypochondrium** <note>the region of the abdomen under the lower ribs</note>. In young girls who are swollen with a lesser pleasure <note>likely referring to puberty or unfulfilled sexual maturity</note>, it detains, suppresses, or discolors the menses, and produces disordered flows. Then, finally, it brings forth paralysis, spasms, palpitations, tremors, and faints, and contracts the nerves. These things I heal daily through the volatile **tincture of Coral**, **oil of Amber**, **salt of Steel** <note>Iron-based remedies</note>, and similar things. Milder cases obey **Narcotics**. More atrocious cases require the greater secrets of **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymiæ arcana," the advanced alchemical preparations Van Helmont championed</note>. What I have already said about the governance of the **testes** and the womb, I have demonstrated through many arguments in my treatise on *Catarrhs*, and likewise on the **Duumvirate** <note>The 'governance of two,' Van Helmont’s theory that the stomach and spleen are the primary commanders of the body's health</note>, to belong with no less privilege to the stomach. Neither "fumes" nor "vapors" ascend from the stomach to the head; therefore, the fable taught in the Schools <note>The traditional Galenic medical universities</note> regarding this is impossible. Likewise, in my treatise on *Fevers* and elsewhere, I have shown how drunkenness occurs by "fumes," and by what path those fumes are carried into the anterior cavities of the brain. I will now teach

the manner in which this happens in Apoplexy, the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, lethargy, etc. Although I have denied that these occur through a connected chain of physical emissions <note>original: "aporrhœarum," or physical particles flowing from one part to another</note>, they should at least be understood to be subject to the action of the governance.

<margin>47.</margin>
To what end should I repeat what I have said in passing before? Namely, that the beard is born from the testes, and that the distinctions, ages, varieties, and colors of the beard depend upon them. Since this is commonly known, I advise that it should at least be understood that this does not happen by a vapor brought there through the service of particular vessels. Rather, one must consider a power which, like light, affects and disposes the whole body—or at least its intended objects—according to the gift and purposes implanted in it as a seed by the Creator. Therefore, a certain power radiates from the testes through the body, into the **Archeus** <note>The internal "master-builder" or vital force that directs biological processes</note>, and even into the sensitive soul, just as the Church commends the female sex with natural devotion.

<margin>48.</margin>
Why then does the beard grow on the chin, and not on the forehead or elsewhere, since that universal outflow of light from the testes is throughout the whole? This matter holds a most hidden root of Philosophy, demonstrated in my treatise *On the Entry of Death into Man*. For it must be known that souls act upon their bodies by the power of a certain vital light of their own. Since this light is extended everywhere through life (in which the soul itself is present everywhere), the soul paints in that light of its own the "ideas" of its conception and command, so that they may thereafter be committed to execution in the organs through the **ministering spirits** <note>vital spirits that act as intermediaries</note>. But those animated lights, or the light-bearing souls themselves, cannot be grasped by us through a direct concept, since they are like immediate clients of another and intelligible world. For this reason, the Most High calls himself the **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical reference to James 1:17</note>. For the senses bring nothing to us from the outside that can paint a concept of the soul in the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination or mental representation</note>. Therefore, in my treatise *On Forms*, I have touched upon this matter—to the extent of my meager ability—within the novelty of such a great paradox, as clearly as I could, to be pondered even more powerfully elsewhere. ...and that the formal substance (which I distinguish elsewhere from earlier ones) consists of certain anonymous lights, created directly by the Father of Lights <note>A biblical reference to God from James 1:17</note>. Therefore, the powers depending on the soul, and certain ministerial "satellite lights," are to this extent also luminous. I have shown, therefore, through systematic demonstration <note>original: "mathesin," referring here to a logical or mathematical proof</note>, that these lights penetrate one another, while still preserving the essence and properties of the primary lights. In lower things, however, where forms and formal powers dwell, these possess their own light in actuality, or can be stirred up by our <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont’s term for the internal vital workman or spiritual force that governs the body’s chemistry and health</note>, in the same way that the power in an egg is activated by warmth during brooding. Thus, there exists in the roots of the hair on the chin a power of growth, duration, and other dispositions, the ruler of which is the masculine force, even if only one testis is present. Indeed, this power of the testes, though absolute, is received only in various ways in different places, according to the manner and capacity of each recipient. 

To show how much this speculation benefits the medical art, I will substitute poisonous powers in place of vital ones. Indeed, they are no less "luminous" <note>Van Helmont uses "light" to describe the spiritual radiation or active principle of a substance</note> than those that are otherwise healthy, if the poisons flow immediately from their own forms. For these are either gifts of the first creation belonging to external simple things, or they are generated within us afterward by an error in living. By the same privilege, the natural powers (such as those of the womb, stomach, testes, and other parts) radiate their lights throughout the whole body and penetrate the light of the Archeus. Even the action of governance depends on its own light; from this, the body is either comforted, weakened, alienated, destroyed, or even perishes. Therefore, poisons born in the <term>precordia</term> <note>The region around the heart or the midriff</note> or elsewhere act by the force of their formal and luminous powers, according to the "endowed idea" <note>original: "idea dotalis," an innate blueprint or quality</note> impressed upon them. They affect the vital light of the **sensitive soul** <note>The part of the soul governing sensation and involuntary functions</note> implanted in the Archeus and the parts of the body, and they penetrate each other by a radical union. This happens either by a permanent contagion of the poison, which transplants the innate, formal, and vi-

<column-break/>

-tal light of the parts; or only for a short time, as in the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "caducis," a historical term for epilepsy</note>, with the freedom to return to normal or not, according to the requirements of its root. Therefore, the head does not merely preside over the lower organs; these also, in turn, preside over the head, which I have clearly demonstrated elsewhere by the example of hanging. For indeed, the spinal cord <note>original: "medulla spinalis"</note>, being enclosed in the middle of the vertebrae, cannot be squeezed by a rope in such a way as to deny passage to the motor spirit of the breath. Nevertheless, at that same instant, memory, intellect, sense, and movement perish because of the closing of the carotid arteries in the throat <note>original: "arteriarum gutturalium"</note>, even before the total exclusion of air. From this, it is sufficiently clear that a certain intellectual light flows continuously from the lower parts to the head. When this light is intercepted, as in hanging or drowning, even though the brain, spinal cord, and nerves are not damaged, all the virtue, power, and light of the soul perish. So too, in a <term>feverish delirium</term> stirred up from the lower parts, the discourse of reason perishes.

<margin>49.</margin>
There is, therefore, a reciprocal governance of the lower parts. I willingly admit that <term>scotoma</term> <note>Dizziness with darkened vision</note>, <term>vertigo</term> <note>Dizziness</note>, deafness, <term>apoplexy</term>, <term>epilepsy</term>, and other evils of that kind arise from the lower parts; however, they do not arise through "vapors" carried to the head. For if they ascended through the esophagus, they would yield nothing but tasteless, distilled water. I have shown elsewhere that not even watery breaths can be carried to the level of the brain, much less into its cavities. Therefore, let the blame and guilt assigned to "vapors" in the aforementioned diseases be considered empty. Furthermore, vapors are not carried from the stomach to the heart and head through the arteries and nerves surrounding the mouth of the stomach. For even the Schools <note>The traditional academic authorities of the time</note> admit that it is not the office of the nerves to draw from the outside. They do claim that the arteries draw in air to cool the heart and to express "sooty wastes." I have shown that neither of these is true. But at the very least, that theory has no place here in the arteries ending in the stomach, since they do not draw cold air from the stomach nor from the abdomen.

# THE UNKNOWN ACTION OF GOVERNANCE #

...one could never hope that it would breathe in such a way, nor that it was similarly weighed down by <term>soot</term> <note>original: "fuligine"; in early medicine, this refers to the smoky waste products of metabolic heat</note>, not even a fresh amount. Indeed, it would hardly be fitting to discharge its sooty wastes in a place where they would be much more harmful to the stomach than if they were kept in their own seats. For if the stomach did not receive its name for nothing, it is the "mouth of the heart" <note>An ancient anatomical term for the upper opening of the stomach, reflecting its sensitivity and proximity to the heart</note>. Because more powerful evidence, signs of life, and more horrible storms of disturbance emerge from the stomach than from anywhere else: therefore, air was not to be drawn from the stomach, and much less was vapor—the fuel and beginning of so many evils—to be discharged through the arteries or as soot into the stomach. That is to say: dizzying, epileptic, and apoplectic vapors, and so forth, are not drawn, nor do they ascend of their own accord through the arteries. For the ineffable Creator directed all the goals of things toward the necessities and requirements of their uses. Finally, therefore, if the aforementioned "reeds" <note>referring to the vessels or passages of the body</note> do not draw noxious and disease-causing vapors, the stomach will certainly much less send or discharge them through the arteries or the nerve. Since otherwise it could very quickly free itself through a belch. For the stomach is not a bellows, that it should have to carry noxious vapors conceived within itself into the "chest of life" against the will of the channels. Furthermore, the stomach has few veins; and it is a foreign thing for these to beg anything from the stomach (as has been proven in its proper place); wherefore vapors are not carried through the veins. For to what purpose would they entice and receive what is outside the design of nature? How would the stomach breathe its vapors into the narrowest vessels, filled with blood, especially those which are not capable of drawing them in? 

For I consider the stomach not indeed according to the manner of Galen <note>Galen was the primary authority on medicine from Roman times until the scientific revolution</note>, as if it were a sack or a bare cooking pot dedicated to the cooking of foods: but a vital organ <note>original: "viscus vitale"</note> which is powerful in taste, possesses a sense of smell, and is woven with diverse appetites, as if it were an animal itself: and henceforth it so rejects certain things that a man would often rather die than swallow a single morsel against the stomach's will. The stomach necessarily serves the whole, even in the lowly service of a kitchen pot. But thus far, the other parts obey it in different ways, and unless they listen seriously, they are punished severely. According to that saying, *whoever among you is greatest, let him be as the least* <note>original: "qui vestrum maximus fuerit, tanquam minimus esto," a reference to Matthew 20:26</note>. Certainly, the stomach is busily occupied in humble ministry: yet the service of the stomach is not therefore vile, no more than it was for the High Priest of the Jews to have acted as a butcher <note>referring to the sacrificial slaughter of animals</note>: but compared to the stomach, it is a certain personification of life, with august majesty. If the nerve, artery, and vein appear inserted into the stomach: they are surely signs of allegiance and retribution, by which the internal organs confess themselves bound to the stomach, rather than being added to it for the sake of the helm, the mast, and the sails <note>a nautical metaphor for governing the body</note>. 

Indeed, I would not truly wish this sovereignty to be deferred to the stomach as if the entire command of that "republic" belonged to its membrane alone. For I make a single marriage and one bed out of the Spleen and the stomach. In which, I assign the role of the husband to the Spleen, for the primary motions, and to the stomach, for the primary sense. The stomach is therefore the completion of the spleen, and the spleen the completion of the stomach; under a single bed for both, it is the sovereignty of a single <term>duumvirate</term> <note>A Roman term for a board of two officials jointing exercising power</note>. Yet I never cease to contemplate, with enough wonder, what things the Lord of all foresaw in the bare meninges <note>original: "Menygnibus," the membranes covering the brain</note>, the womb, the stomach, the pericardium, etc., in the internal membranes: except that God is accustomed to establish His wonders in things that are abject in the eyes of man. Whose name be sanctified forever.

-> # THE DUUMVIRATE # <-

1. *Sleep exists because of a sleep-inducing power, and not from a defect.* 2. *The opinions of the Schools regarding sleep.* 3. *The opinion of the ancients is attacked.* 4. *Contradictions.* 5. *The essence of opiates.* 6. *The impossibility of the [Schools'] thesis is demonstrated by the position of the nerves.* 7. *Sleep arrives while the opiate remains within the stomach.* 8. *From the effect of opium.* 9. *It is taught by sulfur and vitriol.* 10. *Several absurdities accompanying the thesis of the Schools.* 11. *A ridiculous evasion.* 12. *When dreams occur.* 13. *Why a headache arises from excessive drinking <note>original: "crapula"; refers to the physical aftermath of intoxication</note>.* 14. *Pain from the contraction of the membranes <note>original: "menyngum"; the meninges surrounding the brain</note>, without vapor.* 15. *A thesis in favor of the Duumvirate.* 16. *Conclusion.*

<margin>1.</margin> A pagan poet <note>Likely referring to Virgil, who described sleep as the "kinsman of death"</note>, speaking morally—or rather, with a rustic understanding—calls sleep "the image of icy death." But I, knowing that sleep is a natural power, sent down from the sovereignty of the stomach into the brain and commanded by the force of the Governing Body <note>original: "Regiminis"; Van Helmont's term for the vital biological control centers</note> to be carried into execution, believe as a Christian that God (who is always to be hallowed) sent a sleep upon Adam when He intended to fashion the woman from his rib. This was certainly not as a "privative" thing <note>meaning a mere absence of wakefulness</note>, but as an actual, real, and purely positive faculty. Therefore, the power of sleeping is vital, necessary, and accordingly, natural. For I do not believe that God created death, or even its image, within man. Nor was it fitting for an image of death to precede sin and the occasion of death itself. 

<margin>2.</margin> Indeed, the Schools <note>the traditional academic followers of Galen and Aristotle</note> teach that sleep is caused by vapors, raised from the stomach into the brain, which clog or intercept the passages of the senses, motion, speech, judgment, and so on. Even as a youth, I judged these ideas to be ridiculous. For in truth, if this were so, disease would have existed 
<margin>3.</margin> before sin, because sleep would be a disease. It would surely have been a flatulent and vaporous paralysis, and a temporary madness <note>original: "Amentia"</note>, in a body that was then still incapable of suffering <note>original: "impassibili"</note> and possessed of immortal life. It is shameful, therefore, that the foolishness of paganism is still seriously taught in the Schools, especially by Christians who ought to be better instructed. Indeed, the Schools err in their proposed 
<margin>4.</margin> thesis. For those who are sleeping 

<column-break/>

move themselves, turn over, and some even walk about; they feel the bites of fleas and bedbugs while sleeping, such that they are awakened by them; others even speak, and not infrequently respond appropriately. Finally, just as the Schools are poorly consistent with themselves when they confuse sleep and "sleepless catarrhs" <note>Early medicine used "catarrh" to describe fluids "dropping" from the brain</note> as having the same root, causes, and manner of ending: so too, after I exploded the delusions regarding Catarrhs, I also rejected the assigned causes of sleep as empty fables. Lastly, the Schools even do violence to themselves regarding opiates—things which are, as they say, "extremely cold" and which ought to suppress all evaporation (at least more so than coriander is imagined to restrain vapors in the case of catarrhs, etc.). They teach that by their very nature, opiates most promptly bring about sleep, lethargy, and even death—and all the more quickly the greater the "coldness" of the opiate is in quality and quantity. 
<margin>5.</margin> And thus, the more pure opium is taken, and the more one is chilled internally, the more abundant and continuous would be the vapors carried from the stomach into the head (even if the esophagus were closed!). But it is surely a stupid fabrication that sleep is caused by cold. It is not even intelligible how a single grain of opium could cause enough cold in the stomach to actually drive a cold vapor into the head. 
<margin>6.</margin> How, likewise, will it be the property of cold to stir up vapors rather than suppress them? But let us suppose these things were granted through a false rule, and that sleep-inducing vapors are carried upward from food, and that the nerves—the authors of sense and motion—are filled up by these vapors. But I wish they had first considered that the roots of the nerves, or their primary extremities, are continuous with the brain and the spinal medulla; and that the other ends of the nerves terminate in the external muscles, or in the organs of the senses themselves. Therefore, sleep-inducing vapors would first have to materially penetrate and be fully soaked into the substance of the brain and the spinal

...the substance of the spinal cord, and to obstruct both, before they could perform what sleep requires under the **thesis of the Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities following Galenic and Aristotelian medicine, which Van Helmont frequently criticized</note>. And by what path would vapors of this kind turn from the stomach and penetrate through the entire substance of the Brain, until they reached the very innermost and utterly continuous root of the nerves, which is inseparably connected to the Brain? Finally, how could a person, once awakened at the whim of the one exciting them, be dissolved and liberated so quickly from impediments of that sort? Or what would keep those vapors in that same place for so many hours without their own constriction or condensation into water? For if those vapors were once constricted, the way would be open for the spirits <note>original: "spiritibus"; refers to the "animal spirits" believed to carry sensation and motion through the nerves</note> which would immediately shake off sleep. Or what, at last, would prevent new vapors from continually hastening to those same principles of the nerves, and by coagulating there, producing necessary daily **Catarrhs** <term>Catarrh: a traditional medical term for an excessive buildup of phlegm or mucus, believed to "flow down" from the brain</term> and certain **paralyses**? Certainly, if an **Anatomist**, or any man of sound mind, were to contemplate these things even once in a rough manner, he must necessarily wonder at these pagan fables with astonishment, especially because they have no connection with the principles of our constitution. It also happens that someone may wake up many times in a single night, rise, and fall asleep again; and so there would be almost as many obstructions of the nerves at will in one night—indeed, in a single hour. Meanwhile, I pass over the fact that sleep is induced while an **opiate** still materially exists within the stomach, as experience has more than often shown against one's will. Therefore, either the slightest scent of opium alone would have to steam into the Brain, or, while it remained there, <margin>7.</margin> it would have to transmit "deputy" sleep-inducing vapors. For it does not happen sooner. Because before the opium could strike the sense of taste or smell, the opium would be perceived continuously on the tongue, palate, nostrils, and throat, even before sleep. This does not happen. Furthermore, the **sulfur of vitriol** <note>Van Helmont's "sweet sulfur of vitriol" is often identified by historians as an early discovery of ether, which has sedative properties</note>, which is highly sleep-inducing, since it is "fixed" <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance does not evaporate or fly away when heated</note>, is unable to vibrate its own vapors into the head, nor can it send out deputies

<column-break/>

in possession of its powers. Truly, I suspect that the Greek authors on sleep, or those acting like Greeks, while perceiving themselves to be given over to sleep when drunk, estimated that all sleep derived from nowhere else; and that sleep could not creep up except from food and drink, not even in the early morning when the food was already digested. I also find in the Schools that the material causes of **vertigo** differ in no way from the causes of natural sleep. All of these things I have proved elsewhere regarding **Catarrhs** to be mere ignorances and silly consensuses, born from a laziness in investigating and a readiness to subscribe to old ideas. But pray, what force so cold exists in opium that it produces sleep against my will, even when I am sufficiently warmed? <margin>8.</margin> If it is the coldness of the vapors, why do wines after lunch stir up sleep? Is there, then, a single identity of the cold and the hot for the sake of procuring sleep? Why, then, is coldness uniquely attributed to opium? Why are hot things not equally judged to be **narcotics** and **soporifics**? Why did the lethal poppies, celebrated by the Poets for sleep, persuade them to remember no power besides cold? Why is opium bitter? And why is a predominating bitterness judged to be "hot" in the Schools? Therefore, it is necessary that the Schools choose one or the other. Namely: either that the cold of opium is not excessive, and consequently opium does not cause sleep through cold; or that bitterness is a deceptive sign of heat in the Schools. For why is the cold **purslane** <note>original: "portulaca"; a succulent plant classified as "cold" in Galenic herbalism</note>, despite its third degree of coldness, not sleep-inducing? Why is a handful of purslane not equivalent to two grains of opium, since there is more abundant cold and it cools more powerfully in such a large portion than in so little opium? Why does **Nightshade** <note>original: "Solanum"</note> cause madness, but does not produce sleep by its coldness? I, however, find in opium an acrid, sweat-inducing salt and a bitter oil, far removed from the smell of opium, yet nevertheless <margin>9.</margin> sleep-inducing. Indeed, the **sulfur of vitriol** is sweet, like honey, without the smell, vapor, and fury of opium; because it is fixed in the torment of fire, excellently hot, and sleep-inducing. For there are those who wash the powder of **Colcothar** <term>Colcothar: the brownish-red iron oxide residue left after the distillation of vitriol</term> to deprive it of its saltiness. But it is almost ineffective, however much it promises vain things,

...the writers of introductory manuals <note>original: "Tyrociniorum Scriptores," likely referring to Jean Beguin's "Tyrocinium Chymicum," a famous 17th-century chemistry textbook</note> are supported. For it becomes legitimate, and what the philosophers call "produced from the green spirit of vitriol": which, expressed through repeated distillation <note>original: "cohobationem," a process of redistilling a liquid over its solid residue</note> and the ultimate torture of fire, and being notably volatile, is coagulated and fixed. This is achieved by common **sal ammoniac** <term>Sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used in alchemy to make substances more volatile or to "fix" them</term>, which must afterwards be removed from it through repeated distillations of the **spirit of wine** <term>Spirit of wine: concentrated ethanol or alcohol</term>.
