<margin>10.</margin>
Therefore, sleep occupies many who are still speaking after the next three moments. How, then, in these people, will there be a sudden constriction of all the nerves? Why, finally, does sleep creep up more quickly on those lying down than on those sitting, when otherwise the movement of vapors from below ought to be far easier in an upright body than in one lying on its side? Furthermore, even if it were granted that all nerves are equally constricted before sleep (which is as senseless as it is ridiculous), from where are the mental powers lulled to sleep? Unless you have mandated that the soul necessarily placed its lodging in the vault of the Brain, and near the nerves? And that the cavities of the Brain, therefore, during the entire interval of sleep, are filled not indeed with **animal spirit** <note>The subtle fluid believed to carry sensation and thought</note>, but with foreign, raw, thick, and morbid vapors, and that the very Authors of our reasoning take a holiday, sleep, or wander far away for that time? And then all the organs are immediately liberated from there at the sound or whim of someone waking them?

<margin>11.</margin>
But I have heard sleep excused under the title of an "ordinary effect," which would otherwise be morbid if it were not daily and habitual. I laughed at this old woman's invention. First, because sleep—or the punishment for sin—was sent into man even before a hangover <note>original: "crapulam"</note>. Secondly, because an evil that is in itself a disease or an evil is nowhere less of an evil just because it is ordinary. And if that were granted, sleep would never bring solace to failing strengths, but rather perpetual labor.

<margin>12.</margin>
However, after I once saw or felt the light of a certain soul through some

<column-break/>

representation, I understood that sleep occurs while the **Spleen** specifically toils in nutrition, with recreation and pleasure. Then, surely, giving leave to its holiday-making imaginations, it merges itself entirely by delighting in a full rest of fruition—namely, from the perceived sweetness of its own saturation and the liberty of the **stomach ferment** <term>Ferment: in Van Helmont's system, a vital force or "yeast" that drives digestion and transformation in the body</term> restored to itself—it settles into enjoying delights. Therefore, digestion in the stomach is less successful during sleep because it is slower. For this reason, fruition and a holiday from work have always been the first desire in all sensitive nature. Therefore, thoughts in the first sleep are vain and full of mockery, while the imagination of the Spleen or the stomach is drawn away from thinking about vegetative necessity.

These things will soon be elucidated more clearly in this treatise.

<margin>13.</margin>
When a **Humorist** <note>A follower of traditional Galenic medicine based on the four humors</note> is asked by a drunkard why his head aches in the morning, on the left "horn" <note>the temple or side of the forehead</note> above the brow, perhaps to the width of a large silver coin <note>original: "thaleri"</note>? That man responds promptly: it is established through **Anatomy** that the orifice of the stomach inclines to the left side; it has also been taught for many centuries that pain-bringing vapors are carried from the stomach into the head. He claims they hurt because they are sharp, harsh, and biting, left over from the wine; and also that they keep to the vertical line of the same side and are not permitted to wander. Having said this, the **Galenist** raises his eyebrows, shakes his cloak, and congratulates his own soul because the other credulous man thinks himself satisfied by such a deceitful fable. For the fact that a headache in the forehead maintains the alignment of the side from the stomach hides something extraordinary regarding the action of the **Governance and the Duumvirate** <note>The "Duumvirate" is Van Helmont's term for the stomach and spleen acting together as the secondary "center" of the body's life and health</note>. But no one has considered that this could not happen without the actual commerce of vapors. For in the first place, no vapor strikes the head from the stomach; just as there is no sharp, salty, bitter, or harsh vapor, as I have stated elsewhere regarding **Catarrhs**. Since the pain we are discussing is continuous, whether lying down, standing, or sitting, and without the necessity of belching.

From this it is clearly established that the head is no more tormented by aqueous vapors from the stomach than the chin is by vapors from the testicles in bearded men—which does not happen in eunuchs. on one half of the head, and much less subsequently on the right side: rather, they would ascend straight up, and would always affect the whole head equally from the throat, since there are no galleries to lead these vapors, as if through tubes, now here, now there. Why does new food quiet a **Cephalalgia** <term>Cephalalgia: a clinical term for a headache</term>, when from recent food (especially when accompanied by wine) sharp vapors rather than mild ones, like milk, ought to exhale? Therefore, once a pain has already been established, feeding would not foul the pain, but rather stir it up and build a new one. All of which, since they contradict both the Thesis and experience, also prove that the aforementioned pain proceeds from the **Duumvirate** through the bare **action of the Government**, without any vapors. I have wondered many times that no one before me has yet seriously meditated on these things: but rather, following the fables handed down by the ancients, everyone has continually subscribed to them in every way. But in the treatise on the *Delusions of Catarrh*, I have shown these offshoots of vapors from the stomach to be trifles, and therefore also the causes of vapors dedicated to sleep. Finally, I have already proven above that there is an **action of the Government** upon the upper parts no less than the actions of the upper parts have hitherto been thought to affect the lower. Then I also said in passing that a most powerful vital temperament <note>original: "crasin," a mixture of qualities or humors</note> for acting emanates from the **precordia** <term>Precordia: the region of the chest and upper abdomen, often associated with the heart and diaphragm</term> in diseases which antiquity has hitherto dedicated to the head alone.
<margin>15. </margin>
Now, for my Thesis, I establish that the **Duumvirate**, the presiding ruler of the **action of the Government**, dwells in the **hypochondrium** <term>Hypochondrium: the upper part of the abdomen, specifically the area under the ribs</term>—namely, in the **Spleen** and the **Stomach**: parts, I say, which the **Schools** have esteemed as a sewer of the foulest humor and a sack of impure foods. Four things, therefore, in such a great paradox, must be proven; namely:
1. That the Duumvirate commands the whole.
2. That the Spleen and Stomach possess Imagination, Love, etc.
3. That sleep, wakefulness, etc., belong to it.

4. That the lodging of the soul is in that very same place. These four points coincide, as it were, into a single point. The Philosophers, along with the Astrologers, have assigned the Spleen to Saturn, the father of the stars, as the incipient principle of life. The **Galenists** <note>Followers of the Greek physician Galen, whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note>, however—who are accustomed to contradicting themselves in most matters—have made the Spleen partly a sewer for the most perverse, excremental, and counterfeit **black bile** <term>Black bile: one of the four "humors" in ancient medicine, thought to cause melancholy</term>; and partly a receptacle of madness, not indeed because of the melancholic matter itself, but rather because of a certain irrational and animal-like conceptual agitation. # TREATICE ON THE SOUL.

<margin>
1. The treatise on the soul is commended. 2. What turned scholars away from this meditation. 3. Knowledge of the soul should not be delivered as a mere epilogue. 4. The imaginary difficulties of the Schools. 5. Why the knowledge of things must be postponed. 6. Through an example sought from water. 7. Actions of the mind in the body. 8. What deceived those who came before. 9. The Author ceased from his undertaking. 10. Things to be considered regarding the mind.
</margin>

Therefore, the entire empire of the **Duumvirate** <term>Duumvirate: Van Helmont’s term for the dual governance of the body by the stomach and spleen</term>, since it flourishes from the vital power of the soul, can surely be proven abundantly through the fourth thesis. For if it is established that the very seat of the soul is in the Duumvirate, then its sovereignty over the other positions of the members and viscera will also become evident. For this reason, I will treat here briefly the soul, although by other writers before me, the treatise on the soul has been banished outside of Physics, especially in the order of learning the Theory of Medicine: and even though so many precise definitions of madness infest us on every side. Indeed, since I have felt no help

<column-break/>

if a diseased and precordial melancholy flows from it. For many people understand that they are losing their minds, as if it were beginning to happen, and they grieve that they cannot restrain such fantasies, which are troublesome day and night. Thus they seethe, as it were, with a double mental concept. In this way, for example, those whom a rabid dog has bitten, and who have fallen into a fear of water (a disease they have since named **hydrophobia** <note>original: "hydrophobiam," from the Greek for water-fear</note>), blame the involuntary madness which they foresee and predict, even warning those standing by to watch out for themselves. The Schools respond that this happens not because some imaginative power is lodged there, but because a "smoke" of black bile is carried from there into the head, the box of fantastic power. Since these matters are surely of great importance, it is proper to examine them in a specific treatise on the soul, and its seat, throne, and lodging.

from my predecessors—but rather labor and sorrow have passed through my innermost parts before I could lay aside those things I had drunk in from **paganism** <note>original: "gentilitate," referring to Aristotelian or non-Christian philosophical traditions</note>—I have decided, for that reason, that I am not at all bound to the method of those in whose works I have not yet found anything that can or should be applied to the beginnings or properties of nature. Therefore, in my own view of liberty, I have considered that nothing among things to be known is as noble as the knowledge of the soul itself, from which, just as all other knowledge obtains its brilliance, so also all boundaries find their distinct goal. For whoever is unfit at the beginning to comprehend the motions, exercises, effects, and essence of the immortal mind, will also be incapable of understanding the secrets of nature, which are more remote from the mind than the mind is from itself. Therefore, such a person can hardly approach those things which he will see are more suited to him. But he who has first tasted the preludes of the soul, having afterward drunk in the juices of nature, will, upon his return, have a greater capacity than he had in a previous casual reading.

# T R E A T I S E #

...not. Lest I should seem like a lawless man who has fruitlessly turned my pen toward these thoughts before the explanation of diseases, I shall state what moved me to this. For first and foremost (even for physical consideration), I have meditated on the fact that the mind is the peak of human nature and the perfection of established humanity. Therefore, it would be more decent to know one's own soul—that is, oneself from the soul—than to inquire into a rhapsody <note>original: "rapsodia"; here meaning a disorganized collection or medley</note> of bodily properties, and from the notion of these, to wish to know the mind itself. Indeed, it has seemed to me that once the soul is known, even if only slightly, the remaining lower things—placed beneath our feet—are added to us. And with almost no effort, those things are understood which previously, at every step, raised suspicions or moved one to despair concerning the true, the permitted, the similar, the just, the proportioned, the agent, the passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon, the opposite of "action"</note>, priority, the appropriate, change, or otherness; or which, at last, led their followers with closed eyes into fallacy through too much agreement. 

<margin>2. What turned scholars away from this meditation.</margin> 

Hence they were deterred from the labor of investigating, not so much through laziness as through fear of halted progress; and therefore they bolted the door of knowledge against further things. For it is clear and beyond doubt that a man cannot know himself unless he has first drawn in the knowledge of the soul. Indeed, without the soul, a man is like a mere corpse. Thus, the knowledge of the soul itself both seals the fear of God in the soul and brings about the beginning of Wisdom. 

<margin>3. Knowledge of the soul should not be delivered as a mere epilogue.</margin> 

If, therefore, the beginning of Wisdom is stirred up by the knowledge of the soul, then some teaching of the soul must not be delivered as an epilogue to Physics <note>original: "Physices"; refers to the study of natural philosophy or the physical world</note>, according to the custom formerly observed. For it is false that the knowledge of fleeting things <note>original: "rerum caducarum"; things that are subject to decay and passing away</note> facilitates for us the understanding of our mind. Rather, let the experienced know that the knowledge of the mind, even if it has departed far from the concept of sublunary bodies <note>Bodies existing below the moon, i.e., the earthly, corruptible world</note>, nevertheless raises itself up whenever it applies itself to human sciences or any arts whatsoever. For he who once, and even in passing, has experienced the soul's introversion <note>A turning inward of the mind to contemplate spiritual or internal realities</note>, or ecstasy, knows afterward to what things he has applied his soul with desire. Not the other way around. For even if someone has obtained the knowledge of many things, he will not therefore be fit for the introversions of the mind. 

<column-break/>

Therefore, with peace toward all who came before me, I say and meditate that it is clearly necessary that a man first know himself, then learn the fear of the Lord, which will raise him to true wisdom, to which the knowledge of these fleeting things and their defects will be added, like a consequence to premises, or like an adjacent thing to the principal. 

<margin>4. The imaginary difficulties of the Schools.</margin> 

My predecessors, after looking at the essences <term>quiddities: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of things, then looked back at the soul in a backwards manner, chiefly for two reasons. The first of these is that the knowledge of the soul seemed to them far more difficult than any other things whatsoever. The second is that they believed knowledge of the mind could be hoped for and obtained from the investigation of external things and the examination of bodily properties. But even if the first of these is true, the second can in no way be so. For if the knowledge of the soul is of an abstract and spiritual being, it certainly cannot be conveyed into us by any speculation of bodily things. Indeed, God alone is the immediate craftsman and Prince of the mind, and the very life of life. Therefore, knowledge of ourselves cannot be hoped for from elsewhere than from its own source and Ruler. Indeed, the knowledge of abstract spirits is a whole heaven apart from the speculation of fleeting things, since they do not participate in any common symbol <note>A shared characteristic or essential link</note> of principles or properties. Therefore, the essence of bodies contains nothing of science or light whereby the soul might recognize or behold itself, except through negation—which is a kind of despair and banishment of knowledge. Whence also it acquires for itself no light from above, or from the opposite of itself; nor does it strike out for itself a light of understanding as if from steel and flint. This is because the manner of the soul's knowledge must be begged from the Father of Lights <note>A biblical title for God, the source of all truth</note>, and not from elsewhere. Because it was the good pleasure of the divine will that...

# O F  T H E  S O U L #

that man should seek knowledge of himself from nowhere else than from his own beginning and source: which is the principle, middle, end, goal, and highest vertical peak of all Philosophy: to which all other knowledge is merely additional. Indeed, the essential and *a priori* <term>a priori: knowledge that comes from theoretical deduction or causes rather than from observation of effects</term> knowledge of sublunary <term>sublunary: literally "under the moon," referring to the physical, changeable world of the Earth</term> things is just as dark, hidden, and difficult as the very conception of the immortal Mind itself, if the essences of things and their causes are known to God alone. Therefore, it is simply false that knowledge of the Mind is more difficult than the bare knowledge of physical things, or should be postponed for that reason. For all things are equally unknown to us in their depths. Because the "quiddity" <term>quiddity: the inherent nature or "what-ness" of a thing</term> of any beings whatsoever is their precise truth, which is closed off to us <margin>5.</margin> and open only to the Infinite. Therefore, our knowledge is measured only against the outward scale of things. All corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body</term> things are primarily foreign and alien to our Mind. And therefore, they are more remote from the mind than the mind is from itself. Furthermore, other things are not to be known except through the mind, and first within the mind. Proximately, the knowledge of any things whatsoever is only a certain observation, from which we form discourses according to each person's capacity. Wherefore also every observation of this kind, and the discourse derived from it, however polished, is only *a posteriori* <term>a posteriori: knowledge derived from observation or experience of effects</term>, and far less illuminated than the observation we have regarding the mind.
<margin>6.</margin> Indeed, who among mortals has ever known what water is? Which is nevertheless the most obvious, open, visible, and translucent of created things? For a peasant or an uneducated man <note>original: "Idiota"; in this context, a person without formal academic training</note> knows as much about it as a Philosopher. Namely, they conceive it equally through the observation of the senses: that it is a heavy body, liquid, moist, yielding to the finger, fluid, closing back up when the finger is removed, susceptible to heat, and able to be thinned into vapor.
<margin>7.</margin> Yet no one knows the internal "quiddity" of water, or why it is liquid or moist. Just so, we know the vital and intellectual circumstances of the mind, which dispose this its workshop <note>original: "ergastulum"; a term Helmont uses to describe the body as a vessel or workhouse for the soul</note> 

<column-break/>

into various alterations, and not infrequently produce something "seminally" <term>seminally: relating to the 'archeus' or seed-like power that generates form</term> outside its own concrete form. Such as when a pregnant woman’s longing produces the mark of a cherry on her fetus, which seems to bloom every year. That we know even more about the soul than about water is also known through the revelation of faith. Namely, that the mind is a spiritual substance, subsisting by itself even without a body, immortal, living, created in the image of God, immediately by God himself, giving sense and movement to the organs; and which, separated from the body, feels without organs as it pleases, being able even to move things outside itself, and when constrained by the body, can produce a being outside itself (as has already been shown regarding the pregnant woman), possessing understanding, will, and memory, etc. The observations of these properties and functions are far stronger than our knowledge of water. Otherwise, all things, and each individual thing, are equally unknown and impassable to us by intrinsic intellection <term>intrinsic intellection: a direct, internal understanding of a thing's true essence</term>. 
What misled those who came before <note>original: "Anteriores"; referring to previous generations of philosophers like the Aristotelians</note> into thinking that the knowledge of water is easier than that of the mind, proceeded from the opinion 
<margin>8.</margin> that the visible must necessarily be better known than the invisible. But they did not distinguish the notion of observation from the internal knowledge of "quiddity," according to which all things are equally unknown to us. They did not know, I say, that the knowledge of observation does not introduce the intellect into the inner essence of the thing, but only erects a "putative" <term>putative: commonly accepted or supposed, but not necessarily true</term> science. For otherwise, the Intellect would perceive the prior causes in their very essence. Then also they were deceived by the simplicity of water. They confused this simplicity with the "unity of knowledge" (which remains unknown to us). Because the observations of the mind are more numerous and more fruitful—and because the property of each of these denies us knowledge *a priori*—they thought therefore that more impossibilities lie beneath the knowledge of the mind than in that of a simple body. And so, both the number of properties in the mind, as well as the visual frequency of bodies, [made the] difficul-

...[it] brought forth for them. Since otherwise, in the entity of a being, the visible is just as intellectually unknown as the invisible. For I intended to hand down the intellectual doctrine of the mind, so that man might primarily recognize himself, as much as he is able, and then from that image of divinity learn to contemplate things inferior to himself. But when I tried to explain that through mental acts of prayer <note>original: "orationis"</note>, I was not free to do so: because such things might be judged to exceed the token of my lowliness <note>original: "tesseram meæ abjectionis" — Van Helmont often expressed humility or caution regarding his mystical insights due to religious censorship</note>, I willingly omitted that treatise. Let it therefore suffice for others more fruitful than me to have pointed the finger at the fact that a Christian philosophy of nature does not allow one to pursue fleeting, alien, and distant things—whose causes are hidden *a priori* <term>a priori: from the cause to the effect; reasoning from theoretical deduction</term>—while remaining ignorant in the meantime of who I, the contemplator, am; what the nature of the intellect is; and how the intellectual act is formed and sustained. <margin>10.</margin> Especially since any object is not conceived as it is in itself, but according to the manner of the receiver—that is, the conceiver. And so,

<column-break/>

before all else, it seemed to me that the receiver must be weighed: the one who affects the understanding of things—who he is, of what sort, and how the intellect is disposed in the act of comprehension. What, finally, is the "casing" <note>original: "theca" — referring to the vessel or container of the mind</note> of the intellect, and its capacity, vigor, and mode? How, finally, is the power—which is indeed indistinct from itself—drawn out and descended into functions and the organs bound and placed under it? Lastly, I must consider this before I can know if that which is understood is true and good: whether in me, or because of me, the thing has not been changed in its own entity by the act of conceiving, or alienated from its own being, whereby the truth of that entity would have assumed a foreign mask. I entirely judged that these things ought to be elucidated through intellectual acts, which I determined could be obtained nowhere more promptly or happily than through practice <term>praxis: practical application or exercise, as opposed to mere theory</term>. That is, from the mental prayer of silence <note>original: "mentali oratione silentii" — a form of mystical meditation</note>. Others, however, will judge and weigh that practice more justly than I. And therefore, I did not wish to willingly descend into this arena <note>a common Latin idiom for entering into a public debate or conflict</note>.

## THE DISTINCTION OF THE MIND FROM THE SENSITIVE SOUL.

1. *The Treatise on the entry of Death into human nature is commended as necessary for obtaining knowledge of the mind.* 2. *The reader is also referred to the treatise on the origin of forms.* 3. *The immortality of the mind is proved from the Gospel.* 4. *He begins the web against modern Atheism.* 5. *Leonard Lessius <note>A famous Jesuit theologian (1554–1623)</note>, in describing so much, wrote back from Augustine on the immortality of the soul.*

<margin>1.</margin>

In the first place, in the *Book on Long Life* <note>original: "Libro de vita longa"</note>, I demonstrated at length that the entry of death into human nature had its own causes in nature, through forbidden means, and outside the intention of the most glorious Creator. And once death had crept in and been admitted—although it was not from the Creator's intention—it was thereafter continued and inexorable by the necessity of nature. And from then on, it was not only permitted and consented to by the Creator, but even

<column-break/>

admitted as if by a change in the style of nature—indeed, even commanded—under the improvement introduced by regenerating through the divine grace of baptism. In which treatise I demonstrated the necessity of the "sensitive soul" <term>sensitive soul: in Aristotelian and Helmontian thought, the "anima sensitiva" is the soul shared with animals, responsible for senses and passions, distinct from the immortal Mind</term>, which otherwise would have been useless under immortality. From this, naturally, was introduced "the law in the members" <note>A reference to Romans 7:23, describing the conflict between physical desires and the spirit</note>, contradicting the laws of the immortal mind. And thus the entire, central, and inexcusable corruption of all nature was received. I presuppose that this doctrine—new and unheard of in prior ages—must be sought from that source, if only a knowledge of our mind is desired. For just as the mind is now so alienated from itself and its own beginning that it seems to listen to the commands of the sensitive soul—yet in its essence, substance, and reality, it is immutable—so indeed for those beginning,

# FROM THE SENSITIVE SOUL.

...or for those coming to their senses, as it adds knowledge of the means by which the soul has fallen and become utterly degenerate: so too it presupposes the same doctrine as the very basis of that knowledge. Finally, regarding the **Origin of Forms** <note>original: "Ortu formarum" — a philosophical concept concerning how specific types of things come into being</note>, I have shown in like manner how much this frail, sensitive, and mortal soul within us differs from the immortal mind. This difference is undoubtedly infinite: for while the Mind is surely a substance that is not mortal, the sensitive soul is neither a substance nor an "accident" <term>accident: in old philosophy, a property (like color) that cannot exist without a substance</term>. Instead, it is a neutral mortal creature that perishes into nothingness, possessing the nature of light. This doctrine is, in part, consistent with the Gospel, which speaks of the eternal life and death of souls—or which considers the human soul to be the **Image of God**, never to perish hereafter. This stands in contrast to the **soul of a beast** <note>original: "animæ pecudis"</note>, which, along with life itself, returns to nothingness, exactly like the light of a candle when extinguished. For the other part, however, the present doctrine is clearly a paradox, insofar as the sensitive soul is relegated outside the categories of "substance" and "accident." For first, it is hardly necessary to demonstrate that the sensitive and brutish soul—both in beasts and that which is within us—is not infinite or immortal; no one doubts that every generated natural thing is subject to decay by the law of nature. <margin>4.</margin> However, we are bound by faith to believe that the human mind is immortal from then on. And therefore, the fact that the human mind is a permanent substance—or a spirit subsisting and living in itself after separation from the body—

<column-break/>

should not need to be drummed into or demonstrated to Christians, whose intellect is brought into the service of faith. Yet, in our midst and within the Church, a most powerful **Atheism** has recently arisen among hypocrites. By a total denial of faith, this movement extricates itself from the principles by which such insolent rashness might be quieted—especially the rashness of those who deny every Divinity <note>original: "Numen"</note>. <margin>5.</margin> Otherwise, it would not be my place to treat the immortality of the mind, which was written about and demonstrated by **Augustine**, and described and rewritten in many pious words by **Lessius** <note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), a prominent Jesuit theologian</note>; for they have proved the same sufficiently. But they have not yet proved it against those who deny every Divinity. I would therefore cease to chew over the same ground if enough had been demonstrated by them against "first-class" atheists, and if I did not establish a difference in nature between the **Mind** and every soul of living things. This integrity of nature belongs to the knowledge of nature itself. That integrity seeks the designated difference between man and any other created thing, and does so unequivocally and principally according to his most vital part. Without this part, man is nothing but a **stinking corpse**, more worthless than a flint, and destroyed or broken more quickly than any glass. Otherwise, if Christianity stands, the immortality of the Mind stands, as does its substantial nature, just as the mortality (or reduction to nothingness) of other souls stands. This is "annihilation" in the proper sense of the word. And from this arises the true and properly stated difference between them.

# CONCERNING OUR SOUL <note>original: "DE ANIMAE NOSTRAE"</note>

<margin>1.</margin> In ancient times, as soon as miracles ceased, the Jews were immediately swept away into idolatry and a madness for idols. However, the modern age, more wicked in its speech, is gradually and of its own accord sliding toward **Atheism**. For the laity, execrably entangled in daily sins, not only neglect the invisible God—the fountain of all good—but even some who are pledged to the Church <note>referring to the clergy or those in religious orders</note>, "eating the sins of the people" <note>original: "peccata populi comedentes"—a biblical reference to priests who profit from the offerings made for sins</note> in our very midst, mock God and declare they owe Him nothing. This is because they believe nothing.

<margin>2.</margin> They consider faith itself to be a mere **political phantasm**, and thus believe all religions are a matter of indifference. Indeed, they believe religions were introduced only to restrain the common people under civil law; consequently, they think religions are different almost everywhere and are all equally "just," being promulgated by the right of a Prince's statutes or received customs. Otherwise, they argue, one would be free to believe and do anything, were it not for the fact that human commerce and society would perish. Those who believe and babble these things claim that the Priests and religious officials themselves secretly profess the same through their own nefarious abuses.

Boasting that they have reached the "bottom of truth," these people pride themselves on being highly polished and refined intellects. Thus, they laugh at the rest of the upright—those imploring the grace of God through faith, hope, and charity—as if they were simpletons or even fools, "roasting themselves like a broiled fish for nothing" <note>original: "fruſtra ut aſſum piſcem torrentes"—an idiom suggesting the faithful suffer the "heat" of religious discipline for no actual reward</note>. And they go from bad to worse daily, urged on by the devil, who "circles like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour."

<margin>3.</margin> Above all, however, certain bad examples foster **Atheism**: specifically those who preach and swear vows of voluntary poverty, obedience, humility, and charity, yet are utterly devoid of humility or charity. Instead, they are thoroughly ambitious, envious, and greedy; they overflow with wealth and chase their own comforts, so that not only is their "belly their god," but they are a god unto themselves. Indeed, under the mask of hypocrisy, they divert to themselves the alms intended—or meant to be intended—for the poor.

<column-break/>

Thus, their lives are twisted into a mockery of religion, which has plunged even the more judicious and the weaker souls into **Atheism**. Yet the Holy Spirit—who alone can wipe away and sweep out the internal filth from His Church—will eventually reform this madness of error on both sides.

<margin>4.</margin> Finally, even **Scripture** itself has confirmed Atheism when it enters such a malevolent soul. Scripture, which ought to move a person toward filial obedience and the love due to God, is instead snatched away and given a distorted meaning. For they first argue through a "disjunctive" logic <note>an 'either/or' argument</note> and then immediately conclude in favor of Atheism.

<margin>5.</margin> Namely, they say: the Bible professes a single, eternal, almighty, and immutable divinity. Therefore, either the **Chronicles of the Bible** are mere Hebrew fables, or the deity that Christians (or even Turks <note>In this period, "Turks" was a general term for Muslims, specifically the Ottoman Empire</note>) worship today is far different from the God of the Jews. For if a tree is known by its fruit and a man by his works, then the divinity—which Christians, Turks, and Jews alike adore and believe to be the one, perpetually enduring, immortal God—must also be known and believed through His works, which should be worthy of Him.

For truly, however many enemies are read to have rushed upon the people of Israel in the past, they were laid low in small numbers, their minds overwhelmed with panic and terror, or they were killed in mutual slaughter. No matter how numerous their camps were—swarming like locusts, with camels beyond counting like the sand on the shore—nevertheless, wailing in panic, they fled from a mere three hundred Hebrews blowing trumpets <note>A reference to Gideon's victory in the Book of Judges</note>. And they immediately slaughtered one another with the sword, so that not a single survivor remained to report the massacre at home. Indeed, without any help from fighters at all, a single Angel put 180,000 to death with a single sword <note>A reference to the miraculous defeat of the Assyrian army in 2 Kings 19:35</note>.

Therefore, if the things read and worshiped there are true, and if the divinity today is the same as of old and equally powerful, He ought to help the Christians (who are now His own) just as powerfully against their enemies, by whom they are daily besieged and subjugated.

### CONCERNING IMMORTALITY <note>original: "IMMORTALITATE"</note>

...daily. For public **Idolatry**, once accused as the cause of social degradation, has ceased today; instead, the very cause of the Divine itself is being contested. This happens if the Church—the bride of that same God—and the **Sacraments** of His body are disgracefully trampled, and the perpetual Sacrifice <note>original: "jugeque Sacrificium," referring to the daily celebration of the Mass or Eucharist</note> is suspended and mocked with great reproach. Whichever side of this dilemma is taken, it at least convinces the skeptic that either that ancient deity has now failed in being and power, or the new one—the one Christians now worship (among whom there are great divisions across the world, both in their concepts of the Divine and among the believers themselves, hostilely destroying one another)—is not as powerful or as kind to its faithful as the former one once was to his Israel. 

For today, angels and [flaming] swords no longer appear, nor do vast camps slaughter one another in mutual carnage [by divine intervention]. Nor do enemies flee in terror and wailing from armed Christians in chariots, cavalry, and fire-engines <note>original: "machinis igneis," referring to early artillery or firearms</note>. From this, our **Atheists** conclude that all those who believe in an immortal and omnipotent being—that is, a deity—live deceived. And subsequently, they rightly infer further: If even a deity might eventually perish or fail, much more so would the mind of man, born from fleeting parents. These are the things that lead the people of Christ first to neglect divine worship, and finally to a faithless **Atheism**. 

Once the devil noticed that Idolatry and the multiplicity of lesser gods were being spurned by the wise as loose and frivolous means to lure people onto his hook, he spread this more subtle net of **Atheism** and gathered a more numerous prey. God foretold that this Atheism would come through His servants the Prophets.

> *The fool said in his heart, "There is no God." The Atheists are corrupted and have become abominable in their iniquities; there is none who does good. God looked down from Heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any who understood or sought God.* <note>Psalm 53:1-2</note>

Indeed, the Atheist said in his heart: "If I could see God, an Angel, or an evil spirit, or even...

Instead, I agree with **Aristotle**, that all science and all intellectual doctrine arise only from the pre-existing knowledge of the senses. To this, the devil responds: "It is good to remain thus." And God says:

> *For he who desires to see for the purpose of being able to believe is already guilty of sin.*

The Spirit of truth does not enter a soul guilty of sin; and therefore, it is not fitting that you should see the things you wish to see merely so that you might believe. For sin is not a medium for the acquisition of faith. It is a blasphemous and impious judgment to deny God or the Devil simply because one has not been permitted to see either—neither of whom is visible except in a borrowed form. 

Finally, it is a decayed and childish argument to say: "God does not provide for Christians today what He once provided for the Jews; therefore, He is not the same as He was before, or He has been diminished from His former power." For a matter is changed not so much by divine *power* as by divine *will*. Why He might not will now what He once willed is not ours to question—we cannot demand an account from God for His own judgment. Therefore, the argument "God does not do now what He once did, therefore He cannot" is foolish. 

The Hebrew people, from whom **Christ** was to rise, were small and surrounded on all sides by enemies; unless they had been continually supported by the outstretched arm of God and as if by a miracle, they would have soon been annihilated and fallen as prey to a victor. Yet it was decreed that the **Messiah** should rise from them. But the lot and the law for Christians are far different. For the Israelite people, in the hardness of their hearts, measured the grace of God by the abundance of wealth, children, the fertility of fruits, and their peaceful possession. We, however, know that scandals will be necessary in the Church, as well as tribulations, however great; yet these are not worthy of comparison with the expectations of the world to come. The argument of the Atheists is thus refuted. For their intellect admits nothing that is not introduced from the outside through the senses. Their entire faith is derived from science; yet their science is founded only on the present sensible world, on past observation, and on the denial of histories and the succession of ages. Otherwise, the authority of the Sacred Writers ought to be no less than that of the secular ones. Indeed, all the science of the Atheists descends only to the eyes—to sight, numbers, lines, figures, tones, weights, motions, smells, touch, contact, and taste. That is, everything depends on a "brutal" <note>meaning animal-like or purely physical</note> beginning, and they are unfit to understand things that surpass the senses. This is why they exclude themselves from the intelligible world and "kick against the cornerstone" <note>original: "calcitrant contra lapidem Angularem," a biblical idiom (Acts 9:5) suggesting a futile struggle against a fundamental truth</note>. Yet they at least admit they see and know things which they actually do not know. 

<margin>g.</margin> This happens in the theories of the planets. I wish the Atheists would truly measure the world’s circumference—I mean the real distance of Saturn from us. For they will admit, even if they are unwilling, that the distance is so many thousands of miles that their own intellect will contradict the dimensions they see with their eyes. Or they will necessarily be inclined to admit that the triple circuit of Saturn <note>original: "triplicatum Saturni circuitum," likely referring to the contemporary telescopic observation of Saturn's "ears" or triple-form before rings were fully understood</note> relative to its diameter could not have arisen by itself or of its own accord. Rather, there must be some Author of these things, possessing infinite power, wisdom, greatness, and likewise duration. But if the Atheist thinks that orbs of such incomprehensible magnitude, and such regular constancy of cycles, have been this way spontaneously from eternity: at least the perpetuation of that infinite eternity must follow a certain law, order, and organized governance, which required some presiding Being <note>original: "ens præſidens"</note>, everlasting in duration, great, and powerful.

<column-break/>

They are most miserable, therefore, who by the denial of all universal things, exclude faith and the merits of faith. Indeed, let us consider the globe of the earth clothed in waters: or that place without earth and water, where all things fall toward the center by their own impetus. It is such that if two men were there—one from the East and one from the West—they would touch one another at the feet and look upward with their heads, just as we and the **Antipodes** <note>literally "those with feet opposite," referring to people on the other side of the globe</note> do today. The Atheist, I say, believes this, even though his senses did not suggest it to him. For heavy bodies do indeed teach their own propensity for falling downward; but that the sky is "up" in every direction relative to a single center, and that this is a property of the center—a property like no other—the Atheist has not seen, yet he believes it nonetheless. Indeed, whatever he may ever build, he always finds the contrary, yet without that property of the center, he believes in a single natural property of this kind in the universal center. But he does not look anywhere for its creative cause, or anything like it in the smallest detail, and he prefers to exclude it from himself through unfaith. 

Yet at the very least, if God did not exist, or were not present everywhere giving all things to all, it would be just as if everything were thrown into confusion: things would fall up and down, heavy things would rush upward; plants and beasts would perish, or fail to be. Therefore, the constancy of order and the perseverance of species necessarily require some <term>fount-like primary being</term> <note>original: "ens primitivum fontale," a source-being from which all things flow like a spring</note> from which they began, from which they are, and by which they propagate through a continuous thread. This Being governs all things by His will and gives the constancy of continuity and succession, lest all things collapse and be mixed together in confusion. He carries out a universal care, and guards things in their own being. Finally, let the Atheist consider the ebb and flow of water. No water rises of its own accord; yet the water of the sea, in both the flux and reflux of the tide, always rises. He believes this because he sees it; but he does not believe its cause, because he does not see it; nor has his science entered through the senses. For that which [is beyond the] sen...

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF OUR SOUL.

...to signify where the child was born, whom they sought from such a distant journey: unless He had determined that this should be drawn out from the writings of the Prophets, for the honor of God and the instruction of the people. Therefore, if any faith is placed in sacred history, it proves that there is one God, and that the gods of the Nations are demons. It proves that this God would eventually raise up the Messiah, his son, from the lineage of Abraham—born not by the will of man, but from a Virgin alone—who is the **bread of Angels** that descended from Heaven, and who saves those to be saved by grace alone. Since the human intellect cannot comprehend these mysteries, much less foresee them through the help of the senses, it is necessary to draw the Intellect into the service of faith, which it can in no way conceive of by itself. Because the intellect is of limited power, and faith is everywhere of a profound obscurity, the Intellect cannot grasp an infinite boundary of duration, nor the immortality of its own soul. And so, once the sacred texts are finally granted and believed—at least in the manner of historical Chronicles—there shines forth by that very fact the one God: eternal, immutable, immortal, infinite, omnipotent, Good, True, Wise, Creator, Author, Sustainer, Governor, and the life of all things. Once this Divinity is granted, the arguments of

<margin>12.</margin> **St. Augustine** regarding the immortality of the soul conclude the matter; and one must grant eternal life, eternal fire, joy, peace, and even unending grief. There exist also Angels, evil spirits, **Pythonesses** <note>original: "Pythonissæ," referring to spirit mediums or fortune-tellers</note>, or the servants of the devil. However, the concepts of these things are lacking in the intellect, which, according to **Aristotle**, tastes only of the senses. Words are lacking for the tongue, and positive expressions are missing from our languages to explain what the ear has not yet heard, nor the Intellect been able to grasp, nor what has yet descended into the heart of man. This is something that is in itself unprovable through the discipline of the senses or the intellect. For faith, the merit of faith, and the expectation of the righteous, surpass every sense and whatever can ever be

<column-break/>

<margin>13.</margin> conceived by the intellect. Furthermore, if the mind is immortal and destined to enjoy eternal joy, it exists and truly lives when separated by death from its mortal body. Therefore, it is not generated by the body, which in itself—with all its disposition—is a falling, mortal thing, a corpse subject to daily and various troublesome changes. Therefore, the mind is an immortal substance, a life of the nature of **eternal light**, inextinguishable. For this reason, it is neither generated nor does it proceed from a human parent or from perishable seed. Much less does it rise or is it produced from itself; rather, it comes from an eternal beginning, which in itself is life and eternal light, infinite, and neither alterable nor extinguishable. These words belong to faith and are revelations of this eternal light, and therefore they are true forever. But the **carnal man** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:14, describing one who relies solely on material understanding.</note> does not perceive the things that are of God; therefore, his wisdom is foolishness before God, who is order, integrity, essence, the **Father of Lights**, and the total, independent, absolute, and abstract cause of all things. Because of this, all honor is owed to Him by every created thing. Moreover, He created not only the substance of the Mind to be a substantial light in His own likeness or image, but He also made all the living lights of animated beings. These indeed would not subsist outside of their physical form in the abstract; therefore, they are destined to perish with the death of those beings. Thus, they are not substances, even if they are "substantial" or act in the manner of substantial spirits. Nor do they belong to the category of "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not exist on its own, like "redness" on an apple.</note>, as I have demonstrated elsewhere in the treatise on the origin of forms. Therefore, the life of a beast comes from a **vital light**, a living creature that is neutral—somewhere between a substance and an accident. This "neutrality" of beings, hitherto unknown to the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university academics of the time.</note>, is given by the name of the **Father of Lights**. This is so that He does not merely create the burning light of the Sun and the glow of the firefly, but also the souls of all living things whatsoever, of which He alone wills to remain the creator and master.

<margin>1.</margin>
Having already premised what I wrote above regarding the immortality of the soul, I now return to my Lord Jesus for the knowledge of the soul. He alone is the principle of paternal wisdom, the unending end—the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "$\alpha$ & $\omega$"</note>—or the unique goal in which the entire clarity of all understandings exists and must terminate. For once the immortality of the mind is known, the soul must come to know itself as much as it is able.

<margin>2.</margin>
Indeed, since the soul sits at the helm as the Ruler <note>original: "Rectrix," a female governor or guide</note> of the body, surely nothing in the body can be examined that is worthy of the effort (unless I am looking at corpses through Anatomy alone) without the knowledge of life or the soul. Truly, I have many times been indignant with myself for wanting to comprehend external and foreign things, while in the meantime not knowing who I am—I, who dare to contemplate external and sublime things. For the image that the mind carries before itself is not yet understood, nor is it known what kind, or how great, the intellect is.

<margin>3.</margin>
And finally, it is not even understood how an intellectual act is formed. Therefore, I determined within myself that a far different knowledge of the soul must be handed down to Christians than what has been taught until now by the schools of the Pagans <note>referring primarily to the followers of Aristotle</note>. For as much as can be explained in words, the Sacred Scriptures also hand down. And the rest is acquired for free through exercise, by grace itself. Nor does the

<column-break/>

mind admit any other teacher than Him who commanded that He alone be called Father and Master. For in truth, all doctrine that is drawn from a pre-existing knowledge of the senses proceeds from the sensitive, carnal, or earthly soul (which the Apostle <note>St. James, in James 3:15</note> therefore calls "Devilish"). It is illuminated, to be sure, but not by the Mind itself; the Mind, namely, desires only to be illuminated by its own beginning, which is above nature, and not by the observation of the senses.

<margin>4.</margin>
This relates to the state of understanding in Adam, before he took up the learning of the senses. Indeed, he knew the essences and the names of living creatures <note>A reference to Genesis 2:19-20</note> because the Mind, in its divine image, contemplated these things within itself whenever it wished, and recalled them by that very gaze. But after the sensitive soul was born beneath it—in which the immortal Mind was wrapped—the sensitive soul alone took up this stewardship. Since then, the numbed mind hardly ever wakes up, at least not more clearly or vividly than when it applies itself to mental prayer. This may be because it momentarily casts off the reins of the sensitive soul, or because God, demanding to be adored in spirit alone, calls it his delight to converse with the children of men.

<margin>5.</margin>
Truly, the prayer of silence and of profound intellectual humility required someone other than myself—now an old man and an ignorant Physician. But since I have undertaken a physical explanation of the mind, and the mind's essence, "whatness" <term>quiddity|the inherent nature or essence of a thing</term>, and physical nature are plainly spiritual and regard their immediate and supernatural beginning, I was altogether bound to publish a doctrine of the mind and explain it through its exercises, so that the man may be revealed by his works. Therefore, I ask and deserve pardon if I have not declared the matter according to its worth. Divine goodness will supply my defects through another more worthy than I. It is in this Mind that the Kingdom of **God** has established its seat by His good pleasure, and it continues to illuminate every man coming into this world; He has enriched it with the spiritual gifts of the Deity and, by His presence, has excluded the evil demon. It was for this Mind, certainly, that He deigned to die—but not for the fallen Angel. I knew secondly, from the knowledge of nature, that Brutes <note>meaning non-human animals</note> have souls that are more or less prudent and sagacious: yet they are all perishable <note>original: "caducas"</note> and hastening toward nothingness; they perish just like a breath. The light of a candle is extinguished and goes into nothingness. Therefore, the souls of beasts are not spiritual substances in the proper sense of the name, but only living, vital lights of animated beings. These, however, are created by God the Father alone and are dispensed according to the requirement of seminal dispositions. I knew thirdly that every perishable and sensitive soul emanates from seeds only occasionally and by way of disposition; therefore, it shares no similarity or unity with the human Mind. For even if both were created by God, they are nonetheless as far apart as a perishable being is from an immortal one. Or as a light destined to perish by being blown out <note>original: "exsufflationem"</note>,

I knew fifthly that the sensitive soul (as I proved in my treatise *On Long Life* regarding the entry of death into human nature) arose in us from sin and remains naturally thereafter through the successive union of the sexes; nor can the immortal Mind be produced by nature, by man, or by any natural means.

<margin>7.</margin> 1. Because it is a substance. 2. And because it is permanent, and therefore 3. Because it could by no means be made from a perishing entity. 4. Because the Mind must therefore be made out of nothing, after the manner of all substances, without the aid of cooperating nature. 5. And because, for that reason, the sensitive soul was not in us before sin, nor was it necessary.

<margin>8.</margin> Finally, I knew sixthly that from the transgression [the Fall] onward, the Mind was bound to the sensitive soul. For in a body subject to death, nothing was closer or more akin to the Mind in which it might sit. And for that reason, the Mind had immersed itself in that bright and vital beginning, as if in a lodging place, and had been divinely annexed to it until the end of life's term. For I have observed so many instances of madness, fallacies, defects, errors, and the betrayals of men—indeed, even all the insanities that utterly deny all use of the Mind, making one suspect its total absence rather than its presence. I recognized seventhly that the mortal soul, since the Fall, so darkens the Mind within its own lodging, covering it in idleness and holding it as if in a slumber, that it not only fails to rule corporal actions but so obscures the very presence of the Mind that it can achieve nothing at all in this life, as if it were no longer in control of itself.

<margin>10.</margin> For although the Mind continuously breathes forth a vital ray from itself (inasmuch as it is never struck down, grows weary, or sleeps) into its deputy, the sensitive soul: nevertheless, it seemed so enslaved by its own faculties to the perishable soul that it was powerless to enjoy its own intellect freely; instead, it yielded to the insane whim of the sensitive soul. Therefore, easily led astray by the filth of diseases, I was prone to descend [into error], because I saw that "serpents" <note>likely referring to internal parasites or metaphorical "poisonous" thoughts</note>, and certain simple—even domestic—excrements of ours, could in every way alter the use of the Mind. Indeed, its powers and their functions seemed utterly trampled and driven mad, becoming far more wretched than those of beasts, even though we are established in such majesty, made in the image of divinity. For I was incited to this [thought] because it did not seem consistent with equity or possibility that some virulent, perishable Being, unequal to the immortality of the Mind, could kick against the image of **God**: so that every right and prerogative might be lost at the whim of a "rabid dog" <note>a metaphor for uncontrolled physical passions or madness</note>. It seemed wrong that the power of the lowest thing should be extended over the excellence of a being destined for an infinite duration. For it seemed that whatever was immortal in itself ought to be impassible <note>term: <term>impassible</term>—incapable of suffering or being affected by external forces</note> by that which is perishable. Furthermore, the Mind of the Wise is frequently besieged by folly: because nearly everyone labors under their own particular point of vertigo <note>a "weak spot" or tendency toward mental confusion</note>. For whoever loves what is not lovable is ensnared, as is he who fails to maintain the proportion of adequacy among lovable things: already in this, he looks upon plausible things as if they were peaceful, with an affection of dementia. For this is how Eve looked upon the apple: as something beautiful, and therefore as something peaceful. Immediately she took it and ate. 
<margin>11.</margin> And this is so common that the Holy Scriptures say, *The number of fools is infinite.* <note>original: "Stultorum infinitum esse numerum," a quote from Ecclesiastes 1:15 in the Vulgate Bible</note> I rushed headlong into these fallacies of error because I did not yet know the nature of the combination, the necessity, and the bond of the Mind and the sensitive soul.

<column-break/>

Indeed, because the Mind was now connected to a mortal soul, it remained bound to it by the "right of hospitality" <note>original: "jure hospitii"—a legal and social metaphor where the Mind is a guest in the "house" of the soul</note>. So much so, that even if the Mind were impassible in itself: nevertheless, because they were both combined by a conjugal bond of unity and a shared bed—so that the mortal soul alone might enjoy the life of the immortal Mind—it was entirely necessary that whenever the mortal soul suffered anything from perishable, harmful, or hostile things, the Mind itself, though immortal, would also suffer "consecutively" <note>meaning suffering by association or as a consequence of the partnership</note> through that equality of marriage, conjugal unity, and the social right of hospitality. This was not because perishable things gained power over an immortal being that was superior to them and of a foreign nature: but **God** willed the mind to suffer in this way, so that, hindered by the discomforts of its lodging, it might be deprived of the liberty of its own magnitude, and might listen to the distresses and anxieties of its own home. For the immortal life of the Mind is communicated to the perishable soul, its seat and its lodging. Yet this life (since whatever is received is received according to the mode and capacity of the recipient) becomes perishable within the connection, or within that perishable light. And therefore, it can be trampled by perishable things until the life is entirely breathed out. And then the Mind, deprived of its lodging, is not indeed extinguished or annihilated: but it is forced to withdraw because of the unbinding and annihilation of the *syndesmos* <note>term: <term>syndesmos</term>—a Greek word meaning a bond or ligament; here used for the spiritual tie connecting mind and soul</note>. Therefore, whatever the Mind seems to suffer beneath the level of life, it remains a guest itself: but it does not freely exercise its duties, because sensation stands in the middle of the bond. Indeed, I have constantly considered 
<margin>12.</margin> the light of the Sun "married" to the glow of a glow-worm <note>original: "nitedula," a small shining insect</note>: so that from both, a single shimmer might shine. For both the lights of the connection within us are not merely "shining" lights, but living and clearly vital ones. One is undoubtedly celestial and constant: but the other is like that of a little worm. Finally, I imagined the light of the glow-worm to be stained or tinted. Whether this happened through its own error...

# THE CONNECTION BETWEEN THE SENSITIVE SOUL AND THE MIND.

...or finally, because a tinted shell is held out over it: at least the solar light, which is always constant in itself, insofar as it has joined with the already tinted light, shining through the light of the **glow-worm** <note>original: *nitedulæ*; a common 17th-century analogy for the soul's light</note>, assumes and undergoes, as it were, the same stain and tint—not indeed that the Sun suffers, but only its light: which produces vital actions according to the defiled colors of the glow-worm. And when the light of the glow-worm is finally extinguished, the solar light loses its "spouse" and departs to its original source to give an account of the duties performed. In this way, the Mind, though unwilling, endures all the insanities of the sensitive soul which the filth of the flesh holds out before it; and the clear beam of the intellect, unable to penetrate the <margin>¶ 13.</margin> filth, is overwhelmed. This is true even if, in its own root, the Mind is entirely **impassible** <note>term: <term>impassible</term>—incapable of suffering or being harmed by external forces</note>. Moreover, what has just been said about life is interpreted in the same way regarding the other functions of the Mind. It is, meanwhile, certain and manifest that the sensitive soul is the seat of the Mind, and thus its immediate handmaid. Since the governance [of the body] was delivered to the sensitive soul following the **Fall** <note>the biblical Fall of Man, which early modern thinkers believed disrupted the natural hierarchy of Reason over Passion</note>, it thereafter draws into itself all the energy of the Mind through improper habit. It is no different than someone accustomed to cutting bread with their left hand; they can hardly manage to divide it with the right. Therefore, the Mind, through ordinary habit, consents to whatever its partner—the brutish sensitive soul—perpetrates by the breadth of its liberty and the license of habit, using the paternal ray of life. For this reason, in all things and through all the paths of this pilgrimage, we lack the aids of divine grace, for which we must pray often and daily: *Lead us not into the temptations of our lodging* <note>a variation on the Lord's Prayer, viewing the body as a temporary "inn" or "lodging"</note>. This is more clearly evident when the Mind operates in arenas of activity plainly distinct and far removed from the sensitive soul. To this end, we first consider the power of the "impregnated" sensitive soul: namely, how by the help of the mental ray (for as the Mind is the image of **God**, so it also busies itself with creating something from nothing by a mere nod or whim) it creates, by appetite alone, a real cherry outside of a <margin>¶ 14.</margin> tree. First, it is beyond doubt that a thought of this kind is appetitive, or

<column-break/>

fearful, etc., and not yet discursive <note>reasoned or logical</note>, and much less is it nakedly subject to the Mind alone. Second, the cherry thus produced is real, not merely a "cherry-stain." Indeed, it changes colors every year in the fixed cycles by which trees color their own fruits. From this, the action of the **pregnant woman's imagination** <note>referring to the historical belief that a mother's intense desires or fears could physically mark or shape her unborn child</note> becomes more manifest, extricating itself beyond the sense of a mere stain. For instance, a woman in **Brussels**, seeing someone's head struck off in the market, soon gave birth to a decapitated fetus whose head was found near the trunk. And I have recounted elsewhere that this happened in the amputation of an arm and hand, though the arm or hand were not found. At the very least, the sensitive soul in man, illuminated by the ray of the Mind, operates actually and truly; therefore, this is not nearly so common in beasts. If this did not happen frequently, we might easily be cast by critics into the suspicion of having an implicit pact with an **evil spirit** <note>original: *cacodæmone*</note>. For because it is not the sensitive soul alone that works these things, but one illuminated by the ray of the immortal Mind, there is a certain "similitude of creation" which is produced by the living image of its Creator; beasts, likewise, do not emulate this effect. By the mere conception of a passion, a cherry is created out of nothing in the fetus, on that part where the pregnant woman moves her right hand on the outside (if it was the right), or the left (if it was the left). This is because that hand is accustomed to carrying out the commands of the soul. At the same time, the whole "feminine being" of the Cherry is created, outside of its own wood, and indeed perfected—not increasing slowly through ages as it otherwise does in a tree, where a cherry produces its fruit after several years. But suddenly, a cherry, or a mouse, etc., is fabricated in the womb. This fabricating power requires sight, and moreover, a disturbance, etc., so that the power of the soul's "conception" is designated, rather than a work of discourse. For this is not a **true** <margin>¶ 15.</margin> creation, because no new matter is made from nothing; rather, it is a **transmutative creation** of one thing into another, and it is almost instantaneous. While it is already created in the "ideal being" of the concept...

...as an ideal, and clothed in the vital spirit of the mother, the place where it ought to be carried and depicted is soon designated by the hand. In the absence of this hand, the **cherry-seal** <note>original: *cerasi sigillum*; a common early modern term for a birthmark (maternal mark) resembling a cherry</note> is lost, and the creation is brought to nothing. This occurs in things desired. Otherwise, in fearsome events: since these are so much more powerful, the direction of the mother's hand is not required. Namely, a hand or arm of the fetus is amputated, even if the mother's hand remained still, nor is it found among the membranes, like the head. Just as when the fetus is transformed into a monster. But in the case of non-fearsome beasts, the hand is required as a designer of the location for the fetus, so that the whole may be changed. There is a different reason in those fearsome cases. Because in one, only the act is shown, and in the other, a created being. For in the former, it intends only removal; but in the latter, it desires to emulate by creating something.

<column-break/>

Finally, there is this universal principle in such matters: the mother who acts does not intend to do this for her fetus; and so, not in herself but in her fetus, she attaches these images, according to the whim of her hand, and not according to the will of the woman conceiving something desirable or horrible. However, some plausible or fearful conception precedes, with appetite or aversion. And from there, the appetite for those conceptions immediately follows, with desire or dread. I have expanded on these things here so that the power of the divine image in this **mimic-creation** <note>original: *similitudinariæ creationis*; the idea that human imagination mimics God's creative power</note> might lead us into the likeness of creating divine love in the mind. While the mind itself, by its own motion—and not only by the single ray of itself dispersed into the falling soul (as was already stated happens in pregnant women)—and by its own wish, is carried entirely within into the love of God. Ah, would that we were led there!

# ASTHMA

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'A' at the beginning of the text, set within a square frame featuring a detailed woodcut of scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

**B**ecause Asthma has been relegated to the <note>original: *nænias*; literally "trifles" or "funeral songs"</note> nonsense of Catarrh, and remains a condition unrecognized and scarcely cured until now, I am compelled to write about Asthma point by point. To this end, certain points from my previous deductions must be repeated. Namely, that the Lung is permeable through its pores as long as one lives, no differently than all the nerves. This is especially evident in the optic nerves: if one eye is closed, the pupil of the other can be seen to enlarge. 
<margin>1.</margin> 
But in death, these pores are closed, though they are otherwise open in the living; the light visibly perishes from the eyes of the dying because, when the optic channels are closed, the "visual spirit" <note>An early modern concept of a subtle fluid or energy that allowed the eyes to see.</note> ceases and fails to flow there. Hippocrates already knew this in his own age; 
<margin>2.</margin> 
therefore he declared the whole body to be "breathable and in harmony" <note>original: *perspirabile & conspirabile*</note>. Furthermore, I believe it has now been sufficiently demonstrated that nothing "drops down" from the head into the Larynx or the Lung—even though such matter is frequently and copiously coughed up—to such an extent that there is no room left for the fiction of "distillation" or "Catarrh" <note>The author is attacking the ancient Greek theory that respiratory phlegm was actually fluid dripping from the brain.</note>. Indeed, whatever the Cough ejects is produced within the pipes of the Lung by its own fault. Thus, healers have erred until now due to ignorance of which part commands, which part acts, and which part receives, and because of their failure to think about the nature of the matter and the way it is formed. 
<margin>3.</margin> 
It is no wonder, therefore, that nothing has been achieved in healing. For remedies were applied to the head to prevent it from acting, or from sending down matter—or to prevent matter from sliding into the lung of its own accord—even though this matter was never under the head's control. Rather, it resides constantly within the lung itself. Thus, the sick have remained without a remedy because all the care of the physicians was occupied partly with the head—which is innocent in this disease—and partly with precautions and the easier 
<margin>4.</margin> 
ejection of filth. They did not, however, concern themselves with the correction of that **Corrupting Vulcan** <note>original: *Vulcani Corruptoris*; a reference to an internal "alchemical" heat or transformative force that has gone awry.</note> who fashions the aforementioned phlegm out of the Lung's own good nourishment. Truly, ignorance of the primary causes has caused the Schools <note>Traditional medical universities teaching Galenic medicine.</note> to forever direct their healing intentions toward the effect and the secondary symptoms. For while they 

<column-break/>

observed that drinks and food are swallowed straight into the stomach, and that nothing turns toward the Lung, they devised sweets to aid expectoration, insofar as they might make the throat smooth. 
<margin>6.</margin> 
Then they invented thicker syrups, which they thought, by being slowly licked up, would by a greater right slide down toward the Lung. But again, these were all lazy thoughts. For first, in this, the Schools forgot their own positions regarding the head. Finally, they did not consider that if linctuses <note>original: *eclegmata*; thick, syrupy medicines intended to be licked.</note> of this kind were to enter the lung, they would cause more narrowness and distress than the very filth that stagnates and is built up there gradually. At the very least, they would be piling a new evil upon the old. For they would accomplish nothing there, except to cause a blockage through the great narrowing of the passages, and render the patient anxious for the rest of time. 
<margin>7.</margin> 
This is especially true because roses, coltsfoot <note>original: *farfara*</note>, fox lung <note>A traditional sympathetic remedy: using the lungs of a long-winded animal to treat respiratory issues.</note>, sugar, and so on, in no way respond to the curative Requirement. For the condition demands only the restoration of the damaged "transformative faculty" <note>The internal ability of the organ to process nutrients properly.</note>. Those things which look toward easier expectoration only attack the disease from behind and address its effects. Therefore, since the Lung lies open where the ends of the "rough arteries" <note>original: *arteriæ asperæ*; an old term for the trachea and bronchi.</note> terminate and breathe into the chest, it is clear enough that in Asthma there is a constriction of these very pores. Furthermore, they still err because the remedies 
<margin>8.</margin> 
for a Cough differ in no way from the remedies for Asthma, even though both differ immensely and in every way in their root and causes. There is, therefore, a twofold Asthma. 
<margin>9.</margin> 
One is specific to women, depending solely on the governance of the womb; the other is promiscuous, common to both sexes. 
<margin>10.</margin> 
A woman is certainly miserable in both cases, for being excluded from almost all business, she is not even satisfied with a single species of the disease. For this Asthma is so frequent in this sex that the Schools have attributed every "Uterine Rhythm" <note>original: *Arithmum*; likely referring to the complex cycles and movements of the womb.</note> (which is very manifold) to "suffocations of the womb," and have wished to pass over a huge volume of diseases under a single heading. Indeed, I have seen many...

The author also introduces a distinction between general asthma and a specific form of the condition related to the womb in women.</summary>
