# AND COUGH
<meta>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page: "tes" likely completes "mulier-tes" or "affec-tes" (women or affected persons).</meta>

...who, because of the scent of sweet-smelling things, besides headaches and the threat of fainting, would immediately fall into extreme difficulty breathing. I have observed others who, when the North wind <note>original: *Borea*</note> blows, were immediately afflicted with Asthma, even while staying in heated rooms <note>original: *hypocaustis*; rooms heated by underfloor systems</note>. Finally, I have seen others who—due to anger, sad news, drinking sugar, Spanish wine, etc., or even from being scolded—were soon seized by a sorrowful Asthma.

<margin>11.</margin>
Indeed, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the time, which followed the teachings of Galen and Avicenna.</note>, having always concerned themselves only with bodily actions, perpetually worship the "humors." They have blamed "phlegm" <note>original: *pituita*</note> in every case, claiming it flows down into the Lungs. They claim that foul vapors rise from the uterus, which stir up similar conditions in themselves and from the stomach, whereby they squeeze out all the coughed-up mucus, which they name the author of Asthma. For the Schools have given such harmful vapors a "safe conduct" to penetrate everywhere, even to places where air cannot freely pass. This is evident in the voluntary compression or 

<margin>12.</margin>
holding of the breath. Indeed, although these theories only have a place in "moist" Asthma, the Schools, in the same ignorance, have not ceased to attempt all sorts of useless things: enemas, bloodletting <note>original: *phlebotomiam*</note>, cauteries, and laxatives, so that they might satisfy their theory of "drawing away" these fictional vapors, 

<margin>13.</margin>
even in "dry" Asthma. Thus they have neglected the fact that the uterus—by its governing action and a nearly celestial influence—at the whim of anger, sadness, fear, etc., blocks the aforementioned pores of the lung where they open into the chest. This happens like a shadow of death, just as the moon, by its look alone, presides over the waters; this is because the life and power of the uterus rules the whole woman. For this reason, a woman has a different chin, character, flesh, hair, and blood than a man. And again, once the furies and overflows of this governing power cease, free breathing is immediately restored, and usually without any notable coughing up of phlegm. For the uterus does not rule the woman merely 

<margin>14.</margin>
by vapors: but by the pure command of its governance, it rules the whole woman. It is like a foreign guest, depending on the body only for its nourishment, just as mistletoe <note>original: *viscus*</note> grows upon a tree.

<margin>15.</margin>
Furthermore, the uterus lives its own

<column-break/>

life, and knows no enemy to itself except the disturbances of the mind <note>original: *pathemata*</note>. Therefore, it does not serve the soul: but it rages against the mind when it is troubled by disturbances, just as it rages against the body. For the disturbances of the soul alone agitate the uterus into various furies: so much so that it now cruelly strikes at the nerves, then the intestines, the bones, the internal organs, and the membranes. It likewise shakes the heart or the head, the senses, and the mind. Indeed, I have not rarely seen tendons, convulsed with great torment, leap out of their place of their own accord; I have seen marvelous convulsions of the muscles, accompanied by great wailing, and then resolve; indeed, I have even seen it seriously dislocate bones. I have also observed that Apoplexy, Paralysis, the "Falling Sickness" <note>Epilepsy</note>, Jaundice, Dropsy <note>edema</note>, griping pains, migraines, madness, and a great tyranny of diseases have proceeded from the uterus. These have been unsuccessfully treated by the Schools with 

<margin>16.</margin>
"male" remedies <note>Remedies designed for the male constitution, ignoring the specific nature of the uterus.</note>; I would say they were neglected, and somehow attributed only to the "suffocation of Asthma," as if by some singular privilege only the throat obeyed the uterus. Truly, this sex is worthy of much compassion; they were given to us as a help for great necessities, and yet are seemingly worthy of manifold hardship. Since a woman suffers almost all diseases once because of the uterus, and again as a human being, 

<margin>17.</margin>
this innocent and devoted sex endures a double punishment of our corrupted nature through these miserable female individuals. But she is happy at least in that she bears tribulations patiently and is, in this way, closer to the Son of God.

<margin>18.</margin>
There is, therefore, another type of Asthma common to both sexes. Asthma is further subdivided into "dry" and "moist," judged by what is coughed up. Until now, the causes of Asthma and the way it comes to be have remained unknown in the Schools. Consequently, a proper cure for Asthma has remained 

<margin>19.</margin>
unfound. Let God be the witness and judge between me and the Humorists <note>Doctors who believe disease is caused by an imbalance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note>, as to how much I pity the sick who are poorly treated under the unlucky service of ignorance; and who are finally, stripped of hope and drained of their money, miserably abandoned. That is, they are often deceived. For, agitated by useless attempts, they have marveled with me that such sluggish help has been sought for so many centuries and from so many libraries.

<margin>20.</margin>

-> ### ASTHMA <-

Meanwhile, we have seen not a few people cured by an old woman or a quack <note>original: *agyrta*; a traveling peddler of medicine or a "street-doctor"</note>. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the 17th century</note> fall asleep at the complaints of the sick. For they indeed hear their wailing; but like the Levites, they pass by on the road to Jericho <note>original: *quum Levitis transeunt in Jericho*; an allusion to the Parable of the Good Samaritan, where religious authorities ignored a suffering man</note>. And because they do not wish to hear, they listen unwillingly. Namely, they see that their daily patronage of diseases is becoming unfortunate for them. Yet, they do not recede so much as a fingernail's breadth from their predecessors, though they should once seriously repent for the life of a neighbor entrusted to them. To agree with the ancients and these blind leaders has fallen into a kind of laziness. Therefore, they are no longer ashamed to declare patients "incurable" whenever they have not been relieved by bloodletting <note>original: *phlebotomo*</note>, laxatives, sweating, enemas, cautery <note>branding the skin with hot iron</note>, hot baths, or the drinking of acidic mineral waters—that is to say, by things that diminish one’s strength. Concerning Asthma, I shall now first describe several well-known case histories. Those who follow me will examine these same things better and more successfully.

<margin>21.</margin>
A consul of a great city, fifty years old, a generous drinker and a strong man, fell from a ladder on a ship onto his shoulders and the back of his head; he fainted for a long time. Upon coming to himself, he remained well for eight months. Then, having suffered a slight fever for several days, he abandoned his drinking parties because a feverish Asthma seized him. Each attack, lasting through several days and nights, continually threatened him with strangulation. They ended, however, without any obvious coughing up of phlegm. Yet the night preceding an assault of Asthma was sleepless and restless, with a dryness of the mouth, a warning of fever, a strange abundance of urine, and usually three troublesome bowel movements. Then, on the following morning, in a single assault as it were, his breath is cut off as if by a snapped thread. He lifts his shoulders while breathing like wings; he presses both hands against the frame of the bed so that he may lift his shoulders easier and higher. His face turns red, and his eyes protrude. In this way, he spends several days and nights without sleep and struggles continually with imminent suffocation. Finally, when the paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms</note> is finished, he is perfectly healthy: he eats, walks, climbs, hunts, rides, and travels. Indeed, he does not remember ever 

<column-break/>

in his life having a headache or a chest prone to coughing. <margin>22</margin> A young man of 24 years, untainted by any error in health or lifestyle, a scholar, a nobleman, and also devoted to hunting—hence he was swift of foot and a fast runner. This man, coming to Brussels after a journey of three leagues <note>A league was roughly 3 miles</note>, was first seized by Asthma after a moderate dinner with his sister. For three whole days, in fear of suffocation, he agonized between life and death with labors and sweats. Soon after, he was restored without any spitting, and being quickly well again, he returned to his home. Afterward, for two whole years, he did not dare to lie down to sleep; instead, sitting by the hearth, he spent his nights awake for years. For if he lay down, the sleeping Asthma would soon wake up. Frequently, a paroxysm also threatened—indeed, it would begin, but not proceed. One time it would afflict him more cruelly than another. It is worsened by the phases of the moon <note>original: *lunae stationibus*</note>, as well as by changes in the weather, which he senses and predicts beforehand. The attacks infest him more severely and more often in summer than in winter. Indeed, today it urges him more frequently and cruelly than at its first beginning. On the intervening days, however, he walks, runs, rides, hunts, and performs the other duties of healthy men rightly; but at night, he does not dare to lie down. In mountainous places, he feels worse; therefore, he hardly dares to spend the night in Brussels. Furthermore, several hours before a paroxysm, his saliva becomes salty to him; he feels his teeth and gums contract, and his intestines rumble with a great roar. His sides ache on both sides, and he passes abundant, frequent, and watery urine; and his bowels are loosened three or four times. Finally, as if a noose were suddenly thrown around him, the Asthma seizes him; each time, it threatens suffocation throughout the entire attack. Toward the end, at last, he easily coughs up four or five foamy spits without a cough, and he is soon liberated as if the noose had been removed. <margin>23</margin> A certain Canon <note>A member of a cathedral's clergy</note>, a man of a steady and vigorous age, measures the future ferocity of a paroxysm by the magnitude of the preceding signs. For the whole summer, almost...

# AND COUGH.

...while he is asthmatic, he is free of it for the whole winter. But in whatever season he is oppressed by the asthma, his whole body itches, he sheds white scales, and he displays the appearance of leprosy <note>original: *Lepræ*; here likely referring to a severe scaling skin condition like psoriasis rather than Hansen’s disease</note>. He says his mother suffered from a similar itch, as did his sister. Indeed, he says the former died from it, but the latter was cured spontaneously after her second childbirth.

<margin>24.</margin> A certain lay monk of the Order of Saint Francis of Paola <note>The Minims, a Roman Catholic religious order known for extreme humility and strict dietary rules</note> was occupied in tearing down buildings. From then on, whenever a place was swept or the wind stirred up dust elsewhere, he soon collapsed, nearly suffocated. His mind remained clear, but he would lie there at death’s door with his breath almost shut off; thereafter, he could only sleep while sitting up. Furthermore, whenever he ate fish fried in oil (according to his order’s rules and his own appetite), he would immediately collapse, deprived of breath, such that he could hardly be distinguished from someone being strangled. He says he feels the signs of an impending asthmatic attack, which another hunter also reports: that he is made more certain of a future attack and its severity by a precursor of symptoms. This occurs, of course, when the asthma rushes in spontaneously, and not from food or dust.

<margin>25.</margin> A certain citizen, a wise and prudent man, was treated with reproach and public injury by a nobleman <note>original: *Magnate*; a person of high rank or great influence</note>. He was unable to respond with even a word for fear of total ruin. Keeping silent, he hid his feelings and endured the insult; but soon after, asthma arose. Although he was otherwise in good health, it grew more burdensome daily for two whole years. Finally, toward the end, a moderate case of dropsy <note>original: *Hydrops*; an accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, often related to heart or kidney failure</note> extinguished his life within a few days.

<margin>26.</margin> A certain boy, almost from the cradle, struggled with quartan fever <note>original: *quartana*; a form of malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day</note> for two whole years; against everyone’s hope, he recovered through a "crisis" <note>a sudden change in a disease leading to recovery or death</note> and many bowel movements. However, due to a severe "falling sickness" <note>original: *comitiali*; usually referring to epilepsy</note>, he was considered as good as dead. As an adolescent and young man, he was quite agile, but of precarious health. Soon after reaching young adulthood, he felt that he panted far too much while running, which he attributed to a life full of comforts. In his manhood, he felt that even moderate dancing cost him a shorter breath than was right. Around his fiftieth year, however, he clearly suspected himself to be asthmatic; and he felt this had clearly increased 

<column-break/>

around his sixtieth year. For since infancy, he had a notably damaged spleen <note>original: *lienem*</note>, which was frequently painful. So much so, that a single day's ride on horseback was troublesome because of the jolting of the spleen; he was especially exhausted if he spent the day traveling at a courier’s pace. Furthermore, that "falling sickness," although it did not reveal itself except for the gravest reasons—having been dormant otherwise for several years—was not actually convulsive, but rather like a fainting spell. He would feel a certain joy around the opening of the stomach, and soon he would collapse. He rarely had a cough; but since he was a young man, he had frequent hawking. His phlegm <note>original: *Sputum*</note> consisted of bluish droplets, similar to melted tragacanth <note>a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of several species of Middle Eastern legumes</note>. These spittings were rare throughout the summer, but more frequent in the cold, so much so that as old age grew heavy upon him, he hawked a great deal all winter. Finally, now fully asthmatic, he could read through the entire psalm *De profundis* <note>original: "From the depths"; Psalm 130, often used in funeral liturgies or daily prayer</note> in a single breath, without rushing his speech, provided he was sitting down. He even walks on flat ground for a league at a fairly quick pace; but if he climbs a street or even a slight incline at a moderate gait, he immediately salivates, pants, his chest tightens, and his heart soon palpitates with a rapid, irregular pulse. His tongue becomes parched at the back of the throat, and foam forms around his teeth. Furthermore, his knees almost give way along with the asthma, increasing or decreasing according to its measure; whereas before the asthma, his whole leg was agile and strong. However, while sitting or standing, or even walking about the house, he never pants unless he is climbing. Whenever he is refreshed by a large dinner, he pants at night, his chest contracts, and his larynx <note>original: *Larinx*</note> snores with a nearly continuous murmur, as if his throat were tinkling with phlegm. All of these symptoms are soon put to rest by sitting up, and he coughs up several bits of phlegm much more easily; once these are cleared, he lies down again. A meager dinner gives rest to the stomach, and likewise peace to the lungs. He perceives, however, that this asthma has its nest and primary source in a place midway between the mouth of the stomach and the navel. I draw these things out at such length...

# ASTHMA

whereby the seeds <note>original: *femina*, likely a typo for *semina* (seeds) given the context of the following sentence</note> of Asthma are made more manifest.

<margin>27.</margin> Indeed, in the Consul, the Citizen, and the Hunter, as much as in the Canon, asthma resides in a virulent seed, which has obtained the spirit of some internal organ as its root and dwelling place. Moreover, the property of that seed is to contract the pores of the lung, through which it transmits breath into the chest. The necessity of this constriction appears immediately in the teeth and gums. For it affects the whole, because it is dispersed into the **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that Van Helmont believed governed the body's functions</note>, the organ common to the whole body. Therefore, the kidneys milk out the urine, the bowels are loosened, the intestines rumble, the making of blood falters, the heart palpitates: and finally the lung is contracted, not unlike the Scrotum under the urge to defecate <note>original: *sub assellandi cupidine*; a characteristically earthy 17th-century physiological comparison</note>.

<margin>28.</margin> Furthermore, the nest of Asthma is in the **Duumvirate** <note>The "Duumvirate" refers to the stomach and spleen, which Van Helmont viewed as the primary governing center of the body, rather than the brain</note> (concerning which I shall treat in a specific tract), from which, evidently, the governance of the whole depends: for otherwise the evil does not sit immediately in the "inflowing spirit" <note>the air taken in during breathing</note>: which would otherwise be terminated by a single attack: for unless it had obtained a stable root within, it would not recur, nor would it persist.

Then finally, the character of the evil, which sleeps for a time in a stable part, does not seem able to be stabled anywhere else than where the governance of the body depends, and thus it has even assumed the prerogative of the heart. Therefore, Asthma is similar to **Epilepsy** <note>often called the "falling sickness" in this period</note> in this regard: that although it does not strike the mind, nor contract the nerves, nor excite a fainting fit: it nevertheless sleeps in some seat, from whence at last, polluting the Archeus by a certain contagion, it contracts, if not the nerves, at least the lung. To be sure, it regards that organ specifically: indeed, although it may seem to contract the veins, kidneys, and liver with equal pace: yet there is no such manifest injury in these as is felt in the sense of suffocation. All these things are even more clearly established in the Citizen and sixty-year-old man. For since his infancy, he retained a poorly affected spleen, and simultaneously epileptic insults; yet his lungs were otherwise quite free. But he, through the agony of shame, anger, revenge, and the modesty of commanding reason,

<column-break/>

showed that the organ injured in him was that in which the first movements of conceptions are stabled.

<margin>29.</margin> It is permitted, therefore, with philosophical liberty, to name Asthma the **falling sickness of the lung**. Its nest is indeed in the Duumvirate; it is also a disease of the whole, insofar as it moves all members before an attack, and thus shakes the spirit, the ruler of the whole. Nevertheless, it bears fruit in the area of the chest, and regards the lung specifically, as the target of its own property and its proper object: that falling sickness of the lung arises from a poison, which by its own property affects the lung, not unlike how *cantharides* <note>Spanish fly, a toxic beetle used in medicine that specifically irritates the urinary tract</note> affect the organs of urine.

<margin>30.</margin> To be sure, there is some poison which prostrates the head, and the whole man, into epilepsy, much more insolently and wonderfully than that which would bind the lung. Yet the rarity of the affection has not dared to compel it toward the position of a certain epilepsy. Although, in the meantime, whatever heals an adult epileptic

<margin>31.</margin> also heals an Asthmatic. I have also seen a virus rise up from the womb, which bound nothing except the throat, so that for three months an illustrious matron could hardly swallow anything. I arrived, recognized the evil, and immediately the Lord healed her. For on account of emaciation and hunger, she was infested by a continuous falling sickness, and for 37 days she had only a single bowel movement the size of an acorn. In the Consul, indeed, the virus consists in the spleen, and therefore it began with a fever, and always begins so, because it was fermented in that same place by febrile beginnings. But in the hunter, it was around the mouth of the stomach, and when it seized him, he was immune from febrile beginnings. Thus also he begins his paroxysm in the manner of a falling sickness, and his insult is even daily, because a ferment of his Asthma becomes concentric to the organ expressing the rhythm of the heart. In this man, therefore, it converses with the eccentricities of the weather, while in the other, it does not listen to them so readily. For in both cases, it must wait for its own maturity, and mixing with the spirit of the whole. And for that reason, mountainous and summer places bring it to maturity,

<margin>33.</margin> and they hasten the eruption of that seed: which in some, under wintry and swampy conditions, erupts more easily; otherwise it remains silent for a long time, as if requiring a feverish seat, which hastens the impacted poison and ripens it toward the period of its eruption. Therefore, properly speaking, the seed itself is the Asthma, and the "falling sickness" <note>original: *caducus*; a term usually reserved for epilepsy, here suggesting the lung is suffering a kind of seizure</note> of the lung, even if it has long remained silent. However, once it has reached maturity, it is the apple of that tree—the root, the fruit, the onset, and the product of the latent Asthma. And because it rises into action 
<margin>34.</margin> by the force of the vital governance, and by way of "influences," it invades suddenly, no differently than a noose thrown around the neck. For I consider a person asthmatic both outside of a paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or violent expression of symptoms</note> and during one, because the true Asthma is present within them: just as a pear tree is as much a pear tree in winter 
<margin>35.</margin> as it is in autumn when it bears pears. Meanwhile, I believe I have satisfied everyone that at least the aforementioned types of Asthma do not owe their origin to phlegm flowing down into the lung, or to a fictitious Catarrh <note>The "catarrh" theory held that illnesses were caused by waste fluids dripping from the brain into the body</note>, since they invade suddenly and are resolved without any clear coughing up of matter that could have so distressed the lung. Indeed, if anything happens to be coughed up near the end, and even then but a tiny amount, it should not be considered the prior cause or the occasion of the illness; rather, it takes the place of a product—arising, clearly, from the great constriction and the untimely injury inflicted upon the lung. For this reason, I would be cruel if I proposed a remedy for a "dripping head" or a "steaming stomach." Therefore, anyone who wishes to be a person of heart and a Christian will learn from this how fruitless are the solicitations of expectation in Asthma (especially the dry kind) through linctuses <note>syrupy medicines to be licked</note>, lohochs <note>a thick, honey-like medicinal paste</note>, syrups, bloodletting <term>Phlebotomy: the practice of opening a vein to drain blood, which Van Helmont vehemently opposed</term>, and laxatives; or through drinks made of China root, Sarsaparilla, or Sassafras 
<margin>37.</margin> (which they falsely call "drying" remedies); and through stinginess of diet, sweating, baths, and cauteries <note>branding or burning the skin to create a sore</note>—all intended to stop, pull back, evacuate, consume, or turn away the supposed cause of Asthma, whether it be rising from the stomach or materially raining down from the head. It is in vain, therefore, that any indistinct remedies have been

<column-break/>

hitherto attributed to coughs with such lack of discretion, and explored through the vanishing results of mere luck. Finally, in the face of such a great evil, it is vain to beg for "flowers of sulfur" <note>a bright yellow powder produced by heating sulfur until it turns to vapor and then solidifies</note>, however variously they may be refined; and from this, the false remedies of "extracted milk" and tinctures, even though they promise these things more boldly and brilliantly than others, and inject hope through such a plausible-looking apparatus. I have likewise understood the vain fermentations and promises of wine mixed with coltsfoot <note>original: *tussilaginibus*; a plant long used as a cough remedy</note> and other lung medicines. And once 
<margin>38.</margin> the cause was known to me, I finally saw through the section by Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a revolutionary physician who moved medicine toward chemistry, though Van Helmont often found his theories incomplete</note> regarding Asthma, which was established for the author's own boasting, along with his cures made from tartar, sulfur, lemon balm, and so on. But I found things even more foolish than these: nasal sprays, the "phlegm-purging" medicines of the ancients, lozenges, and other things of that sort. At the very least, laxatives and bloodletting are monstrous, because they cause a collapse of strength. I confess, indeed, that by such tricks 
<margin>39.</margin> the attacks are occasionally eased, or delayed and spread out, and that this once deceived me. But afterward, I seriously repented of my stupidities. I acknowledge that I then held up masks and cloaks over diseases; I healed no one, but rather deluded as many as trusted themselves to my ignorance. Therefore, after I stood like useless foam cast upon the shore by the storms of common ignorance, I wondered greatly why the Schools, and the sharpest of such great minds, had not yet been able to say farewell to the false persuasions of their predecessors. Since Asthma is never 
<margin>40.</margin> cut short by any remedy except by the remedy of an "arcanum" <term>Arcanum: a secret, higher-order medicinal power that acts on the vital spirit rather than just physical matter</term> which penetrates through all the paths of the body so that it leaves nothing unattempted: and thus, by a single means, it overthrows the "falling sickness" of Asthma and whatever has fixed its seat immediately anywhere in the hiding places of the body. I except Gout <note>original: *Podagram*</note> and similar diseases, which have found their lodging immediately in the vital spirit. And since, in the meantime, I considered my own worthlessness in the presence of such great geniuses of old, I could not help but immediately fall on my face and praise, in a prayer of silence, the Father of Lights, because He had given to the little ones...

<summary>Van Helmont rejects traditional treatments for asthma—such as bloodletting, laxatives, and herbal syrups—labeling them as "masks" for the physician's ignorance. He argues that asthma is an internal "seed" or seizure of the lung that requires a deep-penetrating chemical "arcanum" to cure, rather than treatments targeting "dripping" phlegm from the head.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of asthma as a disease of the "vital spirit" and "ferments" rather than just excess fluid. Having previously argued against the "catarrh" theory, he now provides clinical case studies and observations of occupational hazards to prove that asthma is a corruption of the body's internal processing of nutrients and air.</meta>

# ASTHMA

[The Lord] grants knowledge, which He had hidden from the Wise of this world. Since it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs and labors, but of God alone who shows mercy. To whom be all honor and glory forever.

<margin>41.</margin>
As for the fact that sweet smells, sadness, and also sweets can cause asthma; I would not want it understood as if asthma occurred from those causes by themselves. While in other women, these same things are pleasing and harmless, in others, instead of asthma, they produce migraines, palpitations, and fainting. For each of these arises from a singular frenzy of uterine madness <note>original: *amentiæ uterinæ furore*; Van Helmont refers here to "hysteria," which in the 17th century was believed to be a physical disturbance or "frenzy" of the womb affecting the whole body</note>.

<margin>42.</margin>
A certain wealthy priest of good life, who had never spent his youth on Wine or Women <note>original: *Venere aut Baccho*; references to Venus (goddess of love) and Bacchus (god of wine)</note>, suddenly became hoarse in his 38th year. He gradually lost his tone and voice, and could only express formed words through his breath. From this hoarseness, he became completely short of breath and died after a year. Upon dissecting the lung, the posterior lobe of the left side was found hard and petrified like a pumice stone; inside, it was as if a clot had hardened through the lung.

<margin>43.</margin>
Where the windpipe <note>original: *aspera arteria*; literally "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea and bronchi</note> branches into four lobes, there were cheesy clots, halfway between cartilage and pumice. Many such small stones were seen scattered through the region of the lung. This good man endured a perpetual asthma, not a recurring one. However, his phlegm did not increase. For the nourishment of the final digestion <term>sixth digestion: Van Helmont’s term for the final stage of metabolism where nutrients are actually turned into the living substance of the organs</term> is coagulated by a foreign ferment <term>ferment: a biological catalyst or "seed" that Van Helmont believed directed all bodily processes</term>, from which rare asthma arises, wavering between moist and dry.

<margin>44.</margin>
Miners, metal-smelters, refiners, coin-makers, chemists, and also craftsmen who work with gold-dissolving acids, white lead, red lead, verdigris, cinnabar, and gilders, etc.—nearly all of these are soon seized by asthma. This is because the Gas <note>Van Helmont famously coined the word "Gas" to describe invisible vapors that possessed specific chemical and vital properties</note> they breathe in with the air ruins the channels of the larynx during the sixth digestion. From this it happens that, instead of the assimilation of nourishment, the whole substance degenerates into waste, according to the condition of the transforming ferment. When this waste is held back and stays there, the aforementioned channels are closed. But because the sixth digestion itself has contracted a stain in its vital powers from the impression of an endemic poison,

<column-break/>

or from a real adhesion of the same, therefore daily—even hourly—a new waste of this kind is born, even unto death. This death is at the door when the expulsive force is not sufficient to blast out the newly created waste through coughing. Thus they are suffocated by asthma. For the Gas of certain minerals suffocates immediately by its nature, no differently than the Sicilian cave <note>original: *crypta sicula*; likely a reference to the *Grotta del Cane* near Naples, famous in early science for a layer of CO2 that would suffocate dogs but not taller humans</note> suffocates a dog. For the smoke of Mercury (which, however masked, is still Mercury) immediately shuts and constricts the larynx. Indeed, because it is terrifyingly poisonous, the throat immediately contracts itself at the presence of the enemy.

<margin>45.</margin>
At the very least, every harmful Gas, by being breathed in, ruins the digestion of the lung. This filth, a witness to the injury inflicted, soon brings the tragedy to its epilogue <note>meaning: brings the illness to its final conclusion, death</note> if it sticks too tightly, because a new offspring of filth is continually being born. Therefore, once the poison of a localized Gas is swallowed, the lung succumbs and soon produces asthma. In the same way, extreme cold, insofar as it overcomes the powers of the lung, produces a moist asthma, because the digestion in that place is lost.

<margin>46.</margin>
Another asthmatic person was suddenly suffocated, even though he was coughing up phlegm correctly. The cause was sought through anatomy. In the lung, almost no waste was found, only a very little; but the right lobe was attached to the pleura <note>the membrane lining the chest cavity</note> at the back. The doctors were content to have found the "knot" of the matter. "Behold," they said, "the cause of sudden death. For the lung could not move itself, and therefore he perished suffocated."

<margin>47.</margin>
While still a young man, I did not believe that the lung (which I then believed had to move necessarily and continuously) could have been so firmly attached to the pleura at the back in perhaps a single hour—especially while he was sitting. Indeed, if a hernia is pushed inward and tightly compressed, it would hardly grow together with its neighbor so unwillingly, even during the rest of the bed. Meanwhile, this continuous growth of torn parts would be by the direction of nature; but not so the pleura to the lung, both of which were distinguished by their own membrane and by the purpose of nature. I looked upon these reckless errors of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university medical authorities of the time, whom Van Helmont frequently criticized</note>, and thereafter...

He transitions from dissecting soldiers to describing specific cases of asthma and how the "Duumvirate" (the stomach and spleen) governs these symptoms.</meta>

-># AND COUGH.<-

I observed this even more clearly after I had dissected soldiers who had been suddenly killed. I saw, for instance, the lung attached to the back of the ribs in men who were otherwise healthy and who had previously shown no difficulty in breathing. Among others, a certain very swift Irishman, a footman of the <note>original: *Marchionis de Winchestræ*; John Paulet, 5th Marquess of Winchester, a prominent Royalist during the English Civil War</note> Marquess of Winchester, who had been killed by a dagger, showed both lobes of the lung attached to the ribs when he was dissected. If you were to blame this on a flaw in his formation or a "monstrosity," you must at least admit it is consistent with birds <note>Van Helmont notes that in birds, the lungs are naturally fixed to the ribs, unlike in most mammals</note>. For while anatomists never find those imaginary humors <note>The "four humors" of ancient medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, they nevertheless promise to uncover every cause of death with their razor. First they are amazed, then they are seriously indignant that death arrived without their permission. Indeed, as if they held hope and a remedy in their knife, they rejoice to have found a part in the corpse to which they can attribute the killing.

<margin>48.</margin>
And then they cry out: "Behold, this noble organ has long since failed through putrefaction!" Yet it is not always in the Physician's power for the sick man to be relieved. In this way, those who practice medicine often cover up their errors and console the heirs with trifles. The relatives are stunned and find solace in the "necessity" of the death—as if a putrefaction of the internal organs could have persisted for many months prior, when a gangrene on the outside of the body kills within a few days. Indeed, the "nest" from which death arrives is gradually disposed toward its end, but it begins to rot (and more quickly than other corpses) from the very moment death is near because it is fostered by the internal heat.

<margin>49.</margin>
I gathered that one asthmatic man died because long before, he had been troubled by palpitations and even an intermittent pulse; the "poison," finally acquiring the properties of asthma, had blocked the pores through which the lung breathes into the chest. For nowhere does the action of the governing power in the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>The Duumvirate is Van Helmont’s term for the partnership between the stomach and the spleen, which he believed acted as the primary seat of the body's vital spirit and governed health</note> shine more brightly than in Asthma, Epilepsy, vertigo, lethargy, Apoplexy, and the like. In these cases, no actual decay is found in the organ itself, nor is any foreign obstruction seen that might fill up the pores.

<margin>50.</margin>
For I noticed an old man who, if he meditated too long in bed, would soon breathe with difficulty; a certain rattling with the sound of phlegm was heard, and he was forced to sit upright so that all the symptoms would soften. Otherwise, even if he coughed up a great deal while lying down, more would immediately be produced. Specifically, as soon as the "mouth of the stomach" <note>original: *os stomachi*; refers to the cardia or the upper opening of the stomach where it meets the esophagus</note> was distressed, the distress of the lung followed, and those impurities were formed incessantly from the closing of the pores. For when the chest is upright, there is greater freedom for the pores, and therefore <term>orthopnea</term> <note>A condition where a person can only breathe comfortably when standing or sitting upright</note> brings relief. Thus, a great offspring of spit was substituted for as long as the constriction of the pores lasted; this experience taught the senses the reasoning faculty.

<column-break/>

<margin>51.</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that this constriction arises from eating certain harmful things is a sign to us that the cause exciting that constriction and the production of phlegm does not depend on the lung, but from elsewhere. From the mouth of the stomach, I say (which now possesses the name of the "heart" <note>The term "cardialgia" or "heartburn" stems from this historical confusion between the stomach's upper opening and the heart itself</note> because it brings on similar symptoms), the first movements arise. For this reason, staying awake with anxious meditation excites a dormant Asthma, because of the difficulties caused to the parts occupied in meditating. In the same way, the vertigo remaining from yesterday's heavy drinking, or from the tossing of the sea, is removed by vomiting. This is not because the "filth" itself contains a rotating motion, but because it hinders the <term>Duumvirate</term> in the mouth of the stomach.

Now I will speak of a sixty-year-old man. At the beginning, he never suffered from breathing trouble except during uphill or rapid movement. Otherwise, his breathing is open, free, and just as he wishes. Therefore, he lacks "Asthma" in the proper sense of the name. For although he has a lung that is tender, impatient of the cold, and fertile in producing much waste during cold weather, he is subject to a cough rather than asthma in respect to these things. But why is his breathing narrowed during movement? Is it from a <term>vomica</term> <note>An old medical term for an internal abscess that has ruptured, usually in the lungs</note> or a hidden abscess? It is clear that it is from neither of these, because outside of movement, he feels no pain in his chest, nor does he draw air with difficulty while at rest.

<margin>52.</margin>
What must be noted in his case is a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every third day (on the fourth day by Roman counting)</note> he had since he was a boy...

...leaving a residue in the Spleen, sometimes provoking fainting fits <note>original: *syncopes*</note>. In such fragile health, and with the lungs in a state of distress—which, due to lack of sleep, cannot bear the labor of thought without producing rattling phlegm—it becomes clear what I have said elsewhere: that the Lung is the organ that dies first in man, and especially so in this man, who has been prone to spitting <note>producing mucus</note> since his youth. What if the lung, through a thousand pores, breathes air into the chest? And if those pores are blocked, would not coughing up phlegm naturally increase during cold spells?

<margin>53.</margin> But at least the doubt is not resolved: why does he not pant as much when walking at a fast pace on a downward slope or on flat ground as he does when climbing a hill at a slow pace? Why then does his heart palpitate? For the Schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities</note> have provided a ready cause: namely, that all motion, by its nature, stirs up "sooty vapors" <note>original: *fuligines*; thought to be waste products of the body's internal "heat"</note>, and therefore more intense motion is accompanied by more sooty vapors; to expel these, faster breathing is required. But they say nothing of value. For besides a false assumption, the same doubt as before remains. Specifically: why does fast movement on flat ground, and even faster movement with a jolting of the entire body on a descent, not stir up as many sooty vapors as slow movement while climbing a gradually inclining street? For the distress of a slow ascent is not felt in the organs or the lungs, but in the legs. Will those copious sooty vapors then be formed in the muscles of the legs to provoke the chest to pant and the heart to palpitate? And will those vapors take the path back from the surface to the center—vapors which nature would prefer to expel through the external pores rather than recall inward? Then let them explain what they mean by the term "sooty vapors." For Aristotle counts only two of them: the moist, which he calls "watery breath" <note>original: *halitum aqueum*</note>, and the dry or oily, which he calls "exhalation." Chemistry <note>original: *Chymia*</note> also adds a third, unknown to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>.

<margin>54.</margin> When the body itself rises from its joined parts in the form of smoke and attaches itself to the sides of the vessels,

<column-break/>

it is called a *Sublimate* <note>original: *Sublimatum*; a chemical term for a solid that has been vaporized and then re-solidified</note>. Thus sulfur, arsenic, camphor, mercury, marcasites, zinc <note>original: *zinetum*</note>, sal ammoniac, etc., give off their own "outflowings" <note>original: *aporrhoeas*</note>, indistinguishable from their original body. Finally, I have added a fourth kind of sooty vapor: when a solid body, by the power of a ferment, is transformed into a gas, or *Wild Gas* <note>original: *Gas sylvestre*; a term Van Helmont famously coined to describe carbon dioxide and other elusive substances</note>. However, since the Peripatetics only recognized the first two, the Galenic Schools also understood both indiscriminately under the name of "sooty vapors." But primarily, I conclude from this that these cannot be watery vapors of smoke: namely, because sweats flow more copiously in summer even when the body is at rest, they would necessarily distress this asthmatic person more than an ascent upward in colder air. Which is false. Therefore, if by "sooty vapor" they mean an "exhalation," it is certain above all that these are not stirred up unless the watery ones have first failed. Since that does not happen in living beings, the Schools necessarily do not understand themselves in their aforementioned reasoning, just as they do not understand the other "column of pulses" demonstrated in the chapter *Blas of Pulses* <note>original: *Blas pulsuum*; Van Helmont used the word "Blas" to describe a vital, pulsing movement or force in nature and the body</note>. Nor, finally, is it clear that both types of "outflowing" are meant by the name "sooty vapors." For if, at an equal degree of heat, dry things cannot rise or be separated from their whole parts in the same way as moist things, it follows that the "sooty vapors" assigned as the cause do not exist and are not given. But come now, let us suppose these impossible and anonymous sooty vapors, which they claim exhale from us through "insensible transpiration" <note>the invisible release of fluids through the skin</note>, though it has not yet been examined whether they belong to the class of vapors or exhalations. This is because the Schools did not know that the entire blood is dispersed <note>original: *diffari*</note> within us by a power far different from that of heat.

<margin>55.</margin> But at least by the "rule of falsehood" <note>a logical method of proving a point by showing the absurdity of its opposite</note>, let us examine where those supposed sooty vapors are stirred up by a moderate upward ascent—vapors which otherwise remain quiet during a faster walk. Are they in the lung itself? So much so that they stimulate it to the necessity of breathing them out? But the lung never moves more or less, whether the legs ascend or descend. Do the Schools <note>The established medical universities of the 17th century</note> therefore understand these to be the sooty vapors of food? But why would those infest the legs after a meal? 

What if they believe sooty vapors are produced more copiously in the heart or the "workshops" of the internal organs? Furthermore, if these sooty vapors are thought to be the odors and vapors from food, the Schools claim that those are carried straight to the head and thus produce catarrhs <note>a "downward flow" of mucus from the brain</note>. 

At the very least, they are in no way carried to the Heart. For it is not only inconvenient, but a brand new invention to claim that the heart is provoked by the smells of food. Nor is the membrane of the stomach so permeable as to allow any exit for belching and gas—which are far thinner than vapors—other than through the gullet and the Pylorus <note>the opening from the stomach to the intestines</note>. Why then, through an ascent where the legs are moved, would so many sooty vapors be made that they seek out the Heart and demand panting? And why do these not arise during a faster motion on a downward slope? 

For if they were formed by chance in the veins and arteries, or outside them, it is still not clear why a slower ascent and motion would produce more sooty vapors in the vessels than a fast motion of those same muscles while descending. If, indeed, the predicted soot is born outside the vessels—besides the absurdity already mentioned—by what path would the sooty vapors proceed so suddenly from there to the heart and Lung? Especially since, in a non-asthmatic person running quickly, if there were any sooty vapors, they would exhale outward through the skin along with sweat more quickly than they would seek the internal parts by a backward motion.

Therefore, there is another cause for why the chest is constricted, the heart palpitates, and the throat becomes parched—even if they breathe only through the nose with the mouth closed—while the tongue foams around the teeth and the knees give way. By this same cause, all those with healthy

Lungs, who are free from every cough and Asthma, are distinguished from one another; for one person is better than another at running faster and further without panting.

Do food and drink, then, produce sooty vapors by which the strength of the knees falters? If this were true, then it would also happen to those without asthma, who actually become stronger after taking food. <margin>56.</margin> But they will say: when the stomach is full, the empty space in the chest <note>the thorax</note> is diminished. Correct. But this is to have retreated from the theory of "sooty vapor" and fled to the "anxieties of space." 

Why then do not all people pant equally from food during a moderate ascent, if the space of the chest is diminished for everyone equally after eating? Or perhaps when descending, or walking on level ground, is the space of the chest extended? The reason for less breathing after food than before has indeed been given by the Schools, but it does not fit the question: namely, why does someone pant while climbing with a modest step who is not breathless during any faster movement on a flat path? 

As for the fact that this tortures him more after a meal, it is rightly argued to be from the unequal narrowness of the space. But the lung is not so compressed by a moderately filled stomach that it becomes breathless from it. Otherwise, why—even when the urine and bowels are emptied and gases are simultaneously released—does this sixty-year-old man still pant and gasp just as much in upward motion? 

Indeed, when fasting (and more strongly after a meal), he feels in upward motion a sort of belt tightening around the ribs, a palpitating pulse, falling rhythmically and interruptedly. Yet nevertheless, he inhales a long breath at will without obstacle—that is, he has an open and free lung, even if he is breathless. At those times, his spit is frequent and foamy. In a cold state, the phlegm is abundant and very similar to dissolved tragacanth <note>a thick, sap-like vegetable gum</note> when coughed up; otherwise, he coughs very rarely. # ASTHMA

I first considered whether some lung defect underlay all <term>Asthmatics</term><note>Those suffering from chronic gasping or respiratory distress</note>. I looked for an external obstruction, perhaps something hardened there, or an internal one—specifically that the <term>aspera arteria</term><note>The trachea or windpipe</note> might be constricted at the external openings where they breathe into the chest. But neither idea pleased me upon reflection, because asthma attacks some people suddenly and then leaves without any notable <term>sputum</term><note>Phlegm or coughed-up matter</note>. Furthermore, the aforementioned sixty-year-old man takes quick, free, and long breaths without any obstacle. Indeed, while sitting—even in smoke—he breathes no less freely than any healthy person. 

I therefore considered whether perhaps the muscles of the legs, being more tightly contracted and raised when climbing upward (whereas they otherwise hang loose when walking on flat or downward ground), might be the cause. I wondered if the rounded "belly" of the muscle, by compressing its own artery during an ascent, contained the more immediate cause of the panting. Could it be that in this motion, the muscles alternately impede the arteries and their pulse, so that the ascent becomes more breathless? 

Finally, I considered whether the breath is held a little more during an ascent than it is during movement on flat or downward ground. Surely everyone compresses their breath more when they intend to move something with greater force. Thirdly, I considered that in an ascent, the breath is interrupted at almost every step; not unlike someone saying "Ha, ha, ha" at every step; whereas otherwise, in downward or flat motion, there is a single and continuous "Ha," not cut short by rest. 

I also doubted whether the Lung suffers from <term>Idiopathia</term><note>original: *Idiopathia*; a primary disease originating in the organ itself, rather than being caused by another part of the body</note>, and whether in upward motion the organ is strained, not so much to expel "sooty vapors" as to overcome a "conceived error" <note>Helmont's idea that organs can "imagine" or react to perceived threats incorrectly</note>. I also observed that a person can walk more easily for seven hours than they can stand for five. When standing, the muscles of both kneecaps are continuously tensed, whereas they enjoy alternating rest while walking. Yet, a person pants more while walking than while standing, because more muscles work alternately while going; whereas while standing, even if they are tensed, they are not moved. From this, I learned that the brisk motion of many muscles causes more panting.

<column-break/>

Finally, although each of these considerations carried some weight, all of them connected together were still not able to satisfy the proposed question: namely, why a slower upward motion causes panting, but a faster downward motion does not. 

Therefore, I added to these the fact that in upward motion, however slow, the straight muscles of the abdomen tense themselves and do not allow the belly to be sufficiently raised. The chest and the ribs are indeed drawn wider during panting; but (as I taught in the section on catarrhs) the motion of the ribs is not the primary or principal cause of breathing, but only an auxiliary one when the principal motion is not enough. Thus, because the belly is not sufficiently distended, the breath is soon shortened, as the body wishes to compensate for the preceding errors and defects. 

Nevertheless, although one may argue for a greater necessity of panting from the aforementioned considerations, they prove nothing as to why there is such narrow breathing in our sixty-year-old man, while in another healthy person, there is none at all. And since the sixty-year-old's lung lacks any obstruction—as is clear from the established signs—it is necessary that its fault be sought elsewhere. This is especially true since he feels compressions in the abdomen, in the region of the stomach, as the causes of his asthma. 

His asthma is therefore caused by a poorly affected Spleen, arising from the <term>duumvirate</term><note>original: *duumviratu*; Van Helmont's term for the combined governance of the Stomach and Spleen over the body's lower functions</note>. This cause (otherwise dormant) is stirred up by upward motion due to the reasons mentioned above. By the action of this internal "governance," the Spleen constricts the otherwise weak Lung by its "mere appearance" <note>meaning by sympathy or reflex rather than physical contact</note>, just as was described regarding "dry asthma." Contributing factors to this include latent <term>comitialis</term><note>Epilepsy, often called the "falling sickness"</note>, pain in the Spleen after horse-riding, the shaking of the whole body during riding, and so on. 

Furthermore, to make a more secure judgment as to whether the lung suffered through *Idiopathia* or through <term>Deuteropathia</term><note>original: *Deuteropathia*; a secondary disease where one organ suffers because of a primary ailment in another</note>, I inquired whether he found sexual intercourse <note>original: *Venerem*</note> to be troublesome. He confessed to me that before the asthma had manifested, intercourse had harmed him; he felt a coldness in his chest from it, a laxity in his muscles, and a threatened <term>Lipopsychia</term><note>original: *Lipopsychin*; a sudden fainting or loss of consciousness</note>. In spontaneous...

Nor does that "virus" strike the heart and lung materially—as an exhalation, vapor, or soot—but rather by the **action of the governance** <note>The "regimen" or vital direction of the body's internal spirit</note>. And since the heart palpitates, the pulse becomes disordered, and a great and frequent gasping is required at the same time, while the area between the navel and the mouth of the stomach feels anxiety—all from a single cause, a single motion, and excited in the same way—it becomes certain that there is a single "virus" that affects the vital power of the heart and the lung. Furthermore, it grows more painful, more obvious, and more cruel every year, because that unpleasant guest sitting in the Spleen becomes more troublesome day by day through old age. And I concluded this more firmly because this Asthmatic complained that for many years his left hand would periodically go numb and feel cold in the palm below the little finger, and likewise his left shoulder would ache immensely, even if burdened by only a light cloak, if he walked for a long time (even at a moderate pace). I will note only one thing here: namely, that the left hand, along the length of the palm, aches with a penetrating cold, and likewise the fingers sometimes go numb due to the troubles of the Spleen. This happens by the **action of the governance**. If the <term>Schools</term><note>The traditional medical universities following Galen and Aristotle</note>, however, should command that this happens because of "hidden vapors," let the Schools at least pave the road by which such vapors might travel there! The "Archer" of this Asthma is therefore in the Duumvirate, but its "Target" is the Lung. There is, therefore, a twofold Asthma: **moist** and **dry**. The former indeed takes its name from copious <term>screatus</term><note>Hawking or spitting up phlegm</note>, and usually occurs through a fault of the lung itself; thus it is continuous, and infests more during cold or damp seasons, in old age, or in states close to weakness and death. **Dry Asthma**, however, is usually interrupted. And just as it violently shakes the whole body (even to the teeth) with a confusion of the vitals, it is necessarily a "falling sickness" <note>An epileptic-like convulsion</note> of the lung, in which the Lung alone suffers a constriction or convulsion of itself, because it causes a tightening of the pores. For in this Asthma, the total <term>Archeus</term><note>The internal "vital chemist" or governing spirit that directs an organ's functions</note> is tainted at its root: some part (namely the uterus, or the spleen, etc.) primarily affects the innate spirit of the lung through the **action of the governance**. Therefore, from an invisible and immaterial sudden storm, the whole body is shaken, and yet is suddenly restored again to unexpected health. In vain, therefore, are openings of the pores attempted in dry asthma—methods unknown until now—and in vain are many easy expectorations expected, because these are palliative and empty helps, as they are focused only on the "products" or later symptoms. Remedies that are usually applied to coughs are likewise empty, since coughs differ greatly from dry Asthma. For although **moist Asthma** usually produces a cough so that it may expel the generated mucus, it is nevertheless entirely different in kind from a cough. <meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s discussion of the causes of asthma, moving from the role of the spleen to the physical obstructions within the lungs and the nature of the "wandering guardian" or vital spirit. # ASTHMA

<margin>63.</margin>...some obstructing phlegm within the organ itself, or a mark impressed by some cold or other injury, from which it produces more mucus and corrupts its own nourishment. Often, such mucus is stirred up not so much by an evil in the organ, but by the weakness of the **wandering guardian**. Although this kind of defect produces a cough rather than <term>Asthma</term><note>A condition characterized by difficulty breathing, which Van Helmont distinguishes here from a simple cough</note>, they easily coincide due to the unequal strength of the lung and its obstruction. The weak guardian easily succumbs to any adverse things offered to it. Such things include smoke, and the <term>Gas</term><note>original: "Gas" — a term coined by Van Helmont to describe the volatile, spiritual essence of substances</note> of minerals, metals, and strong chemical waters; these specifically wound the power of the organ itself so that it does not cease thereafter to produce continuous phlegm from its own nourishment. The presence of these things forces craftsmen of that kind to struggle with perpetual asthma, coughing, and spitting. Finally, asthma is partly dry and partly moist because, on account of certain <term>endemic</term><note>Diseases characteristic of a particular people or region</note> influences drawn in by thin sipping, it affects the tender lung. This emerges and is worsened only by certain endemic injuries or otherwise by a disorder in one's way of life. Finally, <term>Scirrhus</term><note>A hard, firm tumor</note>, <term>Hydrops</term><note>Dropsy, or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, etc., although they produce breathless conditions, they are not true "asthmas" because they are weighed down by an external weight. <term>Icterus</term><note>Jaundice</note>, however, produces a dry asthma through its own <margin>64.</margin> poison. Lastly, remedies for dry asthma are the same as those for long-standing <term>Epilepsy</term><note>original: "Epilepsiæ"</note>. However, great strengthening and restorative medicines are required for moist asthma, both in respect to the Lung and the guardian.

<margin>65.</margin> Now I will add my observations on the cough, because of its proximity to asthma and the cruelties of <term>Catarrh</term><note>The traditional medical theory that mucus "drips" from the brain into the lower body; Van Helmont famously disputed this</note>. For I am prone to be easily seized by a "heavy head" or <term>Coryza</term><note>original: "Corizza" — a head cold or nasal congestion</note>, because my head is weakened by the injuries of distillations and suffers from unequal strength. I have discovered that coryza occurs whenever the **wandering guardian** has driven mucus around or into the <term>ethmoid bone</term><note>original: "os Ethmoides" — the "spongy" bone at the roof of the nose</note>. Therefore, when coryza has arisen, if on that same evening I inhale a sneezing powder made of equal parts black <term>hellebore</term><note>A medicinal plant used since antiquity to treat mental illness and "clear the head"</note> and su-

<column-break/>

-gar, I am usually better the following morning. But if I do this for a long-standing coryza, it does not yield so easily. Indeed, I have benefited so much from that sneezing powder that I can now harmlessly endure the evening air; for this reason, the "fool" in the Poets' writings does not need hellebore in vain. For although there are many emetics, hellebore seems to be particularly beneficial to the head. Therefore, in the beginning, mucus—like salt water—drips through the nostrils and throat on the same side (if not both) where the spongy bone is besieged. The throat, poorly enduring the unusual mucus, usually becomes red with <term>phlogosis</term><note>Inflammation or burning heat</note> and swells up along with the adjacent parts. Then, the mucus becomes thick and yellow, <margin>66.</margin> as if that which is stuffed into the spongy bone, acting as a <term>ferment</term><note>In Helmontian medicine, a "ferment" is a transformative agent that changes the state of matter, often causing disease</note>, continually infects the falling fluid. The wandering guardian, of course, sensing the impacted enemy, first tries to wash it away with thin mucus. Though I was about to speak of the cough, I began with coryza, because if the latter is strong, it provokes and precedes the cough; and I have observed this to be constant. Thus, in the first days of coryza, a certain dry tickling cough, with an itching of the <term>aspera arteria</term><note>The trachea or windpipe</note>, infests the patient, and sometimes causes hoarseness; but not infrequently it is just a tickling in the <term>larynx</term><note>The voice box</note>, felt one or two fingers below the chin. If there is neglect of the remedy, yellow, thick, and plentiful mucus is blown from the nose, and indeed is even knocked out by an easy cough. From this, there was hope that soon the affliction would be resolved of its own accord. But negligence grows, and external injury presses in. Meanwhile, the channel to the organ of smell, or the spongy bone, is entirely hardened by the foreign guest. From this, yellow mucus, copious and sticky, is poured out through the nostrils, which are otherwise quite open. Soon after, similar mucus is exploded out through a cough. However, I have already proven regarding "Catarrhs" that this is generated in the Lung, and does not drip from the head into the windpipe. <margin>67.</margin> And I add: that no matter how much is detained within the larynx and its nearby branches, it is all ejected in the morning through coughing; and then the breath becomes free—indeed, if one is attentive, in the region of the "mirror" <note>This likely refers to the "speculum matricis" or a similar anatomical focal point in Helmontian theory, or perhaps a reflective observation of the breath</note>, it is often suppress-

sa <note>Catchword for "saturatum" or similar on the following page</note>

He then transitions to a personal case study on the common cold (coryza), arguing against the traditional theory that mucus drips from the brain to the lungs.</summary>

# AND THE COUGH.

Bbb 2

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

I have observed with my own tongue whether even the smallest bit of mucus threatens to fall into the throat and is expelled by clearing the throat. I discovered, nonetheless, soon after that a rattling in the <term>larynx</term><note>The voice box</note> and a ringing from the chest are heard, followed at intervals by yellow and sticky mucus. Indeed, the more I cough, the more prone I am to the labor of coughing, and I am forced to cough even more. For I have found that the constant generation of this same mucus occurs within the Lung itself. 

Secondly, I have found that a <term>Head Cold</term><note>original: "Corizza" — a common cold or nasal catarrh</note> harms not only the sense of smell, but also takes away the sense of taste, even though it is separated by a specific organ. It was as if I could no longer taste a clove. I learned, therefore, by my own misfortune, that the defect is not only located around the organ of smell or in the congested bone, but even the neighboring brain has felt a spreading infection, whereby the nerves of taste become partners in the contagion. Therefore, I further discovered that the brain, having caught the infection and being thus contaminated, infects its own **guardian**, who then affects the other neighboring **guardian** in the larynx with its own weakness. 

Because of this, a cough is often born from a Head Cold, and it is extended, promoted, and continued according to the nature of the cold. Often, however, the same injury affects both the guardian of the brain and the guardian of the larynx at the same time with an equal action. That the brain might immediately infect the lung in this sickness by an "action of governance" was shown to me by the case of a certain sixty-year-old man. If he had disturbed his mind with intense contemplation or spent half the night sleepless, he would soon—without any irritation to the guardian of the head—find a rattling arising and phlegm born within himself. This phlegm would not stop being produced until it was pacified by sleep after the restlessness of his mind. 

For it is a matter of organic law: if a "dual-leadership" <note>original: "duumviratus" — a Roman term for a pair of joint magistrates, used here to describe the shared governance of the head and lungs</note> can badly influence the head, the lung, and other parts, the head draws the lower parts into its own service. I also observed this: as often as a cough comes from a Head Cold, the remedies that heal the Head Cold also heal the cough. Such a cough is easily recognized by a slight, slow fever,

<column-break/>

more colored urine, and a more continuous production of mucus. For that fever belongs to a poorly disposed head, which communicates its distress to the lower parts of the body. Indeed, the head has this prerogative: although a cough follows a Head Cold, both end at the same time; then, even if you have cleared the nostrils of all mucus, as soon as a cough arises, mucus immediately flows abundantly from the nostril again. 

There is, therefore, a great harmony of action between the head and the lung. It is not, indeed, that the head deposits its "lot" <note>The physical mucus</note> into the lung; but just as the brain takes away the sense of taste at the same time as the injury to the sense of smell, so also it pulls the lungs into its union. Because both organs are made from the same nourishment, both **guardians** <note>The *Archaeus*, or vital spirit that Van Helmont believes directs the functions of each organ</note> generate a similar mucus, as if a vassal mourns the downfall of his Prince. 

Finally, there is a closer necessity between the head and the lung because both organs conspire in the regime of the guardian serving the same end. These things must be emphasized so fundamentally that healing is directed at the roots—at the "Precedent"—that is, toward the liberation of the <term>spongy bone</term><note>The ethmoid bone in the nose</note>. For a cough born from the "action of governance," which is in the lung only by accident, ceases once the Head Cold is removed. 

If a coughing person sits up, the mucus rattles less in the larynx, breathing is freer, and expectoration is easier (hence the name <term>orthopnea</term><note>A condition where a person must sit upright to breathe comfortably</note>). Whereas, if mucus were actually dripping from above into the larynx, it would hurry downward more while sitting than while lying down. <margin>68.</margin> But this is false; therefore, the premise <note>The theory that mucus drips from the brain to the lungs</note> is also false. For if it fell from the head into the lung, it would descend with less trouble and be received in the lung more easily during the start of a Head Cold, when the mucus is blown out like water. I say it would then easily fill the lung and cut off the breath by its sheer quantity; yet at the start of a Head Cold, there is not yet a cough, nor any difficulty in breathing. Therefore, in a cough, there is no "downward-falling" of mucus from the head into the Lung. Otherwise, I have already treated the cough which arises from the Lung's own sickness and not from a Head Cold.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that a cough resulting from a cold is not caused by mucus dripping from the brain, but by a sympathetic reaction where the lungs produce their own mucus in response to the brain's distress. He cites his own loss of taste during a cold and the effectiveness of sitting upright as proof for this internal "governance."</summary>

As for remedies: First of all, sleep-inducing medicines relieve the cough and the <term>Head Cold</term><note>original: "Coryzzam" — a common cold or nasal catarrh</note>, insofar as they calm both symptomatic conditions. And I overcome a cough with the same remedies used for **Pleurisy**<note>Inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs</note>. There are, finally, other coughs not at all originating from a head cold, but from pleurisy or from a harmful impression of the air—even from untimely extreme cold—insofar as the lung is harmed in its vital growth, much like a **Wandering Guardian**<note>original: "Custos errans" — Van Helmont's term for the Archaeus or vital force that manages body functions and can become "disturbed"</note> at the gates. Moreover, the waste that has stagnated too long around the ends of the <term>windpipe</term><note>original: "asperæ arteriæ" — literally the 'rough artery' or trachea</note> becomes hardened and thereafter causes difficult breathing. And the lung, weary of this guest, gives signs of its weariness by spitting up the tainted waste. And if this is not expelled through coughing, it ends up internally as an abscess or a wasting disease. A sedentary life often brings about this evil. Therefore, exercises that quicken the breath are almost always necessary, by which waste is coughed up and stagnation is prevented by the force of the air. Indeed, they require nothing other than what sea ports require: the ebbing waters washing away the sand. For if any filth remains, the lung cannot help but suffer injury to its vitality and produce many diverse spittles according to the nature of the corruption contracted. Coughs of this kind involve a lingering and foreign filth, and they successively produce more. These then end in the narrowness of breathing called **Asthma**, the erosion of vessels, and of the <term>organ's flesh</term><note>original: "parenchymatis"</note>. Most of these defects, because they testify to a weakness of vital strength in the organ, are restored with difficulty—and even less so in old age. Asthma born from this has as many closed floodgates of air as there are openings dedicated to breathing. This is the difference in degrees between greater and lesser difficulty in breathing. The filth or phlegm produced by these conditions are not so much the original cause of the cough as they are the product leading to new coughs. For they always grow anew, because the hated guest with-

<column-break/>

<margin>69.</margin>
in does not cease to stir up new filth from the final digestion. Such indeed is the sluggishness of this organ, and the power of external things over the **Wandering Guardian**. Remedies, however, whether those that cure the "epilepsy of the lungs" (or dry Asthma) or those for moist Asthma, ought to be restorative and rise to a grander class of medicines. Indeed, they must contain the restoration of the contracted weakness. These are surely the **Greater Secrets** of <term>Paracelsus</term><note>A famous Renaissance physician and alchemist who influenced Van Helmont's chemical approach to medicine</note>, of which I have written elsewhere. Likewise, there are those which sympathetically overcome every disease. For the <term>Secrets</term><note>original: "Arcana" — alchemical medicines believed to have specific spiritual or vital powers to cleanse the body</note> remove any diseases through complete purification; but since they do not infuse new strength into the damaged part, nor remove the bad impression of the indwelling spirit, certainly lost strength can only be restored to some extent through sympathetic remedies. In order that some fruit may be gathered from the things said, I will relate one example from common and domestic experience. <margin>70.</margin> A certain old man wheezed in a wondrous way; he seemed now to whistle through his throat, now to rattle, so that quite often he was forced to remain upright all night and sleep sitting up; he produced less noise and fewer phlegms when sitting than when lying down. The healers therefore tried to restore him with concentrated broths and stronger, more abundant nourishment, lest he waste away from too much coughing up of phlegm, or suffer <term>Phthisis</term><note>A wasting disease of the lungs, now known as tuberculosis</note>, which they said threatened him. Yet he felt better during fasts and during Lent than he did immediately after Easter. The healers blamed now the north wind, now the rain, but not the rich and more potent foods. <margin>71.</margin> I, however, visited the man by chance, and when I seriously calculated each detail for myself, I showed immediately that this generation of phlegm had its own internal cause in the lung; it was not because it dripped down into the lung from above, nor because the lung was languishing from a <term>secondary disease</term><note>original: "deuteropathia" — a condition where one organ suffers as a result of an ailment in another</note>. Furthermore, just as the generation of phlegm happened within the lung itself, so too its abundance or plenty did not come from an increase of...
