### ANCIENTLY CONSIDERED

<margin>20.</margin> [The disease] reveals its alteration. Therefore, once the **Synonia** <term>Synonia: joint-water, now known as synovial fluid</term> has become acidic, it cannot help but stir up pains. Because of the greater or lesser degree of this acidity, the pains, heat, intensity, and characteristics of Gout vary so greatly. This **Synonia** is a certain transparent mucilage, like that which drips from the shins of a slaughtered calf when its feet are cut off. But as soon as acidity is conceived, the Synonia curdles, becomes cheese-like, and turns opaque.

<margin>21.</margin> And thus it is rendered so unfit that, instead of following the usual course of health where it would entirely evaporate, it leaves behind a residue of **dead-head** <term>caput mortuum: a term from chemistry referring to the useless, dry dregs or ash left after a substance has been processed</term>. From this arises a degenerate, diseased birth—the unhappy mother of "knots" <note>gouty tophi or hard lumps in the joints</note>. For the body then suffers the swelling of its watery parts, while the residues from the opaque and hardened Synonia are retained. From this come those monsters: lime and chalk <note>referring to the chalky deposits found in gouty joints</note>. Therefore, that sourness is the cause of the pain; but the pain is the cause of the outflow of nearby blood, which is otherwise good and innocent.

<margin>22.</margin> However, this influx of blood is not a "down-flow" from the head or the liver, sent there through winding paths that would be impossible for the intellect to grasp. And although it may deceive the unwary senses, making them feel as if they sense a flow from above: these are merely the deceptive judgments of the senses. It is just as when a tooth aches, and the increase of the painful cause seems to flow down into the entire side of the head. It is no different than with the pain of a **whitlow** <term>Paneritium: an agonizing infection of the finger</term>, where a swollen gland appears under the armpit. For by a topical remedy, the **toothache** <term>Odontalgia: pain in the teeth</term> goes away, or ceases once the tooth is uprooted, and the gland vanishes as soon as the finger is relieved of pain. This is the origin and root of Gout, and this is its way of being. This is indeed confirmed by what helps and what harms. I do not say this because I approve of that old axiom <note>referring to "contraries are cured by contraries"</note>, which is shameful in itself, nor because I wish to derive healing judgments from it; but sometimes

<margin>23.</margin> errors that have been committed instruct those who wander, if they are judicious and wish to be wise in charity, just as good remedies confirm those who work well. Therefore, whatever initiates, matures, increases, or promotes a subtle acidity in the spirit; that also

<column-break/>

stimulates an attack of Gout. Such things include white wines that are slightly acidic—containing little wine and much vinegar—when drunk in large quantities; likewise, whatever corrupts the bodily fluids, such as asparagus, etc. In the same way, whatever removes acidity from the spirit of life and the fluids before an attack—whether taken internally or applied externally—removes, prevents, or preserves against the attack, or at least mitigates the pains and inhibits the formation of knots.

<margin>24.</margin> But in healing Gout, one must not look at the produced acidity (which is merely the fruit and a secondary effect), but one must meditate on how the **seminal character** <note>the "blueprint" or genetic-spiritual seed of the disease</note> of Gout is to be abolished from the spirit of life. If that remains, nothing has been done that is worthy of a chosen physician.

<margin>25.</margin> For not just any messenger approaches the innermost cabinets of the vital spirit, unless he is a sent friend. Therefore, a purging through the **Coralline Secret** <term>Arcanum corallinum: a high-level chemical remedy, named for its coral-red color, used to strike at the "seed" of a disease</term> destroys Gout in its very seed. This "Secret" is not the color or tincture of coral (as the crowd ignorant of chemical matters mockingly interprets it), because the words of **Paracelsus** <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note>—stating that it is of the "essence of gold"—suggest something else. Nor do the color, sulfur, or tincture of gold move the bowels; rather, this Secret is a material that is metallic in nature, coralline in color, honey-like in taste, and golden in essence. Not indeed that it was ever a malleable metal: but it is the "horizon of gold," an unconfined and fixed body, whose sulfur is sweet and capable of being mixed with our own constituent parts. For in this sulfur, the Almighty gathered all the powers of the Sun, to whom alone all honor and glory is due. He who understands me is rare; yet he knows that what I have said about Gout is true. However, since it is said that "what is not understood does not exist," it may perhaps be helpful to repeat the origin and progress of Gout in a brief summary.

<margin>26.</margin> Those suffering from Gout complain first of all that they feel a down-flow of a burning humor.

### THE DISEASE OF THE LIVING

<margin>27.</margin> And yet, I have already shown more than enough that in nature there has never been any humor of ours except for blood, **Latex** <term>Latex: Van Helmont’s term for the clear, salty serum of the blood, distinct from the four traditional humors</term>, and the secondary or nutritious food—and furthermore, degenerate excrement. None of these "flow down," and much less can such a "down-flow" be felt. Such a Humor exists nowhere <margin>28.</margin> except in the books of the **Galenists** <note>Followers of Galen, whose medical theories dominated Europe for 1,500 years</note>. Therefore, in the very premise of how we feel the disease, there is a necessary error. Thus, **Podagra** <term>Podagra: Gout, specifically in the foot</term> is a "character" disease, seminally inserted into the spirit of life, which, at the limits of its maturity, produces an acidic fermenting fruit that can be fermented along with the spermatic parts <note>parts of the body responsible for growth and structure, like ligaments and tendons</note>. Therefore, Gout does not exist in the blood, and much <margin>29.</margin> less in the excrements. Rather, gouty patients are first agitated in the **precordia** <term>precordia: the area of the chest around the heart and diaphragm</term>, and they feel internal changes from drinks and food as much as external changes in the air; indeed, <margin>30.</margin> they often foresee these changes before they happen. For this reason, they first suffer feverish motions around the workshop of the vital spirit, specifically at the beginning of the **paroxysms** <note>sudden attacks or fits of the disease</note>. For the first motions rise from the precordia and attack the seat of the sensitive soul. For the "character" conceived in the precordia unfolds the patterns of the **Moon and Mercury** <note>original: "Lunae atque Mercurii typos." In Helmontian alchemy, these represent specific archetypal forces or metallic spirits influencing the body</note>; and it is then perfected in the heart. Once the character is formed or matured, it puts on a feverish spirit in that same place, insofar as it infects it. As soon as it has conceived the sourness of the life-symbol or ferment, it is driven away in a foul, feverish motion, and is carried feverishly to the destined places—namely, to the raw "seed" in the **Synonia** <term>Synonia: synovial fluid or joint-water</term> of the joints. It is the spirit, I say, that is thus infected, and *not a humor* (which is to be noted). It coagulates the transparent Synonia into an opaque lump by means of its fermenting acidity. Thus, the heats, pains, and swellings of Gout are distinguished according to the degree of sourness conceived. It is certain that the **Latex** is called forth by the "trumpet of pain" and sent through the veins to wash it away; this has confirmed the errors of the Schools regarding "down-flows," whereby the liver was accused and the head received undeserved blame, resulting in a thousand useless remedies. Therefore, Gout is not the thing that hurts, nor the thing that swells or

<column-break/>

burns; rather, these are its products. For Gout—or **Arthritis**—is not removed just because a foot is taken off by a cannonball; since in sensation, through the organ of sense, there is only a "consensus" of parts. <margin>31.</margin> This is what deceived the sick and the healers who believed them. Meanwhile, a swelling does not prove a "descent" of fluid. For that which follows the pain ought to precede it, if the descent of humor (or the swelling) were the cause of the pain. Add to this that the most burning Gout can occur without any swelling. This is usually seen in **Odontalgia** <term>Odontalgia: toothache</term> or when a thorn is fixed in the flesh—where a local pain mimics the "down-flows" of the upper parts. But what do these things have in common with the fable of **Catarrh** <note>the traditional theory that diseases were caused by fluids "dropping" from the brain</note>? On the contrary, the Schools persist; they inflict **cauteries** <note>burning the skin with hot irons or chemicals</note> on the opposite side, so that they might "pull back" the flowing humor into the opposite leg and drain it through the hole. But in good faith, what do cauteries draw out? Nothing but **pus** and **sanies** <term>sanies: a thin, greenish-flesh colored discharge from a wound</term>. These, however, <margin>32.</margin> are the fruits of the wound itself—degenerations of the blood. Is the matter of Gout then pus, or sanies, or the purulent filth of an ulcer? Does pus ever change into "chalk" <note>referring to the hard, white gouty tophi</note>? Does pus ever rest without causing corrosion? Thus the Schools sell their own dream to the **Tyro** <term>Tyro: a beginner or medical student</term>: that pus descends between the joints, or is fit to be turned into chalk; yet, it would be more likely to make an opening for itself by corroding the flesh. It is even more childish to suggest that something purulent, flowing down toward the right foot, would deflect from its intended target if a wound were made in the left leg. If it "flows down," it either falls down by its own weight or is sent and directed by a commanding part. Meanwhile, I pass over <margin>33.</margin> the absurdities of the process and the pathways, which I have discussed elsewhere. Likewise, I have already banished the idea of humors separating from the blood and "settling down" to the realm of the impossible, along with the humors themselves, in a dedicated book. Primarily, it has been sufficiently established elsewhere that there is no "commanding," "sending," "shooting," or "directing" part of the body. <margin>34.</margin> But if it were to "settle down" of its own accord in a vertical line: surely the humor would not fall in a sleeping person, if the whole body were sleeping on a flat bed, since there is a lack of...

### PURIFIED ANTIQUITY

The plumb line is missing. Nor will the fluid, sliding by its own weight, be turned away from its purpose, even if there is a hole in the opposite leg. <margin>34.</margin> In **Gout** <term>Podagra: Gout, specifically affecting the feet</term>, nature has surely mocked the vain purgings of the **Physicians** <term>Medentes: Those practicing medicine, specifically the Galenic establishment Van Helmont opposed</term>, as well as their weakenings, bloodlettings, scarifications, hot baths, and cauteries, which only drain the strength and shorten life. For it is certain that nature, sensing and fearing the ruin prepared for it, often causes the aforementioned symptoms to be mitigated by such remedies; but soon that peace must be paid for with a more cruel pain and the atrocity of **nodules** <note>Chalky deposits or "tophi" that form in the joints of gout sufferers</note>. Therefore, everything attempted so far has met with an unlucky outcome. Finally, they prescribe dry sweats <note>Sauna-like treatments intended to "sweat out" the disease</note>, certainly with less loss of life, but with an equal failure of success. At last, they offer drinks from the farthest corner of the earth, based on a barbarian foundation <note>Likely referring to Guaiacum or Sarsaparilla imported from the Americas</note>; and as long as they find our local remedies useless, they promise that the humors (which were never seen, named, or even born) can be dried out by these "barbarian" remedies. <margin>35.</margin> But why do they offer these drinks in cases of **consumption** <term>Tabe: A wasting away of the body, often used for tuberculosis or extreme atrophy</term>? Is it not to dry out the "down-flowing" and wandering **ill-tempered humor** <term>Cacochymum: A Galenic term for "bad juice" or unhealthy humors in the body</term>? But first, let them answer the question: does it even exist? Are watery decoctions meant for drying? Then let them prove that these drinks, by some certain privilege, will not dry out the **blood** <term>Cruor: The vital, clotting part of the blood</term>, nor the humors which they call "secondary." Instead, they claim it dries only the three other "dreamed-up" humors in the blood, or perhaps only the **phlegmy excrements** <term>Pituitosa: Relating to pituita, or phlegm, one of the four traditional humors</term>. Finally, let them prove that they will not ruin the required composition and symmetry of the blood. For if decoctions of this kind only dry out what is viscous and sharp, they will at least increase the lumps and nodules, leaving behind a curd of bitterness. <margin>36.</margin> If they do this in cases of **Catarrhs** <note>original: "Catarrhis" - referring to the "down-flow" of fluids from the head</note>, why not in Gout? Or if not in Gout, why not also in Catarrhs? If they dry out the phlegm between the joints, when they are given as a precaution for Gout, how will they not also constrict the phlegm sliding through the veins or the path under the skin into **stones** <term>Tophum: Chalk-stones or mineral deposits in the joints</term> and nodules? If tough phlegm is dried into stones by

<column-break/>

decoctions, will they not increase the harm in **lung-patients** <term>Pulmoniacis: Those suffering from respiratory diseases</term>? And therefore, are they not prescribed and given with a sense of crime? If dry things absorb the wet, I simply do not see how wet things will dry, especially where the decocted drink always remains wet. Finally, at the very least, a catarrhal humor <margin>37.</margin> cannot be anything other than an excrement; but the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic universities that taught Galenic medicine</note> have not considered that excremental things cannot be dispersed without a "dead head" <note>original: "capite mortuo" - a term from alchemy meaning the useless residue left after distillation</note>, nor can they be dried. For I have taught elsewhere that drying is merely the result of heat and cold. Of these, cold (in an increased degree, scarcely tolerable to living things) converts aqueous things into **Gas** <term>Gas: A term famously coined by Van Helmont to describe a "fine" or "spiritual" state of matter, distinct from air</term>; while heat converts them into a drying vapor. Dryness is not an operative quality, nor is humidity; rather, the dry absorbs the wet, and vice versa, the wet moistens insofar as it is absorbed. Moisture is dried not by "dryness," but by the departure of the moisture, absorbed through heat or cold. The Schools, in cases of "flows," forbid hot things, prohibit wines, and recommend barley-waters; and thus in the midst of waters—sometimes moistening and sometimes "desiccating" (as they say)—they strive to dry things out. But they know not what, nor how, nor by what means, because until now, the humor that is the author of such great evils remains anonymous. I, therefore, know neither the motion, nor the method, nor the means by which drinks of this kind could dry anything through true desiccation, much less without doing harm; they achieve the very least of those things which the Physicians promise. Nature, therefore, despises these dreams of the Physicians, and has always made—and will always make—their promises void. I pray to the most good God that He may forgive the sins which we have contracted from ignorance—not a stubborn ignorance, but one born of human frailty. However, I fear that it may happen to <margin>38.</margin> physicians as it does to other men: that an ignorance of the law takes away their inheritance. Finally, just as Gout is truly a **primary disease**, its understanding depends on the science of primary diseases, at the end of which certain things concerning the cure of Gout have been noted.

<margin>1.</margin> Pleurisy is numbered among the "down-flows," or **Catarrhs** <term>Catarrh: From the Greek 'katarrhein,' to flow down. In older medicine, it was believed that excess mucus or "phlegm" flowed from the brain into the body to cause disease</term> by the Schools <term>The Schools: The academic medical establishment of the 17th century, primarily following the ancient Greek teachings of Galen</term>. They define it as a bloody **abscess** <note>original: "apostema" — a localized collection of pus or a swelling</note> in which the pleura—the membrane lining the ribs—is torn away from the ribs, accompanied by a continuous fever and local pain. An abscess is their chosen category for the definition. And so, while they always define a disease by its **disposition** <note>original: "diathesin" — the constitutional state or tendency of the body</note> <margin>2.</margin> and place it among the qualities of the body, here they judge the product or effect of pleurisy—the things that happen *after* the "down-flow" has settled—to be the disease itself; thus, they give it a place <margin>3.</margin> among physical substances. They no longer treat it as an Imbalance, a disposition, or a failure of action, but instead they put forward a material product and an abscess. Finally, they leave it uncertain whether they should attribute pleurisy to a salty catarrhal phlegm <note>original: "phlegmati catarrhone salso"</note> or to blood <note>original: "cruori"</note> driven to that spot.

And they do not explain in the slightest what that furious disposition is which, by its own **agitation** <note>original: "thymosi" — a Helmontian term for a "vital rage" or spiritual fermentation within the body's fluids</note>, tears the pleura away from the ribs. Yet this agitation is prior in nature and movement to the "down-flowing" Catarrh; and the Catarrh is prior to that tearing; and that tearing precedes the Abscess. <margin>4.</margin> Thus, they define the disease by its effect. They also believe that the "down-flowing" Catarrh, by the mere weight of its "false phlegm," actually tears the pleura from the ribs. Furthermore, the Schools fail because they decree no remedy for this phlegmatic Catarrh in pleurisy, and they even forget the already mangled pleura. Indeed, they only provide for the coughing up of phlegm through sugary **syrups** <note>original: "illinctus" — a thick, medicinal liquid meant to be licked or swallowed slowly</note>. To be sure, they see clearly enough that Pleurisy is a sudden disease, and the saltiness of the phlegm could not have produced a corrosion in that place from a distance, or created a cavity which the blood falling there might fill and further distend. They therefore claim that the down-flowing phlegm itself, by its weight alone, tears the pleura from the ribs. As if it did not flow down drop by drop! As if the weight of the phlegm about to flow from above, pressing down perpendicularly, could exert the force of several pounds at once! But they have not yet explained the cavity in which that weight of accumulated phlegm would reside. For even if the patient were as empty-headed as this current foolish assertion of the Schools, such a great amount of phlegm in the skull still could not tear the pleura from the ribs. <margin>2.</margin> They have not yet shown the paths by which there would be a continuity in the passage of the Catarrh from the Brain to the membrane between the ribs; much less how it could achieve this from a distance by its weight. <margin>3.</margin> Nor have they yet named that "Tearer"—that powerful mangler—which could rip the pleura away, considering it is attached to the ribs so stubbornly and by so many fibers on all sides. Or what could stretch the water in a dropsical belly like the skin of a drum. Nor, finally, do they show why that Catarrh flows down to the designated...

### ->THE RAGING PLEURA<-

<margin>6.</margin> ...then a small space, which had been made or held within the common brain. For does not the successive agreement of the Schools, arising from so many and such great lapses of thought, deserve to be held in suspect faith? For it is a work of greater violence to have torn the pleura <note>The membrane lining the thoracic cavity and covering the lungs.</note> from the ribs than the weight of sinking phlegm <note>original: "pituitae" — one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note> could achieve. For as many as have commented on the ninth book of Almansor <note>A reference to the *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes, a standard medical textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> scratch themselves far and wide over the azygos vein <note>The "unpaired" vein that drains the thoracic wall.</note> (that is, the vein without a pair) distributed among the ribs; and thus they forget the flowing catarrh, as well as the weight of that same fluid, having turned their attention only to the depletion of the blood. For in this they consider the remedy—which is the only one they have, and is known equally to peasants—namely, through repeated bloodletting <note>original: "venae sectionem" — literally "cutting the vein"</note> alone, rather than the nature of the disease itself or the supposed causes of catarrh taught by the Schools. Indeed, they have all declined into such absurdity that, having cast aside the consideration of catarrh during treatment, they think the cause first struck that part where the blood, as if by accident, slipped from the unpaired vein into the pleura. For they have always succumbed so greatly to laziness that they mostly overshadow the causes with meditation on the effect. Nor did they ever notice that blood is not carried from the veins of its own accord, just as it does not slip out by its own downward weight. For tearing the pleura from the ribs, sending blood there, and similar actions, are duties of life <note>Helmont refers here to the "Archeus" or vital spirit that governs the body's actions.</note>: they are not the crimes of a leaking liquid. But what will the Schools do, who are accustomed only to subscribe to the Pagans <note>Helmont frequently uses "Pagans" to refer to Galen and Aristotle, whose ancient theories he sought to overturn.</note>, whose doctrine was accustomed to imitate not nature, but Mathematics itself in artificial things? For they see the azygos vein, dilated and led down through the ribs on both sides: and therefore they beg every cause from this. It is no different than if a traveler, sleeping near a river, were found by a corpse in the nearby woods killed by robbers, and therefore that sleeper, as the Guilty party, should have his head taken off and all his blood poured out. Therefore they institute phlebotomy <note>Bloodletting.</note>, and attempt to draw out the blood through revulsion <note>A medical theory where blood is drawn from a distant part of the body to "pull" the disease away from the affected area.</note> from the "guilty" azygos vein, as if it were the proximate, immediate, and containing cause.

<column-break/>

But where now does your Catarrh of phlegm or bile remain, flowing from the head? And which, by its weight alone, tears the pleura from the ribs? At the very least, they intend to pull the blood back through revulsion from the unpaired vein—not only the blood that is flowing, but even that which *might* flow. And on account of this, the said revulsion—just as when some nearer vein is pierced as if it were a mediator of the evil—is called derivation <note>A medical theory where blood is drawn from a site near the inflammation to "drain" the local area.</note>. Ah! how circumspect are the Schools in verbalisms and artificialities, which in nature are nothing but playthings? Since even if the vein of the elbow drains all the blood right down into the *vena cava*, and this consecutively extracts blood from the azygos vein: yet the Schools ought to know that immediately afterward, all the blood is again restored equally into the veins. Thus, even if the entire elbow vein could be evacuated (which never happens), yet soon all the blood would again be equalized throughout the entire network of veins. From this it becomes manifest that the nursery rhymes of Revulsion and Derivation are vain; for even if they were granted, they would still serve their intention for only a very short delay. 

<margin>8.</margin> I ask, therefore, that Doctors consider that in Pleurisy, phlebotomy is not of use because of Revulsion and Derivation, but because of the mere extraction and diminution of the blood and strength. So that nature, forsooth, dreading that evacuation, may desist and cease to send the increase of blood around the pleura. Attend, I say, whether this is not a matter of healing "from the rear" through precaution and prevention of the increase, with such a notable and sudden loss of strength (in a disease where the strength alone must carry the whole burden). I ask, is this going to the connected and nourishing cause, while they turn their entire effort not toward the *making*, but toward the *thing made*? 

<margin>9.</margin> These are utterly foolish ministries drawn from artificial things. For a torrent flowing to a certain boundary is diminished and stopped if its bank is opened to the side, and if it slips by a nearer and more prone journey to a lower place. But how would that help, if the blood can only be depleted by a few ounces, and indeed with...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that pleurisy is not caused by fluids leaking from the brain or blood spilling from the azygos vein, but by vital forces. He dismisses the Galenic practices of "revulsion" and "derivation" as ineffective "nursery rhymes" that dangerously weaken the patient.</summary>

# ->PLEURA<-

...with a notable loss of strength? If the vein is blocked, will not the blood flow again to the designated place as long as the initial cause of movement persists? Would it not have been more appropriate to have stopped the source of the flow? Since from bloodletting <note>original: "vena secta" — the practice of cutting a vein to drain blood, a standard treatment of the time</note>, no other benefit can be expected in Pleurisy than what might be hoped for from exhausted strength? Namely, that nature—greedy for strength, yet lacking and in need of blood—ceases its symptomatic movement toward the pleura <note>The membrane lining the chest cavity</note> as long as it remains weakened. And therefore, as the Pleurisy does not increase during this delay, nature—as if repenting of the "rumor and storm"—thinks of the maturation of pus to be crafted from the blood poured outside the veins. All of these things would follow more successfully if the blood were retained, in which life—that is, strength—dwells. For life is nature, which alone is the healer of diseases; and when she fails, the Physician simply shrugs his shoulders. Therefore, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic medical authorities following Galen and Aristotle.</note> have until now paid no attention to the impelling cause which pours blood outside the veins into improper places, beyond all limit and measure, and which furiously tears the pleura away from the ribs, creating a wound and a cavity.

<margin>10.</margin> These causes, linked together, certainly exist before the effect; yet they persist within that same effect so much that they are materially and efficiently the effects themselves. Toward which effect, the downward flow of "false phlegm" <note>original: "pituitae falsae"</note> from the head (through non-existent channels or continuous paths) and the dreamed-up "Catarrhal flows" are slow and powerless.

<margin>11.</margin> Paracelsus, however, considering this tearing of the pleura and wishing to adapt a cause to it, brought forward other absurdities so that he might defend his insane laws of the "microcosm" <note>The idea that the human body is a miniature map of the universe</note> within us. For he fakes a new kind of salt, never named by him elsewhere, called **Ogertine salt**: although he prattles variously about salts in ulcers and abscesses, even to the point of skin-stripping. And he teaches that this **Ogertine salt** particularly shares the property of Arsenicals (sulfurs); meanwhile, he remains silent about its mines, veins, properties, history, etymology, and the reason for its name. This is because it was dreamed up by him. But at least in this, he has achieved nothing more brilliant: since he stumbles no less than the Schools, 

<column-break/>

being dirty with the same mud.

<margin>12.</margin> Indeed, no one until now has explained why the pleura recedes from the ribs—to which it is attached by a continuous thread of fibers—whether, for instance, it happens of its own accord, or if it is torn away by some other "lacerator." They are content with a settled doubt if they say it is torn from the ribs by the weight of falling Catarrh <note>A term used by ancient medicine to describe a "down-flowing" of harmful fluids from the brain.</note>. Yet in the settling of this doubt, as if at the root, consists the entire healing and prevention of Pleurisy. Indeed, the root of every disease is worthy of the Schools' mute silence (I will show, in a specific treatise, that the very essence of any disease whatever has been unknown in the Schools until now). It seemed sufficient to them if they applied their teaching to external things, to artificialities, to later symptoms, and to the resulting fruits or products: as if the stage of causes and essential roots were ridiculous or useless. Paracelsus also, if he thought he was adding something solid to such a disease and its doctrine—if he did not determine to bring forth that very **Ogertine salt** from the blood from potentiality into act—at least that unusual, anonymous, and unknown salt ought to have brought with it the necessity of its own invention and its own generation, so that at least some place might be given for precaution. This is, after all, what his pretended title of "Monarch of Secrets" <note>original: "Monarchae Arcanorum" — a title Paracelsus often claimed for himself.</note> demands. But everything has remained neglected because the princedom of Healing stood founded upon empty straw. I promise, therefore, that whatever has been built upon it will collapse. For whether fire, the explorer of truth, is placed beneath it, or finally the spontaneous decay of days consumes the straw—at least I know that building will eventually fall.

<margin>13.</margin> I, however, in pleurisy, consider first the "internal motor" or the spur; and then the "Lacerator" of the pleura. And I call both of these together the efficient cause of itself: Pleurisy itself. But the blood flowing there and poured out, and the abscess <note>original: "apostema" — a localized collection of pus</note> born from it, I consider as a product. For this, I will bring common experience as an example. Suppose a thorn is stuck in some part. To which...

# ->RAGING<-

pain follows in an instant; from the pain, soon comes a pulse; from the pulse, a rush of blood: from which arise tumors, fevers, abscesses <note>original: "apostema" — a localized collection of pus or a swelling</note>, etc. Therefore, the "thorn" <note>Van Helmont uses the image of a thorn to describe the initial irritant that triggers a disease</note> sets the rest in motion. Thus, the metaphorical thorn of Pleurisy—and properly speaking, Pleurisy itself—is a foreign acidity conceived in the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is the internal vital spirit or "chief" that Van Helmont believed governed the life and health of each organ</note>. If the Archeus flees from this acidity or drops it into the blood of the *vena cava* <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note>, it is surely expelled toward the azygos vein <note>A vein running up the side of the thoracic vertebral column</note>, or even into the nearby flesh of the ribs: from which an abscess is produced as a result of the Pleurisy. Finally, just as an abscess born from a thorn stuck in a finger is cured only recklessly by bloodletting—promising healing instead only through the removal of the thorn—so it happens in

<margin>14.</margin>
Pleurisy. For just as sourness in the stomach is a pleasing and ordinary flavor, so outside the stomach, all acidity is contrary to nature and hostile. This has been unknown in the Schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities</note> until now. In this way, indeed, come the cramps from acid in the intestines, the "strangury" <note>painful or difficult urination</note> in the urine, the corrosion in ulcers, the scabies on the skin, the gout in the joints, etc. And if you wish to experience this for yourself, take some urine recently passed without pain, mix in at least a few drops of sour wine, and inject it via a syringe. You will experience, against your will, that I teach the truth. In the "latex" <note>Van Helmont's term for a specific watery fluid in the body, distinct from blood or urine</note> (of which more will be said in its proper place), it also excites a "false pleurisy" (which they call "windy" pleurisy, with the same total lack of care in investigation as the rest). But if the Archeus has deposited into the heart of the blood a slight acidity that has attached itself to its left side: it is immediately pushed out of the vessels, rejected by the veins, and creates an abscess wherever it happens to land. But if this happens deeper within the veins, some pestilential suffering arises. This

<margin>15.</margin>
I can prove. Indeed, blood or flesh never turn sour without an actual consequence of putrefaction (which I have proven elsewhere by the example of the flesh of beasts, which putrefy very quickly under the "dog star" <note>The hottest days of summer, or "dog days," associated with the star Sirius</note>, and therefore yield a sour broth). For blood turning sour is immediately clotted, contrary to the nature of the veins and the character of all flesh (as long as it lives). For in a 

<column-break/>

corpse, the blood is preserved from clotting by the vein, but if it falls out of the vein, it immediately turns into lumps <note>original: "grumescit" — to become clotted or lumpy</note>. I have discussed this more widely elsewhere. From this it follows,

<margin>16.</margin>
that once an abscess has formed in Pleurisy, the blood from it cannot be evacuated by cutting a vein <note>bloodletting</note>, no matter how much the names "revulsion" or "derivation" <note>Galenic medical terms for moving "bad humors" away from an organ</note> are boasted about to frighten the diseased and delude the sick. Likewise, bloodletting does not prevent anything from turning further sour afterward. For phlebotomy <note>The practice of opening a vein to let blood</note> has only the power of deprivation <note>It only takes away; it does not add or change the nature of what remains</note>. Nor can the blood that is drawn out prevent the blood that has swallowed acidity inside from depositing it. Rather, a worthy remedy for

<margin>17.</margin>
Pleurisy is held to cause in the Archeus a turning-away from the very idea of turning sour. If, therefore, the sourness of the blood is a sign of its putrefaction, it is certain that the vein neither receives putrid or putrefying blood into itself, nor allows it to rot, if even after death it defends the blood from clotting. Therefore, there is some wandering or pestilential impression in the blood if it turns sour, however slightly. But if the Archeus has been infected by something local that was breathed into the chest, or by an acid poison born within, and it has affected the blood of the veins or other blood intended for nourishment, immediately any part that fears putrefaction repels that same blood from itself. This, I say, is the efficient "spur" <note>original: "calcar" — the stimulus or driving cause</note> and the truth of Pleurisy. And the first of the healers, Hippocrates, seems to have sensed this when he wrote: *It is not the hot, the cold, the moist, or the dry that are diseases: but that which is sharp, bitter, acid, and harsh.* That acidity is the 

<margin>18.</margin>
spur in Pleurisy is evident from this: that in Pleurisy, the urine and the blood drawn by bloodletting turn lumpy even as they come out, or before the blood condenses—which lumpiness, or "cheesification" <note>original: "cascatio" — curdling like cheese</note>, is the effect of sourness. Moreover, when sour "latex" falls into the muscles between the ribs, it causes pleuritic pain, but not the true or constant disease. For this reason, they call it "windy" <note>original: "flatulentam"</note> (although "winds" or gases never reach there, unless a transforming toxin has been taken).

He compares the disease to a physical thorn and criticizes bloodletting for failing to address this underlying chemical "spur."</summary>

# PLEURA

<margin>19.</margin> Just as with gases, it soon produces a remedy through light means: namely, through insensible transpiration <note>The release of vapors through the skin or breath</note>. Therefore, acidity immediately gives birth to pain; and I have said elsewhere (in the book on *Lithiasis*, the chapter on sensation) that the proper companion and cause of pain is **convulsion**. In this convulsion, the pulse—which was previously hidden—becomes manifest, the artery hardens, and pain accompanies it. But because a convulsion is mostly stretched and relaxed at intervals (as the pain of those in labor testifies), it follows that as often as the pleura intensifies its spasm by its own motive *Blas* <note>original: "Blas" — Van Helmont's term for a vital, formative motion or force</note>, some of the fibers are torn from the ribs. While it relaxes itself even a little, the neighboring blood rushes into the place of the wrinkles to repair the break. This, happening repeatedly, is the cause of a great abscess <note>original: "apostema" — a swelling or collection of pus</note>, depending on the frequency and sharpness of the contractions. Furthermore, blood that has escaped the veins, or otherwise exceeds its proper dose, becomes hostile and quickly coagulates because of the "acid ferment" it has conceived. <margin>20.</margin> But if that sourness is dispersed from the infected Archeus <note>The internal "vital director" of an organ</note> into the arterial vein or the venous artery <note>original: "venam arterialem, vel arteriam venalem" — in 17th-century terms, these refer to the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein</note> (which are the vessels of the lung), then by necessity, **pneumonia** of the lung arrives.

Therefore, let the Schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities</note> see and discern whether bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomon"</note> heals the continuing cause and the root. Or rather, whether their whole effort extends only to this: that with a deliberate loss of strength, they might prevent the increase of pleurisy (when it is severe). For in this way, the manner in which diseases arise through motive and vital causes ought to have been explained, if it is necessary for students to be rightly instructed. Physicians must be so advised that, henceforth, each may rightly perform his duty, and the patient may gather the desired fruit of health. <margin>21.</margin> For once the **thorn** is plucked out, the rest easily ceases—unless by chance a long delay has made the abscess itself "thorny" <note>meaning the secondary infection has become as irritating as the original cause</note>. For once an abscess or ulcer is formed, even if they no longer have a root in the body behind them and are not nourished from elsewhere, they stand thereafter by themselves and persist without any other protection. Therefore, one must apply oneself to 

<column-break/>

plucking out the thorn. Such is the persistence of a wasting ulcer: that the ulcer no longer merely *has* a thorn, but has *become* thorny itself. <margin>22.</margin> Thus, pleurisy is produced within us spontaneously when a "guest" from the first digestion <note>The digestive process in the stomach</note> flies like a stranger into a "foreign field"; or otherwise by inhaling a poisonous local air. In such cases, Pleurisy is common among the people. <margin>23.</margin> For in a great heat, a sudden and abundant drink of cold water contracts the pleura, just like any other rushing acid. The "kitchen" <note>The site of metabolic transformation</note> of the pleura is not in its very thin and indivisible membrane, but in the intercostal flesh adjacent to it. For its extreme thinness does not allow a "kitchen" to be hidden within it. Therefore, the blood of the pleura itself is very quickly killed by a violent external rush, whether it be acid or sudden cold. This is because in that external kitchen, the nourishment is not digested and prepared for itself. Therefore, when the blood is corrupted while it is being made into nourishment for the pleura, it immediately turns sour, and true pleurisy begins. 

Men do not perceive that pleurisy is *coming*, but rather that it *has arrived* and is present, when it is generated by that external rush. For natural generations happen as if in an instant. Therefore, the degeneration of blood in the aforementioned external kitchen of the pleura is almost instantaneous. But Pleurisy happening from acidic blood, contaminated from elsewhere, usually has other diseases as precursors. <margin>24.</margin> It is also a property of Pleurisy that nature soon "repents" of its error. And so, out of horror for the mistake admitted, it willingly corrects the fault of its digestion. Therefore, for healing, it is required only that the **thorn** and the product of the confused digestion be removed, both in the surrounding blood and even in the abscess itself. But Pleurisy which is restored <note>treated</note> by bloodletting often recurs after a year, and even more often leaves behind a wasting disease <note>original: "tabem" — consumption or physical decline</note>. This is because the task of the remaining thorn is left to be overcome by the shoulders of nature alone, without help, while the "character" <note>the lingering impression or seed of the disease</note> remains staying in that place. The ancients...

...they perceived that where there is pain and heat, the blood flows to that spot. <margin>25.</margin> But as for the "thorn" <note>Van Helmont uses "thorn" (spina) as a metaphor for the root cause of irritation</note> and the preceding womb-like acidity—and how these cause spasmodic pain—no one (to my knowledge) has yet touched upon it. Yet, it is only from this understanding that comfort ought to be hoped for. One might rightly wonder why the pleura, when it relaxes slightly from its contraction, does not push the blood contained within it back to the places it came from. But it is now clear: the blood thickens into a mass <note>original: "grumescere" — to clot or become grumous</note> immediately because of the acid, and it has learned to stay fixed constantly in this place. Otherwise, tumors often disappear elsewhere quite frequently, because in those cases the blood has not been alienated by the acid. <margin>26.</margin> Furthermore, dysentery distinguishes itself from Pleurisy not so much by the sourness of the material cause, but by the variety of the subject. For the intestines do not have flesh at their back to serve as a "kitchen" <note>Van Helmont often views the muscles/flesh as a site of metabolic "cooking" or heat</note>. Therefore, the intestine has its own "thorn" fixed in its membranes. For besides the double coating of the intestine, a third is fortified by the "cloak" of the Mesentery <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>. And because it does not have a "kitchen" in the flesh outside itself, its membrane does not tolerate an abscess <note>term: "Apostema" — a collection of pus or a swelling</note>. For this reason, the blood arriving to soothe the griping pains does not harden or clot; nor has the blood of the Mesentery yet acquired the fibers by which it might be coagulated or swell into an abscess. Therefore, in dysentery, that blood flowing in to soothe the stinging pain caused by the acid flows out without being clotted. In pleurisy, however, on one hand, bloody sputum is coughed up—not clotted (because it is not yet acidic), having rushed there as if sent to soothe the pain. Neither that blood, nor such sputum, is the "occasional cause" <note>The external or triggering cause</note> of that disease. On the other hand, the blood caught between the pleura and the ribs is made acidic, it clots, it forms an abscess, and thus becomes pus. Therefore, a great deal of blood, hurrying to soothe the pain (for where there is pain, the blood runs to it), penetrates through the pleura into the chest, which is then coughed up by a most troublesome cough. <margin>27.</margin> Thus, Pleurisy does not differ from Pneumonia <note>original: "Peripneumonia"</note> in its occasional causes, nor in its remedy. Specifically, blood is poured into the lung tissue <note>term: "parenchyma" — the functional tissue of an organ</note> near the pleuritic "thorn." For in a cavity <note>original: "vomica" — an abscess in the lung</note>, although the lung

<column-break/>

contains blood and various hostile elements within itself, it is not pneumonia if the "acidic thorn" is lacking. Instead, there are other defects proceeding from the wastes of its own digestion. Therefore, many diseases do not differ in their "occasional material," but in the different agents and properties of the organs and functions. These factors generally do not change the remedies as much as they do the adjacent parts that depend on the power of those properties. It is clear from this how useless <margin>28.</margin> the remedy of enemas <note>original: "enematum"</note> is in dysentery. Indeed, dysentery only affects the small intestines, which are several cubits <note>original: "ulnis" — ells or cubits</note> distant from the thicker [large] intestines that are capable of receiving clysters <note>A liquid injected into the rectum</note>. Thus, in Pleurisy and Pneumonia, they use a bloodletter <note>term: "phlebotomo" — a surgeon who performs bloodletting</note> for the "necessary removal of causes" (as they call it). As if a mere "plethora" <note>An excess of bodily fluids, especially blood</note> of blood (which they nonetheless call the sole and adequate indicator for cutting a vein) were the mother of these diseases. <margin>29.</margin> Furthermore, they have prescribed linctuses <note>syrup-like medicines to be licked</note>, not indeed to remove the cause, but for the easier coughing up of sputum. These include linctuses made from coltsfoot <note>original: "farfara"</note>, from fox lung, etc. For since this animal is almost tireless, they thought that when dying, it bequeathed to its lung a remedy for healing those who are short of breath (for without such "thinking," the authority of the Schools lacks any validity). Yet the organ—the author of the "thorn" in us—remains badly affected while the abscess persists, threatening to turn into pus. And unless it is healed entirely within a fixed number of days (according to Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>), an undoubted wasting disease <note>term: "phthisis" — pulmonary tuberculosis or a general state of wasting</note> must be expected. <margin>30.</margin> Therefore, the entire study of the Schools of medicine does not aim so much at healing as at merely preventing the "increase" of the disease. That is, they do not look at the radical cause, but keep their eye on the later product, lest it turn for the worse. It is the constant habit of the Schools to leave their own burden to Nature, to hope for and delay until the "critical day." For since they recognize almost no remedies besides purging and bloodletting, they only proceed to things that diminish the fluids and the strength, and thus they provide only palliative care regarding the effects,

...the effects and later products of the disease. They relegate the patient to the remnants of kitchen-trickery <note>original: "mangonia" — refers to the deceptive preparation of food or drugs</note> and the prescribed diet, whether they are saved by a more blessed disposition of their own strength, or they fall into more difficult diseases, or, being deprived of hope, are counted among the incurable. For in the same way that I spoke of the linctus <note>original: "loh" — an Arabic term for a licking-medicine or syrup</note> made from a fox’s lung, they recommend for paralysis the brain of a rabbit or a hare, simply because they are fast in their running. They suggest the penis of a stag <note>original: "Virgam cervi"</note> for cold temperaments, because the beast is very lustful. By this logic, if a peasant ate the cooked hand of a lute player, would he perhaps strike the shell of a lute skillfully?

Meanwhile, the Schools require that syrups <note>original: "eclegmata" — medicinal pastes or licking-medicines</note> be swallowed slowly, and they are thus endowed with the name of "linctus," so that the remedy might physically descend to the location of the cough. I wonder, meanwhile, why they have not also prepared a linctus out of a horse’s tail, which spends the whole summer agitated in swatting flies. But the Schools have thought of nothing for the <margin>31.</margin> removal of the "thorn" of Pleurisy <note>Van Helmont uses the "thorn" (spina) as a metaphor for the specific irritant causing the inflammation</note>, for one fault alone: they simply did not know it, and they neglected to investigate it, being content to merely sign off on each other's opinions. 

In the meantime, they make the strength of the sick man even weaker, and they disregard it as if they intended to destroy it through repeated bloodlettings <note>original: "venæ-sectiones"</note>; as if, once the strength is flattened, any opportunity for recovery should then be hoped for. I grieve for the fate of mortals who have found such helpers for so painful a disease—helpers who, being ignorant of the cause, attempt any absurdity, provided they have first debilitated the patient through a lack of blood and strength, leaving nature to swim on its own oars. If, in the meantime, the patient’s own youthful strength helps them, the doctors demand and claim the honor (that is, the payment) for themselves. They then proclaim that they have acquired the right to slaughter two hundred others by the same means. Or, if the exhausted strength succumbs while the surgeon is draining it, and the patient is extinguished by a long wasting-away and a daily, mournful spectacle: at least the Physician may excuse himself by the "cruel and unusual magnitude" of the disease, claiming that despite applying the "best" remedies, the patient nonetheless declined into consumption. None of this

<column-break/>

would happen (for I pledge and promise this upon the penalty of trial) if, having rejected that cursed bloodletting, the "balsam of life" and the strength of nature were preserved, and the radical thorn <margin>32.</margin> were plucked out. Indeed, in this way, the pain, the bloody spit, and the fever cease peacefully at once, and the torn continuity of the tissue is soon healed with new flesh. 

But the causes unknown until now have fathered an ignorance of the remedy. My remedies are those which leave no one behind in Pleurisy or Peripneumonia <note>Inflammation of the lungs</note>. These include: powder of the stag’s or bull’s penis, the blood of a goat, the juice of wild chicory, wild poppy flowers, and more such things. Most of all I praise the blood of a goat <note>original: "cruor hirci"</note>—not indeed the kind for sale, but a goat I hang by the horns; having tied its hind feet to the horns, it is castrated by cutting off the testicles. The blood flowing from there, up until its death, is collected and dried. It is distinguished from the commercial blood (which is nothing but sheep’s blood) because the commercial kind is easily ground and its powder is reddish-purple; the true goat’s blood, however, is ground with the greatest and most tedious difficulty, and its powder is the color of pitch. This grinding is so troublesome not because of any stickiness, but because of its sheer and incredible hardness.

For these kinds of safeguards, being friendly to the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont's term for the vital internal "spirit" or "governor" that regulates the body's functions and health</note> and domestic to human nature, correct the immediate cause within the Archeus. They remove the acidity, dispose the blood for dispersal <note>original: "diapheresin" — the process of resolving or sweating out a morbid matter</note>, and calm the pain because they extinguish the sourness. Once the ferment of the acidity is removed, they resolve as much of the extravasated blood <note>Blood that has leaked out of its proper vessels</note> as possible, and the rest (ignoring the tendency toward pus) they timely cast out through coughing. Therefore, the same remedies are given to those who have fallen from a height, insofar as they disperse blood that has turned into clots from a bruise; that is, they remove the thorn, take away the poison, and thus heal the site. And so, by the correction of a single "thorn," they satisfy all indications at once. For these, the inexhaustible bounty of Divine Mercy has established many similar things. For dysentery <margin>33.</margin> does not require astringents; for under the ordinary judgment...

-> # THE RAGING <note>original: "FURENS" — likely referring to the "Furious Archeus" or the "Raging Fever"</note> <-

...brine: or else, under constipation and constriction, death is soon at hand. Indeed, while I was present and looking on in astonishment, after four hundred and twenty-six fruitless enemas <note>original: "clysteres"</note>, our Chief Physicians finally injected a noble man with a "plaster of white lead" <note>original: "emplastrum diapompholigos" — a lead-based ointment used for skin ulcers</note> dissolved in oil of quinces. This was a remarkable display of the Schools' stupidity. For in fact, without any enema, and after more than eighteen hundred bowel movements, he was cured by me using a remedy taken by mouth. And yet the Schools continue to teach even now that dysentery does not exist except with an ulcer of the intestines; for the healing of which, the aforementioned physicians <margin>34.</margin> would pour in that plaster. As if an intestinal ulcer could be healed by such a plaster! Especially when a simple wound of the intestine is considered incurable. Likewise, if the dysentery were in the small intestines, why do they not apply their plasters to the long gut? For which of the Galenists <note>Followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen, whose theories dominated the "Schools"</note> ever healed an ulcer of the throat, the larynx, or the intestine by means of enemas? When they do not even know how to heal an anal fistula, which they have right at hand, through plasters! Let the Healers remember, I pray, that a natural tear does not sting the eye, just as urine does not sting the bladder. So too, dung in the intestine is unfelt until near the exit, because it is a natural excrement. But an enema, because it is foreign to the intestine, causes pain. Therefore, it is harmful in dysentery. This error flows from the Schools, who define dysentery as an ulcer of the intestines. Yet I have very often seen it cured, even when it was long-standing and almost desperate, and indeed with great safety—namely, by administering certain specific remedies. But truly, I perceive a bloody Moloch <note>A biblical reference to a deity associated with child sacrifice; here, a metaphor for doctors who "sacrifice" patients through bloodletting</note> presiding over the medical Chairs. Look back, therefore, my brothers. For a dire horror will fall upon the world at the sound of the trumpet, when everyone must give an account of his stewardship.
Finally, I shall say what I observed as a sufferer of <margin>35.</margin> pleurisy. On the third day before the Kalends of January <note>December 30th</note>, I was suddenly seized by a fever with a slight shivering, so that my teeth chattered. A piercing pain appeared in the

<column-break/>

front of my side around the breastbone <note>original: "os Sternum"</note>, which hindered my breathing; soon after, bloody spit appeared, and finally, pure blood came forth. I immediately took the "genitalia of a stag" <note>original: "cervi genitale" — likely a dried and powdered preparation used in folk medicine</note> (for it was at hand) and the pain was immediately diminished; soon I drank a dram of "he-goat’s blood" <note>original: "cruoris hircini"</note>. Within four days, therefore, the spitting of blood ceased, though a rare little cough remained with some clearing of the throat. However, the fever persisted. For on the second day, a pain spread around the "waistband" <note>original: "zonam"</note> on the left side, with difficult respiration, an increase in fever, and an intermittent pulse. I had already completed my sixty-third year, and I expected an abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> to clot in my spleen. Indeed, the spleen, gathered into a mass, created a heavy weight. For if I raised my knees high, or lay down on my right side, I felt the globe of a heavy weight falling. And so I suspected that the Pleurisy had been stirred up from the Spleen; which, though it had been driven from the ribs with proper remedies, eventually afflicted the Spleen. I immediately met this with a drink of wine boiled with "crab's stones" <note>original: "lapidibus cancrorum" — also known as "crab's eyes," these are calcium deposits from the stomach of crawfish, used as an antacid</note>. And within a few days, all the pain and the mass of weight vanished. Meanwhile, I was visited by a nobleman who wore boots made of fragrant Prussian leather. From their scent, I immediately felt the pain in my spleen return, and the fever flared up again. From this I concluded that the Archeus <note>The internal "vital spirit" or "governor" of an organ in Helmontian medicine</note> of the spleen was the author of the entire tragedy. Finally, I noted that in the beginning of Pleurisy, opening a vein <note>bloodletting</note> does indeed stop the internal hemorrhage, and the sick seem to feel better. And although the <margin>36.</margin> emission of blood increased their weakness, they nevertheless attribute this not to the bloodletter <note>original: "phlebotomo"</note>, but to the Pleurisy itself. But if the opening of the vein is too late, the blood—already clotted and the abscess conceived from it, along with the destined pus—hastens toward its own end. From this comes the frequent occurrence of "Consumption" <note>original: "Tabes" — a wasting disease</note>, or an annual recurring Pleurisy, following a "cure" by bloodletting. These complications are not seen when the aforementioned remedies are used instead.

After I have already demonstrated that the elements, temperaments, primary qualities, and finally "Tartar" <note>Paracelsus used the term "Tartar" to describe the stony or gravel-like deposits formed in the body, comparing them to the crusts in wine barrels.</note> have been wrongly introduced into the essential causes of diseases by the Schools of both the Ancients and the Moderns, I proceed to teach that the three chemical origins—recently introduced into the medical art—have been falsely thrust in as essential causes of diseases. What then shall the more discerning physicians do, while they clearly behold not only the miserable equipment of their own remedies, but also the unfortunate attempts to help their wailing patients? To such an extent that many have seriously and secretly confessed to me that almost nothing obeys their efforts anymore, and that every healing—of both acute diseases (for all have long since despaired of chronic ones) and even the smallest ailments—is in truth nothing but palliative care, or a mere deception <meta>catchword: of the sick</meta>...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s critique of traditional medicine. # THE THREE FIRST PRINCIPLES OF THE CHYMISTS, ETC.

...[it is] nature itself, to which—unless a certain <note>original: "resurrectio"</note> resurrection of the sick person's nature spontaneously follows—the intended and certain comfort of remedies is expected in vain. Indeed, from this it happens that many an **old woman**, in curing certain defects here and there, is far more successful than the entire **Medical School** with all its discursive theorems, theoretical prescriptions, culinary rules of diet, and its long experience in the deaths of neighbors, confirmed by the multiplicity of its dispensaries. Therefore, since the more ingenious have long been weary of the correction of "intemperance" and the vain expulsion of humors, they now turn elsewhere, seeking a port from the shipwreck. Easily led by **Theophrastus Paracelsus**, they have inclined their studies so that what has not yet been found among the Greeks and Arabs, they might find more happily elsewhere. From here, they have fallen by a steep descent into the fictions of **Tartar** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to stony or gravel-like deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty crystals, which Paracelsus believed were the cause of many diseases.</note>; yet surely their curiosity is to be held in high regard. For even if they did not reach the desired goal, *it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God alone who showeth mercy.* <note>A reference to Romans 9:16.</note> Thus, by right, the Schools now yield from the court; for what will they do if the root of diseases and the method of healing are no longer to be drawn from the elements, qualities, contrarieties, humors, stars, winds, and catarrhs? But since other models of healing have possessed the more modern followers of Paracelsus, it must still be diligently investigated whether the causes of diseases were truly known to Paracelsus himself. For when he, having rejected the teachings of the ancients, perceived well enough that there was no foundation or truth in "complexions" and humors, he began, by various attempts, to inquire into the <term>proximate cause</term> <note>The "proximate cause" is the immediate, direct reason for an illness, as opposed to a distant or symbolic one.</note> of diseases; and for this, posterity owes him praise. Even if he did not <note>original: "rem acu tetigerit" - literally "touch the matter with a needle," a Latin idiom meaning to hit the nail on the head.</note> hit the mark exactly, it cannot be turned into a fault if the **Most High Giver of Gifts** did not yet deign to reveal the truth to mortals in the days of Paracelsus. This man, therefore, had learned from **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary Benedictine monk and alchemist; Helmont suggests Paracelsus borrowed his best ideas from him.</note> that by distillation, water, oil, and salt are separated from most bodies; he began to call these three—

<column-break/>

not only the first universal beginnings of bodily beings, but he also introduced them into diseases and the necessities of healing in such a way that he referred all diseases immediately to one of those three first principles. And this so nearly drove his followers mad that, having cast aside the hope of searching for the truth, they consecrated everything to the **Three Firsts**. <margin>4.</margin> This doctrine took deeper root because three things are actually separated from most bodies, and thus they were not indemonstrable, unlike the humors which arose from fictional beginnings. <margin>5.</margin> But truly an **abuse** was detected when these three beginnings were distorted to explain the origins of any and all diseases. For indeed, because many bodies, dissolved by fire, would give of themselves salt, sulfur, and liquor (which they call **Mercury**), it was thought that all diseases owed their birth to those constitutive beginnings. <margin>6.</margin> **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> first, before the industry of the Greeks was born, because in the *Pymander* <note>A foundational Hermetic text.</note> he had noted that "every triple thing is perfect," consequently foresaw in chemical matters that metals consist of two extremes (namely, body and soul); and these he willed to cohere only by the charm of a certain third thing, or spirit. Thereafter, **Basil Valentine**, a Benedictine Monk, wrote more distinctly: he called the **Soul** of the metal "Sulfur" (or the Tincture), the **Body** indeed "Salt," and finally he called the **Spirit** "Mercury." These things, thus borrowed from Basil, **Theophrastus Paracelsus** (who was younger than Basil by more than a century) subsequently transferred, by a wonderful investigation, into the principles of all bodies. <margin>7.</margin> He seized this doctrine for himself, suppressing the name of the Author, and introduced it into medical speculations by his own license. <margin>8.</margin> Thus, surely, after he had relegated every disease into the catalog of "Tartars" and was not yet satisfied in his own mind, he finally adorned his *Paramirum* <note>One of Paracelsus’s most famous books on the causes of disease.</note> concerning the "Three First Entities" with much audacity. He indeed fashioned these three as if they were the beginnings of all things, and declaimed many things, in general, about diseases; but compelled by necessity, while [trying to] sort diseases into the classes of the first...

In the previous section, Van Helmont noted that while the Paracelsian "Three First Principles" (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) were a step forward from Greek theories, they were still flawed. # THE THREE FIRST CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES, AND NOT THE SAME

<margin>9.</margin> ...of the three, he would reduce them; yet, pressed under the burden, he fell silent. Except in the family of ulcers—where he seemed to himself to have found **Salt**—he remained impoverished and nearly ridiculous regarding the other two principles <note>The other two being Sulfur and Mercury.</note> in both instances. 

<margin>10.</margin> For he had commanded everywhere that the **four elements** should be believed to be nothing but incorporeal "matrices" <note>Molds or wombs that give shape to matter.</note>, and as it were, the guesthouses of bodies. He claimed the "first principles" <note>The *Tria Prima*: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> thus took the place of bodies, so that even the elements of the world have all their substance and subsistence solely from those three. Elsewhere, also unmindful of these, he clung entirely to the elements, and to their "complexions," and finally attributed the inclinations and properties of the stars and of men to them. He also dedicated specific fruits to each of the elements, and degrees of fruits, but not all of them to one element; nor did the fruits any longer proceed from the incorporeal matrices, but rather borrowed their bodies from the material elements themselves. Finally, with the same liberty of borrowing and inconsistency, he taught through *Analysis* <note>The chemical breakdown of a substance.</note> that bodies fall away now into 

<margin>11.</margin> four, and now into only three parts. Indeed, by introducing **Pyrotechnia** <term>Pyrotechnia: The "art of fire," or chemistry, used to prepare medicines.</term> into medicine in this way, he decorated it, as if panting for an eternal name for himself, and hoping for the future, so that he might one day pride himself on the title of **Monarch of Secrets**. Foreseeing the doctrine of **Basilius** <note>Basilius Valentine, a shadowy alchemical figure whose writings Paracelsus was often accused of plagiarizing.</note>—which was not known to the common people—he made it his own by keeping the author's name silent, and thus he expanded his own volumes. Because of this, his **Tartar** <note>Paracelsus's term for metabolic waste that causes "stone" diseases like gout or gravel.</note>, repeatedly losing its universal dominion over diseases, runs in suppressed, 

<margin>12.</margin> subjected to the laws of the **Three First Principles**. At length, having dared to increase his "Three Firsts," he wished that they might even become the mothers and "matrices" <note>The originating sources.</note> of all diseases, of both the mind and the being. This, to be sure, was his invention alone, and not that of Basilius; which, while he strove to scatter it in crowds into the series of diseases, he sometimes attacked confusedly; 

<margin>13.</margin> yet more often he passed it by again, everywhere forgetting his own broad doctrine. For in the *Archidoxis* <note>One of Paracelsus's major works on chemistry.</note>

<column-break/>

he dedicated a small book to the **separation of elements**, to be drawn out from flame, air, water, and earth. And thus far he contradicted his own doctrine regarding the **Three First Principles** and the matrices of the elements, because now there were *four* beginnings, no longer "Three Firsts" and "Lasts," into which—at last, after long labor—the Three Firsts would be reduced as if they were posterior to the elements, and thus no longer rightly "first." For even thus, enriched by one more in number, they would generate far more diseases than recently, when that pretended **Monarch** commanded that there were only three principles of both bodies and diseases. Truly, only and finally he accuses a single **Tartar** as the guilty cause of almost all diseases. 

<margin>14.</margin> But elsewhere, in several peculiar treatises, he calls **Heaven** the maker of all diseases—an assisting and cooperating "angry parent" and avenger. For he says an unknown star (which he calls *zedo*) is the immediate and containing cause of **dropsy** <note>Edema or fluid swelling.</note>. Likewise, he affirms that **consumption**, **gout**, **apoplexy**, etc., have their own peculiar (though anonymous) star, and that each **epilepsy** has its own proper constellation. But in the *Paramiric* books <note>Paracelsus's *Opus Paramirum*, which discusses the five "pillars" or causes of disease.</note>, he affirms the **Three First Principles** are the immediate causes of all diseases. That is to say: everything is confused. Let him who wishes explain and excuse it; for I have not dedicated my life to interpreting the dreams of others. 

<margin>15.</margin> And so, I searched seriously into the nature and species of diseases, and it happened to me no differently than to all others before me, until—having stripped off the doctrines of all authors—I seriously implored divine grace. For then I suddenly knew that to every disease its own **matter** has fallen, which fosters its own **Vulcan** <term>Vulcan: The internal "alchemist" or governing vital heat that directs the growth or decay of a substance.</term> within; which, although it may sometimes imitate the courses of the stars, its "enormontic" <note>original: "enormontica" - a term derived from Hippocrates referring to the vital governing power of the body.</note> cause does not depend on the **Stars**. For all "seeds" possess, as it were, their own Republic, especially their own **vital light**, by which, through their own power, they reflect the analogy of the stars. Let it be ridiculous [to say] that consumption, or dropsy, [comes from the stars]...

<summary>Van Helmont criticizes Paracelsus for his inconsistent theories, accusing him of switching between three and four primary elements and plagiarizing Basilius Valentine. He concludes that diseases are not caused by the stars or Tartar alone, but by a specific internal "matter" and governing spirit (Vulcan) unique to each ailment.</summary>

### THE ESSENCE OF THE ARMY OF DISEASES.

...dropsy, although it is stirred up more severely or mildly under different positions, is brought about by the motion and light of the stars: which, otherwise, such clear collections of filth generate through a manifest occasion, and once these are removed, health follows, even without the favor of the stars. You will read the explanation of this doctrine in my book *On the Plague*, and elsewhere in my writings. I have followed the materials of diseases, with their **Vulcanian seeds** <note>original: "seminariis Vulcanis" — refers to the seeds of disease triggered by heat or alchemical-like transformations</note>, from the first to the last, with all dualities and alterities <note>differences or changes in state</note> regarding human life. May the Almighty grant that, as much as He has bestowed on me, I may report purely for His honor and the neighbor's benefit, and give to the world another person better than me. 

<margin>16.</margin> For **Paracelsus** composed various books on long life, yet he chose death for himself, by divine privilege, comforting his old age with the **Elixir of Property** <term>Elixir Proprietatis: A famous alchemical tonic made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron, which Paracelsus claimed could extend life.</term>, but not by the remedies for long life he himself prescribed; he died in the 47th year of his age. Therefore, the great boasting and inconsistency of this man have kept me little concerned until now. 

<margin>17.</margin> Meanwhile, many difficulties held me anxious for a long time regarding the **three firsts** <note>The chemical principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, until, relying on divine help, I knew that wood and herbs could be distilled without any **caput mortuum** <term>caput mortuum: literally "dead head," the useless solid residue left over after an alchemical distillation.</term>. 

<margin>18.</margin> For I used to wonder long ago that no ash could be obtained from the charcoal of honey, and consequently, no salt of ash. These things I later observed with pleasure through a universal analysis of the body. For it was enough for Paracelsus to have left everything involved in doubt, he who had drunk the discovery of another with a thin draft, and turned a knot into nourishment, making it his own by embezzlement; and striving to fly from the nest to the **Monarchy** <note>Paracelsus often called himself the "Monarch of Medicine."</note> before having sufficient feathers, he fell. 

<margin>19.</margin> For snatching the glory of the discovery for himself, he pleased himself by having repeated the same thing many times in various places, though meanwhile he made little progress in his own works. 

<margin>20.</margin> Indeed, it is ridiculous, and like a fable, that **sulfur** in 

<column-break/>

us should be distilled, sublimated, reverberated, calcined, and resolved, and hence various diseases be caused, solely by the man's audacity, without pledge or surety, of his own great authority. For he does not know, nor dare, to draw diseases into an **Eximolegesim** <note>original: "Eximolegesim" — a Helmontian term for a thorough, lawful explanation or unfolding of a subject.</note>, not yet being fully commissioned for this by his Inventor. 

It is also a childish dream that **salt** should be distilled, sublimated, calcined, or circulated in us, or undergo other tortures; or that **Mercury** should sustain these trials in us, and for every individual change of the variations, produce other diseases, pains, and defects individually, and others again, when complicated with his other two companions—the two beginnings—or masked by different degrees and doses. 

It is likewise nonsense that **Mercury**, on account of the exceptional subtlety of its circulation, would be the cause of all sudden death: which we know is established, cured, and prevented by its own causes. 

<margin>21a.</margin> For first of all, every day several ounces of blood are breathed away for nourishment, without a *caput mortuum*, pain, or defect, indeed without sensation, while they pass, and where they pass. But whatever was once dedicated to expulsion in the form of water, Mercury, or sweat, or whatever was once judged unfit for nourishment, or having already performed its duties of nutrition, is assigned to distillation: that thing is never thereafter distilled, sublimated, calcined, or circulated within us. For the works of **Nature** are too serious, because they ultimately look toward **GOD**. 

<margin>22.</margin> For nature does not **play ball** <note>original: "pila ludit" — a metaphor meaning nature does not toss materials back and forth aimlessly.</note>, so as to receive back into favor excrement once torn away from the commerce of life. It never returns to the same point, because it proceeds and does not take a holiday. 

<margin>23.</margin> Finally, if some watery liquor were redistilled a hundred times, it would [not] therefore be sharper or subtle, but rather, as the seed of the middle life is gradually exhausted, it migrates more and more toward the simplicity of the element. Not
