### THE THREE FIRST CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES, AND NOT OF THE SAME

For the rainwater that has just fallen from above is finer than that which rained at the beginning of creation. If something watery were to exhale from our own warmth, and through imagined returns <note>original: "somniatis reditibus" — referring to the supposed cycles of refinement within the body</note> were to acquire sharpness, that would not be the fault of the refinement of **Mercury** <note>In alchemical theory, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and volatility</note>, but the fault of what has been added to it.

<margin>24.</margin> I truly wonder that so great a **Chemist** <note>original: "Chymicus"</note> was ignorant of the fact that blood does not circulate, nor does it endure cycles of refinement within us; and that it does not persist in us for more than a single course of the Moon; and that for this reason, a woman pays a tax of spent blood <note>A reference to menstruation as a purging of "worn out" blood</note>. For she ought to abound in more blood, both for the growth of the fetus and for the suckling of milk.

<margin>25.</margin> However, so that **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician who founded iatrochemistry (chemical medicine)</note> might better mask his fiction, he supposes that one of the **Three First Principles** <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the building blocks of all matter in Paracelsian theory</note>, once separated, immediately assumes an active reality from its "microcosmic nature" <note>The idea that the human body is a "little world" reflecting the universe</note> within some accidental thing—one being out of infinite possibilities, whose seeds of myriads, gathered into one, it contained. Therefore, because of its monstrous and foreign birth, he claims it becomes hostile to us by that very fact and becomes the cause of diseases. And thus, he suggests there are at least ten times more possible diseases in us than there are species of animals, plants, minerals, and stars—namely, as many as there are species of salts, sulfurs, and mercuries, and their complications in nature. Furthermore, he issues an edict warning that no one should rashly intrude into the art of healing who does not know all things intimately and outwardly—specifically, certainly, properly, and distinctly—through their causes, essences, species, properties, proportions, alterations, and defects.

<margin>26.</margin> This is so that everyone might believe that Paracelsus, who teaches these things, also knew all these things universally and in detail. Moreover, he wants us to reflect the **microcosm** <note>The human body</note> exactly, and therefore that the three beginnings of our body give birth to as many diseases as there are species of created beings. For he casts the science of healing and its **students** <note>original: "Tyrones" — beginners or apprentices</note> into a thousand confusions, obscurities, ignorances, and impossibilities, for one fault alone: namely, so that he might seem

<column-break/>

to be knowledgeable about all things, and that his dreams might be thought true.

<margin>27.</margin> He easily recognized that the medicine of the **Schools** <note>Referring to the traditional Galenic medicine taught in universities, which relied on the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</note> rested on false foundations; nor did he think it would be difficult for him to utterly overturn those Schools. Therefore, he devised for himself the title of "Monarch of Healing." But while he thought the path to destruction was easy, his strength failed him in such great ignorance when it came to building up such a great sovereignty. He introduced the Three Beginnings <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> into diseases for this very reason.

<margin>28.</margin> It is so. Those three are indeed found in many bodies: or (to speak more distinctly) at least three things are separated from many. But a certain absurdity of reckless daring deluded the man, because he did not consider the impossibility of the matter regarding diseases. This is because nowhere—neither in us, nor elsewhere—are those principles separated or separable, except by the corruption of the whole, and specifically through the use of fire. Nevertheless, he judged that their separate management produced diseases in us.

<margin>29.</margin> For the essences of the "firsts" are connected in us through their "middle life" <note>original: "vitam mediam" — a vital force that holds the chemical principles together in a living being</note>, under whose dominion they are restrained, and they always remain what they are.

<margin>30.</margin> First of all, **Salt** itself deceived him, making him appear foolish because it seemed to confirm his concept to Paracelsus in **urine** <note>original: "lotio"</note>, sweat, and tears. He paid no attention to the fact that this salt is not from the "Three Firsts" of our body, but is mere excrement from transformed food and drink. From this point, spurred on into credulity, he was led away into errors by his thinking. For he had noticed that a poorly treated wound pours out "false water"—the body's own fluid impregnated with a foreign salt—or that the blood itself degenerates through its whole, as in an ulcer, **Dropsy** <note>Edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation</note>, etc. And from this, he gathered a plentiful harvest of ulcers and diseases in favor of Salt, which he mistakenly thought was one of the three principles, and not the whole blood converted at once into false water, without any separation of Sulfur or Mercury, through erroneous transformations. He therefore judged that there were as many turns of Mercury, and a part of Sulfur as well, and for his own equipment...

He asserts that while Paracelsus correctly rejected traditional Galenic medicine, his own chemical system was built on "dreams" and a misunderstanding of how the body actually functions.</summary>

# THE ESSENCE OF THE ARMY OF DISEASES.

Confident that his intellectual baggage was sufficient, he would have gladly designated a classification <note>original: "praedicamentum" — a term from Aristotelian logic referring to the categories of being</note> of diseases. But <margin>31.</margin> remaining unequal to the burden, he succumbed. Yet he would have uncovered his own wandering error, had he not been greatly deceived by his own daring. For whether out of hope for ambition or a rush of preconceived notions, he ought to have examined where the remaining **Sulfur** stayed, if the **Salt** in ulcers or in dropsy <note>original: "hydrope" — an old term for edema or the swelling of the body with fluid</note> was torn away from the whole and its two other companions in such a massive separation. He ought also to have been mindful of his own doctrine (erroneous though it be), in which he calls the fluid salt within us—which is present inside—the mere **Saltpeter of the Cagastrum** <term>Cagastrum: a term coined by Paracelsus to describe diseases that arise from a "corrupt seed" or external environmental influences, as opposed to "Iliaster," which is healthy or celestial.</term> Thus, he tries to persuade us that not only the flesh and blood, but the entire body and life itself, are of the nature of saltpeter and the **Cagastrum**. For the blood—just as water produces all fruits—is entirely uniform; yet when imbued with a poisonous or foreign ferment <note>A "ferment" in Helmontian medicine is a vital force that transforms matter, similar to how yeast transforms dough.</note>, it degenerates now into a child of salt, then truly into various offspring of filth, without any memory of a "posthumous" **Mercury** or **Sulfur**.

<margin>32.</margin> Finally, consider how **Paracelsus** finds his cause for diseases. For example: he not infrequently defines a fever as an "earthquake of the microcosm" <note>Microcosm: the Renaissance idea that the human body is a "little world" that mirrors the physical universe or "macrocosm."</note>; which trembling of the earth he sometimes defines as our "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy</note>. At other times, he attributes the trembling of the earth to tremors born from "smothered mercury." Elsewhere again, he defines fever as a disease of **Sulfur** and **Nitre**; boasting that both the cause and the remedy are contained within that essential definition of his. Truly, under an ulcerated abscess, the whole body—once fat in itself—often becomes like a skeleton, and excretes nothing besides pus. Thus, by the power of laxatives, the entire habit of the body often suddenly liquefies into a rotten sludge. What happens through the art of the Physician happens in Diarrhea through a defect. Yet at least the poison is the same in both cases, only applied and tempered differently.

<margin>33.</margin> Consider a patient with dropsy: he might have a waistline of eight feet; yet through the work of an empirical healer, in one day and by a single drink, he was released from the dropsy, and the water perhaps weighed 40 pounds <note>original: "℔ 40"</note>. On the day after next, however, his belly soon swelled again to its former size, and after a few hours, he died. The remainder of him, surely, displayed nothing but skin and

<column-break/>

bones. This is because the flesh and blood had immediately migrated together into the salty water of the dropsy. I saw this wonder in this man: that today his belly had plainly shrunk, and tomorrow it returned again to the previous limit of swelling, tension, and hardness, and then he died. If, therefore, that vast amount of salt was one of the **Three First Principles**, at least 40 pounds of **Sulfur** necessarily should have remained visible.

An ulcerated oak tree continually weeps salty water and wastes away with decay: but if that salt were one of the three "beginnings" <note>The Tria Prima: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> of the oak, the oak would surely grow fat like a torch; it would not waste away dry, decayed, and nearly rejected from the kitchen hearth. Therefore, these principles do not testify to a morbid destruction; rather, they show that the whole body <margin>34.</margin> is affected in various ways, liquefies, and becomes putrid, according to the guidance of various seeds and ferments.

For Paracelsus had learned this from **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years; Van Helmont considered him outdated.</note>, who thought that blood consisted of as many simple parts as it could be resolved into. I wonder, therefore, at the thoughtlessness of **Paracelsus**, <margin>35.</margin> that he did not know that the **Three Firsts** are never separated except by fire, once their final life has been destroyed, while the "symbol" of the seed of their middle life is retained. They are not, therefore, to be called "beginnings" <note>original: "initia"</note>, for they are made, and thus they are born. Much less should they be considered the beginning of bodies while the whole, under the guidance of a foreign seed, retreats through transmutation into another nature. For that man never saw the "Three Firsts" of any solid thing appear in living beings by any degree of heat, nor are they ever made or extorted except by fire.

I am even indignant that it is not known that while these same "Firsts" remain materially under the same weight, they are nevertheless subject to the various transmutations of seeds. He relapsed <margin>36.</margin> in a way into the errors of **Galen**, who thought that the elements essentially remain in mixtures. Thus, he was clearly deluded by his three principles. For there is the same defect in the philosophical principles of both men; principles which teach that life alone works in the living body and upon the body. Yet the subordinate forms <margin>37.</margin> of the integral parts, even of the three...

He uses the example of a dropsy patient and a decaying oak tree to prove that chemicals like salt are products of the body's breakdown, not its original building blocks.</summary>

### THE THREE FIRST CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES, NOR INDEED ARE THEY DEMONSTRATED

<margin>38.</margin> Of the first principles (if these are present before they are created through extraction), they are restrained under the unity of the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that Van Helmont believed directed all biological processes</term> by a higher form or life. These Three First Principles never appear or perform their work—much less do they "sin" through imbalance or become diseased—unless their required obedience to the Archeus is first dissolved. That is to say, they must first be separated by fire, and their "ultimate life" destroyed, while a "middle life" of that specific body persists—a small remnant of the seed whose properties each of those principles mimics in a certain way once they have become a self-subsisting entity <note>original: "ens per se subsistens"</note>. Because he was ignorant of this, **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> thought that all power and the formal operations of things depended immediately on the essence of the Three First Principles. He went so far as to describe the properties of vegetables based on how much of such **Mercury**, **Salt**, or **Sulfur** they contained, and all of it according to his own whim. It was as if these beginnings, though enclosed under a formal Archeus, could operate while the vital Archeus was "on holiday." Just as **Galen** <note>Aelius Galenus (130–210 AD), the Greek physician whose theory of the four humors dominated medicine for centuries</note> attributed everything to the "elements," so Paracelsus, becoming incensed, attributed everything to his three adopted "beginnings." They are like **Charlatans** <note>original: "Agyrtarum" — wandering quacks or street performers</note> who, having obtained a single oil or plaster, extol it as a cure for absolutely every disease, and many others besides. Paracelsus did not, I say, notice that lead, as long as it is lead, has different powers than it does once it has been <margin>39.</margin> changed into sulfur and mercury. Indeed, water, oil, and ash, when sealed in a flask, do not operate outside the containing vessel. The flask, as such, does perform an action; however, it does not do so insofar as it contains three things that could be separated from one another. You should judge the same regarding the "three," as long as they are <margin>40.</margin> enclosed under a common life. Therefore, although Paracelsus investigated nature more closely than Galen—insofar as three specific things are actually drawn out from many bodies, which does not happen with the fictitious elements and humors—both of them stumbled in this: they brought their own "suppositions" into the study of diseases. In truth, nothing in us feels sickness except the vital powers themselves. Life, however, through its seminal **Blas** <term>Blas: Van Helmont’s term for the "spirit of motion" or the vital impulse that drives change in the body</term>,

<column-break/>

moves and alters matter; nothing hurts us materially from within that is not hostile, foreign, or an excrement in respect to life—and therefore, it cannot be made of its own "adopted first principles." For those three are not <margin>41.</margin> originally and immediately subject to the life of the whole, but rather to the "middle life" of that seed from which the three bodily beginnings are said to have come. Truly, the Three First Principles of the flesh, blood, brain, etc., are not immediately subject to the command of the total Archeus, but to the "seminal balsam" of the specific organs. And this does not happen before their birth is made manifest. Therefore, diseases do not owe their origin or the cause of their birth to the birth of the Three First Principles, or any one of them. For they cannot exist, act, or harm unless they are first separated from one another and the integrity of the whole is destroyed (through death), in which they are contained potentially. If, however, they were separated so that they could hurt and harm, surely that would have been done by some disease or internal agent that is contrary to nature and exists prior to them. Therefore, the separation of those three from each other could never be anything but a product, and thus something that comes *after* the disease; nor would it appear earlier, unless a disease were already assumed. Therefore, the principles are not the immediate occasional cause of diseases. For even if the Three First Principles are not the causes <margin>42.</margin> of diseases, this nevertheless does not prove that the salt, sulfur, and mercury of things are not the *medicines* for diseases. For it is not required that a remedy and the external cause of a disease share a "symbol" <note>In alchemy, a "symbol" refers to a shared nature or correspondence</note>. Even so, Paracelsus ordered it thus, so that he might attack Galen's axiom: *Contraries are cured by contraries* <note>original: "Contraria contrariis curantur"</note>. For toxins are not overcome by a "symbol" of <margin>43.</margin> poison, but by a "poison-conqueror" <note>original: "vincetoxico" — likely referring to the plant Vincetoxicum or the general concept of an antidote</note>. For those medical powers are gifts of GOD, which bear no character of contrariety or hostility toward each other, nor toward diseases. Instead, each thing acts out of the gift it was commanded to perform. Indeed, bodies—once freed from their bulk, enclosure, filth, and impediments—unfold the noblest gifts and most excellent **powers** <note>original: "dynames" — from the Greek 'dynameis'</note>. As <margin>44.</margin> has been shown more copiously elsewhere. Furthermore, it has now been sufficiently demonstrated—

He rejects Paracelsus's and Galen's systemic classifications of disease, asserting that medicines work as God-given powers rather than through simple "contrariety."</summary>

### THE ESSENCE OF THE ARMY OF DISEASES.

...it has been demonstrated that nature does not tolerate four elements <note>The ancient Greek theory that everything is made of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. Nor does it allow their meeting for the constitution of concrete bodies; and consequently, there is no opposition or skirmish of elements that leads to disease or remedy. It follows from this that nothing can be called a "quintessence" <term>Quintessence: literally the "fifth essence," traditionally thought to be a pure substance distinct from the four elements</term> in its proper name, if "fifth" implies a necessary relationship to the other four. Therefore, the "quintessence" is indeed a chemical invention: but one belonging to those philosophers who, before me, were ignorant of the true number of elements, their essences, and the fact that such mixtures do not actually exist. If **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note> had known these things, he would undoubtedly have called the essence he labels "fifth" the "fourth," with respect to his Three First Principles. No doubt he thought that every single body was constituted—and likewise resolved, both by art and by nature—into these three, and that nothing else remained. Indeed, in such a state of novelty, he was inconsistent and did not know which side to throw himself toward. For at times he denies that elements are bodies, instead calling them "empty and hollow matrices" <note>original: "matrices," meaning wombs or places where things are formed</note>, the locations and seats of bodies; he claims all bodies are nothing but the Three First Principles, and not elements. Yet elsewhere, following the herd of those who came before him, he teaches that elements remain in individual bodies, are found there, and can be extracted from them unharmed—so that their essences and bodies persist within the mixture, merely crowded together by the act of mixing.

<margin>45.</margin> Certainly, the "Three First Principles" as well as the "Quintessence" are subscribed to today by followers of Paracelsus with just as much lack of substance as the fables of elements, mixtures, and complexions <term>Complexions: in ancient medicine, the specific balance of "humors" (fluids) that determined a person's health and temperament</term> were in the past. For in this recent century, people have begun—without investigation—to give credit and names to the plausible novelties of the Paracelsian invention. However, I have so far seen no one, read no one, nor heard of anyone who was able (much less who dared) to adequately separate the Three First Principles from bodies. Therefore, I establish this proposition:

<margin>46.</margin> **The Three First Principles are a recent invention, contrary to the truth of nature and reality.**

### *The First Thesis.*

Even if the Three First Principles are, in part, drawn out from certain things

<column-break/>

by fire: this does not happen through the separation of those same principles already existing there. <margin>47.</margin> Rather, they are generated right then and there as new entities, through a transformation performed by the fire; something is created that was not there before.

### *The Second.*

A shoot of a tree, while it is still in its herbal state, weighing one pound, will scarcely yield a drachm <term>Drachm: an ancient unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</term> of oil. But that same shoot, becoming woody around October, will yield about seven drachms of oil. And finally, in the following <margin>48.</margin> February, it will yield nearly two ounces of oil—and five times more charcoal and ash than it did previously in August.

### *The Third.*

Things that were not present as constituents from the beginning cannot be "first principles." Instead, they are made and changed into one another as secondary things, artificial and arising from the directions of the seeds <note>Van Helmont believed "seeds" (semina) were the internal blueprints that directed the growth and form of all matter</note>.

### *The Fourth.*

Elemental water becomes oil in vegetables, animals, and sulfurs. Likewise, every oil, when something is added to it, is easily reduced back into water. However, the first principles of other <margin>49.</margin> things cannot be changed into one another, nor can they cease to be what they were before.

### *The Fifth.*

Certain bodies do not contain the "Three," but are composed of only one or two.

### *The Sixth.*

There are certain bodies from which the "Three" have never been separated by any of the techniques used until now, in a way that their weight would always balance the weight of the body from which they were taken.

### *The Seventh.*

Certain bodies are entirely immutable <margin>50.</margin> and inseparable, containing no duality. It is helpful to explain these things a little more accurately for the sake of beginners who easily subscribe to the comments of others. For instance, wood contains water and oil, but not charcoal. The charcoal was not inside it, but is produced by the art of chemistry. It was only present materially, potentially, and remotely. It would never have been made from the wood except by fire. Finally, charcoal—unless it burns in an open fire—is never changed even slightly, let alone turned into ash or salt. In

### THE THREE FIRST CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES, AND WHY THEY ARE NOT SUCH

...in charcoal, a certain fatty substance burns, which is immediately and materially reduced into <term>Gas <note>Van Helmont famously coined the word "Gas," likely derived from the Greek word "Chaos," to describe substances that are neither solid nor liquid and cannot be easily contained.</note></term>, a thing never before observed. This Gas eventually turns into water. But as long as it is Gas, and separated from the solid body (the charcoal), it is not sulfur (for it is consumed and transformed by burning), nor is it salt or mercury (for those would return to mercury and salt, not into an uncoagulable Gas, if they were indeed the first and constant beginnings of things). Therefore, it is something else, outside those three principles. Furthermore, not all the ash remaining from the charcoal is salt. For once the <term>lixivial salt <note>Potash or alkaline salt extracted from ashes using water.</note></term> is removed, that which remains cannot be calcined by any fire, nor can it be turned into salt, sulfur, or mercury. If, however, it is turned into salt by adding other things, it is a sign that the salt is being *made*, not that it *was* already salt; thus, a principle would be "born." Therefore, the salt in the ash does not arise through extraction or separation (by burning away the other two principles), but by <term>transmutation <note>The changing of one substance into another.</note></term> into a new being that did not exist before. For not everything manufactured from a substance is actually inside it. If it were, then bread would contain the blood and bones of many different genera and species. Marble does not contain glass, even though glass may be made from marble when something is added to it. It is one thing to argue about these three principles as if they were the total matter of things and actually constituted them; it is quite another to say that a tree is in a seed, or a fish, bone, or cartilage is in bread. For leather or wood are not stone, even if they are petrified by certain springs. In things that are transmuted, the end result differs in its appearance from how it was at the beginning of the change. I have also demonstrated elsewhere that <term>fixed Alkali <note>Potassium carbonate or similar alkaline substances produced by burning plants.</note></term> did not pre-exist in vegetables; rather, it is "fixed" by the act of burning. Therefore, the doctrine of the "Three Firsts" is insufficient, not only because it forces nature under violent rules, but because if they were truly "Firsts" and earned the title of "principles," they ought to be stable (as was not hidden even from **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose theories of the four elements dominated science until the time of Van Helmont.</note>) and one could not be changed into another. For if wood were composed of salt, oil, water, and ash, then from the ash, by the

<column-break/>

salt of the ash itself, salt would be prepared; likewise, every distilled oil would be changeable into salt, as well as into water by additions. If there were such instability among these three, then they could also have been created by fire during the separation and destruction of the solid body.

<margin>51.</margin>
It is necessary to establish in bodies one first and ultimate, material, and real beginning, which is water; and not three, because those three are the offspring of seeds—bodies made solid from water. Secondly, there is another motivating and effective principle, which is the essential seed, or the very <term>Archeal <note>From "Archeus," the vital force or "internal chemist" that Van Helmont believed directed all biological and chemical processes.</note></term> essence of the seed, which is different from the "form" of a thing. This Archeal essence does not have the character of a beginning in itself, because it is generated in the act of generating, like the goal of generation, which is led toward the perfection of a being through available pathways, simultaneously with the end of generation. These are the two principles of all bodies, as well as their causes. For if every thing exists through its causes and is begun by them, it is vain to believe in other causes and other principles of things in the manner of Aristotle. Therefore, true principles are those which never slip into one another through any rotation of changes. The first is stable, a perpetual, real beginning of bodies, their support and their nursery. It is the ultimate thing into which the finished tragedies of things return. It is not some fictional, lazy, and impossible <term>hyle <note>A Greek term used in Aristotelian philosophy to mean "prime matter"—matter without form or qualities.</note></term>. The other principle is the beginning of the motion of initiation, carrying every property of the things to be acted out upon its stage. Indeed, since species never exist in isolation within their genera, and only individuals exist and subsist in real action, it was necessary for principles to be real and individually existing. Thus, the universality of matter is determined individually by the activity of the "efficient" cause.

<margin>52.</margin>
For this reason, even if we granted the false premise that all bodies were reduced to those three principles by the motion of their own dissolution, it still would not follow that these three are the beginnings of bodies. Because the immediate resolution of bodies does not prove their origin.

it argues against the principles, but for the <term>heterogeneity <note>The state of being composed of diverse or different parts; the opposite of being uniform.</note></term> of the final matter. And the final resolution of matter is merely a witness to the seeds of the concrete body, but not to the principles themselves. Finally, there is no reason why three things should be called "first" if three can return to, or be reduced to, two, and finally into one. Indeed, even if three bodies were seen at the beginning, transforming into one another and passing back and forth, they should be considered three rather than two only as long as two cannot be made from the three. Therefore, where three are found, they are not the material beginnings of bodies, but the <term>beds of seeds <note>Van Helmont used the term "thori seminum" to describe the internal organizing structures or "blueprints" that direct the growth and form of matter.</note></term>. Once these are exhausted, all things spontaneously return to the primeval element of water.

<margin>53.</margin> Furthermore, the fact that those three are not contained in all bodies, and thus are not necessary principles, is clear because Mercury extracted from a metal is so <term>univocal <note>Having only one possible nature or meaning; completely uniform.</note></term>, homogeneous, simple, and indivisible, that it is impossible by either art or nature for salt or sulfur to be drawn from it. Moreover, Mercury is never divisible by any method. It is clear that from elemental water alone, and by the power of the simplest mercurial seed, it coalesced into a body that is indivisible, impenetrable, and inseparable,

<margin>54.</margin> which has no equal among generated things. Otherwise, it would be like water, which, being defiled by no seed within itself, has a similar simplicity throughout and an impossibility of separation. However, if I have occasionally attributed "three" to the element of water, I spoke <term>analogically <note>By way of comparison or metaphor, rather than literal fact.</note></term>; insofar as, besides abstracted spirits, nothing in bodies is so similar that it is not understood to be affected in different ways according to various dispositions, and it is necessary that those dispositions regard some heterogeneity of the being. For it is enough to have also warned in the same place that the heterogeneous parts of water are in the simplest body of the element, indivisible by art, nature, and all ages, and actually impossible to separate, consisting of extreme simplicity. Therefore, although I called them the "three firsts of water" in that place, they are not the three

<column-break/>

beginnings of a composition, as if they existed before the water: but rather three aspects of heterogeneity. Although water contains this heterogeneity by the law of being a body—at the very least being mentally divisible into different parts—since it is actually impossible for them to be pulled apart from one another, there is only room for conjecture that, even though these things are not actually sulfur, salt, and Mercury, they at least correspond to them in some way. Therefore, in water no less than in mercury, there is proof by which the existence of the "three firsts" as separate entities is denied.

<margin>55.</margin> I seem to hear whispers that I have offended many craftsmen who boast with full cheeks of "oil of mercury," "salt of vitriol," and "water"; and that I am accusing them of lying or <term>imposture <note>Deception or fraud.</note></term> while they promise the aforementioned things. I respond that an active imposture produces its own impostor, unworthy of life and happiness; but a passive imposture is worthy of pity. But those who do not yet detect the fallacy by which they are surrounded argue first as follows.

<margin>56.</margin> Gold (they say), a body by far the most constant among <term>sublunary <note>Literally "under the moon"; a term from old science referring to the Earthly realm where things change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note></term> things, is dissolved into heterogeneous parts: therefore, by a stronger reasoning, Mercury must be as well. They are certainly arguing from the lesser to the greater. Again they urge: Nature knows how to compose mercury from the first elements; therefore, it also knows how to destroy it. Moreover, the way of composition is not to make Mercury immediately from the element of water, but through intermediate dispositions of matter, which are dissimilar; thus also the way of corruption in mercury will proceed through those same dispositions in a backward step, and through the heterogeneity of matter.

<margin>57.</margin> Wherefore, thirdly, <term>Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who established the "Three Principles" theory that Van Helmont is here refuting.</note></term> says: "The matter of things which cannot be destroyed by art, is at least destroyed by nature." Because all sublunary things that are not subject to death are at least subject to a "term" or limit.

<margin>58.</margin> To the first I respond: That gold is indeed the most constant of bodies in fire; but it borrows the constancy of its separation from mercury; and thus if its sulfur includes a heterogeneous duality, that does not affect the mercury in the least. For pure Mercury, distinct from combustible sulfur...

To the second point, I say that nature indeed proceeded from the purity of the element of water toward the composition of mercury; yet, once the seed of mercury is admitted and enclosed in the depths of the water, it cannot return to the destruction of that compound. This is because that seed is not mortal, nor fleeting, nor subject to the laws of the sublunary world <note>The realm below the moon, subject to change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note>, as Paracelsus says in *The Vexation of the Chemists*. 

<margin>59.</margin> The reason for this immortality in mercury is that its seed and its fruit, in the constitution of mercury, are already one and the same: Mercury within mercury. Nature does not know how to find a way to destroy a thing so homogeneous, where the seed has become the fruit through a most perfect and <term>anatic <note>From the Greek 'ana', used in pharmacy to mean 'in equal parts'; here it refers to a perfectly balanced, inseparable union.</note></term> union. Since nature cannot penetrate to divide where there is no knot or heterogeneity. I admit, of course, that Mercury becomes a metal through the process of transmutation and the "marriage" of metallic sulfurs; and this metal becomes destructible by reason of the duality of its sulfur; nevertheless, the Mercury of that metal remains indestructible. Hence Paracelsus says in the aforementioned *Vexation*: *“Even if you destroy a metal ten thousand times, it will always rise again from the destructions far more perfect.”* And in the *Archidoxis*, in the book on the separation of elements, the chapter on metals: *“Every one of the elements in the form of the 'oil of metallic destruction' can be reduced again into its original white and malleable metal, except for the element of fire, which contains the tincture or sulfur.”* Therefore, although the mercurial part in metals—and even in the body of mercury itself—might take on the masks of vitriol, oil, salt, or water due to additives, these are nothing but deceptions of the eyes. For Mercury always returns from such states because, according to nature and all its properties, it is always present. I hold, therefore, with the principles of the more abstruse philosophy:

<column-break/>

<margin>60.</margin> *“If Mercury were divisible into heterogeneous parts, the chemical art would not be true, and Mercury itself would be unfit for the work. Indeed, unless I had seen mercury subsisting in this way, I would deny that the art is true. For nature cannot destroy the seed, which cannot die, nor be separated from its matter. Nor can it die through the sublunary machinations of this age. Likewise, it is easier to construct gold than to destroy it; thus it is also easier for nature to construct mercury than to destroy it. Therefore, as many as promise the separations of gold or mercury, yet do not know how to construct gold in any significant quantity—since they do not know what is far easier—let them believe they also do not know what is still far more difficult.”* Therefore <margin>61.</margin> [Roger] Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English philosopher and friar who was an early advocate for the empirical scientific method.</note>, inquiring into the first matter of the art and searching through all the bodies of the world, denies that gold and silver are the matter of the art; because it is plainly impossible to reduce them back into sulfur and quicksilver, from which the <term>son of fire <note>original: "filius ignis." An alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone or the perfected metallic essence.</note></term>, so beloved by philosophers, might be made. 

<margin>62.</margin> Finally, to the third point, I say: those things which are not subject to death, separation, or change are at least subject to a "term" or end. I concede that this is true if we are talking about the dissolution of the world and the "fire of Gehenna" <note>Hellfire or the final cleansing fire at the end of time.</note> at the end of the age, about which I say nothing. Otherwise, the aforementioned assertion contains an <term>idiotism <note>original: "Idiotismum." Here, Van Helmont uses the term to mean a vulgar error or a piece of flawed, unlearned reasoning.</note></term>. For a "term" [an end point] performs nothing naturally; rather, the operation is performed by an active agent in the very point toward which it moves. But such an agent is lacking when it comes to indissoluble things. Finally, neither time nor duration performs anything by itself; only the intermediate dispositions of changeable things occurring in time perform anything. Therefore, whatever does not respond to changeable dispositions responds much less to time or the end of duration—for that end is included only in changeable things, and not in unchangeable ones. If, then, metallic mercury lacks all sulfur—I speak of the noblest union of bodies of the most constant kind—it is permitted to consider this law of the "three firsts" to have failed, like a broken chain. <margin>63.</margin> ...first: but rather a single, entirely material beginning, serving various destinations, ends, goals, and necessities of the seeds, and playing through various possibilities. Therefore, those three principles, where they are found, are not primary, but are made through the dissolution of fire. Their matter is not joined according to a primary existence of salt, sulfur, and mercury, but according to the ends of the seeds. They are not even beginnings, but rather intermediate stages subordinated to the ultimate goal of life. <margin>64.</margin> Finally, I know that from sand, flint, and non-calcarious stones <note>Stones that cannot be turned into lime through heating.</note>, sulfur or mercury can never be extracted. For their seeds were contained in the coagulation of petrifying water, without any destination for fats <note>original: "pinguedinum," here referring to the oily nature of sulfur</note> or mercuries. <margin>65.</margin> However, stones that can be calcined <note>Reduced to a powder (lime) by heat.</note> acquire the nature of salt and the sharpness of lime. But that very thing is a transmutation into a new generation promoted by fire; it is not the extraction, leading out, or separation of something already contained within. This is what the Chemical School <note>The followers of Paracelsus and traditional alchemy.</note> before me did not know. I can prove this. Because I know how to reduce rock, and all stones, into a pure salt weighing the same as the original rock or stone, without any sulfur or mercury at all; and thus, whatever is lost in burning the stone belongs to the nature of a single salt rather than to the three principles. But because this unity of the solid relates to the path of the first reduction into the element of water, and is not obvious to every worker, we are therefore accustomed to speak generally among chemists of things under the name of the three: namely, salt, sulfur, and mercury. Not indeed because I think those are the principles of things, but because they are separated from most things by fire, we use their names <note>original: "etymo"</note> to distinguish the different parts <note>original: "heterogeneitates"</note> of solid bodies. The same thing happens to a rock as happens to coal; for unless both are burned in an open fire, they are never changed into lime or ash. And although coal gives off a flame when fanned, and so far whatever perishes from the coal is sulfur; nevertheless, since nothing in a stone is ignited or illuminated, let it be considered salt rather than sulfur. Therefore, while stone, gem, rock, or sand are skillfully reduced into salt,

<column-break/>

that salt—because of its complete uniformity <note>original: "homogeneitatem"</note> left by the fire—cannot produce or contain sulfur, nor be pulled apart into different substances. Finally, <margin>66.</margin> if glass is made by fire from ash and sand, it is not an extraction of glass from the ash, but a product of artifice and a new generation. For since any body takes its matter immediately from the element of water, joined by the power of seeds: sulfur is indeed the action of the seed, while salt is born in the solid from the spontaneous inclination of the water, though changed by the disposition of the seminal sulfur. Thus those two beings leap forth immediately from two principles of bodies. However, the Mercury of things is nothing but pure water, not yet matured enough by the disposition of the seed and the inclination of the material beginning. And this is so destined by the design or study of nature, so that by reason of the watery principle—not yet fully changed—growth from its own element and communication with its mother <note>Water, as the "mother" element of all things in Van Helmont’s theory.</note> may be granted more opportunely through a shared likeness. Therefore, I do not admit that the "Three Firsts" are the constituents of bodies, nor that they are universal. This is truly characteristic of my strictness, <margin>67.</margin> for I am not accustomed to build universal axioms from any particular case. Let anyone who wishes do that; I prefer to be precise so that I may understand more precisely. For I have found for the most part that those three do not come forth from the bodies from which they are thought to be drawn, unless a third thing is added, either for transmutation or by composition. This should rather be attributed to the arriving seed and the transmutation born from it, and not to "firsts" existing within as necessary, immediate, and universal principles of nature, from which bodies are made and into which they are again resolved. For they cannot provide certain proof that they were in the body before its separation, just as they are expressed by fire; much less that they pre-existed before the body of which they seem to have been parts. It is also clear <margin>68.</margin> that most things are changed by distilling, and they are not in the diversity of the solid in the same state or quantity as they are when they are created through fire. <meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument that Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury are not pre-existing building blocks of matter. He uses the example of "Tartar" (the crusty deposit in wine barrels) to show that fire actually creates these substances during the process of distillation rather than simply releasing them.</meta>

->### THE THREE CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES ARE NOT IN ALL THINGS###<-

This is clear from the example of Tartar. Indeed, by distilling 16 ounces of the best tartar, scarcely one ounce of water is drawn out; of salt, truly, at most two and a half ounces. All the rest is oil: that is, out of 16 parts, nearly thirteen are oily. Yet crude Tartar is not oily, nor does it act as an oily substance, nor does it burn like birch bark: rather, it has the nature of an acid salt. Therefore, through distillation, the nature of the acid salt is changed into oil.

Then again, if the salt of Tartar spontaneously becomes a liquid <note>original: "lixivium," referring to the salt absorbing moisture from the air to become a solution</note>, and oil is joined to it, a soap <term>smegma</term> <note>The Latin term for soap or a cleansing agent.</note> will be made from it; when this is distilled, mostly water will be obtained, and the original oil will cease to exist and will be changed into something else. What indeed is clearer than this mechanical demonstration to show that fire is the creator of these "first principles"? And thus, they are not primary in themselves, nor do they pre-exist in the compound as they appear when separated by fire. Indeed, this is not a bare separation of unlike things, but a transformation of the compound by fire, according to the activity which heterogeneous <note>Parts that are different in kind or nature.</note> parts perform among themselves.

<margin>69.</margin> But surely, if those three were inside every single body, so that no body could be without them—nay, if each kept its original nature—then Salt, I say, would never become Mercury, nor would Mercury in turn become Sulfur, and so on. In that case, Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the famous 16th-century physician who popularized the "Tria Prima."</note> might have apparently thought that every body was originally composed of salt, sulfur, and Mercury. But since there is an indubitable changing of things, through the things themselves and their smallest parts, as well as through the transition of a triple life, those changes cannot denote a fixed identity of the "three," nor any constancy, since their very progression is entirely inconstant and their perseverance unstable.

For from Paracelsus onward, almost everyone has subscribed to his invention; no one has dared to penetrate the condition of those three. They stood amazed at the different parts they saw extracted by fire, whereby, as if they had eaten the lotus <note>A classical reference to the "Lotus Eaters" who became forgetful and lost their way.</note>, they allowed themselves to be led away to wherever Paracelsus called them. But let Paracelsus learn: while blood is made from food, a separation of pure from impure indeed happens, but no separation of the "three principles" occurs.

<column-break/>

<margin>70.</margin> For as often as a being passes through its final life into a new life, the mass is indeed changed into a vital juice <note>original: "succum"</note>, with a division of its different parts, the extinction of its form, and the properties of its middle life. Yet it does not change into or toward the "three firsts"; rather, it proceeds to a radical destruction, with the ultimate annihilation of the prior life. Under which, at last, the seeds draw in a new life for a new generation. This is truly the way of return, or the regression of the "Night of Hippocrates" to the "Day of Orpheus" <note>Van Helmont uses these names to symbolize the cycle of death (night/dissolution) and birth (day/reconstitution).</note>.

At least it is perpetually true that those three are never separated without fire; thus, before the development of the art of fire <term>Pyrotechnia</term> <note>Van Helmont’s term for chemistry, literally "the art of fire."</note>, those things were unknown to the Ancients. Since that fire and its various degrees are absent as a separator within us—and whatever is breathed out of us by the degree of our heat tends toward a "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum," the worthless dregs or ash remaining after a chemical reaction.</note>, unless it is prevented by *Blas* <note>Van Helmont’s term for a vital force or "pulse" that governs the movement of the stars and the functions of the body.</note> and *ferment* (as I taught above regarding the human *Blas*)—the origin of diseases can surely in no way be blamed on one or more of those three principles.

<margin>72.</margin> Finally, I deny that salt, sulfur, and Mercury are the universal principles of bodies. They did not exist before the composition of bodies, nor did they flow together to make a mixture; nor, finally, through the natural resolution of bodies at the end of their lives, have they ever appeared in nature. Instead, they are led out solely by the art of fire, and only from certain things. Insofar as the "seeds" of things are clothed in the material principle of water, and are strengthened by the energy of their own active power, they take on the properties partly of salt and partly of oil.

The Mercury of bodies, however, is nothing but a part of water that is not yet pregnant with the sufficient maturity of the active seed. Therefore, they exist nowhere by themselves, nor do they obtain the power of being foundational beginnings. This is because they do not have their natures or conditions from some prior existence, but partly from the disposition of the "seeds" flowing into the properties of the compound, and partly from the digestion and burning of the fire encountered during separation. For it is manifest that, by mutual transformation, reciprocally...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s critique of the Paracelsian "three principles" (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury). He is arguing that these substances are often created by the chemist's fire or biological processes like fermentation, rather than being the fundamental, pre-existing building blocks of all matter as previously claimed.</meta>

# ESSENCE: ON THE ARMY OF DISEASES #

<margin>73.</margin> They are made from one another. Therefore, these substances are the final products, not the primary ones, regardless of how they are considered. For all vegetables, as long as they are not woody, contain the "spirit of wine" <note>original: "spiritu vini," referring to alcohol</note>, insofar as the spirit of wine is drawn out of them once they are opened by fermentation. But from that same material, once it has become wood, the "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitae," a term for distilled spirits or brandy</note> is no longer drawn out. I say that the spirit of wine is created in vegetables through the chemist’s art—a spirit that was not in them before—arising from the disposition of the rot-prone sap and the sign of vinous fermentation. Therefore, the spirit of wine is not a "principle" of vegetables just because different plants agree in this one spirit and it can be drawn from each; rather, the spirit of wine has the nature of an effect and a product. Similarly, those three substances <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> are things "principled" <note>Resulting products rather than starting causes.</note>, not the "principles" themselves. For will blood lack salt during distillation because it has already secreted urine <note>original: "lotium"</note>, which Paracelsus calls the <margin>74.</margin> "salt of the blood" <note>original: "salem cruoris"</note>? And if salt is one of the "principles," then blood would surely be eternal in its foundation if it lacked a beginning, or something could exist out of mercury and sulfur alone without the principle of salt. This did not seem foreign to Paracelsus while he was struggling with his own doctrine of the "three firsts." In that work, he teaches that the blood and flesh of lepers are deprived of all salt. Thus, his own history of ulcers falls apart if the ulcers of lepers are spontaneous and not to be <margin>75.</margin> disregarded, yet exist without salt. For he wrongly distinguished the salt from a drink from the salt of the blood. Nor did he know the difference between the salt in the external fluid <note>original: "latice," here referring to bodily fluids or water</note> and the salt that is squeezed out of the blood through the torture of the fire during distillation. He was entirely ignorant of where the salt in urine came from, not even suspecting it was the salt consumed. Because the categories of digestion were unknown to him, natural science was obscured by shadows in Paracelsus; and through the ignorance of healers, the days of mortals are shortened, and cemeteries become crowded with mounds <note>original: "gibbosa coemiteria," literally "hunchbacked cemeteries," referring to the many fresh burial mounds caused by medical errors.</note>.

The "fifth essence" <term>quintessence</term> <note>A supposed fifth element or the purest part of a substance.</note> has also been investigated soberly until now, as if it were a glorious thing to have lazily subscribed to the commentaries of others and to have remained stuck in fabulous principles. Therefore, "essence" is called by various names. <margin>76.</margin> For it is most principally understood to refer to God, the most good and greatest, who is the

<column-break/>

true, immediate, and very essence of all things, from which the "being" of things flows and depends, inseparable in nature. However, "essence" used for the actual "being" of things, in the abstract, is the "life" in living things, or the soul. Otherwise, it is the "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or identity of a thing.</note>, because of which each thing is what it is. <margin>77.</margin> But "life" or "form" is not taken as an "essence" by the Chemists because, once the thing has died, it returns to nothing. Therefore, they considered a certain most excellent substance in which the whole "constitution" <term>crasis</term> <note>The specific mixture of qualities or humors that gives a substance its character.</note> and the "actualization" <term>entelechia</term> <note>A Greek philosophical term meaning the realization of potential or the soul of a thing.</note> of the thing resides. An example of this is the light oil in spices; when this is drawn away, the body of the spice remains as something unpleasant. Take Cinnamon, for example: once the oil is removed, it tastes like oak bark because of its astringency. Truly, in dyed things, the essence is the colored liquid extracted from the items. These substances, as they are more active, behave like the "life" or "form" toward the remaining mass. <margin>78.</margin> To such an extent that the name "essence" is clearly metaphorical.

For this reason, most things do not have an "essence" in this way, as I have demonstrated regarding mercury, crystal, stones, and homogeneous things. Then, finally, not rarely, there is greater power and energy in the whole thing than in the separated "essence." This is evident in the magnet <note>lodestone</note>, amber <note>original: "carabe"</note>, and so on. <margin>79.</margin> For many "simples" <note>Natural medicinal ingredients, usually plants.</note> lose their specific property through preparation, and even more through separation and fire. In the hoof of an Elk, or in bezoar stones <note>Stony concretions found in the stomachs of animals, thought to be universal antidotes.</note>, there is something that prefers to belong to the raw, simple state. However, the "forms" or "essences" of herbs refuse to be subject to the Artisan <note>the chemist</note>. For many things are just as effective whether the vegetative force (which they call the soul) has perished or whether it still exists. After they have completely dried out, some bring forth an essence; but many truly (especially water-pepper <note>original: "hydropiper"</note>) lose it. Therefore, however "essence" is taken, the name is improper, and "fifth" <note>referring to quintessence</note> is an unwise epithet. Since the essence they promise either is not equally in all things, nor does it obey the Artisan, or it cannot be drawn from everywhere. Indeed, under other circumstances, in the raw state of things, it laughs at such laborious efforts.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the "three principles" (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) and the "quintessence" are often artifacts of the distillation process rather than inherent building blocks of nature. He contends that the medicinal power of a substance often resides in its whole, natural form rather than in an extracted "essence."</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, quintessence, spirit of wine, distillation, entelechy, blood salt, bezoar stones, medical critique, chemical principles</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument that the "Three Principles" (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) are not the fundamental essences of nature. He is now moving into a discussion of fragrance, "seminal liquors," and how the body’s internal spirit—the Archeus—processes these substances.</meta>

-># THE THREE FIRST CHEMICAL PRINCIPLES ARE NOT THE ESSENCE OF DISEASES #<-

Nor does every fragrance generally reside in the "middle life" of a plant, but rather in the "ultimate life." For the flowers of Jasmine, Lily of the Valley, and others, lose their pleasant scent and medical virtues when they rot; they turn sour and never regain their former fragrance. In other cases, however, the fragrance resides in the middle life—those which preserve their scent through the process of rotting and release it when distilled, 
<margin>80.</margin>
such as roses. This matter deceived Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist who proposed that all things are made of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, and led him to believe that the essences of things rot in this way. Thus, being ignorant, he dictated that essences would remain safe forever in the lowest, manure-filled fields. He did not know that once the duties of the seeds are finished and dead, all things give themselves over to rest and finally seek again their first home in water; or at least, obeying a stronger incoming seed, they allow themselves to be led again into new colonies and new scenes. Indeed, there are many simple substances that find a fragrance in the depths of rot which they did not have before in their own species. Such are musk, civet <note>original: "zibetta," a musky secretion from the civet cat used in perfumery</note>, 
<margin>81.</margin>
ambergris <note>original: "Ambarum"</note>, certain dungs of animals, and rotting wood. Indeed, a variety of "muckiness" <note>original: "Fracedo," referring to the softness or ripeness of rotting fruit or organic matter</note> arises in them, from which the seeds draw fragrance for themselves and transplant it into a new generation. Therefore, if the fragrance is bound to the <term>balsam of the middle life</term> <note>Van Helmont's term for the preservative vital spirit within a substance</note> and is not overcome by rot through the separation of parts, it is more conveniently separated from the corrupted remains. Therefore, a chemical essence is not properly a "fifth essence" <note>original: "quinta," or quintessence</note>, since there are not four other elements in the concrete object, nor is it an extract of the "three principles"; but 
<margin>82.</margin>
it is the seminal part of the sulfur of the compound. I say "of the sulfur," because sulfur is the offspring of the efficient cause, and thus more "formal" <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" gives a thing its specific identity and function.</note>. For cinnamon, while it is without its fragrance, is indeed still cinnamon, just as a fetus or a fool are still humans. I, therefore, call the best part of a thing its <term>crasis</term> <note>original: "crasin," from Greek for "mixture," referring to the specific vital temperament or healthy constitution of a substance</note>, whether the fragrance smells or not. In non-fragrant herbs, however, I call their seminal liquor their *crasis*. I know for certain that from any plant or seed, and likewise from the trunk

<column-break/>

of some, a liquor can be extracted which contains the power of the seed. This liquor, although it is not fit for planting because the seed enclosed within it cannot endure a delay in the earth and evaporates, nevertheless blesses a plant of its own kind with wonderful fertility when poured at the root. 
<margin>83.</margin>
For the seminal liquor contains the *crasis* for propagation, and therefore it is truly essential; yet it is not commonly known, no, not even to the most experienced. Accordingly, I pity the processes of extracting "quintessences" as vain efforts. It is no wonder, indeed, if all the powers of the generated thing shine forth in the *crasis*. At the very least, scented oils, insofar as they are oils, resist our digestion and remain unconquered; they bring little help, since they only refresh us for a short space of time when taken internally for the sake of their scent. But when the oil of cinnamon (and so on) is mixed with its own <term>alkali salt</term> <note>A salt produced from the ashes of the same plant</note>, without any water, through an ingenious and hidden "circulation" of three months, and is entirely changed into a <term>volatile salt</term>, it truly expresses the essence of its simple nature within us and works its way into the very primary building blocks of our being. In other cases, where the medical power is hidden in scents (for strong and stubborn odors overcome our strengths and are scarcely conquered or digested by the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "internal chemist" or vital spirit that Van Helmont believed directed all bodily functions</note>, and thus act upon us in a troublesome way; for the Archeus labors much to destroy them and to impress its own odors upon the substance in which they exist), and especially if they are fermenting, even though they might promise comfort, they do not provide constant relief in healing because they do not persist long enough to penetrate the primary constituents. This is mostly because they easily collapse within themselves and degenerate spontaneously—even more so if they are subdued by our bodily faculties. In this way, musk and spices "die" if the *crasis* departs, even though the physical body remains intact; therefore, the *crasis* of a thing does not at all touch upon the dreamed-of "beginnings" <note>The Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> of things.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the true essence of a substance is its "crasis" (vital temperament) or seminal liquor, rather than the Paracelsian Three Principles. He explains how the body's Archeus struggles to digest raw oils and scents unless they are converted into a volatile salt through alchemical circulation.</summary>

After the more discerning of the healers had implored help in vain from elements, humors, and stars, and had called upon **Tartar** <note>In Helmontian medicine, a term for stony or calcified deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty crystals.</note>, as well as the supposed "principles" of the chemists, to their aid without success, they subsequently meditated (against the will of the Galenic Schools) that headaches, migraines, the pain left over from yesterday's debauchery, as well as vertigo, delirium, asthma, false pleurisies, spasms, cramps, excessive sexual desire, abdominal swelling of the womb, and even the furies of epilepsy, along with several other conditions seemingly distinct, beyond controversy owe their beginnings to gases and vapors. Wherefore, expanding the catalog with equal right to the book <term>On Winds</term> <note>original Greek: "περὶ φυσῶν" (*Peri Physon*), a Hippocratic treatise.</note> by Hippocrates, they poured out their investigations. That old man [Hippocrates] so consecrated all diseases to gases that he indiscriminately confused winds with the principles of life. The happier talents of the Schools therefore began not so much to investigate the nature and properties of gases, as to build further upon the given and conceded hypotheses of gases, and to construct the nature and causes of almost all diseases, and to dedicate them to gases, vapors, and exhalations climbing from below upwards, or thrust down headlong. But when they were unable to extricate themselves entirely from these difficulties, nor could such a firm building stand, resting on no foundation of solid inquiry, the thread of the undertaking was broken, as it were, by too much...

<meta>This page continues the new chapter "On Gases" (De Flatibus). Van Helmont is critiquing the traditional medical authorities—specifically Hippocrates, Galen, and Paracelsus—for their failure to understand the true nature of gas, which he considers a fundamental substance of life and chemistry.</meta>

->## ON GASES ##<-

...twisting. Indeed, Hippocrates constrained **flatus** <note>original: "flatum"; in this context, it refers to both intestinal gas and the "winds" or "spirits" believed to move through the body</note> into a category of either life, death, or even destruction; he wondered whether they were participants in these states and contained their causes, or whether they were stirred up from the heavens by the **Blas** <note>Helmont’s term for a "motive power" or vital pulsating force</note> of the stars—thus promising a mathematical analogy to the celestial orbits—or finally, whether they obeyed sublunary or voluntary laws. He essentially left the whole matter undecided. Consequently, he left the scientific method disrupted. He stood still because the necessity, experience, frequency, and perversity of diseases were not yet so great. For it was not yet known that the **vital spirits** had conceived the light of life, that they were the closest seats of the sensitive souls and of the forms of living beings, and thus contained the mixture <term>crasim</term> <note>The specific "mixture" or temperament of qualities that defines a substance</note> of the entire essence.

<margin>2.</margin> For no one at that time had learned that the matter of that **Gas** <note>Helmont famously coined the word "Gas," likely derived from the Greek "Chaos."</note> was water; thus, no one had yet dreamed that the vital spirit differs from the wind of the world in its entire element. Indeed, the **Schools** <note>Refers to the traditional university medical faculties following Galen and Aristotle</note> would have easily fallen into this pit of "flatulence" and remained there more stubbornly, had they not recognized the uselessness of their protections—purgatives and bloodletting—against these internal winds, and foreseen that they would be acting in vain without the help of those two types of remedies.

<margin>3.</margin> Galen, to be sure, had seen that oils and fats gradually exhale through the action of fire; he thought, therefore, that the winds within us were stirred up by melted fat or by the disorder of digestions, as he was unable to distinguish air, or wind,

<margin>4.</margin> from exhalation, from vapor, and from gas. The Galenic Schools, I say, have hitherto been ignorant of the difference between **Windy Gas** (which is merely air—that is, wind—moved by the *Blas* of the stars), **Fatty Gas**, **Dry Gas** (which is called "sublimated"), **Sooty Gas** (or endemic gas), and **Wild Gas** <note>original: "Gas sylvestre"; this is Helmont's term for carbon dioxide and other gases produced in fermentation that cannot be easily captured or condensed</note> (or the "uncontrollable" gas, which cannot be forced into a visible body).

<margin>5.</margin> Therefore, the darkness regarding natural things remained inexcusable for those ignorant of **Pyrotechnia** <note>The "Art of Fire," referring to early chemical or alchemical practice</note>. This art instructs us at what degree of heat watery substances fly off, and in what degree and order any fat evaporates; and finally, by what separation and by what **ferment** bodies

<column-break/>

depart from one another and rot; what each thing carries away with itself through **analysis**; and finally, by what means the mixtures of the **seeds** <note>Helmont's "Semina" or seeds are the internal blueprints that govern the development and function of matter</note> and the properties of the concrete object refer back to themselves. By this work, finally, everything within us—without the separation of parts—is disposed toward **diaphaeresis** <note>A term for the dissolution or breaking down of substances into their constituent parts</note>.

<margin>6.</margin> They had indeed heard of winds in the belly, and they noticed harmless **rumblings** <term>borborigmos</term> and painful **gripes** <term>tormina</term> <note>Severe, twisting intestinal pains</note> in the stomach and colon. In winter, they noted a plurality of winds, and because of this, they dreamed of an "icy phlegm" in the intestines and thought that warm remedies should be applied to cold diseases. In this, the Schools first entangle themselves when they hand down the origin of vapors and "windiness," and then intend to cure them and drive them out with "contrary" remedies (as they call them).

<margin>7.</margin> For they contradict themselves in their principles, their means, and their method. For if the "windiness" within us were vapors or exhalations, then surely a greater excitation of pains and gas, and a distension of the parts, would follow if warm remedies were used against the winds; this is because vapors must necessarily increase, and the torments would multiply, both because of the distensions and because of the sharpness of the winds.

<margin>8.</margin> And the whole **art of distilling** proves this. Even Paracelsus, though he was a Master of Pyrotechnia, was not immune to the whirlwind of these "winds." This is because he was ignorant of the nature of winds and air, the matter of vapors or gas (which is watery Gas), and their efficient causes, methods, and means—as well as the fact that their matter is water impregnated with a seed. Since he plainly despised the authorities of Philosophy and attempted to bind nature under his own **unlearned views** <note>original: "idiotifmum"; here implying a private, uneducated, or idiosyncratic system of thought</note>, he was also abandoned by the light of nature, by the permission of God, who everywhere makes such attempts come to nothing. No one ever reaches wisdom who thinks he has already arrived. For Paracelsus everywhere constantly persuades us that we ought to feel the diseases and defects of all things, because we are an "extract" of the entire universe in every way. We must, he says, express the universe as a son expresses his parent. Thus, he wants us to contain the winds and their varieties; he also wants our gripes to be equivalent to storms...

<summary>Van Helmont critiques Hippocrates and Galen for failing to understand the chemical nature of internal gases, introducing his own classification of five distinct types of "Gas." He argues that traditional medicine's use of heat to treat gas is logically flawed and critiques Paracelsus for viewing human illness as a mere reflection of macrocosmic weather patterns.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's critique of traditional theories regarding "winds" or gases in the human body. He specifically targets Paracelsus, who attempted to map the four cardinal winds of the macrocosm (the universe) onto the human anatomy (the microcosm).</meta>

->## ON GASES ##<-

...to correspond to the currents of the air. But I would not want men to depart even a fingernail's breadth from the majestic image of God, so that we might reflect the **macrocosm** <note>The "great world" or universe</note> rather than God in His image. For I believe that I am not a man merely to be subject to diseases, and thus reflect the "parts of the world" <note>original Hebrew: *pirke olam*</note> or the "world of separation" <note>original Hebrew: *holam hapiroud*</note>; rather, I know that I am subject to diseases to demonstrate a depraved and mortal nature, while I exist as a man for no other purpose than to represent the living image of God according to His good pleasure.

<margin>9.</margin>
Thus, that man <note>referring to the physician Paracelsus</note> divides **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> <note>Severe, twisting abdominal pains often associated with colic</note> fourfold, according to the four customary cardinal points of the winds. Among these, he places the North primarily in the loins, whose wind in its colic state would blow against the navel; in the navel, however, he places the South, which would blow in its diameter toward the back. Likewise, he disposed the East on the right side and the West on the left, and finally ascribed specific remedies to each of the winds, wrapped in **hieroglyphs** <note>Alchemical or symbolic characters</note> not yet understood by him. Alas! With what a dismal pledge and by what a ludicrous means did that man invade the sovereignty of healing! As if we were each indeed **microcosms** <note>A "little world"; the idea that man contains all the elements of the universe</note>! For at how dear a price does he sell us this idea of the macrocosm! And upon how meager an argument does he found his dreams!

<margin>10.</margin>
When in truth there are no winds in us, nor any matter of winds, except that which we breathe in and out. Otherwise, there is no flatulent **Gas** in us, except by one way, one house, and one passage: namely, from the stomach through the intestines, all the way to the anus. Paracelsus did indeed know some of these things—that winds in the womb, the **pleura** <note>the membrane surrounding the lungs</note>, the head, and the muscles were "old wives' tales"—and yet he wove even greater stories to compose these ridiculous cardinal points of the winds, which he could have transferred with better right to the womb than to the intestines.

<margin>11.</margin>
Which, with great pain, now twists itself to the left side of the abdomen, sometimes to the right, and besets either the navel or inclines itself backward toward the spine and loins. But he would have remained doubtful as to where he might find a fifth wind in the steep womb, and where a sixth, while the womb is carried straight

<column-break/>

upward. And therefore, although he may declaim to the point of boredom about the "star of the womb" in a specific book, he nevertheless drowsily neglected the cardinal points of the world in the wanderings of the womb—even though he seriously calls the womb a "world," albeit one smaller than the **microcosm**. But

<margin>12.</margin>
look here, Paracelsus! Suppose a few yards of intestine are distended by wind, and that wind is enclosed on both sides (for if it is not enclosed, it will neither cause pain nor tension, but will be evacuated of its own accord through its outlet); therefore, it can neither breathe nor be carried laterally in the manner of the winds. My question concerns the name, essence, origin, and remedy of that wind. Furthermore, since the **ileum** <note>the longest part of the small intestine</note> is perhaps distended forty times, as much from the back forward as by a lateral duct on both sides, in which specific twist of the intestine will the four cardinal winds have their position, name, and the property of that name? For in this way, in every single turn there would now be forty South winds, and as many North winds, and so on. If you place them in the twentieth turn, or in every single contortion of the bowel, you ought to have added a reason why they are not in the tenth or twelfth, if you wished faith to be given to you while dreaming these things. But truly, you were not a faithful **Aeolus** <note>The mythical Greek keeper of the winds</note> of those winds.

<margin>13.</margin>
Indeed, noticing that colic often produced contracted muscles of the hands—convulsions, I mean, as well as paralyses—you did not blush to say that winds are carried from the intestines through all the muscles and tendons. And you asserted this all the more licentiously because you find the **Schools** <note>The traditional university medical faculties following Galen</note> prone to every service of vapors and winds for perhaps all diseases. For as long as they could not find rest for themselves in the elements, temperaments, and humors (while the testimony of truth dictated otherwise within them), they sought in their confusion a way to find the cause of diseases through vapors and winds. For perhaps, while the humors themselves had deceived them, they hoped they could not be refuted through the invisible position of the winds. It was surely an invention of the impostor **Satan**, who, since he strives to be the "ape of God" <note>A common early modern phrase suggesting the Devil mimics God’s works to deceive</note>, pretends that the intellect of the credulous is owed to him through faith in things unseen.

<summary>Van Helmont rejects Paracelsus’s theory that intestinal gas follows the four cardinal winds of the universe, arguing instead that gas is a physical substance confined to the digestive tract. He accuses both Paracelsus and the traditional medical "Schools" of using invisible "winds" and "vapors" as a convenient excuse for diseases they do not understand.</summary>
