...and to suffice for all diseases, provided the belly makes its **rumblings** <term>borborygmi</term> <note>original: *borborignuos*; the gurgling or rumbling sounds of gas moving through the intestines</note> ring in the ears. And therefore, I absolutely ought to treat of gases. I truly pity Paracelsus’s great inconsistency on both sides; he both shuts out and cuts off the title of "Leader of Secrets" <note>original: *narchæ Arcanorum*</note> for those who believe him. For he did not know in this place that it is the property of any poison—even when administered under a friendly appearance, such as a purgative—to stir up the **internal governing spirit** <term>Archeus</term> <note>Van Helmont’s term for the vital principle that directs the functions of an organ</note> and excite its **vital motion** <term>Blas</term> <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the rhythmic, active force or pulse of life within the body</note>, according to the Aphorism: <margin>14.</margin> *A convulsion after taking hellebore is deadly.* <note>original Latin: *Spasimus post helleborum lethalis*; a reference to Hippocrates' Aphorisms regarding the dangerous effects of powerful purgatives</note> And he did not know that **colic**, which besides the usual **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> arising from acid, contains moreover the stain of poison and is the author of the convulsion—even if, meanwhile, the wind is not carried outside the **ileum** <note>The final section of the small intestine</note>.

Thus a man, dying with the total extinction of his strengths, leaves his corpse in a state of general **tetanus**, stretched out on both sides; but when he is snatched away by a violent death, his corpse is flaccid. Whence I learned that life is a certain sensation and motion, or *Blas*, <margin>15.</margin> in the flesh, besides the voluntary motion. That life, surely, perceiving poisons and death along with its own extinction, stretches itself out <margin>16.</margin> on both sides when dying. For the life of the muscles still remains surviving—which is most powerful in insects, so much so that even when the head is torn off, flies still fly away. And in a woman long dead, not rarely has the womb cast forth its fetus. Therefore, every convulsion of the muscles—whether from colic, or from taking a laxative poison, or another cause—is not from voluntary motion: but from the natural sensation and motion of the muscles. It is not, however, because gas stretching the intestines effectively stretches the muscles as well, as I have abundantly confirmed in my book *On the Stone* <note>original: *lib. de Lithiafi*</note>, in the treatise *On Sense and Sensation*.

<margin>17.</margin> Insane, therefore, is the decree: *"This is a carminative. This drives out winds; that indeed dissipates gas."* As if the winds departed by means of **charms** or **songs** <note>original: *carmina*; Van Helmont is mocking the etymology of "carminative," which comes from *carmen* (song/charm), suggesting physicians thought they could "sing" the gas away</note>. Physicians must swear off these things. For if the passages and exits are open, the wind in no way needs external help, nor any foreign pusher, to get out. Indeed, what is even more: the griping pains do not always cease, even if the exit of gases is free. Otherwise, if the way is without impediment, the gas—whether the physician wills it or not—will find it: since there is only one continuous path through the intestines.

Those remedies that "drive out" gas ought to have some medium, just as a **piston** <term>pistillum</term> <note>original: *pistillum*; likely referring to a plunger or the mechanism of a syringe/enema</note> pushes forward the contents of enemas. But that piston, in order to properly drive out gas, would have to correspond exactly to the passage of the intestines, both in the narrow and the thicker parts; and moreover, it would need to have its own pushing *Blas*. And yet, enclosed wind hurts less as long as it stays quiet. Thus every "pushing" remedy would necessarily increase the griping pains; and so nature indicates that we must abstain from things that drive out gas.

But perhaps they imagine that "carminatives" possess the power of a whip? And that gases are like cattle? Or do they perhaps admit that they and their carminatives lack an adequate piston? Or maybe carminatives have a voice like one driving away cattle, and the gas listens to the encouragement of the carminative? I know indeed that the <margin>19.</margin> Schools <note>The traditional medical universities</note> are ignorant of the power, property, causes, and manner of both the griping pains and the remedies. For winds are not to be "driven out," nor finally "dissipated." For the latter is impossible, and the former contains a childish fiction. Nor are gases to be restrained by any "charm" <note>original: *carmine*</note> by an honest man, though its name remains sacred in the Schools to this day.

<margin>20.</margin> Gases are not stirred up internally in the womb, because the womb lacks "flatulent" matter, and its digestion is not suited to creating gases. Externally, however, air hardly enters the womb; for lest it suffer a vacuum, its membrane collapses entirely, moist and flaccid. Thus, the entrance is closed to breathing air of its own accord, unless it is injected by force through an instrument. Finally, <margin>21.</margin> external winds do not borrow power from the mouth to enter unusual regions, nor to pierce through the **pleura** <note>The membrane surrounding the lungs</note> with force, and between this and the **intercostal muscles**, stir up a "flatulent" **pleurisy**, and then presently tear the pleura from the ribs, and...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that abdominal pains and spasms are caused by the vital "Blas" (motion) of the Archeus reacting to irritants, rather than the physical pressure of gas. He mocks the "carminative" remedies of traditional medicine as superstitious "charms" that lack any physical mechanism to actually expel gas.</summary>

...that they might create the inflammation of pleurisy. <note>Pleurisy is an inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs.</note>
<margin>22.</margin> Because air has no way to get there; indeed, if it reached that point, it has no **vital motion** <term>Blas</term> <note>original: *Blas*; Van Helmont’s term for the active, rhythmic force of life</note> behind it that could cause any harm. And by whatever way it might have entered, it would have been breathed out before it could do damage. Furthermore, internal gases are not produced in those parts, as both the material from which they would be made and the efficient cause are lacking.
<margin>23.</margin> It is likewise a fiction similar to an old wives' tale that external wind, or a draft of air, could pierce the skin—however porous it may be—as well as the fleshy membrane and the muscles beneath it. This follows the shameful reasoning of doctors who say: "He recently caught a wind, and therefore his parts are unwell."
<margin>24.</margin> I have often heard this assigned as the cause for almost all diseases, from the head down to the heel, much to my embarrassment. The "intemperance of the air" is blamed for defects of the head, eyes, ears, teeth, and throat. For hoarseness, coughs, and all "deflections" <note>original: *defluxiones*; refers to the "catarrhs" or humors traditionally thought to flow from the brain</note>, indigestion, fevers, and even **Pandora’s Box** <note>A mythological reference to the source of all human miseries</note>, air has been held responsible. And this is not just through the touch of cold as an external cause, but as a wind swallowed within and improperly detained there. I shall speak of these elsewhere. For now, our discourse concerns our own internal gases.
<margin>25.</margin> I do grant that unusual cold (acting as a servant of death) can affect some noble or subservient part of the body, insofar as it disturbs its final digestion. From this, the excrements of similar parts, pains, and even various types of abscesses may follow. But in these cases, the power of the cold is only an external, occasional cause; it indicates a need for precaution, but it does not indicate the cure or the quality of the remedy.
<margin>26.</margin> Therefore, let the **trifles of the Schools** <note>original: *Scholarum nugæ*; Van Helmont’s frequent dismissal of traditional university medical teachings</note> be gone. If anyone is to rightly perform the duty of a Physician, he must first know what wind is, and then what **gas** <term>Gas</term> <note>Van Helmont coined the word "Gas" to describe the invisible vapors distinct from ordinary air</note> is, where it comes from, and why it causes pain. Then
<margin>27.</margin> the remedy will be easy for him. Once the cause of the gases is known, one must take care that their source does not turn into Gas. For Gas, once it is created, easily makes a way for itself. But if not—and if the intestine is blocked lower down by a harder obstacle—that obstacle must be loosened. But where there is no blockage of excrement, and yet the **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> <note>Severe, twisting abdominal pains or cramps</note> per-

<column-break/>

-sist, will those things that "drive out winds" <note>original: *ventos pellunt*; referring to carminative medicines</note> not be in vain? And is it not foolish to use things that "disperse" them? If it is not the gas itself, but the matter from which the intestines are constricted—and the intestines themselves that generate the gas—should that not be "weeded out"? I say the cure should not be directed at the gas produced, but at the cause that produces it.
<margin>28.</margin> I see, therefore, that the remedies of dill, caraway, anise, cumin, wild carrot, etc., were not discovered by the Schools (who are ignorant of the causes of griping pains), but became known through divine mercy to the little ones and the poor. The Schools then "begged" <note>original: *mendicarunt*; suggests the academics took folk knowledge and claimed it as their own</note> these from them, as they did many other experiments. Indeed, the origin, essence, matter, property, process, and history of gases have remained hidden from the Schools. Finally, there is no such thing as **volvulus** <note>A twisting of the intestine</note>, **Ileon** <note>Iliac passion, a severe bowel obstruction</note>, or that which bears the barbarian name **Misere-mei** <note>original: *miserere mei*; Latin for "have mercy on me," a historical name for a lethal intestinal blockage</note>, as some sort of twisting or "apogee" of the small intestine.
<margin>29.</margin> For besides the fact that it would be a permanent and necessarily recurring evil, anatomy itself refutes it. Anatomy shows that the intestine is clothed by the **mesentery** <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>—that is, its external covering, its third garment and overcoat—and is bound by that mesentery to the loins so that it hangs there. Therefore, once that bond was broken and the partnership with the mesentery rejected, there would be no further hope of returning the intestines to their original "case" from which they had freed themselves by breaking their prison. Thus, an evil restored by mere chance would necessarily recur soon after, and would always rush toward a worse state. Finally, through the whole tract of the intestine, there would then be no nutrition through the veins and no attraction of **chyle** <term>chyli</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food that is absorbed into the blood</note> into the life-force; yet, meanwhile, this disease often yields to a simple remedy. For if the intestine were twisted beyond its usual coils, what would be that mover? Or what would be the "torturer" that twists it? From the outside, it has none and fears none, because the intestine is covered by the smooth **omentum** <note>A fatty layer of tissue hanging over the intestines</note> and the simple membrane of the abdomen. From the inside, it can only be blocked by excrement (for this, and nothing else, can happen to it).
<margin>30.</margin> Thus the **ileum** <note>The final part of the small intestine</note> is obstructed (where excrement does not yet usually harden) by unusual waste; it is not, however, twisted or loosened from its mesentery casing. And so...

# ON GASES

<page-num>418</page-num>
<header>->ON GASES<-</header>

While the academic Schools are stunned, this disease remains unknown to them in both its causes and its nature. I remember, when I was a young man in Antwerp, a certain Thomas Balbani who was dying of **Ileus** <note>original: *Ileò*; a painful bowel obstruction</note>. Within a week, he had offered eighty thousand Flemish pounds to anyone who could cure him, sending out messengers in every direction. The Antwerp physicians, following the decrees of the Schools, haughtily blamed an "involved intestine"—one twisted like a **Gordian knot** <note>A legendary impossible knot; used here to describe a complex blockage</note>. This was merely an excuse for their ignorance, providing no remedy to the patient. But **Anatomy** <note>original: *Anatome*; here referring to the autopsy</note> revealed their deception and gross 
<margin>31.</margin> ignorance. It was found that hardened dung had become stuck in the small intestine, sixteen finger-widths above the **cecum** <term>monoculum</term> <note>Literally the "one-eye," an early anatomical term for the cecum, where the small and large intestines meet</note>, and much loose waste was floating above it through the **ileum** <note>The final section of the small intestine</note>. It is indeed rare for waste to harden in the small intestine. Because of this, I have never since allowed anyone to perish from this (wrongly named) condition. I have given them several lead musket balls to drink, so that by their weight alone they might push forward that hardened excrement. Indeed, the more and larger the balls swallowed, the safer and swifter the cure follows—provided the patient stands, walks, or is led about with the abdomen held upright. 

Now, I shall further relate the history of gases, though it be 
<margin>32.</margin> a foul one. Truly, every gas is contained within the stomach and the intestines, just as winds exist only in the air, and not beneath water or earth. The birth of a gas requires a certain stomach acid, though not the ordinary ferment of digestion. Because this acid is found nowhere else but in the aforementioned places, gas is generated nowhere else, as will be shown hereafter. 

Finally, every gas is stirred up either from undigested food, from the **chyme** <note>original: *cremore*; the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>, from the waste of food, or from the degenerating "spermatic" nourishment of the 
<margin>33.</margin> intestines. There are thus four types of internal gas within us; a fifth is the external **Tympanias** <note>A type of dropsy or swelling where the abdomen is stretched tight like a drum (tympanum)</note>, which is trapped outside the intestines. A sixth is natural and necessary, or ordinary. A seventh is poisonous, residing in the body's general condition. None of these, however, are vapor or watery breath, for vapor, by its own nature and consistency, immediately and easily turns back into water. 
<margin>34.</margin> Furthermore, none of these gases are "air" or "wind." Since wind (or air) is not part of the composition of solid bodies, as I have proven at great length, it 
<margin>35.</margin> follows that every gas within us is **Wild Gas** <term>Gas sylvestre</term> <note>Van Helmont’s famous term for "gas," derived from the Latin for "wild" or "of the forest," because it cannot be contained or easily condensed</note>, stirred up during digestion from food, drink, and waste. 

One type exists in the stomach and is called a **belch** <term>ructus</term>. It can be 
<margin>36.</margin> tasteless, sour, sharp, fatty-smelling, foul, or "specific." I call it "specific" when it carries the scent of undigested food; thus garlic, radish, and similar things provide their own flavors in a belch. A tasteless or sour belch comes from digested chyme that has been stirred up by the stomach’s weakness. A sharp belch—such as occurs in **heartburn** <note>original: *Orexi*; referring to acid reflux or sour appetite</note>—and fatty-smelling ones are made from foods that have degenerated into a near-fecal nature. 

There is also another gas, stirred up in the small intestines by a defect of the **bile ferment** <note>original: *fermenti fellei*; the "gall" or bile thought to act as a ferment in the lower gut</note>. It is either tasteless, harsh, sharp, bitter, fecal, corpse-like, or rotten, according to the variety of the material and the power of the bile ferment. This gas is called a **fart** <term>peditus</term>, and it never ascends through the **pylorus** <note>The valve opening from the stomach into the intestine</note> into the stomach. If it is rotten or fatty-smelling, it indicates a premature fecal ferment that has "reaped another's harvest" <note>An idiom meaning it has interfered with a process where it doesn't belong</note>. 

There are, moreover, two more gases in us. One is entirely abnormal, held and born both in the intestines and throughout the whole body’s habit. For from a poisonous ferment and external fecal matter, a certain gas arises in the final digestion of the "similar parts" <note>The basic tissues of the body, like muscle or bone</note>. Truly, when poison is taken, bodies swell and puff up. For an acid corruption enters the flesh in an abnormal way; the solid part dies, the indwelling vital spirit is extinguished, and the part is affected by the toxic poison. From this comes a fecal, corpse-like gas, abominable to our nature. In this way, the immediate nourishment of the solid parts is changed into **Wild Gas**, and the whole body (or the specifically affected part) swells. 
<margin>37.</margin> There is also another, tasteless gas in the **ileum** <note>small intestine</note>, which is natural and a useful product...

# ON GASES

...namely, that it is an ordinary and natural thing. And since it occurs in many people and those oppressed by great hunger, I concluded that this tasteless gas was born from the well-disposed, immediate nourishment of that intestine itself. Otherwise, it would be impossible in **celiac passion** <note>original: "coeliaca"; a chronic diarrheal condition, now known as celiac disease</note> and other dissolutions of the belly for such sudden and rapid excretions to occur, if the **Ileum** <note>the final and longest segment of the small intestine</note>, which is closed and collapsed when empty, did not somehow stay open perpetually through the presence of natural gas. This, I say, the academic Schools have never investigated. To which I will add even greater anxieties, unless <margin>38.</margin> the Ileum is naturally and moderately swollen with wind at all times. For otherwise, the labor of certain fibers in the intestines would seem futile if the Ileum did not swell moderately with continuous gas. 

Indeed, there was a boy who suffered from a monstrous hernia at his navel (for his whole navel was transparent like a thin outer skin, extending to the width of half a palm). This clearly monstrous boy, whenever he suffered from **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> <note>original: "tormina"; acute, twisting abdominal pain or colic</note>, allowed us to behold a "storm" within the Ileum. It reached the point where that intestine, as if walking over itself, seemed to boil, twist, and be convulsed. This happened especially whenever new griping pains attacked him. Since these things occurred during his bouts of pain, I also wished to contemplate the economy of the intestines during health, to see what it was like. And then I observed a clearly different, successive movement by which the intestines exercised themselves. For whenever something was transmitted from above toward the anus (it was the consistency of a thin syrup and dark yellow), the intestine contracted with its transverse fibers as if it were being closed off entirely there, pushing the waste down below it. This happened by a successive contraction of the transverse fibers, no different than how a **lute-player** <note>original: "fidicen"; a player of a stringed instrument</note> opens finger after finger and relaxes the previous one. To that extent, it propelled the waste along with the gas, but the gas immediately moved back to its original place. It is truly worthy of great admiration that, by God’s providence, the internal parts do not rest but work thus without our feeling it and without ceasing, even 

<column-break/>

while we sleep. Finally, I observed that as long as the boy lay on his right side, the transverse fibers in the intestine on that same side compressed themselves to push the waste upward into the lower part; yet the fibers of the downward intestine were not working or compressed at all. Thus I saw that gas is not continuously propelled through the Ileum to the anus along with the waste, but rather it bounces back and retreats to the parts of the Ileum that reopen immediately after the waste is moved away. 

From this I gathered that gas of this kind is natural and useful, and not at all burdensome. For this closing of the Ileum is extremely precise before anything thin and slippery can be propelled upward. Having seen this, <margin>39.</margin> I soon concluded: first, that in the celiac passion, it is not only the digestive power that errs because of a corruption of the failing **ferment** <term>fermentum</term> <note>Van Helmont’s term for the vital agents or catalysts that drive biological processes</note>, but also the retentive power of the **Pylorus** <note>the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</note>; and furthermore, that the propulsive power of the intestines then rages with a symptomatic error. 

Second, I concluded that a certain amount of gas is natural to the Ileum, excited by its own **spermatic** <note>Referring to the foundational, life-giving "seeds" or vital blueprints of the tissue</note> nourishment, and thus arising from the **sixth digestion** <note>Van Helmont's system of six stages of digestion, the sixth being the final stage where nutrients become part of the living tissue</note> of that intestine, without stench, sharpness, or discomfort. And thus it maintains itself in a moderate quantity. <margin>40.</margin> However, whatever part of this gas exceeds the proper amount as a superfluity is soon expelled. Thus a fault in the quantity reveals itself spontaneously and is easily banished. <margin>41.</margin> It comes from a superfluity, yet it neither hurts nor bites. 

But if gases are stirred up from foods that are spoiled in themselves, or imbued with a spoiled ferment during digestion, they cause pain by their sharpness and "exotic" impression; and far more powerfully if the intestines are convulsed, especially where a tenacious **mucilage** <note>thick, sticky mucus</note>—the mother of griping pains—is imbued with a spoiled ferment and clings stubbornly somewhere. To propel this (usually in vain), the intestines compress, convulse, and wrinkle themselves. <margin>42.</margin> I call the cause of these massive griping pains a "contracture" whenever the intestine contracts not just transversely or in oblique circles, but entirely along its length; especially because contractures through the transverse and oblique fibers [occur]...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s anatomical and physiological critique of the "Schools" (traditional Galenic medicine). Having previously discussed the natural presence of gas in the small intestine (the Ileum), he now transitions into a critique of Galen's anatomical accuracy compared to Vesalius, before defining the different types of "stercoreous" (fecal) ferments and gases produced in the lower digestive tract.</meta>

# ON GASES

...whether they be daily, natural, and painless. 
<margin>43.</margin> **Galen**, triumphant in his work *On the Use of the Parts*, and held in high regard by the academic Schools, is shown by **Vesalius** in 116 places—or rather, errors—to have never actually seen the dissection of a human body. Just as the Schools will never wash away those factual demonstrations of that great Anatomist <note>referring to Andreas Vesalius, the 16th-century physician who revolutionized anatomy by practicing human dissection</note>: so I maintain that the principal uses of the parts—the targets or "delights" of the formative power—remain untouched and unexamined, but hitherto unknown. Indeed, since Galen, they have seen clearly enough that the straight, oblique, and transverse fibers of the intestine are effective for the propulsion of excrement; yet they did not know in what direction and how each of these fibers bent themselves in their respective duties. For those who have erred rashly by writing at length about the **choroid plexus** <note>a network of blood vessels in the brain</note>, the playful motions of the lung, and the obsolete "uses" of the pulses, have lazily passed over the true service of the pulses and the intestines.

Thus far I have determined the nature of the belch and the fart. Likewise, I have defined the irregular gas found throughout the body, and the natural, required gas of the **Ileum** <note>the final section of the small intestine</note>. For I have never seen a dissected corpse that did not present an Ileum swollen with gas to the onlookers. Now, furthermore, I shall proceed to the gases of **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> <note>original: "tormina"; acute, twisting abdominal pain or colic</note>, which are the authors of diseases and death. In the third place is the gas generated in the thicker intestines, from the **cecum** <note>original: "caeco"; the pouch at the beginning of the large intestine</note> onwards. 
<margin>44.</margin> The Schools truly attended to no other gas except this one, as if gases were only conceived in the Rectum and the Colon. Therefore, they also called the disease of gases "Colic," and they distinguished it strictly into the colic of the colon and of the stomach, into the "sandy" and the "windy," and similar shameful confusions. 

This third type of gas, therefore, arises from a **stercoreous** <note>fecal</note> and putrefactive **ferment** <note>Van Helmont used "ferment" to describe the chemical catalysts of digestion, similar to our modern concept of enzymes or bacteria</note>. It is twofold: namely, from food already putrefied by the stercoreous ferment; and from "spermatic" nourishment that has degenerated, turned cadaverous, and has moreover been turned to dung. For this is by far the most foul-smelling of all. Finally, there is a "foreign" gas, which although it may not act as the cause of griping pains, is nevertheless often a subsequent effect of them; it is generally worse than **dropsy** <note>swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and is called **Tympany** <term>Tympanias</term> <note>a condition where the abdomen is stretched tight and sounds like a drum (tympanum) when tapped, due to gas</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>45.</margin> Now, I call it a "stercoreous ferment" whether it is produced outside the intestine, or has its seat within the **cecum** <note>original: "caeco"</note>, where the excrements of food begin to rot under a specific difference of living things; there they borrow the impression of the stercoreous ferment according to their own species. Nor indeed is this idea of a ferment an idle or dreamed-up fiction, for it produces a specific diversity in both cases: otherwise, there can be no transmutation of things without a peculiar ferment. 

<margin>46.</margin> In this ferment, therefore, oily substances are volatilized, and an inflammable exhalation is excited from the rotting matter. For this reason, the **chemists** <term>chymici</term> <note>early chemists or alchemists</note> subject everything to putrefaction first, so that things which would otherwise remain in the dregs—heavy, hidden, and closed off—might be raised up together with the wateriness of the substance. For meats, eggs, broths, and whatever things spontaneously turn to "carrion" <note>original: "cadaverantur"</note>, produce the most foul-smelling excrements and gases. Thus **Ambergris** <note>original: "Ambarum"</note>, Musk, **Civet** <note>original: "Zibetta"</note>, and spices of that sort—because in their origin they are partly from animal flesh, and because they once obtained the stercoreous ferment of that species—are then easily subdued again by our own ferment and produce the most foul-smelling excrements and gases. 

<margin>47.</margin> Under this heading also fall the excrements and gases which are drawn out by laxatives. Because these are already dripping immediately from a transmuted "corpse" (the food being broken down), they are by far the most putrid—both because of the putrefactive ferment of the laxative "poison," and because of the location in the intestine, quite apart from the inherent horror of the cadaverous matter itself. 

<margin>48.</margin> And so even from this, it is clear that there is some stercoreous ferment in living things: for besides the property of its own species, it still preserves within itself as many diversities as there are receiving objects. This is especially true because dung is not the spontaneous rot of things, nor an artificial putrefaction, but is something determined and specific. The energy of this process, since it does not proceed merely from the food itself, must have an external "author" <note>a source or catalyst</note>, always operating with the same symbol, in the same way, and with the same character. This is most true because the impression follows the **disposition**...

# ON GASES

...not only the healthy state of its ferment, but also the diseased state. This is clearly evident from what follows: a belch, or the original gas in the stomach, as well as the gas of the **Ileum** <note>the final part of the small intestine</note>, will extinguish a candle's flame. 
<margin>49.</margin> However, fecal gas <note>original: "stercoreus flatus"</note>, which is formed in the final intestines and erupts through the anus, is ignited when passed through a candle flame; as it flies through, it catches fire and displays a multicolored flame, like a rainbow. But the gas formed in the Ileum, or the thin intestines, is never flammable; it is often odorless unless it carries a mixture of something else with it, and not infrequently it is sharp, piercing, and stinging in the anus.

Therefore, the gases within us differ in their matter, form, location, ferment, and properties—and thus in their entire species. Gases have their own generic and specific varieties no less than the bodies from which they originate. For gases are by no means mere air. Indeed, gases are distinguished not only by the matter from which they come, but also by the ferment and the "seed" of the gas. To this point belong the things I have taught regarding the origin of **Gas** <term>Van Helmont's coined term for "wild spirit," from which the modern word gas originates</term>, or the **wild spirit** <note>original: "spiritus sylvestris"</note>, which would otherwise remain in its former solid state unless, by the addition of the local ferment and the drawing in of the seed of acidity, it is transformed into gas.

I shall repeat here the generic differences of the gases generated within us, specified by their ferments and the properties of the things from which they arise. Here is the **Schema** <note>The following list serves as Van Helmont's classification system</note>. There are two anomalous gases in us: one is ordinary, natural, and necessary in the Ileum. The other is entirely pestiferous and irregular; having taken in a poison, or having a poison born within, it usually swells the entire habit of the body into a tumor. Then there are four gases in the stomach and intestines. First, there is one of the stomach, which is the belch. This is either **specific**, from undigested food that is hard and persistent; another is **tasteless**, born from nearly digested chyme but caused by a weakness of digestion; the third is **acid**, from digested but hindered chyme; the fourth belch is **bitter**, produced by an irritated ferment of that location. The second gas is that of the Ileum, which has several varieties within itself. Of these,

<column-break/>

the first contains the **fart** <note>original: "peditum"</note>, arising from an abundance of the aforementioned natural gas. The second is **bitter**, which breaks forth from foreign and poorly digested feces; it has something of the premature fecal ferment about it. Next follows the gas of the **colon**, arising from foods not entirely freed from their stomach acid, but corrupted prematurely by the arrival of fecal matter. There is also the **fecal gas**, which is cadaverous, resulting from the resolution and putrefaction of the living and vital nourishment of the solid parts. 
<margin>51.</margin> Finally, outside the channels of the intestine, there is the gas of **Tympanites** <note>abdominal bloating</note>, arising from a disease-causing agent between the outer curve of the intestine and the inner hollow of the **peritoneum** <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. This disease-causing agent has a localized property, though a milder one. The gas generated here is not made of disease-causing matter itself; rather, it is the product of it. It is of the same matter as the natural and ordinary gas of the Ileum—that is, from the immediate nourishment of the intestine. However, it is fatal, both due to a poisonous cause or a radical disease, and by reason of its location, because the resulting disease increases without limit and finally suffocates the patient, 
<margin>52.</margin> just like **Ascites** <note>a condition where fluid collects in spaces within the abdomen</note>.

Having finished the Schema, you will observe that the matter from which gas is made is that solid substance upon which the ferment operates. Furthermore, whoever strives to drive away gas by "propulsion" or "discussion" <note>medical terms for forcing gas out or breaking it up</note>, and thus thinks to overcome the disease, does not remove the cause, but only treats the final effect. To make this more clearly visible to the eye, let us suppose three brothers, nourished on the same food and drink. One of them produces almost no gas. The second, being weaker, produces many tasteless and occasionally acid belches. The third, suffering from an imbalance of the intestines, makes many farts. 
<margin>53.</margin> From this it becomes especially conspicuous that gases are not made from "flatulent foods"—the use of which is so strictly forbidden in the dietetics of the Schools. Rather, just as satiety usually causes more gas than sobriety allows, it follows that the "baggage" is a burden; and a burden presupposes labor, or rather, a weakness of the digestive power. Thus, tart apples, if they are roasted, produce the most gas...

# ON GASES
### Iii 2
<meta>catchword: Belching</meta>

...properties, changes, and defects of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; here Helmont refers to the reproductive drive or the "spirit" associated with the spleen, which he believed governed sexual function</note>, since this is not yet well-known in the Schools <note>the traditional universities following Galen and Aristotle</note>, I will teach concerning the Spleen in its proper place. Here it is enough to have separated the matter, or the power of Venus, from gases. Therefore, a weak digestion produces more gases, which a stronger digestion does not find, even when examining individual things more curiously and transforming them more robustly. <margin>61.</margin> For a straying ferment <note>a "ferment" in Helmont’s chemistry is a transformative agent, like an enzyme</note> draws out of a thing that which is not in it materially, but only potentially. That is, Gas arises from an error of the ferment, which has been alienated during digestion. Truly, gases are not led out of matter as if they had pre-existed there in a solid or clotted state; nor do they come from digestion itself as a primary cause (in the way heat ordinarily draws vapors from water). Rather, they arise because a certain diminished disposition of the ferment occurs during digestion, whence the digestive spirit drives out the gas as an unsuitable guest, as if the *Archeus* <note>the internal "master-workman" or vital force of an organ</note> were correcting the error of the ferment. <margin>62.</margin> Wherefore the resulting indisposition of the matter is prone to change into *Wild Gas* <note>original: "Gas sylvestre"; Helmont’s term for carbon dioxide and other non-condensable gases</note>. Take this example: *Sal ammoniac* <note>ammonium chloride</note> and *Aqua Chrysulca* <note>literally "gold-dissolving water," likely a type of strong acid like nitric acid</note>, which can each be distilled by themselves and endure heat; but if they are joined and become warm, they cannot help but be immediately transformed into *Wild Gas*, or an uncontainable vapor. So much so that if the vessel is perfectly closed—even if it is very strong and large—it will nonetheless burst apart, even in the cold. Similarly, *Saltpeter* <note>potassium nitrate</note> melts in a glowing fire, is cold to the touch, and is a remedy for quinsy <note>a severe sore throat</note>; yet if charcoal is added, both are immediately consumed and fly off into *Flaming Gas* <note>original: "Gas flammeum"</note>. For a *Donkey* and a *Beast of Burden* do not "turn into" a *mule*; rather, the seminal beginnings of both, when joined, produce the mule. In this way, many things which were not materially present before are made anew through additions, ferments, digestions, errors, and alterations. And those things which, under the first ferments, were not materially flatulent, because they were not fully digested and were thus sent away as excrement, when they endure another subsequent ferment, <margin>63.</margin> they pass into inordinate gases. Thus, gas does not pre-exist in foods, and much less

<column-break/>

in the chyme <note>original: "cremore"; the creamy semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>; rather, it is a certain new and monstrous generation, arising from the mixed seeds of things, or from matter improperly transformed when subjected to the action of another ferment. This will be more clearly evident regarding digestions. For in this way, a weaker stomach causes food to putrefy before or during the formation of *chyle* <note>the milky fluid of digestion</note>, and it produces frequent belches, even those smelling of burnt fat <note>original: "nidorosos"</note>, as occurs in fevers. In such cases, frequent belching bursts forth from an empty stomach, which is unusual in healthy people. In this way, putrefaction carries off the color of roses, together with their aroma and water, during distillation—things which otherwise are not raised by the same heat. In the intestines, similarly, there is a specific alienation of the ferments and of the putrefied matter, and specific stages under which gases are generated and break out. <margin>64.</margin> For as long as a grape is enclosed on all sides in its skin, it dries out more quickly, or rots, or changes into a raisin, rather than emitting gas; but if the skin of the grape is damaged even a little, immediately from that wound, a certain preceding ferment of putrefaction falls in, from which it does not thereafter cease to belch out *Wild Gas*, as long as the heat of the boiling ferment lasts; or, at least, until the wine is perfected from the juice of the grape. <margin>65.</margin> For just as flour differs from fermented dough, and a mass of dough differs from bread: so does wine differ from the juice of grapes. And just as flour, if it is cooked, does not produce gas, but once fermented, it belches out gas spontaneously: so foods do not contain gas by their own nature, but the ferments draw it out. It is truly a wonder that the Schools have hitherto perceived nothing of these things, and written nothing; but have handed everything down through the ages as being under the command of heat alone. Furthermore, concerning the properties of the *Gas of must* <note>unfermented grape juice</note> and the wild spirit, I have said enough elsewhere. Nor should it be seen as troublesome that I have brought over to this discussion of gases those things which I have written elsewhere regarding ferments, digestions, and the "crossing over into another’s harvest" <note>a metaphor for one organ's process interfering with another</note>, and the morbid transplantations born therefrom. <margin>66.</margin> A very weak stomach, therefore, gives tasteless belches; one that is less weak gives acidic ones; a corrupt one gives those smelling of burnt fat, bitter, and sharp. But a stronger stomach rightly prepares *well-juiced* foods <note>original: "enchymos"</note>, though not necessarily *onions, garlic, or radishes*, etc.

He uses chemical examples like gunpowder and biological examples like fermenting grapes to show how gas is produced by the interaction of substances.</summary>

Belches, therefore, testify to a certain weakness, and for that reason, they carry the flavors of the foods eaten. However, under the heavy burden of many rich foods <note>original: "enchymi"; referring to foods full of juices</note>, harsh <note>original: "pontici"; an astringent, tart flavor</note> belches come forth, and even reeking ones <note>original: "nidorosi"; smelling like burnt fat or decaying meat</note>, especially if the foods begin to decay like a corpse. This harshness, stirred up by an exasperated ferment, <margin>67.</margin> produces various types of appetite <note>original: "Orexim"</note>. Furthermore, take note of an example showing that gases are generated even from things that are not naturally flatulent. Distilled vinegar, while it dissolves "crab stones" <note>calcium carbonate deposits found in crayfish, used historically as an antacid</note>, or strong acid <note>original: "chrysulca"; literally "gold-washer," likely nitric acid or aqua regia</note> dissolving silver: a "wild spirit" <note>original: "spiritus sylvester"; Van Helmont’s term for carbon dioxide</note> is belched out. Roasting a sour apple stirs up a great deal of gas; but this does not happen if it is allowed to sweeten through ripening on the tree. If, therefore, gas had been materially present in that same apple, it would be necessary for the ripening process to have converted the greatest part of the apple—which was flatulent and pure gas—into the sweet and uniform substance of the apple. That is, into "non-gas." It would mean a mixed body was made from a nearly simple element (as they say). Therefore, the whole apple, whether it is ripe or unripe, consists of the same matter; and indeed, it is not naturally gaseous. A sour apple, toasted in a hermetically sealed glass, forces the vessel to burst because of the gas. Yet a similar apple, sealed in a similar glass with an equal amount of water so that it boils, emits no Gas: but only a watery vapor. Strong acid distilled by itself passes entirely into the receiving vessel without "wild gas": but if a dissolvable metal is added to it, it produces Gas, such that even the strongest glass will burst if it is well-sealed with cement; even though, meanwhile, <margin>68.</margin> none of the aforementioned metal is actually converted into Gas. Not even a hundredth part of the tartar of wine can be distilled by the distillation of its own oil, unless a crack is left in the joints. Otherwise, the "wild gas" suddenly shatters the vessel, no matter how large. If, therefore, Tartar contained gas materially, it would have given it off during its first combustion, or at least during a second distillation; yet the gas is made anew in each subsequent distillation, even from its oil or sulfur alone. This is because there is a hidden acidity of the wine within it, and at the same time a volatile

<column-break/>

Alkali. Whence, from the coupling of both, <margin>69.</margin> "wild gas" is made. For food, not sufficiently subdued in the stomach, putrefies and makes Gas. For it putrefies due to the corruption of the place, which is the "stercoral" <note>fecal or waste-related</note> environment of the stomach; or rather, by an action contrary to nature. For the smallest atoms of food, if well chewed, are easily turned into chyle <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note>; but larger pieces in a weaker stomach, even if they are resolved into chyle on their outer surface and external appearance through digestion, remain undigested at their center. While they feel enough of the heat, they do not equally enjoy the ferment; they remain undigested, they rot under the yellowish heat, and they mostly cause trouble for the intestines. Or, if they retain the original sliminess of the food with a little acidity, they turn into worms (which are always messengers of weakness). Soon, the ferment of the stomach, finding certain things resisting it—and therefore half-cooked and half-rotten—seethes, doubles, and intensifies its sourness. Thence comes a biting, harsh belching, the companion of Appetite. This mass, falling down into the intestine, stirs up foul gases—and stinking ones, from putrefied fat. By mechanical proof: take one <margin>70.</margin> part sulfur, let it boil with double the amount of linseed oil: soon the sulfur putrefies, and it takes on the appearance of the lung tissue of birds, exhaling the odor of human feces, just as it belches out a similar Gas during distillation. Therefore, a mass poorly <margin>71.</margin> digested in the stomach, descending through the intestine, stirs up sharp gases if the sourness is intense, from which come the "Gripes" <note>original: "Tormina"; sharp, twisting abdominal pains or colic</note>. But if any of its mucus sticks to the intestine, the Gripes become more persistent, occasionally accompanied by diarrhea. And they are all the more atrocious the more the acidity is harsh. For from a harsh gas, the colic is small and fleeting; but from food-matter, it is far more persistent, and it changes locations and migrates. But if it comes from sticking and fixed harsh mucus: it afflicts and convulses most cruelly. Therefore, gas does not come from the matter properly speaking: but from the operation of the ferment, which is striving for a new generation contrary to nature, and from the error of the irritated *Archeus* <note>the internal "master-workman" or vital force of the organ</note>. <margin>72.</margin> and diseased states. Moreover, regarding poisons that have been drunk, why do they produce a body habitus swollen with gas? Know that this happens during and after death. For a corpse does not swell because it has acquired new matter, but because life exists chiefly in the internal organs; therefore, the habitus of the body is first contaminated by the poison. <margin>73.</margin> which are read as forbidden to the Jews <note>original: "vetita leguntur Judæis"; referring to the prohibition of leaven/fermentation during Passover</note>). Therefore, a sudden and terrible corruption, striking the flesh, also generates gas and swelling within it. <margin>74.</margin> remaining after death, produces the gas. For it is commonly said that a corpse is about to emerge when the gallbladder <note>original: "fellis cystis"</note> bursts. Nor is this without its own force of truth. Not, indeed, that it is literally true that the bursting of the gallbladder and its eruption brings lightness to the corpse, but bile is a balsam, restraining in the living those corruptions arising from acidity. Therefore, when corruption is present, a failure of the bile is inferred. A fresh belly sinks; but when the juice contained within it is corrupted, the "tree" <note>likely a metaphor for the distended trunk of the body</note> emerges from the depths. Furthermore, I have said that 
<margin>75.</margin> the smaller warm seeds <note>original: "semina minora calida"; carminative herbs like anise and fennel</note> became known to mortals through divine mercy, and their use was introduced into the Schools by the good common people, who were ignorant of the cause and circumstances of gases. Therefore, those seeds inhibit both the corruption and the acidity of the matter, and are thus comforts for the intestines. Learn this comfort by this example: A careless person with a hernia, whose intestine has fallen into the scrotum, soon rises to the size of a head, hardens, and finally turns bluish. Indeed, various milk poultices and warm fomentations of cow dung are tried in vain. And through an opening six times smaller than the swelling of the scrotum, it seems to lose hope of its return because of the hardness. Then, after drinking anise, cumin, fennel, coriander, etc., in wine, the hardness of the swelling soon vanishes and allows

<column-break/>

itself to be pushed back inside. What the clyster <note>an enema</note> and the external poultice did not provide, that silent defect speaks for itself: that the intestines, having wandered out of place around the testicle, immediately take on an unnatural hardness and stir up gases. All of these things soon disappear through the comfort given to the intestinal Archeus <note>the internal "vital governor" or spirit that directs the body's functions</note>; otherwise, they would cause a swift and painful death. Furthermore, I will add something about the natural gas of the Ileum <note>the lower part of the small intestine</note>, which is unknown to the Schools. A noble woman was troubled by a slight pain in the belly; she was walking through her chamber, having dined; soon the pain ascended to the right breast, invaded the shoulder, and a little later killed her. When the corpse was dissected, nothing was 
<margin>76.</margin> observed by the eyes that could be blamed for causing the death. But at the opportune moment, they saw the Ileum distended with a small amount of gas. "Wind! Wind!" I say, the Doctors accused the torturer. When the judgment was brought to me, I reckoned that the pain of the belly had been uterine; it had therefore ascended to the breasts, with which the womb ordinarily communicates; and so it strangled the woman. But as for the gas in the Ileum, I said it was not only innocent, but that in any corpse (even one killed by sudden death), the Ileum is always naturally distended by a small amount of gas, because this is natural, inseparable, and proper to it. For without gas, the intestines would collapse, and excrement would pass through with greater difficulty. Indeed, unless pushed from behind and kept fluid, they would easily fall backward and, as if staying there without progress, would contract too long a delay. 
<margin>77.</margin> If, therefore, some gas is a native inhabitant of the Ileum, there is no place for complaint about gas in griping pains <note>original: "Torminibus"; sharp, twisting colic</note>, and much less for carminatives <note>medicines used to expel gas</note> that drive out and disperse winds. Let the griping pains, therefore, be attributed to a harsh <note>original: "ponticæ"</note> mucilage, more or less bitter, upon whose resolution (if they should stick) or expulsion (if they should flow) the restoration of health is expected. If, in the meantime, a bitter gas should arise, or the Ileum swells more than is right with winds, it easily finds a way for itself. The dismissal of gases does indeed relieve compression and distention; but gas does not cause griping pains of great importance, for they quickly make a way for themselves.

<margin>78.</margin> But if, indeed, from below, due to hardened waste, gas is blocked from exiting: then it is called <term>Volvulus</term> <note>original: "Volvulus"; a painful twisting or obstruction of the intestines</note> and is distinct from the term for <term>Tormina</term> <note>original: "Torminum"; sharp, griping pains in the bowels</note>. IT is now the proper time to show that the massive heap of diseases dedicated to the "Catarrh"—supposedly flowing down from the head even to the very tips of the toes without obstacle—is an old wives' fiction. It was invented by none other than the "Driver" <note>A reference to the Devil</note>, the enemy of the human race, so that if the true causes of diseases were known, their remedies might also become known at the same time. However that may be, it is at least manifest from this that the Schools <note>The traditional medical universities of the time</note> are even today led astray by the errors of the heathens regarding the generation of Catarrh: its supposed pruning, its flowing down, its manner, path, material, means, locations, and organs, as well as the methods of "drawing it back" <note>original: "revulsione"; the practice of trying to pull humors away from a diseased part</note> and its remedies. For whatever you build upon a single absurdity or impossibility is necessarily false and absurd. From this likewise falls the vain hope placed in <term>cauteries</term> <note>The practice of burning the skin to create a "drain" for bad fluids</note>, as I shall demonstrate in the proper place. Natures themselves are the <margin>1.</margin> healers of diseases: but the Physician is their Minister, according to Hippocrates <note>original: "Hippocr."</note>. But concerning those diseases...

...diseases which Nature heals of her own accord. But where she has succumbed, so that she cannot rise again by her own strength, the Physician—chosen by the Lord’s kindness, and for whom almost all diseases are of equal value (for such is the man who has obtained one universal Medicine among many of that kind)—remains no longer a mere servant: but an interpreter, a Ruler, and a powerful master. May the name of my Lord **JESUS** be exalted forever, who always gives His bounty to the little ones, cast down in their humility. For the Nature of the sick person, the chief receiver of morbid impressions and the sensitive mover in opposition to them, succumbs—at least when the "guest" diseases prevail—or at least lives thereafter in a calamitous state near to death itself, unless he is restored to his former state by a Healer. Yet it does not happen that every Physician reaches Corinth <note>A classical proverb meaning that not everyone achieves a difficult or elite goal; original: "Non cuivis tamen Medico contingit adire Corinthum"</note>, unless he is called, elected, practiced, and committed. For in the age of Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note>, the universal heights of healing, which contain the tone of nature within themselves, had not yet become known (indeed, they are still starved and mocked by the common crowd of Physicians today); therefore Hippocrates deserves pardon if he thought the entire business of disease was finished by nature as the Teacher. 

<margin>2.</margin> Furthermore, I have said elsewhere that from the beginning of the fetus onward, an "assisting ruling spirit" <note>original: "spiritum insitum," the innate spirit or internal director of an organ</note> presides over each member: while another spirit flows from the heart, acting as the awakener and comforter of the innate spirit; yet this second spirit is neither determined nor individually disposed unless it has first been subdued by the innate spirit. I have also taught elsewhere that every member is nourished according to the power of its <term>innate ferment</term> <note>Van Helmont used "ferment" to describe the chemical and spiritual catalysts that drive digestion and life processes</note>, and thus no transformation toward new generation can be hoped for except by means of a ferment. Consequently, it is understood from this that all growth and life come from the spirits, and thus the weakened digestion of the members depends on the diminishing of these spirits and their ferment, according to that saying: *My spirit (the sheath of the ferment) shall be weakened, (therefore) also my days shall be shortened:* <note>A paraphrase of Job 17:1</note> Thus, a member which in health

<column-break/>

produces no visible waste, may produce much of it and do so incessantly if it has been struck, injured, diminished, or hindered in the vigor of its ferment. Finally, it follows from this that according to the injury and the variety of the injuring factors, deformity and external irregularity are born. 

<margin>3.</margin> Therefore, diseases do not arise from one single source, namely the human head (from where the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic medical establishment based on Galenic and Aristotelian teachings</note> foolishly imagine all <term>catarrhs</term> <note>Mucus or "down-flowing" fluids</note> rain down), but from the specific <term>idiopathy</term> <note>A disease or condition arising spontaneously or from a cause specific to that organ</note> or proper indisposition of each part, induced upon the local ferments. 

<margin>4.</margin> In this way, wounds that were once healed suffer a relapse, and not infrequently give birth to ulcers and abscesses. And when the direction of the winds changes, even after a long course of years, they become raw again and cause pain. In this same way, coughs, pleurisy, the spitting of blood, and <term>Erysipelas</term> <note>A skin infection, often called "St. Anthony's Fire"</note> recur. For the extreme cold of the mountains, or some other sudden rushing force, the night air, a marshy breeze, or the <term>Gas</term> <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe "wild spirits" or invisible vapors distinct from air</note> belched from mines, often ruins the ferments of the brain or the lungs with a single assault; so that thereafter they become workshops for various wastes during the patient's life. 

<margin>5.</margin> In this manner, certainly, wastes are produced in the eyes, ears, teeth, and throat—not indeed as mucus from the brain—but by the specific error of the part itself. Thus coughs and asthma first begin, and they persevere because the ferment is continuously disrupted. 

<margin>6.</margin> This is not due to mucus flowing down from the head, but because it is generated within the lung through the violation of that place’s ferment. For the lung is most easily affected by external rushing forces compared to the other members: because it is the first of the members to grow old and die. This is evident from the cough of the elderly and the "death rattles" of the dying, even those afflicted by a fault other than that of the lung. For this is specific to the lung, because it always drinks in crude air, and being near the oppressed heart, it stands ready to give up its strength, and for that reason its strength fails sooner. 

<margin>7.</margin> Indeed, I disagree with the Schools most of all because I know this type of vice belongs to the "containing parts" <note>The organs and tissues themselves</note> and not to the "contained liquids" <note>The humors or fluids like phlegm</note>. For products of this kind are certain results of the "root," which are brought forth by the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "master workman" or vital internal semi-spiritual force that governs an organ's functions</note> of the parts when it has been badly tainted.

### ON CATARRHS ###

<margin>8.</margin>
Next, I also disagree in this: I know this to be a local <term>topicum | an ailment restricted to a specific part of the body</term> evil, and not something transmitted by a secondary affection <term>deuteropathia | a condition where one organ is affected as a consequence of a disease in another</term> of the head. Indeed, the coughs of old age occur with little hope of restoration because a tiny amount of waste, born within the lung, resides in the furthest branches of the windpipe <note>original: "cannæ aëreæ," literally the "air-reed" or bronchial tubes</note>. This waste not only obstructs the passages but, by its very presence, disturbs and diminishes the local ferment <note>In Van Helmont’s theory, a "ferment" is a vital chemical agent responsible for the healthy function and transformation of matter within a specific organ</note>. Because of this, new wastes are stirred up every hour—a plentiful supply for coughs. In old age, these are scarcely cured by commonly known means, as these remedies do not penetrate the affected areas; indeed, they have not even gained the power to restore strength. Therefore, waste products of this kind are local defects of the parts. Each part has its own weakness, whether innate or acquired, accompanied by a diminution of the 
<margin>9.</margin> 
vegetating ferment. And so, from this source, all the waste of such parts flows forth. I understand, therefore, that repeated purgings are primarily useless and harmful in these affections, since they are directed only at the products, not at the causes. Furthermore, and most importantly, because waste of this kind does not yield to laxatives. However it may be, these treatments in no way reach the primary flaw and the harmful root within us; instead, they only concern themselves with the consequences. They are unable to touch the prior things, or the roots. Add to this that although laxatives may sometimes seem to help for a day or two—insofar as once the mass of blood from the mesenteric vessels is removed, a smaller supply and nutrition is carried to the lung, resulting in less spitting <note>original: "screatus," the act of coughing up phlegm</note>—nevertheless, laxatives attack the general strength of the whole body, weakening it more 
<margin>10.</margin> 
and more. When the Physicians <note>original: "Medentes"</note> see this as if through a sieve <note>An idiom meaning they see it only partially or unclearly</note>, and realize the patient has not benefited due to the exhaustion of their strength and the wasting of the body, they finally dismiss the sick to be managed by the rules of diet and the sole help of a sober kitchen. Provided they continue to live "medically"—that is to say, miserably—with the help of a cautery <note>A hot iron or chemical used to burn the skin, intended to "draw out" bad humors</note> and the repeated assistance of light laxatives. By this hypothesis, they suggest that at least the kitchen is to be preferred over any 

<column-break/>

untrustworthy drugs from the apothecary shops; and having gained experience, they decree that these drugs should be avoided as harmful. And would that after so much draining of strength, this were enough, and they did not repeatedly try to exhaust the hope, the body, the veins, the strength, and the pockets of the sick with those same safeguards! Would that they were at least mindful of their own axiom: that the most important curative indication should be taken from what helps and what harms. Even if this rule is 
<margin>11.</margin> 
shameful and belongs only to the empirics <note>Practical healers who relied on experience rather than the complex theories of "learned" university doctors</note>, would that they would at least now recoil from the errors they have committed! Nor should they return, in cases of cough and consumption, to remedies which they have found thus far to have benefited no one. For laxatives, bloodletting, nasal drops <note>original: "errhina"</note>, phlegm-clearing medicines <note>original: "Apophlegmatismi"</note>, syrups <note>original: "illinctus," thick medicinal pastes or linctuses</note>, decoctions of China root, Sarsaparilla, Sassafras, the cautery on the coronal suture of the skull, and other untrustworthy aids of that kind brought forward by the Physician, ought to be laid to rest, so that they do not appear to have received their fee for nothing. Would that they had at least learned from their own practice that while they intend the removals, revulsions, diversions, and preventions of the later effects—that is, the waste products—they openly show that the knowledge of the causes remained hidden from them, and they have not cured their patients methodically through the removal of causes. They would have also found that a regulated diet is a fine, feeble, weak, and desperate kind of remedy against such a great enemy that is now an inhabitant, and indeed, a master. It is no wonder, then, that the common people, observing the vanity of these cures, have taken the opportunity to say: *The best medicine is to use no medicine.* For I have often grieved with a certain compassion while reading through hundreds of medical counsels, especially when, in the style of a "New Almansor" <note>Reference to the *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes, a standard medical textbook; here Van Helmont mocks those who follow old texts blindly</note>, they pursue all diseases from the top of the head to the heel of the foot. 
<margin>12.</margin> 
Searching for the "catarrhal" cause from the very beginning (as they think, and boast), they everywhere accuse some natural or acquired particular imbalance <note>original: "intemperiem," a Galenic term for an imbalance of the four humors</note>, yet under a cloud of uncertainty as to whether they should treat it as a disease...

### FOLLIES ###

...whether they established it as a word, or truly as an antecedent cause of the disease for which they were consulted. At the very least, to avoid being wrong, they accused both heat and cold simultaneously in any disease. They complain, in almost all cases, about a solitary coldness of the stomach, or one combined with a heat of the liver. From this, they divine that catarrhs <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, a "catarrh" was believed to be a "down-flowing" of excess phlegm from the brain to other parts of the body</note> arise and slip down into various parts, causing a manifold variety of diseases. They pursue these not only through almost all internal illnesses but even down to defects of the skin. This is how the Schools imbue their students, both in theory and in practice. 

For they claim that catarrhs are the culprits behind defects of the eyes, ears, throat, tongue, teeth, chest, arms, loins, and legs. Thus, coughs, consumption <term>tabes | a wasting disease, often tuberculosis</term>, asthma, pleurisy, pneumonia, apoplexy, paralysis, sudden deaths, abscesses <term>vomicæ | internal collections of pus</term>, and the coughing up of blood have now found their cause established in catarrhs. Finally, the stomach feels the urge to vomit, suffers nausea and indigestion <term>apepsia | inability to digest food</term>, and even the liver and spleen fall ill. For when indigestible mucus has fallen from the head, obstructions, hardness, dropsy <term>hydropes | swelling caused by excess fluid</term>, sores, tumors <term>scirrhi | hard, fibrous growths</term>, fevers, and griping pains of the 
<margin>3.</margin> 
bowels have made a place for themselves among the clients of catarrh. 

Even Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note>, although otherwise triumphant in his discovery of the "Tartars" and the three primary principles, mostly subscribed to these catarrhs. He always clearly recognized the name of "defluxion" <note>original: "flüffen," the German term for flows or fluxes</note>, nodding along under the mistress of 
<margin>4.</margin> 
uncertainty. Indeed, the Schools so adorn this seriously lamentable fable of catarrhs, and pass it from hand to hand to one another, that it takes the place of truth. Indeed, passive doctors, having become fools, declaim to me about their catarrhs until I am bored to tears. For me, it is difficult and even nauseating to try to tear each one of them away from this unaccustomed, supposed doctrine and to bring the true light of Theory—especially since the crowd is of such a mind that, like new clay pots, they hardly lose the scent of what they first absorbed <note>A reference to a Horace quote implying that early education is hard to unlearn</note>. Therefore, I usually remain silent among the great men; I do not declaim on the disease, the causes, the species, nor the medicines. Silent, regarding that easy 

<column-break/>

Theory of the Schools, I seem to be ignorant of everything, departing in agreement with everyone. In some places, however, I say that I have been instructed differently; but these idiots are not capable of understanding Medicine, and I am not their schoolmaster. 

At the very least, I marvel daily that no one until now has noticed such great ignorance among healers, but that the Christian world has dragged these dreams of the Greeks behind itself into a ridiculous, lying worship that is ruinous to human society. To be sure, they establish the primary source of catarrhs in the cold imbalance of the stomach and the hot imbalance of the liver, and they claim the greatest part of sick mortals is subject to this tyranny. 

They say the process happens like this: Because the stomach is incessantly heated by the liver during the "cooking" <note>Traditional medicine compared digestion to a culinary process or "coction" driven by the liver's heat</note> of food, it cannot help but constantly send vapors up to the head. But the brain, being cold by its own nature, acts like a lid to a boiling pot, or like the head of a still <note>original: "fungi alembici," referring to the mushroom-shaped cap of a distillation apparatus</note> into which vapors ascend and are condensed into water. Since this water must naturally flow down, it provides the ample and general material for 
<margin>15.</margin> 
catarrhs. If this falls into the eyes, ears, throat, teeth, etc., the parts rightly grieve that they have the brain as a neighbor and a superior tyrant. But if it rains into the lungs, it is transformed into a cough, sighing affections, and finally into consumption, heart palpitations, and even sudden death. 

If, however, these catarrhs rain down into the stomach, it then pays the penalty for its own fault through indigestion, rawness, vomiting, excessive appetite, heartburn, fainting, obstructions, diarrhea, celiac disease, cholera, colic, wasting <term>atrophias | a loss of muscle or tissue</term>, dropsy, tumors, and all defects of the belly. Indeed, fevers, putrefactions in the veins, and even stones in the spleen, kidneys, and bladder take their beginnings from the mucus of catarrh. But if the catarrhs are diverted into the cavity of the cerebellum, then instantaneous death, apoplexy, and paralysis are immediately present. Yet if by chance the catarrhs turn through the neck into the nerves, arteries, and muscles, then various types of arthritis, pleurisy, and paralysis [ensue]...

...of the parts, and convulsions soon follow. Likewise, they claim that catarrhs generate a varied offspring of surgical defects—pains, abscesses, and ulcers. In truth, beyond the aforementioned imbalances of heat and cold—and the catarrh necessarily born from them—the books, speeches, consultations, conversations,
<margin>16.</margin> lectures, and practices of Physicians resonate with nothing else: thus, the entire axis of healing today revolves around purges, bloodlettings <term>venæsectiones</term>, scarifications, baths, sweats, cauteries, and, in short, nothing but the weakening of the body and its strength, or the "drying out" of catarrhs. For this purpose, they have prescribed China root and Sarsaparilla from the distant East, along with Sassafras wood, to serve as drying agents. They measure dietetics and pharmacy mostly by the yardstick of heat and cold; in this way, they never release patients from
<margin>17.</margin> their hands, but keep them as perpetual clients, like acquired slaves—yet in a state of manifest despair. Because, since these Physicians are ignorant of the causes and roots, and see themselves working in vain, they claim that a cure or healing is impossible, because the "natural cold" of the stomach
<margin>18.</margin> supposedly contradicts the "heat" of the liver; and thus, whatever would benefit the stomach would harm the liver, and vice-versa. Since all these things conspire toward the destruction of mortals, as well as the ruin of the State and families, it has been my duty to utterly overthrow this execrable heresy of medical doctrine. I was duty-bound to do so all the more powerfully because this plague has possessed the minds of all Europeans since the days of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over 1,500 years</note>. The rich, of course, learn this doctrine for a fee, and what they have learned, they teach to others; and so, all diseases are said to be born from catarrhs. I shall speak, therefore, through theses accepted in the Schools.
<margin>19. 1.</margin> The human stomach, as long as it is alive, is actually hot, and its membrane is soaked with some moisture.

<column-break/>

<margin>2.</margin> It is impossible for any watery moisture to be actually hot within us without also raising a vapor from itself by that very fact.
<margin>3.</margin> The upper path from the stomach is the gullet, or esophagus <term>œsophagus</term>, a membrane stretched out like a reed, extending from the stomach to the throat, similar to the membrane of the stomach.
<margin>4.</margin> The gullet, of itself, is entirely moist and is closed (since it would otherwise collapse due to the vacuum) actually and always, not unlike a bladder lacking its own contents. Therefore, the gullet touches itself laterally out of natural necessity, which does not allow for a vacuum. For if the gullet did not contain food, drink, or air, it would necessarily be empty if it were open. That it is not open, nor contains air, is clear from this: otherwise, with every mouthful swallowed, the air that was below it—and which would resist the mouthful—would be pushed down to the stomach, and thus there would be as many burps as there were mouthfuls swallowed. Finally, since the membrane of the gullet is moist, it would necessarily collapse into itself unless it were stretched by some force on all sides; this neither occurs in dissections, nor would it serve any purpose in the living.
<margin>5.</margin> The mouth of the stomach is closed by a natural motion, not a voluntary one. As for the gullet, there is no other anatomical knowledge than that it is narrow,
<margin>6.</margin> closed below, through the Pylorus <term>the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</term> or the lower orifice of the stomach, and compressed in the human neck by many vessels.
<margin>7.</margin> The gullet does not draw in air, nor does it contain it. It collapses, indeed, by the natural motion of its moist membrane and the lack of content.
<margin>8.</margin> The gullet does not open along its length unless it transmits food. If the food is quite dry, it sticks in the passage and does not easily descend unless a drink is added; this could not happen if it contained air beneath the mouthful, unless a burp followed. However, the gullet is open at its beginning around the larynx.
<margin>9.</margin> The gullet is closed at the bottom by an external right <note>original: "jure alieno" - meaning it is controlled by the stomach's mechanics rather than its own</note>, and therefore it does not open unless an external guest enters, or something erupts. Or, during hunger, it may even be opened by an external will.
<margin>10.</margin> No air, and much less vapor, from the stomach
