# FOLLIES. #

<margin>11.</margin> A burp breaks out upward from the stomach without sound. If the heat necessary for the stomach creates vapor, it still does not push that same vapor upward with such violence that it is able to distend and open the locked entrance of the stomach and the throat. Otherwise, if the opposite were true, everyone would be burping constantly. <note>Van Helmont is arguing that if heat constantly produced rising vapors as the Galenists claimed, the physical pressure would result in non-stop burping.</note>

<margin>12.</margin> In the stomach, just as in other vessels that are lukewarm, every watery vapor—at the slightest compression—condenses back into drops more quickly than it can lift and stretch the compressed membrane along its length. Therefore, vapors do not produce burps; only air and the <term>wild spirit | Gas sylvestre</term> do so. <note>Van Helmont coined the word "Gas" (from the Greek 'chaos'). Here he distinguishes between "vapor" (which condenses) and "gas" (which remains airy).</note>

<margin>13.</margin> If we were to assume there is a "hepatic spirit" of the blood, all the veins—through their own heat, whether near the liver or in the furthest branches—would produce catarrhs, a fact neglected by the Schools.

->FIRST CONCLUSION.<-

<margin>20.</margin> From these theses, which are mostly admitted and are clear through Anatomy, the following primarily follows:

<margin>1.</margin> That no vapor is carried from the stomach into the head, and the supposed material for catarrhs is lacking.

<margin>2.</margin> If such blindness has surrounded the world regarding manifest things, what should we not suspect regarding more hidden matters?

<margin>3.</margin> That according to the doctrine of the Schools, a healthy and warm stomach would generate much greater and more numerous catarrhs than a sick and otherwise colder one—which now contradicts the Schools. <note>The Galenists argued that catarrhs were caused by "cold" and "moisture," yet their theory of rising vapors required "heat" to make them rise.</note>

<margin>4.</margin> That we should be focused on cooling the stomach rather than warming it.

<margin>5.</margin> That all mortals would necessarily suffer from catarrhs and be continuously infirm.

<margin>6.</margin> Because everyone is composed of the same throat, brain, and stomach—all actually warm and moist—and of the same shape.

<margin>7.</margin> That every human, like pigs, would naturally burp at almost every step, because the unending heat and moisture would necessarily emit a continuous upward vapor.

<margin>8.</margin> That even if the vapor excited by the stomach were to distend the throat—indeed, if it ascended without a burp—nevertheless, it would all be blown out through the mouth and nostrils

<column-break/>

continually, before it could proceed to the brain through the narrow and closed path of the membrane. Also, that vapor ascending from food in the stomach would necessarily, in every person, smell of the food and its transformations, being offensive to themselves and to those standing by; so much so that if burps are occasionally smelly, the entire breath of every person would also stink continually with the mixed smell of food.

<margin>9.</margin> That since a burp is <term>wild spirit | Gas sylvestre</term>, and far more subtle than vapor, yet it does not strike the brain unless it is forced out through the nostrils with the mouth closed, certainly vapors will be carried to the brain much less.

<margin>10.</margin> That burps are never carried from the throat by a straight path to the brain, but only through the organ of smell; and therefore, they only provide an odor when the mouth is closed; much less will vapor be carried spontaneously from the stomach to the head.

<margin>11.</margin> That for vapor—the material of catarrh—to still ascend to the head or the organ of smell, it would have to be impossible for this to happen unless the mouth were closed. Thus, the material of catarrh would not be possible for one with an open mouth; and therefore, this would be an easy remedy for catarrh. <note>Van Helmont is using irony here to show the absurdity of the traditional theory.</note>

<margin>12.</margin> That since two bodies naturally cannot occupy the same space, and the path from the throat to the brain is narrow and filled (for there is no vacuum in those organs), and is closed and impassable at the top (for the breath, even if compressed, does not exhale upward to the head), therefore vapor from the stomach cannot reach the base of the brain. For example: if a <note>original: "canna"</note> tube is stopped up at the top, even if it is held over warm vapors, it does not allow them to ascend because of the presence of the air with which it is filled.

<margin>13.</margin> Granted that vapor could climb upward, it would still not encounter any flat or concave surface upon which it could condense into drops. Much less would it find something that resembles an <term>Alembic | a distilling apparatus</term> or the lid of a pot; but in the base of the brain, where the vapor is supposedly allowed to ascend, there is a narrow part—a pelvis, or the bottom of a funnel—which has two small tubes toward the nostrils and just as many toward the neck.

All these things the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities following the teachings of Galen and Aristotle.</note> have seen through **Anatomy**, and would know to be inevitable through **Logic** <note>original: "Mathesin"; Helmont often uses this to mean rigorous, mathematical-style reasoning.</note> (if they weighed them); yet they go about, they have eyes and see not; they have ears, and it is to be feared they do not wish to hear.

<margin>16.</margin> Although mucus may slide into the throat and often affect it badly in various ways, according to the different states of the mucus; nevertheless, neither that mucus nor its dripping can be considered a "catarrh" <note>Van Helmont argues that "catarrh" is a misnomer for the brain's natural waste-clearing process.</note>. <margin>17.</margin> How much less should a catarrh be considered the flow of some fictitious humor or a dreamed-up excrement, born and carried through ways, means, places, and paths that are naturally <margin>18.</margin> impossible? But if this were so, there would be an utterly inexcusable storm constantly raging inside healthy people.

<margin>20.</margin> Even if all these points were set aside (which nevertheless cannot naturally exist by necessity), catarrhs would still not flow down. For they do not primarily flow outward between the skull and the skin. <margin>21.</margin> Since the Schools themselves teach that vapors—the supposed preceding material of catarrh—climb from the stomach to the base of the brain, and there strike some flat surface (an imaginary one, not yet found by Anatomy), in whose cavity it supposedly solidifies immediately and, once condensed, falls drop by drop. It is a far cry from the truth that an arriving enemy, a mere waste-product foreign to the brain and the cause of so many illnesses, would pass into water at the lowest level of the brain and then penetrate through the very body of the brain—either in the form of water, or perhaps playing about on that aforementioned flat surface in the form of vapor. <margin>22.</margin> For it does not happen in the form of vapor: as if the vapor reaches from the stomach to the base of the brain and solidifies (as they say) by the coldness of the place; certainly by that same opportunity of cold, it will remain water and will not become vapor again. <margin>23.</margin> If, therefore, that vapor has already become water there because of the coldness of the place, it is not believable that this hostile water is drawn inward, much less that it has become so subtle that it could pierce through the brain, the membranes, the <term>sutures|The joints between the bones of the skull</term>, the skull, and the <term>periosteum|The dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</term> against the will of those receiving parts, just to settle and run under the skin. # ON DELUSIONS.

It has no place, path, custom, or admission for penetrating into the brain through the membranes <note>the meninges</note>, the skull, etc. For an excrement never has a place or a right of deposit there: otherwise, a trepan <note>a surgical drill used to bore holes in the skull</note> would be needed daily for a cold just as much as for pus.
<margin>30.</margin> But why does the catarrh <note>a "running" of fluid or mucus</note> cease to flow as soon as a tooth is pulled? Is it because it has forgotten its way? But if the matter is supplied from below, where, I ask, will it flow? Or in what part will it settle, which previously used to enter through the tiny openings through which the nerves—both internal and external, and both the upper and lower sides of each jaw—enter? Will the stomach perhaps stop, or no longer dare to give off vapors and the matter for catarrhs, once the tooth is pulled? Or does all the matter of catarrhs, even future ones, flow out along with the blood when the tooth is extracted? Or, because the cavity of the tooth is hardened by the flesh that immediately grows underneath, and no exit is given to the outside, will the catarrh therefore cease? But the catarrh was not seeking an exit through the very hard tooth. Why then, in the neighboring parts of the mouth, does it not provoke a necessary abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note>? Why, when one tooth is pulled, does it often descend to another? Is the channel changed when one is pulled? And does it no longer know how to flow down into at least the nerve of the extracted tooth and into the new-grown flesh? Does it think the path through a tooth is easier for itself than through the flesh growing after the extraction? Why does it not keep the path it prepared? And before the flesh grows back, why does it not keep that exit for itself? Truly, that man is miserably deceived by the surgeon who, thinking it flows into the tooth and finding it removed, would be forced to return by the same path to a noble part, which it would then torment in revenge against the surgeon. Therefore, a tooth does not ache because of a catarrh: but either because the gum is exposed and it becomes overly sensitive, or otherwise, the poorly digested matter of its final nourishment putrefies around the root of the tooth.
<margin>31.</margin> Hence the pain. In this, indeed, the digestion of a tooth and a nail differs from the digestion of other parts: because the latter occurs in their own internal "kitchens," while the former occurs in the "kitchens" adjacent to their roots.

# ON CATARRHS

<margin>34.</margin> (proven by mechanical laws to be necessarily tasteless) having first been changed from a vapor by itself, falling down into the stomach, would it cause such great distress to that organ, when a moment before, along with the rest of the chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food</note>, it was pleasing to it? From where does this hostility arise? Does it come from the brain, that sovereign organ, rich in the beginnings of life? But if the vapor merely touches the lowest surface of the brain (as they say) and then immediately thereafter reaches the full size of a drop and falls—and since there cannot be a third party to hold back each individual drop—then this perversity cannot arise from that tiny delay, nor from the contagion of a malignant part, nor finally from a "seed" of harmful matter received there. This is true unless they can show that, besides the condensation of vapor into drops of water, something else intervened. This they have neglected to prove until now.

<margin>35.</margin> But since so many fictions about catarrhal and pulmonary defects have everywhere risen up into huge volumes, consultations, and prescriptions, it is my duty to show that nothing has ever been taught by the Schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities, often followers of Galen</note> more negligently, more stupidly, or more dangerously. For they have hitherto considered no sin to be smaller than homicide committed through carelessness, provided the earth covers the fault and the killers are excused by the traditional axioms. Indeed, I have considered that the demon Moloch <note>A biblical figure associated with child sacrifice; here used to describe a bloodthirsty or destructive authority</note> presides over these academic Chairs, and has hitherto driven the world mad with "Catarrhs." In these theories, the matter, the birth, the location, the efficient cause, the manner of formation, the containing vessel, the path, and the connection of associations are all simultaneously lacking and are false. Therefore, none other than the ancient serpent, the father of lies, has taught these things until now for the destruction of mortals: for truly, whatever flows from the head is mucus and pure excrement <note>Waste product</note>, and is not brought there from the stomach.

<margin>36.</margin> Mucus is white, thick, and viscous when the Guardian of the brain is well-constituted; but when its powers are overturned and wrongly affected, the mucus is watery, sharp, salty, harsh, yellow, tenacious, etc., and it flows down whatever path is more open to it, from the basin or its 

<column-break/>

funnel <note>The infundibulum of the brain</note>. For that which drips in the form of water at the beginning of a *Coryza* <note>A head cold or runny nose</note> is not pure mucus: <margin>37.</margin> but it is a salty fluid <note>original: "latex"</note> with which nature tries to wash away that which has settled as a foreign enemy in the spongy bone <note>The ethmoid bone</note> bordering the brain, as I have said. Furthermore, the yellow and viscous fluid that flows down as the *Coryza* declines is not the same fluid as before, nor has it been detained and thickened there for so long (as the Schools teach), since otherwise the entire cranium, even if empty of the brain, would scarcely suffice as a box for so much waste. For new mucus of this kind is created in moments, far different from the healthy kind in color, stench, viscosity, and sharpness. It is, moreover, ridiculous for this foul mucus to be called "already cooked" or "thickened from the previous fluid," when it grows anew by a foreign vice. That it is a fluid at the start of a *Coryza* is clear: for after two days, the bowels are drier and the urine more scarce. Finally, that fluid, evaporated warmly, has scarcely the means to become mucus; however much mucus the fluid carries with it, it has that much mucilage and no more.

Whatever it is, and whatever <margin>38.</margin> it is that flows down from the brain to the throat, not even a single drop of it enters the lung without first exciting a fear of suffocation at every drop. If a single drop of water, falling into the windpipe by careless swallowing, strikes a fear of choking into the drinker, what would such a great quantity of mucus do, which fills basins in a short space of time? For it is a stray thought to suggest that a few hours of sleep could carry whole basins of mucus into the lung without sensation and without the fear of choking. Long ago, when I was a novice deluded by the Schools, I positioned such patients so that they slept on their faces among pillows, hoping that the mucus would slip out through the nostrils which would otherwise glide into the lung, and thus I hoped for immunity from the effect of the catarrh. But the following morning, my ignorance was mocked by their coughing up of phlegm. Then I discovered that *orthopnea* <note>A condition where one can only breathe comfortably while sitting or standing upright</note>, which positions those breathing with a straight neck, pays little heed to the doctrine of catarrh.

catarrhs, and to prove that theory frivolous. For patients were being strangled while lying flat and horizontal, even though the supposed flow of catarrh-matter should have been cut off by that position. Therefore, I began to observe that any poorly affected limb or organ creates not only a great deal of its own waste, but even harmful waste.
<margin>39.</margin> For instance, when the eye is affected in various ways, a great deal of discharge and sharp tears flow out; likewise, when the throat is blocked by quinsy <note>angina: a painful inflammation of the throat</note>, a viscous thread hangs continually from the tongue. From this, I believed that the lung is held by the same law as other members; so much so, that whenever it is irritated, injured, pricked, attacked by the injury of the air or by an endemic Gas <note>Gas: a term coined by van Helmont to describe vital or chemical vapors</note>, oppressed, or affected, it produces various testimonies of its own distress by its own error. It is not, therefore, that those foul excrements glide down insensibly from the brain (which is usually healthy) through the tiny channels of the windpipe <note>aspera arteria: literally "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea</note>. Then at last I began to wonder why the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established Galenic medical authorities of the universities</note> saw that in a cold <note>Coryza: a head cold or nasal congestion</note> the head's own waste degenerates and imitates itself, yet they did not think meanwhile that the same could happen to the lung just as well as to other members. Thus, whatever is brought up from the lung, they attribute entirely to the brain; and they claim it falls (ridiculously!) into the windpipe without being felt, and is gradually cooked in that narrow passage, mostly without shortness of breath, and is kept there until it matures. Yet sometimes more is ejected by coughing in a single month than the entire capacity of the chest could hold. Therefore, the yellow and ash-colored phlegm of the consumptive are errors of the vegetative power <note>vegetatricis: the internal biological force responsible for growth and nutrition</note> in the lung, and are degenerated blood, which is why a wasting of the whole body follows.
<margin>40.</margin> For this reason, the "cephalic" remedies <note>remedies intended for the head</note> applied are useless and deplorable: the drinks of cooling barley-water, linctuses <note>loch: a thick, syrupy medicine licked from a spoon</note>, syrups, and whatever descends into the stomach by swallowing are all in vain. This is because such things are often formally changed on their journey before they ever reach the affected part.
<margin>41.</margin> For what is more foolish than to offer Indian roots to be drunk for the drying up of Catarrhs? For how will China-root, Sarsaparilla, or

<column-break/>

Guaiacum <note>These were "New World" plants used to treat syphilis and respiratory issues</note> dry anything out when drunk in the form of water? Indeed, what would they dry out, since the dried matter would be no less harmful than the liquid itself?
<margin>42.</margin> Why do they call for "drying" when they only need a remedy that inhibits the matter from forming in the first place? And once it has been formed, it does not require drying, but ejection. Why do the Schools everywhere look at the effects and not at the roots? What if these foreign and barbaric remedies stir up sweat and diminish the bodily fluids to the detriment of the sick man—has the root of the problem been reached? Indeed, by meager nutrition and copious sweating, they primarily diminish the blood, and secondarily cause wasting and weakness. The Schools have falsely translated this into the "drying up of superfluities," thinking that they can encompass the proper quantity of blood, the generation of morbid waste, and its expulsion all under the single synonym of "drying." For will the indisposition and the "transforming Vulcan" <note>Vulcan: the Roman god of fire, used here as a metaphor for the internal "heat" or chemical fire that transforms blood into phlegm</note>—who prepares the wasting phlegm from good blood in the lung—be overcome by this? Will he sleep? Will he be diminished? Will he grow mild? Will he stop? Meanwhile, that Vulcan, even under the extreme wasting of Consumption <note>Marasmus: a severe wasting of the body</note>, gives up none of his fury.

> Turn away, O good God, the slaughter
> <margin>43.</margin> which the ignorant School of Pagans and the crowd gasping for a little profit commit.

Only the erroneous morbid impression must be removed (which I call the internal Corruptor of the lung), which depletes the membranes of the veins, the cartilages of the windpipe, and the entire lung of its nourishment, and incessantly transforms it into various filths in a continuous thread. But if bloody phlegm has come first, and an ulcer is present, learn to prepare the medicines with which Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> cured consumption. I say that to have cured a cancer or any eating sore by means of those things applied to the mouth is to have cured an ulcer of the lung. For whatever heals an ulcer of the thigh or foot by being drunk: why should it not also do the same in the lung? But what will the Schools do? They are ignorant of the causes, ignorant of the remedies, and with upturned noses they mock diaphoretic mercury <note>mercurium diaphoreticum: a chemical preparation of mercury intended to induce sweating</note>—sweet as honey and fixed—and the volatile tincture of Lily <note>Lili: an alchemical term, often referring to a specific antimony compound or a "philosopher's" medicine</note>.

# CATARRHS

44. Likewise, there is the milk, or rather the element of pearls <note>original: "lae, five elementum perlarum." For indeed, unless the whole body is universally imbued with an over-abundant balsam, internal ulcers are never solidified. For the lung, being the first to grow old and the first to die, is recovered from the threat of death with the greatest difficulty, and consequently it scorns the remedies of the common people. Wherefore the continued error of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Galenic medical establishment of the time.</note> follows, who would sooner acknowledge a defect in their own sallow medicines than accuse nature of defects or its most glorious Author of a sleepy omission. They decree, forsooth, that the four lobes of the lung, like bellows, are incessantly drawn apart and compressed for as long as one lives, for the purpose of breathing, so that the breath, or inspired air, is merely drawn within the lung and does not reach further into the cavity of the chest. This has certainly produced no small amount of ignorance in the art of healing. Just as it provides a playful subterfuge for the Physician. For they endeavor, by the unceasing and inexcusable necessity of dilation and compression—or the restless motion of the lung—to excuse to themselves the impossible miseries of ulcers, Consumption <term>Tabis: a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term>, and the rest. Ah! As if they could otherwise cure an ulcerated cancer, or a quiet fistula of the anus or eyes, at their pleasure!

45. I meet this error in this way: In the air there flits a thin dust of atoms; by a continuous necessity, however, we draw breath along with these dusty atoms: and therefore the entire chest would soon be filled with mud, unless we had the lung, in whose windings the aforementioned atoms of dust might be fixed; and thus far the lung does not otherwise unburden itself of its excrements except through hawking <note>original: "fcreationem" - the act of coughing up phlegm or clearing the throat</note>, so that the matter conceived in the lungs, having been ensnared, may be carried out. This is a use which has certainly been neglected by the Schools, who unanimously deny that the lung is pervious <note>permeable or having passages through it</note>. Indeed, the hair in the nostrils detains every fiber flitting in the air and keeps it from being drawn inside: then, the manifold branching of the pipes of the rough artery <term>asperæ arteriæ: the historical term for the trachea or windpipe</term> ensures that the finer dust does not go deep within. Furthermore, that it may be established that the lung is entirely motionless—not only from the use already revealed—this is sufficiently clear: but even more so because <margin>B.</margin> the substance of the lung is entirely incapable of dilation and compression. Therefore <margin>C.</margin> the thin lung of birds (serving the same uses for the bird and for us), because it is firmly attached to the ribs, rejects all dilation and compression of bellows. Finally, <margin>D.</margin> the lung consists of three vessels adequately dispersed throughout the whole (namely, one arterial, one venous artery, and the rough artery <note>The pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, and the bronchial tubes.</note>) with the parenchyma of the blood poured around them, and a membrane like a cloak. These three vessels, however, are channels equally extended through the whole, the first two of which are filled with blood, and are thus incapable of concealing new inspired air within themselves. But the third channel is always open, filled with air, and therefore also incapable of other new and inspired air, unless the contained air yields to the newcomer, enters into the chest, and thus that third channel is perforated, together with the membrane clothing the lung. For this third channel is always kept blown open and patent by cartilaginous rings which are contiguous to one another, not otherwise than the trunk of the rough artery itself. The fourth part of the organ, however, is its parenchymatous flesh, equally incapable of the arriving air. Finally, the fifth is the small membrane, or tunic of the lung. Therefore, none of these is capable of new air, none is receptive of new breath, and there is nothing that can sustain dilation and compression, or motion. It is truly a wonder with how much sleep the Schools nevertheless snore, because they know and admit every single thing just said, yet they do not yet cease to teach even today that the lung is continually agitated in the manner of a bellows. <margin>E.</margin> Furthermore, even if it were granted that the third of the vessels, or the aforementioned channels, were not full of air, but entirely void of all air: from respiration (since it is otherwise open, nor can it collapse into itself like a bladder, the cartilage of the rings forbidding it) at least only so much air...

how much of the organ there would be, if it were to conceive something new within itself. Nevertheless, since we can inspire a portion of air at will in a single breath, consider how large the entire lung is. It is absolutely necessary that air is not merely breathed into the channels of the <term>windpipe</term><note>original: "asperæ arteriæ", literally the 'rough artery', the historical term for the trachea</note>, which would otherwise be powerless to collapse and expand; but from these, 
<margin>F.</margin> it proceeds further inward into the cavity of the chest. Finally, if someone’s intercostal muscles are pierced by a dagger, it is soon revealed that the wound has penetrated; for with a puff of breath, he extinguishes the flame of a candle. If, however, the wound is then closed during inspiration and opened again during expiration, he always blows out the candle's light. This would be impossible to happen unless the inhaled air, having been guided through the lung, proceeded into the <term>thorax</term><note>the chest cavity</note>. And consequently, the lung would remain at rest. This is especially true because there is a double <term>mediastinum</term><note>the membrane or partition between the two lungs</note> in the breast, or an interstitial membrane from the top to the bottom of the thorax, for the sake of protecting the heart from the injuries of the air. This mediastinum divides the right side of the thorax from the left. 
<margin>G.</margin> It is clear, therefore, by mechanical necessity, that the breath is carried straight into the thorax, across the lung, and thus the lung itself remains still. This is equally evident and obvious through the <term>expectorations of pleurisy</term><note>phlegm or fluid coughed up during lung inflammation</note>. Indeed, those things which were previously outside the vessels and putrefied in the ribs and the cavity of the chest are rejected through coughing. It must be, therefore, that the membrane of the lung is very porous, which suffices for transmitting blood and pus. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established academic and medical authorities of the time, often followers of Galen or Aristotle</note> see these things, know them, confess them, and write them: yet they deny that the breath is blown outside the lung into the thorax; instead, they insist the lung itself must necessarily be agitated like a pair of bellows. They grant indeed that the lung has pores through which blood and pus are absorbed in pleurisy; yet they do not want air to be transmitted through those same pores into the thorax: but they just as stubbornly command that the lung itself be moved like bellows. Nor is it a wonder. This is because they contemplate nothing but corpses (in which the pores of that membrane are closed by death), both in what has been done and what is to be done. For the same thing happens to the optic nerves, the spinal cord, the partition of the heart, and the openings of the veins to the intestines.

<column-break/>

The lung of brute animals floats on water, in which it is boiled whole, but when cut into pieces, it sinks, because the windpipe is filled with air. To what purpose (lest it be added impertinently) if boiling water does not have access while it is being cooked: how shall <term>catarrh</term><note>excessive mucus or "rheum"</note> find an entrance there? The same is shown through mechanics. Blow out 
<margin>H.</margin> your breath from your chest as much as you can; measure the circumference of the ribs with a string: then again, inspire air as much as you can, and measure again: You will find by the volume that more air is drawn in than fits the size of the human lung. How much more so, because 
<margin>I.</margin> a large part of the breath escapes this measurement. Namely, as much as the diaphragm has stretched the stomach downward. Try 
<margin>J.</margin> therefore again. Draw in your breath as much as you can, and breathe into a bladder, and you will find the same as before: that the inspired air exceeds the size of the entire lung. Meanwhile, remember that after every 
<margin>K.</margin> expiration, the channels of the windpipe still remain open by their rings, and are still filled with air as before. It is beyond doubt that the chest and belly swell when air is inspired: if therefore the lung could be extended (which it cannot at all), it would at least not be to a tenth part of how much the thorax is extended to accommodate the inspired air. Therefore, the motion of the thorax proves that the motion of the lung is not necessary. If the lung filled the entire 
<margin>L.</margin> cavity of the chest (which it clearly does not), it would be consistent with reason that the elevation of the ribs could dilate the lung: but since air undergoes dilation and compression (as is commonly said), therefore the elevation of the ribs would not draw in an adequate amount of air. Indeed, since that attraction would still be violent (namely, for fear of a vacuum), and contrary to natural and vital motion, it follows also that the motion of the ribs was not ordained for dilating the lung. And since the lung has no principle of its own motion, either in itself or from elsewhere, except from the motion of the ribs (according to the Schools), it follows also that the lung is moved by no mover, but clearly always remains at rest.

<margin>M.</margin> For what greater foolishness is there than to admit that all the small branches of the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"</note> are kept open by a structure of cartilaginous rings, and yet to teach that these same branches—when new air is drawn in—are always being widened, spread apart, and compressed? <margin>N.</margin> Finally, the Schools teach that the diaphragm is sufficient for our ordinary use of breathing; yet, for its function, they substitute the intercostal muscles. Furthermore, it is not uncommon for a belch from the stomach to express odors that were drawn into the lung. Therefore, the lung and the diaphragm are members capable of perspiration <note>meaning they allow the passage of air/vapors through their tissues</note>. It is truly deplorable that the Schools have labored over such harmful negligences and childish mockeries. For if you lie on your back and place one hand on the abdomen and the other on the ribs, and take a moderate or unforced breath, you will easily feel that only the muscles of the abdomen were working. <margin>O.</margin> With the belly raised, the diaphragm is pulled downward, and consequently, the cavity of the abdomen is enlarged by as much as the plane of the diaphragm (which is loose in itself) or its diameter is less than its own semicircle when pulled downward—and by as much more as the ductile looseness of the diaphragm's plane allows. Indeed, if you cinch the ribs with a tight belt and take the aforementioned breath, you will feel the belly rise and fall while the ribs remain entirely unmoved. And consequently, the lung—even if it were otherwise mobile (which it is not)—could thus <margin>P.</margin> remain at rest all day long. But in a sigh, a yawn, a sneeze, and heavy panting, the intercostal muscles are felt (and not before then) to perform their duty as substitutes and helpers. For the ribs are semicircles hanging downward, which the individual intercostal muscles pull <margin>Q.</margin> upward. To this extent, they also become larger by being lifted, insofar as they then become rounder and thus enlarge the cavity of the chest. <margin>R.</margin> Indeed, those who breathe only with a stiff neck draw their shoulder blades and shoulders apart to help the breath, and press their hands on their seats on both sides to elevate the shoulders,

<column-break/>

so that the cavity of the chest may be increased, and the diaphragm may project downward with a greater swelling. <margin>S.</margin> The wife of a nobleman, while struggling to give birth (for the child was coming into the light buttocks-first), broke and tore her <term>pleura</term> <note>the membrane lining the chest</note> between the 7th and 8th rib, without feeling it (for a greater pain obscures a lesser one) due to an abscess, etc. Soon after the days of her recovery, she noticed that whenever she held her breath, whether by singing or straining at stool, if she had removed her bodice, a huge, flatulent tumor would immediately protrude, which would yield to a pressing finger and hurry back inside when the breath was released. And so thereafter, she never slept except with a tight bodice. <margin>T.</margin> From this it is clearly established that the breath is led directly through the lung into the chest cavity. I noted a similar thing in a high-born woman who, since childbirth, had retained a condition where, whenever she held her breath, she showed us one side of her throat swollen like a bladder. <margin>V.</margin> It also pertains to this that I have attentively considered those with lung disease, as well as those breathing with difficulty, and I found that they usually lie more successfully on one of their sides, and can scarcely breathe on the other. For it is beyond doubt that this defect belongs to the lung itself; because on the "down" side of the lung (that is, the one the patient is lying on) and whichever part then touches the rib membrane, the pores through which one usually breathes are crowded together. Furthermore, the pores of both lobes of the lung on the "up" side may be morbidly obstructed—if not all, then at least a large part—and this is to be measured by the proportion of the failing breath. By this argument it is manifest that the lung does not rise and fall like a bellows; rather, it is permeable by pores, through which the air flowing to and from the chest corresponds to the width of the chest's expansion or contraction. This is why people breathe better standing up than lying down. Because the lung is then hanging, it has free pores on all sides which have not succumbed to the defect of blockage. <margin>48.</margin> It is therefore an error of the Schools to teach that the diaphragm is the sole moving member of the lung, and so...

# D O T A G E S . <note>original: "DELIRAMENTA" — referring to the "follies" or "errors" of traditional medical schools.</note>

the proper and primary efficient organ of breathing. Namely, that while the diaphragm contracts toward its center, it causes exhalation; and as much as it relaxes this contraction, by that same amount we inhale. 1. For since every voluntary movement is executed by a muscle, with the tail drawn back toward its head, the diaphragm would then be the first, most irregular, and most principal muscle, and its head would be in its middle, or its center. 2. If, therefore, the diaphragm were the primary executive organ of movement, even if the abdomen and ribs ceased to function, the diaphragm would produce movement by itself. Which is false. 3. Indeed, the abdominal muscles, which are the ordinary muscles, would not move; rather, they would be moved by the diaphragm. 4. Therefore, its own fleshy membrane of the belly would suffice for this duty, and those muscles would have been made in vain. 5. Finally, since every organ of voluntary movement pulls while moving, the chest ought to be pulled inward by the draw of the diaphragm, and exhibit the shape of a clepsydra <note>An ancient water-clock, typically narrow in the middle.</note> on the outside around the diaphragm. 6. Indeed, exhalation would not be a rest from movement, but the very movement of the contracted diaphragm. 7. And so exhalation, even in healthy people, would always be more difficult than inhalation. Since 8. inhalation would not be a movement, but the relaxation or rest of the contracted diaphragm.
<margin>49.</margin> From which I conclude: 1. The use of the diaphragm has remained unknown until now. 2. The use of the lung has also been hidden. 3. The manner in which breathing occurs was unknown. 4. The first and principal organs of breathing were unknown. 5. For the modest respiration and exhalation of breath, the abdominal muscles alone suffice. 6. That the Lung is never moved; and that it serves as a sieve, so that pure air may enter the chest. 7. From this, therefore, it is clear why syrups and linctuses <note>Thick, honey-like medicinal syrups licked from a spoon.</note>, since they do not reach the affected places, are useless remedies. For would coriander, thrown into boiling water, prevent vapors from being made from the water or from ascending? Similar are the things prescribed for combing and rubbing, namely that catarrhs should be led not late, but in the morning, not toward the forehead, but toward the back of the head. And even if the matter always turned out otherwise in practice, and they saw nothing responding to their rules, they nevertheless drew a veil over such atrocious ignorance under the numbness of "impossibility." They cried out, therefore, that there is an imperceptible and ordinary descent of excrements from the brain into the lungs; and they decreed that "licks" <term>illinctus: a syrupy medicine meant to be licked or dissolved in the mouth, like a lozenge</term> would be the ultimate remedy for Consumption <note>original: "Tabis"</note>, since they are carried immediately to the larynx and from there to its thin tubes. That trial was indeed cruel to the dog, but far more cruel and unhappy for mortals. This is because the Schools, at the persuasion of this experiment, have handed down from hand to hand and subscribed to such pernicious trifles. For first of all, what would syrups and licks accomplish in the branches of the windpipe, except the harm of obstructions? To what end, then, would they naturally and ordinarily hasten there, or be sent, or be admitted? Since they cannot be "cooked" <note>processed by the body's heat</note> there, nor changed into anything good, nor can they heal pus or mucus. Finally, if this happened ordinarily, the ordinary phlegm of healthy people would smell of putrefied broth or syrupy licks. And although the first spit-up sometimes resembles the licks, these do not come from the lungs, but from the vicinity of the throat. Nor does repeated spitting express the licks any further, just as repeated spitting otherwise coughs up soot. Then also, those who lick several ounces in one evening...

It is truly a wonder that the Schools <note>note: referring to the traditional academic medical authorities of the time</note>, misled by such a grisly experiment on a dog, did not notice that through the dog's inadvertence—amidst such howling in the slaughterhouse—that colored broth was snatched into the larynx. This is not something that usually happens in healthy people, nor is it observed in those suffering from catarrhs <note>term: catarrh; an old medical term for excessive buildup of mucus</note> (as they call them). Indeed, if a person with bladder stones, while passing urine, even unwillingly relaxes the anus because of the pain, is it therefore a property of the bladder's sphincter that by relaxing itself, it also ordinarily opens the anus? For because of pain, parts of the body sometimes perform their duties poorly and lead other neighboring parts into error with them. Rather, one should trust the histories in which it is written that some were suffocated by a thin feather, and another by a single hair. This is so they may know that the lung is in no way receptive to foreign things without notable harm and distress; indeed, *as those with shortness of breath* know, they cannot even endure fragrant fumigations (*for the reasons recited concerning the human "Blas"* <note>note: "Blas" is Van Helmont's specific term for a vital motion or guiding force in the body</note>). If, therefore, even helpful fumigations are a burden to the lung, what will linctuses be? Even if it were granted that they could reach the lung? For this reason, whenever anything is swallowed, the larynx is firmly closed by the epiglottis—which mimics the shape of an ivy leaf—lest even the smallest thing slip down to the lung. And I have known several who were suffocated because on at least one side the epiglottis was not closed tightly enough, due to a convulsion of one part or a paralysis of the other. 

<margin>§ 5.</margin>
And herein a new error of the Schools is detected: namely, that they assert that linctuses swallowed gradually are admitted into the lung, but not those things which are swallowed abundantly and quickly. Did the dissected dog then "lick" and not rather gulp down the injected broth of herbs? For why did they inject it for drinking if they knew that by licking alone the way lay open to the lung? But if the hypothesis stands—that the lung rejects the company of all foreign things except for pure air, not 

<column-break/>

associated with smoke—it follows necessarily that whether something is swallowed by licking or by drinking, the same care of the guardian epiglottis is always exercised, and the same closure of the larynx is observed. For in that moment, nothing less than the loss of life is at stake. Therefore, linctuses and syrups, although they may make the throat parts smooth for bringing up phlegm, nevertheless primarily harm the stomach and are absolutely of no benefit to lung afflictions. But they say that saliva, by a spontaneous slip and even without sensation, flows into the larynx, and that linctuses would be helpful on this basis. 

<margin>§ 6.</margin>

A *stage-performer* was recently seen, walking on his hands with his feet and body upright, who drank a cup of wine while having his head near the ground. I appeal to Anatomy,

But if any saliva then falls into the larynx through carelessness, a cough does not cease to explode it out immediately. But how, finally, will the lung be helped by *sugar linctuses, soaked with the cadaverous fried lung of a fox or the juice of coltsfoot*, if the lung itself, shuddering at all foreign things, admits them only through carelessness and immediately explodes them with great distress? For will that be enough to restore damaged faculties? Is the root of catarrhs cut down in this way? Certainly, wherever I turn, I do not see the Schools attacking diseases except through the fabricated dreams of the heathens—in imagination, in effects, and from hindsight. And that is because of their ignorance of diseases and causes. Thus, the name of "Physician" has deservedly turned into the jokes of comedians, because they do not think about what they do, what they say, or what they ought to do to satisfy the precept: "Be merciful, even as your Father who is in heaven is merciful." ## On the Nature of Catarrhs

Hence arose the decree that pain (since it is an accident of inherence) <note>A philosophical term meaning pain cannot exist without a physical subject.</note> does not migrate from one subject to another, unless something material, from the brain through the muscles of the vertebrae, by a prone gliding, has given place to the filth of *Catarrhs*, and fits the accepted etymology of *Catarrh*. <note>The word "catarrh" comes from the Greek *katarrhein*, meaning "to flow down."</note> This persuasion of the *Catarrh* must be recognized for what it is, once the mask is removed by *Anatomy*. <margin>59.</margin> For indeed, if the painful matter drips successively from the brain through the neck: it would surely be carried there either through the sinuses of the brain, or through the brain and the membranes <note>original: "meninges"</note>, or between both membranes, or between the hard membrane <note>The dura mater.</note> and the skull, or finally between the cranium and the skin. For the conclusion holds by a sufficient enumeration of the parts. Yet, it is not primarily through the vessels of the brain, because without *Apoplexy* and certain *paralysis* of the whole, this could not subsist: if only the doctrine of the *Schools* regarding these diseases stands firm. For if it were expelled successively from the prior parts to the fourth sinus: the matter of the *Catarrh* into the spinal marrow <note>The spinal cord.</note> could not fail to block it with that foreign and sharp excrement, and then *Apoplexy* and *paralysis* would be born. Secondly, this matter of the *Catarrh* cannot, by sweating through the brain, accumulate and glide between the brain and the thin membrane <note>The pia mater.</note>, so that both membranes maintain a continuous separation from the marrow of the spinal nerve itself: because the gliding *catarrh* would produce a tearing and

<column-break/>

a solution of continuity <note>A medical term for a rupture or break in bodily tissue.</note> in the medullary root of the nerves, along its length. Which is not without many absurdities. Likewise, if the *Catarrh* rained down between both membranes, there would primarily be two small membranes coating the spinal marrow: which the eye has not yet observed. And that being granted, it could not at least disturb the movement of the muscles, or know pain. And so there is an error in the thesis. Because the nerve is indeed the organ for conveying the command of the will, but not therefore the executor of voluntary motion. Especially since a small nerve sometimes hardly exceeds the thickness of a doubled thread: and being inserted externally into the muscle, the impacted catarrhal humor could not bring anything but paralysis to the part, and certainly not the immense pains of a moved muscle. Finally, if the *Catarrh* flowed down between the hard mother <note>The dura mater.</note> and the skull, *Anatomy* teaches that the exit of the nerves laterally through the small holes of the vertebrae is so exact and narrow that by no means is an entrance given for the *Catarrh* from the spinal marrow to the muscles. Finally, if a place were granted to this fiction, what at least would be the cause of the succession, so that the humor, once fallen between the small nerve of two vertebrae, would return to other successive nerves? Does the *Catarrh*, perhaps affected by boredom with one muscle, then desire other clients of its delights? For how shall the catarrhal humor flow down through a tiny nerve without numbness of the limb? Will it enter into the muscle by a foreign grafting all the way to its tail? And from there will it truly recede again to other muscles, which are in a more prone location? Or if a new *Catarrh* is imagined to flow down to other and lower parts with equal succession; how then do the upper parts appear immune from the evil? For since it would proceed from the same source, the brain, and through the same channel of the marrow of the backbone; why does it not rather follow the path already opened? It would settle more in the weakened, prone, and affected part, and commit new adul-

Why does it seek new matter? Why does it seek new lodgings? Is that perhaps a whim of nature, which, with a harlot’s appetite, successively infests and pulls apart new areas? Finally, it has already been discussed above that there is no place of refuge for a catarrh <note>original: "catarrho"; traditionally thought of as a "down-flowing" of cold phlegm from the brain</note> running down between the skull and the scalp, and the muscles clothed in their own membrane. Therefore, there is no path, manner, means, connection, or dependence by which a catarrh truly exists. And since nothing material flows down in such ailments—for which the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university medical authorities following Galen and Aristotle</note> have rashly invented catarrhs—let the lovers of truth know this: that as often as a foreign air, odor, ferment, or exotic seed is received into the "impulse-making spirit" <note>original: "spiritum impetum facientem"; the vital force that directs bodily movement and reaction</note>, so often is that spirit contaminated by the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "master workman" or vital governing principle of an organ in Paracelsian medicine</note> and excluded from the communion of life. Moreover, the character or nature of that conceived seed plays no small part, so that the spirit, defiled by a foreign ferment, is sent to distant rather than nearby places. As will be said in its proper place concerning Arthritis in the "Duumvirate" <note>The "Duumvirate" refers to the author's theory that the stomach and spleen act as a secondary governing center of the body</note>, and elsewhere. Thus, for instance, Mercury, even when smeared on the outside, affects the throat, tongue, and teeth. Furthermore, when this defiled spirit arrives at the place of its mission, it immediately imbues the nourishment of that part with its own ferment; it transplants and transforms it according to the "idea" of the seed, and by successive breaths and foreign dispositions, it disturbs the duties of digestion in that place. From this, it eventually stirs up a copious supply of waste, and not infrequently marks the indwelling spirit there with a lasting stigma upon the life-force. The Schools beg for these explanations from the brain alone, blaming it for their primary invented humors and the settling of "down-flowings." I am therefore far from the theory of catarrh, as I deny the matter, the workshops, the efficient cause, and the manner of its becoming and flowing down; and therefore I separate the causes, the effect, and the healing far from the fictions of catarrh.
<margin>61.</margin> Thus, it is not false, acid, sharp, phlegmatic, or bilious humors that settle down: but as often as the defiled spirit passes to a location, the first thing that arrives there, in a common effort and zeal to wash it away,

<column-break/>

is the "latex" <note>The "latex" refers to the clear, watery part of the blood or bodily fluids, distinct from the "nutritive" blood</note>. For the spirit, depraved by exotic contagion, is carried through the nerves, arteries, and indeed through the very habit of the body. Hence the brain has borne the blame, and the sick feel as if there is a settling of a flowing humor. And because the latex is assigned there through the veins—not as the primary cause of the evil (although by accident it not infrequently nourishes the evil longer), but for relief and washing—the Schools have remained doubtful whether Catarrhs are sent from the head through the nerves or between the skin, or indeed through the veins from the liver, at least in those suffering from gout. Therefore, the phlegm and bile of the Schools do not flow from a fountain or a cataract, as if the head were the sole sewer for these things. Furthermore, they do not fall down because of a downward-sloping position or because of the ease of the paths. For just as in a corpse there are no such defects, but only in the living, so whatever of these things happens proceeds from the "impulse-making" power and the vital beginning. In its economy, an upward ascent is no more difficult than a downward descent. Since none of these things flow in the living by their own motion of gravity, but are indeed directed and sent to certain boundaries. It also happens not infrequently that the latex, contaminated by a foreign salt, then infects the spirit, so that the spirit is not always alienated by an external injury of the air or by its own internally generated breath of contagion; rather, the spirit, being stirred up, assumes a "thymosin" <note>A term used here to imply a spirited or reactive quality, likely derived from the Greek 'thymos' (soul/spirit)</note> for itself from the latex (as it is less alive). And the latex accompanies it, troublesome both in its aforementioned acidity and its quantity, entering like an unruly soldier against the will of the host. For this reason, hot springs, baths, and sweat-houses resolve more defects of this kind—by consuming the latex—and restore health more effectively than the "solutives" and "exsiccatives" <note>laxatives and drying medicines</note> of the Schools.
Vain, therefore, is the story and the matter of Catarrh being raised from the stomach to the head; vain also are the flowings and settlings between the muscles and the skin, and the remedies for unknown causes are to be deplored. Vain also are the cauteries <note>The practice of burning the skin to "draw out" bad humors</note> used to pull back and consume invented humors. However, the history and necessity of the latex is owed its own chapter. You will remember that all the fruits of solid bodies are materially born from water. Let us imagine, then, that the latex is tasteless, but soon becomes sour with the help of a tiny bit of "seed." For example: in the spring, a copious liquid drips from a vine or a birch tree. If the bark is wounded near the ground, it pours out the tasteless liquid of the earth. But if a wound is made in the trunk or branches, that same juice is already slightly acidic. So it happens in the latex, which is tasteless by nature: through the contagion of the vessels receiving it, it finally becomes sour or becomes the heir to a foreign quality. For the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university authorities following Galen and Aristotle, whom the author frequently critiques.</note> have neglected the latex because they confused urine with latex. # THE METHOD OF NOURISHMENT

Therefore, these things vary according to the palate of the Physicians <note>original: "Medentum"</note>. For what is praised as healthy for one person is condemned by another who finds it less pleasing. In this way, pheasants, partridges, starlings, blackbirds, and fattened capons are preferred over quadrupeds; even though the latter <note>mammals</note> bring forth living offspring just as we do, and are thus more familiar to us than birds, fish, and insects—that is, egg-laying animals. So too, rock-fish are preferred to sea-fish, and fine wheaten bread to bran bread. For those who are overly delicate devote themselves to the "pimping" of the kitchen <note>original: "mangonio," referring to the deceptive alteration or "dressing up" of food</note>, so that they might please the sick. These people, destitute of remedies and true science, have enslaved themselves to an otherwise sterile profession, for they end up as teachers of cooks. How tirelessly they survey everything, so that they may exercise their command in kitchens and dining rooms; and so that they may seem to have diligently provided for everyone, they are ready to exercise a tyranny over the sick.
<margin>4.</margin>
As if food and drink were the cures for the more serious diseases! Truly, I have always been remarkably ashamed of this branch of medicine. Indeed, even as a young man, I sensed deep down that healings <note>original: "sanationes"</note> are the effects of medicines, not of foods. Therefore, just as I suspected the weak action of foods, I also guessed that a strict obedience to diet—on the part of both the one commanding it and the one obeying—implied a favored ignorance of the true and adequate remedy, or even a deception <note>original: "imposturam"</note>.
<margin>5.</margin>
On the contrary, he who has fire is able to burn; and he who has a knife is able to cut. So also, he who possesses the fit secret <note>term: "arcanum," a specialized alchemical or chemical remedy believed to have specific healing powers</note> of curing is able to heal, to despise the rules of diet, and to bypass the superfluous industry or flattery of the Schools in this regard. For any error that might otherwise arise from the choice of diet is easily forestalled by the overpowering goodness of the remedy. For if Hippocrates prefers accustomed things (even if they are less healthy in themselves) to unaccustomed things, and says a diet should not be changed easily, safely, or quickly from what one is used to: what then should we think of those chosen, longed-for, and desired foods and drinks? Especially since it has been discovered that when nature dictates from within, a remedy has often shone forth through those very foods,
<column-break/>
to the great shame of the Physicians, especially when they had previously forbidden them.
<margin>6.</margin>
Dietetics, first of all, does not deal with things that are openly harmful: for there is no debate whether it is healthy to eat poisons, or the scrapings of pots, etc. Indeed, it is not even a question of whether it is healthy for a sick person to be stuffed with much food or drink, even if it is nutritious <note>original: "enchismis," referring to juices or nourishing liquids</note>. Or whether gluttony, drunkenness, and a disordered life are healthy acts and suitable aids for preserving or recovering health: rather, the whole of Dietetics is occupied only in the selection of foods and drinks. These, however, as "indifferent" nutrients, exist within the limits of goodness and differ only in the breadth of their neutrality. And for that reason, I have always looked upon Dietetics as a betrayer of the ignorance of causes, of true Medicine, and of the prevailing remedy.
<margin>7.</margin>
How many people are there, for instance, who have often recovered after rejecting the rules prescribed for them? Meanwhile the Physician—while the disobedient patient laughs through his teeth—arrogates the praise for the healing to his own rules? Hence, indeed, this "Art of Healing" is dragged onto every stage, because these dietary rules testify to a poverty of judgment in both the Physician and the patient.
<margin>8.</margin>
From this, Physicians not infrequently hope to find an opportunity to excuse a death, blaming the disobedience of the sick regarding dietary rules not strictly kept. What absurdities, alas, are committed by this trickery, which are not yet sufficiently clear to the world! That while they know nothing, or have nothing with which to drive out the disease and force it to obey them, they should at least be thought to want to remove the "impediments to growth" through the allurements of the kitchen and much fussing?
<margin>9.</margin>
If the observation of a Diet were useful, it would serve either during the illness or during recovery <note>original: "convalescentia"</note>. During the illness, how troublesome, annoying, and impertinent it is! While for the most part the appetite lies prostrate, and yet suggests its own satisfaction so that it does not perish entirely? The preservation of which is of as much importance as the indication of life itself! For in a state of wavering appetite, nature usually suggests to itself the convenient food; and that not rarely, then especially—

especially when it is most unworthy of help. Physicians then struggle against this decree of nature through their rules of diet: from which the sick person should abstain, unless he wishes the entire cause of his death to be attributed to an unfaithful helper. For then, the *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "vital director" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions and healing.</note> rages symptomatically, because it feels itself denied a perhaps familiar food that it desired; and thus they stir up a new dispute within the dispute. Just as a horse passing through water, and not drinking enough to its liking, thereafter retains an anxious difficulty in breathing for the rest of its life. <margin>10.</margin> Truly, a diet imposed by disease, or during convalescence, is also wonderfully troublesome, if not even useless, since nature is already busy of its own accord. Indeed, the prescription of a Diet cannot help but accuse the lack of a sufficient remedy, and is thus an implicit confession of an unfaithful healing. For let the Physician heal as is proper, and as nature promises, as a guarantee of restoration. Surely the Almighty saw and judged that whatever He had made was good. That is, whatever He had intended for <margin>11.</margin> food was good. Or whatever He had ordained as poison, was a good poison. For otherwise the poor man would have great right to complain that God had shared with him in a less fatherly way, because He had denied the means by which the needy, by responding to elegant rules of Diet, could have recovered their health: while to the Rich, He had bestowed health along with wealth. Inasmuch as He grants the means by which they might pay the costs of the <margin>12.</margin> Diet. For indeed, for fifty years now I have experienced for myself that I heal more people, even those not seen, and by scorning the rules of Diet, than many Physicians together who wander about our city. I experience, I say, that I cure all continued and intermittent fevers in a few days, indeed and mostly in a few hours, without admitting the blood-letter <note>original: "phlebotomo" — the practice of bloodletting, which the author rejects here.</note>: but <margin>13.</margin> permitting wine. For the most powerful part of the Diet of Physicians is found in the flattering of the sick, prepared for the sake of the Physician's popularity. Excepting usually the wine. Also, each of the Physicians proclaims those things to be healthy which please him more.

<column-break/>

But lest this be discovered to be a kind of sycophancy, they enjoin strict obedience, so that by this severity of laws they may be thought to hold the reins of life. <margin>14.</margin> Bread especially is held to be the primary food; but other nourishments are only side-dishes <note>original: "concibi, vel obfonia" — items eaten with bread.</note>. I, on the contrary, call the other nourishments the true foods; but bread only a side-dish. For many are found to have lived for a long time on milk alone. The Irish also, men of swift and most ready strength, use *Chambroch* <note>Shamrock or clover.</note>, or trefoil, in place of bread in some places. And some Northerners live to a great age on fish alone without bread, and remain persistent against cold and diseases. "A stuffing of bread is the worst," says the Proverb <note>original: "Adagio"</note>: not only because it is an index of poverty; but because in truth, in a weak stomach, it is most burdensome. <margin>15.</margin> Inasmuch as bread, on account of the ferment it has received (for otherwise it is nothing but paste), melting into a cream, forces the herbs and foods with which it was chewed to melt together (which we experience daily in the digestion of manure) and for this reason alone it is a side-dish rather than a food. But lest I dwell too long on names, it is enough for me, in whatever way it is called, provided the use of bread is known, and its necessity for the liquefaction of foods is most effective. <margin>16.</margin> Furthermore, I have always highly valued sobriety as the hinge of the entire Diet. <margin>17.</margin> Then also, if the appetite were carried toward some object, I have willingly allowed it, yet with the moderation of mediocrity. However, I am not one who does not know that one food excels another, or is more suitable for the sick: but I am little troubled which of the two the sick person takes, provided he has at the same time obtained some good remedy. <margin>18.</margin> Thinking that if a remedy is not strong enough to meet the evil arising from a less suitable food, it will also be far less strong to overcome or expel diseases. Therefore, I have considered those remedies unfaithful and sluggish which are hoped for from the prescription of a Diet. Since, as it is often said, it is easier not to admit a guest than to expel him. And from the correlative: Whoever presumes, by the virtue of a re-

# THE METHOD OF NOURISHMENT

If a physician is certain that his remedy can overcome a disease, he should be equally certain that any complications arising from unsuitable foods will be far more easily overcome by that same remedy. Therefore, I have always considered it a sign of weakness and lack of confidence in a physician whenever he is anxiously preoccupied with the shameful <note>original: "pudibunda"; the author suggests it is beneath the dignity of a high physician to act like a kitchen-maid</note> care of the kitchen. For such a man, lacking a worthy medicine, prescribes a selection of foods and pins his hope on the "critical day" <note>The "critical day" was a traditional medical belief that diseases had set turning points (like the 7th or 14th day) where the patient either recovered or died.</note> just so he appears to be doing something in the meantime and does not receive his fee for nothing.

I have learned this through my own conviction:
1. First, that the nature within us is wiser than any physician, and more aware of its own benefit and harm than all the collective genius of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university authorities of the time, often followers of Galen or Aristotle.</note>.
2. Consequently, nature selects for itself and desires what is most suitable.
3. Just as a beast never died of thirst because it satisfied its craving—unless perhaps it had swallowed poison or succumbed to excessive greed—so too, drinking during fevers overcomes many of the discomforts of dryness.
4. Drinking when thirsty is no less natural than urinating when the bladder is full.
5. Therefore, since the latter does not require a doctor's permission, the former should not require a consultation either.
6. Furthermore, by administering a few drops <note>likely a reference to alchemical or spagyric tinctures</note> along with the drink, which penetrate easily (especially during thirst), I have many times suffocated numerous fevers to the great delight of the patients.
7. A great craving for something that apparently violates "Dietetic rules" is usually dictated by nature itself, which knows its own remedy, whereas the books of the Schools do not.
8. Therefore, we ought to be very little concerned about desired things that are only slightly harmful or unusual.
9. If a remedy is to prevail over a disease, food and drink, in all their variety, cannot contain the inherent strength of a medicinal substance <term>pharmaceutical entity: the active healing power of a drug</term>.
10. If foods are not a remedy, then they can also hardly contain a great harm—speaking of foods as such, that is, as indifferent things.

I have convinced myself of these things and prescribed them to others. To be sure, abstinence and moderation are the best means in Dietetics. And even more so when something is

<column-break/>

eaten with pleasure. According to the proverb: *What tastes good, nourishes.* For the appetite is satisfied by quality, not by quantity. Otherwise, if fullness burdens the healthy, it burdens the sick and weak much more.
2. Let them eat, certainly, but not to the point of filling the stomach cavity, nor according to the dictates of pleasure or taste, but as much as easily suffices to maintain a healthy life. If this is difficult at first for one forming the habit, it will at least not be so for one accustomed to it. For how foolish it is for one groaning through illness to wish his past gluttonies undone. <margin>20.</margin> I would not, however, want anyone to persuade himself that this sobriety of living and "light backpack" <note>a metaphor for a light digestive load</note> can protect anyone from the Plague, accidents, wounds, lightning, or the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>. For external incidents disregard the economy of digestion because they overpower it. Indeed, I categorize "the stone" among external things because it is produced by a foreign ferment <note>The author views stones as a chemical precipitation caused by an outside influence rather than a failure of the body's own nature.</note>.
3. <margin>21.</margin> Since all food must be changed into chyle <note>original: "cremorem" (cream/thick juice)</note>, there must be thorough chewing to facilitate digestion; hence, I perpetually and most severely recommend mastication. Indeed, a single morsel not properly chewed causes more trouble in the body than three that are well-ground by chewing. Birds, because they lack teeth, require a double stomach, even though they are otherwise very powerful at digesting. Every ruminating beast <note>animals that "chew the cud"</note>, held in high regard in the Law <note>A reference to Kosher laws in the Bible (Leviticus 11), where chewing the cud is a sign of a "pure" animal.</note>, seriously impresses upon us the necessity of chewing which must not be despised. Indeed, for that reason, a ruminating beast is chosen as "pure" in the Holy Scriptures.
4. Finally, <margin>22.</margin> whatever is taken during a bout of gluttony <term>crapula: excessive eating or drinking</term> beyond the power of the stomach's ferment, grows hot inside but putrefies and is not even digested to that extent—as is most evident in fevers. However much of the more tender foods are taken during gluttony, they are indeed digested and slip out of the stomach, but they drag down a great mass of undigested matter with them, both because of the tension of the vessel and the carelessness of nature, which is overloaded and lets go of the reins. But if it has been digested,

# THE METHOD OF DIET 451

If food, even that which is by far the most tender, remains in the stomach longer than is right, it is necessarily retained and becomes excessively sour or plainly putrefies. It is drawn down into a bitter excrement by morning, not infrequently rejected through vomiting. This is what the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities of the time, often followers of Galen or Aristotle.</note> have falsely called Cholera. For dyers, with a single dyeing of a vat, can change over a hundred different colors if the cloths were previously treated in different ways. In the same way, a single stray ferment of the stomach—which would otherwise produce a uniform chyle <note>term: chyle (cremor) — the milky fluid of digested food</note>—disposes and determines that chyle into various forms according to the diversity of its parts, if it still contains undigested differences within itself. Thus, although it ordinarily dyes only the digested part of the chyle with its ferment, it does not cease to affect the undigested part, and due to the defect of the receiver, it imbues it wrongly. For this reason, many things go astray in this way in the "kitchen" of the first digestion.

5. Whatever is customary, not harmful, but desired, is assumed; that is also more easily digested when satiety is absent, and is safely admitted in diseases if taken soberly and moderately. This is because ferments easily subdue those things which are customary, and especially if they are craved. Indeed, Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician, often called the Father of Medicine.</note> advises that a very thin diet should be used in acute diseases, specifically until the appetite rises again. For I praise thinner beers, whereas I despise sweet drinks and ptisans <note>term: ptisan — a medicinal herbal infusion or barley water</note>,
<margin>23.</margin> relying on the words of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>. He says: "Barley that is poorly cooked causes windiness; but it causes obstructions if it has boiled a bit better." Therefore our Ancestors, believing that boiled barley was in no way harmless, forced it to sprout (which they then called Malt <note>original: "Maltham"</note>), by which process they prevented both windiness and obstructions. From Malt and hops, they fashion beers.

6. I also urge no one toward concentrated broths,
<margin>24.</margin> crushed meats, eggs, etc., if an acute fever is present, mindful of that precept: *The more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them.* For even if in acute illnesses one lives without food and by 

<column-break/>

drink alone, no danger to life threatens from that. Rather, they recover more quickly this way, and strength and appetite return with much less obstacle. For whenever something capable of putrefying—or "corpse-making"—is cast into a stomach lacking its digestive ferment, the food putrefies and is not digested. And that is the correct explanation of that Aphorism. For I never desired that patients should return from acute diseases fat or fattened, but I intended this one thing: namely, that they should recover, and indeed without their strength being greatly cut down. Therefore, I have drawn the greatest part of the diet in stomach diseases from the Aphorism: *That a sour belch, coming upon greasy ones, is a sign of restored ferment, and is good.* For greasy belches, the spontaneous aversion to nausea, to meat, fish, and eggs, and indeed the burdens of the stomach, have commanded that the sick person be nourished by drinkables alone. For otherwise, through "corpse-making" substances, I had learned to expect strange accidents, failings of the mind, and other inconveniences of that kind. Since then, drinks moisten, they comfort the thirst, and they yield to the heat; they ward off the dryness and weaknesses following from it. By "drink" here, however, I do not mean sips of broths that are abundantly nourishing—those which, in a hot stomach without digestive ferment, spontaneously turn into a corpse—but entirely of those things which putrefy the least: such as bread-water <note>original: "panata" — a soup made of bread crumbs, water, and sometimes oil or butter</note>, and likewise beer tinted with wine, with which a crumb of bread has been mixed at the same time, so that they are food and drink at once. To this I recall what I have taught at length elsewhere: namely, that digestion is caused by its own ferment, and not by heat. Therefore, whenever there is an aversion to meat and greasy belches, it signifies that heat is present and the acid ferment is missing. Attend to this: how easily fresh meat, tied to a hot foot or head, putrefies and immediately stinks. In a feverish stomach, therefore, being quite hot, wise Nature fears a "corpse" being made within itself, and therefore immediately turns away from meats. But to what end...
<margin>25.</margin>
