# THE METHOD OF NOURISHMENT.

Where then does the ferment <note>original: *fermentum*; the author views digestion as a chemical fermentation process rather than just mechanical grinding or heat</note> of the stomach go during a fever? Has it migrated elsewhere? Or is it extinguished? For why would the ferment have departed, since it is welcome nowhere except in its own hiding places? Nor has it perished. For it is vital; and whatever is vital, once it has perished, does not return again from a state of deprivation. Yet the ferment is capable of revival. Therefore, this is what happens: either sometimes the release of the ferment from the Spleen to the stomach does not reach its destination due to some defect in one of the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>The "Duumvirate" is the author's term for the Spleen and Stomach acting as the dual governors of the lower body</note>; or at least, once the ferment is received in the stomach, it is masked by a foreign and febrile odor. Understand it in this way: someone who is hungry and in the best of health, staying too long amidst the persistent fumes of coals, soon perceives nausea arising, an aversion to food, then also a pain in the forehead, and finally vomiting. Just as the ferment of the stomach is covered by the harmful odor of coals, so likewise, by the virulent odor of stirred-up fevers and a foul-smelling contagion, it happens that an aversion to meat is immediately born, insofar as the ferment native to the stomach is covered by that stench. I had concluded these things for myself regarding diet, and I measured the method of nourishment within the few common rules mentioned above, according to the course of nature, before I had obtained 
<margin>26.</margin> greater remedies. Knowing, however, that whatever is converted in the stomach into a type of transparent cream <note>chyle</note> by the power of its own ferment, has taken on the beginnings of the vital juice, although not 

<column-break/>

yet life itself: and because of this, it does not rot so spontaneously. But whatever is either not dissolved, or if it is dissolved in itself but has not yet received the ferment—such as water or salty brine—that very thing is either excrement or easily becomes such, and is prone to corruption. Therefore, in the method of nourishment, one must pay attention most especially to diseases and foods: what the sick person rejects or craves by reason of the illness. For one must serve nature, and by no means command her. That is to say, the ferment, which ought to prepare the foods, should prescribe them; the Physician should not do so according to his own appetite, nor should he take one single form from the authors to fit every shoe. As if the various natures of men did not relate to things in different ways. Finally, exercises, labors, works, rest, sleep, and air should depend on the rules which the importance of the other digestions dictates to us. Namely, so that the juices generated from the "cream" may more successfully reach their own ends. This is the truth of diet, which nature spontaneously indicates and teaches. And let this one thing be perpetual: that whoever has obtained the best secret remedies <note>original: *arcanorum*; refers to "Arcana," the high-level alchemical medicines</note>, just as he soon restores the sick and delivers them from any disease whatsoever, so also he prescribes no different diet for the sick than for the healthy. For to the healthy, all things are considered healthy, because the digestive ferments powerfully draw anything into their own jurisdiction and restrain it. Thus, the digestions themselves should prescribe the rules of Diet.

<margin>1.</margin> **E**verywhere the Art of Healing is dragged onto the stage and made a mockery for the common people. This is because healers refuse to be wise, except according to the custom of the Schools. For what they read, they believe; and what they believe, they hand over to be executed by the faith of the Perfumer <note>original: "Seplasia," referring to the Seplasia market in ancient Capua, here meaning a common druggist</note>, the wife, and the household servants. From this, any ointment-seller or old woman thrusts themselves into medicine and mocks physicians, because not infrequently they excel them in many matters. For in olden times, people used to reserve certain secrets for themselves as a pledge of their fame and family. But after laziness conquered, and profit arranged Medicine like a plow <note>treating it as a mere tool for labor/profit</note>, by the just judgment of God, everything went to ruin. Before the threshold of the apothecary shop, I cannot help but be indignant at the describers of "simples" <note>unmixed medicinal herbs</note>. For although there is no field more spacious, more fertile, or more pleasant in the whole face of the earth, nor where the mind may be more delighted than in herbalism: yet hardly anywhere else has <margin>2.</margin> less progress been made. Indeed, the Arabs, Heathens, Barbarians, Savages, and Indians have observed their simples much more vigilantly 

<column-break/>

<margin>3.</margin> than all the Europeans. Indeed, since the days of Plato (around which time lived Dioscorides, a military man), almost nothing has been added to herbalism: but much has been diminished. Galen, with a lust for plagiarism, snatched this study of another and—suppressing the name—stole the words of Dioscorides, acting quite "un-Dioscoridean" <note>a pun on the name Dioscorides and "adioscorus," implying he was ungrateful or a thief</note>. Meanwhile, Pliny sprinkled these things with many trifles. Being poor in judgment, he was unable to distinguish the plausible from the true and the false; he described many things scraped together from everywhere, so that the name might equal the magnitude of his volumes. Furthermore, to this very day, the more learned part of healers still anxiously disputes merely the appearances and names of herbs. As if, once the face were known, the powers would not speak for themselves; the powers, I say, first handed down by Dioscorides. As if in the first Author, the medical power had reached its end. Meanwhile, things that were of the greatest importance have stood neglected until now. But the more modern writers have begun <margin>4.</margin> to distinguish herbs into sexes, and thinking they have detected many things therefrom, they complained that these things had remained veiled. As if nature labored in jest and not in earnest, or would have been solicitous about sex where she was content with the promiscuous and the androgynous. For sex regards only generation, but not operation, or the relation of equal objects. Therefore, lest she should establish even a point or a jot in vain, she who referred herself entirely to certain ends known to her Creator, wherever there was no need for the marks of sexes for generating: she also disregarded them in her operation. But if of two simples, one is stronger or harsher than the other, that certainly does not denote sex, but degree. For while the same simple rots and is changed into little animals <note>referring to the theory of spontaneous generation of insects from decaying matter</note>, these are not of one sex, but of both. Which certainly would not happen if those simples already had sex or sexual powers within them. For from the same herb in number, insects of both male and female sex are born indiscriminately. <margin>5.</margin> There were afterwards others who observed "signatures" <note>the theory that plants resemble the body parts they cure</note>, like Chiromancy <note>palm reading</note> in herbs: and the root of the Satyrion <note>an orchid, thought to resemble testicles</note> [suggested] this meditation...

I believe by faith that man is not a reflection of nature, and therefore, in turn, nature is not an image, icon, or sculpture of man. <note>The author is arguing against the "Microcosm" theory which suggests man's body perfectly mirrors the universe.</note> God, from the eternal providence of His goodness and wisdom, has abundantly and sufficiently provided for future necessities. Consequently, more study should be devoted to the investigation of their virtues than to disputing any manner of problems. While God composed this simple to be entirely sufficient against the breaking of bones? Whatever you finally add to it, you act as if you were subjecting God to your correction. You err gravely." Likewise, I also judge that GOD has perfectly and sufficiently composed in simples the complete remedies for any diseases whatsoever. I know finally, without fail, that there is no anatomical kinship between us and the **Archeus** <note>term: Archeus. In Paracelsian medicine, the internal "vital force" or "alchemist" within an organism that directs its functions.</note> of vegetables, whether we look at the whole or finally the parts. Indeed, the endowments of simples are from creation: not, however, from the usurpation of possession: for the properties were already inherent in their herbs before sin, death, and necessity. Finally, I believe that God gives the knowledge of simples to whom He wills, out of supernatural grace: not, however, through the signs of nature!

Or what signature do those simples have in turn? I indeed praise my Lord, who primarily created all things for His glory before diseases existed: nor did He mark the simples because of future diseases arising by chance: but for the beauty of the universe, from whence, of course, comes honor to the Lord.
<margin>6.</margin> Therefore, I reject Paracelsus, because he raised such trifles and follies into the principles of Medicine. There were also those who <margin>7.</margin> expanded an immense catalog of diseases into the signs of the **Zodiac**; and since that number was too narrow, they enlarged each of the signs into a triple section. This was so that they might divide all the powers of herbs into 36 parts and drive them into a cramped stable. For the Earth has from itself the **seminal virtue** for producing herbs, which it therefore does not beg from the Heavens. For the entire property of herbs is from the seed, and the power of seeding is taken from the earth, according to the Holy Scriptures: not, however, from the faces of the lights of Heaven. Suppose that 16 or 20 stars make up a constellation, or one of the 12 mansions, and extend across 30 degrees. How, indeed, can so few stars contain the essences, seeds, faces, and properties of perhaps five hundred plants, differing in species and internal properties? Besides the still-empty thousand attributions of so many things, both human and political? Away with those trifles! The properties are in the seeds of the herbs, not in the Heaven or the stars. The powers of the Stars are obsolete, which stood attached to heats, colds, and complexions by an old fable. For the stars differ much more from plants, in whatever way they are taken, than herbs do from mists and frosts, or fish from precious gems. Therefore, let this be the refutation: to have attributed effects to causes which possess nothing at all similar to the cause within themselves. By their own peculiar reckoning, they wander into madness. Mattioli, Tabernaemontanus, Brasavola, Ruellius, Fuchs, Tragus, Dalechamps <note>These are all famous 16th-century botanists and physicians</note>, and other observers of herbs, have until now occupied themselves only with the appearance and visual recognition of plants. As for their virtues <note>The medicinal powers or "essences" of the plants</note>, they all likewise describe them according to Dioscorides <note>The ancient Greek physician whose work was the standard for 1,500 years</note>; they even confine them to degrees of heat and cold, as if they were demonstrating something from a fundamental principle. It is truly shameful to have derived the *crasis* <note>term: crasis (the specific temperament or "mixture" of a substance)</note> of simple medicines from heat,

<margin>9.</margin>
rather than from the sources of their seeds. Dodoens the Frisian (now become a Dutchman), Tabernaemontanus, and a few others, although they followed the same tracks of "degrees," nevertheless added some additions from their own experiences or gathered them from elsewhere. Yet these are still plainly confused, uncertain, and poorly distinguished, inasmuch as they wrote things noted down not from science, but either from common folk-tales or drawn from accidental experiment. There is no one among them all

<margin>10.</margin>

By a certain sign, true sciences are to be sought from nowhere else than from the Father of Lights <note>original: "Patre Luminum" — a biblical reference to God as the source of all knowledge</note>. As I have touched upon elsewhere in passing regarding the "hunting of the sciences."

<margin>11.</margin>
A whole, living animal cannot be crushed without its dung. It is therefore to be lamented that it has not yet been considered that herbs have much "dung" in them, which they have never ejected from themselves; and thus they must be purified with greater caution. Finally, in man, we distinguish the vital blood from the gore <note>original: "sanguinem à cruore" — distinguishing the life-giving fluid from the waste-heavy clotted blood</note> by many marks. In plants, however, it has seemed sufficient

<margin>12.</margin>
to have said: "This plant, in a single subject, consists of diverse and opposite properties." They are satisfied with this, and have not entered deeper than through a few common flavors and uncertain outcomes. For indeed, from the wounded stalk of a poppy, opium drips. Celandine weeps a golden juice, and Spurge a milky one. From the Butterbur comes a gum, from the Chameleon plant, *Ixia*, etc. If you crush these simple plants, they will yield another

<column-break/>

and far inferior juice—namely the "dung" and the "gore" mixed with the vital blood—no matter how much they are clarified. For the beginners <note>original: "Tyrones" — students or novices</note> should learn to distinguish and separate the vital blood from the gore and the *parenchyma* <note>term: parenchyma (the bulk of the plant tissue)</note> of plants, if they ever intend to achieve anything worthy of praise through simple medicines. For it happens that, however strenuously you have worked at extracting according to the manner taught by the Moderns, one drachm of raw Rhubarb, administered as a powder, still effects more than whatever you might extract from a drachm and a half. For the stomach, by its own ferment, dissolves more than whatever the mediators of juices take away in extractions, because they resolve the dregs-like and despised liquor of the parenchyma without distinction. For Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne, a famous Paracelsian physician</note>,

<margin>13.</margin>
when he noticed that the innermost powers of things were not sufficiently examined through Chiromancy <note>Palmistry/Hand-reading</note> and "Signated Anatomy" <note>The study of the "signatures" or physical signs on plants that indicate their use</note> as they call it, called Pyromancy <note>Divination by fire, here used to mean chemical analysis by heat</note> to his aid; but he failed on the way. Specifically, he had drawn a weak lye from the ash of a nettle, which by chance in a bowl had been slightly constricted by ice (for if the lye had been stronger, it could not have frozen). Marvelling in the morning, he cried out: "Aha! Look, I see the shape of the nettle leaves in the ice!" Rejoicing, he established an axiom: namely, that in the ash there remains a "seminal being" <note>original: "ens feminale"</note>, the shaper of herbs, unconquered by fires. That good man declares his ignorance of principles, not knowing first of all that all beginning ice forms jagged points in the shape of a nettle leaf. Secondly, that the *Archeus* <note>term: Archeus (the internal "chemist" or vital force that directs growth)</note> is the shaper of the thing to be generated, which is burned up by fire long before it becomes coal or ash. Thirdly, if the "seminal being" of herbs expressed the lye,

<margin>14.</margin>
it certainly ought not to represent the leaves, but the root, the trunk, the flowers, and the fruit. But the figurative power of seeds lies hidden in the *Archeus*, the Vulcan <note>The inner blacksmith or fire-worker</note> of herbs and of all generable things, who, since he is not subject to eyes of flesh, must be obtained from GOD alone.

It is necessary to pray that He might deign to open the eyes of the soul—He who showed the properties of things at first glance to Adam and to Solomon. St. Teresa, having once seen the Crucified Lord in her mind, felt that her soul possessed eyes, which she thereafter kept open toward life, but which are closed to us through the corruption of nature. For otherwise, we do not know natures from their first principles <note>original: "à priori"</note>, nor do we know the variations of the *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and van Helmont to describe the internal vital force or "master workman" that governs the life and health of an organism.</note> except through bare observation. Many legacies regarding simple medicines <note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb or plant used on its own, rather than in a complex mixture.</note> have indeed been left to us, but they are mostly false and inconsistent. Nor does the reading of books make us experts in properties, except through observation. It is no different than a boy who sings music but does not compose it; he does not know the primary principles of Symphony, because of which the tones had to be arranged in such a way. If this happens in sensible things known by the senses, the logic of which is measured by hearing, what will not happen in medical matters, in which the powers of simples are not accessible to any sense? Furthermore, the descriptions of whatever medicines are handed down in the workshops are read with a lack of knowledge regarding their properties and harmonies. For I speak of an optical <note>meaning "clear" or "visionary"</note> notion, such as the soul has when separated from the body, and such as God grants in this life to whom He wills; and He has hitherto kept such a person far from the assembly of those who offer all their veneration to pagan books. Therefore, the Father of Lights must be entreated to deign to give us knowledge, such as He once gave to Bezalel and Oholiab <note>Biblical craftsmen filled with the Spirit of God to build the Tabernacle (Exodus 31).</note>, for the glory of His name and the pure charity of our neighbors. In this way, the Medical Art would stand upright under any weight. But it is to be feared lest He, who permitted the books of Solomon to perish, reserves this science of simples for the age of Elias the Artist <note>A legendary figure in alchemy and prophecy expected to appear at the end of time to reveal all hidden secrets of nature.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>15.</margin> For the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic medical establishment of the time.</note> have promised an entry to the science of simples through flavors or tastes. They claim to measure themselves by the sharp, bitter, salty, sweet, astringent, sour, and tasteless—by heats and colds—as if they were the craftsmen of all properties. But these proud displays have been made ridiculous by the result. For instance, they claim opium is very bitter, which they have hitherto wanted to be "hot," yet they teach it is "extremely cold." Likewise, they say that sharp Camphor, according to their rules, ought to be hot, yet they preach it is cold without controversy. Similarly, *Chrysulca* <note>Aqua regia or a strong acid used to dissolve gold.</note>, oil of vitriol, sulfur, etc., being acidic, ought to be extremely cold according to the rules of flavors. But I shall show in the proper place that the Schools have not yet looked at the faculties of things even as far as the bark <note>meaning they have only a superficial understanding</note>, and therefore they have bypassed the fountains of the seminal properties. Finally, there is in individual things <margin>16.</margin> a specific flavor which ought to teach the property, if anything among the external signatures <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that the appearance or taste of a plant indicated its medicinal use.</note> can. Indeed, besides its sharpness, there is a peculiar grace in the flavor of Cinnamon, which you will hardly find in any other simple. Thus Gentian, Elecampane, etc., besides their common bitterness, have a specific flavor which cannot be reduced under rules because of the unique individuality of any simples; it alone is the indicator and the distinguisher of individual properties. Furthermore, that simples must be gathered at the time when they are in their vigor is a point common to the Schools, the peasants, and myself. Namely, seeds when they are nearly dry; stalks and leaves, however, while they are succulent and dripping with full blood; roots also while they swell with strength and have not yet been exhausted by generating and ripening—but many, now saturated with rest, meditate on sprouting once the *Archeus* has been awakened. Others advise Autumn; I mostly love Spring. This I have learned by experience in Polypody, Bryony, etc. For the juice of herbs is their blood, which, becoming more and more matured, is either driven into itself, or ends in the nature of fibers, or at least dies off while the vital force meditates on propagating the seed. Therefore, in investigating and selecting simples, nothing has remained more neglected than that which was most desired, and in which, from the beginning until now, there has been no progress. Namely, the Powers of the simples and their immediate subjects have remained <margin>17.</margin> unknown. For those, besides a clear and, as it were,

The visual knowledge of substances demands a desired preparation and appropriation. Knowledge, first of all, presupposes the sciences; it does not rely on traditions narrated at will and transcribed from one to another. True preparation, however, requires not only the boilings of the apothecary shop or simple crushing, but the entirety of **Pyrotechny** <note>original: "Pyrotechniam" — literally "fire-art," the alchemical term for chemistry involving heat</note>. Finally, adaptation, application, or appropriation requires a theory founded in the light of nature regarding man, diseases, and affections, and thereafter their dependencies, mutations, and alterations. It is no wonder, therefore, that the doctrine of simples <note>medicinal herbs or minerals used on their own</note> has stood deserted.
<margin>18.</margin> Amidst such great sloth of mortals, the Almighty has deigned to raise up the **Spagyrics** <note>alchemists who "separate and recombine" substances to purify them</note>, who rightly consider the transmutation, maturity, tincture, and promotion of powers as being of the highest necessity. And thus, having progressed to the harmony of Medicine, these followers have escaped as masters of their wish. For they did not go toward the immoderate measurement, struggle, or flowing of fictional humors <note>referring to the traditional Greek theory of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, nor indeed to the products or fruits of diseases (the pruning of which they knew resulted only in the temporary masking of recurring illnesses); instead, they turned their study to the prior or preceding causes. They knew that the powerful basis of many defects was characterized in the **Archeus of life** <note>original: "Archeo vitæ" — the internal "vital programmer" or life force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine</note>. Therefore, through the purity, simplicity, and subtlety of remedies that possess a symbolic likeness, they attempted an entry into the "middle life." So that if any of these remedies do not penetrate to the primary constituents of our being, they might at least display their dowry at the threshold of these parts, exciting our powers by their pleasing address.
<margin>19.</margin> For nature not only recognizes the actions of agents that enter entirely into the domain of the patients <note>the "patient" here refers to the body receiving the medicine</note> (for such action is merely bodily, like the obedience of the nourishing faculty); but there is also another authority of agents not to be despised, which is the unfolding of a native gift into the very middle life of the **Archeus**, on account of the sequestration of mortality, dregs, and turbulence. By this superiority, such

<column-break/>

agents suffer nothing from their patients, and much less are they altered by resistance or reaction.
<margin>20.</margin> For some remedies prepared in this way, by their silent union, so refresh our faculties that they make us more certain that they came into the world for this very purpose. For some refresh us, as it were, by their fragrance. There are others which, being closed up, are hindered from showing us their benevolence—such as gold and gemstones. Others finally, once their bonds are loosed, are led into a higher grade, happy as if by the favor of growth; having attained the liberty and authority of their powers, they raise us from a fall and console us. Surely they act no less vigorously than lethal Aconite <note>Monkshood, a deadly poison</note> otherwise ruins our strengths. They drive out, to be sure, the bodily and even the fermental virus. This is not to say, however, that any drug can restore anew the powers implanted in the parts once they are extinguished, abolished, and exhausted. Furthermore, it was an error of the schools not to first subject the juices of herbs, along with their pulp, to a ferment before a selection of the best parts becomes possible.
<margin>21.</margin> Then they also neglected to investigate how the juice of things, expressed by a press, remains thereafter without sugar or other additive uncorrupted by the mere odor of a certain sulfurous fire; by whose favor it acquires something balsamic, and transfers the ethereal draughts incorporated into itself to the **great entelechy** <note>original: "magnam entelechiam" — the realization or complete expression of a vital principle</note>. Furthermore, descending to the labors of the apothecary shops: first of all, although extracts seem to relieve a sluggish stomach from labor, I do not value them highly on account of the errors already noted.
<margin>22.</margin> Instead of extracts, I substitute **Magisteries** <note>original: "Magisteria" — in alchemy, a "master" preparation where the full essence of a substance is extracted without losing its soul</note>, by which the entire substance of a thing is reduced into its primitive juice. This method of preparation will generally remain unknown to the common sort of physicians forever. In this backward-step of dissolution, heterogeneous juices are spontaneously separated, usually floating upon one another in different layers, and one "governor" settles there, distinguished by its diversity, containing the **seminal essence** <note>original: "ens feminale"</note>. Secondly, I am troubled by the mixing in shops of so many simples...

<margin>23.</margin> For the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the 17th century, which followed Galenic tradition.</note> hope that if one ingredient does not help, another will; and thus they associate many things together, which are exalted toward the same goal by the public praise of herbalists. To these are joined the sisters of deception: boiling and seasoning.
<margin>24.</margin> Consequently, the Dispensatories <note>Standardized books of medicinal recipes.</note> described by the Schools and used by healers are commended for speed and readiness (indeed, storehouses or "promptuaries" take their name from this readiness) but not for appropriateness or the specific requirements of the patient. That is to say, they possess only general and universal intentions, allowing for the substitution and "dispensation" <note>The legal permission for a pharmacist to swap one ingredient for another.</note> of one thing for another. <margin>25.</margin> The patient thinks that he who swears he has been admitted as an expert and a sufficient practitioner cannot err, deceive, or be deceived. I, for my part, greatly admire the sincere composition found in "simples" <note>Medicinal plants or minerals used on their own, not mixed.</note> which was made by God the Creator.
<margin>26.</margin> In Comfrey <note>original: "consolida" – a plant traditionally used to heal bones.</note>, for instance, I find a full remedy for a broken bone <note>original: "ossifragii"</note>, possessing everything it needs. If you mix into this Armenian bole <note>A medicinal clay.</note>, vinegar, or other foreign things—as I warned above from Paracelsus—you have already corrupted the mixture ordained by God.
<margin>27.</margin> Nevertheless, whenever individual things do not achieve the intended goal, I occasionally admit additions, provided that the things acquire through their union what they do not have in isolation. This must subsequently be confirmed by the teaching of experience. The clearest example of this is in ink and dyes. Indeed, under the penance of my studies, I often considered that since in nature there was a certain proportion of matter to matter, and form to form, the same was also kept from properties to properties, and consequently,

<column-break/>

from effects to effects. But the failure of these soon taught me the composition of simples. There, "alterations" enter immediately from the beginning of the mixed seed, and they mostly destroy themselves—not unlike the seeds of many things crushed and confused together, which shut out the hope of growth. I knew thereafter, through much labor and expense, that the materials of remedies—provided they were raised to a nobler dignity by preparation—could reach a degree of perfection, freedom, subtlety, and purity, and would far excel the decoctions, syrups, and powders heaped under honey found in the apothecary shops.
<margin>28.</margin> For whoever is well-instructed in the exercises of Pyrotechnia <note>The "art of fire," or chemical laboratory work/alchemy.</note> clearly perceives with me that no drug is found in the Dispensatories that does not contain more harm than benefit.
<margin>29.</margin> For the Schools, which profess to follow Hippocrates, even if they recognize that diseases proceed from the sharp, the bitter, the salty, or the acid, they nevertheless mask and season everything with nothing but honey and sugar. They overwhelm the properties of remedies (which are otherwise weak enough in themselves) as if the sole remedy and pinnacle of all diseases resided in sweetness.
<margin>30.</margin> For they respond that laxatives work no less successfully even if sugared; secondly, that they are more pleasing to the palate; and thirdly, that they are thus preserved from decay and rot. Regarding the first point, I admit that poisons have an equal effect whether they are accompanied by sugar or swallowed alone. Indeed, the power of laxatives is entirely sealed in the liquefaction of the body, and in the putrefaction of what is liquefied; therefore, it ought to be infamous as a poison. The response of the Schools is therefore irrelevant, using poisons to answer a question about remedies for diseases characterized by bitterness, sharpness, etc. To the second point, I say the response is futile until the first point is satisfied. They do not yet know that the strengths of remedies are changed and blunted by sugar. Although the taste of aloes becomes more pleasing to many by a drink of honey, they are nevertheless unable to flatter the stomach, which—at the mere sight of drugs covered by the trickery of sugar—shudders...

Furthermore, a substance is more easily smoked <note>The author likely refers to "fuming" or vaporizing a medicine, or perhaps its rapid absorption</note> in a few drops of some liquid and is more willingly digested within the body than when preserved in a large amount of sugar. Finally, when mixed with a suitable liquid, medicines penetrate more deeply and unite more harmoniously than when covered by much sugar. For sugar, though pleasing to the healthy, soon becomes horrific to the sick; in most diseases of the stomach and womb, it is hostile. In others, it not infrequently makes the help of the added remedy ridiculous. For sugar is diametrically opposed to the acid ferment of the stomach, and therefore makes digestion more difficult. Indeed, sugar is clarified with a lye of quicklime and potter's clay. If the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university medical authorities following Galen and Avicenna</note> had known the sharpness of the spirit of honey and the foul dregs of sugar, they would have been content with a more sparing use of them among the sick. To the third point <margin>31.</margin> I finally say: the Schools confess their ignorance in this, that they do not know how to preserve medicines from corruption without seasoning and the castration of their strengths. Therefore, the fraud of syrups is sufficiently detected, which are made only from simple decoctions with honey or sugar added. To this end, it follows that vegetables, when boiled in water, deposit only juice and mucilage. These raw and impure substances inflict their own troubles upon the stomach before they—digested with honey—can make us heirs to their virtues. Especially since the gumminess of herbs, when fried with honey and sugar, becomes unpleasant and troublesome to the stomach, and a notable loss of virtues occurs through boiling. I praise my kind <margin>32.</margin> God, who called me into <term>Pyrotechny</term> <note>The "art of fire," a synonym for chemistry or alchemy</note>, far from the dregs of other professions. For <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: Chymia</note> has principles not born of logical arguments, but which are known through nature and made visible through fire. It prepares the Intellect to penetrate the secrets of nature and places investigation further into nature than all other sciences combined; it penetrates even to the furthest depths of real truth. Because it admits the operator to the first roots of those

<column-break/>

things, with the articulation of the operations of nature and the powers of art, and with the ripening of the seminal virtues. For the Most High is praiseworthy and super-glorious, who gave this science freely to the little ones. I also rarely use remedies from across the sea or sought from the farthest <margin>33.</margin> East, knowing that the Almighty made all nations of the earth healable, and did not wish that goods brought from the Indian shore must be waited for; just as God was no less favorable to mortals before the Indies were known. Therefore, divine <margin>34.</margin> goodness has persuaded me that for local diseases, their own remedies are found at home. And the <term>Spagyric</term> <note>The alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to create medicine</note> theorems have taught me that a tiny liquid may be prepared which keeps the <term>constitutions</term> <note>original: crases; the balanced temperament or essence of a substance</note> of simples uncorrupted, without foreign seasoning. Therefore, they boil herbs in water, wine, <margin>35.</margin> or distilled liquid down to a third or a half, even in a "double vessel" (as they say) <note>A bain-marie or water bath</note>, and piled up under a "diploma" <note>A sealed vessel or specific chemical apparatus</note>. In these, the best strengths—if they do not perish—at least are not drawn out, except for the troublesome and unpleasant mucus of the herbs, which the stomach must digest, even if the decoctions and juices are purified with egg whites and masked with sugar. As such, they are drunk without the separation of the pure part by the invalid, without the unlocking of the closed virtues, without the root of life, and without participation in the correction of defects, rawness, excrement, and violent powers, whose activities our nature cannot bear without grave slaughter. Next, <term>electuaries</term> <note>Medicinal pastes made with honey or syrup</note>, <term>confections</term>, <margin>36.</margin> or <term>pills</term>, whether for strengthening or for purging, teem with even greater miseries than syrups. For without boiling, by crushing or powdering alone, they are connected from many simples ridiculously, ignorantly, and thoughtlessly—things which for the most part oppose, harm, and hinder each other from joining in the mutual work they owe us. For it is not in <margin>37.</margin> nature, as the Schools have looked for in numbers, that strengths come together into one simply because they agree by units.

# THE APOTHECARY SHOP AND...

For in nature, every single thing is unique, lives by its own internal economy, and does not rejoice in marriage <note>original: "conjugio"; here meaning the forced mixing of substances</note>. Thus far, the operation of Healing proceeds into the middle life of the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: the internal vital force or "inner alchemist" that governs the body's health</term>, which, through confusions and connections, if it does not perish entirely, is at least manifestly weakened. Indeed, the failure of success resulting from the embrace of many seeds should have warned the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Galenic academic medicine</note> to abstain from the confusion of so many and such diverse simples <term>Simples: individual medicinal herbs or minerals used as ingredients</term>. How much more so, because under that multitude, many substituted, opposed, useless, and otherwise heavy, impertinent, inept, improper, and therefore languid, exhausted, bad, and dead things flow together, or at least become so. For although the defects and adulterations of simples are more the fault of the merchants than the *Seplasii* <term>Seplasii: an archaic term for perfume and ointment sellers or druggists</term>; nevertheless, not to have discerned them is the mark of a lazy, ignorant, or greedy pharmacist. Meanwhile, it is certain that for the most part, everything is eventually taken in raw, hard, immature, closed, poisonous, impure, bound, and unfit for the communication of its powers, and is further corrupted by mixing. And because the stomach of the sick is on the threshold, it is therefore the first to be offended, because it is weak and unfit for extracting the middle life that is hedged in by so many difficulties. Therefore, with singular labor and care, it was absolutely necessary to anticipate this, so that we might prepare everything for the languishing stomach, if we hope to reach the conceived and desired ends pleasantly. Thus, the use of all confections is horrid, nauseating, and tedious. And so hence comes that proverb: <margin>38.</margin> "It smells of the Apothecary." Also, regarding purgatives, if you remove Scammony and Colocynth <note>Two powerful, often harsh, herbal laxatives</note>, the entire building of the shops' purgatives will collapse, those two columns upon which it rests having been removed. For purgatives—besides Scammony, Colocynth, Euphorbium, Elaterium, Spurge, and such manifest poisons, and those still adulterated, filthy, and horrid—contain absolutely nothing but the chief causes of the diminution of our strength and vigor: unless we suppose those same poisons are present in a mitigated form in aloe, rhubarb, senna, agaric, manna, and

<column-break/>

similar things, which are all the more subject to imposture. I hate, therefore, the preparations of simples whenever washing, boiling, roasting, associating, or calcining <term>Calcining: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to ash or powder</term> causes a loss of power. For Aloe, by <margin>39.</margin> washing, loses its juice, and a mere resin remains as a residue, which by its adhesion to the intestines is a provoker of griping pains and hemorrhoids. Finally, since the genial and chief power of spices lies in their scent, <margin>40.</margin> if this vanishes of its own accord and strikes the sense of smell spontaneously, what will finally happen by boiling and roasting, especially when heat is added? This is what our distillations of fragrant things teach us. Finally, what can be said in the Schools <margin>41.</margin> more foolish than to have reduced Hartshorn <note>original: "Cervi cornu"; deer antler, used as a source of ammonia/calcium</note> to an insipid ash, deprived of all virtue, for great uses? And to have substituted castration, or rather deprivation, in place of preparation? For I have learned that most remedies, by scent and taste, both internally and externally, aid our infirmities: and therefore I have detested the mixtures of many simples, because if you add another scent on top of a healing scent which suppresses the first, cloaks it, converts it into itself, or raises a third thing from both that is neither; I knew then that the specific healing power would be abolished, and the effect desired by the patient rendered void. Therefore, the association of spices and sweets is suspicious to me. Furthermore, I hate most of the other confections of the <margin>42.</margin> shops because they are futile: in which they strive to cloak and blunt the towering and violent power of things with certain ridiculous additions. Indeed, meanwhile, they preach that the innate favor of this kind of medicine is promoted just as much as they take away from the powers by the annexed forces. For they mix in a few grains of cinnamon or other futilities with most things, so that they might subdue the furies of the more violent ones—as if the furies of laxatives could be tamed by a few grains of spices! Who, even slightly instructed in Chemistry <note>original: "Chymicis"; referring here to the burgeoning field of iatrochemistry or alchemy</note>, does not know that in aromatic confections, the first sin is that of plurality? Then, that most of those things are in vain...

<margin>43.</margin> Is it not a sin to err through the rawness, hardness, poor sealing, selection, and substitution of simple ingredients? <note>original: "simplicium" — individual medicinal herbs or substances used as components in a compound.</note> Finally, do these not flow together in doses that are still uncertain, whereby the hoped-for effect is surely prevented? And this, indeed, arises from the error of each individual part. Let me settle this with a single example.

<margin>44.</margin> What, I ask, is in the *Lithontribon* <note>A traditional "stone-crusher" remedy intended to dissolve kidney or bladder stones.</note> that actually satisfies the promises of its name? For what purpose are cinnamon, cloves, three types of pepper, sweet flag, costus, rhapontic, cassia, bdellium, mastic, amomum, hog’s fennel, spikenard, ginger, the wood and juice of the balsam tree, tragacanth, wall-germander, euphorbium, and also the oils of nard and nutmeg included? Do every one of these conspire toward the goal proposed by the name? Or will some new power arise from things mixed together—things that smell of each other's intentions—which might fulfill the promises? Namely, to powerfully shatter a stone in the kidney and bladder? And to immediately resolve all defects of urine? Or would the true balsam <note>original: "opobalsamum"</note> not rather perish among the rest of the dross and rubbish? Furthermore, in opiate confections, the same "deafness" <note>A metaphor for the lack of harmony or responsiveness between ingredients.</note> found in aromatic ones is met with everywhere. To settle this with another single example: For what purpose does the confusion of 65 ingredients in the *Aurea Alexandrina* of Nicolaus <note>A famous, complex medieval electuary attributed to Nicolaus Myrepsos or Nicolaus Praepositus.</note> exist? These simple ingredients have no kinship with opium and mandrake, which are the pillars of the confection. Truly, these gatherings of simples, made at the whim of the ignorant, have infatuated the Schools and exhausted the sick; they have frustrated them with injected hope and exposed the fleeting moments of the opportunity for healing to sale by uncertain conjectures, letting them pass by. Therefore, if you examine the compositions of the apothecary shops without a prejudiced mind—whether in syrups, electuaries, pills, linctuses, lozenges, or others—you will be stunned with a useful wonder that the world has been deluded by the chatter of healers, the foolish stupidities of the Schools, and harmful presumptions.

For as Christians, we believe with the Stoics that the world was brought together for human use. And when I was once contemplating this deeply within myself, it soon

<column-break/>

<margin>45.</margin> seemed to me that human use could have conveniently done without such great poisons. For I have found our colder climates to be more fortunate in this at least: that they lack the monstrous, virulent, and lethal reptiles with which the hotter zones otherwise swarm. Certainly, we have no great necessity for, familiarity with, or abundance of poisons; nor will their use in any way compensate for the many calamities arising from them. Indeed, if the earth brings forth briars and thorns as a curse for sin, it surely carries far greater calamities on its back, troublesome to the lives of mortals, both in the class of animals and of vegetables. Wherefore the text threatens only a very small thing through "briars and thorns" compared to the maximum which man had already explored in the cunning of the hostile serpent. Truly, if it be well investigated, nature has scarcely anything immune that does not have its own toxin secretly mixed into it. For we have no roses or violets that do not deceive us; indeed, beneath such fragrance of scent, they hide the contagions of poison: namely, the signs of putrefaction, the melting away of our body, and the stealing of our strength. Therefore, having entered into an inventory of simple ingredients, we shall find very few that are innocent; indeed, if you look at the fields, the entire globe of the earth is nothing but a single and continuous spider's web. Furthermore, by attending closely, the face of things today seems to be the same as it was before that single sin. And so perhaps from the beginning, there were more poisons, harmful and guilty things, than good things on the earth—yet not a "medicine of extermination" for man. Because Paradise lacked poisons of that kind, even if serpents were present; or perhaps by reason of immortality, poisons would have been as nothing to man in Eden.

But on the contrary, the Almighty saw that whatever He had made (even in the world outside of Paradise) was good in itself and for its own ends. Therefore, I was for a long time deluded within myself, thinking poisons were unworthy of existence. Both because the honor of God did not require their existence, and also...

...that man would have more gladly lacked so many poisons; indeed, I used to think that poisons were created neither for the glory of **GOD** nor for human use. For there are very few innocent things which are safe to use without caution: most, in fact, fight against us with a horrifying tyranny. Some also consume us by burning with their sharpness: many others everywhere, under a friendly appearance, mock us and carry a hidden, deadly enemy within. In general, however, there is nothing that does not teem with filth, and everything is bristling with impurities: consisting finally of rawness, lack of proportion, and an unconquerable persistence of perversity. For although man had been brought into Paradise, the praiseworthy Architect of things knew from eternity that the world would be a home for man: and just as He gave the earth to the sons of men, so He created it and all its contents for the sake of man. Finally, looking into the universe more clearly through Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiam"</note>, I repented of my former rashness and my stupid <margin>46.</margin> ignorance. Indeed, in both aspects, I humbly adored with admiration the immense Mercy and Wisdom of the Architect. For He did not wish poisons to be poisons or harmful to us. For He neither made death, nor a medicine of destruction upon the earth: but rather intended that, by a little effort of ours, they might be changed into great pledges of His love, for the benefit of mortals against the cruelty of future diseases. For in those very things lies hidden a help which the milder and familiar simples <note>Individual medicinal herbs or plants</note> otherwise refuse. For the greater and heroic uses of healers, such horrifying poisons are preserved. For brute beasts hardly feed on them, either because they know the poison intuitively—which is not otherwise betrayed by smell or taste—or because some governing spirit of the beasts preserves those poisons for greater uses, as if they were heirs to the greatest virtues. It is enough, at least, that the beasts leave the most powerful remedies to us, as if by the command of the Most High, who has more care for us than for the cattle. For raw Asarabacca <note>original: "Asarum"; a plant used as an emetic</note>, although

<column-break/>

it induces vomiting with such great distress, and the stomach testifies to the poison present in it: yet how easily that recedes by boiling, and the venom is changed into a deobstruent <note>A medicine that removes obstructions in the body</note>, a diuretic, and a remedy for lingering fevers, because the hidden aroma within it then comes forth? So too Cuckoo-pint <note>original: "Aaron" (Arum maculatum)</note> becomes mild when boiled with vinegar and becomes a cure for great ailments. For this reason, the Schools <note>The established medical authorities/universities</note> instituted "corrections"; but would that they were not ridiculous, not castrations, and not rather the stripping away of strengths! They think, forsooth, that the laxative property flies out of the Asarabacca through boiling, not unlike how every thing decays with its own <margin>47.</margin> rot as the years fail. But at least the root of Asarabacca does not become mild in the same way when cooked in wine as it does if it boils in water. Yet at an equal degree of fire, its laxative property would fly away just the same. Others therefore think <margin>48.</margin> that the rawness in Asarabacca is the cause of the purging; but these people overlook vegetables that are rawer than Asarabacca: and that Hellebore is not "ripened" by cooking if the vomiting were to arise from rawness. They cook Scammony <note>A harsh purgative resin</note> in acidic things to mitigate it: but the common crowd of healers already knows that Scammony is thus "castrated," so that if it is exposed to the acidic vapor of sulfur, it is plainly deprived of its power; and as much of the Scammony's power departs as it has absorbed of the acidity. But I, wishing with a fatherly mind to correct the furious force of medicines, understand that the original strengths of things ought to remain, and be turned inward to their own root, or be transmuted under their simplicity into other endowments, lying hidden there in secret under the guard of the poison: or be newly acquired by reason of an added perfection. In this way, Colocynth <note>Bitter apple, a potent laxative</note> turns its laxative and deadly quality inward, and there emerges from the depths a resolving power, an excellent curer of chronic diseases. For <margin>49.</margin> Paracelsus <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> attempted this with praise in the tincture of the "Lily of Antimony"; yet he was either silent, or did not know, that the same could be done in absolutely all poisons of animals and vegetables, through his "circulated salt." ->All the poison of these substances perishes if they are returned to their "first entities" <note>The *Prima Entia*: a Paracelsian concept referring to the original, pure essence of a substance before it is corrupted or solidified.</note>. This is the pivot point that the Schools do not know; but the physicians chosen by God, whom the Almighty selected from their mother's womb, will know this in the age to come, and He will make a distinction between the sheep and the goats. Therefore, the simple herbs of great power are not to be castrated or killed, but rather improved through Art: either by the extraction of what lies hidden, or by the suspension of their virulence, or the substitution of one for another through specific commanding additions. These things are for those to whom it has not been granted to taste the power of the *greater circulated salt* <note>original: "salis circulati majoris" - a high-level alchemical solvent or catalyst used to transform substances without destroying their life-force.</note>. For certain things, having laid aside their wildness, become mild through additions: they become neutral, namely by taking on participatory strengths from both sides. And therefore, it is not permitted to borrow such additions from the accepted Dispensatories of the pharmacies, which do not teach improvement, or even corrections, but rather the slaughter of things; or they offer nothing but utterly playful <note>i.e., trivial or ineffective</note> correctives. For example, the Marquis Carlo Spinelli, recently Commander of the Ligurians, when he had walked through the city on foot late at night and inspected all the walls, ordered physicians to be called. He told them that he had sometimes suffered from epilepsy and had been cured by me, but that he had subsequently felt vertigo after he had come down in the crossing from Aquitaine to Liguria. <margin>50.</margin> The "Crown of Healers" <note>A sarcastic reference to the group of prestigious university doctors.</note>, on the following morning, gave him a scruple of white Hellebore to drink, and for a "correction" they added an equal amount of anise seeds. Soon, within half an hour, he vomited, and then in vain he invoked my help while I was absent; he accused his murderers, saying: *My Helmont, you told me so—the doctors will kill you.* <note>original: "Helmonte mio, voi me lo dicefti, gli medici t' uccideranno."</note> He fell silent, and after two hours, with his stomach convulsing first and then his whole body in spasms, he died. The physicians sought excuses, and the earth covered their fault. For in this way, the concoctions of the Schools, through their "corrective" dispensatories, carry many foolish things with them in their baggage. Opiates especially have hot things

<column-break/>

annexed to them; laxatives, however, usually have ginger, mace, anise, and whatever might be able to heal the griping pains caused by the subsequent effect of the purgatives. Alas, what unpunished license ignorance has held over mortals! How little they understand their own Hippocrates: *If those things are removed which are fitting (that is, which harm and burden), the sick person feels better and bears it easily.* For indeed, since those things which harm within often weigh scarcely a drachm, it is necessary that every purging which ends in health be an evacuation that is either imperceptible or at least very moderate, and accompanied by a restoration of strength. For this is the kind which the sick bear easily with benefit. Therefore, the "correctives" of pharmacists are useless burdens and a weight described by the Schools without knowledge of things; they are thus destructive at least to the medicines, if not also to the sick at the same time. This part of healing requires a skillful and knowledgeable Secretary of Nature. Because in that part, the most ample riches of medicines and the "golden furniture of Glaura" <note>An alchemical metaphor for hidden, precious wisdom or the perfected state of matter.</note> are found. The Schools once learned from our Philosophers that the most excellent virtues dwell in "simples" <note>Single-ingredient medicinal herbs.</note> over which deadly poisons have been set as guards. From this followed the rashness of those who mixed manifest poisons and open corrosives with antidotes, hoping that through the goodness and quantity of the additions, the malignancy of the poison would be overcome—as if it were fitting for health that a pestilential glove be carried into a guest room filled with healthy air. <margin>51.</margin> For I do not here accuse the viper in the Theriac <note>Theriac was a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "universal antidote" containing viper flesh.</note>, without which, indeed, the medicine is like a dead heap of herbs. For viper flesh is in itself harmless and without poison; indeed, it is an antidote to toxins. But the lozenges prepared from it by boiling leave all the power in the broth which the raw flesh preserved. I complain in this place about the arsenicals, placed by "masters" (as they call them) into the Alexipharmic <note>A medicine intended to ward off poison or infection.</note>.

For the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic medical authorities of the time, often followers of Galen.</note> presume, because of the rarity of such boldness, that they deserve trust, and they have placed the glory of their studies in the authority of possession. Nor is it a permanent rule that the most excellent virtues must always dwell alongside destructive elements in the same subject, such that the virtues are covered by 
<margin>§2.</margin> poisons. Indeed, Arsenic, Orpiment <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, and so on, no matter how much they are fixed or sweetened, are never to be taken internally, even if others have advised otherwise. They are effective only externally; they kill and subdue other poisons of ulcers, provided they themselves have first been brought under control. Therefore, the "corrections" <note>The process of adding ingredients to a drug to mitigate its harmful side effects.</note> of medicines are currently performed without knowledge of their properties, parts, and harmonies. For what does a spice weigh in respect to a poison? If the whole human body, robust and full of life, collapses instantly from the bite of a viper's tooth? Will Monkshood <note>original: "Napellus"; a highly toxic flowering plant</note> become mild by the addition of a clove? Will Bitter Apple <note>original: "colocynthis"; a powerful and painful laxative</note> cease to cause rot and its accompanying griping pains if it is joined with Tragacanth <note>A natural gum used as a binder</note>? Therefore, the corrections found in the dispensatories <note>Pharmacopoeias or recipe books</note> are merely burdens and stupid additions which do not moderate the virulence, but rather cause a loss of strength.
<margin>§3.</margin> For just as poisons have a fermental promptness in acting, we should have labored to preserve the strength and promptness of medicines, but through the applications of Art <note>Refers to Alchemy or "Pyrotechny"</note>, we should direct them toward the necessities of chronic and deeply rooted diseases. This was the only thing remaining in this business: that we break and tame the extreme violence of the substance through fermental propagation. For this 
<margin>§4.</margin> reason, just as I pity the compositions and corrections of the workshops in general, I detest even more the precipitations, vitrifications <note>Turning a substance into glass</note>, and preparations of Mercury, Antimony, Tutty <note>Crude zinc oxide</note>, sulfur, etc. Likewise, I detest the adulterations of spirits made from spices, hot seeds, vitriol, sulfur, and so on; for these are prepared for profit by our "runaway slaves" <note>A derogatory term for dishonest or unskilled laboratory assistants</note> and provided to the apothecaries, more in contempt of Pyrotechny <note>The art of chemistry/fire-working</note> than for 
<margin>§5.</margin> the lack of sick people. I likewise deplore the shameful simplicity of those who offer gold 

<column-break/>

leaf and crushed gems to men with great hope, selling their ignorance—if not their deceit—at a high price. As if the stomach could expect even the slightest help from such things! More subtle, and therefore more to be pitied, is the error of those who corrode and seem to dissolve gold, silver, corals, pearls, and the like through acid liquids; they think that in this way, once admitted into the veins, these things will truly communicate their properties to us. For they do not know—ah, they do not know—that acid is hostile to the veins. Therefore, once the foreign acidity of the solvents has been overcome and transmuted by the body, those metals and stones return to being powder, just as they were before. Even if it is reduced to the finest dust, nothing is digested by the stomach, nor does it share its powers with us. You may see this for yourself: pour Salt of Tartar <note>Potassium carbonate</note> onto things dissolved in some sharp, corrosive liquid, and immediately the dissolved substance will fall to the bottom in the form of a powder. For if "strong waters" <note>original: "aquæ fortes"; nitric acid or other mineral acids</note> do not change metals in their substance—even though they are made transparent where they were previously opaque—then silver can be recovered from them unharmed. By what blindness, then, do they administer stones and pearls, as if they had left behind the original essence of the stone or metal through the use of corrosives? This was the invention of a subtle deceiver, so that he might value his goods highly among the sick. Because ignorant deceivers think that if the solvent cannot be visually distinguished from the dissolved material, then the dissolved material itself has been truly and substantially transmuted. Finally, oils and fats are not effective as balms, ointments, and plasters, except perhaps to give consistency to a drug. For first, a large portion of people do not tolerate oily substances on the skin, because they excite itching, pustules, and swelling. Secondly, because the aforementioned oils are 
<margin>§6.</margin> mostly prepared from herbs whose virtue lies hidden in a mucilaginous and gummy juice; this juice is drawn into the broths by boiling or expressed by a press, but it never truly "marries" with the oils, and eventually hardens when fixed. But I, in...

-># THE MODERN DISPENSATORY<-
->## Ooo 3<-

I more rightly gather the balsam of flowers with honey. However, I admit the simplicity of single oils more readily than those that are compounded. For that reason, I especially reject the clumsy and "deaf" <note>original: "surdas" - likely meaning ineffective or unresponsive</note> compositions of ointments and plasters found in the apothecary shops. Nothing is more foolish than to scorch the powder of vegetables by fixing them under various fats, ignorantly mixed, and thus rendering them useless. If the powder is mineral, it does not mix with the fat; rather, it is so covered and imprisoned within the greases that it becomes worthless, serving only as weight. Indeed, nothing should be mixed into oils, ointments, or plasters that cannot <margin>57.</margin> be resolved into them homogeneously throughout. It is even worthy of a loud laugh <note>original: "cachinno" - a derisive laugh</note> that *Tabarzet* sugar <note>A high-quality white cane sugar, often associated with the city of Tabarzad</note>, or the whitest kind, is commended—not because it is sweeter or more worthy in its own strength, but because it is more expensive and has been boiled more often with a lye of quicklime. In this case, the name of "purity" has created a deception. When crushed flowers, herbs, etc., are mixed with *Tabarzet* sugar, they remain dormant; but with a sweeter sugar, they catch a ferment and, by effervescing, they unlock the powers of the Simple <term>Simple: a medicinal herb used on its own</term>. Soon after, the fermentation is inhibited by the closed digestion of heat, and they become far more powerful. This difference in fermentation depends on the lye, which one sugar possesses in abundance while the other lacks it. I am also accustomed to apply ointments externally with <margin>58.</margin> discretion. Specifically, in ailments where the healing moves from the center outwards—such as in a wound, a bruise, or a burn—I advise they be applied lukewarm. But where an internal ailment seeks external aid—such as dysentery, colic, kidney spasms, or a *scirrhus* <note>a hard tumor</note>—I order the external ointments to be warmed by a heated stone or hot sand. I learned this by watching chaff in a cauldron of warm water, moving up and down

<column-break/>

as if by the heat kindled beneath. Therefore, I first suspected that applied ointments are animated by a potent heat and join their spirit to our blood; then I discovered that in this way the evil is drawn out and the symptomatic impulses are halted. Whatever baths do for the whole body, these heated and warmed ointments accomplish for a specific part, without loss to the whole. For a warming brick drives the scent of the plaster inward and draws out things that otherwise cling sluggishly; likewise, as the spirit makes an onset with the blood, it is drawn out and dispersed by the heat, and another spirit succeeds in its place, drinks in the strength of the medicine, and, as if boiling inward, is rolled back. Regarding the collection <margin>59.</margin> of "simples" <note>medicinal plants</note>, there is also not enough agreement everywhere. They determine that roots should be gathered toward autumn. But for the most part, many plants give more powerful roots in the spring. Spring Polypody <note>a type of fern</note> is especially vigorous. In autumn, however, it shows a gray and black root: namely, one that is exhausted and aged. I believe each thing should be harvested immediately before its state of maturity; for full maturity is the beginning of decline. Therefore, let there be determined spans for the maturity of individual fruits, flowers, roots, leaves, barks, etc. For the sap first flows into plants, which in many then soon dries up or is consumed by the leaves. Thus, the variety of maturities produces a variety of collections. For some leaves are more vigorous than the flowers, while others are more succulent before the leaves appear. Then also there are those which are stronger before the growth of the fruit. Some persist with an evergreen leaf. Therefore, they determine more rightly who harvest the simples according to the requirements of the goal.

Truly, those things which smear over, stuff up, or dissolve, and cause the substance of our body to become salty (as if through tiny points) without a sense of burning or acrimony: those, I say, are what moisten. And that only occasionally, and as if by accident. Therefore, I perceived that whatever dissolves, resolves, and liquefies glutinous things, moistens. Namely, insofar as they remove the obstacles of coagulation and dryness. Therefore, mallow, Marshmallow (<italic>Althaea</italic>), and those things believed to be moistening—insofar as they close the cutaneous pores and thus stop <term>diaphoresis</term> <note>perspiration</note>—have given birth to an error in the Schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities</note>. For such moistening would be nothing but a morbid retention of excrements, and not a dewy moistening of the parts. I also perceived that nothing else dries within us except those things which, by thinning, dispose the body toward exhalation. For in this way sweat, although it moistens the skin and makes the habit of the body swell, <margin>5.</margin> nevertheless merely dries us out. Furthermore, whatever things cause coagulation, I perceived to harden and turn things into lumps rather than to dry them. Therefore, the opposite of coagulation is <margin>6.</margin> resolution <note>dissolving</note>, not moistening. Truly, those things which induce <term>Atrophy</term> <note>wasting away</note> and cause consumption, I perceived that this does not happen by a "drying quality," but because the liquor, which is otherwise nutritious, is secretly withdrawn elsewhere; on which occasion the ferments, connected to heat, accomplish a true drying. <margin>7.</margin> Thus I perceived no other drying in us than that which occurs by the resolution of ferments and the scattering of heat. I perceived, I say, that coagulation itself, or hardening, proceeds from its own coagulum, or the property of the seed, which promotes liquids into

Therefore, I perceived that thirst is not an introduced quality of dryness; but that thirst is a natural sense of diminished liquid, yet not so completely lacking that it signals a beginning dryness. Thus I perceived that preternatural thirst is not an indication of parching. For people drink and distend the abdomen while the thirst remains safe and sound. Therefore, examples of excessive heat and cold are like a sword; they are not to be counted among the occasional and internal causes of diseases to be considered by the Physician. If, of course, according to the theorems, health is expected by the removal of those causes. Wherefore, the speculation of external and antecedent causes is not curative, but only occasionally diagnostic and directive. For when a wound is inflicted, even if the sword is removed, the wound is not healed. Nor is the fire to be removed from the hearth, even if it has sometimes burned someone in that same place. Since the internal causes of diseases are connected occasions, their consideration and removal is truly medical. <margin>9.</margin> But when the Schools saw that fire burns its objects, and similarly that cold mortifies and destroys, and that the human body is moved in various ways by those excellent external qualities, they thought for that reason that effects which had heat attached to them were stirred up by fire. Something dreadful to our vital organs. At the very least, whenever a poison possesses a mild taste, I have sensed within that same simple exterior a great secret, which—once the poison is removed—is born and ordained for <margin>28.</margin> arduous effects. I have perceived thereafter, beyond specific flavors and their pleasantness, goodwill, or horrors, a certain formal property emanating from them; yet this is imperceptible to the tongue and comprehensible only to the *archeus* <note>The "archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "vital director" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions.</note>. The Schools are struck dumb whenever they arrive at what they call "occult qualities." For since they are unable to ascribe their trifles to heats, colds, and their borrowed "complexions" <note>The traditional Galenic theory that health depends on the balance of four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, writers lay down the pen, and physicians shrug their shoulders and raise their eyebrows. They blame this "property," which is known to them by its effect but unknown in its cause; they shield themselves in this ignorance by claiming that the investigation of those properties is impossible for the human intellect—properties they would have otherwise sought out long ago. It is as if they say: "We, the Schools, are the ones who determine how far the human mind can inquire. We therefore decree that no powers of things can be understood or investigated by humans except those which are the primary qualities of the elements, or those arising from them." We admit, therefore, that formal faculties are "occult" simply because they are impossible to know. Certainly, the Schools are quite muddy, watery, airy, cloudy, and fiery! How they reveal themselves to be ignorant of their own subjects and unequal to the practice they profess! For they have enslaved their talents to laziness, so that nothing is more pleasing to them than to resort to making excuses for their ignorance and the "impossibility of nature," with which each man veils his own particular failings. For first, when the Ancients saw some disease cured by a specific and appropriate remedy, they were amazed as if at the miracle of an unusual thing. But thereafter, the Schools thought it sufficient to relegate their own stupors to a general state of ignorance. Nor indeed, even if they had distinguished causes from the elementary qualities known to them, did they say anything un-

<column-break/>

-contaminated or without a cataract in their eye. For who has ever investigated the cause of moisture in water, or of heat in fire, by *a priori* reasoning <note>Reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> any more than the drawing of iron to a magnet? Therefore, the elemental qualities are just as "occult" as any of the others. Indeed, the Schools have been blinded in this because they have proceeded against Gospel doctrine. For the primitive truth <margin>29.</margin> dictates that we should "know the tree by its fruits" <note>A reference to Matthew 7:16.</note>; the Schools, however, insist that the fruit must be known by the tree. I shall say, therefore, through the fruits, in what manner one must arrive at a knowledge of the tree. First, then, for the knowledge of occult causes, some effect is presupposed, as well as its cause; there is no doubt as to what the effect is or what its cause is. What is sought is only the connection between the two: namely, in what way the effect proceeds from the cause, or vice versa, by what way and means the cause produces such an effect. I say the knowledge of the tree and its fruit is presupposed. If we apply these to healing (for if the whole world exists for the sake of man, then the entire physical knowledge of nature serves the physician), the knowledge of oneself must first be presupposed: namely, that the true Physician should know the "tree" of whole human nature and its "fruit," which is health. Likewise, he must know the "tree" of corrupted health, and the very category of depraved health as its fruit. These knowledges are required of the thing's own essence, along with its surroundings. Therefore, so that we may know the tree in its root and properties, it must be done from the fruits; for which reason the fruits must also be known first. Moreover, the fruits of both whole and corrupted health, since they are the targets to which the properties of occult remedies are referred, behave like the tree and the trunk into which the grafts, buds, and seeds of things must be grafted as their own fruits. This is surely what the purpose of Healing requires: that remedies, although they behave as a cause, nevertheless become

The fruits or effects within us: insofar as they bear fruit in our own tree: and thus they are not only the fruits of their own native tree, from which they are taken in the nature of things: but rather they are new fruits, produced by grafting, and thus entirely mixed, arising from the branch or fruit of the grafted tree, and from the vital power of the trunk into which it is inserted. Fruits of this kind surely reveal their tree. Just as in every progression of nature, a sexual duality is required for the production of any fruit. It was no wonder that the class of hidden <term>occult: hidden properties not immediately apparent to the senses</term> things and their applications remained unknown, if hitherto the healthy and diseased states were neglected as being born from the same parent: and thus they referred the entire essence of a disease to external, occasional, efficient, or warring causes: but not to the true and internal tree of illnesses. Let us suppose, therefore, an irritated and almost furious <term>Archeus: the internal "vital director" or spirit that governs the body's functions</term>, which, provoked by occasional causes, pours out its own blood and causes dysentery: or likewise let us imagine the Archeus in some part serving the final digestion, unfairly bearing a conceived mark of pain, and as if moved by fury, stirs up <term>Erysipelas: a skin infection, often called "St. Anthony's Fire"</term>. The question is finding a remedy from a hidden property. The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Galenic university medicine</note> therefore considered applying cooling agents to Erysipelas, insofar as they wished to apply a remedy to the fruit, and not to the corrupted tree. But the fellow-initiates of natural things observed the aforementioned furies, which must be restrained through fear, so that fear is not for the man: but must be struck into the Archeus. Therefore, they killed the most fearful animal, namely the hare. Not indeed with a weapon, so that it might fall in an unexpected death: but by hunting, so that it might perish by the bite of dogs: by which a doubled force of dread is imprinted into its whole being. And so they dipped a bloody cloth in the hare's blood, and kept it dried. And they administered it bit by bit in wine, and the dysentery was cured. Likewise, they applied the dry cloth to erysipelas, and it was healed. Indeed, German soldiers

Likewise, cooling treatments are ridiculous: inasmuch as they try to heal from the effect <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>, they by no means reach the roots, and for that reason, they mostly provoke nature into greater furies. Hence the knowledge of hidden things is wrongly sought from the fruit. Moreover, I knew that seminal beings arise by the <term>phantastic power: the imaginative or image-forming faculty</term> of living things, or of their Archeus, by a similar disturbance. So that from a certain invisible principle, this visible world is continued. In underlying things, however, or non-living things, I noticed that the same things hold themselves similarly by a certain analogous proportion. Since fire is the death of things, if it does not totally destroy the seeds of things, it at least transforms them significantly. Thus, in some cases, preparation transforms the entire matter, as in Masteries <note>term: Magisteries (A chemical term for a preparation where the whole substance is converted into a medicinal form without losing its essential virtues).</note>; in other cases, due to the sequestering of certain parts, it only changes, sharpens, loses, or consumes what is left behind. Such as glass. Which is no longer ash and sand. Often even without fire, additions penetrate the root of the mixture, especially when a ferment intervenes, and then a neutral composite is established. For in this way, from rye bread and honey, ants are generated; from honey and dew, eels; from basil and the decay of stone, scorpions; from a strangled calf and dew, bees. <note>The author is referencing the historical theory of "Spontaneous Generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter.</note> However, those things which are mixed by melting alone often allow themselves to be reduced back to their original state.
