<margin>41.</margin> I have perceived, I say, that planetary powers reside within Metals, provided they are reduced into the nature of a salt or a sulfur; yet this must be done apart from any residue of the substance added to them. In this matter, not every <term>Stentor</term> <note>original: "Stentor"; a reference to the Greek herald with a loud voice, here used to mean that not just anyone—even the loud or boastful—can achieve this difficult task</note> was able to reach Corinth <note>A proverb meaning that difficult things are not attainable by everyone.</note>.

<margin>42.</margin> For after I learned how to unlock bodies through means agreeable to their own radical principles, then for the first time, with a healthy sense of weariness, I began to laugh at my own foolish beliefs with which I once used to dissolve gold. I profited less from its "potable juice" than from a simple decoction of some common herb. Afterward, however, I was able to dissolve gold and play with it until it took on the appearance of butter, resin, or vitriol. But nowhere did I find the virtues attributed to gold, for the reason that it resisted our internal ferments even in those states. I perceived, therefore, that gold is dead without its own proper corrosive. Dead, I say, unless it is radically penetrated by its corrosive—not indeed that it then reflects the nature of the Sun <note>In alchemy, the Sun represents Gold</note> or adds anything to the vital forces, but only that it cleanses the whole body by purging it imperceptibly, in a harmonious tone. Indeed, even pearls are changed by that corrosive into a "spermatic milk," becoming sociable to the first constituents of our body, and thus far a remedy for Consumption <note>original: "Tabis"</note>, Paralysis, etc.

<margin>43.</margin> I perceived at last that the liquor <term>Alkahest</term> <note>A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists</note> would cleanse nature by the power of its own fire. For just as fire destroys all infected things, so the <term>Alkahest</term> consumes diseases.

<margin>44.</margin> Finally, I perceived that the <term>Mercury of Life</term> <note>original: "Mercurius vitae"; a preparation of antimony, not liquid mercury</note>, listed by Paracelsus among the four Secrets <note>original: "Arcana"</note>, besides its fiery power of "Gehenna" <note>hell-fire</note>, clarifies the organs just as <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibium"</note> purifies gold from admixtures. I hold the same opinion regarding the Tincture of the Lily <note>An alchemical medicine, often a red antimony-based tincture</note>, which is a synonym. Meanwhile, Nature desires to rise again under these medicines as if in a new spring; yet, the hope of restoration to our original state is but smoke, since we lack the infusion of new strengths that would prove immortality. For it is appointed unto every living thing once to die. Because there is nothing in nature that is equal to the temple of the image of God.

<margin>45.</margin> And so I perceived that all restorative things work by purifying and, to that extent, by cheering; otherwise, there is no true rejuvenation. I perceived then that the Secrets,

<column-break/>

which heal by dissolving and expelling, do nothing except awaken the indwelling powers within us, which, once the impediments are removed, sprout again as if under a new spring.

<margin>46.</margin> Lastly, I perceived simple substances in which the proper outflow of their own form does not operate, but rather the command and character of a foreign form comes upon them, so that they create a contagion among things that share a likeness; and from this, poisonings or incantations are born. For whatever things are prepared through a voluntary <term>Blas</term> <note>A term coined by Van Helmont referring to a "motion" or "vital force," here specifically the "Blas" of the stars or the human will</note> are mostly propagated to the functions of local motion—I mean they are directed to the nerves—being most fit for stirring up pains or for states of painlessness. For they do not have poisons or ferments through themselves, unless an evil spirit adds them or joins them through things conquered by itself. Then they excel all other poisons, being related to the poison of the Plague.

<margin>47.</margin> Indeed, I also perceived that all poisons (except corrosives) act because of a specific property, emulating the imagination, implanted in the seed, formally innate, and having the powers of a ferment acting equivocally.

<margin>48.</margin> Furthermore, I perceived that any single thing, according to the manner of the receiver and the application, spreads its activities in various ways. For bread works one way inside us and in individual animals, and another way in the stomach, liver, and other "kitchens" <note>The organs of digestion</note>, because of the diversity of ferments. Thus I perceived that meat applied externally soon rots, while inside it is dissolved by ferments and finally assimilated into our own parts. I perceived that barley-meal certainly smears and softens when applied externally, but inside it nourishes, warms, constipates the bowels, and moves the winds <note>gas</note>. For every simple substance, when applied externally, explores its powers with us under our "sixth digestion"; whereas inside, it is usually mastered at the very first steps. A living man, kept long in water, would rot; but dead flesh, washed by a constantly renewed stream, takes on the nature of a balsam. Thus the stomach, although it is perpetually wet, does not rot from it. For Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for centuries</note> was ignorant of the operations of nature because he did not catch the scent of the properties of ferments.

# THE POWER OF MEDICINES

In a wound, oils and plasters are thought to be digested and transformed into new flesh no differently than food in the stomach. But such a person does not know that one cannot reach the **sixth digestion** except step-by-step through the preceding ones. Thus far, <term>cruor</term> <note>original: "cruor"; refers to raw, circulating blood before it is fully vitalized</note> is not formed in the stomach; just as no nutrition occurs from an enema held in the Colon or the borders of the ileum, despite what the Schools whisper to the contrary. For broths soon putrefy in the intestines, and the creation of <term>cremor</term> <note>original: "cremor"; the milky chyle or essence of digested food</note> does not happen there. Far be it from the truth that blood is made if chyle did not exist before it. Nor is the liver the workshop of chyle; much less is "incarnation" <note>the process of turning into flesh</note> performed in the stomach. It is least true of all that flesh or blood are materially made from a plaster. For once the skin is opened, putrefaction is soon introduced to it, just as corruption follows when an eggshell is damaged. From this comes ichor, discharge, pus, gravelly water, fluid, worms, etc. The Surgeon devotes his entire care to preventing these, and once they are removed, flesh grows back of its own accord—not, however, from the applied remedies. I have also perceived that our domestic salts, used for seasoning food, are more suited for dissolving and wiping away filth than for being promoted into nourishment. Oils, truly, are scarcely fit for <term>sanguification</term> <note>the process of making blood</note>: and least of all those which rise by fire <note>distilled oils</note>. Moreover, distilled waters possess meager medicinal strengths. <margin>50.</margin> <margin>51.</margin> <margin>52.</margin> This is because nature everywhere rejoices in nourishment prepared from bodies existing under her own synthesis. Therefore, artificial salts penetrate deeper than oils, which resist blood-making and do not mix. <margin>53.</margin> Consequently, the salts of aromatics, made from their oils, take the place of their "First Being." <margin>54.</margin> <term>Magisteries</term> <note>concentrated medicinal extracts</note> are to be held in high regard because their substance is whole, digestible, and obedient to ferments. <margin>55.</margin> Therefore, nature rejects foods seasoned with "essences" because of the difficulties of fermentation. For all things that are too highly "graduated" <note>refined or intensified</note> drag their "middle life" behind them; they are not easily subdued by ferments. In short: those things which more stubbornly preserve their own "middle life" are not easily overcome by the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "vital director" or governing spirit of the body's functions</note>. They are not only stubborn in digestion, but are persistent

<column-break/>

and act upon us insofar as they are not subdued. <margin>56.</margin> Verdigris, saffron of copper, white lead, precipitate, sublimate, etc., have ascended into virulence through additives. Since these are not admitted into the "root of Mercury," they work only on the outside around the sulfur, and there they are variously disposed by way of the recipient. <margin>57.</margin> Finally, I perceived a sixfold difference of digestions within us. The first three of these are occupied with the disposition of matter destined for nourishment: although they truly transmute it, they are sent ahead as a preparatory arrangement rather than as its vital "betrothal." For in the **fourth digestion**, the vital power is communicated to the <term>cruor</term>. <margin>58.</margin> And thus the dispute is settled as to whether the blood is "animated" <note>endowed with a soul/life force</note>. For the <term>cruor</term> is not truly animated until it becomes *blood* <note>original: "sanguis"</note>. This is drawn through the septum of the Heart into the Aorta for no other purpose than to be endowed with life in that storehouse and informed by the Mind. We are nourished by both, just as life arises from the seed of two sexes. Perhaps the mystery of the **Liturgy** <note>original: "Lithurgiæ"; likely referring to the Eucharist</note> is recognized from this: why a little water is mixed with much wine. So that the water may pass into <term>cruor</term>, and the wine into blood. I perceived the **fifth digestion** to be entirely occupied with the participative communion of life. The **sixth**, finally, works by a dispositive quality, but rejoices in an assimilative ferment that induces "humanity" <note>the state of being human tissue</note>. Therefore, external aids are excited and work by a different quality than internal ones. Obese people are seized by pains and spasms of the tendons, which human <term>axungia</term> <note>fat or grease</note>, smeared on the outside, soothes. For the sixth digestion is entirely assimilative: it strives to change the applied fat into its own vital aura. <margin>59.</margin> But the internal fat of the fatty tissues, already subdued by the assimilating ferment, is kept without action. But the sixth digestion enters into the "middle life" of the external fat that has been smeared on, which our Archeus therefore appropriates for itself. This life, and its properties, are hidden in the ultimate life of the internal fat. <margin>60.</margin> Furthermore, I perceived how...

->THE POWER OF MEDICINES<-

The Spanish Fly <note>original: "Cantharis"; a beetle used historically in medicine to cause blistering</note> produces blisters in the living, but not in a corpse; just as a caustic agent does not raise a scab <note>original: "Escharam"</note> on a corpse, even though it may dissolve the body, much like quicklime dissolves powdered cheese. For the Spanish Fly does not act as long as it remains dry: but it is ignited by the imperceptible madness of the dew <note>likely referring to the moisture of the living skin</note>, not much differently than what happens under St. Anthony's Fire <note>original: "Erysipelate"; a skin infection</note>, a burn, or a caustic. Thus, the Spanish Fly begins its work in the epidermis, and the caustic in the skin—the same process that gangrene finally completes in the physical constitution. For caustics first shrivel the skin, which they then resolve into a mucus once they have become fully saturated. For then, they not only sharpen our internal heat, but they also take on the strength of their own corrosion. Then, I say, they not only create a scab, which arises from the ignition of the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is a Paracelsian term for the vital internal force or "inner alchemist" that governs the body's functions</note>, but they liquefy the whole.
<margin>61.</margin> Finally, I perceived that amulets, charms <note>original: "periapta"</note>, and pendants act by the power of influence and direction, without the evaporation of those elements which reside in more fixed bodies. To be sure, there are other pendants which gradually decrease in strength because they release an "outflow" <note>original: "aporrhoeam"</note> from themselves. There are charms made of bone, horn, animals, and plants. Others are metallic, stony, salty, transparent, or opaque. Metals, however, are rarely amulets unless they are still "open" <note>chemically reactive</note> or exalted by an external force, because they contain a divisible sulfur within them.
<margin>62.</margin> In stones, however, there is great power. Of stones, some are transparent mirrors, while others are opaque—such as Coral, Carnelian, Turquoise, and Jasper. In the translucent ones, the "Evektrum" <note>A term for a visionary or spiritual reflection</note> of life, whether well or poorly affected, reverberates. For life rejoices in being reflected by a bright mirror, by which it is then likened to the intellect, which is altered in its own light to the likeness of objects, in the manner of a chameleon. Not in vain did I also perceive gems to be like well-polished opaque mirrors. Because a native gift, natural to itself from the nature of the mirror, more powerfully reflects the vital ray communicated to it. For continually, and necessarily, something is breathed out of us that is not yet entirely devoid of a participation in life. This very thing maintains the activity of its own sphere around us: which, when it finds a polished mirror, it easily reflects back into the whole from whence it flowed. From this, the "sympathetic" arts first became famous. But later, when it was known that charms were applied by the power of a mirror in their operation, the shapes of mirrors—convex, concave, etc.—were soon devised. To these, the hieroglyphic Heathens <note>original: "Gentilitas"</note> added figures to denote the sign of an occult virtue. From this, superstition grew in posterity, who anointed "Gamahen" <note>carved stones with astrological signs</note>, Talismans, and that kind of demonic buffoonery—thinking that the shape had the power of a cause, rather than merely being a sign. Transparent mirrors, however, receive the "evectric" power, which, although they do not reflect it like the opaque ones, they nevertheless approach more closely to the nature of life, or a shining mirror.
<margin>63.</margin> I perceived finally that the diversity of effects, the purpose, and the appropriation of medicines did not arise from the fourfold fiction of the "complexions" <note>The traditional Galenic theory of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, but from the very powers of the "simples" <note>individual medicinal herbs or minerals</note> themselves. For this reason, the selection, dosage, and preparation of these have been neglected, because they have not been investigated in their root and manner until now. After the sensations of all these things, finally another spirit took away from me the flask which he had given me; and with great sorrow I then
<margin>64.</margin> felt all the necessities of death within me, which are beyond words: whereupon I soon returned to myself. Nor could I receive any comfort, except when I truly knew that all these things had been done only through a dream. And that if I ought to recount the powers of things, I could not do it better than if I myself had sensed all those things as if from within. This one thing at least I still remembered: that things act by the power of the Chemical <note>original: "Chymica"</note> art rather than by the native power of nature, because their beginnings were produced and mixed by fire.
<margin>65.</margin> Chemistry, to be sure, separates the fixed from the non-fixed, which is the first and most obvious sequestration of heterogeneous things. It even fixes many things that were previously volatile, or vice versa. Then, among the volatile things, it separates the fragrant ones.

# THE POWER OF MEDICINES

-> scented from the unscented. <- This distinction was falsely thought to be one of the pure from the impure. Indeed, the action of fire is to burn. It therefore burns the pure as much as the impure. A third separation then occurs through digestions and specific <term>ferments</term> <note>Ferment: In 17th-century chemistry, a substance that causes a chemical change or "ripening" in another.</note>. Thus, parts that cling together with stubborn continuity are separated from one another by the discord of the ferment. For in this way, bodies spontaneously waste away in the fullness of their final life, and their sheltered powers come forth into the light. Furthermore, by boiling and melting, parts previously governed by a single restraint now act upon one another, under which stage they acquire other powers. Therefore, <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymia"</note> brings forth things that would otherwise occur in Nature, or would never be possessed at all. And this is not only in separated volatile substances, but even in the residues, which are therefore reduced to ash through heat.

Truly, if new powers arise through the mixing and co-fermentation of a compound, this is even more remarkable in <term>Spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric: The alchemical art of separating and recombining the essential components of plants and minerals to create medicine.</note> arts; not only because Art imitates nature in all operations whatsoever, but also by the peculiar energy of <term>Epyreuma</term> <note>Epyreuma: An old chemical term for the "burnt" smell or taste resulting from the alteration of organic matter by fire.</note> and melting, which play out various operations under the fire and change the very nature of things. Thus, for instance, the spirit of <term>Saltpeter</term> <note>original: "Salispetræ"; potassium nitrate.</note> raises up a moist sulfur and the embryo of vitriol into a poisonous water; yet the separate spirits of both of these were fit for healing and pleasing to the stomach. Finally, Chemistry brings certain milder things to such a degree that poisons are made from honey, manna, etc. Many things that are violent also become tame under the fire. So much so that fixed <term>Alkalis</term> <note>original: "Alcalia"</note>, if they are made volatile,

<column-break/>

may equal the powers of great medicines. Indeed, by the power of cutting, dissolving, and cleansing—carried even to the threshold of the "fourth digestion"—they fundamentally remove the stickiness of clotted matter in the vessels. For Chemistry dissolves the hardest and most compact things so that, not only forgetting their former clot and their resistance against fire, they return into a manageable juice and hidden things are made plain; indeed, they even become "social" or compatible with us. Nay, it not only prepares the things themselves in this way, but it also creates the means by which bodies may be opened. For thus, clotted things pass into the family of dissolved things; fixed things are changed into volatile ones, and vice versa; raw things are ripened; and heterogeneous things are divided into classes. Finally, sluggish things acquire degrees of power, and many new things emerge which remained unknown to the <margin>66.</margin> Schools of the Gentiles <note>The "Schools of the Gentiles" refers to traditional academic medicine based on ancient Greek and Roman authorities like Galen, which the author rejects.</note>. At last, and at the very peak of its craft, <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Chymeia"</note> prepares a universal solvent, by which all things return into their "first being" and offer up their native gifts; the original stains of bodies are wiped away, and their inhuman wildness having been abandoned, it is possible to obtain great and inexplicable powers. However, how much purity the intellect acquires during this work, only the <term>Adept</term> <note>Adept: One who has mastered the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> knows. Ah, would that the flask, once possessed, had not been taken from me! But God knows why he gave the goat so short a tail. Let His name be exalted forever: and let His alone be the only sanctifying will.

# P R E F A C E

<margin>1.</margin> I have resolved, by the divine goodwill, to make known what has hitherto been hidden from the world—and especially in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established universities of the time, which relied on ancient Greek and Roman authorities.</note>—namely, the causes of diseases, the knowledge of their essences <term>quiddities: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, and their remedies. That is to say, for so many centuries, and by the testimonies of men, the essence of diseases has not yet been penetrated. <margin>2.</margin> Indeed, I have grieved truly and significantly that this ignorance of past ages and of the present century is real, and that it had to be uncovered by me, a useless old man. I was seriously distressed that physicians have been so careless regarding both their own lives and those of their neighbors, and seemed to have studied for profit alone—unless this was <margin>3.</margin> an ordinance of the divine Will <note>original: "divini Numinis"</note>, that as long as the Schools clung to pagan doctrines, they would also persist in the aforementioned darkness. This was to continue until finally, in the fullness of time, there would be someone to open the essence and nature of diseases to his neighbors: and indeed, to do so in the very Chairs of Medicine <note>The "Cathedras" or official seats of university professors.</note> themselves. This is so that, as if at the very source, once the errors of Heathenism <note>original: "Ethnicismi," referring here to the non-Christian Greek and Roman medical authorities like Galen and Aristotle.</note> have been driven out, the truth may shine hereafter, and as many as have not closed their eyes out of stubbornness may come to their senses.

<margin>4.</margin> I propose a matter truly new and plainly wonderful to the whole world and to our posterity. And oh, would that I alone, who first reveal these things, might draw and endure the insults upon myself, so that the life and health of my neighbor might not suffer. For I would have gladly remained silent, nor would I have made my talent public, had I not known this was given solely for the life of my neighbor.

<margin>5.</margin> And while I still contemplate the magnitude of the matter within myself—the succession of so many centuries, the fatal ignorance, and the continued sluggishness or negligence of the body in a matter, I say, of such great importance as is human life—I cannot help but look back many times in amazement, put down my pen, and doubt the deception of my own boldness. Namely, that in the Academies themselves, where fresh, more fervent minds not yet defiled by profit are exercised, disease is still utterly unknown—disease, which is the proper

<column-break/>

object of the medical faculty; the object, I say, of so many lectures founded by Princes. Indeed, I would have utterly <margin>6.</margin> doubted my own boldness, were it not that He who gives such a talent was the internal dispenser of the same, and gave a clarity beyond all demonstration and fear of error. It would have been hard otherwise to persuade and believe myself, unless, compelled from within by the authority and security of a greater title, I had felt obliged to confidently expose myself to the censures of all. For what I teach will at first be incredible among wise men if they judge me at the tribunal of so many centuries—I who gladly confess myself unfit to <margin>7.</margin> reach such a peak of light, unless the knowledgeable contemplate with me more vividly the accustomed superabundance of the divine Majesty. For no one will more clearly recognize the honor of God in this case, and that the present gift comes freely from the Father of Lights, unless they see in my dejected smallness and ignorance that it is the accustomed path for God to reveal to little ones what He has denied to the great ones of the world in the ordinary course. This is for one fault: that by a continued error, they have all immersed themselves entirely in the opinions of the pagans.

<margin>8.</margin> For the wise will discern from this, first, that they should not attack me as a man. Then, finally, they will weigh by their own judgment the scholastic reasons drawn from my bosom. From there, at last, as if led through the principles and theorems of nature, they will hasten of their own accord to far more sublime and clearer beginnings of healing, to which the tenderness of my judgment could not ascend. Truly I warn <margin>9.</margin> and exhort the Wise of this world, that the errors and ignorance of healers did not open themselves to me gradually, nor enter into my soul by degrees, such that I conceived or meditated upon one thing before another. That is, it was not that I first considered the Schools deceived regarding the gathering of elementary mixtures, temperament, complexions, and morbid distempers <note>These are terms from Galenic medicine, which taught that health depended on the balance of four "humors" or qualities.</note>, and from there was tumbled into the errors...

# PREFACE

<margin>10.</margin> ...of Catarrhs <note>original: "Catarrhorum"; a term then used for any bodily discharge or "runny" condition</note>: and only after that would I have sought the roots, causes, and the very essence of diseases and their remedies. But truly, none of these things happened that way. For if these things had become known to me one after another, I would have thought that such progress was merely the result of Reason and imagination <note>original: "phantasiæ"</note>, which are prone to errors and deceptions. But instead, a single flash of light overshadowed my intellectual conception with the whole truth at once—namely, the ignorance of healers, as much in their knowledge of causes and diseases as in their remedies and applications. I knew without a doubt that this talent was given for the benefit of my neighbors, and therefore it must be offered to the Chairs of Medicine <margin>11.</margin> (from whom correction is sought and expected), and it must be seriously <margin>12.</margin> brought forth to them under the threat of a heavy penalty. Therefore, when I had already decided to demonstrate that the essence of diseases was not yet known through their innermost and proper roots, it was night before four in the morning on the ninth of August. It seemed to me—just as dreams are sometimes formed from the crowing of a cock—that I heard, out of my pre-existing concern for writing, a reminder of an Anatomy <note>A reference to a dissection or anatomical study</note>, which I shall mention shortly. While I seemed to have understood these things as a warning, I doubted in a half-awake state how that dissection of a corpse could relate to the treatise I had decided to write on the essence of diseases. And so, while unconcerned, I dreamed that I saw a grave man from abroad sitting at my table, eating fresh Salmon in a sauce of vinegar and pepper, and so greedily that he almost gorged himself on it (since fresh salmon is not found in his own country). I saw that two days later, around evening, a slight fever seized him and his teeth shook; and thereafter he maintained the pattern of a tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typically associated with malaria</note>. That is, four days <margin>13.</margin> after the digestion of that food. This was so much the case that nothing of its residue had putrefied, much less remained, which could provoke a febrile tumult at fixed intervals. For there is a common saying about an "elemental imbalance" <note>original: "elementalem intemperiem"</note> being left behind, which would prepare a morbid impression. Indeed, that—besides the absurdities of imbalances and complexions <note>The "complexion" was the specific balance of humors in an individual</note> demonstrated by me elsewhere—

<column-break/>

seems to signify nothing but a mere "Being of Reason" <note>original: "Ens rationis"; a philosophical term for something that exists only in the mind, not in reality</note>. <margin>14.</margin> This is because the thing making the impression and the thing impressed are indeed actual things and relative terms: but the impression itself, since it is nothing but a relation resulting from the fitting together of the terms, can only hold the place of a "Being of Reason." Therefore, at the very least, an impression or an imbalance cannot remain surviving where the imbalancing thing, or the thing making the impression itself, has ceased to be, and consequently has ceased to do harm. It would be necessary, then, that the impressing thing itself had produced a harmful quality outside of itself, and had deposited it into the subject of the impression as its own product. And since this would happen in an organ participating in life, it would be necessary at least for that product to be entirely and immediately submerged or sheltered within the bosom of life itself; and even more so if it must recur at fixed periods and interrupt the silent peace of health—indeed, by acting hostily, it ought in some way to exhibit signs of a disturbed life. To such an extent did I confirm the essence of diseases more perfectly through this dream. For just as these things do not happen outside of life, so life itself is the very "enormontic" cause <note>original: "causa enormontica"; a term derived from Hippocrates referring to the vital governing power of the body</note>, once it has been disturbed in its place, peace, or quiet. Behold, on the same day as the aforementioned dream, a nobleman whom I had not seen for many years arrived as a guest at my table. Since it was the eve of St. Lawrence, it also happened that boiled fresh Salmon was served, and he ate it, just as I had seen in the dream. Indeed, two days later, he fell into a tertian fever. Furthermore, the dissected corpse, regarding which I had received a warning, pertains to these same goals. ### 92. Frequent sins. The lazy negligence of the schools. 93. How death and disease emerged as natural entities after the creation and took on secondary causes as their own producers. 94. Two objections of the Schools refuted. 95. An omen from inseparable goodness.

<margin>1.</margin> Having first established the integrity of nature—specifically within matter, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital workman" or governing spirit that directs the functions of the body</note>, and life, or the form of vital light, along with seminal and vital beginnings—and having newly discovered the ferments that act as the authors of transmutations; and having likewise rejected the four elements, qualities, complexions, and the mixtures, battles, struggles, and alternating victories among them; and having banished from nature the flowing humors and <term>Catarrhs</term> <note>The traditional medical theory that illnesses were caused by fluids "dropping" from the brain</note>; and finally, having proscribed gases, <term>tartars</term> <note>Hard deposits formed in the body, likened to the crust in wine barrels</note>, and the three <term>Chemical Principles</term> <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> from the army of diseases: it now remained for the defects and <margin>2.</margin> alterations of nature to be considered to the very marrow. Therefore, before I enter more deeply, I have undertaken to prove that diseases have hitherto been unknown in the Schools <note>The established universities and academic authorities of the time</note>, not only in their particulars—whereby the radical healing of them has remained hidden—but moreover, that the very essence of <margin>3.</margin> disease in general has been concealed. It is indeed a cause for grief that while other professions have been so ingeniously refined, in the Art of Healing alone we have stumbled until now upon such deaf principles. Yet in this art, charity toward one's neighbor is commanded under penalty. For all things have remained most obscure, and most are utterly false; those things which would most greatly lead to the goal of healing have been left untouched. Nowhere is subtlety to be found; instead, on every side, there is a vast dullness. So much so that from the aforementioned, anyone may easily conclude that whatever has been taught until now according to the doctrine of the Pagans <note>Referring to Galen and Aristotle, whose ancient Greek theories dominated medieval medicine</note> and against mutual charity is an invention of the evil demon. For this reason, surely, the stability of pagan theorems has persisted through the persuasion of the devil. Yet these theorems, by their very ease, should have been suspect at first glance to anyone of sound mind.

<column-break/>

Thus, nothing more harsh, more inhuman, or more full of cruelty has been undertaken among the arts of mortals through so many centuries than that art which, through the deaths of men under a "concentric signature" <note>Likely referring to the official stamps or collective agreements of medical faculties</note>, performs experiments anew. While the Professors of these things presume that they guard the keys of Science, they neither enter the inner sanctums themselves, nor do they admit others wishing to enter; rather, they ward everyone off with every kind of trickery. *Always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth* <note>original: "Semper discentes, & nunquam ad veritatis scientiam pervenientes." A quote from 2 Timothy 3:7</note>, according to the Apostle.

<margin>4.</margin> My Jesus, my light, my life, my glory, and the helper of my weakness and corrupt nature, you who find an easy way out in your affairs, with whom that is easy which among mortals is as if impossible. You, who have made me undergo all manner of adversity: I offer to you my calamities and the depressions of Justice. You have nonetheless always strengthened me with your invincible right hand; reach out your hand to me, so that if you do not deign to snatch me from the deep pit of so many tribulations, at least by your strength I may not sin against you, and those who hate me without cause may repent. May those who adore your power recognize in me that you alone are God, the helper of the oppressed, and the certain hope of those who trust in you. Let them be clothed in contrition and find grace with you, and let me, a wretch, sing the praises of your greatness after this age. For it is the decay of this age that, by your hidden judgment, the hypocrisy of the powerful, trusting in fraud, shall do, and under the shadow of piety, shall read its own wickedness.

In such a whirlwind of my troubles, <margin>5.</margin> I have set out to note the miseries of mortals and the defects of the errors of the Physicians <note>original: "Medentum"</note> placed before the sight of my mind, under your command. Just as hypocrisy has destroyed me and my fortunes, I may likewise recognize, and primarily so, that the Father of Lies has poured into the pagan schools the cup of ignorance and the poison of Charity and health, with profit paving the way through the worn, stormy path of the Tritons. Indeed, every future student <note>original: "Tyro"</note> will marvel with me that nothing has been treated with such lack of skill as those things which concern the life of mortals.

And finally, they adapted to these qualities fictitious and excrementitious "humors" <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to govern health</note>, which were said to rule a person, whether healthy or sick, so completely as to preside over all human affairs: as if the conditions of mortals, their character, health, appetites, instincts, leanings, failures, strengths, values, defects, the outcomes of fortune, and even the merits of punishment or the adoption into eternal life depended upon them. It is truly horrendous and intolerable that these silly stories have stood for so long, and that such serious and pernicious fables have been fabricated and believed concerning things that do not exist and never will—things which are even regarded as "excrement" by those who assert their existence. Thus, almost nothing has ever been investigated by these Schools that is actually true or good under such principles.

<margin>7.</margin>
Meanwhile, I grieve (and I testify to this again), not because I have found the light of truth through long compassion for my neighbor, but because it has become necessary for me to expose these errors. That is, I grieve because the devil has deceived the Schools, and will continue to deceive them as long as they allow themselves to be deluded by pagan fables and separated from the Schools of Truth. However, so that this may be established, I will declare it in passing as if by a Preface, and by way of a positive demonstration.

<margin>8.</margin>
For truly, "God did not make death" <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 1:13</note>. And that is a matter of faith. Therefore, man became mortal from a source other than God. And since the goal or end of most

diseases is death itself (which is nothing other than the extinction of life), for that reason, disease and death are diametrically opposed to life. From this it follows: that every disease acts immediately upon the life. However, nothing is able to act upon the life unless it is applied to it and mixed with it. But the enemy, disease, is not applied indiscriminately to the life unless it has besieged a part of that life, and thus sits totally or partially within the life itself. Once this is done, that besieged or conquered part of life withdraws from the **vital aura** <note>original: *vitalis aura*; the spiritual "breath" or atmosphere surrounding the living soul</note>, and having been thus conquered and made degenerate, it becomes hostile to the life that still remains, or which is still established in its integrity.

<margin>9.</margin>
It follows from this necessarily that every disease finds its "material" in the organic aura of life, by which it attacks life most closely and deeply. Likewise, it finds its "efficient cause" in that same vital light. And so, disease, being thus equipped with matter and an efficient cause, takes up residence around the life. Meanwhile, it does not matter whether that contagion of disease was drawn from occasional causes, or finally generated within by an error of the life in the **Archeus** <note>term: *Archeus* — the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note>. At the very least, it suffices for this passage that the life itself is the primary object of the hostile disease in both cases. But since life itself is a "luminous being," it does not act except through the organ of the vital aura, or through the Archeus, as a medium between the light of life—flowing from the Father of Lights—and the body.

<margin>10.</margin>
Furthermore, this aura or Archeus does not act except in the manner by which every **seminal spirit** <note>original: *spiritus seminalis*; the formative power within a "seed" or beginning of a thing</note> acts upon the mass placed under it. That is, it acts only through an impressed mark, or a **sealing Idea** <note>original: *Idea sigillaris*; a formative mental image that "stamps" its character onto matter</note>, which knows what must be done and toward what end. Therefore, every single disease has a "sealing mark," and as it were, a "seminal act" that is aware of the things it must do.

<margin>11.</margin>
Therefore, this declaration stands far apart from "elementary imbalance," from "humors," and from their **lack of proportion** <note>original: *ametria*</note>, or from the "struggle and contrariety of the elements" of our composition. Inasmuch as every disease is nothing but the sword of life, wounding or cutting it off entirely. For just as a sword drains life along with the blood...

Thus, finally, disease would migrate from being a quality into the Category of Relation. <margin>31.</margin> Finally, if a disease is an affection that immediately harms an action, they ought at least to recognize from this that the *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a central concept in Van Helmont's chemistry and medicine; it refers to the internal "vital workman" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions.</note> itself—or the "acting impulse"—must be the universal and primary disease of all things when it moves irregularly (for instance, when a small flame blisters a living body, but not a corpse) and for this purpose sets aside and loses a part of itself. I have already threatened to demonstrate this regarding fevers. They ought likewise to recognize that if material causes are sufficient in themselves and primarily to immediately harm the functions (as, for example, a cataract in front of the pupil produces blindness by itself and immediately; just as the severing of a tendon removes motion without the intervention of a *Diathesis* really distinct from the severing wound), then there is no need to invent such a *Diathesis*. Indeed, there is no blockage <note>original: "oppilatio"; a common medical term for an obstruction of the vessels or passages.</note> or *Diathesis* that shuts off the passage of urine if a stone alone does this immediately and materially blocks it. The stone thus contains within itself the whole foundation of the relation so perfectly and really that the *Diathesis*, or the blocking action proceeding from the blocking stone, is nothing but a relation and a mere "being of reason" <note>original: "ens rationis"; a philosophical term for something that exists only in the mind, not in physical reality.</note>, which has no place in the treatment of diseases, nor in true and truly existing beings. Therefore, extrinsic Diseases, such as wounds and whatever intercepts a passage, since they do not arise from a seminal beginning nor 

<column-break/>

foster a cause that excites the *Archeus*, are subjects of a different monarchy. But for <margin>32.</margin> seminal diseases, it is more consistent with nature and motion to suppose that the *Archeus* spirit—insofar as it is the efficient beginning of sensation and motion—is immediately and proximately affected by harmful things, and that the occasional cause and the *Archeus* touch each other at a single point. From this comes Disease. <margin>33.</margin> For the "occasional matter"—whether brought in from outside, generated within, whether it be coagulable, putrefiable, able to be blown away, or hardening—always only occasionally excites the *Archeus* so that it becomes terrified or burns with various kinds of anger. Under <margin>34.</margin> this perturbation, an *Idea* is born, informing a certain part of the *Archeus*. And that composite, made of the matter of the *Archeus* and the aforementioned seminal *Idea* acting as the efficient beginning, is truly every seminal Disease. Therefore, the <margin>35.</margin> Schools, seduced by the liberties of their own dreams, have supposed that because the consideration of causes and principles differs from the consideration of the thing produced by them, therefore, by a formal causing necessity, all causes must remain forever separated from the things caused in their becoming, being, operating, and remaining. They do not notice that, for the most part, the consideration of causes and principles does not differ from the consideration of the thing caused, except through a relation of a mental being—which, though accepted in Mathematics and logic, is not at all accepted in the course of nature. Thus the Schools, <margin>36.</margin> deluded by such fallacies, believed that every efficient cause is by necessity external, and therefore cannot be united with the thing caused. Consequently, they believe the generator is not part of the thing generated. Whereas in nature, the thing proximately generating is always the internal moderator, the vital and presiding Architect of generation: so much so that he directs all things toward their ends and goals, accomplishes all things for himself, and does everything on his own behalf. Therefore, being also deceived <margin>37.</margin> regarding diseases, they believed the morbific cause to be external with respect to the human body, or at least in view of the vital economy. <note>The "vital economy" refers to the internal management and distribution of life forces within the organism.</note>

38. For it is unknown that **generation** <note>The process of coming into being or biological reproduction.</note> means nothing other than the flow of the **seed** <note>original: *feminis*; referring to the seminal or generative principle</note> toward perfection, the ripening of properties, the unfolding of hidden things, and the fulfillment of 39. orders toward their own ends. Therefore, **Aristotle** was the first to deceive the Schools, teaching that **corruption** <note>Decay or the ending of a state of being.</note> and generation succeed one another by turns throughout all of nature, always and by necessity. And for that reason, he made a "mental being"—a mere negative non-being (a naked privation)—into a principle in nature, standing immediately between 40. generation and corruption. Nor could the Schools ever understand that the same craftsman who makes a plant from a seed does not fail during the plant's generation; he does not depart as an outlaw, nor die away as something obsolete. Finally, no other is substituted in his place because of the arrival of a **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> (of which that craftsman remains the immediate executive instrument toward ends foreknown by **GOD**) or the participation in life: but he himself, alone and always, persists throughout the governance of life. From this, surely, they also failed to understand that the thing generated proceeds from causes that are, in reality and in substance, not distinct from the being of the thing—indeed, not even with any difference of causality. This is because the Schools have hitherto speculated more upon demonstrable operations through the senses (I mean mathematics and artificial things, which are foreign to nature) than upon the natures of things themselves, situated in the storehouse of essentiality. For they never noticed that the instrument of art, the craftsman himself, and even the very measures of measurable things, are unable to generate anything "seminally" in nature, or to introduce a seminal, substantial, or essential disposition for the purpose of transforming products. Consequently, they also did not understand **disease** as a **real being** <note>original: *ens reale*; a thing with its own actual existence rather than just a lack of health.</note> and a substantial one, but only as an **accident** <note>In logic, an "accident" is a quality that can change without destroying the subject (like hair color), as opposed to an "essence."</note>. Whereas otherwise, disease is not a **Diathesis** <note>A physical condition or constitution.</note>, nor an accident harming actions, and much less is it the very injury of the action itself proceeding from a duel of harmful causes against our governing powers. Instead, disease is a real being, having material and efficient causes provoked by occasional causes. For if disease and nature (or our faculties) stood in diametric opposition—as they claim—then disease and healthy life could not exist at the same time in the same immediate subject. Therefore, disease cannot be a Diathesis which at least brings detriment to the powers; rather, such a Diathesis would be the fruit of the disease, a consequence following the disease, and the mother and nurse of debilitations. This, therefore, I distinguish from occasional causes and the products of diseases. But the fruit of a disease, when it generates these products of its own, can coincide with life at the same time; therefore, some symptomatic fruits are among the Diatheses, which the Schools have not yet explained. Namely, the failure of digestions, motions, etc. Likewise, debilitations are Diatheses which indeed proceed from the products of diseases (as will be shown in its proper place), yet they are not the diseases themselves. This is because they fall upon the nature into which they were introduced through the foreign seminal violences of the diseased state, and they have been guests thus far in a singular way within life. Accordingly, they cannot have the nature of a disease. This is because a disease cannot dwell together with life in the same point of identity. Rather, disease withdraws from the vital storehouse, just as it separates itself outside of health. Life, however, is in itself a certain integrity of **light**, with which disease cannot cohabit; just as disease does not subsist except in a vice of life, or a degenerate life. This life is indeed separated from the vital light itself, and thus also from the central point of life itself. For just as the light, which is the **Soul** itself, is not life itself, so the light of life is not the disease itself. But the disease sits in the "abscess" <note>A departure or falling away.</note> of the vital **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine.</note>, and thus it also vitiates its light; and therefore, by way of a shared symbol, it participates in life, sometimes rendering life conformable to itself and corrupting it entirely. This is ordinary and manifest in the **Plague**. <margin>41.</margin> It was therefore unknown in the Schools into which **Category** <note>Referring to Aristotle's ten categories of being.</note> they should place disease. I, however, say that disease—

# DISEASE.

## Rrr 3

A disease consists of matter and an efficient cause, no differently than other entities of nature. For the efficient cause is the **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is a term popularized by Paracelsus and van Helmont referring to the internal "vital director" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions.</note>, which, by laboring through the dislocations of its passions and by giving birth to the **Ideas** of its disturbances (for whatever things occur in nature arise and are propagated through Ideas enclosed within seeds: <margin>42.</margin> otherwise the progressions of nature would be foolish, lacking an internal guide), it manages to arrange some portion of its own substance according to the ends which it has proposed in that sort of alienation of itself—ends hostile to itself and to the whole body. And by that very act, when the matter reaches the limit proposed by the efficient Idea, a disease is born. To such an extent that every **seminal disease** <note>A disease that grows from a "seed" or internal blueprint rather than just an external imbalance.</note> consists in a real act causing a disorder of the matter congenial to itself—that is, of the matter making an attack and applied to us.

<margin>43.</margin> I have therefore learned that the entire scope of the **Categories** <note>original: "Prædicamentorum"; referring to Aristotle’s fundamental classifications of being, such as substance, quality, and quantity.</note> is truly present in diseases, in the true manner of other entities subsisting by themselves in nature. In this way, I have not found diseases within the Categories, but rather all the Categories within diseases. Indeed, in all seminal diseases, I find an "occasional matter" which, like a violent guest making an attack, violates the hospitality and the law of the body and disturbs its internal economy. From this, I find that the Archeus itself is disturbed in every single disease; for hence I also consider the other internal matter of the disease: namely, that part of the Archeus which it has defiled by its own wandering. Into this part, it has fashioned the Idea of its disturbance and the seminal efficient cause of the disease.

<margin>44.</margin> Thus, indeed, a true and real entity cherishes within itself the respects of all the Categories. The ignorance of this single point alone has overwhelmed the schools of medicine with a contagion of blindness and **Paganism** <note>original: "Ethniciſmus"; the author often uses this to criticize Galenic or Aristotelian medicine as lacking Christian/divine insight.</note>. It has been believed that every healing is subject to bare qualities, excesses of degrees, relative respects, and actions. Hence they have also fashioned "contrary remedies for contraries" <note>The traditional Galenic principle of *contraria contrariis curantur*.</note>; and they believe no disease is soothed by the goodness of nature, by the mildness of medicines, or by the pacification and repentance of the Archeus that was previously disturbed.

<column-break/>

They believe only through battle, skirmish, and war can the "middle ground" or the temperament of the primary qualities be restored. Thus, since they think every disease is a **Diathesis** <note>A Greek term for a "disposition" or state of the body.</note>, they must likewise believe all remedies are a bare diathesis, or they are deceived in their thesis. From this it follows that the removal of a **stone** <note>original: "calculi"; a kidney or bladder stone.</note> from the bladder can never, by itself, bring about the healing of the patient. For since it is a remedy <margin>45.</margin> that is at least "privative" <note>Meaning it removes an object but doesn't fix the underlying cause.</note>, following which the Archeus is pacified, it is not a Diathesis contrary to the stone. Much less does it prohibit the "antecedent matter" which they suppose is necessarily supplied from elsewhere and flows in without end; this does not cease when the stone is removed by the knife, unless the Diathesis generating the "matter from which" has first ceased. Therefore, according to the Schools, one cut for a stone is healed only for a short time—insofar as the impediments to functions produced and fostered by the stone are removed—and simultaneously insofar as the Diathesis, intervening mentally, is deleted secondarily, by chance, and by accident.

But the matter stands far otherwise. Indeed, a seminal disease is a creature which has made and found its own matters and its own Ideas within us by the hereditary right of the Archeus after the Fall <note>Referring to the original sin of Adam, which the author links to the origin of human disease.</note>; it did not originally exist in nature. Therefore, the root of diseases must have been totally unknown to all Paganism. And since an essential definition must be sought not from the "genus" of the thing defined and its "constitutive difference" (as I taught in the *Book on Fevers*), because of the multiple anxieties of errors and ridiculous theses, but rather entirely from the connected causes of entities in nature: the primitive and ideal cause of diseases has remained unknown until now. It follows that the definition, knowledge, essence, and roots of disease have also remained unknown. And finally, healings have been instituted by accident, with ignorance of the universal condition of internal properties, efficacy, and "otherness."

<margin>46.</margin> I know indeed, as a Christian,

Because disease is not a creature of the first creation <note>original: "primæ constitutionis"; referring to the state of nature before the Fall of Man</note>; indeed, it took root from sin in the impurity of nature, which then, in its own springtime, finally germinated in individuals. For created poisons are not diseases as long as they remain outside of us: but rather, they become so when their **Archeus** <term>Archeus: The internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine</term>, having become a guest within us through the foreign nature of its middle life, has stirred up **seminal Ideas** <term>Ideas feminales: Spiritual seeds or blueprints that give form to matter</term> in our own Archeus, just as fire is struck from a flint. Then, I say, diseases—the precursors of death—are formed within us from an occasional poison. Diseases therefore endure with us because they have provocative occasions subsisting in our nature, until either their occasional matter is consumed, or at least the Archeus is finished with its disturbances or its duty. For diseases did indeed come upon us from sin; and then in nature, now corrupted by sin, ferments grew and the ready compliance of matter followed: and so they entered into the census and catalog of nature, and even today, in a singular way, they persist most deeply within <margin>47.</margin> us. Yet they are always distinct from the rest of created things in this: that the creations of the first constitution have their own existence in themselves, whereas diseases can neither exist nor subsist outside of us. Inasmuch as they proceed, as it were, from the formal light and the vital beginning that constitutes us. Therefore, the natural Archeus and the disease penetrate one another, because they share a material symbol. <margin>48.</margin> For while the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities of the time, specifically those following Galen and Aristotle</note> observed that diseases exist nowhere outside of us, they concluded that our body is the subject in which diseases inhere: and consequently, that diseases are merely "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing</note>: and for that reason, they are stirred up by an elemental imbalance <note>original: "intemperie elementali"</note>, because they grasped this with a very ready and rustic sense. Also for that reason, they hoped they would more than sufficiently overcome diseases through heats and colds. And likewise, they decreed that all comfort, help, and aid which nature, informed by the healer, might require, should not be administered as a kind of help in peace and tranquility; but that it would be valid

<column-break/>

only for, and destined for, wars, struggles, contraries, and discords: by which the hostile elemental qualities in us, having been broken, might be forced back into symmetry. So that they might restrain the injuries of a now-corrupted nature with contrary injuries, and subdue them by taking revenge. This they certainly judged to be so, and they understood it no other way: inasmuch as they knew no other action in nature than that which dominates the sufferer through the superiority of the agent. But truly, those things do not taste of help, nor is the law of Christ (through whom all things were made) conformable to these laws of the Schools. And so (as discussed more widely elsewhere) either Christ is not the parent of nature, or He is an adversary to Himself in nature, or such pagan theorems of healing are merely meddlesome. The Schools, therefore, did not consider that the matter of many beings consists only in the foreign lodging to which they were destined. Wherefore, because of an irregular <note>original: "heteroclitum"</note> mode of existing, they thought disease was a mere accident: separating the matter which the disease displays from the disease itself in a categorical sense. As if an embryo were an accident, because it is nowhere except in the womb. It certainly pleased the avenger of sin that diseases, with their matters—both the occasional and the twin matter internal to itself—should not subsist except in those for whom the diseases were also an atonement <note>original: "piaculum"</note>: and this without respect of the being of one to the other. For the ethnic <note>pagan</note> Schools never thought, nor do the modern ones stalled in pagan beginnings, that this relationship of existence came to them from the condition of sin, and its procreation from the Archeus, when it is moved by disturbances. Because thoughts of this kind never entered into paganism. Nor is it a wonder that the Gentiles did not know the weight of transgression, although through the fable of **Prometheus and Pandora** <note>Prometheus stole fire from the gods, and Pandora opened a jar that released all the evils/diseases into the world</note>, they betray that they learned something from the Hebrews. It is a wonder, however, that they were ignorant that disease, before it becomes ours, proceeds from the intimate beginning of life, and must be incorporated into us; and therefore occasional causes cannot be the connected, constitutive parts of diseases.

## 49.
...diseases: for those causes remain even after life has ended, and yet the diseases themselves cease. But Christians should by no means indulge in such ideas, having been taught by Sacred Scripture; even now, they should consider it a matter of honor to have surrendered their minds, which were once bound to the harmful stupidities of the Pagans. They have indeed noticed a certain kinship between us and some diseases, because, as far as the <term>occasional matter</term><note>The physical substance that triggers a disease, as opposed to the disease's vital cause.</note> is concerned, they are so connected to our body that they can hardly be separated by the judgment of the mind, nor can they be distinguished from the impaired action itself. This is seen in wounds, in diseases of the organs, and in those deprived of the strength of their "seeds." For example, a growth <margin>49.</margin> upon the cornea immediately harms the sight; just as a stone, without any other <margin>50.</margin> medium, blocks the passage of urine. However, the obstruction arising from this is merely a relation and a "being of reason" <note>A logical construct rather than a physical thing.</note>. Just as it does nothing of itself, so it possesses neither the essence of a disease nor a consideration within nature. Nevertheless, the modern Schools have preferred to entrust the essences of diseases to elemental discords rather than admit that natural bodies express nothing other than a connection—unknown to the Schools—between both constitutive causes. Hitherto, for this reason, wretched mortals have groaned under this burden of blindness, expecting healing from those who were entirely ignorant of the constitutive causes of diseases. Therefore, since a disease must contain its own <term>efficient cause</term><note>The active agent that produces an effect.</note> within itself and its own matter, it is easily clear from this that hunger—although it may kill in a few days like a very acute disease—is not a disease. This is because it does not consist of diseased causes, whether it is considered as a sorrowful sense (from the class of symptoms) or as a state of real deficiencies. Indeed, insofar as the acid <term>ferment</term> of the stomach (as discussed in the Treatise on Digestions), lacking an object to act upon but unable to remain idle, attacks and dissolves the secondary humor and the nearby nourishment of the stomach; the <term>Archeus</term><note>The internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note> is present in hunger just as in fullness, and is the cause not of disease, but of health itself. The lack of food-matter indicates a privation, but not a disease. For this reason, it must be

<column-break/>

noted quite accurately that hunger, although it kills cruelly as if it were a disease, is nevertheless not a disease by that title, because the Archeus is by no means diseased in hunger. From this it should be clearly established that every disease primarily and essentially regards its efficient Archeus. For this reason, <margin>52.</margin> it was rightly decreed by Hippocrates—despite the neglect of the Schools—that heat, cold, moisture, or dryness (not even as such, or in combination) are not diseases or their causes; but rather the sharp, the bitter, the salty, the harsh, etc. Perhaps in the age of Hippocrates, the <term>occasional cause</term> had not yet been distinguished from the true disease. He knew indeed that there are two types of excrement in us. One is natural and ordinary, and thus our own; the other, however, is morbid, born of error and a hostile offshoot, which we Christians know proceeded from the power of sin. When the Old Man <note>Referring to Hippocrates.</note> had distinguished this by exotic flavors, he reckoned that if it were not the disease itself, it was at least the adequate occasion for diseases, though not yet distinguished from the disease. He believed that its removal alone would open both valves of healing. But it is astounding that the Schools, who boast of following him as their leader, have through laziness skipped over this text, as well as another from the same Foremost Leader:

> *By which he declared that every movement toward disease, death, and health is efficiently produced by the "impelling spirit" <note>original: "impetu faciente spiritu" / Greek: "enormon".</note>. Likewise, where he said: Natures themselves are the healers of diseases: and consequently, they are also the creators of diseases, if that "enormon" spirit, by its own agitation, performs everything whatsoever that happens in living beings.*

The Schools have certainly bypassed many things of this <margin>53.</margin> sort, which deserved to be held as oracles. Because they were deluded and bewitched by the fictitious four humors, and carried away on a deep ship of sleep, lethargy, and laziness, they neglected the fluids which he himself calls "secondary": as if a disease were not just as possible in those as in the four fictitious primary ones. Thus, they also neglected diseases arising from retained digestions and "transplantations": for even the digestions and fermentations themselves...

<columns>2</columns>

(As I have taught in its proper place) they were utterly ignorant. Alas! How meager is the knowledge that has hitherto adorned those practicing medicine—men who otherwise, if they were true Physicians, the Most High has commanded us to honor.
<margin>54.</margin>
For they considered that a disease flows out as an "accident" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like the color of a shirt, rather than the shirt itself.</note>, produced by an Agent, the **morbific matter** <note>original: "materia morbifica" — the physical substance thought to carry disease</note> (in which they failed to recognize from the start that its own efficient cause resides), and a "patient": which they say is the human body. First and foremost, they do not distinguish the Agent from the matter, which is most intimate to it. Then, they deny that disease is material, since they reckon it a mere quality. Thirdly, they do not distinguish irritating occasions from the internal efficient cause. This is because, following **Aristotle**, they reckon every efficient cause to be external. 4. They separate the constitutive causes from the thing constituted. 5. They are ignorant of the chain of efficient causes and their products. 6. They mostly confuse occasional causes with the diseases and symptoms themselves. 7. Frequently they look upon disease as a **disposition** <note>original: "Diathesin" — a Greek term for a constitutional state or tendency</note> hovering between the series of causes and the human body.
<margin>55.</margin>
8. They prefer that the subsequent disposition itself, arising from the "battle of causes" (as they call it), be the disease—which would then immediately (so they say) harm the actions of the body, whether it be contrary to the vital action in the meantime, or truly the effect of that contrariety which has offended the functions. But I do not look to the impairment of functions as the **essence of the disease**; rather, I contemplate in diseases the operative disturbances extended into the **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine.</note>. For it is not rare for a man to die without any sense of impaired action; he falls suddenly, though he has long been diseased within, or he perishes by a simple failure of nature. Therefore, among other impertinences, I reckon it a mistake to have restricted the essence of diseases to the impairment of functions. For that is accidental to diseases, and comes after them: it does not accompany them perpetually.
<margin>56.</margin>
Indeed, because the spontaneous restoration of weakened powers follows health, the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the time.</note> have measured the essence of diseases as owing an inseparable respect to the impairment and the things impairing the functions. This was done so that these things would be included

<column-break/>

within the very essence of diseases. They thought, for instance, that the entire hinge of healing turned upon "contraries" <note>The traditional Galenic principle of "contraria contrariis curantur" — treating heat with cold, etc.</note>. Yet otherwise, it is entirely by accident if functions are impaired in diseases. Otherwise, who is there who would deny that a disease is not really present during the "silence" of a **quartan fever**, **epilepsy**, **mania**, or **gout** <note>original: "quartanæ, Caduci, Maniæ, ac Podagræ"</note>, even when no impairment of function is observed? Who is there who does not notice in a convalescent person greater obstacles to action and greater weaknesses than at the flaming onset of the disease? It has therefore always seemed stupid to me for a thing to be defined essentially by its later and separable effects. And since disease arises primarily from the **Archeus** making an onset (albeit an erring one), certainly its action will be much closer to the faculties themselves than to the actions of those faculties. Especially since, as long as the strengths of a convalescent are still as if conquered and shattered, there are indeed impediments to strength, as well as impairment and suppression of actions—yet with no disease remaining. And since I have sufficiently demonstrated elsewhere that in natural things, both causes do not differ in their underlying reality from the thing constituted itself: therefore, if the disease were the cause of the impairment of action, as its constitutive difference, it would also be necessary for the disease itself to be in no way different from the impaired action. Which is now clearly false. And it would be false that the cause and the disease are comprised indistinctly under the single title of "that which impairs action"—or else the Schools judge poorly that the thing impairing the action is the morbific cause itself. The impairment of action would then be the disease, and the impaired action would be the symptom itself. For that too is a childish fiction. For first, the disease would be a mere **mental construct** <note>original: "ens rationis" — a thing that exists only in the mind</note>, arising mentally from the relationship of the terms of cause to effect—namely, of the harmer and the harmed. Finally, an error is detected in the definition of disease handed down by the Schools: namely, that disease is a "disposition primarily impairing action." For that would define the cause, and not the disease itself, or the effect of the cause.

# DISEASE.

Thirdly, we must consider whether a remedy ought to remove the very thing that harms our vital action. Such a remedy would either possess a singular monarchy—by which it summons and shakes the harming agent—or the remedy joins itself to nature itself, and that so unitedly, that with combined forces, and as if now joined as one, it stations itself at the opposite boundary against the harming agent. For the first of these is not true. Since the remedy would be as foreign to nature as the disease itself otherwise is, on account of its particular direction and the choice of its movements, which would be rejected by our *Archeus* <note>The 'Archeus' is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal 'vital workman' or spiritual force that governs the body's functions.</note>. For if it were to help in that way, it would possess a power superior to human nature, such that it would obey neither the laws of disease nor of death. Thus, it would expel the cause of disease as easily from a corpse as from a lingering patient. Nor, likewise, does the second option hold place. Because if a remedy were united to nature radically, and by a unifying mixture, it would have a privilege beyond the fate of mere nourishment. Therefore, the impairment of action itself does not fall into the definition of disease. Specifically, because a remedy does not look so much toward the occasional cause <note>The 'occasional cause' refers to the external trigger or material stimulus of a sickness.</note> as toward the internal morbific efficient cause itself. Whence the axiom is verified: *That natures themselves are the healers of diseases, just as they are the creators of them.* <note>original: "Quod naturæ ipsæ sint morborum curatrices, ut effectrices."</note> In both cases, namely, people confuse the disease with the symptom, to the ruin of those to be healed. Since healing frequently lies in the removal of the occasional cause, but never in the removal of symptoms. <margin>§ 7.</margin> And because the removal of the occasional cause is thought to be a material extraction, hitherto only dissolving and diminishing treatments of the body's contents have flourished. <margin>§ 8.</margin> Whereas, otherwise, the removal of the occasional cause looks more toward the correction or pacification of the immediate efficient cause than the tearing away of the occasional matter: inasmuch as from correction—even without the removal of the occasional matter—cessation, unexpected rest, and indeed even healing mostly follow. This frequently occurs in sympathetic cures, and is clearly evident. <margin>§ 9.</margin> The Schools <note>The 'Schools' refers to the traditional academic authorities of the time, often followers of Galen or Aristotle.</note> therefore, deceived by artificial things, and because they thought that every gene-

<column-break/>

ration begins from a privative point of corruption, did not know: that that which already flows in the material seminal beginning of anything, already by that very fact has its real being, though immature, and is through this a "this-something" in itself, and distinct from anything else: and that it acquires through natural generation only maturity and illumination at its peak, on account of a new formal light of acting. Nor indeed does the seed differ from its constitution by an internal efficient cause and matter: but only through an individual alterity <note>difference or otherness</note> of perfection of the formal light, as I have discussed elsewhere regarding the rise of forms. <margin>60.</margin> For the seed, which previously had need of an exciter, once this formal light is obtained, is henceforth moving itself. <margin>61.</margin> The Schools also repeatedly consider disease as if it were a neutral product, flowing through the activity of a cause and the resistance of our nature. But I know that both the formal agent and the patient in a disease are foreign to us in that act. I know, for instance, that the *Falling Sickness* <note>original: "Caducum," referring to epilepsy.</note>, *in the days of silence*, is no less really in us than when it is in full onset. <margin>62.</margin> I know also that disease is a real, substantive entity. It is not a relative thing, nor a bare condition of an agent struggling against a patient, as if they were extremes meeting in the middle. Nor, finally, is it a conformity of proportion or disproportion between extremes. Although this respect of forming a relation, among entities of reason, may be closer to the resulting effect. I know, moreover, that every natural agent is born to produce its like, except that which acts through *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a "vis motus" or "power of motion," both in the stars (Blas meteoron) and in the body (Blas humanum).</note> (for a power as much locally motive as alterative, because it lacked a name, seemed to me to be called *Blas* in the beginnings of Physics.) Thus the Heaven generates meteors, not heavens. And man, through voluntary *Blas*; and likewise the *Archeus* through an ideal and seminal *Blas*, stirs up various alterations. But a seminal agent, when disordered through a foreign *Blas*, brings forth a monster, which is properly a disease. <margin>63.</margin>

<summary>Van Helmont argues that disease is a real, substantive entity rather than a mere imbalance or symptom, driven by an internal 'Blas' or vital motion that has gone astray. He critiques traditional medicine for treating symptoms rather than correcting the internal 'Archeus' or vital workman of the body.</summary>
