# THE UNKNOWN GUEST

For even if a disease, according to its causes, is natural, yet in respect to us, it does not cease to be contrary to nature—both insofar as it began from an exotic *Blas* <note>original: "Blas"; a term coined by Van Helmont to describe a "formative" or "motive" power in nature and the body</note>, and because that *Blas* carries a hostile intent and stirs it up from within itself. Therefore, this monster does not generate an offspring like itself (unless it transfers its seminal contagion through ferments), and thus it creates diseases in others by accident.

<margin>64.</margin> Now, as for what pertains to the efficient cause of diseases: there is a certain efficient cause born within by an "abortive birth" (such as a cataract in the eye, a stone, or feverish matter). Although the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Galenic or Aristotelian academic medicine, which the author often critiques.</note> call this the "morbific, immediate, and containing efficient cause," it is nevertheless merely an *occasional* cause of diseases, and external with respect to the life in which every disease always exists. Therefore, such visible matter cannot obtain the status of a true efficient cause; nor can it even be a part of the intrinsic matter of the disease itself. It remains, therefore, a provoker and an 

<margin>65.</margin> occasional cause of diseases. This is because if the efficient and seminal matter is to immediately touch and penetrate the vital faculties—and thus life itself—it is absolutely necessary that it contain the symbol of life at its very core. Thus, it is a perpetual rule in seminal diseases that just as a disease is never in a corpse, so it cannot but be in a living being.

<margin>66.</margin> Furthermore, some efficient causes are and remain external. For example, iron, having acquired an impulsive force, creates a disease in divided matter, which is called a wound. Similar is the wearing away of the bladder caused by a stone. For although some external efficiencies have their own seminal beginnings by which they are generated (like a stone), yet in respect to the disease they produce, they lack seeds; therefore, they are external and foreign to the disease itself. But internal occasional causes have a seed by which they cherish the disease they have stirred up, and they are often enclosed within the "completed state" <note>original: "in facto esse"; a scholastic term meaning the state of a thing once it is fully formed.</note>. This is evident in fever, an abscess, etc. Finally, there are occasional efficiencies which contaminate by a continuous and fermental propagation, such as ulcers, jaundice, etc.

<column-break/>

And there are internal occasional causes which sleep from time to time, as in the "Falling Sickness" <note>Epilepsy</note>, Gout, Mania, Asthma, fevers, etc. Some of these internal occasional causes work incessantly to alienate the matter of our body from the communion of life. If a ferment is added to these (which Hippocrates calls "the divine" in diseases), "liquefactions" <note>Wasting of the tissues</note> occur. In a fever, however, the occasional efficient matter, according to its twin properties, provokes the *Archeus* <note>original: "Archeum"; the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions</note> toward expulsion, for its own consumption. Therefore, it leaves no other product behind it, unless a new *Idea* <note>A morbid mental or spiritual image formed by the Archeus</note> flows from the frustrated *Archeus* by accident—just as Dropsy <note>Edema/fluid retention</note> follows fevers, etc. Let pains, however, lethargy, sleeplessness, weaknesses, etc., be considered symptoms and dispositions.

<margin>67.</margin> Thus also a foreign seminal efficient cause produces a stone <note>original: "calculum"; a kidney or bladder stone</note>, and there it stops, although thereafter it excites troubles and new movements from moment to moment. The products of the Stone, however, are excoriations and new diseases, which are monsters unlike their parent.

<margin>68.</margin> For properly speaking, the generation of a Stone is not a disease, any more than the stone itself, which in itself is a natural composite, but in respect to us is diseased. Wherefore, it is generated by its own causes of petrification both in the chamber-pot and outside of life. Thus, it is a monstrous and anomalous disease, inasmuch as it is born in us by accident and outside of life.

<margin>69.</margin> Finally, as soon as the effect or product in its "completed state" has lost its occasional efficient cause, that product is no longer the connection of both causes (the original disease), but it has its own causes, which are posterior to the connection of the primary causes.

<margin>70.</margin> For in this way, an Abscess gave birth to an ulcer; this ulcer, in turn, weeps a virulent *ichor* <note>A thin, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer</note>; and this, finally, not infrequently causes excoriation, changes the original ulcer, or stirs up a new one. But the producing ulcer does not concern itself with whether its *ichor* subsequently causes further ulceration or not, because it has no effective intention to produce an ulcer from the *ichor*. For the discharge itself, or *ichor*, is the product of the producing ulcer, which has [already] undertaken its effective and seminal intention...

<summary>This page discusses the distinction between the "efficient" and "occasional" causes of disease, arguing that physical matter like stones or pus are merely triggers (occasional causes) while the true disease resides in the reaction of the vital spirit or Archeus. It explores how diseases can evolve from one form to another, such as a fever leading to dropsy or an abscess becoming a chronic ulcer.</summary>

-> # D I S E A S E . <-

began to exist in itself: but not for the propagation of a new ulcer, which is therefore accidental to it. A stone <note>Latin: *calculus*, referring to kidney or bladder stones</note> also is the product of its own constituent causes, which it encloses and terminates within itself. Because its causes, having been carried to the end of their effect, cease in the product and are enclosed as if buried. Although that stone may be an occasional medium by which the generation of a new stone happens by accretion. Meanwhile, it is accidental to the stone if it produces other diseases more atrocious than itself, or indeed than death itself. In Dropsy <note>Latin: *Hydrops*, an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid</note>, however, the efficient Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont’s term for the internal vital spirit or "master workman" that governs the body's functions.</note> of the kidneys, in the conception of an Idea generated by its own disturbance, shuts the kidneys, and dropsy occurs. Yet the original efficient cause does not cease until the person is suffocated. In that finished act, once the water is produced and sent forth, there is no further intention to produce anything else. Sometimes the product of a disease, since it is an innate monster, has an occasional power of propagation from the property of the efficient Archeus, which is not enclosed or bound in the product, but remains free in the organs of life. From this, naturally, other products bloom forth successively one after another. At the very least, the loss of faculties and life should not be considered so much the products of diseases as their destined fruits, symptoms, and the periods of these things. Meanwhile, a disease produced by a morbid ferment <note>A "ferment" was believed to be a chemical or spiritual agent that transformed matter, similar to yeast in bread.</note> is of no less privilege than the disease that was the parent of that product. That is to say, it does not corrupt a vital part any more sluggishly through foreign efficient causes it has received than that disease in whose primary efficient action the disease itself resides.

<margin>71.</margin> Furthermore, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional academic authorities of the time, largely following Galen and Aristotle.</note> suppose a contrariety of disease with health, with life, and again with the remedy itself. Thus they oppose several contraries to a single term, against the nature of relatives and against their own axiom: that one of the contraries is spoken of in as many ways as the other. For if the doctrine of contraries in remedies stood firm, health ought at least to <margin>72.</margin> emerge from Medicine like a chick from an egg. Or, since contraries ought to reduce each other to nothing,

<column-break/>

health ought to come forth from disease, just as weakness otherwise comes out of disease. For if the remedy is made contrary to the disease, then certainly our vital faculties cannot be contrary to the disease; and consequently, the disease will not be able to hurt the faculties or their actions. And the Schools have erred when they contend that in a crisis, the disease maintains a single combat <note>Latin: *monomachia*</note> with the faculties throughout its entire course. But if the disease were contrary to the faculties and to the remedy itself, they would at least incongruously apply cold things to a fever, which are applied to the vital faculty no less than to the disease. Indeed, if a disease were born from a contrariety of Diathesis <note>A "Diathesis" refers to a physical constitution or predisposition to a certain state.</note>, our action ought not to depend entirely on the spirit making the onset, but on the mere morbific cause; and because it would thus have the principle of its motion within itself, it ought to operate in a corpse as much as in a living person. It would thus be a total skirmish merely between the Diatheses of foreign accidents, defeating each other. Of which struggle, life itself would be only a hateful spectator, without its own inconvenience. What is this other than to have fashioned an inert and cold vital Philosophy? And that the healers of fevers are themselves cold? What if the disease consists in a quality whose warring contrary they wish to be known by sense and to be elemental? Why then are such uncertain, languid, and slow remedies for diseases mixed together? Since the signs, remedies, and simples <note>Medicinal herbs or medicines made of only one ingredient.</note> of manifest contrary qualities are boasted of so openly and promptly in the Schools?

<margin>73.</margin> Therefore, in my view, disease is a substantial entity, generated by Archeal causes, both materially and efficiently. But heat, and cold, and that kind of concomitant sign, I call fruits and symptoms, far removed from the produced diseases. For often a disease moves furiously against us, in which many symptoms intervene, which nevertheless frequently ceases without a product. As is evident in intermittent fevers. For no new disease rises from them. But at least nature intends to shake off a tedious guest; under which effort the fruits and symptoms are produced.

This happens when the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: The internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions and healing</term>, stirred up by an occasional ferment, brings forth a new product: whether the prior disease is concluded within that product or not. Not infrequently, a disease also occasionally produces a "monster" unlike itself. It is either total, due to afflictions of a significant or noble part <note>A "noble part" refers to vital organs like the heart, brain, or liver.</note>. It also happens due to the adherence of a diseased occasion to some solid part. From this, eventually, once the *Archeus* is extinguished in that spot, a "blasting" <note>original: "sideratio," meaning a sudden stroke or localized death/gangrene</note> of that part and soon the death of the whole follows. Or, the weakness is particular, due to a specific *Blas* <term>Blas: A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the "impulse" or "motion" of the stars or the internal vital spirit</term>, affecting some limb through its own "anger" <note>original: "thimosim," from Greek *thymosis*, meaning an outburst of passion or irritation</note>. Thus, from the stomach comes vertigo and headache, etc.; just as from the womb, various parts languish miserably through a shared influence. These are certainly symptoms and fruits of the *Archeus*, but not of its disease: which otherwise naturally hide their own efficiencies within themselves. Just as I have written elsewhere regarding the action of the government <note>The "government" refers to the body's internal regulation.</note>. Finally, the product of a disease differs from a symptom in this: the symptom is a fruit that requires mitigation from the *Archeus* itself, but does not, of itself, require a separate cure. This is because it vanishes along with the disease. However, I find no mention of the "products" of diseases in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Galenic university medicine, which Van Helmont often criticized.</note>; instead, they are either confused with symptoms or attributed to some new "imbalance of humors" <note>original: "intemperiei," referring to the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> or a new influx of fluids.

<margin>75.</margin>

Others are also accustomed to assign diseases to the "containing parts" <note>The vessels or organs.</note>, the causes to the "contained parts" <note>The fluids or humors.</note>, and the symptoms to the "spirit making the attack." They are poorly mindful that they attribute the primary heat and cold to the contained

<column-break/>

humors as if they were the diseases themselves. Finally, if the disease is in the Container and the cause is in the Contained: I ask, what will move the cause and the disease
<margin>76.</margin>
if not the spirit innate within us? Who will fashion a disease out of a cause, if not the spirit? For just as Anger, shame, and agony produce heat through the *Blas*: so fear, pain, and sadness produce cold, without the help of the humors. Moreover, Pepper and heating substances heat the living; but not corpses: just as Spanish fly <note>original: "Cantharides"</note>, spearwort, or celery do not cause blisters on them. But caustics do consume a corpse: and this is not by the effect of their own heat, but solely by the power of the caustic salt, which dissolves solid parts into salt without heat. Just as, for example, quicklime dissolves cheese into a slime. Therefore, caustics generate a scab <note>original: "Escharam"</note> in the living, but not in the dead: in the dead, they merely dissolve it through the simple resolution of their salt. But because in the living, the *Archeus* is simultaneously ignited within, the scab is produced by both agents (namely, the Caustic and the *Archeus*). Finally, Fire burns the living and the dead indifferently: and the living more quickly. Because fire consumes from the outside by burning, and inside the spirit itself becomes caustic by its own ignition. From
<margin>77.</margin>
this fourfold mechanism—namely of Fire, Pepper, Blistering agents, and Caustics—the following notable points flow naturally:
1. That the efficient heat of "heating" substances is actually our own. In pepper, therefore, it is only an occasional stimulus.
2. That a fever is not essentially heat; but from the property of the alterative *Blas*, it possesses both cold and heat as its characteristics. And this is not efficiently: but only occasionally, incitately, and accidentally. The *Archeus* alone is the efficient cause of heat and cold. For the "feverish matter" in a body that is otherwise warm does not suddenly become cold and then hot, so that the whole body freezes and burns in alternation with it. Rather, these are the works and Signatures of life: not properties of the "seeds" of disease in the matter, but mere passions of the body, arising from the heat and cold of the *Archeus*.

And therefore these things no longer occur in a corpse, nor after the disease gains victory, nor even while the disease ceases, even if the occasional matter <note>The physical substance (like a toxin or splinter) that triggers a reaction, but is not the disease itself</note> remains in the meantime.

At the source, through the sedation and pacification of the disturbed *Archeus*. 8. That the *Archeus*, who formed us in the womb, also directs, moderates, and moves all things during life. Therefore, occasional causes are perceived only in the *Archeus*. 10. ...of a [glowing object], by blocking [the pores] it suffocates the fire. Thus also metal, or glass, when ignited and glowing, will shine for a long time at the very bottom of the coldest water; meanwhile, an ignited coal is suffocated in an instant under water. This is because its pores are immediately obstructed. Glowing copper is therefore extinguished more quickly than silver, and silver more quickly than gold. However, ignited glass, because it lacks pores, shines under water as long as gold. Indeed, boiling water suffocates fire more quickly than cold water, because it penetrates the pores faster. In this matter also you must remain: that they should always consider our heat by making a comparison to fire. For even if fire is a being of nature; nevertheless, because it was directed by the Most High for the use of mortals to enter into nature as a destructor, and to be as it were an artificial death: therefore it pursues its own artificial ends: but it has nothing in itself that is vital or seminal <note>The author argues fire is a force of breakdown/death, not a biological force of life/growth</note>. There is therefore no fire in nature, if it has not first risen to the degree required for a destructor.
<margin>79.</margin>
In this regard, it is of little or no use to medical speculation. Truly, our [body] heat is not graduated [like fire], and therefore it is neither fiery, nor does it proceed as if refracted from fire: but it is the formal heat of light, and therefore vital: nor does it subsist in its highest degree in the same way as fire; for it admits a latitude, and its degrees are diversified according to the stimulation of the *Blas* <term>Blas: a term coined by Van Helmont referring to the internal "motion" or "pulse" of the stars and the human spirit</term>. For even if it is from formal light, and lives by it: nevertheless, in both the healthy and the sick, it often ascends further or is suppressed lower through the *Blas*. Finally, it wanders higher through rages, and then immediately casts off the vital light, as if burnt, and assumes a caustic Alkali. This is seen in damp, compressed hay, where fire rises spontaneously. Thus in escharotic <note>tissue-burning or scarring</note> affections, our heat, forgetting its former life, passes into the degree of fire. For by the meeting of light rays and the degeneration of the salts of the spirits, just as in the hay, a true fire is born, and it would consume us if the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions</term> waited for this end of the scene before death. Our heat indeed

<column-break/>

is in fire, insofar as the number two is within forty: yet fire is not in our heat. And so our heat cannot
<margin>80.</margin>
be called fiery. Just as the number two is not the number forty. Furthermore, a morbid occasion <note>The "occasional cause" or trigger of a disease</note> sometimes burdens by weight alone, and by its hateful presence: such as that of an odious guest. Then, often from milder beginnings, a porous quality grows up, from the class of tastes. Thirdly, or finally, it rots. Fourthly, it seizes a foreign ferment. And lastly, the contagion of an infamous poison threatens us with destruction. The dire seminal occasion of diseases either arrives from abroad or arises within. Often also it degenerates in the final stages, which the schools <note>The traditional academic medical authorities, like those following Galen</note> have neglected, because they fell asleep content with their "primary humors." I say that some harmful tares are separated from the innocent vital parts, and the mixed occasion of the disease fluctuates among the proper nutrients, and has joined or adhered to them even more tenaciously, choosing a local bed. In both cases, the hostile properties of the seeds of disease harass their various lodgings by playing about. Therefore, the *Archeus* is affected not by heat and cold, but by an excellent quality of taste and a foreign fellowship, and it fashions the seminal Idea of the disease. And I marvel that the Greek Schools profess Hippocrates as their leader: yet they have despised this hinge of healing in him, and have immersed themselves in mere heats and foolish marriages of qualities. For to Hippocrates, disease arises from a good fluid, or one previously condemned, turned into
<margin>81.</margin>
excrement. Truly, I pardon this due to the lack of distinction of that age. And therefore I call such dross not the diseases themselves, but the occasional causes of them. For excrement, vitiated by its own digestions or in the final kitchens [of the body], or lingering elsewhere too long, is first noted for its sluggishness due to the delay of its slowness: and then, by the activity of the rejected stall, it is corrupted like a troublesome guest. By title, insofar as it is destitute of vital balsam. For our smith, the *Archeus*, when...

# DISEASE

Since [the body] is never struck without cause, nor ever lacks a local transformative ferment <note>original: "fermento locali commutativo"; a "ferment" in 17th-century medicine was a chemical agent of change, similar to an enzyme</note>; therefore, through heat and continuous warmth, it increasingly agitates the waste products born within or brought from elsewhere, and disturbs them toward their destined ends. For this reason, no waste product can remain for long in its original state. One must also entirely despair that nature, once it has rejected something, would ever receive it back as a true citizen, or adopt it again through a renewed reconciliation (such as the fiction that blood is made from phlegm, or yellow bile from scorched blood: and from this, leek-green or rust-colored bile, and finally the melancholy humor). <note>The author is arguing against the traditional Galenic theory that humors can transform into one another to maintain health.</note> For nature cannot help but alter an unwelcome foreign guest—which is perhaps changeable by its very nature—and push it toward its own ends. And if this happens within the "inns" of its own digestion, the waste will be far milder than if it were once carried to foreign hearths and outside its own boundaries. Then, indeed, that adulterated fruit, that fetus placed upon that part, is refused as an alien enemy, ominous and tumultuous, into which a foreign ferment of another harvest is necessarily introduced by restless alteration. Thus, from things retained—which were at first simply troublesome—they become harmful things, and finally, transformed Retained Matters. If a notable flavor is not already present in them, it usually arises soon after, designated by Hippocrates in the cited passage as a morbid signature <note>A "signature" is an outward sign or physical characteristic that reveals the inner nature or ailment</note>. For as long as the nourishing fluid is restrained by the bridle of nature's balsam, it rightfully possesses the flavors of blood and assimilable nutriment: all things are well. But once rejected by the Archeus <note>term: Archeus; the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note>, it soon assumes a foreign character as well as a foreign flavor, and through the agitation of days, the degree of its malignancy varies. This is surely that sharp, bitter, and harsh quality about which the Old Man <note>referring to Hippocrates</note> complains through his oracles, from which almost all diseases gush forth. For this, although small in weight and light in quantity, and scarcely perceptible to the sight: is nevertheless the true occasion of the disease. But the disease sits deeper:

<column-break/>

namely, in the vital beginnings, which are more active and commanding than those things called waste products. For every disease is seminal <note>meaning it grows from a "seed" or internal blueprint</note>, and being fostered by an occasional cause, it begins from a being that is immediately sensitive and subject to desire, full of passions, disturbances, and disorders: so also it sits in no other place than in the source, prince, and ruler of all motions. Yet it does not fight with a single weapon of malignancy: rather, by its own contaminated delay, it may also overwhelm the part itself, or at least deprive it of the continuity and communion of life: if, moreover, it does not weigh it down with the harm of its impression, or threaten extinction by the wasting of the ferment drawn into a similar part. Therefore, disease begins from the matter of the Archeus,
<margin>§ 3.</margin>
insofar as it rages within us through a foreign Idea <note>term: Idea; here meaning a morbid mental or spiritual image that disrupts the vital force</note> arising from a conceived injury, which it judges the occasional causes to have inflicted upon it. Let the accompanying action, resulting from the proper wandering of the efficient cause (such as a headache, delirium, etc.), be called a symptom. But whatever flows as a finished work of the disease, whether because of pain, spasm, the governance of the parts, or fermental action; if it truly subsists in its own root, that is the product of the disease. Of these products, some
<margin>§ 4.</margin>
are the final effects left behind by the disease, such as a scirrhus <note>a hard, cancerous tumor</note> or Dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> resulting from a fever. Or they leap forth while still in the making. Such as the passing of mucus in those with bladder stones. These do not intend the propagation of another evil, nor of morbid matter, nor of subsequent products. These again are similar to their makers, which indeed creep further by the contagion of a ferment: as is familiar in the case of the itch <note>scabies</note>, leprosy, the venereal plague <note>syphilis</note>, etc. But others, by progressing inward, dilate themselves deeply and generate in an anomalous manner. Such as Breathlessness <note>Apnœa</note>, convulsion, etc., arising from the womb or the stomach. And so griping pains made from acids bring forth diarrhea, hemorrhoids, dysentery, and other evils of that kind. Indeed, while the seed of diseases lies quiet, at intervals, from the hidden nursery of the Archeus, something unusual and discontinuous germinates.

# THE UNKNOWN GUEST

Such as the Falling Sickness <note>original: "Caducus"; epilepsy</note>, Gout <note>original: "Podagra"</note>, Madness <note>original: "Mania"</note>, etc.

<margin>Section 5.</margin> Truly, in all of these, there is a manifest error of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university medical authorities, typically followers of Galen or Aristotle</note>, who teach that all of nature is governed by a ruler—that is, a created intelligence that does not err, knows all goals, and acts in the best possible way for their sake. Yet it is beyond doubt that a wound could be closed up without the swelling of the lips, pain, pus, and inflammation: or that a thorn could be driven out of a finger by a much shorter route than the finger rising up into a purulent abscess. For the fat of a hare, when smeared on, may extract a thorn in a single night; the *Archeus* <note>term: Archeus; the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note> does not lack ways by which he might accomplish this very thing safely and quickly (as he does spontaneously in some cases), unless our *Archeus*, being subject to all kinds of passions, should conceive a sort of childish indignation over the smallest injury to the body. It is no wonder, then, that a being of sublunary nature <note>referring to the earthly realm below the moon, subject to change and decay</note>, submitting itself in no way to justice, should succumb to its own disordered passions: since even the whole man, over whom the intellectual mind presides, exceeds the path of right reason in many things.

<margin>Section 6.</margin> Finally, it is notable that in works of art <note>meaning "artificial" or man-made things</note>, the efficient cause is always outside the object. Deceived by this error, the Schools have failed to realize that in natural and substantial generations, the acting agent is internal. For this reason, they relegated the efficient cause to the catalog of natural causes as something external. Indeed, it has remained unknown that both connected causes of natural things (as I have demonstrated in its proper place) do not differ from their effect except by the priority of their flow. This matter has deceived as many as have contemplated nature by way of analogy through artificial crafts. Nor have they been more blind elsewhere than when they introduced this clumsiness of their speculation into the study of diseases. For they have not only made artificial things equal to seminal things <note>referring to the "seeds" or internal blueprints of life</note> in theory: but even in attempting to heal, they have defiled the entire practice of medicine with "contraries" <note>The Galenic principle of treating "hot" diseases with "cold" remedies</note> through great falsehood and confusion.

<margin>Section 7.</margin> For it was thought that to produce and to generate were exactly the same. Meanwhile, "to generate" means to bring forth something from one's own substance; but he "produces" who

<column-break/>

at least joins active things to passive ones, even if he contributes nothing of his own. He also "makes" who acts in any way whatsoever. Furthermore, I often marvel that while the Schools place the benefit of healing in the removal of causes, they could somehow place "Intemperance" <note>imbalance of the four humors</note> within the series of diseases; since a hot and very well-known disease may suddenly and spontaneously slide into cold, and we are able to remove an intemperance of heat immediately at will, without any relief of the fevers.

<margin>Section 8.</margin> Then, since they have never accepted the vital cause—the *enormontic* <note>term: enormontic; from the Greek 'enormon,' referring to the vital impulse or "stimulator" of the body</note> power—as the efficient cause of diseases, they have decided only upon the removal of the "occasional cause" <note>the external trigger rather than the internal source</note>. For the *Archeus*, although he is the true and immediate cause, both according to the matter (which he brings forth from his own bosom in a corrupted state) and according to the seminal and efficient Idea, nevertheless the *Archeus* does not indicate his own removal. On the contrary, the Schools act while they labor at their "cures" with the blood-letter <note>phlebotomist</note>, with purgatives, and finally with every means that weakens life.

<margin>Section 9.</margin> On what basis they do this, let them see to it. Furthermore, in diseases, there is nature standing, sitting, and lying down. **Standing nature** heals its own diseases by its spontaneous goodness: such as healthy fevers. Likewise the quartan fever <note>a fever occurring every third day, often associated with malaria</note>, which is healed by nature's own guidance, and not by the aids of the Schools. And standing nature can also soon walk, which belongs to health alone. **Sitting nature**, although it can stand and finally walk of its own accord, is nevertheless forced to rise before it stands, and therefore it rises with greater difficulty. But if it is tempted to rise by disordered remedies, it is thrown down from its seat and lies on the ground; nor does it suffer a little from being shaken, and sometimes it succumbs from the fall. Indeed, while many use advice to avoid being ill, they mostly accelerate old age and death, and not rarely even deprive themselves of life. But **lying nature** can never rise by itself. Such as leprosy, the Falling Sickness, Asthma, the Stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, Dropsy <note>edema/swelling</note>, etc. Nor indeed is it enough to rise; for unless the nerves are strengthened, they easily relapse.

For after nearly a thousand years of Anatomy, the moderns neither recognize diseases better, nor drive them away more successfully. Thus, the world is deceived with a high brow. For that corruption was not there two days prior, even if the place had been painful long before: so far is it from excusing the healer (even if summoned in time) that it rather reveals his fault: namely, that he should have opportunely dispersed the trapped excrement <note>In this context, "excrement" refers to waste products or morbid matter within the body.</note>. For nothing of the containing parts is destroyed in the living unless it has first been deprived of the commerce of life. Moreover, a part cannot be deprived of the balsam of life <note>The "balsam of life" is a Paracelsian term for the vital preservative force in the body.</note> for long, nor does a dead part wait many hours in the warmth of the body without likewise quickly rotting, stinking, and drawing the whole into a conspiracy with itself. It is clear, therefore, that the corruption found in a dissected corpse occurred only a few hours before, and began only a few days before death. For abscesses, stirred up by malignant gatherings in the lung, do indeed contain the seeds of diseases; but the mortification of internal parts does not precede the day of death by many steps.

I have given a treatise on fevers. And since Dropsy is a not uncommon metamorphosis of malignant fevers, it seemed right to me to connect the treatise on Dropsy to that of fevers. However, later, when I perceived that Dropsy is resolved through the kidneys, I doubted whether Dropsy should rather be considered after the treatise on Lithiasis <note>The formation of stones, particularly kidney stones</note>: or whether, by way of example, I should subjoin it to the trea-

<column-break/>

tise on diseases. Indeed, if the belly swells from a defect of the wash <note>original: "lotii," referring to urine</note>, and thus from a forgetfulness of the kidneys, Dropsy seemed to be referred there. But the Stone <note>Calculus</note> expelled the treatise on Dropsy: therefore it made a singular place for itself. But I shall be less solicitous about the order, provided that my proposed goal of healing is attained with fruit. I have made it plain that the causes of fevers, Lithiasis, Apoplexy, Paralysis, Lethargy, Leprosy, Spasm, Plague, Jaundice, Colic, Diarrhea, and other similar things are unknown. Then, finally, I have already finished demonstrating the same ignorance regarding the knowledge of disease in general. Now, furthermore, I shall show that the same occurs regarding Dropsy, which is for the most part the heir of diseases. In the schools, a triple Dropsy is observed: namely **Anasarca**, which is water under the skin, and what they call **Leucophlegmatia**, as if arising from phlegm, and they mostly confuse this with local edema. Then follows **Ascites**, which is Dropsy by its proper etymology, manifest in the belly and occasionally in the legs. And the third is **Tympanias**, or windy Dropsy, confined to the belly alone. Because, forsooth, from solitary wind, or mixed with a little serosity, it distends the abdomen no differently than water, and finally kills miserably by suffocating. **Tympanites** is rarer and more atrocious than **Ascites**, and is easily distinguished from Ascites from the beginning. Because the patient, rolled onto their side, does not feel the water fluctuating, as is otherwise manifest in Ascites. Truly, Authors hardly distinguish Anasarca from Ascites by causes or location, especially while the latter begins around the ankles, in the same nursery-place as Anasarca and edema. If these rise higher into the belly, then they name it Ascites, the names of edema and Anasarca ceasing: thus a mere degree varies the species of the disease in the schools. But if the whole habit appears swollen, as if poison had been taken, they immediately think that phlegm has committed the crime, and they call it Leucophlegmatia.

## THE UNKNOWN DROPSY

...you to be admitted as an equal into the mouths of the veins and the vital duties. But since [physicians] expend so much effort in drying out Dropsy <note>original: "Hydropisi"; a historical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> that they command an almost impossible abstinence from liquids for an entire year. If dropsy is a defect of a single hepatic digestion <note>The "first digestion" in the liver according to Galenic medicine</note>, why do they classify it among diseases offending by humidity alone, which ought to have been numbered among half-complete digestions? For I shall first dispute concerning the liver, and under that same side-project, I shall uncover the occasional cause of dropsy. I saw a certain simple, tasteless substance (not to be revealed in any way) exhibited by a Physician under the suspicion of a kidney stone <note>original: "calculi renum"</note>, which suspended the urine for eight days, even unto death; yet just before death, it was released, and then it soaked through the blankets. Disease produced another similar case. Indeed, neither in the ureter nor the bladder did any obstacle appear upon dissection. However, he had a triangular left Kidney, free from all obstruction and stone. But the right Kidney was plainly monstrous to him, and scarcely the size of a hazelnut. Therefore, since he had urinated for 76 years without the left Kidney being hindered, I will narrate my experiences to show that the liver is innocent in dropsy.

10. Because the decrees of the schools <note>The "Scholastics" or traditional university-trained doctors</note> satisfied me less regarding dropsy, I was accustomed, even as a young man and without being called, to run to the dissections of those who died of dropsy, so that I might examine the origins of the disease. For I thought: To what purpose have there been Anatomists for two thousand years now, if today the healing of dropsy is no more successful than of old? Why indeed should we be butchers of corpses <note>original: "cadaverum laniones"</note> if we do not learn from the errors of the ancients? If we do not amend the past? For we flee to Anatomy with a prejudiced mind, and we wipe out the purses of the heirs, if we do not inspect the causes of death so that we may learn healings. Indeed, dissection profits the dead man nothing. The heirs also do not spend money to heal the dead through Anatomy; much less to wound him, lest perhaps he should rise again. Nor even so that those who refuse to heal might learn to cure others. But the corpse is opened solely for the sake of the physician, and so that he may learn, the heir pays the tuition <note>original: "didactron"</note>. *Thus you, oh oxen, carry the plows, but not for yourselves.* <note>A reference to a famous Latin verse by Virgil about unrewarded labor</note> But the Physicians, since they scarcely hope to learn more, stand by, dull the minds of the men, and hope at the expense of the heirs to mostly escape the mark of death.

A Lawyer, after long-lasting torments, died of dropsy. In the dissection, however, we saw his liver without a blemish. An Englishman, my neighbor, having been stuffed by eating roasted pig, fell into a long-lasting diarrhea, and soon after lapsed into dropsy and died; upon being dissected, his liver was seen to be blameless. To this also belongs the tragedy of Count Stegrius. In the autumn of the year 1605, returning from England to Antwerp, I found several hundred people with dropsy following a malignant and popular fever: many I healed, and many meanwhile perished under the unlucky attempts of others. Moreover, those people have persuaded themselves that unless all the water is drained from the corpse, the dropsy will migrate into the next heir; and so they are very anxious about dissection. And I affirm for certain that I found no one's liver to be decayed. A certain citizen for a long time suffered pain among the false ribs, nor did he breathe without pain; having tried the conjectures of physicians, he finally died of dropsy: yet the liver appeared without harm. 

The Fiscal Officer of Brabant, from a sudden passing of blood in the urine <note>original: "mictu cruoris"</note>, was long agitated in vain by doctors, and therefore sent away by his family to the springs of Spa; returning, he began to show a hardness on the left side of the abdomen beneath the ribs, and then the leg of that side swelled. The Chief Physicians <note>original: "Archiatri"</note> and those of Louvain, although they saw his urine was very similar to that of a healthy person and indicated from that that his liver was innocent, nevertheless did not desist from the continuous use of laxatives <note>original: "solutivorum"</note>, deobstruents <note>original: "deoppilantium"</note>, and diuretics. Indeed, they even prescribed steel <note>original: "chalybem"; often used as a tonic for the blood or liver</note> against obstructions of the liver, masked in various ways, and finally, with an immense abdomen, he died of dropsy. Nor is there room for the excuse that they were called too late, they who were present from the hour of the bloody urination. But when his corpse was dissected, the liver was found innocent: but the left Kidney...

A chaplain of Brussels, 31 years of age, complained to me of shortness of breath: he showed swollen shins and a tumid belly. He said his scrotum was swollen to the size of a head. When the rupture of the vein, becoming more torn, poured out gore, it suffocated the man. One dropsical man, and the only one I have seen, showed a black and foul bubble in the cavity of the liver. <insert>Bartholomew Cabrol</insert><note>A famous 16th-century French anatomist</note>, an anatomist of Montpellier, says he has cured many dropsical patients by <term>paracentesis</term><note>the surgical piercing of a cavity to drain fluid</note> performed right in the protruding navel, and this in both sexes. # UNKNOWN DROPSY.

<margin>15.</margin> Having discussed the "lethal sin" <note>The author likely refers to a primary internal cause or a "sin" against the body's natural order</note>, I shall now add something regarding the occasional causes. I will resume the case of our fiscal officer <note>A public official or treasurer; here used as a specific medical case study</note>, who, upon dissection, showed nothing remarkable except for blood that had leaked out of the vessels and hardened within the kidney—the occasional cause of his dropsy and death. However, a stone <term>calculus: a kidney stone</term> filling the kidney does not produce dropsy, even if the entire kidney is hidden by stones and retains no functional tissue <term>parenchyma: the functional parts of an organ</term>. Therefore, the obstruction of the kidney as such is not the occasional cause of dropsy; rather, it is the extravasated blood <note>Blood that has escaped from its proper vessels into the surrounding tissue</note>. Thus, a sixty-year-old woman, having struck herself against the corner of a table, contracted dropsy. Thus, those wounded in the abdomen who are poorly healed become dropsical. Thus, extravasated blood resting upon the membranes of the brain <term>meninges</term> soon renders the face swollen with dropsy. Finally, great torments <note>Severe intestinal cramping or "tormina"</note> pour blood out of the veins into the space bordering the curve of the intestine. <margin>16.</margin> Thus those with dysentery, and thus heavy drinkers, take on dropsy insofar as some blood accumulates in the curve of the intestine. I learned this, moreover, in a fracture of the skull and in dropsy of the lung. In the former, the remaining blood inflates the whole head and face as if with dropsy. In the latter, I noticed that the blood settled around the duct of the arterial vein <note>The pulmonary artery</note>. For blood does not degenerate into the form of pus unless it is "cooked" within the cavity of the flesh; but outside the flesh in a free space, blood immediately clots, then soon becomes drier and hardens, and immediately conceives a virulent ferment, from which the *Archeus* <note>In Paracelsian medicine, the internal "vital chemist" or governing spirit of an organ</note> stirs up dropsy. Our fiscal officer certainly taught me that extravasated and clotted blood causes dropsy of the belly; and furthermore, that the kidney is the adequate craftsman, perpetrator, executor, and judge of true dropsy. It confirmed for me that under dropsy, the kidney hardly produces any urine <term>lotium: an archaic term for urine</term>; and conversely, when the kidney is stimulated to return the urine, it drains the entire dropsy from the belly. Therefore, the water reported in the abdomen is by the judgment of the kidney. <margin>17.</margin> Vain, therefore, is the fiction of Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, a famous 16th-century physician</note> that the star *Zedo* <note>A Paracelsian term for an imaginary astral influence</note> is the sole and singular architect of

<column-break/>

dropsy. For the cause is within our innermost parts and the very beginnings of life, and is not to be sought or healed from so far away. For dropsy is not the handiwork of the stars, nor is that the destiny of the stars. <margin>18.</margin> Nor does it matter if Mercury, separated "dead" from its vein <note>Likely referring to purified metallic mercury</note>, truly and perfectly cures the triple dropsy. For "Mercury" is an analogous and fabricated name; it does not designate a star, but a running metal. For what does a metaphorically fabricated name have to do with the fabricated star of *Zedo*? For metallic mercury is neither a star, nor does it kill a star, nor does it hinder its operation, nor does it loosen the conjunction of a star with us (if any existed). For stars are the occasions for meteors; but for diseases, they are only occasions by accident. For they are the primary causes of the seasons and of the *Blas* of the meteor <note>Helmontian term for the "impulse" or moving force of celestial and natural phenomena</note>; but secondarily and by accident, they agitate our bodies, stir up diseases, or ripen the occasional matter. However, accidental causes do not concern healings, but rather precautions, especially where the causes operate through themselves within us, by the proper motion and destination of their own "seeds." <margin>19.</margin> Indeed, the left kidney of the fiscal officer was choked with dry blood; the left part of the abdomen became stretched and hardened immediately, while the right remained healthy. Then the leg and thigh on the left side immediately swelled. Therefore, the tension of the belly is not due to the quantity of water alone; rather, the membranes are stretched by the disease itself, not unlike an artery under a hard pulse. The membranes are stretched and contracted even before there is copious water, by the same "craftsman" who generates the dropsy. It certainly contracts all the pores of the membrane so that they do not transmit wind or liquid. Whereas otherwise in the living (that is, the healthy), the whole body is "perspirable" and "conspirable" <note>Meaning the body's pores are open and the systems work in harmony</note>. The fiscal officer, therefore, first urinated very little, then gradually the dropsy rushed in, beginning on his left side. And so, right from the start, the left leg was besieged by edema, and then the whole swelled. But why does the right kidney not draw the urine?

Thus, the latex is of little value. Just as wind is in Tympania. Truly, dropsy is received as a guest in the inner household and is more intimate to us, attacking the vital principles and the faculties of life before the water is even born. The schools <note>referring to the traditional academic medical authorities of the time</note> are content with these explanations. Come now, examine this with me. But what are the channels by which the liver might deliver the matter or water of dropsy, as if by hand, to the space of the abdomen? If they are those sober veins by which that membrane of the abdomen, or the Peritoneum, is nourished, why at least did the liver choose these veins instead, and afflict these places, when it could far more conveniently drive away such superfluous water through the hemorrhoids <note>veins of the rectum</note> before the liver is burdened by its inconvenience and weight? Meanwhile, it is certain that the fluid, or the matter of dropsy, floats in the veins that are below the liver, since it is not properly secreted <margin>26.</margin> through the urine. At any rate, however it is taken, the liver—now stretched to an immense mass and hardness because of the accumulation of water—is not strong enough to add even a single little drop more to the abdomen without the mouths of those veins opening like a broken floodgate, and the dropsical water receding from the whole abdomen and regurgitating back into the liver. For in the first place, the mouths of the veins ending in the abdominal membrane do not each have valves attached, like suction cups, to keep the blown-in wind and fluid inside. Indeed, all dropsical blood would be nothing but mere water. Which is false. And for that reason, the Kidneys, as if returning to their senses after an absence, have not infrequently reclaimed the water deposited in the abdomen and spontaneously restored health from Dropsy. And she emerged healthy, and lives now as a seventy-year-old. Primarily, thirst—whether it is taken as a sensation of something lacking, or <margin>34.</margin> for the actual defect of moisture—at least in neither way does it dry up the dropsical water. For even if no drink is swallowed, at least the broths, which provide sufficient blood-substance, also give a little bit of urine and liquid, as much as is enough for the subsistence of the dropsy. Finally, neither thirst nor the lack of drinks themselves removes the occasional cause of dropsy (which is mostly extravasated blood); rather, they dry it out more and reserve it for themselves more stubbornly, so that it resists resolution through a feigned abstinence <margin>35.</margin>. But that continual thirst, combined with the hope and persuasion of health, pacified the error or indignation conceived in the *Archeus of the Kidneys*; from which I learned that thirst <margin>36.</margin> arises regularly from the Kidney, and not from the liver; and much less from the smaller branches of the veins sucking from the larger ones, until the defect of moisture is brought to the orifice of the stomach. But just as the defect of blood is restored by foods and purer drinks, so the defect of liquid is compensated by watery things; which experience teaches.

# THE UNKNOWN DROPSY.

Thirst, therefore, proceeds from the moderator of the *Latex* <note>original: "Laticis"; the clear, watery part of the blood or bodily fluids</note>, and not from the blood-making organ <note>the liver</note>. Indeed, the necessity of the *Latex* is as great as the dullness has been until now in overlooking it.
<margin>Note</margin>
Some authors recommend live toads, tied to the kidneys on both sides, to dissolve *Dropsy* <note>original: "Hydropem"; an old term for swelling or edema</note> through the urine. I have at least seen a dropsical peasant cured by tying the sloughed skin of snakes across the belly and kidneys. For an *Idea* <note>a formative, spiritual force in the body's governing spirit</note> of fear is induced in the kidneys, through which they lose their indignation. By the same token, *Thirst* excites an *Idea* of sadness, or of denied appetite; whereby the Kidney forgets its own
<margin>37.</margin>
indignation. From the aforementioned, therefore, the ignorance of the causes of *Dropsy* is sufficiently clear, and with what great obscurity people have sweated over the "imbalance" of the liver and the depletion of waters. How vainly they have thought of diuretics, blister-agents, and laxatives. And it must be noted in this place,
<margin>38.</margin>
that they impiously prescribe bile-purging cathartics <note>original: "Cholagoga"</note> to dropsical patients; inasmuch as these transform the flesh and blood into a foul and yellow dross, without helping the *Dropsy*, but rather destroying the patient. However, a water-purger <note>original: "Hydragogum"</note> differs from a bile-purger. For when the former is drunk, the belly's swelling subsides, and it does not excrete foul matter—unless the force of a bile-purger
<margin>39.</margin>
is added to the water-purger. Therefore, Mercury precipitated according to the prescription of Paracelsus <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> cures every *Dropsy*, not insofar as it purges, but insofar as it passes materially through the intestines and resolves the blood that has leaked out of the veins. But if it should simultaneously provoke vomiting or a bowel movement, that is merely accidental to the *Dropsy*.
<margin>40.</margin>
Note this, therefore: That white bryony <note>original: "brionia alba"</note>, shaved and placed over a bruise where the blood
<margin>Note</margin>
turns black under the skin, resolves that blood into water within a few hours, which it likewise drives out through the skin. Therefore, observe the beneficial power of the water-purger in Bryony, if you remove the laxative poison from it. I have observed, for instance, that if Antimony is turned into a liquid, and afterwards into a powder which purges only through sweat, a remedy is obtained which modestly removes every *Dropsy*, without fear of relapse. Since

<column-break/>

it removes both the occasional cause and the very lack of moderation of the raging *Archeus* <note>the internal "vital director" or spirit that governs the functions of an organ</note>. For remedies of this kind, which are carried through the intestines while their gift remains intact and safe, and which are fit to resolve the occasional cause, free nature from impediments. Whereupon the *Archeus of the Kidney*, noticing the madness of its own past fury, opens the veins, flees, and filters the water as is due and customary; and by an eccentric and opposite motion of the *Latex*, it atones for the stubbornness of its past fury with diligence, grieving that it intended its own destruction. From this it becomes conspicuous
<margin>41.</margin>
that the Kidney's governance over the abdomen and veins has been unknown until now. *Dropsy* is, therefore, a disease
<margin>42.</margin>
arising occasionally from depraved bloody matter, as if by a fermental beginning: at the incitement of which the *Archeus of the Kidneys* forms an *Idea* of indignation. By the power of this, it shuts the ureters and veins, corrupts and diverts the inflowing *Latex*, and transmits this into the space of the abdomen: meanwhile, it so constricts the membranes of the abdomen and their pores that they transmit nothing further, even unto death.
However, *Tympanites* <note>distension of the abdomen due to gas</note> differs greatly from *Dropsy*:
<margin>43.</margin>
for it has another occasional cause, another way of happening, and finally another matter and efficient cause: thus another disposition and another product. For it is not water that is generated, but wind <note>gas</note>. Furthermore, *Tympanites* does not happen by the judgment of the Kidney: but only under the presiding toxic ferment of the spermatic nourishment, sticking in the curve of the intestine and defiling it. Nor has Anatomy yet discovered veins swollen with wind. Nor, because of the griping pains of the intestine, ought the liver to be blamed, although griping pains follow both *Dropsy* and tympanites. If indeed the gases of the intestine were made by the liver, the remedy should be given to the Liver, and not a carminative <note>a herb or drug that relieves gas</note> to the intestine: otherwise the Schools <note>the traditional medical establishment</note> make themselves guilty by their way of healing. For if they were mindful of their own theorem: "That healthy action and weak action belong to the same faculty," they would have known that belches and gas come from the intestine and stomach...

# THE UNKNOWN DROPSY.

## 44.
The convex outer surface of the intestine is no less prone to generating gases than its concave interior. It is from these assimilated but corrupted fluids that **Tympanites** <note>A form of dropsy where the abdomen is stretched tight like a drum (tympanum) by gas rather than water.</note> infests the body. For windiness or gas is created in the intestine by a certain indisposition of the local **Archeus** <note>term: Archeus. In Helmontian medicine, this is the "internal chemist" or vital spirit that governs the functions of an organ.</note>, which then continually turns even non-flatulent foods into gas. Therefore, when in Tympanites the gas is outside, or on the convex side of the intestine, one must consider that the same flatulent indisposition exists outside as exists inside the intestine. 

Indeed, it arises from a similar degenerating nourishment, which the incoming fecal ferment—the Archeus of the place being indignant and poorly affected—converts into gas; not the aforementioned occasional cause itself, but the proper nourishment of the membranes. To this end, a portion of the fecal ferment migrates from the hollow (interior) to the convex (exterior) of the intestine. Therefore, that gas is not tasteless or acidic like a burp, nor does it smell of dung (since it is not made from fecal matter), but from degenerated and cadaverous nourishment.

<margin>folio 44.</margin>
A certain man, on the advice of physicians, underwent a **paracentesis** <note>term: paracentesis. A surgical puncture of the abdominal cavity to drain fluid.</note> at the side of the navel. He was judged to be dropsical, and they sought to draw out water. While I was watching as a young man, the surgeon drew his lancet and suddenly slit the abdomen; the man died instantly. An immensely foul gas was emitted, smelling of a corpse. It is clear, therefore, that the occasional matter—and finally the true matter and internal cause—remained unknown to the physician, despite all the knowledge that honors the profession.

<margin>45.</margin>
The vanity of remedies is also clear, especially those "carminatives" <note>Herbs or medicines intended to expel gas.</note> which do not address the convex side of the intestine. In vain do they imagine that winds are dispersed by "extenuation" <note>Thinning or weakening the substance.</note>. For into what matter thinner than subtle wind do they hope the winds can be thinned? Or what would it profit to grant the wind a subtler state, if it then requires a larger space and increases the pains of tension? For it is a foolish local remedy, drawn from fables.

<margin>46.</margin>
**Cabrollius** <note>Barthélemy Cabrol, a 16th-century French anatomist.</note>, an anatomist of Montpellier, relates that he cured an eighty-year-old man who, on the advice of **Rondelet** <note>Guillaume Rondelet, a famous Renaissance physician.</note>, ate nothing but

<column-break/>

salted foods; and lest he be overwhelmed by thirst, he mixed seasonings or condiments made of vinegar and sugar into his food. He also fomented him twice daily with a lye in which salt, alum, and sulfur had been boiled. Following this, he used cow dung as a poultice. And finally, the man escaped the disease and survived to be a centenarian. For things that consume the "occasional cause" are not given in vain, nor does **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and occultist (1493–1541).</note> commend dungs without reason: since they contain the salts of putrid foods, which are granted the power to resolve the occasional matter of dropsy. Truly, the action of the Archeus is wonderful in both cases—both where he holds the keys shut and where he unbars the enclosures and expels his enemy.

<margin>47.</margin>
Paracelsus, however, approves of his "chief prize" or **mercury** <note>note: original "mercurium". Here referring to a chemical/alchemical preparation of mercury, not just the raw metal.</note>, drawn dead from its own ore, above all other remedies. As for other simples <note>Medicinal herbs or single-ingredient drugs.</note>, he judges them by the degree of affinity by which they touch this metallic mercury. This is a phrase of his own liberty. I myself venerate and look up to the gifts of simples as originating from God, but not insofar as they are "blood relatives" to mineral mercury. I confess, meanwhile, that this mercury has always complied with my wishes. Its acquisition is indeed difficult, but a dose of two grains, administered three or four times, suffices. But once one has obtained **diaphoretic mercury** <note>A preparation of mercury intended to induce sweating.</note>, it suffices for many thousands of sick people, both for the physician himself and for his successors.

<margin>48.</margin>
Finally, I have seen a "false dropsy," which no one before me has mentioned, as far as I know. For I have frequently seen a tension of the belly mimic dropsy due to an inordinate growth of the **liver**. Indeed, even in those dead of consumption and the extremely emaciated, I have seen the liver grown beyond measure, though it was entirely bloodless. Therefore, that mercury kills the "growing power," just as **quicksilver** <note>note: original "argentum tremulum".</note> kills a tree if it is injected into a hole bored all the way to the marrow (the heartwood).

<margin>49.</margin>
It is therefore a property of mercury to extinguish the "accretive" (growth) power of the liver. However, for this to succeed as desired, the mercury must "die" without any companionship of external salts or the association of foreign spirits.

I congratulate him whom fire has taught to understand me. To this I refer the remedy of "dissolving antimony" <term>stibii solutivi: a chemical preparation of antimony used in Paracelsian medicine</term>. For remedies of this kind resolve, consume, and sweep away every "occasional cause" <note>the external or immediate trigger of a disease</note> lurking or detained elsewhere. This is truly the healing of the *Arcana* <term>Arcana: "Secret" or higher-order chemical medicines</term>, which is acquired through the removal of the occasional cause: and any one of these *Arcana* is sufficient, for it indifferently resolves, wipes away, and disperses whatever is enclosed in the body contrary to nature (I except *duelech* <term>duelech: a Paracelsian term for a stony transformation or calculus in the body</term>). For of any diseases whatsoever, even if there are two columns upon which the diseased edifice rests (namely the "occasional matter" and the "matter with the efficient *Archeus*" <term>Archeus: the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</term>), if either one of the columns is removed, the whole structure built upon them collapses. Thus, the Paracelsian *Arcana* remove every disease as a consequence, insofar as they reap the occasional cause. <margin>50.</margin> And then there is another, more hidden path of another *arcanum*: namely, that through which peace, rest, and solace are brought to the *Archeus*, so that he does not produce disease out of indignation, but rather destroys what has been produced; indeed, he even meditates on the 

<column-break/>

<margin>Note</margin> driving out of the occasional cause itself. For just as an embedded thorn is drawn out by the fat of a hare—a common and gentle remedy—otherwise the *Archeus* is immediately angered by the entering thorn, a tumult arises, the place swells, and various wandering symptoms are stirred up, so that finally, by creating pus and putrefying the area, he may exclude the thorn. Yet if he had approached it more mildly, he would have plucked it out, as he does under the influence of the hare's fat. In the same way, I say, there is an *Arcanum* in nature that heals almost every disease, insofar as it removes the indignation and confusion of the *Archeus* and commands peace upon him. Concerning this *Arcanum*, I shall be the first to attempt to open the way. Let the *Archeus* of the Kidneys therefore relax the passages, and let him rise up to drive out the occasional cause, just as he seeks his own end with persistent fury in Dropsy <term>Hydrope: edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term>. And the axiom of Hippocrates will be verified: *That natures themselves are the healers of diseases; the Physician is truly only their minister.* Therefore, from the aforementioned, I conclude that the healing of the "sedative Arcanum" will be far more peaceful and desirable than that of the Paracelsian *Arcana*. For they do more for the preservation of a long life. Concerning which, I shall write in a specific book.

<header>VINDICATION</header>

# VINDICATION

<note>original: "VINDICYA"</note>

even those in the Chairs of authority <note>referring to university professors</note> must eventually be punished with the threat of infernal pain, and shall be judged as guilty of a crime before wise Princes. This is especially true where warnings have proven fruitless and efforts of charity have been made in vain. The more fastidious critics have therefore passed judgment according to their own standards. And most of them were offended, not only because I brought forth and demonstrated things that were new, unheard of, and beyond the grasp of many; but because I was destroying the ancient foundations of healing without teaching other, better ones—as if such a great burden of labor could be measured by a single day. Many, however, wished that I would once and for all "pre-chew" my secrets in private and thrust them into their mouths, morsel by morsel <note>original: "buccellatim"</note>, so that they might learn better doctrines and remedies without any effort. For this reason, several of the more curious wrote to me, praising my work, the labors I had undertaken, and the expenses incurred; yet they could not tolerate that I had left the secret remedies <term>Arcana: powerful, hidden "secrets of nature" in Paracelsian medicine</term> shrouded in thick darkness, nor that I had not revealed the whole of Chemistry and hidden Philosophy, claiming this was against the precept of the Gospel—that I had not "thrown pearls before swine," that is, the undeserving. But truly, on both counts, I have provided as much as I could and as much as was permitted. For I had learned securely through experience that when I returned to my homeland in 1602, I cured several hopeless cases using spirits of salt, sulfur, and vitriol, and through vitriolated emetics, etc., of which there was no trace of memory among the Belgians. Therefore, the Chief Physicians <note>original: "Archiatri"</note> and other more famous men laid a snare for my remedies. For if I had given any of the aforementioned to anyone, they immediately arranged for it to be brought to them, so that they might imitate and surpass me. I myself, therefore, offered chemical medicines for sale publicly through my servants and attendants—those who had already left my service. These men thus earned their bread. But as all things are soon liable to ruin, other fugitives from abroad interfered, thrusting similar goods for sale at a cheaper price. And so they substituted items adulterated with a thousand deceits; whatever was sold at a lower price was considered the best. Hence, today nothing is found among manufactured drugs that is not thus adulterated, and the hope of greater profit daily undermines them even more. Therefore, having been taught by this, I learned that I should no longer travel this path; rather, whatever of the rarer Philosophy is to be published must be presented entirely under the hieroglyphics <note>symbolic or coded language</note> of the more skilled. Let them forgive me, therefore, all who write these words to me: "Please, explain yourself; speak more plainly concerning the preparation of the Secrets." For that is a new method of learning Philosophy, which must be learned in the same way I learned it. For God sells the arts for the price of sweat. Indeed, nothing in the Spagyric <term>Spagyric: the alchemical art of separating and recombining natural substances to create medicine</term> writings was written with the intention that they should be understood indiscriminately by everyone, but rather specifically so that they might *not* be understood. And Chemistry, above all other disciplines, has always observed this unique rule by the command of the Lord: lest roses be scattered before men and swine. For our writings are in the place of exhortations, so that each may profit by his own labors, as much as has been granted to him from above. Finally, the stubborn and the unlearned act with insults and mock me, saying:

1. With what face does this rash, morose old man, this trifler and unlearned person, dare to assert that one and the same "hot" remedy is effective against "cold" diseases? And even to break the axiom of the ancients that is true in the first degree: *That remedies are only the contraries of the opposites?* <note>The traditional Galenic theory that "hot" illnesses must be treated with "cold" herbs, which the author rejects.</note>

2. By what audacity does he say that the abundance of harmful humors can be removed without purging and bloodletting? <note>original: "venæ fectionem"</note>

3. If he thinks the Secrets of Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541)</note> bring a just temperament of the elements to their proper weight, will they therefore reset a broken or dislocated bone? Or have they cured a hernia?

4. What if the Secrets wipe away the "sinning matter" <note>the cause of the disease</note>? How would this help if it is not simultaneously carried out of the body by a dissolving drug?

5. Or what does this have in common with the diseases of the Insane <note>original: "Amentium"</note>, that we should believe every disease can be cut away by one "knife" of a Secret remedy?

<margin>1.</margin>
Health itself does not consist in a just balance <note>original: *temperie*</note> of the body, but in an unimpaired life. For otherwise, the balance of the body is still present in a freshly slaughtered carcass, where death already resides; but there is no life, no health. Health is a single, homogenous integrity of life and an unblemished disposition. It requires the conservation of that integrity in the healthy and its restoration in the sick. And Hippocrates <note>the "Father of Medicine"</note> proved this even then, asserting that nature alone (which is one) is the healer of diseases; the Physician is the servant, and the medicine is the means of leading back a nature that has wandered off course. Therefore, the integrity of health is in a "unison," and there is only one governor of life, not many. It is this governor alone that fares badly in sickness. For it alone is the "impelling force" <note>original: *impetum faciens*, a translation of the Greek *enormon*</note> in both the healthy and the sick, and its rupture alone tears the vital economy. For even if nothing attacks from without, and nothing from the seed of our parents disturbs us, yet of its own accord, that *Archeus* <note>the internal "vital spirit" or "master workman" that Helmont believed governed the body's functions</note> sometimes faints, and thus our integrity is dissolved; and with many...

<margin>3.</margin> Similarly regarding fevers, I have so withdrawn my faith from **solutives** <note>Medicines used to "loosen" the bowels; laxatives.</note> that I only mention them again with a weariness of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established medical universities of the time, which followed Galen.</note>. # TREATISE
# ON DISEASES.

## DIAGNOSTIC INTRODUCTION.

*1. Summary of the entire work. 2. Why such severity was used in restraining the Author. 3. He calls upon God, while feeling deprived of human aid. 4. The poverty and false coloring of Logic were to be uncovered. 5. The nakedness of the study of Aristotle’s Physics. 6. An unheard-of method of investigation. 7. Why the schools have lacked knowledge of diseases. 8. Disease flowed from transgression <note>A reference to the Fall of Man as the origin of illness</note>. 9. Introduction to the knowledge of Disease. 10. A scheme of diseases according to Hippocrates. 11. The Schools, fed on Lotus-flowers <note>A metaphor for being drugged into forgetfulness or apathy</note>, have abandoned their Hippocrates. 12. A core contemplation of diseases.*

---

<margin>1.</margin>
It seemed necessary to have begun with the Elements, qualities, mixtures, complexions, oppositions, humors, and Catarrhs <note>term: Catarrh; here referring to the old medical theory of fluids "flowing down" from the brain to cause illness</note>, in order to demonstrate that the schools have never truly considered the nature of diseases. Therefore, they have been ignorant of the true goals of medicine—namely, the principles of diseases, their theorems, their ways of coming into being, the causes of their adaptation, their relationships, their agreements, their differences, and their specific properties. Likewise, they have been ignorant of the discovery of remedies, their selection, preparation, enhancement, and specific application: that is, they have not known the scientific healing of the sick. For I believed I had to proceed through such beginnings because they have attributed all ailments (with perhaps a few exceptions) to elemental qualities and the innate discords of nature. They blame humors, catarrhs, winds, and vapors—so much so that the knowledge of the schools, having been carried off into smoke and vapors, vanishes into smoke. Finally, through the errors of Tartar <note>term: Tartar; in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony precipitates in the body, but here the author puns on "Tartarus" or hell</note>, it arrived at the underworld, showing that they, enveloped in darkness, have continually faltered in their paths.

<margin>2.</margin>
For I had to uncover those things diligently if young students are to recover their senses hereafter. But it was not enough to have shown errors, lack of skill, laziness, and persistent, constant ignorance, unless I should weigh out true doctrine in place of

<column-break/>

trifles. Indeed, for many years the abuse of axioms remained suspect to me (which I depicted to the life in my book on fevers) before I arrived at a solid knowledge of the truth; and I had long surveyed the truth of Theory before I had found, by searching, some proper medicines which would be sufficient for the initiated.

<margin>3.</margin>
Wherefore, when I was about to speak concerning diseases under such a paradox and weight of matters, and yet found no helper among the ancients or the more recent moderns, I earnestly called upon God, and I even found Him favorable.

<margin>4.</margin>
I determined, therefore, before I wrote, to call upon Logic, so that through its definitions it might demonstrate to me the essences of diseases; through its divisions, their species and differences; and finally, through Argumentation, it might suggest the causes, properties, means, and remedies for knowing and healing. But to my outcries, even made to its face, it was deaf; it was stunned, it heard nothing, it remained mute, and did not help wretched me in the least. Because it is entirely powerless, without sense.

<margin>5.</margin>
Then, therefore, I called to my aid the "Physical Lectures" <note>original: "auscultationes Physicas"; a reference to Aristotle's *Physics*</note> of the schools. Namely, their three boasted principles, the four causes, fortune, Chance, Time, the infinite vacuum, motion, and even the "monster." From this I finally uncovered that their entire Physics is truly monstrous: having beginnings that are fictional, false, and playful—not true principles, much less vital ones, in the sight of the King <note>God</note> to whom all things live. Likewise, it has causes that do not cause. It thrusts forward "beings of reason" <note>abstract concepts with no physical reality</note> that are fantastical and dogmas hedged in by a thousand absurdities. In which I have not yet found a single trace of nature in its integrity: much less its defects, or the alterations of the vital faculties or functions.
