# INTRODUCTION

of such things. Least of all should the knowledge of natural and vital causes, of diseases, remedies, and healings, have been sought from such a structure of principles. Yet I had thought that the science of nature should be looked upon as the target and goal. For whatever I sought from the schools and attempted to handle through Theory; all of it nature immediately laughed at in Practice, and it was regarded as mere pedantry. Nature, I say, laughed at me (to speak more clearly) as a ridiculous figure along with the schools. And at last, she complained to me of such invincible stupidity. Then Logic deplored to me its own powerless nakedness and the vain boasting of the schools. Indeed, Logic—which until now was hailed as the discoverer and investigator of means, causes, terms, and sciences—grieved to have to confess that it was mute in the face of diseases, no less than in the whole fabric of nature, and that it must desert its own professors in such great necessity of hardships. Indeed, the *Physics* of Aristotle <note>The standard natural philosophy textbook of the era, which the author rejects as abstract and impractical.</note> would have laughed at the same time with a single loud cackle at the foolish credulities of the world and of so many centuries, if it were not itself a non-existent fiction, swollen only by the breath of pride.

<margin>6.</margin>
Therefore, since nature exists and is perceived nowhere except in Individuals: it is necessary for me, as I am about to write concerning diseases, to have known the causes of particulars especially well, just as it is necessary for the Physician <note>original: *Medenti*</note>, under the guilt of infernal punishment, to have perceived those causes individually. It seemed to me, therefore, that the "what-ness" <note>original: *quidditates*, the essential nature of a thing</note> of things, both healthy and damaged, had to be investigated by the method handed down concerning the "hunting of the sciences." And yet, since knowledge drawn in this way can be explained, I decided for the Beginner <note>original: *Tyroni*, a novice student</note> that the essential definition must be set forth through causes and their properties. This is nothing other than the connection of causes. It is not, however, the "genus" and "difference" of the thing defined <note>The author rejects the Aristotelian method of defining things by category (genus) and specific difference, preferring to look at actual physical causes.</note>. But this Method of explaining is unheard of, just as Logic has lied about being the discoverer of sciences. Along with it, every faculty serving the philosophy of speech <note>The "trivium" of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note> has lied. For in vain does one recur to the genus of the defined and the differences that constitute a species when dealing with diseases, which were never and nowhere known in that way.

<margin>7.</margin>
Therefore, since it has been ignored until now that things themselves are nothing outside or beyond the connection of matter and the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the active agent that brings something into being.</note>, the schools have consequently lacked a true definition: that is, a proper knowledge of diseases. If, therefore, the essential nature of diseases and the condition of morbid properties flow from their immediate essential causes: necessarily, the knowledge of the aforementioned must also be taken from those same causes. This is because the consideration of causes comes before the consideration of diseases. Thus, I have shown—even to the point of boredom—that the essences of natural things are matter and the efficient cause, connected in action: therefore, the essence of any disease also consists of these two causes, and knowledge must be sought from them through a proper definition.

<margin>8.</margin>
In the first place, a disease is a certain evil in respect to life. And although it arises from sin, it is not, however, an evil in the same way as sin—from a cause of deficiency which lacks form, measure, and order. Instead, disease is from a seminal <note>original: *seminali*, relating to the "seeds" or formative principles of things</note>, positive, actual, and real efficient cause, with its own seed, measure, form, and order. And although from the perspective of life it is an evil, it nevertheless has the nature of a good from its own simple being. For that which is good in itself produces something by accident, by the positioning of which the faculties innate to the parts are occasionally harmed and perish through the *Adastria* <note>A term used by the author to refer to a punishing or reactive power in nature, similar to fate or nemesis.</note>.

<margin>9.</margin>
They are, therefore, defects from an external cause, making an attack upon or beyond the vital forces hidden in the parts; and they are from foreign guests, received within, and endowed with a stronger *Archeus* <note>The internal "governor" or vital spirit that directs the functions of a living organ or organism.</note>. And hence, by the importunity of times, quantities, and strength, they are superior. Finally, they are occasional defects which (since good gives birth to evil by accident, and it flows more often from our own vital powers) are endowed with their own properties, as if with their own seminal beginnings; therefore, they tend immediately toward the conquest of our powers as their end. These I therefore call "powerful diseases" <note>original: *morbos potestativos*</note>.

<summary>The author rejects traditional Aristotelian logic and scholastic definitions of disease, arguing instead that medicine must be based on the specific "seminal" and "efficient" causes of individual cases. He introduces the concept of the Archeus and the idea that disease, while harmful to life, possesses its own organized natural structure.</summary>

# DIAGNOSTICS

->**539**<-

The "potential being" <note>original: *ens potestativum*; a term referring to a disease's power to command or influence the body's functions</note> is not that which the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university medical authorities of the time.</note> call a "disease by consent," which they believe happens through the gathering of vapors. Rather, the potential being contains the governance of a forced faculty, both in respect to the vital authority and the disease-causing being itself. This is because it is born of its own motion and is able to stir up a potential disease of its own class. Just as the Spanish Fly <note>original: *Cantaris*; used historically as a diuretic or irritant</note> stirs up a difficulty in passing urine <note>original: *stranguriam*</note>. This also occurs by the power of internal authority and by the force of parts acting upon other parts. Thus, an apoplectic or epileptic being, while still present in the stomach or womb, shakes the soul; indeed, from there it leads the brain, along with its attendant powers, into its own service, whether it wishes to or not. Therefore, the potential being designates not only the injury of functions, but also the governance of the part and the occasional force of the disease-bearing being, extended into subordinate faculties like a command over vassals. This is true whether the parts are far apart or near to one another. For these are the due tributes of their properties.

<margin>10.</margin> Truly, Hippocrates was the first to suggest that diseases are distinguished by their "inns" <note>locations in the body</note> and their flavors. And would that posterity had maintained this course! But as if inspired by a divine frenzy, that Old Man <note>Hippocrates</note> foresaw the future daring of the following school, and he warned precisely that they should not believe heats, colds, humidities, bitterness, or sharpness to be the diseases themselves; rather, it is the bitter, the sharp, the salty, or the harsh substance itself.

<margin>11.</margin> But he sang these things to the deaf, or to ears remarkably blocked. Indeed, for ages past, prone to the laziness of inquiry and easy belief, they seized upon the itchy theorems of "heat" and "cold" and subscribed to them because of their plausible ease. Thus they said farewell to their Master, who thought diseases should be divided according to their lodgings, and divided our body into three classes: namely, the containing solid (the vessel itself); the contained (the liquid); and the Spirit, which he called the "impelling force" <note>original: *impetum facientem*</note>. This is surely the ethereal and vital Gas <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a spiritualized substance or vital air.</note> which, within us,

<column-break/>

stirs up every *Blas* <note>A term for the "motive power" or "pulsing force" of the stars or the human body.</note> toward either end. Although he did not expressly dictate this division of diseases, he suggested it sufficiently. For he wrote only a few things, and almost everything circulated under his name is attributed to him falsely.

<margin>12.</margin> And therefore, would that posterity had directed the sharpness of their wits according to the mind of that Old Man! Perhaps, by God's permission, they would have grasped the understanding of morbid causes. But afterward, they so subscribed to the authority of Galen alone that they fell into a deep sleep, and they are astonished while being awakened by me.

By the name of "causes," within the very marrow-like integrity of diseases, I understand the matter itself, equipped with its own efficient power—namely, the internal, proximate cause arising from a vital beginning. For this reason, I also name as "external" and "occasional" all those which do not flow from the very root of life. Therefore, I deal with the causes which *are* the disease itself. For bread, once chewed and swallowed, is still external because it can be rejected. So too the chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> cooked in the stomach is still external. Indeed, even after it has become "domesticated" and made an internal citizen of our economy <note>The "economy" refers to the internal management and regulation of the living body.</note>, as soon as it is separated from the living and rushes into the "kitchen of diseases," it must be considered an external thing in respect to life, having become a hostile act.

So too, pestilential air drawn inside, although it has scattered poison within and is internal in respect to the body, is not yet internal in respect to life. Thus, it is not yet the disease itself; it merely contains the "occasion" of the disease within itself, and it will never lay aside that occasionality. But it becomes the Plague <note>original: *Pestis*</note> when the *Archeus* <note>The internal "master-mechanic" or vital principle that governs the body's functions.</note>, having the contagion applied to itself, separates the infected part of itself from the whole. To the banishment of this infection, the rest of the *Archeus* works together and is seriously distressed, lest it be penetrated by the likeness and perish. Something similar occurs in almost all other diseases. For life is not directly harmed except by some poison of its own, proper to itself, which it has permitted to be applied to itself.

<summary>The author argues that disease is not merely a symptom like "heat" or "cold," but a "potential being" that seizes control of the body's vital functions. He critiques the shift from Hippocratic observation to Galenic theory, emphasizing that true disease arises when the body's internal vital principle (the Archeus) reacts to a stimulus.</summary>

# THE SUBJECT OF DISEASE WITHIN THE POINT OF LIFE
## ON THE INHERENCE OF DISEASES.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring floral or vine motifs.</image-desc>

A perfectly healthy life possesses no disease: because health presupposes an integrity <note>wholeness or completeness</note> which disease tears apart. Thus, health and disease are contradictions to one another. Likewise, an extinguished life is not a disease, nor does it admit disease into itself. This is because, properly speaking, that life is a mere nothing, no longer existing; whereas a disease is "this something" <note>original: "hoc aliquid," a philosophical term for a distinct, existing entity</note>. Thirdly and finally, a corpse, however poisonous or infected by rot it may be, is nevertheless in no way capable of diseases. Therefore, although the body while it lives becomes the dwelling-place of diseases, it is not the true internal efficient cause <note>the active force that produces an effect</note> of those diseases. Much less, certainly, do filth or excrement (which are thought to be our constitutive humors <note>the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—traditionally thought to govern health</note>) have any right or property over diseases. Rather, if any part of a disease is to be ascribed to disordered dregs, that part tends entirely toward being an occasional cause <note>an external trigger rather than the internal source</note>. For disease is a being truly subsisting in the body, constructed from matter and an internal seminal efficient power; thus, it separates itself far from mere occasional causes. This is especially true because the internal beginnings of things constitute the being itself, and are inseparably part of its essential "whatness" <note>original: "quidditate," the essence of a thing</note>. Just as if we speak of the human body or soul: each is rightly called "man," though not the whole man.

In this way, the matter of a disease is truly the disease, just as its seminal efficient power is truly the disease, even if it is not properly the whole disease. Therefore, since disease exists only in the living and not in the dead, it is necessary that life be the immediate dwelling-place of disease, its internal subject, and indeed its very maker. But since life does not belong to the body, nor is it essentially proper to the body—for the body without life is a corpse, and disease exists in life—it 

<column-break/>

necessarily follows that all matter, dwelling-place, and efficient cause of disease does not exceed the limits of life. That is, every disease necessarily lives inside the "box" of the Archeus <note>term: Archeus; in Paracelsian medicine, this is the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note>, who alone is the immediate witness, executor, organ, and host of life. Moreover, abscesses, ulcers, filth, excrement, and so on, are only either the occasions of death and diseases, or the later products of the same, raised up for a new scene of tragedy. Nor is it truly a wonder that, together with life, all diseases vanish into nothingness, if life is the immediate subject and dwelling-place of diseases. But I have long wondered why, until now, no healer has known in what the essence of diseases thrives. Instead, they have wandered around elemental qualities, humors, complexions, contrarieties, and dispositions <note>original: "diatheses"</note>. Not once have they noticed that just as filth is not disease, so diseases are not in the filth; rather, they live only in life itself, and being thus enclosed within it, they arise, grow, and perish. Because they are nowhere outside of life, they must be the intimate and domestic thieves of life. So much for the proper receptacle of diseases. Furthermore, since disease is admitted without controversy to be a being existing in us as if in a guest-house, and it possesses its own singular properties and diverse symptoms: disease is necessarily not among the number of accidents <note>term: accident; in logic, a quality that can change without changing the essence of the thing (like hair color)</note>. This is because an accident does not belong to another accident combined with it and distinct from it in its entire species. For acidity or bitterness is not a property of whiteness, blackness, lightness, or heat. Therefore, if disease is a being and not an accident—if, finally, it brings forth from itself not only alterations, various dispositions, and weaknesses, but moreover generates substances that degenerate from the ordinary law of their nature—it must necessarily consist of ma-

He asserts that disease cannot exist in a corpse because it is an internal "thief" that requires the presence of life to function as a subsisting being.</summary>

matter, and by its own internal or seminal efficient cause. Finally, since disease is internal to life itself, it follows by necessity that the matter of disease is Archeal <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the vital internal principle or "master workman" that governs the body's functions.</note>, and its efficient cause is vital. To speak more clearly: every disease is necessarily an Ideal efficient act of vital power, clothing itself in a garment of Archeal matter; and acquiring a vital and substantial form according to the difference of the slowness or speed of the seminal ideals.

These things have hitherto been unknown by mortals, and those things which follow lean even further upon this thesis: **God did not make death.** <note>original: "DEUS non fecit mortem." A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 1:13.</note> And He is always so far removed from death that He refuses to be called the God of the dead. First of all, although death sometimes invades without disease, death usually follows disease; no one should doubt that such death is the daughter of diseases, or the secondary cause from which, and because of which, life is extinguished. That is, death is present. But since God is in no way the author of death—through whom, namely, death entered into man, who was otherwise immortal—and this is no more true at the beginning of the world than it is today: the diligent healer must inquire from whence death rushed in causally from the beginning, and even today, so that it may be established from whence disease drew its integrity.

For although it is obvious enough that death contains, as it were, a privation or extinction of life, it does not in itself, or for its own existence, require any substantial form, much less a vital one. And certainly, disease does not signify, as such, a privation; rather, it is a truly subsisting entity, acting with an act harmful to life and lying in wait for life. Thus, it is also necessary that disease consist of the form of its own "whatness" <note>term: quiddity (the essence or defining nature of a thing)</note>, which life is able to take into itself and be informed by. But since disease arose from the same beginning as death, and God is never the author of death, it follows absolutely that **God is not the author or creator of diseases.**

Therefore, although a disease may have some substantial form, it does not have life, nor a vital light, except what it has borrowed from life itself: namely, insofar as it thrives in the light of our life, or that of cattle. It is not, however, that the disease, for the sake of its seminal being, requires or has obtained from the Father of Lights <note>A biblical title for God (James 1:17).</note> a vital light; rather, in itself, it must be called lethal, and is utterly foreign to the goodness of God the Creator. Therefore, even though God alone creates all forms of all things, and the Father of Lights gives every essential form—namely the vital, the substantial, and even the formal substance—without any competitor alongside Him: yet this has no place in diseases, over whose formation man alone presides. Because the life of man alone contains the secondary causes of diseases and of death.

For this reason, because God the Creator denies that He made death, He also denies making disease. For disease stands in the life of man, and thus its entire essence depends on the life of man; and this not only seminally (as is otherwise proper to the seeds of all things whatsoever), but furthermore and formally, so that the Archeal life—or flesh and blood—are and remain the total formal cause of diseases, or the effective cause of the forms of disease. For He who from the beginning refused to have made death or diseases, will thereafter never wish to have made death or diseases. For the Father of Lights will grant His honor of creating formal lights to no creature—excepting the lethal forms of diseases, of which (as of the dead) God did not wish to be called the God.

Thus man remains the craftsman of his own death (who the day before was immortal), as well as the creator of his own diseases; and in this way, the creator of death. So it is that where God had made vital lights, man creates diseased, dark, and lethal Ideas; and such an Idea is as far removed from vital light as heat is from light. The formal act of death and diseases, therefore, flowed from the action of original sin, and will flow even unto the consummation of the age.

# ON THE POINT OF LIFE AS THE SUBJECT OF INHERENCE.

The very same cause that brought about death at the beginning of the world—that is, the same secondary natural cause that gave death its natural entrance into human nature—is exactly what causes death and disease today. For it would conflict with the Creator's glory to suggest He did not make death at the beginning, and that after it was made by man, He then took upon Himself the glory of knowing how to manufacture it; as if He had to learn that craft from man. Furthermore, what has been said regarding death must be understood with equal justice regarding diseases: for death and disease flow from the same point of origin. Therefore, if it is said that God gives diseases or death, it is not because He now wishes to be the Creator of those things whose manufacture He previously utterly refused. Rather, He is called the author "permissively" <note>original: "permissivè" - meaning God allows these things to happen through natural laws rather than actively creating each instance of sickness.</note>, as the prince of life and death. Just as He is the true and only Author of life, and therefore governs it and takes it away at His pleasure, so He permits one person to yield and another to fall, and allows secondary causes to fall out both directly and irregularly, whereby a man may perish or a disease may flourish. 

But the creation of disease as a "subsisting entity" <note>An entity that exists in its own right with its own form and matter.</note>—composed of matter and an efficient, seminal, and ideal cause that is evil and lethal—does not proceed from God at all. For when He placed it in man's free will to be able to remain without death, or to die the death on that very day, He likewise placed in man's hand the power to manufacture death and disease itself, as the precursor and preparer for death. The entrance of death into human nature, considered as I have explained elsewhere through a notable paradox, proves most exquisitely that disease does not only consist in the vital part of man, but that disease itself is born as a "seminal Idea" from the *Archeus* <note>term: Archeus - In Paracelsian medicine, the internal "chemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions.</note> itself. I will prove this briefly. From the lust of the flesh, the "flesh of sin" was born; and therefore a mortal *Archeus* was born within it. Consequently, the *Archeus*, insofar as it is vital within the flesh of sin, performs every action and produces every formal act that is harmful and lethal—acts which God refused to make,

<column-break/>

but permitted man to forge for himself as the causes of death and diseases. Man is not, however, a "creator" because of this, even though he makes for himself these formal acts (or substantial forms of diseases) which are harmful to life. This was granted to him by the power of the Word: that on whatever day he ate of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, he would die the death and would make for himself the attendants destined for death. This arises from the very nature of death, necessarily acquired in the flesh of sin. Therefore the "act"—which pertains to the essence, existence, and subsistence, as well as the propagation or fertile contagion of diseases—depends entirely on life, comes from life, and exists through life, within which it is also enclosed. 

Wretched indeed are mortals, and by far the most wretched are the sick, who until now have paid physicians a great and dear price, while those doctors remain ignorant of what disease is, where it originates, and in what it consists and subsists. I marvel that those before me did not "scent" these things, nor even the moderns; for their "sacred anchor" <note>A metaphor for a last resort or primary hope.</note> is usually in the hope of a *Crisis* <note>term: Crisis - The turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or dies.</note>, and they have invented many commentaries about Crises to excuse their own ignorance. Indeed, a Crisis in disease proves nothing except the *Archeus*—if they would only believe their own Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>, who said that the "Natures" themselves are the healers of diseases and the only helpers. For the Moon does not cause Crises as a primary cause; rather, the *Archeus* alone does, following the rhythm of the moon. The moon measures the days, and this pertains more to the testing of the *Archeus*'s actions than to causality. For the Moon on the 14th day is always in the opposite position to where it was on the 1st day; therefore the *Archeus*, which emulates the rhythms of the moon, also possesses opposite strengths. The same applies to the 7th day, etc.

I conclude, therefore, regarding the knowledge of disease, that a disease either has its nourishment or at least its provocation from an occasional cause; or it rises up by its own accord and motion, and persists through the contagion of its own "seed." For example, once epilepsy has been concentrated, or gout has taken root, it wakes up of its own accord as often as it pleases. Likewise, after two or three days, or...

## HE PROCEEDS TO THE KNOWLEDGE OF DISEASES.

1. **1.** *Medicine is the most hidden of the sciences.*
2. **2.** *The ignorance of past centuries is therefore excusable.*
3. **3.** *In what place diseases dwell.*
4. **4.** *The origin of diseases.*
5. **5.** *From whence a disease begins.*
6. **6.** *Why a disease is immediately in the being of the first motions.*

8. **8.** *Disease is wedded to the vital being.*
9. **9.** *How all seeds flow forth from the invisible world.*
10. **10.** *The origin of efficient causes, and the properties of seminal Ideas.*
11. **11.** *The true seminal beginnings of all things come from the invisible Idea.*
12. **12.** *How the seminal being receives its fulfillment.*
13. **13.** *The ideal power of seeds is explained by classes.*
14. **14.** *Death and disease, though they arise from the same beginning, differ in that disease has "Ideas," but death does not.*
15. **15.** *The Schools <note>Refers to the traditional academic medical authorities, such as those following Galen or Aristotle.</note> will laugh at these "Ideas": but the Author rebukes the ignorance of the schools.*
16. **16.** *He proves their lack of knowledge by at least one example.*

I do not wish to suggest that the goodness of God has begrudged this doctrine to human health. For from the beginning, throughout the ages of the world, He has dispersed His gift through certain men; the Holy Scriptures also highly commend the physician. But most men, through laziness in searching and a readiness to believe [tradition], have suffocated that endowed light within themselves: and so, by the devil's construction, medicine was always built upon the false foundations of the Pagans. Therefore, medicine—the most difficult of sciences because of the invisibility and deceit of diseases—having grown from ethnic theories, was not penetrable by any sharpness of wit. These difficulties were increased by the discovery and knowledge of so many simples <note>Medicinal herbs or single-ingredient drugs.</note>, and the preparations, appropriations, and applications of the remedies sought from them, according to the varieties and speeds of passing occasions; in each of these, on both sides, there are invisible Actors on the stage. Unless one knows these perfectly, or has obtained a superlative remedy, he will surely lose his arrows on the symptoms <note>original: "posteriora," referring to the effects rather than the cause.</note> rather than the roots themselves. Therefore, the door of healing stood closed to all the world, which the talent I received commanded me to open (for I was remarkably ashamed of this boasting; God be my witness). Therefore, I first had to loosen the hinges and posts from rust, so that I might open the doors for those wishing to enter. I had to expose the single and golden key, hidden until now in the archives of the Vital Governor <note>original: "Archei archivis"</note>, to the pyrotechnic fire <note>Alchemical or chemical laboratory heat.</note> and the light of truth. Let each man enter into the secrets of the hall, as much as has been granted to him from above.

<image-desc>Large ornate initial P</image-desc> I have asserted several times, and not in vain, that the arts and sciences have progressed; but the art of healing, if it has not gone backward, has at least stood still, and circled around the same deceptive point. From this I also gathered that the knowledge of diseases, and the cure depending on it, was humanly most difficult. Into this, so many happy geniuses through so many centuries spent their efforts in vain. And I gather this not from chance alone, or from events: namely, that the notice of diseases has been neglected until now: but because, on the part of the causes, it is entirely invisible and pathless. Wherefore, although I tax the schools with ignorance, I would not have it thought that I do this for the sake of vain glory, nor with a mind for reviling the whole body of the faculty (as that does not belong to me): but solely out of a zeal for teaching mortals.

# HE PROCEEDS TO THE STUDY OF DISEASES

thesis: but rather a "prevaricating being" <note>original: *ens prævaricans*; a being that has strayed from its proper path or duty</note> which is forged from the vital *Archeus* <note>The *Archeus* is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions.</note> itself. Therefore, I do not look upon a disease as an abstract quality. And I have convinced myself of this for a long time: that just as life is, so is disease a native being belonging to life itself. <margin>4.</margin> Disease indeed began from sin. For in the integrity, purity, and vigor of innocence of our nature, there was no death, and much less disease. For death was threatened [as a punishment], not disease, except that the latter was understood as a companion to what was to come. Therefore, disease, no differently than death itself, by its very nature attacks life and its powers, which we therefore call "vital": because by the loss of those powers, a slow or sudden death arrives.

<margin>5.</margin> By faith we believe that death, and every infirmity, entered into man because of sin, and through the concupiscence <note>Strong desire or lust, often used in a theological sense for the inclination toward sin.</note> of the flesh of sin, they were propagated to all descendants. For this reason, the entry of diseases and death could not be learned from the Heathen [philosophers].

<margin>6.</margin> Inasmuch as it was reasonable, all classes of ailments are rooted in that same concupiscence of the flesh through which disease entered. For just as concupiscence in its conception does not sin before there is consent—which forms an idea of its attractiveness—so it is necessary that every disease arising in the flesh of sin consists in a foreign image, or a "seminal idea" <note>original: *idea seminalis*; a formative blueprint or "seed-thought" that directs the growth of a condition.</note> of corrupted nature. It was, I say, consistent with the Law that the being which consented and sinned under the pleasure of desire should also be primarily punished by diseases. This happened in such a way that it would not only succumb to external violence, but through its own "exorbitations" <note>Deviations from a regular orbit or proper path.</note> it would experience the vengeance of sin within the flesh. Namely, that the *Archeus* himself,

<column-break/>

the governor of the flesh of sin, by the same freedom of his passions, might fabricate for himself erroneous images which would be like poison to him. Truly, being subject to the pleasures of desire, the storms of the "irascible" passions <note>The "irascible" faculty refers to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and vigor.</note>, and even to turbulent, spontaneous impulses, he would stand at the brink of his own ruin, which he would forge for himself.

<margin>7.</margin> These images, as the seeds of diseased beings, would thereafter be entirely ready for marriage <note>original: *nubiles*; literally "marriageable," implying a deep union or bonding.</note> within the intimate bed of life. This is truly a "hard saying" <note>A reference to John 6:60.</note> in the ears of those accustomed to hearing nothing but trifles, "heats," and "mud" <note>Likely referring to the four humors or crude materialistic theories of medicine.</note>. <margin>8.</margin> Therefore, if anyone wonders at such great efficacy of the "ideated" *Archeus* and of the seminal ideas, that they should give birth to diseases and death itself: such a person does not yet recognize that the natural beginning of all things whatsoever depends, on the "ideal" side, upon some seed. Therefore, let him consider how light, when united in sublunary things <note>The earthly realm below the moon.</note>—since there is scarcely anything more spiritual than light, inasmuch as it penetrates solid glass and even space itself—sets fire to wood and houses. In the same way, every "idea" becomes a light, both insofar as it is forged by the spirit (which participates in the vital light) and because it becomes luminous by the property of its own essence. Otherwise, <margin>9.</margin> the ideas themselves, insofar as they are conceived, are nothing but the lights of the vital soul reflected back upon its own thoughts: which, therefore, are not conceived except in a luminous spirit, in which they receive the shape of the thing conceived. That is, they become in that place the intellectual idea itself. Thus, although the thought itself is a mere "non-being," yet by the very right of its birth, any conceived thing consists of a conceived matter and a vital light, intelligibly reflected into it. And since the imagination is the "ape of the intellect," although it does not transform itself into the thing conceived in the manner of the intellect; nevertheless, by conceiving this thing, it takes it into itself figuratively, seals its concept, and depicts a certain seminal idea of the imagined thing, with light, efficacy, and every mode of operation. And all of this occurs under its greatest unity and simplicity. So much so that if in prolific seeds...

Why should we not recognize that these same things happen no differently in diseases? Especially while they are being engraved by that stronger form of mental apprehension?

<margin>110.</margin> For the things we conceive teach us that from passions or disturbances—which are non-entities—true, real, and actual images arise: just as the thoughts of a pregnant woman forge a real image, however strange and exotic it may be. <note>A reference to the historical belief in "maternal impression," where a mother's desires or fears could physically mark her unborn child.</note> For this reason, the imagination produces poisons in this very way, which kill the man himself and afflict him with various hardships. To such an extent, just as those images proceed primarily from the imaginative power, whose immediate organ is the **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note> itself: so it is absolutely necessary that he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it. That is, it is necessary for the Archeus himself to conceive primarily and immediately, and to put on that new image, to be affected by it, and—by virtue of a shared symbol—to affect all other things depending on him according to the harmful properties of that idea. And that ferment, once depicted in him by the rushing ether, is the disease. From there, it spreads into the blood (the fluid most closely assimilated), and finally into the similar parts and into the very waste products of the body, according to the property of that idea. Hence, indeed, come the diseases of distribution and digestion. What if ideas are formed by imagining within the indwelling spirit, housed in the brain or the spleen—which even in beasts are the principal organ and source of **Blas** <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the "motive power" or pulsating force of life and the stars.</note> for all motions? Nothing prevents the Archeus himself, implanted in the parts, from fabricating singular and occasionally wandering ideas, not unlike the power of the imagination. In this way, the saliva of a rabid dog, a tarantula, or serpents, and likewise the juice of wolfsbane, monkshood, or nightshade, communicates its own image of madness to us against our will. Therefore, nothing prevents the primary organ of imagining from forming for itself indwelling images that are seminal, fermenting, poisonous, etc.

<column-break/>

<margin>111.</margin> Whatever by its own nature, through itself, and immediately afflicts the vital powers, must by that very fact be of the same lineage and condition as those powers. For otherwise, they would have no shared symbol, no entrance, no harmony, strength, or penetration into one another: and consequently, no application or activity. For since these powers are the invisible and intangible seals of the Archeus, who is himself invisible and intangible, they cannot be touched, much less penetrated or overcome by a physical body. Because powers of this kind, however vital they may be, nevertheless lack extremities by which they might be touched. From which it follows (which has been unknown until now) that every disease (insofar as it thrives in life), because it is of the nature of the vital powers, must be immediately forged and arise from an entity that is born to produce **seminal ideas**.

<margin>120.</margin> And since nothing among created things happens originally by itself, the powers of both diseased and vital states necessarily depend on ideas, either of the generator itself (hence **hereditary diseases**) or of the generated Archeus. But so that this may be more clearly established: In the seed of beasts and man, there is a **formative power** according to the likeness of the generator. Since this power is the disposer and distributor of the entire governance in shaping the body, its activity is disputed by no one. Therefore, the seed has knowledge infused from the generator, accommodated to the ends it must achieve. For otherwise the seed, which in its substance is sterile, becomes fertile through an image excited in lust. Truly, the imagination of the generator first gives birth to an idea, which at its beginning is entirely a non-entity; but by putting on the cloak of the Archeus, it becomes a real and seminal entity. And this occurs in plants as well as in sentient beings. Nevertheless, death and all dead things lack the roots by which they might produce. **S**ince, therefore, both matter and an efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about; here, the trigger for disease.</note> are required for the **essence of a disease**, and the "idea" itself is that morbid efficient cause, both must be explained. First, I shall describe the "whatness" <note>original: *quidditatem*; the essential nature</note> of ideas, their efficacy, and their structure, so that the action and birth of a produced disease may become clear. First, I will declare those ideas conceived by man; then I will treat the **Archeal ideas** <note>The *Archeus* is the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine.</note>; and finally, I will discuss foreign ideas. Lastly, I will hand over the matter of disease, so that from the connection of both causes, the essence of the disease and its immediate nature may be established.

<margin>2.</margin>
First, I have certainly taught elsewhere that the force of the "first motions" is a certain unbridled **imaginative power**, not reduced to the power of the will, and stabled in the **spleen**. I have also taught that the Almighty has housed the faculty of such great power even in mere membranes and almost bloodless pouches; thus, the orifice of the stomach as well as the uterus are rightly and deservedly equated to the heart, namely because of their remarkable temperament <note>original: *crasim*; the specific mixture of qualities</note> for acting and the obedience shown to them in turn by other viscera. By the prerogative of this power, the spleen is situated almost in the middle place between both: yet it is inclined a little lower, because it takes the place of the integral root. Indeed, by its breadth, it reaches the stomach, in respect of which a "duumvirate" <note>A partnership of two governing powers.</note> exists; but it reaches the uterus with its other extremity, namely by its ligaments, being annexed to the loins.

<margin>3.</margin>
Next, I said that although in the beginning the "imagined thing" is nothing but a mere **being of reason** <note>original: *ens rationis*; something that exists only in the mind</note>, it does not remain so. For the **Phantasy** is a seal-bearing power; it is called "imaginative" insofar as it forms images, or ideas, of conceived things and brands them into its own **vital spirit**. Consequently, that idea becomes a spiritual, seminal being, powerful enough to perpetrate things of great moment.

It is helpful to have shown this by the example of a pregnant woman. For if a pregnant woman has conceived a cherry in her imaginative faculty with great desire, she imprints the idea of it upon the fetus (as I have discussed regarding the Plague

<column-break/>

elsewhere)—I say, she imprints a seminal, seal-like idea, which is spontaneously indelible. This is because the idea of it turns green, yellow, and red every year in the flesh, at the same seasons of the year in which these cherries otherwise show the signs of their own changes on the tree.

<margin>4.</margin>
Now, why the idea of a cherry, or a mouse, is not imprinted on the mother but on the fetus, and immediately migrates into a subject different from the one imagining (which often begins to live on its own terms): the cause is the unceasing and genuine affection of the mother, by which she naturally watches more for the fetus than for herself.

Therefore, the mother's internal, natural, and inexcusable solicitude, as if continually brooding over the fetus, directs the idea born from her passions to her fetus by a single ray.

And because the hand is the principal organ of active things: therefore, the solicitude, descending to the hand as if for the defense of her fetus, receives the conceived idea and proceeds further into the fetus.

But since ideas are certain **seminal lights**, they penetrate each other without the violation of union. Therefore, when the idea of the cherry has been conceived and the idea of maternal care supervenes, it is directed to that part of the fetus where the hand touched the mother's body.

For indeed, every care is always for the sake of an end toward which the hand works. The hand, therefore, as the executive organ of the will, depicts the idea of the conceived cherry on that part where the mother moved her hand to herself.

<margin>5.</margin>
From this, it is at least clear at the threshold how a thought, which is a mere non-being, becomes a **real and qualified being**.

Next, it is clear from this that the spirit is primarily imbued with that image; and once imbued with any idea, it thereafter becomes unfit for performing other duties. This is because an idea, once conceived, is a seal for doing only specific things.

Therefore, that character of the seminal image, once impressed upon some part of the **Archeus**, makes it incapable of other duties thereafter. <margin>6.</margin>
According to the saying: *Wine taken in moderation sharpens the wit.* Nor is that moderation to be delivered in ounces according to the gloomy crisis of a physician, while it has been granted by the Wise Man to each according to his capacity. For this reason, the ideas of pregnant women are easily connected to the constituent ideas: which, just as they often corrupt otherwise good morals, and indeed sometimes produce fools, so not infrequently they improve others from the womb.

Soon after, in youth, ideas of self-esteem begin to flourish, which although they are mostly still innocent, yet when the ideas of some passion are associated with them—introduced by the hand of inclinations—then the earlier ideas are penetrated by stronger ones, such as hatred, love, revenge, luxury, etc. But if a notable fear is added, a so vehement idea arises from it that it strikes a violent sickness with perpetual faint-heartedness. However, the mildest of ideas are those of love, joy, and desire, which finally delight with their sweetness and so ensnare the whole soul that it continually gasps for delights and pleasures. must be noted: that Agony is not a gathering of hope and fear alone, but also of anger and fear, anger and dissimulation, hope and anger, hatred and fear, hope and sadness, etc. For just as there is a contrary in concepts alone, so it is in the ideas generated from them. # ON IDEAS

From this, a powerful habit binds the soul, insofar as the ideas conceived in the flowing *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a term from Paracelsian medicine referring to the vital internal force or "inner alchemist" that governs life and health.</note> eventually contaminate even the spirit implanted within the body's parts. Indeed, the inclinations toward supernatural virtue are given as ideas only after the whole of nature has been corrupted by sin.

<margin>11.</margin>
Regarding morality, however, skills and defects are implanted in us by the "seminal ideas" <note>The formative blueprints or hereditary traits passed down from parents.</note> of our parents; or, instilled from childhood through education, they pass into our nature, penetrating our native qualities and merging with them. Furthermore, "affections" are the products of the exercise of inclinations, passions, and feelings, and they do not occur without a new propagation of ideas. Each of these, like a form of life, prepares a local dwelling and a habitual state within us.

<margin>12.</margin>
Passions, moreover, are the internal motions of the mind, around whose restraint the whole of Stoicism <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude as a means of overcoming destructive emotions.</note> revolves. Finally, "disturbances" are passions—ideas mostly stirred up by external causes.

<margin>13.</margin>
The common mother of all passions is desire. For this is in itself either good or evil. For that which is indifferent, or neutral, very easily puts on the corruption of nature and is perverted.

<margin>14.</margin>
The only remedy for evil desires is the resignation of the will. For desire is born in this way: corrupted nature is now naturally turned inward upon itself, and therefore it gladly meditates on things that seem pleasing to it, insofar as it is continually occupied with the objects of the "concupiscence of sin" <note>The strong desire for worldly or sinful things.</note>. And just as fire comes from flint, so desire comes from the pleasing nature of an object. Unless you apply the fear of the Lord (which is therefore the beginning of Wisdom) as a curb by means of a fork <note>Likely a metaphor for a pitchfork or a mechanical restraint used to steer or stop.</note>, or cut down the attractiveness of these concepts in their first sprouting, they find fuel in corrupted nature. The malice then grows—not yet visible because of its smallness—and soon drags the entire soul under its power. It reaches the point where the soul becomes a slave to that appetite, by which it was expelled from its throne of majesty. For instance, if ambition or a greater lust seethes in the "frying pan of desire";

<column-break/>

those things are either possible through hope, without hope, or against hope. If a man persists in desire, these latter two will drive him mad. Since every desire of corrupted nature always has something of foolishness and anxiety attached to it. But if the end of the desire is accompanied by hope, it is at least directed toward an object not yet present, and at that time impossible; thus it has a loathsome expectation and a troublesome companion. For we desire those things which are not. Therefore, desire is painful, mostly evil by its own nature, and far worse by its effect. And finally, it is evil by consequence. Because desires immediately and spontaneously decline into anger, hatred, revenge, moodiness, gloominess, intolerance, arrogance, contempt, and so on. For natural desire always rushes toward the worse, because it descends from *philautia* <note>original: "philautia" — Greek for self-love or excessive egoism.</note>, is formed by a corrupted nature, is mostly occupied with the objects of sin, is accompanied by anxieties, expectations, and troubles, and bends the freedom of the will. Insofar as it reflects upon itself and the future, it gives birth to impatience, affects a false freedom, and resists the "mortification" <note>The spiritual practice of subduing one's bodily desires and passions.</note> of the self. It brings about moodiness, distress, intolerance, and eventually despair. Good desire is always given from above by grace, the product of which is Love, and a brightness of the soul producing perfection. Virtues, therefore, insofar as they come from grace, transcend from the imaginative faculty, with its ideas, into the intellect: and thus they "tint" the soul. Just as the vices of the passions, the exercises of sin, and the withdrawal from the fear of the Lord tint the soul, so that it becomes, as it were, beast-like.

<margin>15.</margin>
Hence the scriptures speak of "ravenous wolves," "offspring of vipers," "tell that fox," etc. <note>References to Matthew 7:15, Matthew 3:7, and Luke 13:32, where humans are compared to animals based on their character.</note> Therefore, committed sins will sometimes be visible in the soul without the need for a searching inquiry. But purely "negative" sins, because they are non-entities and have no actuality, do not tint the soul (such as sins of omission); therefore, these alone will be charged against one in the Last Judgment by verbal reproach, whereas the others will be distinguished by sight alone—

I do this not only insofar as the indispositions of the soul pollute and weaken health, but chiefly under the title that, since disease is the "son of sin," it cannot be perfectly understood if one is ignorant of the faculty of the concupiscence <note>The strong desire or inclination toward sin</note> of sin. From this source, every impulse toward disease is derived into the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital workman" or spiritual governor of the body in Paracelsian medicine</note> through these "ideas." Thus far we have spoken of ideas conceived and fathered by human thought, which shall be treated even more liberally under the chapter on "conceptions."

19. It now remains to explain why ideas made by human means possess such great strength that they often summon disease, or even death, upon the one imagining them. We must therefore summarize from the premises: 1. That ideas are forged in the imaginative faculty through thought. 2. That they imprint an image of themselves upon the spirit of life. 3. That they are the operative means by which the soul moves and governs the body. 4. That they are "seminal images" <note>Images that act like seeds, containing the blueprint for growth</note>. 5. That they are ranked according to the power and strength of the imagination. 6. Which is why a human embryo can be changed into various monsters. 7. That every human, through images of sadness, terror, etc., forms for themselves "seminal poisons" which consume them even unto the plague or other violent wasting.

8. Furthermore, these ideas may even travel outside the body of the one imagining. It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, not only regarding the question *Whether it is so*—namely, that there is a most powerful force in ideas for acting—but also that because they are seminal, they naturally penetrate and work upon anything. Indeed, if there were no directing and formative idea present in the matter of the seeds, formed by the Parent, the seed would remain entirely sterile by itself. Finally, these ideas must exist immediately, not indeed in the human soul, but immediately in the Archeus as it makes its impulse; for without an idea of this sort, the Archeus would remain entirely devoid of all action, operation, and propagation.

<margin>20.</margin>

<margin>31.</margin> In the bean, there concur "shadowy ideas" <note>The author uses "ideas" to mean the invisible blueprints or spiritual patterns that dictate how a plant or organism grows.</note> created at the very beginning of the world and born with it through seminal propagation. It is bound to both scales of the bean, as if to a dual sexual beginning. This is not unlike how the thicker white of an egg adheres to the yolk, containing the *entelechy* <note>The "entelechy" is the realized potential or the "soul" of the seed that drives it to become a complete organism.</note> of the seed. The earth, however, possesses within itself its own *fracedo* <note>A term for a fermenting or "mellowing" quality in the soil that triggers growth.</note> or power of impressing a fermental odor. In respect to this, a motive power is granted to the earth to germinate spontaneously, even without a visible seed being committed to it. Consequently, once the juice of the earth is imbibed, that same fermental power which otherwise belongs to the earth is transferred to the bean. This juice, possessing a fermental ripeness determined by the specific odor of the bean, excites the latent seminal idea within the bean, which then proceeds to act of its own accord. Therefore, the sprout that is born is not what the earth of that place would have produced on its own; rather, from the intrinsic and invisible seminal idea of the bean, a sprout is born which is the bean-herb. Yet, it grows such that the specific power of the bean is bent according to the nature of the ferment of the earth's ripeness. This is why wine varies in different places, even though the vine was planted from the same cutting. In this way, seeds flow toward their destined duties, fruits, and ends. And this is the difference between the entities of creation and the entities of disease. # ON IDEAS

The body forges virulent ideas and impresses them upon itself by the same law through which the imaginative faculty fabricates images agreeable to its passions. It happens, I say, no differently than in the uterus, the heart, the brain, the stomach, or the very seminal power that propagates plants: indeed, it shines forth no differently than in the excrements of simple creatures (for instance, the saliva of a rabid dog). In this way, I say, a cancer is born, and it propagates its own ideas to transform nearby nourishment into its own likeness.
<margin>33.</margin>
For the primary cancer, located in the local <term>Archeus</term><note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "vital director" or spiritual governor of the body's functions.</note>, extends further into neighboring parts through a dependent connection of contagion. However, just as from the beginning until final maturity there is only one single ideal and seminal governor of a bean: so from the beginning of the conceived idea of a cancer until death, there is nothing but that same poison. Yet, since the cancer exists in a sensitive subject, the Archeus thereafter rages anew daily, substituting new ideas and poisons for the old ones. This is not the case with the bean, which begins from a singular starting point and proceeds through a flow into the continuity of its own thread. In created things of the first constitution, although the ideal beginning and the progress of becoming from non-being to being is the same as in diseases: nevertheless, the progress of diseases once they have come into existence differs. Accordingly, the bean also changes daily in its outward appearance by growing, even though the flowering stage does not differ from the germinating stage in its vital beginning. Similarly, in diseases sealed in the Archeus—whether local or influential—the poison is diversified by the varying insanity of this governor. For although the base of an ulcerated cancer, exposed to the air, was the first object where it was conceived and born: nevertheless, when that base is consumed by corrosion, another deeper one always succeeds it, infamous with new contagion, just as if a new bean were germinating daily. Therefore, the disease proceeds not merely from a local center of measurement, but from a physical center: which is the furious and seminal idea of the Archeus. The same judgment and parity applies to all other poisons generated within, such as that already mentioned in surgical cases. For in beasts (as mentioned elsewhere regarding the Plague),

<column-break/>

every specific virus flows only from the idea of an image. Whence the proverb: *the beast being dead, the poison is dead* <note>original: "mortua la bestia, morto il veleno"</note>. In this way, surely, proceed leprosy, the venereal plague <note>syphilis</note>, the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, apoplexy, and likewise all primary diseases. However, ingested poisons are not therefore diseases, nor do they arise as such, until the Archeus, having borrowed the ferment of their contagion, does injury to itself. Then indeed, it does not so much forge foreign ideas for itself by its own fury, as it borrows them from the simple substances ingested, and finally succumbs to them. In this agony, it forms wondrous ideas for itself, which it explains tragically through a variety of symptoms. Thus, a Cancer is not the hollow ulcer that the eyes see, nor its crusted and livid lips which the hand touches; finally, it is not the dark, foul-smelling base of the ulcer, or the gore dripping from it, which the nostrils smell: for even without these, the cancer already existed while still clothed in its own skin. But these are the effects, signs, and symptoms of the being whose fruits they are. Truly, since an effect or product implies an inseparable relationship to the cause producing it: therefore, the disease must be a being containing the causes and properties of its own entity. And for that reason, a Cancerous Abscess is as much a cancer as when it has already become an ulcer. For this reason, primary diseases in the Archeus usually produce an equivocal product. Such is

Or if black bile travels from abroad up to the breasts, why is the milk not full of black bile? Why is it not ordinarily cancerous for those who are breastfeeding? Why, when purgatives like dodder of thyme, Lapis Lazuli, or Armenian stone are taken, does the Cancer not soften in the slightest? For they once distinguished diseases by "idiopathy" <note>A primary disease.</note> and "deuteropathy" <note>A secondary disease caused by another.</note>, and they did so the more unhappily as they did so indistinctly. So much so that the Schools, having run into a wall, transferred these conditions from the category of "diseases" to "symptoms." Such as when a migraine or choking arises from the womb, or a swollen gland in the groin arises from a painful abscess of the foot. They called these "consensual" or secondary affections: but they never recognized them as they proceed from their own "seed." As has been demonstrated by me elsewhere more at length regarding the ignorance of the disease-making essence.

**P**reviously, enough was said regarding how the *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note>, even when well-disposed, can be alienated by human passions and disturbances. Likewise, it can be compromised by the exotic image of a foreign *Archeus* penetrating it, or quickly ruined by the deleterious powers of ingested drugs and poisons.

<margin>1.</margin> But while no fault of ingested things presses upon us, nor do external storms rush against us, nor do disturbances shake us, it has not yet been made clear by what compact, way, or method—or by what persuader and leader—the *Archeus* declines of its own accord. It is unclear how it defiles the good within itself (namely the nutritional and seminal fluid <note>original: "humorem alimentarium, atque spermaticum"</note> which had been maintained in unshaken health with such great labor) and why it immediately corrupts that which was prepared and taken in for the vital society, fashioning from it a dross so hostile that the *Archeus* leads itself, along with its host, to the detriment of life. The schools <note>Refers to traditional university medical authorities.</note> say nothing of these things, except that they have devised "catarrhs" <note>A traditional medical theory that diseases were caused by "runny" fluids dripping from the brain.</note> which are supposedly rollable by their own weight and ductile according to their own whim. I say they make no mention of the nutritional fluid, but only of distilled muscus. For without consideration, they have leaped over this torrent, and the business of healing has remained neglected because they have hitherto neglected the corruptor itself.

<margin>2.</margin> They have indeed rightly judged that nothing is moved by itself; they have acknowledged a First Mover and its intelligences, the moving forms of the heavens. But they have not sufficiently considered the proper movers inhabiting the seeds, which, by their own spontaneous power, would effect their own *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the "inner power of motion" or "vital pulse" in living things and stars.</note> through the ideas provided to them, acting as the primary mobile within us. Much less have they applied this philosophy to diseases and the business of healing. For it was never thought how the seminal entity <note>original: "ens seminale"</note>, the Ruler of life, might intend its own destruction and excite a mortal *Blas* for itself.

<margin>3.</margin> Since every single thing desires to exist and to remain. Away with you, *Aristotle*, with your "meretricious appetite" for impossible matter! For with

<column-break/>

those trifles, your shame has been satisfied elsewhere. *Galen* <note>The famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note>, at the tolling of this bell, has merely fallen into a trance and snores, so that he never even dreamed of this tone. Finally, *Paracelsus* <note>The 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who challenged traditional medicine.</note>, who thought that the essences of things and their liquors never perish, began the dissolution of life from the disorder <note>original: "ataxia"</note> of the three primes <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>. For he scarcely believed that the *Archeus* grows weary; he even asserted that the essences of herbs taken in fodder do not perish in the dung of the fields. Nay, the *Archeus* (he says) is never dissolved because of the failings of old age, but is only suffocated through corruptions grown powerful within nature. And so, he does not think the *Archeus* perishes even then, but that it is obscured, wrapped in foreign things, and departs—violently suspended from its duty of acting—to return to the first sacramental entity. Truly, these things are more worthy of laughter and pity than of refutation. For hitherto, people have only dealt with the products of diseases and the occasional causes brought inside. For *Paracelsus* and his followers introduced "tartars" <note>Hard deposits or stones formed in the body, which Paracelsus blamed for many diseases.</note> as the intimate efficient cause of every disease—which perhaps were not harmful before, except when, brought to their final limit, they became coagulated. But I have previously rejected that man's errors, and I have better instructed a credulous posterity, now that the dye of his lies has been uncovered.

<margin>4.</margin> Because I know that the *Archeus* has its own motive and alterative *Blas*, given to it naturally and proper to it by seminal power. For it is this which, from the first conception, moves, shapes, alters, and increases every animal as well as every vegetable according to the whim of its own destination. Thus, the *Archeus* is the "impulse-maker" <note>original: "impetum facientem," a reference to the Hippocratic concept of *Enormon*.</note> mentioned in *Hippocrates*, outside of which or besides which nothing is moved, felt, or altered in living beings. Finally, I know that the *Archeus* moves itself regularly according to an "idea," either left to it by the parent or acquired from elsewhere.

<margin>5.</margin> Whence I also believed it to be of the same entity and faculty by which all motion and alteration occur in ordered regularity during health, and by which these same things occur irregularly. Therefore, it is necessary...

# ON THE ARCHEOI
<note>original: "A R C H E A L I B U S." The Archeus is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal vital force that governs the body's functions.</note>

I have shown that from the Archeus alone, disease is naturally derived no less than health. Thus, just as life and health exist through images impressed upon the seed, so too are diseases created through similar, yet perverse, ideas.
<margin>5.</margin>
But from where do these "guest" images leap forth, if nothing external strikes them, and nothing internal—not even a hereditary blemish—disturbs them?
<margin>7.</margin>
Indeed, I have already dealt with human ideas regarding affections, inclinations, passions, and disturbances; but I have not yet said enough about the *Archeal* ones, wherein the Archeus, by its own excess, goes astray of its own accord and, like Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note>, voluptuously transforms itself. For just as regular ideas (from which the Archeus derives all its *Blas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont meaning "vital motion" or "astral influence."</note>) are implanted in the seed by the desire of the parent, so too, from the impurity of nature, it has reserved every luxurious and pleasure-seeking disorder for concupiscence <note>Strong desire or lust, often used in a theological sense regarding "fallen" nature.</note>. This is clearly never laid aside as long as one lives in the "flesh of sin," because it is entirely native to a nature defiled by passions. For in this way, the Archeus is in a sense saddened, becomes angry, hates, feels anguish, despairs, and becomes weary of itself—even if the human being has procured no such thing for themselves or felt it within. To be sure, there occur overflows in the Archeus which have been anonymous until now, because they are peculiar to it and not so closely related to human disturbances; from these, eccentric and virulent images give birth to pure poisons. For these are, as it were, spontaneous sorrows which "gnaw at life as a moth eats a garment," according to the Wise Man <note>A reference to the Bible, likely Proverbs or Sirach.</note>. These are the anonymous ideas that bring into the open a disease otherwise latent, or a hereditary character. But if the brain, heart, spleen, etc., are the halls in which the Prince Archeus holds his councils, why should not the principal, original being—the motive force of the imaginative power—also have its own "genial fantasy" <note>A creative or innate imagination belonging to the vital spirit itself.</note>? And in a nature corrupted by concupiscence, there occur irregular wanderings in the being, especially when it withdraws itself from the commands of the soul and prefers to be its own master!
<margin>8.</margin>
Nor does it stand in the way that these passions of the 

<column-break/>

Archeus are not properly felt in the human being—passions which would otherwise seem to be required if they are to produce morbid and "sealing" ideas <note>Ideas that leave a permanent mark or "signature" on the body.</note>. But certainly, the Archeus's own discords, happening without the commerce of the organs and the soul, are by no means felt by the human. This is no wonder, since we are ignorant of most of our dreams; indeed, we would not even know we had dreamed unless a certain mutual transfer of faculties into the "guest-house" <note>The conscious mind or memory.</note> had occurred. For does the parent feel themselves forming the idea that will soon build such a proud edifice? Does one even once think about the mere forming of the fetus, or the things to be done? For in lust, the mind is in a sense alienated and withdraws itself for a time, while the Archeus impresses its own image without the conscious imagination. Therefore, the Archeus, having withdrawn without the assembly of its court, struggles within itself with a certain weariness (for the irregularities of the Archeus do not bind themselves to the rules of passions and mental ideas, while it violently wanders from its duties and even from the command of the mind).
<margin>9.</margin>
From this come ideas that are the authors of sluggishness; and hence the slowness of digestions, negligence, omission, along with a certain distaste for life, etc. Such are the excesses of being, of dominating, of knowing, of having, of taming, of avenging, of enjoying, etc. And so the ideas of these concepts give birth to dissolutions, desires, wastes, and intolerances. From which, finally, come neglects of digestion, distribution, and governance, as well as losses, ticklings, irresolutions, grievances, gloominess, etc. From these at last come Plagues, even unknown monsters of toxins, as well as wasting diseases and the poverty of Atrophies. For such ideas are destitute of counsel and formed outside the usual courts. Therefore, their "marriages" and services are no more regular than their births. Thus the Archeus, having fallen into its own luxurious irregularities, becomes entirely symptomatic and impatient; it rages, as it were, and now abandons the reins of governance (which otherwise can never rest), and now again snatches them up after they have been interrupted,

# ON DISEASES

Sometimes it begins, at other times it operates more slowly, and is seized by a weariness of itself. Indeed, in the midst of a satiety of pleasures, it stirs up torments for itself—a plainly irrational being. For once the exercise of digestion is interrupted, the nourishing fluid in the "sixth" <note>referring to the sixth digestion or station of metabolic processing in Helmontian theory</note>, being detained by too long a delay, conceives an exotic ferment of exuberant digestion and is frustrated in its purpose. From this point again, as if terrified, the **Archeus** <note>The internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions</note>, repenting as it were for its own neglect, moves everything in a preposterous manner. 

<margin>10.</margin> But I am unable to worthily explain the means by which the Archeus creates its own spontaneous eccentricities, nor can I depict their "ideas" with a proper name if they are invisible, imperceptible, and created during the abstraction of the Archeus from its bodily duties. For I do not know the manner in which the seminal beginnings express their gifts, which is plainly unknown to me from the outset. Indeed, I am merely playing with conjectures reached by observing similarities. Truly, I have made conjectures based on the regular patterns in man, which another more judicious than I may explain. It seemed to me, however, that it would not be worth the effort to scrutinize these things deeply according to every individual case; rather, it is sufficient, both in diagnosis and in healing, to have encountered the generated "ideas" and to have removed all **ataxia** <note>disorder or lack of coordination</note> from the Archeus, perhaps by a single **Arcanum** <note>a secret, powerful chemical remedy</note>: about which I shall speak more extensively later. Therefore, intending to give the longed-for peace to studies and to the complaints of the sick, "seek, and you shall find." 

<margin>11.</margin> Furthermore, all "authoritative" diseases—those which grow harsh as if without any contact with filth—support the doctrine already handed down. And of this sort are, first and foremost, hereditary diseases, infused by the parent along with the seed. The "ideas" of these diseases wait patiently for several years before they are manifested in the offspring, or indeed sometimes in a late-born grandson. Secondly, the same is proven by diseases that sleep through long silences of days and then repeatedly recur. Thirdly, concentrated diseases, which I call elsewhere the **Torments of the Night**. And fourthly, the same is explained by diseases of disproportionate power, which I call "unequal strength." 

<column-break/>

As far as hereditary and posthumous diseases are concerned: it is certain that the **morbific idea** <note>the "blueprint" or seed of a disease</note> is transplanted, having been depicted in the seed of the parents. 

<margin>12.</margin> It is not that the parent has a character of some conceived passion or disease set before them as a destined goal while procreating; but (as I cease not to say) the Archeus conceives a pleasure in the act of generation, through which, being abstracted from the body into its own center, it must reflect itself so much more closely into the soul, as if into the other extreme from the body. 

<margin>13.</margin> Whence, looking up at the **vital light**, it cannot help but be invigorated and receive its own seminal image—the cause, namely, of fertility. For it is characteristic of all pleasures that, with self-approval, one contemplates oneself in one's own mirror, and with a plausible joy which has even given birth to **philautia** <note>self-love or vanity</note> and a certain arrogance in the very cradles of nature, yet differing in itself according to the variety of pleasures. For while the Archeus withdraws and abstracts itself, as I have said, it nevertheless cannot help but be in the body as its place. I call it "abstracted," therefore, not indeed from the body, but from its hall or ordinary throne. 

However, this abstracted contemplation of the Archeus does not take place in the heart, as if it were fluctuating in a continuous motion of agitation and pulses; nor are the chambers of the heart the council hall of the abstracted Archeus. Indeed, it is not even in the parenchyma of the heart itself: but the palace is deeper within. Namely, in the **stable spirit** itself, implanted in the **spleen**. This image of itself, conceived under lust, puts on a small particle of the spirit by which it is performed; which, under the **synteresis of Chemistry** <note>the "preservation" or essential spark of chemical life</note>, is the 1/800th part of the whole. And each smallest particle of it, thus depicted, passes thereafter into the **influous spirit** <note>the flowing or circulating vital spirit</note>, domestic to the heart, together with the idea of lust and desire. 

Moreover, the ideas of desire are the sole motivating directors (as I have said elsewhere regarding sympathetic forces), and therefore the conceived image of the human Archeus, through that direction, is inserted into the material seed. 

<margin>14.</margin> Wherefore, just as death began from Venus <note>sexual intercourse</note>, so it is daily accelerated, just as the passing away of a plant begins from the conception of the seed: insofar as from that point it is diminished...

Because it would either rot, dry up, be consumed, or lose its original taint of poison: which,

For just as the virus of the Falling Sickness is intoxicating, sleep-inducing, and in a certain way furious; it first shines forth around the stomach, and then is perceived chiefly in the head, and affects its subjects in a singular way. Nothing, however, is sealed there except ideal characters. <margin>1.</margin> The unheard-of doctrine of the "disease entity" promised by me, I have now described at length, so that physicians may learn to look into disease at its source and unlearn being seduced by pagan opinions. For this reason, disease is not any <term>intemperies</term><note>An imbalance of qualities.</note> of elemental qualities, nor the victory arising from their continuous struggle—as the <term>Galenists</term><note>Followers of Galen, whose medicine relied on balancing the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note> have dreamed until now—nor likewise is disease one of the four fictitious humors exceeding its own <term>crasis</term><note>The healthy mixture or temperament of the body.</note> and

equated to the four elements. Nor, finally, is disease some degenerate matter stirred up by the impression of the elements. But all excrementitious matter is either naked matter preceding the disease (and therefore an occasional cause of the disease), or it is a product of the disease resulting from an error of the parts (and thus a certain later effect of the disease)—although it may then occasionally stir up another disease or nourish and increase another preceding cause. Nor, finally, is disease a noxious quality budding from the poison or contagion of another and harmful matter. Nevertheless, those types of "sins" merely accuse their own presence; they are not the effect that depends on them only <margin>2.</margin> occasionally. Therefore, disease is a certain "born entity," created after some harmful foreign power has violated the vital beginning and penetrated its force, and by penetrating has excited the Archeus to indignation, fury, fear, etc.—of which disturbances, indeed...
