# DISEASES
## Bbbb

For anxieties and distresses excite a similar idea and a corresponding image within themselves through the act of imagining. This image is promptly forged, expressed, and sealed into the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note>; and once clothed in that image, the disease soon enters the stage, constructed of an "archeal" body and an efficient idea. Indeed, the Archeus brings harm upon itself; once it has admitted this harm, it soon yields to its persistence, flees, becomes alienated, or is disturbed and defiled. It is then forced to submit to a foreign command and endure a civil war stirred up within its own home. This is truly a foreign "Icon" or image of that kind, materially imprinted and rising from the Archeus. This is the true <term>morbific entity</term> <note>original: "ens morbificum"; the "being" or "essence" of the disease itself.</note> which is called a disease.

<margin>3.</margin> For although healers are solely occupied with the dissolution, cleansing, and expulsion of harmful occasional matter <note>The physical waste or "triggers" of a sickness.</note>, our pruning of these things cannot change the essence of the disease. Just because a physician labors to banish the harmful occasional cause, it does not follow that the disease must be that very thing which the deceived healer, in a backwards order, intends to expel. For a disease is essentially what it is, whether a physician is absent or present. The physician’s beginning no more determines the disease than it terminates it. The disease does not accommodate itself to the "pruning" of others, but rather mocks it daily.

Therefore, just as health consists in an unimpaired life, so disease <margin>4.</margin> consists in that very life being wounded. Now, life subsists solely and most closely in the seat of the soul; but the soul does not operate outside itself except by the power of its official organ, which is the <term>vital aura</term> <note>original: "aura vitalis"</note> of the Archeus. Therefore, it is a wonder that it has been unknown until now that disease sits immediately in the same <term>vital lodging</term> <note>original: "hospitio vitali"</note> where life itself dwells. More on this later.

For those who hate these truths will hardly believe that every sublunary power is excited and contained in ideas. I have already touched upon this in passing, <margin>5.</margin> but it will be helpful to bind it more firmly. For we know, and believe by faith, that herbs were given the power of propagating their own likeness. This is a proprietary power, a real entity, actually existing, which is manifested in the seed continually and successively. Nor is this power some accidental authority or a naked quality; rather, it is a <term>seminal force</term> <note>original: "vis seminalis"</note> by which the parent plant depicts an idea in its seed, containing the figure and properties according to which the seed itself will excite, delineate, and cause the daughter plant to grow. For in seeds, a manifest image is recognized, which is "knowledgeable" of the things to be done for the new offspring.

<column-break/>

Likewise, the sea does not create, but rather suffers <margin>6.</margin> the horrid tempests which the wind efficiently stirs up. And the wind is not moved by itself or of its own accord, but by the invisible influence of the Stars, according to that saying:
> *The stars shall be to you for signs, seasons, days, and years.* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14.</note>

Indeed, such a great storm of the primary elements breaks forth from an entity that is like light. However, the <term>Blas</term> <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe a "motive power" or "pulsing force" in nature and the stars.</note> of the elements is not stirred up by the mere light of the Stars. For however incorporeal and immaterial the light of the Stars may be, it is not a simple light; rather, beyond the property of solitary light (which is merely to illuminate), it has a motive *Blas* within itself, as well as durations and directions according to locations, strengths, and weaknesses—no less than an alterative *Blas* for every change of seasons and periods.

In ancient times, these things were usually ascribed to the "aspects" <note>The relative positions of planets in astrology.</note> of different lights, which, as such, do not exceed their own efficacy, which is merely to have shone. But to excite such dissimilar stations of the seasons, and even foreseen tempests (that is, before the arrival of the stars at the locations of those aspects), is surely an effect of greater weight than simple light alone. I believe, therefore, that through the diversities of the aspects, spiritual and astral images of the invisible world are formed, which they deposit into the air to excite the *Blas* according to the image of those properties. Since the aspect of the stars is only momentary, and their location unstable, yet the effects persevere for some time. Therefore, it is necessary...

# THE ORIGIN OF THE IMAGE

It is necessary that the celestial alignments, beyond their momentary light, have deposited in the air an idea of *Blas* <note>original: "Blas"; a term coined by van Helmont to describe a specific "motive power" or vital force of motion in the stars and living things</note>, which operates until its own exhaustion, following the irregular rules, barriers, obstacles, spurs, and cycles of time. Therefore, an image of this kind is of the nature of light, so that it may operate at a fixed time; for otherwise, in the course of many years, it would hardly reach us unless it were of the nature of light.

Thus, just as there is in plants a power that awakens a seminal image for the purpose of reproduction, so too in the Stars there is a power of fashioning an idea of motive light, which is the initial beginning of motion, performing whatever has been commanded of it for execution.

<margin>7.</margin> Furthermore, our *Archeus* <note>original: "Archeus"; the internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions</note>, whether it possesses a power similar to the earth or to the Stars, it is all the same, provided we understand that it is characteristic of him to stir up a tempestuous *Blas* within us, following the disobedience of the First-Formed <note>original: "Protoplasti"; referring to Adam or the first human</note>. Whether such a property has grown into him from sin, or whether he awakens it anew by his own will and the sight of his own disturbance, it is equally valid. We need only recognize that every power, whether of a regular life or of a disordered governance, proceeds only from this vital beginning.

<margin>8.</margin> And for that reason, all diseases, and the patterns of these, are certain depicted "conceptions" <note>mental images or seeds</note> created by this invisible Ruler <note>the Archeus</note> to carry out the storms of our calamities. Therefore, in the ether of the Archeus, "aspectual ideas" are painted, formed both from the depth of the "starry Heaven" of the soul itself, and from the errors implanted in the spirits of the seven viscera <note>the internal organs</note>. For in this way, the dread of the Plague creates the Plague. A sudden dread of death has often killed the gout <note>original: "podagram"</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> Likewise, the dread of lost honor, or honor about to be lost, if it lasts for a single day, has repeatedly caused Epilepsy. The sadness of poverty has brought on insanity; in others, it has given birth to the King's Evil <note>original: "Scrophulas"; a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes</note>. Most maniacs have fallen into their state through pride. And the wise man testifies: that sadness gnaws at the life of a man as a worm gnaws at clothes. Now, sadness is a sad thought; but this is a "non-being" because it is a mental entity. Because it is a non-being, it therefore has no

<column-break/>

<margin>10.</margin> power of acting from itself. Therefore, a sad thought gives birth to an *active idea*, and this "something" is made out of nothing, not unlike how a disturbance in a pregnant woman gives birth to a monster and transforms a human fetus into a beast-like one. This is because it is natural to the imaginative power to build images, both in mental and Archeal matters. Sadness, therefore, which is a slow disturbance, gives birth to an idea that consumes and gnaws at life: because such an idea has, for its material, the degenerate vital aura of the Archeus. This degenerate aura then attempts to pervert the rest of the Archeus into its own likeness. And this degenerate aura is corrupted in the "duumvirate" <note>original: "duumviratu"; van Helmont's term for the functional union of the stomach and spleen as the seat of the soul</note>. Therefore, immediately following sadness, there are continuous sighs. These things happen thus by the powers of a sad imagination <note>original: "phantasiæ"</note>. The same also happens in the power of the Archeus's own imagination, whether it be influenced from without or implanted within: both of which (as discussed elsewhere regarding the tomb of the Plague) build most powerful images of the imagination. Wherefore

<margin>11.</margin> from a twofold Archeus, a twofold Archeal disease-causing idea also distinguishes a passing disease from a chronic one. Therefore, those who hereafter pay proper attention will find that every disturbance of the soul that is strong, long-lasting, and does not descend by emanation outside the Archeus of the viscera (which are dedicated to imaginative duties), or outside the duumvirate, produces a diverse or distinct madness through the varieties of ideas. They will similarly find that simple substances, whether degenerated within or taken from without—provided they affect the Archeus itself from the outside—cause the Duumvirate to produce a similar Idea of Madness. This becomes manifest in the slightest contagion of a Rabid animal. Such diseases, concentrated in the vital members that "speak" with the Stars—whence unequal Strength, the Torture of the night, hereditary and periodically repeating ailments—are seen to have an invisible storehouse within, and an initiating principle of a tragedy, from which Ideas are repeated like so many storms, by the command of their maturity or their eccentric peak.

<margin>1.</margin>
After I had discovered that the stomach is the root of the tree—that is, the root of both universal digestion and of any particular digestions whatsoever—I likewise recognized in earnest that the mortal or sensitive soul <note>The "sensitive soul" in 17th-century physiology was thought to govern sensation and involuntary functions, distinct from the immortal, rational soul.</note> dwells there. It is the mistress of any actions within us and the dispenser of life throughout the whole. Clearly, the fabricator of our first concepts is also situated there, as well as the workshop of sleep, no less than of waking and madness. I deemed it consistent with reason that the immortal mind—the image of God—could be stabled or connected nowhere more fittingly than in the aforementioned formal and vital light: namely, in a spiritual principle, which is most closely related to it by nature. And when, having finally investigated the vital monarchy, I perceived and understood through observation that every disease essentially consists in life and rises up from the same, there presented themselves to me the causes of the difficulties in curing diseases—especially those which do not fall silent of their own accord, or which do not hasten by their own impetus to the end of their period, but rather accompany the life which they so bitterly infest.

<margin>2.</margin>
Therefore, among the more long-lasting diseases, I saw that the quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day.</note>, atrophy, <term>cacochymia</term> <note>An imbalance of the humors or "bad juices" in the body.</note>, and likewise weaknesses—and then those which have chosen a bed in the extreme habit of the body (such as Leprosy,

<column-break/>

palsy, Sciatica, spasms, Gout, etc.) as well as those which are bound to one of the internal organs (such as Apoplexy, Epilepsy, Asthma, Stone-disease, Dropsy, Madness, etc.)—are not cured, certainly not for lack of a desire to heal, but truly through a poverty of the remedy alone. I have long labored over that remedy and looked back many times, until I recognized that it must regard the very fountain of life, or the sensitive soul. Therefore, first, I took in hand the quartan fever itself, as it is common, most tedious, and clearly known; and while it scorned the usual remedies of Physicians, it rendered their hope vain. Primarily, I was made certain through this disease that wherever some material morbid product lay hidden, the application of a suitable remedy was equally required; otherwise, a lasting effect, stirred up by that occasional cause, would be feared even in a healthy person.

<margin>3.</margin>
And therefore, from the corollary of this pronouncement, I found that no remedies of Physicians until now—however much they are boasted of by reputation as <term>deoppilative</term> <note>Medicines intended to remove obstructions or "unblock" the organs.</term>, resolving, cleansing, or purging—actually reach their mark. They only arrive, or are carried, at most to the threshold of the spleen, which reveals itself by sensible testimony to be the host of the quartan fever. Thus, being certainly instructed by this, I conjectured that the deoppilative power of the remedy, etc., either soon perishes in the stomach, grows mild, is subdued, or is banished through the intestines, if it has not already perished before then. But if, indeed, some quality of the remedies persists safely through its own vital means, and having been somewhat broken down and more deeply assumed, it penetrates (just as mace or turpentine, in urine, necessarily retain their own flavor by a great Necessity), yet at least it occurs so castrated and weakened that it effects nothing of those things for which the medicines are swallowed. # ON THE PRESERVATION OF THE INTERNAL ORGANS

...they diminish unjust acidity in such a way that they even inhibit and ward off acidity from a wound (all acidity outside the stomach is harmful, morbid, and a companion of putrefaction, as I have demonstrated elsewhere regarding digestions).

<margin>13.</margin> Indeed, the general digestion of the stomach presides over the "kitchens" of each individual digestion. For truly, birds are actually and notably hot throughout their entire bodies, so much so that they tolerate the nocturnal rigors of winter during the day. However, they do not urinate, because they lack kidneys and a bladder. Therefore, whatever a drinking dove drinks, the whole of it departs through <term>insensible perspiration</term> <note>original: "insensilem diapnœam"; the process of losing fluid through the skin or breath without visible sweating</note>. Hence it is clear that the kidneys alone produce urine, which otherwise would be sweat; and urine in man differs not in the matter of the first liquid, but solely by the efficient <term>ferment</term> <note>In Helmontian medicine, a "ferment" is a vitalizing agent that transforms matter</note> of the kidneys. It is also evident that birds, without sweating, eject every superfluous excrement insensibly. Thus, urine differs from sweat by more than just its matter: not only because of the formal essence of urine received from the kidney, but it also receives into itself liquid and staining dregs. These are not drawn upward to the veins in a bird, nor do they sweat, even when exhausted. Therefore, the fact that sweat in man is not exhaled insensibly—as it otherwise is in a pig—is the fault of the human Kidney; just as the fact that liquid dregs are separated and drawn upward from the intestines into the veins is the fault of the Kidney. The use of that traction, on account of <term>duelech</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for a stony deposit or calculus formed in the body</note>, has been shown elsewhere. However, urine is not stained so that it may be ejected more promptly: for urine is sharper and stings more whenever it is without the staining dross. Therefore, just as the Kidney is the cause of urine and the aforementioned things, so it is also the cause of <term>Dropsy</term> <note>Edema or swelling caused by excess fluid; "Hydrops"</note>, insofar as the **Kidney** closes itself through the indignation of its own **Archeus** <note>The internal "master workman" or vital spirit of an organ</note>. If the indignation of this Archeus is restrained by a proper remedy of the stomach, insofar as

<margin>14.</margin> its "duumvirate" <note>The governing partnership of organs</note> presides over the Kidney, then certainly the Dropsy is soon relieved. For the watery fluids of Dropsy are not infrequently driven out from a swollen and tense abdomen through water-

For the water which the **Kidney** deposited in the abdomen, the stomach seeks back from there and casts down through the bowels; and thus it shows that it can command the kidneys in their follies and indignations, so as to lead the watery fluids back to the intestines even through unknown paths. It is certainly not that such purgatives materially and physically go all the way into the abdomen and, by a virulent cathartic force, bring back with them the deposited burden of the **Dropsy**. Not at all. Rather, these are the feats of the stomach alone, and the privileges of the life and the vital duumvirate. The channels are indeed unknown to us:

<margin>15.</margin> but life, the director and mistress of these things, reflects itself toward its seat or center, that is, toward the **soul**. And therefore, from the life of the **soul** itself must be sought the functions of powers, duties, vigors, values, and each of their defects. For the **Soul** distributes all offices to the parts and moderates them through life. Nor does it only distinguish offices by parts—so much so that in the vessel of the stomach itself it has separated diversities both in the orifice and in the pylorus—but it has even connected the powers themselves, starting from a <term>homogeneous</term> <note>original: "homoiomero"; parts that are similar in nature</note> beginning, yet each providing its own scenes. This is certainly nowhere more clearly

<margin>16.</margin> discerned than in diseases, and thus in the defects of the faculties. For these pave the way to **disorder** <note>original: "ataxiam"</note> and the torn discord of unity. Since the immortal mind is believed to be of a single identity, therefore the conditions, inclinations, ferocities, etc., must be ascribed to the mortal soul. This soul, to be sure, follows the material variety of dispositions. Hence come stupidity, barbarism, rages, madness, as well as lustfulness, sagacity, and finally the destruction of sciences and the extinctions of memory, etc.

In order that the roots of life may be more clearly opened, I shall construct into Theses several preludes established by me elsewhere and borrowed from there.

<margin>I.</margin>
The immortal mind, the closest image of divinity, after it delegated the government of life to the sensitive soul—which is mortal and fleeting—even though it handed over its power to this mortal light, it nevertheless remained connected to the same through a symbol of life, bound together as if by a link <note>original: "syndesmon"</note> of immediate cognition. Because that sensitive light of life sits as a guest in the stomach, as if in the root of mortal life, the mind itself therefore chose its couch and throne in that same place. I have more strongly confirmed this elsewhere in my formal treatise on the soul.

The soul has sown its faculties, necessary for life, through the organs of the body. For this reason, the ankle does not see, nor does the ear walk, just as the liver does not transmute consumed food into chyle <note>A milky fluid of digested fat and lymph.</note>.

The vital faculty of the organs, in health, produces healthy actions; and the same, whenever it is corrupted, produces corrupted actions.

However, the vital faculty is not corrupted except by disease.

Which, accordingly, is nothing other than a real and actual vice of the faculty: a positive entity, I say,

<column-break/>

and for that reason consisting of matter and an efficient cause, after the manner of other natural entities.

Since, however, the vital faculty itself essentially encloses the disease within it, it follows from this that the disease itself, in the formality of its efficient cause, is a faculty—not indeed a corrupted one, but a "vicious" one <note>Meaning a faculty that has become harmful or strayed from its natural purpose.</note> which surely corrupts or harms the vital faculty. Thus, disease is a power very similar to the vital faculties, and so intimate that in certain cases—whether lethal and hereditary or centrally rooted—it is united with them.

But a corrupted or injured faculty is either particular to a specific organ, such as blindness, deafness, paralysis, etc., or it is dispersed in every direction by the common vehicle of the flowing Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "chemist" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note>, whether idiopathically <note>arising spontaneously</note>, deuteropathically <note>secondary to another disease</note>, or sympathetically. And truly, in whatever way and by whatever means the faculty is harmed, it is at least discerned, and clearly seen, that a vital vice lies beneath it everywhere, and that every disease is hosted most closely in the vital principle, that is, the Archeus itself.

Universal diseases, for instance, sit in the universal beginning of life, whether the Archeus is infested in detail by some organ, or whether it is stirred up and angered by the fountain of life and the animated root. For although that may vary the appearance of the disease, such variety does not take away the disease-making quality.

The sensitive soul is set over all its vital faculties, whether they are distributed through the organs or fostered by the common Archeus. At the very least, it depends on this: that the healing of almost all diseases consists in, and is perfected in, the radical inn of life. That is, in the seat of the Soul and the center of life. Unless perhaps sometimes some organic part has drunk in for itself a genial...

From this it becomes evident that almost every healing of diseases (I do not even exclude wounds and similar surgical matters) must be sought in the stomach and its *Duumvirate* <note>original: "Duumviratu." A term used by Van Helmont to describe the dual leadership of the stomach and spleen over the body's health.</note>; and thus, it is not inappropriately sought there. For in this way, even external defects are not infrequently removed by an internal remedy of the stomach, which were otherwise attempted in vain with external medicines. It is no wonder, therefore, that remedies hardly overcome the command or rank of the stomach, or are materially dispersed any further.

2. Having briefly premised these things, I shall add several privileges of the stomach: 1. And first, that "genial" and particular right of the stomach, that it cooks primarily for itself; but for the whole body only by accident, indirectly, and by an extraordinary right above the other members. For so the divine ordinance has brought it to pass: that it prepares nourishment from the raw material of food for all others. However, the stomach itself is immediately nourished by the chyle <note>The milky fluid produced from food during digestion.</note> prepared by itself. Not unlike the root of vegetables, which is nourished by the juice of the earth, the <term>Lessas</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the specific nutritive juice or "sap" of the earth.</note>. It is not, however, that the stomach draws blood from the liver for its own nourishment; just as the root of vegetables does not seek back the juice once sent away and dispersed upward from the bark again, to be nourished therefrom. For this reason, the stomach enjoys few veins for a duty of such great mass and a vessel of such great capacity. Because, namely, it is not nourished by blood in the accustomed manner of other members. But it is fed by chyle alone, which it then adapts into the spermatic liquor <note>The fundamental "seed-like" fluid used for tissue repair and growth.</note> suitable for itself. 2. The stomachic veins do not, therefore, diffuse blood outside themselves, nor does a stomach injured by a wound "weep" blood. And the remaining membranes have borrowed this same right for themselves from the stomach. 3. The stomachic veins transmit or suck up nothing of the chyle prepared from food to carry it to the portal vein, as is otherwise the custom of the <term>mesaraic</term> <note>Mesenteric; the veins draining the intestines.</note> veins. And this I have more strongly confirmed elsewhere concerning digestions.

<column-break/>

4. Finally, the stomachic veins do not attend to the nutrition of the stomach. 5. Therefore, the stomachic veins, full of pure blood, have a free, vital power, not disturbed or destined for the suction of chyle or the dispersing of blood. Yet one or the other of these is domestic to all other veins. 6. Not in vain, however, are the veins and arteries, bound to the orifice of the stomach, distended; but the soul, guesting in the thinness of the stomach's membrane—as if it were not there, indeed, hardly bound to the place—breathes the breath of its life into the organs (namely the heart, spleen, liver, brain, kidneys, testes, etc.) in an insensible manner, and by an incredible narrowness and thinness of channels. From here, surely, come sudden eclipses <note>Fainting or loss of consciousness.</note>, apoplexies, epilepsies, dizziness, swoons, etc., whenever the sensitive soul ceases to radiate its light into the organs. 7. For there is in the channel of the stomachic artery a vital power of that soul, for radiating to the heart as long as it is well. But when it behaves wrongly, there are immediately stirred up palpitations, faintings, dizziness, apoplexies, epilepsies, slumbers, wakefulness, madness, headaches, convulsions, etc. Finally, its vital power is breathed by the soul—the moderator of the vital faculties—through the stomachic veins to the liver, and so from the unity of the soul flow various gifts to the individual organs: since always, and everywhere, all things flow from one point, both in the universe and in us. For that mortal and seminal soul, the constant ruler of the body, since it is obtained occasionally from the disposition of the blood: it necessarily also dwells in the organs: as much in the bloody spleen as in the bloodless membrane of the stomach. Just as the brain, the source and judge of sensations, is itself mostly lacking in sensation. And therefore, it also occurs several times in Holy Scripture that the soul of man dwells in the blood. 8. <margin>4.</margin> Furthermore, regarding the fact that in epileptics all sensation falls away, but not likewise motion: this does not prove that the sensitive soul is not the source of both. For even if all intellectual powers are interrupted, and only the evidence of shaking and jumping motion remains as long as that "eclipse" lasts; nevertheless, all those powers are designated as the soul's own, flowing from it into the body. But those powers which the soul itself planted in the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs specific organs</note> inherent in the organs, are under an eclipse, and they riot during the soul's consternation; yet they persist in a darkened state because life is not taken away, nor does the pulse <margin>5.</margin> cease for that reason. Which, as I have shown elsewhere, continues for some time even after death, and <term>Tetanus</term> <note>stiffening or muscle spasms</note> begins a while after death: thus, although the life of the muscles flows from the sensitive soul, it nevertheless obtains a certain peculiar energy and a local station. Therefore, it is less strange or absurd that the muscles should riot with their own motion if they feel the common life eclipsed short of death. <margin>6.</margin> In apoplexy, however, and in <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>, even the motion of the muscles completely fails, except for the motion of the intercostal muscles; for then the sensitive soul undergoes total darkness. For each thing drives us to the astonishment of a miracle or a portent. <margin>2.</margin>
There are, therefore, primarily as many species of diseases as there are <term>morbid ideas</term><note>The author's theory that disease is not just physical matter, but a "corrupt blueprint" or "idea" that infects the vital spirit.</note>. For there are neither more nor fewer: because every disease draws its essential nature from a morbid idea. Consequently, there are just as many species of morbid ideas as there are diversities of "filth" <note>original: "sordium," referring to metabolic waste or impurities</note> within us. Whether these entered from the outside, or were first unfolded within and arose from errors in digestion, or finally whether they began from the nourishment and the vital juice, it is all the same in this context. Furthermore, there are as many morbid ideas in us as there are heirs to <term>authoritative beings</term><note>original: "entium potestativorum," referring to powerful external forces or substances that can dominate the body's internal balance</note>. For example, if a too-violent laxative is taken: even if the substance itself is soon secreted through the bowels, its poison does not cease to remain domestic to the stomach and intestines; so much so, indeed, that a foul diarrhea may persist until death. In this way also, any poisons—once their original matter is gone—sometimes slaughter by a slow killing, leaving a long-lasting plague in one's descendants. This is true whether they are taken from without or generated within. Finally, hereditary diseases and their kin are born with us in the manner of a seed, flowing from their own "ideas." Thus, for instance, <term>Gout</term><note>original: "Podagra"</note>, <term>Epilepsy</term>, etc., unfold their own rhythms and are prolonged throughout life without any visible "filth" or matter. This is because they have found "ideas" that are firmly fixed in the <term>Archeus</term><note>The "internal chemist" or vital governing spirit of the body in Paracelsian medicine.</note>, or the indwelling governing spirit, as if intimately related and clinging to it. Therefore, they infest only at their own boundaries and according to their own native periods.

<margin>3.</margin>
These things having been established and now known, I consequently say that in the task of the **Division of Diseases**, I shall follow the variety of <term>occasional causes</term><note>The external triggers or circumstances that allow a disease to manifest.</note>. I do this so that I might not seem to want to overturn the names and every determination of diseases from the very egg <note>from the very beginning</note>, to the great 

<column-break/>

weariness of the readers. Such readers might either take offense at a total novelty of this kind, or might only be able to follow it with excessive difficulty. Therefore, although I may name the occasional cause in place of the diseases, I would not want it to be understood as if the occasional cause were the disease itself: but rather that the disease, as an invisible entity, is understood to be forged "occasionally" by external matter.

<margin>4.</margin>
Therefore, I establish two primary genera of diseases: namely, **Received** and **Retained**. Moreover, the **Received** are those injected, conceived, inspired, or finally undertaken. I will first explain these four individually. And only then will I treat the **Retained**, as much on the part of the body and its distributions as on the part of digestions and transmutations.

<margin>5.</margin>
The **Received** are those which enter into us treacherously from the outside and provoke or affect the *Archeus*, so that by a counsel harmful to itself, the *Archeus* fabricates a morbid idea within itself and seals it in its own material part. And thus, it becomes the true parent of a true disease. For "Received" things, before their entrance and application, suggested precaution and preservation, but not healing; because, clearly, there was not yet a disease. Nor is there healing, except from disease alone. But once the "Received" things have made even a secret entry, or have been admitted even in passing, they soon overturn the entire economy and peace of the *Archeus*.

<margin>6.</margin>
The **Retained**, however, arise from our own fault and defect. For they are, for the most part, "recrements" <note>waste products or dross</note>, either taken in or generated within us: which, like citizens expelled from our Republic, being enemies of unity and concord, have no part with us in the inheritance of life.

I therefore perceive that since the days of Plato, three patrons of Witches have constantly flourished among the Atheists. And I omen that such a dire blight has persisted until now only by the presidency of that same [Evil] Leader.

->brought forth out of pity and without charge.<- Just as he is no thief who uncovers the hiding places and assemblies of thieves, so let there be no evasion or fear of being held infamous for knowing the means, progress, ends, and cures of incantations. <margin>5.</margin>
I shall therefore speak according to my capacity regarding how much power the Devil possesses in the actions of Witches <note>original: "Sagarum"</note>. And so that this may be established fundamentally, I shall review it through eight Theses.

1. That every vital form is the **vital light** of its own body.
2. That however much the forms of inanimate things differ from souls in the degree and character of that light, they at least all agree in being something essentially luminous.
3. That because they are light, they touch and penetrate one another immediately. Thus, connected forms work upon each other just as one light intersects another. For solar rays, collected through a glass into a cone, though they meet at a single point, proceed from there again; those which were on the right in the glass pass to the left after the cone, refracted by the glass. Yet they preserve the identity of the prior light unimpaired, so that they do not suffer "contagion" or mixing because of the penetration made in the cone. I have demonstrated this elsewhere mechanically through a diagram.
4. That therefore different formal lights, whether in genus or species, immediately penetrate one another like light, and work communicatively and without exhaustion.
5. That all forms of bodies are true lights—not substantial ones, though they are entities—for reasons

<column-break/>

alleged elsewhere concerning "neutral creatures." <note>Van Helmont's term for entities that are neither purely spiritual nor purely material.</note> However, the **Human Mind** <note>original: "Mens humana"</note> alone is a formal substance, immortal and indelible. To this extent, it operates with superiority; it reaches and penetrates every other form inferior to itself (as I have discussed elsewhere regarding the "hunting of the sciences"), especially by 그 title, received into faith and nature, that it is the true **Image of God**, and that the Kingdom of God dwells within it. For this reason, He has placed all things under its feet.
6. That therefore the Evil Spirit <note>original: "Cacodaemon"</note>, by his very creation, does not have the power of reaching any form so as to fulfill his will upon it by the absolute command of his nod. For he is a spirit abstracted from corporeal being, bound, and furthermore, since his sin, a most wretched buffoon.
7. Only the power of moving bodies from place to place remains to him, provided their motion does not result in the destruction of mortals. For he cannot destroy a single window by himself without the help of the freedom of his clients <note>i.e., the voluntary cooperation of witches</note>.
8. Nor does he move the elements by physical touch (since he lacks extremities with which to touch bodies, even those he assumes) to seize or move anything; rather, he moves them by his "nod" alone through an **intuitive gaze**, such as that of the Stars upon Meteors, through Ideas, or as our will moves its own organs. This mutual power was naturally endowed to the Angelic nature, and thus it was left to the Devil. He possesses a certain *Blas* <note><term>Blas</term>: Van Helmont's invented term for a "motive power" or "astral influence" that governs motion in the stars and the human body.</note> of birth, by which he stirs up the storms of the air and the heat of the sea whenever God permits him.

<margin>6.</margin>
For the Devil is so primarily evil, and our enemy, that he cannot will even the slightest good. Therefore, he has no free will in choosing evil <note>meaning he is compelled to it</note>, and in good things he has none at all, unless unwilling and coerced. For "being," "one," "true," and "good" are interchangeable terms. Therefore, from the opposite sense, the "apparent," "false," "evil," and "manifold" are the properties of Satan. Consequently, by his own nod and natural power, he cannot even work anything freely and without divine permission, or without the free cooperation of the Human Mind.

The body bends its knees against its will. For otherwise, as is commonly said, the Devil harms man by the permission of God: this is to be understood either through the aforementioned command, given as if to a Torturer, or by a mutual natural operative force which God bestowed

Therefore, those impressions or "sealing Ideas" which the evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmon"</note> excites in his followers, and borrows from them, he imprints into the filth which he places beneath them so that they may infect them. And so the law calls them Poison-makers <note>original: "Veneficas"</note>, or makers of poisons. For it is not only that they offer poisons to be drunk, but rather that they create poisons out of non-poisons. These are applied both through the locomotive power natural and free to the devil, and also because they are transferred to the intended object with desire alone as the mover and director. As will be discussed more broadly later. Thus the Witch hangs, buries, or offers those filthy things—contaminated by her through an Ideal Being <note>original: "ens Ideale"</note>—or even anoints or washes her hands with that filth and imbues them with dire poisons, so that through contact she may transfer those poisons into the object she wishes to harm. For truly, those seminal, monstrous, and poisonous Ideas, since they have become citizens of another and foreign Archeus <note>the vital internal governing spirit of a living thing</note>, once introduced into the body of the enchanted person, and thus being outside their proper place and subject, the Archeus of the enchanted person is immediately contaminated and corrupted by them. Therefore, since the enemy of nature cannot complete the application by himself (for otherwise all miserable enchanted mortals would succumb to the devil's wish), he excites an Idea of strong desire and hatred in the Witch, so that by these changed mental and free means, he may transfer his will through that which he intends to affect. To this end, he especially prescribes to his "sows" <note>a derogatory term for the witches</note> execrations joined with an Idea of desire and most hateful terror.

# REMEDIES FOR INJECTED THINGS

-> (Medicines or objects introduced into the body by witchcraft) <-

<margin>13.</margin> For man possesses a free will to do harm, through which one person is able to kill another with a knife, and thus destroy any innocent person; this is something the devil cannot do in the same way. Therefore, just as the use of a knife is forbidden to the devil at his own pleasure, so too is the application of poison. And for that reason, it is utterly impossible for him—that is, without a free human being or a servant devoted to him. For indeed, not even a man kills another with a knife unless a desire is added, within free consent and by the command of a resolved will. From this it is sufficiently clear, first, that the devil does not possess the power to create a "seminal idea" <note>term: seminal idea (idea seminalis). In Paracelsian philosophy, this is a formative spiritual force that can organize matter and produce physical effects.</note> that actually and positively exists, such as is granted to the divine image [in man]. Likewise, the devil has not obtained the mutual application of such an idea unless he has acquired a free faculty from elsewhere—one that is not bound, and is ignited through desire or priority. Indeed, that desire, as it is a passion of the one imagining, also creates an idea—not a hollow one, but one that is executive and provides the motive force for an incantation. For this reason, surely,

<margin>14.</margin> That hostile buffoon <note>The author refers to the devil as a "scurra" (buffoon/jester) to diminish his perceived power.</note> requires a touch upon the body to be enchanted, or at least upon something that has been primarily affected, and finally upon the body to be enchanted, so that the received ideas may act upon it through a sympathetic and natural force (such as that by which Vitriol <note>original: "Chalcantum." Copper sulfate or vitriol, used in the "weapon salve" to heal wounds from a distance.</note> naturally heals an absent wound), and thereafter upon the body whose natural effluvia maintain a sympathetic commerce,

<margin>15.</margin> as if they were mediums. Finally, things buried deep or hung up high cause harm; indeed, they unfold their virulent ferocity only upon the first person who enters, even without the Witch's <note>original: "Saga"</note> contact with the body to be enchanted, and without any prior notion, hatred, or harmful desire against the specific person who enters first. But this is a matter of more difficult resolution; namely, a more subtle harm and propagation, which has adopted for its own proof the directions of the gaze of the Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent said to kill with its look.</note> or the Torpedo fish <note>An electric ray known for numbing fishermen through their nets or spears.</note> in nature. For just as the Basilisk, by a visual ray, spreads its venom into an object and not into the place, nor into any other body

<column-break/>

however much closer it may be to itself, but only into that one upon whom it first directed and vibrated the sharpness of its eyes; and just as the Torpedo does not perhaps cast the poison of its sight into someone nearer, but rather and only into the one pulling the ropes from a distance. In this way, namely, the seminal ideas, connected to the filth hung up or buried, are invigorated by the Idea of ignited desire, just as if by the will of the Basilisk or the Torpedo, and they exercise that power only upon a determined object. And although the likeness does not correspond in every respect

<margin>16.</margin> in the identity of both terms, it suffices at least to have demonstrated that there exists naturally, not only in man but even in vile little animals, an attributive and executive power of their intention, by which they resolve to do harm by sight alone, by intention, desire, or hatred. Indeed, this gift

<margin>17.</margin> extends even to whatever things move their objects from a distance magnetically or sympathetically. It is not absurd that these mediums exist naturally within man, attributed in an even more excellent way, since we read that all things are placed under his feet. Wherefore,

<margin>18.</margin> in the same way, by a touch or a simple blow, witches transfer their incantations into an object, though in a far coarser manner than the one previously mentioned. And therefore, the sympathetic medium also hides something similar within itself. And it is far more restricted still when such incantations are bound to gore, pus, or other effluvia; but indeed, they also necessarily touch or strike the object itself. Truly, I have not brought up sympathetic matters here to defame them, but rather insofar as I might demonstrate the mode of application to a medium through them. On the contrary, I do it to show that Witches use natural modes and means, otherwise common in the Torpedo and the Basilisk, so that I may extinguish all hope of diabolical fraud from sympathetic remedies. And so that it may be established through natural things how falsely and lyingly the infernal serpent prescribes for himself adorations and liturgies for those things over which he has no

<margin>19.</margin> power. Furthermore, to strike back at a striking Witch, as the incantation naturally reflects...

### THE FOLLOWING THINGS WERE LEFT BY THE AUTHOR IN A MORE IMPERFECT, UNFINISHED, AND UNCORRECTED STATE THAN THE PRECEDING ONES.

<column-break/>

Since it has now been demonstrated that every disease consists in the life of the sensitive soul and its vital organ, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions.</note>, and since this Archeus contains within itself unity and identity; it must next be taught from this that healing and restoration from all diseases consist in the unity of the remedy. However, the schools of the "Humorists" <note>Followers of Galen who believed disease was caused by an imbalance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> will argue to the contrary, and say, etc.

Now, therefore, having proved the necessity of recovery through the peace of the "occasional causes" with life: and so that almost every individual universal secret <note>original: "arcana"</note> is effective for the aforementioned soothing and pacification of the vital Archeus: it is now finally necessary to descend to the secrets themselves, and not only to administer them by name, but also, as far as charity toward one's neighbor permits, to describe them to skilled <term>Philiatris</term> <note>Greek: "lovers of the art of medicine," referring to aspiring or student physicians.</note>. It is not permitted, however, to make them public so that the ignorant and those gaping only for a little profit may dispose of them, or commit them to the <term>Seplasia</term> <note>A famous street of perfume and drug sellers in ancient Capua; here used to mean common apothecaries.</note> and his wife. Far be it! For I have been taught, etc.

I will say, therefore, as much as the order of charity permits concerning the revelations of the Secrets. In the first place, therefore, nature has produced from the goodness of God singular remedies in the vegetable monarchy, by which diseases are also singularly restored and healed: <margin>N.</margin> which until now **N.** have remained hidden through the laziness of investigation, the greedy desire for gain, and the envy of the demon. Thus, for example, the *Elixir of Property* <note>original: "Elixir proprietatis," a famous alchemical medicine attributed to Paracelsus.</note> according to Paracelsus cures Asthma, Epilepsy, Apoplexy, Paralysis, Atrophy, Consumption, etc. But because this Elixir is not prepared except by a most skilled Philosopher: who, not by thinking but by knowing perfectly, and being doubly chosen for this, has thus attained the title of <term>Adept</term> <note>A master alchemist who has successfully discovered the "Great Secret."</note>. Hence, out of compassion, I will set forth a middle way. Take of clear aloes, the best myrrh, and the best saffron, one ounce of each. For if you take more, you will find it done in vain. Let the first two be ground accurately; but the saffron, because it is not ground unless dried, rather...

<column-break/>

...[the testament] against its own Author: so perhaps they might be despised by the indiscreet and scrupulous as a superstitious means. But surely, as it is permitted by natural law to repel force with force, especially if it happens not so much out of anger or hatred as out of self-defense and the turning away of harm: which distinguishes the moderation of blameless defense. For which reason, as I have already demonstrated, because the most powerful force of an incantation depends on the natural "idea" of the <term>Saga</term> <note>Latin: a witch or sorceress.</note>: so it is also consequent that the aforementioned "repercussion" <note>The act of reflecting a curse back upon the sender.</note> is entirely lawful, on account of the natural idea of the desire by which one wishes and strives to free oneself from the incantation. And so, in this repercussion, no one follows or is provoked by the power of a pact with a <term>Cacodæmon</term> <note>Greek/Latin: an evil spirit or demon.</note>. Indeed, this repercussion alone manifests the entirely natural force of the incantation, as well as the demon's impotence.

Meanwhile, that most unhappy one [the demon], being entirely proud and ashamed to admit his own impotence, deceives his credulous followers, who think that he is the sole master, giver, and ruler of that malignant and harmful activity. Wherefore they also worship him with serious cult and obey him in every scurrility. Therefore, poisons produced in this way—since Satan is unable to infect and prepare them according to his wish, nor to adapt them at his pleasure, and much less to apply them!—he orders it all to be completed through his slaves, so that they become "emanative" poisons, directed toward the specific object of desire. For in this way, poisons which before were either entirely material, or things altogether indifferent, and could not harm unless perhaps swallowed: now, by the casting of "ideas," have become virulent in a formal, seminal, and fermental way.

# CERTAIN INCOMPLETE WORKS FOLLOW.

...let it be gathered into a mass by pounding. Let these be placed in a very capacious and strong glass vessel, and let it be sealed by melting the neck of the glass. Then let it be distilled with moderate heat, lest the vessel shatter, until you see the entire mass has coalesced at the bottom, and a clear oil is circulating with the water upon the walls of the glass. Then let the neck of the glass be opened, and pour in cinnamon water <note>original: "aquæ cinnamomi"</note>, and distill it through moist sand, to which boiling water is gradually added. Continue until nothing more drips from the beak of the alembic <note>A teardrop-shaped chemical still</note>. By this medicine, both quartan fever <note>A malaria-like fever that returns every four days</note> and continuous fever are immediately released. So much so, that one who had received the Holy Viaticum <note>The final Eucharist given to those near death</note> and the Extreme Unction of oil at night, had me as a guest at his table for dinner the next day.

Nature has also produced in the subterranean Kingdom <note>original: "Monarchia"</note> a certain mineral, which because of its uniqueness is called by Paracelsus <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note> the **First Metal** or the **Male Metal**. By its metallic nature, it is necessarily clothed in metallic mercury and sulfur. Namely, a mercury that is liquid and does not stick to the fingers, and a sulfur that is combustible with a blue flame. This sulfur, however, is distilled with its corrosive agent, and is cohobated <note>Repeatedly distilled over its own residue to increase potency</note> so many times until it passes through the alembic in the form of a red oil. This is then finally and most accurately cleansed of every corrosive; it is an oil prepared not indeed by the separation of its salt and Mercury, but the whole is reduced equally <note>original: "anaticè," from the Greek 'ana', meaning in equal parts</note> into the form of an oil. For as long as it remains oily, it cannot be altered or applied to life by the full power of the sensitive soul. Therefore, it must be transmuted into a mercurial juice, which Paracelsus teaches and calls the **Wine of Life** <note>original: "vinum vitæ"</note>. This is because it does not heal diseases in the manner of other Secrets <note><term>Arcana: Secret alchemical remedies believed to have specific healing powers</term></note>, by the scouring and banishing of whatever is harmful; rather, it additionally renews lost strengths in general and restores imbalances of vigor. Therefore, not in vain is it called by Paracelsus the **Essence of the Limbs**, being truly the sole peak and summit of hope for a long life. How much light I have brought to the writings of Paracelsus, only he—

<column-break/>

—knows, who understands Paracelsus as I do. But when this sulfur is not transformed so that it can be turned into blood, or rather restore and renew the innate spirit of the limbs and viscera—even though it is in itself the summit of nature's wonders—it nevertheless merely passes through the first two digestions <note>The stages of processing nutrients or medicines in the body</note> and does not satisfy its calling, for which it shines with such narrow endowments. Thus, it is obvious from this that a long life is only for chosen men: and not even for all of those, not so much because the youth of princes shorten the thread of life in lust and pleasures (and thus the remedy of long life is received according to the capacity of the receiver), but chiefly because **Adepts** <note>Masters of the alchemical art</note> are lacking, to whom alone it is given to shell such Secrets from their husks. I suppose, of course, that this "male metal," because it easily allows sulfur to be sequestered from itself, and this separated sulfur is dissolved in oil of cinnamon or nutmeg, or in the oil that drips from fir resin while it is thickened into the best rosin by boiling. But at least, although the sulfur thus resolved has remarkable powers, because it draws in a foul odor and retains the resistance of melted sulfur, it cannot pass to the innermost parts; it can only act as if in passing, briefly exciting a superficial remembrance of its gift through its touch. Therefore, it is further from the "Wine of Life" than a precious garnet is from a common flint. However, if this melted sulfur is so united in the oil of an aromatic spice that it passes through the alembic (even if stinking), and is then circulated with alkali in the proper manner, and finally passes into a **Volatile Elixir of Salt**, it in some way emulates the powers and virtues of the Wine of Life and the Essence of the Limbs. Indeed, this elixir, rectified in the best spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol</note>, loses all foul odor and resumes something of its genial gift, so that it may at least remove difficult and chronic diseases; even if it does not ascend to the highest perfection <note>original: "entelechia"</note> of the internal organs, so as to be a renewed Essence of the Limbs.

->IN WORDS, HERBS, AND STONES THERE IS GREAT POWER.<-

There is a passage in the Sacred Scriptures which takes "stones" to mean mineral bodies. Words, indeed, insofar as they are commands issued from a supernatural power, rule over created things; because these things are subject to that power, they also obey. Next, the power of "herbs" refers to medicines <note>pharmaceuticals</note>, but does not include herbaceous foods. There is, therefore, a medical force in plants, simple in its nature: yet it is so exceedingly potent that it often rises to a degree of virulence <note>toxicity or extreme potency</note>, because it exceeds the capacity of our own nature; for that reason, it is also hostile to us. Indeed, garden vegetables, legumes, and grains must be entirely subdued and broken down in the stomach—that is, the seat of the soul—where, if they fall upon it with their powers unbroken, they constrain that same seat by the laws of their fresh hospitality <note>The author suggests that raw or "unsubdued" plants impose their own nature upon the body rather than being assimilated by it</note>. Thus, the seat of the soul itself labors around these still-simple raw materials, and by working, it endures the crudities, harms, and troubles of these vegetable guests. For thus far, whatever is not properly subdued in the stomach is sent out through the intestines as useless and harmful excrement, after the aforementioned troubles. For this reason, the harsher plants, while they do not promise nourishment nor are they directly drawn into use as food, are—if they do not cause notable harm—at least totally sequestered and expelled with labor and distress. This has been notably evident in the quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day</note>, which has mocked the promised help of healers and the hope of medicines. For even if the occasional matter of the quartan fever clings only around the Spleen and in the vicinity of the stomach: nevertheless, the medicines of plants have not yet reached the threshold of the quartan fever. Meanwhile, the more robust plants, since they have been allotted a degree above the powers of our nature, are for that reason mostly rejected or "castrated" <note>weakened or stripped of their essential potency</note>: and so, through corrective means, they are plainly alienated and degenerate, and thus pass into a foreign family. In vain, too, have many attempted to separate the 

<column-break/>

virulent powers from the appropriate ones lurking beneath them. As is customary today, such robust medicines are horrid and troublesome, and are not admitted into our innermost parts. This is because they attack and weaken the vital forces, and bring along anxieties as companions in every way. For however much they do not turn into nourishment for us, nor are admitted deeper than to enter the very threshold: yet by touch alone, and by their bare passage—indeed, even by a sort of "deaf glance" <note>an influence exerted without direct contact or mixing</note>—they alter the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: The internal "vital worker" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine</term> by contamination, subjecting it to their own influence and carrying it away. This is the reason why the more robust vegetable remedies are mostly suspected of atrocity and virulence. These things are seen even more clearly in the secret minerals and higher medicines. Indeed, these perform their duties and achieve the goals of their gifts by no mixing of themselves, but as if by a glance alone. For in this way, mothers dip a piece of wool into a mixture of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sew it inside the waistband of garments: knowing, of course, that even if the quicksilver does not breathe out anything outside itself (for it is so homogeneous that it cannot be divided into a heterogeneous part unlike itself), it nevertheless prevents the presence and generation of lice throughout the whole body. I have also described . . . . . . . how common quicksilver is reduced into a snowy mass if the spirit of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note> is distilled from it. This spirit is indeed coagulated above the Mercury and transmuted into alum: yet it is separable from the quicksilver by washing. This becomes a yellow powder, which easily returns to its former state, becoming quicksilver of equal weight to itself. Thus, indeed, the whole spirit of vitriol, most acidic in itself, is turned into an aluminous salt by the bare touch of mercury, and without any radical mixing of the two.

# THERE IS GREAT VIRTUE IN WORDS, HERBS, AND STONES.

And this may be done a thousand times, yet nothing of the weight or nature of the quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note> is lost. For quicksilver, without any participation of itself or from itself—indeed, even without any radical mixing of itself—transforms whatever the sulfurous spirit touches. This radial mixing of quicksilver is even more admirable: namely, if quicksilver is steeped in a great quantity of common water. For this water, although it cannot absorb even the smallest bit of quicksilver into itself, nor convert it to its own nature, nevertheless borrows a property (though not the substance) from the quicksilver. Thus, when such water is drunk, it kills all intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos universos & ascarides"</note>, even those existing where the drink itself never reaches, since the liquid is soon entirely hurried away into the urine. And this water becomes more powerful against worms if it has boiled once with the quicksilver. Thus, a single ounce of quicksilver can infect a measure of water a thousand times, yet remain in its original weight and property. 

In this way, even the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Galenic academic medicine, which the author often critiques.</note> learn against their will that certain agents act freely, always, and with unwearied strength, without any suffering or reaction from the patients <note>In this context, "patients" refers to the substances being acted upon.</note>, and while their own weight remains always the same. For quicksilver acts upon the water and impresses its character upon it; yet it suffers nothing in return from the water. It is manifest, therefore, that a certain medicinal force is transferred, and changes its natural subject, passing into a foreign object by a mere ray, as it were, or by its very presence. Yet, although the foreign object acquires a power exotic to itself, the agent that inspires this beginning loses nothing of its original strength or weight. This happens without any suffering, diminution, change, weakness, or alteration of the quicksilver. Truly, the example brought forward in this place serves as an argument for the nearly infinite power of remedies to be celebrated hereafter. After this matter had been handled often and in various ways through experience among minerals,

<column-break/>

it finally taught me what perhaps no mortal before this had yet seen clearly and inwardly: namely, how the more hidden remedies <note>original: "remedia abstrusiora"</note> operate. It showed that without their own dissolution or destruction, without penetration, admission, mixing, or commutation, they act freely even from a distance upon the dormant or inflamed *Archeus* <term>Archeus: The internal "vital physician" or life-force that governs the body's functions in Paracelsian medicine</term>. They act by the mere sight of them, as it were, or by the irradiation or ejaculation of their forces produced in the medium, while their original weight and properties are still retained and unchanged. 

And so, these *Arcana* <term>Arcana: Secret, powerful medicinal preparations believed to contain the concentrated essence of a substance</term> testify that they are close to infinite goodness, while they gradually scatter almost infinite powers. Therefore, Physicians will not go unpunished when the poor sometimes wail that they were neglected at the Last Judgment—those who could have been cured easily and in passing without any expense. Therefore, *Arcana* can never turn into food: because they keep their own boundaries, as things destined not for food but for medicines; they remain medicines even if taken internally. For they begin in the stomach (which I have elsewhere professedly shown to be the seat of the soul) to display the direct ray of their powers and their endowed virtue, and for what purpose they were destined by God. From there, finally, the radial force, having been sprinkled into the *Archeus*, is scattered into the whole body, and the succeeding health is greedily received. 

Thus, indeed, when these more universal remedies are offered, there occur healings such as I have declared happen at the fountain of nature, and are owed to the same—such as Paracelsus promised, and then Butler <note>likely referring to the Irish alchemist Butler, whom the author claimed to have witnessed performing miraculous cures</note> performed in my sight, namely by the smallest application of "con-fermentation." Certainly, after this speculation drew me under it by deeper contemplation, I recognized most clearly and as if through an optical lens that while filth indeed clings to occasional causes and excrementitious products, stirring up peculiar diseases: nevertheless, I consider the whole disease itself, and its remedies,

# THERE IS GREAT VIRTUE.

In the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "vital workman" or life-force that governs the body's health</note>, that is, when it is altered or pacified: and so by the slightest touch, vibration, darting, or even by radiation or illumination alone (provided they reach the sensitive life in the seat of the soul), healings are perfected and completed, without regard for the occasional causes of disease. And I perceive this more powerfully in the sulfurous remedies of minerals, for instance in the sulfur of Venus <note>Copper</note>, of antimony, and especially in the sulfur of the "Glaure of Augurellus" <note>A reference to the alchemical writings of Joannes Aurelius Augurellus; "Glaure" likely refers to a specific golden or radiant essence</note>, which Nymph has lacked another proper name until now. For sulfurs of this kind, because they are further removed from human nature than the entire cohort of vegetables, and meanwhile obtain distinguished gifts from the Giver: so also they most fully and stubbornly resist being turned aside by the digestive power into the "republic of foods" <note>i.e., being digested like ordinary nutrition</note>, and therefore they keep their genial powers free and unbroken; the <term>crasis</term> <note>The unique temperament or constitution</note> of the minerals remains whole, and more fit for dispersing its ray into the <term>duumvirate</term> <note>The "two-fold power" or governing center of the body</note>, the seat of the soul. Thus indeed <term>diaphoretic Mercury</term> <note>A preparation of mercury intended to induce sweating and purification</note> acquires the ultimate goal of its <term>entelechy</term> <note>The realization of its full potential</note>, through the redness of the ascending sulfur, to which the sulfur of mercury is joined in an indissoluble union. For thus far, the sulfurs of minerals under <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The fire of the furnace</note> attain the extreme completion of the Healers' intention. I therefore urge <term>Tyrones</term> <note>Beginners or apprentices</note> to learn how to strip sulfurs of their foreign and poisonous power: under whose custody, truly, the vital fire is hidden, leading the Archeus most peacefully to the desired goals. There are, you see, certain sulfurs which, once corrected and perfected, the whole cohort of diseases obeys: inasmuch as their plurality is contracted into the unity of the Archeus, as if into a fighting fist. In this way, in the very seat of the soul and the combined duumvirate, we have seen <term>Amentia</term> <note>Dementia or madness</note>, <term>Apoplexy</term>, the <term>Falling Sickness</term> <note>Epilepsy</note>, <term>Paralyses</term>, <term>Vertigo</term>, <term>Asthma</term>, <term>Dropsy</term>, <term>Atrophy</term>, and immense defects annihilated: with nature itself, of course, standing amazed. Therefore, a great virtue in stones is proclaimed by the Sacred Scriptures, which until now is hidden as much in the Academic as in the Chemical Schools, until Kings

<column-break/>

and Republics shall have looked toward the reformation of the Schools. It wearies one of the labor, who hope to hunt for gain through abuse. They know not how to labor, nor do they wish or want to: those who mock the students of virtues: For if ever before, now at least the whole world is placed in wickedness, which has deterred my pen, lest I should sow pearls before swine. Extract the sulfur of antimony, which differs hardly at all from the common sight, except that it verges a little into greenness. Make this <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>Mercury sulfide</note> yet six times; you shall sublimate it by itself, so that the sublimation may serve as the reverberation of the Lily. Take half an ounce of this ground Cinnabar, suspend it for 24 hours in a cask of wine; you will wonder at the effect of a single spoonful taken for several days. And the same Cinnabar is sufficient for many hundreds of doses, being equivalent again if it is resublimated repeatedly.

Concerning the great power of words, I have said certain things frankly, which I admire more than I apply. The use of herbs is indeed very well known, yet their value is not known enough, nor is it adequately defined. And this is not only because of ignorance of their powers: but chiefly because of the clumsy adaptation of morbid causes, the lack of science in relating causes to the effect, and the ridiculous and fabulous dimensions of temperaments and degrees, which others before me have sufficiently unbuckled. For I do not here recount the thousand confusions of simples <note>Individual medicinal herbs</note>, the devastations of faculties, and extinctions of all kinds. But most of all I deplore the lack of the science of applying causes to effects: or the matching of the thing applicable to the thing to be applied. For before all things it must be known, that just as the births and promotions of some things are slow: so proportionally they also have expected magnitudes of powers and varieties of estimations. For as the proverb says: "what is done quickly, also perishes quickly": so neither can a thing be drawn out into a long hope of maturity

For this reason, commendation was made only concerning **words, herbs, and stones**. It is certain, indeed, that herbs can be digested and subdued by our stomach, unless they have malignancy as a companion. Truly, the number of pot-herbs and cereals is small in the class of herbs; which smallness certainly accuses some malignancy, which, when properly separated—then first, and not before—their powers will be of benefit, like the targets of their mission, which poisonous guardians were hiding beneath themselves. Certainly, vegetables act upon us only so long as the stomach works upon them. Nor do they proceed further without first laying aside almost all the strength of the remedy. Whether these are added for the guardianship or covering of their strengths, or indeed for defense, denial, and hindrance: it is at least enough that most of them have attached to them their own cruelty, infamy, immaturity, scabbiness, decay, and the exhaustion of strengths, besides still manifold filth and impurities; since they are deprived of <term>emunctories</term> <note>Organs or channels that carry off waste, like sweat glands or kidneys.</note> dedicated to the evacuation of excrement, it is necessary that their entire nourishment be full of excrement. Indeed, they must be utterly and formally stripped of all their previous qualities before they can become citizens of our Republic <note>The "Republic" of the human body.</note>. For the singular goal of our nature intends only one thing from what is ingested: the process of making blood <term>sanguification: the formation of blood from food</term> for nourishment. Since this blood must proceed not from just anything at all, but only from things truly transmuted and made compatible with our species' seminal nature, it is certainly useless to offer anything from the vegetable lineage for the deeper "families" of digestion, if one thinks these plants retain the original power of their parents. This is confirmed well enough by the quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day.</note> and all diseases occasionally provoked by waste products, which have hitherto held the Schools <note>The traditional medical universities.</note> in contempt. For those Schools have meditated on nothing beyond lettuce and cooked herbs.

To be sure, vegetables are readily available and corresponded to the diseases of the first ages of the world. But for chronic diseases—which are mostly increased by the infamous harshness of vegetable remedies, and which have found their hiding places in the innermost parts of the body and spirits far from the mouth—how difficult it is to achieve resolution through vegetables is attested by entire hospitals, which echo with the continuous wailing of the unfortunate. Therefore, everyone sees at home every day an almost defiant and unceasing disease among their kin, while the healers have become a laughingstock <note>original: "pegmatum fabula," literally a stage-play or fiction</note> because they have done scarcely anything worthy of thanksgiving. Indeed, some of them confess the weaknesses of themselves and their Authors, and many unwillingly flee in secret to unknown chemical remedies, most of which reek of adultery and corruption. They flee back to books, but not to the furnaces: for their apprenticeships promise the most ample fruits, yet every illegitimate and ridiculous thing is boasted of. While the Academics do not understand these things, and on the other hand see the withered Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine.</note> to be so impoverished, they waver and flee to cauteries, acidic springs, and baths. Alas, what an unfortunate refuge for the sick,

<column-break/>

and what a hollow one for themselves, has this great stumbling block of darkness in the Schools produced!

I shall say it, therefore. By the "Text," under the name of "stones" and that "great boasted virtue," I understand all minerals thoroughly, and the marrow of these—the metals—above all others. For these show themselves in no other image than that of stones or rocks. Truly, this is the richest and most constant offspring of nature, and its chief treasure: so much so that the conjunctions <term>syzygies: the alignment of celestial bodies</term> of the Stars are stored within it. Furthermore, to speak more accurately and outside the profound ignorance of the Heathens, the Stars only preside over meteors causally; but metals, by the excellence of their remedies, far surpass the stars. For I have taught, according to the Sacred Text, that the Stars are not causes for us, but only for "Signs, seasons, days, and years" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14.</note>. Nor is it permitted for man to extend the duties of the Stars any further.

For this reason, I have never, by my wish, wedded the number of the Stars to the wandering planets, nor have I restricted the offices and dignities of either to an equality. For just as they are distant from one another in space, so they have disparate duties and the ends of their offices directed toward different things. This one thing, however, I gladly admit: that metals surpass plants and minerals in healing by many miles <note>original: "parasangis," an ancient Persian measure of distance.</note>. Therefore, metals are certain shining mirrors—not indeed by reason of their polish, but rather because whenever they are opened and their virtues are liberated, they act by an endowed light and a vital contact. Thus, metals operate in the manner attributed to the Stars: namely, through the "aspect" and the touch of the *altering Blas* <term>Blas alterativi: a term coined by Van Helmont referring to the internal motion or "gas" that directs change in the body</term>. These things will become clearer through mechanical explanation. For the metals themselves are mirrors—the best offspring, I say, of the lower globe—upon which the entire central force has prodigally poured its treasure for several centuries past, so that it might most richly betroth this liquid of the earth, this fatness, and this offspring of divine providence to the ends which the weakness of nature required.
