There are, therefore, mirrors of Gold, Silver, Mercury, Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Venus <note>Copper</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, and Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and their marcasites <note>metallic ores</note>, not yet enclosed, etc. Now, I call those things "shining mirrors" which have the power of penetrating and illuminating the *Archeus* <note>The vital internal force or "master workman" that governs the body's functions</note> from its errors, furies, and defects: because they restore it to its brightness by a tincture of endowed perfection. For although minerals of this kind are not foodstuffs, nor of the same nature as the human body, they nevertheless possess the internal power of a mirror, and a most effective potency, contiguous to the whole and calmed human *Archeus*. This is such as the *Archeus* was before the *Mind* <note>original: "Mentem"</note> was conceived—which mind, to be sure, was afterwards alienated from its right path, after the sensitive soul (in which the mind resided) drew the government of the body into itself; for that soul was entirely falling and brutal in itself. 

In these shining mirrors, however (to distinguish them from vegetables, which are not shining), there has remained a certain residual type of the former immortality. Thus far, in an imperceptible way, such mirrors are not only communicated, but are also gladly received by the *Archeus*. Indeed, the restoration of the *Archeus* would persist longer if these mirrors were not immediately banished <note>expelled by the body</note>. This is evident in the mechanical preparation of Copper, Iron, etc. I pursue these matters concerning the Tree of Life in my book *On Long Life*, so that there may be a stable remedy, transmutable into human nature, to be taken from childhood, especially as long as the power of growth flourishes. This, I say, surpasses the power of the shining mirror for a long life, though not likewise for a healthy life. Furthermore, whatever else is to be said about stones, it was either insofar as they participate in some metallic tincture, sulfur, or mineral salt. However, insofar as it is a mineral entity, it could be neither food, nor nourishment, nor vital. But before I pass on to the Secrets <note>original: "Arcana"</note> (which in this place is called the great virtue of stones), it is truly helpful to enter into the very seat of the body and look within, to see how much any remedy operates there. To which end

<column-break/>

first of all, that which I have already said above stands in the way. Namely, that the stomach cooks nothing except with the single-minded goal of finally fashioning nourishment for its whole from it. By that very act, it intends to make an alimentary liquor—namely blood—and then the spermatic humor fit for nourishing the primary constituents. This is so that it can be turned into substance suitable for nourishing and increasing the parts: namely, as long as they are applied within the limit assigned to growth. From this, it also necessarily follows that only suitable and edible materials, prepared and digested by the stomach, are transmitted into the further workshops of the digestions. 

For this reason, I have first of all removed every plant infamous for any kind of ferocity from the boundary of the *Mesentery* <note>The membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>: because everything unfit for these purposes is, by that very fact, driven out through the stomach and associated with the excrements. As a truth to defend me, the quartan fever presents itself.

Wherefore, I have first diligently considered that all remedies work according to the gift which the Almighty has bestowed upon them, whether they be vegetable or mineral. But since the most powerful strengths of remedies are not of a food-like or blood-like substance; and much less of an excremental substance (since the intestines are only a bag and a sewer)

That is, as long as it is detained in the stomach on the way, or in the process of becoming excrement. So that, since there is no final middle ground between a food-entity and excrement: at least let there be a mediating middle in the being of the remedy. Namely, as long as the determination is undecided whether the taken remedy is to be driven out along with the excrements. It further follows that each of the remedies, exceeding the limits of food, acts by its touch, in the manner of a mirror. Since, without material mixing of itself, it acts upon the *Archeus* by touch alone. The *Archeus* himself first feels the gift drunk in from the remedy. In that sensation, however, he fashions for himself an *Idea* of the things he must do, following the dispositions of that gift: whence, consequently stirring up peace, rest, or anger for himself, and taking up these produced *Ideas*, he soon disperses them into the viscera (which listen to the action of the governing power) as if by a seal, performing favorable or opposite duties according to the command of the vital Archeus. All things are mirrors and certain shining objects; some act only through their contact, smell, taste, and power. Furthermore, each and every remedy remains external with respect to life: thus far they also wash away and drive out an innate or conceived blemish from the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "governor" or vital force that directs the body's functions.</note>. But they are never strong enough to hold back life from its continuous downward flow, nor to suggest new strengths, nor to create or awaken new powers for immortality. This is because the powers of remedies cannot penetrate with their own substance, or be transmuted into our vital matter, in such a way that they are mixed into our primary constituents through growth. For whatever they do, that whole action is occupied around the Archeus of the stomach, the prince of life and the governor of the helm. It is against this rector of the helm, the center of life and the pilot of the "duumvirate" <note>The "duumvirate" refers to the partnership between the stomach and the spleen/vital spirit in Helmontian medicine.</note>, that all diseases also rage primarily, or through <term>deuteropathy</term> <note>A secondary condition or symptom caused by a primary disease elsewhere in the body.</note>. For thus far, not even an ancient, deeply rooted <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagra"</note> breaks out from the depths of the implanted vital spirit in which it is sealed, unless before its onset it causes distress around the mouth of the stomach, and from there violates and excites the total disposition of the entire body; a certain preceding <term>slight fever</term> <note>original: "febricula"</note> usually betrays this approaching gout. Wherefore, thus far also, the remedy and the disease touch one another, and indeed even penetrate. For who has not observed that the scents of spices, merely tasted, immediately refresh those suffering from <term>fainting</term> <note>original: "Lipothymicos"; refers to those experiencing a sudden loss of consciousness or strength</note>? This is not because those scents, mixed with the air, are an addition to the vital aura, as if they substituted a new vital spirit from themselves in place of the lost one. For the restoration of the vital spirit itself from a spice would be a task of more laborious mass than from the blood. Nor is the pleasant scent of a spice similar to the vital spirit produced from the blood; rather, it is because of the gifts innate to the remedy. Likewise, neither do the oils of Cinnamon, Cloves, etc., refresh the vital spirit of the parts by their material connection (for the spirit of life is not nourished by oil), but those things which are pleasing in smell or taste are so many

<column-break/>

mirrors, which by the touch of their breathing or reflection, as if by a dowry gift, refresh and console the burdened spirit of life. For just as the appearances of certain things move nausea, vomiting, lack of appetite, anger, indignation, etc., insofar as they are visual mirrors; so there are "dotal mirrors" <note>Mirrors acting through an endowed or "dowry" power (dotalis) rather than physical substance.</note> which stir the Archeus into peace, tranquility, sleep, joy, and cessation from sorrow, contraction, pain, etc. There are dotal mirrors of this kind which apply a right and orderly concern for their duties in the Archeus, and move it occasionally. Just as, conversely, there are poisons and deadly things, and there are exalted powers of things, which stir up blemish and wasting, and every concussion in the Archeus. And in this, poisons surpass any remedies: because remedies cannot be so connected to life that life is thereby resuscitated or grows into a more perfect nature. Meanwhile, poisons kill the parts, utterly deprive them of innate strength, and draw them entirely into their own likeness, truly transmuting the vital parts. This is granted to no remedies—to renew the defects of the parts into their pristine youth and bring forth immortality. Because remedies are not identified with the Archeus or the ill-affected member by the deepest union. And so, a remedy is not able to provide a stable effect from the union of the agent with the patient, which is otherwise granted to poisons. There are, therefore, "touching mirrors" which, by touch alone, disperse the gift that the Almighty glories to have bestowed upon things torn and dug from the earth, while the solid body of that mirror remains whole. For just as certain things hung around the neck, worn outside, or tied tightly, plainly take away many languors, or at least suspend them; so certain excellent remedies are stable and produce a stable effect from themselves. There are also others which, not so much by the force of a touching and fostering mirror as by a transitory and easy scent, strike down great diseases—namely, those arisen and nourished solely by the indignation of the Archeus.

# IN WORDS, HERBS, AND STONES, THERE IS GREAT VIRTUE.

There are, to be sure, many things which possess a notable flavor, through which—even if they are not digested by the stomach through a passive transformation—they nevertheless separate the pure from the weak, even if the impurity is far removed from them. Insofar as they draw the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal vital force or "master workman" that governs the body's functions in Helmontian medicine.</note>, as if it were bound and obligated by their specific gifts, to bring about such effects. There are, however, certain "mirrors" which I call "touching agents"; these are mostly fixed, lacking odor and taste, and they stir the Archeus—not so much by cleansing or sequestering impurities, as by soothing its pains, disturbances, and the continuous, successive substitution of the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The "morbid ideas" or mental images that the Archeus conceives, which then manifest as physical disease.</note> that nourish the ailment. 

For <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, while disparaging all fixed metallic and mineral remedies, nevertheless—forgetful of his own rule—commends a <term>diaphoretic mercury</term> <note>A preparation of mercury intended to induce sweating and expel toxins.</note> that is exceedingly sweet, yet fixed and unchangeable in fire. And this remedy, although it scorns all the labor of digestion, nevertheless achieves in diseases as much as a Physician or Surgeon could rightly wish. For on its surface plays the sweetness of its <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustibility and soul.</note>; but the mercurial part, covered by the external sulfur, lies hidden and does not work except through a "mirror," shining through the sulfur, and thus affecting the Archeus according to its pleasure. Otherwise, that sweetness of the diaphoretic is of the sulfur drawn from the "fire of Venus" <note>Likely a reference to copper-based preparations or a specific alchemical heat.</note>. This is of the same flavor as the diaphoretic. Wherefore that fire is <term>anodyne</term> <note>Pain-relieving.</note>, harmlessly sleep-inducing, a pacifier of pain; it sedates all anger, pain, motion, disturbance, and the storm of the Archeus. Likewise, it impresses upon the Archeus the will to dissolve 

<column-break/>

all coagulated things. In this respect, it removes every disease occasionally, materially, and <term>enormontically</term> <note>From 'enormon,' a term used by Hippocrates and revived by Van Helmont to describe the vital energy or "impetus" of the body.</note>, which is attributed to any excrements whatsoever. At least here it is obvious that this diaphoretic mercury, remaining indeed undigested in the stomach and not penetrating within (because it persists unchanged, fixed, and stubborn in the form of a powder), causes all the aforementioned effects—not indeed because it performs them effectively or efficiently itself, but because it excites the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>The "dual-governance" of the stomach and spleen, which Van Helmont believed controlled the body's vitality.</note> which performs all things. For these things must happen in this way, not by actual contact with the excrements (which are bound, proscribed, and led out), but by the impression of its "gift" (for stones truly have great virtue) upon the Archeus. The Archeus is the effector of all healing, just as it is the very origin and fountain of diseases; whence, as I have shown above, every disease proceeds immediately from sin from that day forward.

Now, in the preceding treatise, I have sufficiently demonstrated that disease does not exist except in living things, and not only has it chosen a vital body as its proper subject, but furthermore, the intrinsic organ of life itself is the "smith" of the disease and its internal efficient cause. Indeed, I have demonstrated that the matter and the spiritual aura of the Archeus itself is not only the object against which all the "mirrors" of diseases are first sharpened, but it is also the very matter from which, and around which, the boilings, overflows, and disturbances of that "smith" occur, tending toward its own destruction. That is, to be sure, the foolish offspring of sin; for when man turns away from God, he thereafter stupidly turns all things toward his own [destruction].

# BUTLER. 585

...to turn into destruction. But since every thing in nature subsists from matter and an efficient cause alone (which I have also taught most extensively elsewhere in a specific treatise) and a thing in nature is therefore only required to be defined by its immediate and proper matter, and its internal efficient cause (since the entire essence and existence of a thing are nothing but the connection of those same two causes), it is certainly now clear enough that disease is the very vital matter of the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: In Paracelsian medicine, the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</term>, into which a seminal Character, or the idea of a poorly affected Archeus, is born or inserted. Whether meanwhile the Archeus persists in that abomination of its own away from the right path—I mean a harmful **dislocation** <note>original: "exarthrosi"</note>—or whether it has finally scattered those same Ideas of its wrath into some product and thereafter ceased: it is likewise a disease, since it is accidental to this state whether it is cherished or not by an **enormontic** <term>enormontic: A term from Hippocrates, used here to mean the "impelling" or "governing" cause of motion</term> cause. For the Archeus immediately seals an Idea conceived by itself into some excrement of its own body, which it prepares if it has not previously found it ready for itself. From this, and in this, the disease is thereafter able to subsist by itself. In other places, truly, the Archeus wanders not far abroad, outside the matter it has defiled: therefore it either animates the same by continuous nourishment, or it is admitted into the spirit implanted in the organs by a joining of symbols; from there, as if from a citadel, it either continually attacks the strengths of the limbs, or at least sleeps and wakes at fixed periods, because it has poured itself into the vital principle—the guest and steward implanted in life—and has not merely flowed in the spirit of the fluid Archeus. Furthermore, whatever filth is ingested, admitted, or born from an error in living—whether it follows the family of **pre-disposing causes** <note>original: "causæ procatharticæ"</note> or finally of the product—it is all entirely nothing but occasional: namely, at whose importunities the Archeus itself is moved and represents the true scene of the disease. From this it is especially clear that diseases are just as real while they are silent and sleeping as those which happen to be awakened and meditate in their own paroxysm. I had to, of course,

First, I have truly considered the sixfold invasion of disease, and the freedom of seizing its possession: as if first provoked by an **Evil Spirit** <note>original: "Cacodæmone"</note>, it would accordingly also follow the week of creation. 4. Diseases arise most clearly from disturbances, or passions of the mind. And far more hiddenly, they arise from the luxurious and spontaneous disturbances of the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is a central concept in Paracelsian and Helmontian medicine, referring to the internal "vital director" or spiritual force that governs the body's functions.</note> itself, or those drawn in and born from provoking occasional matter. Of these, there is especially a vast harvest, and a numerous army led against us, which has hitherto not been attributed to its own causes because they were unknown. 5. Diseases break out from the inclemency of the Heavens, the injuries of unstable seasons, and the unlucky drafts of local climates, by which an enemy is brought inside, and a guest is admitted so that he may make himself a family member. 6. Finally, disease enters through external violence, namely wounds, bone-breaks, falls, bruises, burns, frostbite, the stings of asps, etc.
But at least all these things lie in wait for a single life, and its protector the Archeus, from whence they derive their beginning. Therefore, by constantly aiming at unity, we shall contemplate God as the single, most glorious source of life, the Presider, and the sole permitter of any diseases whatsoever: so also shall we worship Him more amply as the giver of the remedy in the unity of His own pattern, according to the occasion.
Wherefore, although I have written elsewhere in passing about <term>Arcana</term> <note>Secret, highly potent alchemical remedies believed to act directly on the vital spirit.</note>, each of which individually mows down almost all diseases with a single scythe—namely, through the separation and cleansing of superfluity—nevertheless, such secrets, as they are prepared with the greatest difficulty, and indeed in secret, ought to remain for all time in the possession of the <term>symmystas</term> <note>Initiates or fellow-priests of a mystery.</note>. Thus, a healing instituted by their help does not so much regard the diseases immediately, as it primarily regards either the preceding occasional cause of the same, or at least the subsequent product of the disease. Likewise, such secret remedies are very scarce, and the greater part of mortals are deprived of them and left destitute of hope. And so it does not seem to me that the infinite Goodness of God willed to be communicated and notified through such a meager remedy. For which reason I conjecture that the time is

<column-break/>

at hand in which Almighty Goodness will manifest to His faithful a hitherto unknown science and essence of diseases. But the aforementioned Secrets He has revealed only to a very few, solely for the glory of His power, lest the commerce of the world otherwise perish. For it is not otherwise credible that the Divine Goodness, after this intimate essence of diseases has been detected, would thereafter hide from the faithful the remedies that are the dowries of His unity, or that the cure of diseases should be deferred to Secrets alone. It is therefore opportune for me to investigate a remedy which, with a single effort, looks toward the "tree" of the corrupted Archeus, in whatever way it has been altered. Since nature is a whole thing before it is a corrupted thing. Therefore life, and the Archeus, insofar as they are simply the cause of being itself, are older than the vice conceived within them. For just as life itself is the immediate cause of any indispositions: so indeed the speculation of the healing and reintegration of a life altered or weakened, without any inconvenience or burden, is more principal, more intimate, rightfully prior, and more noble than the healing which is perfected through Secrets or through the most excellent cleansers. For such Secrets, although they often look more toward and cut off the prior occasion: it is nevertheless secondary to the healing which proceeds from internal causes primarily altered and affected: and which therefore first and most principally require their own calming, by a natural indication, and the most important of all. Indeed, natures themselves have been known from of old as the healers of diseases: just as, under the veiled cloud of an etymology, the "spirit making an impetus" <note>original: "spiritus impetum facientis"</note> was venerated as the vital nature, the maker and procreator of any diseases. Yet from the days of Hippocrates to Galen, and afterwards, the speculation of diseases has remained neglected. Therefore, whatever I have said about the method of healing—by pacifying and calming the Archeus, namely by removing its alienations—has remained thin and impassable until now.

# B U T L E R.

Therefore, by primarily contemplating the <term>Synarthrosis</term><note>A joining or harmony of parts</note>, the peace, quiet, and docility of the <term>Archeus</term><note>The vital life force or internal chemist that governs the body's health in Paracelsian medicine</note>, I will first explain myself through several stories. A certain Irishman named *Butler*, who was once a great man at the court of James, King of England, was being held in the prison of Vilvoorde Castle. He took pity on a certain Baillius, a Franciscan monk and a very famous Anglo-French preacher, who was also imprisoned there. This monk had a terrifying case of <term>Erysipelas</term><note>A severe bacterial skin infection, often called 'St. Anthony's Fire'</note> in his arm. One evening, when the patient was almost in despair, Butler quickly dipped a certain small stone into a spoonful of almond milk and immediately withdrew it. He then said to the prison guard:

> Give this drink to that monk, and no matter how little of it he takes, he will be healthy within at least one short hour.

And so it happened, to the great amazement of the guard; the patient was unaware of how such sudden health had flowed into him, as he did not know he had consumed anything medicinal. For his left arm, which had been immensely swollen before, subsided so quickly that it could hardly be distinguished from the other. The following morning, having been asked by certain nobles, I came to Vilvoorde so that I might be a witness to these acts. I thus formed a friendship with *Butler*. Immediately afterward, I saw an old washerwoman who had suffered from an intolerable <term>hemicrania</term><note>A severe migraine affecting one side of the head</note> for about sixteen years; she was also cured instantly in my presence. Truly, he merely dipped that same stone into a spoonful of olive oil and immediately wiped the stone clean by licking it, then replaced it in his breast-case. He then poured that spoonful of oil into a small flask of oil. He ordered a single drop of it to be rubbed onto the head of the aforementioned old woman. She was immediately cured from that moment and remained healthy for several years, as I can attest. I was stunned, as if I had become another Midas <note>The king whose touch turned everything to gold; here, the author feels overwhelmed by the "golden" miracle</note>. But he, laughing at me, said:

> My dearest friend, unless you reach the point where you can cure any disease with a single remedy, you will remain a mere apprentice, no matter how old you become.

I was easily won over, because I had already learned of the <term>Arcana</term><note>Secret, powerful remedies</note> of Paracelsus

<column-break/>

and was now made more certain of them by sight and hope. But I freely confessed that this new method of healing was unusual and unknown to me. I mentioned, therefore, that a young prince of our court, the Viscount of Ghent, brother of the Prince d'Espinoy, of the House of Melun, was completely bedridden with <term>podagra</term><note>Gout, specifically in the feet</note>. He lay thereafter on only one side, miserable and deformed by many <term>nodes</term><note>Hardened lumps or swellings caused by gout</note>. Butler then took my right hand and said:

> Do you want me to cure that young man? I will cure him for your sake.

But I replied:

> He is of such stubbornness that he would rather die than drink even a single medicine.

> So be it, said *Butler*, for I require nothing else than that he touch the tip of his tongue to the stone you see, every morning. For after three weeks, let him wash the painful and painless nodes daily with his own urine, and you will see him soon thereafter healed and walking about in safety. Go and joyfully announce to him what I have said.

So I returned happily to Brussels and reported what *Butler* had said. But the Lord replied:

> Ha! Tell *Butler* that if he restores me as you have said, I will give him as much as he asks. Ask the price, and I will gladly place the deposit in a secure account for his guarantee.

When I reported this to *Butler* the following day, he grew incensed and said:

> That prince is insane and miserable. Therefore, I shall never help him. For I am not in need of his money, nor do I yield to him, nor am I his inferior.

Indeed, I was never able to persuade him to perform what he had previously promised. Because of this, I began to doubt whether the preceding things I had seen were like dreams. Meanwhile, it happened that a friend, the master and owner of a glass furnace in Antwerp, who was very obese, humbly asked *Butler* to be freed from the burden of his fat. *Butler* offered him a small fragment of that stone to lick once, or to touch quickly with the tip of his tongue every morning. And within three weeks, I saw his tunics...

And immediately that limb was restored to free movement with its former strength, beyond all hope. We all wondered at the miracle of such a sudden outcome. In the evening, therefore, on going to bed, she rubbed four drops of that oil on the afflicted part, and in the morning no trace of the former evil appeared. So much so that she, who previously could hardly go to the market for one day, set out that same morning to the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mother of God in Laken <note>A district in Brussels famous for its Marian shrine</note>, and returned briskly, and brought me water from the spring of St. Anne, located a long distance from there. Hearing this, a certain widowed lady, who had been afflicted in both arms for many months so that she could never lift her hand upward, was restored to full health in a single evening by a few drops of that oil, and remained so. Then I asked Butler why so many women were healed immediately, while I, though I struggled most fiercely with death itself, surrounded by pains in all my joints and organs, felt no relief? He asked, however, what disease I had labored under? And when he understood that poison had given rise to the disease, he said: "Because the cause came from the inside out, the oil ought to have been taken internally, or the stone dipped [in a drink]." For the pain fostered internally was not topical or external. I also observed that this oil gradually lost its healing energy. Because the stone, dipped in it only superficially, had not changed the oil thoroughly through its core, but had only blessed it with a fleeting sprinkling of its scent. Indeed, that stone presented the appearance of fused sea salt to the eyes and tongue; and it is well known to the fates <note>i.e., it is a known fact of nature</note> that salt is not intimately mixed with oil. Butler also healed a well-known Abbess, who for eighteen years had held her right arm swollen with an unusual loss of movement, and her fingers extended and immobile, solely by the touch of her tongue to the little stone.

# BUTLER.

For many witnesses of these wonders immediately suspected some hidden sorcery <note>original: *veneficium*</note> and a diabolical pact. For the common people have long had the habit that whatever their ignorance makes them ashamed not to know, they refer to the deceits of an evil spirit <note>original: *cacodæmonis*</note> as a subterfuge for their lack of knowledge. But I could not incline toward that view, because the remedies applied were natural, possessing nothing beyond an unusual potency. For no ritual, words, or any other suspicious thing was required. Nor is it permitted, according to the human power of understanding, to attribute the Glory of God, displayed in nature, to an evil spirit. For none of those women had sought help from Butler as if he were in any way suspected of necromancy <note>original: *nigromantia*; the practice of communicating with the dead or black magic</note>. Indeed, the cures were first attempted mockingly, without faith or confidence. Nevertheless, the ease and speed of this kind of healing will remain suspicious to many for a long time to come. For the fickle and idle mind of the masses is always ready to judge difficult and unusual things in the same tone; because of its weakness, it is therefore flaccid. It more willingly consecrates such great kindness of restorations to diabolical fraud than to divine goodness—to the Creator, Lover, Savior, Restorer of human nature, and Father of the poor. And this is true not only of the common people, but even of the learned who follow them, who investigate the beginnings of healing incorrectly, being not yet instructed or observing a common and stupid rule. Because they always think like children, never having stepped over their mother’s threshold, fearful at every story. Truly, those who have hitherto not known that the entire scope of diseases is contained within the "life-spirit" <note>original: *spiritum vitæ*; the vital force animating the body</note> making its attack—or if, having read my studies in passing hereafter, they impress this momentum of healing upon themselves—they will nonetheless, because they were accustomed from the very start of their studies to the precepts of the humorists <note>term: *humoristæ*; followers of Galenic medicine who believed health depended on the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, easily fall away from me at last and leap back to the accustomed and ancient dogmas of the Schools.

> *The jar will long preserve the odor*
> *with which it was once steeped when new.*
> <note>A quote from Horace (Epistles 1.2.69), suggesting that early education leaves a permanent impression.</note>

They will easily return again to the vexations of the "down-lying humors." But I, by investigating more closely and being unwilling to attribute the benefits of God to the devil, found first of all that all things in nature consist of an invisible seed <note>original: *semine invisibili*</note>. I say they arise, are sustained, and are governed by a being which first began from a formative imagination <note>original: *imaginante libidine*</note> or a transmitted power, and stands thereafter through the whole duration of its existence. They then become visible, or "this specific thing," only by the clothing and apparatus of the bodies joined to them. Moreover, I have taught that diseases, by a stronger reason, arise from a more invisible seed. Therefore, the "disease-idea" <note>term: *Idea morbifica*; the spiritual or formal blueprint of a sickness that must be destroyed to effect a cure</note> is what must be fought, abolished, and extinguished. Indeed, a sympathetic remedy <note>term: *remedium sympatheticum*; a cure based on the "sympathy" or natural connection between objects, such as treating a weapon to heal the wound it caused</note> has recently been revealed which heals from a distance. On the other hand, he had seen several experiments made by honest men. And so, she thereafter believed that natural causes, although unknown to us, operate in the aforementioned sympathetic healing. Which, nevertheless, not yet being sufficiently understood by some, is still—even now—rejected as one of Satan’s enticements, using this argument: A natural agent, in order to act, must be applied and brought close to the patient; but a sympathetic remedy does not need to be close to the patient. Therefore, a sympathetic remedy is not a natural agent.

I respond: If it is understood that a natural agent must touch the patient immediately—by the "immediacy of the substance"—upon which it acts most closely; yet remotely, by the mediation of other intervening bodies through which that action is communicated to a distant object. The Major premise is granted. For it is enough that the agent touches the patient, or its proper and distant object, immediately by the "immediacy of its power" <note>The author distinguishes between physical contact and the "power" or "virtue" of a substance traveling through the air or other media</note>; and therefore, the Minor premise is then denied. Because the sympathetic remedy must be present immediately, by the immediacy of its substance, to that subject in which the action is first received: but not to the affected part, in which it is received secondarily and ultimately, by the mediation of the assumed organs, wandering or stretched across the interval. For there is no fire in the hand of the one warmed, nor is the Sun of Heaven inside the bedroom. 

In this matter, however, it has become well known today that sympathetic forces are equal to <term>astral influences</term>. Namely, that not only the air, but covered rocks and opaque bodies are subjects and organs capable of this action, no less than of astral influence. For nothing stands in the way of sublunary things to prevent God from being able, or willing, to have made them somewhat equal in this regard. Just as the character of a grandfather shines forth not in the son, but sometimes in a late grandson. Sound, too, may penetrate far through bodies that are adequately closed, etc. Therefore, if

He who endowed His creations according to His pleasure. For it was free for Him to hand down His gifts even to the most abject things, nor can a Christian translate such gifts to the devil without punishment. 

Nor do I speculate on sympathetic matters in this place merely to believe that **Butler’s Little Stone** acts by sympathetic force. And so, it regards the peace and quiet of the Archeus in its simplicity.

The antidote of Orvieto <note>original: "Orvietani"; a famous polypharmaceutical electic or "theriac" used against poisons, named after the city of Orvieto</note>, even when a poison has been taken that rages to the point of convulsions, so thoroughly tramples down all anxieties and imminent fainting spells that it is as if no venom had ever been admitted within. For just as disease is a defect of nature—specifically of the transgressing **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "chemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note>—so the remedy is of pure Divine goodness, which, having descended into nature, must both compensate for and utterly overcome every defect. Therefore, the remedy is far more powerful and concentrated than the transgression; thus it is smaller in quantity and far swifter in its delay. That breadth and nobility of power does not concern a superiority acquired gradually through growth or maturity, but rather a present and effective majesty. Through this majesty, the medicinal thing itself, unfolded by its endowed virtue, releases and restrains the Archeus from its obstructions and furies; at the same time, it impresses an eminent excellence of the helping faculty for which it was created. This is its manner and speed of operation.

Furthermore, regarding remedies of such great goodness and their efficacy: first, it is clear that the little stone of *Butler*, even if lightly dipped into a single spoonful of oil, and if that spoonful of oil is poured into a jug—indeed, into a whole cask of oil—the entire volume will become a remedy. In the same way, a pestilential odor infects a whole vessel with its contagion. If the odor of a sympathetic remedy, sprinkled on a cloth with a few drops of blood, can assist a wound, a bone fracture <note>original: "ossifragio"</note>, or even an ulcer, and calm the entire Archeus agitated from a distance, what wonder is it if the remedy does this when applied to the sick person themselves? Indeed, the remedies of Surgeons do not heal otherwise than by mere attraction to the wounded part. For plasters or oils do not enter into the vital composition of the depths, nor into the nourishment of the wounded part. In topical ulcers, whether innate or formed on the spot—such as **Cancer**, **Lupus** <note>literally "the wolf"; a term used for various skin-eating diseases</note>, etc.—the mere attraction of a powerful remedy is enough to extinguish the virus arising there from the indignant Archeus.

<column-break/>

The judgment is the same and equal concerning abscesses, excrescences, sores, and marks fixed in the place itself, even if they were born elsewhere first but were brought down and finally deposited in that spot. Because the external smearing of the remedy, by a certain consequence of touch, tames the whole Archeus—not unlike how the tooth of a rabid dog, even if wiped perfectly in the wind, nevertheless sometimes brings on rabies. In this way, the remedies of our little stone heal internal affections. Yet they vibrate their effects more and faster if they are taken *by mouth* <note>original: "oretenus"</note>. It is no different than how certain poisons are harmless unless they are brought into contact with open skin. But if remedies of this kind touch the tongue even in passing, it is no wonder that they immediately affect the whole Archeus with their powerful benevolence, and settle the straying Archeus from its fury, soothing it from every exacerbation.

Since that little stone is of the nature of salt, it is in no way dissolved by oil, nor does anything materially depart from it to be received by the oil in which it is dipped, except for a light odor—such as the odor of a pestilential footprint in a time of plague. And it seemed to me that there was a prelude to this little stone in the Holy Scriptures: -> *The perfumer shall make ointments of sweetness, and his works shall not be consumed.* <- <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 38:8</note> That is, even if the stone is dipped in oil, the center of its medicinal virtue is hardly diminished. Therefore, if this excellent remedy is taken internally, it not only changes the blood into a medicine similar to a balsam, but the very excrements of the man (namely the *urine* <note>original: "lotium"</note>) remain tinged with its super-eminent goodness. It is no different than how the eggs of a hen taste of the *buckwheat* <note>original: "fagopyrum"</note> she has eaten, and the *urine* of a nursing infant smells of *anise* if the nurse has taken oil of anise *by mouth*. And just as *urine* smells of eaten *asparagus*, so too the *urine*, by its own washing or anointing, heals every disease settled in the habit of the body. So great, truly, is the goodness of God, that a single little stone suffices for many myriads, so that the Physician may not excuse himself regarding the poor by complaining about the weight of the expenses. # BUTLER.

All diseases are cured by a single remedy, namely by anointing, or by the touch of the tongue, or by taste alone. This is because the tongue is similar to exposed skin, especially if the saliva following the contact is immediately swallowed. That the power of this remedy is so great must be demonstrated not only by its effect on poisons—and thus by its likeness to the pestilential air <note>original: "pestilentis auræ"; referring to the "miasma" or infectious atmosphere believed to carry the plague</note>—but because a remedy ought to be far more powerful than any evil if it is to overcome it, and indeed quickly, and thus it ought to express, to some extent, the seal of Divine Goodness. Therefore, from the indication of Philosophy itself, I immediately conjectured that this remedy primarily requires that it be a body once resuscitated and once destroyed, and then, as if from resurrection, in some way glorified. Thus, it is no longer thereafter capable of being defiled by the vices of sublimation <note>technical chemical processes</note> or by evil arts. From this it follows that it must be a thousand times more powerful than any pestilential poison and operative in a more absolute manner. For while the poison of the Plague is simple and resides in the bodily aura—and though the pestilential poison ferments more easily due to its human affinity <note>original: "symbolum humanum"</note>—it is not therefore a more powerful virus. For a virus produces a virus according to the rule and ferment of the original poison, but it cannot exalt the power of its product above itself. But in a remedy rising again from death, the beneficial goodness of its simple nature is increased a thousandfold; it is diffused by the thin scent of contact, expanded into the medium, and immediately commands the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: In Paracelsian medicine, the internal "alchemist" or vital force of the body that directs health and digestion</term> of the subject, so that it composes itself according to peace and virtue. In this way, it introduces the *Arcanum* <note>a secret, powerful medicinal essence</note>, the foster-child of its own power, which is the true hope and joy of the *Archeus*, existing truly and standing above life itself. Finally, I considered that this remedy does not belong to the vegetable kingdom, inasmuch as that which is easily born possesses too fleeting a lineage, and therefore such things are hardly reborn through Art. For like animals, they easily die under the hand of the artist; yet they hardly 

<column-break/>

rise again from death, since under the trial of fire they either perish entirely and lose their former strengths, or if they seem to rise again, they are rather new entities, entirely cut off from the orbit of their predecessors and parents. Furthermore, whatever Paracelsus promises concerning his four *Arcana* in the *Archidoxes* <note>referring to Paracelsus's work *Archidoxa*, or "Concerning the Arch-Secrets"</note>—that they have a power above the elemental and almost infinite—as for the first, which supposes a *homunculus* <note>a "little man" created through alchemy</note>, it is unspeakable, sodomitical, diabolical, and for no reason to be mentioned. The remaining three are Chemical, to which the promise of extending oneself even unto the tenth generation does not apply. But I speak in this place of a pigment <note>or "tincture"</note> whose works shall not be consumed; nor shall there be a disease or poison resisting it, or as the Text has it: *There shall be no medicine of destruction upon the earth, and the Almighty made all the nations of the earth healthy.* <note>A paraphrase of Wisdom of Solomon 1:14</note> Upon deeper inspection, all diseases, because they flow from the fountain of the *Archeus*, yield either because of suspended amulets and charms <note>original: "periapta"</note>, or because of baths, ointments, and plasters. Of these, not even the smallest anointing occurs with the diseased body; rather, only the scent is offered, or if they are taken internally, they are digested like drugs. Yet they are either soon transmuted in the stomach and immediately put on foreign flavors and types of qualities, so that they fully cast off every lot of their former life—unless they prefer to be judged as disagreeable or poisonous. Indeed, they are then so truly and utterly transmuted that they leave behind the likeness of their former *entelechy* <term>entelechy: the realized potential or "soul-form" of a thing</term>, or are thought to have scarcely possessed it. For this reason, they are taken in great quantities, so that some tiny bit might seem to breathe more deeply into the man. At what great cost this is done, those know who have sometimes discovered that "to live medically is to live most miserably." Therefore, of the things taken in, hardly anything reflects the original being; and if it does, woe to the one taking it. Wherefore, if any power was in the drug, it was surely there before it laid down its own nature and original being. It failed, to be sure, as soon as its scent...

This kind of sympathetic remedy has come forth, I say, first by God's permission and now recently, in wounds, so that from external and more apparent things, we might be led by the hand of our senses to the solace of internal and more hidden diseases. For which reason I passed over to the lineage of minerals, enriched by the long flow of ages. I had to believe, being admonished by the Sacred [Scriptures], that the virtue of stones is great. # B U T L E R.

I recalled that every disease is fashioned and governed by the vital *Archeus* <note>The "Archeus" is a term used by Paracelsus and Van Helmont to describe the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the body's functions.</note>, which is to say, by life itself. I had not yet sufficiently considered that a wandering or straying life could be conquered and subdued by the mere quantity of a remedy. Therefore, I soon reconsidered what I had said before: namely, that the tooth of a mad dog, or of vipers and adders—even if the saliva were first wiped away on a garment—could still kill by touch alone, far beyond any physical quantity of the venom itself. I also considered a certain liquid known to me; if a hand is lightly anointed with it and dried, and then touches a man's chin, the hair of the beard, eyebrows, and the entire head will fall out shortly thereafter. For if poisons of this kind, by a very slight touch, can extinguish life—and even the vegetative life of the hair (which not infrequently grows even after death)—then surely powerful remedies, which restrain the errors of life by touch alone, could smear and pacify the *Archeus* by a simple shortcut, without any perceptible quantity. I was slow to grasp this, partly because I was hindered by the aforementioned errors of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university medical authorities, such as Galenists, whom Van Helmont often critiqued.</note>, and partly because I saw that if a single grain of poison could kill, a drachm would do so more powerfully and swiftly. For I had not yet sufficiently weighed the fact that all diseases proceed from a wandering or angry *Archeus*; thus, a powerful remedy possesses a super-eminent and extraordinary goodness, by which it restores the errors of an enraged and inflamed *Archeus*. Much less had I considered that a powerful medicine ought to be admitted within as if the *Archeus* were unaware of it. Otherwise, if the *Archeus* suspects that its own turbulence of indignation and alteration is being attacked by remedies, or that its downfall is being attempted, it will certainly fall into a fury; it will not admit helpful things, as it is already straying by its own error and will rise up into a greater heat and stubbornness to build its own disease-causing Idea <note>The "Idea" here refers to a morbid mental or spiritual blueprint that the Archeus follows to create a disease.</note>. Therefore, I approached the remedies of *Butler* by the touch of the tip of the tongue alone, or by a weight of half a grain. For the little stone <note>original: "lapillum"</note> of *Butler*, and

<column-break/>

such a powerful and ferment-like remedy, I have called in our native tongue *Drif*, for lack of a better name. This term denotes sand, or virgin earth; likewise, in sentient beings, it signifies a simultaneous repelling of animosity, just as boiling sand shakes out whatever foreign matter has been inserted into it. Therefore, 1. I shall state the requirements of *Drif*, and then I shall declare the method of its composition, as far as is permitted to a *Philosopher* <note>An "Alchemical Philosopher" or Adept.</note>, lest I cast roses before swine. 1. First, as I said, *Drif* requires that it be a certain metallic body. This is because its long endurance signifies constancy rather than rapid corruption. By the long favor of Heaven, it has completed its circuit of generation. It seems directed by a particular destination from the *Almighty* for the relief of the wretched and the poor. 2. *Drif* is not one of those unusual secrets <note>original: "arcanis"</note> bestowed by God only upon a very few Adepts, His certain chosen disciples. For our *Drif* seems intended solely for the solace of the poor. 3. *Drif* requires that it be from a natural body, a participant in metallic kindness, but one which has first been made compliant and opened through death. This is not with the extinction of its powers, like the corpse of one who died naturally, but rather, while retaining the benefits of its endowments, it is unlocked by the *Artist*, freed from its bars, and as if resuscitated: indeed, it is a thing enriched and entirely new, rising fresh from the fire. 4. Thus, it must have risen as if from death, entirely volatile and spiritual, or be sublimated two or three times with other things added to it. 5. But because volatile things perish quickly, are scattered, and dissolve even before they are admitted within to penetrate and bring forth their excellencies from their bosom, or thus be able to pacify the *Archeus*, *Drif* therefore requires that after its volatility is attained, it be connected to some friendly body by which it may be held, so that in its entirety it may be communicable to the human body.

This is a frequent occurrence, seen everywhere and admitted by learned men. Yet the more "sharp-nosed" <note>meaning: overly critical or skeptical</note> critics hesitate, because they cannot understand how much larger things can exit through such a tiny passage. For some excuse the matter by saying that although they seem to be rejected through vomiting, they were never actually admitted inside; they consider them, I say, to be mockeries and delusions of the eyes <note>original: "effascinationes"</note>. They claim these objects appear anew as they exit and are brought in from a distance. They do admit the objects themselves are real. For the insects are alive, the metals can be melted, and the wood burns; they all emerge gradually of their own accord or are pulled out by hand. Martin Delrio <note>A famous Jesuit demonologist (1551–1608)</note> and his followers admit they are carried inside and are truly what they appear to be, and thus they refute the previous opinion. As to the manner of entry and exit, they assert that those things are first crushed by the devil into a very fine powder, then restored inside the body to their original integrity, shape, and condition. Or for pieces of wood and leather to be ground down so many times and again be restored to their original state. For in Brussels, in the year 1599, I saw that an ox, having consumed three types of herbs, vomited up a dragon with an eel-like tail, a leathery body, and a serpent’s head, no smaller than a partridge. The method by which nature might do this is unknown. Equally unknown is the method by which Satan might do it. Therefore, those who refer a work of nature to the devil gain nothing. Whether they truly sin, let others see to it. For at the very least, it was an invention of immense laziness to have referred everything we do not understand to the devil. I find, indeed, a <term>penetration of dimensions</term><note>A philosophical/physical concept where two solid bodies seem to occupy the same space or pass through one another without a visible opening.</note> contiguous to nature, though it is not ordinary. Nor would I wish the devil to be invoked to satisfy our questions through a rash attribution of powers.

<margin>7.</margin>
There is the story of a Polish peasant, recently seen by the son of Master Ericius Puteanus <note>A famous Dutch humanist and philologist (1574–1646).</note>. The rustic man had attempted to open an ulcer in his throat with a short knife, which he carelessly swallowed; he eventually gave it back <note>i.e., it passed out of his body</note> through the right side of his abdomen with much pus, and after many anxieties, he survived unharmed. Likewise at Vilvoorde in the year 1636, a peasant known to me, wishing to fatten a cow, gave her a drink daily in which he had cooked vegetables with bran. Eventually she grew thinner by the day and began to limp in her right leg; when the cow was slaughtered, his wife’s short knife was found, twisted into its boxwood handle, hidden between the ribs and the shoulder blade. For the peasant woman, while chopping turnips, had left the knife among the vegetables, and the cow had swallowed it while drinking. Likewise, Ambroise Paré <note>The famous French royal surgeon (c. 1510–1590).</note> reports of a certain man whom robbers had forced to swallow a knife, which he later returned safely through an <term>aposteme</term><note>An abscess or swelling filled with pus.</note> in his side. Alexander Benedictus—

Likewise, Antonio Benivieni <note>An early pioneer of pathological anatomy.</note> records that a Tuscan woman had swallowed a copper needle, which she excreted healthily three years later near her navel. Valerius de Taranta tells of a Venetian girl (perhaps the same one) who expelled a needle three fingers long with her urine. A certain Capuchin from Liège <note>original: "Eburo"</note>, named Bullonius, with the surname Hampteau, drank a huge spider which he had seen fall into the chalice during the Sacrifice of the Mass; he drank it alive with great aversion of soul. Within a few days, an inflammation arose in his right thigh, and under the first sign of pus, he returned the spider from there, whole (though dead). A young merchant of Antwerp, while playing in Venice with an unripened ear of barley in his mouth, swallowed it in a great fear of suffocation. After three weeks, an abscess appeared on his left side above the waist, and finally that same ear of grain, now yellow in color, was extracted whole with the pus. He himself escaped unharmed. In the works of Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician.</note>, one reads of a student restored by him who passed an ear of grain through his ribs. Writers also commemorate that a fetus, sometimes dead and consumed in the womb, has sent out its bones across the uterus and abdomen, through the navel, and sometimes through the anus. Many such things occur here and there among trustworthy authors. That is, without a wound, knives were transmitted through those membranes. This is equivalent to a "penetration of dimensions" performed in nature, without the help of the Devil. <margin>8.</margin>
A pregnant woman was seized by a <term>longing</term> <note>appetitus - a specific medical concept of pregnancy cravings believed to affect the fetus</note> for eating black shellfish. She ate several greedily, even devouring the raw shells after crunching them twice or thrice with her teeth. Then soon, within the hour, she gave birth to a healthy and full-term infant, but with those same half-chewed shells, and wounded in the abdomen. Therefore, the shells, without any opening of the membranes, immediately penetrated the stomach, the womb, and the afterbirth; or else new shells were generated upon the fetus. But this latter cannot be true. For they were real fragments of shellfish, not merely shaped in imitation of them. Furthermore, appetite is not directed toward the unknown: therefore the appetite for eating shellfish was not the infant's, but the woman's. Thus it was not necessary for new shells to be generated around the fetus. For they were craved by the mother so that they might become nourishment for her, and not for the fetus. Otherwise, by the same argument of identity, whatever things are craved would always be generated around the fetus; and since they would be in no way digested by it, they would always either remain as residues around the fetus or rot in that same place.

<column-break/>

Which is false in both ways: for if it rotted, it would cause a miscarriage; if it were the object craved, it would regularly be found preserved there. Indeed, the fetus is nourished only through the umbilical cord: wherefore those external shells were neither desired by the fetus nor profitable to it. And consequently, they were not made anew by nature for that purpose: but were sent down to the fetus insofar as the appetite was of the womb. Appetite is always directed by its end; but the pregnant woman craves shellfish, not shells, nor even that the shellfish should remain as a whole animal in its original state, in which it is useless to the mother and does not satisfy her craving. Therefore, she had much less occasion for generating new and useless shells around the fetus. Finally, however it is taken, the appetite was not for shells broken twice or thrice. For if the shellfish had been cut out from the shells, she would have chewed the shellfish themselves, leaving the shells behind. Thus the accompaniment and crushing of the shells was accidental to the appetite. I truly believe that just as desire, terror, etc., generate **seminal Ideas**, which the hand of the pregnant woman sends down to the fetus and depicts in a fixed place: so the joy of finding that which was craved leads that very thing to the fetus. In this way, surely, the sadness of a swallowed knife, the horror of a swallowed spider, or a swallowed ear of grain, drives these same things through the membranes of a wound, which are powerless to stop them, without causing death. These things concern objects cast in, entering by the ordinary force of nature, beyond any suspicion of <term>diabolical cooperation</term> <note>the theory that such strange events required the help of the devil</note>. # CONCERNING INJECTED THINGS

A woman saw a soldier whose right arm had been torn off by an iron cannonball during the siege of Ostend <note>The Siege of Ostend (1601–1604) was one of the longest and bloodiest sieges in history.</note>, and he was still carrying that bloody limb around. Soon after, she gave birth to a daughter who was missing an arm—specifically the right one—whose shoulder, still bloody, had to be healed by a Surgeon. She married a merchant in Amsterdam named Hoochcamer <note>original: "Hoochcamer"</note> and was still alive in the year 1638. Furthermore, the right arm was nowhere to be found; no bones or any putrefaction appeared into which the arm might have wasted away in that short hour. Yet, before she had seen the soldier, the fetus had two arms. The torn-off arm could not simply have been annihilated. Therefore, while the womb was closed, the arm was removed. As to who might have removed it naturally, and where it was taken, trivial reasons certainly do not suffice for such a portent or paradox. I am not the one to say these things <note>The author is being cautious about attributing this directly to magic or the divine</note>. I will say only this: the arm was not removed or torn away by Satan. Furthermore, it is a lesser task for a severed arm to be carried elsewhere than it was to tear the arm from the whole body without causing death. 

A merchant's wife known to us, when she heard that thirteen people were to be beheaded in one morning (this happened in Antwerp during the time of the Duke of Alva <note>The Duke of Alba, a Spanish governor known for his harsh "Council of Blood" in the Netherlands</note>), and being led by disordered cravings common to pregnant women, she decided to watch the executions. I find, at least, that human nature does not abhor the "penetration of dimensions" <term>penetration of dimensions: a philosophical concept where two physical bodies occupy the same space</term>, since it is very frequent in the "seeds" of things.

spirit. But once nature was corrupted, that authority of the spirit over the body perished. And so, in the manner of beasts, the woman brings forth thereafter. <margin>11.</margin> there is an energy for penetrating bodies, but it is not subject to human force, art, or will. Therefore, the internal and daily progress of seeds in generations requires a body to penetrate itself through condensation. This is utterly impossible for a craftsman to do. Let us grant that there are pores in water; yet these cannot contain fourteen times as much of their own whole self. It is therefore ordinary in nature for some parts of water to penetrate themselves into one place. And the seeds do this 

<margin>12.</margin> by the power of a certain spirit called the Archeus <term>Archeus: the vital principle or "internal chemist" that governs life processes in Paracelsian medicine</term>. Properly speaking, the Archeus does not imitate an incantation, but incantations follow the rule prescribed by the Archeus, insofar as he works far differently than bodies work upon each other. As in "uterine affections" <note>Hysterical or womb-related disorders</note>, the nerves are stretched spontaneously, tendons leap out of place and snap back again. Likewise, bones are dislocated with no visible mover, the neck rises swollen to the height of the chin, the lungs are blocked from air: unlucky poisons are born within, and the blood plays at strange appearances of filth. How much the penetrations of bodies...

## 607

Regarding the body, our Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is a term popularized by Paracelsus referring to the vital internal force or "master workman" that governs the life functions of an organism.</note> absorbs bodies <margin>13.</margin> into itself, so that they become as if they were spirits. For example, *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid; literally "strong water."</note> by its spirit makes copper, iron, or silver—which are by nature flowing and opaque—so transparent that they cannot be seen; and through filter paper <note>original: *charta emporetica*, used by apothecaries for straining.</note>, which otherwise does not let even the finest powder pass, it carries the metal through, while it still essentially remains in the form of a metal. However, this is not to say that the likeness of the penetration of dimensions fits uniformly with the proposed example of the metal. Because (as I have said) the reasons do not fit such a great paradox, where I willingly acknowledge a mode that is, *from the prior* <note>Indemonstrable by logic or cause alone.</note>, indemonstrable. Just as no one can know in what way the Idea impressed upon seeds shapes, directs, and disposes its constituents. Therefore, we shall hunt for the same thing *from the posterior* <note>Demonstrable by observing the effects or results.</note>. First, let it be established that the devil has no right or power over us against our will, unless by the specific permission <margin>14.</margin> of the Lord. For do you not know that we are the temple of God? and that the kingdom of God itself dwells within us? This matter must be supported from its origin. First, therefore, it is a matter of faith that we are the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit; that the Holy Trinity makes its dwelling place with the Just man. That the delights of God are with the sons of men, to whom He gave the power to become sons of God. Moreover, baptized children, infants, and the just—theirs is the kingdom of Heaven, the fitting temple of God. Yet children are killed by enchantments more easily than others. Therefore, it must be that this happens from some free faculty: since the excellence of the Christian (especially the just) concludes that the devil has no right of entering, or <margin>15.</margin> introducing his own means. Since it is the same to him whether he has harmed through a medium or through himself. There is, therefore, another power of enchantment far beyond the devil: and it is accordingly natural and free. Over a just man, no one has command. But if the power of enchanting were free to the devil, it would be equally free for him to kill by knife or hammer. And thus no one would be immune. Indeed, if the devil could, he would not wish to enter the skin of the just,

<column-break/>

on account of the divine presence of the Kingdom of Heaven. For the devil perceives God present in the just man in a different way than anywhere else. This is the cause of his everlasting hatred toward us. Therefore, he does not enter, even if he could, but circles about like a roaring Lion. Therefore, the Witch <note>original: *Saga*, a female practitioner of magic or a sorceress.</note>, through a natural being, imaginatively forms a free, natural, and harmful Idea. This, Satan is unable to form. This is because the formation of Ideas requires the Image of God and free power: and for that reason, Witches work by a natural virtue, no less against the just and the innocent than against wicked men. Indeed, since enchantments infect children more easily than adults, and women more easily than vigorous men; it signifies a certain natural power, limited to enchantment, which is easily countered by a combative and robust mind. The devil, therefore, offers his clients filth or poisons, so that he may fermentally connect the Ideas formed in their Imaginative faculty. Indeed, he preserves that Ideal poison <note>original: *virus Ideale*.</note>, lest it be scattered by the wind or destroyed by decay when covered by earth. He carries this poison locally near the object to be enchanted; yet to apply it, or to carry it into a man, he is in no way able. And so, next, the human also releases another executive, emanative, and commanding medium to enchant a person, which medium is the Idea of a strong desire. For it is inseparable from desire to be carried toward the things longed for. In all these things, the devil is only a spectator, assisting in the passage. Because in truth, I have already demonstrated that the operative media themselves belong to man alone. For God alone <margin>16.</margin> is the most glorious Creator, infinitely praiseworthy, who created the universe out of nothing. Man, however, insofar as he is the image of God, creates out of nothing certain beings of reason <note>original: *entia rationis*.</note>, or non-beings in their beginning, and this in the proper gift of his fantastic power <note>original: *phantastica dos*, referring to the power of the imagination or *phantasia*.</note>. These, however, are something more than a merely privative or negative being. For primarily, while Ideas conceived in this way eventually clothe themselves in a body, in the likeness of an Image, fabricated through the imagina-

# ON INJECTED MATERIALS

<margin>17.</margin> Looking more deeply into this, it appears that if there were no right of some entity <note>i.e., a legal or natural claim to existence</note> preceding the Idea formed by the **Imaginative power**, it would be unable to clothe itself or assume a body; indeed, it could not even be associated with the body of the **Archeus** <term>the vital internal director of the body's functions</term> through the imaginative faculty. For that which is merely nothing in itself effects nothing, and has a "right" only to nothingness, in a negative sense. Thus, a concept would perish immediately after being conceived and would not produce an **Idea**; indeed, if it were mere nothing, it would immediately pass away into nothingness. But since the **Fantasy** proceeds from the concept to the **Idea** (or formed image), and from there to a **seminal entity**, it follows that the concept becomes "this specific thing" within the **Imaginative power**. That is, the **Imaginative power** creates a certain **seminal entity** <note>original: "ens seminale"</note>, which is the dispositive beginning toward the formality of an entity in potentiality. Just as a spark arises from **steel and flint**, from which a most active fire is produced.

<margin>18.</margin> Thus the **Imaginative power** rubs itself against an object through a concept, from which the **Idea** arises. Therefore, the act of **Imagination** is not so much a thing of nothing that it does not have some foundation within itself, approaching a beginning reality. For the **Imaginative power** possesses for this purpose either images shaped to itself along with the soul (as many believe), or at least images sometimes present, excited through the **memory**, and called back again by remembering.

<margin>19.</margin> I, however, consider these things not because preludes of **Ideas** pre-exist in us before that which is

<column-break/>

imaginatively conceived—as if they were conceived images of a proper name—but because they are made through the contact of the power of the one actually **Imagining** (that is, forming an image) and the object imagined. And so, from its own bosom, the soul nakedly forms an image, which, unless it immediately binds it in the **Archeus**, also perishes and is sterile by that very fact.

<margin>20.</margin> Nor does it stand in the way that in fevers or morbid wakefulness, we experience the shadows of images against our will. These foolish shadows of images wander about, without connection or discourse, before the **Imaginative power**. However, whatever wanders about spontaneously against our will, and without us wishing to imagine—indeed, even bringing us distress—it is necessary that this thing itself pre-exists. Like hidden shadows, before the fantastic force is reflected upon them.

<margin>21.</margin> But such **Ideas** are confusedly recurring from the storehouse of **memory**, having been impressed at some time; it is not that they had pre-existed before every act of imagining. Likewise, it proves nothing that the aforementioned shadows of **Ideas** are confused, often ridiculous, and false, and thus were never before conceived by a healthy **Imaginative power**. For once images are naturally cut off and seriously established, a second, third, and further one is superimposed, and they fold and penetrate one another; hence the confusion. Otherwise, a subsequent image following in order destroys the previous one if it is opposite to it; if not, and if it agrees with the previous one, it is strengthened. Or if there is some slant between the two, both are confusedly undetermined, and they wander as shadows. This certainly in no way helps the supposed pre-existence of **Ideas**. It has always seemed to me that **Ideas** are forged anew through the act of the **Imaginative power**, like a spark made anew by the rubbing of **steel and flint**. Nor does this detract anything from the activity of the **Ideas**, no more than a spark does from a great fire. I respond, therefore, to the first objection: that just as fire is not present in the **steel and flint** before the striking, so neither is there any prelude of entity, or trace of an image, before the concept.

# ON THE MANNER OF ENTRY
## FOR HURLED OBJECTS.

1. *The sole means by which the devil cooperates in hurling is the deception of the eyes, so that they enter invisibly. 2. The motive and determined Blas <note>term: Blas (a term coined by van Helmont to describe a universal motion or vital force)</note> belongs to the devil. 3. How much man contributes to this. 4. The primary healing of injected things. 5. Natural healing. 6. The variety of gifts in simple herbs. 7. The Author proceeds by name. 8. Karichter is commended. 9. Caution regarding herbs. 10. The manner in which Injected things, once expelled, accelerate further rejections.*

I shall now proceed to supply the manner in which Hurled or Injected things enter or are admitted: and at the same time, I will subjoin their remedies. Injected things <margin>1.</margin> first of all enter invisibly. And this one thing is purely diabolical. For that most wretched buffoon <note>A derogatory reference to the Devil.</note>, since he has nothing real left to his own freedom, has only vain appearances: indeed, as the father of lies, he counterfeits real things and makes them appear falsely, as he has since the beginning of the world. In deceptions of this kind, the man who is the slave of the devil contributes nothing. But as to the manner in which Satan makes things that are visible in themselves become invisible—whether he wraps them in his own invisible spirit and grasps the things themselves, or finally does it through the bewitching of the eyes: or even by the very fact that one bodily thing penetrates another (as has already been shown profusely through examples) it perhaps becomes invisible to that extent (for whatever loses the dimensions of a body can also deceive the sight)—at least, I am not a curious investigator of the works of Satan which belong to him by his own nature. It is enough for me that I have shown those things believed to be his are actually proper to man, and that I have uncovered the total and most impoverished misery of Satan. <margin>2.</margin> Therefore, the devil transfers the things to be injected, having been made invisible, to the object, with the Idea of human desire directing the path. For because it is not permitted to the devil in any way to enter into a man, much less to harm him, and least of all with an invisible burden which he himself would wrap around: <margin>3.</margin> Therefore he uses the free *Blas* of the man bound to him. Man, therefore, imprints his own free motive *Blas* into the body that has been made invisible; the devil, however, carries it even to the man into whom it is injected. And just as a knife, through the desire and consent of the one wounding, is fixed into the flesh of the one to be wounded: so this body, made invisible by the devil, is injected into the body of the one to be enchanted, through the Idea of the motive *Blas* of the Witch: with Satan conspiring toward this because of the direction of the striking human.

<margin>4.</margin> The healing of injected things is accomplished partly by remedies famous from the rise of the primitive Church. These work only miraculously: but why they do not always achieve their effect regularly, everywhere, and among all people, I leave to others. I, however, do not touch upon the inscrutable judgments of God, nor the remedies which are outside the court of nature.

<margin>5.</margin> And healing is also obtained partly through certain simples <note>Medicinal herbs or plants used as a single ingredient.</note>, into which Almighty Goodness has instilled a gift from the beginning of Creation for resisting, preventing, and correcting sorceries; and likewise for driving out Injected things. Such as the fumigation of the liver read about in the book of Tobit <note>A reference to the apocryphal Book of Tobit, where a fish's liver is burned to drive away a demon.</note>. And such as that of Solomon, or Eleazar, in Josephus, Book 8, Chapter 2. <margin>6.</margin> Certain...

For indeed, simple substances <note>natural herbs or minerals not mixed with other drugs</note> ward off evil spirits. (O, the wretched crowd of men who display a "slave-worship" <note>original: "dulomania"</note> to gods who are unable to resist the natural efficacy of these simple things!) Some substances finally remove the penetration of formal light, being bound to excrements. Likewise, some at least hinder the touch, entry, or application of evil. Finally, there are many things which correct and destroy such poisons.

<margin>7.</margin> Especially the "immature mineral amber" <note>original: "electrum minerale immaturum"</note> of Paracelsus, when hung from the neck, frees those whom an unclean spirit pursues; this I have seen myself. I remember, moreover, that a drink made from it has released many from sorceries. Furthermore, there is no one who, by wearing that simple substance, has not been protected against the introduction of "Injected" things, or has not been immediately released from persistent "bindings" <note>magical spells intended to paralyze or constrain a person</note>.

<margin>8.</margin> Bartholomew Karichter, Chief Physician to Maximilian II and the first among healers (as far as I know) to pity his neighbor, dedicated a small German treatise to his master. In it, he heals any persons enchanted in any way with just a few herbs. He preferred his "vanguard," the *Daurant* (which is the *Phu* of Dioscorides <note>likely Garden Valerian</note>; it has purple flowers and is the last species of Valerian in the latest edition of Mattioli) above all others. I also highly value Vervain with a purple flower, the leafier St. John’s Wort with a tiny flower, Southernwood, Maidenhair fern, Rue, etc. Likewise, I have found through experience that red Coral

<column-break/>

and its extracted tincture have brought much comfort. One must use the herbs raw and chopped,

<margin>9.</margin> but not cooked. For their power remains whole only in the integrity of the "Concrete" <note>the physical, unified form of the plant</note>. Therefore, the "Ideal force" <note>the spiritual or archetypal essence</note> of the herbs perishes by crushing. Moreover, the herbs are gathered and the roots dug up at the time when they are vigorous, and therefore also just as the Sun is rising. For the "Injected" things are driven out no differently than a snake is driven out by fire. Theologians, indeed, favor consuming the rejected Injected objects with fire, to the disgrace of the evil spirit.

<margin>10.</margin> Certainly, they perish well in this way; however, relapses are not prevented by this method. It is better, therefore, that the expelled Injected objects be wrapped in any simple herbs that possess expulsive power, and thus preserved. For by the same reasoning by which sympathetic remedies heal a wound from a distance, these "endowed" simples ward off Injected things; they detain and restrain them so they cannot be cast in, and they mock the vain labor of the Magician. Therefore, the weakness of the "casting entity" <note>the sorcerer or spirit</note> is rightly suspected, as it cannot introduce the things to be Injected because a certain hindering herb is present and presiding. Thus, the power which carries the Injected things inside is not of the Prince of this world <note>Satan</note> or a most powerful spirit, but of a certain "Ideal entity" that is weaker, which is so easily prevented from all further entry.
