# ON CONCEPTIONS.

->**605**<-

<margin>1.</margin> I have already set forth the introductory remarks. For this reason, I have elsewhere demonstrated that in the Spleen <note>original: *Splene*</note> resides the Imaginative faculty of the primary conceptions; and from there it extends to the stomach, the partner of that "duumvirate" <note>A term used by Van Helmont to describe the functional union of the stomach and spleen as the seat of life and emotion.</note>, and from here it is easily and primarily extended (in the other sex) to the womb.

<margin>2.</margin> The Spleen, therefore, is as much the source of the Ideas conceived in the human Imagination as it is of the Archeus <note>The "Archeus" is the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note> itself. The Archeus has its own peculiar Imaginations, proper to itself (for whether these are phantasies in the true sense of the word, or at least metaphorical, is all the same to me in this place), whose antipathies and self-loves it continually feels,

<margin>3.</margin> and from there it rouses movements derived from them. Certainly, the conceptions of the Archeus immediately achieve the most powerful determinations in the aforementioned places. Because they "smell of their birthplace," they are hypochondriac <note>In 17th-century medicine, "hypochondriac" refers to the upper abdomen (the hypochondrium) where the spleen and liver reside, believed to be the source of melancholy and nervous disorders.</note>, and they bear the marks of primary and undisciplined movements. And although the animated Imagination—which lingers there without the strength of an impression or the inclination of some prejudice—eventually becomes like a dream, indistinct and almost confused (which is why, surely, hair rarely turns gray from mere carelessness), nevertheless, those things which undergo the deliberation of some passion in the very workshops of the primary movements also attract to themselves the aged spirits in the brain. They undergo the contagion of the place, and Ideas are formed and forged that are deprived of judgment, and they give birth in a seminal fashion to affections conforming to their causes. These are surely suspected of hypochondriac madness, confusion, and disturbance. This is why, indeed, "we each suffer our own ghosts" <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*: *Quisque suos patimur manes*, meaning we each endure our own individual destiny or internal demons.</note>. Yet the already mentioned Archeal Imagination neither desires nor waits for the consent of the soul; and therefore it happens imperceptibly and without our knowledge.

<margin>4.</margin> For this reason, surely, the Plague <note>original: *Pestis*</note>—whether it arises from terror conceived in the soul, or finally from a specific fault of the Archeus—always holds its assemblies around the mouth of the stomach. For the Archeal Ideas are most powerful and most fertile in producing diseases, because they are irrational, and they happen

<column-break/>

without our knowledge and against our will; therefore they are also incorrigible and for the most part lawless, and thus they invade us in an ill-omened manner.

<margin>5.</margin> I shall now deal with animated conceptions, as they are more distinct and sensible. Whoever weakens, infatuates, and subsequently enchants themselves by the disturbances of the primary movements and the conceived Ideas of these movements, undergoes a risk due to the aforementioned causes. And although this kind of vice occasionally invades even learned and judicious men, producing moodiness and gloominess, it is nevertheless more common to women, on account of the harmony and proximity of the womb.

<margin>6.</margin> For the womb (though it be a mere membrane) is nonetheless a second Spleen. And therefore, by a kind of instinct proper to women, it immediately covers the fetus with the afterbirth <note>original: *fecundinis*</note> as if with another Spleen from the outside. As I have discussed elsewhere in its proper place. It is not indeed that woman, by this fault of nature, forges hypochondriac Ideas that are accursed to the destruction of others, in the manner of Witches <note>original: *Sagarum*</note>; rather, they are harmful only to themselves, and they, as it were, enchant, infatuate, and weaken themselves.

<margin>7.</margin> For they forge Ideas for themselves, by which they are governed—not unlike Witches driven by a malignant spirit of despair—or are carried away to those things which they would otherwise not want, and they lament their own involuntary madness. Thus, for example, according to the testimony of Plutarch <note>Greek historian and philosopher.</note>, a desire for death by hanging seized all the young women on the Island of Chios; nor could it be stopped except by threatening them with shame after death <note>Referring to a story where the authorities decreed that women who committed suicide would be carried naked through the marketplace.</note>. Since, therefore, the fault of Conceptions also touches men, let the reader turn away his boredom if I must dwell longer on these matters, as I am the first to strike this chord in the art of healing.

<margin>8.</margin> Therefore, if mortals stumble into a presumption of faith, depart from the word of God, and turn to the explanations of their own pleasure—as if gazing at themselves in a mirror of self-complacency—they then forge for themselves wavering Ideas and a neglect of religion, starting first from a single point of doubt,

# CONCERNING CONCEIVED IDEAS

Those who are uncertain and argue about many things drift toward Atheism <note>original: "Atheismum"</note> through a faithless lack of religion. If, however, they fall into superstitions, they forge Ideas consistent with necromancy <note>original: "nigromantiæ," the practice of communicating with the dead or dark spirits</note>, whereby they prepare a soul prone to hellish vanities. The enemy of mortals <note>The Devil</note> very easily associates himself with these people, as they are already out of their minds. This is especially true if a stubborn superstition is packed with a strong desire for hatred or some other sin.
<margin>9.</margin>
Indeed, they forge for themselves Ideas following a voluntary blindness. Above all, this must be remembered again: all ideal images are "feminine" in terms of their real being, produced through the Imagination. Then, on the part of the spirits (insofar as they are vital spirits, and wedded to the feminine concept), they take up the matter or the tablet upon which they are painted; they become an organ fit for carrying out the ends of the Ideas. Therefore, both of these prerogatives penetrate the Archeus <note>term: Archeus. In Paracelsian medicine, this is the internal "chemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions.</note> and alienate it toward the foreign goals of its own disturbances. If, therefore, faith and trusting superstition sin by belief alone, they already forge Ideas through which they think themselves enchanted or incurable, and they become slaves to a desperate madness. For with their strengths cast down, these madmen grow thin and turn pale. But if an undiscerning and disordered scrupulosity <note>An obsessive anxiety about sin or religious rules</note> should torment them, it fabricates for itself an anxious Idea, murky with the fear of Hell, from which their life becomes horrific and all social interaction becomes terrifying, almost as if it were diabolical. For they generate a foolishness which they recognize, confess, and lament, because they are unable to free themselves from it. And at last, they succumb so helplessly that they seize upon the Idea as if it were their soul. But if scrupulosity, before a total victory, returns to the mind for deliberation, and nonetheless in the meantime forges new and disordered Ideas:
<margin>10.</margin>
the unstable person easily migrates to the opposite extreme; as if now shuddering at the former scruple, they take up a "spiritual liberty" accompanied by a presumption of merit and a contempt for others. For however much such a person strives to rise higher, they are merged that much deeper. For presumption is nothing but a vain mad-

<column-break/>

-ness, always hanging upon the judgments of others; yet to most mortals, it seems genuine. For on account of virtues, genius, learning, lineage, riches, beauty, strength, boldness, arts, talkativeness, or even a voice, everyone forges Ideas applauding themselves, which drive almost the whole world mad. Of these it is said: *The number of fools is infinite.* However, the most harmful madness of presumptions is found in politics and in audacity, which not infrequently subjects its followers to the executioner. Truly, rare is the insanity without presumption, unless it be a related stupidity.
<margin>11.</margin>
Indeed, the Ideas of faith, despair, scrupulosity, irreligion, arrogance, self-esteem, etc., because they regard the more abstract and intellectual powers and more directly oppose infused grace, mostly perpetrate a madness so hidden that it is only slowly detected even by spiritual men who are highly practiced. These maddening Ideas are followed in order by those which belong to more bodily disturbances. For first, emulation of jealousy is as harsh as hell, plunging a person into many hardships. Then, the Ideas of lust and fornication, besides madness, also excite many sicknesses.
<margin>12.</margin>
Moreover, all deviations of the disturbances, if they are sudden, strong, frequent, or long-lasting, forge Ideas and infirmities equal to themselves, which are thus durable throughout life. There are, to be sure, those who are of sound mind, but if they fall into the subject matter by which an Idea once drove them mad, they immediately betray their hidden insanity. I say that sudden terror and grief have often extinguished some with unforeseen death; in others, they have at least caused a fainting fit <note>original: "syncopem"</note>. In many women, they have stirred up a flow <note>likely referring to uterine hemorrhaging or chronic discharge</note> that lasts for life. This Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist whose theories Van Helmont often critiques.</note> ridiculously ascribes to the slow star of Orion. Indeed, in certain simples <note>Medicinal plants or substances used in their natural state.</note>, there are naturally infatuating Ideas; not because they destroy the temperament of the brain—for it understands clearly without "temperament" <note>The traditional Galenic balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, bile, black bile), which Van Helmont rejected.</note>, and such temperaments are mere dreams—but because they confer their own Ideal character and impress it upon the spirit, the organ of phantasy, by chance, and rouse ideas conforming to their own. ...is the entrance of arrogance, and the first insanity of the soul. For this reason, it is scarcely read among miracles that a fool born of imaginings is restored to health: indeed, because of unrepentant pride and a refusal to return to the truth, such people generally remain insane. But disturbances, such as love, desire, sadness, fear, and terror, are primarily excited by external things: and therefore they produce their effects not only in the soul, but also in the body.

For in the beginning, individual passions take away sleep, then the appetite for eating, weakening the bodily action first. And finally, through long, excessive, strong, or sudden disorder, these Ideas infatuate the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: the internal vital spirit or "master-workman" that governs the body's functions</term>. Their strength is not to be measured from anywhere else than from their penetration and exquisite merging with a greater or lesser quantity of the *Archeus*. For gradually the soul, apprehending or reasoning, becomes accustomed to following without a struggle where it is often and violently led away—either willingly with approval, or unwillingly, due to the superiority of the apprehensions. Indeed, the soul becomes conscious of that journey, though it be pathless, because it has become accustomed to it. 

And these deviations are manifest, hidden, or unknown; continuous or intermittent. The manifest ones immediately betray the eccentricity of madness, visible in and around everything; but the more hidden and secret ones appear only in certain points and "conceived ideas"—through which, clearly, the soul was once shaken from its place and its judgment shattered. Namely, the Ideas of these things were impressed upon the organ <note>The physical brain or the sensory apparatus.</note> due to long duration or "plausibility" (meaning strength and superiority). In all other matters, however, they seem to think rightly.

I have striven to prove this progression in Ideas with a great train of words <note>original: "syrmate"; a reference to a long, trailing robe, used here metaphorically for a lengthy argument</note>; for which reason I am forced to ascribe a similar birth to Enchantments.

For I have observed how unwillingly the devil tolerates this stone. Moreover, not just any simples heal the bewitched equally, just as they do not all heal hysterical women in the same way: For individual things have their own gifted **Ideas**, and they remove their harmful counterparts. **Southernwood**, **Sage**, and **Rue**, for instance, drive away **Ideas** of fear. **Mugwort**, **nettle**, **Black Horehound**, and **blackcurrant** are effective in cases contracted from grief. **Asafoetida**, **Castoreum**, grains of **Acitis**, and the essence of **Jet** are for cases committed from **Anger**. **Catmint**, **Valerian**, and **Maidenhair** are for cases resulting from an **Idea** of hatred. Furthermore, how much the proposed **Method** deviates from the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Galenic medical establishment of the universities</note>, let them judge for themselves. For they recognize uterine diseases in a crude manner. To be sure, they only know of menstrual irregularities and discharges. For they have become so accustomed to *not* healing their patients that the name of "healing" has fallen into oblivion, and its place has been taken by "**Treatment**" <note>The author suggests university doctors merely manage symptoms rather than curing the root cause</note>. Sometimes they strike the ankle vein for retained menses; but for the flowing menses, they strike the "Liver-vein" in the arm. In both cases, I say, they draw off the blood equally. Because they have found sometimes that nature—as full of danger and fear as it is empty of blood and strength—has ત્યારબાદ ceased for a time from the fury of the flow that had begun. It would be perhaps similar if they made a too-frisky horse go lame by an injury to the tendon. 

But when the menses are failing, the **Schools**—now forgetful of obstructions, and as if suppression involved a necessary **plethora** <term>Plethora: a supposed excess of blood in the body</term>—order a vein to be cut: which is to attack the effect, but not the obstructing cause. They do not know, I say, that detained menses "sin" <note>i.e., malfunction</note> through the fury of the governing power <note>The "rectricis potestatis," referring to the Archeus</note>. Then they repeatedly offer laxatives, and those which are imagined to be "hot in the third degree." Meanwhile, unmindful of these things, they offer **Steel** <note>Iron-based medicines</note>, tormented in various ways. Would that the world knew with what vain protections they harass women, how much they sweat over "un-blocking" treatments throughout the whole Christian world...

# MAGNETIC FORCE.

**Regarding** action that is not locally distant <note>Action at a distance, where one thing affects another without physical contact</note>, wines suggest a demonstration to us. For any wine, even if produced outside neighboring provinces, and likewise flowering earlier elsewhere: nonetheless, it is disturbed while our vines are flowering, and this kind of confusion does not cease as long as the flower has not fallen from the vine. This certainly happens either from a moving cause common to the vine and the wine: or from a particular disposition of the vine, which namely disturbs the wine, and moves it as if confused by a storm up and down. Or conversely, that the wine itself disturbs itself of its own accord, on account of the flowers of the vine. If there is a fore-mentioned conformity, consensus, shared suffering, or shared rejoicing between these two latter things: at the very least, it cannot but happen through action at a distance. For instance, if the wine is disturbed in a subterranean cellar, where perhaps for

<column-break/>

some miles, no vine is nearby, nor is there any communication of the subterranean air with the flower of the absent vine. But if they wish to blame a common cause for such an effect: it is necessary either to recur to the Stars—which cannot be refuted by our pleasures and freedoms of daring—or, I say, we fall back into the confession of action at a distance. Namely, that some one and the same spirit-motor, as yet unknown, rules the absent wine and the far-distant vine, and makes them communicate and suffer together. Moreover, as far as the power of the Stars is concerned: I would not wish, nor would I dare by my own license, to extend the strengths, powers, or ends of the Stars beyond or outside the authority of the Sacred Text. Indeed, the vine flowers earlier in other places; and in rainy or colder years, our own vine flowers later, yet the wine imitates its flower and the stages of its blooming; thus, it does not look to the stars so as to be disturbed at their command. And so, we must not flee to some universal cause or a "world-governing breeze" of nature—lest we recur to impossibilities and absurdities rather than to the closest exchanges of symbol and unity, though these have hitherto been impassable to the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities that followed the rigid teachings of Aristotle and Galen, whom the author frequently challenges.</note>. Furthermore, this appears far more clearly still in Beers. When long ago our grandfathers saw that from barley, boiled in any way, nothing but a useless <term>thin gruel</term> <note>original: "ptisanam"; a medicinal barley water or weak porridge.</note> or porridge was cooked; they realized that the barley ought first to be germinated (which they then call <term>Malt</term> <note>original: "Maltam"; grain that has been soaked and sprouted to prepare it for brewing.</note>), and only then did they brew their beers as rivals to wines. In this process, several notable things coincide. Namely, the vegetable germ is excited in the barley, which then perishes when the barley is dried, losing the hope of growing; it loses this power even more through its change into flour, and then through the subsequent boiling. Yet, notwithstanding these things, it retains a vinous, intoxicating spirit—a <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquæ vitæ"; here referring to the alcoholic spirit or "vitality" of the brew.</note>—which it does not yet possess in actuality, but at last acquires through a number of days by the power of ferment. In the single bosom of a single grain, a single spirit is marked with different powers, and one is "castrated" while the other is left. This indeed shines out far more wonderfully when beer made from malt disturbs itself—just as wine is accustomed to do—while the barley is in bloom. And so, from this, the power is visible

Since there are cities from which pleasant meadows keep the sowing of barley many miles away, they prove the harmony of the beer with itself and the absent flowering barley all the more powerfully. Certainly, the path is far more tranquil for a "magnetic consensus" between certain agents distant from each other than it is to dream of a wandering "water of life" traveling from the beer in the cellar to the flowering barley and then returning to its original vessels in the pantry and the brewery. But magnetism confirms its operation at a distance just as opportunely and clearly through the mark impressed on a fetus by the appetite of a pregnant woman. Suppose a pregnant woman craves a cherry belonging to someone else and scratches her own forehead with her finger. Without a doubt, the fetus is marked on its forehead with the image of a cherry, which thereafter every year turns green, then white, then yellow, and finally red, according to the cycle of the trees. And even more wonderfully, it expresses those same changes of ripeness; for that same fetus, if in Spain (where the cherry blooms at the end of February), would imitate those aforementioned cherry-stages much sooner than it would among us. And so, by this is confirmed not only action at a distance, but also the conformity of the "essences" of the cherry—both in the wooden trunk of the tree and the fleshy "trunk" of the human. It is a kinship of being, revealed to the body through an instantaneous imagination, just as it is revealed in the tree through the successive series of years. Truly, the more learned ought not to reject as the work of an <term>evil demon</term> <note>original: "cacodæmonem"; a malevolent spirit or devil often used by traditional scholars to explain phenomena they did not understand.</note> those things which they are too weak to understand; for truly, things occur everywhere in nature which we, in our insignificance, are unable to explain. It is an act of insolent rashness to refer to the devil the gifts of GOD in nature, simply because our smallness cannot grasp them.

I delayed closing the treatise on <term>Things Injected</term> <note>original: "Injectis"; Helmont’s term for external harmful forces or diseases "thrown" into a person, often via magic or contagion.</note> above, until enough was established regarding <term>Things Conceived</term> <note>original: "conceptis"; internal disorders or images generated by the patient's own imagination.</note>. For I have joined the "Injected" with the "Conceived" because they stand connected at the root of the **Imaginative power**. Moreover, I have shown how much both harm and weaken us; one indeed as a foreign entity, taken from elsewhere, brought from afar, heaping up various calamities; the other, however, born at home within us. And so, I discovered first of all that sympathetic means are bound together. In the year 1639, a small book was published entitled: *The Sympathetic Powder of Ericius Mohy of Hesbaye, by which wounds are healed without the application of medicine to the affected part, and without superstition: winnowed through the sieve of Galenic and Aristotelian reasons.* In this book, it is sufficiently proven according to Aristotle's methods what the title promises: but he neglected the **directing power** which carries the virtues of the sympathetic powder, received on a bloody cloth, to the distant wound. Indeed, the blood from the wound, or the pus and discharge from an ulcer, when caught on a cloth, do indeed receive a balsam from a healing entity—I mean the powder of **vitriol** <note>original: "pulvere vitrioli"; iron or copper sulfate, the active ingredient in the famous "Powder of Sympathy."</note>—a medical power, connected in the aforementioned medium in a determined way: the powers of the received balsam are directed to the wounded object, not indeed by the influential power of the **Stars**, and much less do they fly off to the distant object of their own accord. Therefore, the **Ideas** of the person applying the sympathetic remedy are joined in the medium,

Mohy thought that the sympathetic power flowed from the **Stars**, because it emulated their influences. But I, in truth, take it from a much nearer subject. For this reason, this sympathetic powder works more successfully through the hand of one person than when applied by another. Therefore, I have always observed the process to go best where the remedy is instituted with loving desire and the care of charity: but to succeed with little luck if the operator is careless or drunk. And so, I have since valued these **stars of the mind** more in sympathetic matters than the **Stars of the heavens**.

## ON THINGS INHALED.
<note>original: "DE INSPIRATIS."</note>

The indistinct novelty of these matters has long kept me occupied with <term>Things Received</term> <note>original: "Receptis"; a general category of things taken into the body.</note> in the mind. Now at last I proceed to the third type of "Things Received." I call them **Inhaled Things**. For they enter into us from the outside, and for the most part, they enter along with the air. They come, namely, from caves, swamps, mines, mountains, local winds, snakes, filth, corpses, or even growing things. For these are the exhalations of things, which treacherously and insensibly steal away our life. Indeed, Illyria and Dalmatia were once populous provinces, as was the once-famous Alexandria, and although they possess fertile soil, they are now nearly deserted because of a dire poison that tends immediately toward the end of life. 

Thus the <term>Spagyrist</term> <note>original: "Spagyrus"; an early term for an alchemist or chemical physician who "separates and recombines" substances.</note> daily breathes in a wild and destructive **Gas** <note>Van Helmont is famous for coining the word "Gas," deriving it from the Greek "Chaos."</note> from coals, "stygian" (toxic) waters, and the smelting of minerals; once it is drawn inside, it disturbs the **Archeus** <note>original: "Archeum"; the internal vital spirit or "chief" that governs the body's functions.</note> according to the specific nature of each poison. In this way, the air of a place, infected by troublesome ferments, produces a **Gas** that causes familiar illnesses. These illnesses others have wrongly attributed to the <term>Tartars</term> <note>original: "Tartaros"; in Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to stony or sandy deposits in the body, like kidney stones or gouty deposits.</note> of those places. Truly, over time, any kind of soot or smoke stains the walls of the vessels; from this, under the <term>sixth digestion</term> <note>The final stage of the body's metabolic process in Helmontian theory.</note>, various wastes are forged, which are most suited to rotting the final nutrients and corrupting the vessels. For if the "soot" of salts is packed together in a harmful mixture, it soon melts inside, penetrating and eroding the tenderness of the "reeds" <note>original: "harundinum"; likely referring to the bronchial tubes or vessels.</note>. These are milder, however, than the things collected there as dry smoke. For if

<column-break/>

these vapors occupy the thin branches of the windpipe, they block them and cut off any hope of clearing them. If the wastes of that place grow beneath them so as to block the air from behind, they become permanent guests, packing the part so tightly that they themselves rot and an **abscess** <note>original: "vomica."</note> forms. Those things that enter along with vapors, once the watery parts are consumed, become harshly joined to the similar parts of the body. In this way, many endemic diseases have made entire provinces uninhabitable. 

Indeed, even the sea, salty as it is, is not yet immune to such evils. The shores bear witness to this through the various slaughters of **Scurvy** <note>original: "Scorbutum."</note> and fevers, and most clearly of all at the equinoctial line. Finally, those who tend to the sick inhale cruel things, already fermented through a "symbol" or shared nature. This is also true for those who gild, or who melt lead, copper, marcasites, and so on; likewise for miners, as well as those who separate and smelt minerals. For even if these things do not take life immediately, they at least shorten it and subject it to various calamities. This is the case for those who work with **Cinnabar**, **Arsenic**, **Orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigmento"; a yellow arsenic ore.</note>, sublimates, and **Antimony** <note>original: "stibioque."</note>; or those who prepare **Red Lead** <note>original: "Minium."</note>, **White Lead** <note>original: "Cerussam."</note>, **Verdigris** <note>original: "viridi æris."</note>, or **Cobalt blue** <note>original: "Zaffaris lazurium."</note>, and those who serve painters. 

For these subterranean substances are far more stable than our internal heat can handle; they cannot be tamed, nor mastered, nor expelled—and much less can they be turned into nourishment. Therefore, the products of these substances usually endure throughout a lifetime, unless, by the rising brilliance of a more benign **sulfur**, these very enemies are converted into friends, or they depart in a timely manner.

## ON THINGS INHALED.
<note>original: "DE INSPIRATIS."</note>

For the diseases caused by minerals have been touched by no one except **Paracelsus**; they are neglected by the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional university-taught medicine based on Galen and Aristotle, which Van Helmont frequently criticized.</note>, which always dream up new *Iliads* <note>original: "novas somniarunt Iliadas"; a reference to the Trojan War used here to mean endless, complex, yet ultimately useless academic disputes.</note> based on the commentaries of their grandfathers. Thus, they are very much like the **Levites** passing by on the way to Jericho <note>A biblical allusion to the Parable of the Good Samaritan; Van Helmont suggests traditional doctors ignore the suffering patient to focus on their own status or theories.</note>: indeed, they have scarcely raised their heads beyond the concepts of "heat" and "cold." Truly, I have proven at times that the stomach draws in the odors of things offered in a cup. Indeed, the upper abdomen <term>hypochondria</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, this referred to the region of the abdomen under the ribs, thought to be the seat of various vapors and moods.</note> trembles at the sight of certain drinks, even if they are masked by a pleasant aroma. From this, every <term>endemic</term> <note>original: "endimicum"; here Helmont refers to a localized environmental pathogen or contagion.</note> influence is naturally suited to immediately affect the outer curve of the stomach, and to imprint there odors, "soots" <note>original: "fuligines"; the waste products of internal "combustion" or metabolism.</note>, and ferments. Thus, once wedded to the nutritional fluid, they throw the servants of digestion into confusion and give birth to various wastes. In this way, the **Plague**, along with inhaled endemic pathogens, usually rages primarily around the stomach. For while the passage of the larynx stands subject to the harshness of the air, it must be believed to have received its own defenses from the goodness of God—just as the bladder is armored against urine, and the gallbladder against its own bile. But the membrane of the great mass of the stomach, mostly occupied with its own digestions, is interrupted by these endemic forces and disturbed by an endemic "being" <note>original: "ente endimico"; a "being" or "entity" in the sense of a specific disease-cause.</note>. Therefore, coughs, asthma, ulcers <note>original: "vomicæ"; often referring to internal abscesses or pockets of pus.</note>, palpitations, and many anxieties depend occasionally on these endemic influences impressed upon the curve of the stomach. The same is true for malignant fevers, camp fevers <note>original: "castrensium"; likely typhus, which was common in military camps.</note>, and other diseases that infest the population. **Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a famous French physician.</note>, not content with the doctrine of **Galen**, sought the seat of all fevers below the <term>pylorus</term> <note>The opening from the stomach into the small intestine.</note>, but he did not extricate himself from the idea of fictional "humors"; nor did he ever dream anything of the 

<column-break/>

outer curve of the stomach, or that a light inhaled endemic influence would be enough to transplant the nourishment of the **sixth digestion**. <note>In Van Helmont’s system, the "sixth digestion" is the final process where the blood is transformed into the actual substance of the body's members.</note> Tell me, how does the air or the weather of the seasons touch an "imbalance of humors"? For will the hot air of a summer day produce "bile" or waste from that which a more temperate day would have transformed into vital blood? Will the primary workshop of the humors thus be established in the lungs by every legal prerogative? I have learned that digestions are the substantial generations of the transforming <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is Helmont's term for the internal "vital director" or spirit that governs the functions of an organ.</note>, not of internal heat, and certainly not of the external air. And I have learned that digestions are disturbed when a harmful or at least troublesome endemic influence is swallowed; and the errors of digestion are rarely without a disease-causing product, because it is the nature of digestion to produce something through the act of digesting. I do not deny that intense cold or heat can damage the tender lungs or the brain, just as they burn the skin. But does such harm consist only in a matter of degree, exceeding human nature? There is a certain range in every degree that stays below the level of harm. Now I am looking at **Inhaled Things**. Inhaled mineral particles, however, expect no hope of a remedy from plants <note>original: "vegetabilibus"; refers to herbal medicine.</note>. I admit that fumigations may prevent "soots" from quickly sticking in our airways. But once they have gained possession inside, they will not be evicted by plants. For this reason, I have found no help from "manna of nettle," nor from a decoction of houseleek in the first-milk of a cow, and so on. This I assert with the permission of Paracelsus, and I am confident that those who wish to try it for themselves will agree with me.

-># S U S C E P T A.<-
->### THINGS SUSTAINED ###<-

The fourth kind of **Things Received** <term>Receptorum</term>, I call **Injuries Sustained** <term>Suscepta</term>. These include wounds made by stabbing, cutting, hurling, beating, throwing, tearing, biting, bruising, freezing, burning, or binding. Likewise, bone-fracture, dislocation, shackling, constipation, and in short, whatever falls most closely under the hand of the **Surgeon** <term>Chirurgo</term>. For indeed, ulcers that are not born from a poorly treated wound, but are nourished by an internal principle from the start, belong specifically to the **Physician** <term>Physicum</term> <note>In this period, "Physic" referred to internal medicine, while "Surgery" was a manual craft; Helmont is distinguishing between trauma and internal disease.</note>. This is more evident because any ulcers, no matter how malignant, may be perfectly healed by **Secret Remedies** <term>Arcana</term> <note>original: "Arcana"; specialized chemical or alchemical medicines believed to have "hidden" powers</note> taken by mouth. Therefore, if he lacks these Secrets, the Surgeon will sometimes find himself at a loss, occupied only with manual labor regarding these Sustained Injuries. But because the fullness of time has not yet brought these Secrets into common use, Surgeons have been given the license to invade the territory of the Physician.

Meanwhile, I do not dwell on the difference between diseases of "similar parts" and "organic parts," a distinction so greatly expanded in the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities following Galen and Aristotle.</note>. This is because I measure disease by its **Archeal** <term>Archealibus</term> <note>From the "Archeus," the internal vital spirit or "chief" that Van Helmont believed governed the life and health of each organ.</note> and immediate causes, and not by the impairment of functions. Most importantly, all parts, however organic they may be, do not depart from their own homogeneity. Nor do I think it matters whether many duties converge in one part, or whether there is a singular defect of singular tasks. For if an eye is gouged out, a disease does not follow; rather, it is the death of the visual power. Therefore, the subsequent growth of new flesh <note>original: "incarnatio"</note> effects the healing of the wound, but it does not restore what is dead. Nor do I contradict myself, even if elsewhere I might have said that all

<column-break/>

diseases arise and are fostered by seminal principles. Rather, in this place, I would teach that **Injuries Sustained**—such as wounds from a sword—operate by entering after the manner of artificial things. For the diseases of Sustained Injuries do not exist as long as they are in the process of being made; they only exist as a result of the injury sustained. For Sustained Injuries have this peculiarity: they introduce death rather than disease by their own nature. It is only by accident that a wound cuts through a fleshy part, or the Heart itself, or an artery. And so a wound, at its beginning, threatens death to the part upon which it is inflicted; and these injuries always taste of the nature of artificial things.

For Sustained Injuries originally deceived the Schools. They argued in this way: "The sword wounds; the divided continuum is wounded. But division is nothing but a relationship between boundaries—and yet a wound is a disease. Therefore, every disease consists only in a relationship, or at least in a **Disposition** <term>Diathesi</term>, or the effect of that relationship." This is to say either that disease is a **mental construct** <term>ens rationis</term> (which is what a relationship of boundaries is), or that a real entity arises from a mental construct.

I, however, who do not distinguish internal connected causes from the thing itself, call poisons, foods, the sword, etc., "occasions." I call a wound the absolute or threatened death of the "continuum" <note>The "continuum" refers to the unbroken physical structure of the body.</note>. But when these things have brought their force against the **Archeus** <note>The vital spirit or "internal chemist" of the body.</note>, so much so that it is provoked into a rage by what has been applied to it, I then count what is imprinted by the Sustained Injury among the primary diseases. For as soon as the sword has divided the continuum, the action of a violent "occasional cause" is present, vibrating against the Archeus; and the Archeus soon begins its own storms—that is, Diseases.

## R E T E N T A.
## THINGS RETAINED ##

Having finished the treatise on Things Received, I now proceed to **Things Retained** <term>Retenta</term>. Regarding these, let it be permitted to warn once and seriously: although these are merely the "occasional causes" of diseases, yet I wanted to distinguish diseases according to Things Retained so that I might keep the ancient names of the diseases. To serve as a precaution for what must be said about Retained Things, the chapter titled *A Hitherto Unknown Knowledge of Disease in its Universal State* should suffice...

->### (RETENTA) ###<-

I return the reader to this point: indeed, individual **Retained Things** <term>Retenta</term> <note>original: "Retenta"; refers to substances that should be excreted or transformed but instead remain in the body to cause harm</note> provoke their own invasions into the **Archeus** <term>Archeum</term> <note>The "Archeus" is the vital, governing spirit that directs the body's functions and health</note>, and from there they stir up various differences in diseases. These Retained Things are either taken in from the outside or are born domestically within through internal disorder. For whether these "seeds" are foreign or domestic, they both stir up a notable effect of their own **ataxia** <term>ataxiæ</term> <note>original: "ataxiæ"; a state of disorder, irregularity, or confusion in the vital functions</note> within the Archeus. This is obvious even in a simple tear from the eye. While in a healthy state it is entirely dispersed by the movement of the spirit without feeling or trouble, when the spirit of the eye is poorly disposed, the tear thickens, clots, or is changed into a gnawing **ichor** <term>ichor</term> <note>A thin, watery, or irritating discharge from a wound or sore</note>. Furthermore, Retained Things do not only vary by their own deformity; they are also changed according to the dispositions of the body. For the body, insofar as it is more or less "breathable" (able to perspire), varies the diseases. Some retained materials are dispersed and leave no root behind for a relapse to be stirred up. Yet, they often forget this kindness and leave behind an "occasional matter," and with it, not rarely, adulterated fermental impressions—like offspring that stir up new heirs for themselves, or products within the Archeus. Indeed, even the internal pores sweat, insofar as the whole body is capable of perspiration, and liquids are carried off into "another man's harvest" <note>A metaphor for fluids moving into parts of the body where they do not belong</note>. Because these liquids are carried outside their own homes, they are soon deprived of their common life; they coagulate very quickly (as I said regarding the eye's tear) or remain resolved into a liquid virus <note>original: "virus"; used here in the classical sense of a poisonous or foul-smelling fluid</note>. It is in this way that the matter of coughs, **Dropsy** <term>Hydrops</term>, **Head-colds** <term>Coryza</term>, **Diarrhea** <term>Diarrhœa</term>, **Diabetes**, **Abscesses** <term>Apostemata</term>, and ulcers are born. For the coagulations of certain Retained Things stick more stubbornly and are resolved slowly or never; or they may spontaneously tend toward resolution and liquefaction. Or they may deliver symptomatic impressions into the Archeus, substituted as a perpetual memory of relapses. For in this way, the seeds of diseases prepared to go elsewhere depart distorted. And thus, finally, diseases vary on the part of the **sixfold digestion** <note>Helmont's theory that there are six distinct stages of digestion/transformation in the body, from the stomach to the final tissues</note> being impeded, inverted, suspended, extinguished, or corrupted.

<column-break/>

Diseases of Retained Things also vary on the part of the distribution of what has been digested. For a proportionate distribution exercises the power of "distributive justice" owed to each part. But if they are disproportionate, the distribution is then weak and forced; this is true both in respect to natural functions that never rest, and to continuous perspiration, and therefore because of an unending necessity. Moreover, that disproportion is a spontaneous and, as it were, overflowing distribution, by reason of a symptomatic expulsion, due to the "conspirable" **thymosis** <term>thymosim</term> <note>original: "thymosim"; a state of fury, agitation, or "anger" in the vital spirit/Archeus</note> of the raging Archeus. Or finally, the distribution is disproportionate insofar as it is forced by penury (lack), from which a not uncommon damage eventually attacks the whole. Consider when nourishment degenerates in some part: it is ejected, and thus consumed. Such is the wasting sputum in those with lung disease, the mucous gluten in **the Stone** <term>Calculo</term>, in **gonorrhea** <term>gonorrhœa</term>, etc. For since a part, once the nourishment is defiled and degenerate, is never nourished thereafter but rather scorns and thrusts it away, it nevertheless does not cease—because of the sensation of penury—to continually demand new nourishment from the "dispenser" <note>the digestive system</note>, and to obtain it by its own importunity so that it may satisfy the thirst of its necessity. Therefore, new nourishment is supplied to it many times over, and is taken away from other "roommates" <note>other healthy parts of the body</note>, because there is not enough for everyone. Thence follows leanness, **atrophy** <term>atrophia</term>, **wasting** <term>tabes</term>, and the impoverishment of everything necessary. In this way, indeed, Diarrhea, **Dysentery** <term>Dysenteria</term>, abscesses, ulcers, and purgatives emaciate and exhaust us. For the weak parts are like the **prodigal son** <note>A biblical reference to Luke 15:11-32; the diseased part wastes its inheritance/nourishment</note>, because they consume and uselessly throw away whatever has been distributed to them, having lost it badly, and the other parts mourn that loss.

I wish this to be understood regarding primary diseases: from whose womb, as it were, arise either the dregs of degeneration <term>recrementa</term> <note>original: "recrementa"; the waste products or "dross" left over from the body's processes</note>, giving occasion for new Ideas, or the assaults of diseases. an **adrastia** <term>adrastiam</term> <note>original: "adrastiam"; a term borrowed from Greek mythology meaning inescapable necessity or retribution. That is, if the root of the primary disease has produced something like itself, while the prior **Idea** of the deviation persists) or new branches of diseases are stirred up. At the very least, in both ways, the aforementioned excrements are the products of primary diseases. Primary diseases are either **Archeized Ideas** <term>Ideae Archeizatae</term> <note>original: "Ideae Archeizatae"; Ideas that have taken on the commanding power of the Archeus</note>, specifically from the very substance of the influent Archeus, flowing down into the framework of the body, which it surely devastates according to its own rage. For it then gives birth to the most powerful afflictions, and sometimes even persists throughout life. Thus, the primary diseases of the organs spring forth, nor do they listen to remedies except those of a more profound **syngamia** <term>syngamiae</term> <note>original: "syngamiae"; a deep spiritual or essential union or joining</note>; indeed, they even bequeath inheritances to descendants. I have reviewed **Secrets** <term>Arcana</term> of this kind in my book *On Long Life* <note>original: "lib. de vita longa"; likely referring to Van Helmont's own treatise</note>, each of which represents the majesty of universal medicine.

Although I would not deny that in certain very pure **simples** <term>simplicibus</term> <note>Unmixed medicinal plants or substances used as remedies.</note> there are properties that may heal primary diseases. The **Galenists** <note>Followers of the traditional medical system of Galen, which Van Helmont frequently criticized.</note> laugh at the promise of such generality: but every bird sings according to the shape of its own beak. Everyone speaks of the marketplace according to how they have profited therein. From the things already said, it is now clear:

1. It is futile to intend the healing of a secondary disease unless the primary one, which nourished it, is first rooted out and cast down.
2. The healing of the secondary disease then consists solely in the removal of what was produced.
3. Primary diseases persist even after the generation of a secondary one, if their **Ideas** <term>Ideæ</term> <note>original: "Ideæ"; in Van Helmont’s theory, these are spiritual "blueprints" or seminal images that direct the life of the body or the course of a disease.</note> proceed from the innate spirits.
4. Primary diseases may even cease of their own accord if their Ideas failed during the first attacks.
5. Because the causality, succession, and propagation of disease have been unknown until now, the healing of these diseases has remained ignored.
6. The **Schools** <note>The established university medical authorities of the 17th century.</note> have estimated that secondary diseases, and even the products of diseases, are their causes; and so they directed the entire work of Healing toward the after-effects.
7. They would have proceeded more correctly by removing the product rather than by focusing on "contrary qualities," and they should have sought proper remedies which, with their power intact, could penetrate to the affected places.
8. Whatever succeeded happily in the course of healing is to be ascribed to conjecture and the goodness of nature alone; because, led astray by false persuasions, they wandered about regarding imbalances <term>intemperies</term>, humors, catarrhs, and tartars through **solutives** <note>Laxatives or purgatives meant to "dissolve" bad humors.</note> that do not draw out electively, but rather putrefy everything furiously.
9. They learned certain remedies from old women or peasants which, contrary to the axioms of the Schools, might heal morbid Ideas by a specific gift.
10. They deemed incurable as many primary diseases as persisted by their own **ferment** <term>fermento</term> <note>original: "fermento"; a catalytic principle Van Helmont believed transformed matter and governed biological processes.</note> and did not transplant their vigor into their products. For indeed, primary diseases mostly concern the transmission of seminal causes into Ideas, and they disturb the action of the governing spirit. From this, not only the structure of diseases, but also their critical

deliverances emanate, occurring spontaneously through unusual expulsions, wandering conspiracies, labors, anxieties, and convulsive impulses—especially if they subsist in the matter through a seed and an efficient ferment. By these signs, they distinguish themselves from the family of symptoms. Moreover, I have confirmed the doctrine of primary diseases above through hereditary conditions, the "Unequal Strength," "Torture of the Night," and "Silent Ones," which presuppose not only the necessities of the **Ideas**, but primary diseases as well. Indeed, nature has played in various ways no less in defects than in wholeness; but everywhere through the system of the Universe, she is seen to walk conformably to herself, so that even in abnormal cases <term>heteroclitis</term>, she represents herself everywhere with an analogous consistency. I have now done as much as I promised at the beginning of the work. I have demonstrated the errors of the Schools in **Physics** <note>original: "Physicis"; meaning Natural Philosophy or the study of nature/medicine.</note>, insofar as they concern the faculty of healing: and that they have been ignorant of nothing more than the principles, means, and ends—namely, the essence and causes, the manner of proceeding and becoming, and the means of preparing remedies.

So be it, that everywhere concerning the elegance and order of division, I may have been less precise in such great paradoxes than concerning the essence of the matter. For **Things Taken In** <term>Assumta</term> <note>Food, drink, and air processed by the body.</note> do not sin by a double fault alone—namely, by the error of **Leftovers** <term>Relicta</term> and of **Local Ferments** <note>original: "Topicorum fermentorum"; Van Helmont believed specific organs had "ferments" that acted like chemical catalysts.</note>. Even the digested things themselves are twice-badly affected. For the stomach cooks not only for the whole body, but also for itself. So it is also with several organs: in whose diverse duties of digestions and functions, the **Products** <term>Producta</term> alienate their own errors. 

The stomach, however, clearly lies subject to a double calamity: namely, that of its own digestion, and that of the **Sixth Digestion** <note>Van Helmont proposed six stages of digestion; the sixth is the final transformation of nutrients into the actual solid substance of the organs.</note>. Indeed, every part lives by its own "kitchen," which in the stomach—being subject to the rushing **Things Taken In**—is very easily disturbed, even by any shock of the mind. And so in the **First**, **Second**, and **Third** digestions, obvious, manifest, and frequent stumblings and omissions of the digestions occur. 

In the **Sixth**, however—although the **Products** fail openly on both sides—the **Schools** <note>The traditional Galenic medical establishment, which Van Helmont frequently criticized.</note> have referred these to the four fictitious "heterogeneities" <note>Referring to the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> of the blood. Indeed, and far more absurdly still, the faults of the Sixth digestion are mostly attributed to mucus, carried up by a false vapor of the stomach and distilled from there. For this reason, they have devised that **Catarrhs** <note>Runny noses or "drainage" thought to come from the brain.</note> fall into the "Republic" of the Sixth digestion. But they also contend that **phlegm** <term>pituita</term>, which is generated in the **Liver** along with the blood from a vital origin, is now shamelessly asserted to be a **Leftover** from a casual distillation of their medical art. 

But in the **Fourth** and **Fifth** digestions (being entirely vital, previously purifying everything from inhabitant filth with great care), although the dross of **Things Taken In** is not so open, it is nevertheless not absurd that **Innate Retained Things** <term>Retenta innata</term> are procreated there; for the nature of mortals, now totally corrupt, is nowhere free from all stain. Authors recite little ulcers found in the chamber of the **Heart**; likewise, a woman who died of a four-month difficulty in urinating <term>dysuria</term> showed two stones in the functional tissue of the **Heart**, along with several pustules, to the

<column-break/>

dissectors, and so on. Although surely these prove a fault of the **Sixth** digestion rather than the **Fourth** or **Fifth**. 

But daily palpitations accuse the **Leftovers**, or rather the **Transmuted Things** <term>Transmutata</term>, even if they are not plainly open. It is enough that **Ideas** <note>Spiritual blueprints or images that direct the body's Archeus or vital force.</note> tainted with poison flourish as much as possible and often within the spirit of life—the causes of unexpected death. For the **rabies** of dogs, otherwise introduced through a tooth, corrupts the authors of the spirit’s circuits, because, vitiated by its own character, it infects the chambers of both the **Brain** and the **Spleen**, having assumed the nature of a virulent leftover. 

Simple things also, though taken in only once, often drive one's life to madness: insofar as they contaminate the spirit of the organ with a sluggish poison, such that it degenerates into the strength of a **Leftover** poison. Furthermore, even **biting-irritation** <term>odaxismus</term> <note>original: "odaxismus"; a sharp, stinging, or itching sensation.</note>, or the tenderness of a "tickle," stabled in the naked sensitive spirit, causes that sensation in healthy people as often as it is once set free and carried by a backward motion into the arteries; insofar as it is snatched outside its own heart-center, it riots with a foreign and infatuating poison. 

In the sick, however, the aforementioned origin of the "tickle"—now full of a flourishing, open poison—is translated through the arteries into the head, and provokes **St. Vitus’ Dance** <term>chorea S. From this emerge **itches** <term>psorae</term>, **scabies**, and even **St. Anthony's Fire** <term>erysipelas</term> <note>A skin infection; original: "erysipelata".</note>, and a various crowd of ulcers. Some of these then sustain themselves there by their own poison of a ferment, and thereafter propagate. 

Therefore, the **Flowing Spirit** <term>spiritus influus</term> also suffers its own stains through the **Fourth** and **Fifth** digestions. (as I have taught) produces a twitching of the limbs: and fools become four times stronger than themselves. Truly, if in the **First Digestion** <note>The initial processing of food in the stomach.</note>, if the **Thing Taken In** <term>Assumtum</term> does not match the **ferment** <note>original: "fermento"; Van Helmont viewed organs as chemical laboratories using biological catalysts or "ferments."</note> of the stomach (for many people do not crave, cannot bear, or cannot "cook" <note>Van Helmont uses "cook" (coquere) as a synonym for "digest."</note> most things), then even if the food was good in itself, it degenerates into **Leftovers** <term>Relicta</term>. This often produces no small troubles for the person and stamps those troubles onto the various body parts. There are also the faults of certain people who ingest things that are too much, too hard, foul-smelling, or "rebellious." Rebellious things are those whose "middle life" <note>The vital principle or "anima" of the food itself.</note> cannot be tamed or removed by the ferment of the stomach. Every person recognizes and experiences this against their will.

I have said thereafter that there is a double ferment for the stomach. One indeed for the **First Digestion**, which flows to the stomach from the **Spleen** <term>Lien</term>. The other is truly the stomach's own for the **Sixth Digestion** <note>The final stage where nutrients become the actual solid substance of the body's tissues.</note>, which is native to it from its innate spirit and belongs to its own "kitchen." Both of these, however, are diminished, altered, and alienated by diseases, sorrows, age, and so on. Because of this, eggs, meats, fish, and broths are loathed; they rot inside faster than they can truly be "cooked" into **chyle** <term>chylum</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note>.

> And these **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> calls "impure bodies," which the more you strive to restore with stronger nourishment, the more you harm them.

Indeed, heat then boils more strongly in the stomach, but the healthy ferment is withdrawn from it: therefore, the things ingested are not digested, but instead putrefy. Thus, under "canine hunger" <note>original: "canina fame"; an insatiable, pathological hunger or bulimia.</note>, the spleen’s ferment is doubled. Finally, if it is not the ferment itself that increases, but a foreign acidity, it produces sharp pains in the stomach, compression in the chest, cravings, headaches, cholera, and so on. Similarly, when the ferment of the **gall** <note>The bile.</note> wanders out of its limits, is deficient, or is otherwise corrupted by a foreign poison, products soon emerge that match those corrupted roots. From here surely come Vertigo, Fainting, Apoplexy, Diarrhea, Cholera, as well as bitter or bloody vomiting, Wasting, and more. 

<column-break/>

I warn again, that although I leave the ancient names of diseases in place, I understand—beneath those abstract names—the **Ideas** <term>Ideas</term> <note>Van Helmont believed diseases were caused by "morbid ideas" or spiritual blueprints that misdirected the body's life-force.</note> that perform these acts. In the First, Second, Third, or Sixth digestion, I understand that faulty transformations happen because of these morbid Ideas generated and transformed there. Such **Leftovers** <term>Relicta</term> or **Transformed Things** <term>Transmutata</term> are excreted either by "washing" through sweat or urine, or through the bowels and "insensible perspiration" <note>Sweat that evaporates before it is felt.</note>. The Leftovers of the First digestion pass through the usual drains [the bowels]; those of the Second and Third are regularly driven away with the urine. 

But because disorders occur in most people, there is a place for "Transformed" and "Transmitted" wastes. Transformed things are the produced excrements of primary diseases, or the "fruits" of the things taken in. Because these were once part of the "household" <note>i.e., part of the body's internal systems.</note>, they were birthed by a fault of the transforming **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "master-chemist" or vital spirit that governs the body's functions.</note>. Truly, the **Retained Things** of the **Second Digestion** happen either from a weakness of the ferment or from its excessive wandering. Hence, the residual acidity of the First digestion, not being sufficiently corrected, proceeds to the intestines and causes griping pains. 

Passing further into the veins, it excites various fevers, abdominal contractions, **Dropsy** <term>Hydropes</term> <note>Swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, obstructions of the **mesentery** <term>Mesaraicarum</term> <note>The membranes and veins connecting the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, paralysis of the limbs, and painful urination. However, if the ferment of the Second digestion increases too much or is joined with a corrupted quality, it leads to **Jaundice** <term>Icteri</term>, bitter vomiting, fainting, vertigo, and the like. But if the digested product of the **Third Digestion** lingers too long: even though the blood <term>cruor</term> itself may have committed no fault, the ferment of that "workshop" nevertheless doubles and is alienated through disorder. For as long as nothing is hindered inside, all things proceed to their destined goals, not unlike the water of a flowing stream. 

Blood, therefore, though it is the treasure of human life, if it is detained beyond its just limit, degenerates into menses, hemorrhoids, etc. And generally, whatever the **Schools** <note>The traditional Galenic medical establishment.</note> attribute to **black bile** <term>aträ bili</term> <note>One of the four humors of ancient medicine, thought to cause melancholy and various illnesses.</note>, are nothing more than the **Retained Things** of the Third digestion held within the Third.

Furthermore, since the limbs are not nourished except according to a certain proportion (unknown to mortals) of the **crude venous blood** <term>cruor</term> to the **arterial blood** <term>sanguis</term>, it is inevitable that in the **Sixth Digestion** <note>The final stage of digestion where nutrients become part of the body's solid tissues.</note> a disorder arises. The **Schools** <note>Traditional academic medicine based on Galen and Aristotle.</note> attribute this to the "heat of the liver," and they falsely intend to cure it through cooling agents. For the liver, in itself, is a corpse and is cold, unless it is cherished by the **spirit of life** <term>spiritus vitae</term>. Thus, all heat that comes to the liver is foreign to it. For it behaves exactly like a finger that is naturally well-tempered: if a thorn is driven into it, even if that thorn is cold in both reality and potential, the finger soon swells, throbs, grows hot, and becomes inflamed. In the same way, the liver never grows hot unless it has taken a troublesome **thorn** into itself. Therefore, one must diligently focus on plucking out the thorn, not on cooling it. This "thorn" in the liver is twofold: one is surely from a **harmful Retained thing**; the other is from a **troublesome Retained thing**, namely, an overburdening of the crude venous blood.

For often, because of a **harmful Retained thing**, the liver has "shot out" abscesses and skin defects, which degenerate in many ways along the path of **Transmission** <note>The movement of substances through the body's systems.</note>. These defile the skin so much that whatever crude blood is eventually distributed to it for nourishment is corrupted under the title of "contagion." Such are ulcers which, if they are closed up, threaten a greater harm within. Therefore, in the **Retained things of the Third Digestion**, **Cauteries** <note>The medical practice of burning or piercing the skin to create a "drain" or fontanelle.</note> have not infrequently provided help—a fact ignored by the Schools in their fundamental principles, as they rely on guesswork and the uncertain hope of outcomes. For defects arising from a mere plurality of good, unvitiated blood are rare (as I noted in the book on fevers), and two days of moderation easily bring blood suspected of excess back into balance. Thus, the blood "sins" if it has a "thorn" as a companion; secondly, if it stays inside longer than it should, as I said; and thirdly, if the **crude venous blood** <term>cruor</term> is out of proportion with the **arterial blood** <term>sanguis</term>. Gluttony is usually the mother of these three. Hence the saying: *Gluttony strikes more than the sword.* <note>original: "Plus ferit ense Gula."</note> A plurality of blood also usually arises not because more blood is produced than is right, but because less than is right is consumed, due to

a lack of exercise, a lazy life, an abundance of fat, and so on. This is because they have their own "seed" <note>Van Helmont believed diseases were living "seeds" or archetypes that invaded the body.</note>, and so they often rage even during a shortage of blood. Because of this, the **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "master-chemist" or vital spirit of an organ.</note> of the weaker parts is saddened; it flares up with delay and impatience, and forges various diseases for itself. For the law prescribes a "lunar limit" for the quantity of blood, so that it may be consumed in both sexes and not make a longer stay. This is why, because there is little **sweating** <term>diaphoresis</term> in the cold, coughing up phlegm is more frequent. More food is also taken in during the cold, yet not more blood is fashioned as a result. In summary, in diseases of **Strength** <term>Robur</term>, there is always a vice of the "distributive power." At the very least, it is clear from what has been said that the power of appetite is not measured by the making of blood, nor by the consumption of blood.

-># R E T A I N E D  T H I N G S. 627<-

They speak of fictitious humors <note>original: "fictitios humores"; Van Helmont famously rejected the traditional Greek theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</note>, as if they did not know that the fluids of the human body are, by the hour, fleeting and prone to corruption. I, however, establish that the great storehouse of morbid materials lies in the numerous aversions and degenerations of the fluids that immediately nourish the body. And I do not set a fixed number to these, because I know it is not a knowable thing, where a single matter runs along a continuous thread through a multitude of subordinate dispositions. I am at least amazed that, regarding this process of transformation, the [medical] schools have so far devised or believed in no error, even though several degenerations present themselves clearly to the eye, and every degeneration occasions its own specific diseases. For in this way, vertigo causes sense and motion to stumble, because the degenerate nutritional fluid has associated with itself an inebriating power. But if it should also be sleep-inducing, it becomes a neighbor to **Apoplexy** <term>a sudden loss of consciousness or "stroke," which Helmont associates with the corruption of internal fluids</term>. And if it also becomes stupefying, it already takes on the conditions of the Falling Sickness <note>original: "Caduci"; a historical term for epilepsy</note>. Let those who intend to cure the insane through sleep-inducing drugs also take note. For **Narcotics** <term>substances like opium used to induce sleep or numbness</term> barely bring sleep to the insane even with a quadrupled dose. Instead, they increase the madness; for dementia is nothing but an errant sleep-inducing power: because every insane person dreams while awake. Therefore, narcotics add [additional] dreams to the delirious dreams of wakefulness. For always the sealing character <note>original: "character sigillaris"; a Paracelsian term referring to the essential "stamp" or "signature" that defines a condition's nature</note> in an insane person presupposes the restoration of the limb and the correction of the poison by its own antidote, rather than a narcotic poison. Meanwhile, nothing prevents transformed things from being born erroneously, or digestions from going astray due to the unsuitability of the things transmitted, and producing a result conforming to the hindrance of their own suffering. From this arise painful **diarrheas** <term>loose, watery stools</term>, stirred up by the acid of the First **Chyle** <term>the milky fluid resulting from the first stage of digestion in the stomach</term>, and likewise complicated and double fevers. Nor does it prevent a primary disease from being complicated with its own secondary one, or one born from elsewhere. Just as a primary fever, by producing a byproduct, leads to the resolution of the blood-mass <note>original: "cruoris"</note> into the putrid sludge of a malignant **diarrhea**, matched to the febrile **ferment** <term>an active principle or "yeast-like" catalyst that Helmont believed drove all physiological processes</term>. Finally,

<column-break/>

the transition from the first three [Kitchens] to the Sixth is not necessarily through the Fourth and Fifth. This is because the greatest part of the blood-mass <note>original: "cruoris"</note> never reaches the heart, and much less is it snatched into the left cavity [of the heart]. Because individual parts [of the body] are nourished by blood-mass no less than by [arterial] blood. Hence it happens, indeed, that the defects of the first three kitchens often pass immediately into the sixth. And therefore, the transformed substances of the first three, if they reach the sixth, do not offend by a transmission of their own category, but by transformation alone: because the transmission from the Third to the sixth becomes regular, legitimate, and ordinary. I will add a point about the spleen. If the acidity of the **chyle** <term>partially digested food</term> from the First [kitchen] is immediately carried into the Spleen, a **quartan fever** <term>a form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day, historically linked to the spleen</term> is soon present, namely from the foreign matter coagulated there. But if the sixth [kitchen] is disturbed in the Spleen, since it is the bed of the first concepts: the excrements, or Transformed things which are made from its own nourishment, are mostly endowed with an imaginative power (such as occurs in many simple substances, and most visibly in the saliva of a rabid dog): which I therefore call inebriating, sleep-inducing, or infatuating. For this reason, indeed, the condition of drunkards is manifold even from a single wine. That is, a single wine stirs up different types of madness. For insane poison limps along with a likeness to wine. For the insane poison, with its pre-eminent power, does not follow the conditions of the person: but the conditions of the person themselves are forced to obey the poison. This is clear in the poison of one bitten by a rabid dog. Therefore, poisons that are born from degenerate nourishment in the sixth [kitchen] follow their own nature. For the closer they are to assimilation, the more powerfully they infatuate. For the closer the **ferment** <term>transformative agent</term> of the organ and the irradiation of the indwelling spirit are present to it, the more closely it takes on the Idea of a certain imaginative power, which it finally transplants into a poisonous virus—not indeed so much fatal to life as to the power of that organ. From what has been said, anyone can hereafter construct for himself the scenes of diseases.

-># R E T A I N E D  T H I N G S.<-

<columns>

For it was enough for me to have shown that every primary disease, both objectively and subjectively, falls upon the **Archeus** <term>the internal "master-workman" or vital spirit that directs the body's functions</term>, and thus upon life itself, by which it is directly formed. A secondary disease, however, falls objectively upon the Archeus, but subjectively upon the matter—either the solid parts that contain or the fluid parts that are contained. And so, having shown that diseases are distributed in nature through their causes, roots, and essence, according to their "lodgings" <note>original: "hospitia"; the specific places where a disease takes up residence in the body</note>, I now set down my pen on that matter.

Since sterility is also among the defects that are contrary to nature, I have expanded this treatise to include it. Therefore, it is not coldness, heat, or moisture in either sex that is the cause of sterility, however loudly others may shout this. For first of all, no dryness is possible in living beings; and a faulty moisture of the womb is not a matter of "complexion" <note>the traditional Galenic balance of qualities</note>, but a mere waste product of digestion or transmission. Thus, finally, heat and cold are signs of defects in nature, but not the causes, because these qualities lack seed, vital properties, and the conditions of power. This is why sterility and fertility exist in every climate of the world. Indeed, an Ethiopian woman is far warmer than the warmest Muscovite <note>Russian</note> woman. Furthermore, the excrement-like and superfluous moisture of the womb is an effect of diseases; even if it accompanies sterility, it is not its containing cause. For the internal cause does not differ from the "being" <note>original: "ente"; the actual essence or entity of the condition</note> itself. Likewise, a defect in menstruation is not the cause of sterility, whether that defect involves a total absence or proceeds as an effect of a more immediate indisposition. Those who are not yet of age, or even those before their first menses, have not infrequently conceived, as have more mature women when their menses had ceased. Not infrequently, also, hysterical women, weighed down by many distresses, happily conceive and give birth. Meanwhile, some sterile women remain in perfectly good health. Many conceive just as their menses are beginning, or while they are absent, just as many have been deceived by a conception while the menses were silent. Some women, throughout the entire

<column-break/>

course of their pregnancy—and many for at least a few months—mark their usual menses. Truly, although sterility speaks of a "privative" respect <note>a state defined by what is missing</note>, it is nonetheless a purely positive and diseased "being." For it arises from individual positive defects, because in and of itself, it is an evil of nature. Just as fertility implies a complete and whole cause. Indeed, in a man who is not castrated, not a eunuch, not physically hindered, and not "bewitched" <note>original: "maleficiato"; a term referring to impotence believed to be caused by magic or "binding"</note>, sterility hardly has a place. For this reason, an old man can still father children. From this it follows that the same amount of perfection is neither attributed to, nor required in the male, as is required in the mother. I call those males "hindered" who suffer from **gonorrhea** <note>here used broadly for various seminal discharges</note> or have retained a vice from it; likewise, those who suffer from a notable fault in some internal organ. In a woman, menses that are excessive, deficient, irregular, watery, yellow-black, sticky, or foul-smelling, along with pain in the loins, belly, or hips, and the movement of the womb upward, downward, or sideways, are indeed witnesses and signs of a weak womb—and they may slow down conception, cause stagnation, or trigger miscarriages and "flooding"—yet they do not entirely take away the hope of conception, nor are they the disease called "sterility." For truly, old women are sterile without any of these symptoms. I find the only adequate and co-existent cause for the positive "being" called sterility described in the Holy Scriptures in these words: *God opened the womb of Sarah*. For it is a gift of God, brought down into nature: by which the parchment of the womb, tightly closed in its folds, is opened and dilated at the appropriate moment of union. The **Blas** <term>Van Helmont's term for a vital, formative motion or impulse</term> is, I say, a magnetic, drawing force; through it, following a "fear of a vacuum" <note>original: "metus vacui"; the physical principle that nature abhors a vacuum</note>, that opening is followed by the attraction of the seeds, and the adequate filling of the opened folds. For the aforementioned opening creates a suction through the fear of a vacuum. If this occurs at an improper moment, it happens in vain. For the womb of a virgin shows a width of barely two fingers, as it is wrinkled into itself by very small folds. Its opening, moreover, does not consist in the will of a human, nor in titillation or luxury.
