# P R Æ F A T I O.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' with floral and leaf patterns in the background.</image-desc>
I have already demonstrated elsewhere that **the Schools** <note>the traditional university medical establishments of the time, which followed Galen and Aristotle</note> have passed over the knowledge of diseases and of those things whose neglect is a crime. It is no wonder, then, if nothing has been heard of these matters until now. Indeed, to wish to be wise by departing from the opinions of the Schools was unusual and difficult, as there was a lack of things to substitute in place of recognized errors. There are also few who engage in philosophy solely for the sake of charity toward their neighbor. Most of the older practitioners refuse to learn, as if the Greeks and Arabs knew everything, and they despair that more can be known. Therefore, they have wrapped themselves in their own laziness as if it were a skin. It is common, moreover, for a man immediately after his promotion <note>earning his medical degree</note> to run from house to house, intent only on profit, prostituting salable health in exchange for his visits. Therefore, it is very rare for anyone to be admitted to the inner sanctuary [of medical knowledge]. Meanwhile, many walk to the doors of **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymia"; here referring to alchemy and chemical medicine</note>, boasting of great things, deluded by vain hope.

Truly, I was the first (unless I am mistaken) to write the history of life and death, hoping that God might receive His own honor from the free gift of the **Tree of Life** <note>original: "arbor vitæ"</note> and its fruits, for those whom He Himself preserves for a long life after me. For **Paracelsus** <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who challenged traditional medicine</note>, who treated "Long Life" before me, gave it a title indeed, but was entirely ignorant of the substance. Meanwhile, unless the Lord turns it away, I predict with a justified fear that the life of mortals will be shortened daily, and will finally pass to the grave while still in the "green ear" <note>an agricultural metaphor for dying young, like unripened grain</note>, through the sin of **bloodletting** <note>original: "venæ sectione"</note> and purgations. Unless, I say, God makes almost all things new. For the acquisition of the Tree of Life is most difficult, very laborious, and revealed to few. For it is necessary that he who ascends the Mountain of the Lord be innocent in hands and heart, who has not taken his soul in vain, nor devised deceit for his neighbor. For he alone shall receive this blessing from the Lord. 

<column-break/>

Until finally, in the confusion of the end times, man will dare to teach man those things which otherwise—to preserve human respectability—remain in secret. For today, most of those who practice medicine <note>original: "Medentum"</note> think they know enough if, having been initiated into the pagan doctrine of their ancestors, they at least grow rich and are excused from the deaths of the common people by following the rules of the Writers. Most of them also mock the idea of "Long Life" because they are ignorant: but eventually they will have their fill of their own ways, and their mockery will fall back upon its authors. For in the coming age, God will be weary of such neglect of the neighbor and the poor. Vices, too, succeed one another in a chain through the ages. At one time it was an honor to have drained many cups; at another, for a **gladiator** <note>original: "Monomachum"; literally one who fights in single combat</note> to have killed many. Fraud and deceit flourish today under the title of "shrewdness," and virtue hides as a rarity among the few, although it is continually praised in name only. It will grow strong again when the number of destructive wits withdraws from the lavish leisure of studies and evil curiosities toward the arts and crafts. Surely a tranquility of the times will be born, once the crowd of worms living off others' leisure, covered with the cloak of piety, has been driven away. A coming repentance at last bids us hope for a reformation. For this happy age, I have decided to write about **Long Life**, praising the Lord that my stay here [on earth] has nearly reached its end. In revealing unheard-of things, if I have anywhere uncovered the errors of those who came before me, I have done so by necessity, lest those who follow me strike against the ruts <note>original: "salebras"; rough or bumpy roads</note> and be deprived of the target of truth. For

As I am about to write concerning **Long Life**, it seemed fitting to first provide a treatise on **Time**, because a long life must have an inseparable respect to **duration**. However, I have not established this in the first place as if I wished to measure life by time; rather, to speak properly, I compute the **Duration** of life in relation to days and years, which I shall presently demonstrate are *not* time. These are paradoxes (I confess), but nonetheless they are true doctrine. For I have shown elsewhere that Aristotle was utterly ignorant of the beginnings of nature, and very poor in the matter of Physics; and therefore, he absurdly presented time, place, vacuum, the infinite, fortune, and such abstract considerations—which are entirely foreign to the order of nature—as if they were Physical Principles. I, however, have prefixed to the study of long life a speculation on Time, which has been unknown until now: Wherefore, for its elucidation, I establish this

->CONCERNING TIME.<-

## THE PROPOSITION.

<margin>2.</margin> Time is separated from Eternal duration in no other way than the light of day—when the sun is not visible—is separated from the most brilliant light of the solar body itself.

<margin>3.</margin> For I believe that the way, the truth, the life, and the essence of all things is GOD, most glorious. Likewise, He is the Principle in which all things have their beginning, live, and move. I say, therefore, that even if no body or motion were given, nevertheless time, place, situational arrangement, and distance would remain the same as they are now. Indeed, beyond the heavens, an infinite space is believed to exist, deprived of all body and motion, yet filled with the Spirit, which is equal to that space in its infinite magnitude.

<margin>4.</margin> Similarly, I understand Time to be bound neither to place, nor to body, nor finally to motion, but rather an entity <term>original: "ens," a philosophical term for a thing that exists</term> separated from them. Therefore, I do not beg for Time from the measurement of the motion of the *primum mobile* <note>original: "cœli primi mobilis," the "first mover," which in ancient astronomy was the outermost sphere of the heavens that moved all others</note>. For just as the motion of the heaven occurs in a place, as if it were a certain measure of that place, nevertheless, just as the place is not the motion—even though the motion happens in a place—so also motion is not time, even though it occurs in time. Nor can time be generated by motion, or in the "womb" of motion, if that which is generated is to be similar in kind to its generator.

<margin>5.</margin> Truly, the Year, Day, Months, and Night are not time: but are measures and accidents <note>in logic and philosophy, an "accident" is a characteristic that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note> of things occurring in time, which are entirely foreign and external to time. Thus, indeed, our day is another's night. Meanwhile, the same Time exists everywhere in the whole universe. Spring, summer, autumn, and winter are not time: but alterations of the air, ordered into the change and cycles of things. Likewise, childhood, adolescence, youth, vigor, and old age are not time: but names for the changes of the body and of life.

<margin>6.</margin> For indeed the Schools <note>the "Scholastics," or traditional academic philosophers following the tradition of Aristotle</note>—besides teaching that Time is either the very measure of the "first mover" or at least contained within it (for that has not yet been determined)—wish, moreover, that any indivisible physical point of time should 

<column-break/>

contain within itself, actually and really, infinite mathematical points. Since they already grant an actual, indivisible, real infinite—which in itself is not positively intelligible, and which the Schools therefore deny as possible—within any tiny point of time, they pollute the knowledge of nature with mere dreams.

<margin>7.</margin> It follows necessarily from their given suppositions that any part of time is not actually time, but some mathematical point, indivisible, and thus without duration outside and beyond time. It would also follow that time would consist either of indivisible parts, or be produced from a connection of indivisible and infinite points of duration. Yet, even so, they would not truly be indivisible atoms or points of duration if, through their connection, they rose up into something divisible. They do not realize, I say, that a negative indivisible can never coalesce through connection into some present, actual, long, short, great, or small existence, because it contains within itself a mere nothing in a physical, that is, real, entity.

<margin>8.</margin> Therefore, they contradict themselves in the word "indivisible." They have indeed looked at long and short Time, and thus far have reduced it to a category of quantity. Finally, they have also established the essence and the entire definition of time in "succession," which they claim stands connected by actually infinite and infinitely indivisible points of duration, even in the smallest point of a physical instant.

<margin>9.</margin> Surely in both cases they have devoted themselves too much to Mathematics <note>original: "Mathesi"</note> while they seemed to themselves to have driven nature home. Mathematics, of course, supposes infinite possible points of subdivision in every continuum; meanwhile, nature does not know these suppositions and physics denies them. For physics attends to things as they are, and not as they serve the speculations of the measurement of positions.

<margin>10.</margin> The Schools then separated the consideration of magnitude from the consideration of number, wishing—

<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical critique of the "Schools" (the academic establishment of the time). Having previously argued that Time is a real entity independent of motion, he now attacks the Scholastic and Aristotelian definitions of Time as a numerical measure.</meta>

<header>CONCERNING TIME.</header>

<margin>11.</margin> And they wish Time to be more like a number than a continuum; as if species of apes, insofar as they are similar to humans, should be classified among humans, and not among beasts. It is therefore ridiculous not to have separated Time from number by the breadth of the whole sky <note>original: "toto cælo," a common Latin idiom meaning "by a great distance" or "completely"</note>. They thought at last that numbers cast out the unit—even though the connection of units gives birth to all numbers. In this they are also foolish: they hold zero to be a unit, while a thousand zeros written below one another do not contain even the beginning of a unit.

<margin>12.</margin> Finally, this too is frivolous: that the Number Two <term>original: "Binarius"</term> differs in species from Three <term>original: "ternario"</term>, as this one does from Four, although two Twos make and become a Four. And this happens not through the generation of a new being, but through the melting together <term>original: "colliquationem," a term from alchemy and biology referring to the merging of substances</term> of both Twos. Therefore, I do not recognize distinct "species" in numbers, but only "othernesses" <note>original: "alteritates," the state of being different or distinct without being a different kind of thing</note> that are mixable and reducible. For nature does not allow itself to be coerced under the rules according to the whim of the Schools—namely, the idea that numbers would generate specific "species" from themselves, each of which would be mere individuals of the same number.

<margin>13.</margin> Thus, I know such species and metaphors to be alien to nature. Therefore, the Schools have regarded Time—supposing it to consist in an infinitely indivisible point—as a pillar of Physics. For this reason, I am more confirmed that whatever the Schools take from the Pagans <note>original: "Gentilibus," referring to non-Christian ancient philosophers like Aristotle</note> is a useless ruin <note>original: "labumen," a falling down or collapse</note> of Wisdom.

<margin>14.</margin> Indeed, if in those "actually indivisible" and "infinite" points of duration there were some infinitely corresponding "minimum" that bound the points of Time together through the following of duration (besides many other absurdities), Time would necessarily have to have its actual being before it existed; that is, it would not exist in "being," but all at once in "becoming." Indeed, it would not even "become" in this way, nor exist, nor be able to exist, but would instead perish before it even was.

<margin>15.</margin> Therefore Time (contrary to the prescription of the Schools) is neither long nor short, neither before nor after; it is neither a measure nor a thing that can be measured. It truly grieved me to have to reveal that in the entire Aristotelian *Physics* <note>original: "Aristot. auscultatione Physica," a reference to Aristotle's "Lectures on Physics"</note>, I find

<column-break/>

nothing but thick ignorance packed with absurdities and impossibilities. Therefore, I was compelled to write the truth out of compassion for the Youth who have been led away by credulity.

<margin>16.</margin> First of all, the Schools command that the Time they consider must be the "measure of motions." Yet it is already clear from these exposed falsehoods that time can neither measure nor judge between two motions made in the same duration (if I may speak thus), regarding which of the two is faster. For according to the aforementioned theories, time would necessarily always join itself more closely to the fastest motion, because it is closer and more similar to the "indivisible." Finally, if the succession of time happened by the meeting and help of an "indivisible infinity," and every motion were defined by a limit of duration, and since there is no equality or proportion of the finite to the infinite—least of all where both are considered in view of the same duration—it follows from the doctrine of the Schools that Time would be the incommensurable, vain, false, and incomprehensible measure of the *Primum Mobile* <note>original: "Primi motûs aut mobilis," the "first moved" sphere in ancient astronomy that was thought to drive all other celestial motions</note>.

<margin>17.</margin> To be sure, they define Time as being the measure of motions in relation to duration, as if it were appropriated to motion and succession through "accidents" <note>in Scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt</note>, namely because of duration. Indeed, if motion exists upon something immobile in such a way that Aristotle has inferred from this (though falsely) that the Prime Mover <note>original: "Primum Motorem," the hypothetical first cause of all motion in the universe</note> is necessarily immobile, why do they not also grant stability to duration? Under which, surely, all motions and proportions of successive things ought to be measured.

<margin>18.</margin> For in all seeds <note>original: "Seminibus," used here to mean the internal blueprints or vital principles that govern the growth and life-span of all things</note> from the beginning, there is present not only the principle of any motion, but also its own determined period of duration, proper to each motion; since every variety of any alteration depends on the slowness or speed of motions. Therefore, the duration of motions is included in the seeds essentially, intimately, and originally, as the formal and directive principle of those very things.

<margin>13.</margin> But not that time...

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of Scholasticism. In the previous section, he argued that numbers are not distinct "species" but merely collections of units. He now applies this logic to Time, arguing that it is a fundamental reality (Duration) rather than just a mathematical tool for measuring motion.</meta>

# CONCERNING TIME. 633

Time might be considered some external measure of motion with respect to duration. However, such a consideration—or relationship of proportion—is merely external and accidental to the things themselves, and thus a mere <term>ens rationis (a "being of reason," or a concept that exists only in the mind rather than in physical reality)</term>. It is not something fundamentally or essentially implanted within the seeds of things, as 
<margin>20.</margin> duration is. Finally, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic tradition of the medieval universities, heavily based on Aristotle.</note> assume there are "natural species" within continuous quantities. Yet, the "continuous" and the "discrete" are not things in themselves, but bare considerations of things according to measure. Real things indeed have their own species in reality, but the consideration of them as a mental construct lacks the essential species found in Physics. It is a shameful thing, therefore, that they have placed Time among measures and mental constructs—or even non-entities. 
<margin>21.</margin> It is a shameful thing, I say, for the Schools of Physics to have contemplated Mathematics <note>original: "Mathesin"</note> more than nature itself. It is futile to recognize "species" in numbers by which things in nature might be distinguished, and yet not know that "Unity" <note>The number One</note> is a number. Indeed, "One," in its distinctness from others, is no less a distinct number through its unity than "Ten" is. For there is no reason why two units should constitute a number more than a 
<margin>22.</margin> single unit does; since in the number two <term>binario</term>, both units remain discrete and distinct—indeed, they remain whole in their own being. They have not ceased to be, nor have they vanished into some "third thing" because of their connection. For the number two designates nothing except two units. It is therefore a diseased notion <note>original: "ulcerosum," literally "ulcerous" or "sore-ridden"</note> to claim that two things remain connected in their prior state of being, yet, solely because of that connection, they have generated a new "species" different from each of them. Therefore, Unity is most properly every number, because every number flows from it; thus, every number is nothing but a connection of units. From this, Unity itself is a **type of the Divinity**: because from it all numbers are made, and into it they are again 
<margin>23.</margin> resolved. Truly, as often as the Schools conceived of something through Mathematics, they immediately twisted it into nature under the guise of general rules.

<column-break/>

Thus, by confusedly equating the four supposed elements with four qualities, complexions, and humors, these quarrels were even transferred to the stars; they decreed that all things must agree with their own figments. By this same method, they adapted the "continuum" studied in 
<margin>24.</margin> Mathematics to linear points, and finally even to Time. St. Augustine indeed confesses that Time is something, but that the <term>quiddity (the "what-ness" or essential nature)</term> of Time is unknown; this is because he was imbued with false theses from Paganism. Therefore, I blush again and again that I must explain the essence of Time. But I do not fear this "hater" <note>likely referring to the critics of his work</note>, for he now beholds the truth in heaven.

First, I have removed all "succession" from Time, even though I had already shaken off the yoke of the 
<margin>25.</margin> great authorities of the Ethnic <note>meaning "Pagan" or non-Christian, specifically Aristotelian</note> schools. For at first I meditated on the fact that the heavens stood still <note>A reference to the Biblical story of Joshua, where the sun stood still in the sky</note>, and yet there was no "different" Time while the sun stood still than there is now. Thus, I began to measure that duration without the succession of the heaven's motion. Consequently, I gradually learned that all succession must be separated from Time, and applied only to motion. It is then a madness to think that the Sun once stood still, and yet even today to submerge Time within the motion of the heavens. For even if that stopping of the Sun was miraculous, the duration of that period was not itself miraculous. Then I perceived that Time already existed from the beginning, even when the "day" did not yet exist—that is, before light was born and separated from the darkness. The Heaven, the Earth, the abyss of waters, the darkness, and the day itself existed before the orbit of the heaven defined a "day." In the beginning, 
<margin>26.</margin> I say, of creatures—but not in the beginning of Time. Because that beginning of things includes a certain "While" <term>Dum</term>, so that the sense is: although God decreed from eternity to create things, when <note>original: "dum," which can mean "while" or "until"</note> it pleased His infinite goodness to go forth into external operation, then "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." And yet, that "While" existed before the creature, because God had no need of a created thing, nor of a created duration, nor were the things to be created...

He argues that Time is a real, divine entity that exists independently of the motion we use to measure it.</meta>

# CONCERNING TIME. 654

...they had need of a created duration, since no principle of unequal dignity concurs with a Creator of infinite power. For if a creature did not depend originally, totally, absolutely, and intimately upon God—as if upon the beginning and end of its own duration—then God would not be the immediate and total principle of things. He would not be the immediate life of things; that is, he would not be their <note>original: "α & ω"</note> Alpha and Omega <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, signifying the beginning and the end of all things.</note>. Therefore, I understood from this that if nature had at any time stood rooted in a duration flowing directly from eternity itself, it must still stand so today by those same rules of necessity.

<margin>27.</margin> Indeed, I knew soon after that the Duration which people call "Time" is a <term>real entity (ens reale)</term>. Likewise, if Time existed from the beginning before any creature was made, it cannot be counted among the things created. For no mention is ever made of Time itself being "created" <note>The author suggests Time is a fundamental aspect of God's presence rather than a separate object made during the six days of Creation.</note>.

<margin>28.</margin> I also considered that just as a moving object is in a place, so that the place does not merely surround the object on the outside (as <note>original: "Aristoteles"</note> Aristotle might think), but rather the place penetrates the moving object in every direction. Thus, every internal part of a body is no less "in its place" than its outer surface is. Yet, the reverse is not true: the object does not contain the place.

<margin>29.</margin> In this way—and yet much more abstractly—Duration is indeed internal to things; yet it is not affected, enclosed, or grasped by those things. A place has a certain and determined position which is changeable by the object moving through it, yet the object remains entirely inseparable from the concept of "place." But Duration itself is so inseparable from things that it never moves away or changes from them. Thus, since duration is above and within the being of things, and inseparable from them—indeed, more internal to things than the things are to themselves—

<margin>30.</margin> I have therefore meditated upon a plainly divine duration within time, which in that respect is not to be distinguished from eternity; yet it is distributed to things according to the capacity <note>original: "pro modulo"</note> of each recipient. And thus, I have sufficiently proved the aforementioned proposition.

<margin>31.</margin> For this reason, time neither has parts, nor does it allow for the

<column-break/>

division of itself, and consequently, it knows no "succession" <note>The idea that one moment follows another in a line.</note>. Nor does it prove those dreams to be true which suggest that time receives within itself infinite points, either joined together or broken apart. Indeed, time is not a "great" or "small" duration, any more than it is flat, round, long, deep, short, or wide. This is because it is not truly within the reach of the <term>Categories (praedicamenta)</term> <note>The ten "Categories" of Aristotle used to classify all things; the author argues Time is too fundamental to be categorized like a physical object.</note>. This is because that which exists as "actually infinite" is only one thing: namely God, who is all things. For if goodness, life, truth, and essence are, in an abstract way, God himself within created things, it cannot be denied that Duration likewise represents God in those same things. 

I believe, therefore, that true Time is unmixed, without the stain of the creature, everywhere and always immutable, and in no way successive. So that I might conceive of this more closely, I stripped away from time all physical bodies, all alternation of successive things, and the following changes of motions. Then, for the first time, I clearly understood that Time, in its own being, carries or owes no regard to the instability, variety, or measurement of motions. Indeed, time is what it is, whether motions and changes happen or not. Truly, I found no "duration" relative to motion—nor motion relative to duration—except by accident, and because of a mental measurement of one against the other. This is entirely irrelevant: since time has no succession, it cannot serve for measurement.

<margin>32.</margin> But because we are confined to this <note>original: "sublunari loco"</note> sublunary world <note>The world below the moon, i.e., the Earth, which was thought to be the realm of change and decay.</note> and are wrongly educated by the Pagan Schools <note>Referring to the followers of Greek philosophers like Aristotle.</note>, we are accustomed to considering "priorities" and "speeds" within the duration of time indefinitely. This is because, by a frivolous abuse, we usually measure the determination of motions and moving things according to space. However, if these relationships of "priority" were weighed in the balance of truth, they are merely attributes of motion, and by no means attributes of Time or duration. This is because "priority," "slowness," and so on, only describe a relationship inferred from the parts of motion that follow one another, and...

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that Time is not merely a measurement of movement, such as the rotation of the heavens, but is a divine and eternal duration present in all things. # ON TIME. 635

...and slowness compares the speeds of movements to one another; and so priority, slowness, and so on, do not so much measure time or duration, but only do so in respect to the daily motion <note>The "daily motion" refers to the perceived rotation of the heavens around the Earth every 24 hours.</note>. Indeed, human and indistinct weakness has measured all specific movements against the daily cycle through a certain laziness and dullness of mind. For they do not consider the priorities of movements as the actual duration of time itself, but rather as the universal distance of general movement. And although the duration of time itself is in and present in all things, this is nevertheless entirely foreign to the succession of movements. Hence it began that time was considered as a **successive** and **fleeting** entity through each individual instant. Especially since the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the medieval and early modern universities who followed Aristotelian logic.</note>, imitating the stupidity of the common people, have become accustomed to confounding time with the movement of the heavens. It is no wonder, then, if from such beginnings great Heroes <note>The author uses "Heroes" to refer to the great thinkers and philosophers of history.</note>, considering the essence of time, were unable to conceive of it. For since it involves the <term>actual infinite (actuale infinitum)</term> (which alone is eternal), it is necessarily incomprehensible to the finite mind by its very nature.

<margin>33.</margin> For time was thought to "succeed" and have parts only because parts followed one another in movements. Yet time and motion are disparate things, as far removed from each other as a fleeting and finite thing is from the infinite. For even if motion occurs in time, motion can no more be measured by man through time than man can measure himself through God himself—the one in whom man "exists, lives, and moves."

<margin>34.</margin> For if God willed in the future to make the entire course of the heavens so irregularly disordered that no motion could be matched to it, would time itself therefore become unequal? Or would it cease to be what it is now? Indeed, if the motion of the heavens ceased (as it will one day cease), would time likewise cease? Would the "now" itself no longer be "now"? For what does that which happens in time have to do with time itself? Since time has its being freely, without respect, reflection, or reciprocation toward anything else.

<column-break/>

Truly, time is not given to us as a measure, or so that it may be measurable in itself: but it has its free being in that from which all essence comes. For example: God is in every creature. For "good," insofar as it is "all good" and not just this or that specific thing, is God. But insofar as it is *this* or *that* good, it is not "all good"; and to that extent it has its being in created things. Indeed, just as God is the single good in all things, so in turn all good is essentially this one true good. Similarly, God is present everywhere to all things, and his duration is the duration of each and every thing.

In the same way, the light of the Sun is an entity and something in itself (for it illuminates and warms), yet outside or apart from the sun it is nothing. In the same way, eternal duration in created things is time; which outside of or beyond eternal duration is a mere nothing, in a privative and negative sense. Therefore, as long as there are any created things, time will never cease to be. The Lord said: *You are my son; today I have begotten you.* <note>original: "Tu es filius meus; hodie genui Te." From Psalm 2:7.</note> Because eternity is nothing but a single "now," a single "today." *From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.* <note>original: "Ex utero, ante Luciferum genui Te." From Psalm 110:3. In this context, "Lucifer" refers to the morning star, not the fallen angel.</note> Christ was born from the womb in time, and yet "before the morning star." This is because in time there is no priority or succession.

The word "before," therefore, designates the priority of the succession of movements and the excellence of dignity, but not priority of time. Because from the beginning until the end of the age, there is only a single "now." In this way, the lamb was sacrificed from the origin of the world, and his death saves those who died before the incarnation of the Lord; insofar as that blessed incarnation concerns movement. It certainly saves those who came before, preceding according to the course of life, and in respect to movements compared with each other—but not with regard to duration. *Lest the lion seize them, nor hell devour them.* <note>original: "Ut non rapiat eas leo, nec infernus devoret." A phrase from the Roman Catholic Offertory prayer in the Mass for the Dead.</note> For those prayers for the deceased are offered long after death, even though souls usually undergo their judgment immediately after expiring. Therefore, prayers of this kind would be in vain, and established too late, if time were successive.

# ON TIME. 636

The Church triumphs with the <term>Paraclete (Paracleto)</term> <note>The Holy Spirit, often referred to in Greek-derived Latin as the "Advocate" or "Comforter."</note> as its leader; it knows, therefore, that all future things exist in the same "now" of time, just as if prayers had occurred before death. For the Wise Man asserts that God made all things at once; yet <term>Genesis</term>, writing the history of the six days, says that just as many days were consumed. These accounts would therefore contradict each other if succession were attributed to time. All things were indeed created in the space of six days: yet they exist in a single permanent point of time. For in this way, the Devil foreknew future things in the succession of movements: insofar as they are present in a single "now" of time. The stars are indeed for "times," that is, for the changes of times or the varieties of movements; they are not, however, for the duration of our life, which has a fixed term established by the Almighty.
<margin>35.</margin> Truly, priority is most difficult to separate from time. For although we may abstract time from place, motion, and body, nevertheless, because of contrary habit and the novelty of the matter, it is extremely difficult to break the habit of thinking of "priority" within time. It is no different than if someone accustomed to cutting bread with the left hand finds it troublesome to use his right, even though he performs many other tasks correctly with the right. Nevertheless, this difficulty or lack of habit in understanding changes nothing in the things themselves, nor does it oblige the essence of time to accommodate itself to our errors. For what does the priority of movements in bodies have to do with time itself? Or how does priority, which is due to motion alone, harm time, if through ignorance it has been transferred onto time? But because the priority of movements, in relation to duration, implies an immediate relationship to another movement (namely of days and years) by which we measure all other movements, therefore "priority" has been <note>original: "abusivè," meaning improperly or by a misuse of the term</note> improperly transferred into Duration. Otherwise, it ought first to be established that this movement of the day is time because it happens in time; which being proved, priority could then be referred to Duration, and not otherwise: therefore, never. To me, however, for the distinction of things, it is enough that duration

<column-break/>

does not depend on motion in its essence at all, but bears in and of itself a certain uniform constancy of Divinity, by which it is so permanent that it remains entirely free from all change and succession of priority. It is foreign to, and plainly independent of, things and the successive movements of things: Therefore, duration is to be placed in no <term>category (prædicamento)</term> <note>Referring to the ten Aristotelian "Categories" or "Predicaments" used to classify every object of human apprehension.</note>.
<margin>36.</margin> And since it in no way belongs to the series of relatives, therefore, consequently, duration implies no internal relationship to things, except by accident; and even then, only according to the miserable and deceived discourse of reason, which creates proportions between <term>mobile things (mobilia)</term>; and even then only insofar as they are mobile, in relation to local or transformative motion: but not in relation to their real being. Certain flows of "priorities" and "posteriorities" <note>The states of being "before" and "after."</note> in their movements belong to perishable mobile things, with which they hasten toward the destined ends of their period, and thus toward their own destruction. But what does all this have to do with time? Must Time also run with each and every movement on that account? Certainly then there would be as many times and durations as there are movements. Or if a single time runs universally with each and every movement, and since such time itself would outrun all other movements most swiftly, then the slow course of a crow's life would flow in unequal time with the turn of a spinning wheel. Wherefore they could not flow together under a single duration. Therefore, time has its being or essence as immobile, immutable, indivisible, and unmixed with things; not successive, but simple and free from any intrinsic relationship of its own to the creature. Even though time is more intimate to things than things are to themselves.
<margin>37.</margin> I suppose, therefore, that time is in the thrice-glorious God eminently and essentially: but in the creature dependently, subjectively, and participatively through an outward emanation. The law of
<margin>38.</margin> fate indeed permits the movements of life to follow

# ON TIME. 637

...according to an inherent disposition in moving things, fixed to a certain and prescribed order of destinations. But such attachments and orders do not belong to time itself; they follow, clearly, their own "before" and "after," their own "timely," "opportune," and "late" according to the following of motions and the mutations of those same things, but not of time. 
<margin>39.</margin> For nothing can be thought more absurd than that a single time would move by some succession, follow along, and make itself a servant <note>The author uses the word "vassal" (vassallum) to emphasize how time is wrongly treated as a subordinate to physical events.</note> to infinite points—indivisibly indeed, in its priority—and divided among itself by a suppositional nature: which, nevertheless, would be joined in each single smallest instant, and which, without any extension of their own, would perish successively before they were even connected. And that such a chimera should be the most certain measure of all motions! Indeed, that time, through such an undivided coupling of points and a mutual and unceasing succession, should be forced to move and follow along successively: and that this movement of an infinite, indivisible point should finally be the distinct rule and temperament of all motions. Yet these very dull dogmas are offered to youth in the first spring of their age as if they were Aristotle’s *Physics* <note>original: *naturali Aristotelis auscultatione*, literally "Aristotle’s natural listening," the traditional title for his books on Physics.</note>.
<margin>40.</margin> Priority, therefore, is by no means defined with respect to time, but to fate, related in order to motions: without respect of one motion to another. For local motion does not touch the essence of place: rather, a thing that moves successively through a place expresses only an accidental relationship to the positioning of places; meanwhile, the relationships of the positions or of one place to another remain stable, unmoved, and unchanged, nor do they touch the place in the slightest, whether the thing is moved in that position or not; since the succession of local motion is, on the part of the motion, foreign to the place. Truly, with even greater right, I understand these things to happen with time, because time is not relative by any internal reason, but is something more abstract and closer to eternity in the intellect and in reality than place is. 
<margin>41.</margin> Time, there-

<column-break/>

-fore, knows no succession, neither from the perspective of the motion nor of the thing moved: for succession is nothing other than the proportion of successive things in order to motion; and although duration itself is present in motion, it does not therefore take on the nature of the succession of motions. However, as many as have thought time to be a successive and partible being, they also believed that, with the reins let loose, it would fall and perish with the destruction of the world: and that the *aeon* <note>original: *aevum*, a technical term for the duration of eternal beings like angels, distinct from the "time" of the physical world.</note>, like a new creature, would be substituted in its place without the means of successions. 
<margin>42.</margin> This was surely thought so because the "whatness" <note>the essence or quiddity</note> of time was unknown. For while they say this about time, they reveal that they are not speaking of time at all, and that they are ignorant of its duration: because they only speak of motions, and the change of these things, within the contingency of duration. For even if duration is within and present to things, it nevertheless has nothing in common with things, whether they are burned, submerged, rot, move, sleep, begin, or cease to be; because duration does not look back at things, but remains unbroken and always equal to itself. 
<margin>43.</margin> For perhaps that text led them astray: *After this, there shall be time no longer* <note>original: *Post hac non erit tempus amplius*, a reference to Revelation 10:6.</note>, not noticing that "time" in that place is taken for the days of the year, for the change of the weather <note>original: *meteoron*, referring to atmospheric or celestial changes.</note>, and for the opportunity for repenting, according to a common way of speaking. It does not mean that with the destruction of the world, duration—which is now, always was, and will be—would cease. For the *aeon* assigned to the Angels is in no way different from the duration which they call time. Think of the soul dwelling in the body, which experiences neither day, nor night, nor old age, nor does it have succession: yet it is in one and the same duration, and in the same "now," in which another soul, separated from the body, exists. Indeed, the change of place and condition of souls in no way touches or affects duration, nor binds duration to itself so that it might then change into its own essence. But the same duration of eternity flows emanatively into all things and sustains each one: nevertheless, it does not lose its own simplicity, even when—

<meta>This page continues the author’s philosophical investigation into the nature of duration. He has just argued that time is not a sequence of points but a singular, unchanging reality. # ON TIME. 638

...than that the things participating in it receive it in various ways. For a thing exists in and under duration; if it should fall away from this duration, it vanishes into nothingness.
<margin>44.</margin> For an Angel, in its own substance and being, enjoys continuous time without succession or parts, in which nothing is large, small, long, short, before, after, a measure, or a thing measured. Since, therefore, according to the Schoolmen <note>original: *Scholas*; referring to the medieval Scholastic philosophers</note> there is a duration of this kind for Angels, which they call *aevum* <term>aevum: a technical philosophical term for the "everlastingness" of celestial beings, positioned between the "time" of humans and the "eternity" of God</term>, and they distinguish it from the time of sublunary things <note>original: *sublunarium*; things "below the moon," meaning the earthly realm of change and decay</note>, whether they exist in the Heavens or on earth: and they admit that the works of Angels are measured by successive and discrete time; I conclude that since an Angel cannot exist simultaneously in two durations that differ entirely in their nature—one belonging to itself and the other to its works—both of which are contained within a single "now" of duration, it is necessary that both of these durations melt into one single reality. They differ only by an accidental perspective—that is, by a fictional and mental non-entity. They are, I say, necessarily a single thing in the real act of existence. And thus, time is clearly the same thing in reality as *aevum*, and it remains unchanged for eternity. It is enough for me that the Schools acknowledge some continuous time that is not successive, which they call *aevum*. I am not forced to separate time from *aevum* just because of their mental distinctions.
<margin>45.</margin> For if the alternation of things and motions separates time from *aevum*, by 그 that very fact they are looking more at the alternation itself than at the duration; yet they believe they are attending to the determination and definition of duration. Indeed, this proves that, having been ignorant of the essence <note>original: *quidditate*, literally "what-ness"</note> of time until now, they have in vain separated discrete time from continuous time or *aevum*. Since there is nowhere any necessity for succession in duration, and even more so because they assign certain perspectives to both aforementioned durations which are "a whole heaven apart" <note>original: *toto cœlo*; a common Latin idiom meaning "entirely" or "diametrically opposite"</note> from the nature of duration. These perspectives only give rise to a logical difference—a "non-entity"—which is equivalent to saying

<column-break/>

that the diversity of both durations is, in reality, a mere fiction.
<margin>46.</margin> I prove this as follows: Time is a being. Therefore, it is either the creator or a creature. If it is a successive being, then it is not the substance of the creator or the creature. But if they want it to be an "accident" <term>accident: in philosophy, a property that "clings" to a substance but is not part of its essential nature (e.g., being "green" is an accident of a leaf)</term> (for the Schools have not yet mentioned a "neutral being" between substance and accident), they should at least have described the subject where time "dwells." I will guess then: the subject of time will not be the heavens, for if so, decaying and earthly things would not have their own duration of time proper to themselves; duration would be a foreign visitor, lent to decaying things. Likewise, if one earthly thing participated in Time as an accident proper to itself, another neighboring thing would not necessarily enjoy time. But if they prefer that each decaying thing participates in the Time of the heavens: at least then individual created things would not have a different duration, but each would remain in the same external heavenly duration through participation. Indeed, earthly things would sooner possess all the other manifest qualities and properties of the heavens than they would possess their duration. Therefore, they do not participate in a borrowed permanence of the heavens in duration. But if indeed a proper duration belongs to each individual thing, so that things themselves are the subjects where duration "dwells"—not sought from elsewhere, but as if the determination of duration were essentially included in their seminal beginnings—then the light of Divine Providence <note>original: *Divinæ providentiæ*</note> already appears in time. Thus time is the rule of the created thing, but is not the created thing itself; for "in God we exist, live, and move." So it is also in duration, which is not even created. Otherwise, if time "clings" to individual things like an accident or a companion, then besides countless absurdities, there would be at least as many different times as there are atoms of things. And everyone who now exists together in the same duration would have just as many different essences and existences of durations, and time would be actually divided into infinity. And every accident, by its nature, belongs to some sen—

He further explores whether time is a substance or an accident, suggesting it is a divine rule rather than a created, divisible property of individual objects.</summary>

# DE TEMPORE. 639

<margin>47.</margin> ...its object will not be perceptible to any sense within the duration of time. For this reason, I am forced to recognize in time a certain universality, and at the same time a singularity proper to individual things—something more intimate to things than the things are to themselves. Likewise, I acknowledge a proper rule and determination which grants a precise duration to individual things, yet which is in turn impassive, incomprehensible, or uncontrollable by those things. Therefore, I recognize time as a being that gives and distributes all things to all, according to a destined participation in Eternal Duration—and this to the confusion of atheists! I consider time, therefore, as an emanating splendor of eternity, which no more exists apart from or outside of eternity than the splendor of light exists apart from the light itself. Time, therefore, ought to be for us a hand-leading <note>original: *manuductio*; a guiding hand or introduction</note> to the super-intellectual One—the eternal, the infinite, intimate to every single thing, yet in no way mixed, enclosed, grasped, or detained; in Whom is the essence of all things, to Whom be praise and glory in His eternity!

Therefore, it is a barbaric and absurd pagan saying that "time consumes or devours us," since there is no action or passion <note>meaning "active influence" or "passive being-acted-upon"</note> of time upon us, nor from us upon it. We do not perish by the fault of time, nor is death caused by time any more than by God. For the arrangements of motions are the secondary causes of death, but time is not of the nature of motions. Indeed, divine judgments arrange everything for reasons known to Himself.

<margin>48.</margin> It is surprising, meanwhile, that although the day is the measure of motions, they have prescribed no precise measure for the day itself. They have indeed made subdivisions of hours, minutes, seconds, etc., through the sexagesimal system <note>original: *sexagenarium*; the base-60 system used for time and angles</note>. But no one so far has shown the precise space of one-sixtieth of a minute; for indeed, people have wavered in practice. Furthermore, except for noon <note>original: *meridiem*</note>, there is no stable moment of the day. Even that varies almost everywhere, so much so that the certainty of the meridian point depends not so much on the motion of the sun and the heavens as on the respect of the site of the sphe-

<column-break/>

-re. Therefore, no one has taught a certain or defined "now" or a constant point at which something happened, except by taking eclipses into account. <margin>49.</margin> They imitated the globe of the world when they divided the Sphere by the point of the meridian and the height of the pole: but since the Sun is not always or everywhere visible as desired, they devised wheels, revolved several times a day, which, because they could not move themselves, had a weight hung from them, and thus they measured the day. In this, error soon arose, because the weight, increasing in force due to the length of the ropes, created an inequality. <margin>50.</margin> Even more uncertain is the measurement of days by the forced twisting of steel <note>referring to the mainsprings in early watches</note>; because so far the exact proportion between the strength of the twisted resisting steel and the elongation from the axis within the screw or rope-winding <note>original: *cochleam*; likely referring to a fusee or a similar mechanism used to equalize the pull of a spring</note> is not yet certainly established. For when the north wind blows, the steel is more stubborn than itself and more than usual. Therefore, the proportions of the smallest minutes in motion are not yet fixed. The sixteenth note <term>semifusa: a musical note value, similar to a semiquaver or sixteenth note</term> in Music is still uncertain, because it refers to the pause of a whole note, which can be faster or slower at will. <margin>51.</margin> I first measured the strength and quality of cannons <term>bombardarum: large primitive cannons or mortars</term> and every kind of gunpowder <term>pyrius pulvis: "fire powder," i.e., gunpowder</term> by the measurement of motions in duration. For if a catapult <note>here used as a general term for a heavy engine of war</note> is 200 paces away from a wall to be demolished, firing a 22-pound ball with 10 pounds of gunpowder of a known quality, let it be noted how much the strike of the ball lags after the powder is ignited. Now indeed, by standing at a distance of 250 or 400 paces with a solid ball of the same weight and an equal weight of the same powder, let it be noted whether the sluggishness of the strike corresponds to the proportion of the distance. Let the same trial be made in larger and smaller cannons. Thus, the sluggishness or slowness of the strike will reveal how much resistance the distance of the air creates, how much the quality of the powder accelerates the shot, and how much the hollow in an iron ball takes away—or if it is filled with weighted lead. I, however, have sometimes measured the speeds, powers, and proportions of such motions, and likewise the minutes of the day, with great delight. I hung a weight of one pound from a nail by a thin thread,

# ON TIME. 640

...of one foot in length, and a weight hung free in the air; I moved the weight, however, so that it might beat in the air like the clapper of a bell. I say, therefore, that each and every subsequent beat until the very last will be equal to the first beat in all places. For as much as the first beat is larger, the subsequent ones are smaller, and therefore they can be slower in their motion, but not in their beginning or their end. <note>The author is describing the "isochronism" of the pendulum—the discovery that the time it takes for a swing is the same regardless of the width of the arc.</note> Likewise, whether a single pound or several are hung from the string, they will not for that reason be unequal. But if the string is two feet long, each individual beat will be precisely twice as slow; <note>In modern physics, the period of a pendulum is proportional to the square root of its length, but the author here emphasizes a simpler direct proportionality to explain the measurement of time.</note> Therefore, according to the length of the string, the beats are accelerated or slowed. And so the delay of any motion can be precisely noted. A musician will notice the equality of these beats. Finally, since the motivating force is in both cases a single, equal beginning of motion, moderating the speed according to the distance of the place: for that reason it is necessary that the beat of one pound, as well as of several, be equal. I suppose, then, that a beat of two feet in length is of a moderate pause; therefore, that beat can be subdivided into 16 smaller distinct parts, and it can be observed on a <term>gnomon</term> <note>the part of a sundial or clock that casts a shadow or points to the time</note> how many beats of a one-foot string a quarter of an hour has given: and thus a year will be precisely measured.

<margin>52.</margin> As for what pertains to "critical days" <note>historically, specific days during an illness when a change or "crisis" was expected</note>, the observation indeed has its basis in nature, insofar as our <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "master-builder" or vital spirit that governs the body's health</note> unfolds the rhythm of the heavens. Indeed, the Moon has always proceeded on the 14th day to the place opposite to where it was carried on the first day. For that reason, nature is judged to have obtained the opposing forces of the Archeus: Likewise, the seventh day also has half of the opposition, as well as the square aspect of the moon to its starting point. Accordingly, the 7th and 14th days are bad in respect to the disease, but good in respect to the human Archeus. Therefore, a critical day is rare outside of acute diseases, however much <margin>53.</margin> Paracelsus <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> may have thought otherwise. But I have diligently noted that a crisis never occurs where a physician skilled in his art has removed the disease before the expectation of a crisis.

<column-break/>

For just as nature <margin>54.</margin> rejoices in ordinary motions, and is accustomed to them, and is gladly governed by the unity of the motive power: so when the whole business of a disease rests only on its own shoulders, it summons fixed crises, which otherwise the goodness of a remedy anticipates, or which the wickedness of a remedy delays or destroys. Thus, indeed, the 14th day of a crisis is prolonged into the fortieth. It is, therefore, the duty of a good and faithful physician to ignore crises; and it would have been better for those patients to have lacked a healer, as many as escape through a crisis, and much more so those whose crisis is slower. For let the <margin>55.</margin> Schools <note>the traditional academic and medical establishments of the time</note> boast of "criticals," let them establish a crisis, let them teach that nature "battles" with the disease; let a crisis happen for them without a lawsuit or a judge. <note>The word "crisis" originally referred to a legal judgment or verdict.</note> To me, at least, that similarity of a "battle" seemed impertinent, and the name of "crisis" ineptly borrowed. For fictions of this kind are handed down from hand to hand, by which every active agent is believed to endure a lawsuit solely because of contraries; for once one absurdity is granted, many more soon follow in a chain. For I have taught elsewhere that nature does not know "contraries," nor does a disease "battle." That is, nature broods over a disease, as over an egg, more than being contrary to it: if nature alone is the healer of diseases. And so she matures all things, that she may arrive at the end, and thus she even intends the end of a disease by maturing the means. Thus a disease does not resist nature while it is being matured, any more than an egg, while it is being warmed, fights with the brooding hen. For a destined period is assigned to the seeds of diseases: not indeed one which is owed to the mystic numbers of days, but to the requirements of maturity alone. For if things that are "cooked" and not "raw" are to be moved according to Hippocrates; the wise and gentle Ruler of nature knows his own maturities at fixed moments, which he alone is compelled to perfect—not indeed because of a distinct animosity of diseases in a contest: but, once the filth is matured, it ceases to cling to the solid parts. But to what purpose is such a great commentary on critical days (as a younger man I wrote five books on critical days, which I then offered to Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcano obtuli*; a common Latin idiom meaning he burned his own manuscripts</note>) if it is necessary...

# ON TIME. 641

...that the Healer should be so instructed as to make a dangerous disease harmless, and to shorten a long one—that is, to cut it short—so that it is not prolonged until the crisis? Therefore, a <term>Crisis</term> <note>original: "Crisis, ut judicium sonat" — the word 'crisis' comes from the Greek 'krisis', meaning judgment or decision. In ancient medicine, it was the moment a disease was "judged" by nature to either end in recovery or death.</note>, as the name implies, should be the judge and accuser of physicians, and the testimony of nature alone acting as the bearer: because a Crisis only happens when something sticky is attached or a source of illness is enclosed, and seeks to be separated at full maturity.

<margin>56.</margin>
As for the <term>Climacteric year</term> <note>A "critical" year in a person's life, thought by ancients to be particularly dangerous, especially multiples of 7 and 9. The "Grand Climacteric" was the 63rd year (7 x 9).</note> derived from the multiplication of the number seven by nine—namely, into the 63rd year of life—it is a foolish invention: for "seventy years are the days of man," etc. <note>A reference to Psalm 90:10.</note> Therefore, the Holy Scriptures among Christians accuse this of being a false imposture; and so it is an invention of the Demon, who, as the enemy of our life, seeks to strike down the elderly with the fear of death before their appointed hour. Otherwise, what does the multiplication of one number by another do to the course of life? Indeed, the years hasten and return to their own harvests and maturities. For this reason, the revolutions of years and the numbers of those revolutions look rather to the identity of the returns than to number or life directly, and in no way refer back to a past number, because each year ends in its own precise singularity, and does not reflect back upon the plurality of the preceding ones.

<margin>57.</margin>
Among others, some stupidly look to the "numbering number" <note>original: "numero numerante" — a philosophical distinction between the abstract concept of counting (numbering) and the actual things being counted (numbered).</note>. Truly, as it is pious and Christian to acknowledge life from the hand of the Founder, the Prince of Life: so it is the mark of the lost to have borrowed life from the Planets and numbers. For although God has disposed all things in a certain space according to His whim and good pleasure, it would be foolish to attribute causality to numbers. If plants had the power of producing offspring before the stars were born <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis, where plants are created on the third day and stars on the fourth.</note>, and flourish by the power of the Word, it is shameful for a Christian to have given the powers of human life and its duration and existence to "numbering numbers." Therefore, whether we look at the climacteric year, or the numbered returns of the stars, or the recursive number, or finally the numbering number, it is empty

<column-break/>

chatter, repugnant to the Holy Scriptures, which call life from 70 to 80 years miserable, not because of the years passed, nor because of their numbering number, but because necessities have been ingrained in the seeds by the Prince of Life, who thus decreed it.

<margin>58.</margin>
But they boast about the <term>Sabbatical number</term> <note>The number seven, associated with the Sabbath.</note>, because it is the seventh. This is contradicted by the fiftieth, which is the <term>Jubilee</term> <note>The Jubilee year (every 50 years) in Hebrew tradition followed seven cycles of seven years.</note> and is entirely sabbatical, and even the seventieth year, because as the seven-times-tenth it is more "sabbatical" than the sixty-third; for the ninth year is "enneatic" <note>Related to the number nine (Greek 'ennea').</note>, which contributes nothing to Sabbatism. For if the seventh day is "Critical" <note>In ancient medicine, the 7th, 14th, and 21st days of an illness were considered turning points.</note> because of the positions of the Moon, then it is not because of the number itself; nor does the Moon have anything in common with the climacteric number of 63 years. Indeed:

<margin>59.</margin>
The Astrologers command the 56th year in nocturnal births because of the (truly shameful) doubled coldness of Saturn: and the 63rd year in diurnal births, because of the ridiculous dryness of Mercury and Mars, as being especially dangerous. But these people, besides the fact that they say goodbye to the climacteric year for at least half the time, contradict the text: *Seventy years are the days of man, etc.* Finally, they fall away from numbers when they call upon the qualities of the elements for help, and, in their delirium, transfer them to the stars. If death in the "valley of miseries" is the end of calamities, the Climacteric year ought to be the fiftieth, which is Sabbatical and of the Jubilee.

<margin>60.</margin>
God indeed distinguished the week into 7 days, not because of the mystery or dignities of the number; but because He foresaw that He would hardly be given any time for Himself unless He had commanded it; for which reason He willed that at least every seventh day should be owed to Him, so that we might all be free for Him at least once a week.

<margin>61.</margin>
For it was not that the number contained a sacred mystery, but it testified to the indulgence of His kindness, that He asked for only one out of seven. Come now, if He consecrated the seventh to Himself, why do you add the ninth, which is not consecrated to Him? Why do you marry a profane number (as you say) to a sacred one, so that you may manufacture a climacteric from it? Or for you...

LONG LIFE,

is it permitted to have made days sacred to God? How, finally, if the numbers seven and nine held a mystery within themselves, would you deal with the fact that the number produced by seven times nine makes sixty-three? Since, according to your view on the types of numbers, nothing can be added or taken away without the type itself being immediately changed? God commanded ten days for the unleavened bread before and after the feast; but what authority does that give for the number ten? The Lord commanded a rest for Himself on those days in which He had been beneficial to them, and they are not to be observed by us for that reason alone. Therefore, He did not assign a sacred status to the numbers themselves. 

Thus, that doctrine contains the later falsehoods of the Jews, which were then fashioned from the vanities of Astrologers and the "mad-man" reckonings of the melancholic—rules and arts accommodated to empty whims. I have already cured several such people with remedies for mania, since that kind of stubbornness is not without its own insanity. Finally, therefore, it is established that the "long life" I am treating is not in respect to Duration or time, but rather to the motions flowing from the beginning to the end. The measure of these motions in the constancy of Duration is not Duration itself, but another motion, such as a "day," which measures the lengths of life solely by its own plurality. This is why the Holy Scriptures speak separately, saying: *In those days.* <note>original: "In diebus illis."</note> Likewise, they describe the occurrences of men's affairs by days, but not by the successions of "times" which paganism introduced with an entirely mythical way of speaking; for time has no parts, succession, or otherness.

1. *Life deservedly had to be shortened.* 2. *The consideration of long life flowed from the gift of God.* 3. *Several factions of Paracelsus's disciples concerning long life.* 4. *An objection regarding despair over long life.* 5. *How great the length of life is according to the author.* 6. *Why is the limit of a long life so diverse?* 7. *Long life is proven.* 8. *The insufficiency of Galen is noted.*

<margin>I.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral motifs and scrolls.</image-desc>Almost all of us complain about the shortness of life, yet the span of life is long enough, and the plurality of days great enough, if it is all well-spent. For consider how much sleep, idleness, vain occupations, parents, and friends have divided the span of life with you; you will see that our complaint about the brevity of life is a lie. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher who wrote the famous essay "On the Brevity of Life."</note> once expressed this opinion. Christians, however, who hope for death as an entrance into life, should by no means lament the shortness of life. For the number of the Elect and the reprobate is certain; so that it might be fulfilled more quickly because of the iniquities of many, the day of life had to be shortened, and the number accelerated due to the haste of the Last Day. Otherwise, even if the world were fertile in its entire breadth, it would not 

<column-break/>

suffice to nourish everyone—those already born and those yet to be born—because of the aforementioned haste, if every one of them reached the limit of a long life. 

Furthermore, however much the Just ought to rightly rejoice in the shortness of their life, and conversely, many of the unjust might desire longevity (for perhaps they will be amended in old age), yet since it is clear to no one whether they are considered just in the sight of God—especially since *in His sight no living soul shall be justified* <note>original: "in conspectu ejus non justificabitur omnis vivens" — a quote from Psalm 143:2.</note>—I have therefore judged that everyone should seriously apply themselves to obtaining the ancient blessing promised to those who obey their parents. <note>A reference to the Fourth Commandment: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land."</note> A long life, therefore, has seemed to me to be the very peak of all Philosophy, because it provides a pleasant and most useful meditation. Above all, the death of a person who would be a pillar to mortals, their country, or their family is greatly to be grieved, unless they should die because of some better purpose by the command or permission of God. For everyone is carried by their own will into the love, desire, and longing for a long life, and only the distressing loss of health or fortune brings about a longing for death and a weariness of life for those in despair. But of life...

<page-num>643</page-num>
<header>->THE SHORT ART<-</header>

...of achieving a long life, only despair terrifies those who search for it, because the Schools in the centuries before <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a revolutionary physician and alchemist who rejected traditional Greek medicine.</note> meditated on nothing regarding a long life, as their mute silence teaches us. Just as death crept in by the cunning of Satan, I rightly guess that a long life has likewise been suppressed until now by his deceit, since he is the sworn enemy of our race. Yet the Almighty recently deigned to instill this goal of a long life into the human mind, so that concerning these things, the gatherings of humors, their privileges, and their resting places gradually aspired toward a union of healing. Under this union, they first thought they had found the entrance for remedies, boasting that they had become masters of their wish. Those who followed them found that the subtleties of things, or the purities of medicines, were not yet sufficient to reach such a height that they could enter upon the length of life; this was because, once the duties of our physical growth were completed, these medicines no longer penetrated or mixed themselves into our primary constitution. 

I say that unless they strip away the "dowry" that things acquire by growing before they reach the first threshold, they certainly cannot carry it far inward toward the roots of similar substances. They are still far, however, from being able to hold back the vital powers from their flow toward destruction. For this reason, the more learned followers of Paracelsus thereafter fell away into various factions of opinion and into despair regarding a long life. Others, moved by greater courage and hope, supported more by the promises of Paracelsus than by the evidence of experience, promised many things that the outcomes did not later match, because they, along with Paracelsus, did not know the root of a long life. In such difficult matters, the lazier men also lost heart, saying: *A limit has been set for life, which no one shall pass.* <note>original: "Constitutus est vitæ terminus, quem nemo præteribit."</note> 
<margin>2. silence.</margin>

4. Therefore, they judge as vain whatever the bolder ones have promised regarding a long life. But they do not rightly consider that He who destined the limit of life also simultaneously destined, by that same labor, whatever means were required for that limit of life. Otherwise, the Tree of Life in Paradise would have been in vain, and it would have been in vain for Him to have created Medicine from the earth from the beginning, unless the natural limits of things could be prolonged by healing. For indeed, if I do not use remedies, a limit is set for me which I shall not pass; according to that saying: *Woe is me, that my dwelling is prolonged!* <note>original: "Hei mihi, quod incolatus meus prolongatus est!"—a reference to Psalm 120:5.</note> If Adam did not eat from the Tree of Life, he had a set limit for his life; but if he had eaten, he certainly would not have died. Therefore, there is hope for a long life, but the knowledge of the means alone has been lacking. 

For I am not speaking about a "long life" flowing down from the <term>Scaiolae</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Scaiolae" refers to spiritual or astral forces; the author is dismissing mystical or astrological explanations.</note>; I leave such fables to Paracelsus. Nor, finally, am I the sort of man who extends the years of a long life to the days of <term>Methuselah</term> <note>The oldest man in the Bible, said to have lived 969 years.</note>. But I value the age of <term>Nestor</term> <note>A legendary Greek king from the Iliad known for living through three generations.</note>, or of <term>John of the Times</term> <note>Johannes de Temporibus, a legendary figure said to have lived 361 years, dying in the 12th century.</note>. But Paracelsus calls a life of three hundred years "short"—a name he despises—calling it physical and accurate; indeed, unless it is extended to the "year of fire," he deems it unworthy, and he promises that by the power of his <term>Arcana</term> <note>Secret or "inner" medicinal essences in alchemy.</note>, a Nestorian life will follow with almost no effort. 

But in my view, a long life has a limit of 120 years, and a final limit of three hundred years, seeing as some animals spontaneously reach these ages every day, while man reaches them very rarely, and only in certain unusual places. However, as to why a long life spreads across such a wide range, it is because in both cases it is received according to the capacity of the Receiver. For a modern "Tree of Life" would no longer make me capable of even the smallest dignity or term, because the light of my life has been depraved by many storms, and they have already cut the thread while it was still on the spool. *He will fulfill your desire with good things, and your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.* <note>original: "Implebit in bonis desiderium tuum, & renovabitur ut aquila Iuventus tua." — Psalm 103:5.</note> 
<margin>5.</margin>
<margin>6.</margin>

For it does not say "as the eagle's [youth]," because the eagle’s original youth is not returned. Rather, the eagle is renewed just as the serpent sheds its old age and the stag sheds its horns; although in the meantime they do not cease to grow old during that renewal, so much so that the eagle hastens into white feathers.

He suggests a realistic long life ranges from 120 to 300 years, achieved through a process of renewal similar to animals shedding their old skin or feathers.</summary>

I speak, therefore, of a long life in this way: not indeed one that might be extended until the final Day of Judgment, according to the rash claims of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who challenged traditional medicine and claimed alchemical secrets could grant extreme longevity.</note>; nor do I speak of a "healthy" life that is entirely free from all diseases. Rather, I speak of that life which, under some degree of protection for the vital powers, extends the end of life for a considerable time. If these means were provided to a boy or a robust infant, they would lead them to the aforementioned limit, <margin>7.</margin> provided they continued to use them. What if, after all, certain climates prolong life? Shall this be denied to a medicine whose very "dowry" is long life? For often a person who is forced to use spectacles at the age of 50, later, by some spontaneous internal vigor, sees clearly again in their 80th year. Why then should that which happens in the eyes by spontaneous strength not be achievable for the whole body through the medical art? 

I have always reckoned that whatever was once natural (consider <term>Nestor</term> <note>A legendary king from Greek mythology said to have lived through three generations of men.</note>, for instance) does not contradict the possibilities of nature. Therefore, medical Art is short—lasting only a few years—while life is long, if we look to the hope of life which the loose doctrine of the Pagans neglected.

This treatise on the "entrance of death into human life" precedes the treatise on life for this reason: I am not dealing with immortal life (such as existed by the Creator's intention before the sin of the <term>First-formed</term> <note>original: "Protoplasti," referring to Adam and Eve.</note>), but only with longevity or the prolonging of life. Because the end of such a life is closed and defined by death, death—as the force that moves the limit of life—had to be defined by its causes first. I have not sought to imitate <margin>2.</margin> <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher who argued that the "final cause" (the purpose or end goal of a thing) is the most important cause to understand.</note> in this, who teaches that the "end" is the first of all causes.
