so be it, for with Him <note>God</note> there is no priority of causes, but all coincide in unity; with Him, all things are simply one. Similarly in nature, since whatever is made or generated is necessarily made or generated as female: and thus, up to this point, the female are the primordial principles and natural causes of things, and they act for ends known not indeed to themselves, but to God alone. By the necessity of Christian Philosophy, the <term>final cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" is the purpose or end for which a thing exists or is produced. The author argues that in nature, only God knows this purpose.</note> has no place in nature, but only in artificial things. And so, from this it is verified (as I have proven sufficiently elsewhere) that Aristotle understood natural things even less than he understood artificial things, and he deceived his Schools through artificial examples. He is entirely irrelevant in this place because he reduced artificial things under the catalog of natural causes. Indeed, looking more deeply, Aristotle remains equally ridiculous. For a builder, before the end or the shape of the house is made on paper, presupposes the knowledge of the site, the acquisition of means—finally of lime, bricks, stones, wood, and iron tools: the calculation of these means precedes the shape of the house. And thus, not even the final cause (if there be one) is the first of the artificial causes in the mind of the author. It is therefore foolish to reckon a "being of reason," a "mental being," or a "non-being" among natural causes. Furthermore, I would have gladly hastened to the goal I set for myself regarding "long life," unless death cut the intended thread, placing its own priority before me like an intervening delay. I would have also gladly kept the paradox of this matter among my secrets, had not the treatise on long life demanded its right from death, through which it naturally established its entrance into the human lodging. <margin>4.</margin> It is certainly a paradox, this unheard-of mystery of God, and for that reason I humbly <margin>5.</margin> submit it to the judgment of the Church. In place of a proposition, let it be: that **God did not make death.** For I immediately understand this to be denied for man alone; for otherwise, death was already naturally destined for the brutes before man was created, and indeed from

<column-break/>

the same root through which death entered into <margin>6.</margin> man. Since most beasts live only by mutual slaughter. Finally, death in this place does not signify a naked separation of the soul from the body, as if it designated a mere privation, or as if the meaning were that God did not make "non-being," which is what death is called; for such an utterance would be ridiculous in Holy Scripture. For the word itself ("made") and its negation is the same as that which regards "He spoke and they were made." And so, its negation speaks of the absence of a positive being and not a privation: and it is equivalent to this proposition: **God created man without an inclination toward death**, nor did He make natural causes in him by which he would be mortal. Finally, neither did the <term>Cacodæmon</term> <note>A "bad spirit" or demon (from the Greek 'kakos' and 'daimon'). In this context, it refers to Satan or fallen angels.</note> <margin>7.</margin> make death: *because there is no kingdom of the underworld on earth*, and much less in Paradise. Nor can Satan in any way change the essences established by the Creator, nor invert, abolish, or kill those things which God had made free from death. Death began in us from the Cacodæmon, to be sure, through suggestion and incitement, in a manner plainly accidental and external; nor could he produce a cause of mortality in a subject that was, by the grace of the Creator, incapable of it. Therefore, if neither God nor <margin>8.</margin> the Cacodæmon efficiently made the death of man, then by a sufficient enumeration of parts, **man alone made death for himself**, and applied the causes to himself as a positive being, from which he turned out mortal, and natural death was made. For what the devil could not do, man could do, having the possibility of dying, but not the necessity. For he was in possession of immortality, and he was able not to die, if he had wished, <margin>9.</margin> because death was for him a free contingency; however, because the body of Adam had need of the **Tree of Life**, therefore on the part of the body he was not absolutely immortal, and for that reason he also lacked food. But he was to be immortal from the gratuitous goodness of the Creator. And He who would have preserved Adam from death through grace, and had given the gift of the Tree of Life, would have also preserved the same from any injuries...

...had defended it with these barriers: Therefore, immortality in man would have been continued through the **tree of life**, and he was for that reason banished from Paradise, lest even after eating the apple <note>The "apple" refers to the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil.</note> he should stretch out his hand to the tree of life, and eat, etc. For just as the apple included the cause of death, so the tree of life contained the superiority of life over the causes of death. For it was not fitting for a man, who had brought death upon himself by eating, not to die and thus mock the threatened death; and therefore, he had to be exiled from Paradise.

<margin>10.</margin> Moreover, man was immortal insofar as his **Mind** <note>original: *mens*. The author distinguishes between the divine, immortal Mind and the lower "sensitive soul."</note> was immortal, immediately performing all the duties of the body and giving from itself an immortal life. Indeed, since it is ignorant of destruction and therefore not subject to the disturbances of perishable things, it follows that if it were to govern the immediate economy of the body, it would communicate a similar immortality to its body, at least regarding the excellence of the governing powers—even if, regarding the body's nourishment, man would have gradually failed unless he had been supported by the tree of life.

<margin>11.</margin> Rather, to speak distinctly: All plurality of powers was absorbed into the unity of the Mind. Even today, the Mind is impassible <note>meaning "incapable of suffering or being changed by external force"</note> regarding the duration and alterations of perishable things, because these lack the "bridge" <note>original: *symbolum*</note> through which they might immediately reach or penetrate the Mind. Therefore, so that death might make its approach and entrance into man, it was necessary for the Mind first to cease from its immediate and pristine function of the body's duties, and for another soul—namely the perishable, sensitive, and seminal soul—to enter in as a <term>syndesmon</term> <note>original Greek: $\sigma\acute{\upsilon}\nu\delta\epsilon\sigma\mu o\varsigma$, meaning a "bond" or "link." Here, it refers to a secondary soul that ties the immortal Mind to the physical, mortal body.</note> of the body.

<margin>12.</margin> This soul, which is surely far different from the Mind, is obtained through the **vital aura** in the course of nature from the "Father of Lights," the giver of life (as I have discussed elsewhere regarding the "Origin of Forms"), and it perishes with the death of man. For if the seed of a dog spontaneously flows into a "living soul" <note>original: *animam viventem*</note> exclusively, it was therefore fitting for man to be conceived without seed or manly union—or at least that the human seed would not exist without the disposition of seminal life—but by the common lead of created

<column-break/>

nature, it should terminate in a "living soul" exclusively, the manner of which I shall explain later.

<margin>13.</margin> Furthermore, it will become manifest in what follows that death—that is, the natural, productive cause of death—was situated in the eating of the apple, which (in a dispositive way) produced the **sensitive soul** through the seed (which man would have otherwise lacked), and indeed in the manner of brute animals. Consequently, the Mind deserted the governance of the body, as if shrinking back from the beastly impurity contracted therefrom. For from the moment man created seed within himself for the propagation of his species, he sketched out (at least potentially) by that same act the beginnings of a perishable soul—a covering and shroud for the Mind—so that it might take upon itself the whole ministry of the body. In nature, the Creator had already bound Himself to the seeds of things so that, as often as the seeds of sensitive beings reached the goal of multiplying, the Parent of vital lights Himself would flow in with souls worthy of each individual seed; a point I have followed up on purpose elsewhere in my work *On the Origin of Forms*.

<margin>14.</margin> And so, in the apple, there was the power of producing prolific seed, containing in a brutal manner the seminal <term>Archeus</term> <note>The *Archeus* is a term used in Paracelsian and Helmontian medicine to describe the internal "master workman" or vital force that governs the functions of an organ or organism.</note> that disposes the fetus, and obtaining for itself a perishable soul from the giver of life. For on the same day that they ate of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, "they would die the death" <note>original: *morte morerentur*</note>, because by the arrival of the sensitive soul, another and new generation was made, on account of which the dismayed Mind withdrew itself from the helm of life.

<margin>15.</margin> In this, specifically, stood the necessity of death and immortality. For man would have lacked a mortal soul as long as he had chosen to be immortal; not only because the single immortal Mind was sufficient for ruling the body, and it would not be fitting for the body to serve two masters at once, but moreover, because there was no need for seed that contained within itself the disposition toward a perishable soul. Therefore, the entire seminal disposition for propagating seed existed in the <term>Protoplast</term> <note>original: *Protoplastus*, referring to the first-formed man, Adam.</note> immediately after the eating of the apple, and before a sensitive soul was born either in himself or in his descendants.

<margin>16.</margin> From there, surely...

<page-num>648</page-num>
<header>THESIS.</header>

<margin>1.</margin> The Almighty, out of the immense and spontaneous goodness of His love, specifically loved and raised up man for this purpose: that man might intimately and most closely express His own image. For this reason, He adorned that same image of Himself with such beauty of His divine majesty, and anticipated it with such a kind gaze of His love, that out of His good pleasure He created Eve. He destined her to be the future mother of all humanity—and Adam called his wife’s name Eve after the fall, because she was the mother of all living—who was intended to conceive her offspring, not indeed through carnal copulation in the manner of brutes, nor from the <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Lust or strong physical desire.</note> of the flesh or the will of man, but from God, or from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit alone. This was to be in the same manner by which that Humanity <note>The author refers here to the dual nature of Christ as the model for original human generation.</note> was conceived and born, in which and through which all who are to be saved must be reborn. That is to say, with the mother’s virginity remaining intact and the womb closed, she would have given birth without pain, and Eve was established in a state superior to man.

<margin>2.</margin> This is surely a great and new paradox, which I have undertaken to demonstrate in this treatise. Therefore, at the very threshold, I must remove the obstacles that lie in the way. First, critics object by citing the text: *The earth shall bring forth to you briars and thorns. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions. In pain you shall bring forth children; your husband shall rule over you. By death you shall die;* <note>These are the traditional punishments found in Genesis 3.</note> and consequently, you shall be afflicted by the calamities of disease and old age. They argue that all these things flowed from the curse of the sin of disobedience into all descendants until the destruction of the world, as an irredeemable debt that can be paid by no act of holiness. Because God had established a law for Adam that he should not eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, they claim its transgression flowed into <term>original sin</term> and raised a perpetual curse from the <term>Protoplasts</term> <note>original: *Protoplastis*. A term for Adam and Eve as the "first-formed" humans.</note> upon all posterity. These things have been taught thus far; to which, however, under

<column-break/>

the peace and censure of the Church, I shall humbly join my own concepts.

<margin>3.</margin> First, therefore, I assert the negative contrary. The words of the text do not precisely contain any curses except upon the Serpent and the earth; they are by no means directed at man. If God—with whom there is no change or turning—had once cursed man, man would have remained truly and forever cursed, just like an <term>Evil Demon</term> <note>original: *Cacodæmonis*. A malevolent spirit or devil.</note>.

<margin>4.</margin> For it is foolish to believe that God would curse man in one moment, and then, immediately after the sin and without any intervening act of contrition or penance, bless him with great fertility, give him the whole earth, and place all living creatures under his feet. Indeed, in the very midst of the curse pronounced upon the serpent, He filled the female sex with blessing, saying: *The woman shall crush your head. I will put enmities between you and the woman, and your seed, and her seed.*

<margin>5.</margin> Since this "seed" is not understood to be from a man, it promises the future Messiah, the Savior of the world, born from the seed of the woman. It is far from the truth, then, that He had cursed man in that place.

<margin>6.</margin> Secondly, I deny that a formal law was enacted, and consequently, I deny there was a legal "violation." For it follows that wherever there is no law, there is no transgression or disobedience; and consequently, no curse can fall there. I prove that it was not a "law" through the very words of the text: "And he commanded him saying: From every tree of Paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat." The word "commanded" <note>original: *praecepit*</note> seems to imply a precept or a law; however, this single word carries no more weight for the negative (do not eat) than it does for the affirmative (eat from every tree). It would not have been a sin if they had chosen *not* to eat from every tree in Paradise. Thus, the text did not contain a law or mandate for the inhibition of one tree any more than it did for the permission of all the others. Rather, the text represents a fatherly permission...

<summary>The author argues that God did not actually curse humanity after the Fall, but only the serpent and the earth. He challenges traditional views on original sin by claiming that the prohibition against the fruit was a "paternal permission" rather than a formal legal decree.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s radical re-interpretation of the Book of Genesis. # THESIS.

permission for the affirmative and a grant of it, just as it contained a fatherly warning of caution for the negative. It is just as if a countryman who knows the road said to a traveler: "If you go that way, you will perish and die." In this way, they say the Creator's warning (*do not eat; and on whatever day you eat, you shall die the death*) was not a law, but a piece of advice and a desire for their well-being. The transgression, however, and the act of scorning the warning, certainly contains a sin, but not one of disobedience: for disobedience differs from a scorned warning as much as a law differs from the advice itself. Therefore, the prohibition (*do not eat*) sounds like an admonition, namely, so that he would not bring death upon himself and his descendants with an unquenchable guilt—because death was located in the apple itself, not in the act of violating a command by eating. Thus, this death resulting from eating the apple was natural and forewarned, rather than a curse threatened by law. For threats of death, which was unknown to Adam, could not have terrified him; and thus, threats would have been useless, but a warning was not. Indeed, Adam had not yet seen a corpse, and he who did not know the names of living creatures before he saw them was much less able to know what death was. And Eve would have known least of all what it meant to die in Paradise. Therefore, among the <term>Protoplasts</term> <note>The "first-formed" humans, Adam and Eve.</note>, death was still a non-entity and an unknown; however, there is no concept that corresponds to a non-entity or an unknown, and there is absolutely no fear of it. For that reason, God did not predict death as a threat of terror or a legal punishment, but out of His sheer goodness. This was so that, once they had eaten the fruit He advised against, they would know that GOD had not made <margin>8.</margin> death, but they had made it for themselves. Nor does the text of Chapter 3 stand in the way of these points: *Because you have eaten of the tree, of which I had commanded you not to eat, etc.* <margin>9.</margin> For these words clearly announce the goodness of the preceding warning, not a law. For the same word (*praeceperam*, "I had commanded") which appears before in Chapter 2 (*and He commanded him saying*) signifies only a warning and not a law. Otherwise, they would have been obligated to eat from every tree in Paradise under the same penalty of original sin—a claim which no one of sound

<column-break/>

mind would ever support. For the sin <margin>10.</margin> was great in the suspicion of God's deceit, falsehood, and trickery, and in the fact that they believed the serpent more than God, and that they scorned a fatherly and benevolent warning. But it was not disobedience, because no law had been enacted. It was indeed an act against gratitude, against love toward God, and against a due and rational obligation. Therefore, GOD did not curse them, since they had brought upon themselves the pains of diseases, death, and hardships as a punishment by the act of eating. However, God does not speak of diseases after the fall: because it was enough to have once predicted that death would come while He was warning them not to eat. Finally, the cunning serpent <margin>11.</margin> did not approach the woman because she was the "weaker vessel," but because the warning had been given by the mouth of God to Adam, and was only made known to the woman through her husband's report. For this reason, God first demands an account from Adam. Primarily, it does not constitute a curse upon the man that the earth <margin>12.</margin> would be cursed in its work and produce <term>weeds</term> <note>Original: "zizania," referring to darnel or invasive tares that mimic wheat.</note>, and that he would eat bread in the sweat of his brow his whole life: rather, these things contain a reminder of the loving warning that preceded the fall. Finally, it does not sound like a curse <margin>13.</margin> that the woman should henceforth obey her husband and be subject to him, although in this the intention of the Creator shines through: namely, that He had destined the woman to be the head, the pinnacle, and the final creature above the man. But now, because of a twin sin, she ought to be subject to her husband. For that signifies a deserved penalty rather than a curse, just as a superior is not "cursed" when he is demoted due to an error he committed. But where it is said: <margin>14.</margin> *In pain you shall bring forth your children*, the text expressly confirms the mystery of this paradoxical thesis. For from this it is clearly established: 1. That Eve was not created, nor destined, to perish in pain. Therefore, this announcement is not said to her as a curse: but it is placed before her eyes how much calamity she had caused for herself, in that she would henceforth conceive and give birth in the manner of the brutes.

# THESIS.

If the Adamic or beast-like generation—arising from carnal lust and sexual union—carries death within itself just as it does for animals, then truly innocent descendants would suffer an unmerited punishment. <margin>22.</margin> Finally, if death were caused immediately by a curse or by sin itself, would it not be inappropriate for the text to say, *on that same day you shall die the death*; <note>original: *eadem die morte morieris*</note> why did it not say: *instantly*, in that very moment you shall die? Certainly, a curse does not require twenty-four hours to take effect, nor does sin require an interval of time to merit its guilt and punishment. This was clearly seen when an impure man, attempting to save the wobbling wagon carrying the Ark of the Covenant from falling, paid for his daring with a sudden death. <note>A reference to Uzzah from 2 Samuel 6:6-7, who died instantly upon touching the Ark.</note> But since death consisted in the procreation of forbidden seeds and carnal lust, it presupposed the eating of the apple and its digestion. Therefore, those words—(*on that day you shall die the death*, or, *you shall become mortal*)—mean you shall pay with a doubled death in yourself and your descendants. Our theses strengthen this proposed truth.

<margin>23.</margin> Furthermore, no sin from the first man onward has been considered "original," or passed down irremediably to all posterity, except that which, from the eating of the fruit, thereafter defiled all of nature. This is because it transferred the propagation of the human race into the "flesh of sin," of which God says: *My Spirit shall not remain with man, because he is flesh.* <note>Genesis 6:3</note> <margin>24.</margin> Regarding that sin, if it has not been sufficiently investigated by my predecessors, I will freely add what I believe.

Indeed, in this history of Genesis, several things concur at once: 1. The sin of distrust or evil suspicion, deceit, trickery, and falsehood toward God. For Eve said to the Devil: *Lest perhaps we die*; and thus she doubted that the death she was warned of would necessarily happen. Likewise, there was the sin of despised warning, and that they trusted the Serpent more than GOD; yet it was not "disobedience" in a legal sense, where no law yet existed. 2. The act of eating the apple—not so much because it was forbidden, but because they had been warned to beware of it.

<column-break/>

3. The effect of the eaten apple. For in the middle of Paradise was the tree whose property is called "of life": *Lest he eat, and live forever*; and there was the other tree, whose property was "of the knowledge of good and evil," to which no other was equal. But the rest, except for these two, served only for nourishment. The property and effect of this latter tree, therefore, was to arouse the itching lust of the flesh, or the madness of luxury <note>The author uses "luxury" in the archaic sense of "lewdness" or "lust."</note>. It is called the knowledge of "good lost" and "evil gained." <margin>25.</margin> For they did not know they were naked, and they were without shame—that is, without carnal lust, like children—because they lacked "seed." <note>The author suggests they had not yet developed the biological capacity for sexual reproduction.</note> 4. Carnal union follows: from this, finally, comes a certain beast-like generation, fleeting and mortal, contrary to the intent of God, who did not wish man to be conceived in sins. (*In sins did my mother conceive me*) <note>Psalm 51:5</note>; not indeed because every mother thereafter would eat from that apple, but because soon after the apple was eaten, every conception would only occur from the "will of the blood, the flesh, and the man." Thus, all "flesh of sin" would necessarily proceed from there.

<margin>26.</margin> Therefore, when the immediate cause of corrupted nature and death is ascribed to the sin of "disobedience," or when the immediate cause of corrupted flesh is attributed to the sin of suspecting God of deceit, these are logical fallacies—treating non-causes as causes. <margin>27.</margin> For properly speaking: the total corruption of our nature and the degeneration of the flesh did not flow from a curse, nor did it flow immediately from the accompanying sin. Rather, it flowed from these only occasionally, as a "cause without which it could not be." <term>causa sine qua non | a necessary condition that isn't the direct trigger</term> Our nature was rendered totally corrupt and incapable of eternal glory because of the effective and immediate causalities of lust and brutal generation. These caused the removal of virginal chastity and the loss of all hope that mankind would thereafter be born of the Holy Spirit and of the virgin Eve. <margin>28.</margin> Therefore, "original sin" flows down into absolutely all descendants because, after the virginity of Eve was taken away, the propagation of humans is not possible except from the will of man, flesh, and blood.

—those whom God had otherwise ordained to be generated from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, there is a confusion of causes and an inept application of effects to their proper causes, which has not yet considered: <margin>29.</margin> 1. Why that apple was forbidden with such a loud tone of precaution. 2. Why they estimated as a curse that which was not. 3. Why they ascribed "original sin" to a single act of disobedience as if it were the proximate, containing, and immediate cause. 4. Why they attributed inexcusable death to a curse and a penalty for a broken law. <margin>30.</margin> For even though a grave sin coincided with the original deviation from the generation intended by God—namely, with the impurity of the flesh and the corruption of nature through carnal union—the corruption of nature and the degeneration of our birth did not proceed from the parents' sins of mistrust as an immediate cause. Neither did death. Rather, these proceeded from the effect of eating the apple, as a new product necessarily and naturally depending upon it. That is, death proceeded from its own natural secondary causes existing within the apple, just as the total corruption of nature flowed from it; for both lean upon one and the same root of necessity. <margin>31.</margin> Furthermore, the causes of these natural causes were accidentally linked to the sins of mistrust and so forth in the act of eating. For the sin of suspicion, of bad faith, and the deception of God carried its own guilt, which could be atoned for by the First-Formed Parents <note>original: *Protoplastos*; referring to Adam and Eve as the first created humans</note> through the manner of sin—that is, through contrition and acts of penance, just as with other sins. However, it does not follow that all of nature should therefore have been depraved, or that death and every hardship of the body should enter and be perpetuated in all descendants, no matter how innocent their souls might be. For God occasionally punishes the sins of parents into the first or second generation, but nowhere is it read that He punished the sin of a grandfather who had done wrong five thousand years ago upon all subsequent posterity. Indeed, such a punishment 

<column-break/>

exceeds the love of God toward man, whom He blessed so greatly immediately after the sin. It exceeds, I say, the rules of justice, if the punishment of one innocent of that sin were to be weighed on its scales. <margin>32.</margin> Furthermore, I believe that if God, out of His goodness, had not warned the First-Formed Man of death if he ate from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil—and if the Demon, out of his own innate hostility, had moved the apple from that tree to any other, and both sexes of humans had eaten of that apple—the concupiscence <note>lust or strong carnal desire</note> of the flesh and sexual union would have followed just the same. Thus, even if it had happened without any sin at all, the generation following from the necessity and property of the apple would nonetheless have suspended the Creator's intent, who did not want the sons of God and descendants of Eve to be conceived from the Holy Spirit after her virginity was corrupted. Therefore, death, disease, and the very corruption of nature and the "beastly inversion" would have been "original," and yet not from sin, because the apple contained the natural efficient cause of lust. <margin>33.</margin> For how poorly do these two things agree: "Death proceeded from the sin of the broken law," and thus from a supernatural curse; and those words of the text spoken after the eating of the apple but before the expulsion from Paradise: *Lest he reach out his hand to the Tree of Life, eat from it, and live forever.* <note>Genesis 3:22</note> For no creature has the power to resist a Divine curse. From this, therefore, it becomes clear that the apple contained the natural cause of defiled generation and its own death, and that the Tree of Life likewise naturally contained the preservation of eternal life—that is, a superiority over the necessities of death. 

<margin>34.</margin> Finally, if death had arrived from the law, as a punishment for sin and a curse, it would be false to say that God did not make death; for in reality and immediately, death would have proceeded from God, and not from a natural cause or from corrupted nature. And this would be by a much greater right where the Lawgiver <note>original: *Nomotheta*</note> and the executioner are the same person: the almighty Creator. <margin>35.</margin> Lastly:

# THESIS.

—lastly: Sin is a <term>mental entity</term> <note>original: *ens mentale*; a concept that exists only in the mind</note>, or even a "non-entity," which cannot by itself produce a physical and actual reality. Therefore, death would not have proceeded from natural causes at its beginning if it were merely a result of sin—whereas today, death arises in animals and in us equally through natural means. Thus, death at its beginning would have been an entirely different kind of thing than it is today. Furthermore, it would be ridiculous for the text <margin>37.</margin> to say: *God did not make death*, if He had cursed nature to die simply because of human disobedience. <margin>38.</margin> It is therefore necessary that human death, in its beginning, started and was created through the same "fertile" natural causes by which we die today. Reciprocally, death today attacks through the natural causes of a defiled nature, just as it did <margin>39.</margin> in the beginning. Indeed, even though Adam became mortal because of the apple, his death did not occur until several centuries later, happening naturally from old age as if through secondary causes. Therefore, the law, the violation, the sin, and the curse are absent from the origin of a death that only appears after so many centuries through natural causes, as if they were speaking plainly to us. One must therefore look at the total and immediate cause by which man brought death upon himself within this thesis. <margin>40.</margin> For even though we are now mortal, we do not die when we wish, or when we choose: because death did not come from the will, or from the sin, but from the apple. <margin>41.</margin> Not indeed that death itself was inside the apple like a lethal poison, but there was within the apple the "concupiscence of the flesh," an incentive for lust, and an intoxication of luxury, leading to a beast-like generation in the "flesh of sin"—a flesh that carried within itself the natural causes of defects and the necessity of death. <margin>42.</margin> For this reason, it is likely that even if the Serpent had not been able to persuade man to eat the apple as an act of sin, he would have plucked the apple and thrown it at the root of some other permitted tree, so that the enemy of our life might rejoice in having introduced death by this means. <margin>43.</margin> This is sufficiently gathered from the text, which does not say, "if you eat from that tree," but says: *On whatever day you eat, you shall die*. It is as if he were announcing that this danger of coming death 

<column-break/>

was already predestined. For the world was created for this, and the organs of generation were given to man, because the corruption of nature was foreseen, as was the necessity of rebirth in the Savior and His virginal purity. Let the arguments therefore cease as to whether Eve <margin>44.</margin> ate an apple or a fig. The text calls it an "apple," pleasing to the sight; a fig, however, does not entice in the same way. It was a tree of a unique property, the fruit of which did not exist before—nor is another like it said to exist today among created things. Finally, the words of the <margin>45.</margin> text: *I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions*, are so far from signifying **G O D’s** indignation—and much less His curse—that they instead denote His love toward the <note>original: *devoto sexûs*; literally "the devoted sex," referring to women</note> devoted sex. Indeed, no one is unaware that the more sorrowful the life of the devoted sex is, the closer it is to the life of the Son of Man; otherwise, the tribulations God sends to His Saints, and even martyrdom itself, would be considered curses by the same logic. I will add finally, that just as the works of <margin>46.</margin> the flesh are diabolical, so says the text: *I will put enmity between the seed of the woman and your seed*. I confirm this thesis entirely. For in the first place, the woman of whose seed **G O D** speaks there is the Virgin Mother of God: who, as a Virgin, left no other "seed" as an enemy to the serpent except the "children of light," the children of God reborn from the Holy Spirit. These have no enmity with the eggs of some crawling reptile, but only with the children of the Devil and of darkness, insofar as they guard the seeds of sin. The text therefore promises a future regeneration in the Virgin Mother, calling those who are not reborn the "seed of the Devil" <margin>47.</margin> because they are of the Adamite flesh. Therefore, considering what I have already demonstrated above, Original Sin does not strictly wait for <term>ensoulment</term> <note>original: *empsychosin*; the moment the soul enters the body</note> or the moment of <term>this-ness</term> <note>original: *hæccitatis*; the specific quality that makes an individual unique</note>. For although the soul cannot be guilty of sin before it exists, nevertheless, since original sin exists in the contagion of the flesh, it is immediately in the "concrete subject" <note>the developing body</note> as its recipient as soon as there is a sexual mixture of seeds; according to that saying: *For behold...*

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that Original Sin is a biological transformation. He moves from the general theory of death to the specific mechanism of how the "forbidden fruit" physically altered human reproduction and the vital spirit (Archeus) of Adam and Eve on the very day of the Fall.</meta>

# THESIS.

"I was conceived in iniquities" <note>Original Latin: *in iniquitatibus conceptus sum*; quoting Psalm 51:5</note> (before the arrival of the soul, because) "in sins did my mother conceive me." Indeed, sin exists at the same point where death resides: which is surely in the very mixing of the seeds. For death is immediately present in the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The vital internal force or "master-spirit" that governs the body’s life and health in Van Helmont’s philosophy</note>, but not in the soul. This is proven by the occasional mortal indisposition of the Archeus, which causes a conception to be failed or void, even though it had previously been full of vital hope. And although the material impurity of the individual exists before the flesh is generated from it—and therefore even before the soul arrives—it is not properly called "sin" until the soul has "clothed" itself in it. Therefore, the infection of original sin is of a far different nature than any other sins, which require the soul’s consent. For the soul itself commits other sins; but Original Sin contaminates a soul that does *not* consent, because its original "essence" is the very flesh of sin. For this reason, it is not called the "soul of sin," but the **flesh of sin**, because the soul is contaminated by the flesh. The Devil, however, drew his sin from nowhere else but himself. Therefore, man should marvel at God's mercy, while the Devil cannot. Thus, by the Creator’s good pleasure, the apple contained within itself not only the "lust of the flesh," but also, consequently, the "generation of seed." Yet, the power to propagate the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The lower part of the soul responsible for animal instincts and physical life, as opposed to the rational soul</note> was not inherent in the apple itself. The Arbiter of the world, in creating, willed to obligate Himself to create every living soul in any animated body once the bodily dispositions had reached the threshold of animation. For this reason, the apple, immediately after it was chewed, disposed the blood toward seed, and from there toward a sensitive soul. This was a property unique to that fruit and no other food; so much so that within a few hours, it generated not only seed in our <term>Protoplasts</term> <note>The "first-formed" humans, Adam and Eve</note>, but also the physical conditions required to obtain a sensitive soul from the Creator. What otherwise happens in a fetus over a fixed number of days, and is completed through certain stages of digestion,

<column-break/>

was completed almost instantly in the vital Archeus of our first parents. The text hints at this unique property of the apple when it says that "on the same day" they ate of the fruit, they would "die the death." This is because the apple, even if it anticipated the usual timeline, still required a moment so that after it was turned into vital blood, it might immediately be endowed with a sensitive soul. For those who were formed into man and woman at the very point of creation—and not as children—matured in a short space of time into the ripeness of seed. They aged into the full necessity of death and the properties of secondary causes on that very same day. For this entire line of reasoning falls perpendicularly, like a foundation post, into my thesis, upon which the dizzying business of our mortality has revolved until now.

<margin>48.</margin>
But at the very least, since Eve was made from the rib of the man, this itself implies a mark of modesty and a forbidden carnal union—one which contained "incest" in addition to "debauchery" <note>The author suggests that because Eve was made from Adam's own body, their union was biologically closer than a typical marriage</note>, a fact which was not hidden from Adam. Nevertheless, the Almighty seems to have granted a dispensation for this after the Fall, by permitting marriage. Therefore, it remains to investigate on this occasion whether the act of lust was completed within Paradise. Many maintain that Paradise was free from such filth, because the text says in *Chapter 4*: *But Adam knew Eve his wife, who conceived and bore Cain, saying: "I have possessed a man through God."* But I must beg their pardon. For the opposite appears from the text itself. In the first place, the cited text proves nothing, except that the "deflowering" of true virginity (because it involves blood) does not allow for a simultaneous conception. Therefore, Cain was not conceived during the first act, but outside of Paradise. <margin>49.</margin> Otherwise: 1. "On the same day you shall die the death" designates, according to the truth of my thesis, the disgrace committed in that very place. 2. <margin>52.</margin> At last, with nature now degenerate, it pleased the Almighty to raise up the fall of Adam through birth. And although He has not restored to us the pristine clarity of our intellect, nor the soul’s ready <term>intuitive cognition</term> <note>The ability to know the essence of things immediately without the need for logical reasoning, which Van Helmont believed Adam possessed before the Fall</note>, He has nevertheless raised our dignity far higher. For the Intellect, brought back into the service of faith through grace, proceeds in humble resignation toward the prize of love, upon which we lean and by which we are driven. And the smallest moment of that love is far more glorious than the entire life of Adam in Paradise. For before the Fall, faith—the ancestry of virtues—was unknown, as was especially the surpassing excellence of Divine love; one lived only in the happiness of pure innocence. Therefore, God, by the permission of His foreknowledge and purpose, chose the inequality of bliss emerging from <term>rebirth</term> with a certain prevailing power: because the tribulations of this life are not worthy of the immense things which **GOD**, through His Divine goodness in His only-begotten Son, has prepared. For I would rather know what **GOD** has revealed through the only-begotten Savior of the world, than to have known with a clear intellect the powers of animals and herbs. It is abundantly sufficient for me to have that humanity in **GOD** by which He adopted us as children of God, and made us far more like Himself than Adam would have been in the height of his happiness.

The contrary is clear from this example: therefore, the soul does not come from the father. Yet, it does not follow that the children's souls are borrowed from the mother's soul. For otherwise, from whatever source the soul proceeds, the "formative power" <note>original: "vis formativa" - the internal force believed to shape an embryo</note> would also proceed from that same source. Consequently, not only would offspring always be female and perpetually resemble the mother, but a *mola* <note>original: "mola" - a "false conception" or fleshy growth in the womb thought to occur when the formative process failed</note> would never occur in cases where the exhausted female power lacks the male seed. Furthermore, a pregnant woman's imagination would not be able to transform a fetus already formed in the mother's womb into a monstrous, alien, or even animal-like shape. This is because a seed already possessing a soul borrowed from a parent would no longer be subject to the mother’s "foolish imagination," especially while the fetus is already being nourished in its own sphere and "kitchen" <note>original: "culina" - an early biological/alchemical term for the nutritive environment of the womb</note>. The same argument holds even if we suppose that the soul is generated from the souls of both parents: for whatever is denied individually can rightly be denied collectively. This conclusion also points to the fact that, if that were the case, the seed would already be actually "animated" <note>possessing a soul</note> from its very beginning. It would also mean that from two souls, a certain composite and mixed "spiritual light" would be formed; this contradicts the simplicity of form because it would be a "concrete duality." Thus, the uniform nature of the soul is opposed to duality and to being a mixture of different souls. From this I conclude that not even in animals <note>original: "brutis"</note> is the soul taken from the parents, and much less so in man. Therefore, all souls are created immediately by Life itself and the "Father of Lights," who will grant His honor as Creator to no creature. Thus it is obvious that man cannot produce an immortal mind, nor a Divine image. And so it is clear from this that the Creator's first intention was not that man should involve himself in generation in any way. Rather, the Creator's hand alone should have perfected every fetus—the hand that alone creates all souls, and most specifically that eternal soul thereafter, which it directed toward His own image through essential destiny.

<column-break/>

<margin>13.</margin> Finally, it is naturally necessary that a true image can never be made except by its own proper sculptor. However, there is no "proper sculptor" who does not perfectly know the one whose likeness he intends to carve. But man was created in the "image and likeness of God"; yet he cannot know God, nor express any likeness of Him in mind or word—an ignorance that everyone must admit. Therefore, man cannot be the proper sculptor of the Divine image; and so, any image of God he might manufacture would be utterly monstrous and of limited duration. Consequently, in the Creator's original intention, man was not created to generate man. In nature, the spirit of every generating seed includes (because it contains) the "idea" of the thing to be generated. However, since man is the immediate and true image of God, he cannot in any way pour into his seed the Divine image, which he is completely ignorant of both within and outside himself. But since in <margin>14.</margin> nature "like generates like," man can imprint onto his seed the image of the human body, which was indeed made in the image of God. Thus, the generating man can imprint his own "seal" or "shadow" into the seed, but not the image of God or the substance of the immortal mind. Indeed, I have demonstrated elsewhere that all other souls <note>referring to those of animals or plants</note> are merely "formal lights" and not substances. Therefore, if the mind had to or <margin>15.</margin> could produce the image of God, either the mind would cease to be the image of God itself, or God would not be the Creator of the mind. For this reason, the pure essence of the image of God in the concept of creating or generating required God Himself in every way—as its immediate Creator and sole Father, who is in heaven, and besides whom there is no "paternity" in heaven. Otherwise, there is a carnal paternity in man and animals, which is why the scripture says: *Honor thy father*. And another: *that there is no paternity, except in the heavenly father*. <margin>16.</margin> [Therefore,] the original generation and propagation of life remains reserved for God the Creator. This is especially true since the immortal mind, while infinite in duration, lacks the kind of self-knowledge that would allow it to represent itself so perfectly as to "print" a marked likeness of itself into a seed. For this reason, the immortal mind can never lead a human seed to achieve what the mind itself does not possess: the ability to depict the image of God outside of itself. <margin>17.</margin> Indeed, man was made as a likeness of God <note>original: "simulacrum Dei"</note> so that he might be a garment for the Deity, a casket for the kingdom of God—that is, a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, man was essentially created in the image of GOD. However, after he rashly presumed to generate the image of God from himself—not through some monstrous act, but through something only shadowily similar to himself, following the violation of Eve—he did not actually generate the image of God. God willed that His image remain inimitable insofar as it is Divine. Instead, in the vital "breeze" or spirit of the seed, man generated the dispositions that would eventually receive a "sensitive soul" <note>the part of the soul responsible for senses, reason, and movement</note> from the Father of Lights, the source of all fatherhood. This soul, however, is mortal and perishing, though God in His goodness ordinarily inspires it with a substantial spirit that reflects the image of His own mind. To this point, man has only struggled to generate his own image in the manner of brute animals through the union of seeds, hoping to obtain from the Creator that "animated light" which is called the sensitive soul. From this proceeded a second kind of generation, conceived in a beast-like manner—mortal, incapable of eternal life, following the ritual of beasts, and subject to the pains of childbirth, disease, and death. This state is all the more wretched because this method of propagation dared to overturn the Divine intent for the First-Formed Man <note>original: "Protoplasto," referring to Adam</note>. <margin>18.</margin> Therefore, God's ineffable goodness warned them not to taste of that tree, predicting that they would otherwise die that same day and experience the whole crowd of calamities that accompanies death. Rightly, then, the Lord deprived both parents of the benefit and the dwelling-place of immortality.

<column-break/>

<margin>19.</margin> Death followed, evidently, from this brutal and animal-like marital union; the Spirit of the Lord did not remain with man once he began to be "flesh." Furthermore, because this violation of Eve continues in the propagation of descendants until the end of the world, the sin of despising the Father's warning and the natural transgression—now turned into impurity through an "inverted" generation that is carnal and almost beast-like—is truly called "original sin" <note>original: "peccatum originale"</note>. Consequently, man, being sown in the pleasure of the "lust of the flesh" <note>original: "concupiscentiæ carnis"</note>, will always reap inevitable death in the flesh of sin. <margin>20.</margin> Moreover, the "Knowledge of Good and Evil" which GOD placed within the forbidden fruit contained this lust of the flesh—that is, the hidden, forbidden encounter which is diametrically opposed to the state of innocence.

This state of innocence was not a state of stupidity. Even before the transgression, Adam already knew the essences of all living creatures, and because of this, he was able to name them according to their specific properties and distinguish them essentially at first sight. Indeed, St. Hildegard says in her letter to the people of Mainz: *Adam was formed by the finger of God (which is the Holy Spirit). In his voice, before he sinned, was the sweetness of every harmony and the whole art of music. If he had remained in that state in which he was formed, the weakness of mortal man could not have endured the power and resonance of that voice. But when his Deceiver heard that man, by the inspiration of God, had begun to sing so resonantly—and that through this he was imitating the sweetness of the songs of the heavenly homeland (see how far man has now fallen from that, with his hoarse voice!)—the Deceiver saw the machinations of his own cleverness come to nothing in his anger. He was so terrified that he was tormented by it; and since then, with the various deceits of his wickedness, he always busies himself thinking of ways to disrupt divine praises, not only in the heart of man but also from the mouth of the Church.* Thus she wrote. It is a devout opinion of the Mystics that birds sing praises to GOD. I, however, subject to humble correction, think otherwise.

For if that were true, they <note>referring to birds mentioned in the previous argument</note> would sing all year round, and would not stop as soon as their desire for breeding was satisfied. This argument serves our thesis. Indeed, since only the males sing, and not the females: it follows from their common nature that Adam was more lustful and incontinent, and by his sex more prone to desire than Eve, whose chastity—beloved by God—seems proper to her sex. Therefore, man acquired knowledge through the eating of the apple, because he had lost his radical innocence and in its place made an exchange for the filthy concupiscence <note>uncontrolled sexual desire or lust</note> of the flesh. For before eating the apple, he was not so dull or stupid that he did not know or feel himself to be naked; rather, it was only then that he first declared himself naked, under the brutal effect of shame and lust. 

<margin>21.</margin> For indeed, the Sacred Text is so chaste in every part that the Most High did not wish to call carnal lust by its own name, nor even to accuse it, while he warned of the necessity of death regarding the eating of the apple. This was so that this brutal lust might not become known to man even by name. Therefore, He did not wish "concupiscence" to be named in Genesis because of the ready faithlessness of that people; instead, He called it a loss of innocence evidenced by the acquisition of shame, which He intended to be weighed eventually by the Church in its own context. And so, immediately after his creation, He transferred Adam from the earth into Paradise, and for that reason He also formed the woman in Paradise, lest she—whom He had made and intended to remain a virgin—should witness the mating <note>original: "copula"</note> of brute animals upon the earth. For in the beginning 

<margin>22.</margin> God created the heaven and the earth, and every creature contained within them. However, He made and formed these things materially through a passive and imperative word: "Let it be" <note>original: "fiat"</note>. He spoke that word, and all things were created. Then, over the six days <note>original: "sextiduo"</note>, He made the forms of the established things, and all things were made in an orderly fashion into the life and soul of living beings. In this they differed: to say "let it be," and "to make." For indeed, Adam was formed on the sixth or final day. But on the seventh

<column-break/>

God rested: only afterward did He transfer Adam from the earth into Paradise, and deliberated to make woman from the man’s rib—not, however, from his kidneys, thigh, or belly. Therefore, this occurred on the eighth day, so that it might be the beginning of a new week for a new and supernatural generation of future offspring. For this reason, it can be gathered that woman ascended, entirely outside the law <note>perhaps meaning outside the common biological laws of animals</note>, into a new height of election: a vessel of election. 

<margin>23.</margin> One may, in a sense, guess the quality of human generation as it would have been before the Fall in the virgin Eve from the most glorious Incarnation of the Lord. For truly the Father, to whom the name of all fatherhood is singularly and solely owed, and whom His Son always adores as Father, has indeed always generated His Son from eternity; yet the Father is not read as being the "Father" of the Son's incarnation <note>meaning the biological process was attributed to the Holy Spirit</note>. I venerate this as an immense mystery, and all the more after I perceived His infinite goodness both in the first virginal concept of creation and in the restoration through the regeneration of man. 

The Almighty Father surely willed that the glorious Incarnation of Christ should be conceived from the person of the Holy Spirit, who herself <note>the author uses a feminine phrasing here, possibly reflecting certain mystical traditions</note> was not generated, but proceeds from the Father and the Son from eternity. <meta>This page continues the author’s philosophical and theological exploration of the human soul. Having previously discussed the conception of Christ, the author now explains the relationship between the immortal "Mind" and the "Sensitive Soul," arguing that the Fall caused the Mind to retreat, allowing animalistic instincts and physical diseases to take hold of the human body.</meta>

# IT IS DEMONSTRATED #

At that time, even if the **Sensitive Soul** <note>The *anima sensitiva*, in early modern philosophy, refers to the part of the soul responsible for senses and instincts shared with animals, as opposed to the rational, immortal Mind.</note> had not yet been born, every natural disposition required to obtain it from the Creator was nevertheless present. And since two souls cannot perfectly preside over a single plane of the body simultaneously without conflict—no more than it is permitted to serve two masters at once—the immortal **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*</note> therefore retreated into the innermost depths. Whether this occurred by the Creator’s command, or because the Mind shrank back in weariness from bodily impurity, it thereafter at least delegated the governance of its body to the **Sensitive Soul**, in which it is now bound and enveloped for as long as we live. From this point forward, we generally grow up and live in a brutish manner.

<margin>27.</margin> The **Mind**, however, withdrew into the lodging of the frail soul, and from there inspires its divine gifts <note>original: *charismata*</note> into it, although otherwise it mostly sleeps (perhaps in the same way that coral occasionally loses its color and later recovers it again). Because of this retreat, the body underwent the full **disorder** <term>ataxia: a medical and philosophical term for lack of order or coordination in the body's functions</term> of impurity. The marriage with a mortal soul, which is foreign to the Mind’s original destination, is the reason why the Mind has hidden itself away. Thus, the dispute is still before the judge as to where it has chosen its principal bed. Among **Atheists**, the Mind is not believed to exist because it has submerged itself so deeply by penetrating the frail soul; because mental notions still appear to be subject to the imagination today; and because the sovereignty of the Mind seems to be shaken by the sorceries of certain simpletons, as if it were subject to the whims of diseases. Indeed, the deliriums of fevers, the manias of the melancholic <note>original: *lienariis*, referring to the spleen, once thought to be the seat of melancholy</note>, rabid bites, and the sting of the **tarantula** <note>The "tarantism" phenomenon, where a bite was thought to cause uncontrollable dancing or madness, was often used in these debates to show how physical things affect the soul.</note> have strongly persuaded people toward Atheism. For in the former life, the immortal Mind through itself and immediately established immortality, and also gave perfect knowledge of animals and plants. But afterward, in the brutish filth of procreation <note>original: *generationis*</note>, the **image of God** <note>original: *icon Dei*</note> indeed remained safe in the mind, and its external figure in the body; but such great corruption forced the Mind to retreat to the inner sanctuary of the frail soul.

<column-break/>

Therefore, under the Mind’s happy empire, its immortality flourished; and thus diseases, the declines of old age, and the threats of death were exiled. Consequently, before the **Fall**, man was distinguished from a state of total blessedness only by the *possibility* of sinning, falling, and dying. But in **glorification**, the Mind will again immediately vivify the body, and the body will flow into it. That which before the Fall only shone *upon* the body through its immediate brightness, will, soon after the resurrection, clarify the body through an absorptive transformation. For this reason, the state of the faithful—even if throughout life and even in death itself it is far more wretched than the primitive state—is nevertheless happier insofar as it is fuller in majesty to be more similar to the **Son of God**, incarnate, dead, and glorified, than to have lived with **Adam** free from diseases and finally taken up without a battle; because the rewards of life are in no way worthy of the glory or expectation of the future age.

<margin>28.</margin> Furthermore, the sacred text has compelled me toward a perfect thesis, making **Eve** a "helper similar to Adam," not indeed to fill the name and role of a spouse <note>in the sexual sense</note>, as she is named immediately after the sin. For she was a **Virgin** in the Creator's intention, and was only later filled with sorrows. For as long as the state of purity presided over innocence, the will of the man did not prevail. Indeed, the transfer of the man into **Paradise** prefigured a different lot of living than the bestial one. And so, the "eating of the apple" covers the **concupiscence of the flesh** <note>lust or carnal desire</note> with a most chaste name, while it encompasses the "knowledge of good and evil" under this name, and calls its ignorance alone the state of innocence. Since the attainment of that aforementioned knowledge fostered a most harmful death and the irrevocable deprivation of eternal life. For if man had not tasted the apple, he would have lived free of lust, and offspring would have come forth from Eve as a virgin by the **Holy Spirit**.

<margin>29.</margin> But once the apple was chewed, their eyes were immediately opened, and **Adam** began to lustfully desire the naked virgin, and he defiled her whom God had destined for him as a naked helper, no differently than a Prince...

## IT IS DEMONSTRATED ##

The author is quoting the Vulgate version of Jesus's conversation with Nicodemus.</note> Jesus Christ, descending from Heaven, did not take on the flesh of sin from the Adamic lineage, or from the will of man: but taking the form of a servant, he was made in the likeness of Adamic men, being found in appearance as a man.

However, having been made in the likeness of Adamic man, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Yet he was not made a servant, nor was he made impure. In this Gospel, moreover, he denies the vision of God, or the vision of the kingdom of God, and (6.) entrance into the kingdom of God [to the unregenerate]. For it is not that the beatific glory <term>beatific glory: the direct communication of God to the soul after death, the ultimate goal of human existence</term> is seen without entering heaven, nor is the same thing said twice in vain: but point (a) contains a denial of the participation in the heavens before the resurrection for the souls of the dead, while point (6) denies it even to bodies after the resurrection. It is necessary, therefore, to be born again of water and the Holy Spirit. For just as from the beginning man was created and had not proceeded from the rebirth of the flesh: so whatever is thereafter born of the flesh is flesh. Indeed, water, blood, and spirit are one and the same in Christ (John 5), and these three denote a baptism that is unified <note>original: "indifferens," suggesting a single, undivided efficacy</note> and unique in value.

Therefore, the only rebirth unto life is from water and the Spirit in the sole participation of the virginal body of Christ. Since entering and seeing the kingdom of God is just as impossible for the flesh as it is to ascend into heaven by one's own power.

And this is permitted to no one except the Son of the Virgin, who for that purpose descended from heaven, and who was in heaven while he was speaking these things to Nicode-

<column-break/>

mus, and who a little while later still had to be lifted up on the cross for that same reason. Therefore, he who descended from heaven to be incarnated from the matter of the virgin is the one in whom water, virginal blood, and the Holy Spirit are one. Therefore the Spirit, who makes the corrupt and Adamic man to be born again from water, so regenerates the inner man of the new generation in the spirit that he becomes a true Spirit to be glorified by rising again. The Adamic ones <note>those still in their fallen human state</note> will hear his voice, yet they will not know where it comes from or where it goes; because the regenerating Spirit is God himself in glory, who breathes where he wills, and whose voice you hear now through faith and the Sacrament.

So everyone who is born again of the Holy Spirit becomes Spirit, and is united to him of whom it is unknown where he comes from or where it goes. I call these "earthly things," even if they touch upon spiritual generation and rebirth, because they have certain similarities in sublunary <term>sublunary: relating to the physical world beneath the moon, often used to mean "earthly" or "transient"</term> nature, which not everyone everywhere knows, and therefore they do not believe. For the generations of brute animals occur from watery liquid and seminal spirit.

Yet these things the Lord speaks to Nicodemus are not for that reason plainly "earthly" and naturally intelligible to the common people: because the reason for Divine love in this rebirth is no more conceived than his infinite goodness. That is to say, it remains impenetrable why he wished to adopt man as a son and co-heir of his kingdom, or rather to reduce him into a Deiform <note>God-like in form or nature</note> Spirit, who had been materially born again of water. For that mystery of love surpasses all the intellect of the Angels.

Indeed, no one can naturally understand how to believe and contemplate the actual person of Christ in the old man, the woman, the youth, the sick pauper, the wretched little man, and the naked, unless, compelled by faith, they submit their intellect to the substance of faith.

So we cannot conceive how we, through this rebirth of baptism, all become one in Christ without distinction of sexes or nations, unless we are helped by faith.

# THESIS #

...[punishment]; but even more so, he had to suffer a most bitter and by far the most ignominious death. This death, so cruel and shameful, he calls his "exaltation" <note>original: *exaltationem*. This refers to John 12:32, where being "lifted up" refers to both the physical act of crucifixion and Christ's glorification.</note> in the overflowing goodness of his love. He introduces, as a comparison, the lifting up of the serpent Nehustan. <note>original: *serpentis Nehustan*. This refers to the bronze serpent Moses placed on a pole in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9) to heal the Israelites.</note> Not indeed that the serpent represented the form of the Son of Man more than a gallows represents a cross; but only as a likeness of impure man, fallen into death by the persuasion of the serpent, whose "likeness of a servant" the Lord was to assume. Therefore, the Son of Man had to be exalted, not indeed unharmed upon a gallows, nor like an unfeeling bronze serpent—which, being lifeless, was otherwise quite fit for hanging—but it was necessary for the Son of Man to be exalted alive, full of love, and finally to die on that cross, so that the deserved rebirth could be brought about through his death. For otherwise, without the death and exaltation of the Crucified One, the participation in the rebirth from water and the Holy Spirit would not have followed, nor would death have perished. Thus, by a clearly profound mystery, the likeness of the gallows, the cross, and the Savior was sought, in the likeness of the incarnate servant compared with the bronze serpent. Nor did Israel worship God in the serpent (otherwise Moses, by God’s command, would have been the author of idolatry); nor was a living serpent tied to the gallows, nor even its corpse. Rather, it was only its bronze image, incapable of life; so that by this mystery it would be established that the entire likeness consisted in the exaltation of the gallows and the cross. It shines forth to us that the "flesh of sin" (which the Son of Man represented in likeness) is plainly incapable of life and the kingdom of God, just like that bronze serpent. It is, therefore, simply and absolutely true: unless a person is reborn from God and participates in the immaculate virginity—which the Lord Jesus drew in his most glorious Incarnation from the material substance of the Virgin Mother—the hope of salvation is cut off forever. For this reason, it is also clear from the intent of creation that only a virginal generation was required thereafter. And consequently...

<column-break/>

...the female, impure, bestial, and Adamic generation was drawn and brought forth by the cunning of the Demon from the apple, in which the "fuel of lust" <term>fuel of lust: original *fomes libidinis*, a theological term for the inclination toward sin</term> was contained. Therefore, unless the Adamic flesh <note>The corrupt human nature inherited from Adam after the Fall.</note> dies again, and in its place there is restored in us through the favor of the Holy Spirit (who saves those to be saved freely) the immaculate Virginal flesh of the first intent of our Creator, it is certain that whatever else is done or hoped for will be in vain. For in the beginning, it was enough to be born, because then they would have been born of God. But after the Fall, it is necessary for the Adamic flesh to die and perish, and to be reborn from the Virginal flesh, which the Holy Spirit raises up for us from water, while we desire to be members of that Head and branches of that vine. We are therefore reborn in the Lord's body through grace, to come to the immortal life of the age to come; and so that we may be raised in the participation of virginity, death must intervene, and whatever is Adamic in us must be erased. <margin>48.</margin> *We shall all indeed rise, but not all shall be changed.* <note>original: *Omnes quidem resurgemus, at non omnes immutabimur*. A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 15:51.</note> For only the "changed" will rise, those who rise glorified in the virginal body of regeneration. The Apostle understood this change to mean that because one who is not reborn cannot enter the kingdom of God. Therefore, he who rises without being reborn will consequently not be changed from his former state, even if he rises from death; and thus he will have no entrance to the kingdom of God. This is because through rebirth the whole man becomes Spirit; therefore, he who rises from rebirth will rise in a spiritual nature. Otherwise, one born of the flesh and not reborn of the spirit will indeed hear the voice of the one reborn of the spirit, but he will not know where it comes from or where it goes. This is the transformation of bodies into Spirit, and the change of bodies in the resurrection—that is, the glorification of those to be saved from the resurrection. Other sins, indeed, expiated through penance, are conquered by the victory and triumph of the Lamb; but the loss of that virginity and primitive purity without regeneration retains an eternal stain of impurity and incapacity.

### IT IS DEMONSTRATED ###

<margin>49.</margin> In the same way that the preservation and virginal integrity of the faithful who have been reborn gives to those reborn virgins a Golden Crown <note>original: *Aureolam sive Laureolam*. Therefore, just as Christ is the Father of this virginity, so he is the Father of the future age; for those who are to be saved are his new creation and new regeneration. Truly, "he gave them the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God" <note>This is a translation of John 1:12-13.</note>—born in the most chaste manner of the Holy Spirit. Through the Spirit, it was decreed that every human being should be born of a virgin mother, even before the birth of the brutal concupiscence of the flesh. Christ, therefore, the summit and lover of chastity, distinguishes people by their chastity both in this age and in heaven, and he will decorate them with an inimitable and <margin>50.</margin> eternal privilege. *For a great multitude followed the lamb wherever he went, and sang a song that no one else could sing. These are they who have not been defiled with women.* <note>A reference to Revelation 14:3-4.</note> These are, of course, virgins of both <margin>51.</margin> sexes. *Because there will be neither Jew nor Greek there, but all are one in Christ.* <note>A translation of Galatians 3:28.</note> Indeed, the Almighty has chosen his "eunuchs" who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <note>original: *castratos*. This refers to Matthew 19:12, where "eunuchs" is used metaphorically for those who choose celibacy for spiritual reasons.</note> For this reason, the married are considered "defiled with women," and their mothers are said to have conceived their offspring in sin; in this, they are far inferior to virgins. Indeed, because the Gospel promises mortals not only that the Son of God was incarnated and suffered for their salvation, but also that these two mysteries (lest they otherwise be in vain) are applicable to individuals, I certainly contemplate this application in this way: insofar as man, through the sin of lust, broke God's intent no less than His warning, human nature was thereafter radically corrupted, and there followed from it a second and almost <margin>52.</margin> brutal degeneration of that nature. Therefore, the "joyful news" <note>original: *lætum nuncium*, a literal translation of the Greek *evangelion* or "Gospel."</note> included the abolition of both original sin and the other sins flowing consecutively from it. He, by dying, destroyed our death (not his own, for he truly had no death in him).

<column-break/>

This is not understood as temporal death (for even today the Just man dies, just as before the Passion of the Lord), but as eternal death. Therefore, since man after the Fall could no longer be born, grow, and multiply from GOD, but rather from the "blood of the sexes" and from the "will of the flesh and of man," and could never thereafter rise again by his own power to reassume his lost and pristine purity, nor cease to be so that he might begin to exist again in another and better way; for this reason, the joyful news brought us the certification that Baptism exists for the remission of sins through rebirth from water and the Holy Spirit. This is so that our mind, as if by a new birth of its native lodging through regeneration, might become a participant in the unsullied virginity and humanity of the Lord. This rebirth indeed restores the soul to its original state by taking away the sin or "debt" and its foulness. However, because of the continuation of the Adamic flesh in which the immortal mind dwells, the "ancient possession" or inclination toward sin is not removed, nor is the transmission of corruption drawn from the impure origin of Adamic blood. But we are persuaded to believe that this is really so. For GOD clearly <margin>53.</margin> permits, on a daily basis, that a testimony of that actual grace and purity acquired through true and substantial regeneration in both body and soul be sensibly manifested in the bodies of the baptized. Indeed, it is for this sole end and title that the Mohammadans <note>original: *Mahumetani*. A historical term for Muslims.</note> are baptized to their own shame, because in fact baptism—however illegitimately it may be given and received—takes away from them hereafter their innate stenches <note>original: *fœtores*. Therefore, the true effect of regeneration and its promised character shines through even externally in the defective body during baptism. And for this, the very enemies of the Christian name serve as unwilling witnesses for us. Indeed, the perpetuity of this same effect confirms the baptism...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of purity and the physical body.
