The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. <note>original: *Initium sapientiæ timor Domini*; a quote from Psalm 111:10</note> Now, the fear of the Lord begins with the meditation upon death and eternal life. Yet many, along with the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that emphasized self-control and rationality as the path to happiness</note>, consider the goal of Wisdom to be the knowledge of oneself. But I call the ultimate goal of Wisdom, and the prize of our entire life's course, charity <note>In this context, *charitas* refers to divine, selfless love rather than just modern "charity"</note>, which alone will accompany us when all other things have deserted us. And although the knowledge of oneself, in my view, is merely a means toward the Fear of the Lord: a treatise on a long life must nevertheless begin from here. This is because the knowledge of life presupposes the knowledge of the soul. Since "life" and "soul" (as I have said before) are synonyms. It is an article of faith that man was created in the image of God, out of nothing, into a living creature, and that his Mind shall never perish. Meanwhile, the souls of brute animals perish into nothingness when they cease to live. I have already taught the significance of this difference in my writing on the "origin of forms" <term>The "origin of forms" refers to the philosophical debate over how physical shapes and living essences come into being</term>. But so far, it is not sufficiently clear wherein that likeness to God, our Archetype, is situated. For most people place this exalted Image in the soul alone. I shall say what I feel, though under a humble protestation and submission to the judgment of the Church. So it is: having now somewhat understood the origin of forms, it is right to inquire especially into the human mind. But certainly, no knowledge is more burdensome than that by which the soul comprehends itself; and yet, hardly any is more useful. This is because faith establishes its base upon the imperishable and indelible substance of the soul. I have indeed found many demonstrations concerning this truth published in books: but absolutely none of them explains the "wherefore" <note>The underlying reason or cause</note> in a way that addresses Atheists, who deny a single and constant eternal divinity. Plato indeed established three classes of Atheists. The first class believes there are no Gods. The second class admits there are Gods, but believes they are indifferent to us and ignorant or dismissive of small matters. The th-

<column-break/>

-ird class, finally, is that which—although they believe there are Gods who are aware of even the smallest things—thinks they can be swayed by a tiny little prayer. This type is very common among Christians, even those who profess themselves to be the most perfect today; and therefore they dare to do anything, believing that religion exists only to restrain the common people through fear of the laws, the obligation of faith, and the penalty of hell. For these men heavily impose burdens on the shoulders of others which they themselves do not touch with a finger; they cheat the purses of their own followers, they prostitute heaven for sale to the dying <note>A reference to the corrupt sale of indulgences or spiritual services</note>, and they insert themselves into secular affairs everywhere, to the point that they claim religion cannot exist without the State. My highest wish would be that they might taste, for at least a single moment, what it is to understand intellectually, so that they might feel the immortality of the mind as if by touching it. Indeed, I have not found rules or a method by which I could illuminate another person's intellect. I therefore rightly testify that those who are always studying, as if searching for the truth, yet never arrive at its knowledge, do so because they are puffed up by the letter <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life"</note> and have no charity; they foster a hidden Atheism. I have learned this one thing, however: that the Mind can now understand nothing through the Imagination, nor through figures and images, unless the wretched and troublesome discourse of reason is added. But where the soul comprehends itself, reason fails it, as does the image of itself by which it represents itself to itself. Therefore, the soul can by no means apprehend itself through the discourse of reason, nor through images. For after I had recognized that the truth of essence and the truth of Intellect are one and the same, I knew the intellect to be an immortal thing, separated far from perishable things. The soul indeed is not felt: yet we believe it to be within, never resting, never tiring, nor being agitated by diseases. Therefore sleep, madness, and drunkenness are not symptoms of a damaged immortal soul—

Since even brute animals endure passions of this kind. For it is only right that an immortal thing should suffer at the hands of things that are fleeting. Indeed, just as the Mind is within us, yet is not felt by us, so too its continuous and unshaken operations are not perceptible to the senses. Truly, even if it seems to us that we understand nothing through a total separation from logical discourse and abstraction from all things that can fall under the senses, the mind, or the intellect—and this occurs at the beginnings of contemplations—the soul nonetheless acts in the meantime in its own insensible way and with spiritual efficacy. This is how I have understood it: for a person who is confessing often does not "feel" the effects of contrition <note>Contrition: sincere remorse for one’s sins</note>, and grieves deeply over that very lack of feeling. Yet, if asked whether they would wish to sin, they would perhaps respond that they would prefer to die. Therefore, the operation of the soul—an effect of supernatural faith—is insensible during confession. For intellectual actions belong to another realm and are the subjects of an unceasing Authority. Hence, the mystics teach that in faith alone, without discourse and active thought, the soul performs more work—and even profits more by so working—than the person who prays with many words and stirs up feelings of remorse through logical reasoning. But happy is the one to whom it is permitted to perceive these insensible operations of the soul and to reflect them back, as if by a flowing out, upon the operations or powers of the sensitive soul. For these mostly leave their footprints upon one’s later life and awaken the memory, working thereafter in faith with grace.

Christian Libertines <note>Libertines: Here referring to freethinkers or those who rejected traditional religious constraints</note> and the first class of Atheists mock what they see in us as a fictional "likeness of God," or the idea that we were manufactured in God’s image. Other Atheists of the second and third class believe not only that we were created in God's image, but they imagine within us an identity with the immense, uncreated Divinity. They claim that man differs in substance no more than a part differs from the whole—or like that which had a beginning differs from that which is without origin—but not in essence or internal property. Furthermore, it would imply an imperfection in God if He were able to create something outside of Himself that was equal to Him in substance. For it is established in Philosophy that every individual part of the Infinite must necessarily be infinite. Therefore, a creature cannot be more infinite in its substance than it was equal to the Eternal in its duration. Much less is the soul a part of the divine substance, or essentially similar to it, for in and of itself, the soul is a mere nothing in terms of power, magnitude, duration, glory, and wisdom. If, therefore, it was not made out of God, and much less out of itself, it must have been made out of nothing <note>original: *ex nihilo*</note>. Thus, those who believe the essence of the divine image is located in the soul through an identity of substance err immensely, since they are distant from one another by an infinite degree. Indeed, the soul would, of its own accord, dissolve back into the nothingness from which it began, were it not preserved in its being by divine goodness. Certainly, the damned souls—whom Divine Justice keeps in existence—would wish to be resolved back into their former nothingness. The soul does indeed possess an eternal permanence from that point forward, granted freely by an internal eternity given to it and preserved.

Let it be enough, therefore, that the Mind is a spiritual, vital, and luminous substance. And since there are many kinds and species of vital lights, this light of the mind differs from other vital lights in this: that it is a spiritual substance. The other vital lights, however, are not formal substances—even though they are substantial forms—and therefore they are reduced to nothing through death, no differently than the flame of a candle. But the Mind differs from the Angels in that it is made in the Image and likeness of the eternal God. Therefore, the soul possesses that light and the substance of light from the gift of creation, since it is itself that vital light. But an Angel is not the light itself, nor does it possess a light that is innate and internal; rather, it is a mirror of the uncreated light. And thus, in this respect, the Angel falls short of the perfection of the true divine image. Nor does the fact that the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John <note>A reference to the Biblical passage Matthew 11:11, comparing earthly and heavenly status</note> stand in the way of this. For this reason, the Angel always remains a ministering spirit <note>A spirit that serves God or carries out His commands</note>: but is nowhere read of as a friend, or a son of the father, the delight of the son, the temple of the Holy Spirit, in which the thrice-glorious Trinity makes its dwelling. This, indeed, is the prerogative of the divine image, which the eternal Light impresses upon every man coming into this world.

Indeed, in the year 1610, after a long exhaustion from contemplation, in order that I might obtain some knowledge of my mind, I happened to fall into a sleep. Snatched away beyond the use of reason, I seemed to be in a rather dark hall. At the left hand was a table, upon which was a flask <note>original: "lagena," a large vessel or bottle</note> containing a little liquid, and a voice from the liquid said to me: "Do you want honors and riches?" I was stunned by the unusual voice. I walked about, deliberating within myself what this might signify. Soon, to the right, there was a crack in the wall, through which a certain light struck my eyes, which made me forget the liquid, the voice, and my previous plan. For I saw that it surpassed thought expressible by word. Immediately that crack disappeared. Then, returning sadly to the flask, I took it away with me. I tried to taste the liquid, and with much effort I opened the vial, and struck with horror, I fell out of sleep. But there remained a huge desire to know the soul, in which desire I panted for 23 solid years. Finally, in the year 1633, amid the anxious afflictions of my fortunes, in a vision I saw my soul. It was more than light...

<column-break/>

...in a human figure, the whole of which was a homogeneous "active seeing," a spiritual substance, crystalline and shining. I noticed this, however: that the mark of sex <note>Gender characteristics</note> was only in the husk, not in the crystal. Its seal was an ineffable Light, so reflected in the crystal that the crystal itself became incomprehensible. And this was not indeed through negation or deprivation (for such things are so called in respect to our weakness), but it represented a majestic being <note>original: "ens augustum"</note> which cannot be expressed by words. And it was said to me: "This is what you once saw through the crack." 

Now, I saw these things intellectually in the soul: which, if the eye were to see them, it would then cease to see. Thus the dream showed me that the beauty of the human soul surpasses every concept. At least I understood the vanity of my long desire; and so I desisted from the wish to see the soul. For however beautiful that Spiritual crystal might be: yet my soul retained nothing of perfection for itself from a vision of that kind, whereas otherwise, after an intellectual vision, the mind is adorned with much perfection of knowledge. I knew, therefore, that the mind in that dream-vision had acted the part of a third party, and so it was not worth the effort of such a great wish. Furthermore, as far as the image of God in the mind is concerned, I confess according to my smallness, that I could never conceive of anything, whether it be spirit, or body, or in the intellect, or finally in the phantasy <term>Phantasy: the faculty of forming mental images</term>, or in a mere intellectual vision, which does not by the same labor represent some figure of itself, under which it would stand in the one considering it. Truly, although I had conceived of the mind as an incorporeal and immortal substance, I could not, as soon as I thought of its individual existence, consider it as deprived of all figure; indeed, I could not even think of it without it corresponding to the human figure. For as often as a separated soul sees another soul, an Angel, or an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmonem"</note>, it must know that this being is present to it, so that it may distinguish a soul from an Angel, and likewise the soul of Peter from the soul of Judas. This distinction cannot happen by taste, smell, hearing, or touch; but only by the soul’s own vision, which vision necessarily includes an "otherness" of figure. For since an Angel is in a place in such a way that it is not elsewhere at the same time, it also necessarily includes a certain figural boundary, no less than a local one. Next, I considered the human mind to be shaped in this way: for the human body, as such, cannot give itself the human figure; therefore it had need of an external sculptor who would be enclosed within the matter of the seed <note>The Latin text uses "feminis," which literally refers to the thighs or the inner part of the lap, but in this medical-philosophical context, it refers to the generative fluids or the womb.</note> and had descended into it from elsewhere. But that sculptor, insofar as it were material, could not draw the power of shaping or the image from itself, nor from the mass of the body. It is necessary, therefore, that something precede it, which would be a purely immaterial, yet real and effective beginning, to which the power of shaping would be owed, through a seal-like impression: the <term>Archeus</term> in the seed. <note>The "Archeus" is Van Helmont’s term for the vital internal "master-worker" that directs all biological growth and healing.</note> Therefore the soul of the parent <note>original: "Patrantis," meaning the one performing the act of generation.</note>, while it glides downward and surveys the body of the seed through desire, sketches there the figure of its own seal and the seal of its own figure (which is the unique cause of the fertility of the seed), from which comes such a noble stature of the fetus. For if the soul itself were not shaped in itself, but the figure of the body arose as if spontaneously, an organism missing a limb could not generate anything but a creature missing that same limb. This would be because the body of the parent was not whole, and thus, at least in the indwelling Spirit, it would lack that limb. If, therefore, a figure is inserted into the seed, it certainly receives that 

<column-break/>

image from a more vital and prior beginning. If, indeed, the soul imprints a certain figure on the seed, it will not represent a foreign or strange face, but will depict the likeness of itself. For so also do the souls of brute animals. And although our soul, by reason of its origin, is above the laws of nature, yet once it has entered the threshold of nature and been incorporated into it, it is thereafter compelled to stand by its own laws as well. This is because the progress and end of vital generations are uniform <note>original: "univocus," meaning they follow a consistent, singular path.</note>. Otherwise, it would not be free from absurdities if an operation of such magnitude (such as human generation) happened without the consent and cooperation of the mind. If this is so, it is also necessary that fertility be given to the seed by the soul, through a participation in its own figure and other vital determinations. To be sure, every soul seals the image of itself in the spirit of the seed so that the matter—having been reduced to the required maturity and showing the sketched beauty along with the likeness of the parent—may be able to obtain from the Creator a "formal light," that is, a soul of that species whose likeness is expressed in the figure. For we believe as a matter of faith that our mind is a true substance, not destined to perish; and that the new creation of a substance out of nothing belongs to God alone. Whence there are not many, but there is one unique spiritual Father of all, who is in heaven. If He was well-pleased to adopt only the mind into His image, it also seems to follow that the immense and ineffable God is also of a human figure; and this by an argument from effect <note>original: "a posteriori," a logical method of reasoning from observed consequences back to their origins.</note>. Since the body is like wax, upon which the seal of the mind's image is impressed, the mind has its own image and essential perfection from Him whose likeness it bears. But because the body is frequently defective and like a monster <note>original: "monstro simile," referring to birth defects or abnormalities.</note>, most people have thought that the glorious image of God consists entirely in the power of reason. They do not consider that the image of God consists in the soul in a more immediate and perfect way, and...

On the previous page, Van Helmont argued that the soul must have a "figure" or shape to be distinguishable and to act as a sculptor for the body. Here, he pivots to critique the common theological comparison between the human soul's faculties and the Holy Trinity.</meta>

...thence also in the body, which is formed according to the soul’s master pattern <note>original: "exemplarem characterem"</note>. If an error occurs in this process of shaping, it is not to be attributed to the image itself, but to other causes rushing in from elsewhere. Furthermore, I have already taught, within its proper limits, how much the rational faculty should be allowed in naming the "likeness of God" in my treatise on Reason. Yet, the more learned part of Christians holds that the soul expresses the image of the one and triune God most closely through the uniform simplicity of its substance and the triad of its powers: namely, the **intellect**, **will**, and **memory**. This comparison has always seemed improper to me, as if the mind were the image of God only by some excellent, nearby, or singular value. For indeed, an "image" involves a likeness of figure, but not merely a parity of numbers. Moreover, if the soul in its substance represents the Most Holy Trinity, while the intellect, will, and memory represent the triad of Persons, it would be necessary for these three powers of the soul not to be mere properties or "accidents" <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities that can change without destroying the essence of a thing.</note> of the soul, but rather to be the very unique substance of the mind itself; otherwise, the image fits poorly with the archetype of which it is believed to be the image. Therefore, I considered that it is not merely the mind of man, but the **whole man** who was created in the image of God. For this reason, although the soul in this sense may express a certain ternary in its powers, it in no way expresses "personalities" <note>The distinct "Persons" of the Trinity.</note>. Secondly, no Person of the Most Holy Trinity represents the will alone, nor does the will represent a Person; no Person represents memory, and none represents the intellect as a property separate from the other two. Furthermore, since the three powers of the mind are generally considered as "accidents" of the soul, these certainly cannot express the image or any near substitute for God, except perhaps as a bare triad of accidents heaped into the substance of the soul. In that sense, the soul would denote the image of God less than any piece of wood, which through its analysis exhibits **salt**, **sulfur**, and **mercury** <note>The "Tria Prima" or three primary principles of Paracelsian alchemy, which Van Helmont suggests are more "substantial" than the soul's faculties.</note>—

<column-break/>

—and not merely (like the mind in the aforementioned common comparison) three powers. I mean three substances concluded and diverse within the unity of a solid object, which nevertheless in their connection made only a single substance of wood. Furthermore, **Tauler** <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German mystic known for his teachings on the "ground of the soul."</note> divides the soul into two parts: the **lower** or **outer**, which he calls the "soul," and the other, **higher** part and **ground**, which he calls the "spirit." In this latter part, he says the image of God is specifically represented and contained, because the devil has no access to it, for the "Kingdom of God" <note>original: "Regnum Dei"</note> is there. He assigns far different acts and properties to each part, by which he distinguishes them. But at the very least, that good man destroys the homogeneity <note>The state of being uniform or of one single nature.</note> of the soul, through which it ought most especially to express the likeness of God. Indeed, he has so far not only denied that the image of God is propagated in the whole man, but even in the whole soul. Certainly, I do not easily believe in a duality within the soul, nor do I admit the "otherness" of a binary nature, if the soul is to express the image of the simplest divine nature in its own essence. Rather, it must stand in the simplest unity and indivisible homogeneity as a symbol of immortality and indissolubility, outside of all connection or "otherness." I say, therefore, that the glorious image is not merely *in* the soul; but the mind itself is essentially the glorious image of God. Therefore, the image of God is as intimate to the soul as the soul is to itself. I consider the mind to be a homogenous spirit—simple, immortal, indivisible—a unique being, to which death adds nothing and from which it takes nothing away that is natural to its essence of simplicity. Furthermore, it is a participant in blessedness, because damnation is "accidental" to it, occurring outside its original design and because of a later defect. Therefore, a soul of this kind, when separated from the body, no longer uses memory, nor reminiscence, nor an intuition of the place where it was, or of duration. Instead, a single "Now" contains all things there. For if any memory were to survive in the soul, it would be frustrated for eternity; indeed, it would be a burden.

He contends that the "Image of God" is the very essence of the mind itself, which exists in an eternal "Now" after death, freed from earthly memory and division.</summary>

The same applies to **Recollection** <note>original: "Reminiscentia"</note>: indeed, it only springs into action through the discursive movement of reason; therefore, it has no further place in eternity. There, in the sight of naked Truth—without setting, weariness, or failing—the soul stands beyond the necessities of remembering. The blessed soul would therefore stand outside the aforementioned ternary of powers <note>The "ternary" refers to the three-fold division of Memory, Will, and Intellect, often compared to the Trinity.</note>; thus, it would no longer represent the "Image of God," for which purpose alone it was created. Indeed, by looking more deeply, I do not find **memory** to be a unique and separate power of the soul, but merely a mode of remembering. For those who are forgetful construct for themselves an "artificial memory" with the help of the **imagination** (which acts as a substitute for the intellect), and they learn a memory far stronger than their "natural memory" would otherwise be. 

Furthermore, the **will** departs from the soul along with life, because it joined the soul only as an "accident" <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality that is not part of a thing's essential nature, like the color of a coat</term>. For God, after creation, "placed man in the hand of his own counsel" <note>original: "in manu arbitrii sui," a reference to the Book of Sirach 15:14 regarding free will</note>. This surely indicates that the will, in its own way, is not essential to the mind, but exists by grant—so that it might be like a "talent" <note>referring to the biblical Parable of the Talents</note> and follow the path it prefers to choose for itself. Otherwise, since nothing is more destructive than **free will**—which alone perpetrates every discord between God and man—certainly such a faculty can have no place in the blessedness of eternity. Indeed, once the freedom of choosing is taken away, the will itself perishes. For what use is the power of willing where there is no longer any freedom to "be able" to will? 

But they say: "In heaven, the will is confirmed." This means that those in heaven cannot will anything except what God wills. For those who are in charity cannot help but will the things that belong to charity. This implies that the heavenly citizens are no longer "able" to will on their own; rather, only God wills and nits there. Therefore, the will ceases once the freedom of willing has been dissolved. Since the will of the blessed soul cannot serve or be useful for eternity, it cannot even be brought into action. Such a will would merely be a form of "wishing." But wishing does not exist in heaven, where there is 

<column-break/>

full satisfaction and every abundance of all things desirable. The will would therefore be a burdensome appendage to the blessed soul rather than a benefit. Let it be enough, then, to have earned well through the power of willing in this life, and to have stored up one's "talents" for profit. 

I speak specifically of the *power* of willing; for after this life, the **substantial will** rises and manifests itself, having an essence distinct from that "free power" and "accident" of willing. For just as the power of fantasy <note>imagination</note> dies with life, so also that free power of willing ceases. Thus, I have come to believe that the spiritual substance of the soul itself reflects the Image of God, rather than its "powers." Specifically, consider this: God is an uncreated being, one, incomprehensible, eternal, infinite, omnipotent, good, super-substantial light, and spirit. The soul, however, is a creature—one, undivided, dependent, immortal, simple, and henceforth eternal—a spiritual, luminous substance. 

Finally, in God there are no "accidents"; rather, each individual attribute is the very same, indistinct, and simplest essence of the divine spirit—which even **Plato's *Parmenides*** <note>A famous Socratic dialogue concerning the nature of "The One"</note> understood to some extent. Thus, if the soul reflects the image of God, it will admit no "accident" into itself; instead, its entire substance will be a **simple light** and **Intellect** itself. Just as smoke, once ignited by a flame, is the same as the flame in both form and matter, so too the soul is a naked, pure, and simple Intellect—a light and an image of the Uncreated Light. 

Just as the eye beholds nothing more truly or closely than the Sun (and all other things only because of it), so the blessed soul understands nothing more closely than the Light itself, upon which it totally and immediately depends. And just as our eye cannot endure the direct gaze of the Sun, so the soul cannot understand God—and much less so as long as it uses and is bound to the "means of the powers" <note>the three faculties of memory, will, and intellect</note>. Otherwise, the free Intellect acquires the "form" of the thing understood by the act of understanding, transforming itself into a unity with it (as I have taught regarding Reason). And so, undoubtedly,

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the soul's "Image of God" lies in its essential spiritual substance—a simple light and intellect—rather than in the temporary faculties of memory and free will, which he views as earthly tools that cease in the presence of divine eternity.</summary>

-># THE IMAGE OF GOD.<-

...of the soul <note>Continuing from the previous page's "rum," concluding a word like "memoriarum" or "powers."</note>, the soul principally and primarily contemplates God through understanding, and is thus formed into the true image of God. However, there are others who conceive of the Image of God in the soul in this way: since the Law is the image of God, and the Law is inscribed upon our souls through reason, they conclude that the soul is the Image of God insofar as it is rational. But this is plainly improper—indeed, it is irrelevant. For in that case, the soul containing the Law would merely be a vessel for the Image of God; its very substance would not, therefore, be created into that Image of God itself. For the Law and the soul itself differ no more in essence than they do in their "suppositional" existence <term>suppositionalitas: a scholastic term referring to how a thing exists as a distinct individual or "person" (suppositum)</term>. I truly loathe metaphorical expressions in serious matters. For instance, to say "God created man in His image" would merely denote that God gave man the use of reason. Thus, a person born insane or deformed would not have been made in His image. Furthermore, while the soul was being created, the Law did not yet exist. Moreover, to attribute the Image of God to reason is to be injurious and blasphemous toward God, as I have taught elsewhere regarding reason. For there is no similarity or equality between reason—a fleeting and uncertain faculty—and the eternal substance of God.

Therefore, leaving aside the opinions of others, I shall state my own. The **Intellect** possesses a **Will** coequal to itself—not as a power or an "accident" <note>An "accident" is a quality that can change without changing the nature of the thing itself.</note>, but as the very intellectual light, a spiritual substance, a simple and undivided essence, separated from the Intellect only by its distinct "personhood" <note>original: "suppositionalitatem," referring to the distinct way the Will exists as a person-like entity within the soul</note>, but not at all in its essence. I find, moreover, a third thing in the soul which, for lack of a proper name <note>original: "defectu etymi"</note>, I call **Love**, or a **Desire**—not indeed of having, possessing, or enjoying, but of "complacence" <note>finding delight or restful pleasure in something</note>. These are equal to the other two, equally simple in the unity of substance: they are three "persons" <note>original: "supposita"</note> within the single and indivisible substance of the soul. This Love is not some act of the will; rather, it proceeds from the substantial Intellect and Will as a distinct expression. For even in this life, it happens that we love things which we understand 

<column-break/>

should not be loved, and which we would wish not to love. We also love things that surpass the Intellect and the Will. For in **Ecstasy**, the Intellect and the Will perish and are lulled to sleep, surrendering their kingdom to Love for a time. Indeed, that Love is not a passion, but a dominant essence and a glorifying act. Therefore, in this context, Will and Love exceed the scope of mere "powers," and have nothing in common with the will of the flesh or of man. Rather, they are "essential titles" by which—due to our poverty of names—the **Mind** represents the Image of God. This is because the Intellect then understands God, intends Him, and loves Him with the whole mind in a single, undivided act of love, owing to the total simplicity of its substance.

However, as long as we live in the flesh, we scarcely use the substantial and purely intellectual Intellect; instead, we use the "phantastic power" <note>the faculty of imagination or mental imagery</note>, which is its vicarious quality. For in ecstasy, the Intellect, Will, and Memory often fall asleep, with only the act of Love surviving—yet so distinct from those three that it nevertheless does not exist without the substantial Intellect and Will, which are its equals. Since the soul is entirely "homogeneous" <term>homogeneous: of the same kind; uniform in substance</term> in its substance, it would plainly lose this simplicity if one of the three were outside or apart from the other two. Therefore, when the other two are put to sleep, Love is, as it were, on the surface; or rather, the other two are imbibed and absorbed into Love. In this world, Love is prior to Desire, because it is a passion of the "amative faculty" which proceeds from that "personhood" of the soul (which is truly true Love) and represents the image of a bodily faculty in this life—not unlike the way Intellect and Memory do, as long as the marriage to the body (into which the immortal Mind is submerged) constitutes a "third something." But after death, Love does not create priority or distinction from Desire, nor does it have the nature of a "power," nor is it a habit or act of willing, nor does it exist outside the Intellect; nor does Memory survive as a habit distinct from the Intellect...

remains. Therefore, the **Intellect** is the formal light and the substance of the soul, which intuitively knows, discerns, wills, and desires in its own unity whatever it comprehends within itself, and judges by willing. For it no longer remembers through the repetition of "species" <note>original: "specierum" — in scholastic philosophy, these are the mental images or forms used by the mind to understand objects</note> of a thing once known, nor is it further led to knowledge through external circumstances; rather, there is then a single cognition of all things understood, and an intuitive gaze within itself. Yet, it functions in such a way that it knows one thing more "presently" than another while the Intellect reflects upon the things understood, because it exists in Truth itself and in a distinct Unity. What if the same thing now happens in everyday "artificial memory" <note>techniques used to improve rote recall</note>, namely that the act of recollective memory is not a distinct act from the inductive judgment of the Intellect? Would this not be even more natural to the Mind once it is freed from the turbulent fantasies of earthly understanding? For it is no obstacle to this that memory may perish in wines <note>i.e., through drunkenness</note> while judgment remains sound, or vice-versa. For a drunkard, or a madman, not infrequently remembers everything done before his drunkenness, and everything done during his madness he recalls the next day when he returns to himself. These things are surely distinctly different in the body, according to the "mode of the receiver" <note>a philosophical principle that things are received according to the capacity of the thing receiving them</note>. I also note that even non-living things possess a certain "deaf cognition" <note>original: "surdam cognitionem" — a silent, unconscious form of perception or reactivity in minerals and plants</note>: likewise a sense and an attraction to an object, which have begun to be called "sympathetic." Indeed, such a deaf perception of objects is like sight and intellect to them. Furthermore, there is within them a power, namely a certain vital gift of some goodness and value, destined for the ends intended by the Creator. There is also a third power resulting from both of the preceding: which is a joy at the encounter of helpful things, and an aversion from harmful ones. In these things, a certain affection toward objects is observed. Likewise, a flight from fear, etc. This triple step of the scale is more manifest in the duller insects, just as it is in madmen, over whom no Intellect presides, and only the governing power of the visual light shines forth.

<column-break/>

In these creatures, however, there is additionally the act of virtues and vital functions, for the sake of which, and through which, they are insects. Thirdly, there is in them a far more manifest formal act of joy and aversion. These qualities are, in turn, explained far more clearly in other sentient beings. To these, a certain sensitive **Imagination** belongs, along with a certain discourse of reason, which serves them in place of an Intellect, shining forth more or less in each individual. Thus, sagacity, will, memory, and recollection fall under their apprehension as if by an Intellect: yet with the objects and functions continually changing according to the matter, which is prone to divisions and individualities. There is also in them a power of goodness and an emanating virtue, by which souls incline more or less toward the exercise of their virtues or their wildness. Finally, there is also in them their own complacency, weariness, and "thymosis" <term>thymosis: from the Greek 'thymos,' referring to spiritedness, passion, or anger</term> in the consideration of objects: so united to sensitive souls that it is hardly possible to look upon two persons without soon being more drawn to one than the other. Because these things exist in physical bodies according to the capacity of the receiver, they will for that reason be more clarified in man. I would not wish, however, for the **Image of God** in man to be considered as existing because of some "triad of faculties" <note>referring to the traditional Augustinian triad of Memory, Intellect, and Will</note> which might be found thus far in other things in the system of the world. Certainly, the dignity of the Divine Image is not shared in any way by other created things. For the Divine Image is only the innermost part of the soul, and is as much its own as its own essence. Yet the properties of the soul, whatever they may be, are not the very essence of the mind: but are products and things that follow after the essence. For it is not worthy of the majesty of the Divine Image to be derived from mere qualities. For the properties of other things melt into the essence of the soul by the power of the Divine Image. But if they are considered as attributes, that is due to the wretchedness of common understanding...

...way. For indeed the mind is a single act—pure, simple, formal, homogeneous, and undivided—in which the **Image of God** exists most closely and essentially. So much so that in this Image, all powers not only cast off the nature of "attributes" <note>In theology, attributes are specific characteristics like 'mercy' or 'justice'; Helmont argues the soul's core is more unified than a list of traits</note>, but even gather their distinct modes of existence into an indistinct unity. This is because the soul in itself is a kind of substantial light, and a substance so luminous that it is not distinct in its being from the light itself; and its intellect is the light of the soul in such a way that the soul itself, which is nothing but light, is simply the pure intellect. In this light of its own, the soul, once separated from the body, sees and understands itself entirely throughout its whole being. It has no need of a brain or a heart—organs in which its substance seems only to take on a "lineage of properties" <note>original: "proprietatum prosapiam" — meaning the soul's pure nature gets divided into specific physical functions when limited by organs</note>. 

In the body, of course, the abstract intellect itself is submerged in the bodily organs. When it uses them, it represents and assumes a "qualitative" force <note>A force defined by its qualities or limitations rather than its pure essence</note> called **Imagination**. This arises through a combination of the "phantastic power" <note>the faculty that creates mental images</note> of the sensitive soul <note>the part of the soul responsible for animal functions and sensations</note> and the splendor of the intellect—which has degenerated within the organs—into a qualitative power. For this reason, that faculty becomes exhausted by the act of imagining and gives way, so that a person may become insane or their hair may turn white; however, the mind, once separated from the body, is never fatigued by the act of understanding. 

Indeed, in the living, the imagination is not only prone to exhaustion, but it also does not possess intellectual "forms" <note>original: "species intellectivas" — the mental patterns or concepts used in thought</note> of its own, except those it draws from objects. Thus, the intellectual force, which coincides with the "phantastic" function of the sensitive soul during the act of imagining, follows the nature of the physical organ and the judgment of the sensitive life. This happens just as it regularly does in nature: the result follows the weaker part of its causes. But the soul possesses everything it requires for knowing, remembering, and willing—whether for a single instance or repeatedly—from itself and not from anything external. For in the soul separated from matter, the will does not arise from the thing understood; in fact, there is no "will toward" <note>meaning a desire directed at an external object</note> an understood thing within the soul;

<column-break/>

rather, it is the formal goodness of love. This is not a specific "passion" of the soul, nor a habit, nor a leaning, nor any quality; instead, it is a substantial act of goodness through which the blessed soul is substantially, unequivocally, and homogeneously good—not merely "qualitatively" good. The soul possesses this prerogative because it is the representative image of the Divinity. 

Physical bodies, however—both those believed to be compound and those that are purely simple—spontaneously and perpetually slip away into the attributes of forms; they are ultimately prone to the changes of "heterogeneity" <note>having different parts or qualities</note> and to dissolution. It is now clear, therefore, why the soul's state, dignity, condition, and the prerogative of the divine image are clouded over in the living. 

Furthermore, the desire or love of which I speak here is not a function of the "appetitive power" <note>the faculty of wanting or hungering</note>, nor is it the qualitative power of desiring itself; rather, it is a substantial part of the mind, or rather the mind itself, flowing from the intellect and the will. This is because those three—Intellect, Will, and Love—are indivisibly joined by the Creator under a single unity of the greatest possible simplicity. Yet in living or mortal beings, this desire is separated from the intellect and will in its practical functions, due to the condition of the physical organ and the nature of the sensitive soul. For indeed, we now often desire things that the intellect judges to be undesirable, and which the will would wish not to be desired. 

It is necessary, however, that things whose operations are distinct must also be distinct at their root, according to the way each is separated. In the soul, this happens only through "relative distinction" <note>original: "suppositionalitate relativa" — a term for things that are distinct in relation to one another but remain part of one substance</note>; but in the body, it is according to a corporeal and qualitative nature. And therefore, this substantial desire or love is the soul's innermost essence, consubstantial and coeternal with it. Thus, although there is full satisfaction and perpetual enjoyment of all desirable things in the heavens, this desire in the soul does not cease; for it is the "zeal of delight" <note>original: "studium complacentiæ"</note>. Nor does it cause a "passion" <note>in the sense of a disturbing emotion or suffering</note> in the soul any more than charity itself does, since at their root they are joined as one and the same.

## THE PROPERTY OF EXTERNAL THINGS.

Now that the spiritual beginning of life has been completed, before I come to the corporeal and sensible organs, and other supports of life, I shall propose something concerning locations. First of all, therefore, it is certain that the heavens, after the transgression <note>referring to the Fall of Adam</note>, received no other law, for the earth alone took upon itself every curse. For from this, it is demonstrated sufficiently elsewhere that the heaven is immune from our sins, nor does it act as an avenger of iniquities. But if indeed certain places are prone to death and specific diseases, that is not to be attributed to the rotation of the heavens and the blind influences of the stars; but it is entirely native to the dispositions of the earth. For even if the eastern provinces seem more fortunate, this is not to be attributed to the heaven. Since in its orbit, every part subjected under the same circle is equally eastern. Otherwise, the circle would not lack a beginning, end, and extremities. Therefore, goodness and the fertility of the soil are innate to the earth alone, aided by the continuous nourishment of the stars and the perpetual familiarity of their visitation. Indeed, under the orbit of the Sun, the climates have an ordinary and equal heat: and so all the fruits that ascend through ripeness to the degree of perfection are more fortunate there because of the heat, which elsewhere, due to a lack of heat, are not as perfect. But the heat of the Sun regards fruits, and not long life, which is no less long-lived in cold, mountainous, and northern places than otherwise under the burning zone. Certainly, favors to the soil do not depend on the stars, just as the prolongations of life do not. The stars rotate 

<column-break/>

daily, and beneath them they affect the climates of the earth almost equally every day. However, they receive winter and summer through the approach and retreat of the Sun every year. Meanwhile, tracts of nearby lands vary greatly from one another. Therefore, these are unique gifts of the soil, not of the heaven, which for that reason preserve a stable goodness in those same tracts as if provincial. In the Sacred Scriptures, indeed, the land of promise flows with milk and honey, fertile in wine, rich in grain <note>original: "Cerere" — Ceres, the goddess of agriculture, used here to mean grain</note>, legumes, and tree fruits: and likewise hardly requiring manuring or the weariness of labor. I see then that the other regions of the world owe and pay a tribute to the land of promise. For from the poles on both sides, continuous rains soak the lands, so that the promised soil, without the nuisance of rains, may take for itself the water due to it, and Egypt may repay, with a double interest of crops, the favors of the soil and sky. For the seas and rivers hasten in a hurried course to those places in competition. Indeed, even from beyond the tropic of Capricorn, the Nile carries its melted snows through Egypt to the Mediterranean as a yearly tribute of nature, so that it may irrigate the more fortunate tracts, if not with rain, at least with dew and the cloud-bringing nitreous waters <note>original: "nitreis" — referring to nitrogenous or salty minerals thought to provide life-giving fertility to the soil</note> of the Nile; and with the vapors lifted from the sea through the ground, it repays copious dew all around most abundantly. And so the whole world seems to serve those more fortunate regions. Under the equinoctial line, it rains several times daily, because the tributary waters do not reach there: but are absorbed in the tracts which God once destined for His people, but now for the Barbarians, on account of the transgressions [foretold] by the prophets...

### THE MOISTURE

With one voice, the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the established university faculties of the time, typically following Galenic or Aristotelian medicine.</note> proclaim that "radical moisture" <term>radical moisture: a vital fluid believed by ancient and medieval doctors to be the fuel of life, which slowly "dries up" as one ages</term> is the benefit of life. For they declaim that we live from it and in it, and that once it is consumed, we die. Indeed, those who, along with Aristotle, attribute everything to heat as the active principle, do not tolerate radical moisture as the beginning of life, nor as its dwelling place, unless they abandon the primacy of heat within that moisture. 

To others, however, moisture was more pleasing. From there, terrified by the laziness of further investigation, and lest they should err, they wish our life to depend upon and be prolonged by both moisture and heat without distinction. Thus, they do not name it heat alone, but concretely call it "radical heat" or "primigenial moisture." <note>original: "humidum primigenium" — the first or original moisture present at birth</note> So, they treat the primigenial moisture within us and radical heat as 

<column-break/>

so that a long duration of life may be acquired, as far as it depends on the nature of the place. Finally, there are springs—whether flavorless or mineral—not because they possess longevity "positively," but because they insensibly remove the daily growth of dregs <note>original: "amurcæ" — literally the lees of olive oil, used here to mean metabolic waste or impurities</note>, and thus life is not cut short prematurely by indirect causes. 

Nor does a mild and sweet temperament of the air avail much for this; since in the rugged hills of the Ardennes, Scotland, and Cantabria, and in our own Campania <note>The author is likely referring to the region of the Low Countries (modern Belgium/Netherlands)</note>, a longer life is generally found than in Aquitaine. For Hyères is a valley near Marseilles, shut in by mountains and fertile with the sweetest fruits. There, a most pleasant season of spring is almost continuous. Nevertheless, it has inhabitants of a shorter life, deformed with pale faces, so much so that it has crept into a proverb for the sick and convalescing: *You look like a newcomer from Hyères.* 

For the pleasantness of the fruits removes any suspicion of endemic minerals. Nor indeed does mountain cold alone extend life; yet among the Abyssinians <note>referring to people from modern-day Ethiopia</note>, old age is frequent. Therefore, let the places suitable for a long life be those polluted by no stain of endemic diseases, which moreover have healthy waters and are not infamous for stormy winds.

Thus, they established an equal law for the fish, as if it were absent, regarding the participation in <term>radical heat: the innate warmth believed to be the primary engine of life</term>. But because the soul arrives like a slave to ordained pleasures, and provides reasons even for a non-entity as it pleases, they devised a subterfuge. But they will say that after the period of growth, no more radical moisture is added to the solid parts: hence it is necessary that the true radical moisture, since it no longer sticks to the root, causes the solids to gradually dry out; and thus, as the fuel for heat fails, the heat itself perishes. Primarily, from this they conclude that the death of old age does not happen except because of the dryness of the similar parts. <note>A Galenic term for tissues that are uniform in substance, such as bone, nerve, or fiber.</note> Yet a one-year-old stag is drier than an eighty-year-old man, and it easily extends its life for a century or two. 

Finally, if moisture ceases to be "radical" simply because it reaches its limit or its application to the root—that status is incidental to the moisture, and therefore does not change its essence. For the heat of a fire does not stop spreading into neighboring wood, even if the burning wood has not received any oily kindling from the outside. Finally, the aforementioned excuse does not hold. Indeed, in every case, the solid parts behave like a lamp wick: it is enough to burn as long as oil is supplied to it; and so, if oil were supplied from the outside, the fire would live forever. 

For they teach that the heat of solid parts comes from the element of fire, which they believe is involved in the "mixing of bodies" <term>mistionem corporum: the Aristotelian idea that all things are composed of the four elements</term> and ignited in the fatness of the radical humor. First, this moisture is spermatic and mucilaginous, not oily. Next, if fire passes from the solids to the moisture it ignites: it would be enough for the moisture to be consumed and always replenished from outside, without needing to be incorporated into the root throughout. Indeed, if it passes from the solids to non-solids

<column-break/>

placed near them throughout the whole of life: it could always pass to the non-solids placed near it; nor is the excuse valid that it ceases to be "radical" simply because it is no longer united to the innermost root. Because then, immediately following the period of growth, vital vigor would be extinguished, since the moisture would no longer undergo union with the solids. 

But why do I linger longer in refuting absurdities? It has been more than sufficiently shown that fire is not an element, and that its "mixture" for the sustenance of any bodies is false: because the theories of "mixed bodies" are mere ancient fables. Therefore, if there were any fire in us, it would primarily be in the vital spirit, which always has enough moisture supplied from the blood. For this reason, I truly grieve that in the subject of life and the doctrine of the whole person, there has been such sluggish stumbling until now. For from this I have conjectured since my youth that there has been a completely shameful error—both of commission and omission—in the consideration of defects and diseases. Because no one correctly recognizes what is crooked who has not first known what is straight. 

This, then, is the fictional doctrine of the Schools concerning life, which they strive to establish on the authority of a forged book attributed to *Hippocrates*, called *On Human Nature*, which says: *on the first day of our birth we are at our hottest, and conversely on our last day we are at our coldest.* As if the fate of our heat were different from any other things! For whatever else arises, soon after takes on growth, and eventually declines and fails. Therefore, if according to the mind of the Old Man <note>Hippocrates.</note> heat were most abundant on the first day: life is still not bound to heat.

# RADICAL MOISTURE.

...I have taught you how to investigate the degrees and shifts of heat in the environment. In this sense, I found a man of thirty years who was warmer than any boy, even though he may meanwhile rave about different types of heat. Let them argue about qualities known to the senses as if they were fables, and under potential considerations; I, however, am accustomed to dissecting, opening, inspecting, and evaluating things as they truly are in themselves. Furthermore, Paracelsus, ignorant of the Schools' <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian university system of the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> radical moisture, repeatedly confuses it with the *Mumia* <note>original: "Mumia," a Paracelsian term for the life-force or healing power inherent in a living body.</note> of our body. At other times, he regards it as an internal shadow of our body, from which he claimed shadowy flames <note>original: "Phlagas," a Paracelsian term referring to an internal or astral light.</note> shine forth. Namely, he believed that radical moisture is an image of the human, extended through the whole person and carrying life. Elsewhere, he also considers mercury—one of his three principles <note>The *tria prima* of Paracelsus: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> (which is indivisible in living things)—to be the radical moisture, shared equally throughout the whole. 

For when life is extinguished by the plague (for death takes away the goodness of the *mumia*), the *mumia* indeed ceases, though that same moisture remains perfectly in the body. Finally, although the Schools admit that young people are not infrequently extinguished even when their radical moisture has not yet been consumed, nor from a lack of heat—and thus far they are not particularly concerned about their own thesis, by which they measure life proportionally by heat and radical moisture—they nevertheless stick to the terms of their ancestors because of a habit of agreeing, a laziness in investigating, and a despair of learning. Since they were ignorant that the vital lights are indeed luminous, yet they are indifferent <note>original: "indifferentia," meaning they do not inherently lean toward hot or cold.</note> because of the distinction between the two greater lights. For they can be hot as well as cold. That is, they have not learned that "forms" and "lives" are synonyms. 

But I, always greatly pitying the confused tradition of this moisture, which is of such great importance (even though they admit that both hinges of healing <note>original: "medendi cardinem," the central points on which medicine turns.</note> revolve around this moisture of the root), spent much labor in my younger years on the analysis of bodies to find some certain sign of this radical moisture. And finally, by divine favor, I was at last made certain that nothing 

<column-break/>

of those things exists in nature which are promised by the Schools with such a raised eyebrow. I do indeed acknowledge a primary seminal moisture, which constitutes us; but it is of the exact same species, property, and identity as that by which we grow and are subsequently nourished without ceasing. And so the bones, viscera, nerves, and tendons of children consist of an "indifferent" moisture, and they grow by the same kind as that by which young men are nourished once their growth is complete. 

According to the axiom of the Schools: *We are nourished by the same things of which we consist.* <note>original: "Nutrimur iisdem, quibus constamus."</note> But we consist of the primordial moisture; therefore, we are also nourished by it. I have discovered, however, that as long as the nutritional moisture is admitted homogeneously for growth within the "root of the mixture," it is exactly the same as the radical moisture. If indeed it is no longer admitted into inseparable fellowship later on—because growth ceases—this does not change, corrupt, alter, or alienate the nature of the previous moisture in the slightest. For instance, that which is clearly cast out in abundance through dreams is of the same species as the primordial and radical moisture. 

These two names are distinguished at least in this: the fetus is formed from the primordial. But the radical is that same thing, and additionally that from which we grow and are nourished. For as long as we grow, there occurs not only an application of moisture, but a solid addition and an assimilation of what has been added (for this happens daily under any kind of nutrition); but moreover, there occurs a radical union of the nourished thing with the food. This is soon after sealed by the spirit of life and vitally illuminated by the "form." <note>In this context, the "form" is the organizing principle or soul that makes a living being what it is.</note> Therefore, the "sealing" contains a character that fixes and solidifies that moisture into the homogeneous substance of a similar part <note>A uniform tissue, like bone or muscle.</note> (by whose *Archeus* <term>Archeus: In Van Helmont’s system, the internal "master-builder" or vital force that governs the functions of an organ.</term> the nourishment itself was converted and assimilated); and thus, by transmuting, it passes into the "family" of the container, whereas before it was merely the "content." Under this flow, the true "in-forming" of the soul takes place. Therefore, radical moisture is distinguished from the "dew" of secondary humors only by lot and fortune, but not in nature. # RADICAL MOISTURE.

...moisture is consumed, for the large part during growth, and entirely after growth; nor is it ever united into the root of the mixture so as to become a participant in the aforementioned sealing <note>The "sealing" refers to the process by which nourishment is permanently fixed into the solid parts of the body.</note>, or to attain the status of the containing structure. 

Take, for example, **Quicklime** <term>original: *calx viva*; calcium oxide, which reacts violently with water</term>. When it is slaked, it becomes a **paste** <note>original: *puls*; literally a porridge or pulp</note>, which joins the water most intimately to the lime. But if more water than is proper is poured on, that excess is soon rejected and floats on top. Meanwhile, however, over a number of days—even under the water—this lime dries and turns to stone. Once that hardness is acquired, even if it is then ground into the finest dust, it thereafter keeps the appearance of a powder and spurns the "marriage" with water; it does not take on the nature of the former paste, nor can water be mixed into it "radically" from then on. 

Yet the moisture of the water itself is individually the same, whether it is excluded from the lime mixture or admitted into it. This is because the rejection happens to the water by accident; it occurs not so much through a fault of the water, but by a fault of the lime, or the "root." Furthermore, the aforementioned lime-paste dries out more slowly than a powder of outward moisture is washed away by surrounding waters. 

I have therefore considered that, however much the **Schools** <note>The traditional university system following Aristotelian and Galenic medicine.</note> echo with talk of "radical moisture," the nutritive moisture differs in no way from the radical moisture itself, so long as it turns to paste and solidifies within the root of the mixture, joined by a radical union to the first constituent parts. Because both fluids are the same in matter, power, substance, purity, formal identity, and participation in life. When our solid parts no longer turn to paste or admit the intimate connection of the "root," this moisture at least prevents and delays the dryness of the solid structures as much as it can by continually "bedewing" them. For once that paste of the solids has reached its proper solidity—namely, because the power of growth flowing from the brain is exhausted—then it becomes merely nutritive moisture, whereas before it was becoming "radical." For although old age causes dryness, death does not actually result from a "dry" condition.

<column-break/>

Indeed, one may sooner guess that dryness results from a failure of the vital powers, rather than the failure resulting from dryness. For the moisture of the solid parts—even if consumed equally throughout the whole body in wasting diseases and long-term illnesses—is nevertheless easily restored by proper nourishment, and even more magnificently by taking the "milky element of pearls" <note>A chemical preparation where pearls were dissolved or suspended in a liquid, believed to have restorative powers.</note>. Likewise, ulcers of the lungs are solidified by the "sweet coral-colored diaphoretic mercury" <note>A mercury-based medicine prepared by Van Helmont's chemical methods to induce sweating and healing.</note>; by the power of which, indeed, the epitaph of Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus's tomb in Salzburg bears an inscription claiming he cured various incurable diseases, including "tabes" or consumption.</note> proclaims that wasting disease was often cured. 

I remember that, during the intense heat of July, I pierced the head of a **toad** with a sharp stick and fixed the other end of the stick into the ground so the suspended toad would dry out. It happened, however, that four days later, returning to the same place, I found the toad alive, contracting its thighs as if it had only been there since yesterday. This was because the hole was not straight in the middle of the head, but inclined a little more to the left side <note>The author suggests he missed the "vital center" or "soul" of the animal.</note>. Therefore, I drove the stick into the middle of the head, and returning toward evening, I found the toad not only dead, but entirely dried up. 

From this I became more firmly persuaded: it is not a failure of vital things that comes from the dryness of solids, but rather that dryness exists and increases in us according to the rate at which our vital powers are gradually extinguished. Away, therefore, with the "radical ignorance" of the Schools, by which they cover their own failure under the soil of the cemetery, blaming an "irreparable lack of radical moisture" (as they call it). For it is only the diminishing of the vital powers—which are sealed within the economy of the indwelling spirit—that brings on old age, just as the extinction of death brings on internal calamities. This is to say: *My spirit shall be thinned, and my days shall be shortened* <note>original: "Spiritus meus attenuabitur, & dies mei abbreviabuntur," a reference to Job 17:1.</note>. 

Away, therefore, with the consideration of radical moisture in the pursuit of a long life. Since **Hippocrates** says that natures themselves (the vital powers) are the healers of diseases; when these powers grow faint, the daily hardships of infirmities grow strong, and as the doctors withdraw, shrugging their shoulders, they cry out that life is despaired of...

## V I T A L  S P I R I T.
->(Aura Vitalis)<-

The **Schools** <note>The traditional university establishment following Galen and Aristotle.</note> have not done enough by merely teaching that food is first turned into **chyle** <term>a milky fluid produced in the intestines</term>, then into the juice of the blood, and that a **natural spirit** is then created in the liver. They claim this spirit is refined through a second "digestion" in the heart to become the **vital spirit**, and finally becomes the **animal spirit** in the brain. According to them, the natural spirit is for using the body's parts; the vital spirit is for giving them life and preserving them; and the animal spirit is destined for the functions of the senses, movement, and the mind. In my judgment, they ought to have uncovered the true essence and the actual history of this process more deeply throughout such a long series of studies and repetitive writings. Indeed, they know there is a certain spirit—what **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> called the "impulse-maker"—which holds the tiller of life in its hand. They should have investigated and declared which organs create this spirit, what it actually does, and explained its whole nature, substance, and properties, as well as its manner of formation. I will, therefore, state what I have discovered in this matter.

To lead us into a proper understanding of the **vital spirit**, I would first need to repeat my teachings on the human **Blas** <term>original: *Blas*; Van Helmont’s term for the internal "pulse" or astral-vital force that governs motion in the body</term>; but to avoid being tedious, I will omit that here and refer the reader to my volume *On the Origin of Medicine*. I have also taught elsewhere the method by which "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitae*; high-proof distilled spirit or alcohol</note> is made from any plant or fruit through implanted ferments. The common people know and practice this method when they manufacture "water of life" from grains, fruits, beer, and mead, just as they do from the juice of the vine.

<column-break/>

**Water of life** is a volatile liquor; it is oily (inasmuch as it is entirely flammable) and yet equally "salty" in the way it bites the air—indeed, if held in the mouth for a moment, it burns and blisters the skin of the gums. I note here in passing that two chemical principles are actually a single and indivisible simple substance. I have shown elsewhere how, when one measure of **aqua vitae** is soaked into dried **salt of tartar** <term>potassium carbonate</term>, barely a half-ounce of salt remains, while the rest of the body returns to being "elemental water" just as it was before. From this, it is obvious that water is a substance that is naturally more primary and simple than the chemical principles themselves. While water was not "in action" within the highly refined aqua vitae, it nonetheless becomes the "first element of water" again through this reduction.

Applying this mechanical observation to the study of life, I find that wine—through its vinous part—contains this "water of life." Therefore, it is easily and quickly snatched through the arteries of the stomach directly to the heart, without needing the long "maturing" digestions of the liver and the gall. It is summoned immediately to supplement or remedy a defect in the **vital spirit**. This discovery eludes the opinion of the Schools, which presupposes that the "spirit of the liver" must always come first. Indeed, if there is more "spirit of wine" in the stomach than is proper, **drunkenness** follows; this happens because the spirit of the wine is drawn in more rapidly and in larger quantities than can be comfortably converted into the vital...

->(Aura Vitalis)<-

...that the vital spirit is changed. This certainly proves, above all, its own transformation, as well as the operations of digestion and fermentation. Finally, there is also this notable fact: in wine, there is surely a certain milder spirit, participating in another and more noble quality than that which is immediately drawn out through distillation, which is called **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; high-proof distilled alcohol</note> and **phlegm** <term>the watery, tasteless residue left after distillation</term>.

This is easily seen by the eye in simple olive oil. Indeed, distilled oil—produced without the addition of bricks or tiles <note>Traditional alchemy often used powdered brick or tile to prevent "bumping" or overheating during distillation.</note>, which is called the "oil of the philosophers"—differs greatly from that oiliness which is drawn out by first reducing the simple oil into dissimilar parts, solely through digestion and the addition of the **circulated salt of Paracelsus** <term>Sal Circulatum: a legendary alchemical solvent said to extract essences while remaining unchanged itself</term>. For the circulated salt is separated from the oil, identical in weight and in its original qualities, after the olive oil has been arranged into its own distinct parts. 

For then, a "sweet oil of olives" is separated from the oil, just as the most pleasant spirit of wine is separated from wine; in this way, it is far distinct from the sharpness of the **water of life** <note>alcohol</note>. In us, however, although food and drink may "rot" to some extent (for surely that "rot" is the method and means of changing one thing into another), nevertheless in our digestions, through that kind of putrefaction and the action of the **splenic ferment** <note>Van Helmont believed the spleen provided the vital "acid" or "ferment" necessary for the stomach to digest food.</note>, the spirit of the **water of life** is not drawn out from vegetables, legumes, grains, or fruits. 

For the intention of our nature is not to create **water of life** for itself; rather, there is a far different ferment in us by which things are resolved into **chyle** <term>the milky fluid produced from digested food</term>. It is one thing for matter to rot and be separated into "water of life," and another for it to be digested. For the former is introduced by many means of fermentation, but the latter is acquired only by the specific fermental property of each species. For while herbs rot in water through long soaking—either by their own ferment or one substituted for it—for the extraction of "water of life," their stalks, branches, and leaves remain intact in shape and hardness. Yet those same herbs, when chewed, swallowed, and well-processed within, turn into chyle within a few hours and lose their primary 

<column-break/>

nature as plants. Therefore, I have emphasized elsewhere that there are as many specific digestive ferments, as many varieties of putrefactions, and just as many types of "bread-dung" as there are species of animals nourished by bread. Indeed, there are even more ferments involved in the corruption of bread; for bread rots in even more ways, both spontaneously and by the odor of places and the influences of external agents. And what has been said of bread should be understood of other foods as well. 

The **Schools** <note>Traditional university academics following the ancient Greek physician Galen.</note>, also noticing that nothing would benefit us unless it contained a "prelude to life" in its root, therefore wished for the spirit of the liver—natural in its action—to spread through the blood like a breeze. They thought it was a **vapor**, and thus they confused it with the breath. They were unaware that a vapor is water; it is not, however, a **Gas** <term>Van Helmont's coined term for a "wild spirit" or vital air that cannot be condensed into liquid</term>, a **wild spirit** <note>original: *spiritus silvester*</note>, an uncoagulable breeze, and an ether. 

They thought, therefore, that the vapor exhaling from the blood outside the veins—just as it breathes out from any warm liquid—was that very "spirit of the blood" from which the **vital spirit** would then be materially manufactured. I have discussed these matters elsewhere as a professional. 

Truly, whatever descends into a healthy stomach, if it is processed by the **ferment of the spleen**, it becomes sour with the fermental and specific acidity of our species. And finally, it is turned into **cruor** <term>the raw material of blood before it is vitalized</term>, after the superfluities have been sequestered from it. This raw blood, after the goal of its digestion, is transferred to the heart and becomes **blood** <note>The author distinguishes between *cruor* (raw blood) and *sanguis* (living blood).</note>, which in the Holy Scriptures is called the **red spirit** in which the soul dwells. For it becomes fit to migrate into the **vital spirit**, and its residue undergoes the final digestion of the solid parts, and finally, without that residence of itself, it exhales into the breezes. Therefore, by that very fact, it must be volatile and have assumed the nature of a spirit in the heart. 

Furthermore, that acid of the stomach is entirely converted into salt by the power of the **gall ferment** <note>the ferment of the bile/gallbladder</note>, as I have noted elsewhere regarding digestions. And the actual saltiness is separated with the urine and sweats, because it has turned into waste. But the mass of the raw blood itself, since it cannot pass into the spirit unless by the vital ferment
