Indeed, I have seen it several times and handled it with my own hands. It was of a color like saffron in its powder form, yet heavy and glittering like pulverized glass. Once, a portion was given to me: one-fourth of a single grain. Now, I define a grain as the six-hundredth part of an ounce. This quarter-grain, wrapped in paper, I threw upon eight ounces of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note> heated in a crucible. Immediately, the entire mass of mercury, with a certain sound, stopped flowing and settled, congealed like a yellow mass. After it was melted using a bellows, there were found eight ounces of the purest gold, less only eleven grains. Thus, a single grain of that powder would have transmuted 19,186 parts of quicksilver—equal to its own weight—into the finest gold.

## OCCASIONS OF DEATH.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'I' depicting a figure, possibly a saint or scholar, set within an ornate square frame.</image-desc>

I have compared life to fire and light because it possesses something that appears vital. Indeed, vital forms—whether of things or of life—are themselves lights. Therefore, there will be at least as many occasions of death as there are ways that light can be taken away. First, then, light is blown out; likewise, by compression, the flame perishes, which people call a "lack of air." However, I have demonstrated that this happens due to a lack of the new **Great Element** <term>original: "Magnatis"; likely referring to the *Magnale Magnum*, a term used by Van Helmont to describe a vital, spiritual-physical medium or "gas" in the air</term>, and not because fire is nourished by air. Similarly, fire is extinguished by the constriction of foreign smoke. This is why lamps are extinguished in vaults and mine shafts; light is also blown out by wind or another flame. For often candles are extinguished by a sudden flare-up of flame, resin powder, or gunpowder. Finally, fire perishes from a lack of fuel. Death rushes in similarly in many ways. For either the living body is suddenly crushed and shattered by a weight, or a swift

<column-break/>

Therefore, among earthly things, the aforementioned powder is found, which is in some way similar: it transmutes nearly infinite amounts of impure metal into the finest gold, and by uniting with it, defends it from tarnish, rust, decay, and death. It makes the metal, as it were, immortal against all the "torture" of fire and the alchemist's art, and transfers it into the virgin purity of gold; it requires only the fervor of heat. In this same way, the soul and body are regenerated through baptism and the communion of the unstained Body of the Lord, provided that the just fervor of devotion is present in the faithful. Let the Theologian forgive me if I have spoken "beyond my sandal" <note>original: "ultra crepidam"; a Latin idiom for acting outside one's area of expertise</note> regarding eternal life by way of a parenthesis. For I gladly confess: the regenerated body is not within my jurisdiction. I deal only with the prolongation of the life of the world. I have said this much at least: that real Baptism brings an effect of purity perceptible to the senses, and the most holy communion of the Eucharist has something similar in earthly things, so that we may more easily believe in regeneration.

# OCCASIONS OF DEATH.

...likewise through dislocations of the vertebrae and contractions of those parts of the body intended for purging filth <note>Referring to the organs of elimination and waste</note>. Finally, death occurs because of the exhaustion of the "seeds" <note>The vital generative principles or energies within the body</note> and the failure of powers, being worn out and depleted by old age. It also occurs because of severe disturbances of the mind <note>original: "pathemata animi"</note> and through incantations. Death, therefore, steals mortals away in so many ways every day, even though their life is always simple and uniform. For this reason, there is a distinct and differing consideration for life and for death. Indeed, a sword takes away life; however, the contemplation of preserving life is quite different from that of healing diseases by removing or preventing their causes. To be sure, some causes are external, such as a wound, a plague, a burn, and so forth; consequently, the healing of these does not depend solely on the removal of the causes. For one does not need to destroy the fire in the hearth that burned someone in order for them to be healed, just as a sword does not need to be broken for a wound to close. But for the preservation of a long life, the observation and removal of external causes are no less important than the presence of vital "kindling" <note>original: "fomenti vitalis"; the internal fuel or heat that sustains life</note>. Indeed, even if no infirmities were to infest us, death would not on that account cease to pave the way for its entrance day by day. For although health looks upon life as its foundation, life does not necessarily include health. For a blind man, a lame man, or one suffering from gout <term>podagricus: a person afflicted with gout, a painful inflammatory arthritis</term>, and so on, lives no less than a healthy man. If life ends through disease, that is something foreign to life and happens by accident. Just as a sword contains death, it only does so through its application. Otherwise, death by its nature regards life; but morbific <note>disease-causing</note> causes only become fatal by accident, or through their application to the spirit of life. Hence, the impediments to a long life must be seriously attended to and turned away if we expect longevity. In the beginning, therefore, the meditation on life consists not in something external, but in life itself: namely, how life is preserved in the body. For the sensitive soul <note>In traditional philosophy, the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared by humans and animals</note> has, ever since the time of sin <note>Referring to the Fall of Man</note>, drawn the entire property of life to itself and has become the bond of life with the body. But since the soul

<column-break/>

itself is mortal in its own nature, it is necessary above all that all vital powers, being of the same age as life, be unstable and fleeting. From this, eventually, comes death. To achieve longevity of life, therefore, the first requirement is the healing of diseases—both those that affect the life of the whole body and those that concern the damage or preservation of specific parts and functions, which thus far lie in wait for life. Since there is a uniform conspiracy <note>original: "conspiratio"; here meaning a "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation</note> of the limbs, the primary powers cannot help but eventually falter, even if only the subordinate ones are diminished. In this I depart from Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist known for his radical medical theories</note>, because he thought that every disease must necessarily be removed by a "pharmaceutical for long life." For that good man was just as ignorant of the medicine and use for long life as he was of the essence and properties of long life itself. Therefore, his *arcana* <term>arcana: hidden or "secret" alchemical remedies believed to have great power</term> contribute greatly to a healthy life or to the removal of impurities; yet they do nothing directly and primarily for a long life as an ultimate goal. This is because, just like life itself, the Tree of Life primarily concerns the preservation, restoration, and rejuvenation of the vital faculties implanted in the body parts. In this respect, the *arcana* that remove superfluities differ from the Tree of Life. For those remedies may heal diseases that even mother nature herself could never cure—such as leprosy, the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, paralysis, wasting disease <note>original: "tabem"; consumption or tuberculosis</term>, dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, etc.—but the Tree of Life does not heal these diseases once they have already been admitted. Indeed, if Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> repeatedly said that natures themselves are the healers of diseases, that must be forgiven of his age and his then-beginning art. Otherwise, the *arcana* (which had not yet become known then, and today remain almost hidden) surpass the forces of nature, just as art very often overcomes nature. And this is true not only in the *arcana* that heal diseases, but also in the Tree of Life which restores failing nature. The purpose of the Tree, therefore, is the preservation of life with a certain rejuvenation; but leprosy, the stone, and so on, may persist even with the remedy of the Tree. Therefore, the consideration of the *arcana* of Paracelsus is one thing, and that of the Tree of Life is quite another.

-># OCCASIONS OF DEATH.<-

I confirm this in the following way. Let us consider a young man suffering from any of the aforementioned diseases: his blooming and vivid youth does not, by itself, heal these diseases; therefore, neither does the <term>Tree of Life</term><note>The author refers here to a specific alchemical or botanical elixir intended to extend life, modeled after the biblical Tree of Life.</note>. This is because the elixir only provides the "kindling" or fuel for that blooming life. This fuel is, of course, received according to the capacity of the recipient. Therefore, in the diseased part of the person receiving it, there always remains a disproportion of strength compared to the healthy parts, just as there was before taking the medicine from the Tree of Life. For even if every part of the body participated equally in that medicine, they would not be restored with equal strength. 

First, therefore, the impediments to a long life must be removed entirely. Among these impediments, some actively shorten life, such as diseases, disorders of lifestyle, and so on. Others, however, limit and restrict the Tree of Life in its goodness, preventing it from achieving its ultimate intended purpose. This is true of *our* Tree of Life <note>The medicinal preparation</note>, but not the one from Paradise; and it applies to our fallen, corrupt life, not the life of Adam before the Fall. 

Thus, certain diseases, as well as much deep, intense, and unpleasant speculation <note>Refers to excessive or stressful intellectual labor</note>, disturbances of the mind, and even incantations, act as obstacles, as will be discussed in their proper place. Happy, therefore, and generally long-lived, are those who—far from cares, usury, business, and the tempests of their age—can plow their ancestral lands with their own oxen and live in peace and cheerfulness. Whatever must be considered for the attainment of a long life must be considered in a state of peace and freedom from care, with full resignation to the most gentle will of God. One must reflect, therefore, on how much ridiculous thoughts tire us during fevers, how much serious studies drain our strength, and how much the anxieties of the day ruin our number of days. For in this way, the spirit is thinned and our days are shortened. 

Furthermore, **Venus** <note>A common euphemism for sexual activity or lust</note> holds its own primary place among the impediments to a long life, because it exhausts life's vitality in abundance. Following Venus is excessive and untimely gluttony, which is even more harmful if the drink is noxious. **Tobacco**, fungi, and those things which, because of a hidden, creeping poison, strike down the vital forces, are also harmful. For tobacco does not—

<column-break/>

—settle hunger as if it actually satisfied a deficiency; rather, it works only insofar as it numbs the sense of that deficiency, along with the exercise of the body's functions. Finally, the impediments to life include frequent hot baths, bloodlettings, wounds, and various "solutions of continuity" <note>A surgical term for any break in the skin or tissues, like a cut or ulcer</note>, especially when they are frequent. These things make the generation of the person performing them less flourishing and thus accelerate old age. 

Finally, just as certain climates contribute to a long life, others are obstructive. There are places where an old man is a rarity, and others where old age is held in honor. For local <term>arsenical</term> <note>Refers to toxic vapors or minerals</note> and subterranean conditions reap life while it is still green and in the flower of youth. There are also those places near flooded tracts of land. Indeed, whatever has spontaneously boiled up from rot in the water and been dissolved must be offered up as vapor and swallowed by us. Therefore, the habits of living in marshes that breathe out rot are ruinous; likewise, those places that exhale a half-putrefied salt mixed with filth and dissolved mud. 

I saw at **Antwerp**, for instance, after the **Oosterweel** field was submerged by waves, that the leaves of the lime trees on the city walls were dried up by August and eaten away as if by decay. Before the flood, these were preserved green on the tree until October. The same thing is seen at **Amsterdam**. Meanwhile, at **Leiden** <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum"</note>, the leaves of the trees still mimic the appearance of May. Since the foliage suffers this slaughter from a half-salty vapor, what then must we think will happen to the tender lining of the lungs and the sponge-like tissue of their internal structure? 

Truly, so many enemies of our life lie in wait on all sides that, unless we withdraw far from the harmful contagion of the air, the desired participation in a long life will scarcely be possible, even with the full grant of the Tree of Life. For the original Tree of Life in Eden was for its inhabitants, not for the natives of this "valley of misery." Therefore, whoever wishes to enjoy the goodness of the Tree of Life and profit from the labor of **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sophia"; likely referring to alchemical or divine wisdom</note> should choose a region that commonly supports many old people, and where fierce diseases are rare. Then, finally, one should use the Tree of Life from childhood (or better yet, if the child receives its benefits first through both parents, and then through the nurse)—

IN the eighth year of this century <note>1608</note>, there was brought to me a declamatory speech held at Marburg of the Chatti <note>Marburg, Germany</note>, in which Rudolf Goclenius (to whom the profession of Philosophy had recently been entrusted), paying his first fruits, attempts to show that the healing of wounds through the Sympathetic and Weapon Ointment invented by Paracelsus is purely natural. I read that whole speech and groaned that the history of natural things had obtained such a weak patron.

<meta>This page continues the critique of Rudolf Goclenius the Younger (1572–1628), a professor at Marburg who wrote about the "Weapon Ointment"—a controversial remedy supposed to heal wounds by applying an ointment to the weapon that caused them, rather than the wound itself. Van Helmont positions himself as an arbiter between Goclenius and a Jesuit critic, Jean Roberti.</meta>

### JOHN BAPTIST VAN HELMONT

Nonetheless, the author was pleased with his choice of subject matter, and despite a continued lack of proof, he published an expanded version of the same work in the year 1613. Very recently, a brief "anatomy" <note>An "anatomy" in this context refers to a detailed critical analysis or dissection of a book's arguments.</note> of the aforementioned book was offered by a certain Theologian <note>This refers to Jean Roberti (1569–1651), a Jesuit who argued that the weapon ointment was the work of the devil.</note>, composed more in the style of a witty censure than a formal dispute. My own judgment was sought, however skilled it might be, for the reason that this matter was discovered by Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, and as such, it concerns him and me as his follower. I shall say, therefore, what I think of Goclenius the Physician, and what I think of the Theologian who censured him.

The Physician first proposes and boasts that he will prove that the magnetic cure of wounds is natural; but I found the promiser unequal to such a great task, as he nowhere satisfies his title or promises, even slightly. Collecting a rhapsody <note>A "rhapsody" here means a miscellaneous collection or hodgepodge of ideas gathered from various sources.</note> from here and there, he argues that certain formal powers, which they call sympathy and antipathy, exist in the nature of things. From this premise, he thinks he has sufficiently proven that the magnetic cure is natural. He gathers many things, I say, from the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Persians, conjurers, and tricksters into one pile, by which he might verify the magnetism that is unknown to him. He does this partly to amuse and lead astray minds eager for novelty, and partly so that they might admire the author for having scoured not just trivial writers, but even the rarest ones.

Therefore, the Physician wrongly confuses sympathy (which he cites in various and often fabulous ways) with magnetism; he concludes that magnetism is natural based on sympathy. For I have seen that wound ointment heal not only men, but even horses—and we certainly do not have such a great affinity with horses (unless we are asses) that an ointment could deserve to be called "sympathetic" and common to both us and horses.

The Physician likewise badly confuses sympathy with enchantment <note>original: 'fascino'</note> and binding <note>original: 'ligatione'; a magical practice believed to hinder or "bind" a person’s actions</note>, and both of these with magnetism. Being anxious and lacking solid reasons, he brings forward various obscure effects indiscriminately to

<column-break/>

verify his magnetism. By way of example, I shall distinguish enchantment from sympathy, and both from magnetism.

<margin>1.</margin>
A dog has an antipathy (for sympathy and antipathy are daughters of the same genus) toward a hen: for the dog devours the hen, and the hen flees the dog. But when she has recently hatched chicks, she drives the dog away, even a brave one. This is because the soul of the hen, through enchantment, binds the soul of the dog; the prior antipathy notwithstanding, the hen prevails despite the disparity of her weapons and her unequal strength. Yet in none of this is there magnetism.

Furthermore, the things the Physician brings up regarding seals, characters, <term>gamahēu</term> <note>original: 'gamahēu'; these were stones or talismans believed to have natural markings that granted them magical powers</note>, ceremonies, and mostly vain observations are entirely irrelevant here. They destroy the case for magnetism by making it look suspicious rather than supporting it; my character does not permit me to pass judgment on such things.

Next, Goclenius errs, and indeed he does so as recklessly as he does ignorantly: dreaming that according to the prescription of Paracelsus, if the weapon that caused the wound is bound with the "weapon ointment" <note>original: 'unguento armario'</note>, the wound is cured. For it is in vain to smear the weapon or its point with his prescribed ointment unless the blood on that same sword has first been dried there.

<margin>2.</margin>
For Paracelsus, one ointment is "sympathetic" because it contains blood taken from the wound; but another ointment is surely different, in which weapons not stained with any blood must be plastered. He calls the former "magnetic and sympathetic ointment," but the latter "magnetic weapon ointment." This latter recipe additionally requires honey and bull fat, and not without reason.

Finally, to satisfy his own whims, Goclenius changed Paracelsus’s description, asserting that the <term>usnea</term> <note>original: 'usnea'; a type of lichen or moss found growing on human skulls, used in early modern medicine</note> must be gathered only from the skulls of hanged men. Seeking a reason for his own false invention, he does not fear to dream that vital spirits, through the act of strangling, entered the skull and remained there for a time, until after six years had passed, the moss grew under the open sky. Paracelsus expressly taught the opposite, and it has been proven by use that moss from a skull crushed on the wheel <note>A reference to the "breaking wheel," a form of execution for criminals.</note> is equally effective.

<summary>Van Helmont critiques Rudolf Goclenius for confusing natural magnetism with vague concepts of sympathy, enchantment, and superstitious practices. He specifically corrects Goclenius's errors regarding Paracelsus's recipes for the "weapon ointment" and the medicinal use of moss from human skulls.</summary>

# ON THE MAGNETIC CURE OF WOUNDS.

<page-num>749</page-num>

<margin>3.</margin>...of those killed by animals is no less praiseworthy than those hanged by a noose. For in animals, it is not the "fifth essence" <note>original: "quintum esse"; likely referring to the quintessence or a fifth element distinct from the four physical elements</note> (which perishes along with the inflowing spirit and life), but the <term>mummy-like power <note>Latin: "virtus mumialis." In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to a vital magnetic force or "mummy" that remains in a body after a sudden or violent death and can be harvested for healing.</note></term>—that is, the spirit implanted and fermented together—that is drawn out, surviving in bodies killed by force.

As for what Goclenius has brought forth regarding remedies for restoring memory, just as we recognize them as being in no way suited to the intended purpose, so we do not hesitate to prove them to be irrelevant displays.

Between the Theologian and the Physician, there is no dispute over the fact: both certainly concede that the healing of the wounded man occurs. The dispute lies only in this: the Physician maintains that a healing of this kind is natural; the Theologian, however, wishes it to be satanic, and that by a pact with the original inventor <note>The "original inventor" here refers to the Devil.</note>. Regarding this judgment, the Theologian offers no positive reason in his "anatomy" <note>Referring to Roberti’s critical book "Anatome Gocleniana."</note>: thinking himself satisfied if he has cut down the arguments in his possession, even if he has brought forward no fundamental principles of restoration himself; resting, evidently, in the fact that he has removed the weak reasons of the one asserting it. This requires no effort, no skill, and possesses no authority. For what does it achieve to judge the matter itself based on the futility of the reasons of someone unskilled? And to declare it impious, if he has not dreamed up even one little reason for his own opinion? What if a layman were to praise the priesthood with unpolished reasons, and someone rejected them as undeserved—should the priesthood itself be rejected on that account? How, I ask, does the unskillfulness or rashness of either party touch the things themselves? Certainly, Philosophy does not submit itself to censures unless the weight of the censors is established by reasons.

<margin>4.</margin>And so I, who have undertaken to prove the magnetic cure as natural against the Theologian: first, I thought Goclenius should be excused if he labored in vain in discovering the proximate cause of this unusual effect. What wonder, when the Theologian confesses that he himself does not know it, and therefore

<column-break/>

guesses that Satan is the author? For such is our weakness, that we are destitute of the knowledge of very many and most excellent things. For that reason, we unwillingly turn many things toward the "sacred anchor of ignorance" <note>A metaphorical way of saying people give up and blame God or the Devil when they don't understand something.</note> and refer them to the catalog of <term>occult causes <note>Natural powers that are hidden from the senses or not yet understood by science.</note></term>. For which of the Theologians has ever fully known the demonstration of the cause of laughter, or of another formal property—for instance, the heat in fire? Is it not "begging the question" <note>original: "petitio principii"</note> if you say: "Highest heat belongs to fire because it is of its nature"? Indeed, because the essences of forms are unknown to us *a priori* <note>from first principles or causes</note>, therefore the entire lineage of formal properties is meager and unknown. And whenever we notice some formal passion underlying a thing, the mind, as if exhausted by the investigation in vain soon ceases and rests itself, content with the name of "occult properties." Come now, if you please, does the anatomical censor know the reason why a happy dog wags its tail? Or a lion likewise, when angry? Or why a cat, when pleased, raises its own? What then, if he does not even know the reason for the movement of a tail, will he wonder that Goclenius gave an unsubstantial reason for magnetism? And by his refutation, will he presume that he has more than sufficiently demonstrated that the cure, which is of magnetism, is satanic? Let such rashness of judgment be far from us.

Come now, why do you call the cure diabolical? You should have added the reason for your censure, unless you expect to be denied by others with the same ease with which you proclaim it diabolical. Jurists require only the affirmative to be confirmed; but philosophers require both, lest the ignorance or even the insolence of those denying seem greater than those asserting. <margin>5.</margin> Or do you perhaps claim it is diabolical because a natural reason cannot be understood (by you) to underlie it? I will not believe that you would pass such a sluggish judgment on power based on your own weakness. For you know that the fault is ours—a weakness of understanding—not a fault of the things themselves.

Be busy, therefore, in explaining how you know that God has not directed such a magnetic power into

<columns>2</columns>

...use for the wounded? Show us the letters: as if
<margin>6.</margin> GOD had chosen you to be the secretary of his secret counsel! Truly, however much you wander in various directions, you will eventually find that there is no other reason why you consider this a diabolical cure, except that your own insignificance and your calling cannot grasp it. Is it any wonder
<margin>7.</margin> if no Theologian has scented this out? For after the Priest and the Levite had passed by on the way to Jericho, there followed the Samaritan layman, who took away from the Priests all right to inquire into the causes of things. Therefore, from that time on, nature called not the Theologians to be her interpreters; rather, she chose only the Physicians as her sons—and
<margin>8.</margin> indeed, only those who, equipped with <term>pyrotechnia <note>original: "pyrotechnia"; literally "fire-art," referring to alchemy or early chemistry used to analyze and purify substances.</note></term>, examine the properties of things; by separating the obstacles of the hidden powers—namely, the rawness, the poisonous qualities, and the dregs, which are the "thorns and thistles" from the curse, sown everywhere into virgin nature. For since nature daily distills, sublimes, calcines, ferments, dissolves, coagulates, fixes, and so on, we certainly use these same aids to bring the properties of things out of hiding and into the light, as the only faithful interpreters of nature.

However, for a Theologian to judge what is a deceptive trick versus what is natural, he must first draw a definition from us: lest, as they say, <note>original: "ne sutor ultra crepidam"; a Latin proverb meaning "the shoemaker should not go beyond his last"—warning people not to judge things outside their expertise.</note> the shoemaker slip shamefully beyond his last. Let the Theologian inquire about GOD, but let the natural philosopher inquire about nature.

Certainly, the goodness of the Creator was great everywhere, who established all created things for the use of ungrateful
<margin>9.</margin> men. Nor did He admit any Theologian as an advisor regarding how many and how great the virtues He should instill in things. Meanwhile, I truly do not know how one can be excused from the sin of pride who, because he does not perceive the natural reason—measuring all the works of GOD by his own sharp wits—therefore boldly denies that God gave such virtue to these things. It is as if man, a mere worm, were a master of God and His counsel: he judges the minds of all by his own, thinking that what he cannot understand cannot be possible.

To me, indeed, it seems in no way strange if God gave a virtue to things that is distinct from the body of a physical magnet, yet

<column-break/>

explicable by the name of magnetism alone. Ought not at least one single natural example of that stone (of which I shall soon bring forward more appropriate examples) be sufficient for the positioning of magnetism, so that by its standard, other virtues distributed in various ways among creatures might also be understood? Because it is a new paradox and unknown to you, must it therefore also be satanic? Far be it from us to think so unworthily of the divine majesty of the Creator; nor, certainly, should we flatter
<margin>10.</margin> Satan by deferring such honor to him. For what affects him more sweetly than if the glory of good works is attributed to him, as if he himself had been their author?
<margin>11.</margin> You concede that material nature, by its own magnetism, daily draws "forms" from above and seeks the favor of the heavenly bodies, and that the heavens, in turn, invisibly attract something from below, so that there is a free and reciprocal passage, making a harmonious <term>lyre <note>original: "chelys"; a Greek term for a lyre or lute, here used to describe the harmonious "tuning" or connection of all parts of the universe.</note></term> of all the members into a single whole. Magnetism, therefore, because it flourishes everywhere, contains nothing new except the name; nor is it a paradox, except to those who deride all things and banish to the dominion of Satan whatever they do not understand. Truly, "to the mocker seeking wisdom, it does not exist."
<margin>12.</margin> But I ask, what superstition does the <term>weapon ointment <note>original: "unguentum armarium"; a sympathetic salve applied to the weapon that caused a wound, rather than the wound itself, to effect a cure at a distance.</note></term> possess? Is it because it is composed of <term>skull-moss <note>original: "usnea"; a lichen found on the skulls of those who died a violent death, used in early medicine.</note></term>, blood, <term>mummy <note>original: "mumia"; the vital essence extracted from remains.</note></term>, and human fat? But the Physician uses these harmlessly, and the apothecary sells them for this purpose without penalty. Is it perhaps because the method of use is new to you, unusual to the common people, and marvelous to both, that the effect must be satanic? Submit yourself, and do not be agitated; soon you will be better off.
<margin>13.</margin> For the method of use contains nothing evil. Above all, the intention is good and holy, and it results only in a good end: namely, to heal a suffering neighbor without pain, danger, or the exhaustion of expenses. Do you call this diabolical? Finally, the remedies themselves are natural things, to which I will soon argue that such faculty was granted by GOD...

He asserts that physicians, through chemistry and the study of nature's "magnetism," are the rightful interpreters of these God-given healing virtues.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s polemic against the Jesuit Jean Roberti. Van Helmont is defending the "magnetic" or "sympathetic" cure of wounds (where an ointment is applied to the weapon rather than the wound) by arguing it is a natural, physical process rather than a demonic one.</meta>

# ON THE MAGNETIC CURE OF WOUNDS.

...we will be proven right. I wish that you also had so firmly established your negative stance for us: namely, that God, the supreme good, did not give natural power and mummial magnetism <note>original: "mumialem magnetismum"; in Helmont's theory, "mummy" refers to a vital balsamic force within the body, not an Egyptian corpse.</note> to the sympathetic ointment.

<margin>14.</margin>
This magnetic remedy can by no means be made suspect: since it has no rituals, no words, no characters or seals, nor does it require any ceremonies or vain observations: it does not

<margin>15.</margin>
presuppose specific hours, nor does it profane sacred things; indeed, what is more, it does not even require imagination, confidence, or faith, nor must permission be sought from the wounded person—all of which are attached to superstitious cures.

<margin>16.</margin>
For it is called superstition whenever one relies on faith, or imagination, or both, regarding some power that is either not real, or was not directed to that purpose by the Creator. Therefore, the **Magnetic cure** has nothing of superstition in it. Wherefore, O Theological Censor, even if you make a trial of the ointment full of sarcasm, merely to mock Satan and root out that "implicit pact" <note>An "implicit pact" was a theological term for an unspoken agreement with the devil through the use of suspicious remedies.</note> you imagine, you will nonetheless find the effect to be exactly the same as ours, whether you like it or not—which by no means happens with superstitious causes.

<margin>17.</margin>
Whoever thinks the magnetic cure of wounds is diabolical does so not because it consists of illicit ends or means, but because it proceeds in a manner unknown to him. He, convicted by this same argument, would have to provide the essential causes for everything we are about to say concerning the magnet;

<margin>18.</margin>
otherwise, he will either have to confess that the operations of the magnet are the deceptions of Satan, or at least (which will be safer) he will be forced to acknowledge with us **magnetism**—that is, a certain hidden property, distinguished from other abstruse and commonly unknown qualities by this name because of the manifest excellence of that stone.

<margin>19.</margin>
A magnet placed on a wooden dish and floating in water immediately turns one certain side to the south and the other to the north. Its southern part, if it touches iron, turns it to the north, and the northern part

<column-break/>

of the magnet, having touched the iron, will incline it to the south. With the northern part—that is, its "belly"—it attracts iron, and with its "back," it pushes it away. By rubbing the tip of a compass needle with the northern side from right to left, it will direct it to the south; but if the rubbing is done from left to right, the direction of the tip will be the opposite.

Similarly, the southern side of the magnet varies. Indeed, what is more, if a magnet through its rubbing makes iron magnetic—that is, capable of attracting other iron—and that same iron, now magnetic, is turned upside down and rubbed again against the magnet, it will immediately lose its pulling power. If you have a taste for these things, consult **William Gilbert**, the London Physician, *On the Magnet* <note>original: "Guilielmum Guilbertum... de magnete"; referring to William Gilbert’s 1600 book *De Magnete*, the first great work of modern physics published in England.</note>, than whom no one has written better on this matter, and by whose work the variation of the compass can be restored. The needle which now turns to the North wavers under the equinoctial line; beyond it, however, it tends toward the other pole. I will add this medical point: the "back" of the magnet, just like iron, repels the intestine, cures a **hernia**, and every catarrh of the **nature of Mars** <note>original: "natura Martis"; in alchemy, Mars is the planetary correspondence for iron and masculine, sharp, or inflammatory qualities.</note>; indeed, all forms of magnetism are ordained for the use of man. The power of drawing iron, if it has been "married" to a female "mummy," and then the back of the magnet is applied as a plaster on the thigh and its belly on the loins, safely prevents a threatened miscarriage; but the belly of the magnet on the thigh and the back on the loins wonderfully facilitates childbirth. Our Anatomist <note>Referring to his opponent's logic.</note> will surely illustrate all these things about the magnet with *a priori* reasons and explain the mechanism to us as if it were known to him—otherwise, I shall decree them to be illusions of Satan and not natural effects, using his same argument of ignorance.

I shall now bring forth some examples of similar magnetism, so that we may finally approach the positive reasoning and the refutation of all oppositions with a better-prepared mind. What more should I do? Whatever reasons you have not brought for yourself, I will devise them myself. "Every effect," you will say, "comes either immediately from God the Creator..."

# OF JAN BAPTISTA VAN HELMONT

proceeds from God, and it is a miracle; or from Satan, and it is a prodigy; or from natural and ordinary causes, and then it is natural. But magnetism is neither a miracle nor a natural effect; therefore, it is Satanic. I respond: Although I could show this aforementioned list to be insufficient—insofar as the "inner man" also acts in none of the ways mentioned (which we shall later discuss quite clearly)—nevertheless, I will now skip over the premise and deny the conclusion, specifically the part asserting that the effect is not natural. For that was the very thing that needed to be proven first, so that a *begging of the question* <note>original: "petitio principii"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note> might not be committed. But in this, our Censor was and will remain deficient: to say it is not natural is merely to speak, unless he thinks that speaking and proving are the same thing, or has placed his own authority in the place of reason. For many effects are natural which do not occur ordinarily, namely those happening more rarely. Therefore, for the sake of the Anatomist, I will not only defend the affirmative side everywhere, but I will also explain it with reasons and strengthen it with examples. In this way, the argument just brought forward will collapse under its own weight.

<margin>20.</margin>
There is a book printed at Franeker in the year 1611 by Uldericus Dominicus Balck, concerning the *lamp of life* <note>original: "lampade vitæ"</note>. There you will find, following Paracelsus, the true magnetic cure of many diseases—such as dropsy, gout, jaundice, etc.—by enclosing the warm blood of the sick person in an eggshell and a shell <note>likely a reference to an outer casing or a specific vessel</note>, which is then exposed to be kept warm. If you then give this blood mixed with meat to a hungry dog or a pig, the sickness is soon drawn from you into the dog and departs; just as the leprosy of Naaman migrated into Gehazi by a curse <note>Referencing 2 Kings 5:27.</note>. Will you also judge this to be diabolical—that a neighbor was restored solely by the magnetism of the mummial blood <note>original: "sanguinis mumialis"; here "mummy" refers to the vital balsamic life-force contained in the blood.</note>? Yet they are restored completely and without a doubt.

<margin>21.</margin>
A woman weaning an infant, so that her breasts might dry up more quickly, milks her milk onto glowing coals, and soon the breasts wither. Does Satan perhaps suck them dry?

If someone should defecate at your door, and if you 

<column-break/>

intend to prevent this, pile a fire of iron <note>original: "ignem ferri"; likely meaning a very hot fire or using hot iron tools</note> upon the fresh excrement; soon, through magnetism, the defecator will develop an itchy scab on his buttocks. This happens, namely, by the fire scorching the excrement and driving the sharpness of the burning—as if through a magnetic bridge—into the impudent anus. Perhaps you will call this Satanic, because the end result is an injury. But surely the abuse of powers lies within the freedom of man, yet the use is no less natural.

<margin>22.</margin>
Make a plate out of bismuth, and at one end place a piece of amber; three spans away from there, place green vitriol <note>Iron sulfate.</note>. Soon this vitriol will visibly lose its color and sharpness. Both of these are found in the preparation of amber.

At the very least, this next case will be free of all illusion of Satan. A certain man of Brussels lost his nose in a fight. He went to the surgeon Tagliacozzi, living in Bologna, to have a nose constructed. And since he feared the incision on his own arm, he hired a porter for this purpose, from whose arm he finally had a nose carved out for a price. About thirteen months after his return to his homeland, the grafted nose suddenly grew cold, and a few days later it fell off in a state of rot. By those investigating the cause of this unexpected event, it was found that at the exact moment the nose grew cold, the porter had died. There are eyewitnesses to these things still living in Brussels.

<margin>23.</margin>
Is that not clearly a magnetism of the <term>mummy</term> <note>The vital spirit or essence remaining in organic matter even after separation from the body.</note>, by which the nose—enjoying the right of grafting for so many months with a shared life, sense, and vegetative power—suddenly died across the Alps?

<margin>24.</margin>
I ask you, what is superstitious in this? What is fantastical?

<margin>25.</margin>
The Carline root <note>original: "Radix Carlina"; the Carline thistle.</note> (which is of the Chameleon variety), full of juice and strength, when pulled up and mixed with human mummy as if with a ferment, draws into you the natural strength and vigor from the man whose shadow you press upon <note>referencing an occult belief in capturing a person's vital essence.</note>. But you will call this a deceptive trick because it is a paradox: as if the same leprosy were not transferred from Naaman into Gehazi, and the same jaundice, in number, transplanted into a dog. For a disease is not merely in the category of a "quality"; rather, all categories are present in individual diseases. If...

# ON THE MAGNETIC CURE OF WOUNDS

indeed, it should be permitted to fit names to things, rather than things to names.

<margin>26.</margin> Sun-following flowers <note>original: "Solissequi flores"; likely sunflowers or marigolds.</note> are carried toward the sun by a certain magnetism. This is certainly not because they desire its heat (for on a cloudy and colder day, they still imitate the rhythm of the sun), nor are they followers of the sun merely for its light; for in the dark of night, they turn from the west, where they left the sun, back toward the east. You will not judge this to be diabolical, because another explanation is ready: namely, that there is a harmony between the higher and lower worlds, and a clearly celestial attractive power that is in no way shared with sublunary <note>Meaning "below the moon," referring to the earthly realm in the old Aristotelian view of the universe.</note> things. As if the microcosm <note>The "little world," a common term for a human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>—unworthy of a celestial fate—would notice no revolution of the stars in its own blood or in its *usnea* <note>original: "usnea"; a type of moss, often specifically referring to the moss gathered from the skull of a man who died a violent death, used in sympathetic medicine.</note>.

<margin>27.+</margin> I might speak of love-potions, which require a "mummial" fermentation <note>The "mummy" or *mumia* was believed to be the vital life-force remaining in biological remains after death.</note> so that affection may be drawn toward a specific object. But it is wiser to pass over this, though I will say one thing first. I know a herb found everywhere which, if it is rubbed and warmed in the hand until it grows tepid, and then you hold another person’s hand until it also warms with your heat, that person will immediately burn with love for you for several days. I once held the paw of a certain puppy, and he followed me, a stranger, so closely that he wailed outside my bedroom at night so that I would open the door for him, having completely renounced his former mistress. There are witnesses to this deed of mine in Brussels. For the heat that first warmed the herb—a heat, I say, that was not solitary but stirred by a certain outflow of natural spirits—determines the herb to itself and individualizes it. Having taken up this ferment, it draws the spirit of another through magnetism and subdues it into love.

<margin>28.</margin> I leave aside the cures for many sicknesses which the secret power <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of human blood performs magnetically. For unless blood—indeed, even pus, urine, and the sweat of evaporation—continually took some part of the vital spirit with them, and unless there were in these things a certain participation in the whole while outside the natural body, surely the days of man would not be so short. 

<column-break/>

This, indeed, was the cause of internal calamity.

<margin>29.</margin> Water-pepper <note>original: "Persicaria sive piper aquaticum"</note>, comfrey, flixweed, bistort, adder’s tongue, and many others have this peculiarity: if they are dipped in water while cold (for an oak tree cut while the North Wind blows will become worm-eaten unless it is immediately submerged under water) and allowed to warm up for a little while over a wound or ulcer, and are then buried in a muddy place, as soon as they begin to rot, they also strive to draw out from the sick person whatever is harmful.

And the herbs perform this not while they were growing in the earth, nor even while they remain in their original form (for "the grain must die to bear fruit"), but in the putrefaction of their body. Their virtues, now released as if from the barrier of the body, freely exert their magnetism—which otherwise lay sleeping and hindered—and according to the contagion and impression received from the wounded or ulcerated place, they suck out the remainder of the evil, even from a great distance.

<margin>30.</margin> If anyone, while picking the leaves of the Wild Ginger <note>original: "Asarum"</note>, plucks them upward, they will purge another person—that is, a third person who knows nothing of the plucking—only by vomiting. But if they are twisted while being plucked downward, they will only purge the bowels. Here, at least, no superstition underlies the act. For why should I mention imagination here, since you grant that imagination has no power over a third object, especially when that person <margin>31.</margin> is unaware of the manner in which the picker was acting? Or perhaps you will again blame an "implicit pact" with the devil, that sacred anchor of ignorance? Yet no vain observance lies hidden here, especially when the picker plucks the leaves upward or downward without the person who takes the medicine knowing. Truly, besides Wild Ginger and the tips of the Elderberry tree <note>original: "sambucus"</note>, other purgatives do not have this quality; they act in the same way no matter how they are gathered. But in Wild Ginger, as a whole plant, a magnetic property shines forth, and thus it endows its leaves differently according to the way they are grasped. Not only plants, but almost all created things...

<margin>33.</margin> I knew a noblewoman who, just as one paroxysm of gout <note>original: "podagra"</note> was leaving her, was immediately seized by another. For many months, the gout infested her with unusual recurrences without any relief. She did not know why she suffered such a great and ill-omened relapse of the disease. Finally, she discovered that whenever the heat of the attack subsided and she rose from her bed, if she sat in the chair where her brother—who lived in another city and had also been a gout sufferer—used to sit, the disease would immediately sprout anew. This effect was by no means to be attributed to imagination or anxiety, as both of those occurred long after the effect was felt. Furthermore, if another gout sufferer happened to sit in that chair, no worsening of the disease happened to her. Therefore, the *mumia* <term>mumia: the vital life-force or "balsam" believed to remain in biological matter or objects long-used by a person even after death</term> of her now-deceased brother deservedly rendered that seat suspect of contagion. It moved those flows of illness—which would otherwise have remained quiet—in his sister and in no other gout sufferer, penetrating through all her clothing. It was a **magnetism** toward the uterine <note>Relating to their shared biological/familial origin.</note> *mumia* of the sister, even a long lustrum <note>A period of five years.</note> after his death. Tell me, what "implicit pact with the enemy Satan" is at work here?

<margin>34.</margin> A **sapphire** of a deep blue color, if it touches a plague-boil <note>original: "anthrax"; a carbuncle or lesion characteristic of the bubonic plague.</note> where the pestilence reveals itself, and is rubbed against it for some time, and then removed—the gemstone, though now absent, does not cease to magnetically draw all the poison from the contaminated area, provided the body's strength has not yet been overcome. For this reason (and to our greater faith in magnetism), it is customary to trace a circle around the site of the boil with the sapphire, gradually increasing the size of the circle. This is done so that the exiting poison, which flies out invisibly, does not wander further or infect some noble neighboring part of the body. Indeed, where the poison exhales magnetically from the wasting body—as if drawn through a tube—the entire circle soon turns black and, finally burned into a scab <note>original: "eschara"</note>, it falls away. Meanwhile, the heart is preserved from the deadly contagion. There is no room here for the excuse of saying the poison was drawn in that

<column-break/>

moment when the place was touched by the sapphire, or that the sapphire merely shaped the internal healing at that time, rather than attributing it to the magnetism of the absent gem. Indeed, the sick will testify that they do not perceive relief immediately, but much later, as the venom gradually departs through the magnetic track. Moreover, the site itself will give certain testimony to magnetism: it does not turn black during the drawing of the sapphire, nor through the sapphire's path, but soon after it turns black—burned immediately by the pestilential "aura" <note>An invisible "breath" or vapor.</note> (that is, an arsenic-like vapor) exiting through that path and no other. For where the poison continually exhales, with the venomous rays gathered there into a cone, it is necessary that the site suffer the impact, turn black, and be burned as these things happen over time. They teach us that the poison flows out successively toward the track of the absent gemstone.

You will perhaps reply that every agent requires a certain duration for its impression: that the sapphire did not help in an instant, but left an impression that would gradually overcome the remaining evil, and that the absent gem draws nothing further. Here you should note that every agent of nature acts in an instant, unless there is an obstacle in the "patient" <note>In traditional logic, the "agent" acts and the "patient" receives the action.</note>. In a contaminated body, however, there is no impediment, as the body most quickly demands help and pants for it with every vein.

It would be entirely different if the sapphire had to be prepared, cooked, or altered in the painful spot so that a locked agent could be drawn out from it to then be spread into the body. But since the sapphire remains whole and uncorrupted, it requires only a certain time so that it may couple its influential ray, through the contact of the *mumia*, with the ray of the pestilential aura, by which the absent gem may soon draw it out. I say that for the said coupling—so that the binding of the sapphire's power to the poison may occur—a certain time is required (perhaps one-eighth of an hour) during which the circle is drawn around the boil. For if it were some impression of the sapphire that [acted] gradually within the ven-

Therefore, I ask, what attractive impression does the sapphire leave behind after it is gone, if not a magnetic one? Especially since "attraction" implies an inseparable relationship between the thing drawing and the thing being drawn, and vice-versa.

Indeed, if the sapphire had simply imparted a power from itself into the sick body, after one or two uses it would become weaker (much like the hoof of an elk <note>original: "ungula alcis"; elk hooves were a traditional remedy used to ward off epileptic seizures, believed to lose potency over time</note>, which gradually becomes exhausted as it wards off epileptic attacks). It would lose the faculty it impressed upon the patient—yet this is clearly not the case with the sapphire. For a sapphire is praised as being all the more powerful the more often it has drawn out poison. You might say, perhaps, that the sapphire generated a "quality" in the sick person by which they began to attract and pull out the venom; and although the sapphire is then removed, nature—once set in motion—nevertheless perseveres in the expulsion, following the path where the venom first began to be expelled. First, we must ask: does the sapphire pull by its primary quality (such as heat), or by a formal and magnetic property? For the latter does not require the prior generation of a new quality inside the body, but only the connection of a "drawing power" <note>original: "virtutis tractricis"</note> to perform the pull. Thus, the pulling is done by the absent gemstone. The point is proven: for every natural thing that draws, draws toward itself. Indeed, it draws specifically for this purpose: therefore, a new quality generated *inside* would draw the venom *inward* toward itself, and it would by no means be led *outward* through the pull. Second, did the sapphire perhaps generate a power from itself and impress it only into the skin? Truly, even that cannot be the case; for then it would not be necessary to draw a circle around the carbuncle with the gem; it would be enough to touch any remote and

And could nature not have used its own expulsive power <note>original: "expultrix"; the biological force believed to push waste and toxins out of the body</note> without the touch of the sapphire? If not, then the sapphire does not "attract," but merely strengthens the expulsive power in the patient. The contrary is proven by the fact that the area is not scorched beyond or within the circle, and that developing carbuncles, even if not touched, subside and perish. If the expulsive power alone were strengthened, it would expel the poison in every direction, and not be confined to a specific and chosen spot. Fourth, even before the touch of the sapphire, nature had already shown its strong force in trying to expel the carbuncle. Thus, it is also false that nature, once moved to expel, continues on its own thereafter, since the sapphire otherwise arrived quite late to the beginning of the expulsion. Therefore, however you argue it, it is necessary that the venom is attracted magnetically while the gemstone is absent.

Do you wish for the natural magnetism of the **weapon salve** <note>original: "unguenti armarii"; a famous and controversial 17th-century remedy where an ointment was applied to the weapon that caused a wound, rather than the wound itself, to heal it from a distance</note> to be shown to you more clearly? We judge that to be universally "good" which neither the subject, nor the object, nor the means, nor the intended end would dare to accuse of wickedness. <margin>36.</margin> It has long been the custom for leaders of the Church to wear rings enriched with sapphires, though the use of that gemstone is now almost unknown among them. For to those whom the care of souls is given, it also falls—by law and duty—to stand by those contaminated by the plague. ...earnest study, to be terrified by unjust censures and to shrink back. I have been somewhat long-winded regarding the sapphire because it possesses a power similar to the "weapon salve" <term>unguentum armarium: a controversial medicinal ointment applied to the weapon that caused a wound, rather than the wound itself, believed to heal via magnetic sympathy</term> and shares exactly the same principles.

<margin>37.</margin> Therefore, in this regard, a human being also possesses their own "magnet," which, during a time of pestilence, draws in the poison from contaminated sources from the outside through "insensible transpiration" <note>the process of losing or absorbing fluids/vapors through the skin without visible sweating</note>. For Nature—which is otherwise accustomed to admitting only nourishing juices and skillfully separating them from waste—now succumbs to this magnet of hers, attracts the harmful air, and invites death inside. Against this magnet, there is a contrary magnet (so that this discussion does not prove sterile in any part): namely, the sapphire itself, or even a piece of translucent amber, provided it has first been rubbed over the seven "planetary pulses." These pulses are located in the throat, the wrists, near the ankle bones, and at the "throne of the heart." When worn around the neck in the manner of an amulet <note>original: "periapti vice"</note>, these excel and block the human magnet, serving as the most certain amulets against the dreaded plague <note>original: "diræ luis"</note>. Otherwise, they are entirely ineffective if the rubbing of the pulses has not preceded their use. For the sapphire and amber, which were once just stones, change their "family" through this rubbing; they lose their former names and are henceforth called **zenexton** <term>zenexton: a Paracelsian term for a powerful protective amulet against the plague</term>.

<margin>38.</margin> Will someone judge these things to be diabolical as well, and attribute them to a pact made with the Devil?

It is enough to have brought forward these few, yet sufficient, examples which contain the same principles as the weapon salve. Now, we shall turn ourselves in due time to your arguments.

You accuse Goclenius <note>Rudolph Goclenius (1572–1621), a German professor who defended the weapon salve</note> of being ignorant of Aristotelian doctrine because he suggests that the same "accident" <term>accident: in Aristotelian philosophy, a property or quality (like color or heat) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a "subject" (a physical thing)</term> can migrate from one subject to another. (If only you were as quick at proving your point as you are at refuting others!) Indeed, it is a mark of great stubbornness to think that a scar on a corpse is not the same scar that was on the man yesterday when he was alive. For we would venerate the relics of the saints in vain if only the "impossible matter" of the Aristotelians remained, and if certain accidents—which were once in the living person—did not remain in the corrupted body. Behold, how far this pagan error drives those who recklessly 

<column-break/>

find fault! To think, I say, that something is impossible which is absolutely necessary, is the mark of the deepest ignorance. Consider light: it travels from the sun all the way to the earth, swifter than the blink of an eye, through the smallest atoms of the air, producing new "species" <note>in this context, "species" refers to the visible form or image of a thing transmitted through space</note> of light, and species of those species. To deny this is surely to be blind to the sun itself. For if we did not have the actual light and power of the sun with us, but only the thousandth "species of a species" of that light and power, nothing would grow; nor could fire ever be produced by the refraction or union of rays. Indeed, species of species of light, since they are no more "light" than the species of colors are "colors," would never cause fire. I certainly congratulate myself on my ignorance of such a doctrine, for which Goclenius is accused of being unrefined. Does not a compass needle turn itself toward the pole through glass that has been sealed by a glowing flame (in which no pore can be found)? And is it not drawn toward a nearby piece of iron, while the pole is ignored in the meantime? Therefore, the same "accident" <note>the magnetic quality</note> migrates through the glass, from the magnet into the air, and perhaps reaches the pole itself. <margin>40.</margin> Magnetism, too, is a celestial quality, very similar to astral influences, and is not restricted by distance in space—just like the magnetic salve about which I am disputing.

You laugh because Goclenius gathers the "usnea" <term>usnea: a type of moss or lichen (specifically Usnea cranii humani) that grows on the skulls of those who died violently, highly prized in 17th-century medicine</term> from the skull of a "man of three letters" <note>original: "homo trium literarum"; a Latin idiom for a thief (FUR), who would have been executed by hanging</note>. Nor is there any reason to think there is a "snake in the grass" here, or that the vanity of superstition lies hidden. <margin>41.</margin> For even if a Jesuit, killed by hanging or some other martyrdom, were left to dry out according to the influence and obedience of the stars, his head—being just like the skull of a thief—would produce usnea that is equally useful and to be gathered. For the "seed" of usnea falls from heaven into the "field" of the skull. Sometimes it rains down as a foam, which is called "dawn-dew"; and occasionally a more tenacious slime falls, which is called "star-sperm" <term>sperma siderum: also known as "star jelly," a gelatinous substance found on the ground, historically believed to be deposited by falling stars</term>. At times the sky even rains frogs, spiders, and so on, which upon falling become tangible and vital substances. In some places in the mountains, it rains milk, no less than...

<sig>Bbbb d</sig>
<meta>catchword: than</meta>

<summary>Van Helmont defends the use of amulets like the "zenexton" and the gathering of skull-moss (usnea), arguing that these operate via natural magnetic and celestial influences. He critiques Aristotelian physics, asserting that qualities like magnetism and light can indeed travel between objects without physical contact.</summary>

<margin>42.</margin> ...than blood: quite often, a white and bituminous substance, sent down from the heavens, settles upon stones and bones and becomes **skull moss** <term>usnea: a lichen or moss-like growth, specifically the variety found on the skulls of the dead, which Paracelsian physicians believed contained the vital "mummy" or life-force of the deceased</term>. 
<margin>43.</margin> In some places, this forms a crust upon stones where it turns to stone; in others, it degenerates into moss. To this category belong **dew**, **manna**, **throni**, **thereniabin** <note>original: "thereniabin" — a Persian medicinal manna gathered from shrubs</note>, **star-jelly** <note>original: "nostoch" — a gelatinous algae traditionally believed to be the remains of fallen stars</note>, **nebulgea**, **laudanum**, and similar things. Although these participate more in the substance of the air, the "excretions of the stars" are of a higher lineage than ordinary **skull moss**, 
<margin>44.</margin> and are called "celestial flowers." Many things have been accomplished through them; for since they are enriched with the favor of the heavens and a continuous influence, they do not lack a foundation of extraordinary virtues. Therefore, when the **skull moss** has received its seed from the heavens, but finds its womb and its growth from the **mummified essences** <note>original: "medullis mumialibus" — the vital spiritual residues remaining in the bones of the dead</note> of the human skull—the citadel of the **microcosm** <note>the "small world" or human being, reflecting the "macrocosm" of the universe</note>—it is no wonder if it has obtained astral and magnetic powers that are distinguished and above the common lot of vegetables (though herbs, in their own right, do not lack their own magnetism). 

I shall speak of what I have seen. A certain soldier and nobleman carried a small piece of human **skull moss** that had been healed over <insert>implanted</insert> beneath the skin and flesh of his head. 
<margin>45.</margin> While he was kindly intervening between two brothers who were fighting for their lives, he was struck on the head with a sword and fell to the ground. By this blow, his hat and hair were sliced right down to the skin, as if by a razor; yet he escaped with his skin entirely unhurt. You may judge for yourselves to what cause the protection of the skin should be dedicated. I am not accustomed to torturing my mind with uncertain conjectures: for lightning, though more powerful than a sword, if it strikes a laurel tree, does not shake even a seal <note>original: "vitulum marinum" — literally "sea calf"</note>; nor does it touch a horse whose bit is anointed with seal fat; nor does it strike a stable whose doorposts are greased with such fat. This is trivial experience. Nevertheless, I pass over this and leave this arena to others, though I will first mention a similar example. In the Ardennes, Saint Hubert is venerated, where all who have been bitten by a rabid dog go (just as others flock to the chapels of Saint Domirus and Saint Bellinus). There, a small **tuft of wool** <note>original: "flocculus"</note> from the stole of Saint Hubert is 

<column-break/>

set beneath the skin of the forehead of the person bitten by the rabid animal. From that time forward, they can be harmed by no rabid beast, and the tuft of wool wards off their teeth. 
<margin>46.</margin> You will answer that this is a miracle of God through relics: let it be a miracle. Yet the very tuft of wool shows that God, in His miracles, for the most part goes alongside Nature and observes her customs. For He who can do all things by His word alone also uses means from time to time. Thus, let the sweat on the handkerchief of Saint Paul <note>a reference to Acts 19:12</note> be viewed as a **magnetic ointment**. Indeed, let the sweat of the sick, or even the **insensible effluvium** <note>the invisible vapors or "breath" emitted by the body</note> flowing from them—or the blood of a wounded person placed with a stick inside a jar of ointment—be the means by which the entire harm is immediately drawn magnetically from the sick person. 
<margin>47.</margin> And this occurs more powerfully when that supernatural magnet is of greater efficacy. The principle is the same in both cases, and the method is the same; except that in the material world, it happens through blood and ointment, or physical means; whereas in the supernatural world, it happens through the relics of the friends of God, which are to be greatly venerated for this reason. So that these might become more like a **magnetic ointment**, God, having mercy on us, has caused some relics to incessantly drip a source of oil or balsamic liquor. 
<margin>48.</margin> Supported by this **magnetic remedy** in both cases, we may know for certain that magnetic healing is accepted by God and proceeds in both worlds in a similar order, with equal pace, and under one Leader. This is why recent relics perform more and more frequent miracles when they are moved or touched, etc.; because it is necessary for a magnet to be rubbed and moved if it is to pull anything. 

I return to you, **skull moss** sown from heaven: for he 
<margin>49.</margin> who has recovered from rabies through the tuft of wool and other pious rites is not only left free from the threat of mad dogs in the future; but—what is even more remarkable—he can delay the onset of the poison for another person bitten by a rabid dog for many periods of forty days, until that person can visit Saint Hubert at his own convenience, while the rabid poison remains silent and suspended in the meantime. Nature also gave a relative to this: **Zinzilla** (which is an excretion of the diaphragm 
<margin>50.</margin> turning into an inflammation) kills, when...

<header>JOHN BAPTIST VAN HELMONT</header>

...encircled like a belt <note>The text likely refers to Shingles (Herpes Zoster), which often wraps around the torso like a belt</note>; however, it is cured safely and quickly if the area is externally anointed, even lightly, with the blood of someone who has once suffered from that same disease. Truly, whoever has once recovered from that illness has obtained a balsamic quality in their blood, which ensures they are safe from the same disease in the future; furthermore, it cures the same condition in a neighbor, and by the contact of the blood upon the skin—through the power of **magnetism**—it transplants that blood into a similar healing balsam.

You will say: if the magnetism resides in the **skull moss** <term>usnea: a lichen growing on the skulls of the dead</term>, the remaining ingredients will be in vain. The Physicians respond that some things are primary, others less so; some are for hindering resistances, while others are for exciting the effect, and some promote it by increasing its strength. This, they say, was the necessity of the composition. Therefore, just as it was irrelevant to say: "If the skull moss has magnetism, therefore the human being is eviscerated in vain for the sake of the rest," it would also be absurd to insist: "If the skull moss does not have sufficient magnetism by itself, nor the fat, nor the blood, etc., therefore that magnetic power attributed to the ointment will not be in the whole compound." Since individual parts cannot bring into a composition what they did not previously have in their simple state, I am occasionally forced to take your place and dream up quibbles on your behalf; nevertheless, you ought to have first learned from rustic experiments that a new and unusual quality often emerges in a composition which was not at all apparent in the individual simples beforehand: namely, it was fitting to know that neither **vitriol** <note>iron or copper sulfate</note> nor **gallnuts** <note>growths on oak trees used for making ink</note> are black, yet when joined together, they produce ink.

You will object again: if the skull moss preserves magnetism within itself from the **mummy-like virtue** <note>original: "virtute mumiali" — the vital life-force remaining in dead remains</note> of the bones and the celestial orbit, then it should be collected not only from skulls, but also from the other bones of the skeleton. That too is ridiculous; for nature is also subject to the soil. For instance, fresh pepper planted in Italy <margin>51.</margin> produces only ivy for that reason. **Hellebore** <note>original: "Veratrum"</note> in the region of Trento is robbed of its purging power. And poppies in our land are deprived of their lethal quality, even though our homeland is ten times 

<column-break/>

colder than Thebes itself. Therefore, the skull moss is varied, growing upon the varied "soil" of the bones. For if lightning should melt coins in touched purses, and out of ten companions sitting closely together, it should take away and strike down one from the middle; and this, I say, happens not by chance, but by the permission of Him who willed that not even a leaf fall from a tree unbidden, and by whose help alone all virtues are established; it should not be surprising, then, that one magnetic seed of skull moss should rain down from heaven upon the cranium, and another class of seed upon the rest of the bones. At the very least, the bone of the head is effective against **epilepsy** <note>often called "the falling sickness" in this period</note>, but the other bones are not; finally, the entire brain is consumed and liquefied within the skull, and by the continuous moistening of that liquor (the organ's essence, I mean), the skull acquires other powers which we observe to be absent in other bones.

I know well enough the habits of those who contradict. For when they no longer have any weight to bring against the matter itself, they become more insulting and strike at the man. Wherefore someone will perhaps say: "Magnetism is something new, invented by **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the controversial pioneer of chemical medicine</note> alone; and he was a wicked and ignorant man." Then they add that if such a natural virtue had existed anywhere, it would not have stood hidden for so many centuries, waiting for the arrival of Paracelsus.

I respond regarding the taunts and the scoffs of many directed at a man who is the glory of Germany: they are not worth a nutshell, and the one asserting them makes himself even more unworthy, insofar as he strives to judge not only the living, but the dead as well. For as to what his monuments proclaim concerning his learning, wisdom, and the gifts he attained, there is no reason for me, an unequal praiser, to take up anyone’s eulogy; rather, I weigh the facts themselves. Therefore, the objection is sterile in its pride, which assumes the right to judge not only the living and the dead, but even GOD himself: namely, that He ought not to have poured such a great harmony of nature into Paracelsus, but into someone else (a **Jesuit**, perhaps), and should have revealed it much sooner than the century of **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note>.

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with "atqui" (but yet/nevertheless), which will likely lead into a further rebuttal of the timing of scientific discoveries.</meta>

He also defends Paracelsus against ad hominem attacks, arguing that scientific truths are valid regardless of the person who discovers them or the timing of the discovery.</summary>
