<margin>52.</margin>
But tell me, why did Ignatius <note>St. Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), founder of the Jesuit Order.</note> come so late to establish a society so beneficial to the whole world? Why did it not emerge many centuries earlier? Alas, miserable man, where do you rush in your presumption? Is not God the free giver of His own benefits? Does He not find pleasure in His unmerited gifts? He has provided a whetstone by which we may judge persons: namely, that we shall know them by their works. What the works of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a pioneering and controversial Swiss physician and alchemist.</note> are—and how they are greater than all expectation of nature and the biting tongues of critics—is sufficiently declared, even to his unwilling enemies, by the epitaph placed at his well-deserved tomb by the Most Illustrious and Reverend Prince-Bishop of Salzburg.

# THE EPITAPH OF PARACELSUS,
### which is seen inscribed on stone at the Hospital of Saint Sebastian by the church wall in Salzburg.

> *Here is buried Philip Theophrastus, distinguished Doctor of Medicine, who by wonderful art removed those dire wounds, leprosy, gout, dropsy, and other incurable contagions of the body; and honored his goods by distributing and allocating them to the poor. In the year 1541, on the 24th day of September, he exchanged life for death.*

<margin>53.</margin>
Therefore, Paracelsus is so far from being undeserving because he brought to light a **magnetism** unknown to the ancients, and because in place of the natural studies taught everywhere in schools as sterile theory, he brought another real study—provable by hand through the analysis and synthesis <term>chemical breakdown and recombination</term> of bodies—which is far more fruitful. Indeed, he has by just title snatched the name of "Monarch of Secrets" from all his predecessors, unless we, as ignorant judges, join with his haters to disparage all his good deeds and things gathered for good use. I am a man of this sort: I look with disdain upon whatever earns belief solely through custom. For there is nothing that involves us in greater darkness than the fact that we adapt ourselves to custom, credulously nodding along to rumors and dreams. We must instead go toward freedom; we must enjoy the gifts of judgment, not be enslaved by them.

<column-break/>

You will object: that in sublunary <note>Referring to the earthly realm below the moon.</note> things there is no influential force equal to celestial impressions. But if you stumble here, you rebuke all those who philosophize correctly, who have rightly noted that the "higher motion" exists in the "lower things" in a lower manner, and that an analogy of the lower exists in the higher <note>This refers to the famous Hermetic maxim: "As above, so below."</note>. Do not plants, animals, and the sick man sense and foretell future changes in the weather? Does not the frog, the deeper it digs its lodging for the coming winter, signal that a more monstrous winter is to be expected? From this, indeed, come the meteorological omens—not because these things happen by a premature motion of the heavens that is yet to come, as if the heavens cause that prophetic sensation in earthly things before they even arrive. Far from it. For the firmament only announces future things; it does <margin>54.</margin> not cause them. Truly, within each created thing there is its own "heaven" and its own "heavenly rotation," depending on the being of its seed. In the spirit of that seed—which contains the engraving of the universe—is its own heaven and its own rising stars. Do not think we are trying to destroy Astrology; rather, we are illuminating it. Since each individual thing contains its own heaven, it also contains a **syzygy** <term>alignment or conjunction</term> of heavens. However, because the motion of the Great Heavens is the most known and common, it directs the "particular heavens" (as I will call them for lack of a better word) according to itself. <margin>56.</margin> This is surely the cause of every natural inclination. And when a creature, persuaded by its own internal heaven, wanders away from that motion of the Great Heaven (which is the common norm), <margin>57.</margin> sickness and defect immediately follow. For <margin>58.</margin> a sheep without a leader wanders uncertainly; this is why the sick sense storms and future changes of weather, <margin>59.</margin> while the healthy do not. For if the sea flowed and ebbed only by the guidance of the celestial Moon—that is, by fire-divination <note>original: "pyromantiæ"</note> alone—and not by its own "Moon" of water-governance <note>original: "hydromantiæ"</note>; and if the winds <margin>60.</margin> were stirred up only by the guidance of the celestial Mercury, and not by their own "star of the chaos" <note>original: "astri chaomantici"; in Paracelsian terms, "chaos" refers to the element of Air.</note>, then surely there would be no local provincial winds anywhere, and the same wind would blow through the whole world (since there is only one Mercury and one Moon in the heavens).

<summary>Van Helmont defends Paracelsus as the "Monarch of Secrets," citing his epitaph in Salzburg as proof of his healing powers. He argues that every living thing contains an internal "microcosmic" heaven that interacts with the celestial bodies, explaining how animals and the sick can sense weather changes.</summary>

<header>JOAN. BAPT. HELMONT.</header>

...the wind and the sea would flow everywhere, if not at the same time: at least in the same rhythm, which modern navigation disproves. It is enough, therefore, to have shown here in passing that a celestial and **vital impulsive nature** <note>original: *enormonticam*. A term coined by Van Helmont from the Greek *enormon* to describe the internal power of motion and life within a being.</note> is inherent in things themselves, which nevertheless rouses and regulates itself to the rhythm of the higher motion, so long as it does not wish to be considered stubborn. The Firmament also does not cause future events except <margin>61.</margin> remotely, and that only through the first qualities, acting in the place of some cook: otherwise it would abundantly <margin>62.</margin> declare the works of God’s hands. But the things themselves contain within their **seminal being** <term>ente seminali: the internal spiritual blueprint or "seed" of a substance</term> a particular firmament, by reason of which higher things symbolize with the lower, by the law of friendship and **self-preservation** <note>original: *philautiæ*, literally "self-love," referring here to the natural instinct of a substance to maintain its own existence.</note>: from which we may at least now gather that magnetism and influential forces are everywhere implanted and proper to things: whoever excludes these from sublunary <note>Earthly things existing below the sphere of the moon.</note> things seeks a vain refuge.

You will insist that we must approach more closely, and that it is not yet sufficiently established that there is a quality in sublunary things that rivals the heavens—indeed, such a quality that flows into a far distant and absent object; which is, however, presupposed in the **weapon salve** <term>unguento armorum: a sympathetic ointment applied to the weapon that caused a wound rather than the wound itself</term>: and therefore, that magnetism is indeed a celestial power, but by no means to be attributed to sublunary things, and much less to the fabricated weapon salve. But what else is it (I ask) than to deny magnetism, while being outside or beyond magnetism? For if we universally call every sublunary influence upon another "magnetism," and call that occult adaptation by which the absent acts upon the absent through influence—whether it happens by drawing or by impelling—magnetism for lack of a better term; certainly, whoever denies the influential power of sublunary things upon each other, and demands a counter-instance, seeks an absurdity—namely, magnetism outside of magnetism—and knows not what he denies or asks.

Indeed, I have brought forth examples of the fact in sublunary things, and many instances, such as those concerning the **grafted nose** <note>A famous medical story of the time where a person received a nose graft from a donor; when the donor died, the graft supposedly rotted away simultaneously.</note>, the sapphire,

<column-break/>

smartweed, asarabacca, and many herbs. But you deny them (I know well, because you are ignorant) or you will assert that they do not happen that way, or that they occur by the help of the devil (which is the readier excuse). It is not the custom of physicists to dispute with naked authorities: those who struggle with us must go to the hands—that is, to experience. Investigate, therefore, and prove us liars; otherwise, at least believe: therefore, it is a mark of insolent petulance to deny a fact that is everywhere commonplace because, forsooth, one has not investigated it, nor striven to investigate it: and much more insolent to attribute indifferently to a demon what is everywhere harmonious with nature, as will soon be taught: and that for only one fault: because, forsooth, the "mode" of it cannot be understood through its cause by our **Censor** <note>Likely the Jesuit Jean Roberti, who had published attacks against the weapon salve and Van Helmont's theories.</note>: by a Censor who, by the sharpness of his own understanding and the study of Aristotelian physics, presumes he has surveyed the scope of all nature from every side: by a Censor, I say, who even if he detects nothing superstitious in the ointment, and nothing illicit; yet because of the mode of application, which seems paradoxical to him, damns it as wicked, execrates it, and asserts it contains some kind of diabolical element. But why, I ask? Because, forsooth, a bloody sword or stake is smeared with **mummy-based** <note>original: *mumiali*. In early modern medicine, "mummy" referred to preparations made from preserved human remains, believed to hold magnetic life-force.</note> and magnetic ointment: because he does not know how to maintain the harmony of blood once it has been drawn out with that which is still cherished in the veins: and because he does not believe the action of the ointment can be extended to a far-distant object. But return to yourself: for you will soon understand these things, and believe them, unless you remain stubborn, for now for your sake we will bring the action of magnetism in sublunary things back to the light.

For truly, beyond that class of things and herbs which you undeservedly suspect, I will now show that there is an influence of certain things upon each other, and that it is maintained between distant objects. <margin>63.</margin> A vine that is in flower disturbs wine far away. You will excuse this by saying the same change occurs by the impulse of the heavens: but it is proved that this is not so; for if the heaven caused the flowers in the vine and the turbulence of the wines in the casks, it would be necessary that both occur every single year...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that magnetism is a natural property of earthly matter, not just the heavens, and defends the weapon salve against critics who label it "diabolical." He uses the example of flowering vines affecting wine in barrels as proof of natural "action at a distance."</summary>

--- Page 810 ---
<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's argument that things possess an internal "vital nature" that governs their actions, rather than being simple puppets of the stars. He uses the fermentation of wine and the behavior of magnets to prove that objects have an internal "sense" or "spirit" that directs them.</meta>

# ON THE CURE OF GREAT WOUNDS.

...[natural] forces <note>original: "lis", the conclusion of a word from the previous page, likely "naturalis" or "vitalis".</note> occur at a fixed and defined moment, as it were: which is false. For the vine blooms, and the wine is disturbed <note>Fermentation or "souring" often happened in storage when the vines in the field began to bloom, a phenomenon Van Helmont attributes to a sympathetic bond.</note> before the solstice, and in the same region in another year, long after. Yet, except for a few minutes, the sun and the fixed stars return to the same point every year; therefore, the vine should bloom and the wines be disturbed always at the same time. But if you look for a loophole and say that other planets besides the sun are the cause of this—which do not have the same position at the solstice every year—then at the very least, as the motion of the heavens is most universal, almost all vineyards everywhere would bloom at the same time in the same year: which is false. For just as an **astral nature** underlies the soil, so too a **particular nature** <term>nature particularis: an internal, individual spirit or "Archeus" that governs a specific plant or object</term> is within the vine. This nature, by itself (just as the power of germinating is given to the earth by itself), brings forth the flower, fruit, and seed, and adjusts and moves itself to the rhythm of the most general motion of the heavens. Furthermore, they assert that wines are in no way disturbed in regions where no vines grow; therefore, it is the flower of the vine, and not the motion of the heavens, that disturbs the wine—and it does so from many miles away. Moreover, this effect is more powerful the closer the wines are to the vine.

<margin>64.</margin>
I congratulate public studies and favor the man who knows how **common antimony** <note>original: "antimonium vulgare". A metalloid used extensively in Paracelsian medicine. Van Helmont suggests it has a natural sensitivity to celestial influences during its chemical preparation.</note>, during its preparation, continually directs itself toward the [celestial] influence.

<margin>65.</margin>
I wish to measure the completed measure: therefore I shall have sufficiently proved an influential power, not subject to the distances of place and familiar to sublunary <note>Earthly</note> things. I will prove this even more forcefully in favor of **magnetism** if I teach that the magnet directs itself toward the pole of its own accord, and is by no means "pulled" by the pole. Indeed, one magnet declines from the pole by three degrees, another by six, seven, or eleven; but none (that I know of) marks the pole in a perfectly straight line. Therefore, if the magnet were being pulled, either by the pole or by something near the pole, it would be plucked toward it; but it is not pulled by the pole itself, because whatever pulls, pulls toward itself in a straight line, and not along a diagonal or oblique path. Therefore, if the magnet were pulled by the pole, it would point

<column-break/>

directly to the pole. Thus, magnets—at least those I have seen so far—are not pulled by the pole, nor even by anything nearby. For since that celestial point never rests but is carried incessantly in a circle, if it were pulling the magnet, it would make the magnet restless as well. It would pluck it now a few degrees toward the east, soon as many toward the west, and now upward toward the zenith or downward: which is false. Therefore, the magnet is not pulled, but is carried of its own accord. As for the fact that a magnet might otherwise be carried upward toward the zenith by itself, there is a certain instrument invented by **William Gilbert** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), the English physician who first proposed that the Earth itself is a giant magnet.</note>. The glory of this discovery was recently attempted to be seized for himself by **Ludovicus Fonseca** <note>Possibly a reference to a contemporary claimant or a Jesuit critic of Gilbert's work.</note> at the court of his Catholic Majesty. This instrument, I say, shows the altitude of the pole in every location by a spontaneous elevation within a suspended bronze ring, rather than just the side of the pole.

You will fight for the pole, looking for a path of escape, by saying that the pole indeed pulls the magnet, but according to the various and specific material dispositions of different magnets, it pulls them not straight to itself (which is the nature and "will" of a pulling force) but to a nearby place. This is like saying: "The pole indeed pulls the magnet straight to itself, yet the magnet is not pulled straight to the pole because of some unknown impediment (which you call its 'certain disposition') existing within the magnet, which resists the pole's pull and is more powerful and superior to it"—even though the pull reaches the magnet safely from so many thousands of miles away. Do you see how much you are devoted to escaping the truth? Although you refuse to admit it, you unwillingly assert that there is a **certain motive disposition** dwelling within the magnet (you call it "certain," though it is a fiction to you and uncertain to everyone else) that exists beyond and above the pull of the pole. This is the same as saying that a **directing virtue** exists within the magnet toward some distinct place, rather than it being pulled by the pole.

You will kick back in favor of something near the pole, saying that the magnet is pulled rather than directing...

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s argument regarding the internal "sensation" of objects. # JOHN BAPTIST VAN HELMONT.

...to be drawn not from some single point, but from a whole circle near the pole. I respond that this is a far-fetched excuse; for that circle would have a width of at least eight degrees—ranging from three to eleven degrees—because I have seen magnets with such variation. Therefore, if the power of drawing resided in the entire circle, the same magnet would continually vary; it would deflect now at three, then at eight or eleven degrees from the pole in the same hour, which is false. Therefore, at least in a circle of such width, there would be different orbits, each of which would attract its own magnet. Once this is granted, you fall back into the same pit: namely, that there is a certain disposition in the magnet as to why it is stirred by this orbit rather than another. Consequently, even with these arbitrary fictions, the moving power is nonetheless within the magnet itself.

<margin>66.</margin> It is still not enough to say the pole attracts the magnet; this would happen either because of the elemental and material temperament of the stone, or because of its form. Yet, glass that has been thoroughly washed and cleaned by many rubbings—in which the **mastery of the magnet** <term>magisterium magnetis: an alchemical preparation where the "essence" or "virtue" of a substance is extracted and concentrated</term> was prepared—afterwards observes its own poles. This is because of an "impression" communicated to the glass without any bodily remains. Likewise, steel, after being touched by a magnet and then thoroughly washed and wiped, nonetheless marks the pole. Since these two (glass and steel) have neither an equal temperament nor the same form as the magnet or each other, they demonstrate that the pole does not pull magnets for either of those reasons.

<margin>67.</margin> You might say that by rubbing, a "participation" of the magnet occurred in the pores of the steel or the joints of the glass. A wretched excuse! For fir resin coagulates by itself into the hardness of a stone, and it then attracts iron just like a magnet. Here, at least, the fictional "participation" of a magnet fails.

<margin>68.</margin> A magnet ignores the pole simply by being rubbed with garlic, even while its form, matter, and properties remain preserved. This is because that **spiritual sensation** <note>Van Helmont posits that even "inanimate" matter possesses a rudimentary form of perception or "sensation" that guides its natural functions.</note> in the

<column-break/>

magnet falls asleep because of the garlic. We have already shown this sensation to be the sole cause of the action of formal properties. Surely the pull of the pole would be weak if it could pass through so many celestial spheres, the vast region of the air, through roofs and walls, yet could not penetrate mere garlic juice (or the soot of mercury), while the material root and the unique form of the stone remain the same.

A floating magnet is carried with a certain part toward the North <note>original: "Boream"</note> and another toward the South <note>original: "austrum"</note>. Therefore, if this happened because of a pulling pole, the entire northern side of the stone would always be led by the North Pole. This is false. For if iron touches the northern side, it will not incline toward the North according to its property, but toward the South, even if the dust of the stone sticks to the iron. But if the iron touches the southern side, it turns toward the North. Likewise, the part of the magnet that always inclined toward the North tends toward the South once it passes the equinoctial line <note>The equator.</note>.

One moment more. If a magnet floating in a bowl on a quiet pond is violently turned with its northern part toward the South, the northern side immediately seeks the North <note>original: "Aquilonem"</note> again, as if by a forceful drive. Therefore, if the magnet were being plucked toward the pole by the pole itself, and it were not a spontaneous direction of the stone, then by that same pull, the entire bowl would necessarily fluctuate and be drawn to the northern shore. This is false; for once the direction of the northern side is acquired, the magnet and the bowl stand motionless upon the water. There is, therefore, in the magnet an **influential virtue** <term>virtus influentialis: a power that acts at a distance through a radiating influence rather than physical contact</term> which, without regard for the proximity of the object, is freely carried all the way to the pole in the manner of celestial things. This is a spontaneous radiation of the magnet toward the pole. Thus, if a single natural power has now been found in sublunary things <margin>69.</margin> that radiates toward a very distant object (as in the magnet), it must by no means be ascribed to Satan. It will also be sufficiently proven that many similar powers can be entirely natural, as in the examples provided and the **weapon salve** <note>original: "unguento armario"; a controversial sympathetic ointment believed to heal a wound by being applied to the weapon that caused it.</note>.

And so the magnet, or iron touched by a magnet, since it [turns] toward the pole of its own accord...

# ON THE MAGNETIC CURE OF WOUNDS.

...turn, a certain quality is necessarily extended from the magnet to the pole. Because we know this happens without any physical shedding of particles, we therefore call this quality "spiritual." In this, we disagree with our Theologian, who distinguishes "spirit" as something entirely supernatural and contrary to all physical nature. Physicians, however, use the term merely to contrast it with the denser structure of the body. In this way, we say that the light of the sun, the influence of the heavens, the shock of the torpedo fish, the gaze of the basilisk, and so on, are plainly spiritual qualities. This is because they are not dispersed across a distance through the sharing of a physical evaporation, but are radiated from the subject to the appropriate object by means of an imperceptible light.

These points having been supposed and proven, it is clear enough that while the Theologian still does not understand Goclenius, he has nonetheless criticized him, often without merit. First, he complains that Goclenius would "stable" a spiritual quality within a physical ointment. Second, that this quality is carried to its intended object like a radial light, or by means of a vehicle of traction. Third, that these qualities are carried to a distant and destined object by a certain sensation of the "World Spirit" <note>original: *spiritus mundanus*, a concept in Hermetic philosophy of a universal life force connecting all things</note> (which is the cause of all sympathy). The Theologian interprets this spirit as an evil demon <note>original: *cacodæmonem*</note> by his own law, though I know not by what right. For it is a purer and vital breath of the ether, which sustains the sun and the titanic stars from within; as the poet says, "a spirit within sustains, and mind, infused through all the limbs, moves the whole mass." <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.726–7), often used by early modern scientists to describe the "World Soul."</note> Thus, it governs the world through a certain communion and a conspiracy <note>In the sense of "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation.</note> of parts and powers, according to the consensus of all who philosophize rightly. For 

<margin>70.</margin> example, sun-following flowers feel the sun's path, and the sea marks the stations of the moon. In short, every creature—through life (let us adore the King for whom all things live), essence, existence, and sensation—bears witness to the majesty, generosity, and presence of the Creator. Therefore, our Censor deserves to be refuted, because he has criticized a physician writing in a philosophical style with an altogether intolerable boldness before he even understood him. Indeed, it has always been difficult to maintain a moderate path in all things.

You ask: what is "drawn" from the wounded person? And how does this traction happen through a salve that is absent? I might respond, not unfairly: when you show us why the magnet draws iron and turns itself toward the pole, then I will show you how <term>mumia</term> <note>In Helmontian medicine, *mumia* refers to the vital balsamic force or "spirit of life" contained within the body's tissues.</note> might heal another touched *mumia* by means of *mumia*. But because we have been substituted to repair Goclenius’s insufficiency in this area, we shall soon show by a didactic analogy how the magnetic traction of the salve occurs—provided I have satisfied you as to what is being drawn. It must be noted, therefore, in a 

<column-break/>

wound, that there is not only a "breach of continuity" <note>original: *solutionem continui*, a standard medical term for a physical cut or break in the tissue</note>; but at the same time, a "foreign quality" is introduced. From this, the "lips" of the wound, being provoked, soon seethe and form abscesses; indeed, the whole body is then buffeted by fevers and a variety of symptomatic syndromes. For in this way, an egg whose shell is damaged even slightly will rot, where otherwise it could have been preserved.

<margin>71.</margin> Therefore, the **magnetism** of this salve draws that foreign disposition out of the wound. Thus the lips of the wound, no longer weighed down by any accidental infection, are without pain and soon hasten to grow back together, hindered by nothing. Nature itself is the healer of the wound; the physician is only its servant. A medicine does not "create flesh" in a wound; it does enough if it removes the obstacles. The "Weapon Salve" <note>original: *armorum unguentum*, a controversial remedy of the era applied to the weapon that caused a wound rather than to the wound itself, based on the principle of sympathy.</note> alone keeps these obstacles away securely and abundantly.

You will object: why should the salve attract that aforementioned foreign quality rather than the natural strength and the power of the veins? And since the blood in the salve is healthy, should it not rather impart health to the wounded man, instead of taking on his illness? (Just as has been written regarding the Carline Thistle). I respond: there are different types of magnetisms. Some draw iron, some straw, some lead; some draw flesh, pus, etc. Indeed, the grace of some substances is such that they extract only a pestilential aura.

JAN BAPTIST VAN HELMONT

Indeed, if you join the effect of the healing found in our ointment with your own argument, your own weapon will wound you. From this, since the effect of the ointment is to heal perfectly, briefly, without pain, expense, danger, or loss of strength—it is clear, I say, that the magnetic power within the ointment exists 
<margin>72.</margin>
naturally from God, and not from Satan. For if he were the co-operator in the said healing (as you assert), it would be imperfect, accompanied by a loss of strength, weakness, loss of life, a difficult recovery, or a relapse into some greater misfortune or physical ailment. Just as these traits are tied to diabolical cures, they are entirely absent from the cure of our ointment. All those who have ever been healed by this ointment will testify for us. Satan is never a truth-teller; he never gives good advice except to deceive; indeed, he does not persist in the truth for long. For always, if that enemy brings any bit of good, he mixes in a little more evil. Surely he would observe this same law in this ointment according to his custom, if he were its author or promoter. At the very least, this remedy would fail when a 
<margin>73.</margin>
wounded man is called back, as if from the underworld, who otherwise—stained by mortal sin—would soon lose his life along with his blood through a dangerous wound. You would have to say then that Satan perhaps took pity on our man; or that, having already acquired a right over such a wounded person, he himself put that soul at risk by healing him through the magnetic ointment, when he would rather he perish. Perhaps you think Satan has now become a narrow observer of words and pacts among you, and is no longer a shifter of shapes, a fraud, an impostor, and a total liar. Furthermore, we deny your supposition that blood outside the veins is perfectly healthy; rather, it is already deprived of common life and has entered the beginnings of some corruption. It retains at least a mummial life <note>original: *vitam mumialem*; in Paracelsian philosophy, this is a vital force that remains in a body part or fluid after it has been separated from the body</note>. This is evidenced by putrid blood, which nevertheless remains magnetic within an egg. I pass over, therefore, the absurdity of the objection: that he dares to twist the magnet of the ointment to his own whim, and not toward the purpose for which it was given by GOD.

<column-break/>

### *Positive reasons for magnetism more closely derived through metaphysics and magic.*

It is now time to reveal the immediate cause of magnetism in the ointment. First, by the consensus of the mystical Theologians, we divide man into the external and the internal, assigning to each certain powers of the mind. Thus, 
<margin>74.</margin>
will belongs to the flesh and blood, which is neither the will of the man <note>the rational spirit</note> nor the will of God; and the heavenly father also reveals certain things to the inner man, while the flesh and blood—that is, the external and animal man <note>original: *homo animalis*; refers to the soul governed by physical senses and instincts</note>—reveals others. For how could the service of idols, envy, etc., be rightly numbered among the works of the flesh (since they consist only in the imagination) if the flesh did not also have its own imagination and elective will?
Furthermore, it is confessed that there are miraculous ecstasies belonging to the inner man. That there are also ecstasies in the animal man, on account of intense imagination, is beyond doubt. Indeed, Martin Delrio <note>a Jesuit priest and famous scholar of magic and witchcraft</note>, a priest of the Society of Jesus, admits in his investigations that a certain boy in the city of Lille was led by such violent thought—driven by the same burning 
<margin>75.</margin>
desire to see his parent—that he was snatched away as if by ecstasy, visited her many miles away, and upon returning to himself, remembered everything he had seen and gave many signs to his parent of his true presence.
More similar things occur daily, which I omit for the sake of brevity. It is certain, however, that this was the desire of the external man—that is, of the blood and the animal nature. For the soul, otherwise once untied from the body, is never reunited except by a miracle. Therefore, 
<margin>76.</margin>
there is in the blood a certain ecstatic power <note>original: *potestas ecstatica*</note> which, if ever it is excited by a burning desire, acts by leading out the spirit of the external man even to some distant object. That power, however, lies hidden in the external man, as if in potential; it is not brought into action unless it is excited by a kindled imagination...

...not by burning desire, or by any equal art.
<margin>77.</margin> Furthermore, when blood is corrupted in some way, then all its powers—which were previously in potential—are spontaneously brought into action without a prior excitation of the imagination. For by the corruption of a grain of seed, the seminal virtue, otherwise sluggish and sterile, <margin>78.</margin> breaks out into action. Since the essences of things and their vital spirits do not know how to rot, they emerge safe when the lower harmony of the body is dissolved. Hence indeed, every <term>occult property</term> <note>Hidden or "secret" quality not observable by the five senses.</note>, once the structure of the body is dissolved through previous digestions (which we call <margin>79.</margin> putrefactions), comes to hand free, unhindered, and manifest in action. 

Therefore, when a wound has admitted an adverse quality through the entry of air—from which the blood soon seethes in the lips of the wound and otherwise becomes purulent—it happens that the blood in a fresh wound <margin>80.</margin> already begins some initial stages of corruption because of said "exotic" quality. This blood is then taken up on a wooden stick and smeared with the magnetic ointment. Through this beginning of corruption, the <term>ecstatic power</term> <note>A "standing out" or externalized force that allows a substance to act at a distance.</note> in the blood, which was latent in potential, is led into action. Because this power is drawn back toward its own body by reason of this latent "ecstasy," this specific blood maintains a relationship with the blood of its whole individual person. Then, truly, the magnet in the ointment strives to work; and by means of this ecstatic power (I use this term for lack of a better one), it sucks out the harm from the lips of the wound. Finally, through the <term>mummy-like virtue</term> <note>original: "virtute mumiali"; refers to *Mumia*, the vital medicinal essence found in human remains or blood.</note>, which is balsamic and attractive, the magnetism in the ointment is perfected.

Behold, you now have the positive reason for the natural magnetism in the ointment, drawn from *natural magic*, to which the light of truth assents. <margin>81.</margin> *"Where the treasure is, there the heart is also,"* <note>original: "Ubi theſaurus, ibidem cor"; quoting Matthew 6:21.</note> it says. For if the *treasure* is in heaven, then the *heart*—that is, the spirit of the inner man—is in GOD (who is paradise, who alone is eternal life). But if the *treasure* is fixed in fleeting things, then also the *heart* and spirit of the external man is in fleeting things. There is no reason to bring in a mystical sense here, by taking merely "thought" and

<column-break/>

bare desire for the "heart" instead of the spirit. For that would contain a frivolous meaning: that wherever a man places his treasure by his thought, there his thought would be. Truth itself does not interpret this text mystically, but shows by an added example the real and local presence of *eagles at the carcass* <note>Referring to Matthew 24:28: "Wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered together."</note>. So also the spirit of the internal man is locally in the *kingdom of God* within us, which is God himself; and the *animal heart* or spirit of man is locally around the *treasure*. 

Is it any wonder, then, if the <term>astral spirits</term> <margin>82.</margin> <note>The subtle, "star-like" body that survives for a time after death in Paracelsian philosophy.</note> of animal-like men still show themselves wandering around buried treasure after death? To this phenomenon, the entire <margin>83.</margin> *necromancy* of the ancients surrendered itself. I say, therefore, that the external man is an *animal*, using the reason and will of the blood; meanwhile, however, he is not merely an *animal*, but the true *image of God*. Let the logicians see, therefore, how defectively they define man by the power of *reasoning* alone. More on these things elsewhere.

I will add, therefore, the *magnetism of eagles to carcasses*. For birds are not of such sharp scent that they would travel from *Italy* into *Africa* for carcasses. Nor is scent spread so far and wide; for the vast width of the intervening sea stands in the way, as does a certain elemental property of consumption. Nor should you judge by sight that these birds perceive carcasses from so far away, especially if they lie behind a mountain to the south. But what need is there to press the *magnetism* of birds with more arguments, if God himself—the beginning and end of *philosophy*—expressly establishes the same process of the heart and treasure with the birds and the carcass, and vice versa? For if *eagles* <margin>84.</margin> were led to the food of *carcasses* by the same appetite by which four-footed beasts are led to *pastures*, surely He would have said in one word that *animals* flock to *food*, just as the heart of man to his treasure—which would contain a falsehood. For the heart of man does not go to the treasure to be satiated by it, as *animals* go to *food*. Therefore, the comparison of the human heart and the *eagle* is not about the end goal...

From the former of these suppositions, I conclude: if <term>Satan</term> <note>original: "Satanas."</note> could kill a man guilty of <term>mortal sin</term> <note>original: "peccati mortalis." Therefore, there is a certain power in the witch for this act which is not in Satan; and consequently, Satan is not the principal "efficient cause" or the executor of that homicide. For otherwise, if he were the executor, he would have no need for the witch as a co-helper; instead, he would have quickly removed the greater part of mankind by himself. Surely the condition of mortals would be most miserable if they were subject to such a tyrant and stood vulnerable to his command! Do we not have a God who is too faithful to have subjected the work of His own hands to the whim of Satan? Therefore, in this matter, there is 
<margin>88.</margin> some power clearly proper and natural to the witch which does not belong to Satan. Furthermore, we must weigh more exactly what kind of power this is, how great it is, and of what nature. It is clear first of all that it is not the bodily strength of males; for no forceful physical touch occurs, and these 
<margin>89.</margin> <term>evil-doing women</term> <note>original: "anus maleficae." Literally "wicked old women," a common stereotype in 17th-century witchcraft treatises.</note> are usually weak and exhausted. Therefore, there must be another power, far superior to bodily mass, which is natural to a human being. This power, therefore, had to be placed in that part by which we most closely reflect the Image of God.

<column-break/>

And although all things also reflect that venerable likeness to some extent, yet because man does so most elegantly, most properly, and most 
<margin>90.</margin> closely, therefore the **Image of God** in man prevails, dominates, and commands the "likenesses of God" in other creatures. For perhaps by this prerogative, 
<margin>91.</margin> all things have been placed under his feet. Therefore, if God acts by a nod <note>original: "nutum." This implies a command of the will without physical effort.</note> or by a word, it was fitting for man—if he is truly to be called His image—to perform certain things by a mere nod. Indeed, this is not a new idea, nor is it unsettling, nor is it exclusive to God alone. For Satan, the most dejected of creatures, also moves bodies from place to place by a mere nod, since he has no limbs with which to touch or move them, nor can he seize a new body for himself. This privilege, therefore, ought to belong no less to the internal man, insofar 
<margin>92.</margin> as he is spirit, if he is to represent God—and certainly not as an idle image. If we call this faculty "magical," and you, being poorly instructed, are terrified by this word, you may call it "spiritual strength" for all I care. Indeed, 
<margin>93.</margin> we are not concerned with names; I always look as closely as possible at the thing itself. Therefore, 
<margin>94.</margin> this "magical" power is in the inner man—whether by this term you understand the **soul** <note>original: "animam."</note> or his **vital spirit** <note>original: "spiritum vitalem." For Van Helmont, the vital spirit is the intermediary between the soul and the physical body.</note> is all the same to us now. Since there is a certain proportion between the inner and outer man in all things, there is an appropriate disposition and a proportionate property flourishing in its own way. For this reason, it is necessary for this power to be dispersed through the whole man: more vigorous in the soul, but 
<margin>95.</margin> far more lowly in the flesh and blood. The vital spirit in the flesh and blood performs the role of the soul; that is, in the outer man, it is the same spirit which, in the seed, knows the entire shape of the man—that proud construction and perfect outline—and the ends of the things to be done, because it contains them. This spirit acts as the presiding governor that accompanies the 
<margin>96.</margin> <term>fetus</term> <note>original: "foetum."</note> once it is established, all the way to the end of its life. And although it departs with the soul, at least a tiny portion of it remains in a corpse that was killed by violence, as if...

...which remains perfectly fermented in the same. However, in a corpse that has died naturally and by a failing of nature, both the inborn spirit and the influential spirit have departed together. <margin>97.</margin> For this reason, physicians divide this spirit into the "inborn"—or <term>mummial</term> <note>original: "mumialem." In Paracelsian medicine, "mumia" refers to the vital force or "balsam" that remains in a body after death.</note>—and the "influential," which departs with the previous life. They further subdivide this into the natural, vital, and animal spirits; here, we encompass all of them under a single term. Therefore, the soul, being entirely spirit, could by no means move the vital spirit (which is corporeal <margin>98.</margin> indeed) and much less move or stir the flesh and bones, unless some natural—yet magical and spiritual—force descended from the soul into the spirit and the body. Tell me, in what way would the corporeal spirit obey the command of the soul, unless that command were to move the spirit, and then the body? But immediately, you will object against this "magical mover," saying that it exists within its own natural dwelling; therefore, even if we call it "magical," it would only be a distortion and abuse of the name, since true and superstitious magic does not take its foundation from the soul, as the soul is powerless to move, alter, or stir anything outside its own body. I respond: that power and natural magic of the soul, which acts outside itself by virtue of the image of God, now lies obscured in man and, as it were, sleeps since the <term>Fall</term> <note>original: "praevaricationem," referring to the transgression of Adam in Eden.</note>, in need of awakening (all of which we will soon prove in its proper place). Although this same power remains in us daily as something drowsy or even "drunk," it is still sufficient <margin>99.</margin> to perform its duties within its own body. Thus, the magical knowledge and power—the actor that works by a mere nod—sleeps in man ever since the "knowledge of the apple" was eaten. As long as this knowledge (which belongs to the flesh, blood, the outer man, and darkness) flourishes, the nobler magical power is cast down. But because the entire "knowledge of the apple" occasionally sleeps during slumber, it is for this reason that there are sometimes prophetic dreams, and God himself is often closer to man in dreams through His influence.

<column-break/>

That is to say, where the inner magic, no longer interrupted by the "knowledge of the apple," exerts itself everywhere through understanding. This is evident when it immerses itself into the lower powers, safely leading those who walk in their sleep through places where those who are awake could not climb. <margin>100.</margin> Therefore, the masters of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "cabalae." A tradition of Jewish mysticism that Van Helmont integrated into his Christian-scientific worldview.</note> assert that wisdom is drawn in while sleeping, specifically when the "knowledge of the apple" is stilled. The act of the intellectual soul is always clear and unshaken, and in a way perpetual; <margin>101.</margin> however, as long as the primary agent has not transmitted its power to the limits of the senses, such action has not yet propagated through the whole man. For we, who exist alongside the power of sensing and carnal intelligence, are perpetually distracted by them—alas!—from the higher magical knowledge. We are held in the shadow of cognition rather than in the light of truth. For we, inhabitants of darkness, do not notice that we are understanding except when a certain mutual transfer of faculties has occurred, as if the corners of actions, extended by different agents, are folded together around a center.
<margin>102.</margin> Thus, Satan awakens this magical power (which otherwise sleeps and is hindered by the knowledge of the outer man) in his slaves. He places it in them like a sword in the hand of a powerful person—that is, the witch. Satan brings nothing else to a murder except the awakening of this said "drowsy" power and the consent of the witch’s will, which is for the most part compelled. Because of these two things, the <term>Buffoon</term> <note>original: "scurra." A derogatory term for the Devil.</note> demands for himself—as if the entire deed were owed to him—a perpetual, tenacious, and irrevocable pledge through a pact, perpetual slavery, and devoted worship, if nothing more. <margin>103.</margin> Otherwise, such power is bestowed freely by God the Creator and is entirely natural to man. Indeed, the illusions, the bewitching of the eyes, and the false appearance of ghosts and such things are from Satan alone and are his own specific acts. For his works are merely ridiculous and only false appearances; because the merciful...

### ON THE GREAT CURE OF WOUNDS.

...merciful God does not permit the soul to be capable of anything further, but holds it bound; whereas otherwise, a <margin>104</margin> **witch** <note>original: "saga." In this context, Van Helmont refers to individuals who have "awakened" their latent spiritual powers for evil purposes.</note> might exert real and nefarious acts from her natural faculty. Indeed, no one doubts that through Adam's sin, the gifts of grace—rather than the gifts of nature—were obliterated. Although these same natural gifts were not taken away, they have remained as if restrained by sleep and dazed. For just as man from that time forth became subject to mortality in the manner of his fellow animals, so too were the presiding powers within man obscured; they consequently have need of excitation and of being led out from the <margin>105</margin> darkness. To this end, indeed, do contemplations, continued prayers, vigils, fasts, and acts of mortification look: so that, the sleepiness of the flesh being conquered, they may obtain that agile, heavenly, and ready power in God, and speak sweetly to Him face to face, who demands to be adored only in spirit—that is, in the depths of the inner man. <margin>106</margin> To this, I say, the **art of Kabbalah** <note>original: "ars Cabalae." Van Helmont views Kabbalah not just as a Jewish mystical tradition, but as a method for restoring the soul's original power over nature.</note> looks, which restores that natural and magical power to the soul, as if shaking off sleep.

Through examples in the mathematical style, I shall explain myself further, and I shall take up the very works of witches. Although these acts are nefarious and horrendous, they nevertheless rely upon the same root: a magical power that is indifferent to good or evil. For it does not stain the majesty of the will, nor the discussion of it, even if we discourse occasionally on a thief, a robber, a harlot, an apostate, or a witch. Suppose, then, a witch kills a horse in a stable while she is absent. A certain natural virtue is derived from the spirit of the witch—and not from Satan—which oppresses or strangles the **vital spirit** <note>original: "spiritum vitalem." The subtle substance that carries life through the body.</note> of the horse. Suppose there are two subjects of disease and death: one is the body, in which <margin>107</margin> the disease dwells. And because all entities act upon this as the most passive element, it was thought that the remaining spiritual dominion belonged to Satan. But the other is the impalpable and invisible spirit, which by itself can suffer all diseases. When the spirit suffers, the body also suffers; because 

<column-break/>

the action terminates in the body. (For after the mind has been bound to the body, it always flows downward; just as when the palate is sore, the tongue continually tends toward that spot). But it does not happen the other way around. For there are some material diseases which are only materially "tinged." Indeed, the occasion for death is so manifold that we have no reason for pride. Therefore, the aforementioned act of the witch is plainly natural, even though the excitation of the virtue was made with Satan's help—no less than if, with a sword handed to her by Satan, the witch were to slaughter the horse. That act of the witch is natural and corporeal; just as the preceding one is a natural and spiritual act. For man consists no less naturally of <margin>108</margin> spirit than of body. There is no reason, therefore, why one act should be called "more natural" than another, or why only the body should be said to act, while the spirit is said to be at rest or entirely destitute of its own proper action (inasmuch as it is the image of God). Indeed, the vital spirits, to speak most properly, are what feel, move, remember, etc.; by no means does the body itself or the corpse do so. Every act, therefore, more properly regards its own agent than the body which is the agent's "inn." <margin>109</margin> And so, some **spiritual ray** <note>original: "Radius... spiritualis." A key concept in sympathetic magic where influence travels like a beam of light.</note> departs from the witch into the man or the beast she has decided to kill, according to the axiom: *no action occurs unless there is a proper approximation of the agent to the patient, and a coupling of virtues to one another.* This nearness may happen either corporally or even spiritually, which is proven to the hand by visible testimony. For if the fresh heart of a horse, slaughtered by a witch (for the heart is the seat of the vital spirit), is pierced with a nail, <margin>110</margin> or roasted on a spit, or scorched on a grate, the vital spirit of the witch—without the intervention of any other medium—and then the whole witch herself (since it is not the body, but the spirit alone that feels) immediately suffers immense tortures and pains of fire. This surely would happen in no way unless a coupling of the witch's spirit with the spirit of the horse had been made. For the strangled horse retains a certain **mummial force** <note>original: "vim mumialem." A Paracelsian term for the life-force or "balsam" that remains in the flesh after death, allowing for sympathetic connections.</note> (so I call it whenever it is still in the flesh)...

# JOHANN BAPTISTA VAN HELMONT

<columns>
...the power of the vital liquid—that is, the innate spirit—is fermented together. This kind of spirit is not found in those who die spontaneously from disease or other disruptions of a lower order. The spirit of the **witch** <note>original: "Sagæ." Van Helmont uses this to refer to someone who has projected their harmful intent into another.</note> is a companion to this innate spirit, joined to it. Therefore, in a fresh heart <note>This likely refers to the heart of an animal supposedly killed by witchcraft.</note>, before its own spirit departs through dissolution, a binding of the witch's spirit occurs. This spirit is held fast by an **inserted nail** <note>A reference to a folk-magic practice where a heart was pierced with nails to "torture" a witch and force her to reveal herself.</note>, and the torture of both spirits happens simultaneously. From this, by means of **magnetism** <note>original: "magnetismum." For Van Helmont, this is a spiritual attraction or resonance between two things across a distance.</note> and through the extreme limit of fire, it happens that the witch is agitated in her sensitive spirit.

This effect is changed by the intention behind it: for if **vengeance** <note>original: "vindicta."</note> stirs the experimenter, then the effect is corrupt. But if the trial is made so that the witch is forced to reveal herself, to be subjected to judges, and so that the welfare of the neighbor and herself is procured—inasmuch as by removing such an impious, blasphemous, and harmful slave of Satan, the glory of God, peace, and rest may arise more greatly among neighbors—then surely the effect cannot be condemned.

It must not be thought that the entire spirit of the witch has passed into the horse's heart (for she would thus have departed from the living), but rather that there is a certain identical participation of the vital spirit and light. This is just as the **architectural spirit** <note>original: "architectus spiritus." The organizing force that Van Helmont believed directed the growth and form of a living being.</note> of the whole man is propagated in the seed at any time—sufficient even for many offspring—while the father's spirit remains whole. Indeed, that participation of spiritual light is magical, a rich communication by the **virtue of the word** <note>original: "virtute verbi." A reference to the creative command in Genesis: "let the animals and herbs produce seed."</note>; and one produces a hundred thousand equivalent seeds, and just as many integral feminine spirits, just as a light is kindled from a light.

What the **magnetic spirit** <note>original: "spiritus magneticus."</note> properly is, and the entity generated by the parent of **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiæ." For Van Helmont, the "phantasy" or imagination was a potent force capable of physically altering matter or spirits.</note>, I shall write more extensively later; now I return to the boundaries proposed.

Nor should anyone imagine that this reaction of the heart upon the witch is imaginary, or a trick and mockery of Satan that is plainly superstitious and damnable. For it is infallibly revealed by this sign, and she is forced to come out into the open, whether she wills it or not.

<column-break/>

It has been sufficiently shown above, through other suppositions, that this is opposed to the intention of Satan. For the effect is perpetual, never-failing, and has its foundation in reason and spiritual nature, rather than relying on superstitions.

Does not a stabbed corpse similarly **bleed itself** <note>original: "sese cruentavit." This refers to the *cruentatio* or "ordeal of the bier," a medieval legal test where a suspect was made to touch the victim; if the wounds bled, they were guilty.</note> before the judges in the presence of the murderer, and frequently provide a certain judgment of the crime? This happens even if the blood had already stood still and restricted. Specifically, when a person dies from a wound, the **lower powers**—which are **mumial** <note>original: "mumiales." From *mumia*, referring to the vital force or "balsam" that remains in a body or its parts after death.</note> (for these are unrestrained and not in our power)—imprint upon themselves a trace of the vengeance to be taken. Hence, when the murderer is present, the blood boils up and flows out, as if agitated in anger by the imprinted image of revenge. 

Doubtless, even after death, there remains in the blood its own sense of the murderer's presence and its own vengeance, because it contains its own imagination. Therefore, it is not **Abel** himself, but his **innocent blood** that nevertheless cries out to heaven for vengeance. For this reason, in sieges, the **plague** <note>original: "pestis."</note> usually walks as a companion; because the magical spirit of the outer man has conceived, during conflicts, an earnest-money <note>original: "arrham." A pledge or deposit.</note> of imprinted vengeance. 

Sometimes, indeed, out of desperation and poverty, soldiers and their wives are almost joined together in dying, and they imprecate many misfortunes upon the wealthy. From this, the strongest posthumous impressions are left in the **sidereal spirit** <note>original: "spiritum sidereum." The "star-like" or astral spirit, the middle layer between the immortal soul and the physical body.</note> of the dying (especially in pregnant women). This spirit, wandering in the air soon after death, devises and promptly executes spiritual ways of harming and avenging according to its kind.

Such plagues, however, are wild, sparing no one, and appearing as if sent by God. And because they are spiritual, they implore the help of bodily remedies in vain. I remain silent on this: for it is not entirely safe to express the mutual connection and concordances of **mummies** <note>original: "mumiarum." Again, the residual vital forces in dead matter.</note>; for from that source flowed the entire **necromancy** <note>original: "nectromantia."</note> of the ancients. For that reason also, God forbade in the Law that the bodies of those hanged (even of heathens) should be left on the gallows, lest the sun set upon them. You will answer that the plague...

# ON THE CURE OF GREAT WOUNDS

<margin>119</margin> Likewise, foul odors arise during sieges because of the many types of filth and excrement. Yet, on the other hand, consider the tanners, the dung-carriers, and those who work at rotting glue: all of them (so far from being susceptible to the plague) <margin>120</margin> are for the most part long-lived; God is wonderful in the **spirit of the microcosm** <note>original: "spiritu microcosmi." In Paracelsian philosophy, the "microcosm" refers to the human being as a small-scale reflection of the entire universe.</note>. Do the birds perhaps know why a bull's blood is toxic, but the blood of its brother, the ox, is not? Specifically, when a bull is killed, it bellows in protest and imprints a mark of vengeance and a powerful seal upon its own blood. However, if it happens that an ox is killed and escapes that fury with a single blow, or if it remains in that same fury for a longer time, it leaves the meat unhealthy—unless, its agitation having been <margin>121</margin> calmed first, it is left idle and secluded to return to itself through fasting. Therefore, the bull dies as a more excellent avenger than other living creatures. For that reason, its fat (but not its blood, lest human blood in an external ointment be overpowered by the tincture of bull's blood) is absolutely necessary for the **weapon ointment** <note>original: "unguento armorum." A famous medicinal salve of the era believed to heal wounds by being applied to the weapon that caused them, acting via "magnetic" sympathy.</note>. If the weapons that caused the wounds are present without blood on them, and they are smeared with the ointment, a sure health is to be expected. Indeed, **moss from a skull** <note>original: "usnea." This was a specific type of lichen grown on the skulls of criminals who died by execution, a key ingredient in the weapon salve.</note> and its fellow ingredients are not enough to establish a healing without fresh blood taken from the wound; rather, a more violent **bull-like impression** <margin>122</margin> is required, along with the airy communication of floral honey. From this, it is clear enough that the efficacy of the ointment is not recorded by the assembly of Satan (who could heal even without honey or bull’s blood), but by the communion of natural qualities, with a posthumous vengeance passed down and left in the physical matter.

Our opponents will bark against us, rejoicing and claiming that the proven power of the magnetic ointment could scarcely have escaped being attributed to a witch, Satan, and the spiritual magic of the invisible world—a putative science that is plainly worthless and a damnable error. Nevertheless, it was not any sinister unfairness in the subject matter itself that demanded this treatment, but rather the crass ignorance of others and the wretched condition of human frailty, which tends more readily toward evil, recognizes evil, and is more prepared to be taught by evil than by good. But certainly, whatever we have brought up here regarding Satan and

<column-break/>

**witches** <note>original: "sagis."</note>, there is no reason for others to hope for a conformity of the ointment with witches. For the spiritual power of the ointment and the "phantasy" of the blood are not excited by Satan as a teacher or instigator. Rather, this is what I intended: that there dwells in the soul a certain **magical power** <note>original: "virtutem quandam magam."</note>, given by God, naturally belonging and appropriate to the soul itself, insofar as we are His image and carving. To this extent, it also acts in a peculiar way—that is, spiritually across a distance—and much more powerfully than by any bodily aids. Because the soul is a more principal part than the body, the action appropriate to it is spiritual, magical, and most powerful. The soul, by this same power, governs and moves its own body, though rendered as if **sleepy** <note>original: "somnolenta." Van Helmont believes the Fall of Man dulled our natural "magical" abilities.</note> through the knowledge acquired by eating the apple. However, when that same magical power is somewhat awakened, it can act even outside its own prison toward another distant object, through a medium carried by a mere nod of the will. <margin>123</margin> Indeed, the entire <margin>124</margin> foundation of **natural magic** <margin>125</note> is situated in that; it is in no way found in blessings, ceremonies, or vain superstitions. Rather, all these wicked observances were introduced by him whose constant study has been to defile all good things everywhere with his own weeds. Not fearing the name of **magic** <note>original: "magiæ."</note>, but interpreting it well along with the Scripture, <margin>126</margin> we have conceded that it can be used indifferently for both a good and an evil purpose—namely, through the use or abuse of that power. And so, under that <margin>127</margin> word, we understand the highest innate knowledge of things and the most powerful capacity for action. This was equally natural to us as it was to **Adam**; it was not extinguished by sin, nor obliterated, but became as if sleepy, and therefore in need of awakening. <margin>128</margin> Thus we show that **magnetism** is practiced not through Satan, but through that which does not belong to Satan. Consequently, our innate power has been abusively dedicated to Satan as if he were its patron. The magical power in us sleeps, as it were, because of sin, and therefore it has need of an awakener—whether that be the Holy Spirit through...

# IOANNES BAPTISTA VAN HELMONT

...illumination, as the Church commemorates happened more significantly among the heroic saints, and even happens today in others from time to time; or whether even Satan, because of a prior pledge, rouses this same thing. In these cases, the arousal is like a **waking sleep** <note>original: "soporem vigilantem"</note> or a trance <note>original: "catochum," a term for a cataleptic or seized state</note>, and is therefore imperfect <margin>129</margin> because of the manner, evil because of the end, obscure because of the means, and wicked because of its author. Nor does the shape-shifter <note>original: "versipellis," an epithet for the devil</note> allow the **witch** <note>original: "saga"</note> to recognize that this power is natural to her; he does this to keep her more strictly bound to him, lest she direct the exercise of such a noble power, once awakened, toward anything other than wickedness. Thus, he commands the bit and bridle, and the witch does not know how to awaken this power at her own pleasure, having prostrated herself entirely to the will of another tyrant. Yet man himself, through the **cabalistic art** <note>original: "artem cabalae"</note>, can cause the awakening of such great power at his own pleasure; these men are called **Adepts** <note>original: "adepti"</note>, whose director is the Spirit of God.

This same **magical power** <note>original: "virtutem magicam"</note> exists also in the external man, namely in <margin>130</margin> flesh and blood, though in its own and far more exhausted way. Indeed, it is not only in the external man, but also proportionally in the beasts (for thus Genesis commemorates that the soul of beasts is in the blood, and for this reason declares it unfit for our food) and perhaps in all other things; since individual things contain within themselves a shadow of the whole universe. For this reason, the ancients seriously noted that God—that is, "all things"—is in all things. The magic of the external man, no less than that of the internal, requires awakening; nor does Satan awaken any magic in his "sows" <note>original: "scrophis," a derogatory term for witches</note> other than that which belongs to the external man. For in the internal depths of the soul is the **Kingdom of God**, to which <margin>131</margin> no creature has access. We have taught, moreover, that there is a connection between things acting spiritually, and spirits with spirits; we have shown how they may clash, as in the example of the witch, or be joined in friendship, as in magnetic examples and by the proper reasons for the enchantment and binding of souls, as we see regarding David and Jonathan, etc.

<column-break/>

Lastly, we have endeavored to show that man predominates over all other bodily creatures and can tame the magical virtues of other things through his own **natural magic**. Others have falsely and abusively transferred this predominance to the "right" of charms and incantations. Through this hierarchy, we have more than sufficiently clarified whatever those who philosophize too rustically and corporally have hitherto attributed solely to the dominion of Satan.

Since those who are ignorant of all that has been said must necessarily still doubt many things, we have decided to repeat everything—primarily so that those things we said above concerning the duel of spirits, or their mutual friendly conspiracy, may become clearer. It is worthwhile to define the "weapons" of spirits and their "commonwealth." To this end, one must seriously note the example of a **pregnant woman**. If she violently conceives a **cherry** <note>original: "cerasum"</note> in her mind, a mark of it is soon imprinted on the fetus, on that part where the pregnant woman placed her hand. Nor is it merely an idle image of a cherry or a stain; rather, at its proper time, it blossoms and matures along with other trees, with the markings of its colors and shapes changing accordingly. Truly, the power of the **microcosmic spirit** <note>original: "spiritus microcosmici"</note> is profound and sacred; for outside of a wooden trunk, it produces a real cherry—that is, flesh marked with the properties and power <note>original: "dynami," meaning potential or force</note> of the internal cherry—by mere conception alone. From this, we necessarily understand two consequences. <margin>132</margin> First, that the spirits and, as it were, the essences of all things lie hidden within us, and are only <margin>133</margin> born and drawn out by the **microcosm-making imagination** <note>original: "microcosmicatrice phantasia"</note>. Second, that the soul, by conceiving, generates a certain "idea" of the thing conceived. Just as it previously lay hidden and unknown—like fire in a flint—so by the arousal of the imagination, a certain real idea and essential, "whatness-defining" <note>original: "quidditativam"</note> determination of the cherry is produced. This is not <margin>134</margin> a bare quality, but something like a substance, hovering between the body and the spirit—that is, the soul. It is so spiritual that it is not entirely devoid of bodily condition...

<summary>Van Helmont argues that magical power is a natural human faculty (the "microcosmic spirit") that can be awakened through the imagination, using the "maternal impression" of a cherry on a fetus as proof. He distinguishes this natural ability from the deceptions of Satan, who tricks witches into believing their innate powers are his own.</summary>

# ON THE CURE OF WOUNDS THROUGH MAGNETISM

### THE GREAT CURE OF WOUNDS
<sig>Fffff 3</sig>

...since the actions of the soul, which leans toward the body and its lower orders, are limited [by the physical]; yet they are not so corporeal that they can be enclosed by physical dimensions, a quality which is also characteristic of the **seminal entity** <term>original: "enti seminali," the formative power within a seed</term>, as we have previously recounted. Therefore, when this **ideal entity** <term>original: "entitas idealis," a conceptual form or "thought-life" that takes on a kind of reality</term> falls from the invisible and intellectual world into the **microcosm** <note>The human being viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>, it puts on a body; and then, for the first time, it is confined by the limitations of place and number. The object of the intellect is a naked and pure essence in itself, not an accidental quality, according to the consensus of practical—that is, mystical—theologians. Thus, the **Protean intellect** <note>original: "Protheus intellectus," referring to the Greek sea-god Proteus who could change his shape at will; here, the mind's ability to take any form.</note> as it were, puts on and clothes itself in this conceived essence. But because every work, whether external or internal, must be made in its own proper image: the intellect recognizes, the will loves and desires, and the memory recalls, only through images. Therefore, the intellect puts on this same image of its object; and because the soul is the simple form of the body, which turns itself wherever it goes, the active intellect cannot hold two images at once, but first one, then the other. Therefore, the entire soul descends upon the intellect and the perceived image (which is still fleeting), and it shapes this knowledge of essence into a **persistent image**, or an ideal entity. The defiled mind fell into the wrath of God; and because it was simultaneously debased and stripped of the nobility of its former lot, death found an entrance—not indeed by the Creator's command, but by the degeneration of man. This happened because of that same ideal entity already put on, having fallen into baseness and degenerated from itself. It is proper to thin out this baseness (which emerges even in individual sins) through repentance, either here or in the world to come. Therefore, the entity in the intellect is still light, and finds no consistency anywhere except in the **pregnant state** <note>Helmont often links the power of the "ideal entity" to the literal force of a mother's imagination on her unborn child.</note>; in us, it is only achieved through the will. That is, the intellect always procreates an entity, but does not "clothe" itself in it except through the will, with the exception of those who are pregnant. Therefore, whether we say sin is nothingness or something, at the very

<column-break/>

least, consent to evil never happens without the real procreation of this kind of <margin>136</margin> entity, and its assumption and clothing. This was the cause of the fertility of seeds: namely, the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, moved by lust, produces a "slight" entity; if the soul then clothes itself in this through the will (as the action of the incarcerated mind always wipes downward and outward), it disperses this same entity into the liquid of the seed, which otherwise would be sterile. This action occurs, as it were, through an **alienation of the mind** <note>original: "mentis alienationem," a state where the mind is directed away from itself</note>: namely, as the will departs, through the true magic of the external man, into a certain **ecstasy** <note>original: "ecstasin," a standing-outside of oneself</note>, in which there is a communication of a certain mental light upon the entity, descending into the body of the seed. Whenever, therefore, <margin>137</margin> thought draws the senses and the "will" into "consent," a foul **garment of skin** <note>original: "pellis," likely an allusion to the skins given to Adam and Eve after the Fall in Genesis 3:21</note>—a spurious ideal entity—is born and put on. By this birth, the will is said to be confirmed. Moreover, that ideal entity goes wherever it is directed by the will: in this way, the will moves now the arm, now the foot, and so on. Furthermore, when the said entity is spread into the **vital spirit** <term>original: "spiritum vitalem," the subtle vapor that carries life through the body</term> for the purpose of loving, helping, or harming something, it needs only a slight excitation—whether by the work of God, Art, or Satan—to make a small portion of the spirit travel abroad, having already put on the entity, and perform the duty enjoined upon it by the will. Thus the male deposits the seed <margin>138</margin> outside himself, which is far more fertile because of the entity it has drawn in, and it performs its duty even outside its own trunk. Truly, bodies make up barely half of the world; spirits also, by themselves, have their own half, and indeed the whole world. Therefore, in this entire context, I call those **patrons of magnetism** <margin>139</margin> "Spirits"—not those sent down from heaven, and much less am I speaking of infernal ones—but of those which are made in man himself, just as fire is made from flint. Namely, from the will of man, a tiny amount of the flowing vital spirit is taken, and it assumes the ideal entity as its form and completion. Which...
