<meta>This page continues Van Helmont's exploration of the "ideal entity"—the spiritual blueprint created by the soul—and how it transitions from a purely mental state into a force that can act upon the physical world. He is specifically building toward an explanation of how "sympathetic" or "magnetic" medicine works across distances.</meta>

<margin>140</margin> Having reached perfection, the spirit—which previously was purer than the ethereal breeze—becomes as subtle as light itself. It assumes a middle ground between things that are physical bodies and things that are not. It is sent forth to wherever the will directs it, or at least to wherever the infallible, innate knowledge of spirits sends it, according to the goals of the work to be done. Therefore, the **ideal entity** <term>original: "idealis entitas," a thought-form or mental image that gains a kind of reality</term>, now prepared for its journey, becomes in a way like light; and being almost no longer a physical body, it is bound by no commands of place, time, or dimension. This force is neither a demon, nor a demonic effect, nor is it any conspiracy with such things; rather, it is a spiritual action of the soul itself, entirely natural and native to us. Anyone who truly grasps this wisdom will easily understand that the material world is ruled and constrained on all sides by the immaterial and invisible. Furthermore, all other physical created things are placed beneath the feet of humanity. This is undoubtedly the reason why even **mummy** <term>original: "mumia," the vital essence or "spirit of life" remaining in a body after death</term>, fat, **moss** <note>original: "usnea," specifically the moss that grows on the skull of a person who died a violent death, used in sympathetic medicine.</note>, and human blood—through the imagination residing within them in an ointment—can command the blood of a dog, a horse, and so on, when that blood is brought into a container by means of a wooden rod.

<margin>141</margin> Enough has not yet been said regarding the magnetism of the ointment. I shall therefore resume the topic. It is certain that the magnetism of the magnet, and of other inanimate things, occurs through a natural sensation of **sympathy** <note>The idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and can influence one another through "likeness" or shared nature.</note>, which is the author of all such things. For if a magnet directs itself toward the pole, it must "know" that pole, if it is <margin>142</margin> to avoid making an error in its direction. And how, I ask, can it know if it does not "feel" where the pole is? Similarly, if it twists itself toward iron placed at a distance, ignoring the pole, it is necessary that it has sensed the iron first. Thus, a single object possesses various senses and images. Nor would it be enough for it simply to feel, unless we also added the stings of love and self-preservation; thus, it is endowed with a kind of natural **imagination** <term>original: "phantasia," a creative and formative power inherent in all matter, not just the human mind</term>, from which all magnetisms are produced. Indeed, one type of imagination is directed toward iron, while another is directed toward the pole; for in the former case, its power is spread only through the immediate nearby space. <margin>143</margin> Its imagination is changed again when it restrains a fetus, prevents catarrhs, or treats the intestines;

<column-break/>

and by yet another imagination, the magnet draws something out of glass melted in the fires. For a tiny fragment of it, thrown into a mass of glass while it is being cooked, turns it from green or yellow to white. For although <margin>144</margin> the magnet itself is saturated with a red color and is consumed by the glass-maker’s fire, in the meantime, while it "lives," it attracts and consumes the tinted liquid even from the glowing glass. Thus, its attraction is not only for iron, but additionally for that "airy" part of the glass which <margin>145</margin> would otherwise find it difficult to leave the glass—a fact commonly used by glass-makers. The imagination of **amber** <note>original: "succini."</note> attracts straws and stalks; this is a rather idle form of attraction, but it is a perfect "signature" of the power of drawing. For when amber is "married" to our **mummy** <note>The vital essence of the human body.</note>, it draws more strongly than our magnet and becomes a **zenexton** <term>original: "zenexton," an amulet or medicated tablet worn to ward off the plague or neutralize poisons</term>. Furthermore, when amber is mixed with gums, it draws poison and lead out of a wound through its now-transplanted imagination, varying the pleasure and desire of its "drawing" in both cases. But why should it be a wonder (except to those who, being ignorant of everything, marvel at everything) that <margin>146</margin> inanimate things should possess the power of imagination? Since He who is entirely Life creates all things, did He ever promise that anything coming from His hand would be dead? Nothing exists into which He does not shine His presence: "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world." Indeed, this world which contains all things has the power of a voice. Do we not believe there was great knowledge within the apple? And that by eating it, the **first-formed parents** <note>Adam and Eve.</note> ate that knowledge and conceived it within themselves? And does not knowledge presuppose an imagination of its own kind? For in this way, some simple herbs induce **mindlessness** <term>original: "amentiam"</term>, others insanity, or others a maniacal fury. This does not happen by the destruction <margin>147</margin> of the brain or the scattering of its spirits (for if that were so, the strength and great power of the madman would not remain), but rather by the introduction of the foreign and furious imagination of those herbs, which conquers and subdues our own. It makes our imagination its slave for a time (as in delirium or frenzy) or sometimes forever (as in the case of the permanently insane).

<summary>Van Helmont argues that "imagination" (phantasia) is a natural force present in all matter, including magnets, amber, and herbs, which allows them to "sense" and act upon other objects. He explains that this spiritual power is what enables sympathetic medicine, such as ointments and amulets, to cure wounds or influence the body across a distance.</summary>

# ON THE CURING OF GREAT WOUNDS

<margin>148</margin> Is it not in this way that the madness of dogs <term>original: "rabies," meaning both the disease and the fury associated with it</term> passes into a human? Specifically, a maniacal **phantasy** <note>original: "phantasia," here meaning a powerful, formative mental image or force</note> of fury is transplanted into the saliva. This phantasy, like a victor, soon triumphs over the blood of that animal—even if it has touched it only slightly through an opening in the skin. At that moment, the original phantasy of the entire blood gives way, and it assumes, whether it wishes to or not, the "hydrophobic" phantasy of the foreign stain. From this, finally, comes a **binsic death** <note>original: "mors binsica," a term Helmont uses for death arising from the vital spirit being extinguished by a mental or spiritual blow rather than physical organ failure</note>; that is, from a purely mental sickness, which has been exalted and stirred up by the **magical power** of the dog over the phantasy of the animal, which was not stirred up
<margin>149</margin> but was instead "sleepy." In exactly the same way, the phantasy of the **Tarantula** <note>Referring to "Tarantism," a historical phenomenon where victims of a spider bite were said to fall into a trance and dance uncontrollably</note> is imprinted by a tiny bite, and those whose minds are immediately alienated dance and leap immensely. However, the venom of the tarantula differs from that of a rabid dog in this: the latter acts by an *excited* magical power, and thus by magic in the true sense of the name; 
<margin>150</margin> but the former acts through a *sleepy* magical faculty, just as the difference is clear in **monkshood** <note>original: "napello," or Aconitum</note> and other deadly things that kill in a tiny quantity. This is why no animal protects or defends itself against a rabid dog, because there is a binding magical power against which teeth or horns are useless—something that cannot be said of the tarantula's venom. Therefore, in the "external man," as in our fellow animals, the magical force is as if it were asleep. It cannot be excited in man alone (though it is much easier there), but also in certain fellow living creatures. Indeed, 
<margin>151</margin> the spirit is not enough on its own, since the spirit must observe this law of concord and "single combat" <term>original: "monomachiae," a struggle between two forces</term>. Furthermore, there lies hidden in the entire universe a certain spirit, which we call the **Magnale Magnum** <note>The "Great Magnitude," Van Helmont's term for the universal medium or "ether" that transmits magnetic and sympathetic influences across space</note>. It exists as the go-between, the messenger, and the promoter of actions for **sympathy** and **antipathy** <term>original: "dispathia"</term>; by reason of this, **magnetism** is extended to a distant object, as if through a vehicle. This is proved to the eye: for if you place a light piece of straw upon the string of a **lute** <note>original: "testudinis," literally "tortoise shell," referring to a stringed instrument</note>, hanging with its two ends in the air like a balance-scale, and you pluck a similar string of another lute at a distance, where the tones harmonize in an octave, you will see the straw trembling. But where they agree in unison, then the string of the otherwise 

<column-break/>

quiet lute, impatient of delay, jumps up, dances for joy, and shakes off the hated straw with its leaping. Will Satan be the lute-player for you here as well? <note>Helmont is mocking critics who claim all action-at-a-distance is the work of the Devil.</note> That straw does not happen to jump even if all the other strings of the second lute are plucked together, loudly and up close; nor does the bare tone alone force the other quiet string to jump—otherwise, every tone would achieve that. Rather, only the **intermediary spirit** <term>original: "leno spiritus," literally "pimp spirit," used here in the sense of a matchmaker or facilitator</term>, dwelling in the middle, the faithful executor and helper of natural actions, carries, 
<margin>152</margin> promotes, and causes the sympathy.

Why do we shudder at the name of **magic**? For indeed, nature is entirely magical, and has no power of acting that is not brought forth from the phantasy of its own form—and indeed, brought forth magically. But because this phantasy has a fixed identity in bodies that lack the power of choice, it has therefore been ascribed—ignoranly and crudely, to be sure—not to the phantasy of that thing, but to a "natural property." Thus people offer the effect in place of the cause, out of ignorance of the causes. In truth, every agent acts upon its proper object by "pre-sensing" it, so that it does not scatter its activity blindly, but only into that object. After sensing the object, the phantasy is stirred, dispersing an **ideal entity** <term>original: "idealem entitatem," a thought-form or spiritual blueprint</term> and coupling it with the radiation of the passive entity. This was the magical action of natural things; however, magic and phantasy properly named exist in creatures endowed 
<margin>153</margin> with the power of choice. I shall go through the classes. Therefore, the **formal properties** flowing from the forms of the **three principles**—**Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** (or Salt, Fat, and Liquor)—from which every body is fashioned and into which it is again resolved: and the Mercury or Liquor is as diverse as there are species of things. Let the judgment be the same for Salt and Sulfur. These properties, I say, flow from the phantasies of these forms, which, because they are very corporeal and still cling to the bosom of the elements, are therefore called "formal and occult properties" because of our ignorance of their forms.

<summary>Van Helmont argues that diseases like rabies and phenomena like sympathetic vibration in lute strings are driven by a natural "magical" spirit called the Magnale Magnum. He redefines magic as the natural process by which the "phantasy" or internal blueprint of a form acts upon the world.</summary>

which are otherwise magical effects, propagated by the **phantasy** <note>original: "phantasia," a creative and formative power of the soul or vital spirit</note> of the aforementioned forms: but they are more ignoble and mostly physical, yet they abundantly satisfy the ends they regard. Of this kind are the purging power <margin>154</margin> of the bowels, sleep-inducing powers, etc. Furthermore, there are other more noble properties arising from the phantasy of mixed forms, and these exist in the whole, by reason of the form; such as the magnetism of the magnet, the power of tinctures, and likewise all specific and appropriated things which occur by reason of either the whole homogeneous substance or the form of some integral part, but not of a single principle alone. These are the qualities situated in the flesh, the root, the leaves, and the fruit, and not in any one of the three separated principles <note>Referring to the Paracelsian "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>. Likewise, as long as **antimony** remains in its own form, it possesses the highest powers, which it never attains in its principles; these are also from the corporal bosom. Therefore, the spiritual magic in these is still hidden, and it was thought to be entirely owed to nature, by ineptly distinguishing nature against magic. Thus, a rose leaf has a different virtue than the stalk or the flower <note>original: "anthra," likely referring to the flower's center or the reproductive parts</note>; and that force is in the leaf not because of the "three firsts" <note>Salt, Sulfur, Mercury</note>, but from its "birth-life." When this life is destroyed, the leaf then possesses other virtues; for instance, a grain nourishes during its "first life," but if it loses that life, <margin>155</margin> then it may become prolific <note>original: "prolificet," meaning it gains the power to sprout or reproduce</note>. Thirdly, there follows the **magical virtue** which flows from the phantasy of life of the whole integral being; this is found in beasts and in the "external man." This virtue is more absolute and is already spiritual, though it has not yet been led to its highest peak; nonetheless, through much excitation and a strong phantasy introduced through an entity, it ascends to a great height and very closely emulates the <margin>156</margin> true magic of the "internal man." Moreover, the soul of any beast has the power of creating a real entity and, through the will, of sending the same further away; such a beast is magical, like the basilisk, the dog, and many fish mentioned in Olaus <note>Referring to Olaus Magnus, a writer on the natural wonders of the North</note>, etc. Such also is the virtue dwelling in the blood of many animals; hence, the sacred page <note>A reference to Leviticus 17:11: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood"</note> says that the soul is in the blood when drawn from the vein,

<column-break/>

even when cooked by fire, and perhaps even when clearly putrid through warmth. Lastly, <margin>157</margin> there is the magical virtue abstracted, as it were, from the body, which occurs by the excitation of the soul's interior power. From this come the most powerful procreations, the most august impressions, and the most valid effects. In both cases, <margin>158</margin> nature is a magician <note>original: "maga," the feminine form of magus, suggesting a fertile, creative sorceress</note> and acts through her phantasy: and because the more spiritual she is, the more powerful she is, the term "magical" is an analogous name. <margin>159</margin> Almost every magical virtue requires **excitation**. The lowest kind is excited through a preceding warmth; for a certain vapor is excited—a spiritual breeze—by reason of which the deeply sleeping phantasy is awakened, and a skirmish of the corporeal spirits begins. The middle kind, which is that of magnetism, is excited through a preceding touch. But the highest kind, which belongs to beasts and men, is excited by an intellectual concept. That of the "internal man" is excited only through the **Holy Spirit** and through His gift, the **cabala** <note>Helmont uses "cabala" here to mean a divine, mystical understanding or illumination</note>. That of the "external man," however, is excited through a strong imagination and assiduous, intense speculation—and indeed, in witches, it is excited by Satan. However, the magical power of blood drawn from the vein, in which the soul dwells, is excited—which is yet in potential toward action—either by a stronger, ascending imagination (for instance, that of a mage using the blood as a medium and stabling his ignited entity within it); or, for instance, by the ascending phantasy of the **weapon salve** <note>original: "unguenti armarii," a sympathetic medicine believed to heal a wound by being applied to the weapon that caused it</note>, which acts as the exciter of the property lurking in the blood; or by a preceding destination of the blood toward corruption, through which the elements are disposed toward separation, and the essences (which do not know how to rot) and the essential phantasies, which lay hidden in the potentiality of the properties, come into act. <margin>160</margin> Therefore, in whatever subject the phantasy has obtained a strong appetite toward the spirit of another thing—to move, draw, expel, or <margin>161</margin> repel something in that place—there, and not elsewhere, magnetism, as a natural gift of that thing, magi-

He argues that these powers often require an external trigger or "excitation"—such as heat, touch, or intense imagination—to move from potentiality into action.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s exploration of the "phantasy"—a creative, formative power within nature—explaining how it governs biological processes, heredity, and the "magnetic" healing of wounds through the weapon salve.</meta>

# ON THE GREAT CURE OF WOUNDS.

...we recognize it as magical, established in it by God. Therefore, there is a certain formal property in it, separated from sympathetic and hidden qualities: because their mover, the **phantasy** <note>original: "phantasia," here meaning a creative or formative power within the vital spirit</note>, flows directly not toward local motion, but only toward change <note>original: "alterativum," a motion that changes the quality of a thing</note>. So, let all magnetism be sympathetic or antipathetic: yet not all sympathy will be magnetic.

<margin>162</margin> Returning to our intended goal: I believe it is now well understood that not only does phantasy and magical appetite exist in the blood, but also in the humors, foods, and excrements. Various offspring of diseases reveal this: for pregnant women crave strange things, and young women—driven by the natural sting of an unruly womb—become pale and quickly digest what they crave. This happens not indeed out of reason, nor because human nature demands it by kinship, but because they are seduced by the exotic phantasy of the humors thus foolishly commanding them. When these impurities are expelled, we often restore sudden health to damaged appetites; or we restrain them by saturating the mindless <margin>163</margin> phantasy of those same humors. Therefore, the blood has its own phantasy, which flourishes more powerfully there than in other things. Thus, the Scripture, with high praise, calls blood "animated" <note>original: "animatum," meaning endowed with a soul or life-force</note> while it is still warm and ready to be consumed. 

<margin>164</margin> Because this same phantasy is hereditary, the character, gestures, and conditions of a grandfather shine forth in a grandchild born after his death. Nobility took its origin from well-deserved virtue; hence nobility would be wrongly suspected of increasing by the continuous propagation of the lineage, unless the character and virtues of ancestors were expected to shine out in late-born grandsons. 

<margin>165</margin> Does not the enmity conceived between the wolf and sheep remain even in their skins? <note>Van Helmont refers to the folk belief that a drum head made of wolf skin would cause a nearby sheep-skin drum to tear or lose its sound</note>. For this reason, not only is the animal phantasy imprinted stubbornly in the blood after death, but whoever is covered with blankets made from the skin of a **glutton** <note>original: "gulonis," the wolverine</note> (an animal common in Sweden and very voracious) is forced to dream continually of feasts, greed, and the treacherous hunting of animals—according to the nature

<column-break/>

of that living animal. And so, by the external covering alone, the phantasy of the creature—once living and now housed in the skins—is transferred into the person sleeping beneath. 

Thus, through the service of the blood's phantasy, it happens that blood drawn out and placed on a wooden peg is introduced to the magnetic ointment. For then the <margin>166</margin> phantasy of the blood—otherwise still sleepy and slow to act—is excited by the power of the magnetic ointment. Finding there the balsamic and medicinal virtue of the ointment, it desires to impart the induced quality to its whole self, and from there to draw out every foreign stain by spiritual magnetism. Because it cannot effectively do this on its own, it implores the aid of the **skull-moss** <term>usnea: a type of moss found on the skulls of those who died violently, highly prized in the Paracelsian "weapon salve"</term>, blood, fat, and **mummy** <term>mumia: a medicinal preparation made from preserved human remains, believed to contain concentrated vital spirit</term>. These, combined into such a balsam, become a healer through their own phantasy, acting magnetically while simultaneously drawing out all foreign qualities from the body to which the fresh blood, rich in spirit, was brought—whether it belonged to a man or another creature. 

There is, therefore, a returning and "ecstatic" phantasy on the part of the blood recently and most lately brought; but the magnetic pull, begun in the blood, is perfected by the medicinal virtue of the ointment. However, the ointment does not draw the infirmity of the wound to itself to become a **Pandora's box**; rather, it alters the newly brought blood in spirit, renders it medicinal, and excites its power. From this, a certain medicinal and magnetic virtue arises, which returns to its own "whole," intending to cure the kindred spirit of the blood throughout the entire man. Specifically, it sucks out the dismal impression from the wounded person and, by medicinal power, expels it so that it perishes, driving it outward. This medicinal virtue, the tamer of evil, is partly excited in the blood and partly generated in the same by the ointment—namely, by the ointment's spirit thus commanding the spirit of the blood through its own phantasy, which is a created gift. Otherwise, blood rotting with its powers intact under an eggshell, with the spirit already freed (as if from shackles) through previous putrefaction, draws by means of the dog, mummy, and reactive...

<margin>167</margin> It also transfers the sickness—which resides in the **phantasy** <note>original: "phantasia," the creative or formative power of the spirit</note> and the **star of filth** <note>original: "astro sordium," a Paracelsian term referring to the internal source of impurities or disease</note>—into the dog itself. This occurs for no other reason than because magnetism is achieved without the need for an intervening ointment balsam. We have also noted that if a wounded person has received several wounds at once, it is sufficient to have blood from only one of those wounds; the others will likewise be cured by that single effort. This is because that blood maintains a shared harmony with the spirit of the whole person, and it draws out the hostile quality not only from the lips of the wound but also from the entire man to whom it is <margin>168</margin> communicated. Indeed, a whole person usually becomes feverish from just one wound.

I have until now delayed revealing a great mystery: namely, to show that there is an energy situated in the hand of man, by which he can act outside of himself through his mere will and phantasy. He can impress a virtue—an influence that persists on its own—which then acts upon an object located at a great distance. By this mystery alone, the things I have said regarding the **ideal entity** <note>original: "ideali entitate," a conceptual or spiritual blueprint</note> carried away in the spiritual fuel, and moving abroad to its tasks, will come to light. This explains the magnetism of all things—born both from human phantasy and the property of the thing itself—as well as the magical superiority of men over other bodies.

<margin>169</margin> It is clear and established without controversy that a needle is made from steel which, through the attraction of a magnet, shows the North Pole to sailors. However, steel is hammered into a needle in vain and placed in a mariner’s compass to designate the pole if the proper rubbing of a magnet has not preceded it. Since these things are beyond doubt, it is now appropriate to show how to manufacture a nautical needle by will alone. 

On the anvil where the steel needle is forged, let the **North** <note>original: "septemtrio"</note> be marked by a straight line. Let the blacksmith stand with his back toward the North so that when the steel is drawn under the hammer to make the needle, you draw it toward yourself and toward the North. I say, therefore, that such a needle, made in this way, will indicate the pole without any other help. Furthermore, it will do so without the usual magnetic variation, which is a great mystery. Moreover, a needle that happens to be on the <column-break/> same line by chance, without the blacksmith's knowledge, is useless and does not indicate the pole.

It follows from this that the imagination of the person making it—at that moment, as if at its birth, when the greatest heat of the fire has ceased and while it is still a dull red—impresses this kind of magnetic faculty into the steel, which is the appropriate subject. This does not happen because the heavens impress it at that time; for if that were so, the influence would flow even without the smith’s intention, which is false. If the heavens influenced it at a certain hour and position, then the "science of signs" and "seals of the stars" <note>Van Helmont is dismissing traditional astrology here</note> would triumph, which we pass over. 

Instead, the constellation that flows into the <margin>170</margin> steel (and perhaps every magical seal) flows from the **microcosmic heaven**—that is, from our own internal **Olympus**. Therefore, seals were useless if they were not forged by a magus who was exalted in his phantasy. Indeed, the internal entities and phantasies of things are compelled to yield to ours; through this, "the wise man shall rule the stars," under whose command the Parent of things subjected whatever is enclosed within the heavens.

The things I have brought forward concerning the phantasy impressing itself upon the nautical needle will be proven ten thousand times true by the testimony of many, by my own experience, and by the experience of anyone willing to try it. In this way, the tips of the **asarum** <note>Asarabacca, a medicinal plant</note> and the **elder tree** obey the commanding phantasy of the one who picks them; he impresses his intent into the plant, which then magnetically acts upon the absent leaf. Otherwise, when the leaf is cooked (just as a needle is re-fired) and given as a potion, the power of the impressed phantasy would perish if the magnetism were not fostered by the whole plant. It is true that cooked blood, ready to be eaten, still contains a soul; but that power exists not from the impression of an external human phantasy, but from the gift of its own internal phantasy. 

<margin>171</margin> In this same way, a nail driven into the heart of a horse [that has been bewitched] detains the spirit of the **Witch** <note>original: "Sagæ"</note> and binds it with the **mumial spirit** <note>original: "spiritu mumiali," the vital balsam or essence of a body</note> of the horse. They are scorched together so that she may be betrayed by that torment, as if on a rack, and finally, through a judge, she—hostile to God and ruinous to mortals—may be removed from their company according to the law of God. ->## ON THE GREAT HEALING OF WOUNDS.<-

when the power is directed toward some external object, the **magical soul** <note>original: "anima maga," the aspect of the soul capable of influencing the physical world through will</note> by no means attacks it without a medium: therefore it uses the instrument <note>original: "clavo," literally 'nail' or 'spike,' likely referring to a focal point or tool of transition</note> already mentioned.

Having now proven that man has the power to act or move a distant object by a mere **command of will** <note>original: "nutum," a nod or command</note>: it is also sufficiently confirmed, by the same natural example, that this energy was given to man by God and belongs to him naturally. It has been absurd until now to think that Satan moved, altered, or carried away anything, or applied active things to passive ones through local motion by a mere command; especially since people do not doubt that he was the "prime mover" in said motions, despite having no extremities with which to touch, seize, or transfer—or at least having only an airy body (as they imagine) which lacks a soul. It is absurd, I say, that Satan, after his fall, should have retained a **magical dignity** <note>original: "magicam dignitatem," a natural status or power</note> by which he acts upon anything by a mere command because it was his natural gift; yet to claim that the same natural gift was taken from man, denied to him, and given instead to the demon, the most despised of creatures—or that if such effects proceed from a man, they must be attributed at least to a pact and punishment with the devil. Open your eyes! Satan has boasted greatly in your vast ignorance until now, as if you were offering him the **incense of glory** <note>original: "thymiama gloriae"</note> and dignity, while plucking out your own natural dignity as if tearing out your own eyes to offer them to him.

We have said that perhaps all magical power sleeps and requires excitation: which is perpetually true if the object to be acted upon is not closely disposed, or if its internal **phantasy** <note>the formative or imaginative power within a substance</note> does not entirely agree with the impression of the agent, or even if the recipient is equal or superior in strength to the agent. But on the contrary, where the object is clearly and closely disposed—as steel is to receive magnetism—or is plainly weak and self-conscious (such as a murderer, an adulterer, a thief, or a **witch** <note>original: "Saga"</note>), then the recipient succumbs to magnetism without much excitation, with only the phantasy of the "external man" led into the work and bound to some medium.

<column-break/>

The magus, I say, always uses a medium: for in this way, unless a pregnant woman extends her hand to her leg, forehead, or buttocks, the fetus will not be marked on the leg, forehead, or buttocks. In this same way, the words or forms of the **sacraments** always work: because they act **by the work performed** <note>original: "ex opere operato," a theological term meaning the rite is effective by its own action rather than the merit of the priest</note>. But because **exorcisms** do not always work, the failure is not in God: but only because the unexcited mind of the Exorcist renders the words sluggish. Therefore, no one is a successful exorcist unless he knows how to excite the magical power of his own mind—or can do so even without knowing how.

You will say perhaps that the **weapon ointment** <note>original: "unguento armario," a medicinal salve applied to the weapon that caused a wound rather than the wound itself</note> obtained no other magnetic power than that generated by the phantasy of the one who mixed it: you are wrong. However, even if that were granted, you would be no better off: for it should not therefore be ascribed to Satan. If the ointment were magnetic not by its own inborn phantasy, but by that impressed upon it from the outside by the person mixing it—since there is no closer medium for said magnetism than human blood with human blood—then surely blood alone, as the most disposed subject, would suffice as the ointment, and the other **simples** <note>medicinal herbs or ingredients</note> would be useless, which is false. This is especially true of bull’s blood and honey; where, in the case of bloodless weapons, the ointment of the one applying it would suffice without bull's blood <margin>173</margin>, which is also false. Finally, the magnetism of the ointment would be entirely general, because the mixer would have intended to produce—through his phantasy—an impression too liberal, wandering, uncertain, and weak for all the wounds of all creatures, even beasts. What if he did not intend it for a dog: would the ointment therefore not be able to heal the dog’s wound? Away with that! What does **Armenian bole** <note>a medicinal red clay</note>, what does linseed oil, what does honey, and finally what does bull's blood have by way of a "disposition" toward an equine or human wound, such that the phantasy of the mixer should be impressed upon these as a proper medium and not others? Yet if these ingredients are missing, they will produce a sterile and useless ointment. Therefore, the natural phantasy of the ointment is the cause of magnetism, and...

One thing I shall add: whoever attributes a natural effect, created by God and given to His creatures, to a demon, alienates the honor due to the Creator and shamefully turns it over to Satan. If you were to examine this carefully (if I may say so with your permission), you would find it to be express idolatry. I pray to God, our most merciful parent, that He may pardon the transgressions we have contracted through non-persistent ignorance and human frailty. Amen.

"There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are only one." <note>original: "Tres sunt qui testimonium dant in coelis..." This is the "Johannine Comma," a famous passage from 1 John 5:7-8 used to explain the Trinity.</note> (Speaking soon after of the humanity of Christ): "There are three who give testimony on earth: blood, spirit, and water; and these three are only one." Since we, therefore, possess an equal humanity, it is no wonder if we contain blood and spirit of a similar unity; and thus the action of the blood is purely spiritual. Indeed, in Genesis, for this reason, it is not called by the etymology of "blood," but is marked with the name of "red spirit" <note>original: "spiritus rubei." Van Helmont suggests that blood is essentially a vital spirit that has taken on a physical, red form.</note>. Cease then, whoever you are, from your stubbornness, and recognize a spirit in the blood other than an evil demon—unless you wish to oppose the scriptures.

The Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the universities who relied on the ancient teachings of Aristotle.</note> deny that the Sun is hot. For they want this to be believed on their word, without demonstration. Because they think man is generated by man and by the Sun, they believe it suits nature [for the sun to be cold]. They fear that if the Sun were hot, it would consume itself, its own dwelling, and everything nearby into ashes. For since it is immense and provides warmth from afar, what great destruction would it not commit if it were burning hot in itself? For how could it generate man, and simultaneously all sublunary <note>Everything "below the moon," meaning the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> things? As if, primarily, because the Sun were immensely hot, the substance of the heavens would therefore be combustible! And would it not be more fitting to admit that the Sun is hot without needing fuel, rather than to deny all the senses—namely, that an effect exists produced by no proper cause! I say, to deny heat in a thing which warms with such strength and from such a

The luminous globe of the Sun is said to exceed the diameter of the earth and water 160 times. Outside this globe of the Sun, the rays of light are dispersed, both above and below it throughout the universe. They illuminate all transparent things to their depths, and opaque things at least on their surface. Moreover, I have shown that solar rays united through glass <note>Meaning a "burning glass" or magnifying lens that focuses sunlight to start a fire.</note> are true fire, shining with their own properties. # A TABERNACLE IN THE SUN #

...seen, the Sun also necessarily, as the very center of connected rays, will be by far the most burning. For the fire of the Sun persists without fuel, by the command of God. Just as fire remains at the center of a <term>cone<note>Van Helmont is likely referring to the focal point of a burning lens or concave mirror where solar rays converge.</note></term> where solar rays are joined, it subsists without nourishment. Only <term>culinary fire<note>original: "ignis culinarius." This refers to ordinary, man-made fire used for heat or cooking, which requires fuel (wood, coal) to stay lit.</note></term> displays a light subsisting by itself without the Sun's intervention. Yet, in this it is separated from the Sun: it must be fed to subsist. The Sun, however, because it is of a celestial nature, does not need food; because it is free from consumption, and was so constituted by God that it might burn. The Sun is therefore the most fervent fire, the principal center of created lights in nature. 

Perhaps, when the fullness of its days shall one day come, and the harvest of things is ripe, the <term>Aquaster<note>A Paracelsian term for the "starry" or spiritual water located above the firmament.</note></term> of the heavens—the waters, I say, which are above the heavens—shall, by divine power, take on a ferment and the seed of a combustible thing, and fire shall rain from heaven, and the stars shall fall. For the Sun, breaking the floodgates and barriers of its own globe by divine mandate, will burn the heavens, both those nearby and those far off, and consume the age into ashes. For the heavens shall be changed, they shall grow old, and like wax, they shall one day melt. And the stars shall fall to the earth—not indeed as whole objects (since most are larger than the globe of the earth) but parts of burned matter shall create an abyss of fire upon the center. 

Therefore, the Sun is fire in itself and nearby. However, the further the rays are dispersed through the universe, the more suitable a <term>nourishment<note>original: "fomenta." Literally "kindling" or "fomentation," referring to the warmth that encourages growth.</note></term> they will give to the seeds of things; because the Sun suggests only a general and common light, fit for awakening and promoting <term>seeds<note>In Helmontian philosophy, "seeds" (semina) are the internal blueprints or vital forces that direct the growth and form of all living things.</note></term>, and thus far vital. It is not, however, that it confers life or essence to the seeds of things. In Cairo, Egypt, eggs are cherished by the fire of a furnace, and without any hen to brood them, chicks are born in abundance. Yet the fire of the furnace neither gives nor possesses seminal power, nor does it scorch the eggs; nor, because it warms them, does it cease to be burningly hot at its source. Thus, the solar rays dispersed through the universe are no longer fire, but simple light. Therefore, culinary fire in a certain way disposes itself to an

<column-break/>

emulation of the Sun. For it flames, burns, and consumes things nearby. From a distance, however, it only warms, and from far away it only shines. Indeed, it is not even considered true fire unless it burns at the highest degree, adhering centrally within the cone of light where the rays are connected. It differs from the light of the Sun in nobility, however, because it is not made of the first created things, is not of a celestial disposition, does not subsist without fuel, and therefore does not become universal. 

Just as the Almighty created the Sun as something singular, so in each individual species of sensitive things He created a unique "Sun," as it were, which would suffice until the end of the world and propagate itself thereafter—not indeed as something supremely fervent, but subsisting through the points of dispersed rays, not longing to ascend to further moments of intensity. Therefore, in the tiny particles of specific lights, the <term>formal light<note>The "form" or essential internal light that gives a species its specific identity and life.</note></term> of the species is restrained by divine power, which has constrained each species to a particular momentum of light—general indeed on the part of the Sun, yet individualized by the coordination of my Lord. 

For indeed, the Sun of the species, no differently than the species themselves, shall endure for the age. But because it does not subsist except in individuals, therefore the "Sun of the species" is daily fleeting in individuals, even through every single moment, unless it be nourished by a continued fuel, as it were. Therefore, vital light has some similarity with the Sun, and a part conforming to culinary fire. Specifically in this: that our "Sun" <margin>175</margin> must have <term>vital spirits<note>Invisible, subtle substances in the body believed to carry life and heat from the heart to the rest of the organism.</note></term> as an unending fuel, which are capable of and act as ministers to the dependent and subsequent light. It is not, indeed, that the spirits in themselves and of themselves are hotter than solar rays; for if the light of the Sun is taken away, they immediately fail in heat and light. Yet they "symbolize" with the Sun in that they seem to propagate an ignition and subsist centrally in the heart. For when the <term>Schools<note>The Scholastic philosophers of the universities who relied on Aristotelian logic.</note></term> observed that the heart, of its own accord, hastens into a cold corpse once the spirits are released—cooling immediately—they thought those breathed-in spirits were the beginning, center, and point

# A TABERNACLE IN THE SUN #

...brought back to the primitive Solar effect and heat, not looking back at the fact that spirits are of themselves cold, and their heat perishes in an instant as soon as they are separated from the ray and support of the heart. It is very strange that the heat, to which the whole tragedy of things vital and non-vital is ascribed, has remained unknown and undetermined until now: [namely] whether one prevails over the other in the origin and sustenance of heat. For since neither the Heart, nor its <term>vital spirit<note>In 17th-century medicine, the "vital spirit" was a subtle substance believed to be refined in the heart and carried by the blood to provide life and movement to the body.</note></term>, are originally hot by their own nature and substance; until now, not even once has it been thought from where heat comes to us, or resides in us from the origin of each individual. Since the knowledge of oneself is the most powerful of sciences, in both moral and natural matters: at least <term>the Schools<note>original: "Scholas." This refers to the Scholastic academic tradition based on Aristotle and Galen, which Van Helmont frequently criticized.</note></term> should never have been ashamed to have investigated the fountain of heat and life in things. God knows how much darkness has remained from this in healing and in guarding life. 

Therefore, I have discussed this token with myself from my youth in this way. First, I recognized that fire, as far as it is limited by forms, is neither an accident nor a substance. Much less an element—which I have demonstrated elsewhere with the full sail of philosophy. Then [I recognized] that the Sun lacks its own endowment [of heat]: and the fire of the kitchen is similarly given, as if for a smith, and placed under the hands of craftsmen like death. But where both desert us, we have flint and steel, from which we build fire for ourselves. Namely, from two cold and dead things, we strike out fire. So also the waters of <term>hot springs<note>original: "aquas thermarum."</note></term> under the earth are ignited from volatile salt and sulfur. From which I learned that the spirit of salt must therefore be salty and volatile, and arterial blood is partly salty, and partly fatty and sulfurous: then finally, that there ought to be a concussion of the pulses, not indeed for cooling (as the Schools otherwise dream) but namely, so that just as butter is made from milk through <term>concussion<note>original: "concussio." A mechanical shaking or churning. Van Helmont argues the heart's movement "churns" the blood to create heat, rather than the traditional view that the pulse acts as a bellows to cool the heart.</note></term>: so from the blood comes <term>vital sulfur<note>A Paracelsian chemical concept; sulfur represented the principle of combustibility and oiliness in the body.</note></term>. Which then, through the concussion of the same work, conceives light in the volatile spirit, and <term>formal<note>In this context, "formal" refers to the "substantial form" or the animating essence of a thing.</note></term> or vital light is propagated: just as light is taken from light.

<column-break/>

Namely, the spirit of salt and the sulfur of the blood rub together in the <term>case of the heart<note>original: "theca cordis." Likely referring to the pericardium or the chambers of the heart where this "churning" occurs.</note></term> through the pulse, and formal light is ignited with heat in the vital spirit: from the light, I say, of the innermost and implanted solar spirit, in which is the **tabernacle of the specific Sun**, even until the end of the world. In this human Sun, the Almighty placed His tabernacle, and His delights, His kingdom, with all His charisms. However, the light which is conceived by the concussion is not indeed made anew, as from flint and iron: but is propagated through the attainment of matter, from the specific and human Solar light, or is ignited and dilated. 

Indeed, it is universal there and vital, consisting in points of temperate light: and it is, on the part of production in nature, specific and determined for human life: but it is individualized in every way by Him who placed the vital tabernacle in the Sun of species. From which tabernacle He then **illuminates every man coming into this world.** Because the Lord Jesus is, in an incomprehensible way, light, life, beginning, way, truth, and the whole of all things. For just as life cannot for a moment subsist without the luminous spirit, by which it is illuminated and animated in the habitation of the Sun: so neither the soul, nor life in any way for a single moment, can subsist without the grace of the same eternal light. 

I have conceived, moreover, the quality and intensity of the heat resulting from that light: insofar as the whole human body, weighing perhaps 200 pounds, is warm with actual heat, which without that light of life would soon grow cold and be a corpse. There is therefore as much heat in the heart as suffices for diffusing warmth through as many pounds of water that would otherwise be cold. The life of species, therefore, as it consists in simple and non-united light, contains the mystery of Divine Providence. ## INFANT NUTRITION FOR A LONG LIFE.

It is now clear that life does not come from the stars, but from the <term>seminary power<note>original: "vi seminaria." This refers to the internal vital blueprint or "seed-force" that Van Helmont believed directed all growth and biological function.</note></term> of the parents; whether life is to be short, sickly, healthy, or vigorous is determined by this. Specifically, it is determined by the character of the seed and the lineage, as well as by the abundance and quality of food and the climate. Among the obstacles to a long life are a weak constitution of the fetus and the poor nutrition of the infant. Therefore, once the fetus is conceived and born, one must look to the quantity and quality of its food, since its little body must be nourished and grow large, and thus be established. It is especially well-known that the nutritional juice in a child is adopted into the inheritance of the <term>radical moisture<note>A traditional medical concept referring to the innate fluid that acts as the "fuel" for the flame of life.</note></term>. For Nature destined the milk in the breasts for the food and drink of the infant, which is a form of nourishment held in common with the beasts. Some might think it an insult to God if we were to think of any other food, as if He had not always chosen from among the available means that which was by far the best. But surely, is God a stepfather to nature, or is nature herself a stepmother, because He did not make bread or wine, but only grain and grapes? Nature is guided by the finger of God. This is true. Therefore, He provided milk as an ordinary food, sufficient for living, but not so that it might serve for a long life. For Nature has no longer meditated on a long life since she recognized that her Author shortened life and does not wish everyone to be long-lived. Instead, He gave milk to everyone equally for food. Indeed, He sent an army of diseases into nature so that a thousand premature deaths might lead the foundations of life toward ruin. Nature, therefore, satisfies the boundaries set by her Author through milk, and has given a food fit for beasts. But the doctrine of a long life is very <term>heteroclite<note>Irregular or departing from the standard rules.</note></term>;

<column-break/>

...clearly blasphemous to have said: "Man and the Sun beget man."<note>original: "Homo hominem generat, & Sol." A common Aristotelian axiom in the Middle Ages. Van Helmont argues here that the Sun provides the environment for life, but is not its direct "parent."</note> Since life is not from the Sun, but rather the Sun’s actions provide the fuels and incitements, as well as the obstacles, that serve life in the world below the moon.

and I know that it will remain hidden among the divinely chosen sons of the [medical] art. Therefore, the present doctrine does not look at the ordinary course of nature, but at a new goal. Thus, I do not consider myself harmful to nature if I prefer an unusual food over milk. For in milk, many inconveniences arise. First, when milk curdles, it very often produces frequent vomiting, worms, <term>tormina<note>Severe, griping abdominal pains or colic.</note></term>, fevers, diarrhea, epilepsy, and convulsions; it contains many unexpected occasions for death. For milk in the stomach, obeying the local <term>ferment<note>Van Helmont's term for the chemical and spiritual agent that triggers digestion and transformation within the body.</note></term>, necessarily turns sour before it is converted into nourishment. If a new wave of milk follows this, a hard curd of milk weighs upon the tender stomach; this curd, hardening into lumps, mimics a tough cheese, much like milk not infrequently clots within the breasts and does not break out except with an abscess. Since this curd stubbornly resists digestion—even if it were not also very harmful—it soon putrefies, turns bitter, yellow, or green, contracts a foul smell, and upsets the <term>pylorus<note>The opening from the stomach into the small intestine.</note></term>. From this, the aforementioned disaster of diseases is often stirred up. For the infant has been sucking for a long time and repeats it frequently. The first milk is coagulated, and then more fresh milk is introduced a third and sixth time, and a mixture of it all occurs. An unnatural and alien acidity is stirred up with wailing, and a common curd is formed from everything. In this, the signs of heterogeneity are manifest; there follows from the recent sucking a token of something cheesy, foul-smelling, and putrefied. These vices are almost inevitable; they are the material "sins" of the milk, which the newly born fetus begins to atone for from its origin—as if from birth, the mother were laying snares and threats of death for her own little infant. There are, moreover, other crimes of milk, hidden...

...from a more refined corruption, it is destructive. To be sure, not only are <term>syphilis<note>original: "lues veneris," literally "the Venetian plague," a common term for syphilis at the time.</note></term>, leprosy, plagues, and fevers infamous for their contagion to be avoided in wet nurses, but even a morbid propensity is burned into the child from the cradle by the nurses, just as if it were hereditary. It is certainly a deplorable mark upon one’s life. I knew a certain President who was blessed with six healthy children; however, the seventh—because it was raised by a nurse subject to <term>kidney stones<note>original: "renum calculo."</note></term>—ended its life in sorrowful <term>lithiasis<note>The formation of stony concretions (stones) in the body, such as the kidneys or bladder.</note></term> in its 13th year of age, after a third surgery by a <term>lithotomist<note>A surgeon specialized in the "cutting of stones."</note></term>. Finally, it is not enough that the material diseases of the milk, the hidden wastes of diseases, and hereditary roots are transplanted through the milk into the suckling and most stubbornly incorporated into its life; even the moral seeds of any vices penetrate within with the milk and persist throughout life. I have observed in this way that a nurse who was deceitful, thievish, greedy, and prone to anger transferred her own weaknesses into the boys she nursed. Thus, unusual stupidity, anger, madness, and many passions of the mind (even beyond moral defects) which have long been dormant in families, finally emerge and unfold in the maturity of their days, having been begged from nurses and propagated through milk. Furthermore, the milk in a nurse is also liable to spoil and "become like a corpse" if the nurse has secretly become pregnant, or if she shares in fevers and evils that are naturally inclined to infect the milk in any way. Finally, from hour to hour, the milk undergoes various impressions from all the perturbations of the mind, from which it not only curdles and rots, but also, through an imperceptible quality, takes on deformities which the innocent infant drinks and is then forced to pay the price for. For a nurse does not always restrain her mind in a single consistent tone; rather, she succumbs to being struck by a thousand apprehensions—anger, sadness, agony, envy, lust, theft, greed, and so on—each of which, there is no doubt, poorly disposes the milk both in regard to the body and the soul. Most of these are inevitable, yet dangerous. Whoever, therefore, wishes to study for a long life from birth, let him not expose his children to these kinds of voluntary, unexpected, and certain dangers. All the more so because a medicine

<column-break/>

for a long life, even if it is administered daily drop by drop from the cradle for a long and healthy life, cannot be digested, nor can it penetrate the body, if it is buried within the thick curdled lumps of milk. Indeed, in this way, even poisons in milk turn out to be almost harmless, becoming sterile as if they were castrated. I therefore dislike the nutrition of an infant attempted through milk. Up to this point, I am not accustomed to eating milk unless it is pure and alone, without any other food or drink, until it has been fully digested and passed from the stomach. For our boy, I praise a nourishment which is established by bread, boiled for a while in <term>small beer<note>original: "tenui cerevisia." A low-alcohol beer common in the early modern period as a safe alternative to water.</note></term>, with skimmed honey—or failing that, with sugar—until they both come together into the appearance of a mucilage, a glue, or a jelly. To this, as much small beer is then mixed and diluted as is sufficient to serve in place of a drink. However, one must abstain from <term>dreg-heavy bread<note>original: "pane fecalitio," likely referring to coarse, unrefined, or bran-heavy bread.</note></term> if he is nourished with honey, because it breeds worms. Indeed, if a piece of that bread is cast into a vessel of honey, it turns into ants. In this manner, I ordered the son of a Count, among others, to be nourished from birth; he far surpassed his three brothers in strength, health, stature, intellect, and every virtue, and so he was a man of great hope, had he not fallen in war, his body pierced by a bullet while fighting bravely. For indeed, as the aforementioned food and drink is harmless, not rotting, not prone to curdling, and not resistant to digestion (for whatever is sought from animals rots easily in tenderer stomachs), so it is neither a participant in malice, nor unstable from someone else’s emotional disturbance, nor the heir to an induced vicious impression. Instead, always equal to itself, even and constant, it becomes most familiar to nature; it is not wormy, not sharp, rotten, or foul-smelling; finally, it is not sour, sharp, or fever-inducing. Indeed, it is never harmful, even if it exceeds the proper quantity, for it can be more or less diluted. Thus, the infant grows and matures without diseases, and becomes capable of receiving the remedy for a long-lived life. Therefore, it is also not read badly, according to the letter, concerning the thrice-glorious incarnate Messiah, that *He shall eat honey and butter*. For one indeed contains the glory of the dew with the extract of flow-

## THE SECRETS OF PARACELSUS.

Indeed, we believe through faith that the life of men has been shortened by the divine will; and the sins of mortals have provided the occasion for this. The will or command of the Lord entered into nature and created the reasons for death—which were not found before the Flood—in a kind of successive order. Life was continually changed through successive generations, until at last it was extended to one hundred and twenty years. And finally, seventy years are the days of man: what is beyond this is misery—except in those of great strength, whom He willed to reach eighty years. <note>A reference to Psalm 90:10.</note> This is therefore the short life, the ordinary life, toward which man flows and arrives by the impulse of nature when impediments are introduced; we see from the Sacred Records that this was established by divine decree.

The roots of this short life henceforth have their place in nature. Primarily, the mind—which does not know how to die—does not grow old. The **sensitive soul** <note>The "anima sensitiva," the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared with animals.</note>, however, although it is eventually extinguished like a light, nevertheless the light itself does not grow old, because it does not arrive by parts or degrees. For if the sensitive soul, or the vital light itself, grew old—since nothing can be added to this perishing thing that is of its own nature—I would think of a long life in vain. Therefore, only the **vital powers** age, which are implanted in each organ at the beginnings of generation. I do not look upon these as mere qualities, but I view them as governors, gradually failing in the **airy body** <note>original: "corpore aëreo," likely referring to the "astral" or "sidereal" body that Paracelsians believed mediated between the physical body and the soul.</note>; and therefore the powers of the spirits follow the nature of that body, which is gradually worn away. For sadness gnaws at life, no differently than a moth gnaws a garment; so too do the disorders of life hasten death. Finally, **man is a wolf to man**. <note>original: "Homo homini lupus," a famous proverb suggesting that humans are the greatest threat to one another.</note> These things certainly cut down life while it is still green for many. Yet these 
<column-break/>
are not the *natural* reasons for a short life, nor are they necessities of innate shortness connected to the species. Certainly, beyond accidental chances, we carry the cause of a short life with us even in the midst of our pleasures.

First of all, memory falters; then sight, taste, hearing, and one’s gait grow dull. To **savor** <note>The Latin verb "sapere" means both "to taste" and "to be wise/judicious." The author is arguing that physical taste and mental judgment fail together.</note>, indeed, signifies both physical taste and mental judgment without distinction, because they often fail at the same time. Taste first fails in the stomach because of the **spleen**. <note>original: "lien." In this period, the spleen was thought to provide an acidic "ferment" to the stomach to aid digestion and clarity of thought.</note> On this account, I have elsewhere distinguished sufficiently between the taste of the tongue and the taste of the stomach. Soon, because of the unequal strength of the parts, the innate **ferments** of the "workshops" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the internal organs.</note> fail here and there. When the ferment of the spleen becomes numbed, the power of first concepts wavers, and old men are said to "become children again."

The **Schools** <note>A reference to the "Scholastics" or traditional university academics whose theories Paracelsus and his followers often rejected.</note> indeed grant children a vivid memory because of the tenderness of the brain, which easily receives any **seals** <note>original: "sigilla." Traditional philosophy compared the brain to wax that receives the "seal" of an impression.</note>; they say that as the brain becomes harder through dryness, the impressions of the seals will be all the more difficult, just as they are more stubborn in retaining the marks of concepts because of that dryness. But this comparison used by the Schools is frivolous, as if the brain behaved in the manner of wax, or as if thoughts expressed the turns of a seal. For in the first place, there would hardly be room for ten seals. Indeed, if seals of this kind were so physical that they had to follow the dispositions and alterations of the brain, they would necessarily square themselves to the extension of the space—because a location is more difficult to separate from a body than its being hard or soft. Let the Schools say, then: how much extension does each seal of a concept require in the brain? Does the memory require a larger place in the brain for the seal of a conceived **horse** than...

...which belongs to a mouse or a fly? Therefore, and consequently, the extension of space in the brain for a horse would also be ten thousand times greater than for a mouse; thus, the entire brain would scarcely suffice for remembering two horses. When space failed, I would remember half of a good thing rather than the whole. Indeed, I would remember things that passed a year ago far better than things that happened to me in childhood. For I have seen a boy who learned the second book of the *Aeneid* <note>The epic poem by the Roman poet Virgil.</note> by heart, yet who hardly understood the hundredth verse. Thus, every single word required just as many "seals" and "places" for them. But if indeed the seals of concepts required no place, nor occupied any extension of themselves in the brain, then nothing is "sealed," and nothing is "stamped"—and the comparison used by the **Schools** <note>Refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the universities who relied on Aristotelian logic.</note> is dull. For the **Schools** are far too mired in the mud when they ascribe the duties of the vital or sovereign powers to "primary or secondary qualities." <note>In traditional medicine, these are Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</note> But what are those poor souls to do, if they scarcely dare to venture a finger’s breadth away from these accidents of the body?

Therefore, neglecting the Scholastic considerations of hardness, dryness, and tenderness, I come to the cause of the short life. I have said, naturally, that from the collapsing vigor of the vital powers, life is necessarily and proportionally diminished. But why these powers themselves grow old—as if covered in rust—and gradually cease, I shall explain. It is because the blood and the gore are finally and successively transformed into the nourishment of the parts to be fed; and when the growth of youth is complete, a juice prepared from it is indeed sprinkled into each solid part, and a certain mucilaginous and "spermatic" liquor is glued to them. But it no longer remains with them for long; rather, consumed and worn out by the "ferment" of the parts (which no longer causes it to coagulate as used to happen during growth), it exhales entirely without leaving any residence, dregs, or residue of remains. This, therefore, is the epilogue of the blood. At the end of its tragedy, it is entirely expelled as an exhalation through "insensible transpiration," <note>The process of losing water/vapor through the skin without visible sweating.</note> after it has fulfilled the functions

<column-break/>

of moistening. Therefore, while that liquor—already mixed through the innermost parts and having completed its digestion—exhales as an effluent, it cannot help but have assumed the nature of an excrement. From this, it follows just as inevitably that the **Vital Spirit**, which is inherent and joined to the internal organs, and its innate powers at the same time, are dulled, alienated, and finally extinguished by this continuous and necessary "soot" or vapor.

This, therefore, is the containing and natural cause of the short life. Consequently, the entire consideration of a long life revolves around the preservation of the vital powers. For it is not enough for blood to be present in all the limbs, so that they may be fed by their desired blood at will. Nor, again, is it sufficient for the innate spirit to be refreshed thus far by the inflowing spirit through the continued substitution of nutrition. For nothing is achieved in the arena of life unless the "seminal powers"—I mean the **vital characters**—are preserved from the aforementioned destruction. Otherwise, the spirits are reduced to nakedness and thinned out, whereby our days are necessarily shortened. Since it gradually loses the character of its powers, or the gifts of the seed, the spirit becomes like a **Gas** <note>original: "Gas". This term was coined by Jan Baptista van Helmont, a follower of Paracelsus, to describe a "spirituous" state of matter distinct from air or water.</note> rather than a living being. 

For even if **perpetual motion** fails in figures and machines because there is no subsequent proportion of the greater to the lesser required for one thing to move another; yet surely this has its place in things which do not move themselves, nor are able to grow or be strengthened by moving. Therefore, such things are unworthy of consideration in seminal matters. Since natural generations will be sufficient and constant until the end of the world—so that the species and their strengths persevere intact—they beget from themselves a seed that is by no means diminished. Consequently, if a forty-year-old man generates someone similar to what he once was, his forty-year-old life could be continued in a vigor equal to his youth, unless the flaw of a "broken thread" rushes in from elsewhere, as I have said. Therefore, we must industriously investigate whether there are remains of the **Tree of Life** to be hoped for in nature, or "supplementary substitutions" through which, truly, whatever...

# THE SECRETS OF PARACELSUS.

...finally vanishes from us, it becomes a kind of fuel for those powers, and no longer bears the fate of excrement with its gloomy stench. I am pleased to recognize the quality of our aforementioned incense <note>original: "suffitûs" — here referring to the bodily vapors or "smokes" produced by internal heat</note> not only in the odors of certain sweats; but especially because bedbugs, lice, fleas, and similar insects proceed from it: they are indeed the mere offspring of filth and stench.

It seemed to me a particularly useless question to ask: whether the Garden of Eden and its Tree of Life have ceased to be, or whether they truly persist even today? And in what location? Whether Enoch, Elijah, and John <note>Figures from the Bible traditionally believed to have been taken to Paradise or Heaven without experiencing natural death</note> still live happily there in the company of angels, beyond the inconveniences of old age and infirmities? It is enough for me that the Tree of Life began at creation and that it existed in nature—it was not a fable or a parable. It is sufficient that it was and will be unknown to mortals, and thus the impossibility of obtaining it deprives us of hope. 

In the meantime, I investigate a "substitute plant," though it is inferior in many respects. Indeed, there is no doubt that if there is any plant in this "vale of misery" <note>A traditional phrase for the earthly world</note> which reflects the powers of that primitive Tree, the location contributes its part toward a long life, both in respect to the plant and the person using it. For I trust the climates themselves as evidence that the same plant is ennobled according to the variety of its native soil, and that our life is prolonged by the "drink" of better nutritional juice and sweeter air in certain places. For it is not to be believed that this happens entirely by the favor of the heavens; even at the same degree of distance from the equator, and under the exact same orbit of the sky, those parts situated toward the sunrise produce nobler fruits than those which decline more toward the setting sun. Furthermore, much variety is often found sown close together under the same circle. Yet both parts are affected daily by the same aspect of the sky and the same movement.

For indeed, the hope of certain healers for a long life has been raised by the warnings of Paracelsus. Each man promises himself the "Adept of long life" from his writings, if only he had not described his discoveries with such a great darkness of words. Because of this, many 

<column-break/>

search for the meaning of the obscure novelties of the names he uses. Others, rightly suspecting his simple and shortened descriptions of operations found everywhere, long for a more open method of working. However, no one has attempted to strip away the mask and dig to the bottom of the matter, the very base of the promised truth. For everyone either mocks him, or despairs, or—being too credulous—admires everything with a "suspended nose" <note>A Latin idiom for being skeptical or sneering, though here it suggests a sort of stunned, uncritical amazement</note>. If only they were better than those who have cut off their own path of hope. Yet no one chooses the middle path: namely, of doubting and investigating how much truth the promises contain.

Indeed, Paracelsus promises that he will reach extreme old age through the **Elixir of Propriety** <term>Elixir Proprietatis; a famous multi-ingredient cordial meant to preserve health</term>, and he boasts that it was granted to him by heaven to choose the fate and hour of his own death. But these are vain displays of his "long life," his knowledge, and his choice of death, since he was meanwhile extinguished at the age of 47. His followers are stunned and wonder by what disease or accident he was snatched away while still in the flower of his age—he who was a true master of that **Gold-making Stone** <term>chrysopœia; the alchemist's philosopher's stone</term>, and who everywhere mowed down myriads of the more serious diseases as if with a scythe, or slew them with the "Club of Hercules."

Truly, I act as no man’s apologist. I gladly confess that I have profited much from his writings: and that he was able, through remedies ascending to a "symbol of unity," to cure leprosy, asthma, consumption, paralysis, epilepsy, stones, dropsy, gout, cancer, and diseases of that kind which are commonly incurable. Nevertheless, I have gathered—both from his writings and medicines, as well as from his death—that Paracelsus was ignorant of the "root of long life." For the renovations and restorations in which he often and justly glories are merely the purging of the containing parts, along with the correction and banishment of the contents. Up to this point, he was the champion and healer of almost all diseases. However, his **secret remedies** <term>arcana; hidden or highly potent chemical medicines</term> do not look so much toward a long life as toward a healthy one and its comforts. For hair, nails, and teeth are renewed; although these are the hardest parts, they are the first to feel the flesh...

...feel. And so it is not written in vain that Moses had all his teeth in the 120th year of his age. For insofar as they <note>Referring to the inhabitants of hot climates mentioned on the previous page</note> live obscurely, they have their kitchen <note>original: "culinam" — here used metaphorically for the metabolic heat or preparation of nourishment</note> outside themselves, and they also rot very easily. For perhaps Egypt and the neighboring places possess this by their very nature. Indeed, I remember that the Polish Prince Radziwill <note>Mikołaj Krzysztof "the Orphan" Radziwiłł (1549–1616), who published a famous account of his pilgrimage to Egypt and the Holy Land</note> wrote thus concerning the Memphis Mummy: For three thousand years, without the slightest rot of any limb, bodies of this sort are preserved whole to this day. Moreover, the multitude of these corpses is so great that there are few who can endure the disgust of seeing them all. They are so thickened by the richness of spices and ointments that they shine, hardened in the manner of pitch. Especially the brain, the muscles, and the fleshier shoulder blades: for the chest, hands, and feet, since they have little flesh and are stretched like membrane, do not serve as mummy <note>The medicinal substance "mumia" was often harvested from these specific fleshy parts</note>. As far as can be gathered by the judgment of the nose, much Myrrh must have been mixed into these ointments. At least these ointments preserve a wonderful whiteness in the bones. Outside the caves, a great force of bones lies cast about, from which the mummy-substance has been taken. Among these, we contemplated—not in passing, nor for a brief time—the skulls and lower jaws where the teeth were fixed: we found none at all that had even one decayed tooth or any mark of extraction. Thus, in all the jaws, the teeth were full, whole, and quite white. For among so many hundreds of jaws, there were also aged ones, in which the teeth were short and worn (as is seen in the elderly); but there was none that had any rotten, hollow, or pitted tooth, or a sign of one having fallen out. From this I gather first: that Moses could have naturally possessed all his teeth. 2. That just as cold things harm the teeth, so our cold air is hostile to our teeth. 3. That for this reason the Ethiopian and the Spaniard have white teeth. 4. I find consolation for the Belgians <note>The author, likely Jan Baptista van Helmont, refers to his own countrymen in the Low Countries</note> from the words of the same Prince. In Cairo, they are said to number seven million among the common folk; among the Jews, the number is said to have risen to one million 

<column-break/>

and six hundred thousand, counting women and children. In such a great multitude of people, however, hardly a third part has whole vision. Everyone everywhere suffers in their eyes from the eating of fruits and the drinking of water on top of them. Furthermore, 5. Paracelsus did not trust himself entirely in vain regarding the "elixir of property" <note>original: "elixire proprietatis" — a famous alchemical remedy made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron</note> prepared from saffron, myrrh, and aloe, provided he had not erred in its preparation; rather, he should have fashioned that medicine in the manner of the "Tree of Life." For just as myrrh guards the mummy from the tendency to rot, if an entry for myrrh is granted into our constitution, the authority of myrrh for a long life will not be empty. As for the "renovation" so greatly praised by Paracelsus—which renews hair, nails, and teeth while excluding all diseases—certainly hair and nails, just as they sometimes fall out of their own accord, so they easily grow back at any age, and their renewal is of little importance. I also saw a man and an old woman in their 63rd year of age whose formerly lost teeth were growing back spontaneously, even with the pains of childhood teething. Yet it denoted no longevity of life, because both died in that same year. For the promise of Paracelsus regarding the "return to youth" <note>original: "repuerascentia" — literally "becoming a boy again"</note> through renovation raised many into the hope of a long life. They thought, naturally, that from the regrowth of teeth and nails, a return to youth was necessary—especially since they would cast off the grayness of old age as a sign, and the former color of the hair would return. But their error came from a lack of distinction. Alexander <note>Possibly Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century medical writer</note> mentions that he saw an eighty-year-old man whose new teeth grew in for as many as had failed; but he does not commemorate his longevity for that reason. And although he might have happened to be long-lived at the same time, since one thing does not contain the other in its root or necessary causes, it was a fallacy <note>original: "elenchus" — a logical refutation or flaw</note> to deduce one from the other as a consequence. For Nature, not infrequently, has attempted such renovations of her own accord, during which she meanwhile cuts the thread of long life. For it is not unlike how a pear tree is renewed every year with leaves: yet not that it pro...
