The author critiques Paracelsus’s belief that the physical "renovation" of the body—such as the regrowth of hair or teeth—is a direct indicator of an extended lifespan.</meta>

# THE SECRETS OF PARACELSUS.

### Page 789

From this comes that long-lived tree: the terebinth <note>The turpentine tree, known in antiquity for its longevity</note>, or the cedar, or the fir, which has a shorter life. Indeed, the pear tree does not borrow any power of long life simply because its tree is renewed every year. Therefore, this "renovation" of medicines deceived Paracelsus. For these medicines only prove health, due to the intimate and supreme purification of similar parts; they do not, however, prove that the root of life has been renewed, or that life has been prolonged as a result. For they were deceived because the stag casts off its antlers and the snake its old age <note>refers to the shedding of skin</note>, and yet these are long-lived animals. Thus, they incorrectly attributed this renovation as the cause of a long life. In contrast, crabs, spiders, cicadas, and insects of shorter life very often happen to shed their skin. Conversely, a castrated stag does not change its antlers, because it does not produce new ones; yet it does not cease on that account to be equally long-lived. For the stag does not cast its antlers toward autumn or winter, when the beasts settle themselves for greater rest, but rather while it feeds on the new growth of shoots, in which a renewing power of its own growth exists; this is transferred into stags, but not into oxen. This is because the stomach of the stag, by its own specific ferment, preserves the germinating power of the shoots and translates it into the middle life of the stag. This does not happen in a castrated stag lacking antlers, just as a beard is denied to eunuchs. Therefore, a renovation of this kind is indeed an effect of a more vigorous life, but it is not an inseparable sign of a long life, nor is it a connected cause. For renovation does not have a necessary long life joined to it, nor is renovation conversely attached to a long life. As is clear in the stag, the goose, and so on. Let it be, then, that the individual secrets <note>original: "arcana" — the hidden, powerful chemical remedies Paracelsus was famous for</note> of Paracelsus remove almost all universal ailments, and renew the nails, hair, and teeth; they cannot, however, primarily equalize the unequal strength of some failing part, much less rescue failing powers from death. And least of all can they restore those same powers to youthful vigor. Therefore, such secrets do not regard the powers of the organs, nor the long life that depends

<column-break/>

upon them, but only the highest purification of all the limbs, and the health born from this. To be sure, all diseases—whether they emerge from impurities, hide within those impurities, or finally propagate further impurities by their contagion—are healed by the aforementioned secrets. But those which primarily concern the vital powers are not. Not, I say, those which contain an innate or acquired weakness from disease or old age along with a diminution of powers. For things of this sort return to their original state only through remedies of long life. Nor yet do they return with a perfect and filled reintegration to the original state. For this would otherwise imply absolute immortality. Indeed, those weaknesses which attack from gluttony, Lust <note>original: "Venere" — referring to sexual excess or venereal diseases</note>, etc., are restored only a little bit through the secrets of Paracelsus, and then only if accompanied by a weak nature. For insanities arising from bad physical conformation are restored not at all. Furthermore, those which have arisen from a notable pride of the spirit <note>original: "thymosi" — from the Greek 'thymos', meaning spiritedness or anger</note> are in constant fear of a relapse. Otherwise, however, frenzy, delirium, the falling sickness <note>original: "caducus" — epilepsy</note>, uterine madness, hypochondriacal mania, and whatever arises from some offspring of impurity, are perfectly and completely healed by Paracelsian remedies. Therefore, manias that proceed from notable arrogance are indeed healed immediately, but with the fear of some minor relapse; because these prove a sheer defect of the Imaginative power. Therefore, they so contaminate the seed that, being transferred through several generations, they not infrequently shine forth. Thus also the children of drunkards often retain signs of vitiated powers, as if the children, heirs to the father's crime, must pay the penalties. That is, "the strong are generated by the strong and good." And conversely, "a bad crow, a bad egg." For the children of drunkards are for the most part stupid, sleepy in investigating things, stubborn in their concepts, drunken in their actions, and easily led away into vices. At least I do not doubt that Paracelsus used his secrets, inasmuch as he saw not only successful healings follow, but even that some who used them for a long time were renewed in their hair, nails, and teeth.

-># THE SECRETS OF PARACELSUS.<-

However, since he did not have a long life, his aforementioned secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> will serve as a witness to us, based on my broad judgment. Indeed, a *Will of Paracelsus* is in circulation; but because it contradicts the public record taken from his own epitaph—which can be seen in the Salzburg hospital, on the wall at the Altar of Saint Sebastian, and which records that he left his goods to be distributed to the poor and to be placed in honorable hands—I believe that *Will* was forged by those who hated Paracelsus. Consequently, others of that same ilk assert that Paracelsus, having reached the end of his pact with Satan, died in full health. This contradicts the aforementioned *Will* published by his enemies, in which it is said that he was sickly for several days before his death. Such an act of great guilt <note>referring to a pact with the Devil</note> also contradicts the fact that he was so benevolent toward the poor. There are others as well who say he was taken off by poison. Since the remedies for this were no less known to him than for other diseases and were ready at hand, they suppose he was killed by diamond powder, which ate through his intestines. For my part, I am not at all surprised by the untimely death of a man who, from his youth, was preoccupied with chemical secrets—especially if an excessive curiosity for investigating the sciences, heedless of his own life, troubled him day and night. For which of us mortals would not be infected by the fumes of coals, of "strong waters" <note>Nitric acid</note>, of graduating and arsenical waters, as well as the daily new examination of antimonial substances? Through the long, weary years of experimenting, we who have not yet reached the end of our trials inhale these things, only warned of their malignancy by late experience. For what else would a curious and fearless apprentice do in an art so abstruse, which refuses any teacher other than the "torture of fire"? <note>A common alchemical phrase referring to the intense heat and repeated distillations required to reveal a substance's nature.</note> Here, the theorems of the art are obscured by choice—not so that they may be known in fragments, but rather so they remain unknown. For understanding is given only to the chosen through long preparation of days and works, to those provided with sufficient health and money, and who have not earned unworthiness through the weight of crimes. I grant that there are some universal medicines which, under

<column-break/>

a harmony most pleasing to long life, lead out the bound enemy <note>i.e., the disease</note> insensibly, with an excellent purification of the organs. I likewise grant that there are several "appropriated" medicines, which rival the scope of the universal ones in their specific directions for diseases; they remove the company of foreign impurity, and once a vice <note>a physical ailment or defect</note> has taken hold, they dominate it completely, just as an axe pulls down a tree. This is the index of Paracelsus's secrets:

First is the **Tincture of the Lily** <note>original: "tinctura lili"; an alchemical preparation usually made from antimony, despite the floral name</note>, reduced into the "wine of life" from immature mineral electrum, of which one part is the primary metal and the other is the essence of the limbs.

Next follows the **Mercury of Life** <note>original: "mercurius vitae"; typically antimony trichloride</note>, the offspring of pure antimony, which thoroughly absorbs every nerve of the disease.

In the third place is the **Tincture of the Lily**, also antimonial, of almost the same efficacy as the preceding one, though slightly less powerful.

In the fourth place is **Diaphoretic Mercury** <note>A sweat-inducing preparation of mercury</note>, sweeter than honey; when fixed to the fire, it possesses all the properties of the "Sun of the Horizon." It accomplishes whatever a physician or surgeon could wish for in healing, yet it does not renew the body as powerfully as the previous ones.

More eminent still is his **Immortal Alkahest** <note>The fabled universal solvent of the alchemists</note>, a liquor of unchanging dissolving water, and his **Circulated Salt**, which reduces every tangible body into the liquid of its own concrete form.

Next comes the **Element of Fire** from copper, and the element or **Milk of Pearls**. However, the essences of gems and herbs are far inferior to those mentioned above. Finally, the **Volatile Salts** represent the precise particularity of herbs and stones, but they do not reach the efficacy of the universal remedies.

The **Corallated Mercury** <note>original: "Corallatus"</note>, which is the only purgative administered through the bowels, heals ulcers of the lungs, bladder, larynx, and kidneys by purging them, to such an extent that it even roots out gout. It is, to be sure, the common mercury from which the *Alkahest* liquor has been distilled once; it resides at the bottom, coagulated and able to be powdered, neither increased nor diminished in weight. From this powder, the water of egg whites is to be redistilled until it has acquired the color of coral.

He argues that because these substances are inherently "mineral," they cannot truly integrate with the human "life force," regardless of how refined they are.</meta>

-># THE SECRETS OF PARACELSUS.<-

With a humble spirit, I praise the Lord of all things, because he reveals his secrets to the little ones of this world and perpetually steers the helm, lest these benefits of his fall into the hands of the unworthy. And so, I have found that the secrets of Paracelsus remove diseases, but they do not reach the "root of life" by far. I have also found that mineral remedies, even when brought to the highest degree of refinement, are nevertheless unfit to be transformed into nourishment for our primary constitutive parts. This is because they retain the "middle life" <term>Latin: vitam mediam; the inherent nature or "soul" of a substance that remains even after it has been chemically processed</term> of the solid bodies from which they were drawn. For to that extent, they never entirely set aside their mineral character; indeed, for that reason, they depart far from the requirements of human life. Furthermore, I will not easily be led to believe that the Philosophers' Stone can be vitally united to us, because of its supremely immutable substance, which is incredibly fixed against the tortures of fire and indissolubly uniform. That is to say, it cannot be separated, destroyed, or digested by the body in any way. It is so far from contributing to a long life. History bears me out: no one who possessed that stone enjoyed a long life; instead, for many, life remained short because of the dangers endured while working <note>Alchemy involved frequent exposure to toxic fumes like mercury and arsenic</note>. Furthermore, let the "mangones" <note>deceitful traders or quacks</note> not hope that powerfully nourishing foods will provide a long life. And—

<column-break/>

—indeed, although they may offer strength to those recovering, they later enervate those they have nourished. Caesar also testifies to this. To that extent, more "tender" <note>highly refined or soft</note> foods are easily consumed, making the flesh soft, but they smoke out the vital powers with a greater "nidor" <term>nidor: the heavy fumes or steam produced by cooking meat, believed by early physicians to cloud the internal spirit</term>. The studies of physicians, however, are occupied with culinary delicacies, which they call "dietetics," for they have been led away into error. They act as if a food that produces good juices <note>original: euchymus</note> and is tender might benefit those recovering if given in the proper dose. They have also thought that stronger men, nourished many times over with the same food, would be elevated to the highest increase of strength. For one does not proceed in feeding as one does in arithmetic, where 10 pounds lift nine, and consequently, 100 pounds lift ninety. But it does not follow that he who eats the most and drinks his fill will become more powerful than he who lives more moderately. For nature does not so much observe the proportions of numbers as the proportions of the powers of alterable things to the power of its own *Blas* <term>Blas: Van Helmont’s term for the internal, vital motion or "pulsing" force of life</term>. However it may be, at least it succeeds according to the wishes of the physicians. Since an abundance of blood <note>original: cruoris</note> produces waste products, the physicians are called in, and thus they command rules of diet that will benefit only themselves, and they shorten life in those living "medically and miserably" <note>A play on the Latin proverb *Medice vivere, est misere vivere*—to live according to a doctor's rules is to live a miserable life</note>.

## THE MOUNTAIN OF THE LORD.

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a floral design within a square frame.</image-desc>
Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He shall receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior. <note>Psalm 24:3-5</note> These words sound of eternal blessedness. And so it is. Nevertheless, nothing prevents this figurative and typical speech from also explaining the truth of its own meaning according to the letter. Since it is necessary for the "type" <note>a symbolic foreshadowing or model</note> to correspond to the thing signified by the type. Indeed, I have always observed that almost all the mysteries of God were celebrated on mountains.

<column-break/>

For Abraham was ordered to climb the mountain and there sacrifice his only-begotten son, as a "type" of the sacrifice offered on Mount Calvary. God commanded Moses to ascend the mountain so that He might speak to him. And He gave him the Law. And Moses spoke face to face for forty days and nights. On Horeb, the Lord was transfigured, etc. All these things could have happened in the desert, and the God of hosts could have surrounded Moses with lightning and fires on a plain just as well as on a mountain, so that no mortal would have approached; but a mountain was always chosen by privilege. And a blessing from the Lord is promised in the ascent to the mountain of the Lord. For indeed...

-># THE MOUNTAIN OF THE LORD.<-

For the Lord could have indicated his desires to Moses in a shorter stay; there was no need for forty continuous days and nights, unless that delay itself—by its own weight (for in natural things, delay is required for the proper ripeness and efficacy of matters)—designated some hidden mystery. Naturally, I understand that in mountains lacking endemic malignancy, there is not only the purest air, far removed from dregs and corruption, separated from the common crowd, errors, and defects, and most purified from all filth on account of the cold; but there is also a place where, through the continuity of great things, there is the most ready irradiation of heavenly things, because it is a "drinking of the purest ether" <note>The author uses 'ether' to mean the highest, clearest part of the atmosphere, which he believes has life-giving properties</note>. For I remember that one morning, while fasting in the Alps, I sensed a sweetness in the inhaled air, such as I have never felt before or since in my whole life. It is certain that the Almighty did not create such a great "hump" in nature in vain. It is certain that all the riches of the world are dug out of mountains. Next, the best springs and most famous rivers are turned toward us from mountains by reason of their slope. Finally, all mountain-dwelling nations have tougher bodies and more vigorous lives than others who inhabit pleasant plains. These effects are consistent with their causes: namely, a sweeter and purer air is inhaled there, and every **Gas** <term>A term coined by the author, Jan Baptist van Helmont, to describe vital spirits or vaporous substances</term>, deprived of its filth, returns into the pure matter of water. But why God would raise such a heap, or even the face of the earth itself, or construct so many rocks upon it, or join them into a single stone, yet not enrich it with any mineral (in respect of which he might seem to have piled up such a mass), nor rain down springs, nor yield fruits worthy of such borders—but instead exalted it above all turbulence of air and clouds, the whirlwinds of winds and the portents of lightning, into the most placid quiet of the air: certainly, this seems to me dedicated to a remarkable mystery. For the blessing promised of old mostly concerned a long life, its conveniences, and the fertility of offspring (as in "that you may be long-lived upon the land," etc.). Therefore, the blessing for those ascending the Mountain of the

<column-break/>

Lord, according to the letter, seems to concern the endowments of long life in nature. For He, who alone is entirely life and the Prince of Life, gives long life to no one (at least not through natural means) who has received his soul in vain. Therefore, the blessing of ascending the Mountain of the Lord seems to contain the longevity of life. Thus, those highest mountains, which are read to be granted to nature for the sake of no fruit, and which reach the sweetness of undaunted air, seem to promise a singular image of the Mountain of the Lord and of long life. And this is by some singular prerogative above other mountains, so that by that quasi-right, they hold the name "Mountain of the Lord." Indeed, if it reaches above all occurrences of the lower regions, it promises me singularly that God is there in a peculiar way. For He who was not in the whirlwind of wind, but in the sweet breeze, was perceived by Elijah: He, He (I say) has his domicile there. That is, the Prince of Life gives his blessing there. Not indeed one that is communicated in a few hours, but signaled to Moses on Mount Sinai by the revolution of a forty-day period (specifically through two full moons). Indeed, if someone could dwell continuously for forty days every year around the feast of **Scenopegia** <term>The Feast of Tabernacles; a Jewish festival involving dwelling in temporary shelters</term> on the mountain of rest—having brought the comforts of living to himself from elsewhere—I predict it would benefit him much toward a long life, especially if he is refreshed there daily with a medicine prepared from the **Tree of Life**. This is because on such a mountain, due to the remarkable purity of the air, there is a greater joining of nourishment to the breath <note>Latin: alitus; referring to the vital spirit or the air we breathe</note> and a more inward access to the primary constitutive parts. Finally, although the highest mountains display the privilege of long life, even those less high promise something singular, according to the sensation perceived in the Alps. However, I always reject mountains that breathe out some mineral. For in **chemistry** <term>Latin: Chymicis; specifically the study of minerals and their transformations</term>, "arsenic" has for that reason obtained the name "smoke of metals." But to those who are given the convenience of living on a healthy mountain, not heavy with the fruits of minerals, they would certainly enjoy the benefit of long life, as much as the nature of the place grants.

# TREE OF LIFE

I am forced to believe that there exists a stone that makes gold and silver. This is because on separate occasions, by my own hand, I performed a "projection" <note>original: *projectionem*; the final act of an alchemical work where the "Stone" is cast into base metal to transform it</note> of one grain of powder over several thousand grains of boiling mercury <note>original: *argenti vivi*; literally "living silver"</note>. With a circle of many people standing by, and to the tingling wonder of us all, the work succeeded in the fire just as the books promise. It was not, however, an extract made from gold that would simply replace its own weight in mercury. First, even if that were the case, it would still represent a true and manifold transmutation of one thing into another. Second, goldsmiths and mint-masters know that nothing which is not "mercurial" can enter into metals by melting or be liquefied with them; instead, it would just float on top of the melt. Therefore, third, that extract would have to be "fatter" <note>In alchemy, "fatness" refers to the combustible or oily sulfurous principle</note> than any metal if it were to "tinge" <note>original: *tingere*; to penetrate and color a metal, changing its nature</note> so many thousands of parts. Fourth, that extract would no longer be a metal itself, since it would exceed the perfection of the purest metal by many thousand times. For a metal does not allow for as many degrees of increase in its own perfection as the number of times a gold-making powder <term>chrysopoejus: from the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make)</term> converts a lower metal into true gold. Fifth, he who first gave me the gold-making powder had at least enough of it to be sufficient for changing two hundred thousand pounds of gold. No one possesses ten times more gold than that; and even if he did, he would be destroying it only to construct the same amount of gold again. Sixth, he gave me perhaps half a grain of that powder, and from it, nine and three-quarter ounces of mercury were transmuted. This powder for gold was given to me by a traveling stranger, a friend of a single evening. However, although the Philosopher’s Stone truly exists in nature, for the reasons mentioned before, I have always reckoned that no metallic remedy contains the blessing of the Tree of Life <note>Arbor Vitae: a legendary substance or plant believed to grant immortality or extreme longevity</note>. Meanwhile, I gladly confess that this Stone participates in its beginnings in the life of a zoophyte <term>zoophyte: a plant-like animal, such as coral, once thought to be a link between the plant and animal kingdoms</term> in

<column-break/>

its earliest stages. It possesses a life distinct from the vegetative <note>the life force of plants</note> and sensitive <note>the life force of animals</note> lives; it is a life that has remained unnamed until now. For according to the unanimous writings of the Sages: once the principles of the Stone are joined in the glass egg <note>the "Philosopher’s Egg," a sealed vessel used in alchemical heating</note>, if the "brooding" <note>original: *fotus*; the application of steady, gentle heat</note> is interrupted by a mistake and it happens to cool down completely even for a moment, the principles die off so thoroughly that no hope remains for the future Stone. This happens in a similar way during the brooding of bird eggs. And so, I have judged that these substances must be believed to live with a life equal to that of the Stone’s beginnings. It is a true life, which a true death testifies to. For indeed, that error can never be corrected by any further labor; once it has died in this way, no hope of restoration is left for the rest of the work. Finally, I know that the Tree of Life is sought in vain from animals, however long-lived they may be. In all of them I have found spontaneous death, a frail body, slipping away by the hour—the "way of all flesh." For how shall they give a long life which they do not contain within themselves? Since, even if they are long-lived, they have at least cast off their own life by the time they are taken for medicinal use. At times I looked at stones because they occasionally contained living animals within them—creatures that lived for decades <note>original: *lustra*; five-year periods</note> and were preserved from death without food. Paracelsus <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> asserts that the entire heap of stones, and the whole universe, was once a single stone, or at least a uniform stony liquor, which gradually became distinct into metals, pyrite, rocks, stones, and salts, and gave the beginnings of vitality through many "creeping things" <note>original: *reptilia*; used here for foundational or primitive crawling life forms</note>. And so, if stones perhaps hold toads and salamanders alive for a century without food, snoring as if in a deep sleep, I wondered whether the stones—acting as the casings and wombs of those living creatures—were participants in long life. But Scripture suggested that the life of creeping things is horrid and hateful to us. For this reason, I looked toward more precious gems. Nevertheless, I found no traces of long life in them either, whether they were essences or their "masteries" <term>magistery: in alchemy, a finished medicinal preparation of a substance</term>, because they cannot be immediately assimilated <note>original: *assimilari*; to be absorbed or made similar to the body's own substances</note> to our own first constituents.

<summary>Van Helmont recounts his personal success with alchemical transmutation using a powder provided by a stranger, but concludes that while the Philosopher's Stone is real, it does not provide the biological longevity of the Tree of Life. He explores the concept of "vitality" in minerals and stones, referencing Paracelsus and the phenomenon of toads found living inside rocks.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Van Helmont has established that while alchemical gold is possible, it is distinct from the biological quest for the "Tree of Life," which must be compatible with human nature rather than just metallic nature.</meta>

# TREE OF LIFE

...be likened to, or joined with: or if at last they are joined in some way, and for as long as we grow: at least they are stripped of their pristine longevity, in the manner of other foods; they put on a nature from the strife of the flesh <note>Van Helmont refers to the "strife of the flesh" as the digestive process where external matter is forced to conform to the human body's own nature</note>, and are forced to follow it. I have learned, therefore, that gems, even if they were endowed with medicinal power, contribute to a healthy life: yet they never entirely cast off their mineral nature: and thus they are not mixable with our primary constituents. Indeed, even if they were mixed, they would still not serve a long life. For whatever does not restore the vital powers does not also counter the internal necessities of death, and much less so if it resists a union with our solid parts. Yet aromatic herbs would snatch this palm of victory from their companions—if the tree of life were herbaceous—insofar as they are more pleasing and more spiritual. However, a most highly refined liquor, even one containing the entire essence <term>crasin: from the Greek *krasis*, meaning the specific mixture or temperament of qualities that defines a substance</term> of a herb: nevertheless, it only looks toward specific cures and healing, because the solid substance from which it flowed is not itself a participant in long life. For how can a liquor, which does not know how to preserve from destruction its own solid body to which it was wedded in its smallest parts from the beginning, protect our flesh from death—flesh that is soon to dissolve in hastening rot—when it has been stripped of its own turn? And so from this point, the tree of life began to be held by me as immortal, not subject to old age nor the inconveniences of time, and because it would contain or admit no excrement, much less would it generate the same. Rather, by a certain excellence, it would ward off <note>original: *averruncaret*; a term from Roman religion meaning to avert or ward off evil omens</note> any such things if they should ever happen to fall in, because of its power of propelling and repelling. And since it is the nature of poison to turn good into evil by corrupting it, it seemed right to me to investigate a tree of life in which poisons themselves would die, overcome by the goodness of the tree: for which reason it would also reject things not yet admitted. And those things which had once been admitted, it would correct and overcome. For if it ought not to admit excrement—which is a kind of poison of the lowest degree—it will much more turn away, blunt, and defeat those things which are of a higher and 

<column-break/>

more manifest hostility. For unless it did this, it would assume the name of the "Tree of Life" in vain. I observed that foals born from an old beast of burden or horse are quickly exhausted, sluggish in the vigor of life, and have deeper pits above their eyes than those born from a younger horse. Yet the willow of the ancients gives new shoots, no less fertile if planted than the shoots of a new trunk. Therefore I found that old age passes into the offspring along with the seed of living creatures, but this is not so easily manifest in the "offspring" of trees. Indeed, if long life exists in certain animals, it is so confined that it does not go beyond that individual, and is not communicable outside the species. Finally, I examined dew through an analysis of its parts: for it gave a sugary salt <note>original: *salem saccharinum*</note>, helping great diseases, but truly of no use for long life; for because of the indeterminate generality of its goodness, it contained the properties of food rather than life itself. I finally concluded with myself: that whatever it might be, the thing that would act as the Tree of Life must be an arboreal offspring. Then, this medicine must be sought from a most healthy, fragrant, balsamic, and nearly immortal shrub. And it must be made of the most subtle and purest parts, from the proper gift of its own solid body and its native constitution: and it must resist all kinds of corruptions, whether from an error of art or nature, or those that are acquired. Finally, through art and labor, it must have attained the final goal of perfection and the license to mix with us. For this reason it was especially necessary that this manifold natural gift should not be broken in any way during preparation, nor changed by fire. And so there is a need for a non-burning fire <note>original: *igne non urens*; in alchemy, a "non-burning fire" or "lamp fire" refers to a gentle, constant heat that matures a substance without scorching it</note> for the exaltation of its powers and the sequestration of impediments. So that, namely, for the fulfillment of incorruptibility, or for the maintaining of longevity for us—as much as would be possible for a recipient of corrupted nature—it might make certain mortals participants through the communication of its powers. Certainly, it cannot...

This is so that when at last the nutrients mixed with it have finished their duty, at least their soot <note>original: "fuligo"; referring to the waste products or "smoke" of metabolism</note>, through its own vapor, may no longer wear down and thin out the indwelling spirits, but rather recreate them. Thus far, it should strive for a certain permanence of incorruptibility, and guard it under our middle life, continued and propagated in the nourishing moisture. Therefore, by the grace of its native gift, let it win for itself love with the sealed powers of the indwelling spirits. Let the preparation, therefore, refuse any alteration of its native virtue, and instead provide a deeper entry and application of its power. So much so that, as if beyond the law and beyond the usual, it may be admitted as a confidant into the secret inner chambers of life, to undergo information there. For in certain climates, all things are produced stronger and more excellent because of the nobilities of the alimentary juice; and for that reason, it is certain that they contribute greatly to a long life. For the sweat of some people smells like a goat, while that of others is not far from fragrance. This, I say, is the primary thing to be procured for a long life: lest the nourishing moisture, after it has performed its duties and is carried off through perspiration <term>diaphæresin: the process of sweating or eliminating moisture through the skin</term>, lose that grace, through the lack of which I have described life as short. For I have taught elsewhere that a pig or a goose fed only on fish provides meat which, to the one tasting it, recalls the detestable fat of fish. Therefore, let the medicine of the tree of life be a fragrant, aromatic balsam, pleasing to nature, seasoning the blood with surpassing goodness, and the nourishment now applied in the manner of dew. To such an extent, by the vigor of its own incorruptibility, let the balsamic force be continued even to the furthest limits of its exhalation from the body. Because of this, one must take singular care that fire does not alter this fruit through a separating distillation; but let there be instituted

This vigor the stomachs of men preserved somewhat intact after that, even until the cataclysm of the waters <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>, until through the succession of years and generations, all things gradually fell into ruin. For the entity of essence <note>original: "ens essentiæ"</note>, which was previously sought from foods, no longer came forth, because the stomach was busy extracting only the entity of nourishment <note>original: "ens nutrimenti"; the basic caloric value of food rather than its spiritual essence</note>. Since all things in nature are received according to the manner of the receiving person, the place, and the circumstances. For the friends of Job wept with him for seven days and nights without food, drink, or risk to their health <note>A reference to Job 2:13</note>. Which is now scarcely possible for any mortal today. Thus do we bees prepare honey for ourselves <note>original: "Sic nos nobis mella paramus apes"; a variation of the classical phrase "Sic vos non vobis," implying the author labors for a benefit he himself may not fully enjoy</note>. ->ARBOR VITÆ.<-

They do not contain the "gas" of minerals <note>In the author's chemical theory, "gas" refers to the vital or volatile spirit of a substance; mineral gases were often considered too harsh for the human body.</note> (such as those found in the *Ardennes*, *Asturias*, etc.) nor are they subject to the dampness of lakes: because they reflect the beneficial alignments of the stars and breathe pure air, they may contribute to a long life. Just as a flat field—knowing no provocations of gluttony—adds as much to a long life as satiety [over-eating], which is an enemy of long life, takes away. Indeed, the heavy stuffing of foods fatigues the body's wretched powers, so that they collapse before their time, as if exhausted by labor. While turning these things over in my mind for three whole days—wondering where a medicine for long life might be found—the true balsam <note>original: "opobalsamus"; specifically the Balsam of Mecca, highly prized in the ancient and early modern world.</note> smiled upon me significantly. I do not mean the *Peruvian* balsam, nor the *Brazilian Copaiba* gum, but the true Egyptian one, noted in the Holy Scriptures and primitive, the queenly tear of a small shrub, hardly affordable even for Kings. For indeed, I confess that much perfection is deservedly attributed to this substance. And although it might be sufficiently obtainable, it still falls short of the perfection of the "Tree of Life" because that shrub itself is so short-lived. While I wandered through the various paths of nature to survey the Tree of Life, finally, beyond the light of day and above the dregs of the earth, I saw in a dream the whole face of the earth as it stood deserted and empty at the beginning of creation; then next as it was while it grew green everywhere with its fresh plants. Again, I saw it as it lay hidden under the Great Flood. For I saw all species of plants preserved beneath the waters. Soon, however, after the flood, all entered the path of changes enjoined upon them, to be continued through their species and seeds. I saw, I say, on the peak of *Lebanon*, that the Cedars, by the Word of the most glorious God, remained whole beneath the flood, and a certain number of them still survive there to this day. And immediately after, I returned to myself. During the pause afterward, I considered that the Ark, which was meant to save the human race from destruction, was ordered to be built from incorruptible *Shittim* wood <term>lignum Cetim</term> <note>Biblical acacia wood, which the author here associates with the enduring nature of the cedar.</note>. For the world had lasted perhaps 1,652 years [before the flood]. Noah, however, proceeded slowly in the construction over a hundred solar years. And thus he took wood and beams that would suffer no damage at all throughout that entire century. A leper segre-

<column-break/>

gated from the people, when approaching the Priest, carried *Shittim* wood in his hand to be cleansed. In the Feast of Tabernacles <term>Scenopegiæ</term> <note>The Jewish festival of Sukkot, commemorating the wandering in the desert.</note>, every *Hebrew* carried Cedar and branches of myrrh, so that God might be mindful of the rain for the whole earth, and that He might establish the measures of the seasons and the Stars. Thus I understood that by the cedar, long life—and likewise the blessings of the seasons and the Stars, and cleansing—are designated in a mystical sense; but in this world, they are also actually obtained. For all other vital things soon waste away with old age: but the cedar alone, by a remarkable mystery, through the incorrupt substance of its wood and its healthy growing power <note>original: "sospite vegetatrice"</note>, promises long life because it contains it. For the doors of the temple of *Solomon* were ordered to be made of *Shittim* wood covered with gold, as if the gold were merely a covering or even a cheaper wrapping. Furthermore, it is beyond controversy in the Church of God that the Cedar in *Lebanon*, in the Temple, in the figure of the Ark, in the cleansing of leprosy, and the Feast of Tabernacles represents the mother of GOD, the Virgin Queen of heaven, the incorruptible Vessel, the tree that brought forth eternal life for us in the flesh. The patroness, I say, of the poor, and my own. Moreover, the location of the Cedar in *Lebanon*, rising above the coldest gate of the air covered in snow, designates the unstained integrity of the Virgin Mother of God. And so, if the tree designates the Divine Virgin—especially through so many mysteries combined—it is no wonder that the Cedar signifies the tree of this life even in the temporal world. Indeed, in the days of *David*, the aged cedar was in *Lebanon*, as it was worthy from then on in a mystical sense because of its excellent height. Therefore, either it has been planted there since the flood and the same physical tree perseveres until now, or it has been there long before, perhaps even from the cradle of the world according to the vision of my dream. This, however it is taken, shows that the Cedar scorns the inconveniences of old age. Moreover, it was not planted from a parent Cedar after the flood: for even that parent of the cedar would have been preserved under the flood, and much more easily thereafter than that which has endured from the days of *David* until now. # THE TREE OF LIFE

->THE TREE OF LIFE.<-

Let those who wish look upon the age of that Cedar in Lebanon and say that the modern trees are raised from new buds or fallen seeds. But even if that were granted, today and every day new cedars would have come forth into a great forest. Yet, no new Cedar grows up there. On the contrary, I gather from this that the very same individual cedars persist now that existed before the flood—or even since the creation of the world. Indeed, the Cedar was given as a symbol to the Blessed Virgin. <note>Ecclesiasticus 24:13: "I was exalted like a cedar in Libanus." The author views the cedar as a living link to the era of creation.</note> Furthermore, for our mastery <note>The "mastery" or *magisterium* refers to the alchemical process of creating a medicine.</note>, the fruit of the Cedar is not to be used: because its purpose is not simply to exist within the destination of the Cedar's properties, but only for the propagation of the species, which contradicts the foundation of a long life. Therefore, we must take the *Shittim* wood <note>original: "lignum Cetim"; the wood used to build the Ark of the Covenant, often identified with cedar or acacia.</note> itself, which is so exalted in the Holy Scriptures. Thus, neither the bark, nor the fruit, nor the root, nor the leaves are the ultimate goal toward which nature looked for long life. And so the Cedar is perhaps distinguished from the Tree of Life in Eden by this very fact. Thus, the matter of a tree that knows not how to die has been found—its wood is incorruptible <term>imputrefactibile: incapable of rotting</term>, and because of its many properties, it is destined in a mystical sense for the Divine Virgin, bringing life to the World to redeem it from death. But its preparation is by far the most difficult of all those tasks that fall under the labor of Wisdom <note>original: "Sophia," personified Wisdom or the alchemical process.</note>. For this reason, Monarchs lack long life: because there is no one who knows how to prepare it. For no true Philosopher is a court-singer <note>original: "aulædus"; literally a flute-player in a palace, here meaning a flatterer or "yes-man."</note>, nor does he follow Princes and flatter them; since, being in need of nothing, he scorns whatever a Prince can give. Therefore, only the tree of life recreates failed strength and holds back life for a time in its flux. The difficulty of preparation consists in this: that the wood, without the destruction of its powers, must be resolved through a gentle warmth—like that of the March sun—down to its "First Essence" <term>ens primum: the earliest, most powerful state of a substance in alchemy</term>. In which essence alone is granted to it the fermenting power of preserving and seasoning, so that once it has entered into the primary constituents of our being, it may insinuate itself into familiarity with the indwelling spirits through every organ. Moreover, in the juice of this kind of resolution lies the entire power of the Cedar: namely, the vital power, with every seminal and formal property of long life. 

<column-break/>

For the entire mass of the wood is resolved into a juice; otherwise, if it were distilled, it would be transmuted and become a certain "new creature." This is proven by *aqua vitae* <term>literally "water of life," referring here to high-proof alcohol or spirits</term> distilled from grains or beers, and likewise by oil distilled from woods, or even from olive oil itself. Its practice is as follows: Resolve fragments of *Shittim* wood with an equal weight of the *Alkahest* <term>the legendary universal solvent of alchemy</term> liquor, in a sealed glass under a fostering warmth. And within a week, you will see the whole wood has changed into a milky liquor. Soon, however, around the fifteenth day, two distinct oils float on top, which increase until a month has passed and are separated more clearly. Then, let the oil be separated from the water by manual operation. Next, distill the water in a water-bath, and the *Alkahest* liquor remains in the bottom at its original weight. Then, let the oil be fostered with water for three whole months with gentle heat, and all the oil assumes the nature of a salt and will mix itself with the water. This is the "First Essence" of Cedar. Regarding the length of life, I have little more to say: for I attain these things as an old man and while I myself am dying. My mind breathed something unheard of within, but I shall be buried useless to this life. For the Guardian Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus janitor"; the "doorkeeper" spirit often cited by alchemists as the protector of secrets.</note> has taken away the flask at the command of Him before whom the whole world is like a fungus. Praise be to Him who gave, and who took away what was His own. Deservedly, therefore, the Schools <note>The academic and medical establishments of the time.</note> might rebuke me: "You wretch, a man of little note, a man of great ambition, you have come as a paradoxically slow old man to spread clouds over the world with your praise of the Cedar. The histories and powers of plants are known to our herbalists. But you, to show off an unheard-of fiction about long life, continue to rave paradoxically with your Cedar. Well then, if Cedar has such power for life, why are all Kings not long-lived? From where do you arrive as a new guest? Produce the letters and experiences which you believed. For just as a Lawyer blushes to speak without the law, so does a Doctor without experience. For you cannot deny that decoctions of the leaves, kernels, wood, bark, and roots..." <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, representing the imagined critique from established physicians.</note>

# THE TREE OF LIFE

->THE TREE OF LIFE.<-

...[from the wood], or from the resin of the cedar, they would have long ago produced a continued life. But none of these things are clear through our herbalists. You, therefore, deter others with your hidden method of preparation, and with the grim style of a "smoke-seller" <note>original: "fumivendulæ"; a term for a charlatan or someone who sells "hot air" and empty promises.</note>, you wish to wrap the false mystery of the cedar in darkness. This is a mask of the Alkahest <term>Alkahest: a hypothetical universal solvent in alchemy, believed to be capable of dissolving any substance into its primary matter</term>—assumed only to hide your reckless rashness—at which almost all learned men will laugh, for they do not allow themselves to be led away into new opinions by dreams or feigned ecstasies. This argument arises partly from an ancient hatred toward us, and partly from old-fashioned simplicity. 

As far as my own person is concerned regarding these unusual ways of writing, God knows that I write what I know to be true. I give thanks to Him, for although He had bestowed five talents upon me <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25. Van Helmont often used this biblical metaphor to describe his intellectual gifts and his responsibility to God.</note>, and I had made myself unworthy and had thus far been rejected before Him, it pleased the Divine Goodness to take three from me and leave two still, so that He might wait for me to bear better fruit. He preferred, I say, to impoverish and tolerate me, so that I might not be useful to many, provided He saved me from the perils of this world. To Him be eternal sanctification. 

As for how the argument of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional Scholastic or Galenic medicine, which the author frequently criticized.</note> relies on the appearances of decoctions <term>decoction: a medicine made by boiling herbs in water to extract their virtues</term> and broths, that indeed proceeds from simple ignorance. Since thus far no one has described the powers of things in action. It is therefore certain that although many things become sharper through distillation, and thus more active, yet by that very process they recede and are alienated from the genuine property of their "seeds" <term>seeds/semina: in Helmontian theory, the internal blueprints or vital principles that direct the growth and function of a substance</term>. 

Because Fire is an "artificial death." If it becomes an open flame, it happens through the extinction of the seeds and the Archeus <term>Archeus: the internal "master workman" or life-force that governs the body and its chemistry</term>. Natural death of things presupposes the exhaustion of the seeds. But artificial death, which is not caused by the consumption of flame, separates the volatile parts from the fixed parts, resulting in the dissolution and death of the ultimate life of the compound. Therefore, the original powers are altered and alienated by fire, and a new creature rises from the fire—born from the material disposition, with the properties of the original being inverted by the artificial death it encountered. Thus, in-

<column-break/>

deed, most volatile salts, through melting and coming into contact with oil, are fixed into charcoal, which finally returns to ashes once the fatness is burned away. There are also "fugitive" salts, which, lurking within the fatness of oils, act and labor toward a new product; thus oils, otherwise quite fluid, are changed by the combination of salts. Some therefore become soap-like, others harbor soot. At least all burnt things contract an empyreuma <term>empyreuma: the characteristic smell and taste of organic matter that has been charred or burnt in a closed vessel</term> and are transformed into something else. For nothing of the old remains. 

Because it is the property of fire, not simply to separate, but by its own authority to alter and change things under its power. Therefore, it is not permitted to judge the powers of distillates based on the original compound from which they flow; nor is it permitted to believe that even if the powers of things are not abolished or extinguished by fire, that the original virtues have not been changed by the burning. 

What things are made new by fire are often made worse, yet also not rarely so distinct from their former selves that they become a hundred times better. Finally, there are "simples" <note>Simples are individual medicinal herbs used on their own rather than in a complex mixture.</note> which, by boiling, liquefy their mucilage or gum, and thus transmit their powers into the juice of the decoction. However, they do not retain the same faculty they had in the whole compound; rather, their action is often sluggish. For first they must be digested in the stomach like food. Of which although most, by the property of the "Great Necessity" <note>original: "magni Oportet"; a philosophical term referring to the inherent requirements of nature.</note>, reflect something of their original powers in taste, nevertheless these are either ejected with the waste, or, being wrongly digested and absorbed, they stir up nothing but the strife of unaccustomed "heterogeneity" <note>The presence of foreign or incompatible substances in the body.</note> instead of providing a remedy. Or at least, if they affect the blood and flesh with their scent, they promise only sluggish help—so much so that even the quartan fever inhabiting the spleen <note>Quartan fever is a form of malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day. The spleen was historically thought to be the seat of such "melancholy" illnesses.</note> remains untouched to this day, as a mockery to physicians. But for anything to be admitted into the governance of the spirits and the family of the constituent solids, there is no hope of that through decoctions.

# THE TREE OF LIFE

->THE TREE OF LIFE.<-

So that neither through distillation—which, through the intervention of an artificial death, strips away every vital entelechy <term>entelechy: the vital principle or internal force that guides a living thing to its full realization</term> that the wood contains within itself—nor through the juice, powder, or preserves sought from the Cedar, can we find what we need. These are so foreign to us that, unless they are subdued by the method of the "first being" <note>original: "methodum primi entis"; likely referring to a process of reducing a substance to its primary, most potent state</note>, they promise no familiarity with our nature. Indeed, they are far from surpassing our nature or granting us their own incorruptibility. Therefore, distilled products and raw simples, no matter how noble their powers may shine, have no significance for a long life. For it is necessary that the incorruptibility of the Cedar be preserved exactly, knowing no death, and that its beneficence toward us be not even slightly deteriorated; every foreign impediment must be separated from it. Otherwise, through much struggle of our internal archeus <term>archeus: the vital governing spirit within the body that directs digestion and health</term>, it is turned into a "being of nourishment" rather than a "being of essence" <note>Van Helmont distinguishes between substances that just feed the body ("ens nutrimenti") and those that reinforce its fundamental vital identity ("ens essentiae")</note>. This must be done, however, in such a way that penetration, communication, and harmony with the primary constituents of our being are added to it, along with the refreshment of our inherent faculties. 

Meanwhile, let the Galenic Schools <note>The followers of Galen, representing traditional, herbal-based university medicine which Van Helmont frequently criticized</note> be amazed by this unusual way of preparation and description, and let them laugh at my promises; let them believe they are mere dreams. "Let every bird sing according to its own beak" <note>original: "cantet avis singula juxta suum rostrum"; a proverb meaning everyone speaks according to their own nature or limited understanding</note>; they are free to despise me. For I have long since grown a callus on my ears against those long-standing objections manufactured solely for the sake of profit. I have written about Long Life, and what I know is true. I have not written for beginners, nor are these things to be grasped by simple reading; for "God knows why he gave the goat a short tail" <note>original: "novit enim Deus, cur capræ curtam caudam dederit"; a proverb suggesting God denies certain powers to those who would use them harmfully or who do not deserve them</note>. In the maturity of time, there will be an Adept <term>Adept: a master of alchemy who has achieved the Great Work</term> who will understand that I have spoken the truth. 

As for the opinion acquired through a dream: let such a person read the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, known only to Daniel. Yet the King had ordered all his wise men to be put to the fire unless they could provide an indubitable explanation of the dream. Certainly, dreams of that kind promise a certain internal certainty and are not in vain. Often, He who gives the dream may soon return to it with such certainty of itself that neither death nor 

<column-break/>

hell could introduce a doubt. Although I prefer the Cedar to all other woods, perhaps the Indian varieties offer something not at all inferior to the Cedar of the Palestinian coast. However, I have always given primacy to the authority of the Sacred Scriptures. This is not because the hand of the Lord has bound itself only to the Cedar. But what I have written concerning the Cedar, I have offered as a memorial of honor toward God, who has been favorable to me. Other matters concerning the Cedar shall be buried with me, for the world is not capable of receiving them. 

As for what modern writers boast about the "elixir of property" <term>Elixir Proprietatis: a famous medicinal formula originally attributed to Paracelsus, intended to preserve health</term>, it does not succeed according to the description of Paracelsus. For if three simple ingredients are enclosed in a very large, sealed glass vessel, they give at most a few drops of a milky liquor and some pale oil after two days, and only as much more after two months. Barely a third of the material withstands the fire without threatening a burnt smell <note>original: "empyreuma"; the scorched taste or smell of organic matter overheated in a closed vessel</note>. If it is urged a little more strongly, the vessel, no matter how large, bursts. But if the ingredients are connected with a medium liquor, the result is ultimately nothing. 

Paracelsus was silent (as he was in many other things) about the addition of the liquor Alkahest <term>Alkahest: the fabled universal solvent of the alchemists</term>, with which the entire matter is immediately dissolved throughout, and the medicine succeeds according to his description. For there is a subtle fragrance in this elixir. Because of this, it preserves the liquid matter of our body from corruption, just like a balsam. Often, I have so refreshed those despaired of due to contagious fever with a single drop given in wine, that by noon they dined with me, though at midnight they had received the last rites of holy oil. Truly, in the absence of the "Cedar-being," the elixir of property comes to the rescue. But what of it? It requires the Alkahest. This is not given to those who merely think they know, but only to those who truly know, and indeed to those who are "doubled" <note>original: "duplatis"; possibly referring to those who have achieved a certain level of spiritual and physical mastery, or a specific alchemical preparation</note>. 

Therefore, I will set forth something trivial for the use of the common people for the preservation of a long life. In the year 1600, a certain man serving in the military grain supply as an accountant, burdened with a large and small brood of children, complained that he was 58 years old; and if he should [die...] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the catchword "ceret" completes the Latin word "deficeret" (should fail/die).</note>

<summary>Van Helmont argues that true life-extension requires capturing the "entelechy" of the Cedar through the use of the Alkahest solvent, rather than common distillation. He defends his divinely-inspired knowledge against traditional medical schools and mentions the potency of the Elixir of Property when properly prepared.</summary>
<keywords>Cedar, Entelechy, Archeus, Alkahest, Elixir of Property, Paracelsus, Long Life, Adept, alchemical medicine, contagious fever</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the author’s discourse on the "Tree of Life." Following a theoretical discussion on how certain substances like Cedar fail to grant immortality unless prepared correctly, the author provides a practical, anecdotal proof of his theories involving a distilled preparation of sulfur used as a preservative for the "wine of life"—the human blood.</meta>

# THE TREE OF LIFE

<column-break/>

### THE TREE OF LIFE.

...[he feared] it would happen that his children would go from door to door begging for alms. He asked me for some protection for his life. I, still a young man, pitying his lot, considered how the odor of a lit sulfur candle preserves wines from corruption. Therefore, I persuaded myself that the acid spirit of sulfur <term>acidum sulfuris stagma: likely a form of sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a glass bell</term> necessarily contained this sulfur smoke and its entire odor in such a way that it was nothing other than the smoke of the Sulfur itself, absorbed into its mercurial salt <term>salem mercurialem: in alchemy, the "mercurial" part of a substance represents its fluid, transformative, or vital essence</term>. Then, finally, I reasoned that our blood was the wine of our life; and if that blood were preserved, even if it did not grant a "long life" <note>original: "vitam longam," a reference to the alchemical goal of extreme longevity</note>, it would at least protect us from many diseases of corruption. By this efficiency, a healthy life—immune to disease and tranquil from pains—might at least be prolonged in some manner. Wherefore, I gave him a flask full of the distilled liquor of sulfur, and likewise taught him the art of preparing

<column-break/>

that oil from burnt sulfur. I further ordered that at every meal he should take at least two little drops of that liquor with his first draught of beer, and that he should not recklessly exceed that dose. I judged that two drops contained a great deal of the smoke of sulfur. That man obeyed my warnings, and he still walks through the streets of Brussels in this year 1641. And what is even more remarkable, in that entire forty-year period, he never once lay down for any illness, even though he once by chance broke his leg near the back of the knee upon the ice; yet he always remained free from fever, and stayed lean and thin, even though he lived as an old man in a scarcity of comforts. The name of the old man is Johannes Mass, who served as a valet to Rythovius, the Bishop of Ypres <note>Martin Rythovius (1511–1583), the first Bishop of Ypres</note>, at the time when the Counts Egmont and Horn were beheaded <note>The execution of Lamoral, Count of Egmont, and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn, in 1568 was a pivotal event in the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule</note>; and he was then twenty-five years of age.
